### Series title page

*The Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, and Economical Library of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived through the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with several manuscripts, and corrected with the greatest diligence; continually elucidated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the extensive editions produced during the last three centuries had been completed; furnished with particular analytical indices following each volume and each author of any importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; augmented by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and also by works possessing some authority with respect to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indices: the first, of subjects, by consulting which one may see at a glance whatever each Father has written on any topic; the second, of Sacred Scripture, by which the reader may readily discover which Fathers, and in which passages of their works, have commented on the individual texts of the individual books of Scripture.*

*An edition of the greatest accuracy, easily to be preferred to all others if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the exceptionally convenient format of the volumes, consistently alike throughout the entire work, the low price, and above all this collection, the first single, methodical, and chronological gathering in our library of six hundred fragments and brief works hitherto scattered here and there, collected from works belonging to every age, place, language, and form.*

**SECOND SERIES**, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Edited by J.-P. # [Complete Works of Bruno the Carthusian]

## Volume, or Part II, of the Works of the Divine Bruno, Founder of the Carthusians, containing expositions on all the Epistles of Paul

Reviewed and corrected through the study and labor of P. Theodore Petraeus of Kampen, alumnus of the Cologne Charterhouse; and this by the will of the Most Reverend Father General, minister of the entire order.

> “But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God.” (Psalm 51, verse 10.)

[Col. 0009]

## To the venerable Father in Christ, Lord Hector Hoen, Bishop of Vienne, most prudent Prior of the Trier Charterhouse and Visitor of the Rhine province

Alphonsus, King of Aragon, being a man exceedingly devoted to letters and to those who cultivate them, once, when there was discussion of the loss of precious things, most reverend Father in Christ, solemnly affirmed that he would rather lose the gems, pearls, and diamonds which he possessed and which were renowned throughout the whole world than lose books of any kind. Clearly, he judged books to be the repositories of the sciences, the pastures of souls, and the oracles of the saints; nor did he think that a person could be more harmfully deprived of anything than of these shells and channels of wisdom.

If he valued any books, regardless of their kind, above immeasurable riches—for he believed that no book could be found so foolish that it did not contain at least a morsel of sound teaching—at what price ought the Carthusian clients of their most holy patriarch to value those volumes in which the marrow of religious perfection and that unknown sweetness reserved for the sons of the age are enclosed?

These are truly spiritual storehouses, furnished for the needs of all your members and belonging particularly to the sacred Carthusian family, so that it would need no supplies from elsewhere; if these should fail, however, it would immediately be compelled to seek abundance from foreign orders. These are domestic gardens, supplying the sick and healthy souls alike with health-giving herbs and roots. These are the traces of angelic teaching which the most blessed Bruno, so that his heirs might follow them, left marked out in three monuments after him.

I pass over what lies beyond this. For you can already see, venerable Father in Christ, toward what purpose I began to mention these things: namely, so that you may judge that I have satisfied you by my six months’ labor, to which I devoted my efforts and resources so that the hereditary store of the works of your divine patriarch might at last be cleansed of the dust and squalor of errors, and so that I might restore those traces of heavenly teaching which, through use and the long passage of time, had been almost obliterated.

All this I undertook, stirred by the zeal of the Reverend Father, who rescued the Charterhouse of Rettel in Lorraine from its present ruin and who, with such vigilance, continues to protect the Trier Charterhouse that you would sooner deceive Argus than allow the face of vice to enter it, while Hector Hoen keeps watch.

Since these things are so, just as I do not wish to doubt that all good men are exceedingly moved everywhere by the illustrious and most useful deeds of this man, so I trust that this second volume of the aforesaid Lord Bruno, which I have had reprinted for the benefit of your entire holy order, and which I have now thought fit to dedicate particularly to the Reverend Father, will prove pleasing and welcome to him. Farewell.

Cologne, 30 September 1611.

Your venerable and most devoted servant in Christ,  
**Bernard Gualterus**, citizen and bookseller of Cologne.

[Col. 0011]

# Exposition of the Divine Bruno on the Epistles of Paul (G)*

## Preface of Saint Jerome to the Epistles of Paul

[Col. 0011A] First, it is asked why, after the Gospels—which are the fulfillment of the Law and in which examples and precepts for living are set out most fully—the Apostle wished to send these Epistles to individual Churches.

The reason seems to have been that he might anticipate the beginnings of the nascent Church, when new circumstances arose; cut away present and emerging vices; and exclude future controversies, following the example of the prophets. After the Law of Moses had been given, in which all God’s commandments were read, the prophets nevertheless continued by their renewed teaching to restrain the sins of the people; and, for the sake of an example of living, they transmitted books even to our memory.

Next it is asked why he wrote no more than ten Epistles to the Churches. There are ten, counting the one called “to the Hebrews”; for the remaining four were addressed specifically to disciples. To show that the New Testament does not differ from the Old, and that he was not acting against the law of Moses, he directed his Epistles according to the number of the first commandments of the Decalogue. Just as Moses instituted as many commandments for those whom he liberated from Pharaoh, so Paul teaches in as many Epistles those who have been acquired from the slavery of the devil and idolatry.

The most learned men have also handed down that the two stone tablets represented the two covenants.

As for the Epistle written to the Hebrews, some assert that it is not Paul’s, because it is not titled in his name and because its speech and style differ. They attribute it either to Barnabas, following Tertullian; or to Luke, according to some; or certainly to Clement, the disciple of the apostles and bishop of the Roman Church ordained after the apostles.

They should be answered as follows: If it is not Paul’s because it does not bear his name, then it will belong to no one, because it bears no one’s name. But if that is inconvenient and absurd, it must rather be admitted to be his, since it shines with such eloquence of doctrine.

But because among the Churches of the Hebrews he was held under the false suspicion of being a destroyer of the Law, he wished, under an unspoken name, to give an account of the figures of the Law and of the truth of Christ, lest hatred of a name displayed in the title should exclude the benefit of the reading.

It is certainly not surprising if he appears more eloquent in his own language, that is, Hebrew, than in a foreign language, namely Greek, in which the other Epistles were written.

Some people also ask why the Epistle to the Romans has been placed first, when reason makes clear that it was not written first. He testifies that he wrote it while setting out for Jerusalem, after he had already encouraged the Corinthians and others by letter to gather the ministry that he was about to carry with him.

Some therefore understand that all the Epistles were arranged so that the first place was given to the one that, although sent later, led through the individual Epistles by stages toward more perfect things.

For most of the Romans were so inexperienced that they did not understand that they had been saved by God’s grace and not by their own merits; and for this reason the two peoples were in conflict with one another.

Accordingly, he declares that they need correction, first recalling the vices of their paganism. To the Corinthians, however, he already says that the grace of knowledge has been granted, and he does not rebuke everyone so much as reproach them for failing to rebuke those who were sinning, as he says: “Fornication is heard of among you.” And again: “When you are gathered together, with my spirit, to hand such a one over to Satan.”

In the Second Epistle the Corinthians are praised and exhorted to progress more and more. The Galatians are accused of no crime except this one: that they believed the most cunning false apostles.

The Ephesians are worthy of no reproach, but of much praise, because they preserved the apostolic faith. The Philippians are praised still more, since they did not even wish to listen to false apostles.

In two Epistles likewise he pursues the Thessalonians with every praise, because they not only preserved an unshaken faith in the truth but were also found steadfast during the persecution by their fellow citizens.

The Colossians were such that, although they had not been seen bodily by the Apostle, they were considered worthy of this praise. “Although I am absent in body,” he says, “yet I am with you in spirit, rejoicing and seeing your order” (Colossians 2:5).

What, then, should be said of the Hebrews, whose imitators the Thessalonians—who were praised so highly—are said to have become? He himself says:

“And you, brethren, became imitators of the Churches of God that are in Judaea; for you suffered the same things from your own countrymen as they did from the Jews” (1 Thessalonians 2:14).

Among the Hebrews themselves he also mentions the same thing, saying:

“For you also had compassion on those in bonds, and you joyfully accepted the plundering of your goods, knowing that you have a better and lasting substance” (Hebrews 10:34).

# On the Epistle to the Romans

[Col. 0013]

## Special Prologue to the Epistle to the Romans

[Col. 0013B] The Romans are those who believed from among the Jews and the Gentiles. These people, in proud contention, wished to subordinate one another.

For the Jews said:

“We are the people of God, whom he loved and cherished from the beginning. We are circumcised, descended from the stock of Abraham; we come from a holy lineage; and formerly God was known only in Judaea. We were liberated from Egypt by God’s signs and mighty works; we crossed the sea on dry feet, while the heaviest waves overwhelmed our enemies.

“For us the Lord rained manna in the desert and supplied heavenly food as though we were his children. Day and night he went before us in a pillar of cloud and fire, to show us the way through a trackless place.

“And, to say nothing of his other immeasurable benefits toward us, we alone were deemed worthy to receive God’s Law, to hear the voice of God speaking, and to know his will. In that Law Christ was promised to us; indeed, he himself testified that he had come to us, saying: ‘I was not sent except to the sheep that had perished from the house of Israel’ (Matthew 15:24), while he called you dogs rather than human beings.

“Is it therefore just that, having today abandoned the idols whom you served from the beginning, you should be compared with us, rather than being assigned, according to the authority and custom of the Law, to the place of proselytes? And even this you did not deserve, except because God’s ever-abundant clemency wished to admit you to imitate us.”

The Gentiles, on the other hand, replied:

“For the greater the benefits of God toward you that you recount, the greater the crime of which you show yourselves guilty. For you have always been ungrateful for all these things.

“With the very feet by which you crossed the dry sea, you played before the idols that you had made; and with the very mouth with which shortly before you had sung to the Lord over the destruction of your enemies, you asked for images to be made for you.

“With the eyes by which you were accustomed to behold God in the revered cloud or fire, you gazed upon images. Manna also became hateful to you, and you were always murmuring against the Lord in the desert, desiring to return to Egypt, from which he had brought you out with a strong hand.

“What more need be said? Your fathers so frequently provoked the Lord that they all died in the wilderness, and no more than two men from among the older generation entered the promised land.

“But why rehearse ancient matters, when, even if you had done none of those things, no one would judge you worthy of pardon for this one deed alone: that you not only refused to receive the Lord Christ, whom the voices of the prophets had always promised to you, but also killed him by the most shameful death?

“When we came to know him, we immediately believed, although he had not previously been preached to us. From this it is proved that, if we served idols, this must be attributed not to obstinacy of mind but to ignorance. For we immediately follow him once known; certainly we would have followed him long ago if we had known him earlier.

“You boast of the nobility of your lineage as though it were not imitation of conduct, rather than carnal birth, that makes you children of the saints. After all, Esau and Ishmael are from Abraham’s stock, yet they are by no means counted among his children.”

While they were arguing in this way, the Apostle placed himself between them and settled the disputes of the two parties. He confirms that neither had merited salvation by his own righteousness, but that both peoples had sinned knowingly and gravely: the Jews by dishonoring God through transgressing the Law; the Gentiles by failing to venerate the Creator, whom they ought to have recognized from creation as God, and by exchanging his glory for images made by human hands.

He demonstrates with the most truthful reasoning that both, having likewise obtained pardon, are equal—especially since he shows that the same Law foretold that both Jews and Gentiles would be called to faith in Christ. Therefore, humbling them in turn, he exhorts them to peace and concord.

## Argument

[Col. 0013]

The Romans are a people of Italy. They had been forestalled by false apostles and were being led under the name of our Lord Jesus Christ into the Law and the prophets. The Apostle recalls them to the true and evangelical faith, writing to them from Corinth through Phoebe, a minister of the Church at Cenchreae.

## Blessed Bruno’s Prologue

[Col. 0013D] Paul had not yet come to Rome, but several Romans, partly Gentiles and partly Jews, had received the faith through certain disciples who were preaching there. Among these people there was an improper dispute.

The Jews contended that they ought to be preferred to the Gentiles, while the Gentiles, on the contrary, asserted that they ought to be made more worthy than the Jews.

The Jews’ reason was that the promise of this salvation had been made to their fathers, such as Abraham, David, and the others; and that God had also given them the Law and the prophets, all of which foreshadowed the salvation that was to come through Christ, whereas he had made no mention of the Gentiles in any of these things. Therefore, they claimed, the Jews deservedly ought to be preferred to the Gentiles in this salvation.

The Gentiles, conversely, objected that the Jews ought to be judged less worthy because, if God had shown such care for them as to grant them the things mentioned, they themselves had abused all God’s gifts: by transgressing the Law he had given; by despising the prophets he had sent; and finally by condemning the Savior sent to them to the punishment of the cross.

For this reason, they said, the Jews ought rather to be humbled than exalted. The Gentiles themselves, however, ought deservedly to be preferred, since as soon as they heard the word of God they received the faith. If they had not believed before, they claimed, it was because they had possessed neither the Law nor the prophets, and therefore could excuse themselves.

Since the disciples through whose preaching they had been converted were unable to quell this rebellion, they sent to Paul so that, through the teacher, they might accomplish what their own authority was insufficient to achieve.

Having received this opportunity, Paul wrote this Epistle to them. Its subject is the Romans, or Gentiles, converted to the faith; and he treats them in the following way:

First he restrains the Gentiles, lest, exalting themselves either on account of wisdom or freedom of choice, and thus detracting from Christ’s grace, they should suppose themselves more worthy in the faith than anyone who had received the faith, since faith and salvation are granted solely through God’s grace.

If they exalt themselves on the basis of freedom of choice, they are especially guilty in this respect, since they possessed natural knowledge by which they could recognize their Creator without any teacher; yet, neglecting the Creator, they worshiped creatures. Paul sets forth many other such things to humble the Gentiles.

In humbling the Jews, because he perceived them to be more obstinate, as though they had more excuses to offer, he dwells longer on them. He proves that they ought not to be proud because they had the Law and the prophets, since they had continually offended God by transgressing the very things by which they ought to have appeased him.

He brings forward these and many other matters to restrain the Jews, and proceeds toward this end: to subject both Jews and Gentiles to God’s grace. He teaches that nothing comes to the Jews from their lineage, Law, or prophets, nor to the Gentiles from the ignorance they plead or from freedom of choice.

# Epistle to the Romans

[Col. 0015]

## Chapter One

[Col. 0015C]

> “Paul, servant of Jesus Christ, called as an apostle, set apart for the Gospel of God, which he had promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures concerning his Son, who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh, who was predestined to be the Son of God in power, according to the Spirit of sanctification, by the resurrection of the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord, through whom we have received grace and apostleship, for obedience to the faith among all the Gentiles for his name’s sake; among whom you also are called by Jesus Christ; to all who are in Rome, beloved of God, called as saints: grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

> “First, I give thanks to my God through Jesus Christ for all of you, because your faith is proclaimed throughout the whole world. For God is my witness, whom I serve in my spirit in the Gospel of his Son, that without ceasing I always remember you in my prayers, entreating that somehow, at last, I may have a prosperous journey by the will of God to come to you.

> “For I desire to see you, so that I may impart some spiritual gift to you, to strengthen you—that is, to be comforted together among you through the faith that is mutually yours and mine.

> “But I do not want you to be ignorant, brethren, that I have often planned to come to you and have been prevented until now, so that I might have some fruit among you also, as among the other Gentiles.

> “I am a debtor both to Greeks and to barbarians, to the wise and to the foolish; so, as far as depends on me, I am ready to preach the Gospel to you also who are in Rome.

[Col. 0016C] “For I am not ashamed of the Gospel. For it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and to the Greek. For the righteousness of God is revealed in it from faith to faith, as it is written: ‘But the righteous person lives by faith.’

> “For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of people who suppress the truth of God in unrighteousness, because what can be known of God is manifest among them. For God has revealed it to them.

> “For his invisible attributes, understood and seen through the things that have been made since the creation of the world, are perceived—his eternal power also and divinity—so that they are without excuse.

> “For although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks; instead, they became futile in their thoughts, and their senseless heart was darkened.

> “Claiming to be wise, they became fools. And they exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of corruptible human beings, birds, four-footed animals, and serpents.

> “Therefore God handed them over to the desires of their hearts, to impurity, so that they dishonored their bodies among themselves, because they exchanged the truth of God for a lie, and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever. Amen.

> “For this reason God handed them over to dishonorable passions. Their women exchanged natural use for that use which is against nature. Likewise the men, abandoning natural use of the woman, burned with desire for one another; men committing shameful acts with men and receiving in themselves the recompense that was fitting for their error.

[Col. 0017A] “And just as they did not approve of retaining God in their knowledge, God handed them over to a reprobate mind, to do what is not fitting: filled with every injustice, wickedness, fornication, greed, and malice; full of envy, murder, strife, deceit, and malignity; whisperers, slanderers, hateful to God, insolent, proud, boastful, inventors of evil, disobedient to parents, senseless, disorderly, without affection, without treaty, without mercy.

> “Although they knew God’s justice, they did not understand that those who do such things are worthy of death—not only those who do them, but also those who approve of those who do them.”

## Exposition

[Col. 0017B] As is customary in Epistles, he places a greeting first, saying: “Paul,” who was previously called Saul, deriving from Saul his lineage, name, and cruelty.

The name “Paul,” however, means “quiet” in the Hebrew language. Thus, just as this name was familiar and honorable among everyone by virtue of its authority, so also, by virtue of its meaning, it serves his purpose. For Paul intends to make the Romans quiet and tranquil among themselves.

Or, if “Paul” is rendered in Latin as “small” or “modest,” this again suits the matter well. For he labors to make the Romans, rendered modest and humble through the Epistle, subject to God’s grace.

“Paul,” I say, “servant of Christ Jesus.” Because he is intent in every way on persuading them to humility, he places the name of humility before the name of dignity.

He says: “Paul, servant of Christ Jesus, the King and priest, who alone is able to rule and to save through his evening sacrifice.”

He is also the servant of Jesus, that is, of the Savior, apart from whom no one is sufficient to save. In the same way, following my example, place no confidence in yourselves, but submit yourselves entirely to the service of Jesus Christ.

“Paul,” I say, “servant of Christ Jesus, called through the grace of God,” not through the merit of the Law or of lineage, but through grace alone, for the purpose of being an apostle, whose authority it is right for you to obey.

Or “Paul the apostle,” not secretly, but called by everyone, because everyone now knows that I have been consecrated an apostle by God; therefore I ought to be obeyed all the more.

Both interpretations serve to restrain both peoples, whether Jew or Gentile.

The callings of God occur in various ways. This Paul was called both outwardly through bodily affliction, through the voice of Christ saying, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4), and through inward inspiration.

Paul was “set apart.” He does not specify from whom, but for what purpose—namely, for the Gospel.

“Set apart,” I say, either from the other apostles, because they were appointed preachers to the Jews, whereas I was appointed to the Gentiles.

When Paul had been converted to the faith and had been instructed for several days by the disciples who were in Damascus (Acts 9:27), he immediately began to teach about Christ in the synagogue. Therefore the governor of Damascus wanted to seize him, but the brothers lowered him through the wall in a basket; thus he escaped from his hands. From there he went away to Arabia, preaching to the Gentiles for three years. After this he returned to Jerusalem, where he found Peter and James.

They had previously been greatly astonished when they heard that Paul was preaching to the Gentiles, although they had never seen him. They gave Paul and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship (Galatians 2:9), approving their teaching and saying that they themselves preached the same thing.

They did not consecrate Paul as an apostle—for God himself had consecrated him—but agreed with his teaching, so that those who were converted through them might believe that they belonged to one and the same faith.

Or he was set apart from the Law. For when I was a Pharisee—that is, a keeper—and was among the foremost in the Law, both by lineage and by knowledge, I saw that it was not effective for salvation and separated myself from it.

If I, who was so great in the Law, abandoned the Law, how much more ought you to withdraw from it, since you are far inferior to me?

This final interpretation concerns the Jews alone; the preceding one concerns both peoples.

[Col. 0018B] Up to this point he has commended his own person, both through humility and through authority. Now he begins to commend his preaching, saying:

“Set apart,” I say, whether from the Law or from the other apostles, “coming to preach the Gospel.”

“Gospel” means “good news.” I say, “the Gospel of God.” The New Law is said especially to belong to God, who taught it not through a minister but through his own person.

The Old Law, however, was given to Moses through an angel and through Moses given to the Jews. Therefore it is not said to belong to God in quite the same proper sense as the Gospel, which God promised before it was given, as the one who was going to give it.

For promising belongs to the one who is going to give the promised thing. Thus God promised, while the prophets, as ministers unable to give it, foretold it.

In saying that God promised this from eternity, he indicates that God exercised great care with regard to this Gospel, which he had promised beforehand through the prophets—that is, through those who foresaw future things.

And because there were certain people who foretold the future by a prophetic spirit, while others prophesied by divine inspiration, such as Balaam, yet did not possess this office from God, he specifies “his prophets”: those who received from God both knowledge of future things and the ministry of prophecy.

And so that this prophecy might remain perpetually, it was promised in the holy Scriptures—that is, Scriptures either produced by the Holy Spirit or sanctifying those who act as the Scriptures teach.

Here he begins his commendation of Christ. After the preceding commendation, he says that he received his apostleship from Christ:

[Col. 0018D] “In the Scriptures,” I say, “concerning the Son.”

For every Scripture, even when it treats of the Father or of the Holy Spirit, appears especially to treat of the Son, because whatever was foretold in the Scriptures was brought to completion through the Son.

“Concerning the Son,” I say, not an adopted son, but his own—that is, consubstantial with him and coeternal.

“Who was made,” that is, who received a certain making.

Someone might say: What sort of miracle is this, that the Son, eternal with the Father, should have been made in time?

Against this he says: “He was made,” I say, not according to his divinity but according to the flesh, which he personally united to the Godhead in time.

“Flesh,” I say, assumed from the seed—that is, from the flesh of David—according to the lineage of Christ’s mother, in whom he received the making of the flesh.

“Made for him,” namely for God, that is, for the manifestation of God. For unless Christ assumed flesh, human beings would have little or no knowledge of God.

Christ could likewise be said to have been born from Solomon or Rehoboam. But because promises concerning Christ were made to Abraham and David, he is therefore everywhere said to have been born from one or both of them.

Here there is a reason why he passes over Abraham and gives precedence to David. Through Abraham, the righteous are understood, because he was righteous; through David, sinners are often understood, because he sinned gravely.

But here the discourse was directed toward sinners, whom Paul intended to induce to confess themselves sinners. For that reason he placed David here in the memory of sinners.

Christ was indeed made in time; but [7] from eternity he was predestined—that is, foreordained and appointed—to be the Son of God by assuming flesh.

“Christ,” I say, “according to that by which he remains the Son of God in power,” that is, always with the Father in the same power of divinity.

He was not predestined according to his divinity, but according to his humanity alone. For “to predestine” is said of something that does not yet exist; but the Son of God was always in the beginning.

Yet because two natures are considered in Christ, one divine and the other human, on account of the undivided union of both substances it is often said of the divine nature that which properly belongs to the human nature. Thus here he is called “predestined Son,” something that cannot belong to the nature of the Godhead.

The comparison is with the way in which, when considering body and soul in a human being, people often say of the soul what properly belongs to the body, and conversely, because of their affinity. This manner of speaking applies even more expressly to Christ, since there a human being is called God, and God a human being.

In a human being, however, it is not permissible to call the body “soul” or the soul “body.”

When we refer to Christ in this way, we exclude neither nature. But when we explain the matter in parts, we attribute to the divine nature what belongs to the divine, and to the human nature what belongs to the human. Christ, I say, was predestined to become man: he was not conceived from the desire of the flesh, but according to the Spirit—that is, he was conceived from the Holy Spirit. By “Spirit” I mean the Spirit of sanctification, who sanctified him in his mother’s womb, making him free from sins.

That Christ is the Son of God in power is apparent from the resurrection of the dead: by rising from the dead, he caused the dead to rise with him. He could certainly not have done this unheard-of thing unless he were God [Col. 0019D]. By “the dead” I do not mean all of them, but only those who belonged to our Lord Jesus Christ. For he did not cause unbelievers to rise with him. Hence those who were buried with Abraham at Hebron are said above all to have risen together with Christ.

Through him, Jesus Christ, we have received grace—that is, forgiveness. Paul, in order to commend humility more effectively, places the name of humility before the name of dignity. We have also received apostleship among all the nations. For the Holy Spirit made me the Apostle of the Gentiles, when he said: “Set apart for me Barnabas and Paul for the work to which I have taken [I have taken] them” (Acts 13:2).

We have received, I say, apostleship among the nations, for the obedience of faith—that is, so that we might preach the faith, and, after receiving the faith, teach that one must obey what faith commands, rather than detracting from the grace of God through pride. This ought to be done for his name—that is, for the glory of God’s name.

Among whom—that is, among which nations—you also are, Romans, both Gentiles and Jews, called—that is, called through the grace of God. You were not chosen for faith on account of your own merit, I say, but for the faith of Jesus Christ—that is, in order that you might belong to Jesus Christ. For if the Jews should now object that they ought not to be subject to Paul, since he is only the apostle of the Gentiles, they would be mistaken. Once they have settled among the Gentiles, they belong to his apostleship, just as the Gentiles do. Thus, if foreigners now came to some bishopric, even if they were foreigners by nationality, nevertheless, because of their residence they would be counted as belonging to that bishopric. In the same way, those Jews, because they had joined themselves to the Gentiles, were counted among the Gentiles.

Paul, I say, such-and-such, an apostle of God, writes to all who are in Rome [Col. 0020B]. But, in order to exclude unbelievers, he adds: “To all who are beloved of God”—that is, whom God loves and whom he chose beforehand to become his own. To these, I say, who are called through the love and grace of God to be saints—that is, so that they may be holy—may there be grace, that is, forgiveness of your sins, and peace, that is, tranquillity of mind and perseverance in good things, from God our Father, who is able and therefore has the will; and from the Lord Jesus Christ, who likewise both wills and is able.

Paul, intending to correct the Romans through many and severe reproaches, foretells that he gives thanks to God for the good things they have already received and prays to God with every concern for those things that are still necessary for them, so that they may bear kindly the severity of what he is about to say and become well disposed toward him. It is as though he said: “I am going to say many things to you about your instruction, but first of all I will say what is most pleasing to me and about which I am most concerned: namely, I give thanks to God.”

To give thanks to God is to attribute everything to God and nothing to man. Hence he says: “I give thanks to God”—that is, the good things that I now see in you I ascribe to the grace of God, not to you—“my God,” who is mine in a certain spiritual [special] way, “through Jesus Christ,” whom alone I have as mediator between myself and God. You pass through me to Christ, and through Christ to God. Therefore I give thanks through Christ. You, however, ought to give thanks through me to Christ, and thus to God.

Perhaps some might think that he gave thanks only on behalf of one group—either the Jews or the Gentiles—and that he ascribed their good qualities to the grace of God alone. So that one group might not exalt itself over the other, he says: “On behalf of you Romans, whether you are Jews or Gentiles, I give thanks for all of you, and I ascribe your good faith to God alone.”

He specifies why he gives thanks, saying: “For this reason I give thanks to God: because the faith of God is in you. And your faith benefits not only you, but is proclaimed throughout the whole world.” For when the others hear that the faith of Christ has been received at Rome, which is the head of the world, they accept it by imitating their head.

Truly, I ascribe the already established goodness of your faith to the good grace of God, because I make mention of you in my prayers—that is, when I pray to God for the good things that you are going to possess, I ascribe everything to him. For if the good things that come after faith are ascribed to the grace of God, thanks ought especially to be given to God for faith, which draws a person from sins alone toward righteousness.

And that I make mention of you, God is my witness. If I were to call him as a witness to something false, I would judge myself guilty of falsehood.

Perhaps someone might say: “Because you do not care about God, you lightly call him as a witness to a false matter.” Against this he says: “The God whom I serve.” A servant would not call his lord to testify to a falsehood.

I serve God, certainly, in my spirit—that is, willingly, not under compulsion; or “in spirit,” that is, I serve God not in carnal things but in spiritual ones. He specifies in what service he serves: in the Gospel, that is, in proclaiming his Son. This service was especially pleasing to God at that time: to preach the glory of Christ, the Son of God [Col. 0021B].

For this reason God is my witness that in my prayers I make mention of you—that is, I make God mindful of you—without interruption, because I never cease mentioning you when I pray. He could indeed have prayed once a month, and then it would have been little to say that they had not been omitted at that time. Therefore he says: “Always in my prayers”—that is, I keep making mention of you every day without interruption—not only praying but also entreating, urgently asking God in certain sacred rites and adjurations whether I may be granted a way to come to you.

“May I have,” I say. “How?” That is, I would not care under whatever difficulty this might happen, whether thieves or storms were involved. May I finally have this opportunity. Here he shows that he had long desired it but had been unable to bring it about.

“May I have a way,” at some time—that is, at whatever time it might happen, whether in winter [Col. 0021C] or summer, I would not care. I also pray for this according to the Spirit, so that I may accomplish what I desire. And because many things have an outcome that displeases God, he adds: “According to the will of God.” For unless God willed this, I would prefer not to desire its accomplishment rather than to wish for it.

For this reason I wanted to come to you: because I desire to see you, so that I may impart some grace to you. You indeed already possess the grace of faith, but since other graces would be useful for preserving it, such as the grace of unity, he does not specify which grace, because he would minister to them whatever he saw to be necessary.

“I may impart,” I say, “some grace”—not secular grace, as it would be if he reconciled them with certain rulers of the world, but spiritual grace, that is, grace by which the spirit is nourished for eternal life.

Lest they perhaps think the grace of faith that they had received from Paul’s disciples was useless, because he said that he would give them grace, he says: “I do not mean that I may impart grace to initiate you into the faith”—for you have received sound faith—“but to strengthen you,” that is, to strengthen your faith in those things that ought to accompany faith, namely, that you should have unity and should not judge one another either more worthy or less worthy of the grace of God.

What I mean by “I desire to strengthen you” [Col. 0021D] is: “I desire to be consoled together with you.” When he says “to be consoled together,” he shows that he has grieved over their error. By saying “together,” he indicates that they are to be consoled through his teaching. For both reasons they ought patiently to endure any severe rebuke from Paul: through it they are to be consoled, and Paul has grieved over their error and is concerned to remove it from them.

“I desire,” I say, “to be consoled among you through your faith and mine”—a faith “made mutual,” that is, one that is such as to have reciprocal correspondence, so that just as my faith ascribes everything to the grace of God, so yours may do the same.

Or alternatively: he desires to be consoled through his faith made yours, so that you may believe every good thing to come through the grace of God. “Your faith,” I say, “made mutual”—that is, such as serves its proper purpose, so that, just as I—as is proper to a teacher—instruct by commanding, so you—as is proper to disciples—may learn by obeying.

I certainly desired to come to you, but I could not, because I was prevented. These impediments sometimes came upon Paul through the Holy Spirit [Col. 0022B], but more often through the dangers of thieves or storms at sea. Why I was prevented from coming, my brothers in the faith, I do not want you to remain ignorant.

For if you carefully inquire into the cause of this impediment, it will benefit you for correction, when you understand that I was prevented on account of the sin of your contentiousness. I do not want you to remain ignorant of this: I often planned to come to you, and until now I have been prevented from coming. When he says “until now,” he shows that he had often been prevented, as though he were saying: “Just as I often planned it, so I was often prevented.”

I planned, I say, to come to you in order to have among you what I also have among the other nations: some fruit—that is, either so that, corrected by my teaching, you might bear fruit for the better, or so that I might receive the fruit of my reward because I have laboured among you.

“I may have,” I say, “among you, just as I have among the other Gentiles”—that is, just as I taught the other nations to refer everything to the grace of God, so you too, having been taught by me, may do the same. I cannot cease from teaching you and the other nations, for I am a debtor—that is, I preach out of obligation—for this has been entrusted to me by the Holy Spirit: to Greeks and barbarians.

He calls all nations other than the Greeks “barbarians.” But the Greeks have always pursued wisdom more than the others, and in Greece Paul first established churches among the Gentiles. Among both Greeks and barbarians, therefore, whether Greeks or barbarians, I am a debtor to the wise and to the foolish, because among the Greeks there are wise and foolish people, and likewise among the barbarians.

And just as I am indebted to the other nations, so I am indebted to evangelize you, Jews and converted Gentiles who are in Rome. To evangelize you, that is, is ready—according to what is in me, that is, insofar as it depends on me. See to it that I do not find you unprepared hearers.

It truly is ready in me, for I am not ashamed of the Gospel. A person is ashamed of the Gospel in three ways: either when he foolishly blushes to preach the sufferings of Christ, the cross, death, and so forth; or when, living corruptly, he fears to preach righteousness lest he be reproached for teaching one thing and living another; or when the power of miracles is lacking for confirming his preaching.

But Paul was ashamed in none of these ways. Therefore he says: “I am not ashamed of the Gospel.” For in the Gospel the power of God is present to me, by which I both forgive sins [Col. 0023A] and perform miracles.

This Gospel, I say, is effective for every believer in obtaining salvation through the faith by which he has believed. “Every believer,” I say, namely, the Jew first, in the time when he believed; for the Church of Christ began in Judea. Also for the Greek believer—that is, for the Gentiles—because the Greeks were the head of the nations in knowledge; therefore by “Greeks” he signifies all Gentiles.

Or the meaning is this: the Gospel is salvation for the believing Jew and the Greek first—that is, especially—because it will provide sufficient salvation for both.

Truly, through the Gospel faith is obtained, and through faith eternal salvation. For in the Gospel righteousness is revealed both in knowledge and in conduct: “from faith,” that is, through the faith received from the Gospel, “righteousness,” that is, the performance of good works, through which righteousness eternal salvation is obtained.

Since faith comes through the Gospel, righteousness through faith, and eternal salvation through righteousness, it follows that salvation comes through the Gospel. He adds something further that is relevant, saying: “It is revealed from faith, proceeding into faith.” He does not say this as though he meant different faiths, but to teach that there are many stages in faith.

The Romans indeed had sound faith concerning Christ, but they erred in this: they did not attribute everything to the grace of God. Paul intends to place them at this stage of faith. From faith righteousness is obtained, and from righteousness salvation.

As it is written in the prophet Habakkuk: “But the righteous person lives by faith” (Habakkuk 2:4). Through the prophet he confirms the Gospel. For the prophet says: “Through the faith that is obtained through the Gospel, a person becomes righteous by doing good, and through righteousness he lives in eternal salvation.”

Up to this point he has spoken gently to the Romans, saying that he is concerned for their salvation, so that they may receive the Apostle’s corrections in a composed spirit. Here, however, he first attacks the Gentiles, whom he understands to be more easily corrected, so that afterward he may spend a longer time refuting the Jews. Nevertheless, he begins in this way:

“Truly, righteousness comes from faith, and salvation from righteousness. For, by contrast, from ungodliness—that is, from lack of faith or from idolatry—there follows unrighteousness, that is, evil works; and from unrighteousness follows the wrath of God, that is, eternal condemnation, which is contrary to salvation.”

He says this equivalently: “Truly, righteousness is revealed from faith, and thus salvation. For the wrath of God is revealed against all ungodliness.” The word “against” indicates opposition to ungodliness. And when he says “ungodliness,” this is stronger than if he had said “all the ungodly.” If he had said “the ungodly,” he would indeed have meant all the ungodly, but he would not have said that they were to be punished for each individual act of ungodliness. But by saying “all ungodliness,” he indicates that all the ungodly are to be punished for their individual acts of ungodliness.

Against all ungodliness, certainly, from whose unbelief proceeds unrighteousness—that is, perverse thought or action—and against all unrighteousness the wrath of God is revealed, that is, it is known that the wrath of God will come from heaven on the day of judgment. Then it will be revealed to those who have not believed until that day that Christ is the judge of all.

Or the wrath of God is revealed from heaven because that element itself, in its adornment and structure, shows that the wrath of the one who formed such a creature is to be feared. The wrath, I say, is revealed against the unrighteousness of human beings—of those human beings, I say, who suppress the truth, that is, the true knowledge of God that they naturally possess or are able to possess. They suppress it—that is, they hold it back—so that what nature demanded does not ascend to a fuller recognition of God. They suppress it in unrighteousness, that is, through the evil deeds they perform.

Truly, the ungodly suppress the truth of God in this way, because what can be known of God—that is, what may be known about God—is manifest. If not in the actual exercise of the thing, then at least in them, that is, in their rational faculties and in the potentiality of their intellect. Truly, what can be known of God is potentially manifest in all of them. For God made known in actuality to some of them what can be known of God.

If this was revealed in actuality to some, it is clear that it is manifest in potentiality. Plato and certain philosophers naturally recognized that there is one Creator of all things, though not without the assisting grace of God.

He proves that God revealed this in actuality to certain people, and then gives the manner of the revelation, saying: “Truly, God revealed it to some.” For his invisible things, that is, the invisible things of the divine essence, are seen by the creature of the world and are understood clearly rather than obscurely through those things that have been made.

By “invisible things” he signifies the Father, because he derives his beginning from no one, whereas the Son and the Holy Spirit derive theirs from the Father. He uses the plural number because the weakness of the human intellect is not sufficient to consider God except through temporal intervals, although the things that are natural in him are simultaneous and ought, if possible, to be considered in a single act.

“His eternal power,” moreover—that is, the power of his divine essence—is the Son, who is called the power and wisdom of the Father, eternally with the Father; and “divinity,” that is, goodness. Hence we also call good people divine. Goodness—that is, the divine love of his essence—is the Holy Spirit, who is nothing other than the goodness and love of the Father and the Son.

This power and divinity, I say, are seen and understood through the things that have been made [Col. 0024C]. For a human being cannot understand invisible things except through what he sees. When he looks upon some king of great empire, through that king he somehow understands the far greater king who created him. When he sees virtue or wisdom in someone, he thinks that there is much more virtue and wisdom in the one who gave it to him. In the same way, the goodness or love of God can be recognized through the goodness of a creature.

It would have been sufficient to consider this power and divinity in God by nature, even if people were ignorant of the names “Son” and “Holy Spirit.” For the power and divinity, or love, of God are the same as the Son and the Holy Spirit. The power and divinity of God are understood through the holy things that have been made.

Thus human beings are inexcusable because, although they knew God—if not in actuality, then at least through the potentiality of their natural intellect—they did not glorify God by worshipping and honouring him as God, nor did they give thanks. That is, they attributed the good things of their thought not to the grace of God but to themselves.

They did not give thanks to God. Instead, exalting themselves in their thoughts, they became futile, like smoke, which, the higher it rises, becomes all the more nothing. And because they became futile through pride, their heart—that is, their understanding, which had previously been subtle—was darkened on account of pride, until it became foolish [Col. 0025A].

They became futile, certainly. For they said that they were wise—that is, wise of themselves—and that their wisdom came from themselves, without God’s gift. And truly their heart was darkened. For by saying this and believing it to be so, they became fools. Thus they fell and were hurled from pride into ignorance and from ignorance into foolishness.

So they exchanged the glory of the incorruptible—that is, unchangeable—God, whereas every creature apart from him is changeable and therefore corruptible. They exchanged the glory of that God not for a true human being, but for the image of a corruptible human being.

And, to make an expressed image for themselves, they changed it into the likeness of an image—that is, into an image resembling it—worshipping the creature in place of the Creator. First the Gentiles changed the worship and religion of the Creator into the likeness of a human being; then into the likeness of birds; afterward into the likeness of four-footed animals; and after that into the likeness of serpents [Col. 0025B].

As it has been said: because they became proud in their understanding, they were deprived of understanding. And because they again rejected the Creator, they were punished by worshipping the creature. Again, because they did not wish to glorify God, as nature taught them, but worshipped creatures, toward which nature protested, they fell into sins that are contrary to nature, as follows:

“Because of this”—that is, because they worshipped creatures in a way contrary to nature—“God handed them over, by withdrawing his grace, to the desires of their hearts,” so that they might desire them in their minds. Then he handed them over “to impurity,” that is, to the deed of the impurity they had desired.

For this purpose, I say, he handed them over, so that they might dishonour—that is, contaminate—their bodies with insults, that is, with pollutions which, if inflicted upon them by force, they would regard as a great outrage. “They might dishonour,” I say, “in themselves,” that is, either one against another or each within himself. They understood that this ought to be done, although not by God, because previously they had exalted themselves through their understanding.

What he said above—“They exchanged the glory”—he repeats in order to enumerate the forms of the exchange, saying: “The Gentiles exchanged the truth,” that is, the worship that natural truth asserted ought to be offered to God, “for a lie,” that is, for creatures which they falsely imagined to be gods; and after imagining them, they worshipped them, that is, adored them.

Then they also served them by offering sacrifices and immolating offerings to the creature. In these three ways they exchanged the glory of God: first, they falsely thought that an idol was God; then they worshipped it; third, they sacrificed victims to it.

They served the creature, certainly, judging this preferable to serving the Creator. Yet the Creator loses nothing through their turning away, for he is blessed for ever, whatever they may worship. “Amen,” that is, it is certainly so.

What he said above—“God handed them over to their desires”—he repeats here, in order to compare the punishment of sin with the sin itself. For just as, by denying the Creator the worship that nature demanded, they turned toward the unnatural worship of creatures, so they themselves fell into sins contrary to nature.

He also explains how the sin spread through both sexes, saying: “Because they served the creature and not the Creator, God handed them over, deprived of his grace, to passions of dishonour,” that is, to shameful sins [deeds]. Although the flesh might wickedly desire these things, nature itself suffered violence, since it was not acting naturally within itself.

He enumerates the passions of dishonour, saying: “They were handed over to dishonour.” For the women among these Gentiles exchanged the natural use of the man for that use which is contrary to nature, so that one woman abused another, because they had denied the Creator his natural worship.

Likewise, the males, just as the women, abandoning the natural use of the woman, burned with desire for one another. They desired one another, each inflamed by the fire of lust, and, fulfilling in deed the depravity that their minds had desired, males committed acts with males.

And thus they received the recompense of their error, that is, the punishment of that sin. Because, although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God, they received this recompense not in the loss of property or children but in themselves, because those very people were punished by this penalty.

They ought, certainly, to receive this recompense—that is, it was fitting that they should receive it. Since they despised the Creator and worshipped the creature in opposition to what nature warned them not to do, it was rightly arranged that, for this unnatural sin, they should be plunged into an unnatural sin and the punishment of sin.

And just as, because they sinned by worshipping the creature in an unnatural form of worship, they were punished through unnatural sins, so, because they did not approve of retaining God in their knowledge—that is, because they did not possess God in their understanding, although nature itself rightly demonstrated that he ought to be known; that is, because they sinned through pride by abusing the knowledge of God naturally granted to them—God appropriately handed them over, after they had lost their former knowledge, to a debased mind, because they did not wish to use a sound understanding.

He handed them over, I say, for this purpose: to do things that are not fitting, that is, things that nature itself clearly understood to be unfitting.

First, because they abused the knowledge granted to them, thinking that this good of natural understanding came from themselves and not from God, they were deprived of the understanding granted to them. By abandoning the Creator, they worshipped creatures contrary to nature, and therefore they were punished again through things contrary to nature. But because even afterward they did not repent of their unnatural acts, they were plunged into other evils, as follows:

[Col. 0026D] “The Lord handed them over to a debased mind.” He handed over those, I say, who were filled with every iniquity, because they possessed both all iniquities and each one of them in full measure.

When he said “with every iniquity,” he included everything that follows. But, in order to frighten them more deeply, he enumerates the individual kinds of iniquity, saying: “Truly, with every iniquity, because they were filled with wickedness.”

For they acted wickedly toward their neighbours, taking away their goods or inflicting blows upon them. They were also filled with fornication. He calls fornication whatever is done apart from a lawful wife, who is said to be both the means of producing offspring and the means of avoiding fornication.

They were also filled with greed, unlawfully retaining what belonged to themselves or desiring what belonged to others; and they were filled with wickedness. “Wickedness” is derived either from *nequeo, nequis*—“I cannot, you cannot”—or from the noun *nequam*, “worthless,” because such people cannot restrain themselves from illicit things. But one who cannot restrain himself ought not to be called a person of worth.

They were also full of envy. For although they did not desire the goods of others for themselves, they nevertheless did not want those others to possess them. They were also full of murders, which are committed not only with the hands but also through planning and consent.

They were full of contention, because they quarrelled among themselves with shouting and insults. They were full of deceit, because they did one thing while thinking another. They were full of malice, because, contrary to kindness, they were always bitter in spirit.

They were also whisperers, secretly carrying evil reports about one neighbour to another; and slanderers, taking away the good qualities that existed and imposing evils that did not exist.

Lest these two offences seem easy, since they might not believe that they would be condemned for words alone, he aggravates them by saying: “Whisperers and slanderers, hateful to God.”

I also call them abusive, that is, inflicting shameful insults upon one another; proud, that is, placing themselves above others or desiring to do so; arrogant, unable either to endure equals or to tolerate those greater than themselves—as with Caesar, who did not wish to tolerate Pompey as his superior, and Pompey, who did not wish Caesar to be his equal.

They were also inventors of evils, whether evil customs or instruments of torture; and they were disobedient to their fleshly parents, something that nature teaches even in the case of the young of birds.

They were foolish, that is, undiscerning with respect to good and evil; disorderly both in their clothing and in the immoderate arrangement of their limbs. For through the things we see outwardly, we form judgments about inward things.

They were without affection, that is, without the application of the mind to anything worthy; without a covenant, that is, without the binding together of the spirit. Since covenants serve to nourish faith so that it may always multiply, marriages within the same kinship were prohibited, because that kinship is already sufficiently bound by the bond of relationship.

They were also without mercy, because if they saw anyone in misery, they did not possess toward them the inward compassion of mercy.

In all these things the Gentiles were punished for the sins mentioned above. But because they still did not repent through these punishments, they were plunged into another evil: blinded, they promised themselves impunity for their sins.

Hence he says: “The Gentiles, blinded, did not understand that those who do such things as have been described are worthy of eternal death.” They did not understand in this way, although they had previously known the righteousness of God naturally. They are said to have been deprived of this knowledge because they became proud through it.

They are certainly worthy of death—not only those who do the things described, but also those who consent to those who do them. According to Ambrose, to consent means either to remain silent about something one could reproach or, when hearing such things, to flatter the person doing them.

If, therefore, those who do the evils described and those who consent to them are worthy of condemnation, no Gentile will escape this death.

## CHAPTER II

“Therefore you are inexcusable, O every human being who judges. For in judging another, you condemn yourself. For you do the same things that you judge.

“For we know that the judgment of God is according to truth against those who do such things. But do you suppose this, O human being, who judges those who do such things and does them yourself, that you will escape the judgment of God?

“Or do you despise the riches of his goodness, patience, and longsuffering? Do you not know that the kindness of God leads you to repentance?

“But according to your hardness and unrepentant heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of the righteous judgment of God, who will repay each person according to his works.

“To those who, with perseverance in good work, seek glory, honour, and incorruption: eternal life. But to those who are contentious and do not obey the truth, yet believe iniquity: wrath and indignation.

“Tribulation and anguish upon every soul of a human being who works evil, of the Jew first and also of the Greek; but glory, honour, and peace to everyone who works good, to the Jew first and also to the Greek.

“For there is no partiality with God.

“For whoever has sinned without the law will also perish without the law; and whoever has sinned under the law will be judged by the law. For it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law will be justified.

“For when Gentiles, who do not have the law, naturally do the things of the law, although they do not have the law, they are a law for themselves. They show the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience bearing witness to them, and their thoughts accusing or even defending one another, on the day when God will judge the hidden things of human beings, according to my Gospel, through Jesus Christ.

“But if you are called a Jew, and rest upon the law, and glory in God, and know his will, and approve the things that are more useful, being instructed through the law; if you trust that you yourself are a guide of the blind, a light of those who are in darkness, an instructor of the foolish, a teacher of children, having in the law the form of knowledge and truth—

“You, therefore, who teach another, do you not teach yourself? You who preach that one must not steal, do you steal? You who say that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery? You who abhor idols, do you commit sacrilege? You who glory in the law, do you dishonour God through transgression of the law?

“For ‘the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you,’ as it is written.

“Circumcision indeed profits, if you observe the law; but if you are a transgressor of the law, your circumcision has become uncircumcision.

“If, therefore, uncircumcision keeps the ordinances of the law, will not its uncircumcision be counted as circumcision? And will not that which is uncircumcision by nature, while fulfilling the law, judge you who, through the letter and circumcision, are a transgressor of the law?

“For the Jew is not the one who is so outwardly, nor is circumcision that which is outwardly in the flesh. But the Jew is the one who is so inwardly, and circumcision is of the heart, in the spirit, not in the letter. His praise is not from human beings but from God.”

## EXPOSITION
Up to this point he has sufficiently disparaged the Gentiles according to their former condition, showing that they cannot be excused on the ground of ignorance, since they naturally possessed knowledge of God, of which they were deprived because of sin. But what had been said here only about the Gentiles he now transfers to both peoples [Col. 0029A], that is, to Jews and Gentiles, declaring both peoples inexcusable.

For if a Jew should say that he had been God’s special people, born from the stock of Abraham, that he had possessed the Law and the Prophets, and that, since he was so loved by God, it should not be believed that God would allow one so beloved to perish, even if he had gone astray—and should reproach the Gentile as unworthy of salvation, since God had never at any time remembered him; while, conversely, if the Gentile should say that the Jew was unworthy of salvation because, although he had come to know God through the Law, he had refused to glorify Him, and should consider himself preferable to the Jew because, as soon as he first heard about God, he immediately believed, and because he was not guilty of the sins he had committed through ignorance—the Apostle acts against both positions, saying that the Gentile is inexcusable in his ignorance because he possessed natural [Col. 0029B] knowledge, while the Jew glories in vain either in the Law or in his lineage, since he has always become worse precisely where he ought to have become better: by transgressing the Law, degenerating in faith from Abraham, and doing similar things.

It is as though he were saying: Since those who do such things and those who consent to them are worthy of death, therefore you—every Jew and Gentile who lives and understands in the same way—are inexcusable, you, I say, who judge, that is, condemn, another. For if you, Jew, say that you are to be preferred to the Gentile because you have been beloved by God, whom you say never remembered the Gentile; or if you, Gentile, claim to be excused by ignorance in comparison with the Jew, who dishonored the God made known to him through the Law, both of you are inexcusable: the Gentile because he possessed natural knowledge, and the Jew because the Law and [Col. 0029C] natural understanding taught him about God.

Truly you are both inexcusable, because in the very matter in which you judge the other, you condemn yourself—whether the Jew judges the Gentile or the Gentile the Jew. For if the Law that was given condemns the Jew because he did not keep it, the natural law, likewise not kept, condemns the Gentile. Truly you condemn yourself. For you do the very things that you judge, that is, condemn, in another.

If you, Jew, think that the Gentile ought to be condemned for the reasons mentioned above, but think that you yourself, although committing the same crimes, should be spared because of the Law and your lineage, you are mistaken. Conversely, if you, Gentile, condemn the Jew because he possessed the Law and did not keep it, by this very judgment you condemn yourself as a transgressor of the natural law. Truly, in the matter in which you judge the other, you condemn yourself.

[Col. 0029D] For we, who possess great authority, know that the judgment of God is against those who do such things as have been mentioned—not according to the ignorance that you, Gentile, vainly claim, nor according to the lineage of Abraham in which you, Jew, glory—but according to pure truth, that is, according to the deeds of each person, Jew and Gentile. But you suppose, that is, falsely imagine, this, O man—whether Jew or Gentile—who judge those who do such things as have been mentioned while doing them yourself. You suppose, I say, that you will escape the judgment of God: that from the very basis on which you judge another worthy of condemnation, you yourself will escape unpunished.

First, because they think that God’s judgment takes place according to the dignity or indignity of persons, and not according to their deeds, they fall into this evil: they promise themselves impunity. Then, because of the evil of the impunity promised to themselves, they rush into another evil, namely, that they abuse God’s goodness and patience. This is what he said above: “that you will escape the judgment of God.” He had indicated the same thing earlier when he said: “They did not understand that those who do such things are worthy of death” (Rom. I, 32). In both passages he is dealing with the impunity that they promise themselves. But there he speaks only about the Gentiles, whereas here he understands both peoples.

You despise the riches of His goodness because you first imagine that you will escape God’s judgment. This is said by comparison with a powerful man: if he were to offer food to someone, and the person to whom it was offered, indignant at receiving it, were to throw it away, he would appear to despise not the food but the giver of the food. In the same way, one who abuses God’s goodness by not using it for correction, for which God grants it, is guilty not only of his past deeds but also of having despised majesty.

He calls it the “riches of goodness” because God abundantly gives temporal goods even to the wicked, who would not be worthy of them, so that, considering God’s kindness, they may return to Him. He also gives teachers to instruct them, and understanding by which they may know that it is good to return to God, as well as many other things.

Or do you despise the riches of His goodness, and the riches of His patience because He tolerates you not in one sin but in a thousand, and the riches of His long-suffering because for a long time He endures your correction? You despise them, I say, not knowing that the kindness of God, through goodness, patience, and long-suffering, leads you, so far as it depends upon it, to repentance.

The kindness of God, so far as it depends upon it, calls you to repentance. But [Col. 0030C] according to your hardness—that is, according to your actions stubbornly fixed in evil—and according to your unrepentant heart, because you neither withdraw from evil deeds nor understand that you are doing evil, you treasure up wrath for yourself.

For there are some who are stubborn in evil deeds and yet believe that they are doing evil. You, I say, according to your unrepentant heart, treasure up wrath for yourself, that is, gather for yourself your own future condemnation on the day of wrath, that is, on the day of the common condemnation of the ungodly.

On the day of the revelation of God’s righteous judgment—for on that day even by the ungodly Christ will be believed to be the judge of all, although they have always denied this—every flesh will then see Him. God will then repay each person, Jew and Gentile, according to his deeds, neither sparing the Gentile on account of ignorance nor saving the Jew on account of the Law or the lineage of Abraham.

What he stated as a whole he explains in parts, saying: “He will repay each according to his deeds.” To those who are of good work, that is, who have acted well according to patience—either because they did not abuse God’s patience but corrected themselves while God was bearing with them, or according to patience because they endured with equanimity whatever adversities they suffered for God—to such He will indeed give glory, that is, brightness of body and illumination of soul.

He will also give honor, because they will be among the honored in Christ’s presence; and with the angels of God He will also give incorruption, that is, a permanent state in glory and honor, which they could have possessed for an hour and then lose.

To these, with this qualification, I say, He will give it: to those seeking eternal life, that is, if they work well out of love for eternal life, and not seeking from it temporal profits or the glory of the world.

To those who are of good work He will repay in this way. But to those who are contentious—that is, to those who contentiously prefer themselves to one another—this vice is especially attributed, because they were occupied with it, and he attempts to deter them from it.

To those, I say, who contend and do not submit to the truth when good is urged upon them, as did the Romans, who were unwilling to submit to Paul’s disciples but believed in iniquity, preferring themselves one to another—to such there will certainly be wrath, that is, eternal condemnation, and a wrath that takes the form of indignation.

For when the ungodly have been placed in the fire, they will be gravely indignant with themselves because they acted wickedly. Meanwhile, while that judgment is delayed, wrath will come upon every soul of a human being who works evil: [Col. 0031A] upon the Jew first, that is, especially upon the one who works evil, because he is guilty both of the natural law and of the Law that was given; and upon the Greek, that is, the Gentile, who is accused only on the basis of the natural law.

To the soul of the one who works evil—to the Jew indiscriminately and to the Greek—there will be tribulation, that is, condemnation and anguish. This is what he called “indignation,” because he is describing the evil that would occur both after the judgment and before it.

He does not say in advance what will happen to the good, but what will happen to them after the judgment, in the interim until the judgment comes. There will be tribulation for the one who works evil. But for every one who works good—for the Jew, who first in time worked good, since the Church of Christ began in Judea, and for the Greek, that is, the Gentile, who later in time works good—there will be glory, that is, that brightness and honor by which he will be among the honored; and peace, that is, lasting tranquility in glory and honor.

Truly glory will be given impartially to Jew and Gentile alike, [Col. 0031C] if only they have worked well.

For with God there is no acceptance of persons: He will not save the Jew who acts wickedly because he possessed the Law, nor reject the Gentile who has deserved well because he was not descended in the flesh from Abraham. It is better to imitate Abraham’s faith than to derive one’s line of descent from him. For many descended from Abraham’s flesh have passed over into the Gentiles, while many from the Gentiles, by imitating Abraham’s faith, have made themselves worthy of Abraham’s promises and have been reckoned among the Jews as proselytes.

He proves that God does not accept the person of either Jew or Gentile because He will judge both, and he explains the manner of the future judgment concerning both, saying: Truly, with God there is no acceptance of persons, because He judges everyone—both those who are without the Law [Col. 0031D] and those who are under the Law.

For whoever sinned without the Law, that is, without possessing the written Law, will perish without the Law, that is, will be condemned not for transgression of the written Law but only of the natural law. This was said about the Gentiles.

And whoever sinned in the Law, that is, while possessing the written Law, as the Jews do, will be judged through the Law, that is, they will be condemned for the transgression of the Law that was given, together with their other sins.

The Jew might object that, although he had transgressed while under the Law, he nevertheless should not be condemned but should be spared by God. Against this Paul says: Truly those who possess the Law will be judged by their sin, because they are not righteous before God.

And although before human beings those who are hearers of the Law—that is, those who have merely heard the Law and have not practiced it, as the Jews have—may be respected, it is the doers of the Law who will be justified, whether they are Gentiles or Jews: those who have fulfilled the work of the Law, whether they have heard it or have merely practiced it.

The verse that follows deals only with the Gentiles. It proves that they can be saved through the natural law when they do the same things that are written in the Law, and that they are condemned if they do not do them.

This verse deals with both matters: with the salvation of the Gentiles because of the work of the Law, and with their condemnation if they have not practiced the Law. It is as though someone were objecting to Paul: You say that whoever is a doer of the Law will be saved, but Gentiles ought not to be saved, because even if they do the work of the Law, they do so indiscriminately, not led by reason [or, according to the transmitted reading, *nomine*], but by chance [*casu*, perhaps intended as *causa*, “by a cause”], like those who have been instructed by no Scriptures.

Against this Paul says: Truly, if Gentiles are doers of the Law, they will be justified; and, conversely, if they have done evil, they will be condemned with wrath and indignation. They deserve to be saved for the good and punished for the evil.

“For they are a law to themselves,” that is, they possess the natural law within themselves. They, I say, do not possess a law of that kind—that is, a written law, as the Jews do—and yet truly they are a law to themselves.

For this is what happens: the Gentiles who do not possess the written Law, that is, the Gentiles, naturally do the things of the written Law, that is, the things commanded by the written Law, following the natural law.

Nor do they do the things of the Law indiscriminately, because those who show by their conduct that the work of the Law is written in their hearts abandon evil and cling to good. For this is the work of the Law: to turn away from evil and to do good.

And if you do not believe that the Gentiles can be saved through the natural law, [Col. 0032C] this does not in any way prevent their salvation. For on the day when God judges, it will appear that the work of the Law was written in their hearts.

On that day their conscience—which will then be made manifest to everyone, since there the deeds of each person will be openly known to all—will bear witness for them concerning the good or evil things they have done.

For they will then have many witnesses, since their conscience will be hidden from no one. And just as it will bear witness concerning their deeds, so their conscience will bear witness to their thoughts, because, just as they will be justified with respect to their deeds, so also with respect to their thoughts.
