I speak of thoughts that accuse them if they are evil, or that defend them if they are good—and this in relation to one another. For those that are evil will accuse both the good and one another, while, conversely, the good will oppose the evil.

This conflict will occur in those whose good or evil is uncertain. But in those whose good is certain without any admixture of evil, as in the saints, and in those whose evil is certain without any relief from good, as in the extremely wicked, there will be no struggle of this accusation or defense. Rather, there will be certain salvation for the exceedingly good and unquestionable condemnation for the exceedingly wicked.

This testimony of deeds and thoughts their conscience will give them on that day when God judges the hidden things of all human beings, that is, their uncertain matters, whether good or evil.

He will judge through Jesus Christ, who has been appointed judge of all according to my Gospel, that is, according to what I proclaim: that God will judge all things through Christ.

He has proved that a Gentile can be saved naturally by doing the work of the written Law. Now [Col. 0033A] he begins to prove that it is of no benefit to the Jew that he is called a Jew and has possessed the Law and circumcision, unless he fulfills the work of the Law and of circumcision, saying: The Gentile possessed the natural law, but you, Jew, have possessed both the natural and the written Law.

It must be considered that the Apostle is speaking about the Jew and the Gentiles according to their former condition:

“You, I say, are called a Jew,” that is, you possess this dignified title, by which you are called a Jew.

Before Judas Maccabaeus, only those from the tribe of Judah were called Jews; all the others were called Israelites. But from Judas Maccabaeus onward, because of his virtue, everyone was called a Jew.

“I grant,” says Paul, “that you are called a Jew, because you rest in the Law.” For the other nations are wandering, since they possess no instructions concerning life; but you [Col. 0033B] have rest in knowledge of the Law.

And you glory in God, because it is said that God is known in Israel alone (Ps. LXXV, 1). The other nations are, as it were, without God; therefore you boast and glory.

You also know His will, namely, God’s: what He wishes to be done and what He does not wish to be done.

And, instructed through the Law, you approve what is more useful, that is, you know how to distinguish the more useful things among the useful things of the Law.

You also trust that you yourself are a guide of the blind, that is, of the Gentiles, because if any of the Gentiles should wish to pass over into Judaism, you teach them to observe the Sabbath and the other requirements of the Law, although, because they do not yet know what these things signify, they are blind.

You also trust that you are a light to those who are in darkness. For when they observe the Sabbath while still ignorant of the mystery of the Sabbath, you enlighten them by teaching [Col. 0033C] what these things signify and what purpose they serve, and thus you lead them out of the darkness of ignorance.

You also trust that you are an instructor of foolish Jews, because if there are any who are foolish in the Law, you teach them to be wise.

You also trust that you are a teacher of infants, because if simple people know nothing of the Law that they can even express, you teach them to discuss the Law.

You also possess the form of knowledge, because if someone wishes to consider how great the Law is, he may know that it is as great as your knowledge of it.

You also possess the form of truth in the Law, because you know that both your knowledge of the Law and everything it teaches are true. For we may possess knowledge of Ovid and yet not know that the things narrated there are true.

Therefore, since you are indeed a guide of the blind and enlighten them through the teaching of the Law, you who teach another, why do you not teach yourself?

Thus, although through the Law you ought to advance by rejecting the work of the Law, you are shown to be all the more guilty.

You also, who preach that one must not steal, why do you steal? The Jews frequently stole one another’s possessions. But what is worse, they stole the sound understanding of the Law.

You also, who say that one must not commit adultery, why do you commit adultery? They committed adultery literally; they also committed adultery by placing an adulterated interpretation in the Law, after they had stolen the Law’s sound meaning.

You also, who abhor idols—that is, who judge that the Gentiles who worship idols should not even be called human beings—why do you commit sacrilege, that is, why do you yourself worship idols?

For the Jews often fell into the worship of idols. They committed sacrilege by denying Christ His worship. [Col. 0034A] Sacrilege consists in denying the Creator the worship that the creature naturally owes Him, namely, worship owed to God.

You also, who glory in the Law—that is, who boast that you alone possessed the Law—why do you dishonor God through transgression of the Law?

To transgress the Law is not to do what it commands to be done and to do what it forbids to be done.

But the Jews, by abandoning the Law and doing what was contrary to the Law, dishonored God as far as human opinion was concerned, although they took nothing away from His glory.

Truly, insofar as it lies with you, you dishonor God, because the name of God is blasphemed through you among the Gentiles.

For when the Gentiles see you doing things contrary to the Law, profaning God’s righteousness, sharing in the food of the Gentiles, and doing similar things, they say and think that God instructed you to behave in this way and that He did not carefully choose such people for His worship.

Ezekiel said this, although in different words, about the Jews dispersed among the Gentiles and passing over to idolatry.

Therefore Paul says: What I say—that God is blasphemed through you—I say among the Gentiles, as it is written; for Scripture bears witness to this matter.

And because you have transgressed the Law, your circumcision has become uncircumcision, that is, it is no more valuable for you to be circumcised than for a Gentile to be uncircumcised.

Just as he asserted above that it was of no benefit to be called a Jew or to possess the Law, so here he proves that circumcision is of no value to the one who has not fulfilled the mystery of circumcision.

For that cutting away of the flesh signifies that carnal generation, which is in sins, must be cut away, and that a spiritual generation must thereafter be embraced.

[Col. 0034C] The Jew might say: If circumcision is uncircumcision, it was given for nothing, since it provides no benefit.

Against this Paul says: Circumcision certainly is beneficial, if you observe the law of circumcision—that is, if, in the way circumcision signifies, you cut away all vices from yourself. It is beneficial, then, when its law is observed. But if you are a transgressor of the law of circumcision, by not cutting away the vices of the heart, your circumcision has thus become uncircumcision, that is, it is no more useful to you than uncircumcision is to the Gentile.

Circumcision is itself called the cleanliness of the flesh. Uncircumcision—that is, the flesh that was amputated—is called uncleanness itself, because the flesh itself becomes a resting-place for lust.

And because circumcision, when the law of circumcision is not observed, becomes uncircumcision, therefore uncircumcision, if it keeps the righteous requirements of the law of circumcision, will become circumcision.

But lest anyone dare to contradict this, he presents it as a question, saying:

If uncircumcision—that is, the Gentile, whom you judge to be uncleanness itself, while you regard yourself as circumcision, that is, cleanliness itself—if, I say, uncircumcision keeps the righteous requirements of the law of circumcision, cutting away the vices of the heart even though the flesh has not been amputated, will not the uncircumcision of the one who keeps the Law be reckoned as circumcision?

That is: will it not benefit him in the same way as the Law, when kept by one who is circumcised, benefits him?

And will not uncircumcision, which fulfills—that is, completes—the law of circumcision, and does so by nature, that is, through the natural law, judge—that is, condemn—you by comparison with itself?

You, I say, who are a transgressor of the Law kept according to the letter, because you choose the literal observance and reject the spiritual. You are also a transgressor through the circumcision possessed in the flesh but not observed in the heart.

Truly circumcision becomes uncircumcision. For the one who is a Jew in the outward sense—that is, in name only—is not to be believed to be a Jew. Nor is that circumcision which is outward, and therefore only in the flesh and not in the heart, to be called circumcision.

He again proves that uncircumcision, as has been said, will become circumcision, saying:

The Jew in the outward sense is not a Jew, but the one who is a Jew inwardly—that is, in the presentation of his works—even if he is not called by this name.

And circumcision of the heart is circumcision accomplished in the spirit, that is, spiritually fulfilled, not in the letter, that is, not literally, as a carnal observance. This is indeed spiritual and true circumcision. [Col. 0035B] Its praise—that is, the praise of this circumcision, which is worthy of praise—is not from human beings but from God.

For God alone can give righteousness to the heart; human beings can cut away the flesh and can do nothing else.

## CHAPTER III

“What then has the Jew in addition? Or what is the benefit of circumcision? Much in every way. First, indeed, because the oracles of God were entrusted to them.

“For what if some of them did not believe? Surely their unbelief did not nullify the faithfulness of God? Certainly not! But God is truthful, and every human being is a liar, as it is written: ‘So that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged’ (Ps. L, 6).

“But if our iniquity commends the righteousness of God, what shall we say? Is God unrighteous, who inflicts wrath? I speak according to human understanding. Certainly not! Otherwise, how will God judge the world?

“For if the truth of God abounded through my lie to His glory, why am I still judged as a sinner?

“And why should we not do evil so that good may come, as we are slanderously accused and as some claim that we say? Their condemnation is just.

“What then? Are we superior to them? Not at all. For we have already charged that Jews and Greeks alike are all under sin, as it is written: ‘There is no one righteous, no one who understands, no one who seeks God’ (Ps. XIII, 2).

“They have all turned aside; together they have become worthless: ‘there is no one who does good, not even one’ (ibid., 3).

“‘Their throat is an open tomb; with their tongues they dealt deceitfully; the venom of asps is under their lips’ (ibid.).

“Their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness; their feet are swift to shed blood. Destruction and misery are in their ways, and they have not known the way of peace. There is no fear of God before their eyes” (ibid.).

“But we know that whatever the Law says, it speaks to those who are in the Law, so that every mouth may be stopped and the whole world may become subject to God; because no flesh will be justified before Him by works of the Law. For through the Law comes knowledge of sin.

“But now the righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the Law, testified to by the Law and the Prophets. The righteousness of God, moreover, is through faith in Jesus Christ for all and upon all who believe in Him. For there is no distinction.

“For all have sinned and lack the glory of God, being justified freely by His grace, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus. God appointed Him as a propitiatory offering through faith in His blood, to demonstrate His righteousness, because of the forgiveness of the preceding sins in the forbearance of God, to demonstrate His righteousness at the present time, so that He Himself may be righteous and justify the one who is of the faith of Jesus Christ.

“Where, then, is your boasting? It has been excluded. By what law? Of works? No, but by the law of faith.

“For we hold that a person is justified by faith apart from works of the Law.

“Or is God the God of Jews only? Is He not also the God of the Gentiles? Indeed, of the Gentiles also.

“Since there is one God, who justifies circumcision by faith and uncircumcision through faith.

“Do we then overthrow the Law through faith? Certainly not! Rather, we establish the Law.”

## EXPOSITION

Because he had earlier proved that uncircumcision becomes circumcision, and conversely that circumcision becomes uncircumcision, the Jew might object that, under the former condition of the Old Testament, nothing more had been conferred upon him than upon the Gentile.

To refute this, Paul inserts the Jew’s objection:

Because I said that uncircumcision is reckoned as circumcision, and conversely, he will therefore say to me: What more was conferred upon the Jew in the former condition than upon the Gentile? Or what benefit was circumcision to the Jew, when uncircumcision had the same value for the Gentile?

Circumcision would seem to have been made for nothing and the Law given superfluously if the good of the Law and of circumcision could be possessed without them, as is shown in the Gentile.

The Jew under the former condition certainly had much more conferred upon him than the Gentile, even if he did not observe it. For the fact that he was circumcised and instructed in the other matters contained in the Law was a good preparation and a kind of instruction for understanding the faith of Christ.

But the Gentile possessed no instruction at all apart from natural understanding.

I do not, however, say that the Jew is thereby more worthy than the Gentile in the faith of Christ; rather, he is more prepared for the faith. Therefore, if he did not consent to the faith, he was more condemned than the Gentile; but if he did consent, he did not thereby surpass the Gentile in the dignity of faith.

You ask what more was conferred upon the Jew. Much indeed, and in every way—both according to soul and according to body. Many good things were done for each Jew, both in body and in soul, none of which the Gentile possessed.

In the body, because God delivered them from enemies and gave them the promised land, and so forth. In the soul, because He instructed them through the Law, and they possessed knowledge of God, and so forth. He conferred many similar things upon them, both in body and in soul.

Concerning these Paul says: I could set forth many things to prove that more was conferred upon the Jew than upon the Gentile. But first—that is, because this is the chief point for proving what I intend—I will put forward this: more was conferred upon the Jew because the oracles of God were entrusted to them, that is, placed before them for their instruction—the commandments that God gave in the Law and the Prophets.

The Jew again objects: Through the oracles that were given, no more was possessed by the Jew than by the Gentile, because he did not believe the oracles of God.

Paul truly says that more was possessed by the Jew through the entrusted oracles. For if some of those Jews did not believe the oracles of God and were therefore rejected, what prevents the Jew from having received more than the Gentile? Nothing prevents it, because, insofar as it depended on God, He prepared them for faith, even though they remained unbelieving.

Truly, if some of them did not believe, this prevents nothing, because God did not cease to fulfill what He had promised on account of their unbelief.

Did the unbelief of some of them nullify the faithfulness—that is, the fulfillment—of God’s promises? God left none of the things He had promised unfulfilled. Therefore nothing prevents the Jew from having possessed more, even though some were condemned in unbelief.

I ask whether God’s faithfulness was nullified because of the unbelievers. Certainly not! It is impossible that God’s faithfulness should in any way be or be thought to be nullified.

For although some of them did not believe, God is truthful, that is, the fulfiller of everything He promised.

God is certainly truthful, but every human being, whoever he may be, whether Jew or Gentile, is a liar, that is, a sinner. For when God came to save, He found every human being under sin and, according to his merits, unworthy of salvation.

Hence it is clear that God’s faithfulness and salvation come equally to Jews and Gentiles by grace.

Every sin is called a lie, because every creature, which by nature ought to obey its Creator, makes its nature false when it transgresses God’s command, abandoning the purity in which it was created.

I also assert through the testimony of Scripture that God is truthful. For I say this as it is written about God’s truth in the Psalm: God is undoubtedly truthful.

David says: “You may be justified in your words” (Ps. L, 6), that is: by justifying me, may you appear truthful in your promises.

This is read as part of the continuation of the Psalm, in which David, guilty of many crimes, was dealing with the betrayal of a soldier, the death of his neighbor, unlawful desire, and adultery, so that he might obtain forgiveness for all these things.

He was confident of that forgiveness because of the promise made to him concerning Christ—a promise made only to those who were to be saved through Christ. Therefore he trusts that he will be cleansed from this crime; otherwise he would be unworthy of the salvation to come.

Moreover, it must be noted that David, claiming no merit, trusts that he will be saved solely by grace, and confesses himself to be in sins, although scarcely anyone lived holier than he under the Law. Thus no one can be saved by merit, but only by grace.

“Be justified in your words and prevail against the ungodly when you are judged by them not to be the Son of God, when you overcome them by justifying human beings as you promised.”

Or: “Prevail when you are judged,” that is, when you are made a participant with someone, as with me. For they say that I am not to be saved because of sin, although you have been promised to me.

Here Paul introduces something that appears unrelated to what he began. For it was alleged against him and the other apostles that they taught that it was good to sin, because the more numerous human sins were, the more glorious God would appear when He forgave them all, and because “where sin abounded, grace abounded still more,” and similar claims.

Paul now begins to destroy this allegation, and he does so very appropriately. For here he will prove that all salvation comes from God’s grace and that nothing comes from human merit, saying:

Because every human being was found guilty as a liar, while God, justifying every guilty person by grace, is truthful in His promises, it follows that our iniquity commends the righteousness of God—that is, it makes God commendable, because He justifies human beings from sins by grace alone.

This is certainly true, because the more abundant His grace is in forgiving sins, the more unquestionably commendable God is.

But although He forgives every kind of sin, He does not thereby provide a cause for sinning. Our iniquity commends God; but if this is so, if God becomes more commendable through our iniquity, what shall we say about this?

Something astonishing seems to follow from it. What shall we say, then? Is God unrighteous because He inflicts wrath—that is, punishment—on account of sin, even though that sin makes God more commendable?

This appears contrary to justice. I say that it does not seem sufficiently just that He punishes the sin that commends Him. I say this entirely according to human understanding, that is, according to the understanding of one who thinks carnally.

But I say this on my own behalf: far be it from us to think that God is unrighteous because He punishes sin.

He proves this from the impossible, saying: God is truly not unrighteous in inflicting wrath, because otherwise—that is, if God were unrighteous—how will He judge this world?

It cannot be believed that the one appointed judge of the whole world is unrighteous; that is impossible.

Truly, if God is unrighteous, He will not judge the world, nor will He judge me alone. But He will not judge me concerning sin for this reason: that I increase His glory by it.

For if through my lie—that is, on account of my sin—the truth of God abounded, that is, if God was shown more abundantly, through the truth of His promise, to have forgiven sins, then it abounded to the glory of God Himself.

I say that it abounded to His glory because the more He forgave, the more glorious He was recognized to be in mercy.

If my sin is thus the cause of His glory, why am I still—that is, why am I also in this world, leaving others aside—judged, that is, condemned, as a sinner?

I ought not to be accused of this sin, by which I increase God’s glory. Why, then, should we not do evil so that the good things of God’s mercy may thereby come in greater abundance, as we are slanderously accused by some of believing?

They say that we not only believe this but also say it and preach it to others: Let us do evil, that is, let us sin eagerly, so that good may come, that is, so that God may have sins to forgive in multiplied abundance.

The condemnation of those who slander us in this way is just; that is, they are rightly condemned for this blasphemy. For if I judge that they ought to be condemned for the sin of blasphemy, it is evident that I do not preach that it is good to sin.

Those who held this view of mercy were preaching that God’s grace consisted in mercy.

Because it has already been proved that every human being, both Jew and Gentile, is a liar, therefore, O Jew, tell me: what—that is, for what reason—should we surpass them, namely, the Gentiles, in salvation?

We certainly do not surpass them. Truly, we do not surpass them.

For we have charged—that is, we have proved by suitable causes and arguments—that Jews and Gentiles alike, without exception, are not merely in sin but are so weighed down under sin that no one can rise by himself without the assistance of grace.

He proves concerning the Jews that they are all under sin, saying:

In saying that all Jews are under sin, Scripture bears witness to me. For I assert this as it is written in the Psalm: “There is no one righteous.”

That clause is read in the order of the Psalm: there is indeed no one righteous, that is, no one who abandons evil and does good.

And this is because there is no one who understands. They do not understand because there is no one who seeks God.

For if they sought God, they would certainly understand, and, once understanding, they would pursue righteousness.

No one among the Jews is righteous; rather, they have all turned aside by doing evil among themselves. Nor was this enough for them: they also became worthless, that is, they devoted themselves to the corruption of others.

They turned aside so far that there is no one among them who does good.

I do not say that, once the greater number have been excluded from the good, some remain in the good; rather, “there is none who does good,” extending the statement “as far as one” (Psalm 13), because not even one who does good is left among them. Or, “there is none who does good” until one comes—that is, to Christ through faith. For whoever comes to Christ by faith certainly does good.

There is none among them who does good; rather, “their throat is an open tomb,” which, after receiving corpses, stinks and remains open to receive more corpses. So they stink from their former sins and still gape for the perpetration of crimes; and, since they cannot do openly what they desire, “they acted deceitfully with their tongues” (Psalms 13, 139), thinking one thing and pretending another. “And beneath their lips” (Deuteronomy 32)—that is, in the heart which lies beneath their lips—“is the poison of asps,” incurable, because no one can be healed so long as he consents to them.

The mouth of these Jews is full of cursing. For they cursed Christ, saying that he was the son of a craftsman, and similar things. Their mouth is also full of bitterness (Psalm 9). They uttered bitter words, crying out, “Crucify him, crucify him!” (Mark 15; Luke 23). And their feet—that is, the affections of these Jews—are swift to shed blood. For they shed Christ’s blood first in intention, before doing so in action.

And because they are so wicked, therefore “destruction” is in their ways—that is, in their deeds—their wretched dispersion throughout the world, brought about by the Romans. There is also misery in their deeds, that is, the damnation of their souls, which alone deserves to be called misery. And all this happened to them because they did not wish to know “the way of peace,” that is, Christ, through whom one goes to true peace. And just as they did not know him through love, so neither did they know him through fear. “For there is no fear of God before their eyes,” because, even if by nature they possessed fear of God and remembered well that God ought to be feared, nevertheless at that time they did not have the fear of God before their eyes, but behind their eyes, because they despised him. [Col. 0040A]

Perhaps a Jew would say that these things were spoken about the gentile. Against this Paul says: You, Jew, perhaps think that these things were not spoken about you; but I and all the saints, whose authority must not be resisted, know that whatever the law says—that is, this psalm—without doubt it says to those who are in the law, that is, to the Jews. We say that we know this so that by this statement every mouth may be stopped. For once the Jew has been convicted, there is no one to object, since it is clear to everyone that the gentile is under sin. And thus, after all have been convicted, let the whole world—both Jews and gentiles—become subject to God; that is, let all confess that they are saved by God’s grace alone.

And it is just that the whole world should be subject to God, and no one to the law, because no one will be justified before God by works of the law, even if he appears just in the eyes of men. But everyone who is in the law remains flesh, that is, carnal. Truly, no one will be justified by works of the law. For through the law there is knowledge of sin, not justification from sins. For if some, such as Moses and David, were justified under the law, they did not obtain this from the law, but through faith in Christ, whom they believed in and awaited as Redeemer. Thus all the righteous under the old law were justified not by the law but through Christ, whom they believed in while awaiting his coming.

**Note:** In the first condition of humanity, man fell through pride; God waited for him a long time so that, if possible, he might rise again through natural understanding. After man discovered that he was incapable of this, he said that, if he had a law by which he could distinguish evils from goods, and conversely goods from evils, he might then rise again. God, however, in order everywhere to show man’s incapacity apart from himself, gave a law by which man could distinguish good from evil; yet even then he could not be freed.

God certainly knew beforehand that this would happen to man. But, in accordance with man’s desire, he first left him to natural understanding and afterward granted him the law, so that, when he was not freed by these concessions, he might believe that of himself he was nothing and thus flee to God’s grace. God appropriately granted this grace after natural understanding and after the law, since neither was sufficient for justification—after it could no longer even be imagined that there was another kind of salvation. [Col. 0040D]

And because through the law there is only knowledge of sin, now at last, once this has been demonstrated, the righteousness of God is made manifest without the law; that is, it is openly shown that God justifies believers by grace alone, without any law. The connective expression that follows indicates that this righteousness of God is testified to as being effected by grace through the law of Moses and the other prophets.

Having proved that God’s righteousness is effected without the law, he adds by what means it is effected: namely, through faith and through the shedding of Christ’s blood. He says: The righteousness of God is not effected through the law, but through faith in Jesus Christ, for all who believe. For whoever believes in Christ will be justified from sins, and also above all others; for one who has been justified can never merit so much that, in rewarding his merit, God’s grace does not surpass it.

Truly, all are justified through faith. For there is no distinction, as though one were justified here by merit and another there by grace. There is no distinction because all, both Jews and gentiles, have sinned, as was shown above; and therefore all lack the glory of God—that is, they need to be justified by God, in which matter God appears glorious.

They certainly lacked the glory of God because they were justified freely, without their merit, by his grace—that is, through the shedding of the Holy Spirit, whose grace was given through the preceding redemption, which is in Christ Jesus, that is, through the price paid by Christ’s blood. God the Father set forth this Jesus—that is, he publicly presented him to the world, made man, as a propitiation.

For in Christ God was reconciled to the world through faith—that is, to those who hold sound faith concerning Christ. He is also a propitiation in Christ’s own blood, because neither faith without the shedding of blood nor blood without faith would profit unto salvation. [Col. 0041B]

God therefore set forth Christ to demonstrate righteousness—that is, to show himself just and truthful—because of the remission of preceding sins; that is, so that he might remit the preceding sins of Abraham and of the righteous, in accordance with God’s forbearance. For when their sins were committed, God patiently endured them until, in the time of grace, he should cleanse them from those sins.

God also set forth Christ as a propitiation to demonstrate righteousness—that is, his justification—so that in this time of grace it might be sufficiently shown to all that, since neither natural understanding nor the law that had been given could free anyone from the bondage of sin, God alone could justify. This, I say, was demonstrated so that God himself might be just—that is, truthful in fulfilling his promises—and so that he might be the one who justifies from sins everyone who belongs to the faith of Jesus Christ.

Since, as was proved above, all righteousness is through faith and extends to all, the Jew is not distinguished from the gentile, since all have sinned equally. Therefore, Jew, where is your boasting? You are no longer left anything in which to boast under the law, since there is no justification through the law, but all justification is through faith. Therefore your boasting—that by which you preferred yourself to the gentile through the law—has been excluded, that is, removed.

But through what law has the glorying of your law been excluded? Was it removed through a similar law of works? The old law was a law of works, because in it, too, it was necessary to work by offering sacrifices and observing the other carnal rites, as in a field or vineyard. For if God were to impose upon this law of works another similar law, it would seem incongruous and pointless for him to repel works by works. Therefore he says: Your glory has not been excluded through a law of works, but through the law of faith—that is, through justifying faith, whose law is the Gospel.

Truly, your boasting is excluded through faith, for faith alone justifies, without any work of the law. And at this point he inserts an authority, saying: I and the righteous with me judge that a person is justified by faith alone, without works of the law; that is, although no works of the law have preceded, faith alone is nevertheless sufficient for a person’s justification.

A Jew might say: I grant that people are justified through faith, but Jews alone. Against this Paul says: It must not be believed that God justifies Jews alone through faith. Is God then the creator only of Jews? Is he not the creator of gentiles as well as of Jews? He is not only the God of Jews, but also of gentiles. For if he created gentiles just as he created Jews, it is clear that God wills to save both equally.

Truly, the one who is God of the Jews is also God of the gentiles, since there is one God of all. For if there is only one God, it is clear that the God of the gentiles is the same as the God of the Jews. Since there is one Creator of gentiles and Jews, it is clear that this one and the same God justified the circumcision—that is, the Jews—through faith and not through the law, and justified the uncircumcision—that is, the gentiles—likewise through faith.

Those who lie in wait for the letter say that something more emphatic is indicated by his saying “from faith” than where he says “through faith.” By saying “from faith,” he wishes to indicate that the Jews did not possess even the beginning of justification except from faith. With regard to the gentiles, since there was no uncertainty, he did not express it in this way. But Augustine says that “from faith” and “through faith” are equivalent, although elsewhere the Apostle says that Jews are justified “through faith” and gentiles “from faith.”

And because we say that people are justified by faith alone, without works of the law, do we therefore destroy the law introduced through faith? Far be it from us that faith should destroy the law! We do not destroy it; rather, we establish it, that is, we prove that the law was stable and effective. For unless faith followed, bringing justification, the old law would certainly have been invalid, because neither the reality nor the figure would have come into being. But now it is proved effective by the fact that it prefigured grace, which would justify in this way through faith. [Col. 0042C]

He also wishes to prove by the example of Abraham that the law cannot justify and that faith alone is sufficient. Before he had the law of circumcision, Abraham was justified by faith alone. He says:

## CHAPTER IV

“What then shall we say that Abraham our father found according to the flesh? For if Abraham was justified by works of the law, he has glory, but not before God. For what does Scripture say? ‘Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness’” (Genesis 15:6; Galatians 3:6; James 2:23).

Now to one who works, the reward is not reckoned according to grace but according to what is owed. But to one who does not work, yet believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is reckoned as righteousness according to the purpose of God’s grace. Thus David also speaks of the blessedness of the person to whom God credits righteousness without works:

“Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven and whose sins have been covered. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin” (Psalm 31:1).

Does this blessedness therefore remain in circumcision alone, or also in uncircumcision? For we say that Abraham’s faith was reckoned to him as righteousness. How, then, was it reckoned—as circumcised, or as uncircumcised? Not in circumcision, but in uncircumcision. And he received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of faith that is in uncircumcision, so that he might be the father of all who believe through uncircumcision, so that faith might also be reckoned to them as righteousness.

And he is the father of circumcision—not only of those who are from circumcision, but also of those who follow the footsteps of the faith that was in the uncircumcision of our father Abraham. For the promise to Abraham or to his seed—that he should be heir of the world—was not through the law, but through the righteousness of faith. For if those who are from the law are heirs, faith has been emptied and the promise abolished. For the law produces wrath; for where there is no law, neither is there transgression.

Therefore it is from faith, so that the promise may be firm according to grace for all the seed—not only for the one who is from the law, but also for the one who is from the faith of Abraham, who is the father of us all. As it is written: “I have appointed you the father of many nations” (Genesis 17:5), before the God in whom you believed, who gives life to the dead and calls those things that are not as though they were; who, contrary to hope, believed in hope, so that he might become the father of many nations, according to what was said to him: “So shall your seed be, like the stars of heaven and like the sand of the sea” (Genesis 13:15).

And he was not weakened in faith, nor did he consider his own body already dead, since he was almost a hundred years old, nor the deadness of Sarah’s womb. He did not hesitate in unbelief concerning God’s promise, but was strengthened in faith, giving glory to God, fully knowing that whatever God had promised, he was also able to do. Therefore it was reckoned to him as righteousness.

Now it was not written only for his sake—that it was reckoned to him as righteousness—but also for ours, to whom it will be reckoned, if we believe in him who raised Jesus Christ our Lord from the dead. He was delivered up because of our offenses and rose because of our justification.”

## EXPOSITION

Since there is no justification from works of the law, but only through faith, what then shall we say? Did Abraham, our father according to the faith of gentiles as well as Jews, find anything according to the flesh—that is, according to the observance of the carnal law?

Or it may be understood this way: What shall we say that Abraham our father—that is, the father of the Jews—found from the circumcision of the flesh, according to the flesh, that is, according to the descent of the flesh, although he is the father of all believers according to the institution of faith?

Abraham certainly found no justification from works of the law. He proves this by means of a certain absurd consequence. Truly, Abraham was not justified by the law. For if he is believed to have been justified by works of the law, he has glory before men, but he is not glorious before God, because he was not justified in God’s sight. Yet it is impossible for anyone justified before God to be without glory.

Or it may be understood this way: If Abraham was justified by the law, he has glory to be attributed to his merits, but not before God—that is, this must not be attributed to God’s grace. But for one who derogates from God’s grace to be justified, although he is unjust, cannot coexist with the grace of God.

He proved through the law that justification is impossible; through the absurd consequence stated above he proves that justification is through faith, by the authority that follows, saying: It is impossible to be justified by works of the law, but faith justifies, as Scripture testifies. [Col. 0044A]

For what does Scripture say? This, namely: Abraham believed God, and that belief was reckoned to him as righteousness; that is, through the faith by which he believed God, he merited justification. He says “it was reckoned” because God promised this to him many times and at different times, and Abraham never hesitated on any occasion, but always believed.

Having spoken of Abraham—namely, that he was justified through faith and not through works of the law—he applies this to everyone, saying: This does not happen to Abraham alone—not finding any justification from works of the law—but also to everyone who works, that is, who follows the law of works, the old law, and not grace. To such a person the reward is not reckoned according to grace; that is, he seeks to be rewarded not by God’s grace but according to what is owed, that is, according to what is due to him on account of the merits of his works. [Col. 0044B]

But to the one who does not work—that is, who does not follow the law of works—but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, that is, who makes the ungodly righteous if he believes, his faith, I say, is reckoned as righteousness, because he is justified without any merit, by faith alone, as was shown above in the case of Abraham.

Or alternatively: Although I have said that one is justified by faith alone without the law, nevertheless, for one who works—that is, who has time in which to work—there must be no idleness; rather, he must believe while doing good when grace comes. For reward is not imputed to those who have an age in which to work as grace alone; rather, recompense is made not only according to grace but also according to what is owed. That is, they ought to merit in such a way that by their merit they assist grace.

But to the one who does not work—that is, who has no time in which to work, like children who die immediately—yet believes in him who justifies the ungodly through faith, his faith is reckoned as righteousness; that is, faith alone is sufficient for his justification, since tender age has denied him the opportunity for works. [Col. 0044C]

Just as above he proved by the example of Abraham that every believer is justified through faith, so here he begins to prove by the authority of David that all justification is from grace. For just as faith is through grace, so righteousness is obtained from the grace of God alone.

Thus he says: “Faith is reckoned as righteousness for every believer”—a righteousness that is according to the purpose of God’s grace; that is, all justification is effected through God’s grace, which grace has been purposed and prepared for every believer.

Righteousness is certainly effected through God’s grace, as not I alone but David also says. He says that this is the blessedness—that is, the purity of this present life and eternal life in the future—of the person to whom God “credits,” that is, counts as acceptable to God; or, to whom God “credits,” that is, freely and without merit, righteousness. In other words, it is the blessedness of the one whom God justifies by grace, without works that earn justification.

David says this in the following words (Psalm 31:1): “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven.” He does not specify by whom they have been forgiven, but the following verse indicates that they are forgiven by the Lord.

Those are blessed whose iniquities—that is, in whom the natural tinder of sin—has been forgiven and weakened, so that it can no longer pass into action if they wish to use their strengthened free will. But because the forgiveness of the tinder of sin would not be sufficient for salvation unless past sins were also forgiven, he adds: “And blessed are those whose actual sins have been covered in baptism.” They are said to be covered because God no longer sees them in order to punish them.

Blessed also is the person to whom the Lord has not imputed original sin. Here he does not seem to be dealing much with grace. Nevertheless, it should be understood that the whole psalm concerns the commendation of God’s grace and proves that no one can be justified except through grace.

Since this is how it is read in David, it follows from this authority that blessedness—that is, justification, as has been said—is effected through grace. But since it is effected in this way, let us see whether this blessedness remains in circumcision, that is, among Jews alone, or whether, just as among Jews, it also remains in uncircumcision, that is, among gentiles.

He wishes once again to prove through Abraham—who was justified by faith before he was circumcised—that gentiles are justified by grace just as Jews are. He says: Therefore I ask whether this justification remains in circumcision alone or in uncircumcision, because we say that Abraham’s faith was reckoned to him as righteousness; that is, that Abraham was justified through faith.

Since he was justified through faith, it remains to say how—that is, in what condition—faith was reckoned to him as righteousness: in circumcision, or before he was circumcised, while he was still in uncircumcision, that is, in gentile status?

I ask in what condition; but it is clear that he was not justified through faith at the time of circumcision, but while he still remained in uncircumcision. For if Abraham was justified through faith while still uncircumcised, why should uncircumcised gentiles not likewise be justified if they have faith?

The Jew might object again: If circumcision contributed nothing to Abraham’s justification, why did he circumcise himself after he had been justified?

Appropriately, I say, he did so in order to represent in the flesh the truth that he possessed hidden in his soul, intending rather to teach circumcision of the heart than of the flesh. This is what he said equivalently.

Although Abraham was justified in uncircumcision, he afterward received in his flesh the sign of circumcision and of the justification he had obtained—not so that he might be justified through circumcision, but so that he might thereby be shown to be just. I say “sign,” not something evident to everyone, but a seal containing something hidden, like wax into which a seal is impressed and which contains within itself what does not appear outwardly.

Thus circumcision of the flesh was indeed a sign of inner righteousness, although scarcely any Jews understood it rightly. I say “seal of the righteousness of faith,” that is, of the justification obtained through faith, which faith and which righteousness are in uncircumcision—that is, are considered in Abraham during the time of his uncircumcision.

Abraham was appropriately justified in that condition so that he might be the father—that is, the founder according to the form of faith—not only of the Jews but also of all believers. I say that he is the father of all through uncircumcision, that is, through the faith possessed during the time of uncircumcision. And just as it was reckoned to him, so may the faith of all those believers be reckoned to them as righteousness.

And just as Abraham is the father of faith, so he is the father—that is, the founder—of circumcision, that is, of the justification that follows from faith. I say that he is the father not only of those who are from circumcision of the flesh, that is, Jews, but also of all those who follow the footsteps of Abraham’s faith, doing good by his example through faith—the faith possessed during the time of uncircumcision by our father Abraham.

Truly, Abraham will be the father of all believers, not through the law but through faith. For the promise of this matter—namely, that he should be heir of the world, which is the same as being the father of all nations—was not made through the law, that is, through the merit of the law, but through the merit of faith.

And if it was not promised through the law, it must not be fulfilled through the law. He says this as follows: God indeed promised Abraham, or his seed—that is, Christ—that he should be heir of the world, where it is said, “I will give the nations as your inheritance” (Genesis 17), and so forth.

This, I say, he did not promise through the law but through the righteousness of faith, that is, the righteousness that follows from faith. All who wish to be counted among Christ’s inheritance must possess this faith and the righteousness of faith. Abraham possessed faith in himself, and the righteousness that his children ought to imitate.

Truly, the promise is not made through the law. For if only those who are from the law—that is, Jews—are heirs of Abraham’s promise, then Christ’s faith has been emptied, that is, it is vain, and you have received it in vain, Jews, if the law was sufficient for you to be heirs. You yourselves judge this to be a most serious absurdity: that Christ’s faith should be in vain.

Nor is this all. If Jews alone are heirs, then the promise has likewise been abolished—that is, erased—and made false: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Genesis 17), if this blessing takes place among Jews alone.

Truly, those who are from the law alone do not deserve the inheritance. For the law produces and merits wrath alone, because if any who were under the law performed good works, this was through faith and not through the law.

Truly, the law produces wrath. For where there is no law, there is no transgression; and truly, where there is transgression, there is law. Therefore, because of what was said above, those who are from the law will not be heirs. Rather, those who are from faith will be heirs, so that the promise, made and to be fulfilled according to grace, may be firm for all the seed—that is, for everyone who imitates Abraham through faith—not only for the one who is from the law, that is, the Jew, but also for the one who is from the faith of Abraham, that is, for the one who follows Abraham through faith.

Abraham is the father of us all, both gentiles and Jews, according to the form of faith and righteousness. He is indeed the father of all, as it is written in Genesis. Since this refers to the order of the text from which it is taken, what is written is this: “I have appointed you, Abraham, to become the father of many nations according to the institution of faith”; that is, I have appointed you to become their father through the righteousness established before God, in the good pleasure of the God in whom you believed.

Here Paul’s words follow: God makes those who are dead through sin live, having justified them through faith. He not only gives life, but also by grace calls those things that are not—that is, gentiles, who, because they have not possessed the law, seem to be nothing—as though they were, that is, just as he calls Jews, who boast that they alone exist through the law. [Col. 0047A]

Above he proved through Abraham that all justification is from faith. But so that we may perfectly imitate Abraham in the fullness of faith, he defines the quality of Abraham’s faith: just as Abraham believed that whatever appeared impossible according to human judgment would be fulfilled for him by God, so we too should not hesitate concerning God’s power by setting the law of nature against him.

Thus he says: It was said to Abraham, “I have appointed you the father of many nations.” Abraham believed “against hope in hope”; one might say, against human expectation. Hope is called the certain expectation of a future thing. But he appropriately said “against hope,” because, according to the law of nature, when he saw his own advanced age and his wife’s barrenness, he was completely certain that he would no longer have offspring. Yet against the hope that the law of nature offered him, he believed in the hope that God’s omnipotence suggested, once the law of nature had been broken. [Col. 0047B]

He believed this so that he might become the father of many nations. From a human perspective he could have doubted this sufficiently, since he saw himself to be the father of only one son. I say that he believed everything that had been said to him: that he would become the father of many, not only according to the propagation of the flesh but according to the imitated form of faith.

This, I say, was said to him: “So shall your seed be, Abraham, like the stars of heaven and like the sand of the sea” (Genesis 15:5). By the stars of heaven he signifies Abraham’s spiritual children, conspicuous by the light of their virtues. By the sand of the sea, unfruitful carnal children.

This was promised to Abraham, and after he had received the promise, while its fulfillment was being delayed, he was not weakened in faith. He did not believe less in the firm promise made to him; and, so that he might persevere steadfast in faith in the promised matter, he did not consider his own body already dead. That is, he did not suppose that the natural failure of begetting could alter God’s will, although he was almost a hundred years old and the time of begetting had already passed for him.

He did not consider Sarah’s womb dead either—that is, that his wife’s generative powers had failed, both through the defect of barrenness and through the old age of many years. He was not weakened in faith in the first promise, nor in God’s renewed promise, because God had often renewed the same promise to him.

In that renewed promise, by which God promised that he would give him a son before the year had ended, he did not hesitate in unbelief. He hesitated in wonder, turning the mystery of the matter over in his mind, but he did not hesitate through unbelief, as though he doubted that everything God had promised would be fulfilled for him. Rather, he was strengthened by faith. [Col. 0047D]

For when he could have objected that, since the matter had been promised so many times, its long postponement made him doubtful, he rose stronger in his belief in the promised matter: thereby giving glory to God and attributing nothing of the good of this promise to his own merits, but glorifying God in all things.

He knew this fully and without any hesitation: that whatever God had promised, he was also able to do, in every manner in which he had promised it. And therefore, because he gave fullest credence to God’s promises, not only was the promise fulfilled for him because he believed in this way, but it was also reckoned to him as righteousness; that is, by the merit of such great faith he merited justification.

Since he had now sufficiently expressed the manner of Abraham’s faith, he adapts what he said about Abraham to his own purpose, saying: Because Abraham believed in this way, therefore he was justified.

Yet this was not written here about Abraham only, so that Abraham might be praised for such great faith. What was reckoned to him as righteousness was also written for us, so that we might be conformed to Abraham’s faith. For to us who believe, our faith—as we see in Abraham—will be reckoned as righteousness.

I mean those who believe in him who raised Christ Jesus our Lord from the dead. Just as Abraham believed that he would receive from God what was contrary to nature, so let us not hesitate to believe and confess that Christ rose from the dead, although this is contrary to the ordinary course of nature. For the author of nature could invert it as he wished.

The two statements that follow—“he was delivered up to death” and “he rose for justification”—were not necessary for proving what had already been said, but Paul judged them useful for instructing the Romans, and therefore added them.

“He was delivered up”: he does not specify for what purpose, but it is sufficiently clear that he was delivered up to death. This was because of our offenses, that is, so that he might cleanse us from our offenses. He also rose for our justification, that is, so that, having cleansed us from our offenses, he might make us righteous through the addition of virtues.

He does not say that Christ died for our offenses and rose for our justification in such a way that his death was not the cause of our righteousness and his resurrection the cause of the remission of sins. Rather, he says that he rose for justification in order to show that his resurrection is the cause of our justification in such a way that it is also a sign of a future reality in us—namely, a double resurrection.

The first is the resurrection by which, in baptism, we rise from the death of sin in order to live in righteousness. This is the resurrection of the soul, which was previously dead in sins but now, with free will strengthened, can resist every evil suggestion and know God.

The second resurrection is future and bodily, when, having recovered impassibility and immortality, we shall reign together with Christ, provided that the first resurrection has been preserved intact. The resurrection of Christ and Pentecost, which depends upon that same resurrection, are therefore celebrated at different times because they foreshadow what is still to come, and do not deal only with past events, as the feast of the Nativity does.

## CHAPTER V

[Col. 0048D]

“Therefore, having been justified by faith, let us have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have access by faith into this grace in which we stand, and we glory in the hope of the glory of the children of God.

And not only this, but we also glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces endurance; endurance, probation; and probation, hope. And hope does not put to shame, because the love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.

For why, when we were still weak, did Christ die at the appointed time for the ungodly? For scarcely does anyone die for a righteous person. Perhaps someone might dare to die for a good person.

But God commends his love toward us, because, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us at the appointed time. Much more, therefore, having now been justified in his blood, shall we be saved from wrath through him.

For if, while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved in his life.

And not only this, but we also glory in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation.

Therefore, just as through one man sin entered this world, and through sin death, and so death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned—until the law, sin was in the world. But sin was not imputed when there was no law.

Yet death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression, who is a type of the one who was to come.

But the gift is not like the offense. For if many died through the offense of that one, much more did the grace of God and the gift in the grace of the one man Jesus Christ abound for many.

And the gift is not like what happened through one sin. For judgment arose from one offense unto condemnation, but grace arose from many offenses unto justification.

For if death reigned through one person because of one offense, much more will those who receive the abundance of grace and of the gift and of righteousness reign in life through the one Jesus Christ.

Therefore, just as through one offense condemnation came upon all human beings, so also through one act of righteousness justification unto life came upon all human beings.

For just as through the disobedience of one man many were constituted sinners, so also through the obedience of one man many will be constituted righteous.

But the law entered alongside so that the offense might abound; and where the offense abounded, grace abounded even more, so that, just as sin reigned in death, so grace might reign through righteousness unto eternal life, through Jesus Christ our Lord.”

## EXPOSITION
Since it has been sufficiently proved from what precedes that all justification comes from faith, therefore, having been justified by faith, let us have peace—that is, concord among ourselves—so that neither Jew may exalt himself over Gentile, nor Gentile over Jew, in this new grace. But, in order both to deter them more strongly from discord and to lead them toward concord, he says: “Let us have peace with God.” For if we are discordant among ourselves, we certainly do not have peace with God.

“Let us have peace,” I say, “through our Lord Jesus Christ,” whom we must obey in all things, who consented to be handed over to death for our offenses, and so forth. Through this Christ not only have offenses been forgiven, and life and righteousness been given, but we also have this grace—that is, such an excellent grace that it can drive away diseases and perform miracles. But lest the Jews should suppose that, through the merit of the Law, anyone possessed some rank in attaining this grace, Paul says:

[Col. 0050A] “Through whom”—through Christ—“we have also access,” that is, the first step toward coming to this grace. We attain this grace through faith, just as we attain justification, because faith also justifies; and faith gives us this grace, in which grace we stand—that is, persevere. Much grace was indeed bestowed upon Adam, but he did not stand in it.

And by standing in this grace we glory in the hope of the glory of the children of God—that is, because we most certainly hope that we shall possess the glory which the children of God possess. But we glory not only in hope of this glory; we also glory in tribulations. This is the greatest virtue: to rejoice in what it is natural to fear. Therefore we glory in tribulations, because we know that tribulation produces patience—that is, because the experience and practice of tribulations nourishes [Col. 0050B] patience.

Patience, however, produces testing—that is, purification. For just as gold is purified through fire, so whatever in us must be purified is smelted away in the fire of tribulation. Hence, those who finish their life in tribulation we confidently regard as holy, without any hesitation, because whatever they previously sinned, the fire of tribulation has entirely smelted away. Those, however, who finish their life in peace, however laudably they may have lived—for no one is without some stain—we do not count among the catalogue of the saints without a certain manifestation of miracles.

Testing, moreover, produces hope; for one who has been sufficiently purified can hope with complete certainty. Hope, once possessed after purification, does not put to shame—that is, it does not cause those who hope to blush with shame, as it would make them shamefaced if it were to remain unfulfilled.

Truly, hope does not put to shame, but it will be fulfilled. We know this for certain through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us. For the Holy Spirit, already deifying us in part, gives us assurance: in the future we shall be deified completely, illuminated according to the soul by a greater knowledge of God, and according to the body destined to be incorruptible.

That the Holy Spirit has been given to us is apparent from the fact that the love of God has been poured out in our hearts—that is, the love of God has been enlarged in our hearts, because we are ready both to suffer and to die for him.

Or otherwise: truly hope does not put to shame, but it will be fulfilled. This is evident from the fact that the love of God has been poured out—that is, because God loves us abundantly, and because the love of God burns so greatly toward us. We perceive this in our hearts, which have been enlightened by the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.

He proves, for various reasons, that hope—as has been said—will be fulfilled. First, because, if it were not fulfilled, God would have become man and tasted death in vain, unless by bringing hope to completion he should piously finish what he had begun. Moreover, for this reason also: if, when we were impious and the merit of condemnation alone was in us, he willed to undergo for us, the impious, the difficulty of death, there can be no doubt that he will save us now, when we have already been justified and already lay claim to the merit of salvation. This is easy for him, because he no longer needs to die.

Thus he says: Truly hope does not put to shame, but it will be fulfilled, because, unless what we hope for were brought to completion: “Why did Christ die, righteous for the impious?” Either in place of the impious, because the impious ought to have died for their sin, or for the sake of redeeming the impious.

Someone might say: “Since he died, he is therefore unable to do this.” I answer: he died according to the appointed time, for he rose again on the third day.

Again the adversary says: “You were indeed impious, but by the time of his death you had already been justified.” I say that he died for the impious when we were still weak at the time of his death—that is, when we continued in impiety. The righteous man died in vain for the impious if he now abandons the task of saving those who have been justified. We must not believe that he will leave unfinished the work for which he underwent so great a difficulty.

Someone might say: “Was it really such a great thing to die for the impious?”

“Yes,” I reply. For scarcely anyone—that is, anyone at all—whether worthy of death or about to die soon, dies for a righteous person, either in his place or for his sake. [Col. 0051B] From this it is clear that Christ did something great: with regard to his own righteousness, he was not destined to die, yet he died for the impious.

Therefore I say that scarcely anyone dies for a righteous person; for perhaps someone might dare to die for a good person. If there is doubt whether anyone would die for a good person, it was a great thing for Christ, the pious one, to die for the impious. Scarcely anyone would dare to die for a righteous person; but Christ died for us, and by this God commends his love toward us: for if, while we were still sinners, Christ died—a thing so difficult and so undeserved, a righteous man for us sinners—then, therefore, it must be believed much more strongly that now, having been justified, we who were previously sinners shall be saved in his blood—that is, through the shedding of his blood—and shall be delivered from wrath through him, [Col. 0051C] who no longer needs to be changed from his state, as he did when he underwent death for sinners.

And because we might be justified yet nevertheless fail to recover the peace lost with God, he says: Truly, having been justified, we shall be saved, while we now lay claim to the merit of justification; for when we were enemies and possessed the merit of condemnation, we were reconciled to God through so grave a thing as the death of his Son. If, though previously enemies, we have now been reconciled through the death of his Son, it is much more to be believed that, having been reconciled and having already in some manner merited salvation, we shall be saved.

And he will save us quite easily, because he saves us “in his life.” For he no longer needs to die, as he did previously. One should observe how he sets each thing against its counterpart: sinners justified, enemies reconciled, through death into life. We not only await future salvation, but even while we are here we glory in God through hope and joy in that salvation. “We glory,” he says, “through our Lord Jesus Christ,” through whom we have just now received reconciliation with God, although we were enemies.

Someone might object: “Christ was indeed sufficiently righteous, but his righteousness does not seem sufficient for the salvation of all.” The Apostle proves this by saying:

Since every human being fell through the disobedience of one, it seems fitting and proportionate that, through the obedience of one, the fall of the human race should be repaired—through Jesus alone.

Therefore we were able to be reconciled for salvation. Just as, through one man, sin entered this world—not sent by God, but through a kind of violence—making this world so wretched through sin, so, consequently, through the sin of one man death entered the same man, both bodily and spiritual; and thus death passed from him into all human beings.

And it rightly passed from him into all, because he was the one in whom all sinned. For in Adam’s loins the whole mass of the human race was corrupted by the sin of transgression.

Some extend this verse as far as the much later statement, “Therefore, just as through one,” and so forth. But, as we have explained, it can be sufficiently abbreviated.

Truly all sinned in Adam, even though before the Law almost everyone was unaware of this. For sin was in the world from Adam until the Law. But although this was so, sin was not imputed—that is, no one was judged guilty on account of original sin before Moses, since there was no Law—which, once it came, revealed this sin.

Or let us state the matter in full. This sin was indeed in the world before the Law, but it was unknown for this reason: no sin was imputed, since there was no Law. And although original sin was not imputed before the Law, this can nevertheless be clearly recognized from the fact that bodily death, which was the punishment for original sin, reigned, bringing before itself all its miseries—thirst, hunger, fevers, and the rest.

It reigned, I say, from Adam until Moses, not only over those who added their own sins to original sin, but also over those who did not sin “in the likeness of Adam’s transgression”—that is, who on their own part did not transgress in the same way [Col. 0052C] as Adam.

These are the little ones who did not have time to sin, but were punished solely on account of original sin.

Adam “is the form of the one who was to come,” that is, of Christ. Adam was a form of Christ because, just as Adam is the father of all according to the flesh, so Christ is the father of believers according to faith. And just as Eve was formed from the side of the sleeping Adam, so the Church was fashioned from the side of Christ, overcome by the sleep of death on the cross.

Adam is therefore a form of Christ because God decreed through one Christ to amend what had been sinned through one Adam.

Or let us read it in this way, according to Ambrose: Truly all sinned in Adam, for original sin was in the world until the Law. But although it was in the world, that sin was not imputed, because there was no Law to make this sin known. [Col. 0052D] Yet although this sin was unknown, death reigned as the punishment for it from Adam until Moses, not only over those who sinned through actual offenses, but also over those who sinned in the likeness of Adam’s transgression—that is, who were condemned for the likeness alone, because they were the children of the transgressor Adam.

He showed above that one Christ is sufficient for the salvation of all, because one Adam alone was sufficient for the destruction of all. And just as he compared Christ’s person with Adam’s person, so he sets Christ’s cause—that is, obedience—against Adam’s cause, which is disobedience. He also sets the effect of Christ’s cause—that is, present justification and future eternal life—against the effect of Adam’s cause, namely temporal death and eternal condemnation.

[Col. 0053A] He also proves that Christ’s grace abounds far more greatly than Adam’s sin. For although from Adam we contracted only original sin, Christ’s grace forgave in baptism not only original sin, but also whatever actual sins accompanied it.

The text is connected in this way: The old Adam was a form of the Adam who was to come; but although one person was set against one person, the causes are unlike. For just as Adam’s offense occurred, so also does God’s gift, which is grace, occur. Truly Christ’s gift was not like Adam’s offense: Christ’s gift abounded much more greatly than Adam’s offense, because the offense was one thing, which we call original sin, whereas Christ forgave both original sin and whatever actual sins there were.

He proves this: Truly Christ alone was sufficient for the justification of all. For if, through the offense—that is, through the offense—of one Adam, and through one thing—which he will explain more fully in what follows—that is, through disobedience—if, he says, through this one offense, which we call original sin, many died to sin, contracting that original sin from their first father (he says “many” not because all were not oppressed by this sin, but because not all remained detained in it, laying aside that original sin through the faith they received in Christ); if, he says, through the one offense of one man many died, then much more, in keeping with the dignity of Christ’s person and cause, God’s grace abounded—that is, the forgiveness of sins.

The gift also abounded—that is, strengthening through the Holy Spirit. For after sins have been forgiven, the weapons of the Holy Spirit are necessary, by which we may resist the devil when he gives evil counsel.

“Grace,” he says, “and the gift abounded in grace,” that is, through the grace of one man. He fittingly says “through grace,” because, just as the contracting of original sin occurred by necessity, so salvation was accomplished through grace—that is, through willing action. For no one is saved except willingly.

Just as, he says, the offense of one was spread among many, so it is equally fitting that the grace of one man abounded for many. He does not say that grace abounded for more people than the offense did, but “for many.” For not all have been saved, because they were unwilling.

He speaks of one man who could do nothing less than he willed: namely, Jesus Christ, that is, the Savior and King.

Just as he differentiated Christ’s causes from Adam’s causes, so he distinguishes the effects of those causes by setting them against each other. He says: Just as Christ’s gift was not such as Adam’s offense, so also what occurs through one sin of Adam is not what occurs through Christ’s gift. That is, the effects of Adam’s sin and of Christ’s grace are different, because the sin is single, whereas the gift is manifold.

He proves this by saying: Truly the effect of Adam’s sin and the effect of God’s grace are not alike. For judgment—that is, God’s just sentence—results in condemnation; that is, it condemns Adam’s children on account of one offense, solely on account of original sin. But Christ’s grace results in justification; that is, it justifies his children from many offenses, both actual offenses and original sin.

It should be noted that the first sin did indeed weaken our nature and make it more inclined to fall, but it was not nevertheless the cause of actual sins, which we could resist by natural reason, although our nature had been weakened in great part.

It should also be observed that, although many things are considered in Adam’s sin, such as pride and gluttony, only one is named, because disobedience proves that grace has justified from many offenses. He says:

Truly, through Christ’s grace, human beings are justified from many offenses. For, having received righteousness—which is the greater thing—they will reign with Christ in eternal life. He expresses this equivalently:

Human beings who receive the abundance of his grace—that is, abundant forgiveness, because it includes not only original sin but also all actual sins—and who receive the abundance of the gift—that is, the abundant gifts of the Holy Spirit for strengthening in the good—and who receive the abundance of righteousness—that is, righteous action—for after sins have been forgiven and the Holy Spirit has strengthened them, only then are they permitted to act well—these, I say, having received all this, will reign with God, placed in eternal life. They will receive all these things—grace, gift, and kingdom—through the one Jesus Christ.

And truly through this one, because if, through the offense of one Adam, which was the cause of destruction, death reigned—both temporal and eternal—through the one offense, that is, through disobedience, then much more, in keeping with the dignity of the person, the cause, and the effect, those who receive the abundance of grace, gift, and righteousness will reign in life through the one Jesus Christ.

There is indeed also a likeness here, because Adam is one and Christ is one; and there is the superiority according to the dignity that has been mentioned. Therefore, by analogy and from the greater, I can infer that, just as through the offense of one Adam—an offense passing, as I have said, into all human beings—condemnation came about, so also through the righteousness of one Christ, passing into all human beings according to its power—for Christ gave a sufficient price for all—through the righteousness of one, he says, justification unto life came about.

Above he showed sufficiently that Christ was powerful and sufficient to restore whatever had fallen through Adam, but he had not determined whether in this restoration Christ acted through power or through merit. Here he determines this, saying:

Just as Adam, by earning evil through disobedience, cast all into ruin, so Christ, by earning good through obedience, redeemed all.

The text is connected in this way: Truly all are condemned through the offense of one. For just as, through the disobedience of one man, many were constituted sinners—because not all remained in sin—so also, through the obedience of one Christ, who merited this, many will be constituted righteous. They are called “many” because not all wished to be justified.

Although he now says that Christ justifies human beings from sins, he says that he also justifies transgressors of the Law from the transgression of the Law they received. He introduces this in order to prove that the Jews were more indebted to God’s grace than even the Gentiles, over whom they exalted themselves in this new grace. For the Gentiles were guilty only with respect to natural law, whereas the Jews were guilty both with respect to natural law and with respect to transgression of the written Law.

The text is connected in this way: Christ’s obedience justified many. But the Law caused the offense to abound. The Law, he says, entered alongside, because sin had entered first. The Law entered in order that the offense might abound—not because the Law was evil, but because those whom it would make guilty were under it, commanding without assisting.

The Law was understood in three ways in its own time. For some it existed only as a sign, as in the case of Abraham, who was circumcised not in order to be justified by this, but as a sign of justification already received through faith.

For others the Law was a pedagogue. Just as a pedagogue restrains a child from wandering about and becoming arrogant through disciplinary supervision, so the Law, by threatening punishment, restrained certain people from the act of sin.

For still others the Law was the cause of transgression. In the first two groups—for those to whom the Law was a sign of righteousness or a pedagogue—it accomplished nothing. Those who were righteous, like Abraham, were righteous through faith, not through the Law. Those who restrained themselves from evil through fear did so not through the Law, but through the gift of the Holy Spirit—that is, through the spirit of fear.

For others, however, the Law was the cause of offense, because it became the occasion of transgression. Through the Law the offense abounded, but through grace it was emptied. For wherever the offense abounded—whether under the Law or outside the Law—there grace abounded over the offense, because it not only forgave sins but also granted the ability to act righteously.

Because some were again going astray from the statement that grace abounded where the offense had been, saying that they could therefore sin with impunity and at the proper time, since God’s grace would forgive everything—and that the more sins there were, the more glorious grace would be—Paul determines that God’s grace forgives all sins, however numerous, in baptism. But after people have been justified, if they sin again, their sins will be forgiven not as before by grace, but through the merit of repentance.
