Thus he says: God’s grace certainly abounded under this arrangement: just as sin reigned before justification, leading into death, so also grace, after it has forgiven sins, should reign through the righteousness received and carefully preserved, leading into eternal life, without now turning again toward iniquity. Let it reign, I say, through our Lord Jesus Christ, who, after justifying through grace, gives eternal life.

## CHAPTER VI

“What then shall we say? Shall we remain in sin, so that grace may abound? By no means! For if we have died to sin, how shall we still live in it? Or do you not know, brothers, that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? For we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life. For if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall also be in the likeness of his resurrection.

“Knowing this, that our old man was crucified together with him, so that the body of sin might be destroyed and we might no longer serve sin. For whoever has died has been justified from sin. But if we have died with Christ, we believe that we shall also live with Christ, knowing that Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more; death will no longer have dominion over him. For in that he died to sin, he died once; but in that he lives, he lives to God.

“Thus you also must consider yourselves to be dead indeed to sin, but living to God in Christ Jesus. Therefore let sin not reign in your mortal body, so that you obey its desires. Nor present your members as weapons of iniquity to sin; rather, present yourselves to God as living from the dead, and your members as weapons of righteousness for God. For sin will not have dominion over you. For you are not under the Law, but under grace.

“What then? Shall we sin because we are not under the Law but under grace? By no means! Do you not know that to whomever you present yourselves as servants for obedience, you are servants of the one whom you obey—whether of sin leading to death, or of obedience leading to righteousness?

“But thanks be to God that, although you were servants of sin, you obeyed from the heart the pattern of teaching to which you were handed over. Having been freed from sin, you became servants of righteousness. I speak in human terms, because of the weakness of your flesh.

“For just as you presented your members as servants to impurity and iniquity leading to iniquity, so now present your members as servants to righteousness for sanctification. For when you were servants of sin, you were free with respect to righteousness. What fruit did you have then in those things of which you are now ashamed? For their end is death.

“But now, having been freed from sin and made servants of God, you have your fruit for sanctification, and the end is eternal life. For the wages of sin are death, but the grace of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.” [Col. 0056C]

## EXPOSITION

Since grace must reign through righteousness that is always preserved, until it comes into eternal life, what then shall we say? Shall we remain again in sin, having already been justified through grace, so that grace may abound by freely forgiving again what we have again committed?

Let it be far from us that we should return to sin with so perverse an intention!

Here he begins to speak of a twofold resurrection. The first is the resurrection by which we are justified according to the soul in baptism. Christ consecrated this baptism for us in his death, pouring the water of forgiveness from his side, thereby signifying that we must die together with him in baptism. Just as he died once and did not return to the deeds of the old man, so we too, once justified in baptism and killing there all the oldness of sin, must preserve the resurrection of the soul—for there it rises justified—by walking in newness of life.

For if we preserve the soul’s resurrection in righteousness, we shall certainly possess the future resurrection of our bodies with Christ in incorruption.

Let us return to the text, where he proves that we must not return to sin, saying:

Truly, once justified, we must not remain any longer in sin. For if we who died to sin in baptism—that is, in order that we might no longer work sin—died according to the oldness of sin that we laid aside, how—that is, for what reason—shall we who have thus died together with Christ still live in that sin? That is, how shall we persevere in it?

And truly you ought no longer to live in that sin, because do you not know that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus—that is, through Christ’s institution, or through Christ who consecrated baptism for us—were baptized, that is, washed from sins, into his death? This means into the likeness of his death: just as he died once and lives forever, so we too should die to sins once in baptism and live forever in justification.

Just as he proved that, once justified, we must not sin again, so he also proves that we can keep ourselves well from sin, saying:

Truly, once justified, we have the power, if we wish, not to sin. For we have been buried with Christ—not merely died with him—into death through baptism. Just as Christ, placed in the tomb, had no power according to the flesh to extend hand or foot toward the actions of the old man, so he also gave us, if we wish, in baptism the power never again to return to the oldness of sin.

We were buried for this purpose: just as Christ rose from the dead without again taking up the act of mortality—he rose, I say, through the glory of the Father, that is, through the Word united to him, or for the glorification of the Father’s glory—so we, placed in newness of life, that is, in the resurrection of the soul justified through baptism, may walk forward by making progress in the newness we have received.

Truly, we can walk in newness of life. For we are made like his resurrection. Just as Christ, rising, was a new man, so we too, having laid aside the oldness of sin through baptism, should be new people in the newness of good works.

And truly we shall be made like his resurrection if we have been planted together with him. This cannot happen through ourselves, but through God’s grace we are planted together in the likeness of his death—that is, if we have died together with Christ—in such a likeness that, just as he once laid aside the miseries of the old man and did not return to them, so we too, having once laid aside the oldness of sin in baptism, should not return to it.

For if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, then, by the corresponding unity of death, we shall also be planted together in the likeness of his resurrection, making progress in the newness of our works.

The expression “planted together” is taken from the likeness in which a branch of a good tree is grafted onto the trunk of a bad tree and produces new fruit there. So the newness of justification, grafted onto the trunk of our oldness, should, once the old flavor has been extinguished, produce the fruit of the newness that has been grafted in.

We must indeed be made like Christ’s death, knowing this: our old man was crucified together with Christ, so that the body of sin might be destroyed in us. Our body must be destroyed in that part of it which sinned, so that we may no longer serve sin, but possess authority over sin.

The Lord Jesus could have chosen another kind of death, but he willed to be affixed to the cross, not without a mystery, signifying to us that, just as he had his hands and feet—that is, human senses—affixed, so we too must have not only our deeds but also our senses affixed, so that we may neither think nor do evil.

And we ought, and are able, not to serve sin. For whoever has died in baptism has been freed from sin, and not only this, but has also been justified from sin.

After sufficiently teaching about the first resurrection, which belongs to the soul, and how it must be observed, he adds a discussion of the second resurrection, saying that we shall possess it by the merit of the first, if the first has been carefully preserved.

And, in order that we may be seized more strongly by love for it, he commends it, showing how worthy and beneficial it is. He says:

We are not only justified by dying to sin—and this justification is the first resurrection—but if we have died to sin, that is, with Christ, so that just as Christ died once and never returned to the oldness he had laid aside, so we too, having once died to sin through baptism, must not return to sin. We believe that we too shall live together with him in the second resurrection—that is, having become incapable of suffering and immortal—and that we shall live incorruptibly nowhere else except with Christ, that is, placed in his sight.

If we have died with Christ, we certainly believe that we shall live with Christ, knowing that Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more—that is, he will no longer taste death—for, having died once, he was sufficient for the justification of all.

And not only does he not die, but death will no longer have dominion over him. The dominions of death are hunger, starvation, fevers, and all kinds of misery. The head and completion of all miseries is death. But neither death nor the miseries that are heralds of death will any longer have dominion over Christ, who died once.

Truly Christ now dies no more. For in that he died to sin—that is, for the destruction of sin—he died once; that is, dying once was sufficient.

Therefore, it should be sufficient for us to die together with him once in baptism, persevering in the justification we have received.

He also proves that death will no longer have dominion over Christ. For in that he lives, he lives to God—that is, the life of God. Since God lives eternally and without corruption, there will certainly be no dominion of death in him.

What he said earlier—that we must die with Christ in every respect in order to live with him—he now applies to the Romans, whose instruction he had in view, saying:

Since it is necessary to die together with Christ if we wish to live with him, so—that is, having been instructed in this way—you Romans must consider yourselves to be dead to sin. That is, believe that you died in baptism, so that you may no longer stretch out your hand toward the act of sin.

And if you have died in this way, consider yourselves also to be living to God—that is, living in the justification of the soul that you have received and, by this merit, destined to live in the incorruption of your bodies. All this is in Christ Jesus—that is, through Christ Jesus, who justifies in the present and prepares eternal life for those who remain in justification.

Since he had said above that we are dead to sin and must live to God, and since he saw that a human being cannot in any way restrain himself in this life from venial sins, he determines in which sins we ought and are able to die, knowing that the tinder of sin is naturally present in each person.

But now that free will has been strengthened, we can restrain the tinder of sin so that it does not burst forth into action. In determining this, he says:

Since you are living to God, let sin—that is, the natural tinder of sin—not reign in you. Sin reigns when one consents, acts, and grows accustomed to the work of sin.

Let sin, then, not reign in your body—that is, in what is already yours and, through the strengthening of free will, has been subjected to the rule of reason. I speak of a body that, although justified, is still mortal and, unless ruled by reason, inclined toward the work of sin.

Therefore, you must see to it that, by consenting to your mortality, you do not fail to live to God. Let sin not reign so that you obey its desires—that is, so that you carry out in action what the weakness of your flesh wrongly suggests.

Not only must you not obey it in action, but neither must you present your members in such a way that, through consent, you make them ready and suitable for sin. For just as you must not act wrongly, so you must not consent to evil.

Your members become weapons of iniquity when they are presented to sin. For if you consent to sin, iniquity is armed with your members, so that through these weapons it may accomplish what it wrongly desires.

Do not present yourselves to sin; rather, present yourselves to God—that is, prepare yourselves through good action to be suitable for God. And it is right that you should present yourselves as having been made living in righteousness, as though from the dead, for you were dead in sin.

Do not present yourselves to God only in action; also prepare your members for God in the consent to and encouragement of good things. Your members then become weapons of righteousness. For through these weapons righteousness will accomplish what it rightly suggests and desires.

You ought, and you are able, to present yourselves to God. For although sin is naturally in you, it will not have dominion over you if, with free will strengthened, you wish to make use of it. Rather, you yourselves will have dominion over sin, so that it does not become an action.

Truly sin will not have dominion over you. For you are no longer under the Law, which made people guilty by commanding without assisting; you are under grace, which forgives sins and helps you do good.

Because he again perceives that some are going astray from what he had said—that through grace everything is forgiven—and are sinning in this confidence, because grace is ready and sufficient to release them from everything, he speaks against those who act wickedly in this way.

One must not sin with this intention, because grace does indeed forgive everything; but if someone, by sinning, withdraws himself from grace and becomes a servant of sin, how does he know whether he will be able to return to grace, since he has already been bound under the yoke of sin?

Since we are under grace, which sufficiently purifies everything, what then shall we say? Shall we therefore sin lawfully, because we are not under the Law, which burdens by commanding and does not assist, but under grace, which both forgives sins and helps us to act well?

By no means! This, he says, must be far from us: that we should sin through confidence in grace. For do you not know that you are servants of the one to whom you have presented yourselves for obedience?

You became servants, I say, of the one whom you obeyed—that is, at the very moment when you quickly obeyed. You are servants either of sin, which you obeyed and which leads to death—that is, to condemnation—or servants of obedience, that is, of righteousness, which leads you toward greater righteousness.

For by obeying sin you will become servants of sin, and, having lost your freedom, you will not be able to break the bonds of this servitude.

Therefore it is good that, having become servants of righteousness, you should not turn away from grace, because, once you have become servants of sin, you cannot by your own right return to grace.

Persevere, therefore, in righteousness—not only for the reason already stated, but also for what follows. When, after laying aside the yoke of sin, you became servants of righteousness, if you again slip back into the vomit of your former servitude, you are guilty of instability and justly deserve destruction.

He expresses this as follows:

You ought to persevere in righteousness not only because of what has already been stated, but also because of what follows: “Therefore I give thanks to my God, who freely, without any merit of your own, freed you from the yoke of sin.”

38. I therefore give thanks, because you were once slaves of sin, but now you have obeyed—not under compulsion, but [Col. 0060B] from the heart, that is, proceeding by your own will into the pattern of teaching, that is, the teaching which made you conformable to God. For the image of God in you had been disfigured and blinded; but through my instruction I restored God’s image in you. I speak of that pattern, that is, one as excellent as the restoration of God’s image; into this pattern you were handed over through God’s mercy and our teaching. For by yourselves you were unable to be restored.

Formerly you were slaves of sin, but now, freed from sin, you have become slaves of righteousness; and therefore do not allow yourselves any longer to be reduced to slavery under sin. And now that you have become slaves of righteousness, I speak in human terms, that is, I give you a command sufficiently light, one for which your human capacity is quite sufficient. And [Col. 0060C] I do not command you to do what is spiritual and difficult, because I act thus on account of the weakness of your flesh, that is, because I know that you are still oppressed by carnality and are not yet sufficiently firm in spiritual matters. I speak, then, in human terms.

For this is human: just as you presented your members to serve impurity, that is, lust, gluttony, and desire, and also to serve iniquity, that is, everything contrary to equity, in order to complete iniquity, so now, having at least become believers, present your members to serve righteousness, proceeding into sanctification, that is, into the fullness of righteousness. This is sufficiently human: that in the measure in which you served the devil, you should serve God, to whom you are much more obligated. Truly, because you have become servants of God, you ought to serve righteousness.

For when you were formerly slaves of sin, you were then free from righteousness, that is, strangers [Col. 0060D] to every righteousness, faithfully serving sin. But now that you have become slaves of righteousness, you ought to serve God much more faithfully. Since, out of love for sin, you made yourselves strangers to all righteousness, what fruit—that is, what benefit—did you then have, before your conversion, from those things of which, after your conversion, you are now ashamed? He attacks them by putting the question in this way, so that he may deter them more strongly from slavery to sin.

I ask only about the temporal fruit of sin; for as to their end, it is sufficiently clear: their end is death, that is, at the end of life eternal damnation swallows them up. When you were made slaves of sin, you had no fruit; but now, having been freed from sin by grace and made servants of God, you have your fruit, that is, fruit worthy of the faith you have received. I speak of fruit tending toward sanctification, [Col. 0061A] that is, toward the fullness of righteousness. The ungodly have death, but you have as your end eternal life.

Truly, death is their end; for death is the wage of sin, that is, sin supplies this payment, namely death. “Wage” is used of what a tribune or praetor supplies in the army after reckoning out the soldier’s pay. Death is obtained from sin, but eternal life is obtained through the grace of God. Although some merit is present there, the first justification nevertheless came from grace alone. The ordering of the life that follows also comes from the same grace, which rewards far more abundantly than was deserved. Grace gives eternal life; and this is in Christ Jesus, that is, through Jesus Christ our Lord.

## CHAPTER VII

“Or do you not know, brothers—for I speak to those who know the law—that the law has dominion over a person for as long as he lives? For a woman who is under a husband is bound by the law while her husband lives; but if her husband dies, she is released from the law of her husband. Therefore, while her husband lives, she will be called an adulteress if she is with another man; but if her husband dies, she is freed from the law of her husband, so that she is not an adulteress if she is with another man. Thus, my brothers, you too have been put to death with respect to the law through the body of Christ, so that you may belong to another, to him who rose from the dead, in order that you may bear fruit for God.

For when we were in the flesh, the passions of sins that were through the law were at work in our members, so that they might bear fruit for death. 39 But now we have been released from the law of death, in which we were held, so that we may serve in the newness of the spirit, [Col. 0061C] and not in the oldness of the letter.

What then shall we say? Is the law sin? Far be it! But I did not know sin except through the law. For I would not have known covetous desire unless the law had said: ‘You shall not covet’ (Exod. 20:17; Deut. 5:21). But sin, having taken occasion, through the commandment worked every covetous desire in me. For without the law sin was dead. I, however, was once alive without the law. But when the commandment came, sin revived. I, however, died, and the commandment that was intended for life was found by me to be for death. For sin, having taken occasion through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me. Therefore the law indeed is holy, and the commandment holy, and righteous, and good (1 Tim. 1:8).

Did then what is good become death to me? Far be it! But sin, so that it might appear to be sin, through what was good worked death in me, so that through the commandment sin might become sinful beyond measure. For we know that the law is spiritual. But I am carnal, sold under sin. For I do not understand what I do. For I do not do the good that I will, but I do the evil that I hate. But if I do what I do not will, I agree with the law that it is good. Now, however, it is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me.

For I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh. For to will is present with me, but to accomplish the good I do not find. For I do not do the good that I will; but I do the evil that I do not will. But if I do what I do not will, it is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me.

Therefore I find the law, for me who wishes to do good, that evil is present with me. For I delight in the law of God according to the inner person. But I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive [leading me captive] in the law of sin that is in my members. Wretched man that I am, who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God, through Jesus Christ our Lord. Therefore I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but with my flesh the law of sin.”

## EXPOSITION

Since above he had sufficiently proved that they ought to be subject to grace and that God must be served, lest they should think that they ought to serve God through legal observances—for they believed that it was sin if, even in the time of grace, they neglected the legal requirements—Paul proves that one must no longer serve through those legal requirements. If they abandon them, it is not sin; if they observe them, they are guilty. For the shadow must not be retained after the truth has come. And while he expels the carnal law, he binds them to the spiritual law.

The text is joined as follows: Through Christ Jesus there is eternal life alone. Not through the law; for, “Do you not know, brothers”—to stir them more strongly toward understanding this matter, he both calls them brothers and asks a question. You ought not to be ignorant—for I speak to those who know the law—for, if you consider the matter carefully, you will find the same thing.

I say, “Do you not know?” because whatever law has been established rules over a person, not always, but for as long as the law lives in that person, or the person remains under that law. It is as if some command were established in any city for a fixed number of years: anyone within those years who failed to observe the command would be guilty of violating the established law. But after the fixed years had ended, anyone who acted against the established law would not be guilty on that account, because the period of that law had already passed.

So it was with the law of the Jews: from the time of Moses until the time of Christ, anyone who did not observe it was guilty. But after grace came, the period of that law had passed, and thus the person who abandons it is not guilty. Truly, an established law rules as long as a person lives under the law, or as long as the law lives in the person.

For this is the law of marriage: a woman who is under a husband, joined to him in the marital manner, [Col. 0062D] is bound by the law of her husband while he lives; but if her husband dies, the woman is released from the law of her husband. Since a woman is bound to him while her husband lives, if she has relations with another man while her husband is alive, she will be called an adulteress. But if her husband dies, she is freed from the law of her husband, so that, if she is joined to another man, she is no longer judged an adulteress.

And in the same way—that is, by a similar reasoning—my brothers, you have been put to death with respect to the old law, which was given only until the coming of Christ. You have been put to death through the body of Christ, that is, through Christ who came, who was the body—that is, the reality—of that law, of which the law was the shadow. Nor were you put to death so that you might remain widowed, but so that from now on you might belong to another, namely to him who rose from the dead, through whom you are made sufficiently worthy of commendation. [Col. 0063A]

He rose for this purpose: that through him we might bear fruit for God, that is, through grace, for the honor of God. And only now is it permitted to bear fruit under grace. For when we were in the flesh, that is, held in carnality, then the passions of sins—that is, evil desires—which the sensual person desired, although the rational person nevertheless judged them to be passions, were at work in our members. These passions were made known through the law and increased through the transgression of disobedience, so that they might bear fruit for death, that is, produce the fruit of damnation.

But now, after grace has come, we have been released from the old law, which was for us the law of death, in whose death—that is, the death of sin—we were held, and from which we could not rise with the law’s help. “We have been released,” he says, from the carnal law, so that is, for this reason, we may now serve in the newness of the spirit, [Col. 0063B] that is, renewing ourselves spiritually by doing good every day, according to the saying: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind” (Eph. 4:23), and no longer serve in the oldness of the letter, clinging to a literal interpretation, as oldness is accustomed to do.

Since he had said above that the Jews had been put to death with respect to the old law and must not return to it, because the passions of sins were through the law and through it bore fruit for death, and had also called it the law of death, lest the Jews should wrongly suppose that Paul meant that the law was the efficient cause of sin and compelled people to sin, he proves that the law, insofar as it is concerned, is good. The fact that the Jews sinned more under the law was caused by corrupted nature, not by the law.

The text is joined as follows: Since through the law we bore fruit for death, what shall we say? Shall we say that the law is sin, that is, the efficient cause of sin and something that compels people to sin? Far be it from us to say that the law is sin. If we said this, we would prove the law unjust and accuse God, the giver of the law, of injustice, since he would have given a law compelling people to sin.

Through the law there is certainly not sin, but good: for it is the knowledge of sin. I did not know sin except through the law. Before the law there was indeed knowledge of sin, since Pharaoh’s cupbearer and baker were sent to prison because of sin. But he says that sin was known through the law because original sin was almost universally unknown before the law, and many actual sins were not known to be sins, [Col. 0063D] such as the covetous desire of which he speaks below. The infernal punishment that follows from sins was also not known in the same way, nor was the future reward of those who did not sin. For everyone thought that all would remain in hell, although under unequal punishments.

But through the law original sin was known, and many actual sins previously unknown were also known. Even those things that were known were not thought to be so serious. Future damnation on account of sins was also made known. Therefore he says: “Through the law I knew sin,” both original sin and actual sins, how great they were, as well as the punishment that would follow from them.

Truly, through the law I knew sin. For I did not know this particular thing—covetous desire—to be sin unless the law said: “You shall not covet.” The law is indeed good, because it gives knowledge of sin; yet through the law I possessed nothing good, but every evil, although this was not the law’s fault. He says equivalently: Although the law is good, sin—that is, corrupted nature, or the devil inciting—worked every covetous desire in me, that is, in the will, in action, and through the habit of sinning.

Sin, he says, did this after taking occasion through the commandment, that is, through the law commanded to human beings. “Having taken occasion,” he says, that is, having found an opportunity through the law: first, because human frailty was more inclined toward what was forbidden; and second, because the devil, after the law had been given, attacked the human being more fiercely, seeing that the law had been given as a kind of step by which the human being might return to salvation, whereas previously, possessing him in undisturbed right, he had neglected to trouble him.

It should also be noted that he calls sin corrupted nature. For in each person there are both a sensual [Col. 0064B] person and a spiritual person. The sensual person is that part of the soul, together with the body, which gives sensation to the body; it is so pressed down by the mass of the flesh that through each sense it rejoices with pleasure, loving sweet things through taste, musical things through hearing, pleasing things through sight, agreeable things through touch, and fragrant things through smell.

That part of the soul, however, which is not pressed down in the same way by the flesh—and here is called rationality—contradicts the sensual part and naturally desires what is good. Truly, sin worked evil in me through the commandment. For while I was without the law, sin was dead, that is, corrupted nature was less attacked by the devil; it desired sin less because sin was not forbidden.

Sin was then dead, but I was alive, that is, I seemed to be alive when I was once without the law, because I both knew less and desired sin less, and the devil did not burn with such intensity. Before the law, sin was dead; but when the commandment came, sin, which had been dead, revived, that is, corrupted nature regained its strength, the devil inciting more strongly and, as is the vice of human frailty, desiring forbidden things more intensely.

It revived for this reason: because in the beginning it had lived and original sin had been known while it was still recent. When the commandment came, sin revived; but I died, having become guilty not only of previous sins but also of transgressing the law that had been given. And since through the law sin revived and I died, the commandment that, according to the intention of the giver, had been given to me for life was found by me to be not for life but, reversely, for death. [Col. 0064D]

Not because it compelled me to sin, but because it was the cause without which I would not have been guilty of transgression, and the cause on account of which the devil rose up more fiercely against what the law did not assist but hindered by commanding. He appropriately says, “It was found to be for death”; for the commandment had not been established for death.

He proves that the commandment was for him a cause of death, not through any fault of the law, but through the vice of corrupted nature, which compelled him, saying: Truly the commandment was found by me to be for death. For sin—that is, corrupted sensuality or the devil, having taken the opportunity, or because the persuasion of pleasure toward sin is stronger when prohibition is present, or because the devil pressed forward more ardently—thus, having taken the opportunity through the commandment, deceived me so that I consented to sin; and by that same deception it killed me, rushing me into the act of sin.

And since the commandment was for life, through the fault of sin it was turned into death. Therefore the law is holy, that is, the precepts of the law are holy; and the commandment, that is, the work of the precepts—such as fasting and giving alms—is holy, that is, consecrated and established in goodness. It is also righteous, preserving equity toward one’s neighbor. It is also good, that is, useful to the person who fulfills it. He has now sufficiently proved that the law is good in itself.

But the Jew might say: “I do not care whether the law is good, since it is for me the cause of damnation.” In response, Paul proves that no one is condemned by the law, but rather is nourished in goodness. Corrupted nature, however, is the cause that compels one to sin.

Thus he says: Since the commandment is holy, should what is good in itself be believed to have become death for me, that is, the cause compelling me to death? Far be it! Let what is good be the cause that produces evil! The commandment, which is good, did not become death for me; but sin—that is, corrupted nature, or the devil inciting sin—did so, I say, so that sin might appear, that is, be recognized as sin. Having taken its opportunity from the law, which is good, it worked death in me through what was good, that is, it compelled me to sin more and to transgress what previously had not been transgressed.

It worked, he says, through what was good, so that sin might become sinning beyond its former measure: now sinning under the law, that is, through transgression of the commandment, sinning more than before the commandment was given. [Col. 0065C]

Truly, the law did not work death, but sin did. For we know this from an authority possessing force. We know that the law is spiritual, that is, either given through the Holy Spirit or nourishing the human spirit. In either case it is evident that it is not the cause of death.

The law, then, is spiritual, but I am carnal, that is, clinging to carnality; sold under sin, whom my first parent sold for the taste of an apple. And I am not merely in sin, but also under sin, because even if I wish to rise and labor for a long time, I cannot rise by my own power.

Here he begins to show that the law and the rational person agree in willing the good, yet are overcome by that third element, namely corrupted nature. He proves appropriately that rationality is good and wills good. For just as, if the law were evil, the giver of the law would consequently be blamed, so also, if natural reason opposed the good, the one who had given reason would justly be accused on account of reason’s evil.

Truly, I am under sin. For what I do—whether by abandoning the good, which in fact is to do evil, or by doing evil—I, the sensual person, understand, I, the rational person, ought not to do. Truly, I do evil by abandoning the good which I understand ought to be done. For I do not do the good that I, the rational person, will; and truly I do the evil that I understand ought not to be done. For I, the carnal person, do what I, the rational person, hate.

And now, because the law is spiritual and good, while my rationality wills the good together with the law, it is evident that the law and reason have the same judgment, although carnality prevails. “I do,” he says, “what I hate,” that is, what I do not will. But if I, the rational person, do not will what I, the carnal person, do, then I already agree with the law, that is, by willing the same thing I bear witness with the law that it is good.

Since I, the rational person, do not will what I, the carnal person, do—“now” here has inferential force—therefore I, the rational person, no longer do what the flesh does against my will, but sin, that is, the tinder of sin, which sin dwells in me, that is, continually remains in me, the carnal person. And truly sin dwells in me, because good does not dwell in me.

He says this as follows: I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh, that is, in me as a carnal person. And he proves it: Truly good does not dwell in my flesh, neither through the will nor through action. It does not dwell there through the will. For the willing of good is present with me, the carnal person, that is, it approaches the flesh in a certain way; for no one is so wicked that he does not at least sometimes will the good.

If it is present, then it does not dwell in me: the willing of good is present. But I do not find any way to accomplish that good in my flesh. Truly, accomplishing good is not present in me, the carnal person. For I, the carnal person, do not do the good that I, the rational person, will. Rather, I, the carnal person, do the evil that I, the rational person, do not will.

Or otherwise: Truly, I do not find in myself the complete accomplishment of good. For I do not even do the good that I recognize to be good and therefore wish to do. For not all good things are known to me.

After he had said above, in order to prove another point, “I do not do what I will,” he proves the same thing again by another argument and continues: Since I, the rational person, do not will the evil that I, the carnal person, do, therefore I, the rational person, do not do that evil, but sin—that is, the corruption of nature—which sin dwells in me, the carnal person, does that evil.

He returns to the point from which he may draw the conclusion: “If I do what I do not will.” Since I, the rational person, do not will evil, and the law likewise does not will evil, as has been proved, therefore I, the rational person, find the law to be good, that is, useful to me as a rational person who wishes to do good. The law teaches good, and reason wills good; by agreeing in the good, they recognize one another.

To the person who wishes to do good but does not do it, I rightly say that the evil of carnality is present with me, the rational person; and for this reason I cannot accomplish the good that I will.

[Col. 0066D] Note that Paul speaks figuratively about everyone under his own person, assuming the role sometimes of a person before the law and sometimes of a person under the law. Truly, I find good in me. For I delight in the law of God, because the law wills good and I will it together with the law.

“I delight,” he says, “according to the inner person,” because the rational inner person indeed wills good, even if he is unable to do it. Having just said that the law and rationality will good, he shows that both are overcome by a third element, namely carnality. He shows that this third element must be overcome through grace, and he does so very suitably.

For when he shows that the law is brought low by carnality, and that those who were under the law did nothing good except through grace, he clearly indicates by this that the Jews ought to be entirely subjected to the grace of God and no longer to the law. Again, by saying that rationality, although it willed good, nevertheless succumbed to carnality, he humbles the Gentiles, lest they exalt themselves on account of free will, and thus subjects everyone to the grace of God.

Although according to the inner person I delight in the law of God, I nevertheless see another law in my members, that is, in my carnality. He calls it a law because, just as reason dictates that one should do what is good, so sensuality dictates what is evil. He calls it the law of the members, warring against the law of my mind, that is, against the good things that reason advises.

And it not only wars against it, but also leads me captive into the law of sin, so that I do what corrupted sensuality dictates. This law of sin is in my members, that is, spread through the individual senses.

And since the law of the members leads me captive into sin, therefore I, the rational person, am wretched, because I am a human being, that is, because I am weighed down by carnality. Who will free me, a wretched person, from this body of death, that is, from the death of sins that are in my body—or from the body of death, that is, from this entire mass of sins that leads to death?

The law cannot free me, a Jew; natural reason cannot free me, a Gentile. Since both fail in this, I know that my liberation is the grace of God given through Jesus Christ our Lord. It will certainly free me. Therefore you Jews, submit yourselves to effective grace, not to powerless law; and you Gentiles, likewise submit yourselves to the grace of God, not to weakened reason.

It should be considered that there are two kinds of willing the good in a person. One is according to natural reason, which, weighed down by the corruption of sin, is not sufficient to do the good it wills. The other is willing according to the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, through whom the tinder of sin is subdued, so that we may be able to do good.

The willing of natural reason is what he said above: “I do not do this good that I will.”

He had said above that the inner person and the law delighted in the good through the will alone, not through action, because the tinder of sin was growing strong against these two, attacking both the law and reason. But after God showed that the good of both the law and reason fails in a human being, he finally gave his grace, which strengthened free will, so that now, if a person wishes, he may be able to do good and restrain the tinder of sin effectively.

Since God did not completely separate the human being redeemed through grace from the tinder of sin, the reason was that he left merit to the human being. For if a human being did not sin merely from necessity, because he was unable to do otherwise, there would be no merit by which he ought to be saved.

But in order that there might be an opportunity for merit, he left the tinder of sin struggling against the human being, although weakened and—if the human being wishes—subject to reason. Since, moreover, God did not restore the human being redeemed from sin to as great a dignity as Adam possessed when he fell, this was done so that the human being might not again, through pride arising from sudden and great happiness, fall irreparably.

Therefore, as a reminder of sin and a safeguard of humility, the punishment of sin was appropriately left behind, so that through this too the power of the Holy Spirit might be shown, by whose help the rational person subdues the carnal person, to whom he was subject for as long as he was without grace.

The text is joined as follows: Since the grace of God given through Jesus Christ has freed me, therefore I myself, who before grace was subject to carnality, am now able to do the good I willed. I do not merely will it; I also serve with the mind, that is, I have the power, in accordance with what reason advises, to serve the law of God by doing good. Yet not in such a way that the tinder of sin has been entirely destroyed in me; rather, I have the power to serve the flesh, that is, according to carnality, the law of sin.

In this he also points out a very great miracle: the tinder of sin, against which reason previously had no power, is now subject to reason, if the human being wills it.

## CHAPTER VIII

“Therefore there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, who do not walk according to the flesh. [Col. 0068B] For the law of the spirit of life in Christ Jesus has freed me from the law of sin and death. For what was impossible for the law, in that it was weakened through the flesh, God, sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and on account of sin, condemned sin in the flesh, so that the justification of the law might be fulfilled in us, who do not walk according to the flesh but according to the spirit.

For those who are according to the flesh taste the things of the flesh; but those who are according to the spirit perceive the things of the spirit. For the wisdom of the flesh is death, but the wisdom of the spirit is life and peace, because the wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God. For it is not subject to the law of God, nor indeed can it be.

But those who are in the flesh cannot please God. [Col. 0068C] But you are not in the flesh, but in the spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you. But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, this person does not belong to him. But if Christ is in you, the body indeed is dead because of sin, but the spirit lives because of justification.

But if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Jesus Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies, because of his Spirit dwelling in you.

Therefore, brothers, we are debtors, not to the flesh, so that we should live according to the flesh. For if you live according to the flesh, you will die. But if by the spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you will live. For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God.

For you have not received the spirit of slavery again in fear, but you have received the spirit of adoption as sons of God, in which we cry: ‘Abba’—‘Father.’ [Col. 0068D] For the Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit that we are sons of God. But if sons, then heirs also: heirs indeed of God, but fellow heirs of Christ, if indeed we suffer with him, so that we may also be glorified.

For I consider that the sufferings of this time are not worthy of comparison with the future glory that will be revealed in us. For the expectation of creation awaits the revelation of the sons of God. For every creature has been subjected to vanity, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it, in hope, because creation itself will also be freed from the slavery of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the sons of God.

For we know that every creature groans and labors in childbirth until now. [Col. 0069A] And not only it, but we ourselves also, who have the first fruits of the spirit, groan within ourselves, awaiting the adoption as sons of God, the redemption of our body.

For we have been saved in hope. But hope that is seen is not hope. For what does a person hope for if he sees it? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it through patience.

Likewise the spirit also helps our weakness. For we do not know what we ought to pray for as we should; but the Spirit himself pleads for us with inexpressible groanings. But he who searches the hearts knows what the Spirit desires, because he pleads for the saints according to God.

But we know that all things work together for good for those who love God, for those who are called saints according to his purpose. [Col. 0069B] For those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he himself might be the firstborn among many brothers.

And those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified.

What then shall we say to these things? If God is for us, who is against us? He who did not spare even his own Son, but handed him over for us all—how will he not also, together with him, freely give us all things?

Who will bring an accusation against God’s elect? God, who justifies. Who is the one who condemns? Christ Jesus, who died—indeed, who also rose again—who is at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us.

Who, then, will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation? Or distress? Or persecution? Or famine? Or nakedness? Or danger? Or the sword? As it is written: ‘For your sake we are put to death all day long; we have been reckoned as sheep for slaughter’ (Ps. 43:23).

But in all these things we prevail through him who loved us. For I am certain that neither death nor life, neither angels nor principalities nor powers, neither things present nor things future, neither strength nor height nor depth nor any other creature [or: any creature] will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.”

## EXPOSITION

Since I can serve the law of God with the mind, therefore now, in the time of grace, no condemnation remains for those who are in Christ Jesus, that is, for those who have been reborn in the faith of Christ. This does not mean that they are now always good and, by doing evil, are never so; rather, they are in Christ Jesus in such a way that they do not walk according to the flesh, that is, they do not take pleasure in evils by pursuing carnality.

He appropriately uses the word “walk.” For it is impossible not sometimes to do the things of the flesh. Therefore he did not say, “those who are according to the flesh,” but “those who walk,” that is, those who do not repent of evil but, through habit, take pleasure in it.

Truly, there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. For the law of the spirit—that is, either the law dictated by the Holy Spirit or rationality itself—the spirit, I say, of the giver of life, that is, of the one who grants life here through the virtues, from which eternal life also proceeds; the life, I say, possessed in Christ [Col. 0070A] Jesus, that is, through Christ Jesus, has freed me from the law of sin, that is, from the tinder of sin, and from the law of death, that is, from the act arising from the tinder of sin, so that I would not do what the tinder wrongly advises.

Truly, I have been freed from the law of sin, for through the Son of God—God sent his Son. Not that the Son was absent somewhere, but because he is invisible by nature and became visible through the flesh united to him, he is said to have been sent according to our way of knowing.

God certainly sent his Son, not in sinful flesh, but in the likeness of sinful flesh, that is, in flesh like sinful flesh. For Christ assumed every material aspect of flesh except sin; and through the Son who was sent, he condemned sin, that is, the tinder of sin, which was in our flesh.

“On account of sin,” that is, through the Son who was offered as a sacrifice for the sins of all. Hence Christ was also called “sin.” For a victim offered for sin was called sin, or “for sin.”

Or in another way: he condemned sin, that is, Satan, on account of sin—the sin that the devil committed in the flesh of Christ. For the devil had a right over every human being because of original sin. Since Christ was not guilty of that sin—for he was not born in the desire of the flesh—the devil usurped an unjust right over him. Therefore he lost the right that had been granted to him over all, and thus, because he grasped what had not been granted, he justly lost what had been granted.

He condemned sin for this purpose: so that the justification of the law might be fulfilled in us, that is, the justification which the law foreshadowed but could not complete in us. [Col. 0070C] This is fulfilled in those who do not walk according to the flesh, that is, by following the desires of the flesh, but walk according to the spirit, that is, according to what the Holy Spirit or reason dictates.

He condemned sin, I say, which the law could not condemn. For the law was powerless to free from original sin, and in this matter—that is, in fulfilling justification—the law was weakened through the flesh, because it pursued carnality.

Truly, justification is not fulfilled in those who walk according to the flesh. For those who pursue carnality taste, that is, derive a good flavor from, the things that belong to the flesh. In what follows he will commend the spiritual law at length by contrast, while humbling the carnal law.

What then would someone say if they “set their minds on the things of the flesh”? This is certainly a very great evil. For the mind of the flesh is death—that is, to occupy oneself with what the flesh advises is the death of the soul. [Col. 0070D] For those who follow the Spirit, the justification of the law will be fulfilled. For those who are according to the Spirit perceive—that is, understand and pursue—the things that belong to the Spirit. [46]

And what would someone say about that? Quite a lot, certainly. For the mind of the Spirit is life—that is, living here in the virtues—and it is peace, that is, tranquility of mind and freedom from temptations. Not all who live in the virtues possess this peace, but very few; therefore the mind of the flesh is death, because the wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God. So long as it is hostile to God, it cannot live. But whoever prefers the good of his own carnality to God diminishes the kingdom of God, so far as lies within him, subjecting himself to the kingdom of the flesh.

Truly, the wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God. [Col. 0071A] For it is not subject to the law of God, but to the rule of the flesh. It is not subject because it cannot be subject so long as it clings to carnality. Why should I enumerate each point by saying, “The mind of the flesh is death and hostile to God”? To sum it up briefly: whoever is in the flesh—that is, in carnality—cannot please God so long as he remains there.

Since he had just said that those who are in the flesh cannot please God, lest this should frighten the Romans, who, having previously received justification, had fallen back into certain sins, he soothes them with encouragement, while nevertheless clearly indicating what they must do. “Those who are in the flesh cannot please God.” But you, Romans, are no longer in the flesh, and I do not understand you to be in the flesh; rather, you are in the Spirit. Yet I declare that you are in the Spirit on this condition: if the Spirit of God, whom you received in baptism, dwells—that is, perseveres—in you. [Col. 0071B]

But if anyone—and I do not mean you, but whoever he may be—does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him, namely to God; that is, he has no share with God. Here the Apostle plainly shows that the Spirit proceeds from the Son as from the Father, when he says both “the Spirit of God” and “the Spirit of Christ,” and shows that the Spirit of God and the Spirit of Christ are the same Spirit.

But if Christ—that is, the Spirit of Christ—is in you, your body is indeed dead, that is, it is still subject to mortality because of sin, either because of the punishment of sin or as a safeguard, lest you should again fall through pride. Your body is still dead; but your spirit already lives because of justification, that is, through the works of righteousness which the one justified from sins performs. [Col. 0071C] When he says, “If Christ is in you,” he indicates that Christ and the Holy Spirit are the same in the substance of the Godhead.

Nor will you have life in the spirit only through the Spirit dwelling in you; you will also have it if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you—for this reason, namely, because the Holy Spirit dwelt in him. “If,” he says, “the same Spirit dwells in you, he will also give life to your mortal bodies,” making them immortal for the same reason, namely because his Spirit dwells in you. And he foreshadowed that he can and will do this for you in that he has already raised Jesus Christ from the dead.

For if it is asked why Christ was raised incorruptible before everyone else, the answer is: because he was conceived of the Holy Spirit, because he committed no sin, and because through him all are to receive incorruption. [Col. 0071D] It was fitting, therefore, that he should both precede everyone in this respect in time and receive more than all. Since God has already given life to the soul and will also give life to the body, then, brothers, we are no longer debtors to the flesh—that is, we owe nothing further to carnality, but to the Spirit—because we live through the Spirit and will still be given life.

We do owe the flesh what is necessary for it, such as food and clothing; but we must not live by following carnality. For if you live according to the flesh, you will not be given life but will die. But if through the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you will live, both here according to the soul and in the future according to the incorruption of the body. And you must put them to death, for you are led by the Spirit of God, and you will truly live because you will be sons of God. [Col. 0072A] This is what he says: “Truly, if you put the flesh to death, you will live through the Spirit.” For whoever is led by the Spirit of God—and this means putting the deeds of the flesh to death—these are sons of God, and this is eternal life.

After sufficiently commending the law of the Spirit, he shows how great is the benefit we receive through the Holy Spirit, something he has already partly shown above. Truly, you are sons. For you are no longer slaves, as he says in these words: “You received the Spirit, but not the spirit of slavery, so as to be slaves again and serve in fear.” When you were under the law, you served through fear of the punishments which the law threatened. But whoever serves through fear of punishment escapes punishment but does not merit glory.

You did not receive the spirit of slavery, but you received the Spirit of the adoption of sons, [Col. 0072B] that is, the Spirit through whom you are adopted as sons of God. Taught by this Spirit, we cry out: “Abba” (“Father”). *Abba* is Hebrew, signifying the same as “father,” while *pater* is Greek for “father.” Therefore he placed both the Hebrew expression and the expression of the nations—whether Greek or Latin—to show that both peoples, Jewish and Gentile, ought to serve God in the newness of the Spirit, no longer in the oldness of the letter.

Truly, in the Spirit we cry out, “Abba” (“Father”). For the Holy Spirit bears witness to our spirit, that is, teaches our reason that we are sons of God. Unless the Spirit revealed this, we would not know that we are sons of God. But if we are sons, we shall also be heirs.

See how many benefits we receive through the Spirit. [Col. 0072C] First we are adopted as sons; then we cry out; we are also appointed heirs—not heirs of some paltry inheritance, but heirs of God, because God will distribute his inheritance to us, that is, the sufficiency of every good.

If we ask how we are heirs of God, since ordinary usage has it that one becomes an heir when the predecessor dies, the answer is that God will, in a certain manner, die for us in the future blessedness, according to the fact that now we see him “through a mirror and in a riddle,” but then we shall see him face to face. We shall be heirs of God, but co-heirs with Christ, because we shall receive the same inheritance as Christ—that is, incorruption according to the flesh—in our own manner.

He says “heirs of God,” as of the one whose inheritance it is and who distributes it. He says “co-heirs with Christ,” as of the one who will share the inheritance with us. [Col. 0072D]

We shall be co-heirs with Christ, but I state this condition: if we suffer with Christ, not with the intention of praise or temporal gain, but so that we may be glorified, desiring only eternal glory. We must indeed suffer together with him so that we may be glorified. For I consider—and it is true—that all the sufferings of this present time, that is, the sufferings which are temporal and belong to this brief period, are not worthy of earning the future glory that will be revealed in us, because even we ourselves, who are to possess it, do not understand how worthy and great it is.

Truly, this glory will be revealed in us. [Col. 0073A] For “the expectation of creation,” that is, of the whole Church, awaits the revelation of the sons of God, so that they too may be revealed among the sons of God. Since the whole Church awaits this, we must believe that what it awaits will come to pass. “Expectation awaits” indicates a multitude.

He calls the Church “creation,” for it is especially God’s creation; by justifying it, he also made it a new creation. And because all good things were created for its sake, therefore creation—that is, the Church—awaits this revelation, because it is subject to vanity, that is, to the miseries of the flesh, which are vain. If it eats now, it will soon hunger again; if it drinks, it will thirst again; and so it is with the rest. Because it sees all these things to be vain, it awaits that state in which there will be no change.

It is indeed subject to vanity, but not willingly, because it would not wish to suffer these vanities; and although unwillingly, it nevertheless endures them because of the one who subjected it to these miseries, [Col. 0073B] lest it should perish again through pride. He subjected it, I say, while placing it in hope, so that it might have hope of escaping this vanity. I call this the hope: that, just as in the case of Christ, creation itself also will be liberated from the slavery of corruption—that is, mutability—being transferred from slavery into freedom and from corruption into the glory of the sons of God.

I rightly say that it was subjected unwillingly. For we know that all creation—that is, the Church—groans inwardly and labors in childbirth, that is, struggles with the greatest effort in its works, like a woman in labor awaiting the fruit of her labor. I say that it labors in childbirth “until now,” because from the first righteous person onward the Church has always been in labor, down to the present time.

Creation certainly groans—and not only that creation, but we ourselves also, who possess such great dignity that we are even considered gods. I mean those of us who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, because in the primitive Church we received the Holy Spirit before everyone else and more abundantly, even more abundantly than the prophets who came before. For they did not always speak through the Holy Spirit: sometimes the Holy Spirit departed from them, and they foretold things that were false, as happened at times to Nathan and certain others. But the apostles were never deprived of the Holy Spirit once they had received him.

We ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit and are so worthy, are nevertheless made fragile by God, [Col. 0073C] so that we groan just as creation does. And lest they should think that they groan out of compassion for their subordinates and not for themselves, he makes the matter clear: “We groan,” I say, “within ourselves,” that is, pressed by temptations which trouble us inwardly. [Col. 0073D] The first “we ourselves” indicates dignity; the second, fragility. Through this the Apostle greatly consoles the Church and invites it to patience, saying that the apostles are burdened by the same fragility by which their subordinates are burdened.

He adds the great consolation they possess, saying: “We groan,” I say, “awaiting the adoption of the sons of God,” that is, awaiting our adoption as sons of God.

There are two adoptions. The first is that by which God forgives sins and justifies. The second is that by which, in eternal blessedness, he makes the saints co-heirs with Christ and rewards them. Paul indicates that he understands the second adoption when he says: “Adoption,” I say, “that is, the redemption of our body,” in which adoption our body, now fragile, will no longer be corrupted by any mutability. [Col. 0074A]

By saying “awaiting,” he indicates that he is speaking of a future adoption, not one already possessed. We do not await something that we already possess. It must also be believed that Christ assumed a body together with a soul in order to free both from corruption.

Truly, we await it because we have hope. This hope has great merit, for it makes us saved. He says this in the words “in hope,” that is, by the merit of hope: because we steadfastly hope for something invisible and even inconceivable, by the merit of this we are saved, and in this hope we have been made so by another, not by ourselves. Our fragility would not hope unless it were strengthened by the Holy Spirit, because it would not know what to hope for and thus would possess no merit of salvation.

“We have been saved in hope”: such is the merit of true hope. [Col. 0074B] But that hope—that is, the thing hoped for—which is seen is no longer hope and has no merit of hope. Hope concerns something that is not seen. For example, if we hope that someone will give us money, what we hope for is not yet seen—namely, that we possess the money—even if we see the money itself. But there is no hope concerning something already possessed; one already has its use.

Truly, hope does not concern something that is seen. For how or why should anyone hope for what he sees? It is no longer to be hoped for, but to be used. Something seen should not be called hope; but if we hope for what we do not see, we possess the merit of this hope. For through patience we await the thing hoped for—that is, while waiting, we patiently endure all things, out of desire for the thing we hope for.

And this hope, which has such great merit, is possessed through the Holy Spirit. [Col. 0074C] Nor does the Holy Spirit give us only this. In the same way—that is, just as he gives hope, and through hope patience—so also the same Spirit helps our weakness. For just as without the Holy Spirit we would be weak in hope, so also we would be weak in prayer unless the Spirit taught us.

Truly, the Spirit helps us in our weakness. For we do not know what we should pray for, as it is fitting to know and pray; we do, however, know how one ought not to pray. Certainly we do not know, but the Spirit himself makes petition—that is, he makes us petition and reveals what we should petition for. He makes petition, I say, for us, either in our place or for our benefit, with unutterable groanings.

He calls the groanings unutterable because those who contemplate them would not know how to express, nor would they be able to express, with how many and how great desires they burn. [Col. 0074D]

From the statement that “the Spirit makes petition,” some fell into error, saying that the Spirit is less than the Father and the Son, because one who makes petition is understood to be less than the one to whom he makes petition. They turned Paul’s courtesy into heresy. For just as someone who has taught another how and with what words he should speak to a prince would be said to speak to that same prince through the person he instructed, so the Holy Spirit teaches us what and how we should petition; and through us, whom he has instructed, he is said to make petition—not otherwise.

What he said above—“We do not know how to pray as we ought”—is made clear in Paul himself, who prayed against his salvation that the spirit of Satan given to him for the protection of his humility should be taken away: [Col. 0075A] lest, because he had been caught up to the third heaven and had heard things which it was not permitted for a human being to speak, he should become proud, but through the weakness that pressed upon him he should remember the smallness of the flesh.

The Holy Spirit makes us hope, teaches us to pray, and causes us to be heard. This is what he says: “The Spirit makes petition.” But “the one who searches the hearts,” that is, God, knows—that is, completes and approves—what the Spirit desires, that is, what the Holy Spirit makes us desire. He knows because the Spirit makes petition according to God, that is, the Spirit teaches us to ask for what is good for God to grant.

He makes petition, I say, for the saints, either in their place or for their benefit. The expression “searches” is drawn from that comparison because, just as someone who investigates a matter through careful examination comes to know the matter itself more fully, so God—not because he labors by searching, but as a searcher—knows the hidden things of hearts far better. [Col. 0075B]

The Spirit does not merely give hope, teach us to pray, and cause us to be heard; he also makes every prosperity or adversity that befalls the saints work for good. The sentence is joined as follows: “We do not know how to pray as we ought through ourselves, but through the Holy Spirit we know this, because the same Spirit cooperates in all things, whether prosperous or adverse, for good,” that is, for the benefit of the saints. Or, “all things are made to cooperate by the Holy Spirit for good,” if we take it passively; or, in the active sense, “all things cooperate for good,” and again, through the Holy Spirit. The meaning does not change.

“They cooperate,” I say, “for those who love God”—not for those who love him now and hate him later by sinning, but for those of this kind who love him and have been called by God for this purpose, so that they may be saints. [Col. 0075C] And because not all who are called are elect, he adds:

“Called,” I say, “according to the purpose of God’s foreknowledge,” which can in no way be changed. Truly they were called according to the purpose, and all things cooperate for their good. For God foreknew from eternity that they were suitable for him and worthy of election. And because he foreknew them from eternity, he also predestined them, that is, prepared them at the appropriate time. This preparation consisted in the offering of grace and in inward inspiration.

“He foreknew,” he says, “and predestined them to become conformed,” that is, imitators of the image—namely, the purity—of his Son. For in this world it is possible to imitate the Son of God only through purity; in the future the saints will imitate him through greater purity and unchangeableness.

We say this concerning the divine essence of the Son. [Col. 0075D] For if, by this, we seem to distinguish the Son from the Father when we say “the image of the Son,” we answer that in substance they are entirely the same, but that there is distinction in persons. The Father is without beginning and is from no other; the Son, however, has his beginning from the Father, although he has always existed with the Father, and thus is from another.

But if we are speaking here of Christ according to his humanity, what follows agrees appropriately, since what follows speaks of Christ solely according to the flesh. We shall say: “Let us be conformed to the image of his Son, so that just as he walked in the newness of the Spirit, so may we also walk.”

Nevertheless, we are conformed according to both interpretations, so that the Son himself may be “the firstborn among many brothers”: just as the firstborn Son is Lord of the paternal inheritance, and whatever the other sons possess they possess from him, [Col. 0076A] so Christ is Lord in this inheritance, and whoever possesses anything from it possesses the whole of it from him and through him.

He is also called “the firstborn of the dead” because he was the first to rise from the dead, even as certain saints are believed to have risen incorruptible together with him. But if some have been raised through Christ, they did not rise from the dead, because they are to die again.

Nor did he merely foreknow; those whom he predestined, he also called. For after he had inspired them, he employed callers, prepared inwardly; their calling would be in vain unless the Spirit worked inwardly. And those whom he called, he also justified, by forgiving sins and infusing grace. But those whom he justified, he will also glorify in the future, when they will reign together with him. [Col. 0076B]

Or he says “he glorified” according to the certainty of the future event; according to some, he says this of those who already reign with God with respect to their souls. Since God foreknew, prepared, justified, and finally will glorify his elect, what then shall we say about these things? Is there anything that can oppose this divine disposition?

Certainly nothing can be said against it, because God is for us; and if God is for us, who can be against us? Who can overturn what God has ordained concerning us so that it is not brought to completion?

Truly, God is for us. For he is the one who did not spare even his own Son, but handed him over—that is, arranged for him to be handed over—to death for all his elect. And since he did something so difficult, namely, handing over to death for us the Son whom he loved above all his children, how—that is, for what reason—will he not also give us all the things that remain, together with that Son whom he held far dearer than everything and whom he gave to us at the point of death? [Col. 0076C]

It is not to be believed that the one who gave his Son would deny us things that are lesser than the Son. And since God loved us so greatly that he handed over his Son for us, who will now accuse God’s elect against us?

To accuse is to act against an elect person so as to overturn God’s disposition. Thus Satan, seeing Job abounding in earthly goods, because he thought Job was mentally attached to them, considered that by destroying his possessions he might destroy his righteousness through the impatience arising from the loss of his goods. But because Job was elect, Satan could not do so. [Col. 0076D]

From the beginning, when he said, “I will set my throne in the north” (Isaiah 14:13), he has always labored to destroy the kingdom of Christ, and he still wickedly persists in this. The devil wishes to accuse, but cannot; God can, but does not wish to. For it is God who justifies.

Who also is there who will condemn God’s elect? Satan indeed wishes to condemn, but cannot; Christ could, but does not wish to. This is evident from the fact that Christ Jesus is the one who died for us. And not only this, but he also rose again, so that he might make us rise; he is also at the right hand of God, where he will seat us with him; he also intercedes for us, being at the right hand of the Father, who did and does all these things for us. Is it to be believed that he will condemn us?

Christ is said to intercede not because he cries out with a voice, [Col. 0077A] but because the humanity he assumed, which is before the eyes of God, continually strikes at God and reminds him to complete that purpose for which he willed the Son to assume flesh. It is like an ambassador who, merely by presenting the person of his embassy, reminds the one to whom he has been sent of his mission by presenting himself before him.

Since God foreknew, justified, and so forth, who, then, will be able to separate us from the love of Christ so as to overturn God’s plan? Will tribulation—that is, any affliction of the flesh—separate us? Or distress, that is, anxiety of mind? Or persecution from place to place? Or famine, because he often hungered, to the point that life itself became wearisome to him? Or nakedness? Or danger, that is, the threat of death? Or the sword? Or death itself?

Certainly none of these will separate us, as it is written in the Book of Psalms—and the following words are joined to it: [Col. 0077B]

“For your sake we are put to death all day long; we are considered as sheep for slaughter” (Psalm 43:24)—not sheep kept for bearing offspring, but sheep for slaughter, that is, barren sheep are killed. And if we are killed for your sake, it is clear that we will not be separated from you.

But what concern is it if we are put to death? In all these things—in tribulation, distress, and the rest—we prevail, burning with love for him who loved us. Truly we shall prevail, because neither death—that is, the threat of death—nor life—that is, the promise of life or the glory of the world—nor angels, who perform God’s embassy, nor principalities—that is, the order which also exercises authority over angels—nor powers—that is, the order whose office is to work miracles—

Or, if we wish, we may understand these as evil angels, among whom there are also distinctions of offices. For some have fallen from each order, so that we may say: neither evil angels, whose office it is to carry out embassies; nor principalities, who, among the evil, rule over subordinate angels; nor powers, for evil spirits also perform miracles. [Col. 0077C]

Nor things present—that is, whether they are prosperous or adverse—nor things future, whether the good or evil things of this world; nor strength, that is, the violence of any very powerful being; nor height, that is, the promise of honor—or “height,” such as that in which the devil displayed himself robed in purple and shining with a diadem; nor depth, that is, even if he threatened me with the very abyss while hell stood open; nor any other creature, that is, even if they created a new and unseen creature— [Col. 0077D]

None of all these things will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

## CHAPTER IX

“I speak the truth in Christ Jesus; I do not lie. My conscience bears witness to me in the Holy Spirit: for I have great sorrow and continual pain in my heart. For I myself was wishing to be accursed and separated from Christ for the sake of my brothers, who are my kinsmen according to the flesh, who are Israelites, whose is the adoption as sons, and the glory, and the covenant, and the giving of the law, and the worship, and the promises; whose are the fathers, and from whom Christ is according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever” (2 Corinthians 11:31). Amen.

“But it is not as though the word of God had fallen away [has fallen away]. [Col. 0078A] For not all who are from Israel [by circumcision] are Israelites, nor are all who are the seed of Abraham his children; but ‘In Isaac your seed shall be called’ (Genesis 21:12)—that is, not the children of the flesh are the children of God, but ‘the children of the promise’ (Galatians 4:28) are reckoned as seed.

For the word of the promise is this: ‘At this time I will come, and Sarah shall have a son’ (Genesis 18:10). And not only she, but Rebecca also, having conceived from one intercourse with Isaac our father (Genesis 25:24). For when they had not yet been born, nor had done anything good or evil, so that the purpose of God according to election might remain—not from works, but from him who calls—it was said to her: ‘The elder shall serve the younger’ (Genesis 25:23), [Col. 0078B] as it is written: ‘Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated’ (Malachi 1:2).

What shall we say, then? Is there injustice with God? By no means! For he says to Moses: ‘I will have mercy on whom I have mercy [on whom I have had mercy], and I will show compassion to whom I show compassion’ (Exodus 33:19). Therefore it depends not on the one who wills or on the one who runs, but on God who has mercy.

For Scripture says to Pharaoh: ‘For this very purpose I raised [preserved] you up, that I might show my power in you, and that my name might be proclaimed throughout the whole earth’ (Exodus 9:16). Therefore he has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills.

You will say to me, then: Why does he still find fault? For who has resisted his will? O man, who are you to answer back to God? Does the thing formed say to the one who formed it, ‘Why did you make me thus?’” (Wisdom 15:7; Isaiah 45:9; Jeremiah 18:6.) [Col. 0078C]

“Or does the potter not have authority over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?
