What if God, wishing to show his wrath and make his power known, endured with great patience vessels of wrath prepared for destruction, in order to show the riches of his glory upon vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory?

And these he also called, not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles, as he says in Hosea: ‘I will call the one who was not my people, my people; and the one who was not beloved, beloved; and the one who had not obtained mercy, having obtained mercy’ (Hosea 2:23; 1 Peter 2:10). And in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ there they will be called sons of the living God. [Col. 0078D]

But Isaiah cries out concerning Israel: ‘Even if the number of the sons of Israel were like the sand of the sea, a remnant will be saved’ (Isaiah 10:22). For he is completing and abbreviating the word in righteousness, because the Lord will make an abbreviated word upon the earth.

And as Isaiah foretold: ‘Unless the Lord of Sabaoth had left us seed, we would have become like Sodom and would have been made like Gomorrah’ (Isaiah 1:9).

What shall we say, then? That the Gentiles, who did not pursue righteousness, attained righteousness, namely the righteousness that comes from faith. But Israel, pursuing the law of righteousness [righteousness], did not attain the law of righteousness. Why? Because it was not from faith, but as though from works. For they stumbled over the stone of stumbling, as it is written: ‘Behold, I place in Zion a stone of stumbling and a rock of scandal; and everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame’ (Isaiah 28:26; 1 Peter 2:7).” [Col. 0079A]

## EXPOSITION

I will no longer be separated from the love of Christ, but formerly I was separated; and therefore I grieve greatly. Concerning this grief I speak the truth, being placed in Christ, in whose body it is not permitted to lie. Nor am I truthful in one matter so that I may lie in another. I do not lie in any part; and not only Christ, but also my conscience bears witness to me that I do not lie. I mean a conscience founded in the Holy Spirit, with whom it would not bear false witness.

“Concerning this,” he says, “I speak the truth: that I have great sorrow” because of the affliction of the body, and continual inward pain in my heart. [Col. 0079B] “Pain,” he says, “is mine, and rightly so.” For I myself, who now cannot be separated, was wishing to be not only separated but even accursed—that is, [I wished] the separation of others from Christ for the sake of my brothers. For I wished to separate from God those who are now brothers in Christ, who are also my kinsmen according to the flesh. Although we are bound to love everyone, we owe greater devotion to those of our own household and family.

They are also true Israelites, “seeing God,” whose is the adoption as sons, that is, those who have been adopted as sons of God. Theirs also is the glory of miracles; theirs also is the covenant, the promised Gospel. Theirs also is the giving of the law, that is, the spiritual understanding which the law conveys. Theirs also is the worship, that is, the service of God. [Col. 0079C] To them also the promises of salvation were made. Their fathers also were those from whom Christ was born according to the flesh. According to his divinity he is God from the beginning, remaining over all. He is God, I say, blessed eternally forever. Amen.

For this reason Paul endured more and greater persecutions than the other apostles, because he had persecuted the Church of Christ. He himself bears witness to this when he says: “I labored more than all” (1 Corinthians 15:10). Yet this increase of persecution served him as a safeguard of righteousness and an increase of glory.

Above he sufficiently proved that nothing could separate God’s elect from God. In what follows, however, he wishes to prove that this election of sons takes place not according to the descent of the flesh but through God’s calling.

The text is joined as follows: Formerly I wished to be the separation of the sons of God from Christ; [Col. 0079D] but nevertheless the word of God did not fall away. That is, although I raged greatly against the servants of God and some were overthrown, nevertheless the word did not fall away: the promise of God, by which he had promised that he would redeem Israel, did not perish unfulfilled. For although many who were Israelites according to the flesh were alienated from salvation, all true Israelites were nevertheless elected, and thus the promise was fulfilled.

Truly, even if some have been separated from God, the word of God did not therefore fall away, because not all who are from Israel according to the flesh are to be called Israelites. In the time of Jeroboam many Jews turned to the worship of idols and were reckoned among the Gentiles; [Col. 0080A] they did this many times as well. Many from the Gentiles also adopted Jewish rites and were reckoned among the Jews.

Not all who are from Israel according to the flesh should be called Israelites. Nor should all be called children—that is, heirs—of Abraham merely because they are Abraham’s seed according to the flesh. For Ishmael was from the seed of Abraham according to the flesh, and yet he was not an heir.

Hence it is written: “Cast out the slave woman and her son, for he shall not be an heir” (Gen. 21:12), etc. Thus we do not call those sons of Abraham who degenerate from his faith his sons. For it is customary among fathers to call the one their son who imitates his father. But the one who is opposed to his father’s deeds, the father says is not his son, [Col. 0080B] although he truly knows that he was begotten from his flesh. Not all who are from the seed of Abraham according to the flesh are his sons; rather, those who were born in the likeness of Isaac through God’s promise are called sons of Abraham. For Scripture testifies to this, saying: “In Isaac,” that is, “in the likeness of Isaac, your offspring shall be called.” Nor is this according to the flesh; rather, “he shall be called”—that is, through God’s calling and promise—“your sons”: not so much according to the line of the flesh as through imitation of faith. Isaac, for he was not born according to the law of the flesh—since he was born from an aged father and a barren mother, whose generative organs had already withered through old age—signified that the sons of Abraham were not to be called sons because of the line of the flesh, but in Isaac’s likeness, according to God’s promise. 

The Apostle explains what this means. “In Isaac your offspring shall be called,” he says: [Col. 0080C] What I call “offspring shall be called for you in Isaac” is to be understood in this way: It is not those who are Abraham’s sons according to the flesh who are therefore sons of God; rather, those who are sons of promise—that is, chosen through the promise—are reckoned as Abraham’s offspring, imitators of his faith, just as Isaac was born through the promise. And truly, through the promise. For this is the word of the promise made concerning Isaac, the word which the angel spoke to Abraham, determining the conception of the son promised long beforehand, saying: “I will come at this time”—that is, after a year has elapsed, on this same day—“and when I return, Sarah shall have a son” (Gen. 18:10).

According to Ambrose [Note: The Commentaries on all Paul’s Epistles are not thought to be by Ambrose; concerning this, consult Possevinus’s *Apparatus*.], the preceding text is joined much farther above in another way, as follows: “I desired to be a separation of good things from Christ” [reading uncertain], which I did for my brothers [Col. 0080D]—that is, out of love for my Jewish brothers and zeal for the Law, which I thought Christians were overturning, and therefore I grieved. Nor is it surprising that this was for my brothers, since they are my relatives according to the flesh, and they were the ones who ought to have been true Israelites, and theirs is the adoption of the sons of God—that is, they ought to have been adopted as sons of God, had their wickedness not prevented this. Theirs was the glory of God’s entrusted utterances; theirs was the testament—that is, the Gospel; theirs were the legislation and the service—that is, the worship of God. The promises, too, belonged to them. Theirs were the fathers, from whom Christ was born according to the flesh. [Col. 0081A] But although these promises were theirs, and they did not attain them because their iniquity hindered them, I nevertheless do not say that for this reason the word has fallen—that is, the fulfillment of God’s promise—for although not all who are Jews according to the flesh are included, nevertheless all who were true Israelites received God’s promise.

The following text remains unchanged. “Not only this,” Sarah had the promise, “but also Rebecca.” He appropriately introduces Rebecca, in whose sons it was made clear that someone becomes good solely through God’s election. For if descent is not the reason why Jacob was chosen rather than Esau—since in their election or rejection no merits of their parents and no merits of the sons preceded—then through Rebecca he proves more clearly than through Sarah that Abraham’s sons are made so according to the promise. Sarah had only one chosen son, whereas Rebecca certainly received the promise, having sons from one and the same intercourse with Isaac, our father. This is stated so that it may be known that the merits of the parents neither benefited Jacob nor harmed Esau. He specifies that they were begotten from the same intercourse, lest, if—as certain natural philosophers maintain—they had been conceived at different times, people should suppose that the parents were pleasing to God when they begot Jacob but displeasing when they begot Esau.

Just as he excludes the merits of the parents, so also he excludes the merits of the sons, saying: Rebecca certainly had the promise. For it was said to her: “The elder shall serve the younger.” But before he mentions the promise, he appropriately excludes the merits of the sons together with those of the parents, so that it may be clear that every election is first and chiefly from the grace of God. He says: Rebecca had sons, [Col. 0081C] who, since they had not yet been born, excludes the merits of the sons by this very fact. Yet because they are said to have struggled in their mother’s womb, lest anyone suppose that they could have merited there, he determines the matter by saying: “Or before they had done anything good or evil,” for which one should be chosen here and the other rejected. Therefore, before they had done good or evil, it was said so that the purpose—that is, God’s predestination by which he chose one and rejected the other—might remain; that is, so that it might be shown to endure according to God’s election. This election was not made from works—that is, because Jacob had acted well—but solely from the one who calls, that is, from the grace and good pleasure of God who calls.

This was said because of the statement, “The elder shall serve the younger.” He is not said to serve because Esau at some time served Jacob; rather, he often ruled over him, since he was the stronger in the land. Therefore it is to be understood in this way: “The elder shall serve”—that is, he shall be useful to the younger. For the more Esau persecuted Jacob, the more the merit of patience increased in the one who endured. Thus it is said in Genesis: “The elder shall serve the younger” (Gen. 25:23). This was said to Rebecca before the children were born, and the same thing was later written concerning them through Malachi, long after their death. It is written: “I loved Jacob” (Mal. 1:2), and for this reason chiefly I chose him. But because I hated Esau, I rejected him. For God’s hatred is nothing other than withdrawing grace according to equity.

Just as he appropriately set forth testimony from what preceded in order to exclude the notion that their merits had come first, [Col. 0082A] so also he set forth testimony from what follows, to show that Jacob’s subsequent merit was insufficient and that in himself he was entirely unworthy of God’s grace. Thus it is established that he was chosen through mercy, and it is also shown that grace was rightly denied to Esau because he would not cooperate with grace. The question is asked why Jacob was chosen and Esau rejected, since in neither case had any merit of good or evil preceded: what was the cause of the election of one and the rejection of the other?

The answer is that Jacob was chosen through mercy, while Esau was rejected according to justice. For when God first created man, he adorned him with manifold grace. Because man drove this grace away from himself by sinning, he made himself unworthy of God’s grace. From that point onward God owed man nothing, and thus man was left with no basis on which he could justly complain if he were deprived of God’s grace.

For if it is asked again: Since both could justly be rejected because of original sin, and no merit was found in either for which grace should be given to one and denied to the other, why was Jacob chosen rather than Esau? The answer is that God foreknew Jacob as suitable and willing to cooperate with grace, but Esau as unsuitable because he would not cooperate. Therefore, to one he mercifully granted what he justly withheld from the other because of original sin. This is considered clearly enough in Judas: although God certainly knew that he would perish, he nevertheless permitted him the grace of miracles, as he did to the other apostles, even though Judas was already a thief and had the money box. Yet this was not because God did not know that Judas was irrevocably set upon evil; rather, through him God demonstrated to us that he justly denies all grace to certain people, as to children who die immediately without baptism. He denies them all grace because, if they had time to act and grace were granted to them, they would abuse it and thus be punished far more severely in place of grace; whereas, if they cooperated with grace, they would be saved.

To make this known, God gave certain people grace concerning whom he had no doubt that they would abuse it, so that we might also have it plainly before our eyes that he justly denies all grace to certain people. Again, there is another point: when God created all things, he established some as necessary—for example, the rising of the sun and things of that kind—and others as voluntary, such as man and angel. God therefore chooses one through mercy just as he rejects another through justice, while nevertheless not destroying their voluntary faculty. For although in this world he strengthened many saints with manifold grace, he did not compel them to do good by necessity, nor did he make it impossible for them to turn toward evil if they wished; rather, he assisted them through grace because he saw that they would cooperate with grace.

Conversely, he did not withdraw grace from Judas in such a way that, once grace had been withdrawn, he compelled him—whether he wished it or not—to work iniquity. Rather, this was so that it might be shown what iniquity could accomplish by itself. For if grace given or denied were compelling and necessary, no merit of salvation or damnation would then remain for man. Since Jacob is chosen with no preceding merit and Esau is likewise rejected without merit, what shall we say? Is there injustice with God, who chooses Jacob without merit and similarly rejects Esau without merit? Far be it from us to say that God is unjust for this reason! Truly, in Jacob’s election and Esau’s rejection God is not unjust: in choosing the one he is merciful, and in rejecting the other he is just.

The matter of justice follows below, where, concerning Pharaoh, he adds and proves the matter of mercy, saying: Truly, because he chose Jacob, he is not unjust; for he is merciful.

God said to Moses (Exod. 33:19): “I will have mercy on the one on whom I have mercy”—that is, on the one toward whom I show mercy in foreknowledge, I will show mercy in justification. And on the one toward whom I show mercy in justification, I will bestow mercy in salvation. Here he sufficiently demonstrates that everything proceeds from mercy, because foreknowledge, justification, and salvation all flow from the fountain of mercy. Since everything, as has been shown, is done through God’s mercy, therefore to will the good is not the achievement of the one who wills, as though it should be ascribed to him. Nor is running the achievement of the one who runs—that is, doing is not the achievement of the one who acts—but it is the achievement of God who has mercy. Man can neither will nor accomplish the good unless God’s mercy works in him through the Holy Spirit.

Truly, it belongs to God who has mercy to will and bring to completion, because it does not belong to the one who does not receive mercy either to will or to bring to completion—that is, to reject—which is plainly shown in Pharaoh. For Scripture says to Pharaoh in Genesis—appropriately introducing Pharaoh, to whom God proposed this grace, so that, if he wished, he could act rightly through Moses’ teaching (Exod. 9:16). God certainly knew that Pharaoh would never repent, but in Pharaoh, to whom he granted the grace of instruction and who abused it, he wished plainly to show us that grace is justly denied to Esau before he had merited it, and to all to whom it is denied in this way: for if God were to give them grace, they would abuse it and consequently be punished more severely.

Therefore God also provided Pharaoh with teachers, so that the evils that had previously been hidden in him might then become manifest, as he resisted God in so many and such great matters and did not yield to the prophets and miracles. This, I say, Scripture says to Pharaoh: “For this very purpose”—the phrase continued in Genesis—“for this very purpose in which you were,” that is, you were evil but hidden, “and in this evil I raised you up,” withdrawing grace so that you might appear evil as you were. This was precisely so that I might show my power in you—that is, the signs of miracles, which I would not have shown if you had yielded. I will also show it for this reason, so that my name may be proclaimed throughout the whole earth, on account of the miracles performed in Egypt. Wherever the signs of Egypt were heard, it was said: “Great is the God of the Hebrews.”

Since God chose Jacob according to his will and rejected Esau according to his will, it is therefore evident that God has mercy on whomever he wills because he sees that person will cooperate with grace, and hardens whomever he wills because he sees that person to be unsuitable for grace. God’s hardening means not supplying grace.

Because I said that God has mercy on one and hardens another according to his will, you therefore say and object to me: Why is anything still required of us, so that we should act well, when those who have been rejected cannot act well? Or in this form: Why does God still demand anything of us—why does he complain against us—if we offend, when, once hardened, we cannot avoid offending? There is no basis on which he should complain. Or: what does he require of us, since who can resist his will? Where he hardens us, he seems unwilling that we should act well, and his will cannot be changed.

Paul says all this because he saw the Romans glorying excessively in worldly wisdom and dwelling beyond measure on questions of this kind. Therefore, in order to restrain them more effectively, he attributes everything to God’s grace, so that he seems to leave nothing to free choice. Yet this is sufficiently and appropriately understood, because even the beginning of the will to do good cannot arise from us alone if God’s grace does not inspire it.

Thus he says: You say to me, “Why is anything still required of us?” But, O man clinging to your humanity, who are you to answer God—that is, who are you that, if God should explain the mystery of this matter to you, you could understand it? Or who are you to answer—that is, to quarrel and dispute with God concerning the mystery of this matter? You have no answer to give God concerning this, just as a pot does not have the right to contradict the potter about its own making. The comparison is apt, because just as a potter works from clay, so God finds man as clay, infected with every pollution. You certainly have nothing with which to answer God.

Does the thing formed say to the one who formed it, “Why have you made me so—short or long, shapeless or shaped?” Or does the potter not have authority over the clay, since the material belongs to him? Thus God finds all of you soiled with original sin, as clay. Surely he has the power, from the same lump—which is wholly unclean in itself—to make one vessel for honor, from which one may drink, and another for dishonor, in which the household’s filth may be deposited?

And just as the potter has the power to make from this clay a vessel honorable, as he wishes, and to designate another for uncleanness, since the vessel’s material was unclean, so God, finding the whole mass of humanity corrupted by original sin: if he assigns part of this mass to purity, that is mercy; but if he leaves another part to become filthy in uncleanness, that is equity. To cry out against equity is unjust, as has been shown. If God, following justice, leaves in uncleanness what has been soiled by its own sin, man has no grounds on this matter for contradicting God.

What, moreover, will be said about this? If God mercifully gives grace to those to whom he does not owe it, and they abuse the grace they have received, are not those of this kind rightly rejected? He says this equivalently: If, I say, God wished to reveal his wrath—that is, to make the damnation of the impious manifest to human beings—although it was known to him that they would never cooperate with the grace given, and if he also wished to make his power known—that is, how great a power of patience he uses to make his own endure the persecutions of the impious—through this process God does not work even in the rejected impious without mercy, since the merit of patience increases in his own through the hardening of the wicked.

Wishing, then, to show wrath in the impious and power in the elect, God endured with great patience, both according to the duration and according to the number of their impieties. He endured, I say, “vessels of wrath”—that is, those into whom wrath, meaning damnation, was justly to be poured. Vessels, I say, “fitted for destruction”—that is, for perdition—because of original sin alone, if grace were never given through which they might abuse it.

He endured this in order to show the riches of his glory [Col. 0085A]—that is, his rich glory—in vessels of mercy, that is, in those into whom mercy was to be poured. These vessels God prepared—that is, predestined—to possess future glory. Nor did he merely predestine them: those whom he calls vessels of mercy he also called by sending preachers.

The word “whom” refers to the sense, not to the literal wording. “He called us,” I say—but whom do we mean by “us”? Not only those from the Jews, but also those from the Gentiles, because just as he called the Jews, so also he called the Gentiles.

He proves that the calling of the Gentiles comes from God, saying: Truly, God called the Gentiles, as he says—not Hosea, but the Lord in Hosea. This is what he says: “I will call what was not my people ‘my people’”—that is, the Gentile people, which now is not called my people. “I will call them by grace and make them my people” (Hos. 2:23), and the Gentile people that was not beloved I will call by grace and make beloved, justifying it from sins. And the same Gentile people that had not obtained mercy I will make to have obtained mercy in salvation.

As a sign of the salvation of the Gentiles, Hosea, who was going to preach the salvation of the Gentiles, was commanded by God to take a wife of prostitution, and so forth. “I will call the Gentile people,” he says, “and this will happen in the place where it was said, ‘You are not my people’”—that is, throughout the whole world, where only the Jews were called God’s people. There the Gentiles will no longer be called merely nations; rather, they will be called sons of the living God, who will give them the eternal life that he possesses, to those whom he has called according to election.

Or it may be understood this way: “In the place”—that is, in Judaea—“where it was said, ‘You are not my people,’ there they will be called sons of God,” because apostles were also chosen from the Jews, through whom the Gentiles were converted; and the Church had its first origin in Judaea.

After confirming the calling of the Gentiles by the authority of Hosea, he proves through Isaiah the salvation of the Jews, and appropriately proves it in this way. For the Gentiles reproached the Jews, saying that, once rejected and repudiated because of their fault, they were thereafter unworthy of God’s salvation.

Hosea speaks concerning the Gentiles; “but Isaiah,” he says, “cries out and affirms this on behalf of Israel” (Isa. 10:22)—that is, on behalf of the Jewish people, who were to be honored, although he often reproached them for their evils. This is what he cries out: Even if the number of the sons of Israel should be innumerable, “like the sand of the sea,” nevertheless “the remnant of Israel”—that is, the lowly and rejected, who place no confidence in the carnality of the Law—such a remnant will be saved. Or “the remnant” means those whom God has left for himself and reserved as suitable for salvation; they will be saved.

He determines the manner of salvation, lest they should think that they were saved through the Law. Truly, the remnant will be saved, for it will be through the word—that is, through the teaching of faith—which was “a word that consummates,” that is, which justifies perfectly, something the Law could not do. It will also be “abbreviating”: it will reduce the commandments of the Law, all of which it will bring back to love of God and neighbor, and the sacrifices, all of which it will reduce to the one sacrifice of Christ’s body.

And lest the word be judged unjust because it abbreviates the Law, he adds that this word is “in equity,” because, although it abbreviates the Law, it will nevertheless be equitable and just. This is clear from the fact that the Lord will accomplish this abbreviated word, as was said, with respect to the sacrifices and commandments. Nor will it be only over the Jews, but also over the earth—that is, over the Gentiles.

Or it may be understood this way: “The remnant will be saved” through that word of which it was said: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1), and so forth. That Word—that is, Christ—will consummate and abbreviate the Law in equity, as was said. For the Lord will make this word short—that is, according to the mortal and passible flesh he assumed, by which he was made lower than the angels. In accordance with the saying: “You made him a little lower than the angels” (Ps. 8).

And this Word he will make present upon the earth: what was invisible in the nature of his divinity, through the flesh he assumed he will display visibly to human beings on earth. Truly, through the abbreviated Word the remnant will be saved. For unless the Lord had left us this seed, we would have perished. And I say this not from myself alone, but also as Isaiah foretold when prophesying concerning the same: “Unless the Lord of Sabaoth” (Isa. 1:9)—that is, of the heavenly and earthly armies—“had left us seed,” that is, Christ, whom he established before the ages and gave in time, we would have become like Sodom and like Gomorrah.

Or “seed” means the word of preaching, through which believers bear fruit. Or, unless the ascending Lord had left us seed—that is, the apostles, who would sow the word of faith in us—we would indeed have become like Sodom and like Gomorrah, that is, we would have been utterly imperiled, and deservedly so, because we would have become like them by despising God’s commandments.

Because Paul had said above, concerning the calling of the Gentiles through Hosea (Hos. 2:23), that the Jews might deny that this was said about the Gentiles rather than about themselves—since by often withdrawing from God they too had become “not God’s people”—Paul explains how these words apply only to the Gentiles.

Since it was said above, “I will call what was not my people ‘my people,’” what shall we say? And how shall we understand this authority? We shall explain this in the words of Hosea: the Gentiles, who were not pursuing righteousness—that is, who possessed neither the Law nor the good use of their own reason—“attained” righteousness, not through merit, but through grace, which brought his righteousness to them. This was not carnal justification, but the righteousness that comes from faith.

The Apostle then explains the part of the authority that Isaiah brought forward on behalf of Israel—namely, that not the multitude of the sons of Israel would be saved—by stating the reason why Israel is rejected. He says: The Gentiles attained righteousness; but Israel—that is, the Jewish people—by pursuing the Law of carnal righteousness did not arrive at the Law of spiritual righteousness.

But why did they not arrive? Because they did not believe through faith that they were justified; rather, they presumed that they could be justified as though by works. And because they did not believe through faith that they could be justified, they stumbled—that is, they made for themselves a stumbling block—in the stone, that is, in Christ. He was a stone that would crush enemies and upon which the foundations of the righteous would stand.

I call him “a stone of stumbling,” that is, a stone suited—because of the humility he possessed—to cause the proud to stumble, as it is written in Isaiah: “Behold, I place in Zion”—that is, among the Jewish people—“a stone of stumbling,” that is, Christ, “and a rock of offense” (Isa. 8:14; 1 Pet. 2:7). [Col. 0087A] There is no difference between a stone and a rock, but he calls the sins committed against Christ “stumbling”; he calls the damnation arising from the guilt of sins “offense.”

Although I say that Christ was a stone of stumbling to the Jews, not all stumbled over him. Rather, everyone from Zion who believes in this stone will not be ashamed of having believed in him.

## CHAPTER X

“Brothers, the desire of my heart and my supplication to God for them is for salvation. For I bear them witness that they have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge. For, being ignorant of God’s righteousness and seeking to establish their own, they have not submitted to God’s righteousness. For Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes. [Col. 0087B] For Moses wrote [said]: ‘The person who does the righteousness that is from the Law will live by it’ (Lev. 18:5). But the righteousness that is from faith speaks in this way: ‘Do not say in your heart, “Who will ascend into heaven?”’ (Deut. 30:11)—that is, to bring Christ down; ‘or, “Who will descend into the abyss?”’—that is, to bring Christ back from the dead. But what does Scripture say? ‘The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart’ (Deut. 30:14). This is the word of faith that we preach: if you confess in your mouth the Lord Jesus and believe in your heart that God raised him [revived him] from the dead, you will be saved. For with the heart [or: indeed, with the heart] one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto [Col. 0087C] salvation. For Scripture says: ‘Everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame.’ For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek. For the same Lord is Lord of all, rich toward all who call upon him. For everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved (Joel 2:32). How then will they call upon him in whom they have not believed? Or how will they believe him whom they have not heard? And how will they hear without one who preaches? How will they preach unless they are sent? As it is written: ‘How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace, who proclaim good things!’ (Isa. 52:7; Nah. 1:15.) But not all obey the Gospel. For Isaiah says: ‘Lord, who has believed our report?’ (Isa. 53:1.) Therefore faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ [God]. [Col. 0087D] But I say: Have they not heard? Indeed, ‘their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world’ (Ps. 18:5). But I say: Did Israel not know? Moses first says (Deut. 32:21): ‘I will provoke you to jealousy by that which is not a nation; by a foolish nation I will provoke you to anger.’ But Isaiah dares to say: ‘I was found by those who were not seeking me; I openly appeared to those who were not asking after me’ (Isa. 65:1). But to Israel he says: ‘All day long I stretched out my hands to a people who did not believe but contradicted me’ (ibid. 65:2).”

## EXPLANATION

Lest, because he had just said, “Israel did not arrive at the law of righteousness, but stumbled over Christ,” the Apostle should be thought to say that the Jews were rejected for this reason and could no longer be saved, he says that he prays for them—something he would certainly not do if he knew them to have been rejected by God.

Hence he says: Although the Jews stumbled over Christ, nevertheless, brothers, “the desire of my heart is for them”—that is, I have goodwill toward them, whom I trust will be saved if they repent. And not only is there desire, but also supplication to God is made for them, so that they may obtain salvation.

I beseech God for them for this reason: I bear them witness that they certainly have zeal—that is, love—for God; or “zeal” means indignation against the saints, arising from zeal for God and his Law. Thinking that their own Law must be defended in this way, they persecute the saints. They certainly have zeal for God, but not [Col. 0088B] according to knowledge. For they do not love the Law in this way knowingly, nor are they knowingly indignant on behalf of the Law. Hence blessed Peter says: “I know, brothers, that you acted in ignorance” (Acts 3:17), and so forth.

Truly, it is not according to knowledge, for, being ignorant of God’s righteousness—that is, ignorant that all justification comes from God alone—and seeking to establish, that is, to confirm, their own righteousness, because they thought they were justified through the fleshly works of the Law, they were not subject to God’s righteousness. That righteousness would in fact be theirs, not God’s. In seeking this, they were not subject to God’s righteousness—that is, to God who justifies—but instead, by detracting from God, they ascribed to themselves the righteousness that belongs to God.

Truly, they were not subject to God’s righteousness. For they were unwilling to submit to Christ, who is righteousness for everyone who believes—that is, who justifies everyone who believes. Christ, I say, who is the end of the Law both according to its fulfillment and because, with Christ’s coming, that Law came to an end, and grace now has its place through Christ.

Truly, Christ is for righteousness, for the Law is not for righteousness. For Moses wrote in this way: “The person who has done the righteousness that comes from the Law”—that is, the carnal observances prescribed by the Law—“will live in it” (Lev. 18:5), in that Law. That is, through fulfilling the carnal Law he will obtain only this: that he will not die under the judgment of the Law. For the one who does the Law merely escapes punishment; he is not justified through it.

Concerning the righteousness of the Law he says this. But concerning the righteousness that comes from faith, the same Moses says: “Do not say in your heart”—that is, do not believe in your heart or say with your mouth—this: “Who has ascended into heaven?” (Deut. 30:12) [Col. 0088D] That is, do not even doubt that some have ascended into heaven and that any righteous people who remain will ascend. For to say, “Who has ascended into heaven?” is to bring Christ down from heaven—that is, to deny that Christ ascended into heaven.

Or: Do not say in your heart, “Who has descended into the abyss”—that is, into hell? For to say this is to bring Christ back from the dead, claiming either that Christ, when he died, did not descend into hell, or that he did not bring Abraham and his saints out from there. Both assertions are contrary to faith.

Do not believe this; rather, believe what follows. For what does Scripture say through the same Moses? “The word is near you, in your mouth”—that is, the word of teaching is ready, or Christ, the Word of God, is in your mouth, so that you may confess it and rationally defend it. “And this same word is also near you [Col. 0089A] in your heart” (Deut. 30:14), so that you may believe it.

This word that I say is near is the word of faith—that is, teaching suited to belief. Or it is Christ, in whom it is fitting to believe, and this is the word that we preach. We preach this for the following reason: if you confess the Lord Jesus with your mouth and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead—and whatever impossible things you believe concerning him, including that the law of nature could not resist him—if, he says, you confess and believe this, you will not merely live the present life, as one does through the Law, but you will also be saved eternally.

Truly, if you believe with your heart, you will be saved. For one believes with the heart in order to obtain righteousness—that is, justification from sins. And whoever has been justified is secure concerning salvation. And truly, if you confess with your mouth, [Col. 0089B] you will be saved. For confession is made with the mouth in order to attain eternal salvation.

For this reason he assigned salvation to confession of the mouth, since salvation appears to be the greater thing. To confess this—that is, God—was a great and extraordinary act in the time of the Apostle, when persecution was raging; at that time many who truly believed did not dare to speak openly or to confess.

He proves from the authority of Scripture that belief of the heart justifies, although he does not specify whose Scripture this is. Nevertheless, an equally suitable saying is found many times in the Psalms.

Truly, one believes with the heart unto righteousness. For Scripture says: Everyone, whether Jew or Gentile, who believes in him whom God raised from the dead will not be put to shame, that is, will not blush as though he had believed wrongly. I rightly say “everyone.” For there is no distinction with God:

[Col. 0089C] Jews and Greeks; that is, in his salvation God receives a Jew and a Gentile without distinction, the Jew as a Gentile and the Gentile as a Jew. Truly, with God there is no distinction between Jew and Gentile, for the same Lord is Lord of all. He who created the one also created the other. Hence it is evident that he has an equal will toward both, and, just as he has the same will, so also he has the same power. For he is rich and abundantly rewards all who call upon him.

He proves that confession is made unto salvation. Yet the wording answers what immediately precedes. Truly, God is rich toward all who call upon him. For everyone, whoever he may be, whether Jew or Gentile, who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved. Since they must call upon him in order to be saved,

[Col. 0089D] they must first believe, so that afterward they may call upon him. For how will they call upon him in whom they have not believed? As though he were saying: “They will call because they will believe.” Or how will they believe in him whom they have not heard? That is: “They will believe because they will hear.” But how will they hear without a preacher? That is: “They will hear because he will be preached to them.” And how will they preach unless they are sent? That is: “Because God will send them, they will preach.” Through all these questions he intends that everything proceeds from the grace of God, from the beginning of their calling to their salvation.

For when he says that preachers are sent by God, whom they hear; and after hearing, believe; and then call upon him; and thus at last are saved, he suggests that the whole matter must be attributed to the grace of God. Truly, preachers are sent by God, as it is written in Isaiah:

[Col. 0090A] “How beautiful are the feet,” that is, the coming of those who evangelize, that is, announce peace—peace between God and humanity—and evangelize good things (Isa. V), that is, humility, chastity, and things of this kind.

Since he had said above that they believed because they heard, lest we should suppose that merely hearing was sufficient for possessing faith, without the Holy Spirit working inwardly, he says: “Although I said that they will hear and believe, nevertheless not all who hear obey the Gospel.” Nor do I say this alone; Isaiah, agreeing with me, says the same: “Lord, who has believed our report?” That is, either the things which they heard from us, or the things which we heard from you and announced to them. By saying, “Who has believed?” he implies that many heard, and that, although not all, at least some believed.

And since some believed:

[Col. 0090B] therefore faith comes from hearing, that is, some believe because they hear. Yet sound faith does not arise from every kind of hearing, but from hearing that takes place through the word, that is, according to the teaching of Christ; faith is salutary when it comes in this way.

Although few believed our report, nevertheless I say: “Have they not heard?” As though he were saying: “In the matter of not believing, they are without excuse, because they heard the word of faith.” Indeed, the sound, that is, the fame, of those preachers went out into all the earth. And not only their fame, but also their words—that is, the very things which they themselves preached—were heard to the ends of the earth. Thus I speak of “the earth,” meaning the world, that is, the round-shaped earth. For the words of the apostles were heard in every part of the earth.

They had certainly heard, as has been proved. Nor do I say only that they heard them; I say

[Col. 0090C] that they also understood. He puts this in the form of a question in order to rouse them more strongly, saying: “Has Israel,” that is, the Jewish people, “not understood?”

There are two kinds of understanding. One is the kind by which, when we recognize that something is good, we love and approve the goodness of that thing; this is good understanding. The other is the kind by which we see that a thing is as it is said to be, and cannot contradict it, yet do not love that thing and have toward it the evil will that is all we can possess. This is the evil understanding which the Jews had concerning Christ.

He proves by the authority of Moses that the Jews understood Christ, saying: “Truly Israel understood.” For Moses was the first in time according to the writings, since no one wrote prophecy before him. By saying “first,” he implies that there are many witnesses to the same matter, even though he does not name them. Or “first” may mean “pre-eminent” according to dignity.

Moses, he says, first says this: “I will provoke you Jews to jealousy,” that is, to envy and indignation of spirit, “against a non-nation,” that is, against the Gentile people, which previously was not called my nation, and whom you yourselves used to call dogs. Or “against a non-nation” means against the Gentile people whom I shall make a non-nation: that is, I shall not leave them as they were generated, but shall make them a new creation, regenerated by water and the Holy Spirit.

Nor will I merely bring you so that you may see; I will also send you into anger, so that you may persecute them. I say that I will send you into anger, that is, against the foolish Gentile people, meaning those who were formerly foolish. For although many Gentile philosophers

[Col. 0091A] possessed knowledge concerning worldly matters, they were nevertheless foolish because they were ignorant of the truth of divine worship.

By seeing Moses’ prophecy fulfilled—because they envy the Gentiles who have become Christians, abandoned idolatry, and followed the new law—the Jews understand that the time of which Moses spoke has arrived. Yet their bitterness does not wish to yield to true understanding.

Moses says this concerning the Jews. Isaiah, however, dares to speak of the salvation of the Gentiles and the rejection of the Jews. He does indeed dare. For Isaiah, because he prophesied the salvation of the Gentiles more openly than the others, suffered much at the hands of the Jews and was finally killed by them. Therefore he says:

“He dares,” that is, without fear,

[Col. 0091B] but with boldness he says this: “I was found by those who were not seeking me” (Isa. LXV, 1).

When he says that he was found although he was not sought, which seem to contradict one another, he shows that the Gentiles found salvation solely through the mercy of God. “I was found,” I say, “by the Gentiles who were not seeking me” by the natural reasoning which I had given them in order to understand me; and I appeared openly to them, that is, I was set before them in the sight of all.

I say that I appeared to those who were not asking about me, that is, who were not seeking knowledge of me from anyone who understood. For if they sought me by their own reasoning but were unable to understand, it would have been appropriate for them to ask someone who understood about what they themselves understood less well.

Thus Isaiah speaks concerning the Gentiles. But to Israel, that is, to the Jewish people, he says this:

“All day long,” that is, throughout the whole period through the preachers—or throughout that entire day on which I hung

[Col. 0091C] upon the cross—“I stretched out my hands,” that is, my affections and works, “toward the Jewish people,” who did not believe.

And not only did they not believe; they also contradicted me. The stretching out of Christ’s hands upon the cross signified the love by which he always wished to embrace the Jews, and by which, even upon the cross, he was ready to forgive everything if they repented.

Behold, once again in Isaiah he shows that the Jews understood, since they see this fulfilled which he said. He also shows the salvation of the Gentiles and the rejection of the Jews.

## CHAPTER XI

“I say then: Has God rejected his people? By no means! For I also am an Israelite, from the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin. God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew. Or do you not know what Scripture says concerning Elijah, how he appeals to God against [or: on behalf of] Israel? ‘Lord, they have killed your prophets, they have overthrown your altars, and I alone have been left, and they seek my life’ (III Kings XIX, 10). But what does the divine response say to him? ‘I have kept for myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee before Baal’ (III Kings XIX, 18). So also at this present time a remnant will be saved [or: has been saved] according to the election of the grace of God. But if it is by grace, it is no longer from works; otherwise grace is no longer grace.

“What then? What Israel sought, it did not obtain; but the election obtained it, while the rest were hardened, as it is written: ‘God gave them a spirit of compunction, eyes so that they should not see, and ears so that they should not hear, unto this present day’ (Isa. VI, 9; Matt. XIII, 14; John XII, 40; Acts XXVIII, 26). And David says: ‘Let their table before them become a snare, a trap, a stumbling-block, and a recompense to them. Let their eyes be darkened so that they may not see, and keep their back always bent’ (Ps. LXVIII, 23).

“I say then: Did they stumble so as to fall? By no means! But through their trespass salvation has come to the Gentiles, so as to provoke them to jealousy. For if their trespass is the wealth of the world, and their diminution the wealth of the Gentiles, how much more their fullness?

“For I speak to you Gentiles. Inasmuch as I am indeed the apostle of the Gentiles, I will honor my ministry,

[Col. 0092B] if somehow I may provoke my flesh to jealousy and save some of them. For if their loss is the reconciliation of the world, what will their acceptance be except life from the dead?

“For if the first-fruit is holy, so also is the lump; and if the root is holy, so also are the branches. But if some of the branches have been broken off, and you, although you were a wild olive, have been grafted in among them and have become a sharer in the root and the richness of the olive tree, do not boast against the branches. But if you boast, it is not you who bear the root, but the root bears you.

“You will say, then: ‘Branches were broken off so that I might be grafted in.’ Quite so. They were broken off because of unbelief. But you stand by faith. Do not be high-minded, but fear. For if God did not spare the natural branches, perhaps he will not spare you either.

“See, therefore, the goodness and severity of God: severity toward those who fell, but toward you the goodness of God, if you remain in his goodness. Otherwise you too will be cut off. But they also, if they do not remain in unbelief, will be grafted in. For God is able to graft them in again.

[Col. 0092C] “For if you were cut from a wild olive by nature, and contrary to nature were grafted into a good olive tree, how much more will these, who are natural branches, be grafted into their own olive tree?

“For I do not want you, brothers, to be ignorant of this mystery, lest you be wise in your own eyes: a hardening has happened in part to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter; and thus all Israel would be saved, as it is written: ‘He will come from Zion, he who delivers and turns away ungodliness from Jacob’ (Isa. LIX, 20).

“And this will be my covenant with them, when I take away their sins.

“According to the Gospel they are indeed enemies for your sake, but according to the election they are beloved for the sake of the fathers. For the gifts and calling of God are without repentance.

“For just as you once did not believe God, but now have obtained mercy because of their unbelief, so also these now have not believed in your mercy, so that they too may obtain mercy. For God has enclosed all in unbelief, so that he may have mercy on all.

“O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments and how unsearchable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counsellor? (Wis. IX, 13; Isa. XL, 13; I Cor. II, 16.) Or who has first given to him, that it should be repaid him? For from him, and through him, and in him are all things. To him be honor and glory for ever and ever. Amen.”

## EXPOSITION

Because I say that the Jewish people do not believe but contradict, therefore I say—am I for that reason thought to be saying that God has rejected his Jewish people, whom he had previously chosen? May it be far from us that God should ever reject his people!

Truly, he has not rejected them. For I am an Israelite, and there are many others who have not been rejected. Nor am I an Israelite in such a way that, having been born elsewhere, I transferred into Judaism; rather, I am from the seed of Abraham. Nor am I descended from Ishmael or from the sons of Keturah, but from the tribe of Benjamin.

This tribe was preferred to the others, because those who belonged to it did not fall into idolatry as frequently as the others did. And because I, being from the seed of Abraham, have not been rejected, it is evident from this that God has not rejected his people.

I call that people of God “his people” whom he foreknew, that is, whom he predestined for salvation. He certainly has not rejected them now, just as formerly, when Elijah supposed that everyone except himself had departed from the worship of God; yet many whom he did not know had been preserved by God. So now God has many chosen ones whom we do not know.

Certainly God has not rejected his people. For do you not know what Scripture says concerning Elijah, that is, where it speaks about Elijah—how that Elijah appeals to God against [or: on behalf of] Israel, that is, for the condemnation of the Jews—saying this in the Third Book of Kings:

[Col. 0093C] “Lord, Ahab and Jezebel have killed your prophets; they have also overthrown your altars” (III Kings XIX, 20).

For the faithful among Israel, because they did not dare to gather in Jerusalem for worship, had secretly built altars in caves and forests, and sacrificed there. The idolatrous Israelites had even destroyed these altars from their foundations, and killed those whom they found sacrificing.

“They have killed,” he says, “the other prophets; and I alone have been left in the worship of God, and now they seek my life, so that they may kill me along with the others.” Thus Elijah speaks.

But what does the divine response say to him? This, surely: “I have left,” that is, I have preserved for myself, seven thousand men who have not bent the knee before Baal, that is, who have not worshiped idols.

He does not say “seven thousand” as though that number were fixed among them, so that there were neither more nor fewer there. Rather, because the number seven signifies totality, a definite number is placed in an indefinite matter, so that it may be shown that the number of the elect is known to God, even though it is unknown to human beings.

What he previously said about Elijah he now applies to his own statements in this way: Since many faithful people were preserved in Elijah’s time, although Elijah himself did not know them, therefore—or, because of the similarity, it must be believed that things are so now also—by the mercy of God, just as they were then.

Or in this way: Just as they were unknown then, so now we are not able to distinguish the elect of God.

[Col. 0094A] “So,” he says, “now as formerly, also in this time of grace”—for which reason it is more necessary to believe that God has mercifully preserved elect persons for himself than formerly, when it was not yet the time of grace—“in this time of grace the remnant has been saved,” that is, those whom God left for himself and foreknew to be fit for salvation.

The remnant has been saved, and this according to God’s election, foreseen from eternity. This election was not because of merits, but was of grace, because he both chose by grace and saved by grace.

But if this election is by grace, it is now established that it is not from works, as though works had earned it. Otherwise, if they were chosen because of works, what is called grace would no longer be pure grace, but merit.

He introduces this appropriately concerning grace, so that those whom God has left for himself may not suppose that they were chosen because of merit, just as the wicked were rejected because they deserved evil. In saying this, he serves his purpose well.

He briefly gathers together here the summary of the authorities set forth above,

[Col. 0094B] in order to make clear what he intended by those authorities. He says:

“Because above I said, according to Isaiah, that the Jews do not believe but contradict. I also said, according to the same prophet, that a remnant of the Jews has been saved. What, then, shall we conclude from these statements, which seem to oppose one another?”

We shall say this: What Israel, that is, the Jewish people, sought to establish—namely, its own righteousness—and in that righteousness to be saved, it did not obtain. Israel as a whole did not obtain it, but the election obtained it, that is, those whom God chose from Israel obtained salvation.

But the rest, who were not chosen, not only did not obtain salvation; they were also hardened. And I say this as it is written in Isaiah, although in different words and with the same meaning.

God gave those Jews a spirit of compunction, namely,

[Col. 0094C] an evil spirit which would prick them and compel them to do evil. Or “spirit” means a disposition toward compunction, by which they were pricked through envy and anger against the faithful.

He also gave them eyes, that is, natural reasoning, but in such a way that they did not see, that is, so that they were deprived of the good use of reason.

He also gave them ears, that is, the same reason, as though they could not understand by themselves; they ought to have heard and learned. “They should not hear,” I say, “unto this present day.”

This present day was the prophet’s day; it is also the present day extending to the end of the world, like the saying in the bathhouses: “Today for a price, tomorrow without a price.”

David also says this concerning the hardening of the Jews: “Let their table,” that is, Scripture, by which they ought to have recognized the good, “become for them a snare,” that is, let them be ensnared in it each day by understanding it more badly;

[Col. 0094D] “let it also become for them a trap,” because they were taken captive by the Romans; “and let it become for them a stumbling-block.” He calls their misery, as they were scattered throughout the world, a stumbling-block. “And let it become for them a recompense” (Ps. LXVIII, 23).

Although he could call the captivity and stumbling-block a recompense, he understands “recompense” as eternal destruction, because it will endure.

Or the “table” means this: because they offered God gall and vinegar, whereas he wished to refresh himself with their conversion, let this become for them a snare; that is, let them therefore be ensnared by the Roman siege. The rest remains unchanged.

“And let their eyes,” that is, their reason, “be darkened so that they may not see” and understand the good.

“And bend their back,” that is, the same reason by which they ought to have raised themselves toward knowledge of God; bend it toward earthly things, casting them down more and more into punishments.

Because I said that the Jews were hardened, am I therefore saying that they stumbled in such a way as to fall uselessly and irrecoverably, so that their fall alone remains in them?

Here he intends to restrain the Gentiles, lest they prefer themselves to the Jews, although he called the Jews hardened, because their fall is recoverable and is greatly useful for the salvation of the Gentiles. He says:

“May it be far from us that, although they stumbled irrecoverably, they should therefore fall uselessly! Truly, their fall was not useless; rather, through their trespass—that is, through the trespass of the Jews—salvation has come to the Gentiles.”

For if the Jews had not rejected the word of God, the apostles would not have passed over to the Gentiles. Salvation came to the Gentiles so that the Gentiles might provoke them to jealousy, that is, imitate those Jews who were faithful and whose law is the foundation of the New Testament.

[Col. 0095B] Or understand it this way: Through the trespass of the Jews salvation came to the Gentiles, so that the Jews might emulate them, that is, imitate the Gentiles in the faith of Christ. According to this interpretation he proves that the fall of the Jews is recoverable.

For if their trespass, on account of which the Jews were rejected, is the wealth of the world, that is, was the reason why the Gentile world was enriched by the grace of God, how much more will their fullness, that is, the Jews saved in their fullness, be the wealth of the Gentiles?

By this the recoverability of the Jews’ fall is proved. For if God made the evil of the Jews useful to the Gentiles, much more must we believe that he will make their good far more useful to the Gentiles.

Their trespass is the wealth of the world, and their diminution—that is, the apostles, who, having been chosen from the Jews, diminished the Jewish people in respect of itself—is the wealth of the Gentiles. This diminution, I say, is the wealth

[Col. 0095C] of the Gentiles, for the apostles enriched the Gentiles with the word of God.

He does not say “fullness” because all Jews are to be saved, just as not the whole Gentile world has been chosen, but because many will be saved. Truly, the fullness of the Jews will be saved. For even in the time of their hardening some of them will be saved.

And this I say to you Gentiles: because, as long as I am the apostle of the Gentiles, to whom alone I was sent, I will nevertheless honor my ministry. Since my office requires only that I preach to the Gentiles, I will make it honorable beyond what I owe by laboring among the Jews.

I will honor it, I say, if somehow—since I would care nothing for whatever I might suffer—I provoke my flesh, that is, the Jews who are related to me according to the flesh,

[Col. 0095D] to jealousy, that is, to imitate me in faith, and so, by provoking them, save some of them, that is, so that God may save some of them through me.

He gives the reason why he must labor among them. He seems to have stated the same reason above, but there he added a specification of time, where he said “fullness,” which is understood to occur at the end of the world. Here, however, he introduces the matter for another purpose and without a specification of time, saying:

“Therefore I will labor to save some of them. For if their loss is the reconciliation of the world,” that is, if their hardening was the cause of the Gentile world being reconciled to God, “what,” or what kind of thing, “will their acceptance be at any time, except life from the dead?”

For if God reconciled the world to himself through their evil, much more must we believe that through their acceptance God will make many who are dead in sin live,

[Col. 0096A] when, provoked by their example, they will live in the faith of Christ.

He proves that their lineage does not prevent their acceptance, but only unbelief does, saying:

“I rightly speak of acceptance. For they can indeed merit acceptance. If the first-fruit is holy,” that is, if the apostles and others who were chosen from their people are holy, “then the lump,” that is, the fullness of the Jews, “can also be saved.”

If the Apostle’s lineage did no harm, neither should it harm the others. He calls them “first-fruit” by analogy: just as a small amount of food is tasted, by which it is proved whether the whole lump has been properly or badly prepared, so the apostles were called the first-fruit of the whole mass of the Jews. In them it was clear that their lineage did not hinder the Jews.

He proves the same thing again by another argument. Therefore it is also established that they can rightly be accepted. For their root, that is, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—if their root is holy, the branches can also be holy.

You will say to me again that those branches were broken off. But if some of the branches were broken from the root because of unbelief, while you, although you were a wild olive, that is, barren and alien from the holy root, have been grafted in among them in their place,

[Col. 0096B] you have also become a sharer in the root, that is, in the prophets, in whom faith was rooted. And you have become a sharer in the richness, that is, in the apostles, who possessed the richness of faith and the abundance of the Holy Spirit.

I speak of the root and the richness of the olive tree, that is, of the Jewish people, because the prophets and apostles were born among the Jews.

And if you, alien from the root, have been grafted in, do not boast against the branches that remain, nor prefer yourself to them,

[Col. 0096C] as though you were to be chosen because of merit, while they were to be rejected because of their lineage.

For if you boast improperly, it will be said to you: “Brother, it is not you who bear the root, but the root bears you.” For there is no example of goodness in you, whereas in the root—as in Abraham—there is an example of complete faith.

Because I have now taken away your reason for boasting against the branches that remain, you will therefore say to me, boasting against the branches that were broken off:

“Natural branches were broken off because of unbelief, so that I might be grafted in in their place.”

“This is right, and I grant it,” Paul says. “But they were broken off not because of their lineage, but because of unbelief. You, however, stand in their place solely because of faith.

“Therefore do not be high-minded,” that is, do not grow proud against those who were broken off, “but fear, lest you also be broken. There is indeed reason to fear, because

[Col. 0096D] if God did not spare the natural branches,” that is, the Jews, “perhaps he will not spare you either.” To you, who are not natural but have been grafted in by grace, he seems to owe less; the natural branch was rejected because of guilt.

Therefore observe the goodness and severity of God. Toward those who fell, that is, toward the Jews, observe severity. But toward you, who have been grafted in by mercy, observe the goodness of God.

I speak of goodness on this condition: if you remain in that goodness, cooperating with the grace you have received. Otherwise, if you do not remain, just as the Jew was cut off, so you too will be cut off.

And those Jews, if they do not remain in unbelief, will again be grafted in. And I rightly say “will be grafted in,” for God is able to graft them in again, just as he once grafted them in.

And truly God is able, for he gradually exercises the act of this power even now, by grafting in some, although they are few.

[Col. 0097A] This is what he says equivalently. God is certainly able to graft them in. For if you, a Gentile, were cut from a wild olive, that is, from an unfruitful root—a wild olive naturally belonging to you through long custom—and if you were grafted by grace into a good olive tree, and this contrary to nature, that is, contrary to a custom which through the passage of time had become nature, how much more will these Jews be grafted into their own olive tree, which belongs to them according to nature?

If you, who are not natural, were grafted in because of faith, there is no reason why the natural branches should not be grafted in for the same reason.

Above he proved that God had the power to graft them in by the exercise of his power, because they truly will be grafted in, saying:

“Truly the Jews will again be grafted in.”

[Col. 0097B] For even now, during their hardening, some of them are grafted in according to their portion; and at the end all Israel will be saved.

We understand that some are now being grafted in from what he says: “A hardening has happened in part to Israel.” For if it has happened in part and not in the whole, why should we not say that even now a part of them is being grafted in again?

And, brothers, I do not want you to be ignorant of this: namely, that hardening occurred in Israel so that the Gentiles might enter. This is indeed a mystery, because if the order of events is considered, the cause of the Jews’ hardening and the Gentiles’ illumination is nevertheless not understood.

For this reason I do not want you to be ignorant that this hardening and illumination are a mystery, lest you be wise in yourselves, that is, lest you be able to attribute this to your own wisdom, which is not sufficient to understand the mystery of this matter.

For if this cause were not hidden under a mystery

[Col. 0097C] but were disclosed to you, you would presumptuously attribute it to your own wisdom. But because that wisdom fails in knowledge of this mystery, it recognizes its weakness and marvels at the depth of the divine counsel.

This, I say, I do not want you to be ignorant of: namely, that hardening occurred in Israel. And it occurred only in part; for not all were hardened.

He says that it occurred with respect to human ignorance, which does not know the causes of this mystery, although in God’s providence there is nothing contingent and nothing accidental, since he knows all things and likewise the causes of all things.

Hardening certainly occurred in Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles entered. The word “until” is both temporal and causal. As though he were saying: “The Jews were hardened for this reason, so that the fullness of the Gentiles might enter, and for so long, until it entered.”

Nor is “fullness” to be understood as though every individual among the Gentiles would be saved, but in relation to the fact that previously scarcely any of the Gentiles were saved. It is said that in the time of grace there was a complete salvation of the Gentiles.

And thus, after the fullness of the Gentiles had entered, all Israel would be saved—not all Hebrews, but whoever might be Israel, that is, those who see God.

Nevertheless, some hold the opinion that all Jews will be saved at the end of the world.

He proves by the authority of Isaiah that the Jews are now saved in part and will be saved fully at the end, saying:

“Because I say that Israel will be saved, I do not assert this from myself, but as it is written.” It is written as follows (Isa. LIX, 20):

[Col. 0097D] “He will come from Zion,” that is, from the Jewish people, “who will deliver” with a certain violence and great labor, as happens now in the time of hardening, and who will also “turn away” with a certain ease, as will occur at the end of the world, when the Jews will hasten voluntarily toward salvation.

“He will deliver,” I say, “and turn away ungodliness from Jacob,” that is, from the Jewish people.

Here he does not call their customary idolatry “ungodliness,” but their denial of worship to the Son of God, which the Jews practiced; this he calls ungodliness. For after the time of grace had come, their religious observances were truly idolatry.

He has determined through whom salvation would come to the Jews. He also determines the time when this would occur, saying:

“And this covenant,” that is, this attested promise, “will be fulfilled for them by me,” then, when I take away their sins and justify them. This now occurs gradually, and in the last days fully.

Now some are indeed delivered from ungodliness and become beloved. But others

[Col. 0098B] who do not wish to be delivered are enemies. And this is according to the Gospel, that is, because they envy and disparage the Gospel through which the Gentiles are converted. They are indeed enemies, and this is for your sake, that is, for your benefit. For if the Jews had not rejected the word of God, the apostles would not have passed over to the Gentiles.

Some are enemies. Others, that is, the predestined, are beloved according to election, that is, not because of merit, but because God chose them by grace. They are also beloved for the sake of the fathers—not because of the merit of the fathers, but so that the promises made to their fathers might be fulfilled.

Truly they are beloved according to election and for the sake of the fathers. For the calling of God, that is, their election, and the gifts, that is, the fulfillment of the promises, are without repentance, that is, without change. For just as he promised and chose, so he will fulfill.

Or understand it this way: Truly they are beloved according to election. For the gifts of God, that is, the remission of sins, and the calling of God, that is, the instruction of the faithful whom, after justifying them in baptism, he instructs through teachers—these gifts and this calling of God are without any merit.

For the Jews are certainly chosen without the bodily affliction of penance, which would surpass the merit of penance before God if his gifts and calling were made according to merit.

For just as you Gentiles and certain Jews before the law once did not believe God, but now in the time of grace have obtained mercy, that is, salvation from mercy, and this because of the unbelief of the Jews, so also these Jews now have not believed, being envious of your mercy.

Because they did not receive the word of God,

[Col. 0098D] the apostle transferred it to the Gentiles. “Just as,” he says, “you once did not believe but have now obtained mercy, so these Jews also now have not believed, so that they too may obtain mercy.”

They did not believe because they were unwilling that you should be saved through the mercy of God, so that, just as you obtained mercy, they too might obtain mercy.

God had mercy on you who were unbelieving so that this might be attributed solely to his grace. In the same way he ordained that the Jews, overwhelmed in unbelief, should receive mercy, so that both Jew and Gentile might equally attribute everything to the grace of God and, recognizing their own weakness, might not grow proud.

For God, seeing that both the devil and humanity had fallen through pride, thereafter took great care to guard humanity against pride. Therefore he allowed both Jew and Gentile to be shaken by unbelief, so that the more they recognized their own weakness, the more they might submit themselves to the mercy of God.

Truly the unbelief of the Jews is the cause of their obtaining mercy.

For God has enclosed all people—now the Gentiles, now the Jews—in unbelief, so that, after making all unbelievers, he might fittingly have mercy on all.

For if either group or both groups had persisted in faith, they would certainly have attributed what belonged to the mercy of God to the merit of their own faith.

Do not investigate the reasons why now these and now those are enclosed in unbelief, but marvel with me at the counsel of God, saying:

“O the depth of the judgments of God, by which now the Jews are rejected and now the Gentiles grafted in!”

These judgments are indeed as deep as the wisdom and knowledge of God.

[Col. 0099B] Thus he says: “O the depth,” that is, the profundity, “of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God.”

The wisdom and knowledge of God are called rich because of their great abundance. They are called deep because of their unfathomable depth.

The wisdom of God is that by which he knows himself as great as he is. His knowledge is that by which he knows whatever belongs to creatures.

“O the depth of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments,” that is, no one is sufficient to comprehend the depth of the judgments which he considers within himself.

Someone might say: “As long as God’s judgments are being considered by God, it is true that they cannot be understood; but once they have been carried into effect, they are sufficiently comprehensible.” Paul responds to this: God’s judgments, while they are being considered by God, are no more capable of being comprehended than his ways, [Col. 0099C] that is, the operations of those judgments, are capable of being investigated. He proves this through Isaiah, having first said what precedes: “Truly, the wisdom and knowledge of God are unsearchable.” For who has known the mind of the Lord? Certainly no one has been able to know what God has conceived. And truly, both the judgments and the works of his judgments are unsearchable. For who has been his counselor (Isa. XL, 13), by whose advice he might order his affairs? Or whom would he admit into the counsel of his arrangement? Certainly no one. And just as he has disclosed his mind to no one, so he bestows every good thing out of mercy. For who has given anything to him? Someone might indeed, after receiving grace, merit something in some respect. But who gave to him first, before God gave grace, so that what he gave in this way would not be given to him freely by God, but repaid because he had earned it? These are Isaiah’s words; but the words that [Col. 0099D] follow are Paul’s. Truly, no one gave to him first, because “from him, and through him, and in him are all things.” Through the different prepositions—“from him,” “through him,” “in him”—he indicates the distinction of the persons of the Trinity. Through the same pronoun repeated three times, he indicates the identity of their substance, saying: “From him,” that is, from the Father, whose beginning is from no other; “and through him,” that is, through the Son, who has his beginning from the Father, and through whom the Father made all things; “and in him,” that is, in the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from the Father and the Son and is called the goodness of God, through which goodness created things subsist. “From him,” I say, “and through him, and in him are all things.” Therefore glory and thanksgiving are owed to him for all things, for all the good things that he mercifully gives. And may this glory be [Col. 0100A] “for ages,” that is, eternally. “Amen,” that is, “see that it may be so.”

He could have ended the Epistle here, for he had sufficiently restrained both peoples from becoming mutually proud of themselves and had set forth many arguments to that end. But because, once they had ceased proudly contending among themselves, they still needed reciprocal love, he therefore exhorts them, now calmed after their contention, to serve one another and to support one another, so that through this mutual service the bond of love might grow together and be strengthened in them.

## CHAPTER XII

> “I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercy of God, that you present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God, your reasonable service. And do not be conformed to this age, [Col. 0100B] but be transformed in the newness of your mind, so that you may approve what is the good, pleasing, and perfect will of God. For I say, through the grace that has been given to me, to everyone among you: do not think more highly than one ought to think, but think soberly, and according to each person as God has divided the measure of faith. For just as in one body we have many members, but all the members do not have the same function, so we, though many, are one body in Christ, and individually members of one another. Having gifts that differ according to the grace given to us: whether prophecy, according to the proportion of faith; or ministry, in serving; or the one who teaches, in teaching; the one who exhorts, in exhortation; the one who gives, [Col. 0100C] in simplicity; the one who presides, with diligence; the one who shows mercy, with cheerfulness. Let love be without pretence. ‘Hating evil, clinging to what is good (Amos V, 15).’ ‘Loving one another with brotherly affection, anticipating one another in honor (I Pet. II, 17).’ Not sluggish in diligence, fervent in spirit, serving the Lord; rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation, persevering in prayer; sharing in the needs of the saints 68; ‘pursuing hospitality (Hebr. XIII, 2).’ Bless those who persecute you; bless, and do not curse. Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep; having the same attitude toward one another; not setting your mind on high things, but associating with the humble. Do not be wise in your own estimation. Repaying no one evil for evil; [Col. 0100D] ‘providing what is good not only before God, but also before all people (II Cor. VIII, 21).’ ‘If it is possible, insofar as it depends on you, living at peace with all people (Hebr. XII, 14).’ Do not defend yourselves, beloved, but give place to wrath. For it is written: ‘Vengeance is mine, and I will repay, says the Lord (Deut. XXXII, 35; Hebr. X, 30).’ ‘But if your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink (Prov. XXV, 21).’ ‘For by doing this you will heap burning coals on his head.’ Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.”

## EXPOSITION
