The text is connected as follows: Since all things are from God, through God, and in God, therefore, brethren, I beseech you, [Col. 0101A] that is, I admonish you by everything sacred. I beseech you, certainly, by the mercy of God, that is, by the apostolate entrusted to me—not because I deserved it, but because it was given through mercy—that you present, that is, make ready, not only your souls but also your bodies. I say that you should present them as a sacrifice, that is, put to death with respect to the laying aside of impurities, and living with respect to the adoption of virtues. Nor should it be living only for a time, but holy, that is, holy and enduring in a life of virtue, and, in this life and holiness, not seeking worldly profit or praise, but pleasing God in all things.

And lest, because he had just said, “Present your bodies as a sacrifice,” someone should suppose that the body ought to be afflicted [Col. 0101B] without any moderation, the Apostle therefore adds: I speak of a sacrifice in such a way that your service may be reasonable, that is, so that you may fast and keep vigil with discernment, and so forth.

Someone might now say: “I am ready to present myself to God, so long as the world does not trouble me; but it is hard to resist the world when it compels me.” Paul responds: “Present yourselves as such, and do not be conformed,” that is, do not become conformed to this age by obeying the world in anything, whether it flatters or frightens you. Do not be conformed to the age, but be transformed through baptism—you who were previously deformed through Adam’s fault—or be transformed, that is, be renewed daily, since you have received a new form after being justified. “Be transformed,” I say, by advancing continually in the newness [Col. 0101C] of your mind, that is, be renewed by always doing what is good more and more, so that you may approve, that is, recognize with certainty, what the will of God is—a will, I say, that is good, that is, beneficial to those who do it; pleasing to those who experience it in action; and not pleasing in one respect while displeasing in another, but perfect in all things. I admonish you to present your bodies to God as a sacrifice, without any strict obligation of obedience.

But what follows I say through grace, that is, I command it by the authority of our apostolate. It must be considered why he merely admonishes them concerning what has been said above, while concerning what follows he prohibits them with full authority. For although a prelate may forbid subordinates, by the force of obedience, those things that generate offense, once they do not violate the law they should not be compelled in the same way to pursue what is better. Let them simply do what is good, but let them be admonished out of love. For if they were compelled to greater perfection by the strictness of obedience, the prelate would condemn them more by this than he would help them: if they did not fulfill the command, they would be condemned for disobedience. Therefore they should be drawn toward what is better by admonition rather than compulsion. Thus he says: Through the grace of the apostolate that has been given to me, I say and command everyone—and in such a way that I address each individual who is among you—the following: do not labor to think more highly than you ought to think, that is, more than sound faith requires. Nor do I altogether forbid you to think, but I want you to think soberly. Nor, again, do I want all of you to labor toward the same goal in wisdom, so that you would not be satisfied unless everyone [Col. 0102A] thought in the same way. Therefore let it be sufficient for each person to think according to what God has separately given to each: a measure of faith 69, that is, his gifts measured according to the manner and opportunity of your faith.

For this reason he restrains the Romans from excessive wisdom, because they were investigating the causes of God’s mysteries beyond measure. This fact—that God has not given the whole of wisdom to anyone, but has divided it among individuals in parts—is highly useful for this purpose: that they may serve one another, and that each may in turn accommodate himself to the other. For when one person is ignorant of what another knows, and conversely, each serves the other amid the diversity of the graces received. He then adds an appropriate likeness: just as different members in one body, having different functions [acts], serve one another—the foot serves the hand by carrying the hand to touch [Col. 0102B] what it wishes, and the hand serves the foot by putting a shoe on it—so we too are different members, forming one body, the Church. For just as different members in the same body are animated by the same soul, so all of us in the body of the Church are given life by the same Spirit.

The text is connected as follows: God has given his gifts separately. For just as in one body we indeed have many members, but not all the members have the same function, so we, though many, are one body under Christ the head; but individually we are members, in such a way that one is a member of another—that this eye, for example, should serve that foot, and so in the remaining cases. This mutual accommodation through service is especially suitable for preserving humility and unity.

We are individually members of one another; therefore—that is, because God wanted us to serve one another in this way—we possess different gifts: one prophecy, another teaching, and so forth. For if every individual possessed all the gifts, there would be no reason for one to serve another or to be necessary to another. Thus one would become proud over another, with nothing left by which one might accommodate himself to the other.

I say that we possess different gifts, and this according to grace, that is, through the Holy Spirit, which grace has been given to us by grace, not repaid according to merit. I speak of gifts such as prophecy: whether we have prophecy, that is, certain knowledge of future things or the revelation of any hidden matters—and I say that we possess prophecy according to the proportion of faith. He does not specify whose faith he means, whether ours or that of the hearers; it can be referred to either. According to the proportion of our faith, because God either reveals hidden matters or foretells future things according to what he sees to be appropriate and according to the measure of our faith; or according to the proportion of the faith of the hearers, because God gives preachers as much as he sees the faith and capacity of their hearers to require, so that they may reveal or announce things to them.

Therefore, possessing prophecy according to the proportion either of our own faith or of that of the hearers, let us be members of one another. Or if we possess a ministry of administering temporal goods to the brethren, we ought to be members of one another in serving, according to what has been entrusted to us. If there is one who teaches, “to teach” means that he possesses both the knowledge of teaching and the grace of speech; let the one who teaches, I say, be a member of the other in teaching. Let the one who exhorts be a member of the other in exhortation. To teach is to instruct one who knows less; but even one who knows less may exhort and encourage to good someone far wiser than himself. Thus any peasant could exhort a brave soldier to go to war, although the peasant himself might be ignorant of the art of that war.

Let the one who gives give in simplicity, that is, neither in hope of receiving in return nor out of love for earthly praise, but solely out of love for his neighbor. Let the one who presides preside with diligence, that is, let him care for his subordinates with complete vigilance. Let the one who has something to distribute give simply. But let the one who has nothing to give nevertheless show mercy in his heart; and let the one who shows mercy do so with cheerfulness, that is, not compelled by the commandment of the law, but fervent in the spirit of love.

And because he saw that, by serving one another in this way, they needed love in order to accommodate themselves to one another, he adds concerning it, saying that, so that by these means each may become a member of the other, love should be among them—and this without pretence, so that love may both show itself outwardly and burn inwardly.

Nor should you love in such a way as to cling to your neighbor’s evil; rather, hate his evil 70, but cling to your neighbor’s good, that is, cooperate with it. Nor is it enough for you to possess love among yourselves; you should also be loving toward brotherly affection, that is, toward the existence of good love among your brothers. I say “affection” that is mutually held, in the sense that one person’s love should work in the other; or it may be understood this way: just as I want you to love your neighbors, so I want you to be loving toward brotherly affection returned to you. If your neighbors return some works of love to you, receive them willingly. For there were some who did good to their neighbors but, lest they lose the reward of this merit, did not want to receive anything in return from their neighbors.

And so that your love may always increase, be those who anticipate one another in honor, that is, let each anticipate the other, so that whoever can rise more quickly may rise to the other and embrace his neighbor with every kind of love. And so that the good of brotherhood may grow among you, be not sluggish in diligence, so that with all vigilance one may be concerned to relieve the other’s need. Above he commanded this diligence to prelates; here he commends it to the brethren as a matter of mutual equality. If they do not have anything that they can diligently give, let them nevertheless be fervent in spirit, that is, let love burn in their hearts, even if they lack the ability to act.

And lest contemplatives should think it an evil to descend from the height of contemplation to attend to their neighbor’s needs, Paul says: “In all these things know that we are serving the Lord.” For God greatly loves this kind of service. And when, loving your neighbor in this way, you have devoted yourselves to caring for him, do not await a present reward, but rejoice in hope of the future recompense.

Having shown how they ought to conduct themselves toward the good, he determines how they should conduct themselves toward the wicked, saying: Lest you be frustrated in your future hope, be patient in tribulation, that is, patiently endure whatever you may have to suffer for Christ. But so that you may persevere in patience, devote yourselves to prayer, because, if prayer is useful in all things, it is much more necessary for bearing sufferings, which resist the flesh so greatly.

If tribulations do not press upon you so severely, at least share in the needs of the saints, so that you may make yourselves and your possessions common to the needs of those who suffer. And not only sharing, but also pursuing hospitality, so that you may receive without fear into your homes the saints whom the impious persecute and care for them.

You suffer those who trouble you; but not only this—also bless those who persecute you. Do not bless them once only, but continually; and do not bless them with regard to your own patience while, considering their cruelty, you curse them. Never wish to curse.

And so that your love may be complete, you ought to rejoice with those who rejoice; there is no doubt that this concerns spiritual goods, and, insofar as reason permits, temporal goods as well. You ought also to weep with those who weep, whether someone is afflicted out of repentance or is distressed by excessive bodily pain, although moderation must be maintained in that pain.

But so that you may truly mourn with those who mourn, be of the same feeling, so that you may be afflicted not only in your expression but inwardly in your heart. And let this be mutual, one person toward another. But so that you may feel the same thing, do not set your mind on high things, that is, do not become proud, but associate with the humble, that is, feel the same as those who are despised.

And so that you may know how to associate with the humble, do not be wise, that is, do not be concerned only with what is advantageous in your own judgment; but also provide for others. I mean: do not repay anyone evil for evil. “Be wise,” he says, not merely providing what is good before God, but also before all people, both the faithful and the unfaithful. For the testimony of our conscience alone is not sufficient unless the testimony of outsiders also agrees with it. Therefore what is worthy of praise both before God and before human beings must be done.

And so that your good works may please everyone, live at peace with all people, if it is possible, so that they too may wish to have peace with you. If they do not wish it, let that peace nevertheless be made insofar as it depends on you 71. Or understand it this way: live at peace with everyone, if it is possible, so that your flesh may love those who afflict it. This nevertheless depends on you, because if you wish, you can love everyone according to reason.

And so that you may preserve this peace intact, do not defend yourselves if they inflict evil upon you. I mean that if you do this, then you are beloved. Do not, I say, defend yourselves, but, by enduring with equanimity, give place to the wrath of your persecutors, so that they may rage as they wish.

Or understand it this way: by enduring the wicked, give place to the wrath of God. For God has determined to avenge himself upon the impious in such a way that they may exercise their iniquity according to their desire, so that no misery may be lacking from their condemnation. You must give place to wrath in either of these ways.

For it is written, with the Lord speaking through Solomon: “Reserve vengeance for me, and I will repay the impious” (Deut. XXXII, 35). This must be done because the Lord says so.

Nor should you merely refrain from defending yourselves against the impious; you should also love them and do good to them. He says this as follows (Prov. XXV, 21): “If your enemy is hungry, feed him. If he is thirsty, give him drink.” For by doing this you will heap burning coals on his head, that is, upon his mind: either the fervor of love, because, admiring your patience, he may love and imitate your goodness; or burning coals, that is, a fiery repentance, because, seeing your steadfastness, he may ardently repent so as to deserve to become like you.

And so that you may heap such coals upon the mind of this enemy, do not, through impatience, be overcome by his evil; rather, overcome the enemy’s evil by conquering it with the good of unfailing patience.

## CHAPTER XIII

> “Let every soul be subject to higher authorities. For there is no authority except from God (Wis. VI, 4). And those that exist have been ordained by God. Therefore whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance. [Col. 0105B] And those who resist acquire condemnation for themselves. For rulers are not a terror to good work but to evil. Do you wish not to fear authority? Do what is good, and you will have praise from it. For it is God’s minister to you for good. But if you do evil [wrong], be afraid. For it does not carry the sword without reason. For it is God’s minister, an avenger for wrath against the one who does evil. Therefore be subject, not only because of wrath, but also because of conscience. For this is why you also pay taxes. For they are God’s ministers, serving precisely in this. Therefore render to everyone what is owed: to whom tribute, tribute; to whom tax, tax; to whom fear, fear; to whom honor, honor (Matt. XXII, 21). Owe no one anything, except to love one another. For whoever loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law. For: ‘You shall not commit adultery. You shall not kill. You shall not steal. You shall not bear false witness. You shall not covet’ (Deut. V, 18); and if there is any other commandment, it is summed up in this word: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself’ (Lev. XIX, 18). Love of one’s neighbor does no evil (Matt. XXII, 39). Therefore love is the fullness of the law. And knowing this time—that it is already the hour for us to rise from sleep—for now our salvation is nearer than when we believed. The night has passed, and the day has drawn near. Therefore let us cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light, so that we may walk honorably as in the day. Not in revelries and drunkenness, [Col. 0105D] not in bedrooms and indecencies, not in contention and rivalry (Luke XXI, 34), but put on yourselves [put on] the Lord Jesus Christ. And do not make provision for the flesh in its desires (Gal. V, 16; I Pet. II, 11).”

## EXPOSITION

After teaching how subordinates ought to conduct themselves toward one another, he teaches them that they owe something greater to their superiors, even when those superiors are unbelievers, while preserving the integrity of faith. For there were some who believed that they no longer owed anything to believing masters because they were their brothers in faith. They entirely refused service to unbelieving masters, judging it absurd that one who was faithful should be subject to an unbeliever.

The text is connected as follows: The things stated above are owed mutually by subordinates to one another. But they owe something greater—namely, submission—to rulers. Therefore every soul should be subject to higher authorities, that is, to those exalted according to the will of God. By “soul,” which is a part of the human being, he designates the whole person, to show that rulers must be served not only with the body but also with the will 72.

Truly, every person ought to be subject to the authorities. For there is no authority, whether good or evil, except from God—not in such a way that God permits it unwillingly, because all that exists has been ordered by God, that is, arranged in an orderly manner, not falling through accidental chance.

Since authority and all things have been ordered by God, whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance, that is, God who orders this authority. Nor should you think such resistance trivial, because those who resist in this way acquire condemnation for themselves through that very resistance; that is, this one cause is sufficient for their condemnation.

The ruler must not be resisted. For rulers are not a terror to good work, that is, whoever acts well has no reason to fear the ruler. Even if the ruler is hostile to him because of his good work and persecutes him, he increases that person’s virtue and merit. Therefore the ruler is not a terror to one who acts well, but he is a terror to evil work: the one who acts badly may indeed fear the ruler.

Now, drawing a conclusion from what has been said, he says: The ruler is not to be feared by the good. If you likewise wish not to fear authority, do what is good, and by doing good you will have praise from it, whatever it may be, good or evil. For if it is good, it will praise you for your goodness; if it is evil, it will persecute you while you do good, [Col. 0106C] and you will be praised for the virtue of your patience.

Truly, you will have praise from it. For this same ruler is God’s minister to you for good, that is, for your benefit, if you do what is good. But if you do what is evil, fear him. He must indeed be feared by the one who does evil, for this judge does not carry the sword without reason.

Truly, he does not carry it without reason, for he is God’s minister: an avenger for him, that is, for the harm of the one who does evil. Say “an avenger for wrath,” that is, for carrying out God’s vengeance; or “an avenger for wrath,” that is, as a sign of future punishment, which they perceive through the temporal punishment that they see.

Since this ruler is God’s minister, therefore be subject in mind to this necessity, that is, to the ruler, to whom you will be subject whether you wish it or not, so that you may desire whatever is necessary. Be subject, I say, not only to avoid the ruler’s wrath, but also to preserve your conscience in purity, because unless you submit inwardly to the ruler, your conscience would be polluted by opposing God’s ordinance.

You ought indeed to be subject to the ruler. For this reason—that is, as a sign of this submission—you pay taxes and other obligations. I mean that you pay taxes precisely in this way, serving God through your service to the authorities. For the rulers themselves are God’s ministers, that is, they minister to God through the taxes they receive, which give them the strength and authority to carry out what God has ordained.

Or understand it this way: you pay taxes, and you do well, because these rulers are God’s ministers, serving—that is, whom God has appointed to serve him—in this very matter, in the taxes they receive from you. When God first established Saul as king, he said that he would no longer live from his own labor, but from the labors of his subjects. And because either you serve God precisely by paying taxes, or the rulers serve God precisely in this matter, therefore render to every ruler what is owed.

To whichever ruler you owe tribute, render tribute. To whichever you owe a tax, render the tax. “Tribute” refers to provisions that were paid at home; “tax” refers to what was always carried to the houses of the lords, as the census is today. To the one to whom you owe honor alone, offer honor. To the one to whom you owe fear, show fear and every reverence.

To gather everything briefly, I command universally: owe no one anything—neither tribute nor tax nor anything else—except that you love one another, because I want you always to be debtors of love, so that you never cease from love. Therefore I want you always to love one another, because whoever loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law (Exod. XX, 14).

And truly he has fulfilled the law: “You shall not commit adultery; you shall not kill; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness; you shall not covet” (Deut. V, 18). And if there is any other commandment in the law, it is summed up, that is, fulfilled, in this word: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Lev. XIX, 18). Truly, every commandment of the law is fulfilled in love of one’s neighbor.

For love of one’s neighbor does no evil (Matt. XXII, 39). Whoever loves his neighbor 73 [Col. 0107B] will not commit adultery with that person’s wife; he will not kill him; he will not steal his property, and so forth. And since love of one’s neighbor does no evil, love is therefore the fullness of the law, for whoever does not do evil has fulfilled the law (Gal. V, 14; Jas. II, 8).

We know, certainly, that love does no evil. But we know this about it as well: that it makes us rise from sleep and do what is good. Nevertheless, the force of the continuation and the main point of the sentence depend upon what follows: “Therefore let us cast off the works of darkness.” But he first sets forth certain reasons, from which he may more appropriately draw the conclusion, saying: We know that love does not do evil; and, knowing this also about love, we know that it is already the hour—as if he were saying, “It is the time”—but by “hour” he signifies that time in order to show that it is brief and quickly passing, and that, unless we repent within it, it is irrecoverable.

We know certainly that it is already the hour, that is, from the time we were justified through faith, for us to rise from sleep, that is, from the affliction of the body, which makes us sluggish in doing good. He says “rise” as though he meant that we should devote ourselves completely to good works.

For there are some who, after they have been justified, ought to burn with zeal in the labor of good works, but instead grow sluggish and neglectful, as though secure because of their justification and because they abstain from serious crimes.

Truly, we ought to rise from sleep, for we have believed, that is, received faith, and this faith has brought us near to salvation. But now, through the merit of the things we have done after receiving faith, our salvation is nearer than it was when we merely believed, that is, when grace alone was in us and there was still no merit.

Or understand it this way: our salvation is now nearer in time, that is, the day of our salvation is nearer than it was formerly, when we first believed. For each day we draw nearer and nearer to the future judgment, in which we shall be rewarded.

Truly, our salvation is now near. For the night, that is, the ignorance held in unbelief, has passed, and therefore we must take care lest we fall back into that night. “The night,” he says, “has passed,” but the day of our salvation has drawn near through the rays already mentioned, such as faith, hope, love, and the rest. The virtues possessed in the present are rays of future joy.

And since the night has ceased to exist and the day has drawn near, let us therefore cast off the works of darkness, that is, the works we performed while we were in ignorance; or the works of darkness, that is, works worthy of darkness and worthy not to be seen but always to be hidden.

“Let us cast off these works,” he says, “and let us put on the works of light,” that is, of true knowledge, or works worthy of light and manifestation. These works are weapons by which we defend our faith and overcome the vices that rise against us. Thus, clothed in the weapons of light, let us walk honorably, that is, advance from good to better, like those who are placed in the day, that is, in the knowledge of truth.

Those who are placed in the day ought to cast off the works of night and take up the weapons of light. I mean that we should walk in the day, not remaining in revelries, that is, in gatherings for public banquets, and not remaining in drunkenness by devoting ourselves to excessive drinking.

Nor should we remain in bedrooms, to which one goes because of excessive eating and drinking, where excessive rest is then taken. Nor should we remain in indecencies, that is, in the pleasure of lust; for a drunk person who goes down to his bed is consequently tormented by the torches of lust.

Nor should we remain in contention, for excess in drinking and lust frequently provokes quarrels. Nor should you be in rivalry, that is, in envy. Someone who does not dare to contend envies his neighbor for what he is able to do.

Therefore do not remain in these things, but put on the Lord Jesus Christ, that is, clothe your nakedness with faith in Christ and with the virtues built upon that faith. For because of sin the human being was cast naked from paradise (Gen. V, 16); but this nakedness must be covered with the adornment of faith and the other virtues.

And once you have put on the Lord Jesus Christ, do not make provision for the flesh, that is, do not care for the flesh. I do not forbid the care that necessity 74 demands; but do not make provision for the flesh in its desires, so as to pursue the desires of the flesh.

## CHAPTER XIV

> “Receive the one who is weak in faith, not for disputes about opinions. For one believes that he may eat all things; but the one who is weak should eat vegetables. Let the one who eats not despise the one who does not eat, and let the one who does not eat not judge the one who eats. For God has received him. Who are you to judge another’s servant (Jas. IV, 12)? He stands or falls before his own master. And he will stand, for God is able to make him stand. For one person judges one day above another, while another judges every day. [Col. 0109A] Let each person abound in his own understanding. The one who observes the day observes it for the Lord; and the one who eats eats for the Lord, for he gives thanks to God. And the one who does not eat does not eat for the Lord, and gives thanks to God. For none of us lives for himself, and none dies for himself. For whether we live, we live for the Lord; or whether we die, we die for the Lord. Therefore, whether we live or die, we are the Lord’s. For it was for this that Christ died and rose again: so that he might be Lord both of the living and of the dead. But you, why do you judge your brother (Jas. IV)? Or you, why do you despise your brother? For we shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ [God]. For it is written: ‘As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess to God’ (Isa. [Col. 0109B] XLV, 23; Phil. II, 10). Therefore each of us shall give an account of himself to God. Let us therefore no longer judge one another; but judge this rather: not to place a stumbling block or a scandal before your brother. I know and am confident in the Lord Jesus that nothing is common through him, except that to the one who considers something common to be common, to him it is common. For if your brother is distressed because of food, you are no longer walking according to love. Do not destroy with your food the one for whom Christ died. Therefore let our good not be blasphemed. For the kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit. For whoever serves Christ in this way is pleasing to God and approved by human beings. Therefore let us pursue the things that make for peace and the things that make for mutual edification. [Col. 0109C] Do not destroy the work of God for the sake of food. All things indeed are clean, but it is evil for the person who eats through giving offense. It is good neither to eat meat nor to drink wine nor to do anything by which your brother is offended, scandalized, or weakened. Keep the faith that you have within yourself before God. Blessed is the one who does not condemn himself in what he approves. But the one who discerns and nevertheless eats is condemned, because it is not from faith. Whatever is not from faith is sin.”

## EXPOSITION
Because the Romans were disputing among themselves in serious discord, saying that those who had been converted from Judaism considered certain foods unclean and believed that they ought not to use them, the Jews also slandered the Gentiles because they ate food sacrificed to idols, saying that they still clung to pagan rites. Conversely, the Gentiles, knowing that all foods were clean, used them, accusing the Jews of not possessing complete faith. Thus they were in conflict. The Apostle, wishing to recall them to peace, instructs them not to become stumbling-blocks to one another or to judge one another’s consciences.

That person caused a scandal who, in order to provoke his neighbor’s anger, ate what offended him—or caused him, while lacking faith, to eat what he believed unclean. To judge consciences meant that a Jew, believing certain things unclean, condemned a Gentile, saying that he therefore used food sacrificed to idols because he still clung to idols.

The text is connected as follows: “Do not make provision for the flesh,” but do this: “Receive the one who is weak in faith,” that is, the person who does not possess firm faith because he believes certain creatures of God to be unclean—and this was the Jew. You who are strong in faith must not scandalize him, but receive him. To receive him means to accommodate yourself to his weakness: to abstain from what he abstains from, and thus, by gradually attracting him, teach him the integrity of the faith until he reaches perfection. In this way he removed the scandal.

**75** “Receive the one who is weak, without engaging in disputes about his thoughts”—that is, about the thoughts of the weak person—so that you do not dispute by judging anyone’s conscience of heart, which is known to God alone and not to you.

The weak person truly ought to be received, for there is another who is perfect and able to receive and teach him. Another, however, is weak and needs to be received. He says this as follows: one person believes that he can eat everything, knowing that everything is clean; this person is strong in faith. Another is weak, believing that he cannot eat everything. Now let the one who is weak, unwilling to eat the meats of the Gentiles, eat—that is, let him be permitted to eat vegetables if he wishes to abstain. This is certainly good, and he must not be troubled.

Here he begins to restrain the Romans from judging consciences. Whoever does not wish to eat must be permitted to abstain. But the one who eats, knowing that all foods are clean, must not despise the one who does not eat—that is, the Gentile who eats must not scorn the abstaining Jew, accusing him of imperfection of faith. And the one who does not eat—that is, the Jew—must not judge, that is, must not condemn, the Gentile who eats.

One must not despise or judge the other, for God has received him—that is, both the one who eats and the one who does not eat. He has received them, I say, through the faith which they already have as servants. And since they have been received by God and made his servants, who are you to judge another’s servant? Even the laws of the world do not allow a servant to be judged by anyone other than his own master.

You certainly ought not to judge another’s servant, because that servant, by doing good, remains standing for his master—that is, for the judgment of his master—or, by sinning, falls from his master and is to be judged by him. Even if you plainly know that he has fallen, nevertheless do not judge him, because tomorrow, by repenting, he may become better than you; and a favorable expectation must always be maintained concerning everyone. For even if he has fallen, he may perhaps stand tomorrow—that is, appear strong in goodness. Indeed, you should suppose that he will stand, for God, whose servant he is, is able to make him stand again.

**[Col. 0110D]** Since it belongs to the Lord alone to judge his servant, you ought not to judge him—and, moreover, you ought not to condemn him for this reason. For what he does, he does on the basis of judgment and a sound intention of mind.

He says this as follows: one person—whether Jew or Gentile—judges one day in relation to another, that is, that one day should be observed as a day of abstinence and another should not. Another judges every day to be observed in abstinence. Whoever judges that abstinence should be practiced has a sound view and, therefore, ought to be praised rather than condemned. Whether this person or that, the one who judges that abstinence should be practiced has a sound view; and I wish each person to abound in his own understanding—that is, in what he wisely thinks and does—so that, if he abstains well now, he may later abstain better and pursue the other good things.

It should be noted that, if abstaining were evil, the Apostle would not wish them to abound in this understanding. Therefore I wish them to abound in this understanding because the one who observes a day—that is, observes a day in abstinence—observes it for the Lord, that is, for the Lord’s honor. And the one who eats likewise eats for the Lord, for while eating he gives thanks to God both for possessing a sound understanding concerning God’s creatures and because he is sustained by these benefits.

And the one who does not eat does not eat for the Lord—that is, he fasts for God’s honor—and again gives thanks to the Lord for the abstinence granted to him. This clearly shows that both understand correctly and that neither ought to be condemned for this.

Alternatively, the preceding passage may be read differently: “Do not judge another’s servant.” For one person—that is, a human being—judges one day in relation to another, that is, judges only the present. Another—that is, God—judges every day, concerning the future as well as the present. And since a human being judges the present soundly, I wish each person to abound in his own good understanding. The rest remains unchanged.

Both the one who eats and the one who abstains give thanks to God, and rightly. For none of us lives for himself—that is, no one ought to seek his own glory while he lives—and none of the righteous dies for himself in the same way. Indeed, we neither live nor die for ourselves, but for the Lord. For whether we live, we live for the Lord—that is, we live for the Lord’s honor—or whether we die, we die for the Lord. And because we live and die for the Lord, therefore we are the Lord’s, whether we live or die.

**76** Why, then, whoever you are, do not judge another’s servant? Truly we are the Lord’s, for Christ died and rose again for this purpose: that, through the merit of his death and the power of his resurrection, he might rule over the dead and the living. And since God rules over all, why do you, who abstain from something, judge your brother who eats? Or why do you, who eat, scorn your brother who fasts?

“Do not judge one another.” For we shall all stand before God’s tribunal, to be judged by God. He says “we shall stand,” by comparison with those awaiting the sentence of judgment. He says “tribunal,” as though God were about to sit in the manner of any powerful person presiding from a tribunal.

Indeed, we shall all stand, for it is written: “The Lord says through Isaiah: ‘As I live’” (Isaiah 45:23). Behold the mystery, so that what follows may be believed with complete certainty. When Isaiah said “As I live,” he understood this concerning Christ, who would at some time taste death, and whom the Father would appoint as judge of all when he rose again. Unbelievers considered this false when they saw him dead.

And in Christ’s voice he says: “I truly live.” This will be evident because “every knee shall bend to me,” that is, every creature shall be subjected to me in judgment; and then “every tongue,” that is, every conscience, “shall confess to the Lord.”

And since Scripture says “all,” namely, that all are to be judged by God, it follows that each of us will give an account to God for himself and not for his neighbor. And since we will give an account for ourselves, let us no longer judge one another—that is, let a subordinate not judge a subordinate. By saying “one another,” he indicates that he is not forbidding the judgment of superiors over subordinates, concerning whom they ought to judge; rather, he restrains subordinates alone, lest they presume to judge one another.

After sufficiently showing that they ought not to judge one another concerning consciences, he forbids them to cause scandals to their brothers, saying: “Do not judge one another, but judge this rather: that you do not place a stumbling-block or a scandal before your brother.”

He calls it a “stumbling-block” when someone causes a brother to sin by eating in disbelief, or when he eats with the intention that his brother, abhorring this conduct, will quarrel with and scorn the one who eats. He calls it a “scandal” when the brother is saddened because he sees someone eating what he believes unclean.

Someone who understood that everything ought to be used might object to Paul: “Perhaps you are weak with the Jew, since you say that I offend you when I use God’s creatures.” Paul replies: “Far be this from me, that I should accuse you; rather, believe soundly. For I know, and I am confident in the Lord Jesus”—that is, I testify to you through Jesus—“that nothing is common,” that is, unclean, “through him,” that is, through Christ, who freed us from the Law, under which many things were judged unclean. But since that Law has been abolished and freedom restored, they must no longer be called common—that is, unclean.

“I know certainly that nothing is common except to the one who considers something common.” To that person it is truly common—not because of the creature itself, but because of the weakness of his faith.

“Do not place a scandal before your brother.” For if your brother is saddened because of the food you eat, you are no longer walking according to charity, because you are not caring for your neighbor. To avoid offending your brother, do not destroy him by your food, which is something of little value, whether by causing him to eat with you in disbelief or by quarreling with him.

Do not, I say, neglect him for so trivial a matter—for him Christ died, that is, Christ loved him so greatly that he was willing to die for him. Since food is something trivial, but destroying one’s neighbor is serious, therefore let our neighbor not be destroyed because of food.

Our good—that is, the sound understanding we have concerning God’s creatures—must not be blasphemed. That is, it must not become an occasion for blasphemy, so that through this good we offend a simple brother.

He specifies the matters in which one’s neighbor must not be offended: namely, those that hinder salvation; and those in which one must not be followed: namely, those that take away the soul’s salvation. He says:

“You must not destroy your neighbor because of food, for the kingdom of God is not food and drink.” That is, the use of this food and drink does not grant the kingdom of God, nor does abstaining from them take it away. These things do not grant the kingdom of God. Rather, it is justice—that is, equity maintained toward one’s neighbor, so that we offend him in nothing—and peace, that is, concord arising from preserved equity.

And it is joy, by which one rejoices with another in love; this joy is nourished in peace by the Holy Spirit, that is, according to what the Holy Spirit directs. These, I say, are the kingdom of God, for in these things Christ is served.

Whoever serves Christ in these things—that is, in peace, justice, and joy—pleases God and is approved by human beings. That is, this service is judged acceptable by everyone; and it is not like your eating, by which your neighbor is offended.

Therefore he first said “serves Christ” and afterward “pleases God,” because Christ gave human beings the law of peace and justice; and they cannot please God except through Christ.

Since the service of peace pleases God and is approved by human beings, let us therefore pursue the things that belong to peace. Let us not quarrel with our neighbor, but let us also pursue the things that belong to edification—and this mutually, so that you build him up through your good and he builds you up through his.

What he calls “edification” here is the same as what he said above: “Receive the weak.” Let us pursue the things that belong to edification, not those that belong to destruction. He says this as follows:

“Do not, because of your food, by which your neighbor is offended, destroy the work of God in him,” that is, the faith that God has already worked in him. For if you compel him with excessive strictness, he will abandon the small amount of good that he possesses. Therefore his weakness should rather be nourished than forced by excessive harshness.

Peter observed this very suitably when he still permitted the Jews whom he had converted to the faith of Christ to be circumcised and to observe certain legal practices. If he had compelled them without restraint, they would more quickly have abandoned what they had received from him than ascended so suddenly to perfection. For he knew that they could and ought to be led gradually to perfection, as indeed happened.

Do not destroy your neighbor’s faith because of food—not because food is unclean, for “all things are indeed clean”—but it is evil for the person who eats by causing offense, intending to offend his neighbor.

And you must abstain not only from these things in order to avoid offending your neighbor, but also from every meat and every drink by which your brother is offended. He says this as follows:

“It is good for you not to eat meat, nor to drink wine, nor to do anything by which your brother is offended”—whether he is offended by sinning, or is offended by you and scandalized by becoming saddened, or is weakened in faith by hesitating somewhat. To avoid offending your neighbor, you must abstain from these things.

You indeed have sound faith within yourself; have it before God—that is, it is enough for God to understand your faith. You do not need to perform the work of your faith before the abstainer who is offended. Therefore keep this faith within yourself, not before the one who abstains.

For blessed is the person who does not judge—that is, does not condemn—himself in what he approves, that is, what he believes to be credibly true. But if you use foods that you are permitted to use in such a way as to offend your neighbor, then, in what you approve, you judge yourself guilty of the offense committed against your brother.

The person who does not condemn himself in what he approves is blessed. But the one who distinguishes foods from foods, saying that some are clean and others unclean, if he eats while in this uncertainty, is condemned—not because the food is unclean, but because he does not eat from faith, believing that it is clean. Truly, because it is not from faith, he is condemned; for everything that is not from faith is sin.

## CHAPTER XV

> “But we who are stronger ought to bear the weaknesses of the weak and not to please ourselves. Let each of you please his neighbor for good, for edification. For Christ did not please himself, but, as it is written: ‘The reproaches of those reproaching you fell upon me’ (Psalm 68:10). For whatever things were written were written for our instruction, so that through the patience and consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope. Now may the God of patience and consolation grant you to have the same understanding toward one another according to Jesus Christ, so that with one mind and one mouth you may honor God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore receive one another, as Christ also received you, to the honor of God.

> “For I say that Jesus Christ was a minister of the circumcision for the truth of God, to confirm the promises made to the fathers; but that the Gentiles should honor God for his mercy, as it is written: ‘Therefore I will confess to you among the Gentiles, O Lord, and I will sing to your name’ (2 Samuel 22:50). And again he says: ‘Rejoice, Gentiles, with his people’ (Psalm 17:5). And again: ‘Praise the Lord, all you Gentiles, and magnify him, all you peoples’ (Psalm 116:1). And again Isaiah says: ‘There shall be a root of Jesse, and he who rises to rule the Gentiles; in him the Gentiles shall hope’ (Isaiah 11:10).

> “Now may the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, so that you may abound in hope and in the power of the Holy Spirit. But I myself also am convinced about you, my brothers, that you yourselves are full of love, filled with all knowledge, so that you are able to admonish one another. Yet I have written to you more boldly, brothers, in part, as though reminding you, because of the grace given to me by God, that I should be a minister of Jesus Christ among the Gentiles, sanctifying the Gospel of God, so that the offering of the Gentiles may be acceptable and sanctified in the Holy Spirit.

> “Therefore I have glory in Christ Jesus before God. For I dare not speak of anything that Christ does not accomplish through me for the obedience of the Gentiles, by word and deed, through the power of signs and wonders, through the power of the Holy Spirit, so that from Jerusalem and its surrounding region as far as Illyricum I have fully preached the Gospel of Christ.

> “Thus I have preached this Gospel—not where Christ has been named, lest I build upon another’s foundation, but as it is written: ‘Those to whom nothing was announced about him shall see’ (Isaiah 52:15); and those who have not heard shall understand [alternative: ‘does not have “about him”’].

> “For this reason I was very often hindered from coming to you, and have been prevented until now. But now, having no further place in these regions, and having had the desire to come to you for many preceding years, when I begin to depart for Spain I hope to see you as I pass by, and to be sent on my way there by you, if I may first enjoy your company in part.

> “But now I shall depart for Jerusalem to minister to the saints. For Macedonia and Achaia have approved making some contribution [alternative: collection] for the poor among the saints who are in Jerusalem. For they approved it, and they are their debtors. For if the Gentiles have become participants in their spiritual things, they ought also to minister to them in material things.

> “Therefore, when I have completed this and delivered this fruit to them, I shall depart through you for Spain. And I know [alternative: knowing] that when I come to you, I shall come in the abundance of Christ’s blessing.

> “I beseech you, therefore, brothers, through our Lord Jesus Christ and through the love of the Holy Spirit, to assist me in your prayers to God, so that I may be delivered from the unbelievers who are in Judea, and so that the offering of my service may be acceptable to the saints in Jerusalem [alternative: Hierosolyma], and that I may come to you with joy through the will of God and be refreshed together with you.

> “Now may the God of peace be with you all. Amen.”

## EXPOSITION

Someone who possessed sound faith might say this in response: “If I am, as you yourself admit, of sound faith, believing that all things are clean, while this other person is weak in faith, the more just course seems to be for the weak person to follow the strong rather than for I, the strong, to follow his weakness.”

“It is not so,” Paul says. “Although you are of sound faith and he is of weak faith, nevertheless we who are stronger ought to support the weak and, by sharing to some extent in the weakness of the weak, nourish them toward what is better; and we ought not to please ourselves in everything.

“Let us not please ourselves, but let each person please his neighbor—and this for good, because it is for the neighbor’s edification, since the neighbor must be built up according to charity.

“Let us not please ourselves, for Christ, whom we ought to follow in all things, did not please himself,” that is, he did not consent to weak flesh. Rather, as it is written in the Psalm (68:10), Christ says to the Father: “The reproaches of those reproaching you fell upon me with a certain weight and pressed me down in death.”

It is as though he were saying: “Because I drove from the temple those who were selling and buying, by which they reproached you, they condemned me to death.”

Someone might say: “What difference does it make if it is written in this way?” It makes a great deal of difference, for whatever things were written concerning Christ were written for our instruction, so that through instruction we might have patience, and through patience possess the consolation of the Scriptures, which is greatly useful to those who suffer; and so that through patience and this consolation we might have hope of future recompense.

And because I see that your merits and my teaching are insufficient to obtain these things, I wish God, the giver of patience and consolation, to grant you the same understanding, so that you may all possess true knowledge—and this toward one another—so that what one person rightly understands, the other may also understand in turn.

I say “according to,” that is, through Jesus Christ, so that with one mind, one mouth, one will, and the same confession you may honor God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.

This does not mean that “God” and “Father” signify different beings; rather, in the same being he assigns different reasons, saying that he is to be honored both because he is God and because he is the Father of the Lord Jesus Christ, through whom every good thing comes to us.

“For this reason”—that is, so that you may have the same understanding and honor God with the same mind and confession—“receive one another,” so that each may receive the other with complete kindness, supporting one another for instruction.

“Receive one another,” I say, just as Christ, in his great exaltation, received you. He certainly received you for honor. The greatest honor was the forgiveness of sins; you will increase this honor by granting incorruption.

I speak of God’s honor, that is, honor given by God alone. For God gives, and will give, this honor, toward which our merits are inadequate.

He proves what he has said—“He received you Romans”—for he speaks first about Jews and Gentiles, and first about the Jews:

“Truly Christ received you, O Jews. For I say”—and one ought to believe me—“that Christ Jesus was a minister of the circumcision,” that is, of the Jews. Christ was indeed a minister and, as it were, the apostle of the Jews, to whom he preached in his own person.

This was not because of the Jews’ merit, but “for the truth of God,” that is, because of God’s promises. Therefore he was sent “to confirm”—that is, so that by the act itself the promises of the fathers might be confirmed—the promises made to their fathers.

Or it may be understood in this way: Christ was a minister “for the truth of God,” that is, for the fulfillment of God’s promises, and “to confirm through the truth of the deed the promises of the fathers,” that is, the promises made by the fathers, namely, the prophets, the fathers of the Jews. For God had made promises both through himself, as to Abraham, and more frequently through the prophets.

He proved that God had received the Jews; in proving this he introduced no authority, because it was virtually evident to everyone. He proves the same concerning the Gentiles by authorities, because some people had doubts about this, saying:

“Concerning the Jews I say this. I also say that the Gentiles ought to honor God for the mercy shown to them. And I say this as it is written in the Psalm (Psalm 17:50).”

The word “therefore” has force in the order of the Psalm: it is the Son’s voice to the Father: “O Lord Father, I will confess you among the Gentiles,” that is, I will cause the Gentiles to confess your name. “Nor will I merely confess; I will also sing and rejoice in your name.”

And again Scripture says through Isaiah: “You Gentiles, rejoice with his people” (Isaiah 11:10), that is, with the Jews, who were called God’s special people. Isaiah would invite the Gentiles to rejoice in vain unless he had foreseen their reception.

And again David speaks concerning the Gentiles: “All you Gentiles”—that is, each individual among the Gentiles—“praise the Lord” (Psalm 116:1). “Nor merely praise him, but also show him to be great by good works, all you peoples,” who are found among the individual nations.

And again Isaiah says concerning the same matter: “Jesse, the father of David, shall be the root of his origin,” from which Christ will be born; “he shall rise to rule the Gentiles, and in that king the Gentiles shall hope” (Isaiah 11:10).

Christ rose because he alone among all was free from sin. He rose higher on the third day when, having resumed incorruption, God the Father gave all judgment to this king, his Son.

I urge you to receive one another. But because you cannot accomplish this either by your own strength or by my teaching, I pray that the God of hope—in whom I hope, and in whom you too ought to hope—may fill you with all joy, that is, with the perfection of love.

And, so that you may be worthy to possess this joy, may he fill you with peace, that is, with complete concord. I speak of peace restored through believing, that is, through one and the same integrity of faith, so that the same faith may produce peace in you.

May peace nourish joy. May he fill you, I say, with faith, peace, and joy, so that you may abound in hope—that is, the better you act, the more firmly and abundantly you may hope. And, so that your hope may not be disturbed, may you abound in the power of the Holy Spirit, that is, may the Holy Spirit supply you with abundant strength to persevere in goodness.

Here Paul begins to come to an agreement with certain Romans, praising them for the integrity of their faith, the fullness of their love, and the possession of all knowledge. Yet he touches them somewhat because, although they were wise and therefore able, and although they loved their erring brothers, they had not corrected their brothers’ imperfection; and this was also necessary because Paul, occupied with others, could not devote sufficient time to correcting the Romans.

It is as though he were saying: “Your conscience is certain concerning the integrity of their faith; likewise I myself am certain, my brothers, concerning you, that you yourselves are full of faith and love. You do not quarrel with your brothers, and you are filled with all knowledge, so that you can admonish one another”—that is, instruct the weak faith of others.

And although you are full of love and knowledge, nevertheless I have written to you, brothers, somewhat boldly—that is, with a little boldness—in part, according to that aspect in which, by acting somewhat imperfectly, you have not restrained the quarrels among your brothers.

I wrote not to teach you, since I know that you are wise, but as though recalling to your memory things that I believe you know but do not remember sufficiently.

They might say: “Since you admit that we are perfect, why do you rebuke us?” Paul boldly replies: “Because of the grace”—that is, because of the dignity of the apostolate—“which was given to me by God.” This ministry of mine compels me to admonish you in this way.

Grace was given to me for this purpose: that I might be a minister of Jesus Christ among the Gentiles, that is, that through my ministry I might subject the Gentiles to Christ, sanctifying the Gospel of God. I sanctify it when I do the same thing that I preach.

I sanctify it for this purpose: so that the offering of the Gentiles may be acceptable to God—that is, so that, as one offering the Gentiles, I may be acceptable to God; or so that the Gentiles who are offered may be acceptable to God.

I speak of an offering that is acceptable and sanctified in the Holy Spirit, because through the laying on of hands I give the Holy Spirit, which false teachers cannot do.

And because I sanctify the Gospel, therefore I have glory—that is, I glory greatly—in my apostleship. But this glory is not to be referred to me, but to God, and this in Christ Jesus, that is, through Christ, who consecrated me as an apostle.

Therefore I have glory because I do not dare to speak of anything that Christ does not accomplish through me, his minister, as the false teachers do, who say that they have done things they never did.

I do not speak of what God does not accomplish through me, but I speak of what Christ accomplishes through me “for the obedience of the Gentiles”—that is, either so that I myself may obey him among the Gentiles, or so that the Gentiles may obey him through me.

He accomplishes this through me by word, for Christ speaks in me. He also accomplishes it by deeds, that is, in my works, because what I preach well, I also practice.

He accomplishes it through the power of signs and wonders, for performing these he gives me power. He calls healings “signs,” such as the removal of diseases, and “wonders,” such as raising the dead. These wonders are performed through the power of the Holy Spirit.

Or Christ accomplishes this through me in the power of the Holy Spirit, whom he distributes through my hands.

Thus, I say, he acts so that I have “filled,” that is, fully preached, the Gospel of Christ, beginning from Jerusalem and extending as far as the sea of Illyricum—not by a direct route, but around, by visiting the individual places.

Thus I preached the Gospel, not in Judea, where Christ had been named, lest I build upon another’s foundation, that is, upon the faith preached by the other apostles.

Yet this was not the reason why he did not preach there, but because God directed him to the Gentiles.

“I say, lest I build in this way, but as it is written in Isaiah: ‘The Gentiles to whom nothing has been announced about him shall see’ (Isaiah 52:15) God, ‘and those who have not even heard shall understand.’”

For this reason, because I was preaching to the uneducated and, as it were, stony people, I was very greatly hindered from coming to you, O Romans; for it was necessary that you, who were sound, should build up the weak.

Formerly I was hindered, but now I have no further place in these regions, because everyone has been converted. Yet I have had the desire to come to you for many preceding years, by which you can note how much diligence I have toward you.

When I begin to depart for Spain, I hope to see you as I pass through your midst. For there is no reason for me to remain with you, since you are faithful. I say that I shall see you and be sent on my way there by you, if I may first enjoy your company for a while—that is, if I may remain with you for some time—because I have no further place here and desire to pass on to you.

Therefore I shall first accomplish what must be done: I shall go to Jerusalem to minister to the saints.

When Peter and those who were with him gave Paul and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship (Galatians 2:9), they charged them to make collections in the churches of the Gentiles, from which they might minister to the saints in Jerusalem, from whom the unbelievers had taken everything.

I shall go to minister to the saints, since Macedonia and Achaia—that is, their churches—have judged it good to make some collection to be brought to the poor among the saints who are in Jerusalem.

They approved this not because we compelled them, but because it pleased them. And even if it had not pleased them, they are nevertheless their debtors, and it would have been necessary for them to do it as a debt.

They truly are their debtors. For if the Gentiles have become participants in their spiritual goods, because those saints ministered spiritual things to the Gentiles, the Gentiles ought also to minister material things to the saints.

Since this is what remains for me first to do, therefore, when I have completed it and delivered it—that is, returned this fruit to them under seal—I shall depart for Spain, passing through your midst.

I know that, driven by a long-standing desire, I shall come to you in the abundance of Christ’s blessing—that is, I shall make Christ’s blessing abound in you, imparting to you whatever measure of God’s grace is lacking.

And since I am now about to go to Jerusalem, I beseech you, brothers, through our Lord Jesus Christ, to assist me in prayers poured out for me to God, so that through this assistance I may be delivered from the unbelievers who are in Judea, and so that the offering of my service—that is, the offering in which I serve—may be acceptable to the saints in Jerusalem, presented to them without diminution.

When this has been successfully completed, may I come to you with joy through the will of God—that is, as God has disposed—and may I be refreshed together with you, completing in you whatever I find to be incomplete.

But because neither you nor I are sufficient for this, may the God of peace make peace with all of you. Amen.

## CHAPTER XVI

> “I commend to you Phoebe, our sister, who is in the ministry of the Church at Cenchreae, so that you may receive her in the Lord in a manner worthy of the saints [alternative: sufficiently], and assist her in whatever matter she may need you. For she herself also assisted many, and me personally.
>
> “Greet Prisca and Aquila, my helpers in Christ Jesus, who for my life laid down their own necks; to whom not only I give thanks, but also all the churches of the Gentiles; and greet their household church.
>
> **[Col. 0119B]** “Greet Epaenetus, beloved by me, who is the firstfruits of the Church of Asia in Christ Jesus. Greet Mary, who labored greatly among you. Greet Andronicus and Junia, my kinsmen and fellow prisoners, who are notable among the apostles and who were in Christ before me. Greet Ampliatus, my beloved in the Lord. Greet Urbanus, our helper in Christ Jesus, and Stachys, my beloved. Greet Apelles, approved in Christ. Greet those who are of Aristobulus’s household. Greet Herodion, my kinsman. Greet those who are of Narcissus’s household who are in the Lord. Greet Tryphaena and Tryphosa, who labor in the Lord. Greet Persis, the beloved, who labored greatly in the Lord. Greet Rufus, chosen in the Lord, and his mother and mine. Greet Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, Hermas, and the brothers who are with them. Greet Philologus and Julia, Nereus and his sister, Olympias, and all the saints who are with them.
>
> “Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the churches of Christ greet you.
>
> “Now I urge you, brothers, to watch out for those who create dissensions and stumbling-blocks contrary to the teaching that you learned, and avoid them. For such persons do not serve Christ our Lord, but their own belly; and through smooth speech and blessings they deceive the hearts of the innocent.
>
> “Your obedience has been reported everywhere. Therefore I rejoice in you, but I want you to be wise in what is good and simple in what is evil. Now may the God of peace crush Satan [alternative: Satan] under your feet swiftly. May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.
>
> “Timothy, my helper [alternative: my brother], greets you, and Luke [alternative: Lucius], Jason, and Sosipater, my kinsmen. I, Tertius, who wrote this Epistle, greet you in the Lord. Gaius, my host and the host of the whole Church, greets you. Erastus, the city treasurer, greets you, as does Quartus, the brother.
>
> “May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen.
>
> “Now to him who is able to strengthen you according to my Gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery kept silent through eternal times, but now manifested through the writings of the prophets, according to the command of the eternal God, made known among all the Gentiles for the obedience of faith—to the only wise God, through Jesus Christ, to whom be honor and glory for ever and ever. Amen.”

## EXPOSITION
Having finished the Epistle, he inserts his greetings, saying:

“With those whom I commended above, I also commend to you Phoebe our sister, who is in the ministry of the Church”—that is, who supplies what is necessary to a certain Church—which he established at Cenchreae. This, I say, is what I commend concerning her: that you receive her in the Lord worthily of the saints—that is, either in the manner in which it befits you, as saints, to receive her, or in the manner in which a holy woman ought to be received—and that you assist her in whatever matter she may require your help. It is said that through this Phoebe, who was going to Rome, the Apostle sent his Epistle. He therefore commends her so that the Romans, having heard her authority, might submit to her in everything that she would rightly advise. She ought to be assisted, for she herself assisted many saints, and ministered even to me.

Greet also Prisca and Aquila, my fellow-workers in Christ Jesus. Or: greet them in Christ, since both of them placed their necks on behalf of my life. They helped Paul in many dangers and imprisonments. I alone do not give them thanks, but all the Churches of the Gentiles also, who would not now have their apostle if not for their assistance.

Greet also the household Church—that is, their household.

Greet Epaenetus, beloved by me, who is the firstfruits of Asia in Christ. He was the first from Asia to receive the faith from Paul.

Greet also Mary, who labored greatly among you by recalling you from error. This Mary is said to have informed the Apostle of the disagreement among the Romans; on that occasion he wrote this Epistle to them. She had returned to Rome, and therefore he says that she had labored.

Greet Andronicus and Junia, my kinsmen among the Jewish people, and my fellow prisoners—those who were often imprisoned with me—who are distinguished among the apostles. They are believed to have been among the seventy-two. They were in Christ before me; they were converted to the faith before Paul.

Greet Apelles, approved in Christ.

Greet those who belong to the household of Aristobulus—that is, his household, since he is faithful. Do not greet the master, for he is guilty of unbelief.

Greet those who belong to the household of Narcissus, not all of them, but those who are in the faith in the Lord. For some members of his household cling to their master in unbelief.

Greet Rufus, chosen in the Lord, and his mother, who is also mine: his according to the flesh, mine according to her service to me.

And, to conclude, greet one another on my behalf with a holy kiss—that is, let each one say this to the other—or, on Paul’s behalf, let them kiss one another with a kiss of peace in his place. As I do, so all the Churches of Christ greet you.

Paul therefore greeted by name those persons whom he had approved, so that, when he was now urging the Romans to withdraw from false teachers, they might not perhaps doubt any of those whom he had greeted.

But I ask you, brothers, who have been greeted, to watch carefully—that is, to guard yourselves shrewdly—from those who create dissensions and also stumbling-blocks, throwing people headlong into sin; those who teach what is contrary to the doctrine that you learned from me. And, so that you may watch yourselves, withdraw completely and separate yourselves from them, because such people do not serve Christ our Lord, but their own belly. For they seek what is theirs, not what belongs to Jesus Christ. Such people deceive the hearts of the innocent—that is, of the simple—by smooth words, that is, by seductive words, and by feigned blessings.

You ought to withdraw from them, for your obedience and its good reputation have been spread everywhere, and therefore I rejoice in you. Nevertheless, I want you to be wise and shrewd in what is good, and simple in what is evil, so that you may be like children in malice.

Although I have called you wise, nevertheless, since your wisdom has little power by itself, I pray that the God of peace may crush Satan and his members, prostrate beneath your feet, and may do so quickly.

After saying this, Paul greets them, saying: “May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.”

“Timothy, my helper, greets you, and Luke and Jason and Sosipater”—or, “the father of Sosias”—“who are my kinsmen.”

“I, Tertius, who wrote the Epistle in the Lord, greet you.” This Tertius was the Apostle’s secretary, who inserted his own greeting among those of the others.

Paul returns to his own greetings and says:

“Gaius, my host, and the whole Church”—that is, his household—“greet you.”

“Erastus, the city treasurer”—that is, the city’s financial administrator—“greets you, and Quartus, the brother.”

All of them say: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all.”

For all your good works, let honor and glory be given to God.

I speak of him who is able to strengthen you according to my Gospel—that is, as I preach it to you—and according to the preaching of Jesus Christ, whose preaching is the same as my Gospel. I speak of the Gospel and preaching that have been given according to the revelation of the mystery.

He calls the salvation of human beings a “mystery”: it had always been hidden before Christ’s coming, but through him it was revealed. I speak of the mystery that had been silent through eternal ages before Christ, but which has now, in the time of grace, been disclosed through the writings of the prophets, now finally understood through Christ.

I say that it was disclosed according to the command of the eternal God, to whom this had been openly known from eternity. It was disclosed for the obedience of faith among all the nations—that is, so that all nations might obey the faith.

If you wish to ask why it was formerly silent and has now been revealed, you inquire in vain. I speak of the mystery known to the only wise God, who alone has always known its reason.

I say that it was disclosed through Jesus Christ. To him—namely, to Christ, who is powerful—be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

# [On the First Epistle to the Corinthians]

[Column 0121]

## Prologue to the First Epistle to the Corinthians

[Column 0121C]

The First Epistle to the Corinthians embraces many different matters. The Apostle learned some of them from the report of the brothers; others were indicated in letters from the Corinthians themselves. Some he orders or corrects out of the concern proper to his office, and by various remedies he treats those suffering from different weaknesses.

First, he treats among them the fault of dissension, which many false apostles introduced by splitting the unity of the Church, so that they might make people followers of their own names. The Apostle reproaches them for this in these words:

“Now I mean this: each of you says, ‘I belong to Paul,’ ‘I to Apollos,’ ‘I to Cephas,’ ‘I to Christ’” (1 Cor. 1:12).

He says that he is mentioning these names so that they may be much more ashamed of doing the same thing under the names of false apostles; even if it were done under the name of Paul or Peter, it would still be displeasing.

A second matter is introduced concerning a man who, forgetting the reverence due to his father, was not ashamed to take his stepmother as his wife. Although the Apostle called this deed fornication, he condemned it so severely that, as punishment for the act, he judged the perpetrator of such a crime liable to be handed over to the devil.

The third matter concerns judgments and lawsuits.

Fourth, the rights of marriage are discussed.

Fifth, the counsel of virginity is joined to this as something closely related.

Sixth, the question of permission regarding foods is debated.

Seventh and eighth, instructions are given concerning men cutting their hair, women veiling their heads, and participation in the sacraments.

Ninth, the rivalry arising from the diversity of spiritual gifts is restrained by the example of the members and the body.

Tenth, the hope of the resurrection is confirmed by many arguments and reasons.

Finally, under the heading of charity, care and edification for the collection made to meet the needs of the saints is imposed upon the worshiping community.

A few matters are interspersed among these which either, as some think, depend upon what precedes, or, although they concern distinct actions, are nevertheless minor.

## Argument

[Column 0121]

The Corinthians are Achaeans. They likewise heard the word of truth from the Apostle, but were led astray in many ways by false apostles. Some were drawn in by the verbose eloquence of philosophy; others by the sect of the Jewish Law. The Apostle recalls them to true faith and evangelical wisdom, writing to them from Ephesus through Timothy, his disciple.

## Bruno’s Argument on the Same Epistle

[Column 0121]

[Column 0121D]

Paul had preached to the Corinthians and converted them to the faith. He remained among them for a year and a half, as we believe. He saw that the Corinthians needed advice for a long time and in many matters, because they adhered too strongly to the flesh.

While Paul was present, they adhered simply to his instructions. He had preached to them as to simple people, knowing that the mysteries of the faith, if revealed to them, would harm their carnality more than they would benefit it. Therefore he judged it better to nourish their simplicity in simple matters than to corrupt it through the profundity of God’s mysteries—matters over which they would be more likely to hesitate than to believe.

But after Paul had returned from Corinth, false teachers entered among them and overturned the good simplicity of the earlier teaching. Since their doctrine dealt with worldly arguments, which entirely contradicted spiritual teaching, it began to attract the Corinthians more strongly and to persuade them, because they adhered more to the world than to God. By the craft of human reasoning, it destroyed in them what Paul had built, as they followed the simplicity of faith.

The Corinthians, turning aside from Paul’s instruction, were thrown into many errors. They came to think that the merits of those who baptized benefited the baptized in proportion to their greatness, and harmed them if they were lesser. In this way they attributed to a human being what belonged to God alone—namely, the forgiveness of sins.

As a result, one who had been baptized by a more worthy person judged himself more worthy than someone who had been baptized by a less worthy person. In this, they were certainly dishonoring God. They also erred in that they distinguished the Lord’s body only slightly from other foods.

They erred again because men prayed with covered heads while women prayed with uncovered heads.

There was also another error: they did not believe in the future resurrection, as Paul had preached it.

They were also accused because fornication was heard to occur among them, fornication that even the Gentiles would not tolerate. One of them had taken his stepmother as his wife. They had neither corrected him by admonishing him nor excluded such a criminal from participation in the Church; rather, by their unlawful tolerance, they seemed to consent to this incest.

When Paul learned of these errors, the brothers who were with Chloe—whose place lay within the archbishopric of the Corinthians—sent Sosthenes to him with a letter. Paul wrote this Epistle to them through Sosthenes. In it he deals with the erring Corinthians, enumerating their errors and refuting each of them with appropriate arguments, with the intention of drawing them away from these vices.

# The First Epistle to the Corinthians

[Column 0123]

## Chapter One

[Column 0123B]

“Paul, called an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and Sosthenes, the brother, to the Church of God that is at Corinth, to those sanctified in Christ Jesus, called saints, together with all who invoke the name of our Lord Jesus Christ in every place belonging to them and to us.

“Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

“I give thanks to my God always for you, because of the grace of God that has been given to you in Christ Jesus, because in everything you have been enriched in him, in every word and in all knowledge, just as the testimony of Christ has been confirmed among you, so that you lack nothing in any grace, as you await the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ. He will also confirm you to the end, without accusation, on the day of the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.

“‘God is faithful, through whom you were called’ (1 Thess. 5:24) into the fellowship of his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord.

“Now I beseech you, brothers, through the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you all say the same thing and that there be no schisms among you, but that you be perfected in the same understanding and in the same knowledge.

“For it has been reported to me concerning you, my brothers, by those who belong to Chloe, that there are contentions among you. I mean this: each of you says, ‘I belong to Paul’; ‘I to Apollos’ (Acts 18:25); ‘I to Cephas’; ‘I to Christ.’

“Has Christ been divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?

“I give thanks to my God that I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius, so that no one may say that you were baptized in my name. I also baptized the household of Stephanas; beyond that, I do not know whether I baptized anyone else.

“For Christ did not send me to baptize, but to evangelize—not in the wisdom of speech, so that the cross of Christ might not be emptied.
