“For the word of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to those who are being saved—that is, to us—it is the power of God.

“For it is written: ‘I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and I will reject the prudence of the prudent’ (Isa. 29:14).

“Where is the wise man? Where is the scribe? Where is the investigator of this age? Has God not made the wisdom of this world foolish?

“For since the world did not know God through wisdom in the wisdom of God, it pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe.

“For Jews ask for signs, and Greeks seek wisdom. But we preach Christ crucified: to the Jews, indeed, a stumbling-block; to the Gentiles, foolishness; but to those who are called, Jews and Greeks alike, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God.

“For what is foolish of God is wiser than human beings, and what is weak of God is stronger than human beings.

“See, brothers, your calling: there are not many wise according to the flesh, not many powerful, not many noble. But God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong; and God chose the ignoble things of the world, the despised things, and the things that are not, to destroy the things that are, so that no flesh might glory in his presence.

“But from him you are in Christ Jesus, who was made wisdom for us from God, and righteousness, sanctification, and redemption, so that, as it is written, ‘Let the one who glories glory in the Lord’ (2 Cor. 10:17; Jer. 9:22).”

## Exposition

Paul, and so forth. Since authority was necessary to suppress the pride of the Corinthians, he introduces the name of authority, saying: “Paul”—a name certainly known everywhere.

Paul, I say, called by God, that is, constituted an apostle by divine calling. Or, “called by all,” because everyone already knows him to be an apostle.

“Apostle,” I say, that is, an envoy of Christ Jesus—not presumptuously thrusting himself forward like a false apostle, but an envoy of Christ Jesus; and not sent by Christ to carry out an opportunity for exercising wrath, as Saul was, but sent “through the will,” that is, through the good pleasure, of God.

Paul, certainly, and with him Sosthenes the brother—not because Sosthenes wrote anything in this Epistle, but so that Paul might thereby show that he knew all their errors. Since Sosthenes was one of them and lived among them, he had reported them to Paul. He also includes him to show that Sosthenes had reported their errors not out of ill will toward them, but from a desire for their correction.

Paul, I say, and Sosthenes the brother, write to the Church of God that is at Corinth. “Church,” I say, “to those sanctified,” that is, justified from sins in baptism. And all this is “in Christ Jesus,” not through the merit of those who baptized them.

Because “church” is a collective noun, it is entirely appropriate that it be joined with a plural, so that we say, “to the Church, sanctified ones.” They are sanctified not only through Christ, but also “called saints” through his grace—that is, called for the purpose of being sanctified. In this way it is recognized that both their sanctification and their calling to sanctification come from God, and every merit of the baptized person and of the one who baptized him is excluded.

Paul writes to the Church of the Corinthians together with all—that is, with all the Churches—held in the same errors.

“All,” I say, “who invoke the name of our Lord Jesus Christ,” confessing that the one whom they invoke is the only one who justifies.

I do not mean all the Churches throughout the world, but those “in every place belonging to the Corinthians,” that is, every metropolitan church subject to the Corinthians and fallen into the same error. These Churches belong to the Corinthians in respect of their location, but they are also placed above them in our ordering, because I subject them to the Corinthians in such a way that I nevertheless always apply my care to them, just as I do to the Corinthians.

Paul says this so that the Corinthians might not say: “You have authority to judge only us; we, however, have authority over our subjects.” The same rule is still observed: although the supreme pontiff has subjected Churches to other Churches, he nevertheless examines the error of all, but does so juridically through the metropolitans.

Paul and Sosthenes write this to the Corinthians: “Grace and peace be to you.”

Since some among the Corinthians had preserved the grace given to them in baptism intact by doing good, they did not need the remission that they had already received and firmly retained. Since, however, others among them had destroyed the grace they had received by falling into error, and needed renewed remission, this grace must be wished for differently according to the distinction between the perfect and the imperfect.

Thus we should say: To you who have sinned again, may there be a second grace—that is, may your sins be forgiven again. But to you who have not nullified the justification you received by sinning, may there be grace—that is, may the steadfast preservation of the justification you received remain with you.

The same applies to peace: for sinners, let there be the restoration of peace of mind; for those who do not sin, let tranquility of mind continue.

Grace and peace, I say, be to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Believe that all justification comes from him alone, with every merit of the baptizer excluded.

Because some Corinthians persevered in Paul’s teaching and did not share in the errors of the others, he first speaks to these separately. When they hear that their goodness has such authority with the Apostle, they will be encouraged more strongly toward goodness. He does this also so that they may devote themselves more earnestly to correcting their erring brothers, and so that the erring may obey them without resistance when they hear that the Apostle regards their perfection so highly.

[Column 0126B]

Therefore he says:

“I give thanks to my God”—that is, the God whom I make my own, not by detracting from him, as the false teachers do when they say that the merit of the baptizer harms or benefits the baptized.

“I give thanks to my God always for you,” that is, in all my prayer.

I give thanks, I say, “in grace,” that is, in consideration of God’s grace persevering in you. This grace was given to you “in Christ Jesus,” that is, through Christ Jesus, who supplies this grace to the person reconciled to God.

For this I give thanks: because—that is, because—you have been made rich in everything, since you possess abundantly both each grace individually and all graces together.

You have been made rich “in him,” that is, through Christ, whose mercy alone gives grace.

“In everything,” I say, namely, in every word—that is, in all teaching, whether spiritual, intermediate, or simple—and also rich in all knowledge, whether literal, moral, or allegorical.

You are rich in everything, just as the testimony of Christ—that is, the teaching concerning Christ attested to you through the Scriptures—has been confirmed among you. This testimony, I say, has been confirmed, that is, remains firm among you.

For in the same manner in which you have firmly retained faith in Christ, God has enriched you with his graces. Your confirmation was both the cause and the likeness of this enrichment.

Thus the testimony of Christ has been confirmed among you, so that you lack nothing in any grace—that is, so that you retain every grace as firmly as the strength with which it was delivered to you.

I speak of you who await the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ. Because of the security you possess from the justification you have preserved, you confidently await the day of your dissolution, when he will be revealed to you.

While we live, our soul, enclosed by the flesh, cannot contemplate the divine essence. It will contemplate it more fully when it has been freed from the burden of the flesh. The person who acts rightly awaits this revelation with confidence; the person who acts wrongly seems rather to flee from it than to await it.

You are awaiting Christ, who, just as he confirmed you in the past, will also continue to confirm you to the end—that is, until the day of your dissolution.

I do not say that he will confirm you in such a way that you will be able to refrain from venial sins; rather, he will confirm you “without accusation,” that is, made immune from capital sins.

“To the end,” I say, namely, until the day of the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, who comes to every just person at his dissolution, receiving that person’s soul to be transferred elsewhere.

He specified “without accusation” in this way so that, if they happened to see these people fall into venial sins, they would not mock them and say: “Now the righteousness of those whom Paul esteemed so highly has become apparent.”

He will truly confirm them thereafter, for he promised this, saying: “Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20).

God, who promised this, is faithful and cannot lie. Therefore I trust that he will confirm you. I trust this also because it is through him that you were called.

If, while you were in sin, he called you through mercy, it must certainly be believed that, now that you have been justified and are earning merit, he will confirm you thereafter.

You were called through him into fellowship with his Son—that is, so that, according to your measure, you might remain in righteousness with his Son.

I do not mean an adopted son, but Jesus Christ, God’s own and consubstantial Son.

After strengthening those who were perfect in their goodness, he turns his speech to those who had sinned in the matters mentioned above, saying:

“I praise you who are perfect for your steadfastness; but I beseech you who are in error”—that is, I solemnly adjure you with every strictness—“through the name of our Lord Jesus Christ,” although I still call you brothers, even though you have fallen into error.

He calls them brothers so that, if he did not call them brothers, they would not despair because of the enormity of their sin.

I beseech you, I say, “that you all say the same thing,” that is, that you all confess that God alone can forgive sins.

And by saying this, let there be no schisms among you—that is, no divisions of unbelief. Let there be no schisms; rather, be perfect in the same understanding—that is, in the same will—and in the same knowledge, so that you may both will and know the same thing.

For there are people who will the same thing but do not know the same thing. There are others whose will is different, although their knowledge is the same.

For this reason I beseech you in this way: it has been reported to me by letter concerning you, my brothers—by which he repeats what he said above.

It was reported by those who belong to Chloe, because—that is, because—there are contentions among you: one person contending against another.

Chloe is the name of a place within the archbishopric of the Corinthians, from which this contention had been reported to him through Sosthenes.

He mentions the name here so that the Corinthians would not wish to conceal their error, knowing that Paul had learned of it from the same people who lived among them.

I have learned not only that you contend, but also the words of the contention itself.

This is what I mean: each of you speaks in such a way as to prefer himself to the others on the basis of his baptizer.

One says: “I belong to Paul”—as though saying, “I am separated from him by a much greater righteousness, since my baptizer was superior to his.”

Another says: “I belong to Apollos,” who was the archbishop of the Corinthians.

Another says: “I belong to Cephas,” that is, to Peter.

He does not introduce these names because they gloried in those men, since they had not even seen Peter. Rather, he does so because, if he had inserted the names of the false teachers in whom they gloried, they would have said: “Paul is envious of these men; he does not want us to glory in their names, but would think it good if we gloried in his own name and in the names of his associates.”

To remove this objection, Paul inserted his own name and Peter’s, showing that he did not want them to glory in his name. If they should not glory in the name of Paul, they should glory even less in false teachers.

The unbelieving say: “I belong to Paul; I to Cephas.” But the faithful person says: “I belong to Christ, whose grace alone justifies.”

Since one person says that he belongs to Paul and another to someone else, is Christ therefore divided? Are there now many Christs rather than one? Each person makes his own baptizer into Christ when he attributes to him the forgiveness of sins, which belongs to Christ alone.

Or it may be understood this way: Christ is divided because he distributes the gifts of his grace unequally, justifying less through one person and more through another.

Or, because you err by speaking wrongly in this way, Christ has been divided and separated from you. You divide Christ by making each person his own Christ.

Or you believe that Christ gives grace unequally. But was Paul—whom some of you make your Christ, or on whose merit you rely when you believe that Christ gives more to one person than to another—was Paul crucified for you?

You cannot deny that you were redeemed through Christ, whom Paul did not touch.

Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?

If you had carefully considered the words of baptism, in which you confess God alone, you would understand that all justification comes from God.

Since this good of baptism has become harmful to you in your error, I give thanks to my God that I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius. For this reason I do not wish to have baptized anyone, lest someone say that you were baptized in my name.

I baptized the household—that is, the family—of Stephanas together with Crispus and Gaius. I remember these people, but I do not know whether I perhaps baptized anyone else.

I baptized so few because Christ did not send me to baptize. In this he greatly humbles the ministry of baptizing, when he says that he was not sent for this purpose—something that even any unbeliever can do if necessity demands it.

In this matter, however, the Corinthians were continually preferring one another. He says here that the sacrament of the Church was granted even to an unbeliever in a time of necessity because it is something without which no one can be saved.

But the other sacraments were entrusted only to ministers for this reason: although they contribute to salvation, they are not things without which a person cannot be saved. For the faith of baptism alone, if it is preserved intact, is sufficient for salvation.

Here he concludes his discussion of baptism and begins to speak of his preaching, saying:

“Christ did not send me to baptize, but to evangelize.”

He sent me to preach, certainly, but not “in the wisdom of speech,” that is, not in the verbose wisdom of the world. He did this so that the cross of Christ might not be emptied.

If I followed the arguments of human wisdom—which entirely deny that an immortal being could die and that one who had died could live again—it would be proved completely that Christ had not tasted death on the cross, and thus the price of the whole salvation would be destroyed.

This is why I was not sent in the verbose wisdom of the world, according to whose arguments the cross of Christ can easily be emptied.

If I followed the wisdom of the world, the cross of Christ would indeed be emptied.

For the word—that is, the preaching—of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, that is, to the wise of the world. They are called “those who are perishing” because their wisdom will soon perish and be destroyed, or because they will perish and be condemned on account of this wisdom.

The word of the cross is foolishness to the wise of this world, because human reasoning compels no one to believe that Christ, who was immortal by nature, could die and, having died, live again.

To those who are perishing it is foolishness; but to those who are being saved—that is, to us, who withdraw from verbose wisdom—the word of the cross is the power of God.

For when we consider that the ancient enemy, whose strength had prevailed over the whole human race, was conquered through such weakness as death, we marvel all the more at the power of God: through weakness he destroyed strength.

If he had extinguished a lesser power through manifest strength, God would truly not have sent me in the wisdom of speech.

Thus it is written in Obadiah: “I will destroy,” says the Lord, “the wisdom of the wise” (Obad. 1:8; Isa. 29:14)—either because I will destroy it or because I will condemn those who cling to human wisdom.

I will destroy not only wisdom but also prudence—that is, the foresight by which they cleverly know how to fortify their arguments so that they cannot be broken by any attack.

Some possess the wisdom of an art but do not know how to fortify themselves sufficiently against the quibbles of an objector. I will reject that prudence, because I will not take any of the prudent men of this world into the ministry of my preaching.

Or this may be joined to the place where he says, “those who are perishing.” They are truly perishing, for it is written: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise.” And such prudent people have truly been rejected.

These are the Apostle’s words.

For where is the wise man—that is, the logician who trusts in his argument? And where is the scribe—that is, the ethical teacher who deals with morals? And where is the investigator of this age—that is, the natural philosopher who investigates the natures of all things?

If that logician says, “If she gave birth, she had intercourse with a man,” he is lying, because Mary conceived from the Holy Spirit without intercourse with a man.

If the ethical teacher should teach about morals and the worship of idols, he is rejected, because new morals and a new worship have been introduced.

If the natural philosopher says that it is contrary to nature for a virgin to give birth or for a dead person to live, he is guilty of falsehood.

Since the wise man, the scribe, and the natural philosopher are all rejected, is it not openly evident from this that God made—that is, proved to be—foolish the wisdom of this world?

Therefore God rejects the wisdom of this world. For this pleased God; and when you hear that this pleased God, do not seek the reason for it.

It pleased God through the foolishness of preaching—that is, through both the foolish thing preached and the foolish preachers—to save those who believe in him.

It pleased him to save believers through foolishness because the world—that is, worldly people—did not know God through carnal wisdom.

If some philosophers understood that there is one God who created everything, nevertheless they did not know this in the wisdom of God—that is, they did not understand God’s plan, the order by which he arranged to save fallen humanity through the incarnation of the Word, and so forth.

Or it may be understood in this way: the world did not know God through its own wisdom. This was in the wisdom of God—that is, it pleased God’s wisdom not to mix its own wisdom with worldly wisdom.

He truly saved believers through foolishness, for both the thing preached was foolish and the preachers were foolish.

The thing preached was truly foolish. For the Jews, who had already come to know God through signs, as in Egypt, nevertheless ask for further signs to establish that what is preached about Christ is true.

The Greeks—that is, the Gentiles who do not know God—seek wisdom. They wish what is said about Christ to be proved to them through worldly arguments.

But we, in order to satisfy the Jews, preach Christ as the power of God, because the Jews seek the power of miracles.

To the Greeks, who seek wisdom, we preach that Christ is the wisdom of God.

For those Jews and Greeks who are chosen, both power and wisdom are found in Christ; but for those who are rejected, he is a stumbling-block and foolishness.

This is why we said that believers are saved through a foolish thing.

Now let us explain the text.

God truly saves believers through foolishness, because the Jews ask for signs, having become accustomed to knowing God through miracles. The Greeks seek worldly wisdom because they understand nothing else.

We, however, who are foolish, preach a foolish thing—namely, Christ crucified.

To the Jews he is a stumbling-block, because they are reproached for having crucified their own king. To the Gentiles he is foolishness, because they cannot understand how we can say that the one whom we call God was himself dead.

To rejected Jews and Greeks alike he is a stumbling-block and foolishness. But to those Jews and Greeks who are called—that is, chosen by God—we preach Christ as the power of God, since God could perform no greater miracle than to destroy death through death.

We also preach Christ as the wisdom of God, because no greater wisdom can be found than to destroy pride through humility and strength through weakness.

Christ truly is the wisdom of God. For what belongs to God and is foolish according to human judgment is wiser than human beings. Or it is wiser because human beings cannot grasp such wisdom or act with such wisdom.

Christ truly is the power of God. For what belongs to God and is weak according to the judgment of the flesh is stronger than human beings. Or this is because they do not know how to understand this power. Or because, with all their strength, they can accomplish nothing.

Alternatively, the preceding text may be joined in this way:

The world did not know God through wisdom because the Jews ask for signs and the Greeks for wisdom. We, however, preach Christ crucified: to the Jews, not a sign but a stumbling-block; to the Greeks, or Gentiles, not wisdom but foolishness.

And because the world understands neither power nor wisdom in the cross of Christ, it did not know God. This is the end of the sentence.

Yet although the cross of Christ is a stumbling-block and foolishness to the rejected Jews and Greeks, to those Jews and Greeks who are called, Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God.

The following text is not changed. He has proved in part that salvation comes through foolishness: believers would be saved through a foolish thing preached. He now proves the other part—namely, that God saved believers through foolish preachers—saying:

“God truly saved believers through foolishness.”

See, then, your calling—that is, your callers, through whom you were called to the faith. Consider this, I say, about them: “not many wise,” and so forth. But God chose the foolish things in the ministry of your calling. Or it may be joined to what immediately precedes it in this way: Truly, that thing of God which is foolish and weak is wiser and stronger than human beings. For now look at your callers; you will find them foolish and weak. According to this [Col. 0131B] connection, what follows—that what is foolish and weak of God is wiser and stronger than human beings—refers to proving that the preachers were foolish, just as in the preceding passage he intended to show that the thing preached was foolish. In what follows, too, the effect of this foolishness and lack of wisdom is indicated.

“Consider,” I say, “your calling,” that is, through whom you were called, brothers: among them there are not many wise according to the flesh, that is, according to fleshly wisdom; not many powerful according to the flesh; not many noble according to the nobility of the flesh. The saints say that Paul used the words “not many” because he himself was accomplished in secular learning, wealthy in earthly possessions, and distinguished by Roman ancestry.

Your callers, to be sure, were neither wise [Col. 0131C] nor noble; but God chose the foolish things of the world—that is, those whom the world considers foolish—so that through these God might confound the wise, that is, make the wise of the world ashamed when they see that they cannot withstand the arguments of God’s foolish preachers. God also chose the weak things of the world, namely those who possessed no power in the world, so that through these weak things he might confound the strong, that is, make the powerful of the world ashamed. And he chose the base things of the world, that is, those who could not glory in their ancestry; and the despised things, that is, those in whom there was no reverence arising from their persons. These God chose—and, to enumerate each kind, the things that are not, that is, those who seemed to the world to be nothing—so that through the things that are not he might destroy the things that are, that is, those that appear to be the good things of the world.

And God did all this [Col. 0131D] for this reason: so that no flesh might glory, that is, so that it might be fitting for all flesh not to glory in his presence. For if the preachers considered their own lowliness—or if the nations converted by them understood it—they would attribute nothing to themselves, but refer everything to the grace of God.

Or it may be understood this way (the wording is uncertain): so that the sense may not be distorted thus, “let no flesh glory in the sight of God,” that is, while considering God’s power and its own weakness. Neither the preacher nor his hearers should attribute anything to the teachers, but everything to the grace of God.

Yet although the preachers were foolish and weak, you nevertheless lacked nothing because of this: for you were made faithful in Christ Jesus. And although such great weakness of the preachers is apparent, you still lack nothing. From this it is clear that everything comes from God himself and nothing from the merit of the teachers.

Here the effect of foolishness and weakness is considered most excellently. You, I say, are in Christ Jesus, who was made for us wisdom from God, because God, instructing us through Christ, made us wise in the ministries of God. And in order to make us wise, he was made our righteousness, causing us to live in the righteousness of the virtues. But so that we might live in righteousness, he was made our sanctification. For he sanctified us by remitting sins; and in order to sanctify us, he was made our redemption, that is, he gave the price of his blood by which he might redeem us, so that, having redeemed us, he might sanctify us; having sanctified us, establish us in the righteousness of the virtues; and, for those remaining in righteousness, grant wisdom.

All these things he became for us [Col. 0132B] so that whoever glories might glory not in himself or in the teachers, but in God. In this sense it is written in Jeremiah:

“Let the one who glories glory in this: to understand and know me, that I am the Lord” (Jer. IX, 24).

## CHAPTER II

“And I, when I came to you, brothers, did not come with loftiness of speech or wisdom, proclaiming to you the testimony of Christ. For I judged myself not to know anything among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified. And I was with you in weakness and fear and much trembling; and my speech and my preaching were not in persuasive words of human wisdom, but in the demonstration of the Spirit [Col. 0132C] and of power, so that your faith might not be in the wisdom of human beings but in the power of God.

“Yet we speak wisdom among the perfect: not, however, the wisdom of this age, nor of the rulers of this age, who are being destroyed; but we speak God’s wisdom in a mystery, the wisdom that has been hidden, which God predestined before the ages for our glory. None of the rulers of this age knew it; for if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.

“But, as it is written: ‘What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, what God has prepared for those who love him’ (Isa. LXIV, 4). But God has revealed it to us through his Spirit. For the Spirit searches all things, even the deep things of God. For who among human beings knows the things of a human being except the spirit of that human being, which is in him? So also no one has known the things of God except the Spirit of God.

“Now we have received not the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God, so that we may know the things given to us by God. These things we also speak, not in words taught by human wisdom, but in the Spirit’s teaching, comparing spiritual things with spiritual things.

“But the animal person does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God; for they are foolishness to him, and he cannot understand them, because they are examined spiritually. But the spiritual person judges all things, while he himself is judged by no one, as it is written: ‘For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who will instruct him?’ (Isa. XL, 13; Wis. IX, 13; Rom. XI, 34.) But we have the mind ‘of Christ.’”

## EXPOSITION

I said that your callers were foolish and despised; and just as they were, so I myself, when I came to you, brothers, did not come through loftiness of speech—that is, striving to speak artfully and to use grandiloquent words—although I did not refrain from this on account of ignorance; nor did I come through loftiness of wisdom, in order to preach worldly wisdom to you.

For there are some who possess elevated speech but do not possess an equal mastery of the art; and again, there are others who know the rules of the art but do not have sufficient skill in expression. I, I say, did not come through loftiness of speech or wisdom, proclaiming Christ to you; and I did this by testimony, because whatever I said about Christ I showed to have been testified beforehand in the prophets.

Truly I did not preach in loftiness of speech or wisdom. For although I knew many things, I judged myself not to know anything among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified according to the foolishness of the Gentiles and the weakness of the Jews. I did not set myself above the other preachers on account of the worldly wisdom I possessed; rather, I preached the same foolishness—that is, the cross of Christ—as they did.

I did not come through loftiness of speech or wisdom, nor through the dignity of a person; but I was with you in weakness, that is, in much tribulation, and because of this weakness I was in fear of God and bodily trembling. And although I suffered all these things, [Col. 0133C] nevertheless my speech, which I used in private, and my preaching, delivered in public, were not in persuasive words of human wisdom—that is, I did not devote myself merely to speaking appropriately in order to persuade. Rather, my preaching was in the demonstration of the Spirit, that is, so that it might be proved that the Holy Spirit spoke through me; and in the demonstration of power, that is, of God’s miracles.

Therefore I relied only upon the Spirit and power of God, so that your faith, which I ministered to you, might not be in human wisdom but might stand in the power of God.

And although I judged myself to know nothing among you, nevertheless we speak wisdom—but among the perfect. Since you were imperfect, I could not speak it to you. Yet although we did not speak it to you, we do possess wisdom, not carnal but spiritual, which is far more worthy than the carnal wisdom to which you cling.

He expresses this as follows: “We do indeed possess wisdom, but not the wisdom of this age,” that is, of carnal people, “nor that of the rulers of this age,” that is, either philosophers or evil spirits who rule the people of the world. These rulers are being destroyed, both according to their teaching and because they are condemned on account of their false teaching.

We do not speak the wisdom of this age; rather, we speak the wisdom of God existing in a mystery. Here he calls God’s wisdom that plan by which God determined to save the human race through the incarnation of the Son. We speak this wisdom, hidden in a mystery—not in such a way that everyone can perceive it, as with the mystery of baptism and certain other matters, but as something that has been hidden and revealed through the Holy Spirit to no one except a few.

This wisdom God predestined before the ages, that is, from eternity he ordained that it should come to pass in this way, for our glory—that is, for the glory of all the faithful—so that through it we might all possess eternal glory.

Or it may mean “for our glory,” that is, for the glory of the preachers who minister this wisdom. It was fitting that we who minister to others should understand this wisdom more abundantly than others, since none of the rulers of this age—that is, philosophers or demons—knew this wisdom.

Truly, the rulers did not know it. For if they had known it, they would never have crucified Christ: the devils, who put this into Judas’s heart so that he might betray him, or into the hearts of the Jews so that they might crucify Jesus. They would certainly never have crucified him if, through this crucifixion, they had known him to be the Lord of glory. If they had known, they would not have crucified him.

But they did not know, as it is written in Isaiah. This, I say, is written there: “What eye has not seen” (Isa. LXIV, 4). The passage found in Paul’s text, rather than in Isaiah, is understood in this way: the eye—that is, the sensory person—did not see it by itself; and the ear—that is, the same sensory person, who could not understand it by himself—did not hear it from another teacher. Nor did it enter into the heart, that is, into the very reason of the human being, namely, one who is wise in a human manner. For if a person understood it, then what he previously considered worthless because he did not understand it would enter into him, and he would consider it great.

These things, I say, neither eye saw nor ear heard—things that God prepared for those who love him: that is, how great and how worthy they are.

Or the passage may be read according to the sense suggested by the noun. It is written here that what the eye has not seen, and so forth, is what God prepared for those who love him. This is a sufficiently good relation of the clauses.

Someone might say: If this did not enter into the human heart, how then do you know it? Paul answers: No one of this age knew it; but God revealed it through his Spirit to us who have already stripped off the world.

For the Spirit of God taught this, in which human wisdom is completely deficient. We must certainly believe that God revealed it to us through his Spirit. For the Spirit of God searches all things—not because he himself possesses something unknown, so that he would need to search for it, but because he opens to us everything that must be investigated with the greatest searching. He also opens to us the deep things of God, that is, the higher and more hidden matters of God’s essence, such as how the Trinity remains in unity and unity in the Trinity.

He proves what he has said from the lesser and from the analogous case, as follows: Truly, the Spirit of God alone can search the things that belong to God. For the human spirit knows only the things that are within that human being. And if the spirit of a human being alone knows the things belonging to that human being, it follows by analogy and from the greater case that the Spirit of God alone searches the things belonging to God.

He puts it this way: “The Spirit,” I say, “searches the deep things of God.” For who among human beings knows the things belonging to another human being except the spirit of that same human being, which is in him? No one, certainly.

And since no one knows the things belonging to a human being except the spirit of that same person, so, by a similar reasoning, no one has known the things belonging to God except the Spirit of God, who revealed God’s wisdom to us.

He had indeed said that God revealed it to him through the Spirit; but he had not yet said that they had received that Spirit. He adds: God not only revealed this to us through his Spirit, but we have also received a spirit not of this world, but the Spirit who is from God, so that through that Spirit we may know the mysteries of God, which have been given to us by God through grace.

These mysteries we also speak and make known, not clinging to words taught by human wisdom, but speaking them in the Spirit’s teaching, that is, according to what the Holy Spirit dictates and teaches us. Nor do we speak these mysteries to just anyone, but only to spiritual people, “comparing,” I say, that is, weighing spiritual things by an equal standard against spiritual people. If we have a spiritual hearer, we give spiritual things to him; if he is carnal, we remain silent.

The spiritual person perceives spiritual things; but the animal person, who lives by sensuality alone, like another animal and not by reason, does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God. He does not perceive them because they are foolishness to him: what the Spirit teaches he considers foolish, clinging as he does to carnality. And because they are foolishness to him, he cannot understand the things of the Spirit of God.

The animal person cannot understand because he is examined—that is, his animality is tested and he is convicted of his impiety—spiritually, that is, through those spiritual things granted to him. For God gives certain graces to certain people, knowing with certainty that they will not cooperate with grace; but he does this so that the just condemnation of the impious may be manifest.

Or the expression may be impersonal: “he is examined.” The animal person does not perceive the things of the Spirit because he is examined, that is, an examination and approved knowledge of these things takes place through living spiritually. Those who live carnally cannot understand.

The animal person does not perceive; but the spiritual person judges all things, that is, discerns them by choosing the good and rejecting the evil. The spiritual person himself is judged by no animal person. For the carnal person cannot discern the reason why the spiritual person chooses one thing and rejects another.

Truly the spiritual person is not judged by the carnal. For the spiritual person has the mind of Christ, which the carnal person cannot know. He says it in this way: What animal person has known the mind—that is, the wisdom—of the Lord, so as to know his dispositions? Or who will instruct him about what he ought to do and what he ought not to do?

The animal person certainly has not known the mind of the Lord; but through the Spirit we have received, we possess the mind [Col. 0135D] of Christ. Therefore no carnal person can judge us.

## CHAPTER III

“And I, brothers, could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal people. As little ones in Christ, I gave you milk to drink, not food. For you were not yet able—and indeed even now you are not able. For you are still carnal. Since there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not carnal and walking according to the human manner? For when one says, ‘I am of Paul,’ and another, ‘I am of Apollo,’ are you not human beings?

“What, then, is Apollo? And what is Paul? Ministers of him in whom you believed—and each according to what the Lord gave. I planted, Apollo watered, but God gave the growth. Therefore neither the one who plants is anything nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth. The one who plants and the one who waters are one; but each will receive his own reward according to his labor.

“For we are God’s fellow workers; you are God’s cultivation; you are God’s building. According to the grace of God given to me, as a wise architect I laid a foundation, and another builds upon it. But let each one see how he builds upon it. For no one can lay another foundation besides the one that has been laid, which is Christ Jesus.

“But if anyone builds upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw, each one’s work will become manifest. For the day of the Lord will disclose it, because it will be revealed in fire; and the fire will test what sort of work each one’s is. If anyone’s work that he built upon it remains, he will receive a reward. If anyone’s work burns, he will suffer loss; yet he himself will be saved, but only as through fire.

“Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that the Spirit of God dwells in you? If anyone violates God’s temple, God will destroy him. ‘For God’s temple is holy, and that is what you are’ (II Cor. VI, 16).

“Let no one deceive you. If anyone among you seems to be wise in this age, let him become foolish so that he may be wise. For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. For it is written: ‘I will seize the wise in their craftiness’ (Job V, 13). And again: ‘The Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are vain’ (Ps. XCIII, 11).

“Therefore let no one glory in human beings. For all things are yours, whether Paul or Apollo or Cephas, whether the world or life or death, whether things present or things to come. For all things are yours; but you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s.”

## EXPOSITION

Although we are spiritual people, as has been shown, and teach spiritual things, nevertheless I, brothers, could not speak to you as spiritual people but spoke as carnal people. And because you were carnal, I gave you, as little ones in Christ—that is, tender in the faith of Christ—milk to drink.

By “milk” he signifies the sweetness of doctrine; by “drink,” its ease. I gave you milk, not food, that is, I gave you that doctrine which in your simplicity was to be chewed over and nourished by ease rather than burdened by difficulty.

I did not give you spiritual things because you were not yet able to receive them—and indeed even now you are not able, although you now glory in new teachers. Truly you are not yet able, for you are still carnal.

And truly you are carnal. For since there is now among you jealousy—that is, envy of the mind—and strife in words, are you not carnal? And do you not walk according to the human manner, that is, according to the carnal doctrine of those human beings whom you follow?

Truly you are carnal and walk according to the human manner, because when one of you says, “I am of Paul,” and another says, “I am of Apollo,” are you not human beings, that is, do you not think according to a human manner? Since you say, “I am of Paul; I am of Apollo,” tell me, then, what is Apollo? And what is Paul? And what do you suppose they contribute to you?

This is the true judgment you may form of them: they are ministers of him in whom you believed. They are nothing else except that, by God’s command, they minister to you the things belonging to God, although in different ways.

For just as the Lord gave to each of us, so I planted, that is, preached the Gospel and brought you to the faith; but Apollo watered, that is, baptized you after you had already believed through me. God alone, however, gave the growth of good things through his Spirit.

He continues the metaphor of a planted tree, which one person waters and another plants, while God alone gives the growth. And because giving the growth belongs to God alone, neither the one who plants is anything, insofar as the gift of faith is concerned, nor the one who waters is anything in the remission of sins; but God is everything, since he alone gives the growth of faith and of the righteousness that follows.

An opponent might say: Although they are God’s ministers, they nevertheless differ in merits, and I believe that merits contribute something to me.

Paul answers this: Although one is more worthy and another less worthy, nevertheless the one who plants and the one who waters are one and indifferent in administering; they merely dispense God’s gift, which cannot be increased or diminished by their good or evil merits.

Although the planter and the waterer are indifferent in the fact that they are Christ’s ministers, they nevertheless differ in this: each will receive his own reward, measured out to him according to his labor, that is, according to the measure in which he labored in God’s work. For more is owed to the one who merits more.

This fits the intention well. When he showed that he had merited more than others in the faith of the Corinthians, and that the subjects ought not to glory in him, he added that there was even less reason to glory in those who merited less, and he showed that they were absolutely nothing.

Let us return to the text. Truly he will receive a reward according to his own labor. For we have helped God more than others among you, and therefore we will be rewarded more than others. He says this as follows: “We are God’s fellow workers,” that is, laborers. As servants, by ministering according to the Lord’s commands, we helped God among you by ministering his faith, just as he himself ordained for us.

Truly we helped God among you. For you are God’s cultivation, that is, cultivated land from which the thorns of sins have now been uprooted. You are, I say, God’s cultivation through the removal of evils; and you are God’s building through the placing of virtues, because God has already built other virtues upon your faith.

That you are God’s cultivation and building is through me. For I laid the foundation, that is, faith, upon which the other virtues are founded. I laid it, certainly, as an architect, that is, the master of the structure. For even if I had other fellow workers among you, I was nevertheless the chief there.

I call him a wise architect, that is, one who imparted to each person with discernment what could suffice for that person’s capacity. I did this according to the grace of God. For I could not have founded you in faith unless God’s grace had worked with me; and in order to obtain that grace I had not first offered merit, but it was given to me out of mercy.

I laid a sound foundation insofar as it depended on me [Col. 0138A]; but let another, whose task it is to build upon this foundation, see what he builds upon it. For another is the one who builds upon this foundation. It is as though he said: “What belonged to me—the foundation—I laid; what belongs to you, see that you build well upon it.”

The one who builds upon it is said to do so whether he builds virtues or, if he sins, does not do so in such a way as to destroy the foundation. It is destroyed by mortal sins unless they are removed through suitable repentance. It is also destroyed by venial sins, which we possess not only from necessity, since even “the just person falls seven times a day” (Prov. XXIV, 16), but especially by those venial sins that we admit voluntarily and in which, by consenting to them, we remain unrepentant.

I laid the foundation carefully. But let each one of you see how he builds upon this foundation, for this work is now entrusted to your judgment, strengthened by the grace you have received.

It should be noted that only those are said to build upon the foundation whose faults do not destroy it. For the one who destroys it should rather be said to overthrow it through sin than to build upon it.

You must indeed be watchful regarding the building upon the foundation, lest it be altered. For concerning the foundation I make you secure, because it is one. No one can lay another foundation besides the one that was laid by me; and that foundation—that is, faith—is Christ Jesus.

For your faith concerning Christ, according to Augustine, is Christ in your heart. If anything other than faith is laid down, it is the overthrow of the foundation, not a foundation. The foundation is one and cannot be another; but the structures built upon it are various, because one person builds gold, another silver, another hay or straw upon it.

He puts it this way: If anyone builds upon this foundation—that is, faith—gold, silver, precious stones, these three signify virtues, but virtues distinguished according to their degrees. Or wood, hay, straw: these three signify distinct evils which nevertheless do not destroy the foundation.

All these things will be tested by fire, as he will add immediately. Gold signifies perfect righteousness, so that there is nothing at all in such people that needs purifying. They will certainly pass through fire—not so that they may be detained there by any harshness, but just as pure gold placed in fire [Col. 0138D] suffers no loss and instead becomes more splendid through a greater brilliance, so the perfect do not feel the fire’s injury. Rather, made more approved by the agility of their virtues, they emerge from this fire with the greatest ease.

Silver signifies the righteous in whom, nevertheless, there are some slight things to be purified, since silver placed in fire becomes discolored; the craftsman’s skill restores its color after the fire. So they will indeed suffer the fire, but lightly, because they have committed slight offenses.

Precious stones signify the righteous, although burdened by certain venial sins; nevertheless they have adhered more closely to righteousness. Therefore they will suffer in the fire more than those mentioned above, just as precious stones experience more damage from fire than silver. He said “stones” in the plural because there will be different people in this degree, and they will suffer according to the diversity of their merits.

Through these three, the class of the perfect is signified; through the three that follow, the imperfect are signified.

Wood refers to those who remain in the world. They have wives, children, and possessions; and they must consider what belongs to their wives and children, and therefore labor greatly. For this reason they cannot attend the Church’s prayers as they ought.

Nevertheless, because they do not love the world in such a way as to prefer it to God, they will indeed be saved, but they will be punished for a long time through fire, just as wood is a material that takes a long time to burn and is consumed over a considerable period.

Hay signifies those who are afflicted for some time by fire but, like hay, which quickly disappears in fire, quickly escape. Straw, because through its dryness it burns more quickly than hay, signifies those whose punishment will be brief during their passage through the fire.

If anyone builds these things or those things, each person’s work—whether it is gold, wood, or anything else—will become manifest. And he proves this. For the day of the Lord will disclose this work.

He calls the day of the Lord the period from the hour of each person’s dissolution until the judgment. From the moment the soul is separated from the body, the day of the Lord is present for that person, because he can no longer perform any work except according to God’s will. But while a human being lives, it is the human day and not God’s day, because a person does what pleases him, good or evil, through the freedom of the will.

Truly the day of the Lord will disclose it. For it will be revealed in fire, that is, the work will become public. He calls this fire continuous, like the day. At a person’s death the devil is ready with his fire and his torturers. If anything requires purification, he purifies it through the applied fire.

But if no purification is required—as in the case of blessed Martin—the very escape from the fire reveals the goodness of the person’s work, showing that there was no defilement in the one whom it torments. Yet because this cannot yet be seen clearly, each person’s work will be revealed in the purgatorial fire.

Truly each person’s work will be revealed in fire. For that fire will test what sort of work each person’s is, whether it is gold, wood, or anything else. Truly the fire will test the work of each person.

For there is both good work and evil work; let us consider the good first. If anyone’s work, which he built upon the foundation, remains unharmed, he will receive a reward for the good he built upon it.

The fire will test evil work. For if anyone’s work burns—that is, if it is found capable of burning, like wood, hay, or straw—he will suffer loss and be afflicted by the violence of the fire. Yet although he suffers loss, he himself will be saved. I say that he will be saved, but only as one who will pass through fire.

For what was sweet to commit must first be punished by the bitterness of fire.

He has now distinguished the works that do not destroy the foundation, saying that all who do not destroy it will be saved. He now adds a discussion of those works that destroy the foundation and store up eternal destruction, saying: If anyone does not destroy the foundation, he will be saved; but if anyone violates [Col. 0140A] God’s temple, he will be destroyed.

But in order to pierce them with remorse, he first puts the question in this form: Do you not know that you are God’s temple? God sanctifies you so that you may be his temple. And I say that you are a temple in which the Spirit of God dwells with complete constancy.

If anyone violates himself as God’s temple by destroying the foundation of faith—either in himself through mortal sins or among his hearers by teaching falsehood—God will destroy him in eternal destruction.

And rightly the one who violates it will be destroyed. For God’s temple is holy and must not be violated, and you are that temple.

And because you are God’s temple, take care that none of the false teachers deceive you through false doctrine; and let none of us deceive himself by destroying the foundation of faith.

Let no one, I say, deceive himself. But if anyone who remains among you seems to himself to be wise in this age, that is, in secular knowledge, let him become foolish—that is, let him believe and confess that he is foolish—so that he may deserve to be truly wise. It is genuinely necessary for him to become foolish in order to become wise.

For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. And truly it is foolishness with God. For it is written in Job, where God speaks of worldly wisdom: “I will seize the wise of the world,” that is, “I will enclose them in their very craftiness” (Job V, 13), in the very thing in which they understand themselves to be most crafty and through which they will not be able to resist.

And again, concerning the wisdom of the world, it is written in the psalm: “The Lord knows the thoughts of the wise” (Ps. XCIII, 11). Our translation has “of human beings,” that is, of those who are wise in a human manner. He knows this about them: that they are vain.

Since human wisdom is shown to be foolishness, therefore none of you should henceforth glory in human beings, that is, in those teachers in whom you glory on account of human wisdom.

He proves that one ought not to glory in them, first because they are their servants—the very persons who preach to them, including Paul himself. One may not glory in what is inferior or equal, but only in what is greater than oneself. Second, if there is no glorying in Paul and Cephas, there is much less reason to glory in those carnal teachers who are plainly far inferior to them.

Hence he says: You ought not to glory in human beings. For all things are yours, that is, appointed for your service: whether Paul, Apollo, or Cephas, their head—that is, Peter—or whether the world is yours, for it serves you, even if it ministers necessities to you and brings any hardships upon you for the sake of your righteousness; whether your life is yours, for the present life is granted to you so that you may repent of evil deeds and, afterward doing good, merit reward; whether your death is yours, for it is useful to embrace death for Christ if it should come upon you; whether things present or things future, whether good or evil.

All these things mentioned above are truly yours. For all things are yours; but you belong only to Christ, in whom alone you ought to glory.

Christ, however, is God’s—not because Christ differs from him in substance, but because through Christ, who mediates between us, we are brought back to God.

Cephas means “head”; Simon means “obedient”; Bar-Jonah means “son of a dove.” Since God changed the name Cephas for him and called him Peter, it has consequently become customary to change the names of the apostles.

## CHAPTER IV

“Let a human being regard us as ministers of Christ and stewards of God’s ministries [mysteries]. Here it is now sought among stewards that someone be found faithful. But to me it is a very small matter to be judged by you or by a human day. Nor do I judge myself. For I am conscious of nothing against myself, but I am not thereby justified. The one who judges me is the Lord.

“Therefore do not judge before the time, until the Lord comes. He will both bring to light the hidden things of darkness and manifest the counsels of hearts; and then each person will receive praise from God.

“Now these things, brothers, I have applied figuratively to myself and Apollo for your sake, so that in us you may learn not to go beyond what is written, and that no one may be puffed up against another on behalf of one person.

“For who distinguishes you? And what do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you glory as though you had not received it?

“Already you are filled; already you have become rich; you reign without us. And I wish indeed that you reigned, so that we also might reign with you.

“For I think that God has displayed us apostles as the very last, as men destined for death, because we have become a spectacle to the world, to angels, and to human beings. We are fools for Christ’s sake, but you are wise in Christ; we are weak, but you are strong; you are noble, but we are base.

“Until this very hour we are hungry and thirsty, naked and beaten with blows; we are unsettled and labor, working with our own hands. We are cursed, and we bless; we suffer persecution, and we endure; we are blasphemed, and we entreat. We have become like the refuse of this world, the offscouring of all, until now.

“I do not write these things to shame you, but I admonish you as my most beloved children. For even if you have ten thousand pedagogues in Christ, you do not have many fathers. For in Christ Jesus, through the Gospel, I begot you.

“Therefore I entreat you, brothers: be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ. For this reason I sent Timothy to you, who is my beloved and faithful son in the Lord. He will remind you of my ways, which are in Christ Jesus, just as I teach everywhere in every church.

“As though I were not going to come to you, some have become puffed up. But I will come to you soon, if the Lord wills, and I will discover not the speech of those who are puffed up but their power. For the kingdom of God is not in speech but in power.

“What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in love and a spirit of gentleness?”

## EXPOSITION
Because Paul had just humbled himself so greatly by saying, “and Apollo are yours,” lest the Corinthians should therefore become puffed up, he says that he possesses great dignity, since they are ministers of Christ, and so forth. The text is joined as follows: although I previously said, “I, Paul, and Apollo are yours,” nevertheless every person among the Corinthians should regard us as ministers of Christ—that is, as those worthy to minister Christ and his faith to their subjects—and should also regard us as stewards of God’s ministries. For we distribute ecclesiastical offices, consecrating one as presbyter and another as deacon. Or, “stewards of the mysteries,” that is, of God’s secrets: for we know and speak God’s counsels to the faithful.

Therefore I say, “Let a person regard us in this way,” because here—that is, in this Church of Corinth—already means before the appropriate time of judgment. In this world, because works are hidden, it is not permitted to judge. Or “here,” that is, on the occasion by which I said that we ought to be regarded as ministers and stewards. Therefore it is now asked among stewards which of them may be found faithful—that is, perfect—and whose righteousness may confer something distinctive upon those baptized by him. “Faithful” is said in the same sense as: “found in appearance as a man” (Philippians II, 7).

But whatever the other stewards may think, I nevertheless answer this: it is of very little importance to me, and I regard it as insignificant, that I should be judged by you—that is, that you should condemn me—or that I should be judged by a human day, that is, by a human being who, because of the subtlety of his intelligence, may also be called a “day.” You do not know how to judge me, but neither do I myself judge—that is, reproach—myself in anything, because I am conscious of nothing against myself, and just as my knowledge finds nothing to judge, still less can you, who cannot search out the hidden things of conscience.

But although my conscience accuses me of nothing, I am not thereby justified, because perhaps I consider certain things good which spring from an evil root. Neither a human being nor my own conscience can judge me; but he who judges—that is, he who possesses the power to judge me—is the Lord, and no one besides him can do this. Since God alone can judge, whereas a human being cannot, because he does not even understand himself sufficiently, do not judge me, or anyone else, before the time—that is, now, while hidden things still lie concealed—until the Lord comes to judgment. He will certainly come and bring to light—that is, make manifest—the hidden things of darkness, that is, of sins, because certain things lie concealed among sins. He will also disclose the counsels of hearts—that is, the good works performed from the counsel and deliberation of a righteous heart—and then, at that coming, each person who has acted rightly from the counsel of his heart will receive praise from the Lord.

## Exposition

What he earlier said about the Corinthians declaring, “I belong to Paul,” and “I belong to Apollo,” he now explains, showing how he had said this figuratively, signifying by his own name and by Apollo those about whom they boasted; and he did this as an example of humility. Thus he says:

What I earlier presented you as saying—“I belong to Apollo,” “I belong to Paul”—I did not do for the reason that you were boasting about us. Rather, brothers, I transformed—that is, transferred—these things onto myself, speaking figuratively, while assigning our names to those false teachers. I transformed these things onto myself and Apollo for your instruction, so that you may learn from us not to become puffed up, one against another, on account of something done for oneself or for another—that is, on account of being more worthy than someone else through the merit of the person who baptized him. Or “for another,” that is, for the more righteous teacher whom he had.

I say, do not become puffed up by doing what was stated above. It was written earlier that whoever boasts should boast not in the merit of a human being but in the Lord. You must not become puffed up against another: for who is it that distinguishes you from another, knowing the merits of each? He is surely foolish who presumes to distinguish you. Again, you must not become puffed up, because what do you have from that teacher about whom you boast that you did not receive from me? Indeed, you received more from me, because you received faith from me rather than from him. Again, you must not become puffed up, because if you received it from me, why do you boast about another as though you had not received from me what you received from him? Surely, more from me.

Or otherwise: do not become puffed up, because who distinguishes you from the mass of those lost in Adam, so as to make you a vessel for honor, except God alone? Certainly no one. Again, do not become puffed up, because what good do you have from anyone that you did not receive from God? God is the giver of every good thing. Again, you must not become puffed up, because if you received something from God, why do you boast of it by ascribing it to a human being’s merit, as though you had not received it from God?

I say, “Do not boast,” but I speak wrongly, because you ought rightly to boast: for you are already satisfied—that is, you have enough good things within you. You have already become rich as well, possessing what you can distribute to each person. You also reign—that is, you govern yourselves well without us. All this is said ironically, but from this point seriously. I say, “You reign”—and would that you truly reigned! For this is what I would desire: that you should not need our governance, but should reign in such a way that we too might reign with you—that is, that in the dignity of your life you might precede us in that kingdom.

Certainly I would prefer you to go before me and me to follow you, rather than the reverse, because I am more certain about myself than about you. Again, ironically: you indeed reign, but we do not at all, because I think that you yourselves think this: namely, that God has shown us, the apostles, to be the last—that is, the worst and least esteemed. I say that we are like men destined for death, because we are afflicted for Christ to such a degree that we seem to have been born only for death. Therefore, while you flourish in the world, we are held in contempt.

For this reason also we have become a spectacle to this world: everyone gathers for our oppression, and our misfortunes are their amusement. I say “to this world,” meaning both to evil angels, who rejoice in our affliction, and to human beings. Therefore we are regarded as foolish. But it would be good to imitate this foolishness, because we are foolish for Christ, whereas you are wise in Christ—which, in fact, you are not and ought not to be. We are weak and feeble in the world, whereas you are strong and boast of the world’s power. You are noble, whereas we are ignoble.

Or it may be read without irony: I would that we might reign with you. For I am certain that we truly will reign. I think—and indeed I confidently believe—that God has shown us to be the last apostles, that is, like the last ones, Enoch and Elijah, because at the beginning of the Church we now suffer as much as they will suffer from Antichrist at the end. Hence Paul himself says: “We are those upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (I Corinthians X, 11). Nero was also called Antichrist because, just as he killed Enoch and Elijah, so the latter killed Peter and Paul.

Truly we are the last: for we are destined for death; for we are a spectacle to the world. The rest should be explained in the same way, but ironically. “We are fools, you are wise”; “you are strong, we are weak”: here too there is the same irony.

Nor do we suffer only the evils already mentioned. From the beginning of our preaching until this hour, we hunger and thirst; we are naked; we are struck with blows; we are unstable, driven from place to place; and we labor, working with our hands so that we may have food. We are cursed by the impious, and we bless them. We suffer persecution and endure it cheerfully. We are blasphemed, and we entreat the impious not to blaspheme, or we entreat God to forgive those who blaspheme. They rage against us to such an extent that we have become like the refuse of this world. For they seem to think that the world is polluted by us and cleansed through our destruction. We have indeed become *peripsema*, that is, the cleansing or refuse of all, because everyone would already be cleansed if we did not exist, but they are polluted by us. According to Ambrose, *peripsema* means the refuse of an apple or the slag of iron. Such have we been made from the beginning of the world until now.

Because he had spoken harshly to the Corinthians, he begins again to flatter them, saying: Although I spoke ironically when I called you wise, strong, and noble, I do not write these things to shame you and make you blush, but I admonish you—now gently, now harshly—as my most beloved sons. Truly sons: for even if you have ten thousand pedagogues, that is, teachers—even faithful teachers in Christ—you do not have many fathers, in the faith. Truly, not many, but only me. For I begot you in Christ Jesus through my Gospel.

And since I am the father and you are the sons, I therefore ask you, brothers: be imitators of me, as sons of their father. For this reason, because you are sons and so that you may be imitators, I sent Timothy to you, who is my most beloved and faithful son in the Lord; listen to him. I sent him so that he might remind you of my ways, so that, as I do, you too may walk in all righteousness. These are the ways in which you must persevere, because they are in Christ Jesus, and the whole Church follows them. He says this in the sense of: “As I teach everywhere,” not merely here and there in the countryside, but in every Church.

Through Timothy, the Apostle is said to have sent this Epistle to the Corinthians. Above, he spoke about those who baptized them and sufficiently proved that one should not be preferred to another. He also reproved them for their worldly wisdom, which was held by them in excessively high esteem, and for their contempt of him. Now he turns to the matter of a certain fornicator who had taken his stepmother as his wife. They had neither excluded him from communion with the Church nor grieved over their brother’s sin; rather, they had become puffed up because of it, saying that if he had been baptized by a good man, he would never have fallen into so deep a pit of sin. Thus the merit of the person who baptized him seemed to be at work in those cases, lest they should sin in the same way.

The text is joined as follows: I, concerned for you as a father for his sons, am sending Timothy to you. But some among you are puffed up and, perhaps because of their pride, will not listen to him. Therefore he touches on their pride here, so that he may find them obedient to Timothy in complete humility. You are indeed puffed up, acting as though I were not going to come to you, and you do not respect my coming, which you ought to fear unless you correct yourselves.

Perhaps you believe that I will not come because I am now sending Timothy. But know that I will come to you soon. Yet this does not lie within my own right, and therefore I qualify it: “if the Lord wills,” whose will one may not oppose. I will certainly come, and then I will know—that is, approve—according to the saying: “The Lord knows those who are his” (II Timothy II, 19). I will know not their speech—that is, not the courtliness and artifice of speech to which those who are puffed up by such speech cling—but I will know and praise in you the power, that is, humility, patience, and so forth. These are what ought to be praised, not elevated speech. Therefore I will know the power and not the speech, because the kingdom of God is not in the speech of this world—that is, it is not acquired through it—but in the power of sound faith and good works.

I have set before you two things: speech, which I reject, and power, which I approve. What do you choose—that is, what good thing do you choose? Shall I come to you with a rod, that is, with the harshness of correction; or shall I come to you in love, that is, in gentleness? And indeed in a spirit of meekness—that is, as one accustomed to your hand and glad to serve you? If I find speech, I will come with a rod; if I find power, I will come in a spirit of love.

When he says “with a rod or in love,” he seems to imply that correction is not from love if it is harsh. This is certainly false; but he says this according to the weakness of those who judged everything that opposed the will of the flesh to proceed from anger.

## Chapter V

> “It is certainly reported that there is fornication among you, and such fornication as is not even found among the Gentiles, so that someone has his father’s wife. And you are puffed up, and have not rather mourned, so that the one who has done this deed might be removed from your midst. For I, although absent in body (Colossians II, 5), but present in spirit, have already judged as though present the one who has acted in this way: in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, when you are assembled, and my spirit is present, with the power of the Lord Jesus, to hand such a man over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ. Your boasting is not good. ‘Do you not know that a little leaven corrupts the whole lump?’ (Galatians V, 9.) Cleanse out the old leaven, so that you may be a new dough, just as you are unleavened. For Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed. Therefore let us feast, not with the old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.
>
> “I wrote to you in my letter not to associate with fornicators—not at all meaning the fornicators of this world, or the greedy, or the rapacious, or those serving idols; otherwise you would have had to leave this world. But now I wrote to you not to associate with [*is qui*; variant *si quis*, “if anyone”] who is called a brother among you, if he is a fornicator, or greedy, or serving idols, or abusive, or drunk, or rapacious; with such a person not even to eat. For what have I to do [the source adds the corrupt and uncertain words *non habet est*] with judging those who are outside? Do you not judge those who are inside? For those who are outside God will judge. Remove evil from among yourselves.”

## Exposition

It is certainly necessary to come to you with a rod, because it is reported that there is fornication among you. It is indeed reported universally, that is, according to everyone’s denunciation: since everyone is defaming you—for rumor has also brought this to me—there is no need to await an accuser. Nor is it merely some fornication that must be endured, but such fornication as is not even heard of among the Gentiles, that is, among Gentiles still clinging to their first birth.

It is reported that someone among you has his father’s wife, that is, has taken his stepmother as his wife. They might say: “What is that to us?” Paul replies: “A great deal.” For because a brother sinned, you became puffed up and arrogant, as though you had been justified through baptism better than he, because you had not fallen in the same way. You were not merely puffed up; you also did not mourn by grieving over your brother’s downfall—rather, you did what you ought to have chosen, namely, not to become puffed up.

Nor did you take care that he who had done this deed should be removed from your midst, that is, separated from communion with the Church. He had unlawfully taken his father’s wife for himself, yet while you were present you did not remove him from your midst. But I, although absent in body and present in spirit—that is, by apostolic authority—for the saints also say that the Holy Spirit had made known to him the deeds even of those who were absent, being present in spirit, have already judged—that is, condemned—him as though I were present in body.

I speak of the one who acted in this way with his father’s wife. I have indeed judged him, and you should know that I did so in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, lest you say that his expulsion harms the Church of Christ. Rather, Christ is honored by this, and his Church is not diminished; for it would be infected by the poison of this evil if he were not expelled.

I have judged that, when you are assembled, this man should be handed over to Satan. Or the phrase “in the name of the Lord” belongs to what follows, so that the text reads as follows: I have judged this concerning him: that, when you are assembled in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, and my spirit is present—that is, my authority cooperates with you—

What would the impious man say because your spirit is with us? Paul replies: “A great deal.” For I say that my spirit remains with the power of the Lord Jesus, because God’s power will cooperate with you through me. I have judged, I say, that you ought to hand over to Satan the man who is such.

“To hand over to Satan” means to excommunicate. Just as the devil has every right over a person before that person is justified through faith, so, after someone has been separated because of his fault from the Church’s sacraments—the weapons by which we are fortified against Satan—he is again bound beneath Satan’s yoke. For he can no longer resist by his own strength, and perhaps does not wish to, and he is entirely deprived of God’s assistance.

I say that he is to be handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that is, so that his flesh, which has rejoiced in sin, may gradually perish through the affliction of diseases. For once the devil sees a person without God and weakened, he attacks him freely and torments his flesh with various illnesses. God allows this so that, seeing himself oppressed by so many illnesses after withdrawing from God, the person may confess his sin and, by repenting, return to God, so that his spirit may be saved.

Or it may be understood in this way: “to hand him over to Satan for destruction,” because after he is no longer protected by the Church’s sacraments, he is daily cast from one evil into a worse one. This is the destruction of the soul through the flesh—that is, through the flesh to which he consents when it gives evil counsel. He is not handed over so that he may perish forever, but so that, while weighed down by the burden of his sins, he may grieve over them, repent, and thus have his spirit saved on the day—that is, at the illumination—of our Lord Jesus Christ. Christ illuminates him when he burns with the desire to repent.

This is something the leaders of the Church must carefully observe: they should excommunicate the guilty with the same intention as Paul, namely, so that their spirits may be saved. Since you did not mourn and did not remove him from your midst, it is evident that your boasting is not good. It is evil for someone to boast of his righteousness while neglecting his neighbor’s salvation and infecting himself with his neighbor’s disease.

Truly, you do not boast well. For do you not know that if a little leaven becomes sour, it corrupts the whole lump of dough and makes it sour? So this man—small in number in comparison with the Church—corrupts the whole Church, which has become guilty by sharing in his association. Since this leaven corrupts the Church’s lump, remove him and every evil from your midst; cleanse out the leaven, that is, your inflation or pride. And if there is any other sin, it too must be expelled.

I say “old leaven.” For unless you cleanse yourselves, you are members of the old man. Cleanse yourselves, therefore, so that you may be a dough. Flour bound together by water without leaven is called *conspersio*, a dough or kneaded mixture. Our humanity, which in itself is barren and dry, is represented by dry flour; through the dew of the Holy Spirit it is bound together in baptism, so that, once its dryness has been removed, it may bear fruit, just as flour is joined by water so as to become useful.

Be, I say, a new dough, that is, become members of the new Adam, namely Christ, who renewed you through the Holy Spirit. Now be a new dough, just as earlier in baptism you were unleavened, that is, without the leaven of every sin.
