It is good for you now to be cleansed through repentance—which is a second baptism—just as you were previously cleansed through baptism. *Azymus* is Greek for what is called “without leaven” in Latin. *Zymus* means leaven; *a-* means “without,” as in *acephali*, “headless” or “without a head.”

You ought indeed to cleanse yourselves, for Christ was sacrificed on the altar of the cross. Christ is our Passover, that is, our passage from death to life and from corruption to incorruption. Through him we can now at last cleanse ourselves, whereas previously, bound under the devil’s yoke, we could not.

Here he sends us back to the history in which the sons of Israel, so that they might be delivered from the Egyptian plague, were commanded to smear the doorposts with the blood of the sacrificed lamb (Exodus XII, 7). After the sacrifice of that lamb, they were freed from Egyptian slavery and passed over into the promised land. Among them this feast of the lamb’s sacrifice is called Passover; among the Greeks, *pascha*; among us, “passing over.”

That lamb signified the true Lamb in whom there was no blemish, Christ. Through his shed blood our minds are marked, and so we are delivered from the plague of the destroying angel. The Church gathers daily to eat this Lamb, thereby passing over to the truth of the reality that it now uses under the appearance of bread and wine. Although their appearance remains, we nevertheless believe that they truly pass over into the true substance of Christ’s body and blood; through these we shall pass into eternity.

“Let us feast,” I say, not remaining in the old leaven, nor in the leaven of malice residing within ourselves, nor in the leaven of wickedness, so that we do nothing against our neighbor; but remaining in unleavened bread—that is, in humility—of sincerity, that is, of purity preserved within us, and of truth, so that we may not defraud our neighbor.

Paul had already written to the Corinthians about avoiding fornication. But they, misinterpreting his words, thought that he was commanding them to avoid Gentiles when they committed fornication. Now, because he had already written to them about this crime, he reproves them and indicates how they ought to understand the letter he had sent, saying:

I rightly reproach you for this, because you did not remove that fornicator from your midst. For I wrote to you in the letter already sent that you should not associate with fornicators—not, of course, commanding this concerning the fornicators of this world, that is, concerning the Gentiles who follow not God but the world.

I also wrote to you not to associate with the greedy, the rapacious, or those serving idols—that is, those who either return to the worship of an idol or eat what has been sacrificed to idols under the veneration of an idol. I certainly did not prohibit association with the fornicators of the Gentiles. Otherwise, that is, if I were giving this command concerning avoiding Gentiles, then, if you wished to obey, you would have had to leave this world. It would be better for you to die by rejecting whatever belongs to the world than, through fear, to act otherwise and associate with fornicators.

I wrote this earlier, but you misunderstood it. Now I specify to you what I wrote: you must not associate with such a person. It is to be understood as follows: if someone who is a brother in the faith is called a fornicator, greedy, or a servant of idols—whether through worshiping them or eating sacrificial food under their veneration—or is called abusive, drunk, that is, accustomed to slander and drunkenness, or rapacious, then you must exclude all communion with such a person. To make the prohibition milder, I say: do not even eat with him.

Blessed Augustine notes that when the Apostle says “if he is called” and does not say “if he is,” he understood this distinction as follows: if a brother is guilty of a crime but his fault remains hidden, he ought not to be excommunicated. Judgment must not be passed on uncertainties, but on a crime that has been revealed and proven. Therefore he says “is called.” The person is not to be judged guilty on that account alone.

We ought indeed to judge concerning brothers. For what is it to me—that is, what does it concern me or the Church—to judge those who are outside, that is, the Gentiles? Nothing at all. And since it is not permitted to judge those who are outside the Church, do you not judge—that is, ought you not to judge—those who are inside, in the Church? Certainly, you judge only those who are inside. For those who are outside, that is, the Gentiles, God will judge, and their affairs do not concern you.

Since you must judge the faithful, remove the evil of the fornicator brother from among yourselves. Unless you remove it, you are already contaminated by the guilt of that same crime.

## Chapter VI

> “Does any one of you dare, when he has a case against another, to be judged before the unrighteous and not before the holy? Or do you not know that the saints will judge this world? And if the world will be judged by you, are you unworthy to judge the smallest matters? Do you not know that we shall judge angels, how much more worldly matters? Therefore, if you have worldly lawsuits, appoint as judges those who are contemptible [variant *contendibiles*, “contentious persons”] in the Church. I say this to your shame. Is there thus no wise person among you who can judge between his brother? But brother goes to court against brother—and this before unbelievers? It is already altogether a fault among you that you have lawsuits with one another. Why do you not rather accept wrong? Why do you not rather suffer fraud? But you yourselves do wrong and defraud, and this to your brothers. Or do you not know that the unrighteous will not possess the kingdom of God? Do not be deceived: neither fornicators, nor those serving idols, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor men who have intercourse with males, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor the abusive, nor the rapacious will possess the kingdom of God. And such were some of you [*aliquando*, “once”]; but you have been washed, but you have been sanctified, but you have been justified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God.
>
> “All things are permitted to me, but not all things are beneficial. All things are permitted to me, but I will not be brought under the power of anything. Food is for the stomach and the stomach for food; but God will destroy both it and them. The body, however, is not for fornication but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body. God both raised up the Lord and will also raise us up by his power. Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? Shall I therefore take Christ’s members and make them members of a prostitute? By no means. Or do you not know that he who is joined to a prostitute becomes one body with her? For, he says, ‘the two shall be one flesh’ (Genesis II, 24; Ephesians V, 31; Matthew XIX, 5). But he who is joined to God is one spirit. Flee fornication. Every sin that a human being commits is outside the body; but he who commits fornication sins against his own body. Or do you not know that ‘your members are a temple’ (II Corinthians VI, 16) of the Holy Spirit, who is in you, whom you have from God, and that you are not your own? ‘For you were bought with a great price’ (I Peter I, 18). Glorify and bear God in your body.”

## Exposition

Taking occasion from the fact that he began with lawsuits, he proceeds to correct the evils arising from lawsuits among the Corinthians. If one of them took something away from another, the latter did not patiently endure it; instead, impatiently, he compelled his brother to court. He did not do this before ecclesiastical judges, but, despising them, he defrauded his brother before secular judges, even giving a gift to the judge for the oppression of his brother.

The text is joined as follows: It is indeed permitted for you to judge concerning brothers, but not in the intemperate manner in which you rashly dare to appear before the unrighteous. Or as follows: It is good to remove evil from among you. But why does one of you dare? By saying “dare,” he indicates that such an act of daring is a sin.

Why, I ask, does one of you who has a case—that is, a complaint concerning secular matters—against another brother dare to be judged, that is, to enter into litigation with his brother, before unrighteous judges, that is, secular judges, and not before the saints, that is, the faithful judges of the Church?

They might say: “We fear disturbing the saints from their prayers.” Paul replies: “Not at all. Do you not know that the saints will judge this world at the future judgment? And if this world will be judged by you—that is, in comparison with you—at the last judgment, are you unworthy to judge here the smallest matters in comparison with future matters, namely, the temporal affairs of the Church?”

And just as human beings, so also demons will be judged in our likeness. For do you not know that we shall judge apostate angels, in comparison with you? If we shall judge angels, how much more may we judge worldly matters?

Evil human beings will be judged in comparison with the good, because although they were of the same condition and did not perform the same works as the good, this comparison alone is the sentence of their condemnation.

Demons will be condemned in the likeness of the righteous in two ways: first, because they were created with stronger natures than human beings and nevertheless did not persevere in goodness; second, because they always envy the righteous and are unable to overcome them. The righteous will condemn the evil angels on account of their victory in this struggle.

Now again he reproves them ironically because they were appointing foolish judges, with the result that the Church’s cases were transferred to secular judges. Since, as has been proved, the Church ought to judge between brothers, therefore, if you have worldly lawsuits—that is, disputes among yourselves over temporal matters—he indicates by this that it would be better if you did not have such lawsuits.

If, I say, you have these lawsuits, appoint those as judges—that is, set them over you as judges—who are contemptible, that is, more foolish, in the Church. He says this ironically, because he knew that this was what they did. And when I say, “Appoint the contemptible to judge,” I say this to your shame, not commanding you to do it, but recalling what you are doing so that you may be ashamed.

For when you act in this way, have you become so foolish that there is no wise person among you who can judge between one brother and another? But because you have all become so foolish, brother goes to court against brother, that is, brings a case against him. Nor is the evil of this dispute enough; it also takes place before unbelieving judges because of the lack of ecclesiastical judges.

This evil arises from the lawsuit: you contend with one another and transfer the Church’s rights to unbelievers. Certainly, for this reason it is altogether a fault among you, as is evident to everyone, that you have lawsuits among yourselves. It would be better not to reclaim your property than for so many evils to come upon the Church through your reclamation.

And since lawsuits among you are a fault, why do you not rather accept wrong—that is, endure without complaint the wrong of someone who openly takes what belongs to you? Why do you not rather suffer fraud—that is, the hidden loss inflicted through your brother’s deception—rather than allow the Church to be so degraded by your complaint?

It would be good for you to suffer wrong inflicted by a brother, because you not only refuse to suffer it, but you also do him wrong by taking away his property. You also defraud him: secretly, through your bribe, you forestall the judge for opposition [variant *oppressionem*, “oppression”] to your brother. And you do all this not to strangers but to brothers, whom you ought to support. In doing this to your brothers, you act wickedly.

But do you not know that the unrighteous will not possess the kingdom of God? Therefore, so that you may not be alienated from the kingdom of God, do not err by defrauding and wronging your brothers. Truly, the unrighteous will not possess it. For neither fornicators, nor those who serve idols, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate who submit to intercourse, nor those who have intercourse with males, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor the abusive, nor the rapacious will possess the kingdom of God.

[Col. 0151C] So that the Corinthians would not be frightened by these things and despair—for perhaps they had returned to such practices after baptism—Paul consoles them by addressing them gently. Hence he says: “Do not be frightened by what I have said above. You indeed did these things that I have mentioned; but you were washed from them in baptism. You were also sanctified,” that is, strengthened by the gifts of the Holy Spirit; “but you were justified” by the possession of virtues, “in the name of our Lord,” that is, the Father, “and in the name of Jesus Christ, and in the Spirit of our God,” who proceeds from both—things that were recalled to us in baptism.

Because he had said above, “Why do you not rather accept injury?” they might say: “Are we not permitted to reclaim what belongs to us?” Paul makes the distinction: there are certain things which are lawful, yet which are better left aside for the sake of greater benefit; these are temporal possessions. There are other things which are lawful in such a way that judgment concerning them ought not to be abandoned; these are criminal offenses, which kill the soul.

The passage is joined as follows: “Although I have said, ‘Accept injury rather than bring a complaint,’ I know nevertheless that all these things are permitted both to me and to each of you—that is, to reclaim one’s property, to bring a suit against one’s brother, and so forth. But although they are permitted, all these things are not expedient,” that is, they do not make us more ready for good things but rather hinder us.

He now adds another reason: “All things are permitted to me, but I will not be brought under the power of any judge or of anything else, so as to value it more highly than the peace of my brother.” Or in this sense: “I will not be brought under the power of any judge so as to approach him beforehand by a reward or some service, for the oppression [or: repression] of my brother.” Nor should only these permissible matters be abandoned; things necessary for the body should likewise not become the cause of a brother’s disturbance, such as food, which is prepared for the stomach, while the stomach is sustained by food. Yet although food is so necessary, one must not litigate for it, because God will destroy both this stomach and these foods.

For the sake of these temporal things—which quickly pass away and, if unreclaimed, do not condemn the soul—do not trouble yourselves to have a judgment; but do not allow that fornication to remain uncondemned. The passage is joined in this way: Food is owed to the stomach, but the body is not owed to fornication; rather, it ought in every respect to serve the Lord, and the Lord is owed to the body that serves him. For although the body is naked in itself, God clothes it with the adornment of virtues if it serves the Lord.

Truly the Lord will do good to the body: [Col. 0152B] “for the Lord will raise us to incorruption.” But he first puts forward proof of this, saying: “Truly God will raise us, for he has already raised [106] the Lord Jesus,” in whom he raised our flesh; and he will accomplish this also in us. And if you ask how he raises us, know that it is through his power. He says this to restrain the Corinthians, who doubted the resurrection, as will be made clear in what follows.

He has stated why the body is owed to God; he now gives the reason why it is not owed to fornication, saying: “The body must not be subjected to fornication, because do you not know that not only your souls but also your bodies are members of Christ?” The soul is a member of Christ because, through reason, it fixes its inward eyes upon the contemplation of God. The body is a member of Christ when, through the hand, it ministers to a poor person, and through the feet visits the sick, and so forth.

And since we are members of Christ, shall I therefore take Christ’s members and make them members of a prostitute? Far be it from this! They can indeed become members of a prostitute, because “do you not know that the one who clings to a prostitute becomes one body with her?” A body becomes joined to a prostitute in two ways: first, through that intercourse of flesh by which the two are bound together in a kind of unity; second, through participation in sin.

That they become one body through the joining of flesh he proves because this was more in doubt: truly they become one body, for Moses says in Genesis, “The two shall be one flesh” (Gen. 2:24). He said this, however, concerning lawful marriage; but the same joining and identity [Col. 0152D] of flesh occurs in adulterous intercourse as in marriage. He who clings to a prostitute becomes one body with her, but he who clings to the Lord is one spirit, that is, he is united to the Lord in the identity of spirit. And because fornication is so great an evil, therefore “flee fornication.”

It should be noted that he says, “Flee fornication.” This sin is not to be awaited; rather, before it comes, we must flee from it by whatever means we can. For it is difficult to escape from it after fornication has hurled its fiery arrows. Therefore he said, “Flee,” and not, “Wait for it,” because once it has gained some access to a person, it is no longer within human power to drive it out.

He then adds the reason why fornication must be fled, saying: [Col. 0153A] “For this reason you ought certainly to flee fornication. Every other sin that a person commits is outside the body, but the one who fornicates sins within his own body.”

There are indeed certain sins which bring no pleasure at all to the flesh, such as homicide. If the hand kills, it does not experience pleasure from the act. There are nevertheless other things in which the flesh takes pleasure, such as when food agrees with the palate, or when something is seen that delights the eyes, or something pleasant is heard by the ears, and the like. Yet all these are called “outside the body” in comparison with fornication, because the one who fornicates sins within his own body: through that act the soul itself passes into carnality, for in it all sensuality consents and cooperates and passes into the flesh.

Or alternatively, according to Ambrose, we should understand “fornication” here as adultery alone: “Flee fornication,” that is, adultery, because every other sin is outside the body, that is, outside one’s wife; but the one who fornicates sins in, that is, against, his own body, that is, against his wife. For on account of the sin of fornication a wife may be separated from her husband, and not on account of anything else. The wife is called the man’s body because, since husband and wife become one body, the man is the head while the woman is a portion of the man within that same body.

Or alternatively, according to the innovation of certain interpreters—and this view seems to continue the statement made earlier, that the fornicator must be expelled from the Church—every sin that any human being commits, that is, one who uses reason, is outside the body, that is, outside the Church, which is the body of Christ its head. For sins committed by one who uses reason are venial, and on account of them he is not separated from the Church. But the one who fornicates sins against his own body, that is, against the Church, of whose body he is a member; for the sin of fornication he is separated from the Church.

Again, the reason why they must flee fornication is that it must be fled because “do you not know that your [107] members are a temple of the Holy Spirit?” That is, the Holy Spirit uses your members when through our hand he gives alms to a poor person, and when through our feet we go to visit the sick. Since the Spirit uses your members in this ministry, do not drive him away from you by fornicating.

Again, they must flee it because the Spirit who is in you through continual indwelling must not be driven away once more. You have the Spirit from God himself, and the giver makes his gift all the more worthy of commendation. For all these reasons do not subject your members to fornication.

Or do you not know that you are not your own masters but belong to God? For one who belongs to another must submit himself to that person’s authority. Truly you are not your own: you were bought, and you are servants of the one who bought you. Nor were you bought for a small price but for a great one, namely, the blood of Christ.

Therefore do not fornicate, but glorify God. To glorify God is to proclaim God’s glory by the purity of one’s life. Whoever sees the righteousness of a righteous person glorifies God, through whose causation and assistance he lives in this way.

“I say, glorify him, and bear God.” To bear God is patiently to endure the burden of every adversity inflicted for God’s sake; and, by the example of one’s patience, to bear God to others, so that, seeing this patience, they may rejoice in suffering insult for the name of Christ (Acts 5:41). “I say, bear God,” not only in your soul but also in your body, so that the purity of your body may be worthy to bear the yoke of Christ.

## CHAPTER VII

> “Now concerning the matters about which you wrote to me: It is good for a man not to touch a woman; but because of fornication, let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband. Let the husband render the debt owed to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband. The woman does not have authority over her own body, but the man does; likewise the man does not have authority over his own body, but the woman does. Do not defraud one another, unless perhaps by mutual consent for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer; and return again to the same union, lest Satan tempt you because of your lack of self-control. But I say this by way of concession, not by command. I wish all of you to be as I myself am. But each person has his own gift from [or: of] God: one in this way, another in that.
>
> “But I say to the unmarried and to widows: It is good for them if they remain as I am. But if they do not exercise self-control, let them marry. For it is better to marry than to burn. But to those who are joined in marriage I command—not I, but the Lord—that a wife should not depart from her husband. But if she departs, let her remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband. And let the husband not dismiss his wife.
>
> “But to the rest I say—I, not the Lord: If any brother has an unbelieving wife, and she consents to live with him, let him not dismiss her. And if any believing woman has an unbelieving husband, and he consents to live with her, let her not dismiss her husband. For the unbelieving husband is sanctified through the believing wife, and the unbelieving wife is sanctified through the believing husband. Otherwise your children would be unclean, but now they are holy [clean]. But if the unbeliever departs, let him depart. The brother or sister is not subject to bondage in such matters. God has called you to peace. For how do you know, woman, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, man, whether you will save your wife? Let each person walk as the Lord has allotted to him, each as God has called him, and as I teach everywhere in all the churches.
>
> “Was anyone called after circumcision? Let him not restore the foreskin. Was anyone called in the foreskin? Let him not be circumcised. Circumcision is nothing, and the foreskin is nothing, but the keeping of God’s commandments. Let each person remain in the calling in which he was called.
>
> “Were you called as a slave? Do not let it concern you; but if you are also able to become free, make use of it all the more. For the one who was called as a slave in the Lord is the Lord’s freedman; likewise the one who was called as a free person is Christ’s slave. You were bought for a price; do not become slaves of human beings. Therefore, brothers, let each person remain with God in the condition in which he was called.
>
> “Concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord, but I give counsel, as one who has obtained mercy from the Lord to be faithful.” [Col. 0155A]

> “I think, therefore, that this is good because of the present necessity, that it is good for a person to remain so. Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek release. Are you released from a wife? Do not seek a wife. But if you take a wife, you have not sinned; and if a virgin marries, she has not sinned. Yet such persons will have tribulation in the flesh, and I spare you.
>
> “But this I say, brothers: the time is short. It remains that those who have wives should be as though they had none; those who weep as though they did not weep; those who rejoice as though they did not rejoice; those who buy as though they did not possess; and those who use this world as though they did not use it. For the form of this world is passing away.
>
> “I wish you to be without anxiety. The unmarried man is anxious about the things of the Lord, how he may please God. But the married man is anxious about the things of the world, how he may please his wife, and he is divided. The unmarried woman and the virgin think about the things of the Lord, so that she may be holy in body and spirit. But the married woman thinks about the things of the world, how she may please her husband.
>
> “I say this for your benefit, not to throw a snare over you, but for what is honorable and what provides an opportunity to attend upon the Lord without impediment [or: to observe the Lord]. But if anyone thinks that he is behaving dishonorably toward his virgin, because she is past the age of marriage, and it ought to be so, let him do what he wishes: he does not sin if she marries. But whoever stands firm in his heart, having no necessity, yet having authority over his own will, and has decided in his heart to preserve his virgin, does well. Therefore both he who gives his virgin in marriage does well, and he who does not give her in marriage does better.
>
> “‘A woman is bound by the law as long as her husband lives; but if her husband should sleep, she is released’ (Rom. 7:2). Let her marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord. But she will be happier if she remains as she is, according to my counsel. I think, however, that I also have the Spirit of God.”

## EXPOSITION

Here the matter of that fornicator comes to an end. But on this occasion, since he had begun to speak about fornication, he appropriately responds to the Corinthians, who had questioned him by letter—specifically, whether marriages should be contracted. Did the necessity of the Christian religion compel them to persist in continence? For among them there were certain people who were excessively religious and said that no one who remained in the act of marriage could be saved. But the Apostle, knowing the weakness of their faith, tolerated this in them—not because he believed that they would be saved in that condition, but so that he might nourish the Church in this way, gradually leading it toward perfection.

The passage is joined as follows: Fornication must be fled; yet not in such a way that we destroy marriage, but so that, in order to avoid fornication, each man should have his own wife. And I say this in response to the matters about which you wrote to me, asking whether it was permitted to marry or necessary to remain continent.

This is my answer: It is indeed good for a man not to touch a woman in that manner of intercourse; nevertheless, in order to avoid fornication, let each man have his own wife and each woman her own husband. This I grant. When he says “his own wife,” he excludes those who are not permitted lawfully to take a wife, such as those who minister at the altar. When he says that a woman should have a husband, he excludes those who are not lawfully joined and do not have husbands, in accordance with the Gospel saying: “The one whom you now have is not your husband” (John 4:18).

Although here he places only one good of marriage, namely avoidance of fornication, there are nevertheless other goods: the intention of offspring, fidelity to the marriage bed—that is, that they not fornicate—and the representation of the true marriage of Christ and the Church. For when God first joined the woman to the man, forming her from the man’s rib, he prefigured the Church being joined to Christ, formed from his side on the cross.

Nor should husband and wife come together without intercourse, as certain false preachers teach, living together like brother and sister. Rather, the husband should render the debt to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband. He knows that a woman does not have authority over her own body, so that she may remain continent if she wishes, but the man does; likewise the man does not have authority over his own body, but the woman does. That is, neither has the power to remain continent without the consent of the other.

Therefore do not defraud one another, that is, let neither withdraw from the other in the marital act, unless this is done by the consent of both—and not continuously, but for a time, and for this purpose, so that you may devote yourselves more purely to prayer. If even those who are lawfully married ought to abstain in order to deserve to pray worthily, how much more ought those who fornicate. And this applies to those who not only pray but whose hands also handle the Lord’s sacred things and administer them to the people.

After the time of prayer has passed, return to the marital act, lest Satan tempt you because you abstain from what is lawful, stimulating you toward what is illicit. And I say this because of your lack of self-control. For I know your weakness, which must be nourished more by indulgence than frightened away by harshness.

Although I have granted you permission to take a wife in order to avoid fornication, I say this by way of concession, lest I seem to compel you to this immoderately. I do not say it by command, as though I were making a precept of the matter. For if it were a command, everyone would already be compelled to take a wife.

[109]

And although I thus show you indulgence, I nevertheless wish all people to be as I myself am, so that all might remain continent as I do. From this statement it is understood that Paul was a virgin—and Ambrose also bears witness to this—but some assert that he had previously had a wife.

They also object here that, when he says, “I wish all to remain continent,” he would destroy marriage. But this is nothing: if all remained continent after Paul’s example, they themselves would compel some among them to enter marriage, lest God’s good institution perish. Augustine also rightly says in his book *On the Good of Marriage*, chapter 10, that if everyone were like Paul, the City of God and the number of the brethren would quickly be filled.

Lest, again, because he had said, “I wish you to be as I am,” they should think that they could not be saved unless they became like him through continence, Paul says against this: Although I say that I wish you to imitate me through continence, each of you has his own gift, sufficient for his salvation—a gift that perhaps I do not possess. And he has this gift from God.

One has it in this way, because he is generous in almsgiving; another in that way, being strong in patience or great in prayer. This is what I say concerning married people.

But I say this to the unmarried—that is, virgins of either sex—and to widows of either sex: it is good for them if they remain continent, as many do, and as I also do. But if they do not exercise self-control—that is, if they do not wish to or are unable to remain continent—I say by way of concession, let them marry. I permit such persons to marry because it is better to marry—not, I do not say, than to fornicate, but, which is a lesser evil, than to burn, that is, to be driven and overcome by the desires of lust.

To the unmarried and widows I speak one matter by way of concession and another by way of counsel. But to those who are joined in marriage I not only speak but give a command—not I, but the Lord—that the wife not depart from her husband. This command was sufficiently familiar, so he stated it incompletely, omitting the exception “unless on account of fornication.”

But if the wife departs from her husband, whether on account of fornication or by mutual agreement for continence, I command her to remain unmarried or to be reconciled to her husband. Likewise, the husband must not dismiss his wife, except for the previously mentioned cause of fornication. Here again he states the command incompletely, because he had already stated the exception.

The meaning is this: the husband must not dismiss his wife except on account of fornication; and if he dismisses her for that reason, he must remain unmarried or be reconciled to his wife.

The book of Blessed Ambrose contains the following explanation: the command concerning the husband is not stated in full in the same way as the command concerning the woman because the wife is the husband’s member and is entirely subject to him. Therefore, if she departs from her husband, she is not permitted to cling to another. But the husband, because he has the wife under him and rules over her everywhere, is permitted, if he has departed from his wife for a just cause, to take another, which is not permitted to the wife.

To these matters I do not give a command from the Lord; I merely speak to the rest—I, not the Lord—that is, by my own authority. This is not because the Lord does not consent, but because I do not find his authority concerning this matter in Scripture.

By “the rest” he means those joined by the law of marriage when one is a believer and the other an unbeliever, and conversely. This, then, is what I say: if any believing brother has an unbelieving wife [110] and the unbelieving woman consents to live with the believing man, he must not dismiss her; he must not despise her because she is unbelieving. Conversely, if a believing woman has an unbelieving husband and he consents to live with her, she must not dismiss her husband.

Truly a believing woman ought not to dismiss an unbelieving husband. For often an unbelieving husband has been sanctified—that is, made a believer—through a believing wife living with him and frequently exhorting him toward the faith.

Or alternatively: the believing woman must not dismiss the unbelieving husband, for the unbelieving husband is sanctified, that is, made clean, in the very act of marriage, through the believing wife—that is, through the power of the faith that the woman possesses.

And again, the believing husband must not dismiss the unbelieving wife. For often an unbelieving woman has been sanctified after receiving the faith through her believing husband, who taught her from it.

Or alternatively: the unbelieving woman is sanctified and made clean in the very intercourse, because the faith of her husband prevails.

They ought not to dismiss one another on account of these matters but to remain together. Otherwise—that is, if one dismisses the other—your children would be unclean, that is, illegitimate rather than legitimate. For if the marriage is dissolved, it is not believed to have been legitimate; and therefore, if they separate, their children are not legitimate and are called unclean. But now, that is, if they live together, the children are holy, that is, they are judged legitimate.

Or alternatively: for this reason do not separate, lest otherwise—that is, if it is done differently—your children be unclean, meaning that they remain in unbelief. For if one of the parents, while an unbeliever, should pass over to the faith, the children would cling to the parent who remained in the former sect, in which the children had been born and accustomed to live. Therefore, for love of the children, it is good that the parents remain together. Your children would indeed be unclean through unbelief, but now, if the parents remain together, they are holy, that is, purified through faith.

I command that the believer, whether man or woman, not separate from the unbeliever. But if the unbeliever, whether husband or wife, departs and does not consent to live with the believer, let the unbeliever depart; the believer is not to follow. I say that the unbeliever should be permitted to depart while the believer remains, because the believing brother or sister is not subject to bondage in matters of this kind if they would destroy the believer’s faith. They ought indeed to serve one another according to the law of marriage, but not against the faith.

I say: if the unbeliever departs, let him depart. Yet I would prefer you to live together in peace. For God called us to faith in peace, that is, so that we would not break the marital bond. If he had not wished us to remain in marriage, we would first have had to be removed from marriage and then called to faith.

It should be noted that there are certain conditions in which God calls a person: namely, those whose practice does not contradict the faith. Thus Peter was called while fishing, and after his call he was permitted to return to fishing. There are other conditions from which God calls a person and to which one is not permitted to return after coming to faith, as Matthew was called from the tax office and did not afterward return to the work of the tax office.

From this it is evident that the faith of Christ does not take away anyone’s former condition, provided that it does not destroy the faith. You must therefore live together in peace, because how do you know, believing woman, whether you will save your unbelieving husband? Or how do you know, believing man, whether you will save your unbelieving wife?

Let each of you walk as God has separately appointed for him: the husband, so that he may rule his wife; the wife, so that she may serve her husband. And how else will you know this unless each of you walks as God called each one, so that if he was called while in marriage, he remains in marriage?

If you live together, it may then be known whether the believer will win the unbeliever; but if you separate, how will this be known? And I say that you should remain together in marriage, just as I teach in all the churches.

He says this because certain people charged him with permitting marriages to the Corinthians, who were excessively carnal, while forbidding them entirely in other churches. Just as he has now said that the state of marriage should not be changed on account of faith, so by analogy he permits people to remain in the other conditions in which they were called, provided that the integrity of the faith is preserved.

The statement “as I teach in all the churches” is joined to the following passage [111] in this way: Let the one who was called while married remain in marriage. And, as I teach in all the churches, if someone was called circumcised—that is, in the rites of the Jews that do not violate the faith—he must not be compelled to restore the foreskin, that is, to adopt the customs of the Gentiles, being forced to eat foods to which he is unaccustomed, even though eating or not eating them neither harms nor benefits him.

Again, if someone was called in the foreskin, that is, in Gentile practice, let him not be circumcised, that is, let him not be compelled to follow Jewish rites. Neither person is to be compelled, because neither circumcision nor the foreskin is anything; that is, neither abstaining from nor eating these foods benefits or harms one’s blessedness. Only the keeping of God’s commandments is sufficient for attaining blessedness.

And just as I say this universally concerning the circumcised and the uncircumcised—that each person who comes to the faith should remain in the condition in which he was called—so let him recognize that this condition is God’s calling. For, as I said above, if God had rejected this condition, he would never have called the person to the faith while he remained in it.

Therefore, if you were called as a slave, do not let it concern you to remain in slavery. But if you can in some way become free, make use all the more of that servitude, because the more you are oppressed now, the more you will be exalted in the future.

I therefore say, make use all the more of servitude, because the one who was called as a slave while remaining in the Lord is a freedman, that is, the Lord’s servant. Likewise, the one who was called free is Christ’s servant. “Slave” and “freedman” signify the same thing here, but he gives the slave the more honorable designation in order to attract him more strongly to himself.

Since both of you are Christ’s servants, do not become slaves of human beings in such a way that Christ’s servitude perishes in you. The reason has already been given: you were bought for the price of Christ’s blood.

And although I say, “Do not become slaves of human beings,” nevertheless each brother—that is, each believer—who was called in slavery or freedom should remain in that condition, and in such a way that he remains with God.

Above, in order to avoid fornication, he granted that each person should have his own will. He also gave the Lord’s command concerning married people, that they should not separate from one another. He gave his own command concerning those in whom one partner was a believer, that the believer should not separate from the unbeliever.

But because he had not given a command to remain in virginity, the Corinthians might ask why he had passed over this matter. Paul responds to them.

The passage is joined as follows: concerning married people I have given the Lord’s command; concerning those in whom one partner is a believer, I have given my command. But concerning virgins I do not establish a command, because I have no command of the Lord on this matter. I do not find in the writings that the Lord commanded all people to persevere in virginity.

Since I have no command of the Lord concerning this, I therefore give the counsel stated above: it is good for virgins if they remain as I am, and so forth. Now he approves this counsel, saying: this counsel of mine ought certainly to be followed. For I give it as one who has obtained mercy from the Lord.

Here he calls mercy both the remission of sins and, especially, his apostleship, both of which he received from the Lord by grace. I have obtained mercy so that I may be faithful in the apostleship entrusted to me, for I faithfully administer the mysteries of faith committed to me by God. Since I am faithful in this, there should be no doubt that my counsel is useful.

And because I am faithful, I therefore judge according to the faith that the counsel stated above is good, namely, that they should remain in virginity if they can, as I do.

It is indeed good because of the present necessity, that is, the necessity which presses daily upon married people in raising children, supporting one another, and so forth. The lasting blessedness of virginity, acquired by the merit of virginity, is a greater good than merely avoiding the hardships of the world. But to his weak hearers he presents the temporal advantage of virginity.

Because they were carnal, he knew that they could be led toward the good more readily by bodily utility than by spiritual utility, since they were not spiritual. I judge this to be good because it truly is so. He expresses it thus: it is good for a person of either sex to remain in this condition, namely, in virginity or continence.

[112] Because he had placed the good of continence so highly, the married might think that they ought to dissolve their marriages and remain continent. Against this Paul says: Although I have said that it is good to pursue chastity, if you are bound to a wife, do not seek release; for conjugal chastity is good. This is the opposing statement.

But because widowhood offers a better form of continence, if you are released from a wife, do not seek another wife but remain continent.

Again, lest the unmarried should say: “It is true that married people ought not to dissolve their marriages; but since we are not bound by the law of marriage, do we sin if we marry?” Paul replies: Although it is good for a person to live in chastity, if you, a man, take a wife, you have not sinned; and if a virgin marries, she has not sinned.

But although virgins may marry without sin, nevertheless, if they marry, they will have the tribulation of the flesh proper to such a condition, that is, the burdens that follow marriage: the labor of pregnancy, the upbringing of children, and similar things.

Married women will indeed have tribulation in the flesh, but I spare you who wish to preserve virginity by directing you toward those things which exclude the tribulations of the flesh and the anxieties mentioned above.

After granting that those who do not wish to remain continent may marry, he determines how they ought to conduct themselves in marriage for the salvation of their souls, saying: Since I have permitted you to take a wife without sin, I therefore determine for you, so that you may remain in marriage without sin, that those who have wives should be as though they had none—that is, serving pleasure no more than they serve God.

Those who weep over worldly losses should weep outwardly while inwardly rejoicing through hope. Those who rejoice in temporal prosperity should inwardly fear spiritually, neither allowing themselves to be corrupted by prosperity nor being broken by adversity.

I say that they ought to conduct themselves in this way, brothers, because this time is short and the end is near. Therefore, since the time is short, what remains—that is, the only thing left for salvation—is that those who have wives should be as though they had none; those who weep as though they did not weep; and those who rejoice as though they did not rejoice.

Whatever exists in this world should, because of the shortness of time, appear rather not to exist than to exist. Those who buy should be as though they did not possess: they should use things as though they could not do without them, but should not take pleasure in them. Those who use this world should act as though they did not use it, doing everything from necessity and nothing from pleasure.

The world must therefore be rejected in this way because “the form of this world is passing away.” The world itself will not pass away, but the forms of its substances will be destroyed: thus gold, losing its redness, will return to earth, and likewise the other things.

Once the impious have been condemned, the form of this world will perish in the conflagration of worldly fires, just as the flood was brought about by the inundation of worldly waters.

And because the form of the world is passing away, I wish you to be without anxiety, lest, burdened by earthly things, you incur the loss of heavenly ones. He says “without anxiety” so that married people may, as far as they can, unload themselves of worldly concerns, while those who remain continent may be free from every worldly anxiety.

And so he explains it, saying: “I do indeed want all to be without anxiety, but nevertheless one person is more free for this, another more hindered. For the one who is without a wife—a virgin or a celibate—is concerned, that is, can be concerned, with the things that are the Lord’s, that is, with what pertains to God. It is also possible for him to be concerned with how he may please the Lord.” Where he says, “He is concerned with the things that are the Lord’s” [Col. 0161C], he means those things that suffice for salvation and without which no one is saved. Where he says, “How he may please God,” he means that highest perfection for which this alone is not sufficient—the thing necessary for salvation—unless he has scattered his possessions among the poor, abandoned the world, and, naked, followed the naked cross.

The one who is without a wife is permitted to do this; but the one who has a wife is compelled by necessity to be concerned with the things of the world, so that he may provide for his wife and children, without whom they cannot continue. He is also concerned with how he may please his wife: by giving necklaces, preparing ornaments, and so he is divided, because for the most part he is drawn into the adornment of his wife and the care of his household; only a very small part of him remains for the service of God.

Just as the celibate man thinks about the things that are the Lord’s [Col. 0161D], so also the woman who is unmarried—that is, a virgin or a widow—thinks about the things that are the Lord’s, so that she may be holy both in body and in spirit, that is, through the integrity of both body and spirit. But the married woman thinks about the things of the world, that is, what is necessary for the household, and how she may please her husband in superfluous matters.

And when I commend to you who practice celibacy the good of celibacy, I say this further—that is, I say it in no other way—than for your benefit: not so that I may throw a snare before you by compelling you to vow virginity, only for you afterward to break that vow. Rather, I say this by exhorting you to what is honorable, that is, free from defilement, and what gives you the opportunity to entreat the Lord without impediment from the tribulation of the flesh [Col. 0162A]. For by this you can preserve your purity, since the tribulation of the flesh, which weighs upon married women, does not hinder you from it.

Perhaps parents might say: “Virgins are certainly permitted to marry, but it is our fault that we do not compel our daughters to remain virgins.” Against this Paul says: “Although I have said that celibate persons have the opportunity to serve the Lord without the impediment that married women have, nevertheless, if a father thinks that he appears shameful—that is, fears being disgraced—concerning his virgin daughter who wishes to marry, and if she is not only grown up but beyond the marriageable age, and if it ought to happen in this way because, unless she marries, disgrace is imminent, let the father do what his daughter wishes. For the father does not sin if the daughter marries, when she prefers marriage to chastity.”

Again, because certain fathers forcibly compel daughters who wish to remain committed to virginity to marry, out of desire for a dowry, so that they may have an increase in their family line, and for reasons of this kind, Paul forbids this from happening. The wording is joined together as follows: “Concerning the father who permits a daughter who wishes to marry, I say that he does not sin. For concerning the one who permits a daughter who wishes to remain a virgin, what else shall I say except that he does well? The man who establishes in his heart”—that is, who makes a considered decision—“the man, I say, who is firm and persevering in this, having no necessity for the reason mentioned above, because he does not fear disgrace on account of his daughter, but having power to carry out his own will because his daughter consents, and who has not only established this but also judged it”—that is, has deliberated in his heart [Col. 0162C], considering the burden of marriage and admiring the dignity of virginity—“if he has judged that he should preserve his virgin, he does well, while he keeps her, willing as she is, in virginity.” Since the man who permits her, willing, to marry does not sin, and he does well who preserves in virginity one unwilling to marry.

Therefore, the man who joins his virgin daughter to a husband does well, provided she wishes it; and the man who does not join her to a husband, when she does not wish it, does well—and does better. As I said concerning virgins: she who marries does not sin, and she who does not marry does better. So also concerning women: the woman who is joined to a husband does not sin, but she who remains in chastity will be more blessed.

This is what he says: “A wife is bound to her husband as long as her husband lives. But if her husband should fall asleep, she is released from the law of her husband. And she is permitted to marry whom she wishes” [Col. 0162D], provided it is “in the Lord,” that is, according to the lawful custom of marriage. But although she is permitted to marry, she will be more perfect if she remains as she is—that is, unmarried—acting according to my advice.

What would those people say about this, if you give such advice? To this Paul replies: “My advice must not be despised, because I think that, just as the other apostles do, I too have the Spirit of God, and through the Spirit the grace of advice.”

## CHAPTER VIII

> “Now concerning things sacrificed to idols, we know that we all possess knowledge. Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up. If anyone thinks that he knows something, he has not yet known how he ought to know. But if anyone loves God, he is known by him. Concerning foods sacrificed to idols, then, we know that an idol is nothing in the world and that there is no God except one. For even if there are those who are called gods, whether in heaven or on earth—for indeed there are many gods and many lords—yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things, and we are in him; and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we are through him. But knowledge is not in everyone. Some, through their consciousness of the idol even to the present, eat the food as idol-sacrifice; and their conscience, being weak, is defiled. Food, however, does not commend us to God. For neither, if we do not eat, will we lack anything, nor, if we eat, will we have an abundance. But see to it that perhaps this freedom of yours does not become a stumbling-block to the weak. For if anyone sees the one who has knowledge reclining in an idol’s shrine, will not his conscience, being weak, be built up so that he eats the idol-sacrifices? And will the weak brother, the brother for whom Christ died, perish through your conscience? But when you sin in this way against the brothers and strike their weak conscience, you sin against Christ. Therefore, if food causes my brother to stumble, I will never eat meat, so that I may not cause my brother to stumble.”

## EXPOSITION

There was an error among the Corinthians concerning the use of foods. Some, knowing that everything was clean, ate everything with sound faith. But those whose faith was weak, when they saw people wiser than themselves eating idol-sacrifices, believed that they were doing so in worship of the idol, and said: “It is good that we return to the idol-sacrifices. For if they did not understand that an idol is something, those who are wiser among us would not eat what had been sacrificed to idols.”

Although some of them were thus mistaken, they nevertheless did not want the wiser people to abstain from those foods, and so they struck the consciences of the weak. Concerning this sort of matter Paul begins here, saying: “You questioned me by letter about marriages, but you did not ask me anything about things sacrificed to idols. Nor was it necessary, because we know”—that is, you know and I know; and since we know equally, it was not necessary for you to ask me—and he says this ironically.

“We certainly know concerning these matters,” he says, “because we possess not only this knowledge but whatever knowledge there is.” He now disapproves of this knowledge by means of the evil that follows from it, saying: “Certainly we know, but this knowledge is not sufficiently praiseworthy, because it puffs you up”—that is, it makes you proud against weak brothers, toward whom you do not act out of love but badly—“because love builds up,” nourishing virtues toward the completion of perfection. Therefore your knowledge puffs you up because it is not tempered with love.

He has disapproved of their knowledge on account of the evil of pride that follows it; now he addresses the knowledge itself, showing that they are ignorant precisely in the matter in which they think themselves knowledgeable. “Although I have called you knowledgeable, if anyone thinks that he knows something, like you, without love, that person certainly has not understood how he ought to know” [Col. 0164A]. For the proper manner is that knowledge be tempered with love.

The opposing statement is this: “The one who is puffed up has not understood the proper measure of knowledge. But if anyone loves God”—because he possesses love of his neighbor—“that person is known and approved by God.”

He now defines their knowledge, showing in what respect it should be praised and in what respect rejected, saying: “We know that the one who loves God is known by God. Concerning foods sacrificed to idols, we know”—that is, you who are firm in faith know with me—“that an idol is nothing in the world,” that is, in the creation of the world. God indeed created the stone or wood from which an idol is formed, but he did not create the idol’s form. That form did not come from God’s creation in such a way that it should be called an idol; rather, it came from the craftsman.

You also know that there is no God except one alone; hence it is clear that an idol is not God. Truly, there is only one God. For even if there are those who are called gods, whether in heaven, such as angels, or on earth, such as apostles, according to the saying: “I said: You are gods” (Ps. [XXVXI], 1), it is right to say that they are called gods, since, in a certain sense, there are many gods in truth and many lords among the gods: in heaven, archangels rule over angels; on earth, apostles rule over martyrs.

Although there are indeed many gods, for us there is one God, the Father, from whom all things were created in the beginning, and we, having been created, subsist in him through his governance; and there is one God who is Lord, Jesus Christ. And he rightly added this concerning the unity of Christ with the Father. The Corinthians were hesitating over this matter: through whom were all things made? For the Father established all things in the Son, and we exist in God through Christ as mediator.

But although in these matters we possess sound knowledge, our knowledge is not equally perfect in everyone [Col. 0164C]. Truly, it is not in everyone. Some, whose faith was not whole and whose consciousness of the idol remained even to the present because they believed that the idol ought to be venerated, eat as though it were an idol-sacrifice—that is, what was sacrificed to an idol in worship of the idol.

By doing this their conscience is defiled, since it is weak through the imperfection of their faith. The food they eat defiles them because they see us eating it, but that food does not commend us to God. We will never be dearer to God because of this food. Therefore we ought not to offend in this matter.

Truly, this food does not commend us to God: for if we do not eat it, we will not thereby fall away from God; nor, if we eat it, will we thereby abound in goodness. And since abstaining hinders nothing and eating helps nothing, see, therefore, that perhaps this freedom of yours may cause harm.

It is indeed permitted according to your sound faith, but it is not permitted in such a way that through it a stumbling-block is created for weak brothers, who, by observing us eating idol-sacrifices, sin because they do so in worship of the idol. For this reason I say that a stumbling-block must not be created: if someone who does not have sound faith sees the one who possesses knowledge reclining in an idol’s shrine—that is, in a place where an idol is sacrificed to—namely, the one who has knowledge that every creature of God is clean and is not defiled because of the idol, provided his faith is sound, will not the weak person, seeing this, have his weak conscience encouraged by your example to eat idol-sacrifices in worship of the idol?

And so, through his weak conscience, the weak brother for whose sake Christ died will perish through your knowledge, since he eats on the strength of your example [Col. 0165A].

Nor should you regard this as a small matter, because he is a brother for whom Christ died, and for whose sake you are unwilling to give up a little food that contributes nothing to you. Since the brother perishes through your knowledge, you sin against the brother. By thus sinning against the brothers and striking their weak conscience with your food, you sin against Christ, who died for the weak.

Therefore—that is, because to sin against a brother is to sin against Christ—“if food causes my brother to stumble, I will never eat meat.”

It is indeed true that in eternity no one will use food of the flesh; but he says this in order to deter them more strongly from causing their brother to stumble, when he says: “If food of the flesh were to be eaten eternally, I would reject it so that I might not place a stumbling-block before my brother. For this reason I would not eat meat forever.” Not only so that I might not make my brother sin, but so that I might not scandalize him—that is, at least distress him inwardly.

## CHAPTER IX

> “Am I not free? Am I not an apostle? Have I not seen Jesus Christ our Lord? Are you not my work in the Lord? And if I am not an apostle to others, yet surely I am to you; for you are the seal of my apostleship in the Lord. My defense before those who question me is this: Do we not have the right to eat and drink? Do we not have the right to lead about with us a woman who is a sister, as do the other apostles, and the brothers of the Lord, and Cephas? Or do only I and Barnabas not have the right to do this? Who ever serves as a soldier at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard and does not eat its fruit? Who tends a flock and does not eat the milk of the flock? Do I say these things according to human judgment? Or does the law not also say this? For it is written in the law of Moses: ‘You shall not muzzle an ox while it is threshing’ (Deut. XXV, 4; 1 Tim. V, 18). Is God concerned about oxen? Or does he certainly say this for our sake? For it was written for our sake, because the one who plows ought to plow in hope, and the one who threshes in hope of receiving the fruit. If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great matter if we reap your material things? If others share in your authority, why not we rather? But we have not used this authority. Rather, we endure everything, so that we may not cause any hindrance to the gospel of Christ. Do you not know that those who work in the sanctuary eat what comes from the sanctuary, and that those who serve at the altar share with the altar? So also the Lord ordained that those who proclaim the gospel should live from the gospel. But I have used none of these things. I have not written this so that it may be done in my case. For it would be better for me to die than for anyone to deprive me of my glory. For if I preach the gospel, there is no glory for me, since necessity is laid upon me. Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel. For if I do this willingly, I have a reward; but if unwillingly, a stewardship has been entrusted to me. What, then, is my reward? That, in preaching the gospel, I may offer the gospel without cost, so as not to abuse my authority in the gospel. For although I was free from all, I made myself the servant of all, so that I might win the more. To the Jews I became as a Jew, so that I might win the Jews; to those under the law, as though I were under the law—although I myself was not under the law—so that I might win those under the law; to those without the law, as though I were without the law—although I was not without the law of God but was in the law of Christ—so that I might win those without the law. To the weak I became weak, so that I might win the weak. I became all things to all, so that I might save all. I do everything for the sake of the gospel, so that I may become a participant in it. Do you not know that those who run in the stadium all run, but one receives the prize? Run in such a way that you may obtain it. Everyone who competes in the contest exercises self-control in everything. They do this to receive a perishable crown, but we an imperishable one. I therefore run in this way, not as though into uncertainty; I fight in this way, not as though beating the air. Rather, I discipline my body and bring it into servitude, lest, after preaching to others, I myself should become disqualified.”

## EXPOSITION

He again dissuades them from causing a brother to stumble, saying: “Although your faith is sound, you ought nevertheless to abstain from foods by which the weakness of your brother is offended, just as you see me doing. Although I have the right to receive material things from the Corinthians to whom I preach, I do not wish to provide a stumbling-block to their weakness.”

He first states that he could receive from them by right of preaching, saying: “I could indeed receive material things from you if I wished. For am I not free? Do I not have the freedom that the other apostles have, who receive expenses from their preaching?”

He says this because those false apostles had turned his good into evil, saying: “He does not receive what is necessary from you because he knows that he is not an apostle. For only those who lived with Christ on earth are apostles; but this man did not see him.”

“Truly I am free, like the others. Am I not an apostle?” they would say: “No, because you did not see Christ.”

Against this Paul replies: “I am certainly an apostle. Have I not seen Christ our Lord?” He saw him at the hour of his calling, when it was said to him: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts IX, 4). He saw him again when, as he was praying in the temple, it was said to him: “You will carry my name among the gentiles,” and so forth (Acts XXIII, 11).

“I am an apostle because I saw Christ. I am also an apostle for this reason: are you not my work”—that is, the work of my apostleship—“and this in the Lord, whose grace works in me and in you, without any merit of ours? You are indeed my work in the Lord, because even if”—that is, although—“I am not an apostle to others”—which of course I am—“yet I am an apostle to you. Indeed, especially to you. For you are the seal of my apostleship,” that is, the graces of God have been stamped and expressed in you through the ministry of my apostleship [Col. 0167A].

Therefore you are the proof of my apostleship, and all this is in the Lord, because both my apostleship and the graces given to you have come through the mercy of God.

He said this because the Corinthians had received various graces, such as healings and kinds of tongues, and they preferred that grace to others, although it was the least, as he himself will say. And because, through the graces you have received, you are the seal of my apostleship, this is my defense: through this I am defended and proved to be an apostle before those who question me—that is, who doubt whether I am an apostle—because I did not live bodily with Christ.

After proving that he is an apostle, he proves that by the right of apostleship he can receive material things from those to whom he ministers spiritual things, saying: “Since, as has been proved, I am an apostle, do we not have the right to eat and drink among those to whom we preach? And do we not have the right to lead about with us a woman”—that is, to take women with us everywhere—“who may minister to us from their material possessions?”

He says “a woman,” not in the work of the flesh, but a sister in faith and devout conduct. The apostles took this practice of having faithful women in their company from the Lord Jesus, who therefore wished women to live together with him, in order to show that he came to redeem women just as he redeemed men. Some were therefore doubtful about this because a woman was the cause of the whole of humanity’s destruction.

“Can we not,” I ask, “do this as the other apostles can? Can we not do it also as the brothers of the Lord can—namely, James of Jerusalem and Judas Zelotes, who is called the brother of James—and as Cephas can, that is, Peter, who certainly had women in his company?”

And since all of them have this right, or do only I and Barnabas, who labors with me in the gospel, not have the right to do this—that is, to receive from our subjects as the others do?

He proves that receiving these things is lawful both by human reasoning and through the old law and the gospel, saying: “Truly we ought to do this lawfully. For who ever serves as a soldier in the army while living on his own wages? The law of military service does not allow this. And who plants a vineyard and does not eat its fruit? And who tends a flock and does not eat from the milk of the flock?”

But do I say this according to human judgment—that is, according to human reasoning—and prove that I ought to receive material things from those subject to me? I also say this through the law: does the law not also say this? It certainly does, because it is written in the law of Moses: “You shall not muzzle an ox while it is threshing” (Deut. XXV, 4; 1 Tim. V, 18), in the threshing floor; rather, it shall eat from what it threshes.

A worldly-minded person might say: “What does this have to do with you? This command was given concerning an ox, not a human being.”

Paul replies: “Is God concerned about oxen in the law, so that he should have placed a command there concerning them? God is certainly not concerned about oxen in this matter. But does he not surely say this for our sake? Indeed, for our sake. For these other things also were written for our sake: namely, that the one who plows ought to plow in hope of receiving material fruits, and that the one who threshes threshes in hope of receiving fruits.”

He calls it “plowing” when someone uproots the thorns of unbelief from the good soil of faith and cultivates the unbeliever. He calls it “threshing” when, after people are already in the Church and have received the faith, the preacher threshes them, separating the grain from the chaff, the good from the bad. Both the one who plows and the one who threshes deserve to receive material things.

He proves the same point again by other arguments, saying: “If we preachers have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great matter”—that is, should it be considered of no value—“if we reap your material things from you? And if others”—that is, the false teachers—“share in your possessions, so that they exercise their authority over what belongs to you as they please, why not we rather, who minister sound teaching?”

After proving that he is an apostle and that by the law of ministry he has the authority to receive from them, he finally comes to the point for which he began: “Although we are apostles and have authority by virtue of our apostleship, we have nevertheless not used this authority in order to receive anything from you” [Col. 0168B].

They might say: “Perhaps you had no need.”

“We certainly have need,” he replies, “but nevertheless we endure everything: hunger, thirst, and nakedness. For this reason, so that we may not cause any hindrance to the gospel of Christ,” that is, so that we may not appear in any way to impede the good of our preaching.

Paul feared several obstacles in this matter. If he received from those who were less greedy, they might prefer not to hear the preaching rather than give material things. Moreover, if Paul received, the false apostles would likewise receive. Although they opposed Paul, in this and in certain other matters they followed him, not daring to do what Paul did not accept. If they had an opportunity to receive on Paul’s example, then, because they were gluttonous, they would absolve them from great sins in exchange for a few foods, and on this pretext the Corinthians themselves would sin more securely.

“We do not use our authority, so that we may not cause a stumbling-block.”

For this reason we do not abandon the claim that it is lawful for us. For do you not know that those who work in the sanctuary—that is, in the work of the temple, such as in the curtains or in some repair—eat what belongs to the sanctuary? The sanctuary is so called as though it were a secret place behind the altar.

And do you not know that the priests who serve at the altar take a share with the altar? One portion was burned upon the altar, and another was reserved as food for the priests.

Or, alternatively, let us understand the preceding statement as referring to the gentiles: “Do you not know that those who work in the sanctuary of the gentiles eat what belongs to the sanctuary, and that those who serve the altar of the Jews share with the altar?”

In the same way—that is, according to the same arrangement—the Lord ordained that those who proclaim the gospel should live from preaching, when he says in the gospel: “Eating and drinking what they have” (Luke X, 7), and so forth.

And although the Lord ordained this, I have not used any of these things, whether food, drink, or clothing.

They might say: “Paul is acting craftily, speaking in this way so that what he previously did not accept simply, he may now receive in double measure.”

Paul replies: “Although I write in this way, I have not written these things so that they may thereafter be done in my case”—that is, so that what I did not begin before I may now receive in multiplied form. For this reason I neither did so nor now wish it to be done in my case, because it is better for me to die, not to mention endure want, than for anyone to deprive me of my glory”—that is, of the reward I expect from the gospel.

For if I were to preach with offense to my brother, I would certainly deprive my merit of its glory.

Or it may be understood in this way: “It is better for me to die than that I should die now.” For now I die through many tribulations, but I would prefer to die in even greater poverty than for anyone to deprive me of my glory.

Truly, I must fear that my glory be emptied. For if I preach the gospel in this way—that is, with offense to my brother, out of desire to receive expenses from you—then I have no glory, but my reward is lost.

Truly, glory is not owed to me, because necessity—that is, want—presses upon me and compels me to preach, so that I may thereby obtain support. Indeed, necessity presses upon me, for if I do not preach the gospel, I have woe—that is, the distress of want, specifically hunger and nakedness.

If I preach out of necessity, I have no glory. But if I do this willingly—that is, solely by my own will and not out of desire for expenses—then I have a reward for my gospel.

Or alternatively, this may be referred to what he said above: “I prefer to die rather than for my glory to be emptied.”

Someone might say: “If your gospel were a matter such that, if it were not done, we would not fall away, or such that, if it were done, we would not abound for the better—as, for example, eating idol-sacrifices with sound faith—one could believe that your glory would perish if you preached with offense to your brother. But since your gospel is a matter of such great dignity that through it people are saved, it is not credible that your glory from the gospel should perish because of the offense of a weak brother.”

“It will certainly be emptied,” Paul says. “For if I preach only, and do not turn away from offending my brother, I will have no glory merely for preaching. For there is no merit in preaching in such a way that we do not take care to avoid the offense of our brother.”

Truly, it is not much simply to preach. For the necessity of preaching rests upon me by an office entrusted to me, and the necessity of my office truly compels me to preach. For woe—that is, condemnation—is mine if I do not preach.

From this it is clear that preaching is not of such a nature that its glory cannot perish because of the offense of a brother. If I preach only out of the necessity of my ministry, I have no glory. But if I do this willingly, not so that I may offend my brother out of desire for expenses, then I have a reward from my gospel.

But if I do this unwillingly—that is, compelled by necessity and disregarding the offense of my brother—it is indeed true that a stewardship of God’s gifts has been entrusted to me. That is, God does not dispense his graces any less on account of my sin; nevertheless, I receive no reward.

From this statement—“to me, unwilling and sinning through the offense of my brother, a stewardship of God’s graces has been entrusted”—the saints receive authority for the principle that, although the minister may be bad, the gifts of God dispensed through him are not diminished on account of his sin, just as they are not increased on account of his righteousness.

And because I said, “If I do this willingly, then I have a reward through my will,” let us now say what my reward is—that is, what sort of will must I have for a reward to come to me.

My will must be such that, while preaching the gospel, I may offer it—that is, establish the gospel and lay its foundation—without accepting expenses from the Corinthians, on account of which they would be offended. I do this without expense so that I may not abuse—that is, misuse—the authority granted to me in the gospel.

I have the power to receive expenses from the gospel, but if I offend my brother in this matter, I misuse that authority.

It should be believed that I offer the gospel without expense so that the weakness of my hearers may not be offended. For, even more than the matter of expenses, although I was free from all and owed nothing to any of them, I made myself the servant of all, so that I might win the greater number.

And since I bore the yoke of servitude under everyone for their benefit, it should be believed that I abstain from expenses, fearing the offense of the brother for whose winning I made myself a servant.

Truly, I made myself the servant of all: of Jews, Samaritans, gentiles, and weak brothers.

He explains this as follows: “To the Jews I became as a Jew,” accommodating myself to their rites and abstaining from meats from which they abstained, so that I might win the Jews, who would more readily listen to me because I did not reject their rites.

To those who are under the law—that is, the Samaritans, who possess the five books of Moses but do not have the prophets—I became as though I were under the law, although I myself was not under the law. I did this so that in this way I might win those who were under the law—that is, the Samaritans.

The Samaritans are those whom the king of the Assyrians, after the captivity of the children of Israel, placed in the places of Samaria to inhabit them. They are of Persian origin (2 Kings XVII, 24). They accepted the five books of Moses, although God afflicted them with many tribulations because they had unlawfully seized the land of his people Israel [Col. 0170C].

To those who were without the law—that is, to the gentiles—I became as though I were without the law, sharing their foods and asserting that God had chosen them, although I was not without the law of God but was in the law of Christ. I became such in order to win the gentiles who were without the law.
