I also became weak to the weak brothers, abstaining from lawful foods so that I might not create a stumbling-block for their weakness and might thus win the weak.

And why should I enumerate every particular? I became all things to all: perfect to the perfect, and so in each case, so that I might save all.

I do all these things for the sake of establishing the gospel. If I did not do so, it would be emptied because of the stumbling-blocks of the brothers. I do this for the sake of the gospel so that I may become a participant in it—that is, so that I may receive a share in the reward that the gospel attests to and promises to the faithful.

Here he applies everything that he has introduced about himself. It is as though he were saying: “Just as I became all things to all for the sake of the gospel, so you also should bear with the weakness of the brothers, so that you may become participants in the promised blessedness.”

I said that you must abstain from lawful things for the sake of weak brothers, just as I, your apostle, abstain from lawful things so that I may not cause a hindrance to the gospel of Christ. I do all this so that I may deserve to receive what I await.

He introduces the example of those who, in order to receive a temporal crown, abstain from everything that might hinder them from receiving the crown.

“For do you not know that those who run in the stadium all run, but one receives the prize”—that is, the crown or reward of the race? A stadium is a distance of two hundred and twenty-five paces, so much as Hercules ran in a single breath without stopping to breathe. It is called a stadium from *stando* (“to stand”), because one stands at the end of the race.

Since those who run in the stadium apply themselves attentively to receiving the prize, so run, then, by abstaining from everything that can hinder you, so that all of you may obtain the prize of eternal happiness. For if all run here, where only one receives the prize, you ought to run much more attentively where all of you will receive an eternal prize.

You ought indeed to run in this way, abstaining from everything that might hinder you. For everyone who competes in the contest—that is, in the race—abstains from everything that impedes his running.

Those who run in the stadium thus abstain so that they may receive a perishable crown; but we are to receive an imperishable one. Therefore we ought to abstain much more, in proportion to the greater dignity of the crown with which we will be rewarded.

And because I await an incorruptible crown, “I run in this way, not as though into uncertainty.” The person who runs into uncertainty is the one who acts badly at one time and well at another. When he acts well, he hopes that he will receive the prize; but when he acts badly, he loses confidence.

He calls “running” doing good without the impediment of the tribulation that has been brought upon him. He calls “fighting” the time when tribulation is inflicted and he resists bravely.

“I fight in this way, not as though beating the air,” so that what I say well I do not fail to complete in my actions. For the person who speaks words in vain is said to beat only the air.

Or it may be understood thus: “Not as though beating the air,” that is, not casting my blows in vain, as when someone fights an enemy but, after throwing a blow, does not touch the enemy and is said to beat the air. But I crush the enemy; I do not beat the air. Rather, I discipline my body, that is, I restrain the desires of the flesh, and thus bring the body into servitude, so that the flesh not only does not resist but also serves the spirit.

For this reason I discipline it and bring it into servitude, lest what could happen should happen: that, after preaching to others, I myself should become disqualified and liable to condemnation.

Where he says “lest perhaps,” he rightly shows that God chooses his own in such a way that he does not compel them, lest he destroy freedom of choice in them; for if they should wish to fall again, they are able to do so.

## CHAPTER X
«For I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea (Exod. 13:21). And all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them; and the rock was Christ. Yet God was not pleased with most of them, for they were struck down in the wilderness (Num. 26:65). These things happened as an example for us, so that we might not desire evil things, as they also desired them (Ps. 105:11); [Col. 0172A] nor become idolaters, as some of them did, as it is written: “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play” (Exod. 32:6). Nor let us commit fornication, as some of them fornicated, and twenty-three thousand fell in one day (Num. 25:1). Nor let us test Christ, as some of them tested him, and perished by serpents (Num. 21:6). Nor murmur, as some of them murmured, and perished by the destroyer. All these things happened to them as an example; but they were written for our correction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come. Therefore, whoever thinks that he is standing must take care lest he fall. Let no temptation seize you except what is human. But God is faithful, and he will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can bear; rather, with the temptation he will also provide a way through, so that you may be able to endure. Therefore, my beloved, flee from the worship of idols. I speak as to prudent people: judge for yourselves what I say. The cup of blessing that we bless—is it not a participation in the blood of Christ? And the bread that we break—is it not a participation in the body of the Lord? Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body: for we all partake of the one bread and of the one cup. Consider Israel according to the flesh: are not those who eat the sacrifices participants in the altar? What, then, do I mean? That something sacrificed to idols is anything, or that an idol is anything? But the things that the nations sacrifice, “they sacrifice to demons and not to God” (Deut. 32:17). [Col. 0172C] I do not want you to become partners with demons. You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons; you cannot participate in the table of the Lord and the table of demons. Are we provoking the Lord to jealousy? Are we stronger than he? Everything is lawful for me, but not everything is beneficial. Everything is lawful for me, but not everything builds up. Let no one seek his own good, but that of another. Whatever is sold in the marketplace, eat, asking no questions for the sake of conscience. “The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness” (Ps. 25:1). If someone among the unbelievers invites you to dinner and you wish to go, eat whatever is set before you, asking no questions for the sake of conscience. But if someone says, “This has been sacrificed to idols,” do not eat it, for the sake of the one who disclosed it, [Col. 0172D] and for the sake of conscience. I mean conscience—not your own, but the other’s. For why should my freedom be judged by another’s conscience? If I partake with thanksgiving, why am I slandered for what I give thanks for? “Whether you eat or drink, or whatever else you do, do everything for the glory of God” (Col. 3:17). Be without offense to Jews and gentiles and the Church of God, just as I please everyone in everything, seeking not my own benefit but that of the many, so that they may be saved.»

## Exposition

Since Paul had said, “I chastise my body,” and so forth, lest I myself should become reprobate, someone might ask: Why do you labor so greatly lest you be rejected? For it should not be thought that God lightly rejects us, to whom he has granted baptism, faith, and the other sacraments of the Church, even if we have sometimes acted unjustly. Against this objection Paul proves that the sacraments contribute nothing to salvation if good works are absent. The fathers of the Old Testament possessed in figure the same things that we possess in reality; but because they acted wickedly, the sacraments did not benefit them. Thus they will not benefit us either, if our works are evil.

The text is joined in this way: “For this reason I labor so greatly, lest I become reprobate. I see that the sacraments I have received are not sufficient for me if works are lacking, just as they were not sufficient for our fathers under the Old Covenant, because they acted wickedly.” To make this clear, he says: “I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that our fathers”—that is, the Jews, who preceded us in the worship of God and instructed us, and whose figures brought forth the reality that is ours—“all, without exception, were under the cloud.” That cloud, which was placed between the Egyptians and the Jews as far as the Red Sea, signified divine mercy, which protects catechumens until they come to baptism.

“And all our fathers passed through the Red Sea”; so also we all pass through baptism. “And all our fathers were baptized into Moses,” that is, they were baptized in Moses’ governance: they advanced under the cloud, which separated them from the Egyptians, and through the passage of the sea. Paul says “baptized,” although this word was not then spoken of them, nor was that sea the reality of baptism, since it was only a figure. He uses the name of the signified reality for the sign itself, because just as they were protected under the leadership of Moses, so we are protected much more fully by Christ as our leader in baptism. In baptism he forgives our sins and strengthens our free will, so that it can resist the devil’s evil persuasion.

For this reason he also says “they were baptized”: just as baptism is effective for our salvation, so the passage through the sea would have been effective for them if, believing, they had obeyed God’s commands.

“And all our fathers ate the same food,” namely, manna. I call it spiritual food, that is, signifying the spiritual food of the body and blood of Christ. It is called spiritual because what the food of Christ’s body and blood accomplishes in us, that manna would likewise have accomplished for them unto salvation, if they had persevered in goodness—not because it was anything other than manna.

“And all drank the same drink,” namely, the water flowing from the rock. I call it spiritual drink because it prefigured the drink of Christ’s blood and would have had the same efficacy for them in faith, if they had been good. They did not drink from it only once, but continually: they drank from the rock, that is, from the water flowing from the rock that followed them, because wherever they went in the wilderness, that water followed them. I call the rock spiritual because it signified the spiritual rock, Christ.

Why did they drink not once but continually? Because it is not sufficient for us, who fall daily into sin, to receive Christ’s blood only once. Just as we fall daily, so we continually need its medicine. But that rock from which the water flowed was Christ, from whose side flowed the water of our regeneration.

Although our fathers had so many sacraments, God was nevertheless not pleased with most of them [Col. 0174A], because by sinning they made themselves unworthy of the sacraments that had been given. Truly, most of them did not please God, for they were struck down in the wilderness, provoking God’s anger against themselves by their evil conduct.

These things just mentioned happened not only on their account, but also as an example for us. In all the foregoing, the reality of the sacraments given to us through Christ was prefigured. They happened as an example for us so that we might not desire evil things, as they also frequently desired evil things.

Here Paul inserts himself among them in order to draw them back more effectively, making their sins his own through his sympathy. He now recalls certain sins of the Jews that he saw among the Corinthians, saying: “Do not be desirous of evil things; specifically, do not become idolaters.” Here he separates himself from those with whom he did not agree in idolatry, saying, as it were: “Do not become idolaters, as some of them were.”

The Corinthians were idolaters because either they ate food sacrificed to idols while venerating the idol, or, by failing to care whether they offended a brother through eating such food, they became the cause of a weak brother’s becoming an idolater and were thus liable to accusation of idolatry.

Some of the Jews were idolaters, as it is written of them in Exodus: “The Jewish people sat down to eat and drink” the things they had sacrificed to the molten calf, “and afterward rose up to play” (Exod. 32:6), that is, to dance and perform other acts before the idol. Or “they rose up to play” means that they rose to worship the idol. This appeared as play and mockery in the case of those who had been instructed by so many miracles. [Col. 0174C]

“Nor let us commit fornication, as some of them fornicated with the Midianites, and therefore twenty-three thousand fell” (Num. 25:1). There was fornication among the Corinthians, as in the case of the man who had taken his father’s wife, in whose offense the others also shared by their consent.

“Nor let us test Christ, as some of them tested him,” saying: “Can God prepare a table in the wilderness?” (Ps. 77:19). They perished by serpents poisoning them—or, according to the transmitted reading, *venenantibus*—until Moses raised up a bronze serpent on a piece of wood. Any Jew who looked at it on that day was safe from the serpents’ bite. That serpent signified Christ according to his humanity, as the Gospel itself bears witness: “Just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up” (John 3:14).

The Corinthians tested God when they doubted the resurrection, as though God could not do whatever he wished in his goodness.

“Nor let us murmur”—which the Corinthians certainly did, since some of them said that Paul was not an apostle, and similar things—“as some of the Jews murmured,” such as the sons of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram. They said that Moses had not consecrated Aaron as priest at God’s command, but for the exaltation of his own family; and therefore they perished by the destroyer, that is, by the striking angel.

It should be noted that, because the Jews were inexperienced and unable to grasp spiritual realities, it was appointed for them to serve God through carnal things. Just as, when they offended in their carnal service, they were punished according to the flesh, so we, to whom spiritual realities have been given, will be punished according to the soul if we offend in them.

Not only did the sacraments mentioned above precede us as an example, but all these things—the sins and the punishments of sins—also happened to them as an example for us. If those who remained in the shadow were condemned for transgressing the shadow, how much more will we be condemned if we sin against the reality itself? These things happened to them as an example for us, and they were also written for our correction, so that we might be corrected through their examples.

I say “for our correction,” because the ends of the ages have come upon us. However long these ages may last, we nevertheless have their ends, because the rites given through the Gospel are the final rites. They will not come to an end so long as the world exists.

Or it may be understood this way: “The ends of the ages have come upon us” because all worldly existence has ended—that is, the carnality of the ancient rites—and the reality itself has been handed over to us. Since the earlier sacraments did not benefit our fathers on account of sin, these things have been written for our instruction.

“Therefore”—that is, for this reason—let the one among you who thinks that he is standing, namely, one who rightly understands God’s creatures and thinks that everything is permitted to him, take care lest he fall through causing offense to his brother.

Lest the Corinthians be disturbed by the words “take care lest he fall,” since they knew that even the righteous person falls seven times a day, Paul specifies what sort of fall he means, saying: “Let each one take care lest he fall in such a way that no temptation seize you except what is human,” that is, the delight of sin that comes from the necessity of the flesh, namely, a venial temptation.

As far as you are concerned, see that you act accordingly, because God is faithful and true in his promises and abandons his faithful in nothing. He will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can bear. For he arranges tribulations according to what he sees to be each person’s strength or weakness.

Nor will he merely prevent you from being tempted beyond measure; he will also provide you with an outcome together with the temptation, that is, both an increase of the virtue by which you may persevere and an increase of the tribulation. He will do this, I say, so that you may be able to endure and not fail under tribulation.

“For this reason”—that is, because the person who is standing must take care lest he fall, and because God is present to extend his hand—“flee from the worship of idols.” If you do this, then you will be especially beloved by me.

By “flee from the worship of idols,” Paul means both the weak, who ate food sacrificed to idols while venerating the idol, and those who, although sound in faith, nevertheless caused their brothers’ weakness to be corrupted.

And in order that you may flee from the worship of idols, I am about to speak of a subtle matter. I speak to you not as simple people but as prudent people; therefore judge for yourselves—that is, examine within yourselves, as carefully as you can, what I am telling you.

Let us briefly gather the substance of the argument outside the text itself: You must flee from the worship of idols because, just as the person who participates in Christ’s body and blood becomes, in a certain sense, one with Christ, so the person who participates in an idol by eating food sacrificed to it is incorporated into the devil.

Let us now explain the text itself. You must flee from the worship of idols because the cup—that is, Christ’s blood—is the cup of blessing through which we receive the blessings of graces. Through Christ’s blood, if we receive it worthily, we are both freed from former sins and strengthened against those that are to come.

We bless this cup by praising it because there has never been another cup of this kind, one that both frees us from sins and strengthens us so that we do not sin thereafter.

Or “the cup of blessing” means the cup that God himself blesses and consecrates, and which we bless through our ministry. God accomplishes this through the priest as minister.

Is this cup, then, not a participation in Christ’s blood? That is: are we not united to Christ and conformed to him through the blood we receive?

And the bread—that is, Christ’s true body, which is received under the appearance of bread. I call it the bread that we break on the altar, so that although what is one in reality cannot be divided, by dividing it we may signify that we, who are distinct persons, become one in Christ.

Is this bread that we break not a participation in the Lord’s body? That is: do we not receive God within us through this body and incorporate him into ourselves?

For this reason God instituted this sacrifice in two substances, namely, body and blood: through the flesh handed over on the altar, he showed that he redeems our flesh, which through these sacraments will eventually be transferred into incorruption; and through the blood that he gives, he indicated that he likewise redeemed our soul.

To suggest the soul, since he could not use an incorporeal thing, he fittingly represented the soul through blood, which is said to be the seat of the soul. He did not distribute the sacrifice into two substances so that we should understand them as separate parts of Christ. Whoever receives only the blood or only the body receives the whole Christ; whoever receives both does not receive more through both than through either one.

Just as this body is truly Christ’s flesh under the appearance of bread, so it is worn down, diminished, and divided into parts according to appearance, while in reality it remains incorruptible, indivisible, and incapable of diminution.

Truly, through receiving Christ’s blood and body we are united to Christ, because although we are many, we are one bread. Just as different grains pass into the unity of one loaf, so we are united by faith, hope, and charity.

We are also one body, many in number but joined according to the diversity of members that serve one another in the unity of love. We are all one bread and one body, participating in one bread and one cup—that is, in Christ’s body and blood—through which we are united with Christ by incorporating him into ourselves.

Now let us explain what follows according to Ambrose.

“O Israel”—that is, faithful soul, which gazes upon God—“what I have just shown you spiritually, see also happening according to the flesh”: through carnal participation in food sacrificed to idols, one participates in the devil.

Are not those who eat sacrifices offered to the devil participants in the devil’s altar? That is: do they not participate in the devil by sharing in what is sacrificed upon the idol’s altar? Just as this participation occurs spiritually, so it cannot be denied that it occurs in carnal things as well.

Since I say that those who eat what has been sacrificed to an idol participate in the devil, what am I saying? Am I thought to mean that what is sacrificed to idols is something other than what it was before it was sacrificed? Far be it from me to appear to say that an idol is anything other than stone or wood, or whatever material it was made from!

When I speak of what is sacrificed, I mean that a person is united to the devil through it. I certainly do not mean that what is sacrificed to idols, or the idol itself, is something that it was not before. Rather, I say that the nations that sacrifice these things sacrifice them to demons, and through this they are united to the demons—not through the sacrificed flesh, as though it were something other than flesh, nor through the idol, as though it were something other than what it had previously been.

They sacrifice to demons and not to God; therefore they incorporate themselves into the devil.

Or it may be understood otherwise, if we take the comparison outside the text: just as those who participate in Christ’s body and blood are united to Christ, so, by analogy, those who participate in what has been sacrificed to an idol are united to the devil.

Let us also take this outside the text, so that you may see in carnal things what he shows through spiritual things: “Consider Israel now,” that is, the Jewish people, “according to the flesh,” that is, acting according to carnal rites. Are not those among the Jews who eat sacrifices offered to God participants in the altar, that is, participants in the God to whom they sacrifice upon the altar? In the same way, those who eat food sacrificed to idols are participants in the devil. This, too, is an explanation outside the text.

The following passage is joined in this way: Since I say that the person who eats food sacrificed to idols participates in the devil, what do I appear to be saying? The following text remains unchanged.

For this reason I want you to flee from the worship of idols, because I do not want you to become partners with demons, as those who eat food sacrificed to idols have been shown to be.

You would therefore become partners with demons unless you flee from idols, because you cannot drink the cup of demons and the cup of the Lord. Nor can you be participants in the table of the Lord and the table of demons.

We must flee from the worship of idols so that we may not be associated with demons. We must do so also because, by participating in the table of demons, we provoke—or envy—the Lord, whose kingdom we diminish through ourselves and through those who imitate us.

But are we provoking the Lord? We are envious of him to our own detriment, because are we stronger than he? Whoever envies one stronger than himself acts badly, because he is crushed by that stronger one.

Those who believed with sound faith that an idol and what was sacrificed to it were nothing might say in response: “You seem, Paul, to understand that something sacrificed to an idol is something, since you say that through it we become partners with demons.”

“Far be it from me!” Paul says. “What I plainly affirm is that all these things are lawful for me, and that anyone who has sound faith may eat them in faith. Nevertheless, they are not thereby always permissible, because not everything is beneficial; rather, they may impede blessedness by causing offense to a brother.”

Again, everything is lawful for me according to sound faith, but not everything builds up my neighbor. Whatever destroys him is therefore not permissible. Since everything must be done for the building up of one’s neighbor, no one should seek only what is his own and not what belongs to his neighbor; rather, he should seek what belongs to another, that is, what benefits the building up of his neighbor.

Since Paul has just said that these things are lawful according to faith but not lawful because of the offense caused to a brother, he now determines when these foods may and may not be used.

“So that you may not cause offense in the matters mentioned above, distinguish as follows: Whatever is sold in the marketplace, eat, asking no questions for the sake of conscience,” which he will specify in what follows.

Eat everything, because “the earth is the Lord’s and its fullness” (Ps. 25:1).

But if one of the unbelievers invites you to lunch and you wish to go—which is rightly permitted, because we are not to judge unbelievers—eat whatever is set before you, asking no questions for the sake of conscience. Again, he will specify this conscience; you are not to ask anything.

But if someone says to you, “This has been sacrificed to idols,” do not eat it, for the sake of the one who disclosed it and for the sake of conscience, which he now specifies.

He means not your conscience, since you are sound in faith, but the conscience of another, that is, of a weak brother, lest he be offended by you.

He mentioned conscience first with reference to the conscience of a Jew. If he sees a Christian eating food sacrificed to idols, he will say that one must not adhere to the Christian faith, because Christians are returning to the worship of idols.

Second, he means the conscience of a gentile, who, seeing the same thing, will say: “Why should I abandon my idols, when Christians return to them?”

Third, he means the conscience of the weak brother, for the reason often stated. You must abstain for the sake of another’s conscience.

For why should my freedom—that is, what sound faith permits me—be judged, that is, become judgeable and condemnable, by another’s conscience, namely, by the weak conscience of a brother?

And if I partake of food sacrificed to idols with thanksgiving—that is, eating it in the Lord’s name—why am I blasphemed, or why do I make myself liable to blasphemy, for giving thanks? The weak person or the unbeliever thinks that I am venerating idols when I give thanks to God.

Since no one’s conscience is to be injured, whether you eat, drink, or do anything else, do everything—not as an exercise of your faith’s permission, but for the glory of God, so that no one may justly or unjustly slander the faith of Christ.

And in order that you may do everything for the glory of God, be without offense to Jews, gentiles, and the Church of God—that is, to weak brothers—as was specified above.

Be so, I say, and imitate me also in this matter, just as I please everyone, that is, strive to please everyone in everything, seeking not what is useful only to me, but what is useful to the many, so that many may be saved through me.

And in order that you may be useful to the many, be imitators of me in this matter. If you are imitators of me, you will also be imitators of Christ, just as I am an imitator of Christ.

## Chapter XI

«Be imitators of me, just as I am of Christ. I praise you, brothers, because you remember me in everything and, just as I delivered my instructions to you, you hold to them. But I want you to know that Christ is the head of every man; the man is the head of the woman (Eph. 5:23); and God is the head of Christ. Every man who prays or prophesies with his head covered dishonors his head. But every woman who prays or prophesies with her head uncovered dishonors her head: for it is one and the same as if she were shaved. For if a woman does not cover herself, let her also be shorn. But if it is shameful for a woman to be shorn or shaved, let her cover her head.

A man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God; but the woman is the glory of the man. For man is not from woman, but woman from man. Nor was man created for the sake of woman, but woman for the sake of man. Therefore the woman ought to have authority over her head, and because of the angels.

Nevertheless, neither is woman without man, nor man without woman, in the Lord. For just as woman is from man, so also man is through woman; but all things are from God.

Judge for yourselves: is it fitting for a woman to pray to God uncovered? Does not nature itself teach you that if a man grows his hair, it is a dishonor to him, but if a woman grows her hair, it is her glory? For her hair has been given to her as a covering.

But if anyone seems to be contentious, we have no such custom, nor does the Church of God.

Now I give this instruction—not praising you, because you meet together not for the better but for the worse. First of all, when you come together in the Church, I hear that there are divisions among you, and to some extent I believe it. For there must also be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest among you.

When you come together, then, it is no longer to eat the Lord’s supper. For each one takes his own supper beforehand, and one is hungry while another is drunk. Do you not have houses in which to eat and drink? Or do you despise the Church of God and shame those who have nothing? What shall I say to you? Shall I praise you? In this I do not praise you.

For I received from the Lord what I also delivered to you: that the Lord Jesus Christ, on the night when he was handed over, took bread, [Col. 0179C] and, giving thanks, broke it and said: “Take and eat: This is my body, which will be handed over for [all of] you; do this in remembrance of me.”

Likewise also the cup, after he had eaten, saying: “This cup is the new covenant in my blood; do this, whenever you drink it, in remembrance of me.” For whenever you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes.

“Therefore whoever eats this bread or drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord” (John 6:59).

Let a person examine himself, and thus eat from that bread and drink from the cup. For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the Lord’s body.

For this reason many among you are weak and ill, and many sleep. If we judged ourselves, we would not be judged. But while we are being judged, we are corrected by the Lord, so that we may not be condemned with the world.

Therefore, my brothers, when you come together to eat, wait for one another. If anyone is hungry, let him eat at home, so that you may not come together for judgment. I will arrange the other matters when I come.»

## Exposition

After rebuking them concerning things sacrificed to idols, so that they would not participate in them either by causing offense to a brother or by venerating the idol, Paul turns to another practice they had adopted with excessive shamelessness: men were accustomed to pray in the Church with covered heads, while women prayed with uncovered heads.

To prevent this from happening among them any longer, he prohibits it by appealing to the order of their creation, to the authority of the saints, and to the opposition of nature.

The text is joined in this way: “I rebuke you because you eat food sacrificed to idols either while venerating the idol or while causing offense to your brother. But in this matter I praise you, brothers, because you remember me in everything that I commanded you.”

He says that they remember him because, just as he handed down his instructions to them, they observe them, leaving nothing unfulfilled. But this is all said ironically, because they had scarcely observed any of his command.

Although he praises them in this way, he nevertheless condemns them for the fact that a man, when his head is covered, and a woman, when her head is uncovered, dishonors herself.

He first sets forth the reasons by which he proves that this ought not to be done, saying: “I want you to know that Christ is the head of every man, whether rich or poor,” so that you do not dishonor your heads by such a perverse custom. Man has his beginning from God and not from another.

Just as we have all the senses in the head, and no sense in the body except touch—which we also have in the head—so all our senses ought to agree and cooperate with their head, Christ.

Christ is the head of man; but man is the head of woman, that is, her beginning. Woman was fashioned from man’s rib and thus drew the material of her beginning from man. Man, however, had his beginning from God alone.

Christ is the head of man; God is the head, that is, the beginning, of Christ according to his humanity, and especially his head, because through the divinity united to him God established Christ free from sin.

According to his divinity, God is the head of Christ because the Son has his beginning from the Father, while the Father has his beginning from no one.

Since man has Christ alone as his head, every man who prays in the church—whether he offers the Lord’s Prayer or any other prayer—or who prophesies dishonors his head if he does so with his head covered.

By “prophesying” Paul means either reciting the creed, in which the future resurrection of the flesh and eternal life are proclaimed, or reading in the church and revealing what concerns Christ, whether past or future.

We could say here that Christ is the head of man, whom a man appears to dishonor, insofar as he is concerned, when he acts dishonorably and despises Christ’s commands. But since the following text does not permit this interpretation, we say instead:

A man who prays with his head covered dishonors his own head by covering with a veil the freedom he possesses, since he is subject to no one except Christ. This covering is a sign of shameful subjection.

A man who prays with his head covered dishonors his own head. But every woman who prays or prophesies, as explained above, with her head uncovered dishonors her own head, which she ought always to cover as a sign of her shame, since woman is the cause of all ruin—especially when she presents herself in the Church before her judge. She made every class of human beings hostile to her when she consented to the devil and urged the man to consent to him as well.

Truly, for a woman not to cover her head is to dishonor her head. Not covering the head is one and the same as being shaved, that is, as parting the hair on the forehead, although it is certain that she does not wish to be shorn.

Paul mentions being shaved because he regarded it as unfitting, knowing that women would in no way wish to have their hair cut.

Truly, not covering the head is equivalent to being shaved. For if a woman does not cover herself, let her be shorn. Since she will in no way do this, it follows that, with her head uncovered, she is shaved.

From an uncovered head it necessarily follows that the woman is either shaved or shorn. But if it is shameful for a woman—which would certainly be disgraceful—to be shorn or shaved, let her cover her head, as is fitting.

Let a woman cover her head, but a man ought not to cover his, since man is the image of God, from whom he has his form and beginning, and man is the glory of God. For if he acts well, God is glorified in him.

Man is the image and glory of God. But woman is the glory of man, because she ought to be governed by man; and if she is governed well, he receives glory from the good things the woman has done.

Truly, man is the glory of God alone, and woman is the glory of man. For man is not from woman—that is, in the first creation man did not have his origin from woman, who did not yet exist—but woman had her beginning from man, because Eve was built from Adam’s rib.

Again, man is truly the glory of God alone, and woman the glory of man. For man was not created for woman, as though he were to serve her, since he was created to serve God alone; but woman was created for man, so that she might remain in every form of service as his helper.

Because woman was made for the glory of man and so that she might always be subject to man, she ought always to have authority—that is, a sign that she belongs to another’s authority—over her head. She ought to cover it as a sign of subjection, and because of the angels.

By “the angels” he may mean the teachers of the Church, who are called angels because they are messengers of God, lest, when they see the wantonness of immodest women, they be unlawfully moved toward them.

Or he may mean the angels of God, who are present in all the Church’s sacraments, lest they be offended by such excessive immodesty.

Or “because of the angels” may mean because of the patriarchs and the earlier saints, who prohibited such conduct.

Since Paul had now so greatly depressed the female sex, making it in every respect inferior to man [Col. 0181C], he now raises and consoles it, saying:

Although in the first creation man preceded woman, nevertheless, in the subsequent succession of generation, man and woman are equal, because neither man without woman nor woman without man can generate; rather, each generates equally through the participation of the other.

Yet this does not mean that they can beget from themselves, for everything is in the Lord. The Lord creates a human being through the union of male and female.

Truly, neither man exists without woman nor woman without man: just as woman is generated from man, so man is generated through woman.

Here some people lie in wait for Paul’s words, asking why he said that woman is from man, but man is not from woman, rather through woman. They say that a child is conceived from the seed of the man alone, without seed from the mother, and that the child is merely warmed in the mother’s womb through the woman; they claim that the mother contributes no seed there, but only the nourishment of the womb.

They interpret Paul’s words badly, since “through” can be material in the same way as “from.” Although I say that woman is generated from man, and conversely that man is generated through woman, nevertheless, these things and all things whatsoever are from God, because neither man nor woman can accomplish anything by themselves without God.

[Col. 0182A] The foregoing is read allegorically as follows: The man who was made by God in the first creation, endowed with great strength of rationality, signifies reason, which must always rule sensuality; while the woman, who was not as strong as the man, signifies sensuality, which, when well governed, ought to obey reason. The devil, observing this astutely—that he could not corrupt the man, since he was stronger in reason than he was weakened by sensuality—attacked the woman, whom he perceived to be more oppressed by sensuality than elevated by reason.

Accordingly, we say this: The man ought not to cover his head, because the man is the image of God; that is, through the power of reason he represents God, and by acting through reason he is the glory of God. For God is glorified in servants who act well. The woman, however—that is, sensuality itself—is the glory of the man who represents God through reason: for sensuality, consenting to reason by acting well, is its glory.

And although by “man” we understand reason and by “woman” sensuality, we do not thereby deny that each exists in the other: reason in a woman is called “man,” and sensuality in a man is called “woman.” Nor do we treat here of reason and sensuality in such a way that we cease always to have the actual persons in view. The man ought to be the glory of God, and the woman of the man. For the man is not from the woman—that is, rationality ought not to depend upon sensuality—but the woman is from the man, that is, sensuality from reason.

The man, certainly, is not from the woman. For the man was not created—that is, reason was not given to human beings—for the sake of the woman, that is, so that he should follow sensuality; rather, the woman was created for the man, that is, sensuality was created in order to obey reason. And because the woman was created for the man, she ought therefore to have a sign of authority upon her head, and because of the angels, as has been said.

But although I have preferred the man to the woman with such great dignity, nevertheless neither is the man without the woman, nor the woman without the man; that is, one will not precede the other in the Lord, that is, in blessedness, provided only that they act well. Although in the first creation the man preceded the woman, in salvation one will truly not precede the other. For the statement made above—that the woman is from the man, but the man not from the woman—will do no harm, since in the succession of generation the man is from the woman just as the woman is from the man, even though in the first creation the woman was generated from the man alone; but all things are from God, as has been said. [Col. 0182D]

He proved, according to the order of creation and in accordance with the ordinances of the Fathers, that the man ought not to be veiled and that the woman ought not to uncover her head. He proves the same thing by the nature of each: nature gave the man shorter hair as a sign of freedom, but the woman long hair as a sign of veiling modesty. For although some men have longer hair, this results from art, not from nature. If women have shorter hair, this results from some defect, not from nature.

The text is connected as follows. [129] Above I proved by the order of creation that the woman’s head ought to be veiled. Now you yourselves, Corinthians, judge: I shall prove by nature that this—namely, a woman’s praying to God unveiled—ought not to be done. Judge, I say, whether it is fitting for a woman to pray to God unveiled. Certainly not, because nature itself does not teach you to act in this way; rather, it forbids it. And since nature forbids it, if a man indeed grows his hair long, it is a disgrace to him, because he acts contrary to nature. But if a woman grows her hair long, it is her glory, since long hair was given to her by nature as a covering—that is, as a sign of a covering which ought always to be placed upon her head.

I have proved by the order of creation and by the law of nature that the man ought not to cover his head, nor the woman to uncover hers. But if anyone among you appears contentious and does not agree with our arguments, we shall say this one thing to him: Brother, we do not have such a custom, nor have we had it in the synagogue of the Jews, nor do we yet have it in the new Church of God—that a man should pray with covered head or a woman with uncovered head. And because custom has neither had nor still has this practice, therefore, since you misuse our admonition, I no longer merely persuade you, but by our authority I command that this unfamiliar practice not continue. [Col. 0183B]

After restraining the Corinthians from this evil, he turns to other matters in which they were offending far more seriously. For, led astray by false teachers, they had abandoned Paul’s instruction, which he had delivered to them concerning the reception of the body and blood of Christ. The false teachers had persuaded them that they ought to receive Communion after the meal, since at that hour Christ had handed these sacraments over to his disciples to be shared. Hence they had fallen into many evils. Since there were schisms among them, they dared to approach the unity of Christ’s body; and there was another evil, namely, that they dined and became drunk beforehand, and did this in the church, causing those who lacked such lavish preparations to be ashamed, while supplying nothing to the needy; after these evils, they intruded upon the Lord’s table.

The text is connected as follows: “This foregoing practice I command not to be done”; but he does not approve the other matter, rather he condemns it. This, namely, that you gather for the Lord’s supper, at which you ought to become one: I tell you that by this you are not progressing toward the better, as you ought, but falling toward the worse. And although your evils are many, I first mention this above all: when you gather in the church, I hear that there are divisions and disagreements among you, even though the Church demands unity. And, as I hear, I believe it in part—that is, on account of some among you whom I know to glory in schisms.

I do believe it, certainly, for one must believe it. For religious persons have reported it to me. Or it may be understood in this way: divisions exist among you because divisions must exist—that is, various disagreements—and, what is more serious, heresies. For scandals must come, so that those who are approved and chosen by God may become manifest among you, enduring in temptations, and so that the rejected may likewise become manifest.

Since, therefore, there are divisions among you, when you gather together, you who contradict unity, it is no longer—meaning, because of the sole cause of discord—permitted for you to eat the Lord’s supper, that is, the body and blood of Christ, which the Lord gave to his disciples at the supper. Or “no longer,” that is, in this world, the Lord’s supper is forbidden to you because of your discord, but in the future you will be condemned completely. Because of your divisions, it is not permitted for you to receive Christ’s body.

It is also not permitted to you for this reason: each of you presumes—that is, by presuming, anticipates—his own meal, not merely in order to prepare it, but also in order to eat it. And there is yet another evil: one person, who has no means by which to prepare anything for himself, is hungry. Again, there is another evil: another is drunk. But when you eat in the church in this way, do you not have private houses in which to eat and drink? If you did not have them, it would be more tolerable to eat in the street. Or do you despise the Church of God, in which you become drunk, and shame them—that is, inflict embarrassment upon the poor who have nothing with which to prepare food for themselves? [Col. 0184A]

And because you act so shamelessly, what shall I say to you? Certainly, you are without charity, despisers of God, followers of gluttony, and so forth. Do I praise you in this? Certainly I do not praise you; rather, I condemn you. Or it may be understood thus: I praise you in certain other matters, but in this I do not praise you at all.

After condemning in them the order of conduct in which they had wrongly persisted, he explains how they ought to receive Christ’s sacraments: namely, in abstinence, not in drunkenness, but in sorrow and tribulation.

The text is connected as follows: “I do not praise you because you receive the Lord’s body while drunk”; for it ought not to be received in this way, but in remembrance of the tribulation and death of Christ. But before he comes to this, he commends what he is about to say by the authority of the Lord, saying: “I received from the Lord himself what I have already handed on to you, and now I shall hand it on again”—namely, that our Lord Jesus [Col. 0184C] Christ, on that night (and night is a sign of adversity and sorrow, a night in which he did not feast or become drunk, but was handed over to death for our sins), took bread—that is, the true substance of bread.

And giving thanks to God the Father for this, because, as he had ordained through him, he was redeeming the human race and persevering in obedience to the Father, he broke it. In these words by which Christ gave thanks to the Father, it is said that the substance of bread and wine placed upon the altar passes into the true flesh and true blood of Christ. Giving thanks, I say, he broke that which remains one and inseparable forever; but he broke it when he gave the whole to each individual, so that through this he might signify that we, although diverse in persons, ought to become one in the love of God.

He broke it, I say, and said: “Take”—that is, regard this as worthy of acceptance, and examine carefully the mystery of this sacrament, so that, just as I suffer for you, you too may rejoice to suffer for my name and for your neighbors. “Take,” I say, “and eat.” In this Christ wished to signify that it is not enough for us to believe unless, by tasting, we see how sweet the Lord is; just as eating would not profit us unless we believed.

And what shortly before was bread is now truly my body. This body will be handed over for you unto death, although now I present it to you immortal and incapable of suffering. [Col. 0184D]

It should also be noted that the signs here signify substance in such a way that they indicate no quality there, neither mortality nor immortality. Nor is it surprising that, as Augustine says, he carried the immortal one in mortal hands, since in the Transfiguration (Matthew 17) he who was then and afterward mortal showed himself to Peter, James, and John in the glory of immortality and incapability of suffering.

“Eat,” he says, “my body”; and “do this,” that is, receive it continually. Not in joy and drunkenness, but in remembrance of me, so that, always mindful of my passion and death, you may be willing to suffer and die for me.

Similarly, after supper, just as he had received the body, he took the cup (here he indicates that he likewise gave the body after supper). He took, I say, the cup, saying: “This cup, which shortly before was the true substance of wine—this cup, certainly, is my blood; and in this blood of mine there is a new testament,” that is, a new promise. For the old Law promised bodily things, but this sacrament of my body and blood promises something new, because it promises spiritual blessedness.

It is also a new testament for this reason: it is never to be changed so that other rites may be introduced. And this—namely, my blood—“do,” that is, receive, “in remembrance of me,” that is, with a contrite and humbled heart, not once, but whenever you receive it.

And it is right that you should receive this in memory of me, because whenever you eat this bread—that is, my true body, which retains the appearance and taste of bread so that those receiving it may not recoil from it—and whenever you drink this cup, that is, my blood, which retains the taste and appearance of wine [131], whenever, I say, you receive these things, you proclaim—that is, represent—the death of the Lord, with whom you ought always to suffer and die; doing this until the Lord comes for judgment and presents himself to you face to face. [Col. 0185C]

It should be noted why the Lord Jesus, after supper, having celebrated the old Passover, gave his body and blood—that is, the new Passover—to his disciples. This was done in a sufficiently fitting order. For if he had first celebrated the new Passover and afterward the old, he would not seem by this new sacrament to destroy the old things or to be their end; rather, he would seem to imply that after these new things he would once again restore the old. But in order to show that all the old things find their end in this new sacrifice, and that they are never to be restored, he suitably placed the old Passover first, for its destruction, and set beneath it the new Passover, which was to remain. In this, the end of all the old things was accomplished, since these sacraments are to be received in remembrance and conformity to Christ.

Therefore, whoever eats the bread—that is, the Lord’s body—or drinks the cup—that is, the Lord’s blood—unworthily, that is, in schism, drunkenness, or evils of this kind, will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord, that is, liable to condemnation because he has received Christ’s body and blood unworthily.

But lest a person become guilty, let him test himself—that is, examine and judge himself—not by comparing himself with one who acts badly, as though by doing so he were setting his own righteousness above another’s, but let him judge himself in view of his own weakness. And thus, once tested, let him eat of that bread and drink from the cup. It is necessary that a person test himself in this way.

For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks not forgiveness but judgment—that is, condemnation—upon himself, and deservedly so, because he does not judge, that is, does not sufficiently distinguish, the Lord’s body from other food, just as the Corinthians did not distinguish it; for what he had stated generally above he understood especially of the Corinthians.

From what has been said he draws an inference against them: Because you receive the Lord’s body unworthily and do not distinguish it from other foods, therefore among you, Corinthians, many are weak, suffering from fevers and illnesses of this kind; and many are infirm, deprived of the strength of their limbs; and many are also sleeping the sleep of death.

Because we do not examine ourselves, we are afflicted in this way. But if we judged ourselves—that is, judged our evil deeds, that is, condemned them by the scourge of repentance—we would certainly not be judged, that is, condemned for them by the Lord. For from whatever matter a person judges himself, from that matter he escapes God’s judgment.

And although we are afflicted by the Lord through weakness and infirmity, nevertheless, while we are thus judged and, according to some, condemned on account of our evil conduct, we are corrected by the Lord, so that we others may not sin in the same way. For in the judgment by which God acts against the wicked, he mercifully chastises his own. [Col. 0186B]

“We are corrected,” I say, so that, once corrected, we may not be condemned with the world. Therefore he does not say “with the Corinthians,” but “with the world.” He means that the sacraments received profit those who sin no more than they profit those who remain in the world—that is, in paganism—since those who receive them unworthily are condemned; and because, through the condemnation of the wicked, we are corrected.

Therefore, my brothers, so that you may receive the Lord’s supper worthily and be rightly corrected, when you gather to eat it, wait for one another—that is, each for the other—and do not anticipate the appointed time for receiving the Lord’s supper. For according to the Lord’s tradition, the Church is accustomed to receive Communion in the evening on the day of the supper.

I say that you should wait. But if anyone is hungry and neglects to wait for the proper hour, I would rather that he eat at home than anticipate Christ’s supper before the hour; yet, after he has eaten, he is not thereby to participate in Christ’s table. I want you to wait for one another in such a way that you do not gather for judgment—that is, so that your gathering may not become for you a cause of condemnation.

I have now set these foregoing matters before you because I know that without them you cannot be saved. The remaining matters, without which you can nevertheless be saved, but which are profitable for the increase of glory, I shall arrange for you when I come. [Col. 0186D]

## CHAPTER XII

“Now concerning spiritual gifts, brothers, I do not want you to be ignorant. You know that when you were gentiles, you went to mute idols, being led as you were led. Therefore I make known to you that no one speaking in the Spirit of God says, ‘Anathema to Jesus.’ And no one can say, ‘The Lord Jesus,’ except in the Holy Spirit.

There are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit; varieties of ministries, but the same Lord; and varieties of activities, but the same God, who works all things in all. To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good.

To one, through the Spirit, is given a word of wisdom; to another, a word of knowledge, according to the same Spirit; to another, faith in the same Spirit; to another, the grace of healings in the one Spirit; to another, the working of miracles; to another, prophecy; to another, the discernment of spirits; to another, kinds of tongues; to another, the interpretation of utterances.

But all these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, distributing them to each one as he wills (Romans 12:6; Ephesians 4:7).

For just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, although many, are one body, so also is Christ. For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or gentiles, whether slaves or free; and we were all given to drink of one Spirit.

For the body is not one member but many. If the foot should say, ‘Because I am not a hand, I am not of the body,’ is it for that reason not of the body? And if the ear should say, ‘Because I am not an eye, I am not of the body,’ is it for that reason not of the body?

If the whole body were an eye, where would hearing be? If the whole were hearing, where would smell be? But now God has placed the members, each one of them, in the body as he willed.

And if they were all one member, where would the body be? But now there are many members, yet one body. The eye cannot say to the hand, ‘I do not need your work’; nor again the head to the feet, ‘You are not necessary to me.’

Rather, those members of the body that seem to be weaker are more necessary. And those members of the body that we consider less honorable, we surround with greater honor. And our unpresentable members have greater respectability; while our presentable members have no need of this. But God has so composed the body, giving greater honor to the member that lacked it, so that there may be no schism in the body, but that the members may be mutually concerned for one another.

And if one member suffers anything, all the members suffer with it; or if one member is honored, all the members rejoice with it.

Now you are the body of Christ and members individually. And God has placed some in the Church: first apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then miracles; after that, gifts of healings, helps, governments, kinds of tongues, interpretations of utterances.

Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Are all workers of miracles? Do all have the grace of healings? Do all speak in tongues? Do all interpret?

But desire the better [variant: greater] gifts. And I will show you an even more excellent way.” [Col. 0187D]

## EXPOSITION

Here ends the discussion of the sacraments of the altar. He now turns to teach them about the gifts of the Holy Spirit, concerning which they were seriously mistaken. Those who had received greater gifts boasted against those to whom lesser graces had been granted. But those who had received less despaired because they were inferior in the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

Those who abounded in greater graces attributed this to their own merits and reproached the inferior on account of their merits, thus disparaging the Spirit. They were also mistaken in this: they preferred those graces that were inferior, such as kinds of tongues, to the others and desired them more.

To drive out this error, he instructs them as follows, saying: [133] I set aside the other matters that I shall arrange when I come, but I do not postpone teaching you about spiritual gifts in any way. I do not want you, brothers, to be ignorant concerning spiritual gifts—that is, concerning the gifts of the Holy Spirit—and what you ought to think about them.

By “Spirit” I mean that which causes a person to cease from evil and to do good. But before introducing this, he gives an analogy, saying: Therefore know that the Holy Spirit causes you not to be separated from Christ, since you know that when you were still gentiles—that is, gentiles or living as gentiles—you went to mute idols, being led as you were led by the evil spirit. One person was led to sacrifice, another to burn incense, and another to worship.

When he says “mute idols,” he shows that they were not led by reason, which could sufficiently discern that an idol was not God, but by an evil spirit. And therefore, because you were led by an evil spirit toward evil, I make known to you by analogy that through the Holy Spirit you desist from your former evil.

He says this equivalently: I make known to you that no one speaking in the Spirit of God—speaking in action, thought, and word—for the Spirit, which is an invisible reality, is not known to be in a person except through those things that are seen or heard externally—no one, I say, speaking in the Spirit of God says, in action, word, and thought, “Anathema,” that is, separation from Jesus.

For no one who possesses the gift of the Holy Spirit can do, think, or say anything on account of which he would be separated from Jesus, so long as the Spirit remains in him. In this he greatly lifts the despair of those who had received lesser graces, since he says that the person in whom the Spirit of God remains through some gift cannot be separated from Jesus. [Col. 0188C]

The Spirit not only prevents us from being separated from Jesus; no one can say by word, deed, or thought, “Jesus is my Lord,” that is, “I am his servant,” except in the Holy Spirit, who works through that person. “Jesus is my Lord.” Whoever is not his servant cannot say this, because, if he is not a servant, he lies rather than speaks the truth.

Here he greatly humbles those who preferred themselves to others on account of greater gifts, since he says that nothing comes from human merit, but everything is in the Holy Spirit. Although the Spirit gives indifferently both the turning away from evil and the doing of good, the graces of that same Spirit are distributed separately to different people.

Although there are varieties of gifts, nevertheless the Spirit who gives the varied gifts is one and undivided. And just as there are varieties of gifts, so there are varieties of their effects, namely, ministries. One person ministers in the episcopate, another in the priesthood, and so in the other ranks of the Church. We also speak of ministries in whatever matters we suitably minister to our neighbor.

And although there are varieties of ministries, nevertheless the Lord who gives the grace in which we minister is one. [Col. 0189A]

There are also varieties of activities, namely, the good works we perform in ourselves by praying, keeping vigil, and fasting; and these activities are the effects of the gifts. Although the activities are varied, nevertheless the God who works all things that he sees to be beneficial for salvation in everyone is one.

He expresses this as follows: “The same Spirit, the same Lord, the same God”—not because he understands different substances, but so that he may designate the Trinity in persons and unity in substance.

And although there are varieties of gifts, to each person is given a manifestation of the Spirit, that is, some good through which it is shown that the Spirit works in him, for the common good. For the lesser gift is useful to the one who receives it just as the greater gift is useful to another.

God does not distribute his graces according to human merits. Often a greater gift is given to one less worthy; often a lesser gift is given to one more worthy, according as God sees one person more suitable for exercising one gift and another for exercising another.

He enumerates the graces, saying: There are indeed varieties of gifts. To one—that is, selectively—is given through the Spirit wisdom, that is, knowledge of divine things, and a word of wisdom, so that he may speak graciously what he rightly understands.

To another is given knowledge of human things and a word, so that he may speak readily what he knows; and this is according to the same Spirit, with human merit excluded.

To another is given faith—that is, steadfastness of faith, so that he does not hesitate to die in defense of the faith. Or faith because he knows the sacraments of faith; and this is in the same Spirit. [Col. 0189C]

To another is given the grace of healings, so that through the power of the Spirit he may drive away illnesses; and this is in one and the same Spirit. Since he was weary of attaching the Spirit individually to each gift, he comprehended the remaining graces and finally added that all are given through the Spirit.

To another is given the working of miracles, that is, miracles performed contrary to the law of nature, such as giving sight to a blind person or raising a dead person.

To another is given prophecy, that is, revelation of future things or understanding of the Scriptures.

To another is given discernment of spirits, because he knows by which spirit each person performs or says something.

To another are given kinds of tongues, because he knows how to speak in different languages.

To another is given interpretation of utterances, because he knows how to interpret Greek into Latin, or conversely. Or “interpretation of utterances” means an exposition of allegories.

And although these different gifts are given to different people, nevertheless one and the same Spirit works all these things—the Spirit whom above I called God and Lord. I say “Spirit,” distributing them to each one as he wills, that is, by grace, not by merit. [Col. 0189D]

Here he begins to show the diversity of members in the same head, which is Christ, and how those diverse members become one in Christ the head.

The text is connected as follows: I rightly say that the Spirit distributes to each one, that is, gives different graces to different members. For Christ is one body having diverse members, just as you see that the human body is one and nevertheless has many members, that is, members having different functions; and yet, although the members of the body are many—that is, diverse—they are one body.

So Christ has diverse members in the Church, and yet in him, the head, they are one. Nor is this surprising, because just as diverse members live through the same soul, so all his members are governed through the same Spirit.

Truly Christ is one body. For we were all baptized and made alive in one Spirit, passing into one body of Christ. I say “all” without distinction, whether we are Jews or gentiles, slaves or free.

And just as we were baptized, so after baptism we were all given to drink of one and the same Spirit in confirmation and in the other orders of the Church.

Truly we were all baptized, that is, truly we are diverse members. For just as the human body is not one member but many, so by analogy Christ is not one member but many. [Col. 0190B]

This also conveys the whole meaning. He now infers from what was said above that we, all baptized and given to drink by one Spirit, are one body of Christ. Because we are one, if the foot—that is, an inferior member in the Church—should say, “Because I am not a hand,” that is, an operator of the same kind as another, “therefore I am not of Christ’s body,” it does not follow for that reason that he is not of Christ’s body.

This means that the one who is inferior cannot sever himself from the unity of Christ, because he has another member superior to himself in the same body of Christ.

And just as the foot is not severed because it is not a hand, so if the ear should say—that is, the person whom we ought to understand as being taught through another teacher—“Because I am not an eye,” that is, “Because I do not understand everything by myself, therefore I am not of the body,” it does not follow that for this reason he is not of the body. [Col. 0190C]

Above he had said that the body is not one member but had not supplied the reason. He now adds this as well, saying: Truly the ear, although it is not an eye, is nevertheless of the body, because if it were not for that reason, it would follow that the eye was the whole body.

But if the eye were the whole body, where would hearing be? Behold, there would be deficiency in the body. And if hearing were the whole body, where would smell be? Again, there would be deficiency. By smell we understand the discernment of good and evil.

But so that there might not be this deficiency in the body, God has now placed diverse members, each one of them in one body, distributing graces to them as he willed.

Nor is one member the whole body merely to remove deficiency; it also cannot be so because, if all the members were one member, where would the body be? [Col. 0190D] The body would certainly perish, because if all the members were hands, there would still not be a human body.

Again, if everyone in the Church were apostles, or were all one single thing, they would not even be apostles, since there would be no one to whom they could preach. Since, if one member is called the whole body, both deficiency in the body and the body’s very destruction follow.

Therefore, there are now many distinct members, while the body of these members is one. And because inferior members are necessarily in the body just as superior members are, the eye cannot say to the hand—that is, a superior member to an inferior one—“I do not need your work,” since the removal of one member produces deficiency in the body.

Through this it is sufficiently clear that the one who has received the greater gift has no basis for preferring himself to the one who has received less, since the inferior member produces such deficiency in the body that the superior member would do so as well if it were removed.

Nor again can the head say to the feet, as a superior member to inferior members, “You are not necessary to me,” since the eye needs cleansing by the hand, and the head needs to be carried by the feet to whatever it wishes to taste, hear, or see. [Col. 0191A]

Inferior members are not only necessary; sometimes those members of the body that seem to be weaker are much more necessary. Often even ordinary, uneducated people are more necessary for the administration of ecclesiastical affairs than those who are wiser, according to the needs of the time.

And those members of the Church whom we consider less honorable because they fall, we sometimes surround with greater honor. That is, we ought to support such people with more diligent care and restore them to better things.

Our members that are unpresentable—such as the private parts of the body—and the fornicator who had taken his father’s wife in the Church of the Corinthians, as well as David when he sinned with Uriah’s wife: these unpresentable members possess greater respectability. That is, diligent and honorable care must be shown to them, lest, if they are despised, they despair; for perhaps tomorrow they will be perfected, as was seen in David.

The unpresentable need respectability, but the honorable members do not need any honor bestowed upon them by another. Those who are perfect have no need of another. The honorable indeed lack nothing, but God has composed—that is, ordered—the body so that the honorable members might adorn the unpresentable.

He composed it, I say, by giving greater honor to the member that lacked something, so that we might support the sick member with greater love than the healthy one.

Therefore he composed it in such a way that there might be no schism—that is, discord—in the body of Christ, but that all the members might be concerned for one another, that is, one for another, feeling the same thing, that is, judging the distress of one’s neighbor as one’s own.

And if one member suffers any hardship, all the members should suffer with it; or if one member is honored, all the members should rejoice with it.

And everything I have said about the unity of Christ’s body applies entirely to you, Corinthians, because you are one body of Christ and diverse members dependent upon the member of Christ who taught you the faith.

Or “members dependent upon the member” means dependent upon Christ the head, who is the supreme member of the Church. [Col. 0191D]

Above he spoke of the diversity of Christ’s members and how they are one in their head, Christ. He continues to speak of these same members according to the diversity of the gifts they have from the Holy Spirit, wishing to compare those gifts with one another, showing which are more useful and which less useful: charity and prophecy, which are the greatest, while speaking in different tongues is far below them.

He compares them for this reason: the Corinthians were preferring kinds of tongues—which came last—to all the graces.

The text is connected as follows: You are members dependent upon the member—that is, upon Christ the head—in whom you are one body. And within this unity there is distinction, because God has placed certain people—that is, selectively—in the Church.

First, that is, in the first and most excellent rank, he placed apostles. Second, after the apostles, he placed prophets, that is, men of enlightened understanding who would open the Scriptures. In these three he preserved an order; [136] the remaining offices he mixed together without order.

Then, after the teachers, he placed miracles, namely those who by the power of God would give sight to the blind and raise the dead. After these he placed the gifts of healings, namely those who by God’s gift would drive away illnesses.

Next he placed helps, that is, assistants in preaching, such as Barnabas and Timothy; the legates of the Roman see still perform this office.

After this he placed governments, that is, bishops and presbyters who would govern the churches of the faithful. [Col. 0192B] Finally he placed kinds of tongues, that is, the last gift, which you, Corinthians, desire above all.

And God fittingly ordered the varieties of gifts in the Church. Were all apostles? If all were, there would be not even one apostle; for if all were apostles, there would be no one to whom they could preach the word of God, since all would be perfect.

Again, were all prophets? Then nothing could be revealed to anyone, because each would be a prophet. Again, were all teachers? There would be no one whom they could instruct in morals, since all would be instructed.

Were all workers of miracles? Then there would be no one for whom miracles could be performed. Do all have the grace of healings? No, because there would be no one to heal.

Do all speak in various tongues? Then the gift of God would become cheap and commonplace. Do all interpret, that is, know how to transfer one language into another? If all were interpreters, interpretation would be useless.

Since there are so many gifts of the Holy Spirit, desire—that is, long for—the better charisms, that is, the Spirit’s gratuitous gifts, which among those listed above are the better ones. A charism is so called because it is gratuitous.

And besides those things I have shown above, I show you still an even more excellent way, that is, charity, which is a way and is more excellent than every gift, because all the other things are insufficient for blessedness without charity. [Col. 0192C]

## CHAPTER XIII
«If I speak in the tongues of human beings and of angels, but do not have charity, I have become like sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal. And if I have prophecy, [Col. 0192D] and know all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so that I move mountains, but do not have charity, I am nothing. And if I distribute all my possessions to feed the poor, and if I hand over my body so that I may burn, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing. Charity is patient; it is kind. Charity is not jealous, does not act improperly, is not puffed up, is not ambitious, does not seek its own interests, is not provoked, does not think evil, does not rejoice over wrongdoing, but rejoices with the truth. It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Charity never fails; but whether there are prophecies, they will be brought to an end; whether tongues, they will cease; whether knowledge, it will be destroyed. [Col. 0193A] For we know in part, and we prophesy in part. But when what is perfect has come, what is partial will be brought to an end. When I was a child, I spoke as a child, understood as a child, thought as a child. But when I became a man, I put away the things of a child. Now we see through a mirror, in an enigma; but then face to face. Now I know in part; but then I shall know fully, even as I have been fully known. But now these three remain: faith, hope, and charity. The greatest of these is charity.»

## EXPOSITION

Because he wishes the Corinthians to desire charity more than tongues, he proves that charity is more excellent than speaking in tongues, saying: Charity is certainly more excellent than tongues; [Col. 0193B] for if I speak in the tongues of all human beings, and also speak in the tongues of angels—not that angels speak with tongues, but that by certain signs one angel makes his will known to another—and if I were of such perfection that I understood the angels’ admonitions, 137 or spoke in the tongues of angels—for when angels speak to human beings in an assumed form, they must use human words—and if I spoke these same words.

Or let us understand it this way: If I speak in the tongues of human beings, that is, of those who live humanly, and in the tongues of angels, that is, of those who live contemplatively in this world, but do not have charity, I have become useless, like sounding bronze, which is struck to no productive end so far as it is concerned; or like a clanging cymbal, which delights human ears, while striking and diminishing itself. [Col. 0193C]

And if I have prophecy, so that, with my understanding enlightened, I foretell future things; and if I know all mysteries, that is, the figures of God’s works—for example, the Flood was a figure of baptism, and similarly in other cases—and if I know all knowledge, that is, the meaning of those mysteries; and if I have all faith, so that I move mountains literally—for this was the accomplishment of faith: if a believer said to a mountain, “Move from here and cast yourself into the sea” [Matthew 21:21], it would certainly happen—or alternatively: If I have such perfect faith that I remove mountains, that is, transfer demons from possessed bodies into pigs or something of that kind, but do not have charity, I am nothing, that is, because of faith without charity I am judged to have no merit.

And if I distribute—that is, give to various people—not merely my surplus, but also all my resources, that is, everything which it would be within my power and ability to retain; and if, I say, I distribute not for superfluous things, but for food; not for the rich, but for the poor; and all my resources, however many they may be; and if I hand over my body so that I may burn, as Blessed Lawrence did, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing.
