[Col. 0193D]

Other things are of no benefit without charity. But charity, even if it can be considered in itself, is patient, that is, it possesses the virtue of patience even if at some time it suffers nothing. It is also kind, that is, generous and abundant in love of one’s neighbor, even if it has nothing to give.

After setting out the good qualities found in charity, he removes the evil ones from it, saying: Charity is not jealous, that is, it envies no one. It does not act improperly, that is, it does nothing perversely. [Col. 0194A] It is not puffed up, that is, it is not proud because of temporal or spiritual goods. It is not ambitious, so as to desire worldly honors. It does not seek only what belongs to itself, but gives equal attention to the advantage of its neighbor and to its own. Or: It does not seek what is its own, that is, it does not demand what belongs to it if someone has taken it away.

It is not provoked, that is, it is not stirred to anger. It does not think evil, so as to speak or inflict harm upon anyone. It does not rejoice over—that is, in—wrongdoing. If it sees someone acting unjustly toward a neighbor, it rather suffers with him. But it rejoices with the truth, that is, with the person who speaks or acts according to the truth.

It patiently bears and tolerates all adversities that are inflicted upon it. It believes all things, whatever ought rightly to be believed concerning God. It hopes all things: virtues in the present and glory in the future. It endures all things, that is, if the reward is delayed, it is long-suffering in enduring. [Col. 0194B]

Another excellence of charity is that charity never fails, that is, it endures forever and never passes away. Truly, charity alone does not fail. For prophecies and knowledge, which among the other things seem more likely to endure, are destroyed. Whether there are prophecies, they will be brought to an end in the future. When everything has been made clear to everyone, what would they prophesy? Whether there are tongues, they will cease, for in the future everyone will have the same language. Whether there is the knowledge now possessed, it will be destroyed.

Because some thought that knowledge would endure, he proves that present knowledge will truly be destroyed, because now we know—that is, we know in part, imperfectly. And prophecy will truly be brought to an end. For now we prophesy in part, that is, imperfectly; but in the future, when what is perfect has come, everything that is partial—that is, imperfect—will be brought to an end. [Col. 0194C]

Someone might object: It is indeed true that knowledge is now imperfect, but it will be perfect in the future. Nevertheless, that part of knowledge which exists now will not be destroyed, but will be enclosed within the totality of knowledge. Paul destroys this argument by the analogy he introduces, showing that even the knowledge which exists now will not remain.

Just as a child [138] understands nothing through reason, but through the senses and through certain images—for example, that a stone is hard and solid, and similarly with other things—yet when that same child has become a man, having set aside images and no longer seeking to discern things through bodily sensation, he knows the same things far better through the power of reason alone, so that the sensory and imagistic knowledge which he possessed as a child seems to him, now using reason, to be nothing; so the knowledge of this world imagines God through certain likenesses.

When it sees someone powerful, it considers that God, who created him, is much more powerful, and similarly in other matters. But in the future we shall know God as he is. At present we do not know him as he is, but merely imagine him through certain likenesses. And because then knowledge will be perfect, whereas now it is imperfect; then according to the truth of the thing, whereas now only according to images—therefore he said that knowledge would be destroyed.

Love, however, will not be destroyed, because then we shall love the same one whom we love now, although then more perfectly. Truly, what is imperfect will be brought to an end when what is perfect has come. [Col. 0195A] Just as you see that, when I was a child, ignorant of the power of reason, I spoke as a child, understood as a child, and thought as a child—in all things imperfectly. But when I became a man and exercised the power of reason, I put away the things of a child, because I then understood far better by reason what, when I was a child, I had scarcely known at all through images and the senses.

Similarly, just as children do, we now see—that is, in the present—God through a mirror, that is, not through the truth of the thing as it is, but through a certain likeness by which we imagine God. And not through a mirror that is somewhat bright, but one placed in an enigma, that is, in such great obscurity that the truth of the thing [Col. 0195B] as it is cannot in any way be known. But then, in the future, we shall see God face to face, that is, we shall see God as he is.

And because this will be so, it is evident that present knowledge will be completely destroyed; but charity will remain, since we shall love in the future the same one whom we love now. This will indeed be the case with you: now you know imperfectly, but then you will know perfectly. For I myself now know God in part, that is, imperfectly; but then, in the future, I shall know him as perfectly as I am myself known by God, from whom nothing in me is hidden.

Therefore charity is more excellent, because when the other things are destroyed, it alone will remain. And even now, while it remains in the present together with the other virtues, it is more excellent than all of them. But the text is connected in this way: In the future they will be destroyed, but now [Col. 0195C] faith, hope, and charity remain. By these virtues altogether he means that you can possess faith, hope, and charity quite easily, because there are only these three; and although they are so few, they prepare all glory. And although they remain together, charity is nevertheless the greater of these, that is, among them, or greater than these, namely faith and hope. Since it will remain forever, and is greater even now, therefore pursue charity above all, and not varieties of tongues.

## CHAPTER XIV

«Pursue charity; desire spiritual gifts, but especially that you may prophesy. For the one who speaks in a tongue speaks not to human beings but to God. For no one hears him, but the spirit speaks mysteries. [Col. 0195D] But the one who prophesies speaks to human beings for edification, exhortation, and consolation. The one who speaks in a tongue edifies himself; but the one who prophesies edifies the Church [or, God]. Now I want all of you to speak in tongues, but especially to prophesy. For the one who prophesies is greater than the one who speaks in tongues, unless perhaps he interprets, so that the Church may receive edification.

Now, brothers, if I come to you speaking in tongues, what benefit will I bring you unless I speak to you in revelation, or in knowledge, or in prophecy, or in doctrine? Yet things without a soul that give a sound—whether flute or lyre—unless they give a distinction of sounds, how will it be known what is being played on the flute [139] or the lyre? For if the trumpet gives an uncertain sound, who will prepare himself for battle? [Col. 0196A] So also you, unless through the tongue you give a clear speech, how will it be known what is being said? For you will be speaking into the air.

There are, let us suppose, so many kinds of languages in this world, and nothing is without a voice. Therefore, if I do not know the force of the voice, I shall be a barbarian to the person to whom I speak, and the one who speaks to me will be a barbarian. So also you, since you are zealous for spiritual gifts, seek to abound in them for the edification of the Church. And therefore let the one who speaks in a tongue pray that he may interpret. For if I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays, but my mind is without fruit.

What, then, is the conclusion? I shall pray with the spirit, and I shall pray with the mind; I shall sing psalms with the spirit, and I shall sing psalms with the mind. Otherwise, if you bless with the spirit, who fills the place of the unlearned person? How will he say “Amen” over [Col. 0196B] your blessing, since he does not know what you are saying? For you indeed give thanks well, but the other is not edified.

I give thanks to God [or, my God] that I speak in tongues more than all of you. But in the church I want to speak five words with my mind, so that I may instruct others, rather than ten thousand words in a tongue. Brothers, do not become children in understanding, but be infants in malice and mature in understanding. For it is written in the Law: “In other tongues and with other lips I shall speak to this people; and even so they will not hear me, says the Lord” (Isaiah 28:11).

Therefore tongues are for a sign not to believers but to unbelievers; prophecy, however, is not for unbelievers but for believers. So if the whole Church comes together in [Col. 0196C] one place, and all speak in tongues, but unlearned persons or unbelievers enter, will they not say that you are insane? But if all prophesy, and an unbeliever or an unlearned person enters, he is convicted by all and judged by all. For the secrets of his heart are made manifest, and so, falling on his face, he will worship God, declaring that God is truly among you.

What, then, is the matter, brothers? When you come together, each of you has a psalm, a teaching, an Apocalypse, a tongue, an interpretation. Let everything be done for edification. If anyone speaks in a tongue, let it be by two, or at most three, and in turn, and let one interpret. But if there is no interpreter, let him keep silent in the church and speak to himself and to God.

Let two or three prophets speak, [Col. 0196D] and let the others judge. But if something is revealed to another who is sitting, let the first keep silent. For you can all prophesy one by one, so that all may learn and all be exhorted; and the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets. For God is not a God of dissension but of peace, as I teach in all the churches of the saints.

Let women keep silent in the churches. For they are not permitted to speak, but are to be subject, “as the Law also says” (Genesis 3:16). But if they wish to learn anything, let them ask their husbands at home. For it is shameful for a woman to speak in the church.

Did the word of God go out from you? Or did it come to you alone? If anyone thinks that he is a prophet or spiritual, let him acknowledge that the things I write to you are the Lord’s commandments. But if anyone is ignorant, let him be ignored. [Col. 0197A] Therefore, brothers, desire to prophesy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues. But let everything among you be done decently and in order.»

## EXPOSITION

After proving concerning charity that it is more excellent not only than tongues but also than every virtue, he proves that prophesying is more worthy and more useful in the Church than speaking in tongues. He proves this in many ways, saying: Although I say above all, “Pursue charity,” I nevertheless want you to desire spiritual gifts, that is, to desire spiritual graces. And although all are useful, desire especially to prophesy rather than to speak in tongues.

This is especially to be desired because the one who speaks in an unknown tongue speaks not to human beings—that is, not for the edification of human beings—[Col. 0197B] but to God, that is, only for the honor of God, who gave the tongue. Truly he does not speak to human beings, for no human being hears, that is, understands, what he says. Yet although no one hears, the Holy Spirit speaks mysteries through the one who speaks in an unknown tongue.

It is truly more useful to prophesy than to speak in tongues, because the one who prophesies speaks to human beings for edification. Or let us connect it with what follows, while retaining the same sense: the words “for,” “because,” and “indeed” should answer what precedes. The one who speaks in tongues does not speak to human beings. For only the one who prophesies—that is, who opens the obscurities of the Scriptures—speaks to human beings for edification, that is, to instruct their ignorance [140]; and after they have been instructed, for exhortation, so that they may raise themselves toward better things; [Col. 0197C] and for consolation, so that they may appear strong in tribulations.

But the one who speaks in an unknown tongue edifies himself, as it were; at other times not even himself, because he does not understand—the contrary statement. But the one who prophesies, while opening the Scriptures, edifies the whole Church.

And because prophesying is so useful, I certainly want all of you to speak in tongues, but I want you especially to prophesy. For the one who prophesies is greater in dignity, merit, and usefulness than the one who speaks in tongues, unless perhaps—which scarcely happens—that person interprets, that is, explains in a known language what he speaks in an unknown one, so that the Church may receive edification through his interpretation. This interpretation has the same value as prophecy.

He proves by an analogy [Col. 0197D] from himself that they should not devote themselves to varieties of tongues, saying: Since the Church is not edified by an unknown tongue, tongues should not therefore be greatly desired; nor should they be desired for this reason: if I now, even after you have been converted and have tongues, come to you, brothers, speaking in unheard-of tongues, what benefit will I bring you unless I speak to you either in revelation, or in knowledge, or in prophecy, or in doctrine—that is, unless I speak to you in some form of instruction?

By “revelation” and “prophecy” he understands gifts of God; by “knowledge” and “doctrine,” things acquired through human effort, for they are obtained through diligence. He calls “doctrine” what someone learns from another; “knowledge” is what he understands about the Scriptures through study and his own practice. Or doctrine concerns morals, in which [Col. 0198A] one must act; knowledge concerns the natures of things, for which contemplation alone is sufficient.

He calls “prophecy” a continuous knowledge of future things, not through any figures but through the sole prompting of the Holy Spirit. “Revelation,” however, is a sudden knowledge of future things, as when someone, seized by the Spirit, suddenly foretells the future and then the Spirit departs from him; or revelation is knowledge of future things through dreams, as in Daniel and Joseph, or through events, as Noah knew through the ark.

He proves the same point by an analogy from inanimate things, saying: Although I have given you an example from myself, it was nevertheless unnecessary, because among things without a soul that give a voice, that is, a sound—whether it is a flute or a lyre—unless they give a distinction of sounds, how will it be known what is played on the flute [139] or what is played on the lyre? So also you, because you confuse indistinct sounds, are not understood in what you say.

Again, by another example I prove that confusion of tongues should not be desired. For if a trumpet gives an uncertain sound, although the sound of a trumpet is distinct when it summons to battle, who will prepare himself for battle because of an uncertain sound? Certainly no one.

Or “for” is connected with what follows: a lyre or flute sounding confusedly is not understood. For a trumpet, by analogy, also gives an uncertain sound and is not understood. And just as a trumpet giving an uncertain sound is not understood, so also you, unless through the tongue you give a clear speech, how will the hearers know what is said by you? It will certainly not be known. For you will be speaking into the air, that is, beating the air in vain.

I say that you are speaking “so many,” as it were—that is, just as there are infinitely many kinds of languages [Col. 0198C] in this world—and in each language nothing exists without a voice: each thing has its own word, distinct from those of others. Therefore, because languages are diverse and voices distinct, if I do not know the force—that is, the meaning—of the voice I utter, I shall be a barbarian to the person to whom I speak; and the one who speaks to me will likewise seem a barbarian. Thus you are barbarians to one another.

Or let the verse begin here: “So,” that is, for this reason: because he speaks unknowingly, he is judged a barbarian. You too, since you are zealous for spiritual gifts, that is, desirous of spiritual goods, seek to abound in those gifts which are effective for the edification [Col. 0198D] [141] of the Church, such as prophecy. And do not focus upon varieties of tongues, because you ought to desire those gifts which are effective for the edification of the Church. Therefore the one who speaks in an unknown tongue should pray to God that he may interpret, that is, that he may know how to interpret for his hearers what he speaks in a foreign language.

Or in this way: Let the one who speaks in a tongue pray—that is, speak—in such a way that what he says may be interpreted. One must speak in such a way that interpretation accompanies the speech. For if I myself pray—that is, speak—or pray to God in an unknown tongue, my spirit—that is, the Holy Spirit given to me—or my spirit, that is, my reason, which, although it does not understand, nevertheless knows that what it says is good because it comes from God’s gift—my reason, I say, or my spirit, prays to God within me.

Or “prays” means “speaks.” But my mind, that is, my understanding, is without fruit, that is, without the benefit of compunction, because through what I do not understand [Col. 0199A] I cannot be moved to compunction. Since, therefore, I speak in an unknown tongue, I am without fruit because I do not interpret.

What, then, does this mean—that is, how should one pray? I shall pray, or speak, with the spirit, that is, with the unknown voice given by the spirit—or with reason—and I shall also pray with the mind, that is, with understanding, because I shall utter only what I understand.

Indeed, I shall pray with the spirit and with the mind. For I shall sing psalms with the spirit and I shall sing psalms with the mind. By “singing psalms” he means praying to God with harmonious modulation of the voice. This harmony of different voices in the Church indicates that all ought to praise God in harmony of faith and life.

It is good to pray with both spirit and mind. Otherwise—that is, but—if you bless with the spirit, that is, with an unknown voice alone, who fills the place—that is, supplies the voice—of the unlearned person?

It was customary in the Church for unlearned people, that is, those inexperienced in the faith and even illiterate, when the priest was praying, [Col. 0199B] to respond “Amen,” and “And with your spirit.” But when someone was praying in an unknown tongue, even the more prudent did not know where the prayer ended or where its middle lay, because they did not understand. Thus they could not do even what the unlearned customarily did.

“Idiom” means something proper or particular. From this come the people called “unlearned” (*idiotae*), who are still in the condition of nature, knowing nothing except what they learned from their mothers as children.

Or let “otherwise” be a noun in this sense: Because of what has been said above, you should not pray in a tongue alone. “Otherwise,” that is, for another reason, do not do the same thing, because if you bless well with the spirit, and so on.

Truly no one fills the place of the unlearned person when you pray in an unknown voice. For how will even a wise person say “Amen” over [Col. 0199C] your blessing, since he does not know what you are saying? He does not understand whether, when you are speaking in an unknown tongue, you should bring the prayer to an end or continue it.

In this I reproach you: your neighbor does not understand you. I do not reproach you according to your own person, for you indeed give thanks well, insofar as it depends upon you. But it is wrong because the other person, that is, your neighbor, is not edified, since he does not understand.

Or the preceding words may be connected here: “I rightly said, ‘you bless,’ for you indeed give thanks well, insofar as it depends upon you, but your brother is not instructed.”

Again, by his own example and authority he proves that they should not pursue tongues so intensely, saying: Do not speak in a tongue in such a way that there is no instruction for your neighbor. For I, whom you ought to imitate, sometimes want to speak in the Church—that is, [Col. 0199D] a few words—with my own mind, that is, with understanding, so that I understand what I say.

By this he indicates that they sometimes spoke in such a way that they themselves did not understand each other. I want, I say, to speak with my understanding, so that I may instruct both myself and others, rather than—something I do not want to do in any way—ten thousand words, that is, an infinity of words, in an unknown tongue. I could do this if I wished, and for this I give thanks to God, because I speak, if you please, in the tongue of all of you. But nevertheless, in the Church I want to speak, and so forth.

Paul said that he possessed varieties of tongues so that the Corinthians would not say that he did not have tongues. This is why he reproaches us concerning tongues.

Again, there is another reason why they should not desire tongues: by this they become children. But the text is connected with what follows in this way: As you see in me, speak with your understanding. Likewise, brothers, by pursuing tongues whose meaning you do not possess, do not become children in understanding, speaking what you do not understand; but be infants according to [142] malice. [Col. 0200A]

He says this because they were very malicious in understanding or thought, in word and deed. Be infants in malice, but mature in understanding, that is, desiring perfect understanding, so that you may be able to prophesy.

Again, tongues should not be desired by you because you are believers, and tongues are useful not to believers but to unbelievers. To show that this is so, he first cites the authority of Isaiah (28:11), although he says that it is in the Law, designating prophecy by the name “Law.”

Truly tongues are not for believers but for unbelievers. For in the Law it is written: “In other tongues,” that is, in a [Col. 0200B] variety of languages, “and with other lips,” that is, in other forms of speech, because previously I spoke to this Jewish people about carnal matters, but now I shall speak about spiritual matters, so that, amazed by the novelty of the tongues, they may hear me. Yet even so—that is, despite so evident a miracle—they will not hear me. Believe that this is so, because the Lord says this. The phrase “with other lips” contributes nothing to the proof; it is customary for complete authoritative statements to be inserted.

Paul now draws an inference from the Law just cited. Since different tongues were presented to the unbelieving people, it is evident that tongues are for a sign, that is, a cause of a miracle, not to believers, whose faith does not need miracles, but to unbelievers, who are to be drawn to faith by the novelty of miracles.

The contrary sense is this: Tongues are not for believers but for unbelievers; prophecy, however, [Col. 0200C] is not for unbelievers—it would be foolish to reveal the mysteries of faith to unbelievers—but for believers. And because you are believers, seek prophecy, which is appropriate for believers.

Again, there is another reason why they should not desire tongues: if unbelievers happen to enter while they are speaking in various tongues in the Church, they will think that the speakers are insane.

The text is connected in this way: Since tongues are not for a sign to believers, why should you, who are the Church, be considered insane because of tongues? For if the whole Church comes together in one place and all speak in unknown tongues, while unlearned persons or some unbelievers enter as the speakers cry out amid the variety of tongues, [Col. 0200D] will they not say that you are insane, because you are making a tumult like madmen? They will call them insane because they cry out in a variety of tongues.

But if all in the Church prophesy, opening the Scriptures, and an unbeliever or an unlearned person enters while they are prophesying, he is immediately convicted by all who are prophesying there. Hearing God’s commandments and the mysteries of faith, his own conscience convicts and reproves him. Thus he is judged, that is, he recognizes himself to be subject to judgment and condemnation, instructed by all who prophesy there.

Then the secrets of his heart are made manifest to himself, because in matters where he did not think he had sinned, through the teaching he hears he recognizes himself to be gravely guilty. And so, convicted, falling on his face, he will worship God in order to receive remission of sins, also declaring openly before everyone that God is truly among you who are prophesying—those whom, a little earlier, he would have said were insane because they were making a tumult in tongues.

Because Paul neither wants them to speak in tongues indiscriminately, lest they be judged insane, nor wants them to reject entirely the gift of God, namely speaking in tongues, [Col. 0201A] he determines how they should use this gift and the others: by doing everything for the benefit of their neighbor.

The text is connected in this way: Since we are called insane when we make a tumult in tongues, whereas when we prophesy we are said to have God among us, what should be done, brothers? Will you always prophesy and completely neglect tongues? Certainly not. But when you come together, each one has his own gift.

One has a psalm, so that he may sing or interpret psalms in the Church. Another has teaching, so that he knows how to instruct concerning morals. Another has an Apocalypse, that is, a revelation of hidden things. He gives these three only by way of illustration; the two that follow are given to establish his point. Another [Col. 0201B] has an unknown tongue. Another has the interpretation of the Scriptures, that is, prophecy. Since you have all these gifts, let everything be done among you for the edification of the Church.

Whether you do this [143] or something else; whether someone speaks in an unknown tongue, let it be limited to two—that is, I permit only two people to speak in this way—or at most three. For I do not grant that more than three may do so. Nor should two or three cry out in the same part of the church, but in different parts—for example, one at the front and another at the rear of the church. Or “in different parts” may mean at different times of day, such as one at the third hour and another at the sixth.

Nor should they speak without an interpreter; one should always be present so that what is said in an unusual manner may be interpreted in the language of the people. But if you object that sometimes no interpreter is present, I would rather have the person speaking in a tongue keep silent [Col. 0201C] in the Church than growl like a barbarian without an interpreter. Let him not speak to the Church, but to himself and to God, that is, for his own instruction and for divine praise.

Just as those speaking in tongues are to be limited, so also let two or three prophets speak in the Church, likewise in turn. Others might say: “We know just as much; shall we not prophesy?” Certainly not. Rather, let the other prophets judge what is taught by those brothers, so that if they teach anything wrongly, the others may correct them.

Again, another instruction concerning the prophets: If something is suddenly revealed by the Spirit to another who is sitting, let that person rise and speak, and let the one who was speaking first keep silent. It often happened that the Spirit suddenly seized someone, and concerning this the Apostle gives the command that when [Col. 0201D] it occurs, such a person should be permitted to speak. Let the one who was sitting before speak, and let the other keep silent.

I say this because you can all prophesy, one by one. It is simply necessary to ensure that all may learn, that is, be instructed through the one who is prophesying. It often happens that someone who thought himself wise learns through one who has suddenly been inspired something he did not know. Let them learn, I say, and so let all be exhorted to better things. For this reason I command the first speaker to be silent.

For the spirit of the prophets is subject to the prophets, that is, the Holy Spirit does not compel them to speak whether they wish to or not. Since the Spirit is God, he is not a God of dissension; such dissension would certainly arise if they shouted and quarreled. Rather, he is the God of peace and harmony. This peace is preserved if they support one another in turn.

I say this to you concerning tongues, [Col. 0202A] prophecy, charity, and all the matters mentioned above, just as I teach the same doctrine in all the churches, because they are the churches of the saints.

Or this may be connected with the following text: All men may prophesy, but women never may. I say this just as I teach in all the churches. Indeed, let women keep silent in the churches. They are not permitted by me or by any other teacher to speak in the Church. Rather, I command them everywhere to be subject to men, with whom they would make themselves equal if they presumed to speak in the Church.

I say this concerning women: that they are to be subject, just as the Law also says in Genesis: “You shall be under the authority of your husband, and he shall rule over you” (Genesis 3:16).

They might say: “We do not want to speak, but only to ask questions.” Certainly not. If they wish to learn anything, let them ask [Col. 0202B] their husbands, not in the Church but at home; never in the Church. For it is shameful for a woman to speak in the Church, that is, such speech proves the woman shameful and shameless.

This instruction concerning prophets and women, and whatever else I have taught above, you must not reject out of pride in order to introduce your own innovations. For did the word of God go out from you to the other churches, so that you may now introduce [or, impose] new doctrines? Or do you boast as though the word of God came to you alone, and as though you alone believed in God?

Let no one among you, presuming to be wise, neglect my commandments. But if anyone among you seems to be a prophet, that is, someone who understands the Scriptures, or even spiritual, that is, someone who leads a spiritual life, whoever he may be, let him acknowledge the things I write to you, and that he must obey them, because these commandments are not mine but the Lord’s.

But if anyone, raising himself insolently and scorning to attend to these commandments, is ignorant, I tell you concerning him that he will certainly be ignored by God. Since he ignores these commandments, he will be ignored by God. [Col. 0202C]

Therefore, my brothers, desire to prophesy, as I command, and do not forbid speaking in tongues, as I determined above. Do not forbid it, but let everything among you be done decently, that is, for the edification of the Church, and [144] in accordance with the order I established above, so that only a few speak or prophesy, and in turn.

## CHAPTER XV
“Now I make known to you, brothers, the Gospel that I preached to you, which you also received, in which [Col. 0202D] you also stand. Through it you are also being saved—if you hold fast to the manner in which I preached it to you, unless you believed in vain. For I delivered to you first of all what I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures; and that he was buried; and that he rose again on the third day according to the Scriptures; and that he was seen by Cephas, and afterward by the eleven. Then he was seen by more than five hundred brothers at once, most of whom remain until now, though some have fallen asleep. Then he was seen by James, then by all the apostles; and last of all, as though to one untimely born, he was seen also by me. For I am the least of the apostles, who am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God. But by the grace of God I am what I am; and his grace toward me was not in vain, but I labored more abundantly than all of them. Yet it was not I, but the grace of God with me. Whether then it was I or they, this is how we preached, and this is how you believed.

“But if Christ is preached as having risen from the dead, how do some among you say that there is no resurrection of the dead, and that Christ did not rise? If Christ did not rise, then our preaching is empty, and your faith is also empty. Moreover, we are found to be false witnesses of God, because we have testified against God that he raised Christ, whom he did not raise, if the dead are not raised. For if the dead are not raised, neither has Christ been raised. And if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile. You are still in your sins. Therefore those also who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished. If in this life only we have hope in Christ, we are more pitiable than all people.

“But now Christ has risen from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep, since death came through a human being, and through a human being also comes the resurrection of the dead. For just as all die in Adam, so also all will be made alive in Christ. But each in his own order: Christ the firstfruits; then those who belong to Christ, who believed at his coming; then the end, when he has handed over the kingdom to God and the Father, when he has abolished every rule, authority, and power. For he must reign until he has placed all his enemies under his feet (Ps. CIX, 1). Last of all, death, the enemy, will be destroyed. For he has subjected all things under his feet (Ps. VIII, 8). But when he says, ‘All things have been subjected to him,’ it is undoubtedly except for the one who subjected all things to him. And when [variant: “For when”] all things have been subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subjected to the one who subjected all things to him, so that God may be all in all.

“Otherwise, what will those do who are baptized for the dead? If the dead are not raised at all, why are they also baptized for them? Why do we also endanger ourselves every hour? Every day I die because of your glory [or: for the sake of your glory], brothers, which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord. If, in merely human terms, I fought with beasts at Ephesus, what good does it do me if the dead are not raised? ‘Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die’ (Wis. II, 6; Isa. XXII, 13). Do not be deceived. Evil conversations corrupt good morals. Awake to righteousness, and do not sin; for some have no knowledge of God. I say this to your shame.

“But someone will say: ‘How are the dead raised? And with what sort of body will they come?’ Fool! What you sow is not made alive unless it first dies. And what you sow is not the body that is to be, but a bare grain—perhaps of wheat, or of one of the other kinds. But God gives it a body as he wills, and to each of the seeds its own body. Not all flesh is the same flesh: there is one flesh of human beings, another of animals, another of birds, and another of fish. There are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies; but one is the glory of the heavenly, and another of the earthly. There is one brightness of the sun, another brightness of the moon, and another brightness of the stars; for star differs from star in brightness. So also is the resurrection of the dead. It is sown in corruption; it will rise in incorruption. It is sown in dishonor; it will rise in glory. It is sown in weakness; it will rise in power. It is sown an animal body; it will rise a spiritual body.

“If there is an animal body, there is also a spiritual one, as it is written: ‘The first man Adam was made into a living soul’ (Gen. II, 7); the last Adam into a life-giving spirit. But the spiritual was not first; rather, the animal, and afterward the spiritual. The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man was from heaven, heavenly. As was the earthly, so also are the earthly; and as was the heavenly, so also are the heavenly. Therefore, just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the heavenly.

“Now this I say, brothers: flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God, nor will corruption possess incorruption. Behold, I tell you a mystery: We shall all indeed rise, but we shall not all be changed. In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet—for the trumpet will sound, and the dead will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed. For this corruptible body must put on incorruption, and this mortal body must put on immortality. And when this mortal body has put on immortality, then the saying written will come to pass: ‘Death has been swallowed up in victory’ (Hos. XIII, 14). ‘Where is your victory, O death? Where is your sting, O death?’ The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law. But thanks be to God, who has given us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ (1 John V, 5). Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast and immovable, always abounding in every work of the Lord, knowing always that your labor is not in vain in the Lord.”

## EXPOSITION

After teaching them about baptism, about the body and blood of the Lord, and about the gifts of the Holy Spirit, he finally instructs them about the resurrection of the dead, which some of them believed and some denied. For they believed that Christ had truly risen from the dead; they also believed that those who died at the last trumpet and immediately returned to life with their flesh intact would rise in this way. But they said that those whose bodies had been dissolved into ashes could in no way rise, clinging excessively to natural arguments.

The text is joined as follows: “I teach you in this way about tongues and prophecy. But concerning the resurrection of the dead I make known to you, brothers”—I say, “I make known the Gospel,” that is, the resurrection of the dead, which is the greatest part of my preaching; the Gospel of the resurrection that I preached to you, so that you may not claim that you sinned through ignorance; which you also received, and it ought to be shameful for you to deny again what you once believed rightly; in which you also stand. For unless you believe the resurrection, you stand in the faith in vain [Col. 0205A]. Through this Gospel you will also be saved: for we call the resurrection of the flesh a part of the faith, without which no one can be saved.

I say that you will be saved if you hold fast to this Gospel in the manner in which I preached it to you—and unless this means that you believed in vain, that is, unless you say that your faith is useless, something the Corinthians would in no way admit: namely, that they had believed in vain.

“I deliver the Gospel to you.” For what I delivered to you first of all—that is, among the more important matters of faith—I did not receive from myself, but received from God. This, namely, is the Gospel: that Christ died to erase our sins. And if our sins have been erased, whose punishment is death, why are we held in death? Christ died—and I say this according to the Scriptures of the prophets, who bear witness to the same thing.

Since he is now about to prove the resurrection, he first establishes that Christ truly died, so that a true resurrection might follow a true death. I also delivered this to you concerning Christ: that he was buried, so that it might not be said that, rising immediately after death, he had not truly died. I also delivered to you concerning him that he rose on the third day. And I say this according to the Scriptures, which attest to it.

He proved it through the testimonies of the Scriptures; he also proves that Christ rose through the testimonies of those to whom he appeared after the resurrection. “I also delivered this to you: that he was seen by Cephas,” that is, by Peter. Where and how this apparition occurred, we do not read; it is only written: “The Lord rose and appeared to Peter,” and afterward “he was seen by the eleven apostles” [Col. 0205C], when Thomas was with them (Luke XXIV, 39).

Then he was seen by more than five hundred brothers at once, many of whom remain until this time; and, if you wish, ask them. But some of them have fallen asleep. He says that Christ died, but that these men fell asleep.

Then he was also seen by James, the bishop of Jerusalem, who, having seen Christ on the cross, vowed that he would not eat bread until he saw Christ risen. Nothing is found in the Gospels about these two appearances.

Then he was seen by all the apostles (Acts IX, 3), on the day of the Ascension. “Last of all he was seen by me” (Acts XXII, 17), first on the road, afterward in the temple while I was praying. “By me,” he says, “as though by one untimely born,” that is, born into the apostolate by a certain force and compulsion.

He calls himself untimely born because, born in Christ outside the proper time, he received the apostolate after the Lord had been received into heaven with his flesh. I rightly say “untimely born.” For I am the least of the apostles, and am not even worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God.

And although I was not worthy, nevertheless I am what I am—that is, I am certainly an apostle through the grace of God. Although I was previously a persecutor, from the moment I received his grace that grace was not idle in me; rather, I labored more abundantly than all the other apostles in every kind of suffering. And although I say “I labored,” nevertheless I could not do this by myself; the grace of God worked with me.

By saying that he endured so many and such great things, he sufficiently demonstrates the resurrection, in hope of which he suffers everything.

He returns to what he said above: Truly Christ rose. For “this is how we preach”—whether I or those other apostles; this is an appeal to authority. You also believed in this way, that Christ truly rose; do not deny it.

But if it is preached—and cannot be denied—that Christ rose from the dead, how do some among you say that there will be no resurrection of the dead? If Christ rose—which is certainly true—the resurrection of the dead necessarily follows.

Above he proved this through the authorities of the Scriptures and the testimonies of the saints who saw that Christ truly rose from the dead; from this he inferred that, if Christ rose, the resurrection of the dead will also occur.

He now proves this inference as follows: Truly, if Christ rose, there is also a resurrection of the dead. For if there is no resurrection of the dead [Col. 0206B], neither has Christ risen. This passage is based on similarity, and concerns cause and effect under different aspects.

The similarity consists in this: if Christ could not be held by death because sin—the cause of death—was not in him, neither shall we, justified from sins according to our measure, be held in death. For if we escape death, then we shall rise. Through this similarity—namely, that we have been justified from sins—we shall rise with Christ. But because Christ is far greater than we in righteousness, he will therefore be greater in the glory of the resurrection.

Again, Christ’s resurrection and everything he accomplished on earth had as their purpose the restoration of humanity to its lost blessedness. For if this effect—namely, the resurrection of the dead [Col. 0206C]—does not follow, those causes went before in vain. But Christ rose, and he proves this through many absurd consequences that would follow if he had not risen.

I say that Christ rose. For if Christ did not rise, then our preaching is empty, that is, without a reality, because the thing it preaches would not be so. And another absurd consequence follows from the same premise: your faith is empty, that is, fruitless, if Christ did not rise—something the Corinthians would in no way admit, namely, that their faith was empty.

Again, another absurd consequence follows if Christ did not rise: we would then be found to be false witnesses of God the Father, because we had testified against God. For it does not please God if someone attributes to God what he did not do. This is the testimony, namely, that God raised Christ, whom he certainly did not raise if the dead are not raised.

It is true that the dead rise, as you say. For if the dead do not rise, neither has Christ risen. He had stated the same thing above, but for another purpose. There he stated it in order to prove that the resurrection of the dead is true if Christ has risen and the dead will rise. Here, however, he states it in order to infer the truth of the claim that Christ was not raised unless the dead rise [Col. 0206D].

A Corinthian might say: “I would rather deny Christ’s resurrection than concede that the dead rise.” He again proves through an absurd consequence that Christ rose.

Truly Christ rose. For if Christ did not rise, your faith concerning Christ is vain. That faith which you received did not exist. Truly, if Christ did not rise, your faith is vain. For you are still in your sins. He is read to have risen for our justification. For if he did not rise, neither did he justify us; thus your faith is vain.

And because people are still in their sins, therefore those who have fallen asleep in Christ—that is, those who died in faith in Christ—have perished, that is, they have been condemned.

Again, another absurd consequence follows. If we have hope in Christ only in this life, as you say, without expecting to have a future life, then we are more pitiable than all people, because we shall enjoy neither this life nor another, while we are continually being worn down by afflictions.

Since so many absurd consequences arise from denying the resurrection, it follows that now—that is, from the arguments already given—it is gathered that Christ truly rose from the dead.

Christ, I say, is the firstfruits both in time and in dignity. For even if some were raised before him, they were not raised from the dead permanently; they returned again to the number of those who die. He is first in dignity because he will possess greater glory than all, and whatever the others have, they will have entirely from him and through him.

“Christ,” I say, “the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep.” By saying that Christ is the firstfruits, he intimates that the others who have fallen asleep will follow him in the resurrection.

Someone might say: “It does not seem possible that, through the merit of one human being, Christ, all human beings could rise.” Paul replies: Truly, the others who have fallen asleep will rise through their firstfruits, that is, through Christ, since through one human being came the death of all, and through one human being there will likewise be the resurrection of the dead.

This follows from similarity. For just as all die in Adam alone, so also all will be made alive in Christ alone. If the guilt of Adam alone was sufficient for the condemnation of all, then—to speak only of the similarity while setting aside the greater force of the comparison—why would the righteousness of Christ alone not likewise suffice for the justification of all?

After proving that the resurrection of all will truly take place, he suitably adds a discussion of the order of that resurrection, in order thereby to make them more certain of it and invite them to the same resurrection, saying:

“Although all rise equally, each will nevertheless be in his own order. For whoever has merited more will receive more glory.” Thus Christ will be the firstfruits in time and dignity, as stated above. Then, after Christ, those who belong to Christ will be in glory.

I say that they belong to Christ—namely, those who believed in his second coming, that is, in the resurrection; and they believed in this with integrity of faith and good works, going out to meet Christ at his coming.

He could have said, “those who believed in Christ’s birth or passion.” But he said “at his coming” because he intended to commend the resurrection to them.

And after those who belong to Christ have risen, then there will be the end, that is, the fulfillment of the promised blessedness, when Christ has handed over the kingdom—that is, his Church, which he rules with power.

He says that he will hand it over to God and the Father. Christ will then be said to hand the kingdom over to the Father when he places his Church in the sight of God, so that what it saw here through a mirror and in an enigma it may there see face to face.

He says “to God and the Father” in order to show that he had no beginning from another. He also indicates that he is Creator and extends paternal love toward creatures. When, I say, he has handed over the kingdom, and when he has abolished every rule, authority, and power.

It should be noted that God established differences of offices among the angels, and did all this for the sake of human beings, so that the angels might minister to their salvation. But after human beings have reached perfection and need no ministry, those names will be destroyed among the angels by which they were called according to the diversity of human administration.

For among the angels there are some who hold rule over all the others. There are also others who, with authority, accomplish what is enjoined upon them by those who hold rule. There are others who are called powers because they are workers of miracles.

Likewise, among the evil angels some are rulers over all the others. Others have the power to accomplish what the rulers command. Others are powers, introducing certain new things as though they were miracles. These distinctions too will finally be abolished. For just as the good angels will no longer have anything in which to protect human beings, so the evil angels will no longer have anything in which to harm them.

Likewise, among human beings every distinction of precedence or subjection will be destroyed; among them there will be no inequality of government.

At the end Christ will hand his kingdom over to the Father. But meanwhile, while the end has not yet arrived, he must reign—that is, Christ must rule his Church with power.

He says “must” because this was prophesied in the Scriptures, which necessarily must be fulfilled.

“I say that he must reign until God places all Christ’s enemies under his feet,” that is, in such complete subjection as when some are thrown down beneath the feet of others. Or “under his feet,” that is, subjected to Christ’s humanity. It is signified by the feet for this reason: through the assumed humanity, divinity came to human beings.

And after all these things have been abolished, death too will finally be destroyed, because after sin no longer exists, its punishment—namely, death—will also not remain.

I say “death the enemy,” which human beings also hate and which hates human beings.

Truly, the enemies will be placed under Christ’s feet. For it is written in the Psalm: “God subjected all things under his feet” (Ps. VIII, 8), that is, under Christ’s feet, as has been explained in the Psalm. Nevertheless, the text has, “You subjected them.”

When Scripture says that all things are undoubtedly subjected to Christ, it means all things except the one who subjected all things to him, namely, except divinity. God, who subjected all things to Christ, is not subject to Christ.

But Christ himself will be subject to him—that is, to the Godhead—which subjected all things to Christ. Someone might say: “For the present Christ will be subject to God, until God has subjected all things to him; but afterward he will not be.” “He certainly will,” says Paul. “For when all things have been subjected to Christ, then Christ himself will be subject to God, who subjected all things to him.”

He will be subject in such a way as to be equal—namely, so that Christ may be God in all things, that is, in each of his creatures; and thus be all in all, that is, all things to each individual: perfect blessedness, perfect glory, and peace surpassing even every human desire.

He returns to prove the resurrection of the dead, saying: Death will be destroyed through Christ, and human beings will then rise. Otherwise—that is, if you say that there is no resurrection of the dead—what will those do who are baptized for the dead?

Here he touches upon the wicked custom of certain people who, having heard that a future resurrection would belong to those who were baptized, baptized themselves again, after they had been baptized, in the place of an unbelieving father who had already died, so that the father or mother might thereby be saved in the resurrection.

He brings this forward to shame the Corinthians: if those perverse people had such great faith in the resurrection, how much more ought the Corinthians to believe the resurrection?

The text is as follows: “What will those do who are baptized for the dead in the hope of rising, if the dead do not rise at all? Why are they also baptized for the sake of justifying them, when they are not even justified? If they were justified from sins and rose.”

Or it may be understood in another way: “Otherwise”—that is, if there is no resurrection—“what will those do who are baptized for dead works,” that is, for sins that produce death? They are baptized, I say, in the hope of resurrection. And what will they do if the dead do not rise at all? Why are they also baptized for them,” that is, so that they may be justified from sins?

Or again: “Otherwise, if the dead do not rise, what will those do who are baptized for themselves as dead”—that is, to be put to death with respect to sin—or “for themselves, who have been put to death through sin in relation to God?” The rest is as stated above.

Again, if there is no resurrection of the dead, why do we apostles also endanger ourselves every hour? Our tribulations do not end, and we rejoice to suffer them in the hope of the future resurrection.

Truly, we are endangered. For “every day I die”—that is, I endure the dangers of death—“brothers, because of your glory,” so that you may be worthy of the glory of the resurrection.

Or, according to Augustine: “I die, and I swear this by your glory, brothers”—the glory which I already possess in hope in Christ Jesus our Lord, who has already risen with my flesh into glory and who has also obtained that I might rise with him.

If the dead do not rise, what good does it do me if, in merely human terms—that is, according to the power of human reasoning—or “according to man,” because I was a human being while they were beasts, I fought with beasts at Ephesus?

I certainly fought according to man against beasts at Ephesus—that is, against bestial Ephesians—because by denying the resurrection they say that a human being lives only in this world, which is also what beasts do.

What, I ask, does that struggle profit me unless I am to have glory after death? The Ephesians denied the resurrection; against them Paul argued with great labor, proving that the resurrection would occur.

And since, according to you, no life remains after this one, there is now nothing else to do except, in despair, to eat and drink, because we shall die without living any longer: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die” (Isa. XXII, 13; Wis. II, 6).

The Jews spoke these words when they were being afflicted in the Babylonian captivity and despaired of God’s help. Likewise, those who deny the resurrection despair of God’s help and power.

And because, brothers, one must not despair in this way but must trust in the resurrection, do not be led astray by false apostles who do not possess faith in the resurrection. By saying “be led astray,” he indicates that there are deceivers among them.

Do not believe the deceivers. For their evil conversations not only violate the faith; they also corrupt good morals. Whoever does not believe in the future life, I do not know why he would labor to cling to good morals.

And so that you may not be corrupted by the deceivers, awake for this purpose: that you may be righteous and preserve righteousness. Do not sin any longer; it is necessary for you to awaken.

For some among you have ignorance of God—that is, they do not know God’s equity and faith—and I say this to your shame, so that you may be ashamed of your sins.

After Paul had proved the future resurrection through necessary arguments, through the absurd consequences that follow from denying it, and again through Christ’s power [Col. 0210B], he wishes to prove it through the law of nature, because human wisdom argues more readily according to nature’s passibility [or: possibility].

It is as though he were saying: Although above I sufficiently proved the resurrection, nevertheless, by raising an objection according to the law of nature, someone says to me: “How do the dead rise after they have already been dissolved into dust? Nature does not appear to permit this.”

Again, even if that dust is somehow joined together, with what sort of body will the people who rise come? Can it be believed that such great glory could come to dissolved dust, as you preach?

He answers the first question. Nature readily permits the dead to rise. For that seed—which you, fool that you are, who doubt the resurrection, sow—I say, that seed which you sow is not made alive, that is, it cannot live in any way unless it first dies and decays. You see that the seed must rot so that afterward it may live. Do not now doubt that a human being can live again after death, since through death it is necessary to live.

He proves the other question, namely, the future glory of the bodies, by the likeness of the same seed, saying: Truly, they will come in greater bodily glory. For what you sow is not the body that is to be, but you sow a bare grain; yet the body that will come from the bare grain will have many grains, husks, and stalks.

Likewise, it should not seem absurd to you if we say that our bodies will rise in greater glory than in which they are sown here. You sow a bare grain, for example, as a grain of wheat, or a grain of one of the other crops.

You sow a bare grain; but God gives that grain a body as he wills, glorious in the fruitfulness of grains, ears, and stalks. Nevertheless, he returns to each seed its own body: for if wheat was sown, wheat sprouts; and thus the individual grains rise in the identity of their seeds. This is an example of an improved resurrection, not of a lost substance.

Although all agree in this, that they will possess the glory of the resurrection, they nevertheless differ in that some will possess greater glory and some less, according to the difference of their merits.

Someone might say: Since the substance of all human beings consists of the same elements, it appears that whatever is given to one must be possessed in its entirety by another, since the matter is similar.

Paul refutes this by the likeness of other creatures, so as always to urge them toward what is better. For just as all animals are made from the same elements, the same matter nevertheless does not prevent them from being different from one another.

Among heavenly creatures too, although they are constituted from the same materials, there is a difference of brightness between them. Thus, among human beings also, the fact that the nature of the flesh is the same for all does not prevent them from differing in the glory of the resurrection.

The text is joined as follows: Although all rise in greater glory of the flesh, they nevertheless rise differently. Nor does the same matter of their constitution, common to all, prevent this, just as you see that not all flesh is the same flesh, although all flesh comes from the same matter. The flesh of human beings is one kind, and the flesh of animals another. The flesh of birds is another, and the flesh of fish another [Col. 0211B].

And just as earthly bodies differ from one another, so heavenly bodies differ from earthly bodies. For there are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies; and although they agree in being bodies, they nevertheless differ in this: the glory of heavenly bodies is one thing, and that of earthly bodies another.

And just as heavenly bodies differ from earthly bodies, so the heavenly bodies themselves differ from one another. For the brightness of the sun is one thing, the brightness of the moon another, and the brightness of the stars another.

There is also a difference among the stars themselves: star differs from star in brightness. And just as these creatures differ in brightness from one another, so the resurrection of the dead will also differ among the righteous in the brightness of glory.

Although they differ in the glory of the resurrection, they nevertheless have this in common: here the human body is sown [Col. 0211C] into corruption, that is, so that it may be subject to corruption.

He says that it is sown from the day on which a human being is conceived until the day of the resurrection of all. It is indeed sown in corruption, but it will rise in incorruption—that is, so that it may be free from every corruption—and this rising will take place on the day of judgment.

It is sown not only in corruption but also in dishonor. For a human being is generated in great lowliness of flesh, but then will rise in glory, which will be possessed perpetually.

It is sown here in weakness, for here it is subject to all diseases and various miseries; but then it will rise in the power of impassibility and immortality.

Here the animal body is sown, which must be sustained by the daily nourishment of food, like every animal; but then the spiritual body will rise, governed by the spirit alone, without the use of bodily food.

Truly, an animal body is sown. Since this body of yours is an animal body, the same body will rise as a spiritual body; since it is spiritual then.

Or it may be understood in another way: Truly the body will rise as a spiritual body. For if the body is now called animal, the same body must also be called spiritual. It would not be called animal except in relation to the spiritual, so that “animal” and “spiritual” may have, as it were, the force of relative terms.

Truly, this body is animal, as it is written in Genesis (Gen. II, 7): “The first man”—here called Adam—“was made into a living soul.” He was not made into a soul that gave life to the body, because the body was soon dissolved by death, but into a living soul, that is, one that would live there in the flesh. For unless the body were nourished by food, the soul would not live there.

And therefore it is called living, as though by powers belonging to another, [Col. 0212A] and not life-giving.

And truly, the body will rise as a spiritual body. For the last Adam, that is, Christ, is called Adam because he was born from him according to the line of the flesh. He is called “last,” however, because after him there will not be another Adam who introduces a new generation. For every human being is either a son of the carnal Adam or of the spiritual one.

This last Adam, I say, was made into a spirit that is not living but life-giving. For in that resurrection the soul will give life to the body in such a way that it will live perpetually, needing no nourishment.

He might say: “Although Christ, who was God, could thus be made alive, I shall not be able to do so, since I am merely human.” “Nothing prevents it,” Paul replies. “Although Christ is God, that body which is spiritual did not exist first; rather, first there was the body which [Col. 0212B] is animal, and afterward there was the body which is spiritual. Truly, the first man was made into a living soul, for the first man was made from the earth, earthly, and the second Adam was made into a life-giving spirit. For the second man was heavenly, coming from heaven.

“And just as that first man was earthly, so also are those who belong to the earth, who cling to his earthliness. And just as that second man was heavenly, so also will those who imitate him be heavenly. Since, then, whoever follows what is earthly will be earthly, and whoever follows what is heavenly will be heavenly, let us therefore, just as we have borne the image of the earthly Adam through sin, now bear the image of the heavenly Adam through a life of righteousness, so that, having laid aside the burden of earthliness, we may rejoice in the lightness of heavenly glory.

“Because he had just said that those who cling to the heavenly one would be like him, and had also said, ‘Let us bear the image of the heavenly one,’ we might, on the basis of these words, think that it is sufficient for our salvation merely to lay aside the old man in baptism and assume the new man there. Paul determines that it is not enough to bear the image of the heavenly one in this way, unless we bear it through continual imitation in our works. The wording is joined as follows: ‘Although I have said, “Let us bear the image of the heavenly one, and we shall be heavenly,” nevertheless I say this’—that is, I declare to you, brothers—‘that flesh and blood,’ that is, those who yield to flesh and blood—for some sins arise from carnality, such as soft and luxurious lust, while others arise from a defect of the blood, such as anger resulting from melancholy—and whoever pursues flesh and blood in sin, [Col. 0212D] these cannot possess the kingdom of God,’ that is, themselves in the future glory.

“For the kingdom of God is nothing other than the human beings themselves. In this life no one possesses himself, because there is no day on which a person is not possessed by sin; but in future blessedness each of the righteous will possess himself, where no one will be disturbed by the temptation of the flesh. Truly, flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God, for flesh and blood are corruption, whereas the kingdom of God is incorruption. Corruption, however, will not possess incorruptibility; therefore flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God.

“Because above he had just said, ‘Whoever bears the image of the heavenly one will rise in glory,’ and had again said that flesh and blood would in no way possess the kingdom of God, lest anyone understand these statements as contradictory, he resolves the matter by removing every contradiction, saying: ‘So that you may not interpret my preceding words wrongly, behold, I tell you a mystery’—that is, I disclose to you a hidden matter, so that by disclosing it I may remove your uncertainty concerning it. It is indeed true, as I have already stated, that we shall all rise—that is, we shall all take up our bodies again—but we shall not all be changed, by receiving glory. For some will rise to increase their punishment, and others to glory.

“‘We shall rise in a moment.’ And, to make the suddenness of the resurrection even clearer, he corrects what he had said—‘in a moment’—by saying: ‘We shall rise in the blink of an eye,’ that is, as quickly as the eye moves toward seeing something, or as quickly as one eyelid joins the other. This, however, will take place at the last trumpet—not because the sound of a trumpet will actually be heard there, but because, just as the sound of a trumpet invites victors to the palm of triumph while it brings terror to the defeated, so that sound will be a sign to the righteous that they may receive the reward of triumph, while it will strike the wicked with terror at their punishment.

“‘Last,’ because although Christ has uttered many voices in the world—by which he terrified the wicked and gladdened the righteous—that voice of judgment will be the last, completing glory for the righteous and unending wrath for the wicked. And because he had said nothing further about this trumpet, he adds: ‘I rightly speak of a trumpet. For the trumpet will sound.’ He does not determine whether Christ or an angel ought to sound that trumpet. Or, taking the noun as nominative, ‘that trumpet will sound,’ and at the sound of the trumpet the dead will rise incorruptible—that is, restored in the integrity of their members—although some will be corrupted by the pain of their punishments; but we, the elect of God, will be changed, receiving the glory of the resurrection.

“Truly we shall be changed, for it is necessary—that is, so that the Scriptures may truly be fulfilled, it is unavoidable—that this corruptible thing, namely, the body worn down by so many miseries, put on incorruption. And because something incorruptible might nevertheless exist only for a time and not escape decay forever, he added: ‘This mortal body must also put on immortality.’”

Truly this mortal thing will become immortal. For death has been swallowed up—that is, destroyed and devoured—in Christ’s victory, when by his death he conquered death; or, “in its own victory,” that is, in death’s victory. For by presuming to attack Christ, in whom there was no sin—the cause of death—death itself perished in that very presumption. This authority is found in Hosea as follows: “O death, I shall be your death” (Hosea XIII). And because some were interpreting this Scripture wrongly, saying that it had been written about the death of the soul and not of the body, Paul first gives an explanation of this authority, saying: “When this mortal body has put on immortality.” For it is not the case, as some wrongly suppose, that the soul alone will escape death; the body also will escape it together with the soul. Then will come to pass—that is, that saying written in Hosea will be fulfilled: “Death has been swallowed up in victory,” as has been said.

“The words that follow are said to belong to the same prophet, mocking death itself because it has been destroyed, and saying: ‘Since it has been swallowed up, where is your victory now, O death, by which you subjected everything to your authority? And, O death, [Col. 0214A] where is your sting now—that is, the sin which, in the barb of its tail, carried death like poison?’”

Paul says: “I rightly speak of a sting, for sin is the sting of death,” that is, by its own barb it goads human beings toward death. Because Paul explains what the sting is, the preceding words are thought not to belong to him; or, if they are Paul’s, the meaning nevertheless does not change. For he mocks death, saying: “Now that you have been swallowed up, where is your victory, O death?” The rest remains unchanged.

Lest they should say again, “Once sin has been destroyed, death too will be destroyed; therefore things are well for us now, because through the law we shall destroy sin,” Paul counters: “Sin is the sting of death.” The law, however, in no way weakens sin; rather, it is the power and increase of sin. And this he suitably removes, so that, just as he had proved that the resurrection comes through Christ, he might likewise show through him that there is complete remission of sins.

And because the law increases sin, no thanks are owed to the law; rather, let us all give thanks to God, who has given us victory over sin and death, and this through our Lord Jesus Christ. And because every victory comes from God and through Christ, therefore, my brothers, so that you may be beloved of God, be steadfast in the good while you are at peace. Be immovable also in the faith if adversities should rush upon you. I say this to you who abound in the work of the Lord: work ever more and more excellently. I say this to you who always know that your labor is not in vain—that is, without fruit—but that you will rise in great glory, and this in the Lord, that is, through the Lord who acts mercifully in you.

## CHAPTER XVI

[Col. 0214C]

“Now concerning the collections that are made for the saints: just as I arranged in the church of Galatia, so also do you. On the first day of the week, let each of you set something aside privately, storing up whatever may have seemed good to him, so that collections may not begin when I come. And when I am present, I shall send those whom you approve by letters to carry your gift to Jerusalem. And if it is worthy that I should go, they will go with me.

“I shall come to you when I have passed through Macedonia; for I shall pass through Macedonia. But perhaps I shall remain with you, or even spend the winter, so that you may send me on wherever I go. For I do not wish to see you merely in passing. I hope to remain with you for some time, if the Lord permits. I shall remain at Ephesus until Pentecost. For a great and evident door has been opened to me, and there are many adversaries.

“If Timothy comes, see to it that he is without fear among you; for he is doing the work of the Lord, just as I am. Therefore let no one despise him. Send him on in peace, so that he may come to me; for I am waiting for him with the brothers.

“Now concerning our brother Apollos, I inform you that I urged him strongly to come to you with the brothers; but it was certainly not his will to come now. He will come when he has the opportunity.

“Be watchful, stand firm in the faith, act manfully, and be strengthened. Let everything of yours be done in love.

“Now I beseech you, brothers: you know the household of Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus, because they are the firstfruits of Achaia, and they devoted themselves to the ministry of the saints, so that you also may submit to such men and to everyone who cooperates and labors. I rejoice in the presence of Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus, because they supplied what was lacking on your part. For they refreshed both my spirit and yours. Therefore acknowledge those who are such.

“All the churches of Asia greet you. Aquila and Prisca greet you warmly in the Lord, together with the church in their household; I am also their guest. All the brothers greet you. Greet one another with a holy kiss.

“The greeting is by the hand of Paul. If anyone does not love our Lord Jesus Christ, let him be anathema: Maran Atha. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you. My love be with all of you in Christ Jesus. Amen.”

## EXPOSITION

After arranging, according to the order of right faith, each of the matters that had to be commanded, at the end of the Epistle he admonishes them about certain private matters: namely, that they should assist the saints who were in Jerusalem, whom both the plunder of unbelievers and a public famine had overwhelmed, by supplying something from their abundance.

The wording is joined as follows: “Believe concerning the resurrection of the dead in this way. Concerning the collections that are made to be carried to the saints who are in Jerusalem, do likewise on one day of the week—that is, of the seven-day cycle—as I arranged should be done in the churches of Galatia.”

And lest you think that I intend to assign this collection to my own uses, I command that each of you set something aside privately—not, however, in such a way that he should consider it his own, but storing it up and preserving it intact as though it belonged to another—whatever he has decided to distribute to the poor saints. For this reason I say, “Do it on one day of the week,” so that collections may not first begin when I come.

But, in order to remove every suspicion from you who are inclined to suspect evil, when I am present with you I shall send, not my own envoys, but those whom you approve—that is, whom you yourselves have chosen—to carry your gift, that is, your free offering, to Jerusalem. I shall send them, he says, “by letters,” that is, with my letters, which will be handed over to them as a sign of authorization.

The Corinthians might say: “You carry the gifts of others yourself; why do you disdain carrying ours?” Paul replies: “Certainly, if your gift is worthy of my going, your envoys will go with me, so that I may come together with them and commend your generosity.”

This is what I shall do concerning your gift. I shall also come to you when I have passed through Macedonia, for I am going first to the Macedonians. I rightly say, “when I have passed through,” for I shall truly pass through Macedonia; but afterward I shall perhaps remain with you—that is, if God grants it. Or, to say more, I shall spend the winter with you, so that you may send me on wherever I go when I depart from you.

I shall spend the winter there because I do not wish to see you merely in passing. I shall not see you in passing for this reason: because I hope to remain with you for some time, if the Lord permits. And although I say that I shall come to you, I shall nevertheless remain at Ephesus first, until Pentecost. It is necessary for me to remain there because a great door has been opened to me—that is, because many of the Ephesians are preparing themselves for the faith. And the door is evident because I already see certain signs of faith in them. I must persist there because there are many adversaries who wish to draw them away from Christ.

I shall remain at Ephesus for the present. But if Timothy, carrying this Epistle, comes to you, see to it that he is without fear among you. For whatever he reported to me about you, he reported for your correction. Therefore see to it that you do not trouble him; he ought certainly to be without fear among you, because he is doing the work of the Lord among you, just as I and the other disciples do.

And because he is doing the work of the Lord, see to it that no one despises him; instead, obey his admonitions. And not only must you not despise him, but also send him [Col. 0216B] back to me in peace, so that he may come to me unharmed. For I am waiting for him together with the other brothers.

Apollos, bishop of the Corinthians, had fled their dissension and returned to Paul. The Corinthians had written to Paul asking him to send their bishop back to them. Paul replies that Apollos does not wish to return before they have been properly corrected, saying: “Deal with Timothy in this way. But concerning our brother Apollos, your bishop, I inform you that I urged him strongly to come to you; yet it was certainly not his will to come to you now. He will come when he has the opportunity and has understood that you have been properly corrected.”

But, in order to deserve the arrival of this father of yours, be watchful—that is, take careful heed for yourselves lest you go astray—and stand firm in the faith, so that you may not deviate from sound faith. And while standing in the faith, act manfully, that is, perform good works. Do not do so merely for an hour; rather, persevere in good actions and be strengthened, taking care that everything of yours be done in love—that is, in love of God and neighbor—in which you have until now been exceedingly lukewarm.

I beseech you, brothers, to submit to Stephanas and Fortunatus—and you ought to do so. For you know the household of Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus. You know, I say, that these are the firstfruits of Achaia, for they were the first in Achaia to believe. Corinth is in Achaia.

You also know that they devoted themselves to the ministry of the saints, serving them with their own hands and from their own possessions.
