This, I say, is what I beseech you: that you submit to all who are such, and to everyone who cooperates with them in what is good and who likewise labors in the ministry of the saints.

And so that you may submit to them, know that I rejoice in the presence of Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus. For my relation to them is as though I had them present with me. I rejoice, I say, and rightly so, because they themselves have supplied in me and in the saints what was lacking on your part. They ministered to us in temporal necessities—something that you ought to have done but neglected.

Truly they supplied what was lacking, for by ministering what was necessary they refreshed my spirit, and through this they refreshed yours as well. For if they had not supported us with their possessions, we could not have remained so long in the work of instructing you. And because they refreshed my spirit and yours, therefore acknowledge them—that is, obey them out of love—and all who are such.

All the churches greet you, O Corinthians. Aquila and Prisca greet you warmly in the Lord, together with the church in their household—that is, their entire family also greets you. All the brothers greet you. Greet one another with a holy kiss—that is, kiss one another, removing schisms from among you.

The greeting that follows was written with my own hand, namely Paul’s: “The grace of our Lord,” and so forth.

It was Paul’s custom to close the Epistle himself, in his own hand, so that there might be no doubt that the Epistle had been sent by him. He did this because of the false teachers, who sent forged letters under Paul’s name.

In this greeting he excludes unbelievers, saying: “If anyone does not love our Lord Jesus Christ, I do not greet him; rather, let him be anathema,” that is, separated from God. “Anathema,” I say, “Maranatha.” This word is formed from the Syriac and Hebrew languages, and means “the Lord comes.” It is as though he said: “Let him who does not love Christ be separated from him while the Lord himself comes to judge.” Or, “Let him be anathema,” to his own disadvantage, because perhaps the Lord is coming today or tomorrow to take vengeance on him.

This is my greeting, from which I separate the wicked. May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you, and may my love be with all of you—that is, may you all love me, although I have corrected you somewhat harshly—and may this be “in Christ Jesus,” that is, for the love of Christ Jesus. “Amen,” that is, “so be it.”

[IN THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS.]

[Col. 0217]

## 155. PROLOGUE TO THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS

[Col. 0217B]

In the Second Epistle to the Corinthians, as though in its first part, after recounting his own tribulations, he gives the reasons why he did not go to them a second time. He asserts that he did not act out of some light change of plan, but because, if he had found the disciples persisting in sin, he did not wish to incur sadness by his arrival.

Then, after recognizing the fruits of repentance, he reconciles to the Church the man whom, in the First Epistle, he had ordered to be removed from the fellowship of the saints because of fornication.

Third, he defends the dignity of his office against the false apostles and shows that the ministers of the New Testament surpass them in grace by as much as the Gospel is superior to the law.

He also dwells at considerable length on the matter that he had touched on briefly in the First Epistle: namely, that they should give with a ready and willing spirit what is necessary for the present life to those who lack it, and that through the benefit of spiritual exchange they should trade present things for future ones, so that their abundance might supply the poverty of the saints, and in turn the abundance of the saints might supply their poverty.

At the end he repeats what he had dealt with earlier against the false apostles. He empties out their boastfulness and their glorious proclamations about themselves, whether by comparing the antiquity of their lineage or by listing his own injuries and dangers. He calls them deceitful workers who, in imitation of Satan, transform themselves into apostles of Christ, pursuing every kind of monetary gain under the pretext of preaching.

## ARGUMENT ON THE SAME EPISTLE

[Col. 0217]

After the Corinthians had performed penance, the Apostle writes them a consolatory Epistle from Troas through Titus. Praising them, he exhorts them to better things, showing that they had indeed been saddened but had been corrected.

## B. BRUNO’S ARGUMENT ON THE SAME EPISTLE

[Col. 0217C]

Paul writes this Epistle again to the Corinthians. He had sufficiently corrected some of them through the earlier Epistle, but certain others were still weighed down by the error of preferring false teachers to Paul. They accused Paul of simplicity of speech and exalted the false teachers for their worldly wisdom.

Therefore in this Epistle also he dwells at length on the humiliation of the false teachers and on the commendation of his own apostleship. First of all, he counsels those who were righteous among the Corinthians—whether those who had just been properly corrected through Paul’s Epistle, or those who had persevered from the beginning of their acceptance of the faith—in what is good.

For these men were suffering many things from perverse brothers, whom the false teachers were inciting against the saints. And although he consoles all the good without distinction, when he learned that the man whom he had reproved by name—because he had presumed to take his father’s wife—had been properly corrected, he gives a special command concerning him, that he should be restored to the Church, from which, because of his sin, he had humbly endured being separated.

He also deals more fully in this Epistle with the collections about which he had written to them in the First Epistle, so that those who had abused the brief admonition would not dare to despise the same matter after an admonition repeated and extended at greater length.

In this Epistle, then, the subject is these same Corinthians, whether corrected or uncorrected. Concerning them he acts by consoling the good, so that they may not fail under adversities but may advance eagerly through patient endurance of tribulations toward an increase of virtues.

To the uncorrected, however, he reproaches their error and sin, with this intention concerning both groups: to reduce their differences to a kind of unity—namely, so that the good may advance toward what is better, and the wicked, by abandoning their error, may follow the good in a salutary imitation.

## SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS

[Col. 0217]

## 156. CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0217D]

“Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and Timothy the brother, to the church of God that is at Corinth, with all the saints who are in all Achaia. Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Blessed be God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ (Ephesians I, 3; 1 Peter I, 2), the Father of mercies and God of all consolation, who consoles us in all our tribulation, so that we ourselves may also console those who are in every distress, through the exhortation by which we ourselves are exhorted by God.

“For just as the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so also through Christ our consolation abounds. Whether we are afflicted for your exhortation and salvation, or are consoled for your consolation, or are exhorted for your exhortation and salvation—which produces endurance of the same sufferings that we also endure—our hope concerning you is firm, knowing that just as you are partners in suffering, so also you will be partners in consolation.

“For we do not wish you to be ignorant, brothers, of our tribulation which took place in Asia: we were weighed down beyond measure and beyond our strength, so that we were even weary of living. But within ourselves we had the sentence of death, so that we might not trust in ourselves but in God, who raises the dead. He delivered and continues to deliver us from such great dangers; in him we hope that he will still deliver us, with you also assisting by your prayer for us, so that, from persons of many faces, thanks may be given to God by many on our behalf for the gift bestowed on us.

“For this is our glory: the testimony of our conscience, that in simplicity of heart and in the sincerity of God, and not in worldly wisdom but in the grace of God, we conducted ourselves in this world, and more abundantly toward you. For we write nothing else to you than what you have read and understood [or: understand]. I hope that you will understand to the end, just as you have understood us in part: for we are your glory, just as you are ours, on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.

“And in this confidence I intended to come to you first, so that you might have a second grace, and to pass through you into Macedonia, and again to come to you from Macedonia, and to be sent on by you into Judea. When I had this intention, did I use fickleness? Or do I make my plans according to the flesh, so that with me there should be both ‘Yes’ and ‘No’? But God is faithful: our word that was spoken among you is not both ‘Yes’ and ‘No’; rather, in it there is ‘Yes’ [the text does not have: ‘but “Yes” is in it’]. For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who was preached among you through us—through me and Silvanus and Timothy—was not ‘Yes’ and ‘No’; rather, ‘Yes’ was in him. For however many promises of God there are, in him there is ‘Yes.’ Therefore also through him is the ‘Amen,’ to God for our glory.

“Now the one who confirms us with you in Christ, and who anointed us, is God. He also sealed us and gave the pledge of the Spirit in our hearts. But I call God as witness against my soul that, in sparing you, I did not come again to Corinth—not that we lord it over your faith, but we are helpers of your joy. For you stand by faith.”

## EXPOSITION

In his customary manner he first gives the greeting, saying: Paul—a name expressive both of humility and of authority—Paul, I say, an apostle, that is, an envoy of Christ Jesus, for he proclaims the glory of Christ. An apostle, I say, not through rash presumption, like the false teachers, but through the will, that is, the good pleasure, of God; and with him Timothy the brother, that is, a fellow worker in the work of Christ.

For this reason he includes Timothy, through whom he had sent the First Epistle, so that they may know that everything taking place among them is known to him. Paul, I say, and Timothy write to the church, that is, to the assembly of the faithful. To the church, I say, of God—that is, one in which the grace of God alone works, and not the merits of teachers, as the false teachers boast.

To the church, I say, that is at Corinth. He writes to the church of the Corinthians together with all—that is, with all the saints, sanctified in baptism through Christ—together with all, I say, who are in all Achaia. It is as though he said: “To the church at Corinth and to all the churches subject to it.” For Achaia is the name of the province in which Corinth, the metropolis, was situated.

May there be grace for you Corinthians: for those who have sinned, a second forgiveness; for those who have been properly corrected, or who have not sinned after accepting the faith, perseverance in the grace they have rightly preserved. And may there be peace for them—that is, the good tranquility of mind—from God who is able, our Father, who has a pious affection toward us, and from God who is likewise able, Jesus Christ, who also wills it, because it is his office to save us.

Now, first of all, he gives thanks to God for the perseverance of those who had not fallen and for the correction of those who, having rejected their error, had properly amended their lives. He also consoles them by his own example, so that they may be strong in adversities, whatever they may have to suffer, saying:

“Because I see you laboring in the faith of Christ, I give thanks and say: Blessed be the God of our Lord Jesus Christ and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. He is his God insofar as Christ was man; he is Christ’s Father insofar as Christ is divine, in which nature the Son is equal to the Father—yet having his principle from the Father, not the Father from him.

“If he is the Father of Jesus Christ, and we are Christ’s sons, then through Christ we have God as our Father. The two preceding designations, ‘God’ and ‘Father,’ refer to Christ; the same two that follow refer to human beings. Blessed also be the one who is both God and Father of Christ. He is also the Father of mercies. Although he could have said ‘the giver of mercies,’ he said ‘Father,’ to show that he is both the giver and the one who gives us good things out of paternal affection.

“Father, I say, of mercies, and God of all consolation. All the gifts of God are called mercies, whether they are given in adversity or in prosperity; but consolation is said to exist only where there has been desolation. He could also, if he wished, have said ‘Father of consolation and God of mercies,’ and the meaning would have been the same.

“God, I say, not of incomplete consolation but of all consolation—that is, perfect consolation. In whatever things we are desolate, God is powerful and present to console us, because consolation had now become more necessary for them. For this reason he dwells at greater length on the benefits of consolation, saying:

“‘That God consoles us’—that is, me and my fellow disciples—‘in our tribulation, which we suffer.’ Not merely in some tribulation, but in every tribulation. Wherever we are afflicted, whether the tribulation is easy or difficult according to its measure, the medicine of the one who consoles is present.

“He consoles us, I say, not merely to free us, but also so that we who are afflicted may ourselves console those who now appeared desolate, both by the example of our endurance and by the exhortation of our speech. He consoles us, I say, so that we may console those who are in the distress of tribulations—not merely in some distress, but in every inward or outward distress. We can console them through exhortation.

“He could have said ‘through consolation,’ but to show that he does not merely console in a simple way, but also makes them stronger, he says: ‘through the exhortation by which other saints and we ourselves are exhorted by God.’ Thus, seeing God present with us in tribulation, we may have no hesitation in entering whatever torments arise, and may invite others by word and example to the virtue of patience.

“And truly we are exhorted by God, for just as the sufferings of Christ abound—that is, the sufferings that we endure either for the name of Christ or for Christ’s example, suffering on our behalf—so, just as sufferings abound in us, consolation also abounds copiously through Christ who consoles us. Or, ‘through Christ,’ because we are consoled by the example of his patience.

“Whatever we suffer and whenever we are consoled, this happens not only for our sake but also for your instruction. Whether we are afflicted, this occurs for your exhortation, so that you may be strong to endure tribulations and thus obtain eternal salvation; or whether we are consoled, this occurs for your consolation, so that you may know that you too will be consoled by God in tribulation and may thus obtain future salvation; or whether we are exhorted, all of this occurs for your exhortation, so that by our example and teaching you may be exhorted to better things and thus obtain salvation.

“It must be observed that the words ‘we are afflicted,’ ‘we are consoled,’ and ‘we are exhorted’ are here understood in a passive sense. Truly everything is for your sake, because the tribulation, consolation, and exhortation that operate in you through our word and example produce endurance of the same sufferings that we too endure, though we possess such great authority with God. Therefore do not wonder if God permits you, who are inferior, to be troubled.

“It produces endurance in you, so that our hope concerning you—by which we hope that you will persevere in the good and attain eternal salvation—may be firm, that is, enduring and strengthened by the reality of virtue. He does not say ‘your hope,’ but ‘our hope concerning you,’ to show that his charity is solicitously concerned for their good.

“We suffer, I say, knowing that just as you are—not merely participants in, but partners of—our sufferings, so also you will be partners of the consolation that we expect to come to us and to you in glory. And by calling them partners he greatly encourages them to patience.

“Because he had begun to speak about sufferings, he turns to enumerate the difficulties he suffered in Asia. He does this lest the Corinthians should object: ‘By your example, Paul, you urge us to endure tribulations, although perhaps you have never been afflicted as severely as we have.’

“The wording is joined as follows: ‘I rightly say that we suffer, for we were weighed down beyond measure in Asia.’ But before saying this, he first indicates that everything he is about to say applies entirely to himself.

“‘We were indeed weighed down, and we do not wish you to be ignorant, brothers, of our tribulation that took place in Asia.’ For there at Ephesus, because he had cleansed a girl who possessed a pythonic spirit and had thereby taken away from her masters the profit they derived from her divination, the whole city rushed upon him at their instigation. When he wished to give an account of himself, they shouted together so that he could not be heard: ‘Great is Diana of the Ephesians.’ There they afflicted him with so many blows that he was left in the street as though dead (Acts XVI, XIX).

“This, I say, I do not wish you to be ignorant of: that there at Ephesus we were weighed down beyond the measure of our earlier tribulations [Col. 0222B] and beyond human strength. For human strength could not endure so much suffering. We were so weighed down that we were weary—not, I say, merely of suffering, but even of living.

“And not only were we weary of living, but we ourselves had within us—that is, in our soul—the sentence of death, because, when we consulted our soul about whether we might perhaps escape alive, it answered us with death.

“Lest, because he says that he was weary of living amid torments, he should seem to contradict himself when he says, ‘God consoles us in every tribulation,’ he counters this by saying: ‘We were weighed down to such weariness of life and sentence of death so that we might not trust in ourselves’—that is, attribute nothing to our own strength—‘but trust only in God, who raises the dead.’

“He delivered me from death—that is, from what would have caused another man to die—and he has frequently rescued us from the many dangers that we have suffered. In him we advance by doing good and hope that, just as he delivered us formerly, so also he will deliver us in the future, in this deliverance being assisted by the other faithful and by you through prayer—that is, through the prayer offered for us.

“I say that he is assisted in such a way that thanks are given to God through many helpers on our behalf. Thanks, I say, for the gift he has bestowed—that is, for patience and hope—and for every good gift that is in us. Let thanks be given, I say, from persons of many faces—that is, from persons distinguished by the many faces of their virtues.

“For just as one human being is distinguished from another by the face, so in the Church one is distinguished from another as though by a face through humility, another from this one through patience, and so on. The members of the Church possess faces distinguished by different virtues. From persons of many faces—that is, distinguished by a variety of virtues—let thanks be given to God on our behalf.

“Or otherwise: ‘from persons of many faces,’ that is, from the diversity of ages and sexes. He calls children, young men, and the remaining ages of both sexes ‘persons of many faces.’ Or otherwise: ‘Let thanks be given on our behalf for the gift that is in us.’ Let thanks be given, I say, through many; and what I call ‘through many’ means ‘from persons of many faces.’

“By saying ‘with you assisting on our behalf,’ he sufficiently commends and attracts to himself those whom he values so highly that they are worthy to intercede for the Apostle. In these words he makes them his equals.”

Up to this point he has consoled the perfect among the Corinthians. Here he seems to turn to those who were not yet sufficiently corrected and were clinging to false teachers [Col. 0223A], recalling how worthily he conducted himself among them and how in no way was he burdensome to those from whom he accepted no provisions, saying: “It is certainly fitting that you give thanks for us, for we conducted ourselves among you in simplicity and sincerity.” But before saying this, he puts forward testimony to the matter, saying: “And even if you deny that we conducted ourselves well among you, I do not care. For this is our glory,” that is, “in this I glory greatly in the purity of my conduct, having the testimony of our conscience.” For my conscience bears witness to me that I acted in simplicity—not, like the false teachers, to defraud you of your possessions, but in simplicity, accepting nothing from you—and in the sincerity of God, that is, in purity of faith, not mixing, as they did, falsehoods with truths [Col. 0223B], and not in carnal wisdom: for I did not cling, as they did, to carnal teachings; but in the grace of God, that is, in magnifying the grace of God, from which all good proceeds, and nothing from carnal wisdom. In the grace, I say, of God we conducted ourselves in this world; yet we conducted ourselves more abundantly toward you, among whom I endured greater things, accepting nothing from you so that I would not lose the authority to rebuke you.

The Corinthians might say: “Paul is recalling his conduct for this reason: so that what he formerly did not accept he may now receive in multiplied measure.” Paul replies to this: “Do not think that I recall my conduct among you with the intention of receiving something from you. For we do not write anything else to you in this Epistle than what you read in the previous Epistle, in which I wrote that I would accept nothing from you. Nor do we now write anything other than what you learned about us while we were with you, accepting nothing from you but living by the labor of our hands. And just as you then learned this, so I also hope that you will know to the end that I accept nothing from you, just as you have already learned this about us while we remained among you.” You learned, I say, in part, that is, according to the outward action that you saw; but you did not know the other part, namely, the intention. Therefore I wished to be known as such—that is, as accepting nothing from you—because “we are your glory, just as you are ours,” that is, because I wished to glory in your obedience, and you to glory in our teaching. This glory certainly would not exist if I burdened you by accepting temporal goods from you. For you would prefer to drive away the Teacher [Col. 0223D] rather than support him. This glory of mine in you, and of you in me, will appear on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ, when you will be rewarded for the obedience you have displayed and I for my teaching.

He passes again to another matter. They were accusing him of fickleness because in the previous Epistle he had said that he would come to them, but had not come. They could not, however, accuse him of lying, for he had said: “I will come if the Lord permits.” The text is joined as follows: “And with this confidence”—either because I conducted myself among you simply and sincerely, or because you are my glory and I am yours—“with this confidence, I say, I wished to come to you. Formerly indeed I wished to come, but now I do not.” Certainly I then wished to come so that by my arrival you might have a second grace, that is, because after baptism you had sinned and required a second remission [Col. 0224A]. I also wished to pass through you into Macedonia; and on returning from Macedonia I wished to come to you again, and from you I wished to be escorted into Judaea.

And because I previously wished this, when I had wished to do this—that is, to come to you—did I therefore act with fickleness because I did not come as I had first intended? Or, because I did not come, do I think according to the flesh, that is, do I think of carnal advantage, so that I abandoned the intention of coming because I expected to receive nothing from you? Or, I ask, do I think according to the flesh, so that with me there is “yes” and “no,” that is, affirmation and negation concerning the same matter?

That “yes” and “no” were not with me appears in the speech that was our speech among you while I was present among you, because in that speech which I then delivered there was no “yes” and “no,” that is, no affirmation and negation concerning the same matter. And that this is so [Col. 0224B] God, who is faithful and truthful, knows.

Or otherwise: Truly, “yes” and “no” were not with me, because God is faithful, that is, truthful. But since God promised that he would give teachers of truth, if he appointed me as a teacher of falsehood, he would plainly be guilty of lying. That God is faithful in promising teachers of truth is evident from this: our speech which was among you was not a speech containing “yes” and “no.” Truly God is faithful. For in Jesus Christ—who is Christ Jesus, the Son of God, and who was preached among you through us, namely, through me and Silvanus and Timothy—in that Christ there was no “yes” and “no,” that is, affirmation and negation concerning the same matter; but in him there was always “yes,” that is, truth, whether by denying or by affirming.

Truly, in him there was no “yes” and “no.” For however many the promises of God the Father are, in him there is “yes,” that is, they are true and fulfilled; or likewise, because the promises of God the Father have been fulfilled through Christ, in him there is “yes,” that is, God’s promises are true and fulfilled. Therefore through Christ himself we say “amen,” that is, that it has been fulfilled just as it was promised. And all this is “to God,” that is, for the glory of God and for our glory, because our truth is confirmed by the truth of God.

Although I say “for our glory,” nevertheless glory is owed not to us but to God, who confirms us with you, so that the truth may be in you—and this in Christ. This same God also anointed us with the oil of sanctification in baptism. He also sealed us, that is, he gave us the sign of distinction from others, namely, virtues. He also gave us the pledge of the Spirit, that is, the Holy Spirit, to be for us the earnest of future glory [Col. 0224D]; this Spirit he gave as a perpetual indweller in our hearts. And since the Holy Spirit is in us, it should not be believed that fickleness or falsehood was in us.

After excusing himself for not having refrained from coming to them either through fickleness or because he was thinking according to the flesh, he adds the reason why he did not come, saying: “I did not refrain from coming through fickleness or because I was thinking carnally; rather, I did not come in order to spare you.” And so that you may believe that I did not come in order to spare you, I call upon God as witness to this matter.

The wicked, being careless about offending God, would not be greatly concerned to call God as witness to a falsehood. But Paul, who had placed himself wholly in God, would not presume to make God witness [Col. 0225A] to something he did not understand to be true; otherwise, by acting in this way, he would accuse God of lying. “I call God as witness,” certainly—not only against the body, so that, if I proved false, he might punish me in the body alone, but also in, that is, against, my soul, so that he might destroy it together with the body if I made God witness to a falsehood.

For this reason I call upon God as witness: that, sparing you—that is, so that I might be able to spare you more advantageously—I did not come again to Corinth, that is, any farther than on the first occasion.

Before saying in what respect he spared them by not coming, he defines here what he means by “sparing.” The Corinthians, lying in wait for his words, might say: “You say that you spared us as though you possessed royal power to compel us according to your will.”

“I do not say ‘sparing’ for this reason,” he replies, “as though we lord it over your faith. Faith is a voluntary matter and cannot be compelled by the necessity of domination [Col. 0225B].” One is said to exercise dominion in those positions in which a son succeeds his father by necessary usage. But among ecclesiastical superiors—and even among secular rulers who preside not by a law of succession but by election—it is more properly called service than dominion.

Therefore he says: “We do not lord it over your faith; rather, we are your helpers,” never ceasing to pray to God for your correction. Helpers, I say, of your joy, for we help you in that matter from which you will have lasting joy. Therefore you ought to obey us.

Truly, we do not lord it over you, for you stand by faith. And if you stand, you stand by a matter of the will, not of compulsion.

## CHAPTER II

> “But I determined this in myself, not to come to you again in sadness. For if I make you sad, who is there who can make me glad except the one who is made sad by me? And I wrote this very thing to you so that, when I came, I would not have sadness upon sadness from those over whom I ought to rejoice, having confidence in you all, because my joy is the joy of you all. For out of much tribulation and anguish of heart I wrote to you with many tears—not so that you might be made sad, but so that you might know the love which I have more abundantly for you.
>
> “But if anyone has caused me sadness, he has not caused me sadness, but in part, so that I do not burden all of you. This rebuke, which is made by the greater number, is sufficient for the one who is such, so that, on the contrary, you should rather forgive and console him, lest perhaps the one who is such be swallowed up by excessive sadness. For this reason I beseech you to confirm your love toward him. For this is why I also wrote to you, so that I might learn by experience whether you are obedient in everything.
>
> “But to whomever you have forgiven anything, I also forgive. For what I have forgiven, if I have forgiven anything, I forgave for your sake in the person of Christ, so that we may not be deceived by Satan; for we are not ignorant of his designs.
>
> “When I had come to Troas for the Gospel of Christ, and a door had been opened to me in the Lord, I had no rest for my spirit because I did not find my brother Titus. But, taking leave of them, I departed into Macedonia.
>
> “But thanks be to God, who always makes us triumph in Christ Jesus and manifests through us the fragrance of his knowledge in every place. For we are the good fragrance of Christ to God among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing: to some indeed an odor of death unto death, but to others an odor of life unto life. And who is so capable for these things? For we are not like the many who adulterate the word of God, but we speak from sincerity, as from God, before God, in Christ.”

## EXPOSITION

After explaining how he said that he spared them, he now explains in what respect he spared them, saying: “I did not come to Corinth, but I determined the very thing that I had determined in the previous Epistle.” I determined, he says, in myself—not through the rashness of an inconsiderate decision, but, carefully considering the matter in myself, I determined it after deliberation—not to come to you again in sadness, that is, to make you sad.

He says “again” because in the first Epistle he had come to make them sad, since they had fallen into sin—if not bodily and personally, nevertheless through the Epistle.

Or otherwise: “I had already come once, but for this reason I did not wish to come again, lest my arrival should be a cause of sadness to you.”

Paul did not wish to come because, if he were present, he would have to remove the unrepentant from the Church by the severity of judgment. Being present, he could not use the same degree of leniency, seeing their evils, that he employs toward them through the Epistle. Thus the evil would occur that, when he ought to recall them to the unity of the Church, he would instead separate from one another by the strictness of justice those whom, while absent, he could recall to unity through the gentleness of mercy [Col. 0226C]. And this is what he did.

“For this reason I did not wish to come again: because if I make you sad in any way, who is there among you who can make me glad except the one who is made sad by me,” that is, according to my will, so that, being saddened over his sin, he may repent? If I came, no one would make me glad in this way. For, while I was present, the strictness of justice would frighten you more than it would persuade you to repentance.

He also hints at this, as though he were saying: “You ought indeed to have repented for God’s sake—and, to leave that aside, at least for the sake of making me, your teacher, glad.” And I wrote this very thing, namely, so that, when I come in person, I would not find anyone who could make me glad, and would therefore have sadness upon sadness.

I will have this kind of sadness when I hear that you have sinned [Col. 0226D]; I will have a second sadness if, when I come, I find you uncorrected. And so that I may find you corrected, I now write that I rejoice especially in the one who is saddened unto repentance. I say that I will have sadness concerning you while uncorrected [p. 162], though I ought now to have my first joy concerning you as corrected. And truly I will rejoice as I ought.

For I am confident concerning all of you that I will rejoice over your correction. This is because, while I was with you, my joy was the joy of all of you: as soon as you saw me rejoicing, even without understanding the matter over which I rejoiced, you rejoiced with me out of a pious affection. For this reason I am confident that I will truly rejoice over you once corrected.

Or otherwise: “I am confident in you because my joy is the joy of all of you,” that is, the joy which I await in the future—and for which I pray that you may be worthy to possess God—I am confident that you also will possess.

He says “having confidence in you all” so that those who were sinning would not think that Paul despaired of their salvation.

Because he said, “that I might have sadness upon sadness,” they might say to him: “Did you have sadness?” He replies: “I certainly did. For I wrote to you out of much bodily tribulation, fasting and keeping vigil, so that God might spare you; and out of much anguish of heart, being anxious about your salvation, I wrote to you, afflicting myself with many tears.”

“I do not mention that I was troubled and anguished so that you might be sad with me, but so that you might know how great a love I have for all. I speak of a love shown more abundantly toward you, among whom I stayed longer and from whom I received nothing, living by the labor of my hands.”

Having explained the reason why he did not come to them—a reason suitable for persuading them to correction—he now adds something about the man whom he had ordered to be separated from the Church in another Epistle because he had taken his father’s wife. Since he had heard that the man’s repentance was worthy of pardon, he writes to the Corinthian Church that they should receive him, knowing that Paul had forgiven him.

The text is joined as follows: “I do not wish you to be saddened. But if anyone has caused me sadness”—as did the man who took his father’s wife—“he has not caused sadness to me alone, but also to you, and in part.” For not all of you were saddened, but only the good grieved with their sinful brother.

I say “in part” so that I do not burden all of them, that is, because it is unworthy to impose on all of you the burden of not sympathizing with your brother. He says this ironically concerning those who had become proud over the fall of their brother, with whom they ought to have sympathized [Col. 0227C].

Or otherwise: “He has not caused sadness to me alone, but also to you in part,” that is, according to the share of the good. I except this share so that I do not burden all of you with contempt for the sinful brother, for some of you grieved with him, as was right.

But concerning the one who caused sadness to me and to you, know that this is sufficient for the one who is such, that is, of such frailty that, if he were harassed with excessive severity, he would despair.

For him, I say, this rebuke is sufficient—the rebuke with which you rebuked him by expelling him from the Church because of his sin. I say that the rebuke made against the sinful brother by the many who rightly grieved with him is sufficient for him, so that, acting in the opposite way, just as you previously separated him from the Church, you should now restore him to the Church.

On the contrary, just as you rebuked him more severely and he endured it patiently, so now you should rather forgive him, that is, remit his sin. And lest he think that you are doing this as though you did not care about him, console him frequently through the consolations of the Scriptures.

For this reason, I say, you should forgive and console him, lest perhaps—and this could quickly happen—the one who is such, that is, of great frailty, be swallowed up, that is, devoured in despair, by excessive sadness. For if you restrain him beyond measure, he will despair of salvation, and he will quickly fall back into an even worse sin. Mercy leading to salvation is better than the severity of justice that produces despair.

For this reason, lest he be swallowed up, although I could command you, I beseech you rather out of love to confirm the love that was rightly begun. For it was love that caused you, at my command, to expel him from the Church so that he might be corrected. I beseech you, I say, to confirm this love, that is, to show it to be firm and perfect toward him, by forgiving him and receiving him into the Church—the love that you began when you rejected him.

You ought to forgive him, for this is why I wrote: so that you might complete the love you began, and so that I might learn by experience about you—that is, about you who had shown yourselves experienced when you separated him from the Church in obedience. I wish to learn whether you are obedient in everything: just as you previously obeyed by removing him, so now obey by forgiving him.

And, as I urge you, you ought to forgive, because if you have forgiven anyone anything, I too have forgiven with you.

They might say: “Perhaps you forgave him, but not for our sake.” I reply: “Yes, for what I forgave—if I ever forgave anything—I forgave for your sake.”

Here he restrains his own statement: “If I have forgiven anything” shows that he had forgiven only a few things on behalf of another, so that he might teach us that sins should be forgiven not out of carnal affection, but rather for the fruit of repentance.

They ask again: “What difference does it make if you forgave?” It makes a great difference, certainly, because I forgave this in the person of Christ. The forgiveness had the same effect for the one whom I forgave as if Christ himself had forgiven him in his own person.

You ought certainly to forgive him, both for my sake and so that we may not be deceived, that is, so that we may not be deceived by Satan. For just as he deceives through excessive softness, so the devil also deceives through severity that exceeds measure. Therefore I warn you not to be deceived by Satan, because we are not ignorant of Satan’s designs or of how crafty they are. Here we also understand his power, namely, how he introduces his deceit while the sinner is being disciplined [Col. 0228C].

Paul again shows that their fault was involved when he changed his intention of coming to them, because he heard that they were uncorrected.

“I did not come farther to Corinth, but I came as far as Troas. When I had come to Troas to preach the Gospel of Christ”—for they preached everywhere—and when a door had been opened to me there, in Troas, that is, when their minds were prepared to receive the word of Christ, and this in the Lord, for the Lord was opening their hearts, when I had come in this way, I had no rest for my spirit.”

He says that he had no rest because at that time he was unable to labor in preaching.

“I had no rest because I did not find my brother Titus in Troas.”

Through Timothy and Titus he had sent the first Epistle to the Corinthians. Timothy, however, had returned to Paul, while Titus was still being detained at Corinth, laboring over their correction. The fact that Paul could not preach to the people of Troas because of Titus’s absence was the fault of the Corinthians, whose lack of correction detained Titus.

Paul did not wish to preach at Troas because of Titus—either because Titus had preached to them earlier, and Paul, preaching in his absence, might seem to diminish Titus’s authority, or because Titus was Paul’s interpreter and could express himself in their language more clearly.

“I had no rest, but, taking leave of them at Troas, I departed into Macedonia.” These Macedonians received the Apostle with great honor, so that he was even able to dispose of their possessions in whatever way he wished.

[Col. 0229A] Here Paul begins to magnify himself and his ministry and to disparage the false apostles in many ways, because some of the Corinthians preferred them to Paul.

“I departed into Macedonia.” There I was established as a triumphal victor in Christ, and from there I give thanks to God, who always triumphs over us—that is, makes us triumph—in Christ Jesus, that is, through Christ Jesus, in whom the false apostles do not triumph.

And God “manifests the fragrance of his knowledge,” that is, Christ, through whose humanity we perceive the divine and indivisible essence.

Or he manifests through us the fragrance of his knowledge, that is, our preaching, through which God’s power is manifested in every place where we preach. He manifests it through us, certainly, because “we are the good fragrance of Christ,” that is, if someone considers the purity [Col. 0229B] of our actions, he can perceive the goodness of Christ, whose ministers we are.

We are the good fragrance, I say, and if not to certain unbelievers, nevertheless to God, who sees the interior of our heart. We are the good fragrance, I say, in relation to God, both among those who are saved through our Gospel and among those who perish through their contempt for that same Gospel. In relation to God, we are the good fragrance among both those being saved and those perishing.

But in relation to human beings, to some we are an odor of death. For the unbelievers, hearing from us the faith of Christ, say that they perceive a deadly thing: an odor of death, I say, effective for them unto death, that is, unto condemnation.

But to others, that is, to believers, we are an odor of life. For through our teaching they perceive the life of righteousness, proceeding in this way [Col. 0229C] into eternal life.

God manifests through us the fragrance of his righteousness. And for manifesting these things, who among the false apostles is as capable as I and my fellow apostles? No one is so capable. For we are not like the many—namely, the false apostles—who adulterate the word of God.

Just as an adulterer unlawfully appropriates another person’s property, so the false apostles appropriate for themselves a ministry of preaching that was entrusted to them by no one. And just as an adulterer does not seek the fruit of offspring in his shameful act but only to satisfy his lust, so those false apostles care only that they may acquire temporal goods; they do not care about those whom they teach, whether they perish or do not perish.

We do not, I say, adulterate the word of God, but we speak from sincerity, that is, according to the pure truth of faith [Col. 0229D]. Again, we do not adulterate it, but we speak in Christ, that is, according to the faith and institution of Christ. We speak from God, that is, according to what God inspires us to say, and before God, that is, in the good pleasure of God.

## CHAPTER III

> “Do we begin again to commend ourselves? Or do we perhaps need, like some people, letters of recommendation to you or from you? You are our letter, written in our hearts, known and read by all people, having been manifested as a letter of Christ, administered by us and written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of fleshly hearts.
>
> “And we have such confidence through Christ toward God—not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think of anything as though it came from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God, who also made us capable ministers of a New Testament, not of the letter but of the spirit. For the letter kills, but the spirit gives life.
>
> “For if the ministry of death, formed in letters on stones, was in glory, so that the children of Israel could not gaze upon the face of Moses because of the glory of his countenance, which is being brought to an end, how will the ministry of the spirit not be much more in glory? For if the ministry of condemnation is in glory, the ministry of righteousness abounds much more in glory.
>
> “For that which shone was not glorified in this respect, because of the surpassing glory. For if that which is being brought to an end was through glory, much more will that which remains be in glory.
>
> “Therefore, having such hope, we use great confidence. And we do not act as Moses did, who ‘put a veil over his face’ (Exodus 34:33), so that the children of Israel would not gaze upon the face of that which was being brought to an end; rather, their thoughts were dulled. For to this very day the same veil remains unremoved in the reading of the Old Testament, which is abolished in Christ. But to this very day, when Moses is read, a veil lies over their heart. But when it has turned to the Lord, the veil will be removed.
>
> “‘But the Lord is the Spirit’ (John 4:24). And where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom. But we all, with unveiled face contemplating the glory of the Lord, are transformed into the same image, from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord.”

## EXPOSITION

And because I say that no one is so capable for these things, you say that for this reason we are again beginning—as in the other Epistle, where I said, “I have become all things to all people” (1 Corinthians 9:22), and so forth—to commend ourselves, that is, to magnify ourselves.

Not at all. Rather, we commend God’s ministry in us.

Or do we perhaps need, like some people—namely, the false apostles—letters of recommendation sent from others to you, or from you and sent to others? For those false apostles, so that they might be more able to make profit, when they moved from one place to another, asked those from whom they were departing to commend them by letters to those to whom they were going.

I certainly do not need letters of recommendation. For you are our letter, because you are the seal of my apostleship, since I established you in the faith of Christ.

I call you a letter written in our hearts, for we never forget your faith, but anxiously ask God about your salvation [Col. 0230D]. This letter is known by all, for everyone knows that through me you were converted to the faith; and it is a letter read by all. For if anyone wishes to know what I am like in relation to you, he reads me and comes to know me.

You, I say, have been manifested as a letter of Christ, because your faith and good life display the power of Christ. I call you a letter of Christ administered by us. For since you are my letter, as I instructed you, while I am the letter of Christ, through me you are thus the letter of Christ, whom I dispensed to you.

I call you a letter written not with ink, that is, not in a way that can be erased; or, “with ink,” that is, with some defilement, as the false apostles pollute their followers, but written with the Spirit of God, that is, indelibly. I say “of the living God,” who will also cause you to live forever.

It is not written again on tablets of stone, that is, hardened tablets that do not perceive the word of God, but on tablets that are fleshly, that is, sensitive and receptive of the word of God for the production of fruit.

I say “tablets of the heart,” that is, of the inner understanding. When he says “on tablets of stone,” he refers us to the memory of the Old Law, which was given on stone tablets (Exodus 34:1), signifying the stony hearts of the Jews. For just as a stone receives a carving but perceives nothing, so the hearts of the Jews received the outer shell of the Law, that is, a carnal understanding [Col. 0231B], but did not perceive the spiritual marrow of the Law, namely, its understanding.

He said above: “No one is so capable as I.” Again: “You are my letter, and through me you are the letter of Christ.” And to this he adds such confidence, namely, that he confidently said that he was more capable, and so forth.

We must not attribute this confidence to ourselves, but refer it to God. For because I am capable—because you are my letter—all this God accomplishes. We have this confidence, I say, toward God, and through Christ as mediator. For Christ, according to the command of God, consecrated me as a capable Apostle.

We have this confidence toward God, certainly—not in such a way that we are sufficient of ourselves even to think, much less to do, anything—that is, anything beneficial to us—as though this could come from ourselves, that is, from our own powers, without the cooperating grace of God [Col. 0231C].

And although we are sufficient for nothing of ourselves, nevertheless we are sufficient; but our sufficiency is not merely a sufficiency for thinking, but, as has been stated above, for acting capably. All this sufficiency, whatever its character, is from God.

He has sufficiently commended his own person. Now he commends his ministry, which he will again turn to the commendation of himself, saying: “The God who made us capable ministers.”

He has already shown sufficiently above how they are capable, but now he adds what they are ministers of: “ministers of the New Testament.”

The Old Testament came first, and it was to be abolished by the New, while instructing the carnal according to carnality.

But the Gospel is the New Testament, teaching and renewing the human spirit, and not to be altered by another testament [Col. 0231D].

I call them ministers of the existing New Testament, not merely in the letter, as the Old Testament was, but in spirit and letter.

For the Old Law indeed gave commands in letters, but because it did not possess the grace of the Spirit, it harmed rather than helped. Therefore I say that the New Testament exists in the spirit, because if it existed only in the letter, it would kill.

For the letter kills, but the spirit gives life. The Old Law, which existed only in the letter, is said to kill—not because God, the giver of the Law, or Moses, the minister of the Law, did this, but because of the impious carnality of human beings, who did not deserve to have the assisting grace together with the letter.

The letter kills for this reason: it increases the desire for sin by forbidding it, since it is characteristic of our weakness that we rush more eagerly toward what is forbidden [Col. 0232A]. It also piles up the sin of transgression, which did not exist before the Law was given.

The letter kills in this way, but the Spirit—that is, the Gospel given together with the assisting Spirit—causes one to live in righteousness.

Having commended his Gospel, he pours the same commendation back upon himself, saying: “And because I am a minister of the testament existing in the spirit, I shall rightly have the glory of spiritual administration.”

Truly, the ministry of the spirit will be glorious for me, because the ministry of death was glorious for Moses.

He says this as follows: “For if the ministry of death,” that is, the Old Law, which brought death both through greater desire and through a new transgression, “if this ministry of death, formed only in letters and not made fruitful by the assistance of the Spirit”—formed, I say, “on stones,” for the Law of Moses was given on stone tablets to signify the stony hearts of the Jews [Col. 0232B]—if this ministry was effective for Moses in possessing glory, I say that it was in glory to such a degree that the children of Israel could not gaze upon the face of Moses because of the glory of his countenance, which glory is being brought to an end.

For we know that this glory of Moses’ face soon passed away.

If, I say, the ministry of death was glorious for Moses with such great glory, how will the ministry of the spirit—that is, the Gospel, with which the Holy Spirit is administered through my hands—not be much more effective for me in possessing glory than it was for Moses?

He does not say this to prefer himself to Moses by merit, but only in the dignity of the ministry. Through the hands of Moses mere commands were given, without grace; but through Paul both commands and, through the laying on of his hands, the assisting grace of the Holy Spirit were given, so that a person could perform what was commanded.

The fact that he says the Jews could not gaze upon Moses’ face signified that they could not grasp the spiritual understanding of the Law, which the face—that is, the understanding—of Moses perceived clearly.

Again, the fact that the glory of his countenance was brought to an end signified that the things he administered were temporal, not permanent, and that the glory he possessed on their account was temporal.

Truly, the ministry of the spirit will be glorious for me, for to administer the spirit is to administer righteousness. The ministry of righteousness, moreover, is effective for possessing glory.

For if the ministry of condemnation—that is, of the Old Law, which produced both sin and the transgression of sin—if this ministry of Moses is in glory [Col. 0232D], much more does the ministry, that is, the administration, of righteousness abound in glory for me.

It abounds for this reason: my glory is permanent, while that glory is transitory. Above, where he said “the ministry of death,” he understood death as sin. Here, however, by “condemnation,” he understands the punishment of sin.

Truly, my ministry abounds in glory much more. For “that which was glorified”—that is, that which shone forth in this respect, namely, in Moses’ face—ought not to be called glorified because of the surpassing glory, that is, in comparison with the more excellent glory that is mine.

Or otherwise: that which shone forth in Moses should not be called glorified in this respect, that is, in relation to my portion, because of the surpassing glory that belongs to my portion and not to Moses’ portion.

Truly, my glory is surpassingly excellent, for mine remains, whereas his passes away [Col. 0233A]. And truly, that which remains is in glory for me: if the Old Testament, which is being abolished, was for Moses through glory—that is, was in glory—then much more is my Gospel, which remains, sufficient for me to possess glory.

It should be noted that he first says that he ministers the spirit, and through the spirit righteousness; then he says that this remains. Moses, however, ministered the letter against the spirit, condemnation against righteousness, and what is being abolished against what remains. And just as condemnation is the effect of sin, so righteousness is the effect of the spirit.

Up to this point he has preferred his own ministry to the ministry of the old law, everywhere depressing those false apostles who were bringing back the old law. For if Moses is a minister of death and condemnation, how much more so are those who are [Col. 0233B] so greatly inferior to Moses in dignity?

Because we await an excellent glory, therefore, possessing such a hope—namely, the hope of lasting glory—we use great boldness, not repressing the word of God through fear of any difficulty. We do indeed use boldness; and we do not act like Moses, who placed a veil over his face (Exodus 34:33), so that the children of Israel would not look intently at his face. This veil is now removed through our Gospel. For in the Gospel whatever was closed up in the figures of the old law is opened.

Someone [167] might say: “Why do you say that the veil of the law has been removed, when the law is obscured now just as it was before?” Paul answers this objection: The veil of the law has indeed been removed, but the understanding of the impious has been dulled by the sin of unbelief.

And [Col. 0233C] rightly has it been dulled. For from the time when the law was given up to the present day, that veil itself, just as it formerly was, remains unremoved when the Old Testament is read. For when the figures of the old law are expounded to unbelievers, their unbelief closes their hearts, and thus the veil of the law is not revealed to them. This is not because our Gospel does not remove that veil, but because they do not approach Christ. In Christ—that is, through faith in him—this veil is removed.

There is indeed a veil over the Old Testament, not because the Old Testament has not been opened through the Gospel, but because, even to the present day, when Moses is read and expounded to them, a veil of unbelief is placed over their unrepentant heart. This veil has been removed in Christ, to whom they do not wish to turn.

This veil has been removed [Col. 0233D] in Christ, to whom they do not wish to turn.

That this is how the statement should be understood is suggested by the following text: “A veil is over their heart,” because they do not approach Christ. But when they have turned to the Lord, after the veil of the heart has first been removed—that is, once they have acquired the disposition to repent—the veil of understanding will then also be taken away, and they will openly recognize the mysteries of the law.

Indeed, because they will turn to the Lord, the veil will be removed. For the Lord is spirit. Where, however, the spirit of the Lord is—that is, “the spirit is the Lord,” understood intransitively; or “the spirit of the Lord,” understood transitively, for God gives himself—where, I say, the spirit of the Lord is, there, once the veil has been removed, is freedom of understanding. And if the Lord is spirit, while the spirit removes the veil because it is freedom, then, when they have turned to the Lord, the veil will be removed.

[Col. 0234A] Where the spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom.

But we possess the spirit of the Lord—we certainly do. For we, the disciples of Christ, with unveiled face, that is, with an enlightened mind, contemplate from the height of the virtues in which we have been placed. Or “we contemplate” means that, through a mirror, we do not yet behold perfectly. Or, in either of these senses, we contemplate the glory of the Lord, that is, the essence of the Godhead.

We are transformed into the same image, because Christ has taught us through the spirit to understand the Scriptures as subtly as he himself understands them. We shall be transformed more fully when we recover the same freedom from suffering and immortality.

I say that we are transformed from the brightness of virtue, proceeding into greater brightness. Or we are transformed from the brightness of faith and hope, which exists now, and transferred into the brightness of the reality itself, so that we may see God as he is.

We are transformed, I say, from brightness into brightness [Col. 0234B], as by the spirit of the Lord—that is, in proportion as the spirit of the Lord is able to accomplish this more worthily and more excellently.

## CHAPTER IV

> “Therefore, since we have this ministry, according as we have obtained mercy [from God], we do not falter, but renounce the hidden things of shame, not walking in craftiness nor adulterating the word of God, but by the manifestation of truth commending ourselves to every human conscience before God. For even if our Gospel is veiled, it is veiled among those who are perishing, among whom the god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers, so that the illumination of the Gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of [the invisible] God, may not shine. For we do not preach ourselves, but Jesus Christ [Col. 0234C] our Lord. We, however, are your servants through Jesus. For the God who said, ‘Let light shine out of darkness,’ himself has shone in our hearts for the illumination of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.
>
> “But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, so that the sublimity of the power may belong to God and not come from us. In every respect we suffer tribulation, but we are not oppressed. We are made poor, but are not destitute. We suffer persecution, but are not forsaken. We are humiliated, but not confounded. We are cast down, but do not perish. Always carrying about in our body the dying of Jesus Christ, so that the life of Jesus may also be manifested in our bodies. For we who live are always being handed over to death [Col. 0234D] because of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be manifested in our mortal flesh. Therefore death works in us, but life in you.
>
> “But possessing the same spirit of faith, as it is written: ‘I believed, therefore I spoke’ (Psalm 115:1), we also believe, and therefore we speak, knowing that he who raised Jesus will also raise us with Jesus and establish us with you. For everything is for your sake, so that grace, abounding through many in thanksgiving, may abound to the glory of God.
>
> “Therefore we do not falter. Although our outward human being is being corrupted, nevertheless the inward one is renewed day by day. For this momentary and light affliction of ours is producing for us, beyond all measure, an eternal weight of glory [Col. 0235A], while we do not contemplate the things that are seen but those that are not seen. For the things that are seen are temporary, but the things that are not seen are eternal.”

## EXPOSITION

And therefore, because we contemplate the glory of the Lord, proceeding from brightness into brightness, we, possessing this ministry of the Gospel, do not falter. It was not handed over to us because of our merit, but according as we obtained mercy from God. We do not falter in this ministry, whatever adversities may thrust themselves upon us.

Rather, we renounce not only open but also hidden things of shame—that is, sin, which brings shame upon the human being. I say that we do not walk in craftiness to extort money, as the false apostles do from their subjects, nor adulterate the word of God, as the false apostles do. Instead, by preaching through the clear manifestation of truth [Col. 0235B], we do not, like them, concern ourselves with speaking suitably for persuasion, but commend ourselves by the purity of our speech and life—not to outward appearance, as they do, but to every human conscience.

For although they attack us in words, nevertheless within themselves they praise our purity. I say that we commend ourselves before God—that is, in what is pleasing to God—though the false apostles care little or nothing about pleasing him. Or let it be understood in this way: Since this is the case with us, I say this before God, so that he himself may be our witness, since he alone knows our hidden things.

Because he said there, “in the manifestation of truth,” someone might object that the Gospel has been hidden from certain people [Col. 0235C]. Against this he says: Certainly, we evangelize in manifestation. Even if our Gospel is veiled, know that it is veiled among those who are perishing—that is, in their sin, among those who perish through unbelief.

Among these perishing people he has blinded their minds, because he is still “the god of this age” for unbelievers—that is, the devil, who rules those who belong to the world—according to the statement: “The prince of this world will be cast out” (John 12:31).

Or let us say that “the god of this age” means the one who governs not only heavenly but also earthly things. For some people were mistaken in thinking that God governs only heavenly things, while earthly things roll on solely through the chance of fortune.

Or let it be understood thus: “The god of this age.” For people of the world make various gods for themselves. One worships greed, another pleasure, and they are blinded by such a god.

He blinded them so that the illumination of the Gospel—that is, the Gospel once illuminated—might not shine, but remain veiled for them. I say “the Gospel of the glory” [Col. 0235D] of Christ, that is, the Gospel in which Christ is shown to be glorious. Christ is the image of God, that is, he represents God to us.

He is not an image in the sense that the Son is different from the Father in substance. Rather, he is called the image because whoever sees the Son also sees the Father. He is the image of the invisible God. And because God, in the nature of his Godhead, is invisible, it was necessary that through Christ what is invisible in its own nature should become visible.

We truly evangelize the glory of Christ. For we do not preach ourselves. Or this may be joined with what precedes: Truly, we do not walk in craftiness, as the false apostles do. For we do not preach—that is, by preaching we do not commend ourselves, that is, what proceeds from ourselves—but we preach Jesus Christ our Lord.

We preach ourselves as servants, not only [Col. 0236A] of Jesus but also of you, through Jesus—that is, in order to build up in you the love of Jesus. And rightly do we say “through Jesus,” because God has shone in our hearts, opening his mysteries to us, so that we might be taught to evangelize you.

God shone forth—the God who said, that is, who by a mere word caused light to shine from darkness. For when in the beginning the whole mass of creation was dark, undifferentiated by any variety of forms, he said: “Let there be light” (Genesis 1:3). By this word he expelled the darkness and caused that mass, which had been confused into one, to shine by distinguishing it through various forms.

This God, I say, shone in our hearts for the illumination of knowledge—that is, so that he might illuminate us with the knowledge of the glory of God, that is, of the divine essence. He could illuminate us concerning this only in the face—that is, in the knowledge and faith—of Christ Jesus [Col. 0236B]. For unless Christ had shown himself visible to us, in whom the whole Godhead is present, we would by no means have been capable of understanding the knowledge of the glory of God.

He has sufficiently commended himself according to the spirit; now, according to the body, he greatly debases himself, and through this debasement commends the Gospel entrusted to him. For unless he understood the glory of his Gospel to be marvelous, he would never have been willing to suffer so many and such great things for it.

God has illuminated us with knowledge of the divine glory. Although this is so worthy, nevertheless we possess this treasure of the glory of God in earthen vessels—that is, in our bodies.

He rightly calls it a treasure. For a treasure is something that is cherished and distributed. He calls bodies vessels of the spirit because the spirit would accomplish nothing without the ministry of the limbs [Col. 0236C]. With the hand, for example, we extend something to the poor, and likewise in other matters.

They are called earthen because of their fragility, since our bodies are subject to every kind of corruption. Therefore we possess this treasure in earthen vessels, so that the sublimity of God’s power may be evident: that in all who act well, God’s power alone may be exalted and magnified, and that it may be clear that nothing comes from us, who are earthen.

It was therefore fitting that God’s treasure should be stored in a fragile vessel, lest, if there were any human power, a person should rashly claim for himself what belongs to God.

We truly are earthen, and God’s power is in us, who are fragile. For in every place and circumstance we suffer bodily tribulation; nevertheless we are not oppressed in spirit, but rather are enlarged.

“We are made poor”—that is, we are made poor outwardly—but we are not destitute of God inwardly [Col. 0236D]. *Aporos* in Greek, “poor” in Latin.

We suffer persecution from place to place, but we are not abandoned by God. We are cast down—that is, laid prostrate by blows or hurled down from a height—and nevertheless we do not perish.

To conclude, we are always carrying about in our body, here and there, the dying—that is, the things that bring about death: namely, tribulations that are approaches to death. And we ought to suffer willingly, because this dying is Jesus’ dying, which he himself endured for us; and we carry it about in imitation of him, so that the life of Jesus Christ may be manifested not only in our souls but also in our bodies, once immortality and freedom from suffering have been restored to us.

He continues to dwell upon the abasement of his body, showing that he suffers all these things to commend his Gospel [Col. 0237A] and the glory of Christ, saying: I speak rightly of carrying about the dying. For we are always being handed over.

He does not say “always” because he could die more frequently than once, but because every day he suffered such things as human strength could not escape except by dying. Yet through the power of the spirit, Paul was restored to something better.

He calls the tribulations by which he gradually approaches destruction “the dying.” He calls “death” the final blow by which he is dissolved.

We, I say, are handed over to death. Above he said this in imitation of Jesus; here he says “because of Jesus,” that is, out of love for Jesus.

I say “we,” who, although we die in this way, nevertheless live—that is, we could live in the glory of the world, and far better than your false apostles if we kept silent about what Christ commanded.

Or let it be understood thus: We, according to the body, are handed over to death [Col. 0237B], yet through the death of the flesh we live more fully, according to the justification of the soul.

Or thus: We are handed over to death with respect to the injury inflicted upon the body, yet we live, not failing through the power of God.

We die because of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may be manifested in our flesh, just as in our soul. He had said the same thing in the preceding verse [170], but he repeats it in order to resolve what might be objected here.

The life of Jesus will be in our flesh. For if you object that our mortal flesh cannot become immortal, since the flesh of Jesus also became so, I reply that in our mortal flesh the life of Jesus will indeed be made manifest, and through Jesus the flesh that is mortal will certainly become immortal.

Since, then, we are handed over to death, death works in us what belongs to it, by putting our bodies to death. But in you [Col. 0237C], who have rejected our imitation and cling to the false apostles, there is life—that is, you suffer nothing, but to your own detriment.

Or let it be understood thus: Since the life of Jesus will be manifested in those who are put to death, this death works—that is, does a useful work—in you, namely, the life of Jesus. For if death works the life of Jesus in you, then the present life that you love works in you the opposite of the life of Jesus, namely, condemnation.

Or thus: Since through death we shall possess the life of Jesus, death works in us what is good, and through our death life works in you, because through the merit of our death you live in faith and righteousness.

Someone might say: “You would not need to be put to death by God if you kept your righteousness quiet and did not assert the faith of Christ before human beings.”

Against this Paul says that he cannot keep silent about the faith of Christ, because he has the spirit, and through the spirit he has faith. Since he has faith, therefore he speaks; and since he speaks, he is put to death.

He proves by the authority of David, speaking in the person of the martyrs, that he ought to act in this way, saying: We are therefore perplexed, cast down, and put to death because we possess the spirit that gives faith—the same spirit that David and the other saints possessed, or the same spirit that you possess, if you are willing to suffer for Christ.

For the power of the spirit fails no one except the person who has first failed himself.

We, I say, possess this spirit, and therefore we believe because of what we believe—that is, because we believe. We also speak before human beings what we believe.

Because he had mentioned tribulations, he did not add: “Because we speak, we have been humiliated by blows,” although this follows from what has been said.

We believe, and therefore we speak, acting as it is written of David: “I believed, therefore I spoke”—that is, “because I believed, I spoke.”

By believing and speaking we have the best confidence, knowing that God, who raised Jesus, will also raise us, to be placed with Jesus in rank and immortality; and there he will establish us—that is, he will settle us to remain forever.

He says that he will establish us with you, whom he is prepared, if you are willing, to raise together with Jesus. He therefore says “he will establish us with you,” so that they would not think that they could be reconciled with the Apostle through no righteousness of life of their own. He shows that each person will be rewarded not according to the dignities of positions of precedence but according to the fruits of works.

By also saying “with you,” he strongly draws them toward a desire for righteousness [Col. 0238B].

Therefore I say that he will establish us with you. For we suffer everything and labor for your instruction, so that grace, which abounds in me, may abound in you.

How grace abounded in Paul is sufficiently clear. I say that grace, which abounds in me, may abound in this particular thing, namely, thanksgiving, being multiplied through you to the glory of God.

He rightly ought to be glorified by us, since he gave us abundant grace. He does not say, “May grace abound in you,” but by urging them through this to give thanks to the glory of God, he makes the point sufficiently clear. For they would give thanks to God in vain unless the grace of God abounded in them.

Just as he said that he suffered all these things to the glory of God, so now he turns everything toward the benefit of the Corinthians [Col. 0238C], saying: “Therefore”—that is, because we suffer everything for your sake—even if I now remain silent about the glory of God, we do not falter for your benefit alone, whatever tribulations may be inflicted.

Someone might say: “It is remarkable that you claim not to falter, when we see you being corrupted by daily tribulations.”

To this he replies: Certainly, we do not falter, but we are renewed.

Although our outward human being is so worthless—our flesh, that is, which is always forced to obey our command, namely, the spirit—although this human being is outward, suffering rains, heat, and every adversity, although, I say, our outward human being is being corrupted, nevertheless the praiseworthy human being who is inward, where he ought to be strengthened by the distress of the outward human being, is renewed day by day [Col. 0238D].

The more the outward human being is corrupted, the more the inward one is renewed—that is, continually. Or “from day to day” means proceeding from virtue into virtue.

I say that we do not falter, and rightly so. For whatever our tribulation may be, great or small, the part of our tribulation that exists in the present is momentary—that is, it passes exceedingly quickly—and is not intolerable but light.

Such tribulation, I say, produces in us an eternal weight of glory: “weight” in contrast to “light,” “glory” in contrast to “tribulation,” “eternal” in contrast to “momentary,” and “in sublimity,” that is, in heaven, in contrast to what he said about the present.

It is called a weight because of the likeness to what is placed on a balance: what has weight on the scales is more valuable, while what is light is inferior.

Therefore we judge the things we suffer to be light and almost nothing, because we do not contemplate—that is, do not desire—the things that are seen, but the things that are not seen.

For this reason we despise the things that are seen [Col. 0239A], because the things that are seen are temporary. For this reason we desire the things that are not seen, because the things that are not seen are eternal.

## CHAPTER V

> “For we know that if our earthly house of this habitation is dissolved, we have an edifice from God, a house not made by hands but eternal in the heavens. For in this we also groan, desiring to be clothed over with our habitation, which is from heaven—if indeed, once clothed, we shall not be found naked. For we who are in this tent groan, being burdened, because we do not wish to be stripped but to be clothed over, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life.
>
> “Now he who accomplishes this very thing for us is God, who has given us the pledge of the spirit [Col. 0239B]. Therefore, being always confident and knowing that while we are in this body we are absent from the Lord—for we walk by faith and not by sight—we are confident and have the good will rather to be absent from the body and present with the Lord [God]. And therefore we strive, whether absent or present, to please him.
>
> “For we must all be manifested before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive according to what he has done through the body, whether good or evil. Therefore, knowing the fear of the Lord, we persuade human beings; but to God we are manifest. And I hope that we are also manifest in your consciences.
>
> “We do not commend ourselves to you again, but we give you an occasion to boast on our behalf, so that you may have an answer for those who boast in outward appearance and not in the heart [Col. 0239C]. For whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God; whether we are sober, it is for you.
>
> “For the love of Christ urges us, judging this: that if one died for all, then all have died; and Christ died for all so that those who live may no longer live for themselves but for him who died and rose for them.
>
> “Therefore from now on we know no one according to the flesh. And even if we knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him in that way. Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation; the old things have passed away, and behold, all things have been made new (Isaiah 43:19; Revelation 21:5).
>
> “But all things are from God, who reconciled us to himself through Christ and gave us the ministry [Col. 0239D] of reconciliation. For God was indeed in Christ, reconciling the world to himself, not reckoning their transgressions against them, and he placed in us the word of reconciliation.
>
