> “Therefore we act as ambassadors for Christ, as though God were exhorting through us. We entreat you on behalf of Christ: be reconciled to God. He made him who knew no sin to be sin for us, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.”

## EXPOSITION
Someone might say: “What can be known about the eternity of invisible things unless they are shown?” Paul certainly says so. As long as we are held in our earthly dwelling, we cannot see them; but once we have been dissolved, we shall immediately receive them. He gives the reason why we cannot see them: namely, because we are still held in mortality. He also indicates the time when we shall possess these things—[Col. 0240A] only after dissolution—saying: “Truly, the things that are not seen are eternal.” For we, who must be believed, know that, 172 that is, that if our earthly house, namely our body, is an earthly material and dwelling-place—for it is from the earth and dwells in the earth—our house is so called because the soul dwells in it as someone dwells in a house. If, I say, our house of this very brief and wretched dwelling is dissolved, after the tribulations mentioned above that we have endured for Christ, this, I say, we know: that it will indeed be dissolved. And when it is dissolved, we have an edifice prepared by God, that is, an immortal body built for us by God. This does not mean that God did not make the mortal body; rather, He ordered that it should grow together through the ministry of male and female. But He will make the mortal body immortal without such a minister. [Col. 0240B]

We have, then, an edifice, namely a house, “not made by hand,” that is, not made through another’s ministry, but eternal and abiding in the heavens. By “house” and “edifice” he signifies the immortal body. Truly, we shall have an eternal house in heaven. For we groan—not on account of what we suffer, nor because we fear obtaining immortality, but by groaning we desire to come into this, that is, into this immortality. “We groan,” I say, “desiring to be clothed over”: we are already clothed with the justification of the soul, and over this we wish to put on our dwelling, that is, the immortality of the body, which is a dwelling coming to us from heaven. For immortality is reserved for us in heaven. [Col. 0240C]

Yet I say that we shall be clothed over on this condition: if on that day we are found clothed with the justification of the soul, which was given to us in baptism as our first garment. Someone might say: “Just as all are clothed, so all alike and indiscriminately will be clothed over even if they are naked.” He excludes this possibility. Those who are clothed will indeed be clothed; but those who are naked will not be clothed with the immortality of the body, because they lack the righteousness of the soul.

Here he marks two kinds of good people: the contemplative, whom he mentioned above, and those who remain in the active life while nevertheless preserving the righteousness of God. Of these he proceeds to say: “Truly, the perfect groan, desiring to be clothed over with immortality.” For even we who are less perfect, who are in this tabernacle, to whom it is good to be in the flesh and to nourish it—the flesh is called a tabernacle because in it the soul must serve as a soldier for God—even we, such people, [Col. 0240D] groan, desiring likewise to be clothed over. Although we are weighed down by that body, we nevertheless do not wish to be stripped of it, that is, separated from the soul. Rather, if it were possible, we wish to be clothed over with immortality without death being inflicted, so that the body which is now mortal, without tasting death, might suddenly be swallowed up by the life that comes upon it and thus become immortal.

And although I say, “We groan and desire to be clothed over,” this does not originate from us. Rather, the one who effects this desire in us, and effects it so that it may itself—that is, this desire—remain in us, is God. He, I say, makes us desire this.

Alternatively, the preceding verse may be read in this way: “We ought to groan with desire for that dwelling which is from heaven.” For we also groan with desire for earthly things. He says this as follows: “We who are in this tabernacle,” that is, in this flesh which we nourish, although weighed down by the mass of this flesh, nevertheless groan because—that is, for this reason—we do not wish to be stripped of these bodily things; but we would suddenly wish to be clothed over with immortality, so that what is mortal might be swallowed up by life. This meaning is not changed. [Col. 0241A]

And although we groan from love of earthly things, it is nevertheless God who effects this in us: that we desire to be clothed over with the dwelling that is from heaven, preferring heavenly things to earthly things. I mean God, who will truly make us immortal. This can be believed from the fact that He has already given us the pledge of the Spirit, that is, the Holy Spirit, who is the earnest and beginning of immortality, which He will perfect in us.

And because God effects this in us, therefore “being confident, we are confident.” “Being confident” indicates continuance; “we are confident” signifies that we are still engaged in the same activity. “Being confident,” I say, “always and knowing well.” For some are confident about what they do not know; they know, but at some point they are not confident. We, certainly, are always confident and know that, while we are in this mortal body, we are foreigners, that is, separated from the Lord. [Col. 0241B]

A foreigner is one who is journeying toward a place which he has not yet reached. Thus the saints in this world journey toward God, whose face they have not yet grasped. Truly, while remaining in the body, we are foreigners from the Lord. For here we walk by faith. Faith is spoken of in relation to a thing that is not seen; we do not walk by sight, that is, by the actual operation of the thing itself.

“We are confident,” I say, “and are confident.” Although the flesh certainly resists, we nevertheless confidently persist; and with confidence we possess good will. Some are confident without good will; others have good will but are nevertheless not confident. We have, I say, the will rather to be away from the body, because it is the nature of the flesh never to wish to be dissolved. Therefore he says: “We would rather be separated from the body and be present with God than remain with the body and not be present with the Lord.” [Col. 0241C]

And therefore, in order that we may be present with the Lord, we strive—that is, we labor—to please Him, whether, while we are still absent from God in this life, or when we shall be present with God in glory. We labor to please Him both here and there. And it is necessary for us to please Him. For it is fitting, that is, necessary, that “all of us should be manifested before the tribunal of Christ,” that is, before Christ. By “tribunal,” which is the judge’s seat, he indicates judgment, so that each person may “receive,” that is, carry away from there, what belongs to his own body. This does not mean that he will not also carry away what belongs to the soul; rather, “what belongs to the body” means what he did while he lived in the body.

He shall receive what belongs to him according to what he did, provided that he had time in which to act. For as infants baptized by grace alone will be saved, so unbaptized children will be condemned because of original sin alone. He shall receive what belongs to him according to what he did, whether what he did was good or evil. [Col. 0241D]

Here a question arises: since he says “according to what he did,” the benefits performed for the dead might seem to be rendered ineffective. But against this it is said that, if the dead person piously arranged that this should be done for him, or if, by acting charitably toward his neighbor, he earned this benefit, the dead person is said to have done what he either arranged to be done or merited.

Because all of us shall be manifested before the tribunal of Christ, therefore, knowing that the Lord must be feared, we persuade people to fear the Lord, so that they may bring back good from the judge’s presence. [Col. 0242A]

Someone might object to him: “You persuade people of this less for their benefit than for your own commendation.” Against this he says: “We persuade people in this way; but we are manifest to God” as to the intention with which we persuade, whether for the benefit of people or for our own commendation. Nor are we manifest only to God. “I also hope that we are manifest in your consciences,” because although you curse us with your mouths, inwardly you think well of us.

And while saying that we are manifest to God and to your consciences, “we do not again commend ourselves to you” (as you objected in another letter), but rather we give you an opportunity, that is, an occasion, to boast on behalf of us, your teachers. For in the excellence of your teacher you surpass others. I mean on our behalf, so that you may have something to answer to those who boast “in the face,” that is, in the eyes of people, and do not boast in their own hearts but are tormented within their own consciences. These are the false teachers. [Col. 0242B]

Truly, you have an opportunity to boast on our behalf. For whatever we do, we do either for the glory of God or for your benefit. Since he says: “Whether we exceed in mind”—that is, whether we rise beyond human nature so as to hear things which it is not lawful for a human being to speak—or “whether we are sober,” that is, whether we set aside the intoxication of God’s secrets and soberly accommodate ourselves to your weakness, as when he gave instructions concerning marriage and similar matters. If, I say, we are sober, this sobriety is beneficial to you.

And it is good for us to be sober in this way, for “the love of Christ,” even if we were unwilling, “presses us” to adapt ourselves to you. He wishes to show that Christ alone is sufficient for justification and salvation, and that the old law, which the false teachers strive to restore, is of no benefit but causes great harm. Thus he says: “The love of Christ presses us, since we judge this: that if one”—namely, Christ—“died for the redemption of all, then all died” through the death of that one, in original sin. [Col. 0242C]

He did not die only so that we might die to sin, but so that through His death we might live for righteousness. He says this as follows: “Christ died for all,” and therefore “those who are dead to sin and who live for righteousness should no longer live,” attributing what they possess of life to themselves, as was done under the old law, “but should live for Him,” that is, for the glory of Him who died to put sin to death in them and rose again for those same people, so that they might rise again in righteousness.

Since in Christ’s death we died to sin, and by His rising we rose to righteousness—that is, because Christ is sufficient for every justification—therefore, from that time onward, after Christ suffered and rose again, “we know no one,” that is, we do not approve anyone, who walks according to the flesh, that is, according to the carnal rites of the old law. [Col. 0242D]

Someone might object: “Why do you thus condemn the law which Christ approved and observed?” Paul replies: “Although,” that is, even though, once, at the time when the figures still had to be observed, we knew Christ walking according to the flesh, that is, carrying out the rites of the old law, nevertheless now, after grace has been given, although we once knew Him, we no longer know Christ according to the flesh.”

And because we now know no one according to the flesh, therefore the old things have passed away. He first indicates the point from which he will draw his conclusion, saying: “If there is any creature in Christ,” that is, if a person receives in Christ, through the renewal of the soul, something new—something made new—after putting aside the oldness of sin, it is clear that the old things have passed away. “And behold, it is evident: all things have become a new creation in Christ.” [Col. 0243A]

The objector might still say: “Even if Christ does this, nevertheless He should not be followed, because He abolishes the law given by God; He does not work from God but against God.” But in the very matter by which the adversary wished to weaken his arguments—namely, by asserting that Christ did not do this according to God—Paul confirms his case, saying that God works through Christ to abolish the old law.

“All things have become new in Christ.” All these things which Christ works are from God, and God works this through Christ. For He reconciled the human race to Himself through Christ, that is, through that man who was the middle point in which two extremes, far different from each other—namely, man and God—were joined. And God gave us, me and the other apostles, the ministry of reconciliation, so that we might minister to people how they were reconciled to God through Christ, if they wished, after being reconciled to Christ, to be reconciled to God. [Col. 0243B]

Since God could again perform this work through the man Christ in such a way that the whole divinity did not dwell in that man, Paul determines how God acted through Christ: namely, with the fullness of divinity dwelling bodily in Him. He also determines how Christ Himself became the minister of reconciliation: namely, by the word alone, so that He might preach it to the Gentiles. But Christ was the minister of reconciliation as the one through whom and in whom the reality itself was accomplished.

I rightly say that God reconciled us to Himself through Christ, “because God was in Christ,” that is, the whole divinity was in that man. “God,” I say, “reconciling the world to Himself,” that is, the people of the world, through Christ. He reconciled them in this manner: “not counting,” that is, not exacting payment for, but forgiving, their trespasses from them, that is, from the world. [Col. 0243C]

And He gave us the ministry of this matter in such a way that He “placed in us the word of reconciliation,” that is, so that we might preach the reconciliation accomplished through Christ, so that people, reconciling themselves to Christ, might be reconciled to God.

And because God placed in us the word of reconciliation, therefore we “carry out God’s embassy.” Do not despise this embassy of ours, because we carry it out “for Christ,” that is, by Christ’s authority, knowing that contempt for me is contempt for Christ. And because we carry out this embassy for Christ, “we beseech you, brothers: be reconciled to God,” turning away from evil and doing good. [Col. 0243D]

“Be reconciled,” I say, “for Christ,” that is, out of love [Col. 0244A] for Christ, who loved you with such great charity. And do not despise our entreaty; rather, regard it as being made through us by God exhorting you. That is, know that my entreaty is God’s exhortation.

It is good and worthy that you be reconciled to God, who made Him—namely Christ, who knew no sin, though He knew it by knowledge rather than by experience of the deed—sin for our redemption. Christ was made sin according to the punishment of sin which He bore. Thus we might call an innocent man who was hanged a thief, according to the punishment of theft which he suffered, although the act of theft was not in him.

Alternatively, Christ was called “sin” because that victim which was offered for sin was called sin. Thus Christ, because He was offered for the sin of all, is called sin. [Col. 0244B] God, I say, made Christ sin for us, so that we might become not merely righteous but righteousness itself—not a false righteousness, nor the righteousness of the law, but the true righteousness of God, and this “in Him,” that is, through Christ.

## CHAPTER VI

“While cooperating, we also exhort you not to receive the grace of God in vain. For He says:

‘At an acceptable time I heard you,  
and on the day of salvation I helped you.’

Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation. We give no one any cause for offense, so that our ministry may not be blamed. Rather, in all things let us present ourselves as ministers of God: in great patience, in tribulations, in necessities, in distress, in blows, in prisons, in [Col. 0244C] seditions, in labors, in vigils, in fastings, in chastity, in knowledge, in long-suffering, in gentleness, in the Holy Spirit, in unfeigned love, in the word of truth, in the power of God; through the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left; through glory and dishonor, through ill repute and good repute; as deceivers and yet truthful; as unknown and yet known; as dying, and behold, we live; as disciplined and yet not killed; as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as needy, yet enriching many; as having nothing, yet possessing all things.

Our mouth is open to you, Corinthians; our heart is enlarged. You are not restricted by us, but you are restricted in your own hearts. [Col. 0244D] Since we have the same recompense, I speak as to children: be enlarged yourselves.

Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers. For what participation has righteousness with iniquity? Or what fellowship has light with darkness? What agreement has Christ with Belial? Or what share has the faithful with the unbeliever? What agreement has the temple of God with idols?

For you are the temple of the living God, as God says:

‘For I shall dwell in them,  
and I shall walk among them;  
I shall be their God,  
and they shall be my people.’ (Lev. XXVI, 12)

Therefore:

‘Come out from their midst  
and be separated,’ says the Lord,  
‘and do not touch what is unclean;  
and I shall receive you,  
and I shall be a father to you,  
and you shall be sons and daughters to me,’  
says the Lord Almighty.” (Isa. LII, 11; Jer. XXXI, 9)

## EXPOSITION

“We beseech you, cooperating.” We cooperate so that you may become the righteousness of God, through the ministry of the Lord’s preaching among you. Alternatively, we cooperate with you through instruction and prayers to God. We exhort you not to receive the grace of God in vain, as though he were saying: “You have indeed received the grace of God, but see to it that you did not receive it in vain,” that is, uselessly for yourselves.

I rightly call it “grace,” for now it is the time of grace. The Father says to the whole Christ together with His members, which is the Church: “I heard you,” that is, I fulfilled what you asked by forgiving sins. “I heard you,” I say, “at an acceptable time”—acceptable both to God, who was pleased at that time to show mercy to humanity, and to humanity, because at that time it rejoiced to have been freed from the death of sin. “I heard you,” by forgiving sins. [Col. 0245A]

“I also helped you,” strengthened in good works in the same acceptable time, “on the day,” that is, placed in the brightness of true knowledge. It is called the day of salvation because through true knowledge there is a path to eternal salvation. This is read in Isaiah (chap. XLVIII, verse 8).

Now Paul explains when this acceptable time is to be understood: God said, “At an acceptable time,” and behold, brothers, now—that is, from Christ’s Passion onward—is that acceptable time. And behold, now is that day of salvation on which it is acceptable to God to hear and to help.

Therefore we exhort you in this way: giving no one any cause for offense, that is, conducting ourselves in character, speech, and appearance so that we cause no one offense in any of these matters. We give no cause for offense so that our ministry may not be blamed, that is, so that our apostleship may not be blameworthy. It certainly would be, if I did not show in myself what I teach well. [Col. 0245B]

We give no cause for offense, but we present ourselves as ministers of God. And so that we may remain in this, may God grant that we present ourselves in everything we say and do as truly ministers of God, as newly born, namely, in great patience—that is, by suffering in many ways, in body and soul—presenting ourselves as ministers of God.

He sets out the aspects of patience. I say “in great patience,” possessed in tribulations, so that however our body is afflicted, we may endure it with equanimity. Patience is also possessed in necessities, so that we do not fail through any deprivation. Again, patience is possessed in distress of soul, in blows to the body, and in prisons. Patience is also shown in seditions which unbelievers stir up against us. [Col. 0245C]

Again, patience is possessed in labors, for we labor with our own hands so as not to burden anyone (I Thess. II, 9). Patience is also possessed in vigils, for he often had to keep watch while disputing about the faith. Patience is likewise possessed in fastings, because he often had to fast, sometimes under compulsion, sometimes from want, and sometimes voluntarily.

All the matters mentioned above are aspects of patience; the remaining qualities are concurrent with it. Let us present ourselves as ministers of God “in chastity,” so that we may be chaste in mind and body. Let us also present ourselves as ministers of God “in knowledge,” so that we may be adequately instructed in all things. [Col. 0245D]

Alternatively, we may make chastity and knowledge a single member: let us be ministers of God “in chastity and knowledge,” that is, in chaste knowledge. Let our knowledge not be deceitful, like the knowledge of the false teachers.

Let us also be ministers of God “in long-suffering.” If the crown is delayed, nevertheless we patiently endure the burdens. Let us likewise be ministers of God “in gentleness,” that is, in mild and gentle meekness, possessed in the Holy Spirit, not in flattering smoothness. [Col. 0246A]

Again, let us present ourselves as ministers of God “in unfeigned love,” so that we truly love God and our neighbor, and “in the word of truth,” so that the words of our preaching may sound with pure truth, not like the false teachers who intend to deceive with lying words.

Let us also be good ministers “in the power of God,” so that through signs of miracles I may prove myself to be a competent teacher.

Let us also present ourselves as ministers of God “through the weapons of righteousness,” possessing righteousness in place of weapons “on the right and on the left,” that is, in prosperity and adversity, so that we are neither led astray by prosperity nor cast down by adversity. The matters that follow are aspects of the right or the left. [Col. 0246B]

I say “on the right,” through glory: if some people glorify us, as when they wished to build altars to him, let us present ourselves in that glory as ministers of God. “On the left,” through dishonor: when they disparage us, saying that we preach falsehoods, let us present ourselves in that dishonor as ministers of God.

Again, through ill repute, which is an aspect of the left: when it was said to him, “You are mad, Paul” (Acts XXVI, 24). And again through good repute: when his preaching was extolled by others. Through both of these let us present ourselves as ministers of God. [Col. 0246C]

Let us present ourselves as ministers of God when regarded by some as deceivers and by others as truthful. Again, when regarded by some as unknown to God and by others as known to God, let us present ourselves in both circumstances as ministers of God.

Again, when regarded as dying—that is, by some as falling into crimes—and yet, according to others, behold, living in righteousness, let us present ourselves in both circumstances as ministers of God.

Again, when regarded as disciplined, according to those who, after the blows inflicted upon us, would say, “Behold, they will no longer dare to speak,” and according to others as not disciplined, who would say, “They will never on that account keep silent about the word of God.” This discipline would be a killing; therefore he says, “not killed.” In both circumstances let us present ourselves as ministers of God. [Col. 0246D]

Again, when regarded by some as sorrowful, because we are saddened by adversity in body or spirit, and by others as always rejoicing in body and spirit, let us present ourselves in both circumstances as ministers of God.

According to some, let us also be regarded as needy, either in bodily or spiritual goods; according to others, as enriching many in spiritual goods. In both circumstances let us present ourselves as ministers of God.

Again, according to some, let us be considered as possessing absolutely nothing good, whether temporal or spiritual; according to others, as possessing everything—that is, possessing God. In both circumstances let us present ourselves as ministers of God. [Col. 0247A]

I say this in order to humble the false teachers in your presence. “O Corinthians, our mouth is now open to you”: we speak at length and with sufficient fullness about our glory, although in the earlier Epistle I presented myself as everyone’s servant. And indeed our mouth could rightly be open, because our heart has been enlarged. Whatever I say about our glory, my conscience recognizes all of it as present in me.

And because our mouth is open and our heart enlarged, “you are no longer restricted by us.” Since I taught you plainly, having found you inexperienced, you say that it is my fault that you are restricted in love. But it is certainly clear from our example that you are not restricted by us; rather, “you are restricted in your own hearts,” that is, the source of this narrowness and restraint lies in your hearts. [Col. 0247B]

Alternatively, with a few changes to what was said above: We exhort you not to receive the grace of God in vain. To prevent this, do not give anyone any cause for offense through an evil deed or example, so that our ministry—that is, our teaching—may not be blameworthy because of your giving offense.

Do not give offense, but let us present ourselves in all things so as to attract them more effectively to the good, inserting himself among them when he says, “as ministers of God.” On this interpretation, “as” retains its proper force. Nothing that follows is changed, except that what was explained as applying to Paul is said to apply to them as well.

And because, O Corinthians, I now give you many and extensive commands, “our mouth is open to you” by giving many instructions, although earlier you reproached me for having admonished you about only a few matters. Nor is it surprising that, with open mouth, I give you many commands, because “our heart has been enlarged,” that is, I find in myself everything that I hand over to you for practice. [Col. 0247C]

And from this it is already evident that you are not restricted by us if you practice only a few things, but that you are restricted in your own hearts. Do not, however, be restricted; be enlarged in love, like the other churches, and you likewise. I say this to you as children. In hope, at least, you already possess the same recompense that we possess, namely, heavenly glory. Be enlarged also in the commandments of God.

Do not be yoked with the false teachers who are unbelievers. By the yoke he signifies the old law, which heavily oppressed those who observed it. You ought not to bear the yoke with unbelievers, because you are righteous and they are unrighteous; you are light and they are darkness; Christ is in you and Belial is in them; you are faithful and they are unbelievers; you are the temple of God and they are temples of idols. [Col. 0247D]

“What participation has righteousness with iniquity? Or what fellowship has light with darkness?” Certainly there ought to be no fellowship between members where there is a difference between the heads: Christ is our head, while Belial is their head.

“What agreement, moreover, has Christ with Belial? Or what share has the faithful with the unbeliever? What agreement has the temple of God with idols,” that is, with those impious people who, like an idol, are seats of demons? For just as the demon gave responses through an idol, so he gave responses through them.

I rightly call you the temple of God, for you who are faithful are the temple of the living God, because He lives in you while He makes you live in goodness. And I say this as the Lord God says through Ezekiel, although in different words.

God says this: “I shall dwell in those faithful people,” justifying them through faith, “and I shall walk among them,” advancing them from virtue to virtue. And thus it will appear that “I shall be their God, and they shall be my people.” For whoever sees their righteousness will say: “These are the people of God, and God dwells in them.” [Col. 0248A]

Paul now draws from this authority another passage taken from the same Ezekiel. In that passage, during the Babylonian captivity, he persuaded the Jews to come out and separate themselves from the evil works of the Gentiles. If they did so, he promised them liberation from God, saying: “Therefore,” namely, so that you may be the people of God, “come out from the midst of the impious”; do not do what they do.

Separate yourselves from them also in your will, not merely in your actions. This must necessarily be done, because the Lord says: “Do not even touch what is unclean,” that is, do not even take pleasure in their uncleannesses, so that they may at least be pleasing to you.

And if you do this, “I shall receive you.” After receiving you, I shall be a father to you, and you shall be sons to me, or even daughters, who are adorned by their parents with greater care. You ought to believe and do all these things, because the Lord Almighty says them. [Col. 0248B]

## CHAPTER VII

“Therefore, having these promises, beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God.

Receive us. We have wronged no one. We have corrupted no one. We have defrauded no one. I do not say this for your condemnation. For I have already said that you are in our hearts, to die and to live together. I have great confidence in you; I have great reason to boast on your behalf. I am filled with consolation; I abound in joy in all our tribulation.

For even when we had come into Macedonia, our flesh had no rest, but we suffered every tribulation: battles outside, fears within. But God, who consoles the humble, consoled us through the arrival of Titus. And not only through his arrival, but also through the consolation with which he was consoled among you, when he reported to us your longing, your weeping, and your zeal for me, so that I rejoiced all the more.

For although I saddened you in the letter, I do not regret it. And if I did regret it—seeing that the letter, although it saddened you for a time—I now rejoice, not because you were saddened, but because you were saddened unto repentance. For you were saddened according to God, so that you might suffer no loss through us.

For the sorrow that is according to God produces repentance leading to lasting salvation, whereas the sorrow of the world produces death.

For behold, this very thing—that you were saddened according to God—how great a diligence it produced in you, and also a defense, indignation, fear, longing, zeal, and vengeance. In every respect you showed yourselves to be pure in the matter.

Therefore, although I wrote to you, it was not on account of the one who did the wrong, nor on account of the one who suffered it, but to make manifest before God the concern that we have for you.

For this reason we were consoled. In our consolation we rejoiced even more abundantly over the joy of Titus, because his spirit was refreshed by all of you. And if I boasted to him in any respect about you, I was not put to shame. Rather, just as we spoke everything to you in truth, so our boasting to Titus also proved true. His affections for you are all the more abundant, as he remembers the obedience of you all, how you received him with fear and trembling.

I rejoice that in every respect I have confidence in you.”

## EXPOSITION
179. “Therefore, since you are going out from the midst of the ungodly,” says the Lord, “you shall be to me as sons and daughters,” and so forth. Therefore, dearest brothers, since you have these promises—that is, the promises stated above—so that we may grasp them, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and from every defilement of spirit. By defilements of the flesh he means lust, drunkenness, and the like; by defilements of the spirit, anger, envy, and the like, which infect the soul itself without any contagion of the flesh. Thus let us cleanse ourselves from sins in both respects, thereafter perfecting sanctification—that is, so that, cleansed from evils, we may be perfect in virtues. Let us accomplish this in the fear of God—that is, not in fear of human beings, so that we may seek to appear righteous in the face and not in the heart, as the false apostles do, but in the fear of God. Nor merely in fear of punishments, so that we may escape punishments by this alone, but in the fear of God, so that we may fear offending God; and this fear is called love.

Or the passage may be divided otherwise: “Let us cleanse ourselves from defilement of the flesh,” so that the sentence ends there, and then, “we, cleansed, perfecting the sanctification of the spirit,” that is, according to what the spirit—or that faculty of reason—teaches; or “perfecting the sanctification of the spirit,” that is, of reason, or of the Holy Spirit. The meaning is the same. The same applies to “in the fear of God.”

And so that, once cleansed, you may perfect sanctification, “receive us”—that is, accept our example. Or, without ending the sentence there: “You who are perfecting sanctification, receive us,” that is, imitate us, as has been said. You ought indeed to receive us, for we have injured none of you by reproaching you—saying that you were dogs or something of that kind—nor by boasting about myself on the basis of Abrahamic ancestry, as the false apostles do. Again, we corrupted none of you by teaching perversely or depraving you by a bad example, as the false apostles do, who, mixing falsehoods with truths, corrupt your faith, and do so also by the evil example of their lives. [Col. 0249B]

Nor did we take advantage of anyone among you, as the false apostles do. When they cannot openly extort anything from you, they draw it out by fraudulent seduction, obtaining it by deception rather than by request. When I say that you were corrupted and led astray by those false apostles, I do not say this for your condemnation—that is, I do not intend thereby to condemn you as rejected by God. You can know that I do not say it for your condemnation from the fact that I previously said in this same Epistle that you are in our hearts, where he says: “You are our Epistle, written in our hearts.” For if I intended you to be condemned, I would never have inserted you in our hearts. But you are in our hearts “for dying together and living together”: that is, I desire you to die with me to sin and to live with me to righteousness. [Col. 0249C]

Or he may be speaking to the more perfect: “You are in our hearts for dying together,” so that I desire you to die with me in the present tribulation, in order that you may thus be with me for living together in eternity. Therefore I say, “Receive us,” because I have great confidence in you concerning future blessings, so that you may promptly assent to the exhortation I am about to give. I also have great glorying on your behalf. For I glory greatly before other Churches in the good correction of your conduct, setting you before them as an example.

Therefore I have great confidence in you concerning the future. For I am already filled with consolation in every tribulation, whatever its kind—whether easy or difficult, whether within or without—and I am not consoled in any manner concerning your correction, but to such an extent that I overflow with joy. I rejoice more over your correction than I grieve over all our tribulation. [Col. 0249D]

They might say: “Are you suffering tribulation?” I answer: “Indeed I am.” For elsewhere he also says: “When we had come into Macedonia, our flesh had no rest, but we suffered every tribulation. Outside”—that is, in the body—“there were conflicts,” while they afflicted me with whips; “inside”—that is, in the mind—“there were fears,” lest the faithful should be scandalized by my sufferings and judge that I ought not to be followed because I had been condemned.

Or otherwise: “Outside”—that is, from those who were outside the Church—“there were conflicts” assailing me, as has been said; “inside”—that is, in the Church—“there were fears,” lest the simple should be led astray by false brothers. Thus I suffered greatly, both outside and inside. But God, who comforts the humble—that is, the afflicted—comforted us through the arrival of Titus. [Col. 0250A]

For I rejoiced at the reception of the brother who would share in our tribulations. But I was consoled not only by his arrival, but also by the consolation with which Titus himself was consoled by you. Through his comfort I understood your correction. And therefore, while rejoicing at his return, I was consoled at the same time, recognizing your correction in his consolation.

Titus consoled me, I say, by reporting your longing to us—how greatly you desired our arrival. He also reported your weeping, that is, that you were washing away your sins with tears. He also reported your zeal, that is, your indignation against the false apostles, for my sake, because they reject me. [Col. 0250B]

He reported these things in such a way that I now rejoiced more over your repentance than I had previously been saddened by your impenitence. Or, I rejoiced more over your conversion than I grieved over my own tribulation.

We should understand this as follows. When the Apostle had sent his first Epistle to the Corinthians through Timothy, they were moved more to indignation than to repentance, judging it presumptuous that the Apostle dared to rebuke them with such severity. When Paul learned this through Timothy, he repented that he had written to them. But while Titus remained longer among the Corinthians and repeatedly reread Paul’s Epistle, they, under Titus’s admonition, produced fruit worthy of repentance. When the Apostle heard this, he rejoiced more over their repentance than he had previously grieved over their impenitence. [Col. 0250C]

This is what he says: “Truly, through Titus’s report it came about that I rejoiced. For although I saddened you by the Epistle previously sent, I do not now repent, after hearing Titus’s report, although earlier I had repented after hearing Timothy’s report. At first I repented when I saw that the Epistle previously sent had saddened you to indignation, even if only for a time. Therefore I now repent less. For now I rejoice—not because you were previously saddened, but because you have now been saddened to repentance.”

I rightly rejoice over you who have been saddened to repentance. For you were saddened according to God: abandoning evil and adhering to good, and doing so according to God, so that you now suffer no loss from us in anything, since even that earlier sorrow, which I feared might become a detriment to you, has been corrected according to God. [Col. 0250D]

Truly, you suffer no loss from us in anything. For your sorrow, which is according to God, produces in you repentance that is effective for stable—that is, eternal—salvation. Sorrow according to God produces salvation; but worldly sorrow—which still exists among some of you who do not wish to be saddened unto repentance—produces death, that is, stable perdition. This is appropriately added to terrify those who had not yet repented.

Truly, sorrow according to God produces repentance unto salvation. For it produces solicitude, defense, and the other elements of true repentance. This is what he says: “For behold, this very thing”—so small in comparison with the salvation it produces—“namely, your being saddened according to God: behold how great a solicitude for progress, always toward what is better, it produces in you.” [Col. 0251A]

The items that follow are joined together, serving chiefly as ornaments of the discourse. It also produces in you defense, because, now possessing zeal for God, you defend me against the false apostles who reject me. It also produces indignation, for you are greatly indignant against those who led you astray. It produces fear as well, for you are always fearful lest you fall again into the snare. It produces desire, for you desire an appetite for good things and zeal—that is, imitation—of the righteous. It produces vengeance. For if anyone sins in your Church, you immediately avenge his offense through the repentance imposed upon him. [Col. 0251B]

To gather your good qualities briefly: “In everything you have shown yourselves to be undefiled in the matter,” that is, in ecclesiastical religion. Or, “undefiled by the matter of the world,” that is, by sin.

And because you have shown yourselves undefiled in everything, my intention in the earlier Epistle now becomes apparent. Although I wrote to you, I did not write solely because of the one who committed the offense by taking his father’s wife, nor again solely because of the one who suffered the offense by being dragged before secular judges. Rather, I wrote to make manifest our solicitude, the solicitude we have for you—and this before God, that is, according to God’s good pleasure. For it pleases God that I should be solicitous for your salvation. Or I say “before God,” meaning with God as witness, who knows my conscience. [Col. 0251C]

For when Paul dealt with that fornicator, he did not direct his speech to that man alone, but to the whole Church, intending that the many should not be infected by the pollution of one. And because our solicitude for you has now been made manifest, since it has reached completion, we have been consoled.

In our consolation we rejoiced both over your correction and over Titus’s joy, and we rejoiced more abundantly than we had previously grieved over your sins or over my tribulations. And although we were consoled more abundantly by your correction and Titus’s joy, we rejoiced still more over Titus’s joy than over your correction. [Col. 0251D]

The construction is similar to: “Virgil is more learned than Horace and Lucan; nevertheless, he is more learned than Lucan than Horace.” Therefore the Apostle rejoiced more over Titus’s joy than over the Corinthians’ correction, because if Titus’s joy had not existed, he would not have believed that they had been corrected.

Moreover, if Titus had not rejoiced over this, he would have been completely disheartened and would have ceased entirely from laboring either in the Corinthian Church or elsewhere. Hence he gives the reasons himself: “Therefore I rejoiced more over Titus’s joy, because his spirit has been refreshed by all of you,” even by those who had not yet been corrected, concerning whom he had good hope that they would be corrected through those who had already been corrected well. His spirit would have utterly failed in instruction if he had found the Corinthians incorrigible. [Col. 0252A]

Therefore I rejoiced still more over Titus’s joy because, as I had gloried before Titus in you, O Corinthians—for when he hesitated to come to you and accused you of inhumanity, I said that you were kind and would receive him honorably—if I gloried in you in any respect, I was not put to shame in this. For just as I had foretold him, so he found you; and therefore I was not ashamed to have spoken as I did.

Our glorying about you that had been expressed to Titus thus became truth, just as, while we were with you, we spoke everything to you in truth—that is, just as, remaining among you, I truthfully spoke to you about others, so now I truthfully spoke to Titus about you. [Col. 0252B]

Therefore I rejoice still more over Titus’s joy because his affections are now more abundantly directed toward you who have been corrected than previously toward you who had not been corrected. I mean Titus, who remembers the obedience of all of you—that is, how devotedly you obeyed him and us—and who also remembers how you received him, with fear of mind and trembling of body, namely, with every kind of reverence. [Col. 0252C]

And seeing how worthily you received him, I rejoice that I have confidence in you—not merely in this matter, but also in everything that I may command you to carry out. [Col. 0252D]

## CHAPTER VIII

> “We make known to you, brothers, the grace of God that has been given in the Churches of Macedonia: that amid much testing through tribulation their abundance of joy and their deepest poverty overflowed into the riches of their simplicity. For I bear them witness according to their ability, and beyond their ability they were willing, with much exhortation beseeching us for the grace and fellowship of the ministry that is performed for the saints. And they did not act as we had hoped, but gave themselves first to the Lord, then to us by the will of God, so that we asked Titus that, just as he had begun, so he might also complete this grace among you. But just as you abound in everything—in faith, in speech, in knowledge, in every solicitude, and also in your love for us—so that you may abound in this grace also. I do not speak as one commanding, but by the solicitude of others also testing the goodness of your love. For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ: that although he was rich, he became poor for your sake, so that through his poverty you might become rich. And in this I give advice. For this is useful to you, who not only began to do but also to desire it from the previous year. Now, therefore, complete it in deed, so that, just as the willingness of the will is prompt, so also may be the completion from what you have. For if the will is prompt, it is accepted according to what one has, not according to what one does not have. For it is not that there should be relief for others and tribulation for you, but that, by equality in the present time, your abundance should supply their want, so that their abundance may also be the supply for your want, that there may be equality, as it is written: ‘He who had much did not have too much, and he who had little did not have too little’ (Exodus 15:18). But thanks be to God, who has given the same solicitude for you in Titus’s heart. For he accepted the exhortation, but, being more solicitous, went to you of his own accord. We also sent with him our brother, whose praise in the Gospel is throughout all the Churches. Not only is he praised in the Gospel, but he was also appointed by the Churches as our companion in this journey for the grace that is administered by us to the glory of the Lord and in accordance with our determined purpose, avoiding this: that anyone should reproach us in this abundance that is administered by us to the glory of the Lord. For we provide what is good, not only before God but also before human beings. And we sent with them our brother, whom we have often tested as being solicitous in many matters, but now much more solicitous, with great confidence in you—whether for Titus, who is my companion and your helper, or for our brothers, the apostles of the Churches, the glory of Christ. Therefore show to them, before the face of the Churches of God, the proof of your love and of our glorying about you.” [Col. 0253A–D]

## EXPOSITION

For from this one matter I understand what you will do concerning the future. He now speaks at greater length about the collection, which he had mentioned briefly in the First Epistle, persuading them both by the example of other Churches and by many arguments.

The earlier passage is joined as follows: “When we had come into Macedonia, our flesh had no rest.” Yet although at first we had no rest, God gave peace and grace in the Churches of Macedonia. This is what he says: “We make known to you, brothers, the grace of God that was given in the Churches of Macedonia.” [Col. 0253D]

He appropriately calls almsgiving the grace of God, understanding that the grace of God in ministering to the poor is greater than the varieties of tongues and certain other graces. Concerning this grace I make known to you that, amid much testing through tribulation—for the Churches of the Macedonians experienced many severe tribulations—their abundance of joy existed. [Col. 0254A]

By “abundance,” I mean that they rejoiced greatly, because they were considered worthy to suffer insult for Christ. Their poverty also abounded. For unbelievers were impoverishing the faithful. Their poverty, I say, was “deepest,” that is, greatest—or “deepest,” meaning most worthy.

Their poverty abounded because the more they gave, the poorer they became. I say that it abounded into their riches because, although they were poor in possessions, they were rich in administering alms. I say “into the riches of their simplicity.” For they gave in simplicity, not thinking that on this account they could sin more freely. [Col. 0254B]

It certainly abounded into riches because they were willing according to their ability and beyond their ability. To give according to one’s ability is to retain first what is necessary for oneself and then distribute among the poor what is left over. To give beyond one’s ability is to reserve absolutely nothing for oneself.

And because they were willing according to their ability and beyond their ability, I bear witness to them. They were not compelled by us; rather, with much exhortation they entreated us—that is, they adjured us by every sacred appeal—saying: “Do not be anxious about us, because we are laborers; and we shall be adequately supported by our work, even if nothing remains for us.” [Col. 0254C]

They entreated us to accept grace from them—that is, alms—and fellowship, that is, their possessions, which they intended to share with everyone. I call this fellowship of the ministry, that is, of the administration, which ministry was to be conveyed to the saints who were in Jerusalem.

Here it should be noted that the saints are first to be supported from our abundance; from whatever remains, any needy persons may be supported.

They entreated us, and they did not act as we had hoped—that is, not with the intention that we should endure their many vices—but first they gave themselves to God, correcting their vices. Then they gave themselves to us by offering provisions for the brothers, and this by the will of God. For this is what God wills: first to devote oneself, and afterward one’s possessions.

They gave themselves in such a way that we asked Titus that, just as he had begun well, so he might also complete among you the other graces, and this grace as well, following the example of the Churches of Macedonia. [Col. 0254D]

We did not ask Titus only to complete this grace among you, but also that through him you might abound in this grace. “To complete” applies to Titus; “to abound” applies to the Corinthians.

Or otherwise: We did not merely ask Titus to complete this among you; I myself also ask you that, just as you abound in every grace—namely, in faith, for you possess a sound faith abounding in good works; in speech and knowledge, because you have ready speech for exhortation and knowledge for understanding; in every solicitude, because you are earnestly concerned to act ever better; and in love, that is, in your love extended toward us—so I ask that you abound also in this grace of almsgiving. [Col. 0255A]

I do not say this as one commanding, that is, I do not establish a command concerning this matter, lest, if you should fail to obey the command, you should be guilty of disobedience. I do not speak by command, but I say this while testing your good disposition—that is, your reason together with your will.

For you ought rationally to consider what you give, namely temporal things, and what you will receive in return, namely eternal things. And, together with reason, there ought to be a willing desire to give most freely. I test, I say, the good disposition of your love through the solicitude of others—that is, through the fact that you are concerned to supply the need of the needy brothers.

Or I test your love through the solicitude of others—that is, through the fact that I make Titus and the other disciples solicitous concerning you. [Col. 0255B]

And indeed you ought to abound in this grace. For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ: that is, you know that, although he was rich—God, rich in the wealth of his omnipotence, eternal—he became poor in time for the sake of saving us.

Nor did he merely wish to become poor; he became poor, living in every poverty of the flesh except the poverty of righteousness. He became poor so that, through his poverty—that is, through the merit of his poverty—you might become rich in righteousness.

And in recalling to you the kindness of the Lord Jesus shown toward you, I give you advice concerning salvation. And I rightly call it advice. For this—that is, abounding in almsgiving—is useful to you, who not only began to do it but also began to desire it from the previous year.

Note that doing first increases willing afterward. For doing is not enough unless it proceeds from the will; but willing is enough even when there is no opportunity to do. You began long ago to will it. Now complete it in will and deed, so that, just as the mind of the will is prompt—that is, the discernment of the will, which above he called a good disposition—so also the mind may be prompt to complete it. [Col. 0255C]

And although I urge this, I say that it should be completed from what you have, that is, according to what you possess and are able to provide for the brothers. Therefore I say “from what you have,” because, if your will is prompt to give, it is accepted according to what it possesses, and not only if it gives according to what it does not possess.

What he says, “according to what one has,” and “according to what one does not have,” is the same as what he said above, “according to one’s ability” and “beyond one’s ability.” For the one who reserves what is necessary for himself and distributes what is in excess is said to give according to what he has. But the one who retains nothing for himself, distributes everything, and follows the naked cross naked, gives according to what he does not have. [Col. 0255D]

But because he saw that they were not capable of this perfection, he urges them toward what is easier.

Someone might object: “You compel us to give, so that, while others become rich from what is ours, we may afterward become needy.” Not at all. Give according to what you have, not according to what you do not have. For I do not command this so that, through your gifts, there may be relief for others and, once relieved, they may grow idle in leisure, while you suffer tribulation because they have relief.

I do not command this, but I ask that your abundance—which is in temporal things—supply their want in the present time. Let this be done by equality: not so that you give them only as much as you reserve for yourselves, but enough that you may be equally secure from want. [Col. 0256A]

Therefore let your abundance supply their want, so that their abundance also—the abundance of the perfect, which consists in virtues—may be the supply for your want. For although you are rich in earthly things, you are poor in heavenly things.

Let your abundance supply them in such a way that equality may be established reciprocally in eternal good: just as the saints in this world share in the fruits of those who labor, so in the future those who now minister to the saints may share in their reward.

Nor do I mean that equality should be established so that the imperfect receive as much as the more perfect. Rather, there is equality in this: each will receive his own coin, that is, perfect and sufficient blessedness. [Col. 0256B]

It was not established that some human beings should labor while others devote themselves to prayer, so that those who pray would be supported by the labor of others, while those who labor would be saved by the prayers of the others.

Let there be equality, I say, as it is written figuratively concerning future equality: “He who had much did not have more than the one who had little, and he who had little did not have less,” that is, he did not have less than the one who had gathered much. For the one who has much heavenly glory does not abound in such a way that the one who has less is in need. Rather, for both the one who has much and the one who has little, abundance is equal, because each has what is sufficient, although there is a difference between them in glory.

Literally, this was written about the manna that the Jews gathered. The one who had gathered much, even if more than a full *gomor*, did not have more than a *gomor*; and the one who had gathered less than a *gomor* did not have less than a full *gomor* (Exodus 15:18). [Col. 0256C]

Above I said that I asked Titus. Concerning this I give thanks to God, who gave Titus’s heart the same solicitude for you as exists in my heart. I rightly say “the same,” because he readily accepted the exhortation made on your behalf; but although he accepted it kindly, he went to you of his own accord, being more solicitous for you than my exhortation required.

We also sent with him, namely with Titus, our brother whose praise is in the Gospel. Some say that this brother was Luke, others Barnabas. If we say Luke, his praise is in writing the Gospel; if Barnabas, his praise is in preaching the Gospel throughout all the Churches. For every Church praises him. [Col. 0256D]

Not only is he praised in the Gospel, but he was also appointed by the Churches as our companion in our journey. This seems to refer more particularly to Barnabas. When the brothers who were in Jerusalem sent him with Paul to the Gentiles to preach, the Holy Spirit said to them: “Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them” (Acts 13:2).

He calls it a journey because, when he is sent from Judea to the Gentiles, he leaves his homeland and travels to foreign places. He became, I say, a companion in this grace of almsgiving, which was likewise to be preached. This grace is received by us and administered by you to the saints who are in Jerusalem. You ought to rejoice over this, because it is administered to the glory of the Lord. [Col. 0257A]

And truly God is glorified in this administration. Even if I were to say nothing about the Lord’s glory, you ought to minister, if for no other reason, in order to fulfill our will, by whose teaching you are sons of God.

I speak of a will that must indeed be followed, because it has been determined—that is, ordained by God that I should will this. For God arranged that I should will it in this way.

We sent Titus and another brother with him, avoiding this: that anyone should reproach us in this abundance of alms, which is administered by us to the saints in Jerusalem. For this reason Paul sent so many suitable witnesses to receive the collections, lest, if he carried this out through a suspicious person, they should reproach him, saying that he retained some of the abundance of the alms for his own uses. [Col. 0257B]

I say that no one should reproach us, and rightly so. For in acting in this way we provide what is good not only before God but also before all human beings. No one will be able to suspect anything blameworthy when he sees so many suitable witnesses.

From this statement of Paul it may be understood that someone who presents himself in such a way that an unfavorable suspicion can arise concerning him sins even if he is not guilty of the matter, because, acting less prudently through his negligence, he arouses guilt in his brother.

With Titus and the other brother we also sent our brother whom we have often tested as being solicitous in many matters. We do not name this brother, but we believe him to be Apollos, their bishop. In the First Epistle, when Paul asked him to go, he refused (1 Corinthians 16:12), having learned that they were still uncorrected. But now, having learned through Titus that they had been corrected, he returns to them. [Col. 0257C]

I say that he was solicitous; but you should know that he is now much more solicitous for your salvation, having great confidence in you—whether because of Titus, who commended your correction to him, or because of those who are our brothers, that is, both Titus and the others.

I speak of Titus, who is my companion in everything and especially a helper among you, and of those who are our brothers, the apostles—that is, the envoys—of the Churches, for the glory of Christ, that is, to preach the glory of Christ.

And because we have sent such approved persons to you, show your love toward them and, to say more, display toward them the manifestation that is your love. For if you show yourselves ungrateful, it will be evident that you ministered to Titus and the others out of fear, because you were in your sins, and not out of love. But the kindness you now show toward these men will be a manifestation of your love, because it will prove that what you did previously was done out of love. [Col. 0257D]

Also display our glorying about you that we have expressed to them. For I have greatly gloried and promised that you would receive them honorably. Display it, I say, before the face of the other Churches, so that you may be their face and model, after whose likeness the other Churches may be formed.

## CHAPTER IX

> “Concerning the ministry that is performed for the saints, it is superfluous for me to write to you. For I know your prompt will, on account of which I glory about you before the Macedonians, because Achaia also has been ready from the previous year, and your zeal has stirred up very many. But we sent the brothers so that our glorying about you might not be emptied in this matter, so that, as I said, you may be ready; lest, when the Macedonians come with me and find you unprepared, we should be ashamed [or, according to another reading, ‘I should be ashamed’]—not to say that you should be ashamed—in this substance. Therefore I considered it necessary to ask the brothers to go ahead to you and prepare this promised blessing, so that it may be ready, [or, according to another reading, ‘thus,'] as a blessing and not as avarice. But I say this: He who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and he who sows in blessings will also reap from blessings. Let each give as he has determined in his heart, not from sadness or compulsion. ‘For God loves a cheerful giver’ (Ecclesiasticus 35:11). God is able to make every grace abound in you, so that, always having every sufficiency in everything, you may abound in every good work, as it is written: ‘He has scattered, he has given to the poor; his righteousness remains forever and ever’ (Psalm 111:9). He who supplies seed to the sower will also supply bread for eating. And he will multiply your seed and increase the fruits of your righteousness, so that, enriched in everything, you may abound in all simplicity, which through us produces thanksgiving to God. For the ministry of this service not only supplies what is lacking to the saints, but also abounds through many thanksgivings to the Lord, with those glorifying God through the obedience of your confession in the Gospel of Christ and through the simplicity of your fellowship with them and with all, and through their entreaty for you, as they desire you because of the surpassing grace of God in you. I give thanks to God for his unspeakable gift.” [Col. 0258A–C]

## EXPOSITION

I exhort you to show your love toward them. For writing to you about the ministry—that is, about those collections, which ministry is to be transferred to the saints—is, I say, superfluous for me; I have judged it unnecessary.

It is superfluous because I know that your will is prompt to minister. Since you are ready, I glory about you before the Macedonians, saying that not only Corinth but all Achaia under Corinth has been ready to minister to the saints from the previous year, and that your zeal—that is, your imitation—has stirred up very many to do the same. [Col. 0258D]

We should observe with what subtlety Paul first, by the example of the Macedonians, induces the Corinthians, and now, conversely, induces the Macedonians by the example of the Corinthians.

And although your will is prompt, we nevertheless sent these brothers to you so that what we glory about you before others might not be emptied—that is, destroyed—in this matter, namely, in your prepared administration.

We sent them, I say, so that, as I said in another Epistle, you may be ready, lest, when the Macedonians come with me to you and find you unprepared, we should be ashamed in this substance, that is, in the unprepared alms.

I say that we should be ashamed, not to say that you should be ashamed. For if you are unprepared, you will rightly be ashamed. He calls the alms “substance” because through them we subsist in the present life. [Col. 0259A]

And because I did not want you to be unprepared, I considered it necessary to ask these brothers to go ahead of me to you and prepare the blessing of the alms—not to prepare it when I come, but to have it already prepared. I call this blessing one promised by you; see to it that you are not unfaithful to your promise.

I say that they should prepare a blessing, as a blessing—that is, a generous gift—and not as avarice. For if they give little, it will be judged more an act of avarice than a gift.

I want them to prepare it, and I also say the same thing in my own voice. I exhort you to give abundantly, because he who sows sparingly—that is, he who gives alms avariciously—will indeed reap, that is, be rewarded, but sparingly. [Col. 0259B]

He calls giving alms “sowing,” because, just as the one who sows loses for the present what he will receive multiplied in the future, so the one who gives alms loses for the present what he will gather a hundredfold in glory.

He who sows sparingly will reap sparingly; and he who sows in blessings—that is, in abundant giving—will certainly reap from blessings, that is, abundant rewards.

And although I urge you to give so abundantly, let each one give as he has determined, that is, as he has placed it in his heart, according to the judgment of his own will. Let him not give from sadness, so that he grieves at giving, or from compulsion, so that he gives with a forced will. He might be compelled to will it and yet do so without sadness. But, I say, let him give not from compulsion, but from cheerfulness.

For God loves a cheerful giver, who gives a cheerful gift cheerfully.

He adds reasons why one should give cheerfully, because, in addition to temporal goods and virtues in the present, heavenly glory in the future will abound according to the merit of almsgiving. He says: “Give cheerfully, because God is able to make every grace abound in you”—that is, an abundance of temporal things, virtues, and future glory—“so that, always having every sufficiency, you may abound in everything,” that is, in each of these graces. [Col. 0259C]

Having, I say, every sufficiency and possessing the desire for all these graces, you may abound in every good work, so that you may give alms abundantly and cheerfully, both for clothing and for food, without any complaint.

I say that you should abound in this good work, as it is written in the Psalm about the righteous giver of alms (Psalm 111:9): “He has scattered”—that is, he has distributed his goods not to one person but to many, and not with the intention of receiving anything in return—“he has given,” not to those who were not in need, but to the poor. Therefore his righteousness—that is, the merit of his righteousness—remains forever. [Col. 0259D]

Someone might object: “I would rather reserve something for the future than distribute it now and later suffer want.” In answer to this, Paul explains further what he meant above by “every grace,” saying: You ought certainly to abound in every good work, because he who supplies seed to the sower—that is, temporal goods to the giver of alms—will also provide bread for the following year, not for excess but for eating. He will also multiply your seed, so that you may have abundant means for repeating your almsgiving. Here is grace in temporal matters. He will also increase the harvest of your righteousness, that is, the merit of the righteousness possessed by you without any distribution of alms. He will increase, I say, the growth of the harvest of your righteousness, causing the merit of private righteousness to grow through the merit of almsgiving. He will increase it so that, enriched in all things—both in the multiplication of seed and in the increase of righteousness—you may abound in merit for every simplicity, that is, for perfect and straightforward expenditure.

Now he again adds several benefits that arise from almsgiving, saying: This simplicity produces through us thanksgiving to God, because we give thanks to God for your administration. Here is one benefit. And rightly do we give thanks, because the ministry of this service—that is, the administration of your simplicity—not only supplies what is lacking to the saints, but also abounds in the Lord, that is, in the Lord’s glory, through thanksgiving offered by many. It also abounds through the testing of this ministry, because everyone approves and magnifies such administration.

By many, I say, glorifying God in the obedience of your confession—that is, in the fact that you made confession of faith in the Gospel of Christ in which you believe—and in obedience, because, possessing faith, you confess and immediately obeyed Christ. They also glorify God in the simplicity of your sharing, that is, in the fact that you straightforwardly make your own possessions common. I mean sharing made with those saints and with all. They also glorify him in the supplication of those whom you serve. I mean supplication made on your behalf: of those, I say, who desire to see you—not because you give them temporal goods, but because of the grace of God which they know to be eminent in you.

And because so many benefits result from this administration, I give thanks to God for, that is, concerning, his gift which he bestowed on you, namely, the grace of almsgiving. A gift, I say, that is unspeakable—that is, such that it may be proclaimed to all as an example. Or, “an inexpressible gift”: for it is impossible to declare how many benefits arise from this gift.

## CHAPTER X

“But I myself, Paul, entreat you by the gentleness and moderation of Christ—I who, when present, am humble among you, but when absent am confident toward you. I ask that, when present, I may not need to be bold with that confidence with which I am thought to act boldly against some who reckon that we walk according to the flesh. For although we walk in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh. For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but powerful through God for the destruction of strongholds, destroying arguments and every height that raises itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing every understanding into captivity to the obedience of Christ, and being ready to avenge every disobedience when your obedience has been fulfilled.

“Look at what is according to outward appearance. If anyone is confident that he belongs to Christ, let him consider this again within himself: that just as he belongs to Christ, so do we. For even if I should boast somewhat more about our authority, which the Lord gave us for your edification and not for your destruction, I shall not be ashamed. But I do not wish to seem as though I were terrifying you by letters, since, as they say, ‘His letters are weighty and forceful, but his bodily presence is weak and his speech contemptible.’ Let such a person consider this: that what we are in speech through letters when absent, we shall also be when present in deed.

“For we do not dare to insert ourselves among, or compare ourselves with, certain people who commend themselves; but we measure ourselves by ourselves and compare ourselves with ourselves. We, however, will not boast without measure, but according to the measure of the rule which God measured out to us (Eph. IV, 7)—the measure extending as far as you. For we do not stretch ourselves beyond measure as though we had not reached you. For we have reached you in the Gospel of Christ, not boasting without measure in the labors of others, but having hope, as your faith grows, of being magnified among you according to our rule, and of evangelizing in abundance in the regions beyond you, not boasting in another’s rule concerning things already prepared.

“‘But he who boasts, let him boast in the Lord’ (1 Cor. I, 31; Jer. IX, 23). For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom God commends.”

## EXPOSITION

After sufficiently admonishing those who had been corrected by his manifold commendation of the grace of almsgiving, he proceeds to rebuke those who had not been corrected and who still preferred the false apostles to him. Here he greatly depresses those false apostles, commending his own authority in many appropriate ways. He does not do this to seek his own glory, but intends only that, once the false apostles have been discredited, the Corinthians should no longer cling to them and should rejoice thereafter in clinging to him, who has been so gloriously commended.

The wording is joined as follows: “I exhort you who have been rightly corrected concerning the grace of almsgiving. But I do not give this admonition to you who have not been corrected, whom I know to be unworthy of the grace of God. Rather, I entreat”—that is, I adjure you by every sacred obligation—“I myself, Paul.”

Notice that he says “I myself.” For the Corinthians were saying that, as long as Paul had been present, he had spoken to them quite humbly and had said nothing that harmed anyone, perhaps because he was afraid; but now, while absent, he was threatening them imperiously, as though he possessed imperial authority over them. Therefore he says: “I myself, Paul, now acting imperiously, who formerly acted humbly, entreat you by the gentleness and moderation of Christ.”

He says “gentleness” because Christ freely forgave everything without judgment. He says “moderation” because, when he acted in judgment, he judged moderately, seasoning justice with mercy. “By the gentleness and moderation of Christ I, Paul, entreat you—I who was considered humble and patient in all things among you.” That humility, according to your opinion, was only outward and not in the heart: “I was pretending outward humility while inwardly nurturing pride.”

While I was present, according to you I was humble; but now, being absent, I am confident—that is, I act confidently and imperiously toward you—as though I would not dare to act in this way toward other churches. I do not merely entreat as one making a request, but I ask as though demanding something owed: “that I may not need to be bold when present,” that is, that you should correct yourselves so that, when I am present, I may not dare—that is, according to your opinion, presume boldly—to act against you.

I say “against certain people” who are still uncorrected and who think that we walk according to the flesh. Paul would walk according to the flesh if, either because he loved temporal goods which he received from them, he spared them, or if, conscious of wrongdoing, he feared suffering for Christ.

I rightly said “as though.” For we truly do not wage war according to the flesh. He calls his preaching warfare. Someone might say: “You possess some special gift of God, by which you can so transcend the flesh; but because we do not possess that gift, we must follow the flesh.” In answer he says: “We do not wage war according to the flesh.” We certainly walk in the flesh, for we suffer the burden of the flesh just as you do; yet we overcome it.

We truly do not wage war according to the flesh. For the weapons of our warfare—that is, of our preaching and of our entire life—are not carnal. He calls the weapons of warfare the miracles by which he confirmed his preaching. He also calls virtues and every good work weapons.

“The weapons of our warfare are not carnal.” For if we followed the flesh, those weapons would immediately abandon us. But our weapons are powerful through God—that is, through God or for God’s glory. They are powerful for the destruction of strongholds, so that by these weapons we may easily destroy any very strongly fortified heresies or philosophical arguments.

Our weapons truly have the power to destroy. Indeed, we are also engaged in the act of destroying: wherever there is an act, power cannot be absent. Nevertheless, the wording is joined there as follows: “We do not wage war according to the flesh; we,” I say, “destroying arguments,” that is, carefully devised reasonings.

We also destroy every height of physical science that raises itself against the knowledge of God, such as those who, by the law of nature, argue that a virgin could not give birth or that a dead man could rise again. And we do not merely destroy; we also bring every understanding of every kind of unbelief into captivity, because, after overcoming unbelievers, we remove the devil’s yoke from them and make them captives under Christ’s yoke.

We bring them into captivity by leading them into the obedience of Christ, so that those who previously served the devil wickedly may henceforth serve Christ well. When he says “every understanding” and “every height,” he does not mean that he converted every individual unbeliever, but that from every kind of unbelief he drew some people to the faith.

We bring them into the obedience of Christ. But if some are unwilling to be brought into it, we are ready to avenge every disobedience—that is, by apostolic authority to condemn every disobedient person. He has this ready because neither a bad conscience holds him back nor temporal advantage seduces him.

Someone might say: “Since you are ready to avenge, why do you not avenge?” I shall indeed avenge, but not now; rather, when your obedience has been fulfilled—that is, when, through patient waiting, I have separated from among you the wicked those who are going to obey the faith willingly.

Paul’s subtle moderation must be carefully observed. He postpones the vengeance upon the reprobate, seeing in this waiting of his the salvation of the elect. For if he tolerated the reprobate without vengeance and thereby became liable to condemnation, nevertheless by patiently bearing with them he judges them kindly, lest, while uprooting the darnel, he uproot the wheat with it.

Because we do not wage war according to the flesh, I have proved this by the fact that we destroy the height of worldly science and take rebels captive into the obedience of Christ. These arguments are not so evident to individuals; but now look at them and recognize the same thing: namely, that we do not walk according to the flesh.

Look, I say, at the things that are according to outward appearance—that is, things according to bodily perception and visible without any obstacle. Or understand it this way: “Look now at those who are according to outward appearance,” that is, those who pretend to be good outwardly but inwardly are wolves.
