If any false apostle is confident, not in God but in himself—for he is presumptuous, not elect—if anyone, I say, is confident that he belongs to Christ, that is, that he himself is an apostle of Christ, let him consider not only this but again, likewise, within himself, examining it carefully: that just as he belongs to Christ, so do we.

Indeed, just as he belongs to Christ, so do we. In fact, we are more so than he. He expresses this as follows: If I should boast somewhat more about our authority—the authority by which I can separate the uncorrected from the Church and exercise the other powers of an apostle—which authority the Lord gave me but did not give to your false apostles, he gave it to me for your edification, that is, so that I might build you up in faith and virtues; he did not give it for your destruction, as some wrongly suppose, namely, that I am a destroyer of the Church. If, I say, I should boast somewhat more, I shall not be ashamed of it, because my glory is truly greater.

Someone might object: “Since you ought to build up and not destroy, do not force us impatiently, lest you destroy rather than build.” To this Paul replies: “Although you object that, while I ought to build up, I destroy, nevertheless know that what we are when absent through letters, we shall be when present in deed. And this is so that I may not be thought to be terrifying you while absent through letters.”

He rightly says “as though terrifying.” For if, while absent, he threatened something which, when present, he feared to fulfill, this would not truly be terrifying but only appear to be terrifying. “I am thought to be so,” I say, “because they themselves say: Paul’s letters are weighty”—that is, burdensome and full of severity—“and forceful,” that is, threatening strength and a certain command; “but his bodily presence is weak.”

Against this statement that they are forceful, they add that his speech when present was contemptible, that is, very humble and unpolished, whereas now it is weighty. Therefore, so that I may not be thought to be terrifying you, let the person who is such—that is, who calls me contemptible and weak—consider this: what we are when absent in the word sent through letters, we shall also be when present, not only in word but in deed. For what we threaten by letter, we shall exercise in word and action when present.

We truly shall be when present in deed what we are when absent in word. For we are not like your false apostles, who insert themselves shamelessly—that is, thrust themselves forward—not sent by God. Nor do we dare to insert ourselves, usurping illicitly what has not been entrusted to us.

Or, “We do not dare, being inserted by God, to compare ourselves with certain people,” namely, false apostles who, not commended by God, commend themselves, carrying commendatory letters back and forth. We do not dare to compare ourselves with them in such a way that we neglect the measure of our office as though it were incomplete.

Some, having been regularly inserted through election, afterward by acting perversely compare themselves with the perverse. We did not dare to insert ourselves; rather, we measure ourselves within ourselves, so that we may not exceed the measure entrusted to us by God by usurping what belongs to another, as those do who insert themselves.

We also compare ourselves with ourselves, leaving nothing of the duty entrusted to us unfulfilled. We compare ourselves with ourselves, not remaining within the proposed boundary. And although we measure and compare ourselves with ourselves, nevertheless we shall not boast without measure.

Or the construction may be extended this far without supplying “we are thus”: “Measuring ourselves and comparing ourselves with ourselves, we shall not boast.” We, who could rightly boast, shall not boast without measure, but according to the measure of the rule by which I have properly regulated myself and my subjects.

Then perhaps someone would say: “You have appropriated this measure to yourself.” Against this Paul replies: “The measure which God measured out to us.” The other might again say: “But not as far as us.” “I mean a measure extending as far as you.” And indeed we have reached as far as you.

For we do not stretch ourselves beyond measure as though we had not reached you according to the measure measured out to us by God. We truly do not stretch ourselves beyond measure. For in the Gospel of Christ, by preaching, we have reached as far as you according to God’s measure.

Someone might again object: “You have entered into another’s labor.” To this he replies: “We have reached you without boasting in the labors of others.” That is, I have not built upon another’s foundation. “Without boasting,” I say—and the negative is not to be doubled by extending it to “without measure.” We truly have reached as far as you.

For also beyond you—we may understand him as saying: “Not boasting without measure, but having hope of your faith growing,” that is, of being magnified among you through your growing faith. For when the fruit of your faith has been seen, it will be said: “Great is the teacher and founder of this faith.”

“I hope to be magnified among you according to our rule,” that is, according to the fact that we have regulated your life with complete equity. We also have hope of evangelizing in those regions which lie beyond you, and this in abundance. For I shall evangelize in many places.

Or “to evangelize in abundance” may mean in abundance of signs and speech. We do not hope to boast according to another’s rule—that is, according to another’s governance—in places that have already been prepared, that is, evangelized by other apostles. I do not wish to boast according to another’s rule.

Likewise, whoever boasts should see to it that he boasts in the Lord, who measures out his portion to him; he should not rashly claim for himself what God has measured out to another. Everyone who boasts ought to boast according to the Lord’s measure.

For it is not the one who commends himself—that is, the one who thrusts himself without God into another’s governance, like the false apostles—who is approved by God, but the one whom God commends and to whom he distributes his own measure.

## CHAPTER XI

“Would that you could bear with a little of my foolishness; but indeed, bear with me. For I am jealous over you with the jealousy of God. For I betrothed you to one man, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ. But I fear that, just as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning (Gen. III, 4), so your minds may be corrupted and fall away from the simplicity that is in Christ Jesus.

“For if the one who comes preaches another Christ whom we did not preach, or you receive another spirit which you did not receive, or another Gospel which you did not accept, you would rightly bear with him. For I think that I have done nothing less than the chief apostles. For even if I am unskilled in speech, yet not in knowledge; but in every respect I have been made manifest to you.

“Or did I commit a sin by humbling myself so that you might be exalted? Because I preached the Gospel of God to you without charge. I robbed other churches, receiving support for your service; and when I was with you and in need, I was burdensome to no one. For the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied what was lacking to me; and in everything I kept myself, and shall keep myself, from being burdensome to you.

“The truth of Christ is in me, because this boast of mine will not be silenced in me in the regions of Achaia. Why? Because I do not love you? God knows. But what I do, and what I shall do, I do in order to cut off the opportunity of those who seek an opportunity, so that in the matter in which they boast they may be found to be like us.

“For such men are false apostles, deceitful workers, disguising themselves as apostles of Christ. And no wonder. For Satan himself disguises himself as an angel of light. Therefore it is no great thing if his ministers also disguise themselves as ministers of righteousness; their end will be according to their works.

“Again I say: let no one think that I am foolish. Otherwise, receive me as foolish, so that I too may boast a little. What I am saying, I am not saying according to the Lord, but as though in foolishness, in this substance of boasting. Since many boast according to the flesh, I too will boast.

“For you gladly bear with fools, since you yourselves are wise. For you bear it if someone enslaves you, if someone devours you, if someone takes from you, if someone exalts himself, if someone strikes you in the face. I speak according to dishonor, as though we had been weak in this respect.

“In whatever anyone dares—in foolishness I speak—I also dare. Are they Hebrews? So am I. Are they Israelites? So am I. Are they the seed of Abraham? So am I. Are they ministers of Christ? I speak as one less wise: I am more.

“In many labors, more abundantly in prisons, beyond measure in blows, frequently in deaths. From the Jews five times I received forty lashes less one. Three times I was beaten with rods. Once I was stoned. Three times I suffered shipwreck. I was in the depths of the sea a night and a day, often on journeys, in dangers from rivers, in dangers from robbers, in dangers from my own people, in dangers from the Gentiles, in dangers in the city, in dangers in the wilderness, in dangers at sea, in dangers among false brothers; in labor and hardship, in many vigils, in hunger and thirst, in many fasts, in cold and nakedness.

“Besides those things that are external, there is my daily anxiety, the concern for all the churches. Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not on fire? If I must boast, I will boast of the things that concern my weakness.

“The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed forever, knows that I do not lie. In Damascus, the governor under King Aretas guarded the city of the Damascenes in order to seize me (Acts IX, 24); and through a window I was let down in a basket through the wall, and so I escaped his hands.”

## EXPOSITION

“I say that whoever boasts should boast in the Lord; and would that you could bear a little of my foolishness”—that is, patiently endure a little of my boasting, which among the reprobate is called foolishness. I would indeed admit that it was truly foolishness if by it I were seeking my own glory; but by commending myself I intend only to draw you back from the error of the false teachers.

Why, then, is it called foolishness, although it is not foolishness? I speak as one making a request: “Would that you could bear with me.” But not only this: I also command, “Bear with me,” not resisting my authority, as children bear with a father and disciples with a teacher.

You ought indeed to bear with me, for I am jealous over you—that is, I love you with fervent movement of spirit. And this jealousy, that is, this love, is not for myself, as though I wished you to be credited to me, but the jealousy of God, because I want you to belong to God alone.

This is drawn from the likeness of one who loves another man’s bride, not for himself but for the bridegroom’s advantage and honor. Thus John, when Christ was thought to be the bridegroom of the Church, loved the Church, that is, the bride, not for himself but for Christ the bridegroom, saying: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom stands and hears him” (John III, 29).

“Jealousy” is the movement of the spirit either toward anger or toward love. I truly am jealous over you with the jealousy of God, for I betrothed you. This betrothal of the Church, beginning with baptism, lasts until the day of the resurrection of all, when the Church will be given in marriage to her bridegroom Christ, who will then receive her in his embraces; from the beginning of faith he pledged her to himself with the ring of the Holy Spirit.

I betrothed you to one man; and if to one, then not to me. And to one man—that is, to a legitimate husband, not like the one of whom it was said: “The one whom you now have is not your husband” (John IV, 18).

I betrothed you to one man, that is, to Christ, so that I might present you to that one man as a virgin, that is, uncorrupted in deed by sin. A chaste virgin, that is, one free from agitation, who does not consent to iniquity even in the will.

I indeed wish to present you to Christ; but I fear that, just as the serpent deceived Eve by its cunning (Gen. III, 4), so your minds, deceived by these false apostles, may be corrupted and, once corrupted, may fall away from the simplicity of faith, which simplicity is in Christ Jesus. For Christ’s faith consists in simplicity, not in the crafty doubleness of unbelief.

He greatly humbles the Corinthians by comparing them to Eve, while comparing their teachers to the poisonous serpent. “I fear that they may be corrupted.” But so that you may not be corrupted by them, you ought not to tolerate them.

For if the one who comes—that is, the false apostle who comes from himself and not from God—or “the one who comes,” that is, the one who sells himself to you—for he advertises his preaching very effectively—if such a person preaches another Christ whom we did not preach to you, or if you receive from him another Spirit whom you did not receive from us, or if you accept from him another Gospel which you did not receive from us, then, if these things were so, you would rightly bear with him.

But because they do not preach another Christ, do not bestow the Holy Spirit whom you received from us, and do not preach another Gospel, they ought not to be tolerated by you. You ought to tolerate me, not them.

For, to say nothing of them, I think that I have done nothing less by which I might be less distinct from the chief apostles—that is, from Peter and from those who appeared to be pillars. The false apostles falsely set themselves above me on the basis of their teaching, although they are not even disciples of those apostles.

Here he cleverly answers those who objected that, because he was not an apostle, he did not receive support from preaching as Peter and the others did. I have done nothing less than they. For even if I have seemed to you unskilled in speech, because I spoke to you simply, nevertheless know that I am not unskilled in knowledge.

But why do I say this? In every respect, both in knowledge and in speech, I have been made manifest to you, so that I am unskilled in nothing. I truly did nothing less than the chief apostles; indeed, I did more than they.

He says this secretly, as though reducing himself under a certain appearance of inferiority, in the following manner: “Or did I commit a sin by humbling myself, depriving myself of what the right of preaching demands, so that you might be exalted through my humiliation? For unless I had humbled myself in this way by accepting nothing, you would have preferred to reject the word of God rather than minister to me.”

“Or did I sin because I preached the Gospel of God to you without charge,” that is, accepting nothing from you?

They might ask: “Where, then, did you live from?” He replies: “I robbed other churches, receiving support from them for your service,” that is, for administering the Gospel to you.

They might again say: “Perhaps you had no need.” And he replies: “When I was with you, although I was certainly in need of everything, I was nevertheless burdensome to none of you.” When he says “burdensome,” he strongly accuses them of avarice.

They might again ask: “How, then, did you supply your need?” Paul answers well: “The brothers who came from Macedonia supplied what was lacking to me; and so, in everything, both clothing and food, I kept myself from being burdensome to you, and in the same way I shall continue to do so.”

And in this—that I shall truly continue to keep myself in this way—the truth of Christ is in me. It is as though he said: “By the truth of Christ I affirm that I shall keep myself in this way.”

“The truth of Christ is in me,” concerning this—that is, because this glory of mine, namely, that I shall keep myself in this way, will not be taken away from me. This glory will not be taken away from me, not only in Corinth but also in the regions of Achaia.

They might again say: “You act this way because you are hostile to us.” Paul replies: “It certainly will not be taken away. But why? Will you say that I do this because I do not love you? God knows that I love you.

“But what I do and shall do—namely, accepting nothing—I do in order to cut off the opportunity of those false apostles who wish to obtain from me an opportunity for receiving. For if I were to receive, then they would as well.

“I say that I cut off this opportunity so that they may be found to be like us, receiving nothing, although they boast greatly that they do something like us in this respect, even while they persecute us.

“Or understand it this way: I cut off the opportunity of the false apostles who want an opportunity for receiving in the very thing in which they boast, namely, in receiving. For they seek no other glory than that some people may be found to imitate us in this, receiving nothing.”

Paul’s subtlety must be observed. If Paul received, they too would immediately receive. Once they lived from the Corinthians’ goods, they would appear to possess authority to preach to them. If they preached with such authority, they would undoubtedly corrupt their faith. In this way Paul’s example would become nourishment for the corruption of the Corinthians.

Someone might say: “You say that they may be found to be like us. Can the false apostles be found like us?” Paul answers: “Certainly. For such men are deceitful workers, because they disguise themselves as apostles of Christ, receiving if those apostles receive, abstaining if they abstain, and imitating them in other matters as well.”

It is no wonder if they disguise themselves as apostles of Christ, because Satan himself, their head, often disguises himself as an angel of light. And because Satan passes himself off as an angel of light, it is no great or astonishing thing if Satan’s ministers—that is, the false apostles—disguise themselves as ministers of righteousness. The end of both Satan’s ministers and the ministers of righteousness will be according to their works.

Above he boasted of his apostleship, entrusted to him by God. He also boasted that he had labored more than all the others, preaching the Gospel of God without charge, and of other matters in which he could rightly boast.

Now, however, he proceeds to recount certain things concerning the glory of his ancestry according to the flesh. Yet, as he clearly indicates, he considers this no glory at all. Nevertheless, it was necessary for him to boast of his carnal ancestry.

For when the false apostles exalted themselves in such matters, unless Paul possessed the same things, they would boast that the privilege lacking to Paul belonged to them, and thus they would more easily subvert the faith of the foolish Corinthians. Paul therefore shows that these things are present in himself and contribute nothing to him, while he censures those who boast of a matter in which there is no fruit.

The wording is joined as follows: “Earlier I said, ‘Would that you could bear with my foolishness.’ Now I speak again about the same thing, so that no one may think me foolish because of the boasting already mentioned.”

Otherwise—that is, if you accuse me of foolishness because of the previous boasting—receive me now as foolish, while I boast of carnal descent, which is far inferior to the glory mentioned earlier.

He says “as foolish,” for he is not truly to be judged foolish: by boasting of carnal descent he does not seek his own glory in it, but only the building up of the Corinthians. This is clear from the fact that he himself rejects the glory of the flesh.

Receive me as foolish, so that, like the false apostles, I too may boast—that is, recount the glory of the flesh. This kind of boasting is a small matter and is not to be dwelt upon as true glory.

I rightly call myself foolish, because what I say about the glory of the flesh I do not say according to God, before whom humility is commended and the glory of the flesh is brought low. But I speak as though in foolishness.

He says “as though,” because he is not truly foolish, since he does not believe the glory of the flesh to be real. I speak in foolishness by dwelling on this—that is, on carnal glory—as though it were the substance in which we ought to stand and plant our feet. This is ironic, because he understands that no one should stand in the glory of the flesh.

Someone might ask: “Since the glory of the flesh is not according to God, why do you dwell upon it?” For this reason: because many—that is, the false apostles—boast according to the flesh, I too will boast, that is, I will recount a few things about the same glory.

I will boast both because many boast in this way and because you tolerate them—that is, bear their heavy burden. You tolerate, I say, fools, namely, those false apostles who boast in foolishness. You tolerate them willingly—that is, compelled by no one, because this is what you wish—even though you yourselves are wise. This is ironic: although you claim wisdom for yourselves, your tolerance of their foolishness does not agree with it.

He explains in what ways they tolerate them, saying: You certainly tolerate them, for you bear it if one of those false apostles brings you into slavery—that is, forces you to serve him as slaves. You also tolerate it if one of them devours your goods. For those false apostles consumed their possessions greedily.

You also tolerate it if one of them takes you—that is, captures you for himself by deceit, meaning that he deceives you. You tolerate it if one of them exalts himself, saying that he is descended from Abraham while you are dogs. These two things—deceiving and exalting himself—were useful for devouring their possessions and reducing them to slavery.

You tolerate it if one of them exalts himself and, by exalting himself, strikes you—that is, reproaches you for being uncircumcised and for similar things. He strikes you not secretly but in the face, presuming to reproach you before your eyes.

He strikes you, I say, according to the baseness of your ancestry, which he reproaches you with. You tolerate such men; but we do not, as though we were weak in this respect—that is, unable to boast according to the flesh.

But we are not weak in this matter, because in whatever any one of them dares to boast, I too dare in the same way. When he says “dares” and “I dare,” he indicates that this is presumption rather than true glory.

And when I say “I dare,” I say it in foolishness, since wisdom advises one neither to prefer himself to another nor to depress another. Truly, in whatever anyone dares, I also dare.

For if they are Hebrews—that is, eloquent in the Hebrew language—I am so as well. Hebrews are said to derive their name from Heber, meaning prudence, because this language was reserved for him.

If they again boast that they are Israelites, I likewise am an Israelite. People could be Hebrews and Israelites and yet not be of Abraham, as proselytes, because they passed from Gentile status into circumcision. Therefore he added: If they are the seed of Abraham according to the flesh, I likewise am.

After matching himself with them in the glory of ancestry, he moves on to the glory of ministry. The false apostles would not have found it sufficient to boast of ancient descent unless they also boasted of being disciples of Christ. Therefore he says:

If they boast that they are ministers of Christ, preaching Christ, I likewise administer Christ. I say “I also”; indeed, I am more a minister of Christ than they. And I say this as one less wise, since I place myself above them and humble them.

What he means by “I am more” he explains in parts: I have been shown to be more a minister of Christ in many labors, which I endured more frequently than they, both by working with my hands and by enduring immense dangers.

I have also been shown more to be a minister of Christ in prisons than they, who sometimes allowed themselves to be imprisoned so that they might appear to be apostles of Christ.

I have also been shown to be a minister of Christ in blows endured beyond human strength. And I have frequently been shown to be a minister of Christ in deaths—that is, in punishments sufficient to inflict death on anyone, and sufficient to kill me according to human nature, except that the Holy Spirit preserved me.

He enumerates the blows, saying: “In blows”—rightly do I say this—for from the Jews I received forty, that is, forty strokes less one (Deut. XXV, 3). Nor did this happen once, but five times, that is, on five occasions.

The Jewish custom was as follows: if someone acted against the synagogue, he was to be punished with forty blows, provided that they dealt with him without mercy; but if they were merciful, they could remit as many of the forty blows as they wished. Now, because they could not make Paul desist from preaching the word, according to their custom they led him into the synagogue; and, so that they would not be judged utterly merciless, with cruel cunning they still spared one blow from the punishment. Three times also I was beaten with rods by the Gentiles in Macedonia (Acts 16:22). Once I was stoned by the Ephesians (Acts 14:18), when I freed a girl from a Pythonic spirit (ibid., 9). Three times also I suffered shipwreck—that is, three times I was shipwrecked at sea. I was in the depths of the sea both night and day. It is not recorded whether, like Jonah, he was thrown into the sea and there preserved by God, or whether he endured continuous shipwreck in the depths—that is, in the middle of the deep sea—through both day and night. He suffered these shipwrecks while crossing by ship to preach.

He was also shown to be more a minister of Christ in his frequent journeys: in dangers—that is, through the dangers of rivers, whose force I endured; and through the dangers of robbers, who beat and robbed me; and through dangers from my own people—that is, those I suffered from the Jews; and through dangers from the Gentiles—that is, those I suffered from the Gentiles. And through dangers often inflicted on me in the city; through dangers endured from robbers or wild beasts in the wilderness, while I crossed wooded places for the sake of preaching; through further dangers, often endured at sea, hitherto passed over; through dangers also which I often suffered from false brothers. Through all these things mentioned above I was shown to be more a minister of Christ than they.

I was also shown to be a minister of Christ in labor and hardship—that is, in labor attended by hardship—when I suffered fevers or other illnesses, yet was still obliged to work. In labor, I say, also in many vigils, because, after preaching all day, I worked at night to earn my living. Or he was often watchful in prayer. I was also shown to be a minister of Christ in hunger and thirst, and in many fasts, endured sometimes voluntarily and sometimes from necessity.

I was also shown to be a minister of Christ in cold and nakedness, because, if cold forced me to suffer, it was nakedness that aggravated the cold. These matters of which I have just gloried I endured in the body. But besides those things endured externally—that is, in the body—there is something that afflicts me inwardly, namely, daily concern for all the churches: that is, every day I am anxious about the condition of the whole Church. This concern is my pressing burden; it presses upon me continually, pricks me, and gravely torments me. “Pressing burden” is more than “concern.” For “pressing burden” denotes an affliction of body and soul; “concern” belongs to the soul alone.

I am truly concerned for everyone: when one of the brothers is weak, falling into sin or even suffering from bodily illness, and I am not immediately made weak—that is, I do not judge his weakness to be my own by suffering with him. And when one of the brothers is scandalized either by food or by something else, am I not immediately set aflame—that is, am I not burned by anguish of soul on account of the scandalized brother?

I have gloried above in the things that belong to my weakness, and I will still glory in the same things, if I must glory—as indeed it is necessary, so that the false apostles may be humbled and the Church built up. And in these things in which I have gloried and will glory, God knows that I lie in none of them—God who is the God and Father of my Lord Jesus Christ, and who through Jesus Christ is intimate with me; he is God, blessed forever, through Christ Jesus and through my preaching.

Concerning this, I say, I do not lie: at Damascus—that is, near Damascus—the governor of that people, I mean the governor under King Aretas, who ruled there, hired through the entreaty and payment of the Jews, guarded the city of the Damascenes in order to seize me. For Paul, having been baptized by Ananias and having remained for some time at Damascus, was declaring in the synagogue that “this is the Christ” (Acts 9:22–24), and so forth. Moved by this zeal, the Jews conferred with the governor of the city so that Paul, who was considered guilty, might be arrested. The governor wanted to seize me, but I was lowered through a window in a basket by the brothers over the wall—for the house in which he was staying adjoined the wall—and so I escaped the hands of that governor (Acts 9:25). He did not escape because he was afraid to suffer for the name of Christ, but so that what the divine voice had said about him might be fulfilled:

> “This man is an instrument chosen for me, to carry my name before kings and the children of Israel” (Acts 9:15).

“For I will show him how much he must suffer for my name.”

## CHAPTER XII

> “If it is necessary to glory”—although it is not expedient—I will come to visions and revelations of the Lord. I know a man in Christ fourteen years ago—whether in the body or outside the body, I do not know; God knows—caught up to the third heaven. And I know that such a man—whether in the body or outside the body, I do not know; God knows—was caught up into paradise and heard secret words that it is not permitted for a human being to speak. Of such a man I will glory; but of myself, nothing except in my weaknesses. For even if I should wish to glory, I will not be foolish, since I will speak the truth. But I refrain, lest anyone should think of me above what he sees in me or hears from me. And lest the greatness of the revelations should exalt me, a thorn in my flesh was given to me, an angel of Satan, to buffet me. For this I besought the Lord three times that it might depart from me, and he said to me: ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for power is perfected in weakness.’ Therefore I will gladly glory in my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may dwell in me. For this reason I am pleased with myself in weaknesses, in insults, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses for Christ. For when I am weak, then I am strong.

> I have become foolish; you compelled me. For I ought to have been commended by you. For I did nothing less than those who are excessively apostles, although I am nothing. Yet the signs of my apostleship were performed among you in all endurance, in signs and wonders and mighty works. For what is it in which you were treated less favorably than the other churches, except that I myself did not burden you? Forgive me this wrong. Behold, this is the third time I am ready to come to you, and I will not burden you. For I do not seek what is yours, but you. For children ought not to store up treasures for their parents, but parents for their children. But I will most gladly spend and be spent myself for your souls, even though, loving you more, I am loved less.

> But be it so. I did not burden you, but, being crafty, I caught you by deceit. Did I take advantage of you through any of those whom I sent to you? I appealed to Titus and sent a brother with him. Did Titus take advantage of you? Did we not walk in the same spirit? Did we not follow the same footsteps? Do you think that all this time we have been excusing ourselves to you? We speak before God in Christ. And everything, beloved, is for your edification.

> For I fear that, when I come, I may not find you as I wish, and that I may be found by you as you do not wish; that perhaps there may be among you quarrels, jealousies, hostilities, dissensions, slanders, whisperings, conceits, and disorders; that, when I come again, God may humble me among you, and I may mourn over many of those who sinned previously and did not repent of the uncleanness, fornication, and shamelessness that they committed.”

## EXPOSITION

Above I gloried in my weaknesses. If it is necessary to glory again—as it is certainly opportune on account of the false apostles [interpolation]—if it is necessary, it is not expedient: that is, this glory makes me expedient for nothing. If, I say, it is necessary, I will come to visions, and so forth. Or the sentence may be joined in this way: Although it is not expedient for me, I will nevertheless come to visions and revelations of the Lord, and in them I will glory.

He says “visions and revelations” because what he saw was revealed to his understanding. Some, however, had visions—such as Pharaoh and Nebuchadnezzar—without having the revelations of those visions. Now, speaking of himself in the third person, he recounts the visions, saying: “I know a man”—namely, myself—“placed in Christ, caught up,” and so forth. This happened fourteen years ago, now completed. He would not yet have disclosed what he had kept silent for so many years unless contempt for his ministry had pressed him vehemently.

“Caught up, whether in the body I do not know, or outside the body I do not know; God knows.” If Paul was caught up in the body for this vision, the body was not moved spatially; but the soul, which is weighed down in the flesh and imprisoned by the mass of the flesh, so that it perceives nothing unless first awakened by some bodily sensation, was so liberated at the time of the revelation that it perceived nothing of the fleshly mass. The body itself, moreover, is believed to have been so regulated that its own weight did not disturb the soul’s agility.

But if the soul was outside the body, then, freed from the weight of the flesh, it could be led wherever God willed. Whether it was led elsewhere or remained in the same place makes no difference, because, once by God’s will it no longer perceived the weight of the flesh, it could see him whom in the future it will see as he is.

“I know such a man caught up to the third heaven,” that is, to the vision of the third order. A vision is called “heaven” because it is concealed from many and disclosed to few.

The first heaven, that is, the first vision, is called the vision by which God shows certain hidden things bodily—for example, to Gideon in the dry fleece and the wet threshing floor (Judges 6:38), and to the Maccabees, who saw fiery armies in the air, prefiguring war (2 Maccabees 5:2).

The second heaven, that is, the second vision, is when something is shown not through a bodily object but through an image. Thus images of every kind of reptile were shown to blessed Peter when he was told, “Kill and eat” (Acts 10:11); the things represented by those images were not present there.

The third heaven, that is, the third vision, is distinct from the two mentioned above. It is when something is shown neither through the object itself nor through an image of the object, but is disclosed in simple truth according to the object’s own nature. In this third manner the mysteries of God were made manifest to Paul—not through an object and not through an image.

Or alternatively: just as Dionysius the Areopagite reduces the nine orders of angels into three, calling angels, archangels, and virtues the first order; principalities, powers, and dominions the second; and thrones, cherubim, and seraphim the third, so perfectly did Paul see and know the mysteries of God as this third order contemplates God.

Or alternatively: let us call the first heaven the bodily creatures of heaven—the sun, moon, and so forth; the second heaven, incorporeal beings such as angels; and the third heaven, the divine essence, to the knowledge of which Paul was caught up.

“I also know such a man, whether in the body or outside the body I do not know; God knows.” This I know: that is, I know that he was caught up into paradise, meaning into such a delightful rest of mind that he perceived nothing of the fleshly mass. For paradise is called a garden of delights.

And this man, so caught up, heard secret words that it is not permitted for a human being to speak—that is, words which, insofar as he is human, no one is capable of understanding. Blessed Augustine says that these secrets were that he saw how the Trinity is in Unity and Unity is in the Trinity.

And of such a man, who was so caught up and deemed worthy to hear, I will glory; but of myself—that is, according to my powers—I will never glory in anything except my weaknesses. Therefore I say, “I will glory.” For even if I should wish to glory, whether in those revelations or in my weaknesses, I will not be foolish, because I will speak the truth in everything.

But even this is not yet enough to make it permissible to glory in every truth. It must be added that I will speak the truth and, through this, advance the edification of the Church. He states the same thing below: “Although I could thus glory, I refrain”—that is, I speak sparingly concerning glory—“lest anyone should think of me above what he sees in me.”

For he sees me as a human being oppressed by miseries; but because, on the other hand, he sees miracles performed through me, he may think of me as above the humanity he sees in me, like those who wanted to build altars for him (Acts 14:12). Or he may think of me above what he hears from me, when he hears that I thirst, suffer cold, and am subject to other miseries.

I refrain from glorying, and rightly so, because, lest the greatness of the revelations exalt me into pride, a thorn in my flesh was given to me—namely, an angel, that is, a messenger of Satan, the prince of demons. He sent him so that he might buffet me: if, on account of the greatness of the revelations, I wished to raise my neck, temptation would strike me with a blow. Thus what Satan intends as punishment, God orders for my perfection.

Some say that “the thorn in the flesh” means every kind of temptation; others say that it means only the temptation of lust. For this reason—that is, because Satan buffets me—I asked the Lord three times, “three” being used for an indefinite number, that this angel might depart from me. And the Lord said to me as I prayed: “Because you are tempted in this way, Paul, this is my grace; and this grace is sufficient for you,” that is, it is sufficient for your salvation. For if this grace—namely, the guardianship of humility—were lacking to you, every grace bestowed upon you would be rendered ineffective. This grace, I say, is sufficient.

For every power is perfected in weakness rightly endured. The power that has an opposing weakness with which it lawfully contends, so that it may afterward be crowned, is perfect.

Up to this point these are the Lord’s words. Now Paul speaks: “Because power is perfected in weakness, I will therefore gladly glory from now on in my weaknesses, so that, by the merit of weakness rightly endured, the power of Christ may dwell in me”—the power which must be perfected in weakness.

For this reason—because through this the power of Christ will dwell in me—I am now pleased with myself in my weaknesses: in insults, which I gladly endure in word and deed for Christ; in necessities of food and clothing; in persecutions, by which I am driven from place to place; and in distresses of soul, all endured for Christ.

Therefore I am pleased with myself in weaknesses because, when I am weak in body, then, through the weakness of the flesh, I am spiritually strong.

I have now gloried in many ways, and in commending myself I have become foolish, as has often been said: exalting myself and humbling another. But you compelled me to this foolishness. You compelled me to commend myself. For I ought to have been commended by you, and because you did not do so, I had to do it myself.

Indeed, I ought to have been commended by you because I did nothing less than those who, according to you, are apostles beyond my measure. According to you, they are above me; but although in your judgment I am nothing, the signs of my apostleship were performed among you, by which I am truly proved to be an apostle.

They were performed, I say, in all the endurance I displayed among you; in signs, by healing the lame and giving sight to the blind; in wonders, by raising the dead; and in mighty works, such as cures of fevers and similar illnesses. Or “in mighty works” may mean humility, sobriety, and the other virtues.

Truly I did nothing less than they. For what is it in which you were treated less favorably than the other churches, so that they should be preferred to you, except this: that I myself, though I ought to have done so, did not burden you by accepting anything from you?

“I beg you to forgive me this wrong”: I was wrong because I spared you, whereas no one else spared his own churches in this way. And just as I did not burden you in the past, so in the future I will not burden you, I who am ready to come to you. Behold, this is the third time I have made preparations. I will not burden you because I do not seek what is yours, but you yourselves.

And rightly I do not seek what is yours, because carnal children ought not to store up treasures for carnal parents, but parents for their children. Although spiritual children owe this to spiritual parents, I provide you not only with what a spiritual father owes his children, but also with every tenderness of a carnal father.

I do not seek what is yours, but I will most gladly spend on you spiritual things, and, if I possess any material things that you desire, those as well. Beyond this, I will also spend myself for your souls—that is, I am ready to die so that you may be saved—even though, while loving you more, I am loved less by you according to both spiritual and carnal law.

Although I love you more and am loved less by you, nevertheless, let it be so—that is, let this be conceded. I do not now care to pursue you on account of it.

You will object to me again that, craftily restraining myself from accepting anything from you in person, I intended through my representatives to receive more and more craftily. He says this as follows: “I did not burden you”—as has been proved—by accepting anything from you in my own person; but you will say that, since I was crafty and did not wish to accept anything myself, I caught you by deceit: what I refused through myself, I extorted from you through others.

Or the entire passage may be understood in another way, so that it says only this: “I indeed”—as has been shown—“did not burden you; but be it so,” that is, you will concede what you cannot deny: that I did not burden you in my own person. Nevertheless, you will object that, since I was crafty, I caught you by deceit.

It is said: “I certainly did not deceive you, because, if I had done this, I would have deceived you through one of those whom I sent; but I deceived you through none of them.” He says this as follows: “Did I take advantage of you through any of those whom I sent to you?” Certainly not.

He would have taken advantage of you if he had instructed his disciples to gather for him, by commending him, whatever they could obtain by craft. Truly, I took advantage of you through none of those whom I sent—neither through Titus nor through anyone else.

For he says: “I appealed to Titus to go to you, and with him I sent a brother.” This brother is believed to have been Barnabas, who was both a brother and a fellow worker in preaching. For we read that the apostles gave Paul and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship (Galatians 2:9).

I certainly sent Titus. But did Titus take advantage of you? Certainly not. Did Titus and I not walk in the Lord’s word in the same spirit—that is, with the same will, or filled with the same Holy Spirit? And did we not follow the same footsteps—that is, perform the same works? For just as footsteps are signs of walking, so works are signs of the will. Whatever Titus did, I did also, and nothing else.

When I say that I accepted nothing from you, along with the matters stated above, do you think that, through this commendation—that is, from the time when I began to commend myself—I am in some way excusing us before you, as though we were guilty of something? Do you think that we are not speaking these things according to the truth or for your instruction, but merely to conceal our guilt?

Know, however, that whatever we say, we say before God—that is, as though in God’s presence. If God himself were present, there would be nothing I needed to alter out of fear of falsehood. We speak before God, placed in Christ. We speak these things not only because they are true, but also for your edification, so that, built up by them, you may not be led astray by the false apostles.

O beloved, this is why we speak all these things. Here he rightly supplied the phrase “for your edification,” which was lacking above, where he said, “Although I may glory, I will speak the truth.”

I devote myself so earnestly to your edification because I fear that, when I come, I may find you not as I wish—that is, uncorrected—and that I may then be found by you as you do not wish me to be: punishing your faults through the strictness of justice.

He first explains the statement “that I may not find you as I wish,” and then the statement “that I may be found by you as you do not wish,” saying: “See that I do not find you as I do not wish,” namely, that perhaps there may be among you quarrels—quarrels in which, out of affection for those who baptized them, they argued with one another.

Let there also not be jealousies—that is, envy, by which one envies another—concerning the merit of the one who baptized them. Let there not be hostilities among you, in which one forced another to bring a case before unbelieving judges. Let there not be dissensions, for this was the source of discord and hatred among them.

Let there not be slanders, by which you detract from the good qualities of your neighbor and impose evils that are not present. Let there not be whisperings, that is, secret defamation of one’s neighbors. Let there not be conceits, meaning that the one who is an eye in the Church should not despise the one who is a foot. Let there not, on account of this conceit, be disorders, in which one presumes to injure another with blows.

Take care that these things do not exist among you, lest, when I come again, God may again humble me—that is, afflict me—among you if I find you uncorrected.

When he came the first time, he found them all unbelievers; he was indeed humbled before them and afflicted by various vexations. But now he will be humbled more grievously if he finds those whom he made believers still apostatizing.

“May God humble me, and may I mourn over many.” For even if there are three, they appear many. He says “many” of those who sinned previously, before the Epistle was sent, and who, after being admonished by the Epistle, did not repent of the evils mentioned above.

He says “over”—that is, “of”—uncleanness, since every sin of the flesh may be called uncleanness; but he calls the lust that is against nature “uncleanness” by antonomasia. They did not repent either of fornication or of the shamelessness they practiced—that is, which they possessed in their behavior and habitual conduct.

He calls it fornication when a man has relations with a woman outside the law of marriage. He calls it shamelessness when there is a shameless way of life. For a man who behaves intemperately with his wife is shameless.

## CHAPTER XIII

> “Behold, this is the third time I am coming to you, and ‘every word shall stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses’ (Deuteronomy 19:15). I have already said, and I say beforehand, as though present with you and now absent, to those who sinned previously and to all the others, that if I come again I will not spare. Do you seek proof of Christ who speaks in me? He is not weak among you, but is powerful in you. For although he was crucified through weakness, he lives through the power of God. For we also are weak in him, but we will live with him through the power of God among you.

> Examine yourselves to see whether you are in the faith; test yourselves. Or do you not recognize yourselves, that Jesus Christ is in you? Unless perhaps you are rejected. I hope that you recognize that we are not rejected. But we pray to God that you do nothing evil—not so that we may appear approved, but so that you may do what is good, while we appear to be rejected. For we can do nothing against the truth, but only for the truth.

> For we rejoice when we are weak and you are strong. This also we pray for: your perfection. Therefore I write these things while absent, so that, when present, I may not act harshly according to the authority that the Lord gave me for building up and not for destroying.

> Finally, brothers, rejoice. Be perfected. Encourage one another. Be of the same mind. Keep peace, and the God of peace and love will be with you. Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the saints greet you.

> The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with all of you. Amen.”

## EXPOSITION

He showed what he meant by “not as I wish.” Now he shows what he meant by “that I may be found by you as you do not wish.” The wording is nevertheless joined there: “Lest, when I come,” and so forth.

They might say to him: “Are you really going to come?” Paul replies: “Behold, this is the third time. I do not say that I will come; I am already coming to you in this preparation.”

And when I come, I will not tolerate you, but every word will stand—that is, it will have to stand—whether the word of those who accuse or of those who defend. A word is said to stand when it is proved to be true.

It will stand, I say, “at the mouth of two or three,” not of just any persons, but of witnesses—that is, of those who are competent to give testimony.

They might say: “You threaten that you will come, but when you have come, what will you do?” Paul responds: “I will certainly come and will not spare, because when I was present I foretold to you that I would not spare any longer, and now, absent, I foretell the same through the Epistle, as though present—that is, with as much power as I exercised when I was present among you.”

I foretell this, I say, to those who sinned before the Epistle was first sent and have not yet been corrected, and to all the others who fall into sin. I foretell that—that is, I foretell that if I come again, as I intend, I will not spare again, as I spared you previously when you sinned through ignorance.

They might say again: “Whatever threats he makes now, when he comes he may still be easily appeased.” To this Paul replies: “You do not sufficiently believe that I will not spare. Or do you seek a test of Christ”—that is, do you remain uncorrected so that you may test the power of Christ’s vengeance—“who speaks in me?”

For what I say is not from myself, but from Christ. It is safer for you to correct yourselves than, scorning correction, to experience the Lord’s powerful hand.

This Christ is not weak among you—that is, he did not appear weak to you by failing to work miracles—but is powerful in you: his power has been manifested to you through the miracles that Christ performed through us in your midst.

Christ is truly powerful. For even if you object that, having been condemned on the cross, he appeared powerless, I admit that he was crucified, but through weakness—that is, according to the weakness of mortality and passibility which he assumed in our flesh. Yet although he was crucified in this way, he lives—that is, he acts with power—through the power of God, according to his divinity, whose power did not depart from him and in whom all the fullness of divinity dwelt bodily.

Christ truly lives through the power of God. For we, far inferior to him, will live through the power of God. He says this as follows: “We are indeed weak in him”—that is, in likeness to him, so that just as he suffered for us, we too may suffer for him. Thus we are weak, but we will live—that is, we will act with power—in you through the power, that is, through the power of God, which we have as something familiar in him, namely, in Christ.

But, so that we who live through the power of God may not act more strictly among you, examine yourselves—that is, investigate yourselves with careful consideration. Examine yourselves, I say, to see whether you still remain in the faith that you received through me.

For if they trust in the merits of those who baptized them and restore the old things, they are not in the faith, because they detract from the grace of God.

Examine whether you are in the faith. And, having been found in the faith, test yourselves—that is, having made yourselves approved through good works, adorn your faith.

But if you are not in the faith, you alone are condemned. Nothing is required of me, because you recognize yourselves—or do you not recognize yourselves?—in the fact that Christ Jesus, that is, faith in Christ Jesus, has been placed in you through my ministry, unless perhaps—as can easily happen—you are rejected, that is, rejected by God, because you have shown yourselves unworthy of the sacraments of the faith.

They might say: “It is no wonder that you are rejected, since you yourself are rejected.” To this Paul replies: “Whatever objection you raise, I nevertheless hope that you recognize this about us: that we are in no respect rejected.”

And although we are in no respect rejected, but are found approved in every respect, we do not want you to be evil, like certain superiors who rejoice in the faults of their subjects, so that their own worthiness may appear through the exercise of their authority.

We are not like that. Rather, we pray to God that you do nothing evil; and we do not pray this so that we may appear approved. If a superior punished the fault of a subject by virtue of his authority, he would then appear approved.

This is not what we pray for, but that you may do what is good, while we, finding nothing in you deserving punishment, may be rejected—that is, may appear rejected. A superior is not truly rejected, but appears rejected, when he finds nothing in which to exercise the authority of the judgment entrusted to him.

There are again certain superiors who, although their subjects are good, nevertheless harass them through the command of the authority they have received. Paul responds to these: “For this reason we pray that we may not be rejected while you do what is good, because we cannot do anything against the truth”—that is, where true justice exists, it is not lawful for us to attack it—but we can act for the defense of the truth if someone attacks it either by his actions or by his words.

For this reason we pray that you may do what is good, because we rejoice when we are weak and our authority has no occasion to act, all having been perfected. But you are powerful, possessing a clear conscience, and therefore not fearing our judgment.

We not only rejoice in this, but also pray for it: that you may be powerful—that is, that you may attain the perfection of your justice. And because we rejoice and pray for this, I write these things to you while absent, so that, when I am present, I may not act more harshly according to the authority of my apostleship.

If I were to act by authority, this should not be burdensome to you, since the Lord gave me this authority for your edification and not for your destruction.

After correcting them sufficiently concerning the things they had done, he turns to correct them concerning what remained for the future, saying: In the matters mentioned above, conduct yourselves as I teach; and henceforth—that is, in the future—brothers, rejoice. That is, act in such a way that you may always expect joy from your conduct and may truly rejoice.

“Be perfected,” and, being perfected, encourage the imperfect toward perfection. You, however, who are imperfect, be of the same mind as those who are perfect and encourage you; and keep peace with them—that is, do not misuse their correction, but receive their commands with all moderation.

For if you are of the same mind and keep peace, God will be with you—the God of peace, who rejects those who are divided and chooses those who are united. The same God of love will also be with you, because it is not enough to have peace unless love according to God follows.

And so that the peace and love of God may be with you, greet one another with a kiss: let one kiss another, with all contention among you put to death. With a kiss, I say, not one performed only with the mouth and not with the heart, but with a holy kiss in which no spark of anger lies hidden in the secrecy of the heart.

And you ought to greet one another in this way because all the saints greet you, commending love to you by their example.

Paul’s own greeting follows: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ”—that is, our Lord Jesus Christ giving grace, by which he forgives sins; “and the love of God”—that is, God the Father, whose love for the salvation of human beings willed that the Son become incarnate; “and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit”—that is, the Spirit proceeding jointly from the Father and the Son.

Or “the fellowship of the Holy Spirit” means the Holy Spirit communicating his gifts to you. “Be with all of you. Amen.” And so that this may happen, labor yourselves, and may God grant it.

# [ON THE EPISTLE TO THE GALATIANS]

[Col. 0279]

## 203 ARGUMENT OF THE EPISTLE TO THE GALATIANS

The Galatians are Greeks. They first received the word of truth from the apostle, but after his departure they were tested by false apostles so that they might turn back to the Law and circumcision. The Apostle recalls them to the faith of the truth, writing to them from Ephesus.

## PROLOGUE OF BLESSED BRUNO ON THE SAME EPISTLE
[Col. 0279D] Galatia is indeed a region in Greece, and Paul had spent some time there, preaching the word of God to the Galatians, whom he had also established in the faith. As long as Paul remained with them, they conducted themselves quite honorably in the faith; but after Paul had departed from there, false teachers (whose work consisted in persecuting the Church of Christ) entered among them, wickedly destroying what Paul had piously built up. They said that Paul should not be believed, nor his teaching maintained, because he had neither lived with Christ [Col. 0280D] on earth, nor been taught or chosen by him, nor even instructed by Peter or by those who had lived with Christ. These false teachers also greatly diminished the grace of God, saying that it was insufficient for salvation unless circumcision and the other requirements of the old law were observed. In this respect they accused Paul of having taught wrongly, since he was destroying the law which, as was known to all, God had given through Moses, and which Christ himself had observed while living among human beings. Saying these things to people who were simple, they seemed to offer plausible arguments.

By these deceptions they had already been so thoroughly led astray that, unless Paul’s concern quickly intervened through this Epistle, they were preparing to be circumcised and to observe the other legal requirements. In this Epistle Paul deals with the commendation of his own person, which the false teachers were disparaging. He also deals with the destruction of the old law—not because he disapproves of it, since it had been necessary to observe it—and with the commendation of Christ’s grace. These are the three subjects treated here.

He commends himself in this manner: although they objected that he had not seen Christ and had not been chosen or instructed by him, he proves that he was chosen and taught by Christ in a manner far more worthy than the other apostles. Christ chose and taught them while he was living as a mortal among mortals, according to the weakness of their carnal understanding; for they were still carnal and could not grasp the mysteries of divinity. Although they had received the Spirit, he had not yet been given except only for the remission of sins. Jesus himself clearly indicates this when he says: “I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. But when the Spirit has come” (John XVI, 12), and so forth.

Those apostles, then, were still taught by the mortal Christ as though they were carnal; but Paul, already made immortal, already seated at the right hand of the Father, chose, called, and taught after the Holy Spirit had been given. Thus it appears that in the respect in which Paul seemed inferior, he is much more glorious than the others.

He disapproves of the old law in this way: he shows that it was given for a particular period and that, when grace came, it immediately reached its end, like a shadow when the body arrives. While it lasted, the law was nothing other than a heavy yoke, an unbearable and useless burden, because it could justify no one. After destroying the law, he commends Christ’s grace as that which alone is sufficient for salvation, and without which no one could have been saved, either before grace was given or afterward. He deals with all these matters intending to draw back the Galatians, who wished to Judaize, so that they would neither do so nor continue listening to the false teachers.

# EPISTLE TO THE GALATIANS

[Col. 0281]

## 204 CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0281C]

“Paul, an apostle not from human beings, nor through a human being, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead, and all the brothers who are with me, to the churches of Galatia: grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, who gave himself for our sins, in order to rescue us from the present evil age, according to the will of God and our Father, to whom be glory for ages of ages. Amen.

“I am astonished that you are transferring yourselves so quickly from him who called you into the grace of Christ to another Gospel, which is not another Gospel, except that there are certain people who are troubling you and wishing to overturn the Gospel of Christ. But even if we, or an angel from heaven, should proclaim to you a Gospel other than what we proclaimed to you, let him be accursed. As we said before, so now I say again: if anyone proclaims to you a Gospel other than what you received, let him be accursed.

“For now, am I persuading human beings, or God? Or am I seeking to please human beings? If I were still pleasing human beings, I would not be Christ’s servant.

“For I make known to you, brothers, the Gospel that was proclaimed by me: it is not according to a human being. For I neither received it from a human being, nor learned it, but through a revelation of Jesus Christ.

“For you have heard of my former way of life in Judaism: how beyond measure I persecuted the Church of God and ravaged it, and advanced in Judaism beyond many of my contemporaries among my people, being more abundantly zealous for my ancestral traditions.

“But when it pleased him who set me apart from my mother’s womb and called me through his grace, to reveal his Son in me so that I might proclaim him among the nations, immediately I did not submit to flesh and blood. Nor did I go up to Jerusalem to those who were apostles before me, but I went away to Arabia, and again returned to Damascus.

“Then, after three years, I went up to Jerusalem to visit Peter, and I remained with him fifteen days. But I saw none of the other apostles except James, the brother of the Lord. Now, concerning what I am writing to you, behold, before God, I am not lying.

“Then I came into the regions of Syria and Cilicia. I was personally unknown to the churches of Judaea that were in Christ. They had heard only that the one who once persecuted us now proclaims the faith which he once ravaged; and they glorified [glorificabant] God in me.”

## EXPOSITION

“Paul,” and so forth. At the beginning he briefly gathers the three matters with which he is chiefly concerned: the commendation of himself, the disapproval of the law, and the approval of grace. He says:

He places the name Paul—which had become known throughout the whole Church—at the beginning as an assertion of authority. “Paul,” I say, “an apostle,” not from human beings choosing him, nor through a human being consecrating him, as they objected concerning Ananias. Therefore he says, “not from human beings, nor through a human being.” Some are chosen not by human beings but by God, yet are consecrated through a human being, and the reverse also occurs.

Or the meaning may be this: “Paul, an apostle, not from human beings” choosing or consecrating him, “nor through a human being,” that is, not through Christ while mortal and living in human form, but through Jesus Christ after he had been raised. In what follows, “who raised him,” we appropriately understand “the one who was raised.” They might say: “Even if Christ destroys the law, we do not believe him, because he disagrees with God, who gave the law.” Therefore the Apostle adds, “through Christ who was raised, and through God the Father, who raised him from the dead.” The Father would have wished him to die in vain if he could have justified a human being by another means through the law. But because he saw that the law was ineffective, he excluded the law, so that through Christ’s grace he might perfect what the law failed to accomplish.

“I, Paul,” I say, “and all the brothers who are with me, write to the churches of Galatia.” He joins the brothers to himself in the greeting because the false teachers objected that Paul alone stood for the destruction of the law, whereas Peter and the others tolerated it in their own churches. When he says that he was made an apostle not by a human being but by Christ who was raised and by God the Father, he has sufficiently commended himself in this respect.

“May grace be with you,” O Galatians—that is, may those who have sinned receive a second remission, and may those who have remained in righteousness receive perseverance in grace. May peace also be with you, that is, tranquility of soul, from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, both of whom are able and willing to give it.

Now he will commend Christ’s grace by contrasting it with the law and disapproving the latter. He says: “Christ gave himself,” not another sacrifice, because nothing apart from him would have sufficed. “Himself,” I say, because he was so great: he says “himself” to distinguish the person, and “he” himself to indicate his greatness.

He gave himself to erase our sins. If the law could have destroyed them, this would be considered monstrous, because the Father would then have handed over his Son to death unnecessarily. Nor did he wish to die merely to remove preceding sins; rather, once sins had been destroyed, he wished to rescue us from the present age, in which he saw that no one could remain without sin.

This indicates Christ’s greatest power: in the furnace of sins he rescues us from the burning of sin. “To rescue us from the present evil age,” that is, from conformity to the present world, which does not attract us and which captures us all the more because eternal things seem less visible. “To rescue,” I say, as though by the force of a good way of life, from the age—but an evil age, that is, evil according to sin. Christ rescues his own from the world.

That Christ gave himself over to death happened according to the will of God [Col. 0283D] and our Father. Because he saw that the law was useless, he handed over his Son to death out of compassion in order to save us. And because Christ gave himself over to death for our sins by the will of God, know from this that glory belongs with God to Christ for the remission of sins, not to the law in this present age; and it will remain through the successive ages of these ages.

“Amen,” that is, truly it is so: glory belongs to Christ, not to the law. “Amen” is sometimes affirmative and sometimes optative.

And because Christ gave himself for our sins according to the will of God and emptied the law of its force, “I am astonished,” therefore, “that you are transferring yourselves”—that is, so vehemently, after abandoning all my commands. And “so quickly,” for only a short time has passed since I departed [Col. 0284A] from you.

“I am astonished,” I say, at this: “that you are transferring yourselves.” To press them down more severely, he speaks in this way. Inanimate things, such as stones, are transferred; irrational creatures are led; human beings are driven by reason. But he judges these people to be inanimate. Hence, later, he calls them senseless.

“I am astonished that you are transferring yourselves from him”—that is, from God—who called you, not on account of the merit of the law, but through grace. He called you both by inwardly inspiring you and by providing preachers, “into the grace of Christ,” that is, so that you might be participants in Christ’s grace.

“You are transferring yourselves,” I say, “to another Gospel.” According to them, he calls the old law a Gospel. Yet that Gospel is not another Gospel distinct from ours, except that there are certain people who are troubling you—that is, the false teachers, who, by teaching the old law carnally, make you dissent from the Gospel of Christ, although spiritually understood it has the same meaning as ours.

“They are troubling you” is said by comparison with disturbed water, in which nothing can be clearly discerned. In the same way these men had disturbed the understanding of the Galatians, so that they no longer distinguished evil from good. “They trouble you, and wish to overturn the Gospel of Christ.”

“Overturn” is said by comparison with someone traveling along a road who is turned back by an obstacle behind him. In the same way, these false teachers wanted to turn the Galatians back. Having received the faith of Christ through Paul’s Gospel, the Galatians had already been directed well along the path of good works, but the false teachers wanted to turn them away from it.

When he says “they wish,” he indicates that the Galatians had not yet consented to them in action, although they had consented in their assent. “They wish to overturn it.” But even if “we”—that is, I myself, or Peter, or an evil angel—should come from heaven, that is, in a splendid form, so that he may more easily persuade them—for if he emerged from the darkness of hell, presenting himself as grim and deformed in order to deceive, he would not be so suitable for the purpose—or even if a good angel came from heaven and proclaimed something other than what we proclaimed to you, that is, something beyond our proclamation, whether he were an apostle or an angel, I would dare not only to separate him from the body of Christ, but also to let him be accursed, so that he himself might be the separation of those who are separated.

Here he cleverly responds to those who objected that he did not tolerate Jewish rites in his churches, not understanding that Peter tolerated them not because he approved them, but lest he frighten away the immaturity of their faith, which was to be nourished by such concessions rather than destroyed by excessive severity. Peter tolerated this only among Jews. But Paul, who preached to the Gentiles, had no reason to indulge them in practices in which they had never participated. Moreover, afterward it would have required more difficult labor to destroy these practices so that the faith of Christ might be firm.

And since we would not tolerate either an angel or an apostle preaching anything else to you, if any false teacher proclaims to you something beyond what you received from me, let him be accursed. “And now I say this again” concerning the false teachers, just as a moment ago I spoke of us and of the angel.

Or the meaning may be this: “I told you when I was with you that I would excommunicate all the false teachers; so now I say it again. If anyone proclaims to you a Gospel beyond what you received, let him be accursed.” I say, “let him be accursed,” and I say this and the preceding things out of zeal for Christ. For am I now persuading human beings—that is, am I speaking persuasively according to human will—or God, that is, for the glory of God?

As if he were saying: “I say, ‘Let him be accursed,’ and so forth, for formerly, before the faith, I persuaded human beings by preaching the law; but now, in the faith, I persuade them toward the glory of God. Therefore I no longer persuade human beings, since I do not seek to please them. For am I still seeking to please human beings?”

If he were preaching the law, which a human being could perform by his own power, then he would please human beings. But he does not wish to please them, because if he were still pleasing human beings by preaching the law, he would no longer be Christ’s servant, since by attributing something to the law he would detract from Christ’s grace.

Or the meaning may be this: “Am I now persuading human beings, or God?” If he preached the law, he would be persuading human beings, since a human being can readily perform what the law commands: cutting off the foreskin, sacrificing an animal, and things of that sort. But if he said that a human being was saved through these acts, he would take salvation away from God and ascribe it to the human being. The rest remains unchanged.

He now begins to respond to what he said above: “not from human beings, nor through a human being.” The wording is closely connected: “Therefore I do not seek to please human beings, but Christ, because my Gospel is not according to a human being, but from God.”

“And therefore I make the Gospel known to you, brothers”—not the old Gospel, but that which was proclaimed by me. I make this known to you concerning it: it was not handed on to me according to a human being. He proves this as follows:

“Truly it was not according to a human being, since I neither received this Gospel from a human being who consecrated me for this ministry, nor learned it from a human being.” Someone could be consecrated by God and nevertheless afterward learn those commandments from a human being. But Paul says: “I neither received it from a human being nor learned it, but through a revelation of Jesus Christ”—that is, through Jesus Christ openly revealing it to me, speaking not in parables as he taught the other apostles while he was still mortal in the flesh and they were weaker in understanding.

Truly I did not learn it from a human being, either before or after my conversion. He first demonstrates this concerning the time before his conversion, saying:

“You have heard of my former way of life”—that is, the manner of life I led during the time of unbelief—in Judaism. You have heard “that,” that is, how I persecuted the Church of God beyond measure, beyond the measure of persecutors; for no one was so violent toward the servants of God.

“I persecuted it,” he says, “and ravaged it.” According to some, he ravaged it because, while many wished to convert, he was still breathing threats and murder and drove them back. He also compelled many who had already become believers to deny the faith.

“I ravaged it,” he says, “and advanced in Judaism.” My law advanced more and more through me and reached greater strength. “I advanced,” he says, “beyond many of my contemporaries,” who were young and energetic, as I was.

By “contemporaries” he means not proselytes, but those of my own lineage, sons of Abraham just as I was, and brought up in the law. I was, he says, “a zealous one,” that is, an imitator and lover, not only of the law but also of my ancestral traditions.

For the prophets, in addition to the law, gave certain traditions, such as Zechariah’s fast of the first month and the fast of the fourth month (Zechariah VIII, 19), and so forth. They were “my traditions,” he says, because I practiced them so diligently that they seemed almost to be my own.

And since I persecuted the Church of Christ in this manner, it is evident that before my conversion I did not learn the Gospel.

He adds that he did not learn it after his conversion. “I persecuted the Church of Christ in this manner, but when it pleased him”—through grace, not through merit—“him,” I say, who so powerfully set me apart from my mother’s womb, from which I would never have emerged unless his mercy had drawn me out, and who called me so mercifully through his grace to the faith.

Or the meaning may be this: “He who set me apart from my mother,” that is, from the Synagogue, in which I had been raised and taught as a child—not merely from the bosom or lap, but from the very womb of the Synagogue. For I was a Pharisee among the leaders of the law. He set me apart from it and called me to the faith through his grace, not because I had possessed zeal for the law.

“He called me,” I say, “in order to reveal his Son in me.” [Col. 0286B] Whoever considers my calling will understand that all salvation comes from Christ and none from the law, which did not benefit me.

Nor did he call me merely to reveal his grace in me by comparison with myself; he also called me so that I might proclaim him among the Gentiles and make God’s mercy known.

When this pleased God concerning me, “immediately I did not submit to flesh and blood,” that is, to the Jews who were persuading me wrongly. They are nothing other than desirous flesh. “And blood” means the soul not governed according to reason, but desiring shameful things through the movement of the blood.

Nor did I immediately go to Jerusalem to the apostles who preceded me, because they had preceded me in the faith, so that I might be taught by them. Rather, I immediately went away to Arabia. This Arabia is the region in which Mount Sinai is located, near Egypt, in the desert.

“And again I returned from Arabia to Damascus. Then, after three years, I went to Jerusalem,” not to question them as though I were less wise, but solely to visit Peter. I remained with him fifteen days. If I had needed instruction, such a short period would not have been sufficient for me to be taught.

I saw Peter there, but at that time I saw none of the other apostles except James, the brother of the Lord, who was bishop at Jerusalem. Thus it is evident that after my conversion I learned nothing from them.

“As for what I am writing to you”—namely, that I learned nothing either before or after my conversion—believe that I am not lying about these things. Behold, I speak them before God. If God were visibly present, he would find no falsehood in my speech.

Then, after seeing Peter and James, I came into the regions of Syria and Cilicia. I was personally unknown to the churches of Judaea that were in Christ. If they had not seen me, it is evident that I learned nothing from them.

I was unknown to them personally, but they had heard about me.
