They had heard this: that Paul, who once persecuted us—that is, during the time of unbelief—now proclaims the faith of Christ, the faith which he once ravaged. When they heard this about me after my conversion and heard me preaching in this way, they glorified God and magnified his mercy.

## CHAPTER TWO

“Then, after fourteen years, I went up again to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus also with me. I went up according to a revelation, and I set before them the Gospel that I preach among the Gentiles. Privately, however, before those who seemed to be something, lest perhaps I should be running, or should have run, in vain.

“But not even Titus, who was with me, although he was a Gentile, was compelled to be circumcised—not even because of the false brothers who had secretly entered, who slipped in to spy out our freedom which we have in Christ Jesus, in order to bring us into slavery. To them we did not yield in submission even for an hour, so that the truth of the Gospel might remain with you.

“But from those who seemed to be something—whatever they once were makes no difference to me, for God does not accept a person’s status [Deut. X, 17; Rom. II, 19]—from those, I say, who seemed to be something, I received nothing. On the contrary, when they saw that I had been entrusted with the Gospel of the uncircumcision, just as Peter had been entrusted with that of the circumcision—for he who worked through Peter for the apostleship of the circumcision also worked through me among the Gentiles—and when they recognized the grace that had been given to me, James, Cephas, and John, who seemed to be pillars, gave the right hands of fellowship to me and Barnabas, so that we should go to the Gentiles and they to the circumcision; only we were to remember the poor. This was something I was also eager to do.

“But when Cephas came to Antioch, I opposed him to his face, because he was reprehensible. For before certain people came from James, he ate with the Gentiles. But when they came, he withdrew and separated himself, fearing those who were of the circumcision. And the rest of the Jews joined him in this hypocrisy, so that even Barnabas was led by them into that hypocrisy.

“But when I saw that they were not walking correctly according to the truth of the Gospel, I said to Cephas before them all: ‘If you, although you are a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how can you compel the Gentiles to Judaize? We are Jews by nature and not sinners from among the Gentiles.

“‘Yet knowing that a human being is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ, we too have believed in Christ Jesus, so that we may be justified by faith in Christ and not by works of the law. For by works of the law no flesh will be justified’ (Romans III, 20).

“But if, while seeking to be justified in Christ, ‘we ourselves also are found to be sinners, is Christ then a minister of sin? By no means! For if I rebuild again the things that I destroyed, I establish myself as a transgressor.

“‘For through the law I died to the law, so that I might live for God. I have been crucified with Christ. I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh, I live in faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me.

“‘I do not reject the grace of God. For if righteousness comes through the law, then Christ died for nothing.’”

## EXPOSITION

Then, after fourteen years had passed from his first arrival, he went up again to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus also. He says that he went up according to the location of the place. Paul came to Jerusalem a second time bringing with him suitable witnesses—Barnabas from the Jews and Titus from the Gentiles—because the churches in which he preached objected that his preaching differed from Peter’s and from that of the others.

Wishing to remove this uncertainty, he went up to Jerusalem with witnesses, not because he himself was uncertain about anything, but so that it might become certain to those who doubted that he did not disagree with Peter. He went up not merely because he wished to do so, but also “according to a revelation,” that is, because God revealed to him that this ought to happen.

And then he did not learn from them, but compared the Gospel with them, saying: “This is how I preach, and this is what I preach. Is it not also how you preach?” Someone might say: “You concealed some things that you preach to the Gentiles.” Paul replies: “Certainly not. I compared with them the Gospel that I preach among the Gentiles.” I did not suppress a single word of it; I compared it publicly with the whole Church.

“Privately,” that is, separately, I compared it with those who seemed to be something—that is, with the apostles. He did not do this privately with them in order to exclude the others or to deal with them in secret; rather, his speech had first been public before everyone, and now it was before these men.

Or the meaning may be this: “I compared the Gospel with them privately, with these men—the apostles—having been separated out, lest I appear unable to defend my Gospel without their support.” I compared it in this way lest perhaps something that could happen should occur: lest I be running, that is, lest I be thought to be running, or to have run, in vain, unless by this comparison I proved my Gospel.

Nor did I prove it merely by comparing it with theirs. Not even Titus, who was with me, although he was a Gentile by nation, was compelled to be circumcised. By saying “compelled,” he indicates that the false teachers had worked very hard against Paul to have Titus circumcised.

Not only was Titus not compelled to this, but neither did we yield to submission even for an hour. For he says: “He was not compelled to be circumcised,” and this was not even because of the false brothers who had secretly entered.

The unbelieving Jews, to whom Paul would not respond because they were unbelievers, hired false brothers with a reward, through whom they might attack Paul. These men, he says, secretly entered in deceitfully “to spy out our freedom,” that is, the faith that makes us free from the yoke of the law—the freedom that we have in Christ Jesus.

They spied it out in order, if they could, to bring us into slavery, that is, into the old law, which is a burdensome slavery. Through this he greatly commends the faith of Christ, because he calls it freedom, while he lowers the status of the law by calling it slavery.

Because of them, he says, we did not yield even for an hour to submission, that is, to the law, which subjects those who yield to it to slavery. We did not yield so that the truth of our Gospel might remain with you: so that, just as we preached that the law was useless and that grace was sufficient, you might always believe.

At another time, when Paul came to Jerusalem in order to remove every suspicion concerning him, he had Timothy, who had already been circumcised, circumcised again—not because he believed that circumcision now contributed anything, but because certain people had alleged that he himself had said that the law had always been useless. To prove that this allegation was false, he presented Timothy for circumcision.

But on this occasion he absolutely refused to have Titus circumcised. If, when he had now come to Jerusalem to prove that circumcision was worthless, he had circumcised Titus, the churches of the Gentiles would have said: “Behold the falsehood of Paul, who, whether he wished it or not, had to circumcise Titus at Jerusalem.”

Through this comparison of the Gospel he shows that after his conversion he was not found inferior to Peter and the others. He also adds that before his conversion he had been far more worthy than they under the law, although he cleverly treats the dignity he had before the faith as though it were of no importance to him.

The wording is connected in this way: “I compared the Gospel with them, and after receiving the faith I appeared irreproachable, like them. But what they once were”—that is, what Peter and the others were before the faith, when they seemed to those who were wise according to the flesh to be something—“what they were, and what I was under the law, makes no difference to me,” that is, contributes nothing to my case.

It is true that at that time I was more worthy than they, but I do not care about such glory. He says “those who seemed to be something” with reference to those who judged Peter and the others to be great and Paul to be nothing. Therefore he passes over what they were at that time.

For I know that God does not accept a person’s status: God does not esteem a human being on account of status, lineage, wealth, or knowledge.

I say that what they formerly were is of no importance because this alone is sufficient for my commendation: Peter and the others who were said to be something contributed nothing to me, that is, corrected me in nothing. They benefited me in nothing when I compared my Gospel with theirs.

Or “but” may connect the statement in this way: “What they were before the faith contributes nothing to me; but the fact that those who seemed to be something contributed nothing to me is sufficient for my commendation.”

They certainly contributed nothing to me. On the contrary, desiring fellowship with us, they gave the right hands of fellowship to me and to Barnabas, my disciple. He says this as follows: “They contributed nothing, but on the contrary, when they saw that the Gospel of the uncircumcision had been entrusted to me by God”—that is, the Gospel of the Gentiles, entrusted to me with the same dignity with which the Gospel of the circumcision, that is, of the Jews, had been entrusted to Peter.

He says “on the contrary” according to the opinion of those who judged Paul inferior to Peter.

I rightly say “when they saw,” for they saw that the same God who worked through Peter—that is, who worked miracles through him for Peter’s glory and commendation in the apostleship of the circumcision—worked in the same way through me, that is, for my commendation among the Gentiles; for I was the Apostle of the Gentiles.

When they saw that the Gospel had been entrusted to me, and when they recognized the same thing through its effects, seeing the grace that had been given to me—for I converted more people to the faith than they did—they recognized this, James, Cephas, and John, who seemed to be pillars, that is, supports of the Church.

These men were more honored than the others because Christ always admitted them to his more private matters; before them he was transfigured on the mountain (Matthew XVII, 2).

These men, I say, recognizing this, gave the right hands of fellowship to me and Barnabas. They understood that we were not inferior to them but equal, not disciples but associates. The joining of right hands was a sign of concord, by which the ancients mutually bound themselves in alliance.

They entered into fellowship with us in such a way that we would preach among the Gentiles, while they would preach to the circumcision. They imposed on us only this one particular obligation: that we should remember the poor who were in Jerusalem, since they could not be helped except through us.

I not only wished to benefit the poor; I was also eager to do so, so that I did this very thing—that is, I did no less than they had requested.

After he showed that they had contributed nothing to him, and that he was rather necessary to them because of the matter of remembering the poor, he adds something greater: although he himself was irreproachable, he also shows Peter to have been reprehensible. He says: “When I compared my Gospel with Peter and the others, they contributed nothing to me; rather, I contributed to Peter.”

For when Cephas came to Antioch, I opposed him. I opposed him not secretly but to his face, that is, in the presence of the Church. I opposed him because he was reprehensible, if not in understanding, then at least in example.

Paul therefore opposed Peter to his face because Peter was not sinning against himself in a matter concerning which he should have been corrected privately. Rather, he was sinning through a cautious hypocrisy, corrupting the Church. Anyone who sins publicly must be rebuked publicly; for those who had seen the offense needed also to see the correction of the offense.

Peter was certainly reprehensible because, before certain converts from the Jews came from James—James held the episcopal see at Jerusalem—Peter ate with the Gentiles without making any distinction concerning foods. This was how he acted beforehand.

But when those men came, he withdrew from the table of the Gentiles. He did not withdraw secretly, but separated himself, that is, he arranged a Jewish table apart from the gathering of the Gentiles, either in another house or at another table. He feared offending those who were of the circumcision, that is, the Jews, if he shared food with the Gentiles.

The rest of the Jews joined him in this hypocrisy. He did not believe that there was any real distinction between a Jew and a Gentile; he merely pretended this for the avoidance of scandal. They joined him in this hypocrisy, so that even Barnabas, my disciple, was led by those Jews into the same hypocrisy and refused to share with the Gentiles.

Peter, not considering simply that this corrupted the faith of the Church, avoided offending his Jewish brother through this hypocrisy. But when I saw that Peter and those who were with him were not walking correctly—not walking correctly, I say, in order to confirm the truth of the Gospel, since they had preached that the Jewish rites were now useless and should not be observed—I said to Cephas before them all. This was necessary because his hypocrisy was a corruption of the whole Church.

I said: “If you, Peter, although you are Jewish by birth, live—that is, customarily live—like a Gentile, judging nothing to be unclean, and no longer live like a Jew, condemning foods as unclean according to those rites; if, I say, you, a natural Jew, do not Judaize, how do you compel the Gentiles, who have never Judaized, to Judaize by your example, even though you do not preach this openly?”

For unless Paul had publicly corrected him in this matter, and unless Peter had therefore acknowledged that he was reprehensible, not only the Jews but also the Gentiles would have thought that faith was useless without the law.

Up to this point he has sufficiently proved that he is not inferior to Peter and the others, but rather necessary to them and their corrector. Now he turns to disapprove the law, showing that it must in no way be observed. He says:

The Gentiles certainly ought not to Judaize, because we are Jews by nature. If we now Judaize, we act uselessly. He says this as follows:

“We are Jews by nature,” born in Judaism and always devoted to the work of the law. We are Jews, “and not sinners from the Gentiles,” that is, we have not sinned in the manner of the Gentiles, worshiping idols and doing similar things; the Jews had not done this.

Yet although we are Jews by nature, we are not justified by works of the law. Knowing that no human being is justified by works of the law except through faith in Jesus Christ, we Jews, like the Gentiles, believe in Christ Jesus so that we may be justified solely by faith in Christ and not by works of the law.

Therefore—that is, because we Jews are justified by faith alone and not by the law—“all flesh,” that is, every Gentile obedient to the flesh and ignorant of God, will not be justified by works of the law, even if he performs them. If works do not benefit a Jew, much less do they benefit a Gentile.

He calls the Gentile “flesh” because he has never been engaged in the worship of God according to the law, but has always lived according to the works of the flesh.

Or the meaning may be this: if a Jew is not righteous through the law, much less is “flesh,” that is, a sinner from among the Gentiles, righteous through it.

He proves the same point again by an impossible and absurd consequence. He says: “I declare that we shall be justified by faith in Christ.” If this is not so, then what he says is the following:

“If we, seeking to be justified in Christ”—that is, through faith in Christ—“are ourselves also found to be sinners,” I do not mean that we are merely thought to be so according to the opinion of fools, which I do not consider; rather, if, while seeking justification through faith in Christ, we ourselves are found to be sinners like the Gentiles because we abandoned the law and turned to faith in Christ—if this is the case, then Christ is a minister of sin.

For Christ himself taught that the law was not to be observed, but that all justification came through faith. But because he shrank from calling Christ a minister of sin, he says this with astonishment:

“Does any senseless person dare to say that Christ is a minister of sin? By no means! Let it be far from us that Christ should be a minister of sin!”

Christ is truly not a minister of sin. For I destroyed the law, which I do not rebuild, lest I make myself a transgressor. For if, by rebuilding the law that has been destroyed, I am therefore guilty of transgression, then it properly follows that Christ, because he excluded the law, is not a minister of sin. For this is what he says: If I rebuild the legal observances that I destroyed, teaching that they must be observed, then I certainly make myself a transgressor of the law that I restore. Indeed, the law itself commands that it be disregarded after grace has come, as it says there through Moses: “God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers; you shall listen to him as to me (Deut. XVIII, 15).” As though he were saying: “Listen to me in the meantime, until he comes. When he has come, abandoning me, take refuge in him.” He therefore says “I rebuild” because certain people were charging him with having previously foolishly taught that the law was not to be observed, but now, corrected, of restoring the law. Truly, if I rebuild the law, I make myself a transgressor of the law. For I abandoned the law by means of the law itself, which commands that it not be observed once grace has come.

He does not say “I abandoned it,” but “I died to the law,” that is, I destroyed the law in such a way that I would never again return to it, just as there is no return from death to life. I died to the law so that I might live for God, that is, through God’s grace. In truly abandoning the law, one lives for God through faith; for one ceases from evil and does good. He expresses this as follows: “I have been fastened to the cross of Christ,” that is, I have my faculties fixed by the power of Christ’s cross, so that, as long as I remain in Christ’s faith, I may not stretch out hand or foot toward an evil deed. “I have been fastened to the cross of Christ,” that is, to the glory of Christ, who fastened me thus; and through this we are enabled to cease from evil.

If Christ had wished, he could have chosen another kind of death, but he wished even the kind of death itself not to be without a mystery. He prefigured this in the fastening of his limbs, which, according to the old man, had endured suffering and mortality up to the day of the cross. Thus, just as his limbs, once fastened, could not, according to the power of the human being, extend themselves toward certain actions, so on that cross he fastened the man of righteousness in such a way that, as long as he did not violate the faith of Christ, he could not turn aside toward an act of injustice. “I have been fastened to the cross”: ceasing from evil.

“But I live”—now it is no longer I, who existed according to the law, who live; rather, Christ lives in me. That is, I myself live, having been made Christ through conformity; and through this aspect we have the means to do good. Certainly I live for God through faith, through love, and through surrender.

[Col. 0292C] This is what he says: “I live”; but what I now live, placed in the flesh—although the flesh attacks the spirit, nevertheless the spirit lives in me and puts the desires of the flesh to death—is a marvelous way of living in the flesh. Since I live in this way by faith, that is, I live through faith in the Son of God, and not through the works of the law, but through the love of Christ, who loved me, joining the man personally to himself. I also live through surrender, because Christ handed himself over to death for me, redeeming me from death, which could not be accomplished through the law.

And because I live through faith, and not through the law, I therefore do not restore the law. Yet he puts it this way: “I do not reject the grace of God,” because restoring the law would be rejecting grace. I therefore do not restore the law, because righteousness does not come through the law. [Col. 0292D] For if righteousness came through the law, then Christ died for nothing—that is, needlessly—to justify us, since righteousness is obtained through the law; but you would not be willing to admit that Christ died needlessly.

## CHAPTER III

“O foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you not to obey the truth, before whose eyes Jesus Christ was proscribed and crucified in you?” This alone I wish to learn from you: Did you receive the Spirit from the works of the law, or from hearing with faith? Are you so foolish that, having begun with the Spirit, you are now being completed by the flesh? Have you suffered so many things in vain? If indeed in vain. Therefore, does he who supplies the Spirit to you and works miracles among you do so from the works of the law, or from hearing with faith? As it is written: ‘Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness’ (Gen. XV, 6; Rom. IV, 3).”

Know, therefore, that those who are from faith are the sons of Abraham. But Scripture, foreseeing that God justifies the nations by faith, announced beforehand to Abraham that “all nations will be blessed in you” (Gen. XII, 3). Therefore those who are from faith will be blessed together with faithful Abraham. For all who are from the works of the law are under a curse. For it is written: “Cursed is everyone who does not continue in all the things written in the book of the law, to do them” (Deut. XXVII, 26).

But since no one is justified before God by the law, it is clear that “the righteous person lives by faith” (Habac. II, 4; Rom. I, 17). The law, however, is not from faith, but “the one who does these things will live by them” [Col. 0293B] (Lev. XVIII, 5). But Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us, because it is written: “Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree” (Deut. XXI, 23), so that the blessing of Abraham might come to the nations in Christ Jesus, so that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith.

Brothers, “I speak in human terms”: even a humanly confirmed testament no one rejects or sets aside in favor of another (Hebr. IX, 17). The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his offspring. He does not say “and to offspring,” as though referring to many, but as referring to one: “and to your offspring,” who is Christ.

Now I say this: the testament confirmed by God, the law, which came four hundred and thirty years later, does not annul so as to abolish the promise. For if the inheritance comes from the law, then it no longer comes from the promise. But God granted it to Abraham through a promise.

Why, then, the law? It was established because of transgressions, until the offspring should come to whom the promise had been made, ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator. But a mediator is not of one party; God, however, is one.

Is the law therefore contrary to the promises of God? Certainly not! For if a law had been given that could give life, then righteousness would truly come from the law. But Scripture enclosed everything under sin, so that the promise might be given to believers through faith in Jesus Christ.

Before faith came, however, we were being guarded under the law, enclosed within the faith that was to be revealed. Therefore the law was our pedagogue toward Christ, so that we might be justified by faith. But when faith came, we are no longer under a pedagogue.

For you are all sons of God through faith in Christ Jesus. For all of you who were baptized in Christ have put on Christ. There is neither Jew nor Greek; there is neither slave nor free; there is neither male nor female. For you are all one in Christ Jesus. But if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to the promise.”

## EXPOSITION

And since righteousness comes through faith and not through the law: “O foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you so that you do not believe the truth?” You have the truth within you, namely the faith of Christ, which truly justifies, and yet you do not believe it. He calls them bewitched, accusing them of folly; for they are no different from old women who believe that certain sorcerers can corrupt by a mere glance whomever they wish.

“I call you bewitched, before whose eyes”—because you possess and know the truth itself—“Jesus Christ was proscribed, even in your own sight.” One is called proscribed who is driven from his kingdom and inheritance. They were driving Christ from his kingdom and inheritance when they were withdrawing from Christ themselves, in whom he ought to reign and who were his inheritance.

Not only was he proscribed; Christ was also crucified in you. For Christ was no more despised in the eyes of the Jews and Pilate than in yours, who despise him in this way.

Or in another way: “Before whose eyes Christ was proscribed” in others whom you corrupted by your bad example, and also in yourselves, who reject Christ from yourselves. And although he has been thus proscribed, nevertheless he himself was crucified for you, and ought not to have been so proscribed. He has inserted this point clearly.

Now he returns to the earlier argument: O foolish people, although I have now sufficiently proved that faith is effective and that the law has been annulled, and although you are foolish, nevertheless I will make you yourselves confess and prove that righteousness comes from faith and not from the law.

He says this as follows: Many other considerations occur by which I could prove this, but this one alone is sufficient, and this is what I wish to learn from you: Did you receive the Holy Spirit from the law, or from faith? Not from the law, because you, being Gentiles, did not possess the law. And he does not state it simply in this way, but adds: “from the works of the law, or from hearing with faith,” disparaging the law, whose works were burdensome, and commending faith, which is obtained very easily from hearing alone.

And since you received the Spirit from faith, are you now so foolish that, having begun to be saved through the Spirit, you are now being completed by the flesh—that is, through the carnal law? You are being perfected, that is, brought to completion. You are utterly foolish when you assign to the Spirit what is lesser—namely, beginning—and attribute to the flesh what is greater—namely, completion.

And because you seek completion through the flesh, you have suffered so many things in vain. You did indeed suffer many things from unbelievers, but in vain. I say that you suffered so many things in vain—yet only on the condition that this is in vain, that is, if you are incorrigible. For if you repent, forgiveness is at hand. And by saying this he reveals their hope.

He proved through those whom he showed to possess the Spirit through faith alone, since they had never possessed the law. Now he wishes to prove from his own case [Col. 0294D] that, although he had possessed both the law and faith, nevertheless he received the Spirit through faith, not through the law. Unless he proved this, he would leave room for doubt.

Therefore he says as follows: Since you received the Spirit from faith and not from the law, then tell me whether Paul, who supplies the Spirit to you—that is, through whose hands you received the Holy Spirit—and who works miracles and wonders among you, received the Spirit from the works of the law or from hearing with faith. You can judge from your own case by analogy: he received it from faith, not from the law, although he had possessed both. The Spirit is obtained from faith. Righteousness is obtained from faith, and the promise is obtained from faith.

The text is joined in this way: The Spirit is obtained from faith, just as righteousness is obtained from the same faith. Righteousness certainly comes from faith. For Abraham believed God, that is, he had faith, and this believing was counted sufficient for him to obtain righteousness.

And because Abraham had righteousness through faith, know therefore that whoever is from faith and not from the law—as Abraham also was not then from the law—is, through faith, a son of Abraham, that is, righteous, because he is an imitator of Abraham’s faith.

Not only are the Spirit and righteousness obtained through faith, but blessing is also found in faith, as it is read there: “O Abraham, in you”—that is, in the likeness of your faith—“not only Jews but also all nations will be blessed.”

But before he introduces this authority, he explains beforehand how the phrase “in you” is to be understood, saying: Scripture in Genesis, foreseeing—that is, showing that God had foreseen—thus, from eternity God deliberated, foreseeing, I say, this: namely, that God justifies not only the sons of Abraham’s flesh, but also the nations. He justifies them, I say, not from the law but from faith. That Scripture, long before the time of grace, foretold—that is, showed that God had foretold to Abraham—that in you, through imitated faith, all nations will be blessed (Gen. XII, 3).

It should be noted that, although he ought to prove the matter from blessing, he says, “He justifies from faith,” understanding that wherever righteousness precedes, blessing necessarily follows. What he calls blessing here he understands also as promise, testament, and inheritance.

Moreover, it should be observed that, in a fitting order, the Spirit is first obtained from faith, then righteousness, and finally blessing. For after faith the Spirit is immediately given, without whom no one can act well. Then, through the Spirit’s assistance, works of righteousness follow. After righteousness comes blessing, that is, the recompense of righteous works.

And because Scripture says that through faith, with righteousness mediating, one obtains blessing, therefore those who are from faith—that is, who place their existence in faith—although David and many others were under the law, nevertheless had their existence from faith. Those who are from faith will certainly be blessed with Abraham, not circumcised but faithful—that is, not through the law but through faith.

Nor should this be passed over: Abraham was justified by faith before he was circumcised. Truly, blessing is obtained from faith alone; for from the law one obtains not blessing but rather a curse.

[Col. 0295D] For all who are—that is, who believe that they subsist—from the works of the law are under a curse. And he proves this: They truly are under a curse, for it is written in Deuteronomy, that is, in the abridgment of the law, when Moses briefly recapitulated the law that had been given and, after gathering all the commandments, said: Everyone who does not continue in all that is written in the book of this law—not merely continue in it by intention, but in such a way as to do all these things—“shall be cursed” (Deut. XXVII, 26).

And by saying this Moses was saying the same as if he had said: “I do not hand this law over to you so that you may obtain justification in it, but to restrain your hardness. And know that you must flee to grace, so that the grace of Christ may annul the curse of the law.” Peter himself also says that the burden of the law is so great that even their fathers were unable to bear it.

He has now proved, through Abraham and Moses, that righteousness is obtained from faith, and likewise blessing (Acts XV, 11); he proves again through Habakkuk that both are from faith. And one should consider how he always places faith before the law: through Abraham, who existed before the law; through Moses, the giver of that same law; and through Habakkuk, who lived under the law itself.

Justification is obtained from faith. But since no one is justified in the law—not, I say, according to human opinion, but before God—it is manifest in Habakkuk, who says that a person is made righteous from faith, and that the righteous person lives, that is, obtains the promised blessing. And if the righteous person lives from faith alone, then not from the law.

Someone might object: It is true that a person must be justified through faith, but nevertheless the law assists faith and is, in some way, necessary for faith. He answers as follows: The righteous person lives from faith, not from the law. But the law is not from faith—that is, it does not depend on faith, nor is it any aid to faith. But do you wish to know what it accomplishes better? This: Whoever does the things that the law commands will live by them, that is, what he has will be forgiven him; but nothing will be increased for him on the merit of the law.

Since he had said above, “Cursed is everyone who does not perform the commandments of the law,” someone might say: Since Moses says this, although we are in faith, it is nevertheless necessary for us to observe the law, lest we incur the curse of Moses.

Paul responds to this: Although Moses cursed everyone who does not perform the law, do not therefore cling to the law; for Christ redeemed us from that [Col. 0296C] curse of the law. Moses also understood this when he pronounced the curse. Christ redeemed us by becoming, for our redemption, not only cursed but also a curse.

For if one of those who crucified Christ wished to curse someone, he would curse him by saying: “May this happen to you as it happened to that crucified man.” Truly he became a curse for us, because it is written in Deuteronomy: “Everyone who hangs on a tree is cursed” (Deut. XXI, 25).

But Christ, hanging on the tree, was not cursed because of the guilt of his own crime, but was cursed in this one respect: that he endured the punishment of the curse. For Moses had commanded that if someone were condemned as guilty, he should be cursed in the very act of condemnation.

Or the phrase may be understood in this way: “Everyone who hangs on a tree is cursed.” When God first created the man, he blessed him if he should persevere in obedience; but because he sinned, he cursed him. This curse was nothing other than stripping him of the impassibility and immortality that had been granted to him.

Christ, however, assuming the flesh of the old Adam, was cursed because he was passible and mortal. This became evident in him when he hung on the tree; for he could not suffer if he were impassible.

A Gentile might object: Even if Christ removed the curse of the law, since we did not possess the law, it benefited us nothing.

Paul responds to this: Christ redeemed us so that, just as among the Jews, so also among the nations there might be blessing—that is, the promise of Abraham, to be possessed in Christ Jesus, not through the law. It would become a promise, I say, so that we might receive the pledge, that is, the thing frequently promised.

[Col. 0297A] I mean “the promise of the Spirit,” that is, the promise made to us through the Spirit; or “of the Spirit,” because we have already received the Holy Spirit, through whom we are already partly deified, as the earnest of blessedness to come. We receive it, I say, not through the law but through faith.

What he has just proved through the authority of the law and the prophet—namely, that blessing is received through faith—he proves again through the law of human custom, saying: Just as a testament legally made by any human being cannot be destroyed, so the law cannot annul God’s testament.

And if they object that the law is older than this testament, and that the old ought not to be destroyed by the new, they say nothing, since this promise was made to Abraham long before the law.

The text is joined in this way: What I have just proved through authorities, brothers, I now state according to human custom—that is, I affirm by human practices—in this way: A human testament, even if it belongs to some insignificant person, nevertheless, once confirmed—that is, legally made, with witnesses present, the testator dying, and so forth—is not rejected by anyone as though it were to be left unfulfilled. Nor does anyone establish another testament over and above it.

And just as no one destroys a human testament, so the law does not invalidate God’s testament.

Before setting this out, he first establishes that God’s testament truly was made, and then that the testament preceded the law. No one rejects a human testament; but the testament was made by God, because the promises were spoken to Abraham.

He does not say that the promises were different promises, but that the same thing was promised through many repetitions and at different times. The promises were spoken to Abraham, and through Abraham they were spoken to his offspring, that is, to Christ.

Just as when fertility in children and an increase of inheritance are promised to a father, although his son does not yet exist, the promise is nevertheless made to the son through the father, so the promise was made to the offspring.

He says this and does not say that it was made to offspring, as though the nations were to inherit through many, but as through one: “In your offspring the nations will inherit”; and that offspring is Christ. The relation is good, in which what is proper follows.

Here he has shown that God’s testament was made to Abraham; now he shows that the testament is older than the law. I say that the promises were made to Abraham; but I say of the same thing that this testament was confirmed by God, for God swore that he would fulfill it.

This testament, I say, the law does not invalidate, the law that was made four hundred and thirty years later. For if the testament of any human being is not invalidated, how much more will the testament of God—which he promised with an oath, to so great a man as Abraham and after so great an antiquity of time—not be invalidated!

The law does not invalidate it so as to abolish the promise, that is, so that the promise might be abolished.

When he says that the law does not invalidate it, we should understand “invalidate” to mean that the law itself would justify and grant the blessing, just as it was promised to happen through faith to Abraham. The promise would truly be abolished if the testament were invalidated by the law.

For if the inheritance is obtained from the law—which nevertheless cannot be the case—then, if it is from the law, it is no longer obtained from the promise. For if it is not from the promise, God, who promised, is false. And if that were so, then it would in no way be obtained.

But God, who promised, is true. Therefore it is obtained from his promise and not from the law. If it is from the law, it is not from the promise; but it is obtained from the promise. It is truly from the promise, because God granted the inheritance to Abraham through the promise. Therefore it is not through the law.

And because I prove through the law that neither righteousness nor blessing is obtained from it, you will object to me: What use was the law? It seems to have been given in vain, since it neither justifies nor saves.

Paul truly says that it neither justifies nor saves, but it is not therefore useless, because it was established on account of transgressions. For it added the sin of transgression that had not existed, and it was necessary that transgressions should abound. “Where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more” (Rom. V, 20).

Or in another way: The law was established to prevent transgressions; for the law, by punishing the guilty, makes a person fear sin.

Again someone might say: If it was established on account of transgressions, then the law is useful and must be observed.

Paul says, Not at all, because the law was established for a time, until the offspring should come, that is, Christ, of whom he says, “In your offspring,” and so forth, to whom he had made the promise—that is, to whom the promise had been made.

I say that the law was ordained—that is, it was not to remain, but was arranged in time according to its proper order. First there was the natural law; then this written law; finally grace.

I say that it was ordained through angels, that is, through Moses and Aaron, who were God’s messengers to the people; or through heavenly angels, through whose ministry the law of Moses was delivered.

Again someone might say: What was made through angels ought not to be destroyed.

Paul responds: It was so ordained through angels that it was in the hand—that is, in the power—of the mediator, Christ. For whatever angels there may have been, they wished this: that when faith came, the law should be abolished.

And because he had just spoken of a mediator—for one who is in the middle, joining two extremes, appears to be different from those things he joins—someone might think that Christ, while mediator between God and man, was not God but something other than God, the one who joined man to God. Or, if he were God, someone might think there were two gods: one who, as mediator, joined the two extremes, and another God to whom the human being was joined.

[Col. 0298D] To remove this, he adds: “I speak of the mediator.” A mediator, I grant, is not the mediator of one thing alone, but of two extremes, since he would not be called “in the middle” on account of one thing. And although he is not the mediator of one but of two, it does not therefore follow that there are two gods; there is only one God.

Or alternatively: The law was placed in the hand of the mediator; but this mediator is not of one party alone—that is, of the Jewish people—but is one who belongs equally to the Gentiles as to the Jews. This is evident from the fact that he is God to the Gentiles just as much as to the Jews.

He draws the inference from what came before: Since no one rejects a human testament or sets another above it, and since the testament was made before the law, the law therefore does not destroy the promises of God.

But he presents this by way of a question: Must it be admitted that the law is contrary to the promises of God, so that through the law one obtains what is promised through faith? Certainly not! The law is not so opposed to the promises of God that it brings about the blessing promised through faith.

The law truly is not contrary to the promises of God in such a way that it could give the blessing. For if a law had been given that could give life—that is, give the promised blessing—then righteousness would truly come from the law. For unless righteousness preceded, the blessing could not be obtained; but righteousness does not come from the law.

For Scripture “enclosed,” that is, showed that everything had been enclosed. Or Scripture—that is, the same law—by adding sin, as though forcibly, enclosed and showed that everything had been enclosed under sin.

Everything was therefore enclosed under sin so that those who were enclosed might believe, and so that, once they believed, the promise—that is, the promised blessing—might finally be given to them, not from the law but through faith in Jesus Christ. For it could have been thought that, although they believed, they would nevertheless not receive the blessing as a reward for faith.

**Note:** It therefore enclosed everything under sin so that they might believe. For unless human beings were so bound under the bond of sin that they could not even draw breath by their own strength, they would never flee to mercy, which consists in faith.

But although the law cannot give life, it was nevertheless opportune. For before faith came, we Jews, placed under the law, were being guarded—that is, under the guardianship of the law we were being nurtured—for the grace that was to come.

I say “enclosed under the law,” that is, constrained in prison like slaves. For it threatened punishment; it did not promise rest. We were being guarded, I say, in order to pass from this guardianship into that faith which, then veiled in the figures of the law, was to be revealed through Christ.

And because we were being guarded under the law for faith, therefore the law was our pedagogue, nurturing us so that we might be placed in Christ; in Christ, that is, so that we Jews might be justified through the faith of Christ and not through the law.

A pedagogue is called the one who nurtures a child and always follows his feet. Likewise, the law was our pedagogue, nurturing our childhood and simplicity, just as a child is usually brought up through beatings and threats. We were children under a pedagogue.

But when faith came—that is, the maturity of conduct—and we had become adults, we Jews were no longer under the pedagogue, that is, under the law.

For this reason we Jews are no longer under the law: because you all, Galatians, are Gentiles and are sons of God through faith, no less than we are. And if, through faith, you are no less before God than we are, we would observe the law in vain, since it is proved through us to contribute nothing to us. For if we Jews abandon the law because it is useless, it would surely be insanity for you, who never possessed it, to take hold of it.

I rightly call you sons of God in Christ Jesus. For all who have been baptized in Christ—that is, in the institution of Christ Jesus—have put on Christ. He says “put on.” Through sin a human being is naked and suffers both deprivation and disgrace; but in baptism, coming to Christ, he puts him on both to cover his nakedness and for glory.

I rightly say “all”: for there is neither Jew nor Greek, neither slave nor free, neither male nor female—that is, in the faith of Christ there is no difference of nation, condition, or sex. For you are all one body through faith in Christ Jesus.

But if you belong to Christ, since Christ belongs to Abraham—for it was said above, “and to your offspring, who is Christ”—then through Christ you Gentiles are Abraham’s offspring. And if you are offspring, then you are heirs of his blessing, not through the law but according to the promise.

He continues to dwell on what he proved above. Just as he proved that one must not return to the law, because it was a pedagogue and, once perfected through faith, there is no need for a pedagogue, so he now proves the same thing through other arguments: namely, that Jews ought no longer to work under the law because the law served in the place of a guardian and steward, and the maturity of faith has no need of such a guardian and steward.

He proves this by the analogy of a ward whom a dying father arranges to be under a guardian and steward until maturity of age makes him worthy of freedom.

A guardian of a child is one who protects him against an attacker, so that he cannot be disinherited. A steward of the child is either the same person or another, but for a different purpose: namely, because he manages and administers the ward’s goods, pays taxes, and answers for him in legal matters.

The law is similarly called a guardian and steward. For people possessing little knowledge of divine things, and therefore also wretched and like wards, first needed the law to constrain them as slaves, so that, nurtured under this discipline, they might pass over to the perfection of faith.

At that time the law was their guardian through the precepts it gave, saying: “Do not do this or that. If you do, you will surely die.” Thus, through the commandments it gave, the law guarded and defended them against invading vices, from which they abstained through fear, though not yet through love.

The law was also the steward of the same people, through the sacrifices by which they were brought before God so that they might be cleansed from sins.

The text is joined in this way: Not only by what was said above—namely, because I prove that the law was a pedagogue, that one must not remain any longer under the law—but also by this, that the law served in the place of a guardian and steward. Since we no longer need them, it is unjust to observe the law.

Or it may be joined in another way, as an opposing statement, thus: Because we are one in Christ and through faith are Abraham’s offspring, it is indeed true that for these reasons we ought no longer to observe the law; nevertheless, the law was necessary while we still needed a guardian and steward because we were wards.

According to this continuation, the reason that had not previously been given will now be supplied.

## CHAPTER IV

“I say, then: As long as the heir is a child, he differs in nothing from a slave, although he is lord of all; but he is under guardians and stewards until the time appointed by his father. So also we, when we were children, were enslaved under the elements of the world. But when the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, made from a woman, made under the law, to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons.

And because you are sons of God, God sent the Spirit of his Son into your [our] hearts, crying, ‘Abba’—that is, ‘Father.’ [Col. 0301A] Therefore he is no longer a slave but a son. And if a son, then also an heir through God.

But at that time, when you did not know God, you served those who by nature are not gods. But now, since you have come to know God—or rather, since you have been known [come to be known] by God—how are you turning back again to the weak and impoverished elements, to which you wish to be enslaved anew? You observe days, months, seasons, and years. I fear for you, lest perhaps I have labored among you in vain.

Become as I am, because I also have become as you are. Brothers, I entreat you: you have done me no wrong. You know that it was because of an infirmity of the flesh that I evangelized you long ago, and you did not despise or reject your trial in my flesh; rather, you received me as an angel of God, as Christ Jesus.

Where, then, is your blessedness? [Col. 0301B] For I bear witness to you that, if it had been possible, you would have torn out your eyes and given them to me. Have I therefore become your enemy by telling you the truth?

They court you improperly, but they want to exclude you so that you may court them. But always court what is good in goodness, and not only when I am present with you.

My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you, I would like now to be present with you and change my voice, because I am perplexed about you.

Tell me, you who wish to be under the law: have you not read the law? For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one from a slave woman (Gen. XVI, 15), and one from a free woman (Gen. XXI, 2). But the one from the slave woman was born according to the flesh, while the one from the free woman was born through the promise; these things are spoken allegorically.

For these are the two testaments: one indeed from Mount Sinai, producing slavery, which is Hagar. For Sinai is a mountain in Arabia, which is joined to the present Jerusalem and is enslaved with her children.

But the Jerusalem above is free, which is our mother. For it is written: ‘Rejoice, barren woman who do not give birth; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not labor, because the children of the deserted woman are many more than those of the woman who has a husband’ (Isa. LIV, 1).

But we, brothers, are children of the promise according to Isaac. But just as at that time the one who was born according to the flesh persecuted the one who was born according to the spirit, so also now.

But what does Scripture say? ‘Cast out the slave woman and her son. For the son of the slave woman will not be heir with the son of the free woman.’

Therefore, brothers, we are not children of the slave woman but of the free woman, with the freedom with which Christ freed us.”

## EXPOSITION
He had indeed said that a pedagogue was no longer necessary, but he had not stated the reason why. Here he adds it, saying: Although you now no longer need a pedagogue, being one in Christ, nevertheless I say that you once did need one, as you see that, for however long the heir is a child according to his father’s arrangement, he remains a child—whether for twenty years or fifteen. Although he has been designated heir, he differs in nothing from a slave, because he is often restrained and beaten by his guardian. Although he is destined to be lord of all, he differs in nothing; that ward is under guardians who protect his inheritance lest it be violently taken away, and under administrators who conduct his lawsuits and manage his inheritance. He is certainly under them until the time appointed by his father—that is, as long as his father has determined that he should remain under another’s authority. For it was customary for a boy to remain under a patron until the age of twenty-two, so that he might not dissipate his property unlawfully.

Since Paul does not adapt every detail of the comparison, it is good for us to adapt the individual points. For however long—which was from the first man until Christ—the one who was to be heir, namely the Jewish people, to whom salvation had been promised, remained a child in the knowledge of God throughout that entire period, until Christ. While he was a child, that people differed in nothing from a slave. If it performed the commandments imposed upon it, it avoided punishment; but if it did not, it was tortured most harshly, like a slave. Meanwhile it differed in nothing from a slave, although it was destined to be lord of all the goods of the inheritance. Thus that people, oppressed by the servitude of the Law, was to be established as lord of the heavenly inheritance if it passed from the Law to faith.

A child differs in nothing from a slave, but is under guardians and administrators—that is, under the Law, which protects him through commandments and acts on his behalf through sacrifices. He is certainly under them until the time appointed by God the Father, at which time he would be transferred from the servitude of the Law to the freedom of faith. And just as a child who is an heir is under guardians and administrators, so also, when we were children in the knowledge of God, we were not free, but were serving under the elements—that is, under the legal ordinances. For just as a boy advances through the elements of the alphabet to knowledge of letters, so through the Law one had to advance to the knowledge of God, which was to be possessed in faith.

“Element” is so called either as though it meant an elevation (*elevamentum*), since through it one is raised to knowledge; or as though from *elimo, elimas*, and so forth; or as though from *hylementum*, for *hyle* means “matter.” We were under the elements of the world—that is, under what the Law promised as worldly things and taught as carnal things.

Previously, then, we were children. But when the fullness of time came—or, “the time of fullness”: it is called fullness because whatever had been awaited in the preceding ages was then completed—then perfect justification came, which had not existed before; then present and complete salvation came, which Abraham and the other saints had awaited until that day.

Or alternatively: After the fullness came—that is, the end and completion of the time which God had determined should first pass away—then God sent his Son. Since the Son of God was everywhere wholly and present, this “sending” meant nothing other than that he who was invisible was displayed visibly in the form of a servant. I say “the Son,” whom he humbled so greatly that he willed him who was uncreated and everlasting to assume a new created nature from a woman. He was also made under the Law, because he lived under the Law and fulfilled the Law, when a victim was given on his behalf. He was therefore under the Law so that, by paying the price of his blood, he might redeem those who were under the Law.

For unless he had been made under the Law and kept the Law, he could not free from the Law and destroy the Law, just as it was necessary that by tasting death he should destroy death. He came to redeem us, and so that, once redeemed, we might receive adoption as sons—that is, that we might be sons receiving adoption, namely the eternal inheritance which the grace of God adopted for us.

When he says “made from a woman,” the question arises: since God was everywhere wholly present, how was he present more particularly in the Virgin’s womb? The saints offer the following comparison concerning this matter. Just as the soul, while it is in the body, gives the body sensation, governs it, and makes it live, but, when separated from the body, is wholly present elsewhere in the same way, although it does not perform its function there, so the divinity, although wholly present elsewhere as well as in the Virgin’s womb, nevertheless does not thereby perform elsewhere the same work that it performed in the Virgin’s womb.

Above we ought to have noted that, just as that child, if he dies before reaching mature age, loses his inheritance, so whoever is unwilling to pass from the Law to the maturity of faith becomes deprived of the inheritance.

The Galatians might say: “You Jews will indeed receive adoption as sons; but what benefit will that be to us?” To this Paul replies: “It is not only we who are sons, but you Gentiles are likewise sons.” He proves this by saying that God sent the Spirit of his Son—that is, the same Spirit whom the Son possessed, or whom the Son gave. He sent him, I say, into our hearts, mine and yours—the Spirit, I mean, who cries out, or causes us to cry out: “Abba” among the Jews, “Father” among the Gentiles.

And since both are sons and cry out, therefore no one is now a slave, but a son. Since he is a Son, he will also be heir of the blessed inheritance. And that this will indeed happen, I testify to you by God. Or it may be understood this way: He will be heir through God—that is, through the mercy of God, not through the Law.

Now he recalls to their memory the former condition they had in the worship of idols, proving that they abandoned the idols to no purpose if they accept the Law. For the Law is now idolatry, since grace has come. Whoever thinks that the Law is necessary for justification, by detracting from God and attributing to the Law what belongs to God, attributes to the Law what idolaters attributed to an idol—that which belonged to God. If they now accept the Law, their condition will be worse than before. Then they would have acted through ignorance; now, knowingly and deliberately, they will put their hand into the fire.

The wording is joined as follows: “Now you are sons, but then, before your conversion, you were serving those who were not gods”—and, even if they were gods in people’s opinion, they were not so by nature. Then you served them in this way; but now, when you have come to know God—which corrects what he said about their ignorance—and when he says “when you have come to know,” Paul is also correcting himself: rather, “when you have been known,” that is, approved by God, how, or for what reason, are you turning back again to the elements, to those weak legal ordinances, weak because even in their own time they were unable to justify anyone, and needy in their weakness because they required external assistance?

This little thing that the Law accomplished could not be accomplished except through the assistance of the faith that was to come. Why do you now wish to serve those elements again? From now on the Law will be for you what the idol formerly was.

Indeed, you are turning back to the Law. For you are now observing days—that is, Sabbaths—you are also observing months, that is, the renewals of the moon; and seasons, that is, the Hebrews’ fasts appointed for particular times; and you are also observing years, that is, the seventh year and the jubilee according to Hebrew custom.

And because you are acting in this way, I fear for you—that is, I fear nothing in you so much as this. I fear, I say, lest perhaps—which could happen quickly—I have labored among you without cause, that is, without the fruit of benefit.

But so that it may not happen that I have labored in vain, be as I am, unconcerned with legal observances, since I too was formerly devoted to the Law, as you now wish to be, and abandoned it. Now see how foolishly you wish this.

Or alternatively: “Be as I am, because I am as you are,” living as a Gentile. The false apostles had charged Paul with hating the Galatians and therefore with not having disclosed the whole truth to them. Now he excuses himself on this matter and praises them for their former conduct, in which they had shown themselves exceedingly kind toward Paul. He also flatters them in this way because, after a few words, he is going to attack them more harshly.

The wording is joined as follows: “Be as I am, and I beg you to be my brothers,” having a loving affection toward me. “For you have done me no wrong in any respect. Why should I, because I hated you, have concealed the truth? You have done me no wrong. But I know—and you know very well—that I evangelized to you because of weakness of the flesh,” though not of the spirit. For although I was weak and contemptible according to the flesh, I appeared strong through the power of the Spirit in miracles.

I preached because of weakness—not for a short time, but for a considerable period, so that my weakness might have become a burden to you. And although such great weakness oppressed me, you nevertheless did not despise me when I preached, nor did you reject me when I first came to preach—the trial you experienced in my flesh.

For in my weakness God was testing you, as if he were saying: “If they reject Paul’s weakness, they are guilty; if they receive him kindly, they are worthy.” To reject is more than to despise, just as to cast away utterly is more than to disregard through endurance.

You did not despise me, but received me as an angel of God and as Christ Jesus. And since this shows that there was no cause for hatred but much cause for love, anyone who suspects that I am hostile to you is mistaken. And since you were so kind in receiving me, where, then, is your blessedness, by which you formerly obeyed the Gospel so completely?

And indeed it was blessedness, because I myself bear witness to you that, if it had been possible, you would have torn out your eyes and given them to me. By “if it had been possible” he understands what it would have been appropriate to do.

And since you were bound to me by such great force of love, it is therefore not to be believed that I have become your enemy. You think this because I am telling you the truth. If I concealed the truth and stroked you with flatteries, you would judge me to be your friend.

I am not your enemy; but they are zealous for you—that is, they love you, but not well. They are zealous for you because they wish to exclude you from the faith of Christ, so that, after they have led you more completely into their error, you may become zealous for them and they may imperiously demand from you whatever they wish.

But do not be zealous for them. Be zealous for me and for any good person, never for evil—even if I should happen to urge it—but always for good. And be zealous for me not only when I am present with you, but also when I am absent.

He further proves by the words of that same Law what he had already proved above, namely that the Law is not to be retained. For, as he later shows, when the freedom of faith comes, the servitude of the Law must be rejected.

The wording is joined as follows: “Be zealous for me and for any good person. But do not be zealous for them. If you wish to be zealous for them, tell me, my little children.”

The construction extends to this point. He calls those who had previously been sons according to the integrity of faith “little children,” using the diminutive because, by wishing to cling to perverse people, they had been greatly diminished in the goodness of their sonship.

“My little children, for whom I am again in labor”—that is, concerning whose instruction I labor with the greatest effort. “To be in labor” refers to the suffering a mother undergoes in giving birth, before the child is brought forth.

“My little children, for whom I am again in labor”: formerly, when you were unbelievers, I endured much labor among you. I am in labor and suffering for you until you are re-formed in Christ, in the faith in which you were formed, because you have at least consented to those false apostles.

He does not say, “until you are re-formed,” but “until Christ is formed in you.” For Christ has been disfigured and has lost his form in you who have been led astray. Or, “he has been disfigured in you,” that is, in your likeness. For when others hear how you disparage the faith of Christ, they say, on the basis of your example, that the faith of Christ is insufficient for salvation.

To frighten them more strongly, he intensified his statement when he said, “until Christ is formed”—as if he were saying, “whom you have disfigured.” I call you “little children,” but, although absent, I shall call you little children. Nevertheless, I now wish to be present with you and so change my tone of voice, because if I now call you little children, when present I would call you alienated people who insult God, and many other reproachful names.

Although Paul would have said these things if he had been present, he nevertheless did not wish to write them in the Epistle, knowing that the Epistle would remain and trusting in their correction; he did not want their reproach to endure—and rightly so, since they needed correction.

If I were with you, I would change my tone, because now I am ashamed—that is, I am truly embarrassed on your account. For I had praised your faith before other Churches, and when they hear of the corruption of your faith, they think me guilty of lying; over this I am ashamed.

“My little children, tell me.” Or, if one prefers, the construction need not be extended so far in this way: “Be zealous for me,” which you ought certainly to do, “because you are my little children, for whom I am again in labor,” and so forth. The meaning of the words does not change.

And because I am ashamed on account of you who have been led astray, now tell me and answer me: “You who wish to be under the Law, have you not read the Law?”

He presents them with a dilemma from both sides. It strikes them because, if they have not read the Law, it is foolish to pass over to something they do not know. But if they have read it, since the same Law, when faith comes, forbids itself to be retained, those who wish to retain it are exceedingly foolish. He proceeds, nevertheless, with the second part of the dilemma, namely, the case in which they have read the Law.

They might say: “What follows from our having read the Law?” Therefore I ask whether you have read that the Law itself openly indicates that it is not to be retained. For it is written in the Law that Abraham had two sons.

Abraham certainly had many sons, but these two provided an appropriate figure for faith and the Law. These words, however, are not found in exactly this form in Genesis, though words of equal force are found there. Moses described these two sons in full, all the way to the end, which he did not do with the others.

Since Paul does not follow the allegory in every individual detail, it is good for us to explain it in the same words. Abraham, whose name is interpreted as “father of many nations,” having two sons—that is, two peoples—signifies God having two sons, namely the Gentile and the Jewish peoples. This does not mean that every individual in either people is a son of God, except those who are found worthy in either people.

Abraham had two sons: one from a slave woman, namely Ishmael from Hagar, and one from a free woman, namely Isaac from Sarah. The son from the slave woman signifies the Jewish people, the son of the slave woman—that is, of the Law. They are rightly called sons of the slave woman, since they served like slaves, through fear of punishment and through love of carnal things in carnal matters.

The son from the free woman signifies the faithful people, who serve God in the freedom of faith out of love, not out of fear or for temporal things, but for eternal things.

Although both were sons of Abraham, they were born in different ways. The one who was from the slave woman, namely Ishmael from Hagar, was born according to the flesh, because Hagar was young and fertile. Similarly, the legal people were born from the slave woman—that is, from the Law—according to the flesh, because they served in carnal matters and out of love for carnal things; if they sinned, they immediately feared being punished in the flesh.

But the son who was from the free woman, namely Isaac, was born from Sarah not according to the flesh. Sarah was an old woman and barren, but he was born through God’s promise. For God, as he had graciously promised, caused a son to be born through his power from a barren and decrepit woman.

Similarly, the faithful people who were from the free woman—that is, who were born from faith, which is free through love and not like the slave woman through fear—were born through the promise, because God had mercifully promised that he would bring about salvation through faith.

It was therefore through the promise because this people does not serve God for the desire of carnal things, which it sees, but out of love for spiritual things, which no one has seen, yet which it trusts it will possess solely through God’s promise.

All these things—namely, that Abraham had two sons, one from the slave woman according to the flesh and the other from the free woman through the promise—were spoken allegorically, that is, they are to be understood in another sense than the literal one given here. He himself, however, does not explain the allegory of each individual detail, but only that of the slave woman and the free woman.

They truly were spoken allegorically. For these two women, the slave woman and the free woman, are—or signify—the two Testaments, the Old and the New.

One Testament, namely the Law, generates sons into servitude, because they served both from fear of punishment and for the sake of carnal things. I say that this one was given on Mount Sinai, for the Law was given there in the desert.

“Sinai” is interpreted as “commandment,” and by the mountain we understand the height of pride, so that we may say: “Generating into servitude on Mount Sinai,” that is, in the pride of commandment. For the Jews, who alone possessed the Law, were proud, saying that they were God’s people and that others were not a people but dogs.

One Testament was given on Mount Sinai, which is Hagar—that is, the Testament is signified by Hagar. The grammatical reference is appropriate, since what follows is a feminine noun. Hagar is interpreted as “alienation,” indicating by the very name that the Old Testament was to be alienated and destroyed.

The same thing was signified by the fact that it was given not in the land of promise but in the desert: by the works of this Law they would never come into the true land of promise.

It truly generates into servitude, for Sinai is a mountain in Arabia. By the fact that, while they were in captivity, they received this Law, it was signified that the Law, given in captivity, generated them into servitude, and that by the works of the Law they would never come into freedom.

The allegorical meaning indicates the same thing. For Arabia is interpreted as “humility” or “affliction.” Thus we say: “Sinai is a mountain in Arabia,” that is, commandment and pride are found among the afflicted—or, which is the same thing, among the humbled.

For the fact that they took pride in the commandment and were very often afflicted by the Law like evil slaves shows that this Law had generated them into servitude.

Sinai is a mountain in Arabia, a mountain that is joined to—or assimilated to—Jerusalem, that is, to the Jewish people who saw God, because at that time the other nations did not know God.

I say “Jerusalem which now is,” that is, which sees and worships God in the present, not in spiritual things, and therefore will not see him in the future.

That mountain is joined to it, not because its roots extend all the way to Jerusalem, but because it is assimilated to the Jews. Through Mount Sinai their pride is signified, by which they took pride in the commandment; through Arabia their affliction is signified, by which, when they sinned through the Law, they were afflicted in the manner of slaves.

It is joined to Jerusalem, which now is and which serves through fear of punishment, not through love. It serves, I say, with its sons—that is, with proselytes who pass from paganism to circumcision. Or the whole Synagogue together serves with its own sons. Here it serves in one kind of servitude, there in another.

The Jerusalem which now is serves. But that Jerusalem which is above, which seeks not carnal but spiritual things, is free, because it does not serve out of fear but out of love; nor does it seek temporal things, but eternal things.

This is the Church of faith, which is the Jerusalem above and our mother. For the Church has brought us forth into the freedom of faith.

She is truly free, for she rejoices, breaks forth, and cries out. She is truly a mother, for her children are many. Thus he says: “Our mother is free.”

For it is written of her in Isaiah: “Rejoice, you barren woman, Sarah, who now do not give birth; break forth and cry out, you who are not in labor” (Isaiah IV, 1)—that is, you who do not even suffer the pains of giving birth.

Therefore rejoice, because your children, barren Sarah’s children, are more numerous than the children of her, Hagar, who now has a husband. Hagar had Abraham as a companion in cohabitation, but not in love. Sarah lacked Abraham’s cohabitation, yet possessed him in love, because he honored and loved her as his legitimate wife.

Isaiah, who lived many ages after Abraham, would not have spoken in this way about Sarah and Hagar without reason.

How, then, is this to be understood literally? She is truly free, for Isaiah says: “O barren Church! For there are some barren women who later give birth through grace, such as that same Sarah and Elizabeth.” Therefore he adds: “You barren woman who do not give birth, rejoice in your heart.”

Break forth also in outward joy and cry out—that is, invite others to rejoice with you. I say, you who not only do not give birth, but do not even experience the pains of giving birth—that is, who in the time of the Law, without hope of giving birth, do not strive toward it.

He has proved that she is free; he also proves that she is a mother. The wording nevertheless corresponds to what immediately precedes. Therefore rejoice, and so forth, because the children of the barren woman—that is, of the Church, which in the time of the Law was abandoned by God in terms of cohabitation, though not in love—are more numerous.

Even in the time of the Law, God loved the freedom of faith more than the servitude of the Law.

Her children, I say, are more numerous than the children of that Law which now has a husband. For at that time the Law generated many, but those who were faithful, such as Moses and the prophets, saw their hardness and did not even think of teaching them spiritual things, since they saw them daily transgressing carnal commandments.

At that time the Law had a husband, namely God, in terms of cohabitation, but not in love.

There are two mothers: one free, the other a slave. But we, brothers—that is, I and every faithful person—are children not of servitude but of promise, that is, through the grace promised by God, according to, or in the likeness of, Isaac, who was born not through the law of the flesh but through the power of the divine promise.

He shows that we were born in the likeness of Isaac because the same signs whose figure had preceded in him are seen today in the children of the Church.

And yet the connection of the text is contrary in the following way: Although we are children of promise, nevertheless, just as at that time, in the time of Abraham, the one who was born according to the flesh—that is, Ishmael—persecuted the one who was born according to the spirit, namely Isaac, so also now.

For Ishmael, being older, beat Isaac while he was still young, because he saw that Isaac would be his lord and heir. So too now those who are carnal persecute and afflict those who are spiritual. Just as Isaac was afflicted by Ishmael, so we who are spiritual are afflicted by those who are carnal.

Thus, brothers, it is evident from this that we are not children of the slave woman. Formerly we were slaves under the Law, but now we are children of the free woman, that is, of grace.

But he inserts something, saying: “Those who are according to the flesh persecute us, but this is not to be feared. They themselves will be cast out, while we will enter into the inheritance.”

This is what he says: “What does Scripture say?” In that same Moses it is found that, when Sarah saw Hagar and her son growing proud against her and Isaac, she said to Abraham: “Cast out the slave woman and her son” (Genesis XXI, 16).

Similarly, the children of grace say: “Lord, cast out the slave woman,” that is, the Law, “and her son,” that is, the Jewish people. For the son of the slave woman—that is, of the Law—will not be heir in the promised blessedness with the son of the free woman—that is, of faith—just as the son of Hagar the slave woman was not heir with the son of Sarah the free woman.

Therefore, brothers, we are no longer children of the slave woman, as has been explained, but of the free woman—through whose freedom, that is, through the freedom we possess, Christ, who possesses that same freedom, has set us free through it.

## CHAPTER V

“Stand firm, and do not again submit to the yoke of servitude. Behold, I, Paul, say to you that, if you are circumcised, Christ will benefit you nothing. I testify again to every person who circumcises himself that he is under obligation to perform the whole Law. You are severed from Christ, you who seek justification in the Law; you have fallen away from grace. For we, through the Spirit and by faith, await the hope of righteousness. For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision has any force nor uncircumcision, but faith, which works through love [affection]. You were running well; who has bewitched you [hindered you] from obeying the truth? Consent to no one. This persuasion is not from him who called you. A little leaven corrupts the whole lump (1 Corinthians V, 6). I am confident about you in the Lord that you will think nothing else. But whoever troubles you will bear the judgment, whoever he may be. But I, brothers, if I still preach circumcision, why do I still suffer persecution? Therefore the offense of the cross has been abolished. Would that those who trouble you would also cut themselves off! For you have been called to freedom, brothers; only do not give freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, but through the love of the Spirit serve one another.
