For the whole Law is fulfilled in one saying: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matthew XXII, 39). But if you bite and devour one another, take care that you are not consumed by one another. But I say in Christ: Walk by the Spirit, and you will not fulfill the desires of the flesh. For the flesh desires against the spirit, but the spirit against the flesh. For these oppose one another, so that you may not do whatever you wish. But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the Law. Now the works of the flesh are manifest: fornication, uncleanness, immodesty, lust, service of idols, sorceries, enmities, quarrels, rivalries, anger, fights, dissensions, factions, envies, murders, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these. I warn you, as I warned you before, that those who do such things will not obtain the kingdom of God. But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, long-suffering, gentleness, faith, modesty, self-control, chastity. Against such things there is no law. Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires (1 Peter II, 11). If we live by the Spirit, let us also walk by the Spirit. Let us not become desirous of empty glory, provoking one another and envying one another.”

## EXPOSITION

Although Christ was under the Law, the Law nevertheless did not rule over him who had no sin; rather, he did everything solely in freedom. And since we are children of the free woman and have apprehended freedom through Christ, as is plainly gathered from that same Law, it is madness that one who is free through faith should make himself a slave through the Law.

Therefore, because you are free, stand firm—that is, persevere in this freedom of faith—and do not again submit to the yoke of servitude, that is, do not again be worn down by the burden of the Law. “Again” is appropriate, because if you, already faithful, are circumcised, it is the same as turning back to the idols whom you formerly served.

They might say: “We do not wish to accept the whole Law, but only circumcision, which Abraham had, since he existed before the Law.”

Paul replies against this: “Do not submit to the yoke of the Law, because Christ”—that is, faith in Christ—“will benefit you nothing if you are circumcised.” And behold, I, Paul, whose authority is proclaimed everywhere, say and affirm this to you: if you are circumcised, the faith of Christ will benefit you nothing.

Not only because Christ will benefit you nothing, but also because of the unbearable burden of the Law, you ought not to be circumcised.

For he says: “I testify again”—either as I once testified when I was under the Law, or “again,” that is, a second time I bring this forward to dissuade you from the same thing which I dissuaded you from above. I testify to every person who circumcises himself that he is under obligation to perform the whole Law.

Circumcision demands that the remaining works of the Law follow, just as faith, after baptism, demands that works of faith follow. Do not think that you can be circumcised without bearing the burden of the Law in every respect.

Truly Christ will benefit you nothing; for if you are circumcised, you have been emptied of Christ—that is, faith in Christ has become empty for you.

They might say: “We would rather be emptied of Christ than fail to be circumcised, as God commanded.”

Paul replies: “Not only have you been emptied of Christ, but you have also fallen away from the grace of God, all of you who seek justification in the Law,” that is, who seek justification through the Law.

Here he carefully determines how he forbids circumcision: namely, so that through it they may not seek justification. Yet he allowed Timothy to be circumcised in order to remove suspicion from himself, while both Paul and Timothy understood that circumcision contributed nothing to righteousness.

Truly no one is justified in the Law. For we alone who are of faith await the hope of righteousness—that is, the blessedness hoped for on the basis of righteousness. And that our expectation is certain is evident from the fact that we await it through the Spirit, who indicates that we should hope in this way.

Therefore we have the hope solely from faith. For in Christ Jesus—that is, in faith in Christ Jesus—neither circumcision has any force nor uncircumcision, but faith alone. Yet faith must not be idle; it must work, not abusively, but through love of God and neighbor.

Faith alone has force in Christ, and in this faith you were running well—that is, you were working through love. But who hindered you by persuading you not to obey the truth which you learned from me?

But so that you may obey the truth, do not consent to any of the carnal people, because their persuasion is not from him—that is, it is not according to God—who calls you by his grace to the kingdom.

Therefore do not consent to them, because a little leaven—that is, either even the smallest consent, or mere persuasion, or those few people who are persuading you wrongly—corrupts the whole lump and makes it sour. The lump may mean either the whole Church or all their good works.

A little leaven certainly corrupts the whole lump; but you will not be corrupted. For I am confident in you, and this confidence is in the Lord—that is, through the grace of God working together with you—that you will think nothing other than what is sound and what I taught you.

You will think no other thought. But the one who troubles you—that is, who makes the purity of your faith turbid by mixing in unbelief—will bear the judgment, that is, will endure condemnation, even if he is Peter or an angel from heaven.

Now he responds to what the false apostles themselves had charged: that previously he had indeed destroyed circumcision, but that, after being corrected at Jerusalem by Peter and the others, he was now preaching circumcision.

He proves this false by saying: “They are troubling you, but I am not troubling you. If, however, brothers, I still preach circumcision, as they charge—still, that is, because when I was a Jew I preached it—if, I say, I still preach it in that way, why do I continue to suffer persecution from the Jews, as I have suffered from the beginning of my preaching?”

For, as they charge, if I preach circumcision, then the offense of the cross has been abolished. The Jews were offended by the fact that I preached that a person is justified through the cross alone. But if I were to add circumcision to the cross and say that justification comes from both, the Jews would be appeased toward me.

I am not troubling you; they are troubling you. And would that not merely the skin of the foreskin but those who trouble you might be completely cut off!

Paul does not mean the cutting off of bodily members. Rather, just as severed testicles do not procreate, so may these people be cut off, so that they may not be able to generate anyone in their error.

They certainly trouble you while they wish to bring you back into the servitude of the Law. For you, brothers, have been called into the freedom of God.

Only take care of this: do not give your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, that is, do not believe that, because of your freedom, you are permitted to sin more freely. Do not do this, but serve one another through the love of the Spirit—that is, act through spiritual love.
*[Source pagination follows the translated commentary in order: [Col. 0302A]–[Col. 0311C], with printed pages 219–225 retained as its sequential page boundaries.]*
He takes the opportunity to show them the ease of the new law, which is fulfilled in one saying, and on this same occasion again rebukes them for their detraction, saying: “Serve one another through love.” For the whole law is fulfilled in one saying, namely this: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself,” as we explained in the Epistle to the Romans (Rom. III). The law commands love; but if, despising the law, you bite one another by speaking against one another, and not only bite but also devour one another—that is, entirely consume your neighbor’s goods through envy—see that you are not consumed, that is, devoured by one another: you, because you speak against your neighbor, and he, because he speaks against you.

After sufficiently proving that the law is not to be observed, he now begins to commend faith and grace. The text is joined as follows: “See that you are not consumed according to the persuasion of the flesh, by biting and devouring one another; but I say to you: Walk by the Spirit,” that is, perfect yourselves by doing good according to what the spirit—that is, reason—urges you. “Walk,” I say, “by the Spirit,” and this in Christ, that is, doing only what is permitted through Christ, and nothing else, so that one acts according to reason. If you are in Christ, you will walk according to the Spirit.

Another good also results from this: although you perceive the desires of the flesh through its opposition, you will nevertheless not carry them out in action. Yet, even though you do not carry them out, the flesh still desires against the Spirit, and thus you feel the conflict. Or let us put it another way: I rightly speak of “the desires of the flesh,” for the flesh desires against the Spirit, and the Spirit—that is, reason—desires what is against the flesh. Truly, the flesh and the Spirit desire against one another. For these two—that is, flesh and Spirit—are opposed to one another, not flesh to flesh or spirit to spirit, but mutually: the flesh against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh. They are opposed in such a way that you do not do all the things you wish, whether you are carnal or spiritual. For no one is so just that he does not sometimes fall; and no one is so wicked that he does not at some time restrain himself from something that the flesh urges him to do.

He said that if we live, we can walk by the Spirit. For if we follow the Spirit, we do not carry out the desires of the flesh, because the flesh fights against the Spirit. He now wishes to distinguish this struggle of flesh and Spirit, saying: “The flesh is against the Spirit; the Spirit fights against the flesh.” For if you are led by the Spirit—that is, by reason—you are no longer under the law. The law was established to restrain sinners; but if you act according to the Spirit, you no longer sin, and whoever does not sin is free from the law. Whoever is led by the Spirit is not under the law; but whoever is led by the flesh is held captive under the law.

He expresses the same thing equivalently: the works of the Spirit bring no one under the law; but the works of the flesh are manifest, and there is no need to reproach them. Their disgrace and captivity are known to everyone. Therefore he does not take care to condemn the works of the flesh, because their names alone sufficiently indicate their foulness. The works of the flesh, I mean, are these: fornication, uncleanness, shamelessness, and lust.

He calls it fornication when one is polluted with prostitutes or with married persons; uncleanness is that foulness which occurs contrary to nature, as well as in incestuous kisses and polluted touching. He calls it shamelessness when someone is not a fornicator or unclean, but is not modestly restrained in speech, dress, or the movement of his limbs. He calls it lust the excess of the flesh, whether in gluttony or in intercourse. Such lust may also occur with one’s wife, if one uses her excessively.

[Col. 0312D] The works of the flesh also include the service of idols, sorceries, enmities—that is, prolonged hatreds—quarrels in words, and rivalries, whereby an envious person strives to appropriate another’s good for himself. There are also angers, that is, sudden disturbances of the mind; and from anger arise quarrels, when the matter is pursued with blows.

Again, there are dissensions, which often arise in the Church. There are also sects, for which the Greek has *haireseis* (“heresies”). There are also envies, that is, the evil jealousy of the mind: although a person knows that he will not obtain his neighbor’s possession, he nevertheless envies him and would not want him to have it.

Again, there are murders, drunkenness—that is, habitual drinking beyond measure—and revelries, and things like these, which I now warn you about, just as I warned you previously when I first preached to you, so that you might avoid them. For those who do such things will not obtain the kingdom of God, if they are found persisting in this conduct.

These, then, are the works of the flesh. But the works of the Spirit are as follows. He does not say “works,” but, to commend them, says “the fruit of the Spirit.” For it is beneficial and proper to enjoy these works. The fruit of the Spirit, I say, is love, that is, love of God and neighbor. From this love proceed joy and peace. He calls joy a cheerful conscience; peace is concord with all, arising from love.

The fruit of the Spirit is also patience, that is, hope. For if the reward is delayed, one nevertheless hopes no less and does not await it impatiently. The work of the Spirit is also endurance, by which we tolerate whatever adversities we suffer; goodness, that is, a pious affection of the mind, even when one has nothing to give; kindness, that is, generosity in sharing what one possesses; gentleness, whereby one is so approachable and agreeable to everyone; faith, by which one rightly believes in God; moderation, that is, restraint in words and actions; self-control, by which a person restrains himself even from what is permitted; and chastity, whereby one uses permitted things chastely, as a husband uses his wife.

These are the works of the Spirit, and against such things there is no law. As we said above, you are not under the law. These are the works of the flesh; these are the works of the Spirit. Those who belong to Christ perform the works of the Spirit. He says this as follows: “Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh,” because, so long as they are in Christ, they cannot incline any of their senses toward vices. I mean those who struggle against vices and desires. He understands vices as actions and desires as the will.

Let us crucify not only the flesh, so that we may not do evil, but let us also walk by the Spirit—that is, let us advance by doing good according to what reason admonishes us. It is right that we walk by the Spirit, because we live by the Spirit; and if we live by the Spirit, having been justified, it follows that we should also walk by the Spirit. A person lives through the justification of faith; he walks when he performs what faith requires.

And if we live and walk, let us not become desirous of empty things in this walk—that is, of worldly glory. It is not a sin to be praised when we act well; but if we desire to be praised, let us not become desirous of empty glory. I speak of those who desire this by provoking one another, because pride, which cannot tolerate an equal unless it is preferred above everyone, becomes angry and provokes conflict. And if we do not dare to provoke one another openly, let us at least not envy one another inwardly—that is, one another.

## CHAPTER VI

> “Brothers, if someone is overtaken in any trespass, you who are spiritual should restore such a person in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself, lest you also be tempted. Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ. For if anyone thinks himself to be something when he is nothing, he deceives himself. Let each person test his own work, and then he will have glory in himself alone, and not in another. For each person will bear his own burden. Let the one who is instructed in the word share in all good things with the one who instructs him. Do not be deceived. God is not mocked. For whatever a person sows, that he will also reap. For the one who sows in his flesh will from the flesh reap corruption; but the one who sows in the Spirit will from the Spirit reap eternal life. Let us not grow weary in doing good; for in due season we shall reap, if we do not grow weary. Therefore, while we have time, let us do good to everyone, and especially to those who belong to the household of faith. See with what large letters I have written to you with my own hand. For all who want to please in the flesh compel you to be circumcised, only so that they may not suffer persecution for the cross of Christ. For those who are circumcised do not themselves keep the law, but they want you to be circumcised so that they may boast in your flesh. But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world. For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision counts for anything, nor uncircumcision, but a new creation. And upon all who follow this rule, peace and mercy be upon them, and upon the Israel of God. From now on let no one trouble me. For I bear the marks of the Lord Jesus in my body. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, brothers. Amen.”

## EXPOSITION

After correcting and instructing the whole Church in common, he now admonishes the leaders separately, so that they may instruct sinners subject to them with gentleness. Conversely, he admonishes those subject to them to listen to their leaders with an even temper and complete obedience, saying: “Because you live by the Spirit, walk by the Spirit.” But you who are spiritual—that is, leaders—for every perfect person, even if he lacks an official position, is nevertheless a leader in relation to the imperfect—you, I say, who are spiritual: if someone is overtaken in any trespass, and it is no wonder that he sins, since he is human, for “overtaken” means not that he sinned deliberately, but that he did not know how to guard himself—you, I say, leaders, restore such a person in the spirit not of anger but of gentleness.

He now passes from the plural to the singular, speaking similarly to each individual leader: Correct the delinquent with gentleness, whoever you are, leader, considering yourself, lest you also be tempted in the same way. For God often mercifully arranges matters so that the person who angrily recoils from his neighbor’s fall is himself cast into the same fall, or into something worse.

And do not merely instruct the delinquent; also bear one another’s burdens—the leader the burden of the subordinate. Bear them, I say, by sharing his suffering, praying, and fasting, so that forgiveness may be granted him. Thus, by supporting one another in turn, you will fulfill the law of Christ. For Christ, who knew no sin, carried our sins on the cross and thereby brought this law upon himself: that one person should in this way bear the sin of his neighbor.

Consider yourself, lest you also be tempted. For if anyone acts without due reflection and thinks himself to be something, although in himself he is nothing—and if there is anything good in him, it is by grace—he deceives himself by thinking this way; that is, he is his own deceiver.

Do not be deceived, but let each person test, that is, examine, whether his work is worthy of approval. Then, having been approved, he will have glory only in himself—that is, with himself, in his conscience—and not in another, that is, not through the consideration and contempt of another. He ought to glory in himself, not in another. For each person, whether just or sinful, will on that day bear his own burden—that is, his own bundle, which his works deserve to gather, whether good or evil.

Or perhaps the discussion concerns only the sinner. You, as a just person, should not glory in the contempt of the sinner. For each sinner will bear his own burden, that is, the weight of his sin.

Having instructed the leaders concerning the kind of persons they should show themselves to be toward their subordinates, he admonishes the subordinates to obey their leaders reverently, saying: The leader should instruct the subordinate with gentleness.

But the one who is catechized—that is, instructed—even if not by the example of good works, at least by the word, should share with and obey the one who catechizes him in all the good things that he does and urges. I speak of the one who catechizes him, that is, who instructs him. I say: Share with those who instruct you, and do not err—that is, do not excuse yourselves by saying that one need not obey those who teach well in word but do not act accordingly. Do not fall into this error, because God is not mocked—that is, he cannot be deceived by a superficial pretext. If he could be deceived, he would be mockable. But truly he is not mocked, because whatever a person sows, that he will certainly reap.

And truly he will reap what has been sown, because the one who sows in his flesh—that is, who performs the corruptible desires of the flesh—will certainly reap corruption from the flesh, because he has sown corruption. But the one who sows in the Spirit—that is, according to reason—will reap spiritual things from the Spirit, namely eternal life.

After instructing the leaders separately and then the subordinates, he again admonishes the whole Church together, saying: You leaders, instruct your subordinates with gentleness. You subordinates, share in every good thing with those who instruct you. But let all of us, leaders and subordinates alike, do good equally and not grow weary in doing good.

Nor ought we to grow weary in working, because we shall reap the reward of our work in its proper time—that is, at the opportune time—if we do not grow weary in reaping. And because we shall reap without growing weary, therefore, while we have time for working—that is, in this world—let us do good to everyone, but especially to those belonging to the household of faith. For first we ought to provide what is necessary for the faithful, and afterward, if anything remains in abundance, also for unbelievers.

From this point the Apostle wrote the Epistle in his own hand, so that the Galatians would not doubt that this Epistle was Paul’s, since here he was destroying circumcision, about which the false apostles had told the Galatians that Paul now taught circumcision. Thus he says: So that you may believe these instructions to be mine, see with what letters I have written to you, from this point onward with my own hand, so that, by recognizing my handwriting, you may be certain that this Epistle is mine. And you ought to obey what I have written, not what they have written.

For all who wish to please those Jews in the flesh—that is, through carnal arguments—compel you to be circumcised. They compel you, certainly, because by persistent speech they urge you toward something they cannot prove by arguments. They compel you to be circumcised with this one aim: that they may not suffer persecution from the Jews because of the cross of Christ, which they preach. For the Jews readily allowed the cross of Christ to be preached together with circumcision.

Truly, they do this only so that they may not suffer persecution, because they do nothing out of love for the law. He says this as follows: These false teachers who are circumcised do not keep the law, but for this one reason they want you to be circumcised: so that they may boast before others in your circumcised flesh. For they say to them: “See how much increase your law has received through us.” Thus they boast in the flesh.

But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ. For I neither seek nor preach glory except that of the cross. “Through whom”—through the cross. For according to Priscian, *crux* (“cross”) is of uncertain gender; and according to Haimo, in Greek it is masculine, and therefore the translator did not wish to change the grammatical reference. “Through whom,” that is, through the cross, or through Christ crucified—the meaning is the same.

The world has been crucified to me, so that the world offers me nothing more of its delights. I too have been crucified to the world; and if the world offers me anything, the cross of Christ has so strengthened and bound me that I cannot turn away from it.

Therefore I glory only in the cross, because in Christ Jesus neither circumcision is of any value nor uncircumcision, but only a new creation—that is, faith, which renews the mind and also makes the flesh free from sins. He did not add “uncircumcision” because he thought it contributed anything to faith, but to show that in Christ circumcision contributes no more than uncircumcision.

I glory only in the cross; and upon all who have followed this rule of the cross, so that they glory only in it, there is peace—upon those Galatians who have not sinned—and mercy, that is, a second forgiveness, upon those who have fallen. And not only upon them, but also upon all Israel—not the Israel that is of the flesh, but the Israel of God.

Seek glory only in Christ. From now on—that is, concerning circumcision, which I exclude—let no one trouble me. Or understand it this way: You have troubled me in the past, but from now on, see that no one troubles me. You ought not to trouble me, for I bear in my body the marks of the Lord Jesus Christ.

A mark is called a *stigma*, a sign made with a heated iron. Here Paul, enduring chains and other sufferings for Christ, bore in his body the marks—that is, the signs—that he was a soldier of Christ.

May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, brothers. Amen.

# ON THE EPISTLE TO THE EPHESIANS

## ARGUMENT OF PAUL’S EPISTLE TO THE EPHESIANS

The Ephesians are Asians. After receiving the word of truth, they persevered in faith. The Apostle praises them highly, writing to them from the city of Rome, from prison, through Tychicus the deacon.

## PROLOGUE OF BLESSED BRUNO ON THE SAME EPISTLE

Ephesus is a city in Asia. This is not the Asia that divides the world, but a certain province in Greece, having seven cities, of which Ephesus is the metropolis. To these cities John, exiled to the island of Patmos, wrote the Apocalypse.

After hearing the word of faith from Paul, these Ephesians believed and commendably performed works of faith. While the Apostle was in prison at Rome, he wrote this Epistle to them, carefully taking precautions lest, because they had persevered well in faith, they should become proud and attribute this to their own virtue. What the mercy of God had begun in them, the Apostle was piously bringing to completion.

In this Epistle he treats the benefits of God. He discusses them in this way, showing that they arise not from human merit but from God’s good pleasure. He also shows that God’s benefits are such that no one rises to such perfection in them that there is not still something left for him to ascend toward. For just as a person always has somewhere to fall, so he always has somewhere to grow.

He also discusses how fathers ought to preside over their sons and sons submit to their parents. Likewise he speaks of masters and servants, and of wives and husbands, and how, according to their condition and sex, they ought to serve one another in mutual union.

He treats the benefits of God in this way so that the Ephesians may not find in the good they do an occasion for pride, since they hear that they possess nothing from themselves but everything from the mercy of God. Again, he does so lest they grow sluggish in doing good when they hear that they can still find further growth in the service of God.

As Paul was departing from them, he summoned these Ephesians together and said to them: “Behold, I have delivered sound faith to you; see that you do not make it void. For from now on I am free; but if you act wrongly, God will require this from you” (Acts XX:27). Because of these words and others like them, they were more diligent in taking precautions for themselves.

# EPISTLE TO THE EPHESIANS

## CHAPTER I

> “Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ through the will of God, to all the saints who are in Ephesus and the faithful in Christ Jesus: grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
>
> “Blessed be God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ, just as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, so that we should be holy and blameless in his sight in love. He predestined you for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ, for himself, according to the purpose of his will, to the praise of the glory of his grace, with which he favored us in his beloved Son. In him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace, which he made abound toward us in all wisdom and prudence, making known to us the mystery of his will, according to his good pleasure, which he purposed in him, in the dispensation of the fullness of times, to restore all things in Christ, things in heaven and things on earth, in him.
>
> “In him we have also been called by lot, having been predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will, so that we might be to the praise of his glory—we who first hoped in Christ. In him you also, when you heard the word of truth, the Gospel of your salvation, received it. In him also, when you believed, you were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise, who is the pledge (*arrha*) of our inheritance, for the redemption of the acquired possession, to the praise of his glory.
>
> “Therefore I too, hearing of your faith which is in Christ Jesus and your love toward all the saints, do not cease giving thanks for you, making remembrance of you in my prayers, so that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give you the Spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him, with the eyes of your heart enlightened, so that you may know what is the hope of his calling, what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance among the saints, and what is the surpassing greatness of his power toward us who believe, according to the working of the might of his power, which he worked in Christ Jesus, raising him from the dead and seating him at his right hand in the heavenly places, above every principality, authority, power, and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the age to come. He subjected all things under his feet and gave him as head over the whole Church, which is his body and the fullness of him who fills all things in all.”

## EXPOSITION

“Paul,” and so forth. Paul is the apostle of Christ Jesus, whom Christ Jesus consecrated as Apostle to the Gentiles. From this it is evident that he is your Apostle. Paul, I say, the apostle of Christ, not through his own merit but solely through the will and good pleasure of God. Thus you too should attribute whatever good there is in you not to your own merit but to the grace of God.

Paul, I say, the apostle, writes by the will of God to all the saints—that is, to the more perfect, who have been sanctified in virtues. He also writes to the faithful, that is, to the less perfect, who nevertheless have preserved the integrity of faith. He writes to the faithful in Christ Jesus, that is, to those who keep the faith of Christ Jesus.

He speaks to the saints and faithful who are in Ephesus. Paul wishes this for them: may enduring grace be yours—you who have not sinned—and may those who have at least fallen in venial matters have the grace of a second forgiveness. May peace also be yours from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, as has often been explained.

To show that every benefit comes from the mercy of God, he first gives thanks to God for his benefits, saying: “Blessed be God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.” If he is the Father of Christ, and we are sons of Christ through faith, then through Christ he is our Father. Our blessing of God is nothing other than praising and magnifying his glory. God’s blessing of us, however, is our exaltation and the advancement of our salvation.

Here he now sets forth two divine elections concerning us. The first is the election by which he chose from eternity what we would become; the second is the election in time, when he mercifully infused into us the Spirit who cooperates with us. He joins to these the completions of both elections.

He first sets forth the one that is completed later in time, in which we are to recover immortality and freedom from suffering. Because this is more worthy, he places it before the election completed when the soul is freed from the burden of sins through the mercy of God, saying: “Blessed be God who blessed”—that is, exalted—“us.”

He used the past tense to designate what is future, in order to show that he is as certain of this future blessing as someone is certain of what he sees to have passed. He also speaks this way because he understood that the saints already reign with Christ according to their souls.

“God blessed us with every blessing.” “Every,” because it is sufficient. “Blessing,” I say, “spiritual.” Although this blessing is made according to the body, it is nevertheless spiritual, because just as the human spirit will be sustained by the mere vision of the glory of God, so the body will be satisfied by the nourishment of seeing God.

“Blessing,” I say, already possessed by some according to their souls and to be fully honored by all the saints, not on this earth but in the heavenly places, so that this blessing may be commended also by the dignity of its place. “He blessed us,” I say, “in Christ Jesus,” that is, through the working of Christ Jesus, in whom the Father works all things.

Having shown the fulfillment of one election, he adds the election that is fulfilled at this time according to the justification of the soul, determining that the fulfillment mentioned above comes from the mercy of God through election. He continues: “Thus God blessed us by grace, just as by grace alone he chose us before the foundation of the world.” Here it is clear that no human merit preceded.

He chose us, I say, in Christ himself, in whom he made all things, or in order that we might remain in him. He chose us for this purpose: that we should be holy and blameless—holy through the establishment of good things, blameless through the cleansing away of evil. We were to be such in his sight, that is, so that we might behold him alone and pay attention to nothing in the world. Or “in his sight” means “that we might be seen by him.”

He chose us, I say, in love, that is, in love alone. Having spoken of the election that is fulfilled here according to the justice of the soul, he adds the election whose fulfillment he has already placed first, saying: He chose us to be holy, because he also predestined us—that is, ordained us beforehand from eternity, or prepared us in time—for the adoption of sons that we were to possess.

He did not wish to say “immortality,” but, in order to attribute everything to the grace of God, he said “adoption,” that is, the incorruption of sons granted to us solely by God’s adoption. This adoption, I say, is to be obtained through Jesus Christ. We are to come into him, so that, just as he is immortal and free from suffering, so also may we be immortal and free from suffering.

He predestined us according to the purpose of his will, that is, according to his will that had been purposed. “Purposed” means either ordained in this way from eternity, or offered to all who are to be saved, unless their fault should impede it. He predestined us, I say, solely by his will, to the praise of the glory of his grace—that is, so that his grace might be praised, in which grace there is a manifold glory.

There are certain graces of God, such as the temporal things that he mercifully provides; these are not things in which one should glory. But in incorruption there is manifold glory. We ought to have said this because at first he begins generally with blessings that are given publicly to all the just. Then he descends to those given to the apostles. Third, he adds those which God gave to the Ephesians.

Having set forth the two elections and first mentioned the completion of the more worthy one, he adds the completion of the other, saying: “In this grace he favored us,” that is, made us acceptable, “in his beloved Son,” that is, in faith in his beloved Son. Because he loves the Son, he also loves us as sons of his Son.

In this Son we have redemption—not through a worthless price, but through the blood poured out by the Son. In him we also have forgiveness of sins. All have redemption, because a sufficient price for the redemption of all was given, if they wished to accept it. But only those have forgiveness who have shown themselves worthy of Christ’s redemption.

We have forgiveness according to his riches, that is, according to his grace, in which he is rich because he forgave both original and actual sins, whether they were few or many, all without distinction.

Having listed the benefits given publicly to the saints, he descends from this common level to the apostles, saying: This grace abounded in us apostles, above—that is, more than in the others. And this was fitting, because others were to receive from them.

It abounded, I say, in all wisdom and prudence. By wisdom he means knowledge of divine things; by prudence, as it were, foresight, by which Paul knew well how to provide for his churches. “All” does not mean that they knew everything, but that whatever was necessary for them, whether divine or human, was readily available to them.

It abounded so greatly that he made known to us apostles the mystery—that is, the secret—of his will, namely the order of human redemption. It is called a mystery, as though a secret, because it is permitted to be seen not by everyone but by a few.

He would make this mystery known, namely, that he would restore all things according to his good pleasure, not according to human merit, because there was no human merit on account of which he might have good pleasure in Christ, whom he purposed—that is, ordained—from eternity. Or “purposed” means that God openly set forth his good pleasure, if he should will it.

He purposed it in the dispensation of the fullness of times, that is, in the fullness of time. For the time of grace is called the fullness of times. Or it is called this because all things previously foretold and awaited were completed in him through Christ. Or “fullness” means the end and completion of the times which God had established should precede the time of grace.

“Fullness,” I say, suitably dispensed. For first God wished to test human beings, so that it might be shown that through free choice and natural law they could accomplish nothing. Then he gave the written law, through which they again proved unable to escape sin. And after humanity had recognized itself to be powerless on every side, God finally and appropriately supplied grace, by whose help a person could do what he could not do by himself.

He restored all things in Christ—that is, through Christ—things in heaven that were imperfect and things on earth that had been corrupted by sin. For God made and redeemed humanity for this purpose: that, through humanity’s salvation, he might restore the number diminished among the angels.

For this reason Christ also took flesh: to restore corrupted humanity to righteousness. But this restoration is understood in different ways. Christ was the cause of the restoration of the angels, though not their necessity. The angels were pure, although diminished by the loss of certain companions. Christ, however, was both the cause and the necessity of the restoration of human beings: the cause, so that through him the loss among the angels might be made good; the necessity, because unless humanity were restored by Christ, it would remain lost through sin.

He restored, I say, the things that are on earth, in such a way that they remain in him. For unless they remain in his faith, their restoration will be nothing.

Or understand it another way: he restored in Christ the things that are in heaven, that is, the saints whose souls already reign with Christ in heaven; and the things that are on earth, in him—that is, the just, who, although they are still held by earthly conduct, are already in him through the purity of their life.

The Ephesians might say: “You apostles have indeed been called to such a height that it would be foolish even to suppose that we could reach it.” Paul replies: We apostles too have been called in this Christ, not through our merit or nobility of birth, but by lot—that is, by divine election. “Lot” is called divine election, as when human judgment fails, people turn to God’s choice.

We were called not only by grace but also predestined—that is, prepared—according to his purpose, that is, according to what his goodness purposed concerning us. His goodness, I say, which, just as it works these things in us, so works all things in each person according to the counsel of its will, that is, according to its will acting with counsel and discernment.

Or understand it this way: he not only calls us by grace, but also works in us all the things that follow the calling, according to the counsel of his will, as has been said.

We were called and predestined so that we might be to the praise of his glory, that is, so that we might glorify God with praise worthy of him, who wishes to be praised by us. This is not because our praise contributes anything to him, but so that he may have a reason for doing good to us.

We are, I say, those who hoped in Christ before you. We preceded you only in time; but if you wish, we do not precede you in glory. Indeed, perhaps you will precede us, since the gifts of God depend solely on election, not on lineage or priority in time.

He now descends from the apostles to the benefits of God bestowed upon the Ephesians, saying: In this Christ you were called just as we were, and predestined—not through your merit, but when you heard the word of truth, because by grace alone he sent preachers to you and caused you, inwardly inspired, to hear.

You were not only called; in this Christ, when you believed, you were also sealed, so that you might appear as belonging to the army of Christ, by the Holy Spirit. The Spirit, I say, is the Spirit of promise—that is, either the Spirit whom God promised us, or the Spirit who, already deifying us according to the soul, promises us the immortality of the body in the future.

This Spirit is the pledge—that is, the earnest and beginning—of the inheritance promised to us and to be possessed in future glory. You were sealed for redemption, that is, so that you might appear among those whom Christ redeemed. Redemption, I say, of the acquired possession. Through this redemption we acquire God, and God acquires us [the text apparently omits *nos*, “us”].

You were called and sealed, and so forth, for the praise of his glory, that is, so that his glory might be praised through you.

He now determines his purpose, saying: Because you were called, believed, and were sealed with the Holy Spirit, therefore I—and the saints who are with me—give thanks for you, and in giving thanks I do not cease.

Here he makes it clear that they should not become sluggish through confidence in their righteousness, but should work at every hour toward an increase of perfection.

I, I say, do not cease, hearing of your faith which is in Christ Jesus. This refers to the less perfect, concerning whom he said at the beginning, “the faithful in Christ Jesus.” I also hear of your love toward all the saints. This refers to the more perfect, concerning whom he likewise said, “all the saints.”

I do not cease giving thanks for you, making remembrance of you in my prayers, for the good things you are to receive. It is as though he said: Just as I understand the good things you have already received to come from the grace of God, so I think of all the things you will receive.

I make remembrance of you so that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ—who, according to his human nature, is Christ’s God—and the Father of his glory—for Christ, according to the divinity that is glory in him, is the Son of God—may give you the Spirit of wisdom and revelation, so that you may understand the mysteries of God when they are revealed.

Wisdom, I say, and revelation possessed in the knowledge of him, so that you may know God and his mysteries.

He may also grant you enlightened eyes—not, I mean, of the body, but of your heart. Here he touches upon the foolish error of certain people (especially pagans) who, in their primitive [Col. 0322D] faith, accustomed as they were to handle their idols, which they held in their hands, 234 imagined in their blind minds that God was something of this kind, something that could be seen with the eyes of the flesh and touched with the hands. May he grant you enlightened eyes, so that you may know what a thing hope is—that is, how worthy and how powerful it is. Not only the thing hoped for, but merely to hope is blessed. What is the hope of his calling—that is, of the thing to which he calls us—or of those who are called, that is, his elect. And what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance—that is, how worthy his inheritance is, in which there are riches, meaning no want but complete abundance. In it there is also glory, meaning enduring joy without any mixture of pain. I speak of the inheritance to be distributed among all the saints. And so that you may know what is the greatness [Col. 0323A] of his power—that is, his great and incomprehensible power. Although this greatness is to be manifested through all the saints, it will nevertheless be pre-eminent in us apostles, who believed before the others. And that God works this power in us, I prove by the fact that he has already worked it in Christ. He says this as follows: I affirm that this power is to be manifested in us according to the working of the power of his might—that is, according to his power working potentially—which power he exercised in Christ. And he explains this power, proving by this that he both can and will work in us in the same way. He exercised his power in Christ, raising him from the dead, by which he will also raise us, and it is apparent that he is able to do so. And, having raised him—that is, Christ—he set him at his right hand, that is, [Col. 0323B] at an equality with himself in the heavenly places, and thus above every principality, authority, power, and dominion.

Here we have four orders of angels; and from what follows, “every name,” we understand the remaining orders. The name that is named—that is, that can be named—not only in this age, but also whatever will be named in the future. He added this lest someone object to him: “According to the little that you now know about the angels, I grant that Christ is placed above them; but according to what you will know more fully about them in the future, Christ’s flesh will not be placed above them.” Against this he says: He has placed him above all, not only above what is named in this age, but also above everything that will be known about the angels in the future, and he has subjected everything to him [Col. 0323C]. For some are placed above many who, although inferior, are nevertheless not subject to them. Hence he says: “He subjected all things beneath his feet” (Psalm VIII, 8), that is, with such complete subjection that the one who is laid beneath the feet—or beneath the feet, that is, beneath the humanity of Christ—[has had] all things subjected.

Someone might say: “And what do you prove by this, if he placed the raised Christ above all things and subjected all things to him?” “By this,” Paul says, “I prove it well: God gave Christ himself as head over the whole Church; and this Church is the body of Christ himself. Do you suppose that he remains glorious in the head but inglorious in the body?” The Church is his body, and his fullness is Christ, who is fulfilled through it. For unless the righteous are raised, proceeding all the way to the final righteous person, the body of Christ remains incomplete. Although Christ is fulfilled by the fullness of the Church, he himself is nevertheless all things—that is, every perfection—in all, that is, in each of its members, because the members themselves cannot fulfill him except through him.

## CHAPTER II

“And you he made alive together, when you were dead in your offenses and sins, in which you once walked according to the age of this world, according to the prince of the power of this air, the spirit who now works in the sons of unbelief; among whom we also all once lived in the desires of our flesh, doing the will of the flesh and of our thoughts. And we were by nature children of wrath, just as the others also were [Col. 0324A]. But God, who is rich in mercy, because of his exceedingly great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead in sins, made us alive together with Christ, by whose grace you have been saved. And he raised us up together and made us sit together in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus, so that in the ages to come he might show the abundant riches of his grace in goodness toward us in Christ Jesus. For by grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not from yourselves; for it is God’s gift, not from works, so that no one may boast. For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared so that we might walk in them. Therefore remember that once you Gentiles in the flesh—who were called uncircumcision by that which is called circumcision, made in the flesh by human hands [Col. 0324B]—were at that time without Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel and strangers to the covenants, having no hope of the promise, and without God in this world. But now in Christ Jesus you, who once were far away, have been brought near in the blood of Christ. For he himself is our peace, who made both one and, by abolishing the middle wall of the dividing barrier, the enmity in his flesh, abolished the law of commandments in decrees, so that he might create the two in himself as one new man, making peace, and reconcile both in one body to God through the cross, killing the enmity in himself. And coming, he proclaimed peace to you who were far away, and peace to those who were near, because through him we both have access to the Father in one Spirit [Col. 0324C]. Therefore you are no longer strangers and foreigners, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household, built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the chief cornerstone. In him the whole construction, joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord; in him you too are built together into a dwelling-place [tabernacle] of God in the Holy Spirit.”

## EXPOSITION

Above he said that the Ephesians were called by God’s election and sealed with the Holy Spirit, and that he prayed for them so that what God had mercifully begun in them he might perfect by daily increase. After declaring them so worthy in this newness of grace, he recalls to them the former [Col. 0324D] state they had possessed in sins, so that, remembering their uncleanness, they would not dare to presume except upon the grace of God, as though they had acquired some newness by their own merit.

Again, he recalls to them their state of unbelief for this reason: when they see that God’s grace has drawn them from unrighteousness to righteousness, they may be certain that, if they now labor as righteous people, God—who bestowed grace upon them when they were unrighteous—will grant it much more abundantly and willingly to those who have already been justified, if they wish to merit it.

The text may be joined as follows: We apostles believed, and you likewise believed; or in this way: God raised Christ from the dead, and likewise raised you from the death of sin; or we can construe it with the verb that follows below: He made Christ head over the Church, and he made you alive together with Christ. However it is joined [Col. 0325A], the sentence nevertheless remains suspended where he says: He gave Christ as head over the Church, and he made you its members.

You, I say, when you were dead in offenses and sins. You were dead because you were so buried with sin that no human power could escape its snare. He calls them “offenses” when, by failing to do what God commands, we abandon it. He calls those acts “sins”—fornication, theft, and the like. “Your sins,” I say, that is, those which, by becoming accustomed to them, you had already made almost your own.

He explains how they had been in sins, saying: In those sins you once—that is, in the time of unbelief—walked, that is, you were precipitated from evil into worse, according to the age of this world, that is, following worldliness, which is never concerned with God but always occupied with worldly things [Col. 0325B]. And, to make the sin even more serious, he adds that they walked not only according to the age of the world but also according to the prince of the spirits—that is, according to the devil, who is prince and holds authority over the other evil spirits; or “according to the prince of the spirit,” if we understand it collectively, as meaning the prince of demons; or “according to the prince of spirits,” that is, of the other demons.

For just as among the good angels some are set over others and some are subject, so the same distinctions exist among the evil spirits, although one alone is believed to be set over them all. “The prince,” I say, “of the power of this air,” that is, he who has power in this air. For he often stirs up winds and storms in the air by which he may harm human beings and the fruits of the earth, such as the wind which, coming from the region of the desert, overturned the house and crushed Job’s children [Col. 0325C] (Job I, 19), although it is believed to have been sent only by God’s permission.

God arranged for these evil spirits to dwell in the air for this reason: if they were on earth together with human beings, they would corrupt the fruits of the earth and afflict the people themselves intolerably. By calling them spirits, he wishes to make people watchful, so that they may act carefully, because the enemy who threatens is invisible. By saying that they are in the air, he again warns us of the same thing, because the one lying in wait is near.

The devil, who is their prince, now works in the sons of unbelief, when God’s grace has freed you from him—that is, in those regarding whose salvation we despair. For the Spirit signified to Paul in whom he ought to labor and in whom he ought not, since he knew that their heart was impenitent. Or: “in the sons of unbelief,” who despair of salvation. For when they hear that they will rise again and ascend to heaven, they judge this foolish and therefore refuse to convert.

And since God’s grace has drawn you from such great sins to righteousness, see to it that, at any time, by presuming upon yourselves, you do not diminish God’s grace. That they can attain an increase of perfection, he indicates in what follows, as though answering the Ephesians who objected to him: “We were previously weighed down by so great a burden of sin; it is not permitted us to hope for any perfection, and it is enough if in some way we can be saved.”

To remove this objection, Paul makes himself and the apostles equal with them, because before faith they too had likewise been in sins, though in a different manner, as the following passage will show. Hence he says: In those sins we apostles also, just as all you Ephesians—including Peter—once, that is, before faith, lived. Truly in sins; for we lived in the desires of our flesh, desiring what the flesh suggested. And not only in desires, but also doing the will of the flesh in deed, such as eating to excess and indulging in luxury. We also did the will of our thoughts, in matters in which the flesh does not take such delight—for example, laboring for worldly glory—or, at the prompting of greed, enduring much in order to amass much.

And not only were we involved in these actual sins, but we Jews were also children of wrath, that is, born to endure punishment, “by nature,” that is, on account of original sin—“we Jews, just as the others,” although at that time we falsely supposed that through circumcision we were cleansed from Adam’s sin. The wrath of God is nothing other than punishment.

If we connect this with what he said—“We believed, and you believed”—or with “Raising Christ, he also raised you,” then the sentence is well completed here. But if the construction is extended farther down to “made alive together,” the sentence is not yet finished when it says: “When you were dead, he made you alive together with Christ.” It was God who made you alive together. Or, if the sentence ends there, we shall continue it in this way: We indeed were in sins, but God, who is rich and abundant in mercy—for his mercy is over all his works (Psalm CXLIV, 9)—God, certainly, because of his exceedingly great love, that is, his incomprehensible love, with which he loved us [Col. 0326B].

They might suppose: “He loved us after we had been justified, but not that he loves anyone in sin.” To this Paul replies: I say that he loved us even when we were dead in sins. Lest it seem absurd that God is said to love a human being in sins: he always loves his creature everywhere, but he hates the evil that is in it.

God, I say, because he loved us, made us alive together—that is, he made us live through the righteousness of the soul—with Christ, that is, in the likeness of Christ, so that, just as he is righteous, so also are we righteous. By whose grace, namely God’s, you also, just as we, have been saved—that is, made alive through the righteousness of the soul. Or, if the construction remains suspended below, so that we say, “He made us and you alive together with Christ,” then we shall say that “by whose grace you have been saved” refers to future salvation.

He made us alive together in the first resurrection of the soul, and he also raised us together in the second resurrection of the bodies [Col. 0326D]. Because of the certainty he possesses concerning what will happen, he signifies the future by the past tense. And having raised us together with Christ, he made us sit together with him, so that we would already reign in rest. He made us sit with Christ in the heavenly places, so that this blessedness might also be commended by its location.

He made us sit with Christ in Christ Jesus, and with him and through him. For this reason he made us alive together and made us sit with him after raising us, so that through this he might show in the coming ages—that is, in the future ages—the riches of his grace, that is, his rich grace, abundant in us. I speak of grace made in goodness, that is, solely from his good pleasure, because no prior merit preceded the deserving of grace. “Goodness,” I say, made toward us, that is, which surpassed us, because it is so great that our understanding is not sufficient to grasp it [Col. 0327A].

And all this, I say, is in Christ Jesus; for in him and through him God works all these things in us. God therefore wished these things to become known to those who would come after, so that a human being might understand how much he could hope for—if he wished—from God’s goodness.

Now he introduces what appears to be a human merit, namely faith, and shows that it is not a merit. Truly, it is by goodness that you have been saved, that is, justified. I grant also that you may add “through faith”; for faith is not from yourselves, as though you had merited having faith. Truly faith is not from yourselves, since it is God’s gift and not from your works. Therefore God wished everything to be from grace and nothing from works, so that no one might boast. Seeing the fall of the angel and that of humanity to have arisen from pride, he wished especially to guard human beings against pride.

And just as faith is from God’s gift, so are the works that follow faith from God’s grace [Col. 0327B]. I rightly say this so that no one may boast in faith; for even in the works that follow faith, God did not leave human beings anything of which they could boast. He says this as follows: We are his workmanship, God’s own work, created when we were nothing in the good, in Christ—that is, through Christ Jesus—for good works, which works God prepared for us so that we might walk in them, progress through him, and grow.

Or “workmanship” may be an ablative: we are created in Christ through God’s workmanship, that is, through God’s work. Nothing is changed by this.

Above he said: We were in sins just as you were. Now he defines this by saying that the Jews had not sinned as gravely as the Gentiles. Nevertheless, although before faith even the despised Jews detested the Gentiles, God, without distinction of persons, made them equal—not with those who had previously reproached them, but with the saints and the perfect.

By this he proves both that they are greatly indebted to God’s grace and that, if they wish, they can safely labor for an increase of righteousness. He says: Therefore, so that none of you may boast, remember that once, in the time of unbelief, you Gentiles were such as you had been born in sin, in the flesh, that is, in works of the flesh. You, I say, who were called “uncircumcision,” that is, uncleanness itself, by that circumcision—that is, by the Jews—which is called circumcision, that is, cleanness itself.

And this amounts to nothing, because this circumcision was in the flesh, not in the heart, and was made by the hand of anyone at all, not by the Holy Spirit. Remember also that at that time of unbelief [Col. 0327D] you were without Christ, because Christ was not promised to you. You were also alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, that is, from the Jewish people; for at that time they did not live together with you—or, if perhaps you lived among them as proselytes, you were strangers to the covenants, that is, unstable, being led now toward the law and now away from it.

He says “covenants” in the plural because Moses had his own covenant, Isaiah his own, and each prophet his own covenant. At that time you also had no hope of the promise made to Abraham, for at that time it was not permitted the Gentiles to hope for salvation. And you were without God, worshiping idols. You, I say, were in this world, that is, clinging to worldly things.

Formerly you were such, but now you, who once were far from God and from the Jews, have been brought near [Col. 0328A], both groups in Christ Jesus, that is, through Christ Jesus. And he specifies how this occurred through Christ: in the blood, that is, through the shedding of Christ’s blood.

He proves this concerning both groups, but first concerning the Jews, saying: You have truly been brought near to the Jews, because he himself is our peace, that is, he made us—Gentiles and Jews—peaceful together. He makes the two, that is, Jew and Gentile, one through unity of faith, conduct, and sacrifice.

He made them one in this way: by abolishing the middle wall, that is, the wall placed in the middle that separated one from the other. This wall existed on the side of the Jews as their observances, and on the side of the Gentiles as the worship of idols. He abolished this wall of theirs when he abolished both idolatry and the Jewish rites.

He calls the wall a barrier. According to some, a barrier is a wall firmly joined and connected. This wall was a barrier—that is, strong and difficult to destroy—because the Jews defended their rites by the authority of the law and the prophets. The Gentiles, through philosophy, defended their own practice, in which they had become wickedly accustomed to live. Or “barrier” is said of a heap of stones gathered together without mortar.

In this way that wall was a barrier, that is, weak and easy for Christ to demolish, like a dry heap of stones; and, by abolishing the middle wall, he abolished in his flesh, which he assumed, the enmity between the two peoples. For once the rites of the Jew and the Gentile had been destroyed, there was no longer any basis for their being enemies of one another.

He shows how he abolished the enmity on the side of the Jews, whose system offered the stronger opposition; but because the Gentiles had no such system, he added nothing concerning them. He abolished the enmity by abolishing the law of carnal commandments through decrees, that is, through commandments established by deliberate judgment. Thus he abolished on the one side the law and on the other the idol, so that he might create the two—that is, Jew and Gentile—both in himself.

And because he could still create them in himself while they remained divided, he adds: Let him create them, I say, making peace, that is, reconciling them to one another. He then explains in what he made peace: making peace, I say, in himself as one new man.

He calls him “new” because he is the man of grace and therefore new. For if he were legal, he would be opposed to the Gentile; and if, again, he were Gentile, he would be opposed to the Jew, and neither would agree with his enemy.

He has proved that the Gentile has been brought near to the Jew; he proves that the same Gentile has been brought near to God, saying: And therefore he abolished the enmity so that he might reconcile both to God—that is, Jew and Gentile—joined together in one body, that is, in the Church. He adds the manner of reconciliation. He reconciles them, I say, by Christ himself killing in himself the enmity that existed between God and humanity. He did this in himself through the cross, that is, through the death of the cross [Col. 0328D].

All these things would have been of little benefit unless they had been proclaimed. Therefore he adds: And Christ himself, coming in the flesh, proclaimed through the apostles the peace restored with God to you Gentiles, who had been far from God, because you were without Christ and without God in this world. He also proclaimed peace to those—that is, to the Jews—who were near, because they worshiped God.

He caused this to be preached because through Christ himself both Jew and Gentile have access to God the Father, both placed in one Spirit of faith, whereas previously one had been in the spirit of the law and the other in the spirit of an idol. And because, placed in the same Spirit, we both have access to God, therefore you Gentiles, Ephesians, are no longer strangers to the covenants, as they used to reproach you.

And you are no longer foreigners, that is, you are no longer called proselytes. For although at that time they were stable in the law, they were nevertheless always called newcomers. You are not strangers but fellow citizens—not of those who reproached you, but of the saints, that is, of all the perfect.

And you are not foreigners but members of the household, that is, natural members of a household—not of their household, but members of God’s household. You, I say, are built above the present foundation. Today piety is built; tomorrow humility will be built upon it. And thus you are built above the foundation, that is, the teaching of the apostles and prophets, upon whose teaching the Church was founded.

Or “above the foundation” means Christ, upon whom the apostles and prophets themselves were founded. You have been built, I say, with Christ Jesus existing as the stone—because of its firmness—chief, that is, bringing your righteousness to completion; angular, that is, joining the two peoples, Jew and Gentile, to himself.

We do not know with certainty where this stone was literally situated. Nevertheless, we believe that it existed, since it could not suitably be placed until the completion of both walls; but at the top, with marvelous fittingness, it cemented the two walls together. This stone signified Christ, who joins Jew and Gentile in the perfection of faith.

Just as Christ is the supreme completer of righteousness, so he is also its beginning. He says this as follows: In this stone the whole construction, built through faith, grows through activity [Col. 0329C] into a holy temple, so that the human being may be a temple in which God dwells. “Holy,” I say, “in the Lord,” that is, through the Lord.

In this same stone, Christ, you Gentiles are also built together with the Jews into a dwelling-place, that is, so that you may be a dwelling-place of God. You are built together, I say, in the Holy Spirit, that is, through the Holy Spirit, who purifies you for God.

## CHAPTER III

“For this reason I, Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus for you Gentiles—if indeed you have heard of the stewardship of God’s grace that was given to me for you. For according to revelation the mystery was made known to me, as I wrote above briefly (Wisdom I, 19), so that, when you read, you may be able to understand my insight in the ministry [elsewhere, mystery] of Christ. This mystery in other generations was not made known to the sons of men as it has now been revealed to his holy apostles and prophets in the Spirit: that the Gentiles are co-heirs, members of the same body, and fellow-partakers of his promise in Christ Jesus through the Gospel, of which I became a minister according to the gift of God’s grace, which was given to me according to the working of his power.

To me, the least of all the saints (I Corinthians XV, 9), this grace was given: to proclaim among the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ, and to enlighten all concerning what is the stewardship of the mystery hidden from the ages in God, who created all things, so that the manifold wisdom of God might be made known to the principalities [elsewhere, princes] and powers in the heavenly places through the Church [Col. 0330A], according to the predetermined plan of the ages, which he accomplished in Christ Jesus our Lord. In him we have boldness and access in confidence through faith in him.

For this reason I ask that you not lose heart in my tribulations for you, which are your glory. For this reason I bend my knees to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named, so that he may grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner person; that Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts; that you, rooted and founded in love, may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth, length, height, and depth; and also to know the clarity of Christ that surpasses knowledge [Col. 0330B], so that you may be filled into all the fullness of God.

Now to him who is able to do all things more abundantly than we ask or understand, according to the power that works in us, to him be glory in the Church and in Christ Jesus throughout all generations of the age of ages. Amen.”

## EXPOSITION

To make them more indebted to God’s grace, he says that God made him an apostle for their sake; he is also imprisoned for the same people; and God revealed his mysteries to him for their benefit. You are built together in Christ; and for the sake of this matter—that you too may be built together—

I, Paul, a prisoner of Jesus Christ, whose affliction ought not to cause sorrow. A prisoner, certainly, for you Gentiles; for if I had not preached for your salvation, I would by no means be in chains. For you, I say, provided that you have heard of the stewardship of God’s grace, that is, of the grace—namely, the apostolate—entrusted to me through God’s grace.

I speak of grace administered by God, because God wisely ordered within himself why he appointed me an apostle. Or, I speak of the grace which I dispense to you and to the other churches. If, I say, you have heard of the grace that was given to me for you, that is: just as you truly believed that I am your apostle, so truly believe that I am imprisoned for you.

This grace was certainly given to me because the mystery, that is, the secret of God, was made known to me according to revelation, that is, so that I might know how to speak of it as something revealed. It was made known, I say, as I wrote above to you in a brief discourse, where he says: “He himself is our peace,” and continues truly up to: “Therefore you are no longer strangers.”

I wrote it in such a way that you can understand it well. You can do so by reading it attentively, that is, if you read through it carefully. I say that you can understand not only the mystery, but also my insight as it exists in the mystery. This is the same as “in the mystery of Christ,” because I know the new mystery and also know how to open it prudently.

This mystery was not known to the sons of men in other generations, that is, in other ages. Or, if it was known to some, it was not known as it has now been revealed to his holy apostles. Nor should I seem to boast in this, because it was revealed in the Holy Spirit also to the prophets, that is, to all who were enlightened in their understanding, namely, that the Gentiles are co-heirs with the Jews in the future age; and that they are members of the same body, that is, of the body of Christ; that is, that they are also fellow-partakers in the promise made to Abraham.

They are co-heirs, I say, and members of the same body and fellow-partakers in Christ Jesus, who made the two one in Christ, and this through the Gospel, by whose preaching they come to faith.

The Gospel is not mine but his, and I became a minister of that Gospel. Nor did this happen through my merit, but according to the gift of God’s grace. I did not again earn this grace so as to possess it; rather, it was given to me according to the working of his power, because his power worked many things through my weakness.

It was given to me. And to whom was it given? To me, certainly, the least of all the saints, this grace was given: namely, to proclaim among the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ, that is, riches beyond comprehension [Col. 0331B]. It was also given to me to enlighten all concerning this: what a worthy stewardship—that is, what a worthy fulfillment—is the mystery hidden from former ages.

Yet it was hidden in God, that is, existing in the knowledge of God, who could not have been ignorant of it, since he created all things. Therefore I was to proclaim and enlighten, so that through the Church—which is established in our preaching—the manifold wisdom of God might be made known to the principalities and powers, that is, to the orders of angels existing in the heavenly places.

For the angels, not knowing the salvation of human beings, marvel at and praise God when, through the preaching of the apostles, they see their conversion and understand their salvation. The wisdom of God is manifold because he converts one by gentleness of speech and another by severity, in diverse ways among diverse people.

It is manifold, I say, manifested according to the predetermined plan of the ages, that is, in the ages predetermined by God’s ordering. This predetermined plan—that is, what he had predetermined to do in the ages—he carried out, that is, fulfilled, in Christ Jesus our Lord.

In him, that is, through Christ, we have confidence to approach God. And not only confidence, but we also have access to God, without fearing rejection, but in confidence—that is, trusting in our admission. This confidence is possessed through faith in him, namely, in Christ, in whom and toward whom we believe.

He has mentioned that he was consecrated by God as an apostle for their benefit, that he was also imprisoned for them, and that God’s mysteries had been revealed to him for their instruction [Col. 0331D]. For this reason, because all these things were done for you, and because you too have access to God through faith in Christ together with us, for this reason I do not merely pray but, as though asking for what is owed, request and require of you that you not lose heart in my tribulations.

Paul wishes to fortify them beforehand by this exhortation, because he feared that perhaps they might hold in contempt, on account of the teacher’s tribulation and affliction, what they had learned from one who was treated contemptuously. I speak of my tribulations, endured for you. For God permits me to be afflicted so that he may make the quality of your faith apparent through my trial.

God did not test Abraham and the others because he was ignorant of what would happen, but so that he might show their faith to the world as worthy of approval [Col. 0332A]. This tribulation is your glory. For if you draw strength for good works from my tribulation, then you are worthy of glory. But if, because I am afflicted, you lose heart, you are worthy of disgrace.

And for this reason—that is, so that you may not lose heart, because it is pleasing to me that you should not lose heart—I bend my knees. Just as the body is raised and humbled by the knee, so by the raised and bent knee the exaltation and humbling of the mind are signified. Paul certainly bent the knees of his flesh in order to indicate humility of spirit.

I bend my knees to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is also our Father, since we are children of Christ, whose Father he is. From this Father—that is, from his institution and example—comes every fatherhood, that is, all those who are fathers to us: those whom we have in heaven as angels who watch over us, or those whom we have on earth as bishops and as the various fathers of the Church.

Fatherhood is not simply present in this way, but is named—that is, all those who are fathers to us by the dignity of their virtues are so called. Or it may be understood in this way: “Fatherhood is named,” that is, our guardian fathers are called fathers only in name, that is, merely by designation, not substantially—for God alone is Father in substance.

I bend my knees to God so that he may grant you according to the riches of his glory, that is, abundantly and gloriously, with power. I speak of granting you to be strengthened with power, that is, so that you may be strengthened in goodness. And do not believe that this power in you is your own, but that it comes through his Spirit, so that you may ascribe everything to God’s grace. He grants power, I say, not outwardly but in the inner person.

For this reason God established the power of righteousness in the soul [Col. 0332C]: if it were in the body, which is exposed to every adversity, then, like the body, the power would quickly fail. It is much better situated in the soul. Concerning this Christ says: “After they have killed the body, they have nothing more that they can do to the soul” (Matthew X, 28).

He grants you the Spirit, and he grants you to have Christ dwell in your hearts—not that he sits there bodily, but through faith. Although where the Spirit is, there is Christ, neither expression is superfluous, because the Spirit is present through love and Christ through faith.

I bend my knees for this reason: so that you may be rooted and founded in love. From the likeness of a tree rooted deep below, and abundantly bearing fruit from the abundance of moisture by which its roots are richly supplied in the depths, he says “rooted,” that is, bearing fruit in love, and “founded,” [Col. 0332D] that is, established upon a foundation on which the building of God’s house may be firm and grow.

So that you, I say, rooted and founded, may be able to comprehend in understanding and usefulness, with all the saints—that is, as all the saints comprehend—what is the breadth, length, height, and depth.
