The breadth, extending from the right to the left of Christ’s cross, signified the breadth of love, by which he prayed even for his enemies. The length of the cross, from the head to the feet, signified the perseverance of love, because “having loved his own, he loved them to the end” (John XIII, 1).

The height of the cross, that is, the part which rose above the head and on which Pilate wrote the inscription, signified divine regard, indicating that Christ suffered not out of love for the world but to do the will of his Father, who is in heaven.

The depth was the part of the cross that was fixed in the earth. This depth signifies the hidden grace of God, by which he multiplies good things for his own without their knowing why he does so [Col. 0333A].

Nevertheless, we understand these dimensions as existing within them when we explain the passage in this way: May you comprehend what is the breadth—that is, how broad you ought to be in love, so that you do good even to those who hate you; and the length—that is, how constant and persevering in love you ought to be, so that, if it is necessary, you do not fear to die for God or for your neighbor; and what is the height—that is, how you should do every good thing with regard to heaven, not with regard to the world; and what is the depth—that is, the hidden grace of God in you, by which he justified you without merit and advances you, so that you may also be able to know the love of Christ, that is, how [Col. 0333B] Christ has loved you.

I mean a charity surpassing every kind of knowledge. For no knowledge is sufficient to comprehend how great Christ’s charity is. Or understand it this way: “that you may know the charity of the knowledge of Christ,” according to knowledge. For we often love what we do not know; but if we possess knowledge of the thing we love, we are inflamed much more strongly to love the goodness of the thing known. Therefore he says “the charity of the knowledge of Christ,” that is, according to the knowledge possessed concerning Christ. I mean a charity of knowledge surpassing the charity of ignorance. What is unknown is loved less.

“May you comprehend and know,” therefore, so that you may be filled by proceeding into every— that is, into the fullness of all the good things of God, that is, possessed from God. I bend my knee so that you may comprehend [Col. 0333C] and know. Now God himself is powerful to do all things whatsoever are appropriate. I mean that he can do them abundantly, beyond what we ask or beyond what we understand. For no human being would dare ask this of God: that he should make his Son God into a human being; yet he did so. Nor could anyone understand by what order of mercy he restored the lost human race, or the countless good things he does. Therefore he rightly says, “beyond what we ask or understand.”

And that he is so powerful to do this we can prove by proceeding according to the power which operates in us. For when the things he has bestowed upon us—the power of miracles and many other gifts—are considered, we clearly infer from these that, by his will, he is powerful thereafter to complete all things in us.

To him who is thus powerful to act—to him alone [Col. 0333D], and not to human strength—be glory in the Church, that is, in the consideration of the good things he bestows upon the Church, and also in Christ Jesus. For glory is owed not even to Christ, considered as man, for the good things he accomplished, but to God. I mean glory that remains through all generations. For from Abel, the first righteous man, no generation has passed that did not contain people in whom God would be glorified. I mean the generations of the world, from its beginning to its end. I mean the world of worlds, in which many ages are contained. To him be glory. Amen: certainly, so it is.

## CHAPTER IV

“I therefore beseech you, I who am imprisoned in the Lord, to walk worthily of the calling with which you were called, with [Col. 0334A] all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in charity. Be diligent to preserve the unity of the spirit in the bond of peace (Rom. XII, 10). One body and one spirit, just as you were called in one hope of your calling. One Lord, one faith, one baptism. One God and Father of all, who is over all, and through all, and in all of us. But to each one of us grace has been given according to the measure of Christ’s gift. Therefore he says: ‘Ascending on high, he led captivity captive and gave gifts to men’ (Ps. LXVII, 19). But what does ‘he ascended’ mean except that he also first descended into the lower parts of the earth (John III, 15)? He who descended is also the one who ascended above all the heavens, so that he might fulfill [Col. 0334B] all things. And he himself gave some as apostles, some as prophets, and others as evangelists, and others as pastors and teachers (1 Cor. XII, 28), for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of ministry, for the building up of Christ’s body, until we all attain unity of faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to a perfect man, to the measure of the fullness of Christ’s maturity; so that we may no longer be children, tossed about and carried around by every wind of doctrine, in the wickedness of men, in craftiness aimed at the deception of error. But speaking the truth in charity, let us grow in all things into him who is the head, Christ, from whom the whole body, joined and connected through every supporting joint, according to the operation measured out to each [Col. 0334C] member, produces the growth of the body for its own building up in charity.

“This therefore I say and testify in the Lord: that you should no longer walk as the Gentiles walk in the vanity of their mind, having their understanding darkened, alienated from the life of God through the ignorance that is in them because of the blindness of their hearts. They, despairing, have handed themselves over to shamelessness, to the practice of every impurity, in greed (Rom. I, 21–31). But you have not so learned Christ, if indeed you have heard him and have been instructed in him, as truth is in Jesus. Put off [al.: to put off], according to your former way of life, the old man who is corrupted according to the desires of error (Col. III, 8). Be renewed [Col. 0334D] in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who has been created according to God in the justice and holiness of truth (Rom. VI, 48). Therefore, putting away falsehood, speak the truth, each one with his neighbor (Heb. 12; 1 Pet. II, 3), because we are members of one another. ‘Be angry, and do not sin’ (Ps. IV, 5). Let not the sun go down upon your anger. Do not give place to the devil. Let the one who was stealing steal no longer (Jas. IV, 7); rather, let him labor, working with his hands at what is good, so that he may have something from which to give to the one suffering need. Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth; but if there is any good speech for the building up of faith, let it give grace to those who hear. And do not grieve the [Col. 0335A] Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption. Let all bitterness, anger, indignation, shouting, and blasphemy be removed from you, together with all malice. Be kind and compassionate toward one another, forgiving one another (Col. III, 12, 13), just as God in Christ forgave you.”

## EXPOSITION

After admonishing them in various ways not to become puffed up over the good things of God’s grace, and not to grow sluggish but always to remain vigilant in progressing toward what is better—both admonitions seeming to concern the more perfect—he turns to moral instruction, which appears to pertain more to the less perfect. First he instructs everyone in common, then he treats separately the conditions of sex and age.

The text is joined in this way: Because God is [Col. 0335B] powerful to do for you more than we ask or understand, “therefore I beseech you”—that is, I adjure you by everything sacred—“I who am imprisoned in the Lord,” that is, for the sake of the Lord, whom to offend while he is in chains is no small fault. “I beseech you,” I say, to walk through the steps of the virtues worthily of the calling with which you were called. For you were not called to fulfill the desires of the flesh, but to mortify the flesh according to the spirit.

That is, walk with all humility, both held in the mind and displayed outwardly. For it is a fault to be humble within while pretending pride outwardly, since in this way one gives an occasion for people to speak evil of oneself while concealing a virtue by whose imitation one’s neighbor could have been instructed. To be humble outwardly while being proud within: no one doubts that this is culpable.

Walk in all humility and in [Col. 0335C] all gentleness, so that you may be tractable and approachable toward everyone, and with all patience preserved amid every adversity, bearing with one another, each with the other, if one has caused the other distress. Or “bearing with one another” means showing compassion toward one’s neighbor if perhaps he has fallen, and helping him through prayer and fasting. Bear with one another, I say, in charity, not in expectation of revenge.

I say that you should be diligent to preserve unity among yourselves, so that you may have the same willing and the same refusing. I mean the unity of the Spirit—that is, preserve the unity which the Holy Spirit dictates—in the bond of peace. Peace, preserved outwardly, is the bond and nourishment of spiritual unity.

And in order to preserve this unity, be one body, that is, one in action. And be one spirit, [Col. 0335D] that is, one in will. Thus be one in body and spirit, just as the thing to which you have been called is one. He says this as follows: You have been called in one hope, that is, to one hoped-for reality. I mean the hope of your calling, that is, the hope worthy of your calling.

Again, you ought to be one body and one spirit because you have one Lord ruling over you, and your faith is one and without distinction, and your baptism is one, justifying all equally—not, as some say, more or less worthy according to the merits of the different people who baptize. There is one God, that is, the creator of all, and one Father of all, who governs you according to the affection of sons.

He—the Lord God and Father—by ruling, creating, and loving is over all in power. He is also through all places, and it is in no way possible to escape from him. Although he is thus commonly over all and through all [Col. 0336A], he is nevertheless more familiarly in all the elect, giving his graces.

Here the Trinity can be understood: “over all,” the Father; “through all,” the Son; “in us,” the love of the Father and the Son, that is, the Holy Spirit.

Because he had said, “We are one body, one spirit; we have one Lord, one faith,” lest they should consequently think wrongly that everyone is equal in this new grace—so that there is no superior, no subordinate, no servant, no lord—he clarifies this by saying: Although we are one and have one God and one faith, nevertheless the grace of God has been given to each of us, not the same grace to all, but according to the measure of the gift, that is, of Christ the giver.

To one this grace, to another that; and often there is diversity within the same grace [Col. 0336B], because one has less and another more of the same grace.

For this reason, to establish the point—namely, that the Holy Spirit is the giver of graces—he says in the Psalm (Ps. LXVII, 19): The man Christ, ascending on high, that is, above the heights of heaven, led captivity captive. That is, he restored to himself, in the man, the human nature that had previously been expelled from paradise and heaven, bringing it captive back to the heavens from the place from which it had been taken—the place that was naturally its own through sin—and to the homeland previously destined for it, had it not sinned.

For man, created in purity, had paradise as a place of habitation, so that after obedience had been completed he might be transferred from there to heaven. But because he sinned, lost the promised heaven, and was driven from the place of his habitation—that is, from paradise—he was taken captive on this earth. Sin made this earth natural to man [Col. 0336C], just as justice, so long as he remained in paradise, had made paradise natural to him.

Again, after destroying human sin, Christ led human nature captive from this misery, which had already become natural to it through sin, because he brought it back to its former homeland, the heavens, after removing it from its natural place. But the more wretched the first captivity was, the more glorious the second is.

Ascending on high, Christ gave gifts to men, because he sent the Holy Spirit into the hearts of the disciples. And because he gave gifts, it was proved that Christ is the giver of graces.

What understanding should be drawn from the statement “ascending on high,” he wishes to explain, though without departing from his purpose. I say “ascending.” But what [Col. 0336D] does it mean—that is, what is to be understood by the Lord’s ascending? “He ascended” and “he ascended” mean the same thing, unless we understand that, if he ascended, it follows that before he ascended he descended, that is, he was in a lowly place. For if he ascended, it follows that he ascended from a lower place to a higher one.

I say that he descended into the lower parts of the earth, that is, into hell, which is certainly believed to be in the earth, but in its lower part. Thus he proved that the one who ascended had first dwelt in a lowly place as a true human being. Knowing that Christ is the giver of graces and is human as we are, we may confidently ask him for his graces; for unless he had shared in our humanity, he would be much less inclined to answer us.

And because he first ascended, therefore the one who descended and the one who ascended above all the heavens is one and the same undivided Christ, man and God.

Or otherwise [Col. 0337A]: What does it mean that Christ’s humanity ascended, except that first his divinity descended into the lower parts of the earth, that is, among human beings, in order to unite humanity to itself? If he descended as far as the sphere of the sun and moon, he would still be below; but to descend to the earth was lower still.

And although one appears to be the ascender—that is, the man—and another the descender—that is, God—nevertheless the one who descended and the one who ascended above all the heavens is the same one, a single person in distinction. Thus again this accords well with the purpose: Since we see such great power in him that the man-God has ascended above the heavens, we can confidently ask from him who is capable of all things.

He ascended in order [Col. 0337B] to fulfill all things through his gifts, in accordance with what he himself says: “Unless I go away, the Paraclete will not come to you” (John XVI, 7).

After proving that Christ is the giver of graces, he shows the diversity of gifts. I rightly say, “to fulfill all things.” Indeed, Christ himself gave some—distinctly from others—as apostles. He gave some as prophets, who would reveal the Scriptures; others as evangelists, that is, preachers; and others as pastors and teachers, that is, bishops, who feed their subjects from the table of Christ’s body and teach from the New and Old Testaments.

He gave different people different offices for the work of ministry because, if he gave everything to one person, and one person were not sufficient for everything, Christ’s ministries would remain incomplete.

I mean a ministry [Col. 0337C] effective for the perfection of the saints, that is, so that those who are already righteous may ascend to perfection. I also mean a ministry effective for the building up of Christ’s body, that is, so that from those who are still unbelieving Christ’s body—the Church—may be built up.

Those whom he had admonished—not to think that, because of the unity of the Church, they ought to be equal—might say: “It is of little benefit that we have received the faith if we must always remain in subjection.” 245 He consoles them concerning this, saying: “Let it not be burdensome to you if some are subjected and others placed above them. For the end of this diversity will soon come.”

I mean a diversity that will not last any longer than until, as he says according to the desire of the saints, we attain: “Let us all attain unity of faith,” that is, those who have one faith concerning Christ, and [Col. 0337D] “unity of the knowledge of the Son of God,” that is, unity in the good works that follow faith, through which the Son of God is known.

Or “in the unity of the knowledge of God,” so that we may not labor under uncertainty concerning the knowledge of the Godhead, until we attain “to a perfect man,” that is, until we become a perfect man, having received impassibility and immortality.

I mean “to a perfect man,” specifically, “to the measure,” that is, to the goal of Christ’s maturity. I mean the maturity of fullness, that is, the maturity in which Christ possessed fullness—namely, after the resurrection, when he became impassible and immortal.

Or otherwise: Let us attain to a perfect man, as has been said, and to the goal of Christ’s maturity, thirty-three and a half years—the age that was the fullness of maturity.

For once that point has been reached, the flesh has nowhere [Col. 0338A] to grow, neither in increase of strength nor in stature. All of us, whether younger or older, will rise again at the same point of maturity at which Christ left the world and rose again.

Therefore he gave some as prophets, others as teachers or pastors, so that although we once were such as children, from now on we may no longer be children in understanding. Nor should we be tossed about by ourselves, acting now well and now badly, or be carried around by others, now this way and now that, by every wind of doctrine.

He alludes to an analogy: the sea signifies the world; the wind, the seducers; the ship, the Church, which is driven now below and now above by the persecution of evil people.

I mean doctrine made in the wickedness of men, for such seducers are exceedingly wicked. I also mean doctrine fashioned in craftiness: they secretly lead [Col. 0338B] the simple astray. I mean craftiness directed toward the deception of error, that is, so that they may deceive us through their error.

Let us not be tossed about, but let us grow in charity, that is, in love of God and neighbor. Let us not merely hear the truth—that is, doctrine pure from falsehood—but also practice it in our works. Let us grow by proceeding through all good things in cooperation and agreement.

Let us grow, I say, in him who assists us, in whom we can grow sufficiently, because he is the head—that is, the height toward which we must always ascend—and because he is Christ, our king. From Christ the head the whole body of the Church is joined together by faith.

But since that is not yet sufficient—for members can be joined in the same faith without following one another, just as pieces of wood may merely be joined together, so that if one is pulled the other does not follow—it would be evil [Col. 0338C] if the members did not follow the head. Therefore he adds that the body of the Church is joined together by faith and connected by charity.

Love is the nail by which they are bound together without division. I mean joined and connected through every joint of faith, charity, and all the virtues. I mean a joint that is the cause of mutual service, so that one member may serve another.

I mean service performed according to the operation apportioned to each member of the Church. For one member serves more and another less, according to the ability given to it.

The whole body, I say, thus joined and connected produces the growth of the Church’s body. It produces growth according to the increase of righteousness in the faithful, and it is effective for the building up of its own body—that is, the Church of which it is a member—just as was said above concerning unbelievers who are built up toward faith. I mean growth and building up effected in charity, that is, according to love of God and neighbor.

Or let us construe it this way [Col. 0338D], without changing the meaning: “From whom the whole body, joined and connected through every joint of service, produces the growth of the body for its own building up.” I mean that it does so according to the operation distributed to the measure of each member, and all this in charity, because God gave some as apostles, others as evangelists, and others as teachers, and this for your perfection.

Again, because he joined and connected the whole body of the Church through the joint of faith and charity, therefore I say and command this to you [Col. 0339A]. I do not merely say it; I also testify in the Lord. That is, in this admonition of yours I call God as witness, so that from now on he may require nothing further of you through me, but, if you sin, may require it from your own hands.

Paul spoke these words to them when, after summoning the Church of the Ephesians, he said: “You will no longer see my face: stand in what I taught you. For I am henceforth clean from your blood” (Acts XX, 25). See what you have done, because it will be required from your hands.

I testify, I say, in the Lord, that you should no longer walk as you once walked and as the Gentiles still walk. When he says “now,” he signifies that they previously walked in this way.

Do not walk as the Gentiles walk, in vanity—that is, in the worldliness of their mind. For the mind of the world is vanity. The Gentiles, I mean, have understanding—that is, natural reason—darkened by darkness, so completely that everything is darkness and there is no light.

The Gentiles, I mean, are alienated from the life of God, that is, from the eternity in which God lives. They are alienated from it in knowledge and participation, as he himself says: “Alienated through ignorance,” because they do not know the life of God. This ignorance is in them because of the blindness of their hearts, that is, because their heart has been blinded.

For when the word of God was first preached to them, they had the capacity to understand. They had the capacity not to understand as well, but because they chose to remain ignorant, they were blinded to such a degree that they are now incapable of recognizing what is good.

He does not say these things because the Ephesians had actually gone astray in anything, but because he feared that they might easily be drawn back to the rites of the Gentiles in which they had lived before the faith. That they had not gone astray is inferred from the fact that shortly afterward he will call them saints.

They are “blinded and despairing.” For when they hear, “Man will rise in glory and will reign together with Christ,” they despair, thinking this frivolous. And therefore they handed themselves over—not merely consenting and proceeding by will into the practice of every impurity, but practicing more wickedly what they had wickedly desired.

I mean “into the practice of impurity,” namely, into greed. For the more impurely they acted, the more avid they became for impurities.

Or otherwise: They handed themselves over to impurity and to greed. The Gentiles walk in this shameless and impure way; but you have not so learned Christ, whom you ought to follow.

I say this, however, on the condition that you have heard—that is, understood—that Christ, and that you have been instructed in him, that is, in his teaching. It is certainly true that you heard him and were instructed in him, not in falsehood, but as truth is in Jesus.

For I mixed no falsehood into what I taught you about Christ, unlike the Nicolaitans, who preach that Christ did not disapprove of the common use of women and who confuse Christ’s truth with other falsehoods.

And because you were instructed in Christ according to the truth, therefore put off the old man. Or understand it this way: You were indeed taught in Jesus to put off the old man—not to put off the flesh derived from him, which is put off once through death, but put him off according to your former way of life, that is, according to the oldness of sinful action.

Put him off [Col. 0340A] also according to the desires of error, whether desires arising from error or plunging one into error; the old man is corrupted in his very action. For the more frequently he sins, the more that same flesh is weakened and disfigured.

Or let us properly follow the text with the same meaning: Put off the old man who is corrupted, not only according to his action, but put him off also according to the desires of error. Put off the old; put on the new man.

And therefore be renewed, for through baptism they have already once been made new. He says: Be renewed again in the Holy Spirit, who illuminates your mind. Or understand it intransitively: Be renewed in the spirit of your mind, that is, by following your spiritual mind; and thus, renewed, put on the new man.

He is called “new” because he makes all things new. The new man has been created [Col. 0340B] not according to the law of the flesh, but according to God, conceived and born from the Holy Spirit. I mean: Put on Christ in justice preserved toward your neighbor, and in holiness, that is, possessing yourselves for sanctification to God.

I mean holiness and justice not of pretense but of truth, so that we do not pretend to be righteous while being wicked. Therefore—that is, because the old man must be put off and the new man put on—let us assume the members of the new man, putting off the members of the old; specifically, putting off falsehood, which is a member of the old man.

Let each one speak truth with his neighbor. Truth is a member of Christ. We ought to speak truth with our neighbor because we are members of one another, that is, each of the other. Thus whoever defrauds his neighbor commits fraud against his own body, again putting on the new man.

Be angry against the sin of your brothers, and in being angry do not sin in such a way that, through contempt for sin, you rashly fall into contempt for your neighbor. Sin must be hated in such a way that the creature of God is loved no less.

You will not sin in being angry if the sun—that is, the divinity illuminating you—or the sun, that is, your enlightened reason, does not set, that is, is not destroyed, “upon” or because of your anger, so that anger does not overcome reason.

“Let the sun set upon anger” is said by analogy with those who, placed in a valley, would have a great mountain above them, over which the sun would set for them while the height of the mountain turned the sun away from the valley.

Or otherwise, as if he were saying: “I see that you cannot completely restrain yourselves from anger. I tolerate this in you. Be angry, but do not sin,” that is, do not bring your anger to completion in action. This will be useful to avoid if the sun does not set upon your anger, that is, if your anger is laid aside before evening comes.

They might say: “You command us not to sin; but how can this be done, so that we do not sin?” To this he replies: In order that you may escape sin, do not give place—that is, opportunity for sin—to the devil within you, but flee him.

“Do not give place to the devil”; rather, let the one who was previously stealing steal no longer. Literally: Let him labor, that is, choose to labor, working with his hands—not at homicide or anything of that kind, but at what is good and useful. Let him labor so greatly that he may have something for himself and something from which to give to his neighbor who is suffering need.

Again, another point [Col. 0341A]: “Let no evil speech proceed,” that is, let no evil speech proceed from your mouth. But if there is any speech that is good and useful for the building up of faith, that is, so that it may build up one’s neighbor in faith, let it proceed. Yet let it be such that it gives grace to those who hear, so that it is pleasing to those who hear it, both in place and in time.

You who are set over others, teach, as has been said. And you who hear, do not grieve—not only those who instruct you, but the Holy Spirit who speaks through them. I mean the Spirit of God.

See how serious the fault is: if you offend the preacher and the Spirit speaking in him, then you offend the Spirit and God. Thus whoever offends the preacher offends God.

Do not grieve the Spirit in whom you were sealed. For you are wax, and the seal of the Spirit has been impressed upon you. You were sealed for the day of redemption, that is, of baptism, in [Col. 0341B] which you were redeemed from every sin.

Do not grieve the Spirit, but let all bitterness of spirit be removed from you, and anger, that is, sudden agitation of the spirit, and indignation. If an ignoble person is excessively favored over you who are noble, do not become indignant.

And let shouting be removed, so that you do not cry out disorderly in quarrelling, and blasphemy directed against God or neighbor. For whoever says, “Why did God do this?” appears to have said that God did not act well.

To remove everything briefly: let these things, together with all malice, be removed from you. Do not be bitter or blasphemous, but be kind, that is, generous, each giving to the other. And if you do not have anything to give, at least be compassionate in spirit, forgiving one another—that is, pardoning each other—as God forgave you your sins in Christ, that is, through Christ.

248 ## CHAPTER V

[Col. 0341C]

“Therefore be imitators of God, as most beloved children, and walk in love, just as Christ also loved us and handed himself over for us as an offering and sacrifice to God for a fragrant aroma. But let fornication, and every impurity, or greed, not even be named among you, as is fitting for saints; nor obscenity, nor foolish talk, nor vulgarity, which has no bearing on the matter, but rather thanksgiving. For know this and understand that every fornicator, or impure person, or greedy person—which is the worship of idols—has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God. Let no one deceive you with empty words; for because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the sons of distrust. Therefore [Col. 0341D] do not become their partners. For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord; walk as children of light. For the fruit of light consists in all goodness, justice, and truth, proving what is pleasing to God. And do not share in the unfruitful works of darkness; rather, rebuke them. For the things they do in secret are shameful even to mention. But everything that is rebuked is made manifest by the light. For everything that is made manifest is light. Therefore he says: ‘Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will illuminate you.’ See therefore, brothers, how carefully you walk—not as foolish people, but as wise (Col. III, 5), buying back the time, because the days are evil. Therefore [Col. 0342A] do not become imprudent, but understand what the will of God is (Rom. XII, 2; 1 Thess. IV, 5). And do not become drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery, but be filled with the Holy Spirit, speaking to yourselves in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your hearts to the Lord, always giving thanks for everything in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ to God and the Father. Be subject to one another in the fear of Christ. Let wives be subject to their husbands as to the Lord, because the husband is the head of the wife, just as Christ is the head of the Church (1 Cor. XI, 3), he himself the savior of his body. But just as the Church is subject to Christ, so also let wives be subject to their husbands in everything. Husbands, love your wives (Col. III, 18; 1 Pet. III, 1), just as Christ also loved [Col. 0342B] the Church and handed himself over for her, in order to sanctify her, cleansing her by the washing of water in the word of life, so that he himself might present to himself a glorious Church, not having spot or wrinkle or anything of this kind, but so that she might be holy and without blemish. Thus husbands also ought to love their wives as their own bodies. He who loves his wife loves himself. For no one has ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ also does the Church, because we are members of his body, of his flesh and of his bones. Therefore a man will leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two will be one flesh (Gen. II, 28; Matt. XIX, 5). This mystery is great. But I speak concerning Christ and the Church. Nevertheless, let each of you individually [Col. 0342C] love his own wife as himself, and let the wife fear her husband.”

## EXPOSITION

And because God forgave sins, therefore be imitators of God as most beloved children, forgiving one another. Do not imitate him only by forgiving, but also walk in love, so that one may love the other, just as Christ loved us.

He certainly loved us; for he handed himself over for us as an offering and sacrifice to God for a fragrant aroma. In the Old Law, offerings were called the showbread, lamps, and things of that kind. A sacrifice, however, was what was slaughtered on the altar.

In Christ, the offering consisted of all the good things [Col. 0342D] he did until the day of his death. He was called a sacrifice, however, when he offered himself upon the altar of the cross. That ancient sacrifice was said to be a most pleasing fragrance to God because it prefigured Christ’s sacrifice; in itself, however, it was foul-smelling.

Be imitators of God, not fornicators. He says this as follows: Let every fornication, every impurity—as we have often explained—or greed not only be absent, but not even be named among you. That is, do not thoughtlessly present yourselves as such that someone could at least form an evil opinion of you.

I say, let these things not be named among you, as is fitting for saints—which you are—not only before God, but also in providing what is good before human beings. 249 By calling them saints, he indicates that he is not writing these things because they have sinned, but solely so that from now on they may take care [Col. 0343A] of themselves.

Let fornication not be named among you, nor obscenity, nor foolish talk, nor vulgarity. He calls “obscenity” the touching and kissing of women; “foolish talk,” the behavior of those who labor to speak attractively to women in order to persuade them.

“Vulgarity” is combing and adorning oneself in order to please those who judge such behavior to be courtliness. This vulgarity has no bearing on the matter, that is, it serves no useful purpose. Therefore let it not be named among you, but rather thanksgiving—that is, conduct yourselves honorably, so that those who see your good qualities may give thanks to God because of you.

These things should not be named among you because whoever is such a person has no inheritance in the kingdom of God. Or understand it this way: They should not be named among you not only because they have no bearing on the matter, but also because they take away the kingdom [Col. 0343B] of God.

He says this as follows: Know this, understanding it—that is, examining it with subtle understanding—that every fornicator, or impure person, or greedy person has no inheritance. For to be greedy is, specifically, the worship of idols. Since a greedy person loves money more than God, he makes money into his god.

The fornicator, I say, together with such people, has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God. And lest you be alienated from the inheritance of the kingdom, take care.

Let no one deceive you with empty words, that is, false and lying words. He says this on account of those Nicolaitans who persuaded people that whatever was carnal did not displease God.

See to it that no one misleads you. For because of these things forbidden above comes wrath, that is, God’s vengeance, upon the children of distrust—that is, those concerning whose salvation we despair, or those who despair of God’s salvation. And because God’s wrath comes on account of these things, therefore do not become their associates, that is, of fornication, uncleanness, or greed. You should not participate in these things because now it would be more difficult for you to sin than formerly; for then you acted through ignorance, but now, knowingly, you would be putting your hand into the fire.

This is what he says: “You were once,” that is, before faith, “darkness,” that is, ignorant; “but now you are light in the Lord,” that is, enlightened through the Lord. Therefore walk as children of light ought to walk. I say, walk in all goodness possessed within you, in righteousness maintained toward your neighbor, and in truth, so that you speak true words. He says this because such walking is not merely a work, but the fruit of light, that is, the fruitful work of those who have been enlightened.

Walk as children of light, proving—that is, examining with sound judgment—what is pleasing to God. And so that you may do what is pleasing to him, do not participate in the works of darkness, that is, of those who are darkened. I mean works that are fruitless and useless. Do not participate in them, but rather reprove the works of darkness. You should not participate in them because it is shameful even to speak of, much less to do, the things that they do in secret. “For whoever does evil hates the light” (John 3:20).

Reprove the works of darkness. He now adds: “But all things that are reproved by the light,” that is, censured by those who have been enlightened, “are made manifest” through confession; and, when he is reproved, the sinner repents that he has acted wrongly. It is useful when they are made manifest. For everything that is thus made manifest through confession is light, that is, it already begins to be in the light of righteousness, when the sinner repents that he has acted wrongly.

Or otherwise: “All things that are reproved by the light”—as has been said—are made manifest to those who are reproved. Previously they were ignorant of the weight of their sin, which they recognize through reproof. But everything that is thus made manifest is light, because, inasmuch as he now recognizes his sin, he is in a certain sense enlightened and draws near to righteousness.

To confirm this, namely, that darkness becomes light through manifestation, the Holy Spirit says in my text—for this authority is not found elsewhere in Scripture—that is:

“You who sleep through ignorance in sin, rise through recognition of sin, or through confession; and, having recognized your sin, rise from the dead,” that is, from sins which produce death. Or “from the dead,” that is, from the number of the dead, namely, sinners, by producing fruits worthy of repentance; and thus, when you rise, Christ will enlighten you by pouring out grace.

He said above: “Reprove the works of darkness.” For the things that are reproved become light from darkness through manifestation, and because such great benefit follows from reproof—that what is dark becomes light—therefore, brothers, reprove the works of darkness. And so that you may reprove freely, see how you walk carefully, lest what you reprove in others be found in you.

Walk carefully, not as unwise people. For whoever reproves in another what is in himself acts unwisely, since what displeases him in another pleases him in himself. Not as unwise people, but as wise, that is, first cleansing your conscience and then freely reproving the evils of your neighbor.

Walk carefully, I say. I mean, redeeming the time. According to blessed Gregory, to redeem the time is to wash away past evils with tears. When we act wrongly, we lose time; but when we correct through repentance the evils we have committed and thereafter act well, we redeem the time we lost.

Or “redeeming,” that is, preparing time for yourselves. We redeem time when we prepare ourselves to do what is good. For just as one who acts wrongly loses time, so one who acts well indeed has time, but does not redeem it. Rather, by preparing himself so that he may be fit to act well, he is said through these preparations to redeem time.

See that you walk carefully and redeem the time, because the days are evil, that is, people are evil in these days. And because the days are evil, do not become imprudent, that is, reproving without foresight, but understanding, that is, correcting your neighbor’s evils with insight and prudence. Understand, I say, what the Lord’s will is. For God’s will is that one should humbly accommodate oneself to one’s neighbor rather than frighten him away through excessive harshness.

Do not become imprudent, and do not become drunk with wine, in which there is wantonness together with drunkenness; but be filled with the Holy Spirit. This is what he says:

“Be filled with the Holy Spirit, speaking to yourselves,” that is, with understanding of what you utter. Speaking, I say, in psalms. A psalm is that song which is produced by the movement of the hands upon the instrument called the psaltery. Hence he says: “Speaking in psalms,” that is, in things that pertain to the instruction of mortals.

Speaking in hymns. A hymn is praise of God with song. Here he also calls hymns either praises of God or the deeds of the saints, likewise directed toward the glory of God.

Speaking also in spiritual songs. A song is rejoicing over a heavenly good, and therefore he says “spiritual,” since monks especially use such songs, expressing in them their desire for future blessedness.

Speak psalms, hymns, and songs not only with understanding, but also by doing what you speak. This is what he says: “Singing in hymns and songs, and psalming,” that is, acting well in psalms. To sing in hymns and songs is to act according to their meaning.

I say, sing and psalm to the Lord in your hearts, that is, out of love and not as though compelled; also giving thanks always to God and the Father, who both created and loves. Giving thanks, I say, for everything, whether adverse or prosperous. Giving thanks, I say, in the name, that is, for the glorification of the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.

I mean that you should be subject to one another in fear, that is, in the love of Christ.

After giving these precepts publicly, he admonishes separately the sexes and the various conditions, explaining how they ought to be joined to one another. The text is connected as follows:

“I say, be subject to one another; but women should be subject to their husbands with another kind of subjection, subject to them as to the Lord.” Therefore they should be subject to their husbands as to the Lord, because the husband is the head, that is, the ruler and origin, of the woman, just as Christ is the head of the Church, governing the Church that he formed from his side. For just as woman came from the rib of man (Genesis 2:21–22), so the Church came from Christ’s side.

Christ himself is also the savior of his body, that is, of the Church, for he saves it; but a husband can rule a wife, though he cannot save her. And although they differ in this respect—that Christ saves the Church, whereas a husband does not save his wife—subjection should nevertheless not on that account be less. But just as the Church is subject to Christ, so women should be subject to their husbands in everything that is proper.

Let women be subject to their husbands. But you husbands—I do not say, be subject to your wives, but love your wives; and not sparingly, but as Christ loved the Church. He certainly loved her, for he gave himself over to death for her, in order to sanctify her from sins, cleansing her with the washing of water.

Here he shows that water is necessary for absolution. “Cleansing,” I say, “in the word.” “Word” means the utterance of the Trinity. I say “in the word of life,” that is, in that Word in which the life of righteousness is received. Or “in the Word of life,” that is, Christ, who in baptism restored to us the life of righteousness.

He sanctified her so that on the day of the wedding he might present the Church to himself, glorious in the beauty of virtues, having neither spot, that is, anything criminal, nor wrinkle, that is, deceitfulness, nor anything of that kind which might appear either a spot or deceit; but so that she might be holy through the establishment of virtues and immaculate through the removal of vices.

As Christ loves the Church, so husbands should love their wives. They should love them in such a way that they love them as their own bodies. Truly, in this way: “He who has touched his wife loves himself.” For a wife is the flesh of her husband, and therefore he ought to love her.

No one has ever hated his own flesh; rather, he nourishes it with food and cherishes it with clothing. Even the martyrs, who handed their flesh over to the fire, will be said to have loved their flesh, since they wished it to suffer for a time so that afterward it might rest forever. It is like a sick person who hands his flesh over to a physician to be burned and cut, so that through the hardship of a single day he may have bodily health resting in peace for a long time.

I say that he nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ nourishes and cherishes the Church, namely us, who are his Church. Therefore he nourishes us, his Church, of which we are members of the body of Christ, that is, of the Church.

I mean that we exist as some of his flesh. These are the weaker, less strong members of the Church. Others exist as some of his bones, that is, as the stronger members of the Church.

Christ had flesh, according to the weakness by which he was wearied and afraid. He had bones, that is, reason, according to which he said: “The spirit is willing” (Matthew 26:41). Thus today in the Church some are called flesh and others bones.

In this word he also sends us back to the first creation, when Adam, seeing Eve created, said: “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh” (Genesis 2:23).

For this reason, because the wife is the husband’s flesh, “a man will leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two will be one flesh.” Since a man is the flesh of his father and mother, from whom he derives his origin in the flesh, the husband is said even more to be the flesh of the woman, according to the nature of creation, in which woman was formed from man.

And according to the power of that union, in which they wonderfully pass into unity of flesh, physicians say that if the blood of a man and woman who have been carnally joined is placed in the same vessel, it mixes inseparably. But if the blood of those who have not had intercourse is likewise placed together, it does not mix in this way; rather, the man’s blood remains by itself and the woman’s by itself, as it had been placed before or afterward.

Because they are one flesh, therefore the husband ought to love his wife. Moreover, this is so because the statement “a man will leave his father,” and so forth, is a great thing, that is, a great sacrament.

For what he says—“A man will leave his father”—signifies that the Son of God left the Father, when he, who by the nature of his divinity was invisible like the Father, made himself visible under the form of a servant. Again, he left his mother, that is, the Synagogue in which he had been nurtured, and clung to his wife, that is, the Church, whom he betrothed to himself with the ring of faith.

This, I say, is the sacrament. But I say that the reality of this sacrament exists in Christ and in the Church, as has been said. Even if every other reason for marriage were absent, marriage ought nevertheless to be celebrated solely because of the dignity of the reality of which it is the figure.

But although the reality of this sacrament exists only in Christ and in the Church, and not in husband and wife, nevertheless each of you should love his own wife—not another man’s wife—as himself; and the wife should not only love her husband but also fear him.

Thus husbands should conduct themselves toward their wives, and wives toward their husbands.

# CHAPTER VI

[Col. 0347A]

“Children, obey your parents in the Lord (Colossians 3:20), for this is right. Honor your father and your mother, which is the first commandment with a promise, so that it may be well with you and you may be long-lived upon the earth (Exodus 20:12; Ecclesiasticus 3:9; Matthew 15:4). And you fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but raise them in the discipline and correction of the Lord.

“Servants, obey your bodily masters with fear and trembling, in the simplicity of your hearts, as you would Christ. Do not serve merely for appearance, as though pleasing human beings, but, as servants of Christ, do the will of God from the heart. Serve with good will, as to the Lord and not to human beings, knowing that whatever good each person does, he will receive this from the Lord, whether he is a servant or free.

“And you masters, do the same to them, relinquishing threats, knowing that both their Lord and yours is in heaven, and that there is no partiality with him (Romans 2:11; Acts 10:34; 1 Peter 1:17).

“Finally, brothers, be strengthened in the Lord and in the power of his might. Put on the armor of God, so that you may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil; for our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against rulers and powers, against the world-rulers of this darkness, against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places.

“Therefore take up the armor of God, so that you may be able to resist on the evil day and stand perfect in all things. Stand, therefore, with your loins girded in truth and clothed with the breastplate of righteousness, and with your feet shod in preparation for the Gospel of peace. In all things take up the shield of faith, with which you may be able to extinguish all the flaming darts of the most wicked one.

“And take the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, praying through every prayer and supplication at all times in the Spirit, and watching in him with all perseverance and supplication for all the saints; and for me, so that speech may be given to me when I open my mouth, to make known with confidence the mystery of the Gospel, for which I am an ambassador in chains, so that in it I may dare to speak as I ought.

“But so that you also may know what concerns me and what I am doing, Tychicus, the most beloved brother and faithful minister in the Lord, will make everything known to you. I have sent him to you for this very purpose, so that you may know what concerns us and so that he may comfort your hearts.

“Peace to the brothers, and love with faith, from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Grace be with all who love our Lord Jesus Christ in incorruption. Amen.”

## EXPOSITION

You also, children, obey your parents, but in such a way that it is “in the Lord”; for parents are not to be obeyed in matters that are contrary to the faith. “Obey,” I say, “for this is right”—namely, “Honor your father and your mother,” which is the first commandment on the second tablet.

Two tablets were given to Moses. On the first were placed three commandments pertaining to God: “You shall love your God”; “You shall worship the Lord your God”; and “You shall serve him alone.” Also: “You shall not take the name of your God in vain,” and so forth.

On the second tablet were placed seven commandments pertaining to human beings. This commandment—“Honor your father”—was placed first among the other six. It was also given with a promise, because immediately after the commandment the promise of the commandment was added: namely, that it may be well with you who honor your father, and that you may be long-lived upon this earth and long-lived in the true promised land, because you remain there.

Children should obey their parents. And you fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but raise them in discipline, teaching them what they ought to learn, and in correction, so that, if they sin, you may correct them as is proper. “In the discipline and correction of the Lord,” that is, discipline and correction carried out according to the Lord.

Children, obey your parents; you servants also, obey your masters, even bodily masters. Obey, I say, with fear of the soul and trembling of the body. In the simplicity of your hearts, that is, without any deceitfulness, obey them as you would obey Christ.

I mean that you should not serve them for appearance, that is, so that you may seem devoted in your master’s presence but proud behind his back. I say, do not serve for appearance as though by this you pleased human beings, but, as servants of Christ, from the heart and not under compulsion, do the will of God. That is, just as it would be good for you to do God’s will, so serve them with good will, as to the Lord and not as to human beings.

He therefore says “as to the Lord,” because, since servants have become servants on account of their own sin or that of their parents, if they patiently endure this punishment for sin, they appear to obey God more than the human being who, because of sin, reduced them to this condition.

Serve them as the Lord, knowing that each person, whether servant or free, will receive from the Lord who rewards him whatever good he has done.

Servants, obey your masters; and you masters, do the same to them—not that you should serve them, but that you should piously reward their labors. Do the same to them, relinquishing threats, that is, do not harass them with threats, knowing that their Lord and yours is the same in heaven; and knowing that there is no partiality with God. For he does not love a servant less than a free person; the only requirement is that he be good.

[Col. 0348D]

After giving particular admonitions to the sexes and the various conditions, he returns to a common admonition for the Church, fearing their failure and knowing that they would not see his face again.

Thus children should conduct themselves toward parents, servants toward masters, and conversely. But you brothers, in common and henceforth—that is, in the future—be strengthened, that is, be strong in the Lord. And in order to be strengthened, stand in the power of his might, that is, become powerful through his strength.

Here he calls the armor that follows “strength,” by which they are powerful against their enemies. But so that you may be strong and powerful, put on the armor of God, so that, clothed in God’s weapons, you may be able, like combatants, to stand against the wiles of the devil, that is, against the devil lying in wait for you.

And so that you may not be negligent in this struggle, note that our struggle is not against flesh and blood, that is, against a visible enemy. When he says “struggle,” he indicates that the battle is close at hand.

But our struggle is against rulers, that is, evil spirits who rule over other spirits; and also against powers, that is, those spirits who have power over the rulers; and against the rulers of the world—not because they rule this world, but because they rule the darkness of this world, that is, those darkened by sins. They rule only these, not others.

And our struggle is against spiritual forces, that is, against invisible enemies. I call them spiritual forces of wickedness, for these spirits are most wicked. This struggle, however, is in the heavenly places, that is, it is not for earthly things, but so that they may take heavenly joys away from you.

Or, according to Augustine, it is against spiritual forces dwelling in the heavenly places, that is, in the air.

And because the struggle is against rulers and spiritual forces, therefore take up the spiritual armor of God, that is, the virtues, so that by these weapons you may be able to resist on the evil day, that is, in this present time, which is called an evil day because the saints are afflicted by temptations in it.

And not merely to resist, but also to stand perfect, with righteousness brought to completion. I say, stand in all things, in adversity as well as prosperity.

And because the armor of God is necessary in this struggle, therefore take up the belt, breastplate, shield, and so forth. This is what he says:

“Stand in the struggle with your loins girded,” that is, having a belt around your loins by which wantonness may be restrained. “Girded,” I say, “in truth,” lest you perhaps display chastity outwardly while possessing lust within.

Or gird your loins in love, since the love of God is a belt of the loins, putting wantonness to death in us.

Stand also clothed with the breastplate of righteousness, that is, let righteousness be your breastplate, receiving every blow without injury. He does not say that truth is the belt of the loins and righteousness the breastplate because it would not also be good to say the reverse.

Stand also with your feet shod, that is, with your affections properly fortified. I do not say merely in the Gospel, but in preparation for the Gospel, so that I may first show in you what you will evangelize to others. For this preparation is good.

I mean the Gospel of peace, that is, the Gospel through which peace is restored between God and humanity.

I say that your feet are shod, taking up in all conflicts the shield of faith, that is, faith as your shield and protection.

In this shield of faith you may extinguish all the flaming darts of that most wicked adversary.

Take also the helmet of salvation, that is, let the hope and desire of eternal salvation be your helmet, with which you cover this head. For just as the head is the more worthy member, so future salvation is the more worthy object of regard.

Take also the sword of the Holy Spirit, which is the word of God. With this sword, namely the word of God, the enemies are struck and fall.

I mean that you should pray through every kind of prayer and through every supplication. Prayer is the simple request, such as: “God, help me.” Supplication is made with adjuration, such as: “By your Passion, deliver us, Lord.”

Pray, I say, at all times, not merely with the tongue but in the spirit, that is, from the heart.

And in it, that is, in prayer, be watchful with all perseverance and with every supplication made for all the saints, and also made for me, so that speech may be given to me when I open my mouth, that is, so that the grace of speech may be suited to my opened mouth.

And so that speech may be given to me with confidence to make known the mystery, that is, the secret, of my Gospel. For the revealing of this mystery I serve as an ambassador, placed in chains.

May it be given in such a way that I may dare to speak in the Gospel as I ought, since I will not come to you again.

Thus I have taught you what you ought to do. But so that you may also know the tribulations that concern me and what I am doing amid them, Tychicus, the most beloved brother and faithful minister in the Lord, will make everything known to you.

I have sent Tychicus to you for this very purpose, so that through him you may learn what concerns us and so that he may comfort your hearts when you hear that I am suffering for the name of Christ, for whose sake every burden is light and every yoke is easy to bear (Matthew 11:30).

This Tychicus was the one through whom he sent this Epistle, intending to console them by both means, the letter and its messenger.

Peace and love with faith be to you brothers, that is, and faith from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

Grace be with all who love our Lord Jesus Christ. They love him, I say, in incorruption, that is, with integrity of love. This is said by comparison with a bride, who proves that she loves her husband when she preserves her integrity for him.

Or otherwise: Grace be with them in incorruption, that is, in the hope of incorruption, namely, eternal life. Amen.

# [IN THE EPISTLE TO THE PHILIPPIANS]

[Col. 0349]

## ARGUMENT OF THE EPISTLE TO THE PHILIPPIANS

The Philippians are Macedonians. Having received the word of truth, they persevered in faith and did not accept false apostles. The Apostle praises them highly, writing to them from prison at Rome through Epaphroditus.

## PROLOGUE OF BLESSED BRUNO ON THE SAME EPISTLE

[Col. 0349D]

Philippi is a city in Macedonia; hence its inhabitants are called Philippians. They were among those whom Paul praised so highly in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians, saying: “They gave themselves first, and then their possessions” (2 Corinthians 3:5).

Paul had lived among these Philippians for some time, preaching the word of God to them, and through him they received the faith of Christ. After strengthening them in God’s commandments, he departed from them.

[Col. 0351A]

But when he was in chains at Rome, because of the absence and tribulation of their shepherd, the persecutors of righteousness and the false apostles, corrupters of truth, thought that an opportunity had been given them to attack the Philippians whom Paul had instructed. They supposed that the Philippians would more easily yield to persecution because of the affliction and contempt suffered by their teacher, and that the false apostles could more readily pervert their faith while Paul, who would have confirmed them, was absent.

Understanding this twofold struggle—namely, that of the persecutors and that of the false teachers—Paul wrote this Epistle to them. In it he deals with that double struggle in such a way as to establish that they ought willingly to suffer persecution for the faith of Christ, since they hear their Apostle rejoicing in chains, judged worthy to suffer disgrace for the name of Jesus; and since they also know that Jesus suffered for their salvation.

For these and other reasons he commends patience to them together with humility. Again, he so disparages the doctrine of the false apostles that he calls it dung and gives many reasons why they should not be heeded.

In this way, dealing with both struggles, he intends through this Epistle to arm them for the battle, so that they neither yield to persecution nor consent to error.

# EPISTLE TO THE PHILIPPIANS

[Col. 0351]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0351B]

“Paul and Timothy, servants of Jesus Christ, to all the saints in Christ Jesus who are at Philippi, with the bishops and deacons. Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

“I give thanks to my God at every remembrance of you, always in all my prayers making supplication for you all with joy, because of your fellowship in the Gospel of Christ from the first day until now, confident of this very thing: that he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion until the day of Jesus Christ.

“It is right for me to feel this about you all, because I have you in my heart, and because, in my chains and in the defense and confirmation of the Gospel, you are all my companions in joy. For God is my witness, how greatly I long for you all in the bowels of Jesus Christ.

“And this I pray: that your love may abound more and more in knowledge and in every kind of perception, so that you may approve what is excellent, that you may be sincere and without offense until the day of Christ, filled with the fruit of righteousness through Jesus Christ, to the praise and glory of God.

“But I want you to know, brothers, that what concerns me has turned out rather to advance the Gospel, so that my chains have become manifest in Christ throughout the whole praetorium and in all other places, and so that many of the brothers, trusting in the Lord because of my chains, dare much more fearlessly to speak the word of God.

“Some indeed preach Christ because of envy and rivalry, but others also because of good will. Some do so out of love, knowing that I have been appointed for the defense of the Gospel. Others proclaim Christ out of rivalry, not sincerely, supposing that they are stirring up affliction for my chains.

“But what does it matter? So long as Christ is proclaimed in every way, whether through pretense or through truth, in this I rejoice, and I shall also rejoice. For I know that this will turn out for my salvation through your prayer and the assistance of the Spirit of Jesus Christ, according to my expectation and hope, because I shall be put to shame in nothing. Rather, with all confidence, as always, so now also Christ will be magnified in my body, whether through life or through death.

“For to me, living is Christ and dying is gain. But if living in the flesh means a fruitful labor for me, I do not know what I should choose. I am constrained between the two: I have a desire to depart and to be with Christ, which is much better; but to remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake.

“And, trusting in this, I know that I shall remain and continue with you all for your progress and the joy of faith, so that your rejoicing in Christ Jesus may abound in me through my coming again to you.

“Only live in a manner worthy of the Gospel of Christ, so that, whether I come and see you or, being absent, hear about you, you may stand firm in one spirit, striving together for the faith of the Gospel, and in nothing be terrified by your adversaries. This is for them a cause of destruction, but for you of salvation, and this is from God.

“For to you it has been granted for Christ’s sake not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him, having the same struggle that you saw in me and now hear about me.”

## EXPOSITION

“Paul,” and so forth. Here he did not add titles of dignity, knowing that the Philippians had no doubt about Paul’s apostleship. They confessed him to be their teacher and Apostle, since they were working in faith as Paul had handed it down to them.

But he intended to commend humility to them, inserting the name of humility together with patience when he called himself a servant. Hence he says: “Paul and Timothy.”

He did not add Timothy because Timothy had written the Epistle together with Paul, but because he shared Paul’s intention. He also added him because, as he indicates below, he was soon going to send Timothy to them. Since they were to obey Timothy in all things, it was fitting to commend him in advance by Paul’s recommendation.

“Paul and Timothy, servants of Jesus Christ.” In the same way, preserve your service to Christ with complete humility and patience.

Paul, I say, and Timothy write to all the saints who are at Philippi. Saints, I say, in Christ Jesus, that is, sanctified and strengthened in the faith of Christ Jesus.

When he says “to all the saints,” he understands the community of the Church, that is, the subjects. In the same greeting he joins the leaders to them, saying:

They write “to all the saints,” that is, to the subjects, “with the bishops,” that is, with both the bishops and the deacons in the same Church.

Here by “bishops” we understand presbyters. Since there are not several bishops in the same city, the wording requires that several bishops be supposed [the printed argument is problematic]. Or, even if the region of Philippi had contained different cities, it would be absurd to pass from bishops to deacons while omitting presbyters.

Nor is it absurd if priests are called bishops, since, according to Augustine, any head of a household may be called a bishop because he exercises oversight over his household.

Paul, I say, and Timothy write as follows: “Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ,” as has often been explained.

Here, at the beginning, while commending humility to them in the twofold struggle together with patience, he deals with the matter up to the later passage where he says: “But I want you to know,” and so forth.

It is as though he said: Hearing of your faith and patience, I give thanks to my God, that is, to the one who kindly favors me through you.

We call God “our God” when he graciously grants what we ask. I give thanks, I say, to my God at every remembrance of you, because whenever I hear anything about you—since the things are worthy of the faith of Christ—I give thanks to God, not at some remembrance but at every remembrance of you.

Hearing, I say, something good about you in every respect, I give thanks to God at every remembrance of you, making supplication for you all, because no one makes himself unworthy of my intercession. And I do this with joy. If they were sinning, I would indeed pray for them, but in sadness.

Since, however, they are perfect, it remains for him to pray for them with joy.

“I make supplication,” he says, “in all my prayers.” For I never pray without including you. He means prayers not made rarely but always, that is, continually celebrated.

I give thanks, I say, always, that is, for your fellowship manifested in the Gospel of Christ. For you shared in the Gospel of Christ by believing as soon as you heard it, and also by performing works of faith and preaching the faith of Christ to others together with me.

Or otherwise: “I give thanks because of your fellowship,” that is, because you presented your possessions in common to all the saints. Fellowship, I say, carried out in the Gospel, that is, according to the Gospel of Christ, because you first gave yourselves to God and afterward your possessions to the saints, and because through these things and through fulfilling all the commandments you have shared in the Gospel.

Fellowship, I say, begun from the first day of your conversion until now, that is, until the present day.

I give thanks while making supplication for you, and I am confident of this very thing, that is, I ask with complete confidence that I shall obtain it. Yet I am not confident because of your own strength, but because God, who began the good work in you, will himself bring it to completion.

Therefore he says “began” and “will bring to completion”; and, as above, “I give thanks,” so that he may show that the beginning and the end of their righteousness are wholly from God’s grace.

He also says “confident” because, if God’s mercy began a good work in those who were evil, it is much more to be believed that he will bring it to completion in those who are already righteous.

He will bring it to completion, I say, until the day of Jesus Christ. At each person’s death, insofar as it concerns the one who dies, the day of Christ begins. From that point onward he does nothing except Christ’s will, whereas while he lived he had his own day, doing whatever good or evil he wished.

Or, if by “the day of Christ” we mean the day of judgment, then the statement will refer to testing. In this way he will continually bring the good work in you to completion, that is, he will do this in the righteous until the day of Jesus Christ, that is, as long as the world endures.

Confident and making such supplication as is right—that is, I pray for you no less than your righteousness and kindness, by which you honorably received me, require. It is right for me, I say, since I am ungrateful for no one’s favor but kindly repay it.

As it is right for me not only to make supplication but also to feel this about you. For I feel your tribulation through the force of compassion, as though I were enduring it in my own flesh.

I mean all of you, because you are all perfect. I feel this, I say, because I have you not merely on my lips but in my very heart. I am inwardly afflicted by your tribulations.

I have you in my heart both while I am in chains and while I am engaged in the defense and confirmation of the Gospel.

I have you in my heart in my chains, remembering that you suffer persecution just as I do. And I have you in my heart in the defense of the Gospel, that is, in defending the faith against the false apostles who strive to pervert it.

I have you in my heart, remembering that you contend with the false apostles to protect your faith. By mentioning both their chains and their defense, he strengthens them in both struggles.

I also have you in my heart in the confirmation of the Gospel, that is, whenever I confirm the faith of simple Christians through the Scriptures and so forth. I remember that you likewise confirm the faith of the simple.

And just as I remember your tribulations, so you also should share in my humility. For patience without humility accompanying it is useless. Such as I have you in my heart—that is, I have all of you as companions of my joy and of my reward in eternal joy—for just as you will share in my tribulation, so you will share in my joy. Truly, I have you in my heart. For God is my witness how—that is, with how infinite a longing—I desire all of you to be, not at the feet of Christ but in the inmost parts of Christ Jesus; that is, not among the lower members, but among those most beloved by God, who are called his inmost parts.

And because I desire this for you, therefore [Col. 0354D] I pray that your charity, advancing, may abound more and more, tempered by all knowledge—that is, by complete discernment. Knowledge is necessary for charity because, if it is without discernment, it will often recoil from something venial in one’s neighbor to such an extent that, by rebuking intemperately, it provokes a quarrel, or stir up some greater offense; whereas, if it acted with discretion, it would correct its neighbor more effectively through gentleness. Therefore he says, “Let your charity abound in all knowledge.”

And because those who possess knowledge often forget to put it into practice, he adds, “and in all perception”—that is, in every act of attentiveness—so that we may always attentively remember knowledge and have it ready at hand. Let it abound in such a way that you prove—not only distinguish good from evil, but also approve and choose as worthy—the better things, that is, the better among good things. Let your proving be such that you are sincere—that is, pure in yourselves—and without causing offense to your neighbor, thus proceeding toward the day of Christ, so that nothing requiring cleansing may be found in you on the day of judgment.

I say that you will then be filled, on the day of Christ, with fruit—that is, with the reward of your righteousness, which you possessed here. I say that you will be filled through Jesus Christ, the distributor of that fruit. I speak of righteousness possessed for the glory and praise of God—that is, so that God may be called glorious and praiseworthy in his saints.

Or in this sense: Be such as you should be for the day of Christ. I mean that, while you live, you should be filled not with righteousness—which would lack the capacity for action—but with its fruit, that is, with works of righteousness, so that both righteousness and the works of righteousness may be active in you. I say that you are filled through Jesus Christ, from whom all righteousness comes. And this is for the glory and praise of God—that is, so that you attribute everything to God and nothing to yourselves.

The glory of God is called the splendor of the deity. We understand the praise of God in those things that we see with bodily eyes. “Sincere”: if we derive it from *sin* and *caera*, the middle syllable is lengthened; the nominative singular is *sincerus*, with the two plural forms *sinceri* and *sinceres*, as with *diaconus*, *diaconi* and *diacones*. If, following Isidore, we derive it from *sine* and *carie*, the middle syllable is shortened, and it lacks a singular form.

Up to this point he has treated together of both struggles; here he begins separately to discuss the struggle with persecutors, saying: “Hearing good things about you, I give thanks. I pray with joy, trusting in you. I want you, brothers, to know what concerns me.” He informs them of these things in order to lead them by his example to patience and humility.

“I want you to know,” I say, “what concerns me.” “Concerns” is used because evils surround me on every side. Or “concerns,” because outwardly I am afflicted in the body, but inwardly, in the soul, I gather strength.

“What concerns me,” I say, “has turned out rather for the advancement of the Gospel than for its harm,” contrary to what they themselves had thought—that, when Paul was bound, the word of God had also been bound. It has turned out for its advancement, so that my chains—that is, the usefulness of my chains—became manifest in Christ, that is, in the glorification of Christ’s name. I say that they became manifest in every praetorium and in all the other places—that is, among rulers and among those of lower rank.

Even if it is not known everywhere that Paul is in chains, nevertheless the usefulness of his chains [Col. 0355D] is spread everywhere, while the faith of Christ is extended through him and preached everywhere. Or in this sense: It has turned out for the advancement of the Gospel, so that these very chains of mine became manifest in Christ—that is, the chains that I suffered for Christ. They became manifest, I say, in every praetorium and in all the other places. For everywhere they were saying, “See the steadfastness of Paul, who, even in chains, does not cease preaching the faith of Christ.”

They became manifest in such a way that many of the brothers, growing confident in the Lord because of my chains—that is, on account of my chains, in which I boldly preached—trusted in my example and dared to proclaim the word of God to the Gentiles more abundantly and without fear, whereas previously they had not dared to do so because of fear.

These are the good brothers. “But some,” that is, those distinguished from the good, preach Christ perversely and out of envy, because they wish to diminish Paul’s reputation; yet in this way the word of God is not bound. And if they do not think that they can claim Paul’s praise for themselves, they preach also out of rivalry, competing to make themselves equal to Paul in the praise of preaching.

But some who are good preach Christ, although they do not endure tribulation, out of the good will they have toward all, because they would like all people to come to knowledge of the truth. Others, likewise good, preach Christ out of charity—that is, out of the personal affection they have for me—knowing that I have been placed in chains for the defense, that is, on account of the defense, of the Gospel.

Or in this sense: Knowing that I have been placed—that is, appointed by God—in the defense of the Gospel, so that I might defend the Gospel, they preached [Col. 0356B] out of personal affection, saying: “Our beloved Paul, because he is bound, cannot now instruct his churches; let us take his place, lest perhaps those false teachers overthrow what he has built.” Thus even personal affection contributed to the advancement of the Gospel.

But some perverse men, just as the former preach out of personal affection, so these proclaim Christ out of rivalry—that is, out of personal hatred—not sincerely, that is, not in purity. They suppose that in this way they will stir up pressure, that is, an aggravation of my chains, meaning of me who am placed in chains.

These perverse men had disputed with Paul, and Paul had defeated them. Now, however, they preached what they had heard from him, so that when they were asked, “Why are you preaching the words of that condemned Paul?” they might answer, “We did not receive them from ourselves; we received them from him.” Thus, they thought, he would bear the punishment for their words, and the unbelievers, provoked by these words, raged more violently against Paul.
