Someone might object on the basis of what he said above: “My chains have turned out for the advancement of the Gospel.” In the case of the good, who were stirred by his example to preach, they were indeed beneficial; but in the case of those who preached out of envy and rivalry, your chains were of no benefit.

Paul answers: They were indeed beneficial even in their case. For what harm does it do, provided only that Christ is proclaimed, whether on an occasion for stirring up pressure against me, as the false teachers do, or in truth, as the good do? I do not care who the proclaimer may be; I care only that the hearers advance in faith.

I rejoice in this: Christ is proclaimed by occasion—that is, by the opportunity they have to stir up pressure against me—and I rejoice in this also, that they stir up pressure against me. Nor will I rejoice only now; I shall always rejoice in the same thing. I rejoice and shall rejoice in God, for I know that this—that is, that pressure is stirred up against me—will result in my salvation through your prayer interceding for me, and through the supply—that is, the support and sustaining strength—of the Spirit.

For just as a column placed in the middle supports a house so that it does not fall, so the Spirit supports me. I speak of the Spirit of Jesus Christ, that is, the Spirit whom Christ gives. For whom I suffer, I say, this will result in salvation according to my expectation and hope—that is, bringing no less salvation than I expect and hope for.

“Expectation” is called endurance in bearing something, though without certainty. “Hope,” however, is a confident awaiting. Therefore he says “according to hope,” because I shall not be put to shame—that is, I shall not be ashamed in anything, as though I should fail in the Gospel of Christ because of the tribulation pressing upon me.

I shall not be put to shame, but, just as Christ was always glorified in the past, so now—that is, in the future—he will be glorified, not only in the soul but also in the more fragile part, that is, in my body. He will certainly be glorified either through life or through death—that is, in the life of the body and in death.

I ought to glorify Christ through life, for to live is Christ for me—that is, I do not live for anything else except to glorify Christ. I ought to glorify him through death, for Christ is gain for me in dying—that is, by accepting Christ himself, I gain if I die for Christ.

Or in this sense: Through death I ought to glorify Christ, for dying is gain for me—that is, in death I gain, receiving in heaven the recompense for my labors. And since dying is gain for me, it remains that I should choose death.

An opposing interpretation: Yet although dying is gain, living in the flesh is for me the fruit of labor—namely, this, that Christ will be glorified through my life. And because dying is for me the gain of such blessedness, while living in the flesh is the fruit of glorifying Christ, behold—that is, see—I do not know which of the two I should choose, life or death. I do not know because I am constrained.

Or not only do I not know, but I am also constrained, having a desire for the two things: to be released and to remain in the flesh. But to be released and to be with Christ is much better, so far as I am concerned. To remain in the flesh, however, is necessary for your sake, so that Christ may be glorified through me in you.

And I am confident of this—that I shall be necessary and useful. I know that I shall remain, and shall remain for a long time, for the advancement of all of you and for the joy of your faith—that is, so that you may rejoice in the merit of your faith. The righteous have joy from faith when they no longer fear adversity and are secure concerning their reward.

I shall remain for your advancement, so that your rejoicing—that is, your exultation, or thanksgiving, for *gratulor* signifies both “I rejoice” and “I give thanks”—may abound in Christ, that is, in praise of Christ Jesus, because of me, that is, in consideration of me. I say that it will abound through my coming to you again. It will certainly abound, but meanwhile see only to this: that you conduct yourselves worthily of the Gospel [Col. 0357D] of Christ—that is, in the way the Gospel you received both requires and teaches.

Conduct yourselves worthily in such a way that, whether I come and see you or, being absent, remain wherever I may be, I may hear this about you: that you stand in the one Holy Spirit who justifies you. And because they could stand in the same Spirit—one in humility, another in chastity—without having charity among themselves, he therefore adds, “of one mind in charity,” and “working together by patiently enduring tribulations for the faith of the Gospel,” that is, the faith that you learned in the Gospel.

I shall also hear that you are in no way terrified by your adversaries. The very thing that is a cause for them—that is, their desire to terrify you—is a cause of destruction for them, but for you, who stand unafraid, it is a cause of salvation.

And this—that you are not terrified—is given to you by God. It is given to you for Christ—that is, on account of Christ’s merit—not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him. I speak of you as having the same struggle as you saw in me when I was among you, and as you now hear that I am enduring in Rome. You should imitate what you see me enduring in humility, following patience and humility.

## CHAPTER II

“If, therefore, there is any consolation in Christ, if any comfort from charity, if any fellowship of the Spirit, if any compassion and mercy, fulfill my joy by being of the same mind, having the same charity, united in soul and intent on the same thing. Do nothing out of rivalry or vain glory, but in humility regard one another as superior, not each looking to his own interests [Col. 0358B] but to those of others. Have this mind among yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus. Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings, and being found in appearance as a human being. He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross. Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth. And every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father.

“Therefore, my most beloved, just as you have always obeyed—not only in my presence, but much more now in my absence [Col. 0358C]—work out your salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God who works in you both the willing and the accomplishing, according to his good will. Do everything without grumbling and hesitation (I Peter 4:9), so that you may be blameless and innocent children of God, without reproach in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation, among whom you shine like lights in the world, holding fast the word of life, for my glory on the day of Christ, because I did not run in vain or labor in vain.

“But even if I am poured out upon the sacrifice and service of your faith, I rejoice and rejoice together with all of you. And in the same way, you also should rejoice and rejoice together with me.

“I hope in the Lord Jesus to send Timothy to you shortly, [Col. 0358D] so that I too may be encouraged when I learn what concerns you. For I have no one so united with me who will sincerely be concerned for you. For all seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ (I Corinthians 13:5). But you know his proven character: that, as a son serves his father, so he served with me in the Gospel.

“I hope, therefore, to send him to you as soon as I see what concerns me. I trust in the Lord that I myself shall also come to you shortly.

“But I considered it necessary to send Epaphroditus to you, my brother, fellow worker, and fellow soldier, but your apostle and minister of my need, since he was longing for all of you and was distressed because you had heard that he was ill. For indeed he was ill, even to the point of death; but God had mercy on him—and not only on him, but also on me, so that I would not have sorrow upon sorrow.

“Therefore I sent him more promptly, so that, when you saw him, you might rejoice again, and I might be without sorrow. Receive him, therefore, with all joy in the Lord, and hold such a man in honor, because for the work of Christ he came close to death, surrendering his life in order to fulfill what was lacking on your part in your service to me.”

## EXPOSITION

Above he said: “The chains that concern me have turned out for the advancement of the Gospel”; and, “What you also suffer is a cause of salvation for you,” and thus it has been granted to you to suffer for the merit of Christ.

From these points he now draws the conclusion, saying: Since my suffering has also advanced the Gospel, and what you likewise suffer for Christ is a cause of salvation for you, therefore, brothers, fulfill my joy—the joy you have already begun since you suffered reproach for Christ.

He understands “fulfill my joy” to mean this: that they should suffer for Christ in such a way that they always have humility accompanying their patience. Here he will urge them more explicitly to possess humility together with patience, lest, if they suffer for Christ, they therefore set themselves above the others as though they were more worthy. For patience without humility is useless.

“Fulfill my joy if there is any consolation for you in Christ”—that is, if you seek consolation from Christ in any matter. Or, leaving Christ aside, “if there is any comfort from charity,” that is, from brotherly love, and if you wish to have it, then fulfill my joy.

Or in this sense: If any consolation is given to me among you in Christ—that is, on account of the love of Christ—and if there is any comfort of charity—that is, of brotherly love—among you for me, in that you wish to console me through brotherly charity, then fulfill my joy.

And if there is among you any fellowship of the Spirit—that is, if you have fellowship in the Holy Spirit with the other churches—and if there are in you any inmost feelings, that is, any pious affections of compassion, meaning the exhibition of mercy, fulfill my joy.

“Inmost parts” is used here as a designation for mercy. A pious affection, even if it produces no action, is called mercy; the effect of mercy, however, is called compassion. Therefore he appeals to them so earnestly because he wishes them to maintain humility, without which he considers their patience ineffective.

I say, “Fulfill my joy” in such a way that you are of the same mind—that is, that your neighbor’s prosperity should be as pleasing to you as though it were your own. Be of the same mind, I say, possessing the same charity—that is, equal love toward every neighbor.

Although it is sometimes appropriate to have greater intimacy with certain people, as Christ had with John, this should not be called charity but greater intimacy, which is possessed according to the fact that some people are more suitable for certain things and others less so.

You should also be of the same mind in your neighbor’s adversities, so that you feel his distress not only in your mind but in such a way that it pierces you as though it were your own. I mean that you should be united in soul, possessing an equal disposition of compassion toward every neighbor. Again, do nothing out of rivalry, so that one who suffers more does not contend to set himself above another who suffers less.

Or, do not make arrangements concerning ecclesiastical affairs out of rivalry, and do nothing for the sake of vain glory—that is, for worldly glory—but be such as to regard others as superior to yourselves, so that each person considers the other superior to himself. Let this not be a pretended humility, but let it be in humility: just as one places another before himself, so let him have the same humility in his heart, considering the person whom he places before himself to be his superior.

And how should one regard another as superior to oneself? He gives the instruction, saying: Regard one another as superior to yourselves. Do not each of you look to the good things that are your own, but look only to the good things that belong to others. For if, setting aside your own qualities, you attend to those of others, you will regard them as superior to yourselves.

To commend both humility and patience to them, he explains how great Christ’s humility and patience were, saying: I rightly speak of humility, for you should have within you what you see not only in me but especially in Christ Jesus. And do not merely possess it; also perceive it—that is, test it through experience. Therefore he says “perceive.” For many people think that they can endure everything for Christ, but if they should actually come to the test, they would fail.

“Perceive,” I say, humility and patience in yourselves, which you see especially in me and in Christ Jesus. Christ Jesus, although he was in the form—that is, in the equality—of God the Father, invisible, coeternal, and consubstantial with him, knew himself to be equal to God. And in this knowledge there was greater humility. For if he had humbled himself while ignorant of his own height, his humility would not have been so commendable, because of that ignorance.

Knowing that he was equal to God, he did not regard it as a seizure, as though he were usurping something belonging to another. Or understand the same sentence in this way: Although he regarded himself as equal to God, he did not commit seizure, as did the wicked angel, who said, “I shall set my throne toward the north, and I shall be like the Most High” (Isaiah 14:13), and as did the human being to whom the serpent said, “You shall be like gods” (Genesis 3:5). Each of these committed seizure by wickedly wishing to appropriate to himself what properly belonged to God. Christ, however, did not commit seizure, because he regarded it as his own possession.

And although Christ was in the form of God, he nevertheless emptied himself—that is, emptied the splendor of his deity—when he placed it beneath the form of a servant. He emptied himself, I say, that is, the deity itself, while remaining the same one with the Father. For he assumed what he was not in such a way as to remain what he was, and in this there was great humility.

If some king, having lost the right of kingship, should be humble, that would not be a great thing. But if, while possessing the right of kingship, he withdraws himself from it in humility while remaining what he is, his humility is praiseworthy.

He emptied himself, I say, taking the form of a servant. The humility is incomparable when the Lord chose to be a servant. Again, he could have taken the form of a servant without corruption, so that he would not experience the miseries of the flesh. Therefore he adds “being made”—that is, receiving a new created nature—in the likeness of human beings. For he was passible and mortal in the same way as other human beings.

Again, he could have been in the likeness of human beings, possessing hands and feet, without conducting himself as a human being. Therefore he adds, “and in appearance”—that is, in the way he conducted himself—he was found as a human being by the tempter, the devil. For the devil was investigating whether he was God or a human being; but when he found him hungry, he thought that he was merely a human being.

And he was not only made in the likeness of human beings, but also humbled himself—he who was so great—while nevertheless remaining in the glory of his deity. He humbled himself, I say, becoming obedient to the Father in everything, even unto death—not a death worthy of such a person, but death on a cross. This kind of death was more disgraceful than any other.

When he says “death,” he commends his patience. When he says “of a cross,” he commends his humility.

Therefore—that is, because he obeyed God in such great humility and patience—he himself, by his merit, and God together with him, exalted him—that is, placed him in great majesty—at his right hand. And to him, thus exalted, he gave a name—that is, honor—which is above every name, that is, higher than anything that can be named.

It is so far above every name that, at the name—that is, to the honor—of Jesus every knee should bend, that is, everything should be fully subjected to him, just as the one who bends his knee is subjected.

I say “every knee,” because the knee of those in heaven—that is, of the angels—and of those on earth—that is, of human beings—and of those under the earth—that is, of the demons and the souls who are there—will bend. And every tongue will confess.

This will occur on the day of judgment, when the wicked will confess Christ whether they wish to or not.

They will confess, I say, that the Lord Jesus Christ is in glory—that is, in equality with God the Father according to his deity—and, after the Father, first with respect to his humanity, above every creature.

Christ was so patient and humble, and through both qualities he was so exalted. Therefore, my most beloved, work out your salvation—that is, your exaltation—joining humility to patience within yourselves.

I say that you should do this just as you have always obeyed me while I was among you. So now, with fear of soul and trembling of body—for the one who stands must always fear lest he fall—work out your salvation, so that you may not be said to have obeyed only in my presence, but so that your obedience may be proved much more now in my absence.

Therefore never be secure, but always act with fear and trembling, because God is the one who works in you—even leaving nothing to you—both the willing; and after he has given you the willing through grace, he likewise works in you the accomplishing.

Nor does he do this on account of any prior merit of yours, but solely according to his good will. God works everything in you; you, however, cooperating with God, do everything without grumbling, lest, if it is necessary for you to suffer for a long time, you should grumble impatiently against God, as though he were allowing you to be afflicted unjustly.

Also do everything without hesitation—that is, do not say, “Tomorrow I shall keep watch; tomorrow I shall fast; I shall begin to suffer for Christ in this way.” Therefore act so that you may be without complaint—that is, so that there may be nothing in you concerning which a person could justly complain against you.

And act so that you may be innocent children of God—that is, so that simple sonship of God may be present in you through innocence—and so that you may also be without reproach, meaning that no occasion may appear in you by which you might seem blameworthy, even if there is no actual fault in you.

They might say: “It is difficult to live without reproach among so many who envy righteousness.” To this he replies: It is indeed true, because you dwell in the midst of a generation that is crooked and perverse in itself—that is, a generation that perverts others—yet among them you shine through faith and good works like lights in the world.

For just as the sun and moon illuminate the world, so your righteousness illuminates their darkness. You, I say, hold fast the word of life—that is, the Gospel of Christ, in whose faith eternal life is possessed.

You hold it fast in the manner of a vessel that properly retains the liquid poured into it and offers it to others. So you also preserve the word of God within yourselves and minister it to others.

You hold it fast, I say, for my glory. If I am to have glory from the fact that you hold fast the word of life, you much more are to have it, since you earn it. I speak of glory that I shall have on the day of Christ, when Christ will reward his own. I shall certainly have my glory, because I did not run in vain or labor in vain.

He “ran” with respect to those whom he converted easily. He “labored” with respect to those who were more difficult to approach in faith. I both ran and labored among you, and I do not regret it. But even if it should be necessary for me to be offered for you, I rejoice together with you in this.

He says it in this way: Even if I am offered upon the sacrifice of your faith and upon the service of your faith—that is, I have offered your faith to God like a sacrifice of sweet fragrance—and upon your service, meaning your good works by which, after faith, you have served God; but if, after these labors, it should still be necessary for me to be offered for you, I rejoice in this and rejoice together with you—that is, I give thanks.

Or, I rejoice together with all of you, who ought to rejoice if it is God’s will that I be offered for you. But you, reciprocating this for me, so that you too may likewise be offered for me, should rejoice and rejoice together with me, who have armed you for such a worthy cause as being offered for Christ.

Again: I know that I am building you up through this Epistle for patience and humility. I hope in the Lord Jesus shortly to send Timothy to you. My purpose is that, when I learn what concerns you, I may be encouraged and secure concerning you; for I fear that, because of the struggle pressing upon you from both sides, you may be disturbed.

Therefore I will send Timothy to you especially, for I have no one so united with you and so sincerely concerned for you. Truly, no one else; for all who are now with me seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ. I shall send him to you because he is concerned for you. Receive him honorably and thus recognize him.

He does not simply say “him,” but “his proven character,” that is, one whom I have found thoroughly tested and reliable. For I have tested him in many matters. I rightly call him proven, because he served with me in the Gospel as an obedient son serves his father. And because he loves you with sincere affection, he served me as a son serves his father.

Therefore I hope to send him to you as soon as I see the outcome of the things that concern me. This is why he speaks in this way. For Nero had decided that he would soon pronounce judgment concerning him, whether he would kill him or spare him. He hoped to escape because he had instructed many members of Caesar’s household in the faith, and they were working for his release.

For this reason he added: “But I trust in the Lord that I myself shall soon come to you.” And although I say that I shall come and that I shall send Timothy, nevertheless, in the meantime, I considered it necessary to send Epaphroditus to you, my brother and fellow worker in preaching, and my fellow soldier in tribulation.

He is your apostle—that is, either your envoy, because you had sent him as an envoy to Paul, or your apostle, that is, your preacher, or your bishop—and the minister of my need, that is, the one who ministered at the time of need what you had sent me.

Therefore I considered it necessary to send him to you, although he was necessary to me, since he was longing for all of you and was sorrowful—not because he himself had been beaten, but because you had heard that he was ill, and he did not want you to be saddened on his account.

While Epaphroditus was ministering to Paul, the guards seized him and afflicted him severely with blows. I say that he was ill for this reason: indeed, he was ill even to the point of death, but God had mercy on him. And not only did he have mercy on him; through him he also had mercy on me.

And because you were grieving over him, I therefore sent him more promptly than I otherwise would have done—for he was necessary to me—so that, when you saw him, you might rejoice again. Formerly, when he was among you, you rejoiced. And I sent him so that I might be without sorrow, because I am sorrowful over you, who are sorrowful on his account.

And because he loves you so greatly, and you love him, we send him to you. Therefore receive him with all joy—not with citharas and pipes, but with joy possessed in the Lord—and hold such a man in all honor, since he has suffered so much for you and loves you so greatly.

And this is just, because he came close to death for the work of Christ that he was carrying out in me, surrendering his life in order to fulfill toward me what was lacking in your service. You were indeed sending money, but apart from him there was no one who dared to minister to me.

Through this Epaphroditus Paul sent them this Epistle.

## CHAPTER III

[Col. 0363D]

“Finally, my brothers, rejoice in the Lord. To write the same things to you is not burdensome for me, but necessary for you. Beware of the dogs; beware of the evil workers; beware of the mutilation. For we are the circumcision, who serve God in the Spirit, glory in Christ Jesus, and place no confidence in the flesh—although I myself have confidence in the flesh.

“If anyone else seems to have confidence in the flesh, I have more: circumcised on the eighth day, of the people of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews, according to the law a Pharisee (Acts 23:6), according to zeal persecuting the Church of God, according to the righteousness that is in the law conducting myself without reproach.

“But whatever things were gains to me, these I have considered losses for the sake of Christ. [Col. 0364A] Indeed, I consider everything to be loss because of the surpassing knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord, for whose sake I have suffered the loss of all things and consider them refuse, so that I may gain Christ and be found in him, not having my own righteousness, which comes from the law, but that which comes through the faith of Christ Jesus, the righteousness that comes from God through faith, in order to know him and the power of his resurrection and the fellowship of his sufferings, being conformed to his death, if somehow I may attain to the resurrection that is from the dead.

“Not that I have already received it or am already perfect. But I pursue, if somehow I may take hold of that for which I have also been taken hold of by Christ Jesus. Brothers, I do not consider myself to have taken hold of it. But one thing I do: forgetting what lies behind and stretching myself toward what lies ahead, I pursue the appointed goal, toward the prize of the heavenly calling of God in Christ Jesus.

“Therefore, whoever among us is perfect, let him think this; and if you think anything differently, God has revealed [will reveal] this also to you. Nevertheless, let us proceed according to that which we have attained, so that we may think the same thing and remain within the same rule.

“Be imitators of me, brothers, and observe those who walk as you have our example. For many walk—those of whom I often told you, but now tell you even weeping—as enemies of the cross of Christ. Their end is destruction, their god is their belly, and their glory is in their shame; they set their minds on earthly things.

“But our citizenship is in heaven. From there also we await a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, who will reform the body of our humility, conforming it to the body of his glory, according to the operation of his power by which he is able also to subject all things to himself.”

## EXPOSITION
After he had sufficiently instructed them in the struggle against persecutors, always commending humility together with patience, he instructs them in another struggle which the false teachers were bringing upon them, disparaging the law and exalting faith. As though he were saying: “Just as I taught you, be patient and humble toward persecutors; henceforth—that is, concerning the other struggle which the false teachers bring upon you—I instruct you as follows, my brothers: rejoice in the Lord,” that is, do not seek joy elsewhere, as those men wickedly teach in carnal things. [Col. 0364D] Place all your joy in the Lord. For he alone justifies, and none of those things which the false teachers preach contributes to this. Therefore rejoice not in carnal things, but in the Lord.

And so that you may know how to rejoice in the Lord, for me, who am ready and diligent in instructing my children, it is not burdensome—although perhaps others would be reluctant to repeat what they had already said, since words quickly slip from the memory—but to write to you, so that, while the writing remains, the memory of my traditions may endure in you. It is not burdensome for me. It was necessary for you that I should not consider it burdensome, but should write.

But so that you may rejoice in the Lord, beware of the dogs—that is, protect yourselves from those false teachers who are rightly called dogs. For just as a dog fawns upon someone whom it is accustomed to see, even if that person comes to destroy the house or to kill the dog itself, while it [Col. 0365A] barks at those whom it is not accustomed to see, even if they come to feed it or to benefit the house, so these false teachers fawn upon the carnal people to whom they are accustomed, although in this there is both their death and the destruction of the house, that is, of the Church. But they bark at preachers of the truth simply because they are unaccustomed to such people, although these preachers come to give them life and to build up the house of God.

And concerning such false teachers he says: “Beware of the dogs,” fawning upon accustomed carnality and barking at unfamiliar spirituality. They are not satisfied with contradicting the truth; they are also evil workers, sowing weeds over the seed. Beware of these evil workers, lest they lead you astray by false doctrine.

Beware also of the concision, [Col. 0365B] those who, like skin that has been cut, have a body cut and mutilated, and so possess every understanding cut off and separated from what is good. They are not merely themselves mutilated; they are also the concision of others whom they lead astray. Truly those carnal people are the concision, whereas we alone, the spiritual, are the circumcision—that is, purification. We are purification not only because we have been purified, but also because by doctrine and example we are the purification of others.

The cutting away of that superfluous skin signified that every superfluity must be circumcised from the heart. They, however, with the skin cut away, possess an uncircumcised heart; but we, holding to the reality—that is, circumcision of the heart—neglect their shadow.

We, I say, are the circumcision, who serve God not in the flesh, which is something base, but in the more excellent part, [Col. 0365C] namely, in the spirit. For as spirituality surpasses carnality, so our service surpasses theirs. We serve God in the spirit and glory in Christ Jesus: that is, Christ Jesus is our glory and our joy, and we have no glory in anyone else.

Thus we glory in Christ Jesus—not merely by refusing to glory in the flesh, but by having not even the slightest confidence in the flesh, that is, in the carnal things which they commend.

They might say: “Perhaps you yourself have nothing in which you could place confidence in the flesh.” For they say of themselves, and so forth. To this he replies: “I neither blush at nor place confidence in the flesh, although I possess—or could possess—confidence, if there were any confidence to be placed in the flesh. I certainly would have confidence, if there were any in the flesh. For if anyone appears to place confidence in the flesh”—here he means someone else, someone altogether different from himself, who trusts only in [Col. 0365D] Christ—“I could place confidence in the flesh more than he could.”

“More,” because I was circumcised on the eighth day according to the law; that other person perhaps was circumcised already as an adult, when he passed over to Judaism. Circumcision performed on the eighth day signified that through the righteousness of which circumcision was the figure we were to return to that eighth day which we lost through Adam’s sin. In remembrance of that eighth day we celebrate the Lord’s Day.

This world proceeds through seven days; when the world has ended, this eighth day will begin and will have no end throughout eternity. Since those who were not of Israel were also circumcised on the eighth day, such as the children of proselytes, he therefore adds: “I am also of the stock of Israel.” For again, some were Israelites on one [Col. 0366A] parent’s side and Gentiles on the other, as David, who on one side was descended from Ruth.

For this reason he adds “a Hebrew of Hebrews,” because again some of Benjamin had fallen into idolatry. He says, “born of the tribe of Benjamin.” He also says, “a Hebrew born of Hebrews.” I was also a Pharisee—that is, distinguished according to the law, both in understanding and in fulfilling the law.

*Phares* means “division”; hence *Pharisee*, one who is divided or separated, because they were separated from the people and distinguished in the law, in understanding, and in contemplation.

I was also a persecutor of the Church of God according to zeal—that is, because of zeal and love for defending the law. So that I might appear superior to all those others in the law, I lived according to the law without complaint. I guarded myself in such a way that no one could complain about me.

I say “without complaint” according to a righteousness not [Col. 0366B] the true righteousness, but the righteousness which is in the law and which a person can adequately perform by himself. For anyone can cut away that skin, slaughter a goat, and perform things of that sort.

And because I was so great in the law, if there were any glory in the flesh, none would have had more than I, so pre-eminent was I in the law. Yet those things which had previously been gains to me—for it was a gain to perform the figures while the truth was still awaited—I have now judged losses.

These things, which were formerly gains, I have now judged losses, that is, things destroying the true good, for the sake of embracing Christ. For as long as I remained in the shadow, I could not grasp the body, that is, Christ.

But although I say that I abandoned these former things for Christ’s sake, nevertheless, even if I say nothing about Christ, I regard all things as [Col. 0366C] refuse in comparison with the true good, solely because of the surpassing knowledge which I have now attained in the Scriptures.

Previously, while I was in the law, I seemed to possess knowledge of the law, although in truth I did not possess it. But when I came to Christ, then for the first time I possessed true knowledge of the Scriptures, far surpassing the knowledge which I had previously thought I possessed.

I speak of the knowledge of Jesus Christ my Lord—that is, the knowledge which Jesus Christ distributes to those who come to him. According to Ambrose, he called him “his Lord” because he was moved by love.

For the sake of grasping this Christ, I not only judged all these carnal things to be loss, but also made this judgment evident to others. Nor do I merely regard them as loss, but even as dung. For they defile everyone who clings to them.

I regard them as dung so that I may [Col. 0366D] make Christ my gain: by abandoning those things, I gain Christ for myself, to possess him more fully in the future. I also regard them in this way so that, in the meantime, while I do not yet fully receive Christ, I may be found a member in him, that is, in his body.

I say that I no longer possess my own righteousness—my own, certainly, because it is the righteousness that comes from the law. Anyone can perform the works of the law, namely, anyone who possesses that righteousness which comes from faith in Jesus Christ, that is, which we possess because we believe in Christ Jesus.

Someone might say: “You call the righteousness of the law your own, but you present the righteousness which comes from faith in Christ as though it were not yours.” Paul replies: “It is not mine, but the righteousness which comes from God.”

I speak of a righteousness possessed through faith and thus continuing in faith. Someone might think: [Col. 0367A] “It is true that faith comes from God, and that righteousness cannot be possessed except through faith; but once righteousness has been obtained, faith is no longer necessary.” Therefore he says that just as righteousness originates through faith, so it must continue in faith and not apart from it.

Above he said that through Christ the surpassing knowledge is possessed even in this world. Now he adds that through him a much greater knowledge is possessed—but this will be in the future, when we shall see the Lord as he is.

This righteousness is in faith. I speak of a righteousness capable of enabling us to know him in glory as he is, not as now through a mirror, and of attaining the power of his resurrection—that is, of rising in immortality. Our resurrection is the power of his resurrection, for his resurrection brings about our rising in the same [Col. 0367B] way.

Again, it is a righteousness capable of granting fellowship in his sufferings, so that, just as he suffered for us, we may suffer for him. He calls the sufferings of Christ those which he endured in his whole bodily life before the cross.

It is also capable of bringing about conformity to his death, so that in every way we may be conformed to his death. Just as he died for us out of love alone, so may we rejoice in dying in his love.

The words which we have explained signify this, although they are constructed in the following way: “I may be found in him”—I say—“conformed to his death.”

Someone might say: “Why do you wish to be conformed to his death, when your righteousness would be sufficient, without death, for attaining glory?” To this Paul replies: “For this reason I wish to be conformed to his death: if somehow I were not concerned by whatever kind of suffering or death by which I might obtain this. If [Col. 0367C] somehow,” I say, “I may attain.”

A servant and a master meet one another: the servant by serving well, the master by rewarding well. Thus Paul meets Christ when he dies for him, just as Christ died for Paul.

“I may attain,” I say, striving toward the resurrection. Or it may be understood thus: “If somehow I may attain the resurrection,” so that by “attaining” we may recognize the desire of the saints. This is the resurrection from the dead.

We shall rise outside the company of the dead, but the wicked will not rise from the dead, because they will die from day to day. Therefore I say “if somehow,” because I do not understand that I have already received anything of that glory toward which I strive, or that I am already perfect in the knowledge of Christ, whose knowledge we now approach by faith as someone uses a [Col. 0367D] mirror for knowledge of any object.

I have not yet received it, but I pursue it as something not yet possessed and which I desire. I pursue it, I say, “if somehow”—as was said above—“I may grasp him.”

He says this from an abundance of affection: “I may grasp him,” as though he were saying, “If I could attain him, I would enclose him in my embrace.”

“I may grasp him,” I say, in the manner in which I was grasped by Christ Jesus, when, just as Christ knows me perfectly as I am, I may know him as he is.

Or it may be understood thus: “I may grasp Christ in that degree of glory in which I was grasped by Christ Jesus,” when he called me on the road, so that I might embrace him in whatever glory he then possessed.

Therefore I say “I may grasp him,” because I, brothers, even though I was taken up to the third heaven, nevertheless [Col. 0368A] do not consider that I have grasped Christ except through the mirror of faith.

I do not consider that I have grasped him, but I pursue one thing—that is, one reality. Concerning this one thing he cried: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I will seek” (Psalm 26:4).

The person who always works the same good follows the One. The person who sometimes does good and sometimes evil follows two.

I pursue the One, forgetting what lies behind—that is, temporal and carnal things. Or it may be understood thus: “Forgetting what lies behind,” that is, former merits; and “stretching myself toward what lies ahead,” that is, toward what is better because eternal, or toward those merits which are prior in usefulness, even if later in time.

They are called “last” and “first” because the preceding things would be useless unless these followed and gave them their force.

I stretch myself with every desire, in flesh and spirit, toward what lies [Col. 0368B] ahead, proceeding thus toward the goal—that is, toward the thing appointed for me, namely, the prize, that is, the reward of labor.

I speak of the prize of God’s calling, to receive which God calls me. I speak of a heavenly calling, that is, one to be possessed in the heights of heaven, in Christ Jesus, who distributes this prize to his contestants.

In these words he inserts both certainty concerning the thing he awaits and commendation of it. By “goal” and “calling” he signifies its certainty; by “heavenly,” “of God,” and “in Christ Jesus,” he signifies the dignity of that thing.

For I, Paul, have not yet received anything, nor am I yet perfect; but I pursue in order to grasp, stretching myself toward the goal, the prize of the heavenly calling. Therefore, all of you who are perfect, [Col. 0368C] think this same thing: namely, that you have not yet received Christ in that manner, nor are you yet perfect in his knowledge.

He does not say this in the second person, but, as is his custom, he inserts himself among them in order to lead them more effectively, saying:

“Let all of us who are perfect think this.” What he said above—“not that I have already become perfect”—seems opposed to what he says here, “we who are perfect,” but there is no contradiction.

There he was speaking of perfection in the knowledge of God, in which no one in this world is perfect. Here he is speaking of perfection in virtues, which we can possess in this world and in which there are many degrees. Paul was more perfect than another person, and anyone who leads a life without a criminal stain is called perfect. [Col. 0368D]

And because he said that we should consider ourselves imperfect—at the corrupt reading *ne ideo de solemni* [reading uncertain]—he adds: “And if you think differently”—that is, less perfectly—“God, who has already revealed to you what you understand, will also reveal to you what remains to be understood.”

Or it may be understood thus: “If you think differently,” that is, if you have already attained some degree of knowledge, God will reveal this to you and will thus bring about what remains.

Or again: “Let us consider ourselves imperfect; and if you think differently from what you ought to think, having been deceived by carnal people, God will reveal to you how you ought to think, since he has already accomplished something in you.”

They might say: “And because, as you say, we are imperfect, we cannot stand; nor is it surprising if we fall.” To this Paul replies: “Although we are not yet perfect, nevertheless we ought to think,” that is, understand, “the same thing—all of [Col. 0369A] us.”

Not the same thing in carnal matters, but that same thing to which we have attained by faith in our understanding; and we must remain in the same rule, that is, in the same uprightness of life.

But so that you may remain in the same rule, brothers, be imitators of me. If you object that I, whom you do not see, cannot be imitated, I answer: “Observe,” that is, carefully consider, “those who walk according to the faith, just as you still, I believe, have in your memory the pattern of us, the way in which we taught and lived when we were among you.”

Just as someone recalls the face of a person once seen, so you should recall the pattern of our teaching and conduct.

Therefore I say: those who walk according to our pattern. For many walk in the manner of evil people. When I was with you, I often told you that these people were enemies of the [Col. 0369B] cross of Christ.

Since they say that a person is justified by something other than the crucified Christ, they are certainly enemies of Christ’s cross. Then I told you this; now I say the same thing with grief and tears, both because of their condemnation and because of your seduction.

In order to withdraw the Philippians from agreement with such people, he condemns the false teachers among them, while approving his own position, saying: “The end of those enemies of Christ is destruction,” that is, eternal condemnation.

“Their god is their belly”—the container is named for what it contains, that is, food. For they believe that they are purified through food; they attribute to food what belongs to God.

Or it may be understood thus: “Their god is their belly.” They do not preach out of love for God, but in order to fill their bellies. “Their glory,” of those who set their minds on earthly things—that is, who pursue and teach carnal things—“is in their [Col. 0369C] shame.”

They are said to be mutilated. They may also be ashamed when rational people believe that they are justified through the sacrifice of an irrational goat.

Their end is destruction. But our will—and not merely our will, but also our manner of life—is in heaven, since we who love the cross of Christ have set earthly things aside and long for heavenly things.

Therefore, because our manner of life is in heaven, with this confidence and security we await for judgment the Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ.

He will reform the body of our humiliation, that is, of our abasement. For through sin we cast ourselves down from the glory in which we had been created.

He will reform this body, I say. When he first created the human being, he fashioned him in great glory. In the resurrection, however, [Col. 0369D] he will reform our body in still greater glory, configured to the body—that is, placed in the same form in which his body will be—not to the body of mortality which he previously possessed, but to the body of his glory. At the resurrection he will reform our body in still greater glory, configured to the body—that is, placed in the same form in which his body will be—not to the body of mortality which he previously possessed, but to the body of his glory.

He received the glory of immortality at the resurrection, and in this same glory of immortality he will reform our body.

It should also be noted that our humiliation was his glory. Because he is powerful to reform it, he adds: “He will reform it, acting according to the working”—in which working he is able not only to do this, but also to subject all things to himself.

## CHAPTER IV

“So then, my beloved and most greatly desired brothers, my joy and my crown, stand firm in the Lord in this way, beloved. I urge Euodia and I beg Syntyche [Col. 0370A] to be of the same mind in the Lord. I also ask you, true companion, help them, for they labored with me in the Gospel, together with Clement and the rest of my fellow workers, whose names are in the book of life.

“Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice. Let your moderation be known to all people. The Lord is near. Do not be anxious about anything, but in every prayer and supplication, with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known before God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus.

“Finally, brothers, whatever things are true, whatever things are honorable, whatever things are just, whatever things are holy, whatever things are lovely, whatever things are of good report—if there is any virtue and if there is any praise [Col. 0370B] of discipline—think about these things. What you have both learned and received and heard and seen in me, think about and practice; and the God of peace will be with you.

“I rejoiced greatly in the Lord that at last, after so long a time, you have revived your concern for me, just as you were concerned before. You were occupied, however. I do not say this because of want, for I have learned to be sufficient in whatever circumstances I am. I know how to be humbled, and I know how to abound. In every place and in all things I have been instructed, both to be filled and to hunger, both to abound and to suffer want. I can do all things in him who strengthens me [strengthened me].

“Nevertheless, you did well by sharing in my tribulation. You yourselves know, Philippians, that at the beginning of the Gospel, when I departed from Macedonia, no church shared with me in the account [Col. 0370C] of giving and receiving except you alone, because even in Thessalonica you sent something for my needs once and twice. Not that I seek the gift, but I seek the abundant fruit that accrues to your account.

“I have everything, and I abound. I have been filled by receiving from Epaphroditus what you sent, a fragrant odor, an acceptable sacrifice, pleasing to God. And my God will fulfill every desire of yours according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus.

“To our God and Father be glory throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

“Greet every holy person in Christ Jesus. The brothers who are with me greet you. All the holy people greet you, especially those who are of Caesar’s household. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit [Col. 0370D]. Amen.”

## EXPOSITION

And because he will reform us who have our manner of life in heaven, he therefore says: “My brothers, conduct yourselves with us in this way.”

He calls them brothers “beloved” because of their good conduct already accomplished, and “most greatly desired,” either because they greatly desire me or because they are greatly desired by me.

He calls them his joy in the present, for it is good for him to rejoice in their perfection; and his crown in the future, because he trusts that he will be crowned on their account.

“Stand firm in the Lord” in this way: either as I taught you or as you have stood until now. You have been beloved because of what has happened in the past; remain beloved because of the good that lies ahead.

He gives this exhortation to them collectively. But he urges Euodia, as though she were quick to agree, and he begs Syntyche, who seemed less [Col. 0371A] easy to persuade, to be of the same mind—namely, in the unity of faith.

He says “of the same mind” not concerning the law, but “in the Lord.” These two women had ministered to the Apostle and to his disciples in preaching. But because of feminine fickleness, what they had done for the Apostle they were doing also for the false teachers, thinking that they were acting rightly; and for this they are rebuked by Paul.

“I also ask you, O true companion, who are my equal in preaching the Gospel, help them by teaching them, so that they may no longer err”—and this is fitting—because they labored with me in the Gospel by ministering to me from their own resources. They also labored with Clement and my other fellow workers by ministering in the same way.

Their “names,” that is, their merits, by which they are worthy to be named before God, are in the book of life. The book of life is called the divine mind, in [Col. 0371B] which the good have been memorably written from eternity.

This Germanus was Paul’s fellow worker in preaching.

I admonish these persons by name; but collectively I give this command: “Rejoice,” not in the law and not in carnal things, but in the Lord, as I admonished at the beginning. Rejoice not for an hour only, but always rejoice in the Lord. Again I say the same thing: “Rejoice in the Lord.”

If he said “rejoice” only once, it would not seem that he wanted this rather than something else. But because he intends to urge this more strongly, he never says too much about what can never be done too much.

Rejoice in the Lord in such a way that your moderation may be known to all people, as an example of goodness. He calls moderation a kind of measure, so that they may be measured in such a way that they neither seek joy beyond the Lord nor presume to rejoice below what is fitting.

The person who adds carnal things to faith seeks joy beyond the Lord. The person who seeks joy in his own powers [Col. 0371C] stops below what is fitting. The person who seeks joy in his own powers stops below what is fitting.

They might say: “It would be good to add the law to faith for the worship of God.” To this Paul replies: “Be moderate in this way, because the Lord is near,” that is, he is always ready to assist the moderate.

Again they might say: “If we retained the discipline of the law, it would be useful for correcting the disorderly.” Paul again replies: “Do not be anxious about anything,” that is, do not doubt God’s help, since the abolition of the law hastens toward you.

Or let us understand these words more broadly, so that they answer both struggles. It is as though he were saying: “You are attacked from both sides, but rejoice always in the Lord, because you are worthy to suffer for his name both from persecutors and from false teachers. Again I say: [Col. 0371D] Rejoice.”

There is a twofold struggle and a twofold exhortation. Rejoice in such a way that your moderation—that is, the restraint of your patience—may be known to all people.

To be moderate, know that the Lord is near and does not abandon those who hope in him. And because he is near, do not be anxious about anything; that is, do not doubt on account of persecutors.

Do not be doubtful, but ask in every prayer and supplication, and with thanksgiving. Prayer is spoken when something obtainable is requested in the form of a plea. Supplication is spoken when we ask by adjurations for something which appears difficult to obtain.

The giving of thanks is also useful for obtaining future things, just as ingratitude is harmful.

Ask in such a way that your requests may be made known before God—that is, may be known and approved by God. A request becomes known before [Col. 0372A] God if the person who asks is righteous and if what he asks is suitable.

Requests are said of matters which are sometimes opportune and sometimes pass away, such as rain during drought or heat during the harvest.

Do what you are able to do, and in what you fail, may God in his mercy supply the deficiency.

He says this as follows: “The peace of God,” that is, the God of peace—and appropriately, since they were enduring a struggle, he names God here as the God of peace—“the peace of God which surpasses all understanding.”

The human intellect is not sufficient to grasp it. May this peace guard your hearts, that is, your wills, and your minds in Christ Jesus, who is the guardian of every good.

Some understand the same thing, but do not will the same thing. Others will the same thing, yet do not understand the same thing.

I have instructed you concerning the past. Concerning what remains—that is, the [Col. 0372B] future—brothers, think about whatever things are true and whatever things are honorable.

These two, “true” and “honorable,” are understood in relation to faith, one of which cannot exist in faith without the other. For if truth is in faith, so too is purity; if faith is false, it is also adulterous. Nevertheless, the words are not superfluous, because “true” and “honorable” designate different praises in faith.

Think also about whatever things are just toward your neighbor, whatever things are holy in yourselves, whatever things are lovely—that is, because of which your religion is loved—and whatever things are of good report, that is, about which people speak well.

I say “of good report” if there is any virtue in them. Or, if there is not such great virtue, let there at least be some praise of discipline; Christian discipline alone is sufficient for making a person appear praiseworthy.

Think about [Col. 0372C] all these things, which you both learned from me and received from me. It would be shameful for you to abandon what you began well. You also heard that these things were in me, and when I was with you, you saw them in me.

Think about and practice these things; then the God of peace will be with you, cooperating with you.

Thus I admonish you concerning the future. Concerning the past, however, I rejoiced greatly in the Lord, namely because, after much time had passed, you at last revived your concern for me—and then only once, no more.

When I was with you, you flourished in relation to me. Now you have flourished again, not only in ministering, but also in being concerned for me. My poverty was as grievous to you as if you yourselves were in need of the same things. I say “being concerned,” as once, when I was with you, you were concerned for me. [Col. 0372D]

He appropriately says “you have flourished again.” Just as fruit is expected from a flower, so fruit is expected from this administration.

You have flourished again at last, but previously you were occupied; therefore you are excusable if, being hindered by other matters, you did not minister.

I rejoiced, certainly, but I do not say this as though it were because of want, which would have been burdensome to me. For I have learned to be sufficient in whatever circumstances I am.

I know how to be humbled, that is, to be made poor. I also know how to abound. The person who is not broken by poverty knows how to be humbled. The person who knows how to command subjects with authority knows how to abound—not for his own glory, but for the benefit of the Church.

I know how to be humbled and how to abound. For I have been instructed—that is, accustomed—everywhere, that is, in every place, whether there are few or many people, whether poor or rich.

And in all circumstances I have been instructed both to be [Col. 0373A] satisfied and to hunger; and, to speak more broadly, I know how to abound and to suffer want.

Although I say, “I know how to suffer,” and so forth, nevertheless I can do all these things not by my own strength, but in him who helps me and has strengthened me by his grace.

And although I said that I did not rejoice because of want, nevertheless I am not ungrateful for benefits. You did well by sharing in my tribulation, that is, with me in my tribulation.

I say that I know how to abound and to suffer want. But you, Philippians, know these things, because when I departed from Macedonia at the beginning of the Gospel, no church shared with me in the account—that is, in the consideration—of giving and receiving, so as to consider that I was giving spiritual things to them and that I ought to receive carnal things from them.

Or the reverse: that they were receiving spiritual things from me and ought to give temporal things.

[Col. 0373B]

No church shared with me, I say, except you alone, who sent to me in Thessalonica once and twice—not in order to gather a treasure, but for my use, that is, enough to meet my needs.

They might say: “He praises us so that he may induce us to give.” To this Paul replies: “I do not praise you for this reason, because I seek a gift,” that is, in order that you may give to me, “but I seek abundant fruit in the account,” that is, in the administration resulting from your proper account.

It is as though he were saying: “I do not seek from you out of a desire to receive, but so that I may present myself as suitable material for your generosity, so that it may be able to bear fruit.”

I do not seek a gift because I have everything that is necessary, and I abound in those things. I abound because I have been filled by receiving from Epaphroditus what you sent, a fragrant odor to [Col. 0374A] God.

Prayer is signified by incense, which is called a fragrant odor to God. This almsgiving was no less pleasing to God than devout prayer.

You sent this same offering, acceptable to God—not merely acceptable in some way, but well pleasing to God. An offering was called a sacrifice because it was offered for enemies who had been defeated or were to be defeated.

Even if these people had slain themselves by blows or fasts in order to overcome the temptations of the invisible enemy, they would not have pleased God more than this ministry.

I have been filled by you; and may my God fulfill every desire of yours—not according to what you have deserved, but according to his riches.

May he fulfill it in glory, and this in Christ Jesus, the distributor of glory. Because you have filled me in this way, I pray for you.

To our God and Father, for these things and for all the good things we accomplish, may there be glory [Col. 0374B] throughout the ages that follow these ages. Amen.

Greet every holy person in Christ Jesus. He says this of his disciples, in case they should happen to pass by and see them.

The brothers who are with me greet you. He says this again of his disciples who were with him.

All the holy people greet you. He says this of converts.

Most of all, those who are of Caesar’s household greet you. He wished to signify to them that some members of Nero’s household had been converted through him, and he thought that through their assistance he might escape and visit them.

**Sign of the Epistle.** May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, so that you may serve God in spiritual things, in which you also always rejoice. Amen.

## [ON THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS]

[Column 0373]

## INTRODUCTION TO PAUL’S EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS

The Colossians, like the Laodiceans, are Asians; and they too had been led astray by false apostles. The Apostle did not come to them, but corrects them also by a letter. For he had heard the report from Archippus, who had also received the ministry among them.

Therefore the Apostle, already in chains, writes to them from Ephesus, through Tychicus the deacon and Onesimus the acolyte.

## BLESSED BRUNO’S PROLOGUE TO THE SAME EPISTLE

[Column 0373C]

These Colossians were Asians, related to the Laodiceans, to whom John writes in the Apocalypse together with the other churches, and to whom Paul likewise wrote an epistle, because they were similarly being tested by false apostles. He ordered that the Epistle to the Colossians be read in the church of the Laodiceans, and conversely.

Paul had not preached to these Colossians, nor had he [Column 0373D] come to them. Rather, Archippus, a disciple of Paul and perhaps the son of Philemon, to whom Paul writes concerning the reconciliation of Onesimus, had preached to them and converted them to the faith.

After they had thus advanced in the faith, a certain Epaphras, born from the same people and also instructed by Paul in the faith, came to them, affirming what Archippus had preached to them. His fellow citizens gladly listened to him, and through him received an increase of faith.

While they were flourishing in the faith and walking [Column 0374C] according to the teaching of Archippus and Epaphras, false teachers arrived, preaching the law to them.

The people, still inexperienced and thinking that these teachers ought to be heard no less than the earlier teachers, were almost beginning to agree with them.

But Epaphras, hearing that the Apostle was near Ephesus, went across to him, informed him of the whole matter, and asked him to confirm by a letter sent to them both his own preaching and that of Archippus, and to condemn the party of those who contradicted them.

On this occasion Paul writes this Epistle to them, in which he deals with Christ and the law. The former preached Christ; the latter preached the law.

He treats the matter by approving the faith of Christ with many clear reasons and by rejecting the law as no longer necessary to be observed.

He treats both subjects with this intention: to confirm [Column 0374D] those in the purity of the faith which is Christ.

## THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS

[Column 0373]

## CHAPTER I

[Column 0373D]

“Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God [Col. 0374D], and Timothy, a brother, to those who are at Colossae, holy and faithful brothers in Christ Jesus [Col. 0375A]. Grace to you and peace from God our Father. We give thanks to God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, always praying for you, having heard of your faith in Christ Jesus and of the love which you have for all the saints, because of the hope that is laid up for you in heaven. You heard of this hope in the word of the truth of the Gospel, which has come to you, just as it is also in the whole world, and bears fruit and grows, as it does among you, from the day on which you heard and came to know the grace of God in truth, as you learned from Epaphras, our most beloved fellow servant, who is a faithful minister of Christ Jesus on your behalf. He also made known to us your love in the Spirit.

Therefore, from the day on which we heard, we too have not ceased praying for you and asking that you may be filled [Col. 0375B] with the knowledge of his will in all wisdom and spiritual understanding, so that you may walk worthily of God, pleasing him in every way, bearing fruit in every good work, and growing in the knowledge of God; strengthened with all power according to the might of his glory, in all patience and long-suffering, with joy giving thanks to God and the Father, who has made us worthy to share in the lot of the saints in the light. He has delivered us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love. In him we have redemption and the forgiveness of sins.

He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature, because in him all things were created in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible [Col. 0375C], whether thrones, dominions, principalities, or powers; all things were created through him and in him. He is before all things, and all things subsist in him. He is also the head of the body, the Church; he is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead (I Cor. XV, 20), so that he himself might hold first place in all things. For in him it pleased the whole fullness of divinity to dwell, and through him to reconcile all things to himself, making peace through the blood of his cross, whether the things in heaven or the things on earth.

And you, although you were once alienated and enemies in your understanding, in evil works, he has now reconciled in the body of his flesh, through death, to present you holy, spotless, and blameless before him, provided that you remain [Col. 0375D] grounded and steadfast in the faith, and immovable from the hope of the Gospel which you have heard, which has been preached in all creation under heaven, of which I, Paul, have become a minister. Now I rejoice in sufferings for you, and I complete what is lacking in the sufferings of Christ in my flesh, for his body, which is the Church, of which I have become a minister according to the stewardship of God that was given to me for you, so that I might fulfill the word of God.

The mystery that was hidden from ages and generations has now been revealed to his saints. God wished to make known to them the riches of the glory of this sacrament among the nations, which is Christ in you, the hope of glory. We proclaim him, admonishing everyone and teaching everyone [Col. 0376A] in all wisdom, so that we may present everyone perfect in Christ Jesus. For this I labor, contending according to his activity, which he accomplishes in me with power.”

## EXPOSITION

Paul, and so forth. Since authority was necessary here, he did not omit the title of dignity, saying: “Paul, an apostle,” [273] not of the Law, but “of Jesus Christ.” I say, an apostle “by the will of God.” Know that whoever contradicts me also contradicts the will of God; whoever contradicts Archippus and Epaphras, my disciples [co-workers], likewise contradicts me and God.

“Paul,” I say, “and Timothy the brother write to those who are at Colossae.” To these, I say, who are “holy,” that is, consecrated and confirmed in the righteousness of faith. “Holy,” I say, “and faithful brothers” [Col. 0376B], that is, less perfect. I call them holy and faithful “in Christ Jesus,” because if Christ Jesus is sufficient for your sanctification, you seek to take hold of the Law in vain.

He places Timothy with himself in the greeting because Timothy was known to them and they held him in great authority. Here, however, authority alone was needed. They were not contradicting Peter or Paul, or anyone preaching Christ; they simply thought that those false teachers were from Paul in the same way as the genuine teachers were.

“Paul,” I say, “and Timothy write in this manner: Grace to you and peace from God our Father,” as has often been explained.

Now, first of all, he commends their faith, which Archippus and Epaphras had handed down to them, saying: “Having heard of your faith, we give thanks to God.” I certainly would not give thanks for it if it were imperfect. “But we give thanks [Col. 0376C] to God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ,” whose faith has been handed down to you. Just as I agree with it, so do Christ and his Father, God. See that you do not, as negligent disciples, despise me as your teacher, for if you despise me, you despise Christ and his Father, God.

“We give thanks,” we say, “praying for you,” so that you may advance in the faith which you received; I certainly would not pray for this unless I approved that faith. I say, praying not rarely, but always. See that you do not make the labor of my prayer fruitless.

He immediately adds why he gives thanks, commending their faith as Archippus and Epaphras had handed it down to them, saying: “We give thanks, having heard that your faith is in Christ Jesus,” and having heard the good effect of your faith, namely, the love which you have for all the [Col. 0376D] saints, with whom you share out of your love.

He speaks of love as possessed because of hope, that is, because of the hoped-for reality. This hope is laid up, that is, hidden and reserved for you in a place so worthy as heaven. By saying that it is hoped for, laid up, and hidden, he commends the merit of those who hope in God for what they have neither seen nor heard. When he says “in heaven,” he shows the dignity of the hoped-for reality from the place in which it will be.

They might say to him: “This hope is obtained from the Law.” To this Paul replies: “You have both heard and understood the hoped-for reality in the word of truth.” This truth was not in the Law, but in the truth of the Gospel. For the word of the Law is a word of falsehood, whereas the Gospel is a word of truth.

Again they might say: “We would rather not obey you than accept a matter we have never heard of.” To this Paul replies: “The Gospel [Col. 0377A] has come to you,” having already passed through many churches. “Do you wish to reject what the whole Church holds?”

Again they might say: “It has indeed reached us, but not in its entirety as it has reached others.” To this he says: “It has indeed reached you, just as it has reached the whole world.” For, in this same faith which they handed down to you, the whole world follows after Christ.

I say that it has come and is present, that is, it remains in the whole world in this manner; it bears fruit through good works and grows both in number and in the knowledge of God. It is not different from what was handed down to you, but is just as these men established it among you.

They might say: “It is indeed growing among us from the time we began to hear those who have recently entered.” Paul says: “Certainly not. It has grown from the day on which you heard the faith from Archippus [Col. 0377B] and recognized, through the testimonies of the Scriptures, the grace of God approved for you, which is in the faith.”

For the grace of the Law consists in the hand of the woman who cuts away the skin of an old woman.

“I speak of the grace of God in truth. Believe me, because this is the true grace of God. The grace of the Law was a shadow. You heard it, I say, and you learned it; and it would certainly be shameful for you to abandon what you had learned. Conversely: you learned it, I say, from our most beloved Epaphras, who serves Christ in the Gospel just as Peter or I do. Therefore, do not listen to him less.

They might say: “You call him a fellow servant; but he ministered something else to us, which he did not learn from you.” [274] Paul says: “Certainly not, because he is a faithful minister, adding nothing and taking nothing away.” I say, a minister “of Christ Jesus,” either because he ministers Christ [Col. 0377C], or because Christ appointed him as a minister, or because he is a minister to Christ’s honor.

And since he is a minister, he is certainly so on your behalf, because you are his people; unless it were for your love, I believe he would not minister. He also made known to us—not your hatred or disagreement, but that your love is in the Spirit, that is, that you despise carnal things and love spiritual things.

Having shown why he gives thanks, with approval of the faith they received, he adds that he prays for them, inserting a condemnation of the Law, saying: “And because he made known to us that your love is in the Spirit, therefore we pray for you, and we do not cease praying from the day on which we heard of your faith and love.”

I say that we pray and ask, that is, seeking with confidence as though it were something owed to your righteousness [Col. 0377D], that you may be filled with the knowledge of his will, that is, that you may fully know the will of God.

I say, “filled in all wisdom.” Here he uses “wisdom” as though it meant knowledge; and what he says, “in all wisdom,” has the same force as “in all knowledge of the active life.” Be filled also with all spiritual understanding, so that, just as in bodily matters, you may understand the will of God in spiritual matters.

So that, understanding his will, you may walk in every way, that is, act well. “Walk,” I say, “worthily of God,” that is, so that you may be worthy to have God. Or, “worthily of God,” so that God may judge you worthy to dwell in you. I say that you should walk in this way, pleasing him. Or: “Walk, pleasing him in every way,” which has the same meaning.

Nor should you wish to stop while walking, but should bear fruit in every good work, that is, have increase. I say that, by bearing fruit in this way, you should grow in the knowledge of God [Col. 0378A], that is, in the knowledge of the divine essence, which no one can possess unless he first does what belongs to God. For one does not ascend from knowledge to works, but from works already performed to knowledge.

This knowledge of God and the knowledge of his will, which he mentioned earlier, are far different. There he said what God wills and does not will, something readily apparent to anyone; here, however, he speaks of knowledge of the divine essence, which the purity of life reveals. He proceeds appropriately. First the will of God must be understood; once it is understood, one must walk in it, and one must not stop there, but must bear fruit for the better. Then at last the entrance to knowledge of the divine essence is opened. Once one has reached it, only perseverance remains.

Thus he says: “After you have borne fruit [Col. 0378B] and grown in the knowledge of God, be strengthened,” that is, made strong and persevering, “in every virtue,” that is, humility, temperance, and whatever virtues there are.

“Strengthened,” I say, “according to his power,” that is, strengthened in the way in which he is powerful enough to strengthen you. I speak of “the power of his glory,” that is, the power by which he glorified you. For when you were in the darkness of sins, he glorified you by justifying you; he will more easily be able and ought to complete you now that you are just.

I speak of being strengthened “in every virtue,” namely, being strengthened “in all patience and long-suffering, with joy.” Because he saw these two virtues as especially necessary for perseverance, he therefore adds “in all patience,” that is, so that we may endure reproaches as well as the bitterness of evils. Whoever does not wish to suffer argues, [Col. 0378C] strikes back, and thus love perishes.

He also adds “in long-suffering.” For whoever is not long-suffering in endurance, when his reward is delayed, casts off God’s burden, and thus every virtue perishes in him. Again, it is bad to be patient and long-suffering unless one does so willingly; therefore he adds “with joy,” so that they may not be saddened but rejoice in suffering and in waiting a long time.

He wishes now to condemn the Law to them, saying that he and the other apostles, who were born under the Law, had been in darkness then and had abandoned the Law, giving thanks to God because he had called them to the faith. If those who were naturally under the Law could neglect it and cling to the faith, it is foolish to confuse the purity of faith by mixing it with the Law in those who were never under the Law but received the faith.

Therefore he says: “We do not cease praying for you and giving thanks [Col. 0378D] to God the Father, who has made us worthy to share in the lot,” that is, the participation in the inheritance of the saints, namely, the inheritance which the saints will possess. I say that we have been placed “in the light,” that is, in true knowledge. Or, “in the light,” that [275] is, in Christ, who illuminates us.

He calls him Father with reference to different possessors—not because the portions there are separated, since all have one blessedness. He calls the inheritance of the saints a “lot” because it is not given through human merit, but by lot, that is, by divine election.

He adds how he made us worthy of this lot, saying: “He placed us in the light,” having first “delivered us from the power of darkness,” that is, either of demons, sins, or disgrace. He calls it “power” because human strength by itself could not escape it.

After rescuing us, he transferred us, that is, transformed us, into the kingdom [Col. 0379A] of the Son, so that his Son might reign in us. I say, the Son “of his love.” For all the others were sons of wrath. Everyone was born in sin, but he alone is the Son of love, because he is free from sin. Of him the Father says: “This is my beloved Son,” and so forth (Matt. III, 7).

He adds the manner of this deliverance: “In this Son we have redemption.” For the price of blood, given on the cross, was sufficient for all. Through him we also have the forgiveness of sins in baptism.

This Son, according to the divine nature, is “the image of the invisible God,” that is, the complete representation of the Father, because whatever is in the Father is wholly in the Son—not an image in the sense that it is something different, except with regard to the distinction of persons, but complete identity in substance. We may construe the phrase as “the invisible image [Col. 0379B] of God” or “the image of the invisible God.”

From these words we have the Son consubstantial with the Father. For if everything that is said of the substance of the Father is said also of the substance of the Son, he is plainly consubstantial with him.

I say, the Son is “the firstborn of every creature,” that is, begotten from the Father before every creature. He alone is begotten; the others are created, not begotten as he is. Nor was he himself created. From these words we also have that he is co-eternal with the Father.

He was truly begotten before every creature, because all things were created in him, that is, through him, in accordance with the saying: “You made all things in wisdom” (Ps. CIII, 24), that is, in the Son.
