I say “all things,” because the visible and invisible things in heaven—such as angels, the sun, and the moon—and the visible and invisible things on earth—such as the spirits of animals [Col. 0379C] and all earthly bodies—were created in him.

I rightly say “in heaven,” because whether thrones, dominions, principalities, or powers, all things were created through him; and through him in such a way that created things are contained in him, that is, within the extent of his power. For he is in all things and already beyond them.

He is before all things in dignity according to both natures, and all created things subsist in him, that is, they have existence through him. For just as they could not exist except through him, so created things could not endure except through him.

Christ himself is the head, that is, the beginning and government, of the Church. He says this in the following manner: “The head of the body, the Church.” Just as the human body has all its senses in the head, so the Church has all its powers in Christ, its head, beginning, and ruler.

Someone might object [Col. 0379D]: “Why do you call Christ the head of the Church, since Abel and many righteous people existed before him in time?” He removes this objection in the following way: “He is truly the head of the Church because he is the beginning of the Church.”

Although many saints preceded Christ’s flesh in time, they would never have been saved unless they were members of Christ the head through faith. Thus he could be the head of the Church because he is “the firstborn from the dead.” For he was the first of all to rise from the dead.

He is also “firstborn” because he possesses the whole inheritance of the Father; and whoever possesses any part of it must receive it from him. Just as the firstborn son possesses his father’s whole inheritance, and no one receives anything except from him.

Nor is the firstborn to be rejected, as Esau was; rather, he is firstborn in such a way that he holds first place among all creatures. For he has been appointed prince of all [Col. 0380A], and therefore holds first place, because it pleased God the Father that the fullness of all good things should dwell in the Son himself, as John says: “From his fullness we have all received” (John I, 16). And it pleased God through this Son to reconcile all things to himself, both Gentiles and Jews.

Yet I speak of all things that remain in him. Whoever does not remain in him will be deprived of reconciliation.

It pleased him to reconcile, making peace between the world and himself—or between Jews and Gentiles—with blood, not poured out in some other kind of honorable death, but through the blood of his cross, the most contemptible kind of death [276].

“Making peace,” I say, with God, whether concerning the things that are in heaven, that is, the saints whose souls already reign in heaven, or concerning the things that are on earth, that is, those who are still pilgrims on earth.

Or in this way: “Whether the things that are in heaven [Col. 0380B],” that is, angels, “or the things that are on earth,” that is, human beings. Before Christ there was discord between angels and human beings; but once a human being was justified, he immediately had peace with the angel.

At last he descends to the point he had intended from what preceded, saying: He made peace with us Jews, and likewise reconciled you Gentiles.

“You,” I say, “although you once,” that is, in the time of unbelief, “were alienated from God through ignorance,” and “were enemies,” that is, were hostile to God, “in your understanding,” that is, by your will. You were also enemies in evil works.

Or: although you were enemies in your understanding, nevertheless he reconciled you. “Now he has reconciled you in the body”—not yet immortal, but in the body of his flesh, that is, still mortal. If he did this in a mortal body, what will he do in an immortal one? Much more indeed.

He reconciled you in the body through death. For in order to reconcile you, he willed to suffer death, that is, so that he might present you holy through the establishment of virtues, spotless through the removal of evils, and blameless before God himself. His scrutiny—for whose eyes all things are exposed—would not find in them anything to censure.

I say that he presents you in this way, provided that you remain grounded and firm in the faith; and if you remain steadfast, as far as it depends on you, and immovable if a persecutor presses upon you, from the hope, that is, from the hoped-for reality.

I speak of the hope of the Gospel, that is, the blessedness which the Gospel promises as something to be hoped for. You heard this Gospel from our disciples. You ought not to reject it, because all the righteous receive it.

He says this as follows: “The Gospel was preached to all creation [Col. 0380D] and remains in all creation in this way.”

He calls the righteous “creation” by excellence. Although all are creatures of God, the righteous are called “creation” by a certain privilege, because in them the first generation, which existed in the sin of the flesh, has been erased through baptism, and the newness of faith has generated them as new sons in Christ.

Therefore he says: “In all creation,” that is, in all the righteous who have been made a new creation in the faith of Christ. I say “all,” not of one region, but wherever there is anything under heaven.

Or in this way: “The creation which is under heaven,” that is, which still journeys in the world and, shortly thereafter, is to be transferred above the heavens by the merit of faith. By this word he sufficiently commends the faith to them.

Now he sets forth his authority, which was necessary for their confirmation, saying: “Of this Gospel [Col. 0381A] I, Paul”—whose authority may not be opposed—“have been made by God,” certainly not its giver, but its minister. To magnify the Gospel, I now suffer, placed in chains, and I rejoice in these sufferings for your instruction.

If they saw Paul shrinking from suffering for the faith, they would condemn the faith on the basis of Paul himself, since he would show by his example that one ought not to suffer for it.

“I rejoice,” I say, “and while rejoicing I complete what is still lacking in the sufferings of Christ and remains for me to fulfill.” He calls his sufferings Christ’s sufferings both because Christ appointed him to suffer in this way and because he suffers for Christ’s name.

He says that he completes them because he is going toward death, in which the sufferings reach their completion.

Or in this way: “I complete what is lacking in the sufferings of Christ.” Christ endured many sufferings, suffering reproaches [Col. 0381B], afflictions, and scourging, and finally death. Paul likewise endured reproaches, beatings, and many afflictions, and hastened toward death, so that, just as Christ died for him, he might die for Christ.

“I complete the sufferings of Christ”—not to the detriment of the reality, nor in reproaches alone, but “in my flesh.” For I offer my very flesh to punishment, and I do this for his body, namely, by multiplying Christ’s body.

He did not simply say “for the Church”; but when he says, “for his body, which is the Church,” he greatly commends the faith, which makes a person a member of this body whose head is Christ.

“Of this Church,” again, “I have become a minister according to the stewardship,” because I know how to distribute [Col. 0381C] to each according to his measure: to one a greater grace, to another a lesser [277]. I speak of “the stewardship of God,” either because I dispense God himself, or because God appointed me as steward, according to the stewardship that was given to me for you.

The phrase “which was given to me for you” may seem superfluous, since he had already said “according to the stewardship.” But stewardship was entrusted to certain people who, overtaken by martyrdom, had no time to exercise it; Paul, however, both received the office of stewardship and was given the opportunity to exercise it.

Although he had not been among them, he nevertheless says that the stewardship was given to him for them, because they belong to his apostolate and were taught through his disciples.

It was given to me [Col. 0381D] so that I might fulfill the word of God, which he both spoke from eternity and foretold in time through his prophets.

Paul asserts that he possesses great authority before God when he says that through him what had been foretold so many ages earlier was fulfilled, and that it had remained unfulfilled until him—namely, the salvation of the Gentiles.

I speak of “the word of God,” that is, the mystery which was hidden from former ages, and hidden from ages in such a way that it was also hidden from generations, meaning that everyone who belonged to the former generation was ignorant of this secret.

A few had known it then, and these had been justified through faith in the one who was to come, as Abraham was. It was formerly hidden, but now, in the days of grace, it has been revealed to his saints, namely, Christ’s saints—not to all, but to those whom God willed.

This was apparent when the disciples rebuked Peter [Col. 0382A] because he had received the Gentile Cornelius, since they had not yet fully understood God’s mystery concerning the salvation of the Gentiles.

God wished to make known to them “the riches of glory.” He calls them riches because God’s gifts are infinite; of glory, because glory is present in all of them.

I speak of “the riches of this sacrament,” of which I have become a minister. I speak of the sacrament “among the Gentiles.” For the salvation of the Gentiles was hidden from almost everyone; but the salvation of the Jews is not called a mystery, because Christ had been openly promised to them in the Law, whereas among the Gentiles there was no God. This sacrament is Christ, who was promised in the Law under a mystery.

I speak of Christ as “the hope of glory in you,” that is, in whom you may hope for every glory, the forgiveness of sins, the righteousness of life, and future glory.

We proclaim him as such a hope [Col. 0382B] of all future glory, admonishing everyone with complete confidence and teaching everyone. We admonish the one who has strayed from the truth or contradicts the faith. We teach the one who knows nothing or who still has only a simple understanding.

We admonish and teach “in all wisdom,” that is, both concerning bodily matters and concerning spiritual matters, so that we may present not only a Jew but every human being—not a Gentile less perfectly than a Jew, but every human being equally perfect in Christ Jesus, who alone is sufficient for perfection.

In him, that is, in this matter, so that I may present every person perfect, I not only admonish and teach, but also labor, contending.

He labors by fasting and keeping vigil, and by such means he contends against persecutors by enduring them, and against the false teachers by strengthening the faith [Col. 0382C].

I labor and contend, acting according to his activity which he accomplishes in me through the power of miracles. That is, God cooperates with me in labor and conflict just as he does in the working of miracles; by this even unbelievers confess that God’s power is in me.

## CHAPTER II

“For I want you to know what concern I have for you, for those who are in Laodicea, and for all who have not seen my face in the flesh, so that their hearts may be comforted, instructed in love, and in all the riches of the fullness of understanding, in the knowledge of the mystery of God the Father and of Christ Jesus, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden.

I say this so that no one may deceive you [Col. 0382D] with lofty speech. For although I am absent in body (I Cor. V, 3), nevertheless I am present with you in spirit, rejoicing and seeing your order and the firmness of your faith, which is in Christ.

Therefore, just as you received Jesus Christ our Lord, walk in him, rooted and built up in the faith, as you were also taught, abounding in him in thanksgiving [278].

See that no one deceives you through philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ; because in him the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily, and in him you have been filled, who is the head of every principality and power.

In him you were also circumcised with a circumcision not made by hand, in the stripping away of the body of the flesh, but in the circumcision of Jesus Christ. You were buried with him in baptism, in which you also rose through faith in the working of God, who raised him from the dead.

And when you were dead in transgressions and in the uncircumcision of your flesh, he made you alive together with him, forgiving you all transgressions, wiping out the bond of the decree that was against us, which was opposed to us; he removed it from our midst, fastening it to the cross.

Having stripped principalities and powers, he led them forth openly and confidently, triumphing over them in himself.

Therefore let no one judge you concerning food or drink, or concerning a festival, or a new moon, or Sabbaths, which are a shadow of future things; but the body belongs to Christ.

Let no one deceive you, wishing to do so through humility and the religion of angels, concerning things he has not seen, walking vainly inflated by the sense of his flesh, and not holding fast to the head, from whom the whole body, supplied and constructed through its joints and connections, grows with the growth of God.

Therefore, if you have died with Christ to the elements of this world, why, as though living in the world, do you make distinctions? ‘Do not touch, do not taste, do not handle’—things which all perish by use, according to the precepts and teachings of human beings.

These things indeed have an appearance of wisdom in superstition and humility, but they are not for feeding the body, nor are they of any honor for the satisfying of the flesh.”

## EXPOSITION

[Col. 0383C] Therefore I labor and contend because I am concerned for you, and I want you to know what kind of concern I have, that is, how boundless my concern is for your confirmation, and for those who are in Laodicea. Through the letter sent to them, he armed them against the same matter.

I am also concerned for your neighbors, all who have not seen my face in the flesh. They have seen me by reputation; therefore I am concerned so that their hearts may be comforted, that is, their own hearts.

I say that they are instructed by me in love, that is, in the love of God, so that, remembering that Christ suffered for them solely out of love, they may be inflamed by love for him and hasten to meet him by suffering.

I say that they are instructed in love and instructed in knowledge of the mystery of God, so that they may know certain mysteries—or secrets—of God. Or, for example, how the Trinity [Col. 0383D] exists in Unity and conversely, or something of this sort. For if someone comes to know any mystery of God, through this very knowledge he will certainly increase in love for God.

And because human understanding cannot penetrate to invisible things except through visible things, he first says that they are instructed in love and “in all,” that is, passing through all the riches of the fullness of understanding.

“All riches,” so that they may know something about all things, although not perfectly; “fullness,” so that they may have complete knowledge of each thing. Or “fullness,” so that they may possess all the riches completely concerning three or four matters, so that their knowledge may be full concerning everything.

Instructed through all the riches of the fullness of understanding, they are brought to the knowledge of the mystery of God the Father and Christ Jesus. For in order to reach the height of divine knowledge, we must first [Col. 0384A] consider bodily things, which lie before the eyes; then incorporeal things within us, that is, souls. Through souls, we ascend again to incorporeal things in heaven, such as angels; and from angels we ascend to God, understanding him to be purer, more spiritual, and incomprehensible than the purity of creatures.

In this Jesus Christ are “all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge”: wisdom concerning spiritual things and knowledge concerning bodily things, stored up as in a treasure. He himself is the treasure. From his fullness all are enriched without diminution.

I speak of “treasures hidden,” that is, revealed to few.

They might say: “We have not seen these treasures, so that we possess wisdom and knowledge in both matters.” To this Paul replies: “Even if you find in Christ the treasure of every good thing [279] [Col. 0384B], you nevertheless seek in vain to add the Law to the faith.”

In Christ are the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. I say this concerning Christ—that all the treasures are in him—so that no one may deceive you with loftiness. For those false teachers devote themselves greatly to lofty words.

I speak of loftiness of speech, because this loftiness exists only in language, not in meaning; the faithful possess simplicity in their words and loftiness in their meanings.

Therefore I say: “Let no one deceive you concerning the future,” for you have not yet been deceived.

“And although,” that is, although I am absent from you in body, “nevertheless,” that is, still, “I am present with you in spirit.” Many saints possessed this grace, such as Martin and Nicholas; Paul is believed especially to have possessed it, so that, while absent, he knew through the Spirit what his Church was doing or what it was preparing to do.

“I am with you in spirit, rejoicing.” In this word he intimates that they have not yet fallen. I say that I rejoice over your perfection and see your order, that is, how suitably you adapt yourselves to each matter in its proper order.

For it is not enough to do good things if they are done without order, as with the person who fasts in disordered clothing or with undisciplined speech and thereby condemns himself in his fasting.

I also see the firmness of your faith, that is, your confirmed faith, which is in Christ and not in the Law. Because you have been confirmed in the faith, I rejoice with your order.

Therefore, just as you received not the Law but the Lord Jesus Christ, so walk not in the Law but in him. For they could have received Christ and yet walked in the Law.

Walk, rooted according to the fruit of pious action, and built up so that you may be a house for God to dwell in. This is appropriately said concerning prelates, in whom God, seated, distributed his graces to their subjects through the hands of the prelates.

Built up today and tomorrow super-built, and thus always increasing in good work. Rooted, I say, and super-built in him, and confirmed in the faith, so that you may persevere in the good.

I speak of the faith not as another faith, but as the faith you learned—for I do not hand down another. Be confirmed also in the act of thanksgiving, which is of great value for obtaining what is future.

And it is right that, having been confirmed, you should give thanks, because you are already abounding in many good things received in that Christ.”

I say, walk. But in order that you may walk freely, see that no one deceives you. In saying this, he looks back to what he said above: “Let no one deceive you.” I mean, let no one deceive you through philosophy, as they reckon it, and which I call an empty deception. It is deception because there is no truth in it; empty, that is, without usefulness. For there are many falsehoods in it, such as those of the poets, which are useless.

I call philosophy an empty deception existing according to human tradition, that is, according to those who are wise in human terms—namely, according to the Law. Before Christ, the Law was indeed a tradition of God. But when the Truth came and God willed it to cease, the Law was no longer God’s tradition but the tradition of men. I call it a tradition of men and a deception practiced according to the elements. He calls the same Law “elements” because, just as children first learn through the elements, so that they may afterward advance to the perfection of letters, so those legal elements were called “elements” because the carnal people, unable to grasp spiritual realities, were instructed through carnal things, in order that, having become accustomed to these, they might afterward pass over to serving God in spiritual matters. I call them the elements of the world, because both the commandments were carnal and those who received them were carnal. This philosophy is according to the elements of the world and not according to Christ, whom you received and learned.

Truly, those who teach the Law are not according to Christ, because in Christ himself there is all fullness—a truth not believed by those who seek some righteousness outside Christ, namely, in the Law. In Christ himself all the fullness of divinity dwells. He says well, “dwells,” because divinity is in Christ in such a way that it remains in him eternally. “The fullness of divinity,” that is, complete and perfect divinity, in no respect imperfect.

All of it is in Christ, because whatever graces existed in anyone at all are in Christ, and there is an even greater grace in him, because in him divinity is said to have become human: just as the soul is united to the body, so divinity itself was personally united to that man. Divinity is everywhere in different ways. It is in every creature, since no creature can exist or endure without divinity. It is also in the saints by grace. Both these modes were present in Christ, and yet more abundantly, because—as was said—just as the soul becomes human in a man’s flesh, so divinity became human in Christ. The fullness of divinity dwells bodily in Christ, that is, in a fulfilling manner—not that divinity became a body, but because shadows had preceded, and in Christ there was the truth of those shadows, since he was the fulfillment of everything that had been foretold or prefigured.

He proves the same point again. Truly, those who teach the Law are not according to Christ. For you have been filled with every good thing in him, that is, through Christ—something they say cannot happen without the Law. Christ is the head, that is, the beginning and governance, of every principality and power. Through these two remaining orders, let us understand the matter. In these words he shows that Christ can fill all things, because, if he can fill angels, there can be no doubt about human beings.

He wishes to show that everything commanded by the Law is found in Christ, saying: In Christ you have not only been filled, but also circumcised, with a circumcision not made by hand, as in the Law, in the stripping away of the flesh’s skin. Nothing else is done there except that the foreskin of the flesh is cut off. But you have been circumcised with Christ’s circumcision, by which Christ purified you.

Or let us construe it this way: You have been circumcised with a circumcision not made by hand. I say, with a circumcision made in the stripping away of the body; and that body was of flesh, that is, it was overcome by sensuality. For you have stripped off the body according to carnality, so that it may now obey the spirit—by a circumcision not made by hand, but in Christ’s circumcision, by which Christ cut away from you every excess and the vices dependent upon it. In this circumcision you have been circumcised and purified.

We are stripped of the body of flesh in baptism, in which sins are laid aside and the human free will is strengthened by the righteousness it has received, so that it can now, if it wishes, do good. We have not only been circumcised through the laying aside of sins, but also buried with Christ in baptism, where our will is to be strengthened. We have therefore been buried because Christ, once buried, did not return again to the acts of the old human being; so we too, if we are willing to use reason, strengthened in baptism, will not return again to the practice of the oldness of sin.

In Christ you also rose, insofar as concerns the justification of the soul. You rose, I say, through faith in God’s operation, that is, through the faith which God works in you. Christ’s resurrection works a double resurrection in us: the first, which we have already attained, according to the soul; the other, which we await when the body has been restored to immortality.

And that we shall have a future resurrection of the bodies, he proves by Christ’s resurrection, which is both the cause and the figure of our resurrection, saying: Just as you rose in the first resurrection of the soul, so he will also give you life together with himself in the immortality of your bodies. But he first gives the proof of this, saying: God, who raised Christ from the dead, will likewise raise you, although you were dead—that is, although you were so powerless that you could in no way revive yourselves for righteousness through your own strength.

Dead, I say, in offences, that is, in the violation of the natural law. An offence is so called when what is owed is neglected. You were also dead in the foreskin of your flesh, that is, in original sin, which the foreskin appropriately signifies, since it is the seat of generation. We contract this original sin because we were begotten in the desire of our parents.

[Col. 0386D]

Although you were dead in this way, he nevertheless gave you life together with Christ. He speaks of what is future in the past tense, showing himself to be as certain of this future event as of something already past. “He gave you life together with him” means that he placed you with him in the same dignity of place. For he could give you immortality and yet place you somewhere other than with Christ.

He gave you life together with him, I say, forgiving you Gentiles all your transgressions, both original and actual. Thus he freed you from original sin through faith, just as he also freed us Jews, who were falsely thought to be liberated from it through circumcision. He says this as follows: Blotting out in the same way the bond of the decree, that is, of the Law, in which God had decreed what he wished to be done. This bond was against us Jews.

A bond is called a handwritten document, because it is divided in two so that the memory of the deed may be preserved on both sides. The devil had one part of this bond, by which he accused the Jews before God of transgressing the Law; the Jew had the other part, by which his own conscience likewise accused him.

Thus he says: The bond—that is, the memory of sin—which came from the decree, that is, from the Law, and was hostile to us: this he blotted out. And he did not blot out only the bond, but also the decree itself, that is, the Law itself, which was contrary to us, because the devil provoked us more strongly, we reached toward what was forbidden with greater eagerness, and the Law added the sin of transgression.

He removed the decree itself, I say, from the midst, that is, from the community, so that he left neither Jew nor Gentile with any obligation to retain it. For he could take away the sin of the Law while leaving the Law itself. He removed it from the midst, fastening it to the cross—that is, he fastened the Law itself to the cross so that it would no longer be held, when, as he was dying, he said: “It is finished” (John 19:30). He showed that this was the end and completion of everything that had preceded in the Law, and that the shadow was no longer to be retained after the Truth had arisen. I say, he fastened it to the cross. For on the cross—as we have said—he brought the Law to an end, when everything had been completed as it had been foretold.

They might object: How can you say that we cannot be justified except through Christ, since Abraham and the other holy people who preceded him were justified without him? Paul proves that they too were similarly liberated through Christ, saying: Just as he liberated those who were contemporaries of himself from the Law and from the sin of the Law, so he himself, stripping principalities and powers, [did so] in the lower regions.

He does not say “from whom he stripped them,” but by the expression “stripping” he signifies that Christ brought his spoils back from the lower regions. Stripping them, I say, he led them away, like a victor carrying off booty through the midst of those who were plundering it. He himself, I say, triumphing over those infernal principalities confidently, that is, without doubt concerning his triumph. He triumphed in himself, not through an angel or any minister, but through himself. That he triumphed is manifest to angels and human beings.

For Christ forgave all transgressions. He removed from the midst both the sin of the Law and the Law itself. Therefore see that no one afterward brings you under the Law. And to frighten them still more, he says: Let no one judge you, that is, make you liable to judgment, that is, condemnable. Let no one judge you—even if not on account of the whole Law, at least on account of some part of it—for you would be condemned for observing even the smallest tradition.

He says this as follows: Let no one judge you in food, whether food avoided because of uncleanness or consumed because of purity; or in drink, likewise either consumed or avoided; or in a part of a feast day that is observed. Among them a feast day was a complete matter, having various parts: the new moon, the Sabbath, the departure from Egypt, the entrance into the promised land, and so forth.

Hence he adds: or in a part of the new moon, that is, of the renewal of the moon; or in participation in the Sabbaths, which the Jews were accustomed to celebrate. By saying “or,” he separates each part, so that he may show that even the smallest part is sufficient to condemn the one who observes it. If he had joined them with “and,” he would seem to say that one was judged for observing all of them together, and not merely one.

“Neos” means “new,” and “mene” means “moon”; hence “new moon,” the renewal of the moon. Its celebration was a sign of the renewal of our body, which we await in incorruption. The new moon and the Sabbath ought no longer to be celebrated, because they are shadows of future things, that is, they prefigure the future Truth, just as a shadow seen nearby indicates the presence of a body.

He says “of future things” according to the time of the Law, when the shadow was present and the Truth was future. These things are shadows of future realities. But Christ is the body, that is, the Truth and fulfillment of all these things. Or, “the body is Christ,” meaning that the fulfillment belongs to Christ; for it is his task to fulfill what had been prefigured.

Because he had said, “Let no one judge you,” he adds the ways in which they had to fear being condemned after being led astray, saying: But in order that you may not be judged, take care: let no one deceive you in an affected humility of speech, that is, in an outward display of hidden things, and in a simulated religiousness of dress or fasting.

I say, let no one deceive you in a religiousness of angels. For, when appearing to human beings, the angels of God would not display themselves as more humble or religious than these false ones appear to the eye. Or, “of angels” means of true preachers, who are God’s messengers to the people, whose authority these false ones hypocritically claim for themselves.

Let no one, I say, deceive you in either this way or that, desiring—that is, loving—to perform in himself and persuade you to accept things that he has not seen, that is, things he has never understood, because he sees the figures but does not know the Truth.

He is one who walks in the sacraments of the Church which he has received, and this in vain. For the baptism of one who detracts from the faith will profit him nothing. Although he displays humility outwardly, inwardly he is puffed up with his own understanding, because he subtly boasts that he perceives what the simplicity of others is not sufficient to grasp. This disease of arrogance reigns especially among heretics.

I say, he is puffed up with the understanding of his flesh. For he judges each thing according to the senses of the flesh, understanding nothing otherwise than as his bodily eyes and ears supply it. In this he does not differ from mute animals, which also have perception of things according to what they see and hear.

He is therefore puffed up and does not hold the head, that is, he does not agree with his head, Christ. He does not hold Christ as head who seeks his vitality from somewhere other than the head; and just as a member is not a member of the head if it receives its strength from elsewhere—which cannot happen—so one who abandons the unity of faith cannot be joined to Christ.

[Col. 0388D]

From this head the whole body of the Church is constructed through the joints of faith and the other virtues, and it is supplied so that what one member supplies may be supplied by another through bonds, that is, through charity, which is the nail and sinew connecting one member to another.

For just as, in the human body, members first constructed—that is, gathered together—would not follow one another unless they were joined, that is, unless each were fitted into its proper place; and therefore it is necessary that joined members be connected by sinews, and then at last one member supplies another; so in the body of the Church we, who are different members, are constructed into one and, gathered together according to the distinction of virtues, are joined through faith, and so forth.

But because one member has not yet been bound to another, love is necessary, so that the diversity of the members, connected by this nail, may cling to one another and serve one another. The body, I say, thus constructed and supplied grows both in the number of its members and in the increase of virtues, until it comes to the increase of God, that is, until it is increased to the measure God has established, until the number of the brothers is fulfilled with the last righteous person added.

He now attacks somewhat sharply certain people among them who had already begun, even if not to act, at least mentally to consent and to distinguish between alternatives, saying: “Why should we follow those people rather than these?” and things of that sort. Hence he says: Since the whole Church grows through Christ into the increase of God, why then do you distinguish, as though uncertain whom you ought to adhere to, Christ or the Law?

But he first states why they ought not to distinguish, saying: If you have died with Christ, because Christ’s death has worked in you the death of sin. You have died, I say, to the elements, because previously you worshiped the elements—the sun, the moon, and the rest—which is exactly what you do if, after receiving grace, you retain the Law.

I call them the elements of this world, because both those who worship them are worldly and the things worshiped are worldly. If, I say, you have died to the elements, so that you ought not even breathe toward the worship of these things, why, as though you were still alive in the world—that is, carnally, as before in the worship of the world—do you distinguish, saying: “Do not touch a corpse,” or something of this kind, whatever the Law forbids to be touched? “Nor shall you taste pork,” or anything similar. “Nor shall you handle” those things which it is not permitted to touch, such as handling the private parts; all these things are for destruction, that is, they bring about condemnation.

Not, however, by being done once, but through habitual practice—that is, if someone, neglecting the traditions of the Law, keeps these things as a regular practice.

[Col. 0389C]

When I say that these things are for destruction, I say this not according to myself but according to the commandments and teachings of men, that is, of those who are wise in human terms. He calls them commandments because they compelled people to do these things by the mere command of their authority. He calls them teachings when they seemed to bring forward certain arguments to prove what they urged.

These are human commandments, which also possess—that is, seem to possess—the appearance of wisdom, although they are far removed from it. I say that they possess the appearance of wisdom in superstition. Superstition is a false religion added on top of true religion. Those who added the Law to the faith they had received are therefore rightly called superstitious.

I say that, in superstition and outwardly simulated humility, these things seem to possess an appearance of wisdom. They are also, according to their own words, for not sparing the body. For they say that we do not keep the Law so that we may indulge ourselves more freely in what is pleasant to the body, whereas they, following the custom of God’s Law, say that they do not wish to spare the body.

They also claim that these practices are not undertaken for any honor. For they say that they humble themselves according to the Law because they do not seek to be honored by the people as we do. They also claim that these things are not for the satisfaction of the flesh. For they say that, in order to observe the Law, they wish to mortify the flesh, while we destroy the Law so that we may be permitted to stuff our bellies with everything.

Or, alternatively, if the words “for not sparing the body” and what follows are to be understood as seriously spoken by Paul, the meaning is this: These things seem to have an appearance of wisdom, but in fact they do not. They are also for not sparing the body, and it is foolish that, in something by which they condemn the soul, they do not at least spare the body.

They are also not for any honor. By imposing the Law of the faith of Christ as though it were necessary, they dishonor God. They also dishonor David and the other saints who said that there was no righteousness in the Law, since, by imposing the Law upon the faith, they contradict the testimony of those saints.

They are also not for the satisfaction of the flesh. Yet it is the height of madness to condemn the soul while afflicting the flesh.

## CHAPTER III

> Therefore, if you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, sitting at the right hand of God; savor the things that are above, not those that are upon the earth. For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. But when Christ appears, your life, then you also will appear with him in glory.
>
> Therefore put to death your members that are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust, evil desire, and avarice (Ephesians 5:3), which is the service of images [idolatry]. On account of these the wrath of God comes upon the children of distrust [unbelief], among whom you also once walked, when you lived in them.
>
> But now put away all these things yourselves: anger, indignation, malice, blasphemy, filthy speech from your mouth. Do not lie to one another, stripping off the old man with his acts and putting on the new (Ephesians 4:23), the one who is renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of him who created him, where there is neither Gentile nor Jew, circumcision nor foreskin [male nor female], barbarian nor Scythian, slave nor free, but Christ is all and in all.
>
> Therefore, as God’s elect (Ephesians 6:11), holy and beloved, put on a heart of mercy, kindness, humility, modesty, patience, bearing with one another and forgiving one another. If anyone has a complaint against someone, just as the Lord forgave you, so also do you. Above all these things, have charity [some copies add: continual charity], which is the bond of perfection.
>
> And let the peace of Christ rejoice in your hearts; into this peace you have also been called in one body, and be thankful. Let the word of Christ dwell in you abundantly, teaching and admonishing yourselves in all wisdom, in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing in your hearts to God in grace.
>
> Whatever you do in word or deed, do everything in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, giving thanks to God and the Father through him (1 Corinthians 10:31).
>
> Women, be subject to your husbands, as is fitting in the Lord (Ephesians 5:22; 1 Peter 3:1). Husbands, love your wives, and do not be bitter toward them.
>
> Children, obey your parents in everything; for this is pleasing in the Lord. Fathers, do not provoke your children to indignation [anger], lest they become dispirited [fainthearted] (Ephesians 6:4).
>
> Slaves, obey your carnal masters in everything, serving not for the eye, as though pleasing human beings, but in simplicity of heart, fearing the Lord (1 Peter 2:18). Whatever you do, work from the soul, as for the Lord and not for human beings, knowing that you will receive from the Lord the reward of an inheritance. Serve the Lord Christ.
>
> For whoever does wrong will receive what he has done unjustly (Romans 2:11). And there is no acceptance of persons with God (Ephesians 6:9; Acts 10:34).

## EXPOSITION

And because you have died with Christ, you no longer live for the world. Therefore seek the things that are above, that is, the delight of heaven and every righteousness that leads to what is above. Whatever does not belong to the world is said to be “above.”

Seek, I say, if you have risen with Christ—that is, because through Christ you have attained the resurrection of the soul. You are both able and obliged to seek the things that are above. “Above,” I say, namely where Christ is seated at the right hand of God, that is, resting and judging in equality with the Father.

Christ, seated at the right hand of the Father, is the cause, sign, and certainty that we shall rise with Christ. And do not merely seek these things, but savor them, that is, taste in advance the sweetness of the things that are above. Savor, I say, the things that are above and not those upon the earth.

You ought not to savor the things that are upon the earth; for you have died to earthly things. You ought to savor the things that are above. For your life is in God, and in such dignity that it is with Christ. I say that this life is hidden, that is, not revealed to everyone but to a few.

Many have gone astray in this statement, saying that it is foolish for a human being to labor for something that has not been revealed to human beings. At present your life is hidden; but when Christ appears, coming for judgment—Christ, I say, who is your life, in whose eternity eternity is prepared for you—then, when Christ appears, you too will appear with him, to be placed in glory.

Having sufficiently rejected the Law and adequately commended faith, as in the Epistle to the Ephesians, he adds moral instruction, first teaching the Church publicly, then instructing the sexes, ages, and conditions, saying: Because your life is in God and you are destined to appear with Christ in glory, therefore put to death the members that are yours upon the earth, that is, those clinging to earthly things.

He calls these sins “members,” since they are members of the body of sin, as he indicates in what follows. Put to death your members, namely fornication, such as having intercourse with another man’s wife. Another member is uncleanness and lust, that is, a lustful will, and desire. And because desire may be spoken of good things, he added “evil,” as in desiring another person’s property.

Put avarice to death in yourselves as well. It consists in unlawfully gathering and retaining possessions, and avarice is the service of idols. For one who puts God second so that he may increase his money, despising God, worships money.

On account of the things mentioned above wrath comes, that is, God’s vengeance, even upon the children of unbelief. If those who had not received the faith were condemned for such things, what do you suppose will happen to you, who, after receiving the faith, have renounced all these things?

In these members of the body of sin you too, like the other unbelievers, once walked, when you lived in them, namely during the time of unbelief.

Formerly you walked in them. But now, having become believers, put away both the things already mentioned and all that follows: anger, that is, a sudden disturbance of the mind; indignation, that is, being indignant at those inferior to you on account of some success.

Put away also malice of both mind and body, and blasphemy against God and neighbor. Put away every filthy word from your mouth. And do not lie to one another, so that one may deceive another.

In short, I forbid all such things: strip off the old man, that is, the habit of sins, together with his acts. For some lay aside the habit of sin but occasionally fall into an act of sin when compelled by weakness. Yet they do not resume the habit of sin, even though they have committed the act, because after their fall they hasten to repentance.

Strip off the old man and put on the new, that is, the habit of virtues—the one who is renewed daily, growing in the newness of righteousness. He is renewed, I say, striving toward the knowledge of God, because he continually grows in knowledge of the divinity insofar as he ascends in virtues.

He is renewed, I say, according to the image, that is, the purity, of the one who created him, conforming himself to him according to his capacity. In this new human being there is neither male nor female, that is, no one is received or rejected on account of sex.

There is also neither Gentile nor Jew, that is, it does no harm to have been a Gentile, and it does no good to have been a Jew. “Gentile” and “Jew,” I say, by birth. And because some Jews passed into Gentile status and some Gentiles passed into circumcision, he therefore adds that there is neither circumcision nor foreskin, because it is no more advantageous to have been circumcised than to be uncircumcised.

Likewise, there is neither barbarian nor Scythian, the latter being more barbarous than barbarians. There is neither slave nor free; for in the body of virtues a slave is received as a master.

Social status neither harms nor benefits in the new human being, because every substance is God’s good creation; but qualities, such as righteousness or unrighteousness, which are added by us, either benefit or hinder.

There are neither Gentile nor Jew there, but Christ, that is, the virtue that comes from Christ, is all things, that is, every perfection. And thus Christ is “in all,” that is, in each person, as all things.

And since the new human being must be put on, therefore put on the members of the new human being. He says “put on” both for the sake of adornment—for we had been disfigured by the nakedness of sin—and for the repelling of the cold of wickedness.

Put on, I say, as God’s elect, that is, those whom God chose from eternity and in time by calling them to faith through ministers. Elect, I say, and holy, that is, sanctified in goodness by the establishment of virtues. And, in both respects—that is, in election and sanctification—beloved, put on mercy.

And to encourage them more strongly he says expressly: “A heart of mercy,” so that pious affection may overflow in the very bowels. With mercy of mind, put on this member of the new human being also: kindness in giving, humility in speech and gait, modesty, that is, moderation in all things, and patience when adversities press upon you.

Bearing with one another, that is, carrying one another’s burdens through alternating prayers and fasts. And if anyone among you has a complaint, that is, a just demand for anything, against a brother, forgive one another, not reducing the debt as though it were a price and loving the person less than usual, but, just as the Lord forgave you by remitting the debt and adding love, so also forgive one another.

Put on patience and the rest. Above all these things—that is, above and more worthily than all these—have charity. Or understand it this way: “Above these things,” that is, labor more earnestly to possess charity than to possess the things already mentioned.

To have charity is the bond, that is, the binding together, of perfection, namely of the other virtues which make a person perfect. For all the virtues gathered together without charity are like scattered dust, which is easily dispersed at the wind’s impulse because it lacked cement. So virtues gathered without the cement of charity easily yield to any temptation.

And so that you may be perfect in charity, let peace—that is, outward concord—be in you. I say, let it be the peace of Christ, that is, the peace which Christ had in the world and taught people to have. Let it be in you in such a way that you have peace with everyone in your hearts, not by compulsion but willingly; and let it be in your hearts in such a way that it rejoices there, that is, rejoices in its daily increase.

To this peace—to possessing it—you have been called by God in one body, that is, not merely so that you may come to the unity of the body, but so that you may remain in that unity. Let peace be in your hearts. And be thankful, that is, always giving thanks to God for the benefits conferred upon you. Be thankful, I say, teaching and admonishing yourselves.

But he first states in what they ought to teach and admonish one another, saying: In order that you may teach and admonish yourselves, let the word—that is, the teaching—of Christ dwell continually in you, whether “about Christ” or “which Christ taught.” And let it dwell so that you may have abundance in all wisdom, that is, in every kind of historical, moral, and allegorical understanding, teaching yourselves by studying the Scriptures and, being well taught, admonishing one another.

Exhortation is highly effective, even concerning matters that we know well. Teaching and admonishing, I say, in psalms, in which moral goodness is contained; in hymns, in which praise of God or of the saints is referred to the glory of God; and in spiritual songs, that is, songs concerned with the joy of spiritual goods.

And do not merely teach and admonish, but also sing to God, that is, for the glory of God, not only with your lips but also in your hearts. Sing, I say, in grace, that is, in consideration of God’s grace, by which, forgiving your sins, he justified you.

To summarize briefly what you ought to do: Whatever you do in word or deed, all of it, whether in conduct or in thought, do it in the name, that is, for the honor, of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Or alternatively: Whatever you do in word or deed, do everything—that is, make it perfect—not done for human praise, but do it in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.

I say that you should always give thanks to God and the Father through Christ himself, through whom he has conferred every good thing upon you. For thanksgiving is highly effective in obtaining what is requested.

After admonishing the Church in general, he instructs separately the sexes, ages, and conditions, saying: Bear with one another, but you women, be subject to your husbands more than the others, as is fitting. For it is fitting for a woman to be subject to a man. Yet be subject in the Lord, that is, according to the Lord. For if they wish to subject you to adulterers, do not submit to this.

You men, love your wives and do not be bitter toward them. Excessive harshness sometimes produces sin.

And you children, obey your parents in everything, provided that it is in the Lord, not in the worship of an idol or in murder. I say, obey because this—that is, obeying a parent—is pleasing to God.

And you fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, lest they become fainthearted, that is, of small courage in enduring, and, struck by you, strike you in return.

And you slaves, obey your masters in everything, even those who are carnal. Do not serve them for the eye, that is, only while you are in their sight, as though by this service you were pleasing human beings alone; but serve them in simplicity of heart, fearing in this the Lord God, who established you as slaves on account of your sin or that of your parents, as we read concerning the sons of Ham (Genesis 9:25).

Do not object that your masters repay you badly. Know that you will receive from the Lord God the repayment of an inheritance, that is, the inheritance repaid to you, because you patiently endured the yoke imposed upon you by God.

And when I say that women should be subject, men should love, children should obey, and slaves should serve, serve the Lord Christ in all these things, lest, on account of service to human beings, you despise God.

You slaves, work in this way, because whoever does wrong—whether slave or master—will receive what he has done unjustly, that is, the reward of his injustice in the future. I say “whoever does wrong” because with God there is no acceptance of persons, so that one person is accepted because he is free and another rejected because he is a slave.

## CHAPTER IV

[Col. 0394D]

> Masters, provide your slaves with what is just and fair, knowing that you too have a Lord in heaven. Devote yourselves to prayer, being watchful in it with thanksgiving, praying also for us, that God may open to us a door of speech, to speak the mystery of Christ—for which I am also imprisoned—so that I may make it manifest, as I ought to speak.
>
> Walk in wisdom (Ephesians 5:15) toward those who are outside, redeeming the time. Let your speech always be seasoned with the salt of grace, so that you may know how you ought to answer each person.
>
> Tychicus, the dearest brother and faithful minister and fellow slave in the Lord, will make known to you everything concerning me. I have sent him to you for this very purpose, so that he may learn what concerns you and comfort your hearts, together with Onesimus, the beloved and faithful brother, who is one of you. They will make known to you everything that is being done here.
>
> Aristarchus, my fellow prisoner, greets you, and Mark, the cousin of Barnabas, concerning whom you have received instructions. If he comes to you, receive him.
>
> Jesus, who is called Justus, also greets you. These are the ones who are from the circumcision. These alone are my fellow workers for the kingdom of God; they have been a comfort to me.
>
> Epaphras, who is one of you, a servant of Jesus Christ, greets you. He is always anxious for you in his prayers, that you may stand perfect and complete in every will of God. For I bear him witness that he has much labor on behalf of you, and of those who are in Laodicea and in Hierapolis.
>
> Luke (2 Timothy 4:11), the dearest physician, and Demas greet you.
>
> Greet the brothers who are in Laodicea, and Nymphas, and the church that is in his house. And when this letter has been read among you, arrange that it also be read in the church of the Laodiceans. And say to Archippus: “See to the ministry that you received in the Lord, so that you may fulfill it.”
>
> The greeting is by the hand of Paul. Remember my chains. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you. Amen.

## EXPOSITION
Servants, obey your masters; and you, masters, grant your servants what is just, according to what they deserve and what is equitable—that is, reckon them to be human beings equal to yourselves, knowing that both servants and masters have the same Lord in heaven.

Having admonished these persons, he returns again to the public instruction of the Church, saying: You, servants and masters, act thus toward one another. But let the whole Church devote itself to prayer, keeping watch—whether by nightly vigils or by being diligently watchful in prayer—always engaged in thanksgiving, praying also for us when you pray for yourselves. Or “also”: let the whole Church offer a common prayer for me, that God may open for us a door for the word—that is, lips through which the word proceeds. I say, let him open it for speaking the mystery of Christ, that is, the salvation of the Gentiles, which until Christ lay hidden under a mystery. God would open his mouth for himself if his word were made gracious to its hearers. For because of the arrangement of words and the subtleties of meanings, a mouth will never be opened unless the Spirit works in the hearts of the hearers. For this reason—that is, because I speak the mystery of Christ—even after many afflictions I am still bound in order to speak, so that I may make that mystery manifest, speaking as I ought to speak according to the place, the time, and the capacity of my hearers.

And just as I speak the word of Christ, so also preach it yourselves. Walk toward those who are outside—that is, toward unbelievers. I say, walk in wisdom, that is, with complete discernment in preaching. I say, redeeming the time—that is, procuring for yourselves the opportunity to walk in wisdom. It would be redeeming the time if they invited someone to dinner and there won his goodwill, so that they might more easily lead him to what they desired.

So that you may walk in wisdom, let your speech always be in grace—that is, gracious to its hearers—and seasoned with salt, that is, tempered with wise discernment. Or it may be understood thus: Let your speech be seasoned with salt, so that it may always be in grace—that is, in praise of the grace of God—and never in the law. Let it be seasoned with salt in such a way that you know how you ought to answer each person who asks, according to his simplicity or his prudence.

Thus I instruct you concerning the matters mentioned above. Everything that concerns me—my chains and the rest—Tychicus, the dearest brother and faithful minister, will make known to you. Believe him, because he will minister nothing beyond what is faithful; and he is a fellow servant in the Lord, because, as I do, he serves the Lord in the Gospel and suffers for him. I sent Tychicus to you for this purpose: to make these things known and also to learn what concerns you, so that through him I might know it and he might comfort your hearts, desolate because of my chains.

Tychicus will make these things known together with Onesimus, the dearest and faithful brother. Listen to him, because he was born among you. These two will make known to you everything that is being done here. He commended them for this reason, so that you would believe them as you believe him.

Aristarchus, my fellow captive, greets you; like me, he is held captive in chains for the Gospel. Mark also greets you, the cousin of Barnabas. Concerning both of them you received instructions from me not to receive them. But if both of them now come to you, receive him—receive both of them, reconciled to me. This Mark, unwilling to obey Paul on a certain mission, separated from him; Barnabas, however, led too strongly by natural affection, departed with Mark (Acts 15:39). But Paul, lest they preach anything contrary to the faith after being separated from him, wrote to the Churches that they should not listen to those who, though recently corrected, had been with Paul; and therefore he wrote again concerning receiving them.

Jesus also greets you, the one called Justus, who has a testimony of righteousness from everyone. Mark, Barnabas, and Jesus are of the circumcision; and these alone of the circumcision are my assistants in preaching the kingdom of God. They also became a comfort to me in my chains.

Epaphras greets you, who was born among you. I mean, he is a servant of Christ Jesus and is always concerned for you in his prayers. For you, I say, that you may stand perfect in what you have received, not that you may receive something else; and that you may stand complete in every aspect of the will of God—that is, fully knowing the whole will of God.

He is truly concerned for you; for I bear him witness that he undergoes great labor, keeping watch and praying for you, and for those who are in Laodicea and those who are in Hierapolis. These Churches were near the Colossians.

Luke, the dearest physician, greets you. He was an evangelist. Demas also greets you.

Greet the brothers who are in Laodicea. Greet also Nympha, that matron, and the church which is in her house. She was accustomed to minister to preachers, and Paul feared that, having been deceived, she might minister to false preachers.

When this Epistle has been read among you, see that it is also read in the Church of the Laodiceans, and that you yourselves read the one from Laodicea.

And say to Archippus, your bishop, who, because he was despised by you, withdrew from his office: “See”—that is, take care—“carry out the ministry that you received in the Lord, so that you may complete it, because now that we have been corrected, we are ready to obey you.” For it is right that the obedience of those who deposed him through contempt should restore him. This Archippus, angry because they had listened to the false preachers against him, had said that he would no longer exercise the episcopate among them.

The greeting is written in my own hand—I mean, mine, not the secretary’s, but mine, Paul’s. He adds something before the greeting: Remember my chains, so that you may minister to me in my chains; or, so that by my example you may suffer for Christ.

This is the greeting: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you. Amen.”

[IN THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE THESSALONIANS.]

[Col. 0397]

## Argument of the First Epistle to the Thessalonians

The Thessalonians are Macedonians. Having received the word of truth in Christ Jesus, they persevered in the faith, even during the persecution of their fellow citizens. Moreover, they neither received false apostles nor accepted what was said by the false apostles. The Apostle praises them highly, writing to them from Athens through Tychicus the deacon and Onesimus the acolyte.

## Prologue of Blessed Bruno on the Same Epistle

[Col. 0397B]

The Thessalonians are in Macedonia. Having heard the word of faith from Paul, they believed, receiving abundant grace at the very beginning of their faith. But after Paul had departed from them, some of them—as they had learned from him—remained, as Paul’s imitators, steadfast in the good; others, however, were gradually corrupted, slipping into the pit of fornication. They also began to be idle, unwilling to work, and inquisitive, diligently investigating the rumors of the city. They also fell into error by doubting the resurrection of the dead. For this reason they afflicted themselves excessively at the death of their friends, thinking that they would not rise again.

Since there were two groups among them—one walking directly in Paul’s path, the other, as has been said, straying from the way of truth—Paul sent Timothy to them from Athens. When Timothy returned, Paul learned through him with certainty the faith of some and the error of others, and wrote this Epistle to them. In it he addresses both groups, the perfect and the erring: praising the good for the perfection of their faith and exhorting them to increase in the good works they had begun; and drawing the erring away, with appropriate arguments, from inquisitiveness, idleness, fornication, and the doubt they held concerning the future resurrection. His purpose in this matter is sufficiently clear: the good are to strive for growth, while the others, abandoning their error, are to conform themselves in faith and action to the perfection of the good.

# First Epistle to the Thessalonians

[Col. 0397]

## Chapter One

[Col. 0397C]

> Paul, and Silvanus and Timothy, to the Church of the Thessalonians in God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Grace to you and peace. We give thanks to God always for all of you, making mention of you in our prayers without ceasing, remembering the work of your faith, and your labor, and your charity, and your endurance in hope of our Lord Jesus Christ before God and our Father, knowing, brothers beloved by God, your election, because our Gospel was not given to you in word only, but also in power, and in the Holy Spirit, and in great fullness, as you know what kind of men we were among you for your sake. And you became imitators of us and of the Lord, receiving the word amid great tribulation with the joy of the Holy Spirit, so that you became an example to all believers in Macedonia and Achaia. For from you the word of the Lord has been spread, not only in Macedonia and Achaia, but in every place your faith toward God has gone forth, so that we have no need to say anything. For they themselves announce concerning us what kind of entrance we had among you, and how you turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God, and to await his Son from heaven—whom he raised from the dead—Jesus, who delivered us from the coming wrath.

## Exposition

“Paul,” and so forth. As is his custom, he places the greeting first, saying: “Paul, and Silvanus, and Timothy.” He includes Silvanus with him in the greeting because Silvanus worked with him in their conversion and possessed authority among them. He includes Timothy because Paul writes this Epistle to them at Timothy’s advice, after Timothy had returned from them. He also includes Timothy so that they may know that nothing taking place among them is hidden from Paul.

Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy write to the Church of the Thessalonians—the Church, I say, existing in God the Father and in the Lord Jesus Christ; that is, the Church has its existence from God the Father and Jesus Christ. Let it therefore persevere in the faith of him from whom it has already received the name of election.

This, I say, is what they write: “Grace to you and peace.” At the beginning he addresses the part of them that had preserved the integrity of faith, magnifying their faith and the graces granted to them at the beginning of their faith, so that through the Apostle’s praise they may be encouraged toward better things. He says: “Having heard the fruit of your faith, we give thanks to God”—not rarely, but always—and for all of you who have persevered in what I handed on to you.

We give thanks, making mention of you—that is, asking God to remember you—in our prayers, which are offered without interruption, because prayer is continual and I omit none of you. He then explains why he gives thanks: “We give thanks, remembering the work of your faith.” Although the works of faith are many, faith has this chief [principle]: to confess what one believes. These people, however, did not fear to confess Christ in the sight of persecutors.

We also remember your labor. For, impoverished by unbelievers, they worked to obtain the means by which they could live. We also remember your charity. They loved their neighbors so greatly that they shared with those who were idle the fruits of their own labors. We also remember your endurance. They suffered many things from unbelievers.

I say, your endurance in hope—that is, in the thing hoped for. For the thing you hope for produces such patience in you. I say, in the hope of our Lord Jesus Christ. The fulfillment of this hope belongs to Christ; this hope is held before God and our Father. For they hoped with such confidence as though they already had God before their eyes.

Having commended their faith and charity, he says that God granted them more remarkable graces at the beginning of their faith than to the other Churches. He says this to stir them up, making mention of them in his prayers, knowing their election, brothers beloved by God—that is, knowing that because he loved them, he chose them. And after election he loved them still more. For this reason he placed “beloved” before “election,” to show that their good qualities arose from God’s love.

Knowing, I say, your election—namely, that our Gospel was given to you not merely in speech, so that only words would be spoken in your conversion, but in the power of miracles and in the Holy Spirit. At the very reception of the faith you possessed many graces; and you possessed them in power and in the Spirit, in such great fullness of miracles and spiritual graces.

We know that these things—the powers of miracles and the graces of the Holy Spirit—were present in you, just as you yourselves know what was visible concerning us: what kind of men we were among you—that is, how greatly afflicted we were—and that this was for the sake of winning you yourselves, not for any other advantage.

Thus our Gospel came to you, and you immediately became imitators of us; and because you were imitators of us, you therefore became imitators of God, whom it is glorious to imitate. I say, imitators in enduring great tribulation, receiving—that is, in receiving—the word. For as soon as you received the word of faith, you immediately began to suffer with faith.

I say, tribulation received not unwillingly, but with the joy of the Holy Spirit, because the abundance of graces that was in you caused you to rejoice in tribulations. You became imitators of us, so that you became an example of endurance to all believers in Macedonia and Achaia, who had believed before you. For when they saw you preceding them toward the crown, they praised the speed of your faith while condemning their own slowness.

You became an example to them; for the word of the Lord was spread by you—that is, it was made known through your example—not only in Macedonia and Achaia, but also in every place adjacent to them. And not only the word of the Lord, but also your faith made great progress. This faith is toward God—that is, having rejected the glory of the world, it desires God alone.

It made such progress that we have no need to say anything about our entrance among you or about your conversion. There is no need for us to say anything because they themselves announce concerning you, to the glory of your faith, what kind of entrance we had among you—that is, how difficult it was. For we suffered much in coming and while among you, yet you did not reject the word because of me.

They also announce concerning you how perfectly you turned to God from idols, in which there was only appearance and no truth. I say, you turned not merely to believe, but also to serve the living God—that is, the eternal God who will give you eternal life—the living and true God, in whom there is truth, just as there is appearance in an idol.

Nor did you turn merely to serve him; you also turned to await his Son, who will come from heaven for judgment. They act so well and are so secure that they rejoice to meet the judge, not fearing punishment but confident of the reward.

God raised this Son from the dead and made him Jesus for us—that is, Savior—whose resurrection brings about our resurrection. This Son delivered us from wrath—that is, from the vengeance that will come upon the ungodly. He delivered us, certainly, in baptism, forgiving sins.

## Chapter Two

> For you yourselves know, brothers, our entrance among you, that it was not in vain, but after we had first suffered and been shamefully treated—as you know—in Philippi, we had confidence in our God to speak to you the Gospel of God amid much anxiety. For our exhortation was not from error, nor from impurity, nor in deceit; but just as we were approved by God to be entrusted with the Gospel, so we speak—not as pleasing human beings, but God, who tests our hearts. For we were never found in flattering speech, as you know, nor in an occasion for greed—God is witness—nor seeking glory from human beings, either from you or from others, although we could have been burdensome to you as apostles of Christ. But we became little ones in your midst, as though a nurse were cherishing her own children. So, longing for you, we desired to hand on to you not only the Gospel of God but also our own lives, because you had become very dear to us. For you remember, brothers, our labor and toil: working night and day so as not to burden any of you, we preached the Gospel of God to you. You are witnesses, and God also, of how holily, justly, and blamelessly we behaved toward you who believed. As you know, how we exhorted and consoled each one of you, as a father does his children, we bore witness that you should walk worthily of God, who called you into his own kingdom and glory. Therefore we also give thanks to God without ceasing, because when you received from us the word of the hearing of God, you received it not as the word of human beings, but, as it truly is, the word of God, who works in you who have believed [another reading: “in him”]. For you became imitators, brothers, of the Churches of God that are in Judea, in Christ Jesus, because you also suffered the same things from your fellow countrymen as they did from the Jews, who both killed the Lord Jesus and the prophets, persecuted us, do not please God, and are hostile to all human beings, forbidding us to speak to the Gentiles so that they may be saved, thereby always filling up their sins. For the wrath of God has come upon them to the end. But we, brothers, having been separated from you for a short time—physically, not in heart—hastened all the more eagerly to see your face, with great longing, because we wanted to come to you. I, Paul, indeed desired to come both once and again, but Satan hindered us. For what is our hope, or joy, or crown of glory? Are you not before our Lord Jesus Christ at his coming? For you are our glory and joy.

## Exposition

Earlier, by saying what kind of entrance he had made and what kind of brothers they were, he had twice indicated the difficulty of his entrance among them. Since he had not explained it, he now inserts it quite skillfully, saying: “I do not need to tell you what kind of entrance we had among you; for you yourselves, brothers, know well our entrance among you, because”—that is, the fact that—it was not in vain, that is, useless.

It would have been in vain if he had suffered for worldly things, or if he had suffered in order to rise again, or if he had produced no fruit of faith in them. It was not in vain, but rather, in coming, we suffered in Philippi the bitterness of tribulation and were also treated with insults—that is, afflicted with shameful words. We suffered and were treated with insults, as you yourselves know.

We, I say, suffered and were treated in this way among you amid much anxiety—that is, concern about domestic matters. For we were in great need and were anxious lest, seeing our contemptuous treatment, you should despise the word of God in us. Although we were in such great anxiety, we nevertheless had confidence to speak the Gospel of God to you. We had this confidence, I say, in our Lord; for because of the excessive difficulty, human strength failing within us, we were compelled to consult God.

Therefore we had confidence because our exhortation to you was not from error—that is, from persuading you to error, teaching you to err in the faith—nor from impurity, like those Nicolaitans who persuade people that women should be held in common. Nor was our exhortation in deceit—that is, in deception. For it could have been neither from error nor from impurity and yet still have been in deceit, if we had intended to obtain something from them.

It was not in deceit, but just as we were approved—that is, examined and found acceptable—by God, so that the Gospel might be entrusted to us by him. Just as we were approved, so we speak; that is, God found no less in us than he had foreseen he would find. We speak, I say, not merely without pleasing human beings, but not even pretending to please human beings; rather, we seek to please God, who tests our hearts—that is, before whom our will is also open.

[Col. 0402A]

Truly, we did not speak as though pleasing human beings. For we were never found in flattering speech, as you know, and I call you as witnesses. Nor were we found in speech motivated by greed, or even in an opportunity for it, so that anyone could at least suspect this of us; and God is witness to the matter.

Nor were we seeking glory from human beings, either from you or from others. We were not seeking an opportunity for greed, although we could have been burdensome to you by receiving temporal goods from you as apostles of Christ.

Not seeking glory, we became little ones in your midst—that is, humble within your community. For there was no one to whom I did not condescend. Little ones, I say, as a nurse condescends to an infant and endures much from him—not a nurse hired for pay, but one who cherishes her own children, toward whom she is little solely out of love, seeking nothing there except the children.

As a nurse cherishes her children, so, longing for you, we desired not your possessions, but eagerly wanted to hand on to you not only the Gospel of God, but also, if necessary, our own lives. Since you had become so dear to us, we became little ones, like a nurse.

For you, brothers, remember our labor and toil. One might labor without laboring to the point of exhaustion; but often he labored for God so that, being more weary, he might cease rather than withdraw voluntarily. I rightly speak of labor and toil. For we preached the Gospel of God among you, working night and day, as much of the day remained after preaching and prayer.

We worked in this way so as not to burden any of you. And that I did so, you and God are witnesses: how holily toward myself, how justly toward my neighbor, and blamelessly—that is, innocently and without any evil—we behaved toward you who believed.

Since we behaved holily and justly toward you, you know this as well as you know how we bore witness to each one of you, exhorting you and consoling you in your tribulations as a father would console his children.

We bore witness that you should walk worthily of God—that is, that you should be worthy to have God; or, that it should be fitting for God to dwell in you. This is the God who called you into his kingdom—that is, so that he might now reign in you, who previously were the kingdom of the devil—and into the glory that is to be possessed in the future.

And because you have been called into the kingdom of God, we therefore give thanks to God without ceasing: because, when you received from us the word of hearing—that is, when you received the word of God from hearing alone—you received it not as the word of human beings, but as it truly is, the word of God, who works daily in you who have believed.

And truly he works in you. For you, brothers, became imitators of the Churches of God that are in Judea—Churches, I say, that are in Christ Jesus. You became imitators in this respect: you also suffered the same things from your fellow countrymen as they suffered from the Jews.

It is not surprising that those Jews persecuted them, since they killed the Lord Jesus and the prophets. They also persecuted us; in this they certainly do not please God, although by persecuting us they suppose that they are rendering service to God.

Those Jews are also hostile to all human beings—that is, to the benefit of all human beings—forbidding us to speak to the Gentiles so that they may be saved. They forbid this in order always to fill up their sins, until they have been justly and sufficiently proved, and the ungodly come to the fullness of condemnation.

They forbid this because the wrath of God—that is, blindness—has come upon them to the end, when God will remove the veil from their hearts, and then the remnant will be saved (Romans 9:27; 11:5). Or “to the end” means until death, when they will be handed over to everlasting fire.

And because you suffered the same things, therefore, brothers, we were desolate because of our separation from you.
