The cause of our desolation arose from us—not because we were grieving over a fall, but because we were afraid. We were desolate for a time—that is, from the time we sent Timothy to you until through him we heard of your steadfastness. By saying “for a time,” he indicates that they had not sinned.

We were desolate with mouth removed—that is, with our speech removed from you—and with our presence removed, though not with our heart removed. Nevertheless, we hastened all the more than before to see your face, with great longing.

I rightly say “with longing,” because we wanted to come to you, and we had already begun the journey. I, Paul, indeed wanted to come once and again, whatever the others might have feared; but Satan hindered us.

Satan did this so that, once the consolation of the teacher had been removed, he might more easily pervert you. God permitted it so that, having overcome temptation, you might be more glorious. Satan hindered us because you are our hope, and so forth.

Or it may be understood thus: We wanted to come because what is the hope we are to have in the future, or what is the joy then prepared for me, or what is the crown of glory? I say, what is that joy and crown of mine? Will you not be placed now before our Lord Jesus in the purity of your life? You are a crown prepared for me at his coming.

Truly, you will then be my joy and crown, because even now, while I am weighed down by the flesh and understand less clearly, you are our glory and joy.

## Chapter Three

> Therefore, no longer able to endure, we thought it good to remain alone in Athens [*solis*; another reading, *solos*, both “alone”]; and we sent Timothy, our brother and God’s minister in the Gospel of Christ, to strengthen and exhort you concerning your faith, so that no one might be shaken by these tribulations. For you yourselves know that we are appointed to this. For even when we were with you, we foretold to you that we would suffer tribulations, as indeed has happened, and you know it. Therefore I, no longer able to endure, sent him to learn about your faith, lest perhaps the tempter should have tempted you and our labor should become useless. But now, when Timothy came to us from you and announced to us your faith and charity, and that you always have a good remembrance of us, desiring to see us, just as we also desire to see you, therefore we were comforted, brothers, in you amid all our necessity and tribulation through your faith, because now we live, if you stand in the Lord. For what thanksgiving can we render to God for you, in all the joy with which we rejoice because of you before our Lord God, praying night and day all the more earnestly to see your face and complete what is lacking in your faith? May God himself, our Father, and our Lord Jesus Christ [another reading omits “Christ”] direct our way to you. And may the Lord multiply you and make your charity abound toward one another and toward all, just as ours does toward you, so that he may strengthen your hearts blamelessly in holiness before God and our Father, at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ with all his saints. Amen.

## Exposition

Because you suffered the same things, because we were separated from you, and because you are our joy and crown, therefore we could no longer endure. He says “endure” because, until Timothy consoled them and learned through him how they stood in the faith, he endured as though fearing the fall of a heavy burden.

No longer able to endure, we—myself and Silvanus—thought it good to remain in Athens alone; that is, we were deprived of the consolation of Timothy, who was necessary to us. Here he indicates that he sent this Epistle from Athens.

We remained in Athens and sent Timothy, our brother and minister of God in the Gospel of Christ. I commend him to you; listen to him. We sent him, I say, to strengthen you, so that you might advance toward better things. I say “to strengthen and exhort” for the sake of preserving your faith, so that it might neither err nor fail.

I say “to strengthen,” so that none of you might be shaken by these tribulations, which both you and we suffer. When he says “that no one may be shaken,” he indicates that they had not yet been shaken and that he did not wish even one of them to be moved from the faith.

Nor should you be shaken. For you yourselves know well that we and you have been appointed to suffer adversity. You certainly know this. For when we were with you, we foretold that we would suffer tribulations, and it has happened exactly as I said; you know well that it has happened.

Therefore—that is, because I suffered tribulations, lest the tribulation of the teacher should become the cause of your falling away—I, no longer able to endure, sent him to learn about your faith, so that through an envoy I might learn your faith.

I sent him lest perhaps the tempter should have tempted you—that is, the one whose office it is to tempt—and lest our labor should thus become useless because you had succumbed to temptation.

Long ago I sent him. But now Timothy has come to us from you, and he has announced your faith, which you hold firmly, and your charity, by which you show that you love us all. He has also announced that—that is, the fact that—you have a good remembrance of us, as you ought; that you always desire to see us, just as we also desire to see you.

When he announced this, we were comforted, brothers, in you. That is, we were comforted because he announced these things about you, and not for some other reason. For the same thing could have been announced to him and he could have been comforted for another reason.

We were comforted in you through faith—that is, because of your faith, which stands firmly. Or, “through your faith” may mean: I swear by your faith that I was comforted, for I would not swear falsely about something so important.

I say that we were comforted in every necessity—that is, poverty—and in all our tribulation, which I suffer from persecutors. For not even my affliction can disturb the joy I have concerning your steadfastness.

Therefore I say that we are comforted: because now, even in tribulation and poverty, we live—that is, we believe ourselves to live in joy—if you stand in the Lord, which is certainly true, because you do stand. The word “if” is confirmatory.

We rightly live for this reason: what thanksgiving can we render to God for you who remain in faith and charity? I say that we can render it because we are placed in all the joy with which we rejoice because of you, existing before our God. Or: we rejoice before our God because of you. For what pleases God is that, forgetting my own tribulation, I rejoice with you over your good qualities.

He says “render” because Paul counts the good things that God bestows upon the Churches as things bestowed upon himself. We rejoice, not merely giving thanks, but also praying night and day more earnestly than before, when we had not yet heard of your perfection. We pray that we may see your face and, by being present with you, complete what is still lacking in your faith.

When Paul first handed the faith on to them, because they were still simple and not capable of grasping the mysteries of God, he initiated them according to what was necessary for the faith. But because they are now perfect, if he were present among them he would open the Scriptures and the mysteries of God. These things would previously have been excessive for their simplicity, just as now they are lacking for their perfection.

We pray to see your face. May God himself, our Father, and the Lord Jesus direct our way—that is, make our journey to you direct.

Whether I come or do not come, may the Lord always multiply you according to the growth of the members, and make your charity abound toward one another—that you all love one another mutually within the Church—and toward all, that is, so that your charity may extend even to unbelievers.

May he make it abound, just as we abound in charity toward you. I say, may he make it abound in order to strengthen your hearts, so that your will may be confirmed in every good thing. I say, your hearts are to be strengthened without blame, so that there may be no injustice there, and strengthened in holiness, so that you may be sanctified and confirmed in good works.

I say, in holiness held before God and our Father—that is, in what is pleasing to God the Father. I say that your hearts are to be strengthened in the coming—that is, in consideration of the coming—of our Lord Jesus Christ. For whoever always remembers well Christ’s coming for judgment will fear provoking him by sinning.

Or it may be understood thus: “strengthened in the coming” means strengthened until the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. I mean Christ who will come with all his saints, who will judge the world with him.

Or “strengthened with all his saints” means that he may strengthen you in the same way as he strengthened his saints. “Amen,” that is, may it be so, so that you may be strengthened in this way.

## Chapter Four

> Therefore, brothers, from now on we ask and exhort you in the Lord Jesus that, just as you received from us how you ought to walk and please God, so you may walk, in order to abound more. For you know what commandments I gave you through the Lord Jesus. For this is the will of God: your sanctification (Romans 12:2; Ephesians 6:17), that you abstain from fornication; that each of you know how to possess his own vessel in sanctification and honor, not in the passion of desire, like the Gentiles who do not know God; and that no one overreach or defraud his brother in business, because the Lord is an avenger of all these things, as we foretold you and testified. For God did not call us to impurity, but to sanctification. Therefore, whoever rejects these things rejects not a human being but God, who has also given his Holy Spirit in us. Concerning fraternal charity, we have no need to write to you. For you yourselves have been taught by God to love one another (John 13:34). Indeed, you do this toward all the brothers throughout Macedonia. But we exhort you, brothers, to abound more, and to make it your aim to be quiet, to attend to your own affairs, and to work with your hands, as we commanded you; and to walk honorably toward those who are outside, and to desire nothing belonging to anyone. But we do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who sleep, so that you may not grieve like the others who have no hope. For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, so also God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep through Jesus. For we say this to you by the word of the Lord: we who live, who remain until the coming of the Lord, will not precede those who have fallen asleep. For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God; and the dead who are in Christ will rise first. Then we who live, who are left, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet Christ [another reading: “the Lord”] in the air; and so we shall always be with the Lord. Therefore comfort one another with these words.

## Exposition
Up to this point he has highly praised the part consisting of the perfect and exhorted them toward an increase of perfection. Now he begins to instruct that part which seemed to be corrupted by fornication, curiosity, idleness, and doubt concerning the resurrection [Col. 0406D], saying: “I praise you perfect ones in this way, and invite you to increase.” Henceforth, therefore, brothers—that is, addressing the other part—we ask you, as though for something owed, and we beseech you, adopting a gentler approach, while requesting what it is permissible to command: we beseech you, I say, in the Lord Jesus, if you wish to rejoice because of him, that just as you received from us how you ought to walk and please God, so you should walk. “To walk” is said of those things which arise from love, without which a person cannot be saved; “to please” refers to those things which, arising from love, a person adds beyond what is required, such as preserving [296] virginity or possessing nothing in the world. If he did not do these things, he could nevertheless be saved. You ought to walk, as I believe you do walk, although I admonish you in this way. We ask and beseech you to abound more than before in walking and pleasing, having been admonished by me [Col. 0407A].

And you ought to abound. For you know what commands I gave you through the Lord Jesus—that is, how worthy they were—he instructing me in this way. Worthy commands, certainly, I gave you. For this is the will of God: your sanctification; that is, that you should be sanctified, with every vice removed from you. This, I say, is your sanctification: that you abstain from fornication, so that you do not corrupt your neighbor’s wife. And that each of you know how to possess his own vessel—that is, his own body. For just as a soldier is in the military camp, so the spirit ought to serve God as a soldier in the body: with the hands, by ministering to the poor; with the feet, by visiting the sick; and similarly with the other members.

He says “possess” for this reason: the body ought to be so subdued by the spirit that it is possessed like a servant of reason, carrying whatever is imposed upon it [Col. 0407B]. I say “possess” in sanctification, so that it may become holy through the habitation of virtues; and “possess” in honor, so that it may not incline toward an act of shamefulness; and not in the desire, so that it may not even desire a shameful act, much less perform it. By “desire” I mean being in passion. For it is a grievous passion of the soul to live in desire of the flesh. To live in the passion of desire is what false Christians and the Gentiles who do not know God do.

Abstain from fornication and adultery. This is what he says: “Let no one overreach his brother in any private matter involving his wife, nor defraud him in the same matter.” He would “overreach” if he violently seized another man’s wife. He would “defraud” if, through the seduction of payment or entreaty, he subverted [Col. 0407C] his neighbor’s wife so that she consented to him.

The words of the book do not indicate this meaning sufficiently clearly, but what precedes and follows seems to intend it. Alternatively, those earlier words may be altered: “Abstain from fornication with prostitutes, so that each of you may know how to possess his own vessel”—that is, his own wife, who is the body of the husband—in sanctification, that is, in purity, and in honor; not in shamefulness and not in the passion of desire—that is, so that he is not excessively carnally attached to his wife, as the Gentiles who do not know God are.

What follows is not altered: “Therefore let no one defraud his brother,” and so forth, because the Lord is the avenger of all these things, both fornication and adultery, as we foretold to you when we were with you and testified with the testimonies of the Scriptures.

[Col. 0407D] Truly, the Lord is the avenger of these things. For God did not call us to practice uncleanness, but to possess sanctification; and because he did not call us to uncleanness, God called us to sanctification. Therefore whoever despises this precaution—namely, abstaining from fornication and adultery—does not despise a human being but God, who calls us to sanctification. He also despises his guest, the Holy Spirit. This is what he says: “God gave his Holy Spirit in us.” If you despise him as God, you lose what has been despised along with God.

We have instructed you in this way concerning fornication and adultery. But concerning brotherly love, we do not need to write to you, because you yourselves have learned from God—either through his inward inspiration or through the teaching of the Gospel—to love one another, where he says: “This is my commandment [Col. 0408A] (John XV, 12),” and so forth. Therefore it is again unnecessary to write to you, because you were doing that commandment of love toward all the brothers throughout the whole of Macedonia.

But although it is unnecessary to write to you for this reason, nevertheless we ask all of you, brothers, to abound in love more than usual, and to take care that you remain quiet: not so curious throughout the city, investigating rumors; and that, remaining quiet, you attend to your own business, lest, neglecting your own affairs, you concern yourselves with those of others. In these words he forbids the vice of curiosity.

And that you remain quiet, work with your hands, so that you may have what you need, lest, being idle, you illicitly consume the labor of others. Here he prohibits idleness. “Work,” I say, [297] just as we previously instructed you. Work, because we instructed you; and walk honorably toward those who are outside [Col. 0408B]—that is, in the sight of unbelievers—so that they may have nothing for which they can disparage you. Therefore work also so that you desire nothing belonging to anyone else; that is, having the means supplied by your own labor, do not covet another’s possessions, which poverty arising from idleness compels a person to desire.

Now he resolves with appropriate arguments the doubt they had concerning the resurrection, saying: “It is not necessary to write to you about love; but concerning those who sleep, we do not want you to be ignorant, brothers.” He calls the dead “those who sleep,” to show that God raises the dead as easily as it is easy to awaken someone sleeping from sleep.

Therefore we do not want you to be ignorant concerning those who sleep, so that you may not grieve excessively over the deaths of relatives, like the Gentiles and also false [Col. 0408C] Christians, who do not have hope of the future resurrection. And since you despair of the resurrection, you must not grieve in this way, because, if we believe that Jesus rose—and, to prove that his resurrection was real, he first says, “Jesus truly died and rose again”—if, I say, we believe this, then we must likewise believe that God will bring with Jesus those who, by living through Jesus, have slept through Jesus; that is, those whose life and death were in Jesus. He will bring them, I say, with him—that is, with Jesus—without suffering, immortal, in glory.

He destroys the false opinion of certain people who said that bodies could rise on that day while still intact, but that those which had been dissolved into ashes could never rise again, saying: “Truly, those who have slept will be brought with Jesus.” For this we tell you in the word of the Lord. God revealed this to us [Col. 0408D]: namely, that we who are alive at the coming of the Lord, and who remain after so many evils, will not precede those who have slept.

He presents himself as though he will be living at the last day, because the persecution of the apostles and of the faithful who will exist under Antichrist will be compared with a similar difficulty. Hence he says elsewhere: “We are those upon whom the ends of the ages have come (1 Cor. X, 11).” We, I say, who remain at the coming of the Lord, will not precede those who have slept in the resurrection, those who slept before us, such as Abraham and the others.

In this verse he has accomplished both things: he has confirmed the truth of the resurrection of all, and he has shown that the resurrection of those about whom they were uncertain would take place first.

Here, however, it must be noted that he confirms only the resurrection of the righteous. Truly, we who remain will not precede those who came before [Col. 0409A], because the Lord Christ himself will descend from heaven with a command and with authority. Formerly he descended in obedience and humility; he will also descend with the voice of an archangel.

Whether “archangel” here signifies Christ sounding with his own voice, or some particular angel, we do not know who will utter that voice at which the dead will rise. “With the voice of an archangel and with the trumpet of God.” For that voice will be like a trumpet, which awakens its own and terrifies its adversaries. Thus that voice will invite the saints to the palm of victory and terrify the ungodly toward punishment.

In this way, I say, Jesus will descend, and then the dead who have long been in Christ, such as Abraham and the others, will rise first. And afterward, following them, we who are alive at that time and who remain amid all the persecutions of Antichrist will be caught up together with [Col. 0409B] those who came before us in the clouds.

For the clouds will carry us to meet the Lord in the air, where he will judge all things; and from then on we, the elect, will always be with the Lord. We will be so, I say—that is, with our bodies restored in incorruption.

And because the truth of the resurrection has been confirmed for you by these words, therefore comfort one another with these words: one the other, saying, “Truly we shall rise without suffering and shall be with the Lord,” and so forth.

## CHAPTER V

“Concerning the times and the moments, you do not need us to write to you. For you yourselves know carefully that the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night (Rev. III, 3). For when they say [298], ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction will come upon them, like labor pain upon a woman with child, and they will not escape.

“But you, brothers, are not in darkness, so that that day may overtake you like a thief. For you are all sons of light and sons of day; we are not of night or of darkness. Therefore let us not sleep as the others do, but let us watch and be sober. For those who sleep, sleep at night; and those who are drunk, are drunk at night.

“But since we belong to the day, let us be sober, putting on the breastplate of faith and love, and the helmet of the hope of salvation (Eph. VI, 17). For God has not appointed us to wrath but to the acquisition of salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ, who died for us, so that whether we are awake or asleep, we may live together with him.

“Therefore comfort one another and build one another up, just as you are doing. But we ask you, brothers, to recognize those who labor among you, who preside over you in the Lord and admonish you; and to hold them in the greatest abundance of love because of their work. Be at peace with them.

“And we ask you, brothers: correct the unruly, comfort the fainthearted, support the weak, and be patient toward all. See that no one repays evil for evil to anyone, but always pursue what is good, both toward one another and toward all.

“Rejoice always; pray without ceasing (Ecclus. XVIII, 22; Luke XVIII, 1); give thanks in all things. For this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for all of you.

“Do not extinguish the Spirit. Do not despise prophecies [Col. 0410A]. Test everything; hold fast to what is good; abstain from every appearance of evil.

“May the God of peace himself sanctify you in every way, so that your spirit and soul and body may be preserved blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. He is faithful who called you, and he will also accomplish it.

“Brothers, pray for us. Greet all the brothers with a holy kiss. I adjure you by the Lord that this letter be read to all the holy brothers. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you. Amen.”

## EXPOSITION

After he had sufficiently and clearly confirmed the resurrection of bodies, he proceeds to speak about that final day, which will be for the righteous unto glory and for the ungodly unto punishment, so that those who were living in the sin of fornication, curiosity, and idleness might repent through fear of that day [Col. 0410B], and through desire for the future glory might join themselves to the fellowship of the good.

The text is connected in this way: “Because you were ignorant concerning the resurrection of the dead, we wrote to you; but concerning the future times up to the day of judgment”—that is, how many periods of time, whether a hundred or a thousand years, will be future up to the day of judgment—or, “concerning the times,” that is, whether judgment will take place in summer or winter, by day or by night; and “concerning the moments,” that is, at what hour of the day or night, of summer or winter. Concerning these things, brothers, you do not need us to write to you.

You do not need this because you yourselves know it carefully—that is, through diligent investigation of the Scriptures—this very thing which we know from them: namely, that the day of the Lord will come just as a thief comes in the night.

He does not call it “day” because he knows definitively that judgment will take place during the day [Col. 0410C], but because at that judgment everything will be as though in daylight—that is, in open manifestation—things that had previously been hidden. He says that it is the Lord’s day because then everything will begin to happen by the Lord’s will and command, whereas now many things in this world do not happen by God’s will but by his permission.

The day, I say, of the Lord will come like a thief, so that its coming will be all the more hidden because it comes in the night. If a thief comes by day, we can more easily guard ourselves against him; but if he comes at night, the night itself, providing opportunity, assists the thief’s wickedness.

Therefore that day is said to come like a thief in the night because, just as a wealthy man, surrounded in the evening by great abundance, may be robbed by a thief during the night and find himself stripped in the morning, so those who neglect to prepare themselves for that day in their sins, rich too late in worldly possessions, will be found stripped in the morning, deprived of temporal things and handed over to eternal fires.

The day of the Lord here is understood chiefly as the day of judgment, although this day of the Lord begins at each person’s death.

[299] It must also be noted that, for the ungodly who are unwilling to prepare themselves, that day will come like a thief in the night; but for the righteous, who are always watching, whenever it comes, it does not come like a thief, because they will then be increased rather than diminished in any respect.

Truly it will come like a thief, because when those lovers of the world say, “We have peace in the present and security concerning the future,” then sudden destruction will come upon them—that is, unforeseen damnation. I say “sudden,” like pain that suddenly comes upon a woman who has a child in her womb [Col. 0411A].

He does not specify what she has in the womb, but it is sufficiently understood that this is spoken of a pregnant woman. He compared it to the pain of a pregnant woman for two reasons: because that pain is sudden, and because the pregnant woman cannot determine a certain hour for herself, but gives birth wherever she is overtaken; and also because of the greater distress of this pain. Thus on that day destruction will come unexpectedly and will be full of every anguish.

Lest this destruction seem temporary, like the pain of a pregnant woman, he adds: “Destruction will indeed come upon them, and the ungodly will not escape that destruction, remaining in it forever.”

Because he has just terrified them with such severity of words, in what follows he soothes them, saying that they are not among those upon whom this destruction ought to come. The ungodly indeed will not escape sudden destruction, but you, brothers, are not in darkness—that is, in ignorance and the obscurity of sin—so that that day may overtake you like a thief.

It would overtake them if it found them unrepentant in their sins. Truly you are not in darkness. For you are all sons of light—that is, begotten in the light of faith—and you are sons of day—that is, generated in good works—because just as light precedes, day follows; so faith comes first and good works follow.

You are sons of light, and not sons of darkness—that is, of ignorance—and not sons of night—that is, of the density of sins. For just as darkness precedes night, so ignorance of the truth comes first, and through ignorance one enters the density of sin.

And because we are sons of light and of day, not of night and darkness [Col. 0411C], therefore let us not sleep—that is, let us not be sluggish like unbelievers and also false believers—but let us watch, that is, let us be diligent in doing good; and let us be sober, that is, let us not be intoxicated by love of temporal things.

We ought to watch and be sober because those who sleep—that is, who grow sluggish—sleep at night, that is, because of the night, meaning the density of sins in which they are. Those who are drunk with love of temporal things, forgetful of heavenly things, are drunk at night, that is, because of the night, meaning—as has been said—the density of sins.

Those who are drunk are drunk at night; but let us who belong not to night but to day be sober, that is, not blinded by love of temporal things. Let us, I say, be sober, clothed with the breastplate of faith.

And he rightly compared faith to a breastplate, because just as many hooks in a breastplate are linked together into one, so in faith there are many things necessary to believe, yet linked together into the same unity [Col. 0411D].

Let us also put on the breastplate of love, by which we love God and our neighbor, and let us be secure; rightly protected by faith and love against every attack of the enemies. And let us put on this helmet, namely, the hope of future salvation, so that just as a helmet protects the head, our mind may likewise be enveloped by hope of future blessedness.

We ought to hope for salvation, because God has not appointed us to wrath—that is, to destruction—but has appointed us, through the things mentioned above—faith, love, and hope—to the acquisition of salvation; that is, so that through these we may acquire perpetual salvation. Salvation, I say, which is to be possessed through our Lord Jesus Christ.

He sets forth the merit of Christ, by which he earned this salvation for us, saying: “Christ died for us, so that we might live together with him [Col. 0412A] in eternal glory.” Whether we are awake—that is, whether we are found alive at Christ’s coming—or asleep—that is, whether we are found dead.

Therefore—that is, because he gave us faith, love, and hope for the acquisition of salvation—comfort one another, those who know these things, and build one another up, those who are ignorant, just as I believe you also do.

After he had sufficiently praised the part of the perfect concerning faith and the good that comes from faith, and had admonished the other part concerning correction, [300] he now alternately builds up the subjects and the prelates, teaching how subjects ought to conduct themselves toward prelates and prelates toward subjects [Col. 0412B], saying: “I admonish the good to labor for increase and the erring to withdraw from sins.”

You, however, brothers, who are subjects, we ask you to recognize those who labor among you—that is, the prelates, who labor for your salvation by fasting, praying, and teaching. He says “recognize” so that you may minister to them in the things they need. I say, recognize those who labor and who preside over you as the Lord has ordained, and who admonish you toward better things.

Recognize them not only for this reason, but also hold them in greater abundance of love than you have been accustomed to. And have peace—that is, concord—with them if they rebuke you more sharply, because of their work; that is, knowing that the work of their ministry requires them to compel you, when you go astray, toward the way of righteousness.

Thus we ask the subjects. You, however, brothers, who are prelates, we ask you to do this: correct the unruly with harsher correction—that is, the curious who wander through the city; comfort the fainthearted [Col. 0412C], those who have little courage amid the passion of tribulations.

Or “the fainthearted” means those who, because of the enormity of their crimes, have little confidence in God’s mercy and despair. Support the weak—that is, those whose faith is weak and who despair of the resurrection. Support them in order to heal the weakness of their faith, just as a physician receives a sick person.

And be patient toward all: toward the unruly, the fainthearted, and the weak, lest, if they contradict you, you therefore lay hands upon them for a quarrel. They might say: “We tolerate them, certainly, but we will no longer teach them.” To this Paul replies: “Be patient, and while being patient see that no one returns evil for evil,” by withholding a word of instruction, even if it was previously heard impatiently.

Instead, always pursue what is good—that is, what is useful [Col. 0412D] for the instruction of the Church. Pursue it, I say, toward one another—that is, among yourselves in the Church—and also, by going beyond yourselves, toward all, teaching unbelievers as well.

And always, whether it is necessary to suffer or not, rejoice, and pray without interruption of the appointed hours, so that you do not neglect the established times of prayer. Or: pray without interruption so that, whether you sleep or remain awake, you always pray.

According to this interpretation, the saints say that the person who does not offend in anything is always in prayer; whether awake or asleep, he always longs for Christ.

And in everything that you do or say, give thanks to God, whether adversity weighs upon you or prosperity caresses you. Pray and give thanks, because this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for all of you: that you all pray and give thanks.

He says “in Christ Jesus,” that is, in the institution of Christ Jesus. Since this is God’s institution and will, it is necessary to pray and give thanks. What he says there—“Rejoice always,” and so forth—concerns the prelates; and “all of you rejoice and pray” concerns the subjects.

You, however, prelates, do not extinguish the Spirit, by concealing from your subjects those things which the Holy Spirit has supplied. And you, subjects, do not despise prophecies—that is, revelations of the Scriptures made to you by the prelates.

And although I say, “Do not despise,” nevertheless test everything—that is, first consider it in a reasoned manner, lest you be deceived through the admixture of falsehood. After you have tested it, hold fast to what is good—that is, what is useful—and abstain not only from what is evil but also from every appearance of evil; that is, from whatever retains some semblance of evil, even if it is evil.

For this reason he especially said “from the appearance of evil,” because those heretics borrowed the expressions of the faith in order, through equivalences of words, to lead the simple into error.

You, prelates and subjects, do what you can; but may the God of peace himself perfect in you what is lacking: namely, may he sanctify you in every way, and in the sanctification given by him preserve you steadfastly.

This is what he says: “May he sanctify you, and may your spirit, soul, and body be preserved entire”—that is, not corrupted by any defilement of evil. Your spirit, that is, your reason, must be preserved so that it does not wish to consent to sensuality; your soul, that is, your sensuality, so that it does not give evil counsel to reason; and your body must be preserved blameless, so that it is not polluted by the work of any shamefulness.

“May it be preserved” in—that is, until—the coming, or at the coming, that is, in expectation of the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.

[301] Pray and do the other things that follow, because God is faithful, who called you by grace and who will also do it; that is, he will complete in you that to which you have been called.

We labor in this way for you, and you, brothers, pray for us. And greet all the brothers from our love with a holy kiss, so that one may kiss the other.

## [ON THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE THESSALONIANS]

[Col. 0413]

## ARGUMENT OF THE SECOND LETTER TO THE THESSALONIANS

The Apostle writes a second letter to the Thessalonians and informs them about the last times and the overthrow of the adversary. He writes this letter from Athens through Titus the deacon and Onesimus the acolyte.

## PROLOGUE OF BLESSED BRUNO ON THE SAME LETTER

[Col. 0413C] He writes this letter again to the Thessalonians because, in the preceding letter, from Paul’s words where he had said, “We who are alive will be caught up to meet the Lord in the air,” and so forth, they had formed the suspicion that, while they themselves were still alive, Antichrist and the day of judgment would come. As a result, they were exceedingly terrified.

But since it was harmful for them to be terrified by a falsehood, Paul decided to write to them again, lest, if this ambiguity were not clarified, they should later discover—after Paul’s days—that what they thought Paul had thus foretold had not occurred, and should accuse Paul of lying both in this matter and in everything he had taught, and thus withdraw from the way of truth that he had handed down to them.

Moreover, another evil could arise from this uncertainty: if Satan, seeing them believe that judgment was near, were to show himself in the air adorned with a diadem and, asserting that he was Christ coming to judgment, deceive the Thessalonians—concerning whose corruption he worked all the harder because he knew them to be more perfect—or, by appearing in dreams, mock them in the same way [Col. 0413D].

For this reason also he wrote this letter again, because those curious and idle people had not been corrected by Paul’s command. He wrote again because the persecutions for endurance, with which he had armed them in the earlier letter, had not ceased but perhaps had increased.

These three matters—persecutions, the day of judgment, and those who had not been corrected—provided his subject. He armed them to endure all things, showing that glory would be future for the righteous who are afflicted, and damnation for those who afflict them. He also established by certain and evident signs that the day of judgment would come.

And concerning those who had not been corrected, he commanded that they be separated from communion with the Church, although he did not write to them personally about this, but wrote to the Church concerning them.

He acts in this way with the intention that those who suffer for Christ may persevere in suffering; that those who were terrified, thinking that judgment was near, may not be frightened by a falsehood; and that those who still remained uncorrected may at least, through shame at having been cast out from the communion of others, repent.

After prefacing the salutation, he says:

## SECOND LETTER TO THE THESSALONIANS

[Col. 0413]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0413D]

“Paul and Silvanus and Timothy, to the church of the Thessalonians in God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

“We ought always to give thanks to God for you, brothers, as is fitting [Col. 0414D], because your faith is growing greatly and the love of each one of you for one another is increasing, so that we ourselves boast of you in the churches of God because of your patience and faith, and in all your persecutions and tribulations that you endure as an example of God’s just judgment, so that you may be considered worthy [Col. 0415A] of the kingdom of God, for which you also suffer.

“If indeed it is just before God to repay [302] tribulation [retribution] to those who trouble you, and to you who are troubled rest with us at the revelation of the Lord Jesus from heaven with the angels of his power, in flaming fire, taking vengeance on those who do not know God and who do not obey the Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ.

“They will suffer eternal punishments in destruction, away from the face of the Lord and from the glory of his power, when he comes to be glorified in his saints and to be marveled at in all who have believed, because our testimony concerning you was believed on that day.

“For this reason we also always pray for you, that our God may deem you worthy of his calling and may fulfill every good intention of his goodness [Col. 0415B] [“of his goodness” is absent in some copies], and the work of faith in power, so that the name of our Lord Jesus Christ may be glorified in you, and you in him, according to the grace of our God and of the Lord Jesus Christ.”

## EXPOSITION

Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy write to the church of the Thessalonians existing in God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. As we explained everything in the preceding letter, he first praises them highly for their sufferings, setting forth the glory of those who suffer and the punishment of those who inflict sufferings, thereby arming them for endurance. He says:

“We ought to give thanks to God”—that is, we do not merely give thanks, but are always debtors of thanks to God for you, because you are brothers. I say that we ought to give thanks as is fitting [Col. 0415C], because God’s gifts are great and many; therefore it is necessary to give great and manifold thanks.

This is so because your faith is growing greatly—or, it is growing beyond what it previously was. Or: it grows beyond the tribulations that it surpasses entirely. And therefore it is necessary to give thanks because the love—that is, the affection—of each one of you for one another has increased. This must be understood as referring only to the perfect.

Your faith grows greatly and your love abounds, so that even we ourselves, who would not boast in the churches of God about a small matter, boast of you—that is, in the manifestation of your perfection.

I boast of you before the other churches because of your patience, by which you suffer all things for Christ, and because of your faith, preserved in its integrity, with faith and patience maintained.

I say that this patience and faith are held in all your persecutions [Col. 0415D], when you are driven from place to place, and in the tribulations, when you are afflicted with blows and insults. You endure these persecutions and tribulations as an example of God’s just judgment—that is, by God’s just judgment.

For it is just that the saints should be afflicted so that they may be purified, and that the ungodly should have power over the righteous so that their ungodliness may be brought to completion. You endure in this way by a just judgment, so that you may be an example of just judgment.

In you we can provide others with an example of how just God’s judgment is. You endure for this reason, so that you may be considered worthy of the kingdom of God—that is, of the kingdom in which God reigns at present—or so that you may be worthy to be received into God’s future kingdom.

As I understand it, you endure so that you may be considered worthy for the sake of that kingdom; and, in order that you may be considered worthy of it, you suffer according to your understanding and will [Col. 0416A].

He proves that God’s judgment is just—the judgment by which the righteous are afflicted for purification and the ungodly prosper for the completion of their iniquity—through the experiences and end of both the righteous and the ungodly.

He proves it through their end because, from the things that are visible, he could not give adequate reasons why the righteous should be afflicted and the ungodly prosper. In accordance with what David says in that psalm, “How good” (Ps. LXXII, 16): “I considered in order to understand why punishment is assigned here to the righteous and prosperity to the ungodly; but understanding this is difficult.” That is, if I attend only to the things before me, the present things, God’s judgment is just, by which the righteous are afflicted in the present for purification, while the ungodly prosper for an increase of ungodliness.

Nevertheless, I say that it is just on this condition: if it is just before God [Col. 0416B]. For in the eyes of human beings, who judge according to appearance, it seems unjust that the saints should be afflicted and the wicked prosper.

If, I say, it is just before God to repay tribulation in the future to those who now trouble you, and to repay rest in the future to you who are now troubled, then it is just that you, the righteous, should be purified here through tribulations, and that the ungodly, through the allowance of prosperity, should be prepared for future tribulation.

He will repay you rest to be enjoyed with us [303], for you will be in the same glory in which we apostles are.

Now he determines the manner of the glory of the righteous and the damnation of the ungodly, so that he may gladden the righteous and terrify the ungodly, saying: “He will repay tribulation to the ungodly and rest to us at the revelation of the Lord Jesus”—that is, when the Lord Jesus, who is now hidden from unbelievers [Col. 0416C], will be revealed to everyone in judgment.

Jesus, I say, will come to judgment from heaven. By saying “from heaven,” he indicates the power of the one who comes. He will come from heaven with the angels of his power.

In that coming the angels are called angels of power because then they will powerfully bring both the good into rest and the wicked into fire. But in the present, they sometimes allow even those over whom they preside to be afflicted by the ungodly; then this will not be so.

In these words he equally gladdens the righteous, to whom he will come for salvation, and terrifies the wicked, to whom he will come for punishment.

He now adds what is directed solely toward terrifying the wicked, saying: Jesus will come from heaven in a flame of fire—that is, in a fiery flame. That flame is especially called fire because the flame of present fire is tempered by an admixture of water and the other elements; but the future flame will be so terrifying and harsh that it will not appear to be tempered by any admixture of the elements.

Christ is said to come in a flame of fire, not because a flame will surround him, but because, when he arrives, that flame will arise, just as any prince is said to come with fire and slaughter because, when he arrives, many are killed and many things are burned.

Fire, I say, that gives vengeance—that is, punishment—to those who do not know God, meaning those who have not had faith; not to them alone, but also to those who, although they have had faith, nevertheless have not obeyed the Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Both groups—those who do not know God and those who do not obey the Gospel—will suffer eternal punishments in destruction, that is, in the place of punishments, cast away from the face of the Lord [Col. 0417A], so that they may no longer see him; and cast away from the glory of his power, according to the saying: “Let the ungodly be taken away, lest he see the glory of God” (Isa. XXVI, 10).

He says “they will suffer” by that analogy because they cannot give the saints whom they afflicted any greater gift of joy than the punishments that they themselves will suffer.

In these words he terrified the ungodly. In what follows he gladdens the righteous, saying: The ungodly will suffer punishments when Christ comes to be glorified—that is, so that he may appear glorious in rewarding his saints.

For even if in this world he appears glorious in the saints through miracles and certain other things, then he will be glorified in them to a far greater extent, when he surrounds them, rescued from every disturbance, with unfailing glory.

And he will not merely come to be glorified, but also—which is greater—he will come to be marveled at in all who have believed; that is, in those who will be saved by faith alone if they have not reached an age at which they can perform works.

Therefore he will repay you rest, because our testimony on that day—that is, the testimony we gave you concerning that day, when he will repay rest to the saints and tribulation to the ungodly—was believed by you. This testimony, I say, was believed by you, because you rightly believed our testimony. It was a testimony concerning you, because you correctly set your backs beneath whatever burden we imposed, believing and practicing what we taught.

On that day, then, may the Lord deem you worthy—that is, make you worthy—of his calling. We also always pray for you that, in the future, he may deem you worthy, and that in the present he may fulfill every good intention—that is, that you may have a fully good intention in all things—and that he may fulfill in you [Col. 0417C] the work of faith.

To confess Christ in the sight of persecutors is the work that faith demands. It is the work of faith, I say, in power, because when someone confesses the faith before a persecutor, the power of steadfastness is then necessary.

We also pray that the name of our Lord Jesus Christ may be glorified in you in this world, as you act according to the faith, and that you may be glorified in him in the future when he rewards you—not according to your merit, but according to the abundant grace of our Lord Jesus Christ.

[304]

## CHAPTER II
“We ask you, brothers, by the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and our gathering together to him, that you not be quickly shaken from your understanding. [Col. 0417D] Nor be terrified, either by a spirit, or by a word, or by a letter supposedly sent by us, as though the day of the Lord were imminent. Let no one deceive you in any way. For unless the apostasy [dissension] comes first, and the man of sin, the son of destruction, is revealed, who opposes and exalts himself above everything that is called God or worshiped, so that he sits in the temple of God, displaying himself as though he were God. Do you not remember that, when I was still with you, I used to tell you these things? And now you know what restrains him, so that he may be revealed in his own time. For the mystery of lawlessness is already at work; only let him who now restrains continue to restrain, until he is removed from the midst. And then that lawless one will be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of his mouth and destroy [Col. 0418A] by the manifestation of his coming—the one whose coming is according to the working of Satan, with every power, signs, and lying wonders, and with every deception of unrighteousness for those who are perishing, because they did not receive the love of the truth so that they might be saved. Therefore God will send them an operation of error, so that they may believe the lie, so that all may be judged who did not believe the truth but consented to unrighteousness. But we ought always to give thanks to God for you, brothers beloved by God, because God chose us as firstfruits for salvation in sanctification of the Spirit and faith in the truth, in which he also called you through our Gospel, for the acquisition of the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore, brothers, stand firm and hold fast to the traditions that you learned, whether through our word [Col. 0418B] or through our letter. May our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God our Father, who loved us and gave us eternal consolation and a good hope by grace, encourage your hearts and strengthen you in every good work and word.”

## EXPOSITION

After arming them sufficiently for patience, he establishes the matter by giving certain and evident signs of the future day, on account of which they had been terrified, thinking that day to be near. It is as though he said: “By hope of the future recompense we arm you in this way for patience; but, so that you may not be quickly shaken, we ask you, because you are brothers—we ask, I say, by the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ,” that is, “if you wish to have Christ as your Savior at that coming,” “and by the coming of our gathering together to him,” [Col. 0418C] that is, “if you wish to come with the gathering of the faithful to meet Christ,” or “of the gathering that is to come into that same state which Christ possesses, namely incorruption.” This, I say, is what we ask of you: that you not be quickly shaken.

It would be “quickly” if they were shaken throughout the whole period of their life. “Be shaken,” I say, “from your understanding,” that is, from what you perceived and understood through me as your teacher. Nor be terrified as though the day of the Lord were imminent, because in truth it is not imminent. “Be terrified,” I say, neither through an evil spirit signifying this to you in whatever manner, nor through a word—that is, through the teaching of those false teachers—nor through a letter sent by deceivers as though it were from us. For they marked letters with Paul’s name, so that by this kind of fraud they might deceive Paul’s Churches. [Col. 0418D]

We ask that you not be terrified, and that no one ever deceive you by the means already mentioned or by any other means, so that you believe the day of the Lord to be imminent, because this day will not be imminent unless the apostasy first comes.

Ambrose calls it “the apostasy,” because the Roman—that is, the Christian—empire, however it may be changed, whether at Constantinople or elsewhere, will not hinder this, provided only that the Christian empire endures. For, I say, this Christian empire will be dissolved: there will no longer be kings who punish heretics and destroy invaders of the Churches, nor will the world be subject in unity of faith to the Roman pontiff, who possesses spiritual empire. Rather, the world will depart from both Christian empires, the secular one, represented by kings, and the spiritual one, represented by the pope. Then first the beast will be prepared [Col. 0419A] upon which Antichrist will mount—that is, the unbelievers who will eagerly cooperate with such a head, the members of Antichrist, in the destruction of the faith—and after this apostasy has occurred, Antichrist will come at his proper opportunity.

But if he came now, while the world for the most part obeyed the Roman pontiff in unity of faith and Christian kings still defended the faith, he would find the beast upon which he could mount unprepared, and he could not advance in his own way. Yet when that apostasy is to occur, the faith will endure, even if only among a few, in the see of blessed Peter. The holy writers say that Peter obtained that prayer of Christ in which Christ said to him: “I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail” (Luke 22:32).

Others call it “the apostasy,” leaving aside the secular empire, when people will depart from the unity of faith and enter various paths of error. Then the rider Antichrist will come, with the beast spread out for him to mount. “Unless,” I say, “the apostasy first comes, and after the apostasy has occurred the one who is now hidden has been revealed—the man.”

Against what he is about to say, he calls him “man,” excluding him from every divinity. “Man,” I say, “of sin,” because just as Christ is the man of righteousness, so this one is the man of all sin; and “son of destruction,” that is, begotten for the destruction of his own, just as Christ was begotten for the salvation of the just. He also opposes Christ both in name and in deed. Hence he will be called Antichrist.

He is one who exalts himself above everything that is called God—that is, whatever is called God by designation but is not God substantially, such as the saints, according to the saying: “I said, You are gods” (Psalm 81:6). He also exalts himself above everything that is worshiped as God and is truly God. He exalts himself so that he sits in the temple of God—literally, in Jerusalem—in which Christ taught, asserting that he himself is the true God and that Christ was a deceiver and magician. “Sit,” I say, “in the temple of God, displaying himself as though he were God.”

Unless, I say, these signs have preceded, the day of the Lord will not first be imminent. You must also believe that the day of the Lord cannot otherwise be imminent, because you do not remember that, when I was still with you, I told you that these things would precede the day of the Lord. By saying “when I was still with you,” he indicates that he had delivered these teachings to them around the time of his departure.

It was Paul’s custom at first to nurture the simplicity of the Churches with simple teachings; but when they had already become mature, and he wished to depart, he then first revealed to them the hidden mysteries of God. [Col. 0419D]

After the apostasy has occurred, Antichrist will come. You know well what now restrains him, so that he does not come at present: this restrains him, so that he may be revealed in his own—that is, in the time suitable to him. But if he came while the unity of faith and the Christian empire endured, he would be revealed at a time not his own.

He will truly be revealed in his own time, for even now, though it is not his time, the mystery of lawlessness is at work—that is, mystical and veiled lawlessness through the preceding members of this abominable head. Only this remains for his revelation: that he who now holds back—that is, restrains him from coming, namely the Christian empire and the unity of faith—should restrain him until the unity of faith and the Christian empire are removed from the midst, that is, taken away from the community.

This is said by analogy with the expression: “This man has been removed from the midst,” that is, taken away from the human community. Or it may be understood this way: the only thing delaying Antichrist is that he who now holds the Christian empire and the unity of faith should hold them until the lawlessness now hidden under a mystery comes into the midst, that is, into the public community. Thus, just as faith is now public and lawlessness hidden, in the time of Antichrist faith will be hidden and lawlessness public, because his members will no longer be more ashamed of impiety than of piety, and those who possess the faith will be very few.

And then, after the one who now restrains him has been removed from the midst, or after lawlessness has come into the midst, then, I say, that lawless one will be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the Spirit of his mouth. Blessed Ambrose says that Jesus will show himself to Antichrist, and that when Jesus cries out, this impious one will be killed; but what he will cry out, we do not know. Others say that Michael will kill this Antichrist by terror alone. Jesus will indeed kill him, and afterward destroy him, condemned both in body and in soul. [306]

He will destroy him by the manifestation of his coming, that is, when he comes to judgment in the great brightness of glory. I speak of him whose coming is according to the working of Satan; for just as Christ came through the working of the Holy Spirit, so this one will come according to the working of Satan.

“Its working,” I say, which he will carry out with every power, namely with signs and wonders. He calls the lesser signs “wonders” (prodigia), and the greater ones “miracles.” “Signs and wonders,” I say, “that are lying,” either because they will not truly exist in reality but will appear to exist through magic, or because they are lying even if the miracles are real: what they intend to prove will nevertheless be proved false by the outcome of the matter—namely, that Antichrist is not God. The miracles have preceded for the purpose of proving that claim.

His coming will also be accompanied by every deception of unrighteousness, because he will deceive by every kind of impiety. “Deception,” I say, directed toward those who are perishing, because the righteous will not be deceived. They perish deservedly, because they did not receive the love of truth—that is, Christ, who is pure truth and in whom there is such love that he gave himself over to death for us. They did not receive him so that they might be saved [Col. 0420D] through him, from whom all salvation comes.

And therefore, because they did not wish to be saved, God will send them an operation of error—that is, the erroneous worker, Antichrist—so that they may believe the lie, and so that all may be judged, that is, condemned, who do not believe the truth, that is, Christ, but consent to unrighteousness, that is, to Antichrist.

Because he had said above that Antichrist would come with every power of signs and wonders, and with every deception, so that all who did not believe the truth but consented to unrighteousness might be condemned, Paul consoles them concerning this, lest they be terrified by these words and fear that he would come in their own days. He says that they will not see the day of Antichrist.

The text is connected in this way: “When Antichrist comes, those who consent to unrighteousness will be judged; but we ought always to give thanks to God” [Col. 0421A]—as we explained above—“for you, because you are brothers beloved by God,” that is, those whom God loved.

He says that they should give thanks especially because God chose us—me and you—not as the end of the Church, into which Antichrist will come, since he will come in the last times, but as firstfruits, that is, as among the first established in the faith. He chose us, I say, to possess eternal salvation by placing us in sanctification of the Spirit. For through the Holy Spirit he justified us in baptism, and this sanctification is the way to that salvation.

And in order to sanctify us, he placed us in faith in the truth, so that we might confess Christ, who is pure truth, just as Antichrist is error and falsehood. In possessing this faith, just as he chose us, so also he called you through our Gospel, so that everything might be yours by grace. [Col. 0421B]

He called you, I say, not to idleness but to the acquisition of glory, that is, so that by acting as faith requires, you might acquire glory with worthy works. “Of the glory,” I say, “of our Lord Jesus Christ,” that is, the same glory which the Lord Jesus Christ possesses; he called you to acquire it.

One must consider how he has placed everything in an inverted order. First they are called; then they confess the faith; those confessing the faith are sanctified through baptism; and for those who have been sanctified—if they persevere—eternal salvation is reserved.

Since, therefore, brothers, you have been called in sanctification of the Spirit and in the acquisition of glory, stand firm—that is, be strong in the good work you have begun—and hold fast perseveringly to the traditions of the life of faith and conduct that you learned from me, whether through my word, when I preached to you, or through our letter sent to you.

I admonish you: stand firm and hold fast. But so that you may be able to hold fast, our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God and our Father, always joins will with power. “Father” is the name of loving will; “God” signifies power. He loved us and gave us eternal consolation. In the present tribulation he begins to console us, continuing that consolation into eternal rest.

He also gave us a good hope, which is especially and uniquely to be called good. For the hope of heavenly glory is to be called good above all things that are hoped for. He gave us this hope by grace, when he forgave us our sins; in baptism he granted us hope of possessing glory, namely by freeing us from sins.

He, I say, is the God who has already granted so many good things by grace. May he encourage your hearts—that is, your wills—to stand firm in the state in which you are and to labor for increase; and may he strengthen you, that is, make you strong and persevering, in every good work and every good word, so that you may lack no perfection.

## CHAPTER III

“Finally, brothers, pray for us, so that the word of God may run and be glorified, as it is also among you, and that we may be delivered from unreasonable and evil men. For faith is not possessed by all. But God is faithful, who will strengthen you and guard you from evil. We have confidence in you, brothers, in the Lord, that the things which [variant: “whatever”] we have commanded, you both do and will do. May the Lord direct your hearts in the love [Col. 0422A] of God and [some add: “in”] the patience of Christ.

“We command you, brothers, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, to withdraw yourselves from every brother who walks disorderly and not according to the tradition that they received from us. For you yourselves know how you ought to imitate us, because we were not restless among you, nor did we eat bread from anyone without payment, but in labor and weariness, working night and day so that we might not burden any of you. Not as though we lacked authority, but so that we might give ourselves to you as an example for imitation.

“For even when we were with you, we commanded you this (hoc; variant haec): if anyone does not wish to work, neither should he eat. For we have heard that some among you walk restlessly, doing nothing but acting meddlesomely. To those who are such we command and entreat in the Lord Jesus Christ that, working quietly, they eat their own bread.

“But you, brothers, do not grow weary in doing good. If anyone does not obey our word through the letter, mark that person, and do not (non; variant ne) associate with him, so that he may be ashamed. Do not regard him as an enemy, but admonish him as a brother.

“May the God [Lord] of peace himself give you everlasting peace in every place. May the Lord [God] be with all of you. The greeting is by my hand, Paul’s, which is the sign in every letter. This is how I write: The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen.”

## EXPOSITION

I have instructed you concerning the preservation of patience, knowledge of the last day, and the coming of Antichrist. Now, brothers, finally—that is, concerning another matter—I exhort you to this: “Pray for us, so that the word of the Lord may run,” that is, so that through us it may encompass many in the faith, “and may be glorified in all things” through the integrity of faith and the execution of pious work.

For in some people the word of the Lord runs: they believe sufficiently quickly, but because they remain in vices, it is not glorified in them. “May it be glorified,” I say, “as it has been glorified in other Churches and among you.”

Pray also that I and those who preach with me may be delivered from importunate men, who afflict whomever they seize with much importunity, and from evil men. He indicates a twofold evil: importunity, namely being importunate in persuading people toward evil.

Therefore I say, “Pray that we may be delivered,” because faith is not possessed by all—that is, because not all are yet faithful, but many persecute the faith. Or it may be understood this way: “Pray that we may be delivered from unreasonable and evil men, because faith is not possessed by all of them,” that is, there is no one among all of them who possesses faith.

And lest, because he had said “Pray that we may be delivered,” they should say, “What hope is there for us, when our teacher is so greatly afraid for himself?”, he answers: “Although I have said, ‘Pray that we may be delivered,’ nevertheless I trust that the Lord is faithful, who says to those suffering for his sake: ‘Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age’” (Matthew 28:20). God, I say, is faithful, and he will strengthen you—as I say nothing about myself—in the good in which you stand, and will guard you from evil, so that you do not fall.

Wishing to persuade them of something new [Col. 0423A]—namely, that they should withdraw from those idle and meddlesome people who had refused to be corrected by the earlier letter—he wins them over by praising them for what has already been mentioned, saying:

“We have exhorted you concerning the observance of patience, the day of judgment, and prayer to be made for us; but we have good confidence in you in the Lord, because whatever we commanded, you are now doing and will do in the future.”

And so that you may do good, may the Lord direct your hearts, that is, make your wills straight, in the love of God, so that, just as God loved you, you may love him, and in the patience of Christ, so that, just as Christ suffered for you, you may also suffer for Christ.

We say that we know you will do whatever we command from God, and we issue this command to you. Know that this is God’s command, not ours, except insofar as we announce it to you, brothers, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ—that is, if you care for and honor the name of the Lord Christ.

We issue this command so that you withdraw yourselves from every brother who walks disorderly, that is, who abandons the natural order. Even the Gentiles regard as disorderly the neglect of one’s own affairs and concern for those of others, as certain meddlesome people among you do.

I say “brother,” but one who does not walk according to the tradition that they received from us—that is, according to the manner in which we handed it down to them, while they promised that they would preserve it as they received it. Therefore I simply say, “as they received it from us who handed it down to them,” and I do not explain this tradition, because you yourselves know well how you ought to imitate us.

Lest they should go astray and say, “We know that we must imitate you in prayer, fasting, and vigils,” he specifies what he means by saying: “Imitate us in this: that we were not restless among you,” that is, running about the city inquisitively; “nor did we eat bread received from anyone as idlers”; nor did we eat our bread for nothing, that is, without labor and in idleness. Rather, we worked night and day, in labor and weariness—that is, laboring to the point of exhaustion.

He puts night first because he was especially free for work at night, while during the day he devoted himself especially to prayer and preaching. We worked so that we might not burden any of you by receiving necessities from you.

Paul did not wish to accept anything from these people, just as he did not accept anything from the Corinthians, though his intention was different in the two cases. He refused from the Corinthians because they were greedy. He refused from these people but preferred to work, so that he might give them in himself an example of labor after idleness had been driven away.

“We worked so that we might not burden any of you.” Yet not as though we lacked the authority to receive from you if we wished, but so that we might give ourselves to you as an example for imitation, so that, abandoning idleness, you might live from labor according to my example. We intended, certainly, to give you an example of working.

For even when we were present with you, we commanded you this: if anyone, remaining idle, does not wish to work, neither should he eat from the labors of others.

For this reason I command that one who refuses to work should not eat, because we heard that some among you walk restlessly, doing nothing but acting meddlesomely, carefully investigating the rumors of the city.

To those who are such—that is, doing nothing and being meddlesome—we issue a command with God’s authority, and we entreat them in the Lord Jesus Christ—that is, we command and beseech them, if they wish to be saved in Christ—to work themselves, with idleness driven away and in silence, not being meddlesome about rumors, and to eat their own bread, that is, not another’s, but bread earned by their own labor.

But lest, because he had said, “Let each one eat his own bread,” those who were accustomed to serve the poor should think that they should no longer minister to them, he says: “Although I have said, ‘Let them eat their own bread,’ nevertheless you, brothers, in doing good to brothers who are in need, do not grow weary of doing good, because their own labor cannot suffice for everyone.”

“We command them to work,” and so forth. But if any of them does not obey this word of ours, commanded through the letter, mark him—that is, tell me who he is—and in the meantime do not associate with him, so that, when you do not communicate with him, he may be ashamed, that is, become ashamed of his sin.

And although you do not associate with him, nevertheless do not regard him as an enemy, so that you hate him; rather, correct him out of love as a brother. [309]

And so that you may be perfect in all the things I have commanded you, may the Lord of peace himself give you everlasting peace, that is, here and in the future, and in every place, that is, among household members and strangers.

And so that you may have true peace, may the Lord be with all of you.

“The greeting is written by my hand.” My hand, I say, Paul’s; this is the sign, written in this manner, in every letter that I send. By this sign distinguish the letter, so that those false teachers who used to tell you that I understood the day of judgment to be near may not fraudulently bring you their own letter under my name.

This, I say, is the greeting: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen.” [Col. 0424D]

# [IN THE FIRST LETTER TO TIMOTHY]

[Col. 0423]

## ARGUMENT OF THE FIRST LETTER TO TIMOTHY

He instructs and teaches Timothy concerning the ordering of the episcopate, the diaconate, and all ecclesiastical discipline, writing to him from Laodicea through Tychicus the deacon.

## BLESSED BRUNO’S PROLOGUE TO THE SAME

[Col. 0423D]

It was the custom of the apostles that, after the people of any city had been converted to the faith through their teaching, they did not remain there, but, having consecrated a bishop there to instruct the believers in what must be held after faith, they moved on to gather other peoples into the faith.

Following the pattern of this practice, Paul, after the Ephesians had been converted, consecrated Timothy for them as bishop, a fellow worker in the Gospel, so that, while Paul went on to convert the Macedonians, the Ephesians would have Timothy to instruct them in every matter, lest Paul’s labor among them should perish when they were left without a teacher.

Paul was the first to convert these Ephesians to the faith. Later the evangelist John presided over them as bishop, after Timothy had been recalled by Paul to the work of the Gospel.

Paul writes this letter, together with the three that follow, to individuals: two to Timothy, the third to Titus, and the fourth to Philemon. He writes the remaining letters to Churches.

After Timothy had been consecrated bishop of the Ephesians, as has been said, false teachers rose up against him, saying that, although the new law had been introduced, circumcision and the ancient rites of sacrifices were nevertheless to be observed with it.

When Paul learned this, he directed this letter to Timothy—not because he doubted that Timothy might in any respect agree with the false teachers, but so that Timothy’s teaching, strengthened by Paul’s authority, since Paul taught the same things as Timothy, might possess greater authority [Col. 0426A] and reverence. The Ephesians would hear Timothy teaching the same doctrine that had been delivered to Paul by Christ.

In this letter Paul treats of ecclesiastical order. He teaches that false teachers are to be expelled from the Church and warned not to teach perversely; and if they do not cease for that reason, the people must be warned not to listen to them.

Paul also teaches Timothy here about the priestly and Levitical order: how members are to be chosen and tested. He also teaches about the order of widows, and how they ought to minister in the Church. He teaches that teaching must never be entrusted to women, even if they are extremely wise.

In teaching about ecclesiastical order, Paul intended that the Ephesian Church, and every Church together with it, should preserve the order according to the measure of his teaching.

# FIRST LETTER TO TIMOTHY

[Col. 0425]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0425B]

“Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ according to the command of God our Savior and of Christ Jesus our hope.

“To Timothy, a beloved son in faith: grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.

“As I asked you to remain at Ephesus when I was going to Macedonia, so that you might command certain people not to teach otherwise, nor to devote themselves to myths and endless genealogies, which provide questions rather than God’s edification, which is in faith.

“The end of the commandment is love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith. Some, having departed from these things, have turned to empty talk, wishing to be teachers of the law, understanding neither what they say nor concerning what they make assertions.

“But we know that the law is good, if anyone uses it lawfully, knowing (scientes; variant sciens) this: that the law is not established for the just but for the unjust and disobedient, the impious and sinners, the wicked and defiled, patricides and matricides, murderers, fornicators, those who lie with males, kidnappers (plagiariis; variant plagariis), liars and perjurers, and whatever else is opposed to sound doctrine, which is according to the Gospel of the glory of the blessed God, which was entrusted to me.

“I give thanks to him who strengthened me, Christ Jesus our Lord, because he considered me faithful and appointed me to the ministry. I was formerly a blasphemer, persecutor, and insolent man; but I obtained the mercy of God because I acted ignorantly in unbelief.

“But the grace of our Lord abounded exceedingly, with faith and love that are in Christ Jesus. The saying is faithful and worthy of all acceptance: Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners, of whom I am the first.

“But for this reason I obtained mercy, so that Christ Jesus might first display in me all patience, as an example for those who would believe in him for eternal life.

“To the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, the only God, be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

“This command I entrust to you, son Timothy, according to the preceding prophecies concerning you, so that you may serve as a soldier in them in the good warfare, possessing faith and a good conscience. Some, having rejected this, have suffered shipwreck concerning the faith. Among them are Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom I handed over to Satan, so that they may learn not to blaspheme.”

## EXPOSITION

“Paul,” and so forth. When he is about to write to his disciple, he puts the greeting first, saying, “Paul.” This name is indeed one of humility, for Paul means something like “little.” But here, where authority is needed, it is also a name of authority, since the name Paul was very well known.

Therefore, in order to refute the false teachers more effectively, he says: “Paul, an apostle,” that is, an ambassador or one sent. Although all the saints are ambassadors of God, the apostles are especially called this; beneath them is found every class of saints, while above them is Christ alone.

“An apostle,” I say, “of Christ Jesus,” because the apostles alone were sent by Christ. The other saints were sent by the apostles, as Timothy was sent by Paul. For if Paul is an apostle of Christ, it is clear that whoever contradicts Paul also contradicts Christ, who sent Paul; and whoever contradicts Timothy, sent by Paul, offends both Paul and Christ.

“Paul,” I say, “an apostle of Christ Jesus according to the command.” In other letters he says “according to the will,” but here, to indicate greater strictness, he says “command.” For we wish certain things that we do not command; but whatever we command to be done, we both wish and appear to prohibit lest it not be done.
