Hence he says: “According to the command of God the Father.” For God the Father commanded me to become an apostle. “Of God,” I say, “our Savior,” that is, the one who saves those who obey his command, but separates the disobedient from salvation.

Therefore those who do not obey Timothy’s command must be afraid, because they obey neither me nor God, who commanded me to be an apostle, and thus they are separated from God’s salvation.

“According to the command of God the Father,” I say, “and according to the command of Christ, king and priest.” I speak of him as man, who also sacrificed himself on the altar of the cross to cleanse us from sins, and gave himself to be sacrificed for us daily on the altar.

He is also king, because he gives good things and rules in goodness. “Of Christ,” I say, “Jesus,” that is, Savior, who at present saves his own from evils and in the future will give them eternal salvation.

“Of Christ Jesus,” I say, “the author of our hope,” that is, of the recovery of impassibility and immortality, which we hope to recover through him, who lifted our flesh, united in himself to the Word of God, above every creature, leaving nothing above it except the divinity joined to him.

Hope is said not of things that we possess, such as justification from sins in baptism, but of things that we believe we shall possess, such as immortality and impassibility through Christ. Hope is the expectation of a future good together with desire. [Col. 0427B]

“Paul,” I say, “an apostle,” in this way and in this way, wishes, commands, or something similar, for Timothy, his son, who imitates him well, whom he begot in faith, because when Timothy was an unbeliever Paul made him faithful.

“Son,” I say, “beloved” in a particular and special way, because although every believer ought certainly to be loved, there are nevertheless some among them who, by the privilege of love, ought to be loved especially.

Paul, I say, commands Timothy—his own son, or you, Timothy—“grace, mercy, and peace.” In his other letters he generally places only grace and peace, signifying by “grace” what he signifies here by “mercy,” namely the remission of sins. It is called grace because sins are forgiven freely, without payment or our merit.

It is called mercy because sins are forgiven through God’s mercy. Therefore, “mercy,” that is, remission of sins, and “peace,” that is, the tranquility of soul which the saints possess here, tasting through it the sweetness of eternal peace—may these, I say, remain with you perseveringly.

He does not wish this because he does not know that Timothy’s sins have been forgiven and that he himself has a share among the saints, but so that he may remain in these things.

These two things, mercy and peace, are to be wished for every believer and may come to them. But the third, grace, is to be wished for prelates alone and may come to them. For through grace they receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. The Spirit is not given by prelates, but through their ministry, without distinction of merit, whether the prelates are just or unjust—provided only that their consecration is pure—to those whom they sanctify, if they are suitable persons in whom the Spirit ought to dwell; “for he will not dwell in a body subject to sins” (Wisdom 1:4).

If it is asked why those subject to sin do not deserve to receive the Holy Spirit, when the Spirit is given through the ministry of prelates who are themselves sinners—provided only that their consecration is just—the answer is that the Spirit is given by God and not by the prelate. The prelate could not give what he did not possess, yet the Spirit is given through the prelate’s ministry.

Nor did God choose to give it through this ministry without reason. If the Holy Spirit were given without ministers, everyone would boast that he possessed the Holy Spirit through his own presumption, and thus the ministers of the Church, even those who were just, would fall into contempt.

Christ left an example of this matter. After raising Lazarus, he said to the disciples: “Unbind him and let him go” (John 11:44), showing that no one can be released except through ministers, to whom these ministries have been entrusted.

“Grace, mercy, and peace,” then, be with you from God, who, since he is God, can do these and all things. “From God,” I say, “the Father,” who, in being Father, possesses will and loving affection toward you and every son.

May this same grace, mercy, and peace also be with you from Christ Jesus, who, since he is king and came to save, likewise possesses the will to do so. “From Christ,” I say, “our Lord,” whom, because he is Lord, is evidently able to do this and all things.

After completing the salutation, he begins the Epistle, saying:

“O Timothy”—understand, “Act thus,” as I asked you. When he says “as,” he indicates the degree. It is as though he said: “I have admonished you in many ways, through frequent repetition, that you should persist in teaching; and just as I admonished you in every way, so act with every kind of diligence.” When he says “I asked you,” although, as one who was his superior, he could have said, “I command you as a disciple,” he greatly commends Timothy, suggesting that he was such a man that he should not be restrained by command, but encouraged by a certain dignity of equality.

“As,” I say, “I asked you to remain in Ephesus in order to establish the ecclesiastical order there, when I, after converting the Ephesians, was going to Macedonia in order to convert the Macedonians by the word of preaching”—in this work you too would have been necessary to me, and you offered to go with me of your own accord. Yet, seeing that a greater necessity pressed upon us, I left you [Col. 0428C] to instruct the Ephesians.

Here he first begins to speak about rejecting the false teachers, saying: “Remain,” I say, “for this reason: to warn.” We use *to announce* among equals; *to warn* is used when a superior addresses subordinates. You were to warn certain people, namely those teachers who introduced a distinctive doctrine and withdrew from communion with the Church. You were to warn them, I say, “not to teach otherwise”—that is, not to teach anything alien to my doctrine, by which I taught the Ephesians and which you still teach. For if, when warned by you, the teachers were unwilling to desist, you were to warn the subordinates not to attend to their doctrines or listen to them.

The pattern of this practice is still preserved in the Church. First, the perverse superior is prohibited by the Church. If he does not cease in his disobedience, the subordinates are subsequently forbidden to obey him.

“Not to attend,” I say, “to the fables of the false preachers,” who say that circumcision and the ancient sacrifices must be maintained under the new law. That is called a fable in which there are only words, but no reality; so it is with their doctrine. Their words were indeed bare of the truth of the matter, because circumcision and the practices they taught could not save.

“Attend,” I say, “to fables and genealogies”—that is, discourses composed about their ancestry. For they say that salvation was promised only to those born according to the flesh from Abraham and David, and not to others. “Genealogies,” I say, “without limit”—that is, prohibited, so that no one should put confidence in them. Or “without limit” means having no boundary or end at which they can stop, once they have been established as proven, as they claim. For if anyone considers the matter, he will see [Col. 0429A] that many sons of Abraham according to the flesh were rejected, such as Esau; and he will also find many who were not born from Abraham’s flesh, whom God nevertheless chose, such as Job.

These genealogies produce questions—that is, disputes—and no solutions. This, I say, they produce rather than edification, which they in no way provide. For here the discussion is more concerned with those who do not participate. They do not provide the edification of virtues. What kind of edification is it? Not that which comes through circumcision, but that which is in faith—that is, through faith. For every justification comes from faith, which is laid down as a foundation; and upon it, as upon a foundation, the other virtues are built.

He proves that God’s edification is in faith, saying: “If from faith proceeds a good conscience”—that is, hope; “from hope,” however, comes a pure heart; and from a pure heart, charity. Charity, moreover, is the end—that is, the fulfillment of the whole commandment, whether of the new or of the old law. For if, in this manner, the fulfillment of every commandment follows from faith, then all God’s edification is in faith and nowhere else. But the fulfillment of the whole commandment is in faith; therefore God’s edification is there also. For he sets it down in inverted order as follows: “Truly, God’s edification is in faith.” For the end—that is, because the fulfillment of the whole commandment of the old or new law—is charity, namely love of God and neighbor, and upon this commandment the whole law and the prophets depend (Matt. XXII, 40). Whoever fulfills this commandment, namely charity, has undoubtedly fulfilled both the new and the old law.

Or let the passage be read continuously in this way. When above he says “that they should not teach” and “that they should not attend,” he indicates that some were both teaching and attending perversely. Thus he says: Although those false teachers teach otherwise than I do, nevertheless the end—that is, the entire fulfillment of the law—is charity, just as I teach. Therefore, what they teach about the ancient observances is not to be reintroduced.

Charity proceeds from a pure heart—that is, from a pure understanding: when someone possesses a pure intellect and preserves himself in the purity with which God purified him in baptism, understanding that he must love his Creator and offend him in nothing.

Charity also proceeds from a good conscience—that is, from hope. This does not mean that conscience is identical with hope, but that there is such an affinity between them that the person who has no scruple of a bad conscience, who examines himself everywhere in his mind and finds nothing that bites at him, may finally hope. For one who sees himself to be a sinner must fear concerning sin, not hope.

Charity also proceeds from an unfeigned faith. We believe that Christ is true God and true man, not pretending that he is either a man without God or God without man. Some false teachers also say that Christ had not a true body but an airy one.

Or understand it this way: “I speak of our faith,” strong and inviolable, “not feigned”—that is, not fragile in the manner of a clay vessel, as is the doctrine of the false teachers.

Having commended his own position, he condemns the position of his opponents, saying: “From which”—namely, from charity, a good conscience, and faith—“some, having gone astray,” that is, those who introduced a distinctive doctrine and, separated [Col. 0430A] from the truth, therefore went astray. Separation from the truth is indeed error.

Having gone astray, they turned not to faith but to empty talk, speaking things that are vain and useless, saying, namely, that circumcision must be maintained. It was not enough for them to speak this vanity among themselves; worse still, they wanted to be teachers of the law—that is, they taught that the carnal observances of the law must be maintained.

And they did this quite shamelessly, understanding neither what they themselves said—that is, circumcision, which they taught—nor why it had been maintained in the flesh under the old law: namely, to signify that circumcision of the heart must be maintained in the time of grace, and not circumcision of the flesh.

Nor did they understand the Scriptures of the prophets, from which—that is, through which—they affirm that circumcision and the ancient sacrifices they speak about must be maintained in the time of grace, or conversely. They did not understand the things that the prophets say in order to prove that what they teach must be maintained. Nor did they understand what circumcision and sacrifices signified, whose mysteries they were when they were performed, although they themselves affirm that these practices must still be maintained.

Because he has condemned the position of the opponents by saying “not understanding,” and so forth, this alone would not have been enough unless he had also commended his own position and inserted the reason for that commendation. For one might object to him as follows: “If the doctrine of the false teachers is perverse, but yours too is not to be approved as better, why do you judge that one should adhere to you rather than to them?”

To refute this, after condemning the position of the opponents, he adds an approval of his own, saying: The false teachers do not understand the law, but “we know”—that is, we understand—the law. And someone adds something further that is relevant to the argument, saying: “We know” not only the law, but we also know this about the law: that the law is good—that is, useful and spiritually justifying when understood according to the way we understand it.

According to their carnal understanding, however, it is rather not good, because it justifies no one and is cruel. Therefore, what they understand from the law is not to be reintroduced.

The law is good if someone uses it—that is, its meaning—legitimately, according to what the law itself teaches and commands, namely, that it be understood spiritually.

“We know” about the law that it is good, knowing this also about the same law: that the old law was not established for the just—that is, for one justified under the new law. Nor was it established under the old law itself for anyone who was just. For the law was given either to punish the guilty or to restrain someone who wished to sin, so that he would not transgress. But one who is just does not need to be restrained; he has no will to sin and should not be punished by the law. For there is no stain in one who has been justified.

Therefore, even for those just men who lived under the old law, insofar as they themselves were concerned, it would not have been necessary to keep the law. Nevertheless, they rightly made use of it, lest, if they rejected the law, it should fall into contempt, and so that by their authority those for whom it was necessary on account of their sins might observe it more devotedly.

The just also kept the old law so that, by fulfilling it, they might testify to what it prefigured concerning Christ and the time of grace.

The law was not established for the just, but for the unjust—that is, for the Jews, [Col. 0431A] to whom, before the law was given, Moses had given moral commandments; by failing to observe them, they became unjust. For the unjust, I say, and not the submissive—that is, for the Jews who were unwilling to submit to God, who gave the law through Moses, so that they might turn away from injustice.

He explains whom he calls “unjust” and “not submissive,” saying: “The law was established for the impious”—that is, for those irreligious in mind and opposed to God—and for sinners, meaning those who think irreligiously and act irreligiously; and for criminals, that is, those who, seeing others sacrifice to idols or perform similar acts, were pleased to transgress in the same way.

The law was also established for the defiled—that is, for those who were compelled by the violence of tortures to sacrifice to idols. These four kinds of sin are principally committed against God. The other things that follow are committed against oneself and against one’s neighbor—not because all sins are not against God, but because the four mentioned above appear to offend God in a particular way and without any intermediary.

The law was also established for parricides—that is, killers of fathers, to whom they owed much, since they were human beings, but owed their fathers still more for that reason—and likewise for matricides and murderers; for fornicators, that is, those who defile themselves by adultery or by any kind of fornication; and for those who lie with males, which is worse, since it is not enough for them to defile themselves unless they also corrupt others; and for kidnappers—that is, those who inflict wounds upon their neighbor; or “kidnappers,” as though from *plagiosipis*, meaning one who inflicts a wound upon a living thing, as when someone steals a father’s son from him or commits a similar act.

The law was also established for liars, who devote themselves to deceit; and for perjurers, which is a little worse than lying. For these and similar persons the law was established.

Besides these, it was imposed upon anyone who does anything else contrary to what has been mentioned and contrary to sound doctrine—that is, to the natural and moral law. For moral commandments endure in the new law just as they did in the old.

Thus he says: “Which is sound doctrine according to the Gospel”—that is, it follows the new law. He calls it “the Gospel of glory,” meaning the Gospel that preaches the glorious God. Or “the Gospel of glory” means the Gospel that gives eternal glory to those who follow it.

“Of the glory,” I say, “of the blessed God.” For the saints will have from him the kind of blessedness that God possesses. One is called blessed when nothing is lacking to him; and for the saints, when they are with Christ, nothing will be lacking.

The name “God” needs no adjective, such as “blessed” or any of these terms. But in order to indicate what kind of glory God will have and will give to his own, he added “blessed,” as though he were saying: “The glory that God has and gives, both to himself and to whomever he gives it, is sufficient.”

And because sound doctrine and the Gospel correspond to one another, only these things must be maintained, and circumcision and the ancient practices must not be reintroduced.

Here he begins to show that, because he departed from the old law, all good things were bestowed upon him; for as long as he adhered to that law, he continually rushed into the precipice of evils.

Thus he says: “The Gospel was entrusted to me”—that is, the mercy of God foresaw me as suitable to whom the Gospel might be entrusted. The Gospel is called “good news”: *eu* means “good,” and *angelium* means “message”; hence an angel is called a messenger.

Therefore, because God entrusted the Gospel to me, I give thanks to him and not to the law for this benefit and for the things that follow—he who judged me faithful.

Here some say that Paul’s words are deceptive, as though he were saying: “I therefore give thanks to God because, although I was unfaithful, he made me faithful.” And because he judged me worthy to become faithful—that is, because the providence of God, which cannot be deceived, predestined me from the beginning—he strengthened me once I had become faithful; that is, he made me strong, so that neither death nor the sword could separate me from his charity.

And after he entrusted to me the Gospel of peace, appointing me to the ministry—that is, to the very work of preaching—for the Gospel is entrusted to many superiors, who nevertheless, being sluggish, do not minister to their subordinates what has been entrusted to them.

“I was placed in the ministry of Christ [Col. 0432B] Jesus”—that is, for the honor and glory of Christ Jesus our Lord.

Or: “He strengthened me in Christ Jesus our Lord,” who appeared to me while I was breathing out slaughter on the road.

I became faithful, and so forth, after abandoning the law and submitting myself to the grace of God. Previously, when I was under the law, it drove me into every evil. For at that time I was a blasphemer, calling Christ a man without God, the son of a carpenter, and saying similar things.

I was also a persecutor of all kinds of just people (Acts IX, 1). I was also abusive, because if I could seize anyone, I afflicted them with insults and blows. But although I was so perverse under the law, as soon as I abandoned it I obtained mercy—that is, the remission of sins.

I obtained this mercy because I did what I did in ignorance—that is, I sinned unknowingly—and because I did not know Christ, I therefore remained in unbelief.

Here we read “because,” for it would not be sufficient to the argument to say that, because he sinned unknowingly, he therefore obtained mercy.

The passage may nevertheless be read in another way as relevant to the argument. Someone might say: “Formerly, while you were under the law, you preached that the law had to be maintained. But now, having abandoned that same law, you preach that the law must be abandoned. Which version of you should be believed—the one under the law or the one not under the law? We are uncertain.”

Against this he says: “I was not to be believed when I was under the law, because I acted in ignorance; and because I was ignorant, I therefore remained in unbelief.”

Nor did I obtain only mercy—that is, remission of sins—but “the grace of our Lord abounded in me beyond mercy,” because he both remitted my sins and gave me many other graces, such as knowledge of the divine essence, and so forth.

Or otherwise: While I was a persecutor of Christ’s Church, I had great zeal for the law; nevertheless, the grace of God has now abounded in me, because if I had had to suffer as much for the old law as I suffer for Christ, I would certainly have failed. The rest is to be understood as stated above.

“Grace abounded,” I say, “with faith and love,” because faith and love of God have continually increased in me. This faith and love is in Christ Jesus—that is, it is possessed through Christ Jesus and not through the law.

It is easy for you also to obtain this mercy which I obtained. For Christ Jesus came into this world so that sinners might be saved.

Before saying this, however, he places a commendation of the matter he is about to discuss, as follows: “This word which I proclaim to you is faithful”—that is, it is such that faith should be placed in it and that it is rightly credible. It is not only faithful but also worthy of acceptance—that is, it ought to be accepted.

For many statements are credible but not worthy of acceptance because they are useless. This statement, however, is both credible and acceptable because it is useful.

It is worthy of acceptance not only once or at one time, as the old law was, but always—that is, both in the present and in the future, and according to the body and according to the soul—because it saves in every time and according to both.

This, I say, is the statement: that Christ Jesus came into this world, so contemptible a world, in which he had to suffer so many miseries [Col. 0433B]. He came, I say, to save sinners. If they could have been saved through the law, God would have sent his Christ into the miseries of this world in vain.

Among these sinners I am the first—that is, the chief and worst—of all who adhere to the law. For God found the Jews, who adhered to the law, worse than any who were without the law.

What he stated above absolutely, he now states with its cause, saying: Although I was the worst among sinners, nevertheless I obtained mercy, so that Christ Jesus might first—that is, in the greatest sinner, or “first,” meaning supremely—display all patience in me, not merely patience in one matter but patience of every kind.

For he endured me while I was blaspheming, persecuting, and inflicting insults upon the saints. He displayed every kind of patience in me, as an example to those who would believe in him—that is, so that through me he might teach that, because of the enormity of their crimes, no one should despair of believing in him.

For they will believe in him for eternal life—that is, so that through this faith they may possess eternal life.

And since Christ came to save sinners, for which the law was insufficient, therefore to Christ, the King of the ages, let honor and glory be given; for thanks for this is owed neither to the law nor to anyone other than Christ.

Or the passage may be connected in this way: Christ displayed all patience in me. But to Christ, the immortal King of the ages—that is, the unchanging one, who is always the same—and the invisible one—that is, whose divinity no creature is sufficient to understand—to this God and Creator alone, who alone can save, to this great and such a one, let honor and glory be given.

“Honor” is said with reference to virtues such as humility, prudence, and the like, which a human being can possess. “Glory” is said of those things that belong to God alone and not to human beings, such as rising on the third day and similar things.

“Honor,” I say, and glory be given to him throughout the ages that follow the present ages. And this prayer of mine is “Amen”—that is, certainly it will be so.

Since all salvation comes from Christ Jesus and none from the law, therefore, O Timothy, my son, I commend this commandment to you, so that it may be clear in every respect that you can spare or tolerate no one in this matter.

For this is the commandment which it is not permitted to transgress, and which is commended to you with the greatest obedience: “Wage war,” by excluding the false teachers from the Church; “wage war” also by arranging another ecclesiastical order; wage, in every respect, “the good warfare.”

If he had waged war once or in one matter, he would have fulfilled what he had said, “wage war.” But in order to show that he wanted Timothy to wage war always and in every matter, he added “the good warfare”—that is, the useful one. For it will be useful for you to wage war in this manner.

“I commend,” I say, “that you wage war according to those prophecies”—that is, according to every vision and understanding that you have concerning God. For prophecy is vision, and a prophet is called one who sees.

“I urge you to wage war according to the prophecies that preceded you”—that is, according to what you were taught previously in the sacred Scriptures. Timothy, born of a Gentile father and a Christian mother (Acts XVI, 1), was entrusted from childhood to be instructed in the sacred writings. Thus he says, “according to the prophecies that preceded you.”

Or otherwise: “I commend to you that you wage war according to the prophecies that preceded you”—that is, concerning you. For, taught by the spirit of prophecy, I took you up for the work of the Gospel.

See to it that, by degenerating from the faith, you do not make the Spirit who taught me to choose you a liar.

You must wage war both because it is good and useful and because you are well able to do so: you possess faith, through which you have been fully justified, and you also possess a good conscience. For no one can object to you, who preach, that you teach well but live badly.

Now he briefly returns to the false teachers, saying: “Some rejected a good conscience from themselves.” For one who acts and teaches perversely has no basis on which he can be of good conscience. And because they rejected it, “they suffered shipwreck concerning the faith”—that is, they broke their ship, going around the faith and not entering into it.

Among these false teachers who suffered shipwreck are Hymenaeus and Alexander, leaders of those who wanted to reintroduce circumcision. “I handed them over to Satan” (I Cor. V, 5)—that is, I separated them from the Church by excommunication.

Not so that they might perish forever, but so that in this way they might learn not to blaspheme—that is, so that, corrected and repentant in this manner, they might cease from their perversity and, no longer blaspheming, might be taken away again from Satan and received into the bosom of the Church.

Note that to excommunicate is to hand over to Satan: when someone is excommunicated, he is handed over to Satan, whose he was before he was justified through baptism.

## CHAPTER II

“I ask, therefore, first of all that supplications, prayers, petitions, and thanksgivings be made for all people, for kings, and for all who are placed in positions of authority, so that we may lead a quiet and peaceful life in all piety and chastity. For this is good and acceptable before God our Savior, who wishes all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. For there is one God and one Mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a redemption for all. His testimony was confirmed at its proper times, and for this I was appointed a preacher and apostle (II Tim. I, 11). I speak the truth; I do not lie: a teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth.

“I therefore wish men to pray in every place, lifting up pure hands without anger and dispute. Likewise, women also [or: but women] should adorn themselves in respectable dress, with modesty and sobriety, not with braided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly clothing (I Pet. III, 3), but with what befits women who profess piety through good works.

“Let a woman learn in silence with complete submission. But I do not permit a woman to teach (I Cor. XIV, 34), nor to exercise authority over a man, but to be in silence. For Adam was formed first (Gen. I, 27), then Eve; and Adam was not deceived, but the woman was deceived and fell into transgression. She will be saved through the bearing of children, if they remain [variant: if she remains] in faith, love, and sanctification with sobriety.”

## EXPOSITION

After Paul admonished Timothy to wage war, he consequently indicates in what matters he commands him to wage war, saying: Since Christ came into this world to save sinners, and appointed me to the ministry of preaching this matter, so that you too may be saved through him and so that my preaching may bear fruit in you, therefore—that is, because of these things already stated—I ask you to pray.

For unless God works through the Holy Spirit in your hearts, my word will be useless. “I ask, therefore, first of all”—that is, most importantly, before all things—that supplications, and so forth, be made.

Because the Apostle saw the celebration of the Mass prevail in every kind of prayer—in it, remembrance is made of Christ’s Passion, through which the whole human race was redeemed—therefore, although one should pray in other ways as well, he placed this kind of prayer first because he saw that it prevailed, saying: “First of all”—that is, before all things—“I ask that supplications be made.”

He calls those prayers “supplications” which precede the consecration of the Lord’s body, that is, those said near and before the body of the Lord is consecrated, as at the beginning of the Mass; they are called supplications as though they were spoken near the consecration.

“I ask that prayers, petitions, and thanksgivings also be made.”

He calls “prayers” those petitions during which the substance of bread and wine placed upon the altar passes into the body and blood of Christ.

He calls “petitions” the prayers made after communion, such as: “Complete in us, Lord, what your holy things contain.” That is, after you have fed us with this body and blood of yours, it remains, as though by obligation, that you complete what you piously began, feeding us in heaven with the unfailing food of your glory, which we taste beforehand here upon the altar.

A petition is so called as though it were a prayer concerning something that is already owed by mercy or merit.

He calls “thanksgivings” such words as are said at the end of the Mass: “Let us bless the Lord. Thanks be to God.” By saying this, we indicate that everything he has given and everything he will give eternally must be referred to the grace of God.

“I ask that these things be done for all people,” so that they may be saved according to the will of God.

If someone asks why the Apostle commands prayer for all people, when some have been rejected by God, so that the one who prays for them seems to offend God, who rejects them, the answer is that God, in his goodness and clemency, does indeed wish every human being to be saved. For, insofar as it depends upon him, nothing is lacking in God; rather, the injustice of the impious turns aside God’s goodness.

Therefore, two wills are considered in God. One is the will of goodness and clemency, by which he wishes all to be saved; the other is the will of God’s justice, by which he rejects the wicked and chooses the good.

According to God’s will of goodness, the Apostle commands prayer for all, so that what God piously wills, we too may will by following his piety, and so that we may pray for God’s will to be done. If this did not happen, we would seem to disagree with God’s clemency.

Or let us read the preceding passage in another way, without introducing the foregoing mention here. “I ask that supplications be made”—that is, those adjurations such as occur in the litany, where God is adjured by his Passion, by his Resurrection, and similarly. It is as though someone were to adjure God for the conversion of some exceedingly wicked person, something that would seem scarcely capable of being obtained from God.

But when that impious person had been converted through the prayers of a just person, the just man would make prayers for him, asking God in faith to give him the virtues that follow. Once these had been received, petitions would remain—as was said—for the heavenly glory that is owed to one who already possesses the virtues.

For all these things—conversion, possession of the virtues, and the granting of heavenly glory—thanksgivings follow. This was done by the presbyter Justin, who, having received the spirit of Laurence in heaven, offered God a sacrifice of praise in thanksgiving.

“I ask that this also be done for all people,” as was said.

Because some might perhaps think that one should not pray for rulers and tyrants who oppress the Church [Col. 0436C] of God, he adds: I say that one should pray for all, so that I do not exclude even the persecutors of the Church. Pray also for kings and for all who are in secular positions of authority, whether dukes or consuls.

And your praying for them will benefit not only them but also you: namely, so that, when they cease from their tyranny, we may lead a quiet life, free from persecution. This is not quiet in only one respect, but peaceful in every respect.

The tranquility of the Church greatly benefits certain more delicate persons who preserve their justification in the peace of the Church. If torments were to seize them, they might perhaps fall away from the faith. Therefore he says that one must pray for kings and rulers.

“Let us lead,” I say, “a peaceful life in all piety”—that is, religion—and in all chastity—that is, integrity of faith. If persecution should erupt, this integrity would not remain complete in everyone. Therefore I urge you to pray for all.

For it is good—that is, useful for the advancement of the Church—to pray for all; and it is such a good that it is acceptable and pleasing to God. It does not please him at one time and displease him at another, but is acceptable in such a way that it remains always before God—that is, always in the sight of his good pleasure.

I speak of God our Savior, who, just as he saved us, wishes all people to be saved according to the will of his goodness, as was said above. And he wishes all to come to the knowledge of the truth—that is, to the true faith, through which there is a path to salvation.

He proves what he has said: Truly, God wishes all to be saved. This is evident from the fact that there is one God—that is, the Creator of all. Since God is the Creator of all, there is no reason why he should deny his goodness to one creature and give it to another, while the impious person denies it to himself by acting impiously, even though God’s goodness toward all remains whole and intact.

It is also evident that God wishes all to be saved because there is one Mediator between God and human beings, and not many mediators. Thus it is clear that, because he wishes equally to advance all, he became the Mediator of all.

Christ is called the Mediator because he made two extremes, wholly separated from one another—namely, God, in whom there is all justice and no injustice, and the human being, in whom there is all injustice and no justice—concordant through the humanity he assumed, justifying the human being.

He proves again that God wishes all to be saved, saying: This Mediator, although glorious in his divinity, became a human being—a thing so lowly and so full of disgrace that he would never have become one unless he had wished to save human beings.

This Mediator is Christ, offering himself to God as a sacrifice for us, and the King directing us toward salvation.

This is Jesus, the Savior, as his name indicates: the Savior of all. Christ Jesus gave redemption, giving not gold or silver but himself as the price for redeeming all.

Although that price did not benefit everyone, because some persisted in impiety, Christ nevertheless gave a price sufficient for the salvation of all, if all had wished to be good.

And because he gave redemption for all, he wished equally to save all. His testimony to this—that is, to the fact that he wishes all to be saved—was confirmed because Christ confirmed what the prophets had testified before him concerning him as Savior, fulfilling everything that the prophets had foretold about him.

These things were confirmed through fulfillment at their proper times—that is, at fitting times: Christ’s birth at one time, and at other times his Passion and the other events concerning Christ.

For unless the testimonies of the prophets had preceded Christ, little or nothing would have been believed about him. He himself indicates this when, appearing after his Resurrection to two disciples, he says: “O foolish ones and slow of heart to believe in all that the prophets have spoken” (Luke XXIV, 25), and so forth.

He also says elsewhere in the Gospel: “In this is the true saying: one is he who sows and another he who reaps” (John IV, 37). The prophets indeed sowed, but Christ, together with his apostles, gathered the fruits of the seed.

To prove the same point—that God wishes all to be saved—he brings forward his own authority, saying: “In this”—that is, in preaching this matter, namely, that God gave himself as the price for the salvation of all, together with the other things stated above—“I was appointed a preacher by God,” so that I might preach this to all.

And I was appointed a preacher of great dignity, because I was also appointed an Apostle for this preaching. And without doubt I speak the truth; I do not lie in any respect. I have also been appointed a teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth—that is, I have already taught many disciples who are faithful and preach the truth.

For if my disciples are true, it is clear that I, their teacher, am not a liar. When he calls himself a preacher and an Apostle, these are not words of arrogance, but are intended to strengthen belief in his statements through this authority.

Since it has been sufficiently proved that one must pray for all people, therefore I wish all men and women to pray, so that they may be saved according to the will of God.

I wish men to pray not only in church but also in every place, having pure hands, and so forth. Here he teaches what kind of preparation they should make for prayer.

He calls pure hands pure affections: they should not wish God to give them anything that it would be unlawful for God to give, but above all they should seek salvation.

“Pure,” I say, “lifting them up” through the increase of good works and pious prayer, and doing this “without anger”—that is, without hatred of one’s neighbor. For whoever hates his neighbor tears himself away from the unity of the Church.

“And without dispute”—that is, without distrust—pray, having become such persons that, because of fear of sin, you do not need to dispute whether God will give you what you ask or not.

It is as though he said: Pray with love of God and neighbor.

I also wish women to pray together with men, likewise existing without anger and dispute, in clothing—not clothing that adorns them, but “adorned,” that is, clothing adorned by them. Their reverence should be so great that even their garments may appear adorned, because holy women use them.

Let them remain with modesty, doing everything as bashful women, and with sobriety in food, drink, and words. Along with the other virtues, he especially commends these two to women because he saw them suffer particularly from the disease of immodesty and intemperance.

I speak of women adorning themselves not with braided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly clothing—that is, not devoting themselves to the adornment of their bodies, but through the good works they perform outwardly professing piety—that is, making the religion of their minds public through good works displayed outwardly.

In prayer I wish men and women to be alike; but in teaching or asking questions I wish them to be different. Let a woman learn and listen to the word in church, not by asking questions or responding, but let her remain silent. If she is uncertain about something, let her ask her husband when she has returned home.

Let her learn in silence with complete submission, standing behind the men with her head veiled and her gaze fixed upon the ground. For when we assemble in church, we are brought before the Judge whom we provoked to anger through the woman’s seduction. Remembering this, since she was the cause of the whole ruin, the woman ought to be very much ashamed in the presence of the Judge.

I permit a woman to learn. But I do not permit a woman in any way to teach a man spiritual doctrine, nor to exercise any spiritual authority over a man, but always to remain not only silent in asking or answering questions, but also silent in conversing with anyone in the church.

Therefore a woman ought not to rule over a man, because Adam was formed first, and then Eve. The order of their creation signifies that the man ought to rule over the woman, not the woman over the man. For although [Col. 0439A] God could have created the woman before the man, or at the same moment as the man, he deliberately made her later in time than the man; therefore the woman still ought not to rule over the man. Indeed, Adam was not deceived in the way the woman was, namely, into believing that by tasting the fruit she would become God; rather, he was deceived in this respect: because the woman whom God had given him as a helper persuaded him, he supposed that both things could be achieved—both to comply with his wife and, after repenting of the crime committed, to obtain forgiveness from God.

Adam was not deceived, but the woman was deceived, believing that she would become gods, as the serpent had suggested, in the transgression—that is, in the act of sin, namely, in eating the fruit. And for all these reasons the woman ought always to be subject to the man, not placed above him. I speak of spiritual authority; for if she has [Col. 0439B] servants, she may rule them properly with secular authority. A woman may also preside spiritually over women, but never over a man.

Yet lest anyone should think that a woman could not be saved because she was the cause of universal destruction, and because Paul himself had so thoroughly condemned woman, he adds concerning her salvation, saying: Although the woman was deceived, and the man was not deceived, nevertheless the woman will be saved. Not only a virgin or a celibate woman, but also one who proceeds through the bearing of children—that is, a married woman as well.

I state this condition: if she has remained in faith, possessing sound faith, and in love of God and neighbor, and in the sanctification that she received in baptism. I say that she must remain in these things with sobriety—a qualification he repeats because women are especially accustomed to sin in this matter. [Col. 0439C] For this reason he said that married women could be saved: if he had spoken only of virgins or widows, it might have been thought that he understood married women to be unable to be saved; but since married women are to be saved, this also establishes the salvation of virgins and widows.

Or let us connect the passage differently: Although I do not permit a woman to teach in the Church, nevertheless she will be saved—that is, she will be able to merit salvation—through the bearing of children; that is, by spiritually instructing her children at home, she will be saved on this condition: insofar as it depends upon her, her children remain in faith, love, and sanctification, with sobriety, as has been said.

## CHAPTER III

> “This saying is trustworthy: If anyone desires the episcopate, he desires a good work. For the bishop [Col. 0439D] must be irreproachable, the husband of one wife, sober, well ordered, prudent, chaste, hospitable, a teacher, not given to wine, not violent, but moderate, not quarrelsome, not greedy, but presiding well over his own household, having children subject to him with all chastity. But if anyone does not know how to preside over his own household, how will he care for the Church of God? He must not be a recent convert, lest, puffed up with pride, he fall into the condemnation of the devil. He must also have a good testimony from those who are outside, so that he may not fall into reproach and into the snare of the devil.

> “Deacons likewise must be chaste, not double-tongued, not devoted to much wine, not pursuing shameful gain, holding the mystery of the faith in a pure conscience. And let these also [Col. 0440A] first be tested, and so let them serve, having no accusation against them. Women likewise must be chaste, not slanderers, sober, faithful in all things. Let deacons be husbands of one wife, presiding well over their children and their own households. For those who have served well acquire for themselves a good standing and great confidence in the faith that is in Christ Jesus.

> “I am writing these things to you, son Timothy, hoping to come to you soon. But if I am delayed, so that you may know how it is necessary for you to conduct yourself in the household of God, which is the Church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth. And manifestly great is the mystery of piety: he was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, appeared to angels, preached among the nations, believed on in the world, taken up in glory.”

## EXPOSITION

[Col. 0440B] After admonishing the community of the Church to pray, and thereby giving a public command for everyone, he adds certain separate commands that do not concern all people, namely, commands concerning the priesthood and the diaconate. He indicates what sort of men they should be and how they are to be promoted to these orders.

Because he saw that this command seemed burdensome and difficult to some, he commends it before presenting it, saying: This saying that I am about to give is trustworthy—that is, it ought to be believed and is burdensome to no one. This, then, is the saying that I commend: the bishop must be irreproachable.

Here he signifies a priest by “bishop.” [Col. 0440C] It would be superfluous for him to instruct the Ephesians about ordaining a bishop when Timothy, who was the bishop of the Ephesians, was exercising the episcopate there; it would be absurd to appoint another bishop in the same place, and this must not be believed. Moreover, if he gave a command concerning deacons while passing over the priestly order, which precedes it, the arrangement would seem discordant and disordered.

Nor is it surprising that he signifies a priest by “bishop,” since in this same Epistle he signifies a bishop by “presbyter.” And because anyone wishing to become a bishop must be irreproachable, therefore, if anyone desires the episcopate—that is, to exercise oversight over those entrusted to him—he desires not gold, wealth, or worldly pleasure, but a work: a good work, that is, one useful both to himself and to those over whom he exercises oversight.

And [Col. 0440D] a bishop is so called from “overseer”:  *scopos* means “intention” or “aim,” while *epi* is interpreted as “over.” And since one who desires the episcopate desires to perform a good work, it follows that the bishop—that is, the one wishing to become a priest—must be irreproachable, because if he is liable to reproach, then, so long as he remains so, he cannot perform a good work.

He calls irreproachable the man who is guilty of no criminal offense and who, even if he has committed no crime, guards himself in such a way that no occasion for crime appears in him, from which he might be suspected of being criminal.

This bishop, that is, the man wishing to undertake the priesthood, must have been the husband of one wife: he must have had only one wife, for as long as it was permitted him to marry. This does not mean that he must have her as his wife while in the episcopate, nor that a man who had no wife should be rejected; rather, it is more a matter of accepting him. He denies the priesthood to a man who has had several wives because, after being released from his first wife and contracting a second marriage, he showed that he could not remain continent; but a continent man may become a bishop, whereas one who is incontinent may not.

And in order to be irreproachable, [Col. 0441A] the bishop must be sober both in word and in deed. He must also be prudent, knowing how to bring forth from the treasury of his heart the new and the old law.

He must also not be addicted to wine, dissolved by continual drinking. He must not be violent with bodily violence, for he has spiritual weapons with which he ought to fight against his adversaries, namely, the word of God; therefore he ought not to use bodily weapons. He must not be violent, but moderate—that is, a guardian of complete moderation.

He must not be quarrelsome—that is, he must not return insult for insult, but be patient in all things. He must not be greedy either, lest greed prevent him from distributing the Church’s goods to the poor, whose patrimony they are, not the bishops’ private property.

He must also [Col. 0441B] have presided well over his household, having properly restrained his private family from every vice. He must not merely have restrained the rest of his household, but must also have children subject to him—that is, he must not have been deceived by paternal affection when disciplining his children.

I do not mean that he corrected them after they had committed a vice, but that he did so with all chastity—that is, with every integrity preserved—because he was so strict in guarding his children that they were not permitted to reach the act of crime. It is good that a man who knows how to preside over his own household in this manner should be promoted to the priesthood.

But if someone does not know how to preside over his private household, in which only a few things must be ordered, how will he [Col. 0441C] have care—that is, diligent guardianship—of the Church of God, in which so many and such great matters must be managed? in which only a few things must be ordered, how will he have care—that is, diligent guardianship—of the Church of God, in which so many and such great matters must be managed?

In addition to the foregoing, he must not be a recent convert—that is, one newly converted. Otherwise, if he is promoted to the priesthood while still inexperienced in the faith, he may become puffed up with pride, saying to himself: “If I had not now been converted, there would be no one besides me who knew how to preside over the Church.” By becoming proud in this way, he may fall into judgment—that is, the condemnation of the devil, who was condemned through pride—so that this recent convert likewise may be condemned through pride.

Nor are these things alone necessary for him. [Col. 0441D] He must also—that is, it is necessary that he—have a good testimony, not only from the faithful but also from those who are outside, that is, outside the faith, namely, unbelievers. This is so that he may not fall into reproach. For if unbelievers should now see him made a priest and preaching the word of God, they might insult him, saying: “You who only recently were stealing, committing adultery, and so forth, now proclaim yourself our teacher!” In such a man’s mouth even good things are contemptible.

When he hears this, he may be inflamed with anger and return the insults; and in this way he may fall into the devil’s snare, since the devil works by such devices to entrap him. Therefore the man promoted to the priesthood must, even while he was an unbeliever, have conducted himself among his own people without complaint.

We have said what sort of men presbyters ought to be. Deacons likewise ought to be sober, and so forth, although he does not repeat the remaining qualifications. By saying “likewise,” he indicated that these requirements are to be understood in the ordination of deacons as well, since that order differs little from the priesthood in dignity.

Deacons, I say, [Col. 0442A] must be chaste—that is, guardians of chastity—and not double-tongued, that is, not sowers of discord among the brethren. They must not be devoted to much wine, although wine may indeed be used soberly. They must not pursue shameful gain, so that they neither lend at interest nor engage in commerce. They must also possess the mystery—that is, the secret—of the faith, so that they may know those secrets of our faith that the simplicity of the common people is not sufficient to grasp.

For the office of deacons is to proclaim the word of God to the people. As a sign of this, the Gospel is handed over to them for reading. Therefore those who are going to teach the faith ought to know the mysteries of the faith.

Even if they possess all these qualities, nevertheless, before they are ordained they must first be tested by those questions with which candidates are customarily examined before receiving orders, such as: “Do you wish to preserve chastity?” and similar questions. These men, then, must be tested; and likewise the priests, concerning whom he had not previously mentioned this.

Only then, once ordained, should they [Col. 0442B] serve—that is, distribute the Church’s resources for necessary uses, such as food for the poor and similar needs.

It was also established in the primitive Church that those seven deacons should administer ecclesiastical and household affairs and serve the poor (Acts 6:2), and so forth, so that the apostles, freed from such concerns, might devote themselves more fully to preaching. Hence, even now, when this is rightly done, the ministries of the Churches are distributed through the hands of deacons.

I say that they must serve without having any actual crime, or even any suspicion of one. They must watch over themselves so vigilantly that the enemy has no occasion either to suspect or to accuse them of anything criminal. “Having no accusation” means the same as what he said above, “irreproachable.”

Here [Col. 0442C] he inserts a command concerning women, speaking before and after his discussion of deacons. Unless what is inserted in this way pertains somehow to deacons, the order seems inappropriate. To judge that what he says about women has been inserted appropriately, we explain it as follows:

The women who are married to those being promoted to the diaconate must likewise be chaste; that is, they must be required to profess chastity, just as their husbands are. It would be better for them to remain with their husbands in conjugal chastity than to live immodestly after separating from them.

Therefore their husbands must not be received into the Church unless their wives also profess chastity. These women must not only be chaste but also not [Col. 0442D] slanderers, unless their wives also profess chastity. These women must not only be chaste but also not slanderers, because if they devote themselves to slander, it would have been better for them to remain with their husbands, who could correct them.

They must also be sober in food, drink, and clothing. They must likewise be faithful in all things—that is, guarding intact in every respect the justification from sins that they received through faith.

Or it may be understood in this way: Let them be faithful in all things, so that if anything ecclesiastical is entrusted to them—for example, serving the poor—they may carry it out faithfully.

Let the deacons also be—that is, let them have been—the husbands of one wife, presiding well over their children and their households, as was explained concerning the bishop.

Or, if one prefers, “women” may mean deaconesses, namely, nuns. They too must likewise be chaste, and so forth, as has been stated.

And lest anyone should think that it would be difficult [Col. 0443A] to prepare himself in this way in order to obtain the diaconate, he says: “Let it not be burdensome for you to become such persons and such persons in order to ascend to this order,” because those who have served well and religiously in the diaconate will thereby acquire for themselves a higher rank—a good one, that is, one useful to them—namely, the presbyterate or episcopate.

And if they should happen to die without receiving a higher rank, because they served well in the diaconate they will acquire great—that is, manifold—confidence in good things, namely, heavenly things: in the faith, that is, in being justified by the faith that is in Christ Jesus.

Or it may be understood in another way, so that we take “faith” to mean a particular faith. In this way they will acquire confidence in the faith that is in Christ Jesus, that is, in the person of the Son. This does not mean that complete faith exists in one person, but in three persons. He calls it a particular faith in Christ because, through redemption and the other things proper to the person of the Son, the man trusts that he will be saved.

I am writing these things to you, son Timothy, concerning the priestly and Levitical [Col. 0443B] order and so forth, while nevertheless hoping—although I am now writing to you—to come to you soon.

When he says that he is writing even though he will soon come, he implies by this that there is great necessity that the things he commands in writing be observed. “I hope indeed to come to you soon; but if I should be delayed, I am writing so that through this you may know how it is necessary for you to conduct yourself in the household of God”—that is, with what vigilance you ought to guard the faithful, among whom God dwells as in a household.

And because a household might be understood as consisting of only a few, he adds: “Which household is the Church,” that is, the household in which God has summoned many to the faith. He says “the Church of the living God,” that is, of the God who gives his Church the eternal life that he possesses.

According to some, this Church is a pillar [Col. 0443C] through those who are firm and upright in the faith; they are called a pillar insofar as they stand firm in themselves. They are also called the foundation of the truth insofar as they support others who are weak in faith. Unless the latter were strengthened by the example and exhortation of the former, they would waver in the faith.

In this Church there is the mystery—that is, Christ. And this mystery of piety, that is, of the whole religion, is great, because there is no end to its greatness. This mystery is manifest in it—that is, it appears through the many miracles that God performs through the members of the Church.

Christ is called a mystery by analogy. Under the old law, certain mysteries were hidden in the temple and the people were not permitted to see them. Likewise, although many things may be seen in Christ, many things in him remain hidden, and no creature is sufficient to comprehend them all.

A mystery is called a matter wrapped in [Col. 0443D] secrets. This mystery—that is, Christ—was manifested in the flesh, because through the Word of God made flesh, the divinity was in a certain way made visible through flesh; apart from flesh it was entirely invisible.

For this reason this mystery—that is, Christ—was justified, not because he had sin, but because that man whom God assumed was made righteous in the Spirit—that is, through the Spirit, namely, through the divinity united with him. For whereas other human beings are conceived from the desire of the flesh, Christ was conceived from the love of the Father.

This mystery also appeared to angels: [Col. 0444A] Christ made himself known to angels through the things that he accomplished on earth after becoming human. When they saw these things, the angels greatly advanced in their knowledge of God, for not all the mysteries had been revealed to them.

This mystery was also preached among the nations by the apostles. It was believed in the world as well, for the world now believes in Christ. It was also taken up in glory, where he sits at the right hand of the Father, with angels coming to meet him on the day of his ascension.

## CHAPTER IV

> “Now the Spirit plainly says that in the last times some will depart from the faith, attending to spirits of error and teachings of demons, speaking lies in hypocrisy and having their conscience branded, forbidding marriage and abstinence from foods that God created to be received with thanksgiving by the faithful and by those who have known the truth. For every creature [Col. 0444B] of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected that is received with thanksgiving. For it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer.
>
> “By setting these things before the brethren, you will be a good minister of Christ Jesus, nourished by the words of faith and of the good doctrine that you have attained. But avoid foolish and empty [old-womanish—that is, fruitless] myths (2 Timothy 2:23). Exercise yourself, however, toward piety. For bodily exercise is useful for a little while, but piety is useful for all things, possessing the promise of the life that now is and of the life to come.
>
> “This saying is trustworthy and worthy of all acceptance. For it is for this that we labor and are reviled, because we hope in the living God, who is the Savior of all human beings, especially of believers. Command and teach these things. Let no one despise your [Col. 0444C] youth, but be an example of the faithful in word, in conduct, in love, in faith, and in chastity. Until I come, attend to reading, exhortation, and doctrine. Do not neglect the grace that is in you, which was given to you through prophecy with the laying on of the hands of the presbyterate [or: presbytery]. Meditate on these things; be occupied with them, so that your progress may be manifest to all. Pay attention to yourself and to doctrine; persist in them. For by doing this you will save both yourself and those who hear you.”

## EXPOSITION

[Col. 0444D] Lest Timothy should now object to Paul: “Since, as you say, there is such a great mystery in the Church, I need not watch over it very much, because it will be sufficiently guarded by this mystery,” Paul replies: Know that the Church of Christ must be preserved with all vigilance, because in the last times some will depart from the faith.

I did not receive this lightly from just anyone; rather, the Holy Spirit said it to me plainly, not under any figures: in the last times some heretics will depart from the faith of Christ, attending to spirits of error—that is, demons speaking through the mouths of deceivers. They will attend not only to their arguments but also to their teachings—that is, to the assertions of those same demons’ doctrines—speaking lies in hypocrisy, that is, in a pretence of goodness, although they are truly evil.

They have their conscience—that is, their mind, conscious of every evil—branded, that is, marked outwardly with a [Col. 0445A] visible burning. that is, marked outwardly with a visible burning. “To brand” derives from *caveo, caves* (“I beware, you beware”); for a brand is the burn-mark placed upon thieves when they are caught, so that those who see them may beware of them, knowing by this sign that they are thieves.

By this analogy he says that they have a branded conscience, because they emit outward signs of their deceitful mind by forbidding marriage. This is the burning that reveals to us the evil of their conscience: they forbid marriage, that is, they command people not to marry. They also command people to abstain from foods that God created to be received by the faithful, and to receive them with thanksgiving, because thanks must be given to God the Creator for these things—lest, if we were to receive them without a blessing, the devil should perhaps enter together with them, as has often been heard.

He certainly [Col. 0445B] created them to be received by the faithful, and by those—that is, also by such persons—who have known the truth, namely, that every creature of God, insofar as it has been created by God, is good and useful to everyone who believes this. If something is harmful to someone, such as a snake, this happens because he has not believed that this creature of God is good for him.

Thus, if someone were now to believe that it was not good for him to eat even permitted meat, and yet ate it, he would sin, because he would be using something whose goodness he doubted.

The faithful have also known that nothing is to be rejected. He defines what he means by “not to be rejected”: namely, that which is received—that is, which is to be received—with thanksgiving. For not every kind of flesh is to be eaten.

To receive, I say, and to give thanks is good, because that creature which is taken as [Col. 0445C] food because that creature which is taken as food is sanctified through the Word—that is, through the Son of God. For through the Son he created all things, and through the Son he sanctified all created things. It is also sanctified through prayer—that is, both through the blessing that precedes it and through the thanksgiving that follows.

**Note:** When Paul instructs Timothy about the time of Antichrist, he implies that the members of Antichrist will precede their head by a long period. He also implies that this instruction was made for the whole Church and for all future ages.

By setting before the brethren the things said above—namely, that marriage should not be disparaged, that foods which God created for the faithful to receive should not be condemned, and the other matters previously mentioned—you place them openly before them. Although by doing this you may seem to some [Col. 0445D] to be overly lax that foods which God created for the faithful to receive should not be condemned, and the other matters previously mentioned—you place them openly before them. Although by doing this you may seem to some to be overly lax and indulgent toward the flesh, nevertheless you will be a good minister of Christ Jesus, that is, more useful to those who go beyond proper measure through excessive strictness and forbid marriage and the use of bodily things.

You ought to set these things before them both because in doing so you will be good—that is, useful—and because you are able to do so. For you have been nourished—that is, placed beyond rudiments and childish nourishment—and have been instructed in the words of faith. You know in whom and how it is necessary for you to believe.

You have also been nourished by the words of good doctrine—that is, you have learned useful instruction in morals—which doctrine you have fully attained through me, who both baptized you and sufficiently taught you what still had to be taught.

Timothy was handed over by his faithful mother as a boy [Col. 0446A] to learn sacred letters, but he was not baptized until he was baptized by Paul. Therefore Paul says that he was nourished in the faith, knowing that one must believe in Christ. He was also nourished by good doctrine, that is, by moral instruction.

Set such things before the brethren. But foolish myths that contain no truth—for example, those concerning the prohibition of foods and marriage—and also empty foolish myths, that is, useless ones, which, although they retain an appearance of truth—for example, the restoration of circumcision—are nevertheless entirely without benefit: do not merely forbid such myths, as I warned you earlier, but avoid them if someone wishes to discuss them privately with you.

Do not devote yourself to them alone either. Rather, exercise yourself—not partially, but your whole self, both body and soul—toward piety, that is, toward the teaching and guardianship of religion, so that you may be entirely free to devote yourself vigorously to piety and may not wish to afflict your flesh beyond measure.

For this bodily exercise, through [Col. 0446B] fasts, is indeed useful, but in comparison with piety it is of little value. What good does it do for a prelate to afflict himself so severely that, through the weakness of his flesh, he is unable to devote himself to instructing those subject to him?

The affliction of the body is of little use. But piety—that is, through the piety of compassion, to devote oneself to instructing one’s children—is useful, not for certain things only, but for all things.

He therefore reproves Timothy in a certain way concerning bodily affliction, because he knew that Timothy fasted so much and abstained from drinking wine that his stomach was weakened as a result. Therefore, later on, he commands him to use wine.

This piety possesses the promise of the life that now is—that is, the avoidance of evil and the increase of righteousness, which may be possessed in this life. It also possesses the promise of the future and everlasting life.

This saying, which I said directs one toward [Col. 0446C] piety rather than afflicting the body in such a way that piety is hindered, is trustworthy and worthy of all acceptance, because when the body is strengthened, piety—which is useful for all things—is nourished.

That exercising oneself toward piety ought to be accepted is evident from this: we labor in this—that is, in piety—seeking food by the labor of our hands. We are also reviled by unbelievers because we hope in the living God, directing ourselves toward him, who will give the eternal life that he possesses to those who hope in him.

One ought rightly to hope in him who is the Savior of all human beings, granting temporal salvation to the good and the wicked, because “he makes his sun rise upon the just and the unjust” (Matthew 5:45). Although he is the Savior of all, he is especially and above all the Savior of the faithful, to whom he will give eternal life, which he will deny to the impious—although in this world he saves even them in temporal goods.

Since exercising yourself toward piety is good, and we also labor in the same thing, [Col. 0446D] you ought to imitate us in this world.

Therefore, by devoting yourself to piety, command those who know but are slow to act—namely, command them to observe the precepts set forth above. If there are also those who do not know, teach them. Do both with such severity and purity that no one despises your youth; let the honesty of your life and conduct make your age, though youthful in years, mature in character.

Let no one despise you, I say; rather, be an example to all the faithful in word: addressing everyone with humility; in conduct, becoming all things to all; in love—that is, in love of neighbor; in faith—that is, remaining in justification; and [Col. 0447A] in chastity, rather, be an example to all the faithful in word: addressing everyone with humility; in conduct, becoming all things to all; in love—that is, in love of neighbor; in faith—that is, remaining in justification; and in chastity, which is the jewel of virtues in a young man.

For this reason he instructs a young man concerning chastity, since youth is an age more inclined than others to desire indulgence. And so that you may be an example to the faithful, attend to reading—that is, turn over the sacred page continually—until I come.

After I have come to you, I will admonish you sufficiently. For a living voice encourages anyone more than reading; nevertheless, many know enough who, unless they were stirred by reading, would grow sluggish while their instructor was absent.

Therefore he says: Attend to reading, and attend to exhortation—that is, exhort those who are instructed but slow to act. Attend also to doctrine—that is, teach those who do not know.

And so that you may be more attentive in these matters, [Col. 0447B] do not neglect the grace of the Holy Spirit that has been bestowed upon you. I call it pontifical grace, which was given to you through prophecy—that is, through foreknowledge. For, instructed beforehand by the spirit of prophecy, I saw that you were suitable for pontifical grace.

This grace was given to you with the laying on of the hands of the presbyterate—that is, of the bishop who, when consecrating you as bishop, laid his hands upon you.

Or “of the presbyterate” means “of the presbyteral office”: although one person lays hands upon and consecrates you in particular, nevertheless the other bishops who stand by consecrate the same man together with him.

**Note:** The Holy Spirit is given through the laying on of hands. This is not done because the Spirit could not be given without it; rather, hands are laid on so that the one being consecrated may learn through this to display complete submission to God and to his consecrator.

Hence the consecrator has this precedence over the one whom he consecrates: the consecrator will never afterward be judged by the person whom he consecrates. [Col. 0447C]

That prophecy of which he spoke cannot now take place in precisely the same way, because bishops are not now spiritual in that manner. Nevertheless, it takes place according to what can now be done: the one to be consecrated is presented to the consecrator, and he is questioned about faith and other matters, as the Order prescribes.

And, in order to preserve the grace that is in you, meditate on these things that I urge; be occupied with them through action, so that by meditating and acting your progress may be manifest to all and they may advance through your example.

And so that you may be able to progress in this way, attend carefully to yourself, correct your life, and examine yourself from every side. Attend to doctrine—that is, teach others. For if your life is praiseworthy, it will commend your preaching.

Therefore [Col. 0447D] persist in these things—that is, in directing your life and teaching those subject to you. By doing this, that is, by persisting in these things, you will save yourself. By attending to yourself, you will also save through your doctrine those who hear you.

## CHAPTER V

> “Do not rebuke an older man, but exhort him as a father; younger men as brothers; older women as mothers; younger women as sisters, in all chastity. Honor widows who are truly widows. But if any widow has children or grandchildren, let her first learn to govern her own household piously and to repay her parents in turn. For this is acceptable before God.
>
> “But she who is truly a widow and desolate should hope in God and persist in supplications and prayers night and [Col. 0448A] day. For she who lives in luxury is dead while living. Command this also, so that they may be irreproachable.
>
> “But if anyone does not care for his own, and especially for those of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.
>
> “Let a widow be chosen who is not less than sixty years old, who has been the wife of one man, bearing testimony in good works: if she has brought up children, if she has received strangers in hospitality, if she has washed the feet of the saints, if she has assisted those suffering tribulation, if she has followed every good work.
>
> “But avoid younger widows. For when they have become wanton, they wish to marry in Christ, incurring condemnation because they have made their first faith void. At the same time they also learn to be idle, going around the [Col. 0448B] houses incurring condemnation because they have made their first faith void. At the same time they also learn to be idle, going around the houses—not only idle, but also talkative and inquisitive, saying things that ought not to be said.
>
> “Therefore I want younger women to marry, bear children, manage households, and give the adversary no occasion for reviling. For some have already turned back after Satan.
>
> “If any believer has widows, let him assist them, so that the Church may not be burdened and may be sufficient for those who are truly widows.
>
> “Let presbyters who preside well be considered worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in word and doctrine. For Scripture says: ‘You shall not muzzle the ox while it is treading out the grain’ (Deuteronomy 25:4; 1 Corinthians 9:9). And: ‘The laborer is worthy of his wages.’
>
> “Do not receive an accusation against a presbyter except under two or three witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15, 45). Rebuke sinners before everyone, so that the others may also have fear.
>
> “I testify before God and Christ [Col. 0448C] Jesus and his elect angels that you observe these things without prejudice, doing nothing by inclining toward either side. Lay hands quickly on no one, nor share in the sins of others. Keep yourself chaste.
>
> “Do not continue drinking only water, but use a little wine because of your stomach and your frequent infirmities.
>
> “The sins of some people are manifest, going before them to judgment; but the sins of others follow afterward. Likewise, good works are manifest, and those that are otherwise situated cannot remain hidden.”

## EXPOSITION

And lest Timothy, whom he had thus instructed [Col. 0448D]—“command,” “teach,” and so forth—should teach indiscriminately, without attending to differences of age and sex, Paul adds how each age should be taught, saying:

Although I say “command” and “teach,” nevertheless take care not to rebuke an older man with severity because of his age, but exhort him with such care as you would show a father. Exhort younger men as brothers, older women as mothers, and younger women as sisters.

Because Timothy was young, when he spoke of younger women he added “in all chastity.” It is entirely right that, in addressing young women, a young man should be admonished concerning complete chastity, so that he is not stirred toward them even by the slightest titillation of the flesh.

After instructing Timothy concerning the discretion with which he ought to teach, he adds a command about widows, determining which should be supported from the Church’s goods and which should not.

He says: Exhort younger women in this way; but honor widows [Col. 0449A] who take refuge in the Churches in the manner in which they ought to be honored—that is, by giving food and clothing only to those who are truly widows and unwilling to return again to worldly things, so that they might wish to marry again. This also applies to those who are desolate, as he explains below.

He calls desolate those who have neither children nor parents able to support them, or with whom they themselves might use their possessions, if they have any, and provide for them.

Honor, I say, those who are truly widows. [Col. 0449B] But if any widow has children or grandchildren, then, because she is not desolate, let her learn—before receiving the Church’s resources—to govern her own household, that is, her children and grandchildren.
