And if she still has parents, let her learn to repay her parents in turn, those who supported her when she was an infant. Let her, I say, do good to her parents, because this—that is, both governing her own household in particular and caring for her parents—is acceptable before God, more so than abandoning her parents in distress.

A widow who has children should not transfer her care to the Church. Rather, the woman who is truly a widow, unwilling to return to marriage, and who is desolate, having no children or grandchildren, should hope in God—that is, be supported by the Church’s goods—and should persist there in supplications and prayers night and day.

Otherwise, this verse may be understood as determining who is truly a widow. I say that true widows are to be supported by the Church; but, so that you may not be deceived concerning them, know that she is truly a widow and desolate who hopes in God, and not in sons or grandchildren, and who persists in supplications and prayers night and day. She who is truly a widow hopes only in God, or, “let her hope.” But that widow who lives in carnal pleasures [Col. 0449C], living for the world, is dead to God, and such a woman ought not to be received into the Church.

Also prescribe this concerning widows: since they are truly widows and desolate, they must also be blameless—that is, neither having committed a crime nor giving anyone an occasion to accuse them of anything. A widow who has children or grandchildren must govern them. For if any widow does not care for her own people whom she ought to govern, and especially, before all others, for the members of her household—that is, her children or grandchildren—such a woman has denied the faith that she promised to God. For it is clear that, not caring for her neighbor, she has not loved her neighbor, and thus she does not love God either. “For whoever does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” Since she does not love God either, she has plainly denied the faith [Col. 0449D]. She is even worse than an unbeliever, who has never possessed the faith, because she is guilty of the agreement she made with God and has thus rendered it void.

Or it may be understood this way: Let a widow govern her children and grandchildren. But if any one of them drives away his widowed mother, who wishes to be supported by them, this is equivalent to saying: “If anyone does not care for his own people, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.” This, then, is the widow, if she possesses the qualities mentioned above.

Nevertheless, a widow is not to be chosen for admission into the Church if she is under sixty years of age. She must also have been the wife of one husband, lest, by marrying a second, she appear guilty of incontinence. She must also have been devoted to good works, and have a good reputation in the Church: if she has raised children through spiritual instruction; if she has received the poor as guests; if she has washed the feet of the saints—that is, if she has performed every work of piety for preachers [Col. 0450A], not fearing the threats of persecutors who condemned all who ministered to the saints; if she has also assisted those suffering tribulation—that is, the saints imprisoned. To sum it all up: if she has pursued every good work, let her be chosen.

Let widows who are sixty years old be chosen. But as for younger widows, who are not yet that age, I want them to marry; and therefore avoid them—do not accept them into the ministry of the Church. Avoid them for this reason: if you receive them, when they have become wanton—that is, when, through excessive abundance, they have grown lascivious—they want to marry. And this “in Christ”—that is, legally, not as prostitutes. Such women incur condemnation because, by breaking their vows, they have also annulled the first faith which they had promised at baptism, when they had said that they renounced the devil [Col. 0450B]; by breaking the vow of continence which they had made, they have again handed themselves over to him, openly indicating that, when they were in need, they fled to the Church’s support not out of love for continence.

They not only [p. 328] want to marry, but, having gathered together, they learn to go around the houses. And this is because they are idle—and not merely idle, but also talkative, investigating the rumors of the city. They also speak inquisitively and with great eagerness about things that ought not to be discussed, namely, every kind of immodest matter. Since through idleness they fall into such great ruin, I therefore want younger widows, who have not reached the prescribed age—I repeat, I want them to marry, bear children, and be heads of households, so that they may have people to occupy themselves with and may not remain idle in their customary way.

Thus I want them not to give the adversary—that is, the unbeliever [Col. 0450C]—any occasion for slander, that is, an occasion which is very welcome to him for slandering believers. For this reason I prefer that they marry rather than be received into the Church. For some have already turned away from what they vowed when they promised continence, going back after Satan.

But if these widows do not find someone whom they can marry, I want that, if any believing man has such widows—whether a mother, sisters, or daughters—he should assist them, and that the Church not be burdened with supporting them, so that it may be sufficient for those who are truly widows and desolate.

Having given his instruction concerning widows, he indicates in what ways presbyters are to be honored by the people, saying: “Prescribe these things concerning widows.” Prescribe also that presbyters be considered worthy of double honor: spiritual honor, so that one may yield to them [Col. 0450D] and obey their instructions; and bodily honor, so that their material needs may be adequately supplied by their subjects.

These are the presbyters who preside well—that is, whose leadership is useful to their subjects, because they either devote themselves to instructing them or pray for them. Although this double honor is owed to every presbyter, it should be given especially to those who labor in the word of faith, teaching what ought to be believed, and in doctrine—that is, in instruction concerning conduct.

He said that double honor should be shown to presbyters. Since he saw that one of these honors, namely the spiritual one, could in no way be denied, he added nothing to prove it. But the other honor—namely, supporting the priest from the people’s resources—he saw that certain greedy men would deny. He therefore proves it by the authority of the Old and New Testaments, saying: “Just as I prescribe [Col. 0451A] that presbyters are to be considered worthy, for Scripture says: ‘You shall not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain’” (Deut. 25:4; 1 Cor. 9:9).

It was customary among the ancients—and it still is in some regions—for oxen and other animals trained for this work to tread down the grain laid out on the threshing floor. Yet this was especially the oxen’s task, so that, once the harvest had been crushed in this way, the grains might be separated from the chaff. Moses therefore commanded that the mouth of the ox treading the grain on the threshing floor should not be tied, but that it should freely eat from what it was working on. In giving this command, he intended something else as well: namely, that the preacher who threshes in the Lord’s threshing floor should receive sufficient support from his labor from those for whose instruction he works.

The Lord also says in the Gospel: “The laborer is worthy of his wages” (Luke 10:7)—that is, the preacher should receive from those among whom he labors in instruction whatever is necessary for him [Col. 0451B].

Because the Apostle again saw that, when a presbyter reproved the vices of his subjects, some people reacted badly and wanted to corrupt the presbyter’s life, he added, so that this should not be rashly believed: “Let a presbyter be honored in this way by his subjects: do not accept an accusation against a presbyter concerning a crime unless it is supported by two or three witnesses.”

If he is summoned concerning a debt or any secular matter, let him answer each person individually. But now, because people have fallen further and further into worse ways, a presbyter is permitted to answer even without a larger number of witnesses, unless he is challenged concerning heresy.

“Let presbyters answer on the testimony of two or three witnesses.” But if they are sinners—that is, if presbyters are proved to have sinned in the matter for which they are accused—rebuke them before everyone, so that, just as their crime is public, the repentance for their crime may also be public. Otherwise, if they repent privately, those who were discovered by everyone to have sinned might not be thought to have repented.

Rebuke them before everyone for this reason also: so that, when the other priests see this, they may fear to sin, knowing that they will be punished with a similar penalty if they sin [p. 329] [Col. 0451C]. Or “the others” means the subjects, who, when they see how strictly their superiors are corrected, may fear more for themselves, since they are subject to authority.

But so that no presbyters may be found guilty of sin in this way—for it is no small evil that those who ought to be examples of goodness to others should be discovered in wickedness—I prescribe that no one be ordained priest without a prior examination [Col. 0451D].

And so that you may not neglect this command for any reason, I adjure you before God the Father, so that, if you do this, God may require it not from me but from your hand. I also testify before Christ Jesus, who is to be the judge of all, so that at the judgment he may accuse not me but you concerning it. I also testify before the elect angels, by whose ministry the good will be separated from the impious on the day of judgment, so that on that day they may be witnesses to me in this matter and may not therefore exclude me from the portion of the righteous.

I testify to you, I say, so that you may observe the things I am about to say: do nothing—that is, promote no one to the priesthood—without prejudice, that is, without a prior examination. Here “prejudice” is understood as a preceding judgment; but in the canons, “prejudice” means a hasty sentence [Col. 0452A].

Once you have examined someone by means of this prior judgment, if you find him unworthy of the priesthood through the examination, do nothing by turning aside in another direction from what the examination has shown, so that you do not afterward, deceived in some way, ordain as priest the man whom you found to be evil by examining him.

But if he has been tested and found worthy according to what has now been seen, nevertheless lay hands quickly on none of them—that is, do not ordain him immediately. Rather, delay for a suitable period, so that, if something is perhaps hidden in him which the examination did not discover, it may be found through the passage of time.

By doing nothing without prior judgment, and by not acting rashly in ordaining anyone, you will not share in the sins of others. For if you did not examine him, or ordained him too quickly, you would become a participant in all the crimes that the unjustly ordained man might commit in the priesthood [Col. 0452B].

And so that you may examine others carefully and ordain them worthily, keep yourself chaste—that is, sound in every virtue.

Since he had admonished him concerning chastity, on account of which he did not use wine—and his stomach was therefore becoming weak—lest he believe that he ought to abstain entirely from wine, Paul says: “Do not continue to drink only water.” By saying “continue,” he indicated that he had previously used water.

“Do not continue to drink water, but use wine not merely once; make it part of your regular practice. Use, I say, wine, but moderately—that is, observing restraint—not for the sake of drunkenness, but for the sake of your stomach, that is, because of the illness that frequently afflicts your stomach; and because of your frequent infirmities—that is, because of the repeated attacks and exacerbations of the same illness [Col. 0452C].

A feverish person always has the disease in himself, although at one time he suffers it more severely and at another more mildly; but he suffers the fever’s attacks of heat intermittently, not constantly. In the same way, Timothy continually had the nature of the illness in his stomach, but he suffered the attacks of the illness at intervals and with great difficulty.

It is therefore necessary to examine a person before a presbyter is ordained, because certain sins of certain people are manifest, preceding them to judgment. Before one comes to judgment or investigation, certain sins of those who are to be tested have already come before that investigation, having become sufficiently known through reputation alone. There is no need to investigate what is already public.

But in the case of some, sins follow after investigation has been carried out: before the investigation took place, their crimes were hidden, but through the investigation they were brought to light. For the sake of these hidden crimes, investigation was necessary.

Similarly, certain good deeds of those who are to be tested are manifest and require no examination; conversely, the good deeds of the same people which are of another kind—that is, which are not manifest—cannot remain hidden in an investigation. It was appropriate to investigate in order to discover these good deeds.

And because in some people sins are hidden, while in others [p. 330] good deeds are hidden, it is therefore necessary to examine those who are to be ordained, so that those who are found to be bad may be rejected, while those who are good may be promoted [Col. 0452D].

This is the judgment of blessed Augustine. Ambrose, however, joins the words to what follows in this way:

“I urge you to use wine, in which [Col. 0453A] it is good for you to be obedient. For although not everyone sees that you are doing well in this, do not therefore be afraid. It is true that some good deeds are manifest, while certain deeds of another kind—that is, deeds which are not manifest—cannot be hidden on the day of judgment.

Thus, if you do not now appear to be acting well by using wine, because everyone previously knew that you abstained from it in order to preserve sobriety, do not be concerned. Although it is not evident now, on the day of judgment it will be manifest that you acted well when, in obedience to me, you used wine.”

That some good deeds are manifest and others are not is shown by the contrary case, because the sins of certain people are manifest, preceding them to judgment, while in the case of others they follow afterward, as has been explained.

Likewise, this is read according to the order of the text [Col. 0453B].

## CHAPTER VI

> “Let all who are under the yoke regard their masters as worthy of all honor, so that the name of the Lord and the doctrine may not be blasphemed. But those who have believing masters must not despise them because they are brothers; rather, they should serve them all the more, because they are believing and beloved, since they are participants in the benefit. Teach and exhort these things.
>
> “If anyone teaches otherwise and does not assent to the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ and to the doctrine which is according to godliness, he is arrogant, knowing nothing, but sick about questions and quarrels over words, from which arise envy, strife, blasphemies, evil suspicions, and conflicts among people of corrupt mind who are deprived of the truth, supposing that godliness is a means of gain.
>
> “Godliness with contentment is indeed a great gain. For we brought nothing into this world, and there is no doubt that we can take nothing out of it. But having food and clothing, let us be content with these things. For those who wish to become rich fall into temptation and into the devil’s snare, and into many foolish and harmful desires which plunge people into destruction and ruin. For greed is the root of all evils. By craving it, some have wandered from the faith and entangled themselves in many sorrows.
>
> “But you, O man of God, flee these things. Pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, charity, patience, gentleness. Fight the good [Col. 0453D] fight of faith; seize eternal life, to which you were called and for which you confessed the good confession [faith] before many witnesses.
>
> “I charge you before God, who gives life to all things, and Christ Jesus, who bore witness under Pontius Pilate by making the good confession, that you keep the commandment without stain, blameless, until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ. In his own times the blessed and only powerful King of kings and Lord of lords will show him, who alone possesses immortality and dwells in inaccessible light; whom no human being has seen nor can see; to whom belong honor and eternal dominion. Amen.
>
> “Command the rich of this world not to be high-minded, nor to hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in the living God, who gives [Col. 0454A] us all things abundantly for enjoyment; to do good, to become rich in good works, to give readily, to share, to lay up for themselves a good foundation for the future, so that they may seize true life.
>
> “O Timothy, guard the deposit, avoiding profane novelties of words and oppositions of falsely named knowledge, which some professing have fallen away from the faith. Grace be with you. Amen.”

## EXPOSITION

Because Paul again saw certain slaves who had been converted to the faith becoming indignant and unwilling to serve their unbelieving masters, thinking it absurd that, if someone were a believer, he should serve an unbeliever—and likewise unwilling to serve believing masters, saying that, since all believers are brothers in Christ, all [p. 331] ought to be made equal in condition [Col. 0454B]—he refuted the evil of this opinion by saying:

“Just as I previously instructed you concerning those who are to be ordained presbyters, observe this also: command all who are slaves under the yoke of unbelieving masters to regard their masters as worthy of all honor,” while preserving the faith in every respect.

He signified unbelievers by the word “yoke” because unbelieving masters oppressed slaves more harshly than believing masters did. They must therefore submit to their masters in this way, lest, if it were otherwise, the name of the Lord be blasphemed. People would say that God was unjust, since he had changed their conditions and had not made free the slaves who had become slaves because of their own sins or those of their parents, as happened with Ham, the son of Noah, together with his descendants (Gen. 9:25), because he had exposed his father’s nakedness.

They must therefore also serve their masters so that the doctrine—that is, the preaching—of the saints may not be blasphemed and become contemptible, as though it took away from masters what belonged to them [Col. 0454C].

But those slaves who have believing masters must not despise them because they are brothers in Christ. Rather, they should serve them—not by paying greater debts, but by serving them with greater love—because they are believers, beloved by God, and participants in God’s benefit, that is, in the righteousness possessed in the present and in future blessedness.

Teach these slaves, who do not know, that they are subject to their masters; and exhort those who know but disdain serving, because they are proud.

But if some false teacher teaches otherwise—namely, that slaves ought not to serve their masters—and, when prohibited by you from teaching this, does not assent to the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ and does not assent to the doctrine that is according to godliness, he is to be rejected.

For God’s doctrine is pious: it does not change conditions and takes away from no one what belongs to him [Col. 0454D]. It is also pious for this reason: by this teaching it strongly invites and attracts masters to the faith. If it took their slaves away from them, they would judge the doctrine intolerable and reject it.

It is also pious toward slaves, because, since they became slaves on account of their own sins or those of their parents, if they patiently endure this punishment for sin, they deserve to be justified through humility; but if they refuse it, they are condemned through pride.

If anyone, I say, teaches otherwise and, though prohibited, does not desist, let him be rejected as proud and knowing nothing, although he thinks that he knows something and asserts that all human beings are of the same condition.

Knowing nothing, I say, but sick—that is, dissolute and weak—about the questions which he raises and cannot resolve, and about quarrels over words, that is, about apparently conflicting statements, such as: “If the Son makes you free, you will truly be free” (John 8:36), and: “Give to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s” (Luke 20:25), although these statements are not in fact contradictory [Col. 0455A].

From these quarrels over words arise envy, because masters envy slaves who become proud. Strife also arises, because masters contend with slaves in words. Blasphemies arise as well, because, as has been said, God and his doctrine are thereby blasphemed. Evil suspicions also arise, because masters think that preachers accept gifts from slaves. Conflicts also arise among those who preach this, because they contend with those who preach it.

I say “of people,” that is, of people ruined in their corrupt minds—people who have a corrupted understanding [Col. 0455B] and who are also deprived of every truth in their words.

I say “of people” who still suppose that godliness—that is, Christian doctrine—is a means of gain: people who think that through their doctrine they are thereby permitted to gather wealth for themselves. But they think this falsely, because godliness is not a means of temporal gain. Rather, it is a great gain: godliness is a great and incomparable possession together with contentment—that is, with food and clothing, which ought to be sufficient for each person.

For we were born naked and brought nothing into this world, and there is no doubt that, when we leave the world, we cannot take anything away from it. But lest, because he had said that we entered the world naked and would return naked, he think that we ought to live naked in the world, he says against this:

“Although we brought nothing into the world, nevertheless, while we remain in it, let us have food and clothing with which to cover ourselves—not things in which we may indulge—and let us be content with this food and clothing.”

For we see [p. 332] that those who wish to become rich fall into temptation of the mind and, through this, into the devil’s snare—that is, into the work of temptation. After they have become rich, they also fall into many desires, for they desire houses and estates. These desires are useless and not merely without benefit but also harmful, because they plunge those who desire them into destruction and, after death, into eternal ruin [Col. 0455C].

Truly, these desires plunge people in this way. For desire for wealth is the root of all evils—not because each individual evil is committed through desire for money, but because there is no kind of evil in which some [Col. 0455D] evil has not been committed through desire for riches.

By craving this desire, some have wandered from the faith, denying God through their desire for riches. In order to increase those riches greedily, they have exposed themselves to many sorrows, tormenting their bodies and souls by sea and land. Those who devote themselves to greed go astray.

But you, O man of God, Timothy, flee these desires—flee them—and pursue righteousness by distributing your possessions to needy neighbors, something greed never does.

Pursue godliness as well. For if you possess so little that you cannot give to your neighbor without becoming needy yourself—which you would do if righteousness did not compel you—nevertheless share with him out of godliness.

Pursue faith also, which some have denied because of greed. Pursue charity as well, that is, love of God and neighbor [Col. 0456A]. Pursue patience too: patiently endure if anyone takes away your possessions. Pursue gentleness also: do not quarrel, as greed does.

Pursue these things and fight the fight. The wording indicates frequency. The fight, I say, is the fight of faith, which is good and useful: to fight for the faith of Christ. And seize eternal life, to which you were called from unbelief through grace.

You also confessed—when you were ordained bishop, before the many witnesses who ordained you together with me—the confession from which you ought not to depart, because it is good, that is, useful, to you and to your subjects, if you persevere in it.

Earlier I warned you to flee greed and to pursue what is opposed to greed. In order that you may do this, I not only warn you but also command you, joining a command to the admonition, so that, if you transgress this, you may be convicted [Col. 0456B] as guilty of disobedience.

I command you, I say, these things before God the Father, so that God, who gives life to all things, may require nothing further from my hand. See, therefore, that, by fulfilling what I command, you live in him through whom all things live.

I also command you before Christ Jesus, who, as judge of all, may require none of these things from me on the day of judgment—Christ Jesus who gave testimony under Pontius Pilate. For when Pilate asked him, “Are you the Son of God?” he answered, “You say so,” because I truly am the Son of God (Matt. 27:11). In the same way, Timothy, confess Christ even if torments or death threaten.

He gave testimony, I say, namely, the good confession, that is, the useful one. For what is so useful for redemption as the fact that he was and confessed himself to be the Son of God? Certainly, if he had denied it, he would not have been crucified, nor would he have redeemed the human race. It was therefore useful for him to confess that he was the Son of God [Col. 0456C].

Pilate was called Pontius from the island of Pontus. Since heretics might otherwise be able to turn the statement into a reference to another Jesus or another Pilate—for many people could then be called Jesus—Paul therefore added “Pontius.”

I command you, I say, to keep this commandment, which you can no longer pass over without guilt. I call the commandment unstained because no stain can be found in any part of my doctrine. In the doctrine of heretics, although some good may be put forward first so that they may deceive more effectively, a stain is nevertheless soon found inserted in it.

I call the commandment not only unstained but also blameless, because, if anyone pays sound attention, no opportunity for criticism can arise from it.

Keep it, I say, until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ—that is, until the day of your death. For when a believer dies, God is said to come to him on that day, because then God receives him into glory, having left him, as though alienated from himself, amid the world’s miseries while he lived.

As long as the righteous [p. 333] person is detained in the world, God seems not to come to him, because there he permits him to suffer. But when the righteous person is released from the flesh, God is said to come to him, since he receives his soul into rest [Col. 0456D].

Timothy might perhaps say: “I would wait for God if his coming were not delayed.” Paul says against this: “Good man, wait, because God will reveal the one whose appearing he will show at his appointed times.” For when he sees that the time is suitable, he will come to you [Col. 0457A].

He gives the reason why Timothy ought to wait, saying: “You must keep this until God comes, because he is blessed and will give you blessedness if you wait; and he alone is powerful and will make you powerful over all persecutors. He is also King of kings and will make you a king, because, when you are with him, you will fear neither persecutor nor temptation. He is also Lord of lords and will make you rule over your enemies.”

Note that some are powerful and yet do not rule over others.

This is the God who alone possesses immortality—that is, immutability, because he always remains in the same condition—and who also dwells in light. He speaks of God by comparison with someone who might dwell in a shining region.

He dwells, I say, in light because [Col. 0457B] every true light dwells in him. The light is inaccessible—that is, no one can approach in order to understand that light. He himself specifies this when he says that it is inaccessible, because no human being has seen, according to human capacity, what light in God is, or what God in the light is; nor can anyone, even in the future, see it according to the human condition.

To this God belong glory according to his divinity, honor according to his humanity, and dominion according to the judgment by which he judges and will judge all. The dominion, I say, will endure forever. I desire that glory and honor be his. “Amen”: certainly, it will be so and cannot fail.

Note that he says, “No human being has seen God.” This must be understood with reference to what human beings are by nature. For Paul was caught up to the third heaven [Col. 0457C], where he heard things that it was not permitted a human being to hear, although Paul was a human being both before and after he was caught up. And since the same thing happened to the evangelist John, a human being, precisely as a human being, is not sufficient to see the light of the Godhead.

For the human soul, imprisoned and weighed down in the flesh, cannot see or think anything except when it is awakened by some bodily sense—sight, hearing, or something of that kind. If, as long as the soul is shut up in the prison of the flesh, it can do nothing unless it is awakened through bodily senses—and it is clear that these senses scarcely understand even a little about God—then it must be believed that, as long as the human soul is in a human being, it does not surpass the bodily senses in knowledge of God.

But if Paul’s or John’s soul saw concerning God what it was not permitted a human being to see, it must be believed [Col. 0457D] that either his soul entirely left the body during that hour, or, if it remained in the body, that it surpassed all the bodily senses and, in this respect, was outside the human condition. At that time the bodily senses were, as it were, dead. Hence visions are shown more often to people who are asleep than to those who are awake. For while a person sleeps, the bodily senses perceive nothing; the soul alone remains awake [Col. 0458A].

Because Paul had said above, “Let us have food and clothing with which to cover ourselves,” lest Timothy therefore think that only the poor should be received and that the rich should be driven away from the Church, he says against this:

“Although I said that we ought to be content with food and clothing, nevertheless do not reject the rich. Instead, command the rich of this world not to be high-minded”—that is, not to become proud because of their riches—“nor to hope in the uncertainty of riches,” that is, in uncertain wealth, as though someone who possesses it today might perhaps not possess it tomorrow, “but to hope in God.”

He adds the reason: God gives us all things abundantly, not merely for use but also for enjoyment—that is, so that we may use them with pleasure.

We use the word “enjoy” of something that is pleasant and useful; we use “use” of something which, although useful, has a bitter use—for example, many medicines which taste bitter but are beneficial [Col. 0458B].

Command the rich also to do good and to become rich in good works, which are more valuable [p. 334] than gold and silver. Command them also to give their possessions readily to the poor. And not only this: command them to share their goods with the poor, so that they do not make their riches more their own than the property of the needy.

By distributing their possessions in this way, command them to lay up for themselves a foundation—that is, virtues upon which they may be firmly founded. For someone who is chaste today but incestuous tomorrow has his virtue as though on slippery ground and not on a foundation.

I call the foundation good—that is, useful—for the future, so that by means of it those who are founded here in virtues may seize eternal life [Col. 0458C].

And so that you may practice sound observance concerning the rich and concerning all that I have commanded, therefore, Timothy, guard the deposit—that is, the gift of the Holy Spirit entrusted and committed to you.

And so that you may guard it well, avoid novelties—that is, altered equivalents of the words of our faith—because they are profane. For heretics change the words by which we confess God’s faith, introducing equivalent expressions, until they have gradually deceived the unwary believer through these equivalent expressions. He therefore commands that novelties of words be avoided.

Avoid oppositions as well, that is, the disputations of sophists. These oppositions are said to belong to knowledge falsely so called. It is falsely called knowledge, because by its true name it would be called ignorance.

By promising this false knowledge—that is, boasting that they possessed it—some have fallen away from the faith, that is, have perished, because they did not wish to enter into the faith.

And so that you may guard this deposit, grace be with you. Amen—that is, certainly this will be so; nevertheless, see that you persevere.

# [INTO THE SECOND EPISTLE TO TIMOTHY]

[Col. 0457]

## ARGUMENT OF THE SECOND EPISTLE TO TIMOTHY

Again he writes to Timothy concerning the exhortation to martyrdom and the whole rule of truth; concerning what will happen in the last times; and concerning his own passion, writing to him from the city of Rome.

## PROLOGUE OF BLESSED BRUNO ON THE SAME EPISTLE

The preceding Epistle is said to have been sent from Rome by Paul to Timothy [Col. 0457D]. For if it is established that he sent the first one from Rome, it is also established that he sent this second one from Rome [Col. 0458D]. After Paul came to Rome, he did not depart from there until he suffered martyrdom for Christ [Col. 0459A].

Paul wrote this Epistle again to Timothy while he was in chains at Rome. He had indeed heard many good things about him, but nevertheless that he was somewhat lax and, through fear of sufferings and death, was not, as he ought to have been, intent upon preaching. Therefore in this Epistle he speaks to him about sufferings and death, setting his own sufferings before him together with Christ’s sufferings and death [Col. 0460A]. He shows what great fruit proceeds from these sufferings and commends them to him in many ways, with the aim that, thus encouraged, Timothy might be ready to suffer and die for Christ and, as though voluntarily rushing toward death, preach the word of God with complete devotion.

# SECOND EPISTLE TO TIMOTHY

[Col. 0459]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0459B]

> “Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ through the will of God, according to the promise of life which is in Christ Jesus, to Timothy, my beloved son: grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.
>
> “I give thanks to my God, whom I serve from my forefathers with a pure [good] conscience, because I have unceasing remembrance of you in my prayers, night and day, desiring to see you, remembering your tears, so that I may be filled with joy.
>
> “I receive the recollection of the unfeigned faith that is in you, which first dwelt in your grandmother Lois and in your mother Eunice [variant: Eutice]; and I am certain that it is also in you [p. 335].
>
> “For this reason I remind you to rekindle the grace of God which is in you through the laying on of my hands [Col. 0459C]. For God has not given us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and sobriety.
>
> “Therefore do not be ashamed of the testimony of our Lord, nor of me, his prisoner; rather, labor together with the Gospel according to the power of God, who saved us and called us with his holy calling—not according to our works, but according to his purpose and grace, which was given to us in Christ Jesus before eternal times.
>
> “But it has now been manifested through the illumination of our Savior Jesus Christ, who indeed destroyed death but brought life and incorruption to light through the Gospel. For this Gospel I have been appointed preacher, apostle, and teacher of the Gentiles.
>
> “For this reason I also suffer these things, but I am not ashamed [Col. 0459D]. For I know whom I have believed, and I am certain that he is powerful enough to preserve my deposit until that day.
>
> “Have the form [holding the form] of sound words which you heard from me in faith and love in Christ Jesus. Guard the good deposit through the Holy Spirit who dwells in us.
>
> “For you know this: all who are in Asia have turned away from me, among whom are Philetus and Hermogenes.
>
> “May the Lord grant mercy to the household of Onesiphorus, because he often refreshed me and was not ashamed of my chain. Rather, when he came to Rome, he diligently sought me and found me.
>
> “May the Lord grant him to find mercy from the Lord on that day. And how much he ministered to me at Ephesus, you know better.”

## EXPOSITION
Paul, etc. Paul, apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, as was explained above. “An apostle,” I say, “according to the promise of life.” Life has indeed been promised to those who contend lawfully; this promise I rightly pursue by contending lawfully. You, however, encouraged, pursue the promise of life with me—not of the present life, but of that life which is in Christ Jesus, that is, eternal life. For if we contend lawfully, we shall certainly have eternal life.

Paul writes this to Timothy, his most beloved son: “Grace, mercy, and peace be with you from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord,” as we explained above. Here Paul first speaks gently to him, so that he may more effectively lead him into what he is trying to persuade him to do, saying:

“I give thanks to God, whom I serve, having been instructed by my forefathers,” that is, by Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Paul belonged to the tribe of Benjamin. “I serve,” I say, “with a pure conscience”: for my conscience finds no fault with me. So you also should have a pure conscience, and thus you will be able to preserve the grace entrusted to you.

“For this I give thanks,” namely, that I remember you without ceasing in my prayers—that is, because God has made you such a person that He wills, and that it is fitting, for me always to remember you—so that I cannot even pray once without remembering you, night and day, that is, continually, desiring to see you. For if I were to see you, you would certainly not fear death while I was present. I say that I remember your tears, which you shed, because at Ephesus I would have left you in peace, although you wished to cross over with me and endure chains and deaths. See to it that, just as you did in my presence, so now, on seeing my letter, you voluntarily offer yourself to sufferings and death. For this reason I desire to see you, so that I may be filled with joy. If I were present, you would certainly not fear death; and I would rejoice greatly at this.

“I have received a remembrance of that faith which is in you, sincere”—that is, neither fabricated nor fragile—which first dwelt in your grandmother Lois and in your mother Eunice. Since you have an example of faith in your foremothers and in the female sex, as though faith were already natural to you, you ought for this reason to be especially fervent in faith. Faith was in your mother and grandmother. I am certain, however, that faith also dwells in you—but would that it were fervent!

For this reason, because I see in you both faith and an example of faith, as though they were natural to you, I remind you to revive the grace of God that is in you through the laying on of my hands. For when I consecrated you bishop through the laying on of my hands, you received the grace of the Holy Spirit. I want you to stir up that grace, which has been somewhat dormant in you—that is, awaken it—and, with that grace burning within you, rejoice in suffering and dying for the name of Christ.

Remember that God gave us the Holy Spirit—not a spirit of fear, but of strength, that is, of steadfastness, so that we might endure everything courageously—and the Spirit of love for God. He also gave the Spirit of sobriety, that is, self-control. For self-control nourishes love, and love nourishes strength; where love is, there certainly is no fear. Perfect love casts out fear.

See, therefore, that just as you were my companion in receiving the grace of the Holy Spirit, so you may be an imitator of my sufferings. And since you received with me the Spirit of strength and love, do not be ashamed of the testimony of our Lord Jesus Christ. If you are reproached because you worship one who was crucified, confess openly that this is indeed whom you worship. Nor should you be ashamed of me, his prisoner. For if someone again reproaches you, saying, “Look, your teacher has been condemned in chains,” do not therefore be embarrassed, but labor with the Gospel and preach with me according to the strength of God—that is, by following the steadfastness nourished by the love of God.

God freed us from the yoke of the devil and called us with His holy calling—that is, to be holy. He called us to this holiness not on account of the merit of our works, but according to His purpose—that is, according to His providence, by which He mercifully foresaw that we would become suitable for Him. And just as the calling was not based on any merit, neither was the providence; it was according to the grace that was given—that is, ordained to be given—to us in Christ Jesus before eternal times, that is, from eternity, before these times of ours, which revolve through the ages.

Long ago this grace was promised to be given to us. But now, in the time of Christ, it has been manifested—that is, fulfilled—as it had been promised, through the illumination of our Savior Jesus Christ, that is, through Christ, set before us in the light of knowledge through the humanity He assumed for Himself.

At this point Timothy might perhaps say: “I do not wish to die, but to remain in this illumination.” Paul answers this: Do not fear death, because by dying Christ destroyed death; and, once death had been destroyed, He also illuminated—that is, revealed and made known—life, not a passing life, but incorruption, that is, incorruptible life, in which we shall be impassible and immortal.

He illuminated it, I say, through His Gospel. In this Gospel I have been appointed by God as preacher, apostle, and teacher of the nations. Because of these many offices, it is right that you should not be ashamed to imitate me. For this reason—that is, because I taught this Gospel to the nations—I have suffered much. I am now suffering these chains as well; nevertheless, I am not ashamed, that is, I do not blush, but rejoice in suffering for Christ. So you also must not be ashamed.

For this reason, though I suffer, I am not ashamed: because I know whom I have believed in—that is, in whom I have placed my faith—namely, God. Or in this sense: “I know whom I have believed in,” that is, to whom I have entrusted my sufferings and works; and I am certain of their reward, because He to whom I have entrusted them is able to preserve my deposit—that is, what has been entrusted to Him—until that day when all are rewarded.

And because you see that God guards what is deposited with Him, you too, following His example, guard the deposit—that is, the episcopal grace entrusted to you. This deposit is good, that is, useful, if it is guarded. Do not suppose that you can guard it by your own strength, but through the assisting Holy Spirit who dwells in us.

And in order that you may guard the deposit well, have “the pattern of sound words” which you heard from me—that is, conform yourself to me so fully that you may seem to be Paul. Have my pattern in preserving faith and possessing love; and this faith and love are in Christ Jesus.

It is especially necessary that you guard the deposit because all the disciples who are in Asia have turned away from me, abandoning me; and you know this well. Among them are Philetus and Hermogenes.

He specifies them by name so that, if they should come to him, he would not suppose them still faithful and thus allow them more easily to persuade him and deceive him, as though speaking on Paul’s behalf. Ephesus was in Asia.

These men turned away from me, but Onesiphorus remained. Therefore may the Lord grant mercy not only to Onesiphorus but also to his household—that is, a recompense for the mercy he showed me—because he often refreshed me, both by consoling me in the faith and by supplying what I needed; and he was not ashamed of my chain. See to it that you too are not ashamed, but embrace it.

He was not ashamed; rather, when he came to Rome, he diligently sought me, and, having sought me, found me. And because he found me, may the Lord the Father grant him to find mercy—that is, the fruit of this mercy—from God, that is, from Christ the Judge, on that day, the day of judgment.

In Rome he ministered to me in my chains in this way. How much he ministered to me at Ephesus, you know better than I do—more than what he has now done, or perhaps more than the other disciples know.

## CHAPTER II

“Therefore, my son, be strengthened in the grace that is in Christ Jesus. And what you have heard from me through many witnesses, entrust to faithful men who will be competent to teach others also. Labor as a good soldier of Christ Jesus. No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in worldly affairs, so that he may please the one to whom he has shown himself approved. Moreover, the athlete is not crowned unless he has competed lawfully. The farmer who labors ought first to receive from the fruits [to partake of them]. Understand what I say, for the Lord will give you understanding in all things.

“Remember that the Lord Jesus Christ has risen from the dead, from the seed of David, according to my Gospel, for which I suffer even to the point of chains, as though I were a criminal; but the word of God is not bound. Therefore I endure everything for the sake of the elect, so that they too may obtain the salvation that is in Christ Jesus with heavenly glory.

“Faithful is the saying: For if we have died with Him, we shall also live with Him; if we endure, we shall also reign with Him; if we deny Him, He too will deny us; if we do not believe, He remains faithful, for He cannot deny Himself.

“Remind them of these things [I remind them], testifying before God. Do not engage in disputes about words, to the ruin of those who hear. Take care to present yourself approved to God, a worker who cannot be ashamed, rightly handling the word of truth. Avoid profane and empty talk, for it advances greatly toward ungodliness, and their speech spreads like cancer.

“Among them are Hymenaeus and Philetus, who have fallen away from the truth, saying that the resurrection has already taken place, and they have overturned the faith of some. But the firm foundation of God stands, bearing this seal: ‘The Lord knows those who are His,’ and, ‘Let everyone who invokes [names] the name of the Lord depart from iniquity.’

“But in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and earthenware; some indeed for honor, others for dishonor. Therefore, if anyone purifies himself from these things, he will be a vessel for honor, sanctified [and] useful to the Lord, prepared for every good work.

“Flee youthful desires; pursue righteousness, faith, hope, love, and peace with those who invoke the Lord [the name of the Lord] from a pure heart. Avoid foolish and undisciplined questions, knowing that they produce quarrels. The servant of the Lord must not quarrel, but must be gentle toward everyone, teachable, patient, correcting with restraint those who resist the truth, lest God perhaps grant them repentance for the knowledge of the truth, and they may recover from the snares of the devil, by whom they are held captive for his will.”

## EXPOSITION

Because you are more necessary on account of the defection of some, and because you are also admonished to be steadfast by the example of those who persevered, therefore you, my son Timothy, “be strengthened,” that is, be strong and do not be afraid. “Be strengthened,” I say, “in the grace that is in Christ Jesus,” that is, in pontifical doctrine, the grace of which God bestowed upon you. Or, “be strengthened in grace,” that is, in the remission of sins and the eternal life that must be preached. For this is the grace that comes through Jesus Christ.

And so that, once strengthened, you may advance further, entrust also to faithful men what I commend to you to teach—that is, appoint under yourself preachers who will preach with you to the people of God. Let them be sound in faith; and, since they are faithful, they ought to be such as are competent, both by knowledge and by the grace of eloquence, to teach others entrusted to them.

To such men, I say, entrust what you heard from me—that is, what I taught you—confirming it through many witnesses, that is, through the many testimonies of the Law and the Prophets. For what I taught you about faith in Christ I showed to have been entirely foreshadowed in the Law and the Prophets.

Lest Timothy should think that he could now rest after appointing preachers under himself, Paul says against this: Although you have appointed some to teach others, do not therefore become sluggish; but labor as a soldier of Christ Jesus—that is, remember that you serve in Christ’s camp. Labor is fitting for a soldier, not idleness.

“Labor as a good soldier,” that is, a useful one. How he is good he determines in what follows, saying: If you are a good soldier, you will not entangle yourself in worldly affairs.

For no one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in worldly affairs—that is, he does not devote himself to the examination of secular cases, but to spiritual matters. The world has secular judges who judge temporal matters; bishops, however, ought to devote themselves to spiritual instruction.

Or let us understand it this way: One who serves God does not entangle himself in worldly affairs by conducting his preaching as a business and selling it, demanding payment from his hearers. Therefore, one who serves God does not entangle himself in these things, so that he may please Him, namely God, whom he has shown himself likely to please by living well and giving a good account of himself through his past life.

He proves the point from what is less: one who serves God does not entangle himself in worldly matters in order thereby to please God. For even—what is less—the one who competes in the arena, that is, in some contest, such as the wrestling school or the stadium, is not crowned, that is, does not receive praise or the prize, unless he has competed lawfully, according to the rule of that contest.

Lest Timothy should think that, because Paul had forbidden him worldly affairs, he was to receive nothing temporal from his subjects, Paul says: Although I forbid you worldly affairs, I nevertheless want you to receive temporal goods from the fruit of your preaching. For you labor in the cultivation of the Lord’s field, and therefore ought to receive from the fruits of that field, that is, temporal goods which the field—that is, the people—can give.

Let him receive, I say, first from the fruit what is sufficient for him; and if anything remains, let the poor receive it secondarily. Or “first,” that is, let him receive much from it, because the thing he ministers is greatly worthy. To receive from preaching what is sufficient is not a worldly business.

Or let us join the words in this way: I say, do not entangle yourself in worldly affairs, nor is it necessary for you to do so, because from the fruits of the preaching in which you labor you will receive what is necessary for you.

He says this equivalently, lest Timothy should judge it absurd to live from preaching, since Paul did not do so but lived by the work of his hands. Paul says: Understand what I am saying—that you should receive what is necessary from the fruit of preaching—and understand the reason why I do not receive what I command you to receive.

The saints give this as the reason: Timothy was weak, and if he worked with his hands, he could not devote himself to preaching; Paul, however, was strong and industrious and sufficient for both tasks. Therefore Paul himself received nothing, and for this reason he wanted Timothy to receive.

You will certainly be able to understand this reason, because the Lord will give you understanding both in this matter and in everything.

Labor, as I previously instructed you, in the manner of a good soldier. And, in order that you may labor in this way, remember Christ’s resurrection—and that you too, if you labor well, will rise with Him. Having hope of rising, I say, remember that Christ Jesus rose from the dead.

Christ alone rose from the dead, because afterward He neither experienced the condition of mortality nor could He die again. Lazarus and all who were raised from the dead, however, suffered death again.

Timothy might perhaps say: “He was God and was therefore able to rise.” Paul answers: I say that Jesus rose from the seed of David—that is, according to the fact that He was human—for according to the flesh alone He was David’s son.

He certainly rose according to my Gospel—that is, according to what I preach—and it must be believed because I am an apostle sent by God. Or understand it this way: Christ was from the seed of David according to my Gospel; because He rose, I labor in preaching it even to the point of chains.

Because I preach in this way, I am confined in chains as though I were a criminal—that is, as though I had been caught in some crime. It is as though he were saying: I suffer punishment and, what weighs more heavily, reproaches. If they thought I was suffering for righteousness, it would be a consolation to me.

I am indeed held in chains, but the word of God is not bound, because I preach even in chains. See, therefore, that fear does not bind the word of God in you also.

You ought to remember that Christ rose, because, since I remember His resurrection, I believe that I too shall rise. Through Him I endure all chains and reproaches.

Someone might say: Even if you did not endure these things, purity of life and sound faith would be sufficient. He answers: I endure them for the sake of God’s elect, so that they too may be saved; so that those chosen beforehand by God may obtain salvation—that is, justification from sins in the present—which salvation is in Christ Jesus.

They may obtain, I say, this salvation with heavenly glory, because through the remission of sins that takes place here one reaches eternal glory.

This saying, then, which I have spoken—that one must labor in hope of the resurrection—is faithful and entirely worthy of belief. It is faithful and entirely worthy of belief that, if you labor lawfully, you will rise as Christ did.

For if we have died with Him, abandoning the works of the old man Adam, we shall also live with Him, made impassible and immortal like Him. While Christ lived in the world, He possessed all the works of the old man except sin. He hungered (Matthew 4), thirsted (John 19), and became weary, as is clear in the Gospel of John (John 4:6), when He spoke with the Canaanite woman at the well (John 4); He was truly mortal and capable of suffering.

But after He endured death for all, He no longer extended either hand or foot toward the works of the old man; He became impassible and immortal.

If, then, we die with Him in baptism—which He consecrated on the cross for the justification of human beings, pouring water from His side—so that, justified through baptism, we might no longer extend our senses toward the works of the old man, that is, toward the miseries of sin, we shall live with Him, made impassible and immortal with Him.

But if we do not become participants in this death, we shall not become participants in His life. If we merely die with Him, we shall live with Him.

But if—what is greater—we endure as martyrs, for whom dying to sins was not enough, but who also wished to suffer for righteousness, then, because we endure, we shall reign with Him. That is, we shall not merely live, but a palm and a kind of triumph will be granted to us in accordance with the dignity of martyrdom.

Although being with Christ is sufficient for everyone, there are nevertheless distinctions of dignity in that blessedness.

Truly, if we die with Him, we shall live with Him. For if we deny God by doing evil, He too will deny us by not granting eternal life. To deny God is not to grant eternal goods.

Timothy might perhaps say: “It seems unbelievable that God would deny, on account of sin, one who has confessed faith in Him.” Paul answers: Even if we do not believe that God will deny the one who denies Him, He nevertheless remains faithful—that is, truthful and worthy of belief—who said: “Whoever is ashamed of me before human beings, I too will be ashamed before my Father” (Luke 9:26).

He remains faithful in such a way that it is impossible for Him not to be truthful. For He cannot deny Himself, that is, that He is God; for if He were to lie, He would certainly not be God.

This—that is, that you should die with Christ and thus teach others in the hope of living with Him—I remind you of, testifying to you about it before God, lest God should later require Timothy’s blood from Paul’s hand.

And although I remind you of this with such strictness, nevertheless do not quarrel over words by teaching immoderately what I teach.

Or understand it this way: Remind others of this—that they must die with Christ in the hope of living with Him—testifying to them of these things before God, lest their blood be required from your hand.

And in reminding them, do not quarrel over words, for disputing is useful for nothing except the ruin of those who hear. If foolish people hear various persons quarreling, they think that those who are louder have the more righteous cause. It belongs to fools to cling to fools. But if neither of the disputants prevails by shouting, simple people are left uncertain about which one they should follow more closely.

Do not quarrel, but take care to present yourself wholly—both in body and soul—as approved, that is, praiseworthy, to God.

To be approved, you must be a worker who cannot be ashamed, because you are not ashamed to preach the cross of Christ, and so forth, rightly—that is, without contentiousness and with all restraint—handling the word of truth.

In order that you may rightly handle the word of God, avoid profane things, that is, things utterly abominable. Also avoid empty talk, that is, talk which, even if it is not so profane, is nevertheless useless.

Avoid it for this reason: these empty words will greatly advance the persuasion of ungodliness, and the speech of those who speak emptily spreads gradually like cancer. This disease first occupies a small part of the flesh, but gradually increases more and more until it kills.

So heretics first subtly introduce something that seems neither beneficial nor harmful; then, by alternating arguments, their teaching gradually grows into the greatest heresy. Among such empty talkers are Hymenaeus and Philetus, who have fallen away from the truth of faith.

He specifies what their heresy is, so that if they should perhaps come to Timothy, he may guard himself against them. They say that the resurrection has already taken place, either in those who rose with Christ or in baptism, in which we rise from the death of sin to the life of virtues.

The threefold immersion signifies Christ’s three-day burial; the raising up signifies Christ’s resurrection. By saying this, they overturn the faith of some.

But although they overturn it, the foundation of God nevertheless stands firm—that is, those in whom faith has been well founded, and who in turn have been founded by God in faith. This foundation, I say, is firm and bears a seal.

This is said by comparison with a courageous commander who gives a sign to his soldiers by which they may be distinguished from others. So God marks His own, so that, seeing the sign, the devil may pass them by, knowing that he has no association with them.

The sign is this: “The Lord knows those who are His.” Paul presents this from God’s side, signifying God’s election among the righteous, saying: The Lord knew from eternity who would be His.

In what follows he speaks according to Isaiah, treating the power of free choice and saying: Let every person who, through the freedom of choice, is able—and who invokes the name of the Lord in faith and works—depart from iniquity.

Through divine election and free choice, which by good works responds to divine election, those who will remain in righteousness are marked with these two signs. For God foresaw each person whom He elected as one who would become good, and at the same time foresaw the good works that person would perform.

Whoever, therefore, is marked by God’s election and by the good works of free choice becomes God’s.

Do not therefore wonder if this happens in God’s house: some depart from the faith while others persevere in it. For even in any great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver. Just as in God’s house some are more perfect and others are perfect under them, so in the same house there are also wooden and earthen vessels, just as in God’s house some are evil and others worse.

Some of these vessels are for honor, in which good beverages are stored; others are for dishonor, for receiving urine and similar things. Nevertheless, just as the more honorable vessels are necessary in the house, so also are the dishonorable vessels.

Thus in God’s Church both the evil and the good are each necessary in their own way. For if there were no evil, there would be no merit in the good. If there were no persecution, where would the patience of the good be?

Since vessels are either for honor or for dishonor, and there is no middle category, therefore, if anyone purifies himself from these things—that is, if anyone does not become a vessel for dishonor—he will be a vessel for honor to God.

I call such a vessel sanctified, that is, justified from sins, and also useful to the Lord, because it is prepared to perform every good work.

Avoid profane things; and not only this, but also flee youthful desires—that is, those desires that incite unstable youth. Flee these, but pursue righteousness, that is, equity toward everyone; faith in God; chastity of body and soul; and peace, that is, harmony, with those who invoke the Lord from a pure heart.

Do not flee only youthful desires, but also avoid foolish questions, in which there is no knowledge and none seems possible. Avoid also those which, although not so foolish, are nevertheless without fruit for Christian discipline, such as dialectical questions, knowing that questions of this kind produce quarrels.

The servant of the Lord—which you are and ought to be—must not quarrel. Rather, he must be gentle, that is, moderate in all things and toward everyone; teachable, that is, teaching others with readiness; and patient under whatever may be inflicted upon him.

He must correct with restraint those who resist the truth, not with contentiousness. He must correct them in this way so that God may perhaps—that is, at some time—grant them repentance.

For perhaps at some time they will repent of having acted wickedly, coming in this way to know the truth of the faith; and, having recognized the truth of the faith, they may recover from the snares of the devil—that is, from the sins with which the devil had ensnared them. They are held captive by that devil as long as they remain in sins, held, I say, to carry out the devil’s will.

## CHAPTER III

“But know this, that in the last days perilous times will come. For people will be lovers of themselves, covetous, boastful, proud, blasphemous, disobedient to parents, ungrateful, wicked, without affection, without peace, slanderers, incontinent, savage, without kindness, traitors, reckless [insolent], blind, swollen with pride, lovers of pleasures rather than of God, having indeed an appearance of piety but denying its power [truth]. Avoid such people.

“For among them are those who enter houses and lead captive little women, burdened with sins and driven by various desires, always learning and never arriving at knowledge of the truth.

“Just as Jannes and Jambres resisted Moses (Exodus 7:11), so these also resist the truth: people corrupted in mind and disapproved with regard to the faith. But they will not advance further, for their folly will become manifest to all, just as theirs also became manifest.

“But you have followed my teaching, conduct, purpose, faith, patience, love, endurance, persecutions, and sufferings—such as befell me at Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra, and such persecutions as I endured—and from all of them the Lord delivered me.

“Indeed, all who wish to live devoutly in Christ Jesus will suffer persecution. But wicked people and deceivers will advance from bad to worse, erring and leading others into error.

“But remain in the things you have learned and which have been entrusted to you, knowing from whom you learned them, and because from infancy you have known the sacred writings, which are able to instruct you for salvation through faith that is in Christ Jesus.

“For every Scripture inspired by God is useful for teaching, for refutation, for correction, and for instruction in righteousness, so that the person of God may be perfect, equipped for every good work.”

## EXPOSITION

Avoid foolish questions; avoid also people who have an appearance of piety, and so forth. But before he states this, he first gives the reasons why such people must be avoided, saying:

You should know not only that what was mentioned above must be done, but also this: in the last days—that is, near the end of the world—perilous times will come. That is, at that time perilous teachers will persist in teaching and afflicting those who do not consent to them. Those who believe them will plunge into many dangers.

At that time people will be lovers of themselves, that is, indulging their own flesh in the following ways. They will be covetous, that is, lovers of money. They will also be boastful, wishing to place themselves above others. They will be proud, unlawfully glorying in honors they have acquired.

They will also be blasphemers against God and His teaching. They will be disobedient to parents, whether carnal parents—which is wicked—or spiritual parents, such as bishops and priests.

They will be ungrateful: if someone teaches them good things, for which they ought to be grateful, they will trouble their teachers instead. They will also be wicked, committing murder and similar crimes.

They will be without affection, having no loving disposition toward their neighbor, even if they are unable to give anything. They will be without peace, that is, without harmony, always engaged in quarrels.

They will be slanderers, imposing accusations upon the righteous, although they themselves are incontinent and rush indiscriminately into every crime. They will be savage, that is, cruel and without any gentleness.

They will be without kindness, that is, without generosity, not distributing their possessions to those in need. They will also be traitors, handing the righteous over to death.

They will be reckless, that is, shameless in their insults, and, even when reproved, impatient of reproof. They will also be swollen with pride, inflated in mind, even if they possess neither honor nor hope of honor.

Such people will be lovers of pleasures—that is, of every form of luxury—more than lovers of God, whom they seem to love in no respect.

You must carefully beware of these people. They have an appearance of piety, that is, they pretend to be religious, but deny the power of that piety, namely love, which is the power of the whole of religion. For love is strong as death. Or “power” may mean the truth of religion, which they deny in their conduct. Avoid such people.

Timothy might say: “Why do you warn me about people who will exist near the end of the world?” Paul therefore says: Avoid them, because among those who will exist in the last days are those who enter houses, and so forth.

It should be noted that, from the time the world began, God has had His kingdom in it, and the devil his own. God began to reign in Abel, and the devil in Cain.

God completed His kingdom by assuming flesh and carrying out the works that followed—remitting sins and so forth—insofar as it could be completed in the present. He will complete that kingdom fully in the future by granting eternal life.

Just as God will bring His kingdom to completion in goodness, so the devil will bring his kingdom to completion in the perfection of iniquity near the end of the world through Antichrist.

And just as God wished the patriarchs and prophets to precede Christ’s coming, so many members of Antichrist will precede their head, Antichrist himself.

Against these members Paul instructs Timothy, saying: Among those whom I have described are false teachers who enter houses. They do not dare to teach in public squares, lest their teaching become known among the hearing of good people. But, so that they may deceive more freely, they teach privately in houses; and thus they lead little women—who are easily deceived by every wind of teaching—away as captives, having made them captives by that particular persuasion.

They have been taken captive by God and handed over under the authority of the devil. Or, for the height of reproach, just as he calls women “little women,” so he calls men “little women,” that is, soft people who yield to every wind of teaching, so that, having heard the name of their reproach, they may blush more quickly and be converted to the Lord.

He calls them little women burdened with sins while they are deceived by the devil. These women are driven by various desires because they are always learning and never arriving at knowledge of the truth—that is, they are always laboring and never reaching perfection.

Such people do not teach only in private houses; they also resist the truth openly, just as Jannes and Jambres, the two magician brothers in Egypt, resisted Moses before Pharaoh by performing through their enchantments certain things that Moses performed, though not everything (Exodus 7:11).

These people, I say, are corrupted in mind, that is, perverted in understanding and conduct, and they err with regard to the faith. Because they do not enter into it, they are rejected by God.

Since Timothy might be frightened by these things just foretold, Paul consoles him, saying: Such men will indeed come; but do not be afraid, because they will not make further progress. Their folly will ultimately become manifest, just as that of Jannes and Mambres; therefore they will not advance any farther. But you, as though he were saying, must and can make progress: for you have attained my doctrine in knowledge, my instruction in the ordering of life and in conduct, and my purpose: for just as I have set eternal life as the goal of my labor, so you too have followed the faith, because you truly believe as I do; and endurance in hope, because you are prepared, as long as it pleases God, to endure with me. You also have love of God and neighbor, and patience—that is, the virtue itself, even if there were no need to perform anything—and the actions of that patience, namely persecutions from place to place and the sufferings of torments.

[Col. 0470B] You know also what happened to me at Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra, and, beyond these, what persecutions I endured in many places. But what is there to fear from this? For the Lord rescued me from them all, and so he will rescue you from whatever you may have to suffer. You must be stirred up to self-restraint by my example and that of all religious people. For all who wish to live piously, that is, religiously, in Christ Jesus, will suffer persecution; therefore do not be troubled if you suffer something. Those who live piously will suffer; but evil men, evil in themselves and deceivers of others, will indeed make progress in worldly [uncleanness], but all this will be punishment and condemnation for them. I mean those who err in themselves and therefore are evil, sending others also into error [Col. 0470D] and therefore being deceivers. They will err; but you remain in those commandments which you learned from me and in those things entrusted to you—that is, in pontifical grace—knowing and remembering from whom and from how great a teacher you learned these things. For if you remember my authority, false doctrine will become contemptible to you.

And I want you to remember this also: you have known the sacred writings from infancy, having been handed over to the schools by your mother, who was faithful. These writings can fully instruct you for attaining the salvation of eternal life, to which one comes through faith, and that faith is in Christ Jesus. Truly, the sacred writings can instruct you for salvation, because every Scripture inspired by God—that is, spiritually understood according to God—is useful for teaching those who do not know, for reproving, that is, convicting, [Col. 0471A] those who contradict the faith, for correcting sinners who do not deny that they have sinned, and for educating those who are still inexperienced and simple. I say that it is to be educated in righteousness, that is, so that they may be justified by putting off the rudiments of unbelief. Thus, I say, let him be educated so that, as far as depends on the teacher, the one being educated may be a complete man of God—complete in such a way that he is equipped for every good work.

## CHAPTER IV

“I testify before God and Christ Jesus, who is to judge the living and the dead, and by his appearing and his kingdom: preach the word; be urgent in season and out of season; reprove, beseech, rebuke with all patience and teaching. For there will be a time when they will not endure sound doctrine; instead, according to their own desires, they will heap up teachers for themselves, itching in their ears. They will indeed turn their hearing away from the truth, but they will turn to fables. But you, be watchful in all things, labor; do the work of an evangelist; fulfill your ministry; be sober. For I am already being poured out, and the time of my release is at hand. I have fought the good fight; I have finished the course; I have kept the faith. Henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the just judge, will give me on that day—not only to me, but also to those who love his appearing. Make haste to come to me quickly. For Demas has deserted me, loving this present age, and has gone to Thessalonica; Crescens to Galatia; Titus to Dalmatia. Luke alone is with me. Take Mark and bring him with you, for he is useful to me in the ministry. But I sent Tychicus to Ephesus. When you come, bring the cloak which I left at Troas with Carpus, and the books, but especially the parchments. Alexander the coppersmith did me much harm; the Lord will repay him according to his works. You also avoid him, for he strongly resisted our words. At my first defense no one stood with me; everyone deserted me. May it not be charged against them. But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me, so that through me the preaching might be fulfilled and all the nations might hear, and I was delivered from the mouth of the lion. The Lord delivered me from every evil work and will save me for his heavenly kingdom; to him be glory for ever and ever. Amen.

“Greet Prisca and Aquila, and the household of Onesiphorus. Erastus remained at Corinth. I left Trophimus sick at Miletus. Make haste to come before winter. Eubulus greets you, and Pudens [variant: Prudens], and Linus, and Claudia, and all the brothers [the variant lacks ‘all’]. The Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Grace be with you. Amen.”

## EXPOSITION

Because the Scripture of God, which is known to you, is useful for teaching, reproving, and correcting, I therefore testify to you before God, lest he require this of me any longer. And before Christ Jesus, who will judge the living and the dead: those whom he finds living at the hour of judgment, who will be dissolved and rise again in an instant. He will also judge the dead before the day of judgment. [Col. 0472A] Or, he will judge the living and the dead, that is, the righteous and sinners.

I also testify to you by the appearing of Christ himself, so that you may be prepared as one who expects the Judge to come every day, and so that through fear of him you may do what I exhort. I also testify to you by his kingdom, in which the saints will reign together with him, so that through love of reigning with Christ you may diligently do what I command. This, I say, I testify to you: preach the word, that is, the doctrine of God, and in preaching be urgent in season with those who willingly listen. Be urgent also out of season with those who at first are difficult to bring to hearing, but afterward, once they understand the reasoning, listen willingly. Reprove also, that is, convict, those who contradict the faith. Beseech the righteous also, so that they may always advance toward what is better. Rebuke those caught in sins with the necessary severity.

[Col. 0472B] Do these things with all patience, so that you may willingly endure whatever is inflicted; but do not do so in a way that makes you cease teaching. Rather, always persist in teaching. I urge you to teach with such insistence because there will be a time near the end of the world when people will not endure sound doctrine. If at that time the Church is not strengthened by apostolic teaching, the faith will perish. They will not endure sound doctrine, but will heap up teachers for themselves according to their own desires: if they are lustful, a lustful teacher, and likewise in other matters. I mean people who then itch in their ears, that is, desire to hear new and unheard-of things, among which truth will not exist. They will indeed turn their hearing away from the truth, but they will turn to fables, in which there is no truth of the matter.

They are so intent upon fables; but you be watchful, that is, guard yourself with every care, [Col. 0472C] and labor in all things, if you can, to convert them. And so that your labor may be suitable, do the work of an evangelist, that is, of a preacher: namely, practice what you preach. Act in such a way that you fulfill your ministry, that is, the office of a preacher—not stopping short of it, but doing everything belonging to a preacher, laboring for others and completing in yourself by your deeds what you have taught others.
