And although I exhort you in this way to do the work of an evangelist, nevertheless be sober—not excessively devoted to abstinence, lest, weakened by excessive fasting, you be unable, as is fitting, to apply yourself to preaching. I urge you with such insistence because I am already being poured out, that is, being sacrificed, and gradually failing each day in chains; and the time of my release, that is, the day of my death, is at hand and near. I know that this day is near because I have fought the fight—his use of the repeated form indicates the frequency of the struggle—the good fight, that is, one useful to the Church of God. I fought by suffering whatever had to be suffered, and I finished the course, that is, the rapidity of doing good, where it was not necessary to suffer in the same way. I have indeed finished it, because my righteousness has risen so high that it has nowhere further to rise. In fighting and in running I have kept the faith.

And because I have now finished the course, therefore henceforth—that is, in the life that remains for us in the future—the crown of righteousness is laid up for me, that is, one earned through righteousness. The Lord will return this crown to me as something owed on that future day of repayment, and he cannot deny it to me, because he is a just [Col. 0473A] judge, and justice requires that it be returned to me. To me indeed, but not to me alone: also to all who love the appearing of his judgment, that is, who have a pure conscience. For those who are conscious of evil in themselves do not love the coming of the Judge; they fear it. By this he greatly encourages Timothy, saying that the crown of righteousness is prepared for those who love the coming of God.

Having instructed Timothy in the things that had to be done publicly, he gives him certain personal commands, saying: Since the day of my release is near, make haste to come quickly to me, for you are necessary to me. Demas deserted me by apostatizing, loving this present age, and he went to Thessalonica. Crescens, however, another disciple who remained in the faith, [Col. 0473B] went to Galatia. Titus went to Dalmatia. And so, with the others dispersed, Luke alone is with me.

Come, I say, and when you come, take Mark and bring him with you to me, for he is useful to me in the ministry. Perhaps the Apostle intended to send him on some mission. But I sent Tychicus to Ephesus, where you are bishop. When you come to me, bring the cloak which I left with Carpus at Troas. Bring the books also, and above all the parchments, which I need in order to send letters.

The cloak was a garment granted by the Romans to the people of Tarsus because they had come under Roman rule voluntarily and not through war. He therefore ordered it to be brought so that he might prove that he was a Roman citizen, as he had claimed before Festus. Or the cloak was another garment which he requested to be brought against the cold, since he was going to spend the winter in prison.

While you are coming to me, beware of Alexander, for this Alexander the coppersmith—a name indicating his rank—showed me much harm. I do not care about it, because the Lord will repay him according to his works. You too must avoid this Alexander, for he strongly resisted our words. Come, then, because you are necessary.

At my first defense, when I defended myself in the presence of Nero, none of the disciples was present with me; everyone deserted me. I pray that this not be charged against them. They deserted me, but the Lord stood by me, and by standing beside me made me strong. He did so, and to such an extent, that the preaching might be fulfilled through me, since I did not yield to his threats. If I had consented to him, the preaching would have remained unfulfilled. Therefore he also strengthened me so that the nations might hear these things, and might also hear that I was delivered, because I did not consent, from the mouth of the lion—that is, Nero, or the devil attacking me through Nero.

And not only from the lion: the Lord delivered me from every evil work, so that I might do nothing evil. Having delivered me, he will save me, transferring me into his heavenly kingdom. To this Lord be glory for ever and ever. Amen.

After receiving this letter, greet Prisca and Aquila and the household of Onesiphorus. Erastus remained at Corinth, and I left Trophimus sick at Miletus. Since so many are absent, make haste to come to me before winter.

As for those who are with us, Eubulus, Pudens, Linus, Claudia, and all the brothers greet you. And I greet you. May the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, and grant that grace may be with us—that is, that the love begun between me and you may continue. [Col. 0474C] Amen.

# [IN THE EPISTLE TO TITUS]

[Col. 0473]

## ARGUMENT OF THE EPISTLE TO TITUS

He admonishes and instructs Titus concerning the establishment of the presbyterate, spiritual conduct, and the avoidance of heretics who believe in Jewish traditions; he writes to him from Nicopolis.

## PROLOGUE OF BLESSED BRUNO ON THE SAME EPISTLE

[Col. 0473D] After converting the Cretans, Paul consecrated Titus there as archbishop, so that he might instruct them in whatever matters he considered appropriate. When Paul had gone to Nicopolis—as this Epistle seems to indicate in what follows—he wrote this Epistle to Titus. For he had heard that Titus was exercising the episcopal office too simply, because he was not expelling heretics, or any other perverse people, from the episcopal Church by pontifical authority, as was fitting. He did indeed warn them that they were acting wrongly and ought to desist; but when they did not cease from the evil they had begun, although pontifical dignity required it, he did not restrain them but endured them humbly.

Why, then, does Paul write this Epistle to Titus? He discusses in it the pontifical office, [Col. 0474D] instructing him what sort of bishops he ought to consecrate throughout the cities of his archbishopric. He dwells especially on this instruction: that Titus should use pontifical power and authority. For although being simple is good, excessive humility in a bishop causes harm to the governance of the Church. Therefore he admonishes Titus to teach, exhort, and reprove with episcopal authority, and, if any heretics refuse correction, to drive them from the Church.

Thus, in discussing the episcopal office, he intends to make Titus a perfect bishop, so that by his example he might make bishops who are excessively simple-minded more vigorous and cause them to use episcopal authority.

# THE EPISTLE TO TITUS

[Col. 0473]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0473D]

“Paul, a servant of God, but an apostle of Jesus Christ according to the faith of God’s elect and the knowledge of the truth which is according to godliness, in hope of eternal life, which God, who does not lie, promised before the times of the ages; but in his own times he manifested his word in the preaching entrusted to me according to the command of God our Savior.

“To Titus, his beloved son according to the common faith: grace and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Savior.

“For this reason I left you in Crete, so that you might correct what is lacking and establish presbyters throughout the cities, just as I also directed you: if anyone is without accusation, the husband of one wife, having faithful children who are not under accusation of dissipation or insubordination. For a bishop must be without accusation, as God’s steward: not arrogant, not irascible, not given to wine, not violent, not greedy for shameful gain, but hospitable, kind, prudent, sober, just, holy, self-controlled, embracing the faithful word which is according to doctrine, so that he may be able to exhort in sound doctrine and to refute those who contradict it.

“For there are many who are disobedient, vain talkers, and deceivers, especially those who are of the circumcision, whom it is necessary to refute. They overturn entire households, teaching what ought not to be taught for the sake of shameful gain. One of them, their own prophet, said: ‘Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy bellies.’ This testimony is true.

“For this reason rebuke them sharply, so that they may be sound in the faith, not attending to Jewish fables and commandments of people who turn away [variant: turn others away] from the truth. To the pure all things are pure; but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is pure. Rather, both their mind and their conscience are defiled. They profess to know God, but they deny him by their deeds, being abominated (abominati; variant: abominabiles, ‘abominable’) and unbelieving, and rejected for every good work.”

## EXPOSITION

“Paul,” and so forth. As is his custom, he places the greeting first, saying: “Paul, a servant of God,” that is, simple and humble in the manner of a servant. Here he indicates that simplicity is indeed good. A servant of God, certainly, but nevertheless an apostle of Jesus Christ, that is, acting and restraining each person as the authority of apostolic exaltation requires.

You, therefore, following my example, should be simple in such a way that excessive humility does not obstruct pontifical authority. He did not say “a servant of God and an apostle of Christ” in order to deny that he is also an apostle of God and a servant of Christ. Rather, he said this to indicate that God the Father directed Paul, through Christ, into the ministry of the apostolate.

An apostle, I say, according to the faith of God’s elect. For he continues by preaching the faith held by the prophets and by all who are God’s elect. He is also an apostle according to the knowledge of the truth, that is, according to what he recognized through the true knowledge of God. I do not mean just any truth, but that which is according to godliness, that is, the truth which follows the worship of God.

I speak of faith and knowledge of the truth proceeding toward the hope of eternal life, [Col. 0476A] because through the faith we have received and through the truth we have recognized, we hope to attain eternal life. And not without reason, because the life he promised—that is, predetermined to give—cannot be doubted. He promised it who does not lie and cannot lie, because he is God.

He did not promise it in time; rather, so that the diligence of the promised matter might be considered in God, he promised it before the times of the ages, that is, from eternity he predetermined it before the times that roll through the ages. He promised it, I say; but he manifested it—that is, fulfilled what he had promised to his own—in the appropriate times as eternal life. Abel saw something of it, Abraham more perfectly, and then the prophets gradually knew more of it as redemption drew nearer. John knew more than all of them, pointing out eternal life with his finger, that is, Christ.

But God manifested eternal life most clearly in the time of grace, namely his Word, that is, the incarnate Son, born and revealed in other ways also. He manifested this Word in the preaching entrusted to me, that is, through the preaching committed to me. It was entrusted to me according to the command of God, that is, because God so commanded. I mean our Savior, God.

Paul, being such as this, writes to Titus, beloved in a particular way.

To Titus, I say, his son according to the common—that is, catholic—faith, in which I begot him, not according to the flesh. For “catholic” means common or universal. Or he wishes Titus, his son, to think according to the common, that is, ordinary, faith, and not according to the private doctrines of heretics.

May you have grace, Titus, both according to the remission of sins and according to the episcopal office. May you also have peace, that is, as much tranquility of mind as can be possessed here. May these things be given to you by God the Father, who is able and willing to give them, and by Jesus Christ, who likewise is able and willing, our Savior.

Having completed the greeting, he addresses Titus in this way: O Titus, I left you consecrated as archbishop of Crete for this purpose, that is, for a purpose which, if accomplished, will be pleasing to me. The purpose is this: that you correct, that is, by correcting what must be corrected, complete what is lacking. This was said concerning conduct.

And by correcting conduct, establish presbyters, that is, bishops, throughout the individual cities subject to your archbishopric. Establish them, I say, in the manner in which I also appointed you. When he says, “just as I appointed you,” he indicates that while Titus was with him, Paul instructed him concerning the consecration of bishops.

Appoint as bishop one who is without accusation, that is, without any criminal act or the infamy of one. Let him also be the husband of one wife, as we explained elsewhere. Let him have faithful children, that is, children whom he has instructed in sound faith, and not children accused of luxury, so that no bad report may even have arisen from this. For if he allowed his children to live luxuriously, he set an example showing that he would not correct the children of the Church well.

Or let him not have children who are unsubmissive, that is, disobedient to him. For if he appeared lax with his private children, he showed that he would not sufficiently restrain the Church entrusted to him.

Therefore I want one who is without accusation to be appointed bishop. For a bishop must be without accusation and without a criminal act, as God’s steward, that is, as one who dispenses God himself to those to whom he preaches. A bishop must also not be arrogant, that is, not desirous of placing himself above others. He must not be irascible, but must govern his spirit well. He must not be given to wine, that is, devoted to much wine.

He must not be violent, that is, one who strikes with bodily weapons, for he has the weapons of the Holy Spirit; or one who strikes the consciences of his hearers, lest he preach something from which a perverse opinion may arise. He must not be greedy for shameful gain, that is, not entangled in worldly business.

Rather, he must be hospitable, receiving the poor into his lodging; and, having received the poor and everyone else, kind, that is, generously ministering his possessions. He must be sober in food, drink, and clothing; just also toward his neighbors; holy toward God; and self-controlled, so that he may be an example of self-control to others.

In addition to these things, he must be one who embraces—that is, diligently and constantly handles—the faithful word, that is, the truthful word, but not every truth: rather, the word which is according to doctrine, that is, which is suitable for preaching. For there are many truths to which it would be a fault for a bishop to devote himself.

Therefore let him embrace this word, so that both through practice and through knowledge he may be able to exhort the faithful in sound doctrine. Through practice and knowledge he must also be able to refute those who contradict sound doctrine, that is, convict unbelievers who attack the faith.

It is necessary that he be able to refute in this way, because there are many [Col. 0477C] who are disobedient to bishops. There are also vain talkers, speaking useless things; and in this vain speech they are deceivers, that is, they possess the skill and cunning to deceive their hearers through empty talk. They could speak vainly without the cunning of deception.

Above all, those who are of the circumcision, the Jews, deceive. It is therefore necessary to refute them, because they are the chief deceivers. Those who came from the circumcision overturn not only the master of the household, but also entire households, that is, every family, teaching, for the sake of shameful gain, things which ought neither to be believed nor taught.

There truly are evil deceivers among the Cretans. A certain Cretan, one of their own—that is, a native of their people—confirms this; therefore he is more worthy of belief. This prophet, that is, one who saw by careful consideration the vices of the Cretans, was named Epimenides. He said this about them:

“Cretans are always liars; they are beasts, thinking in a bestial manner, and evil—that is, as they think, so they act cruelly. They are also lazy bellies,” that is, people given to luxury and burdening themselves with food, and therefore slow to every good thing.

So that there might be no doubt about the truth of this, since the man who said it was a pagan, Paul asserts it, saying: This testimony which Epimenides gave concerning the Cretans is true. For this reason, because they are liars and so forth, rebuke them—namely, the Cretans—sharply, that is, with severity and pontifical authority, so that they may remain sound in the faith.

They must not attend to Jewish fables, because what they teach about restoring circumcision is fable and does not possess the truth of the matter. They must not attend to these things because they are fables and because they are human commandments, not God’s. Formerly, under the Old Law, God did indeed command circumcision and the other things; but after the time of grace came, God commanded that these things no longer be done.

Therefore he says: Let them not attend to commandments not of God but of people who turn away from the truth, because they do not wish to receive the spiritual understanding of the Law.

From what follows he indicates that such people taught that one ought to abstain from certain foods, saying: One must not attend to the fables of the Jews, who judge certain foods unclean, when all things customarily used as food are pure to the pure, that is, to those who receive them in purity and holiness.

[Col. 0478B] God created these foods for the sustenance of those who serve him; therefore they are pure and worthy for those who serve God with a pure heart and in pure conduct. Every creature also, insofar as it was created by God, is pure. It is not necessary here to discuss everything.

To those who are pure in conscience and faith, all things are pure; but to those whose conscience is defiled and who are unbelieving, even what they consider pure is not pure for them. Since they do not believe in the Creator and possess a defiled conscience, it is unjust for them to use any creature of God. Nothing is pure for them. Rather, their mind—that is, their understanding, namely their faith—and their conscience are defiled; therefore nothing is pure for them.

Perhaps someone might say: Why are these people defiled when they confess God? Paul answers: I know that they confess with their mouths that they know God, but what does this profit? By their deeds they deny God.

They certainly deny him, since they are detestable, that is, ill-omened—or, redeemed from the number of human beings by God. They are also unbelievable, that is, incapable of believing because of the excess of their impiety. They are also rejected for every good work, because they perform nothing that has the appearance of goodness. Often, indeed, some unbelievers do things which, although not truly good, nevertheless appear to be good.

## CHAPTER II

“But you speak the things that are fitting for sound doctrine: that old men be sober, chaste, prudent, sound in faith, in love, and in patience; that old women likewise be in holy conduct, not slanderers, not enslaved to much wine, teaching what is good, so that they may teach the young women to love their husbands, to love their children, to be prudent, chaste, sober, caring for their households, kind, submissive to their husbands, so that the word of God may not be blasphemed.

“Likewise exhort young men to be sober. In all things present yourself as an example of good works, in doctrine, integrity, and seriousness. Let your speech be sound and irreproachable, so that the one who is opposed may fear [variant: be overcome], having nothing evil to say about us.

“Teach servants to be submissive to their masters, pleasing them in all things, not contradicting, not defrauding, but showing complete good faith, so that in all things they may adorn the doctrine of God our Savior. For the grace of God our Savior has appeared to all people, teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly desires, we should live soberly, justly, and piously in this age, awaiting the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ.

“He gave himself for us, so that he might redeem us from every iniquity and cleanse for himself an acceptable people, a follower of good works. Speak these things, exhort, and rebuke with all authority. Let no one despise you.”

## EXPOSITION

The rejected act perversely in this way; but you should not act in this way. Rather, speak what it is fitting to speak: sound doctrine. Speak this to old men, so that old men may be sober, not devoted to drinking. Let them also be chaste, that is, continent. Let them be prudent, so that they may know how to teach the younger. Let them be sound in faith and sound in love, so that they may love everyone else as they love their own household.

Let them also be sound in patience, not suffering insults in such a way that they are unable to endure reproaches. Likewise admonish old women to be in holy conduct, that is, conduct which indicates their holiness, and not to be slanderers, that is, not to bring accusations against anyone—a vice particularly characteristic of old women.

Let them not be enslaved to much wine, but let them teach what is good. Nor should they teach in the church or teach men; rather, I speak in such a way that they should teach the young women prudence—specifically, that they love their husbands and not adulterers, and that they love their children with all care, nurturing them.

Let them teach the young women to be prudent, chaste, and sober both in food and in adornment, and to care for the household, that is, to labor with their husbands to manage the family well. Let them also teach them to be kind in distributing alms and submissive to their husbands, not exercising authority over men.

Admonish that all these things be done so that the word, that is, the preaching, of God may not be blasphemed. For if women were arrogant toward their husbands, if they were unchaste, and so forth, foolish people would suppose that such conduct belonged to Christian doctrine, and for that reason they would blaspheme the word of God.

Likewise exhort young men to be sober and temperate. But so that you may correct everyone suitably, present yourself as an example of good works to others—not in some works but in all works. Present yourself, I say, as an example to them in doctrine, so that you may teach what is useful to your hearers; and in the integrity of all virtues, so that you may be complete and upright in good things; and teach with seriousness, that is, with severity and pontifical authority.

Let the word of your doctrine be sound, containing no admixture of unbelief; let it also be irreproachable, so that no occasion for reproach can arise from it. This is useful so that the one who is opposed, that is, the unbelieving adversary, may fear to speak evil of us, having nothing from which he can speak evil.

Exhort servants also to be submissive to their masters, so that they do not become arrogant against them. Rather, let them please their masters well in all things commanded them, not contradicting them in anything and not defrauding them either of goods entrusted to them or of labor commanded them—for example, wasting their time when they ought to work—[Col. 0480A] but showing in all their actions that the Christian faith is good, that is, useful. By acting in this way, they adorn in all things the doctrine of God our Savior.

For when servants who have become faithful do not steal but serve their masters more devotedly, the doctrine of God is thereby adorned and praised, since it instructed faithful servants to be submissive to their masters.

Therefore I urge you to labor in all things, whether they are servants or masters, old or young, because God appeared for the salvation of all. He appeared when the Word of the Father, having become flesh in the Virgin’s womb, made himself visible to human beings. I say that the grace of God appeared, that is, God through grace, not because of human merits but through mercy alone. I mean our Savior, God.

And just as he appeared for our salvation, since we have now been justified through faith, so he appeared for the salvation of all people. Therefore you must labor in all things.

And because God’s appearing would not be sufficient for salvation unless we were instructed by the same one, he says that God appeared through grace, teaching all of us this: that, denying ungodliness, that is, the worship of idols, and denying worldly desires, that is, desires supplied by the world and whose cause is the world, we should live soberly—that is, temperately in ourselves—and justly toward our neighbor, and piously toward God.

We should live in this way even in this fragile body, in which it is scarcely possible to live justly, awaiting, by living soberly, justly, and piously, the blessed hope, that is, the blessedness hoped for, and awaiting the appearing of the glory of Jesus Christ—that is, when Christ, who first appeared in humility in order to instruct us, will come in glory to judge the world.

I mean Christ, the great God and our Savior, because then at the judgment, whether they wish to or not, they will confess him to be the great God and Savior of the saints, coming with great power and majesty—those who until that day never confessed that Christ is God.

Between these two appearances, Christ Jesus gave himself for us, in order to redeem us from every iniquity, that is, both from the weakness of the flesh and from the power and suggestion of the devil. Before Christ redeemed us on the cross, we could not resist the devil, his suggestion, or the weakness of our flesh. Unless God delivered us from this danger, even if he cleansed us from all sins, it would nevertheless profit us nothing unless he also gave us the power to resist the devil’s suggestions and the weakness of the flesh.

For if the devil was able to overthrow the first man, created with such great strength, how much more easily can he overthrow one weighed down by so many miseries of suffering and mortality?

He also gave himself to cleanse us from every sin, whether original or actual, in baptism. I mean us, made an acceptable people for himself after the cleansing of baptism, a people zealous for good works. First he rescued us from the dominion of the devil and from the weakness of the flesh; then he cleansed us from every sin—and he did both in baptism. Afterwards, by the performance of good works, he makes us acceptable to God.

Speak and teach those who do not know these things just mentioned—namely, that God appeared through grace and will come in judgment with glory, and so forth. Exhort those who know them, so that they may prepare themselves worthy of the second appearing. But if, after being admonished, they refuse to obey, rebuke them with all authority, that is, with episcopal severity, so that no one despises you—that is, so that your excessive humility does not produce contempt for pontifical authority.

## CHAPTER III
> “Remind them to be subject to rulers and authorities, to obey commands, to be ready for every good work; to slander no one, not to be quarrelsome, but moderate, showing every gentleness toward all people. For we ourselves were once foolish and unbelieving, [Col. 0481B] wandering astray, enslaved to various desires and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful and hating one another. But when the kindness and humanity of God our Savior appeared, he saved us—not from works of righteousness that we had done, but according to his mercy—through the bath of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out upon us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Savior, so that, having been justified by his grace, we might be heirs according to the hope of eternal life. This saying is trustworthy. And concerning these things I want you to affirm strongly, so that those who believe in God may take care to devote themselves to good works. These things are good and useful for people. But avoid foolish questions, genealogies, quarrels, and [Col. 0481C] disputes about the law. For they are useless and futile. Avoid a heretical person after one [or: the first] and a second admonition, knowing that such a person is perverted and sins, being self-condemned. When I send Artemas or Tychicus to you, hasten to come to me at Nicopolis. For I have decided to winter there. Carefully send ahead Zenas the lawyer and Apollos, so that nothing may be lacking for them. Let our people also learn to devote themselves to good works for necessary uses, so that they may not be unfruitful. All who are with me greet you. Greet those who love us in the faith. The grace of God be with all of you. Amen.”

## EXPOSITION

Lest Titus, because Paul had said that they were subject to every authority, should suppose that the people entrusted to him ought to be subject only to him and not to the authorities of the world, Paul removes this misunderstanding by saying: “Remind them”—the Cretans—“to be subject to the rulers of the world,” such as kings and the other authorities, by paying them the tribute and taxes owed to them.

Remind them also to obey commands—that is, the orders of their rulers—and yet not for a wicked work; rather, let them be ready for every good work commanded them by their rulers. For if their rulers ordered them to go to the worship of an idol, or to anything wicked, they ought not to go: “For we must obey God rather than human beings” (Acts 5:29).

Remind them also not to slander any of their masters, and not to be quarrelsome—that is, not to contend against their masters—but to be moderate and well-disciplined, showing every [Col. 0482A] gentleness and humility not only toward their masters but also toward all people.

For this reason I want everyone to obey even unbelieving masters: perhaps those who are unbelievers now will soon become believers, as we did. For we ourselves were once—that is, shortly before—foolish, even if we were wise according to the world. And because we had no understanding of the knowledge of God, we were therefore unbelieving, possessing no faith in God.

We were also wandering astray—that is, sinning—and enslaved to desires. For if we desired money or honors, we served these ambitions with great labor in order to obtain them. We were also enslaved to the various pleasures of the flesh, that is, according to all the senses. Whatever the eye saw or the ear heard, the hand labored to grasp.

He says that we were living in malice because, although we were capable of evil, we inflicted it upon our neighbors. He says that we were also living in envy because, when we could no longer do more, we envied our neighbors. He says that we were hateful to others, and conversely hating others, going toward one another—that is, in repayment of hatred.

Such were we formerly. But when the kindness of God—that is, God acting through kindness—and the humanity of God appeared, he indicates why and through what this happened: namely, on account of kindness and through humanity. God, because of his kindness, appeared to the world through the humanity united to the Word of the Father.

He says “of God our Savior,” because he appeared for us, and likewise for the salvation of those who are still unbelievers. Nor did this happen because of works of righteousness that we had once performed—that is, we had never earned this, that God should appear—but according to his mercy God saved us through the bath of regeneration, that is, through baptism, in which the first generation, which exists in sins, is destroyed, and a second, spiritual generation is received.

He says also “through the bath of renewal.” For baptism, because it comes first, makes us such that, growing daily toward what is better, we are renewed more and more, in accordance with the saying: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind” (Ephesians 4:23).

Hence he says “of regeneration” through the removal of evils, and “of renewal” through the establishment of good things. Both regeneration and renewal are the work of the Holy Spirit: through the Holy Spirit sins are forgiven and virtues are received.

God poured out this Holy Spirit upon us abundantly—that is, sufficiently [Col. 0482D] for the forgiveness of all offenses. He poured him out, I say, through Jesus Christ our Savior; this is understood according to his humanity. For God, who was in that man, gave the Holy Spirit through that man, so that, justified by the grace of that same God, we might be heirs of eternal life. And this is “according to hope,” that is, according to what we hope for while we remain held in this world.

This saying that I have mentioned—namely, that we are saved through the bath of regeneration and will become heirs of eternal life—is trustworthy and fully credible. Therefore, concerning the things I have mentioned, I want you, Titus, to confirm the Cretans, so that, believing these things firmly, they may take care to devote themselves to good works. If they are doing good works today, let them strive to surpass today’s good works by doing better works tomorrow.

Those who believe in God should also take care to surpass others by giving an example of good things. And these things—namely, devotion to good works—are good for those very people and useful for those who imitate them.

Confirm the Cretans in these matters. But avoid foolish questions, genealogies, quarrels that contend with one another about the interpretation of the Scriptures, and disputes about the law—that is, matters that appear to contradict one another. Whatever is of this kind, avoid it. For such questions are useless, without any fruit, and—what is worse—futile, that is, without truth. Avoid these questions.

Avoid also a heretical person, that is, one divided from the unity of the faith. Avoid him, I say, if he has proved incorrigible after one—that is, a first—and a second admonition. For if, after being admonished twice, he has not repented, such a person—that is, a heretic—[Col. 0483B] is perverted. He does not act through ignorance, but knowingly and deliberately puts his hand into the fire. Such a person sins by his own judgment—that is, by his own deliberate decision, with no one forcing him—and therefore is condemned by God.

Note that from this passage it is gathered that if someone falls into error imprudently and does not defend his error, he is not to be judged a heretic. Only the person who asserts and defends as incorrigible what he believes wrongly concerning the faith—and this is the worse course—is a heretic.

If for this reason we deny that the Simonians are heretics, since they know that they are acting wrongly and do not approve their conduct but are blinded by ambition, the following objection is made: their intention when purchasing the gifts of the Holy Spirit with money is unknown. For hidden things of the heart have been revealed to God alone. Yet, according to what we see in their outward actions, we judge their inward dispositions.

Because we see them remaining in the episcopate, which they obtained by payment, we judge them as people who believe that the Holy Spirit can be possessed by money. If they say that they purchased only temporal benefits and not consecration, and therefore are not Simonians, they hold a far worse opinion.

For it is written: “Let him who has separated himself be called anathema.” Just as body and soul cannot be separated so that one of them may live, so a temporal benefit cannot be separated from a spiritual one in a bishop. The same must be understood of ecclesiastical orders and temporal honors.

After teaching Titus about ecclesiastical matters, Paul writes to him about certain private matters, saying: “When I send Artemas or Tychicus to you, Titus, hasten to come to me at Nicopolis; for I have decided to winter there.”

Before you come, send Zenas, learned in the law—whether divine Scripture or secular law—and Apollos with him. Send them ahead carefully, that is, well provided for, giving them what they need. I say “carefully,” so that nothing may be lacking for them.

If you ask where you should obtain these things, I also want our Cretans now to learn to devote themselves to good works, improving from day to day. Let them devote themselves in this way: by administering what is necessary for the preachers’ needs, so that these Cretans may not be unfruitful toward their teachers, but may supply whatever is necessary for their use.

“For the laboring farmer ought first to receive a share of the fruits” (2 Timothy 2:6).

All who are with me greet you, and you should greet those who love us in the faith—that is, the faithful. May the grace of [Col. 0484C] God be with all of you. Amen.

# [IN THE EPISTLE TO PHILEMON]

[Col. 0483]

## ARGUMENT OF THE EPISTLE TO PHILEMON

He writes a personal letter to Philemon on behalf of Onesimus, his slave, sending it to him from the city of Rome, from prison, through Onesimus himself.

## BLESSED BRUNO’S PROLOGUE TO THE SAME

[Col. 0483D] Paul writes a personal letter to Philemon, whom he had converted to the faith, while bound in prison at Rome. Taking occasion from this—that a certain slave of Philemon, Onesimus, while still an unbeliever, had secretly fled from his master and secretly carried away some of his master’s money—Paul addresses him. While absent from his master, Onesimus came to Paul in prison at Rome. There, having received the word of faith, he was baptized by Paul and thereafter served Paul, perhaps also from the stolen money. Wishing to reconcile him, Paul sends the slave back to his master with this Epistle. In it he deals with Philemon, entreating him by many and varied arguments to forgive the slave for what he had done. In this matter Paul intends to instruct us that we ought to pray for an offender if he has repented, and that the offender should be spared by the one who possesses authority, if he has fled for refuge to mercy.

# EPISTLE TO PHILEMON

[Col. 0483]

[Col. 0483D]

> “Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus, and Timothy the brother, to Philemon, our beloved helper, and to Apphia our most beloved sister, and to Archippus our fellow soldier, and to the church that is in your house. Grace to you [Col. 0484D] and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. I give thanks to my God, always making mention of you in my prayers, hearing of your love and of the faith that you have in the Lord Jesus and toward all the saints, so that the fellowship of your faith [Col. 0485A] may become evident in the recognition of every good work that is in Christ Jesus. For I have had great joy and consolation in your love, because the hearts of the saints have found rest through you, brother.

> “Therefore, having great confidence in Christ Jesus to command you concerning what is fitting, I appeal to you rather on account of love, since you are such a person as Paul, an old man, and now also a prisoner of Jesus Christ. I appeal to you for my son, whom I begot in chains, Onesimus, who was once useless to you but now is useful both to me and to you; I have sent him back to you. You, then, receive him as my own heart [my most beloved son]. I had wished to keep him with me, so that he might serve me on your behalf in the chains of the Gospel.

> “But without your advice I wished to do nothing, so that your good might not be as though compelled, [Col. 0485B] but voluntary. For perhaps he departed from you for a time for this reason, so that you might receive him forever—not now as a slave, but in place of a slave, as a most beloved brother, especially to me. How much more to you, both in the flesh and in the Lord? Therefore, if you consider me a partner, receive him as you would receive me.

> “But if he has harmed you in anything or owes you anything, charge it to me. I, Paul, have written this with my own hand. I will repay it—not to mention that you owe me even yourself. Yes, brother, may I benefit from you in the Lord; refresh my heart in Christ [the Lord]. Confident in your obedience, I have written to you, knowing that you will do even more than I say. At the same time, prepare lodging for me. 354 For I hope that through your prayers I shall be granted to you.

> “Epaphras, my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus, greets you, and Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke, my fellow workers. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Amen.”

## EXPOSITION

“Paul a prisoner,” and so forth. In order to move Philemon more quickly to mercy, Paul suppresses here the titles of his dignity—such as “apostle of Christ”—and introduces instead the names of the sufferings that he endured, saying: “Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus,” whom it is more serious to offend because he is being oppressed by imprisonment.

Paul would seem to Philemon to be contemptible, or Philemon would seem to have no compassion at all, if, hearing that Paul was imprisoned, he closed the heart of mercy toward the slave for whom Paul was pleading. Paul was not imprisoned on account of his own fault, but for Christ Jesus.

And so that Philemon might forgive more quickly the more people he saw pleading with him, Paul says: “Paul and Timothy, brothers, write to Philemon,” in a certain spiritual fellowship. They write not only to the beloved, but also to “our helper,” who does not cease to help and support our faithful people from his own resources.

Paul and Timothy also write to Apphia, Philemon’s wife, “our sister” according to the faith and, by a certain special bond of affection, “most beloved.” The Apostle writes to the woman so that, seeing the Apostle do for her what was not customary toward her sex, she might approach her husband and bend him toward sparing the slave.

They also write to Archippus, the son of Apphia and Philemon, “our fellow soldier,” for he serves God with us in preaching. This is the Archippus who established the Colossians in the faith. Paul greets him in this Epistle so that he might kindly urge his parents to forgive Onesimus.

They also write to “the church,” that is, the household summoned to the faith of Christ, which is the church in your house. Thus he greets the entire household, calling it by so honorable a name, “the church,” so that the whole household might intercede with Philemon on behalf of Onesimus, saying: “To all of you—the father of the household, the mother, the son, and the household—may there be grace,” that is, forgiveness of sins, “and peace,” that is, tranquility of mind. May these things, I say, be yours from God our Father, who both can and wills, and from the Lord Jesus Christ, who likewise both wills and can.

To make the Apostle more likely to be heard, he says: “I hear of your love,” that is, your love of God and neighbor. He also hears of “the faith” by which Philemon perseveres in the faith of Christ. He placed love first because he intended to move him to forgive his neighbor.

This love he has “in the Lord Jesus,” in him who is the foundation of love, and he also has it “toward all the saints,” that is, toward all who have been sanctified through baptism. Therefore love and goodness ought also to be shown toward Onesimus, who has been sanctified in the faith.

Hearing this, Paul gives thanks to his God, always making mention of Philemon in his prayers. For Paul gives thanks for the good things already granted, and prays that they may always increase, so that “the fellowship of your faith”—that is, your faith, which shares your good things with the saints—“may become evident,” so that all may see it to be present, “in the recognition of every good thing.” That is, through faith may you advance toward every good thing, and may that good be recognized by all. Thus he prays for the increase of Philemon’s love.

For Paul has had great joy, and with his joy consolation, in Philemon’s love—that is, in the administration of his love. He has both rejoiced and been consoled because “the hearts of the saints”—that is, those converted through the preaching of the saints—have found rest through Philemon, who administered to them.

O brother Philemon, they have had great rest through you, because you drove away their cold and hunger. Therefore—that is, because you have been accustomed to show such love toward the saints—Paul, having great confidence, not merely because he has deserved such confidence, but “in Christ Jesus,” can command Philemon.

For Paul can, if he wishes, command him by the authority of his apostleship, received from Christ Jesus, concerning what is fitting—that is, concerning what is useful to Philemon. Paul can compel him to do what is useful, if he chooses; but, setting aside a command, he appeals to him on account of love rather than commands him on account of authority.

And Philemon ought to be entreated by Paul because he is such a person as Paul—that is, an old man. Similar age urges an old man to agree with an old man. But what invites him even more strongly to listen is that Paul is now, at the time when he makes his appeal, a prisoner of Jesus Christ. Whoever does not hear him in his chains certainly offends Jesus Christ, for whom Paul is imprisoned.

“I appeal to you,” he says, “for my son whom I begot in chains.” Just as parents who begot a son in prison would value him more because he was born amid their hardships, so Paul commends Onesimus, whom he baptized while imprisoned, and who was not ashamed of the faith of Christ because of Paul’s chains. After presenting this extensive commendation, he adds his name at the end.

“I appeal,” he says, “for the son whom I spiritually begot, namely Onesimus, who was once useless to you, having secretly fled from you when he was an unbeliever, but who is now a believer and was useful to me by serving me in my chains, and through this is useful to you. Whatever good he did is owed to you, since he is your slave and perhaps your money was involved.”

Paul sent Onesimus back to Philemon with this Epistle. “You, then, receive him as my own heart,” that is, know that he is in my heart. If you do not receive him, you reject my heart.

Paul had wished to keep Onesimus with him, for he would have been necessary to him, serving him while he was detained in “the chains of the Gospel,” that is, the chains he suffered on account of the Gospel that he preached. This service would have been for Philemon’s benefit. For if Philemon’s slave, taken away from him, had served Paul, he would have acquired a reward for Philemon, who was his master.

But although Onesimus was necessary to Paul, and would have been useful to Philemon if he had been taken away to serve Paul, Paul nevertheless wished to do none of this without Philemon’s advice. He did this so that Philemon’s good might not be “as though from necessity,” that is, something he wanted or did not want but was compelled to do, but voluntary.

Philemon ought to receive him because he departed from him for a time, perhaps for this reason: so that Philemon might now receive him as one who would remain with him forever. If Onesimus had persisted in unbelief and had always stood before Philemon, he would have been with him only in this world, which is short; for Onesimus would have been counted among the impious when he died, while Philemon would have been with the just. But now, because Onesimus is faithful, he will remain with Philemon both now and in the future. Paul says “perhaps” because God’s ordering is uncertain to human beings.

Philemon should no longer have Onesimus merely as a slave, but as a most beloved brother in the Lord, “in place of a slave.” Or the meaning may be that he should have him as a brother, more than as a slave—that is, more than he would have had a most beloved slave. Onesimus is certainly most beloved to Paul. If he is so dear to Paul, to whom he is a brother only in God, how much more ought he to be dear to Philemon, both in the flesh, according to which he is his slave, and in the Lord, in whom he is Philemon’s brother?

Since Onesimus is so dear to Paul, Philemon should receive him as Paul himself, if he wishes to have Paul as a partner. For if he hates one who is his neighbor, certainly he does not love God; and one who does not love God ought to have no fellowship with him.

Perhaps Philemon might say: “Let him return what he took, and I will forgive him.” It is indeed just to release him, but Christian religion does not forbid demanding the money.

Paul answers this: “Receive him. But if he has harmed you in anything by withdrawing from you, or if he owes you anything that he carried away without your knowledge, do not for that reason show him any less mercy. Charge all of it to me, as though I were the debtor.”

Philemon should and may charge it to Paul. “I, Paul, have written this with my own hand. I will repay you what Onesimus owes.” Paul says “with my own hand” because he placed certain signs in his letters so that no one who saw them could doubt that they were his.

Philemon should not refuse to charge to Paul what Onesimus owes, “not to mention,” he says to Philemon, who is hardened and unwilling to forgive, that Philemon owes Paul not merely this but also himself. Paul had authority over those whom he had converted to the faith, including authority over their possessions.

So that Philemon would not dare to offer a denial, Paul adds an adjuration, saying: “Brother Philemon, may I so benefit from you in the Lord if you forgive Onesimus.” This resembles Horace: “So may the powerful goddess...” (3.1). Therefore, “refresh my heart,” that is, Onesimus, “in Christ Jesus,” that is, for Christ’s sake. Do this, namely, refresh him.

Paul has written all these things to Philemon, confident in his obedience. He is confident that Philemon will obey him in these matters, and knows that Philemon will do for Onesimus what Paul says, and even more than he requests. Philemon will not merely forgive him, but, after restoring his favor to him, will provide whatever he may need.

“Do this. At the same time, together with these commands, prepare lodging for me. For I hope that through your prayers I shall be granted to you.” By saying that he will come, Paul also induces Philemon to show mercy to the slave. If, when Paul arrived, he found the master without mercy, he would correct him more severely.

“Epaphras greets you in Christ Jesus,” or “my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus,” since he suffers captivity together with Paul for the sake of Christ Jesus. Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke, Paul’s fellow workers, also greet Philemon.

“May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit,” that is, with Philemon and his household. Amen. As at the beginning, so at the end, Paul greets everyone, so that he might soften everyone’s feelings toward Onesimus.

# [IN THE EPISTLE TO THE HEBREWS]

[Col. 0487]

## ARGUMENT OF THE EPISTLE TO THE HEBREWS

First it must be said why the Apostle Paul, in writing this Epistle, did not follow his usual practice of setting out either his name or the dignity of his office. The reason is that he was writing to those who had believed from circumcision, as the apostle of the Gentiles and not of the Hebrews. He also knew their pride, and, demonstrating his own humility, he did not wish to put forward the merit of his office.

The apostle John likewise, for the sake of humility, did not place his name at the beginning of his Epistle, for the same reason. This Epistle, therefore, is said to have been sent by the Apostle to the Hebrews in the Hebrew language. Luke the Evangelist is said to have composed it in Greek after the Apostle Paul’s death, preserving its meaning and arrangement.

## BLESSED BRUNO’S PROLOGUE TO THE SAME

[Col. 0487D] There were churches in Judea established in the faith of Christ. Christ himself had preached to them, and they had received the faith through the teaching of his apostles, to whom, when he ascended, he had entrusted the establishment of churches. They rightly believed concerning Christ his incarnation, death, resurrection, and the rest. But they were greatly mistaken in this: they observed circumcision and certain legal prescriptions, believing that no one could be saved without them, and thereby detracting from the eminence and faith of Christ.

In addition, they produced many plausible arguments, namely, that Christ had been born under the law and had observed the law in every respect. Whenever he was accused of relaxing the law, he gave reasons that he did not violate it in anything. Thus, when they objected to him that by healing on the Sabbath he did not observe the Sabbath, he gave this reason: “If, on the Sabbath, you lead away an ox or an ass that you have loosed to water without violating the law, how am I violating the law by loosing a human being from a demon?” (Luke 13:15.)

They did not remember that Christ had brought that law to an end when he celebrated the old Passover and immediately afterward consecrated the new Passover—namely, the new sacrifice—handing his body and blood to his apostles and showing that whatever had preceded had been a shadow, whereas now he was handing over the truth for the first time.

They continued to hold circumcision together with faith in Christ because they had seen Christ observe the law, and because Peter and the others, who had preached to Jews attached to circumcision and such legal observances, had not compelled them to abandon these practices. They feared their impatience, since they would rather abandon the whole faith than renounce the practices to which they were accustomed.

For Peter and the others knew that, having thus nourished them in infancy, they could not otherwise lead them to the maturity of perfection. For this reason, then, they retained circumcision together with faith in Christ.

But Paul, seeing that Christ was useless to them so long as they held the law together with faith, according to what he says to the Galatians—“If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing” (Galatians 5:2)—wrote this Epistle to them out of an abundance of concern, although he was solely the apostle of the Gentiles. He acted according to what he says to the Romans: “I will magnify my ministry, if somehow I may provoke my flesh to emulation” (Romans 11:14), and so forth.

Therefore, because he was not their apostle, he did not wish to place the titles of his dignity before the Epistle, as he usually does in each of his letters.

[Col. 0490A] He also kept these things silent because they hated him, since he persecuted the law and everywhere destroyed it. Hence they often accused him, charging him with saying that the law had not been given by God and had always been useless.

Therefore, in order to clear himself of these accusations, it was necessary for him to purify himself in Jerusalem according to Jewish rites and, after being purified, to go up into the temple (Acts 21:26; 24:18), and to circumcise Timothy his disciple (Acts 16:3).

If, when they hated him as a persecutor of their law, he had placed the titles of his dignity before the Epistle, they would have objected at the outset, saying that they ought not to listen to their enemy, even if he argued reasonably. To avoid these objections, he made no mention of his dignity.

It was as if he were saying: “No authority of mine compels you; rather, attend to the authorities of your law and your prophets, and from the law and the prophets themselves you will understand that the end of the law is in Christ.”

Because he did not place his name at the beginning, as he did elsewhere, some said that this Epistle was not Paul’s. Others said that it belonged to Barnabas, others to Luke, and others to Clement.

Jerome argues against them as follows: If, because it is not titled with Paul’s name, it is not Paul’s, then, because it is titled with no one’s name, it must belong to no one.

Luke translated this Epistle from Hebrew into Greek. Its subject is the eminence of Christ and the uselessness of the law, demonstrated through that same law and through the prophets, which had their end in Christ. The legal observances were of no benefit to anyone even at the time when they ought to have existed, except through faith in the one who was to come. Christ, however, is sufficient for justification, so that he does not need the help of the law; and if the law is mixed with faith, it makes faith void.

With this purpose he speaks of Christ and the law: so that the Jews may abandon the legal observances and seek and receive justification in the eminence of Christ.

Toward the end of the Epistle he also instructs them concerning morality, because, as was always a natural vice among the Jews, they were excessively indulgent in food and lust.

# EPISTLE TO THE HEBREWS

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0489D]

> “At many times and in many ways God formerly spoke to the fathers through the prophets; in these last days he has spoken to us in the Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom he also made the ages. He, being the radiance of glory and the representation of his substance, and sustaining all things by the word of his power, having made purification of sins, sits at the right hand of Majesty in the heights, having become so much superior to the angels as he has inherited a name more distinguished than theirs.
>
> “For to which of the angels did he ever say: ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you’? And again: ‘I will be a Father to him, and he will be a Son to me.’ And again, when he brings the Firstborn into the inhabited world, he says: ‘And let all the angels of God worship him.’ And to the angels he says: ‘He makes his angels spirits, [Col. 0490D] and his ministers a flame of fire.’ But to the Son: ‘Your throne, O God, is forever and ever, and the scepter of uprightness is the scepter of your kingdom. You loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, anointed you with the oil of exultation [joy] above your companions. And: ‘You, Lord, in the beginning founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands. They will perish, but you will remain; and they will all grow old like a garment. You will change them like a cloak, and they will be changed; but you are the same, and your years will not fail.’
>
> “But to which of the angels did he ever say: ‘Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet’?” (Psalm 109:1–2.) “Are they not all ministering spirits sent for service on behalf of those who are to inherit salvation?”

## EXPOSITION

[Col. 0491A]

“In many portions,” and so forth. At the beginning Paul intends to prove that Christ, the Son of God, must be heard, comparing him with the prophets. If the prophets had to be heard because God spoke through them as through an instrument, then the commands of Christ must be observed much more, since God spoke in him, as in the Son.

He again compares Christ with the angels, because if the words of the angels, spoken through the prophets, were observed, the words of Christ must be observed all the more, since he has become far superior to the angels.

All these things that he sets forth beforehand point toward the conclusion [inference] stated below, where he says: “Therefore we must pay much closer attention,” and so forth.

It is as though he were saying: “Observe what has been spoken by the Son. For God, who formerly spoke to our fathers”—that is, to the earlier Jews, who are our fathers both according to the flesh and in the worship of God—“spoke to the fathers through the prophets.”

The things they spoke were not the prophets’ own, but belonged to God, who spoke through them as through an instrument.

They strongly opposed Paul on this point, saying that God was unchangeable. It could not be denied that God had given the law; therefore the law ought to be unchangeable, since it had been given by the one who could not change.

“Formerly,” I say, “God spoke to the fathers through the prophets at many times,” that is, many times, if we do not insist on the exact placement of the word. He spoke many times because he spoke to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and to each of them on many occasions.

He also spoke in many ways: sometimes through dreams, as to Daniel; sometimes with an open voice, as to Moses; sometimes through inward inspiration, as to David.

Or *multifariam* (“at many times”) means by a different kind of speech: to one in a dream, to another with an open word, and to another by inward inspiration. For this reason he spoke in different ways. If everything had been heard only in a dream, what had been heard in that way might have been thought empty. But when one received an open utterance, another a dream, and another an inward inspiration, and all bore witness to the same thing and concerning the same one, they gave more certain faith through the many ways in which the matter was understood.

“At many times” (*multifariam*), I say, means through many kinds of speech, and “in many ways” means through different manifestations, as in the burning bush to Moses, in the dry and wet fleece to Gideon, and similarly in many other cases.

God, who formerly spoke to the fathers through the prophets, has spoken to us in the Son.

With reference to that earlier time he uses the present participle “speaking,” while with reference to what was almost present he uses the past tense “has spoken.” He signifies that the Son speaks the same thing that God spoke through the prophets, except that in the prophets the truth was hidden and still had to be fulfilled, whereas in the Son the truth was open and fulfilled.

When he says that God, speaking to the fathers, has spoken to us, the children of those same fathers, he indicates that God did not speak different things to the same people. If he had spoken to the Jews through the prophets but through the Son only to the Gentiles, one might suppose that he had spoken different things to different peoples.

“He has spoken to us in these last days,” since many still remain who both heard and saw him speaking.

Or it may be understood in this way: “He has spoken in these days,” as has been said.

I say that he has spoken in the last days because this speech of God through the Son was the final form of his speaking, not to be altered later by any new form of speech. He who formerly spoke through the prophets has spoken finally because, by speaking the truth in the Son, he was going to destroy the shadow that he had spoken through the prophets.

And if you listened to the prophets because God spoke through the prophets, observe all the more what you have heard concerning God in the Son.

Now he begins to magnify the Son, speaking sometimes according to his humanity, sometimes according to his divinity, and sometimes according to both substances together.

He says: God the Father appointed this Son—that is, firmly established him—as heir of all things, that is, as the permanent possessor of everything. He is not an heir in the sense that his Father had died, as happens under human laws, but an heir according to what the same Son says: “Everything that the Father has is mine” (John 16:15).

This appointment was made in him insofar as he is human, although according to his divinity all fullness existed in him from eternity.

Through him he also made not only the heavenly things but the ages—that is, all the worldly things that you see—according to the saying: “You made everything in Wisdom” (Psalm 103:24).

This is said of the Son according to his divinity.

The Son, then, is “the radiance of glory,” that is, of the divine substance of the Father. That divinity is called “glory” by excellence, and in comparison with it nothing appears glorious.

The Son, I say, is the radiance of glory because, just as a ray signifies that the sun shines, so the Son is the ray who makes the Father known. Yet he is not something other than the Father, just as a ray is not something other than the sun.

This is said of the Son according to both natures, but especially according to his divinity.

The Son is also “the representation of his substance,” that is, the full manifestation of the Father’s essence. “Representation” does not mean that he is different from the Father, but that he is the same: the Son has the same substance as the Father. This is said according to the divine nature alone.

He also sustains all things, because just as they could not have been created except through the Son, so, once created, they could not continue to exist except through the Son.

He sustains all things “by the word,” that is, by will alone, just as we would judge any king powerful who governed his kingdom by his word alone.

He sustains all things, I say, “by the word of his power,” that is, by his powerful word.

All these things still meant nothing to them, because they might say: “What benefit is it to us if all things were made through him, if he is the radiance of glory, and so forth?” To this Paul replies:

[Col. 0492D] “The Son,” I say, “who makes purification for sins,” that is, cleansing human beings from sins; and that he can purify is demonstrated by what precedes: all things are said to have been made and sustained through him, and he is of the same substance as the Father, and so forth. The Jews also confessed this in the time of the Law, when they said to Christ himself: “Who can forgive sins except God alone?” (Mark 2:7). Here they plainly showed that no one could be saved from sins through the Law.

“Making purification for sins”: this was said of the Son according to his divinity. Since the Son is such and such, he sits at the right hand of Majesty, that is, at the equality of the Father’s greatness. For “Majesty” means the essence of God. Nor does he sit in that paradise from which Adam was driven; rather, he sits in the heights of heaven, placed at the Father’s right hand. This is said according to his humanity.

Now he compares the Son with the angels, yet in such a way as to place him far above them, saying: “The Son,” I say, “having become so much better than the angels as he has inherited a more distinguished name,” that is, greater honor after he rose and ascended. It is “more distinguished” because, while he was still capable of suffering and mortal, he had a different name: the angels ministered to him (Matt. 4:11); but after ascending, he possessed a much more distinguished name. And because it could be “more distinguished” without yet being above the angels, he says “more distinguished” in such a way that it is above those angels.

Truly he inherited a name superior to the angels. For the Father’s voice said to him: “You are my Son” (Ps. 2:7), which he said to none of the angels. But for greater confirmation he says this in the form of a question: “To which of the angels did he ever say”—that is, neither before they were confirmed nor after they were confirmed through the fall of the others—“I say, did he say: You are my consubstantial Son, not an adopted son; for I have begotten you today” (ibid.), that is, in eternity?

Because of the weakness of our understanding, when he used “today”—a term indicating the present time—he put “I have begotten” in the past tense, lest, if he said “Today I beget you,” we should suppose that he was not begotten eternally from the Father. Therefore he said “I have begotten,” in accordance with our weakness; “today,” according to divinity, in which there is nothing past and nothing future, but everything there is present today.

And again: “To which of the angels did he ever say this?”—or, without the question. Again the Father says this concerning the Son. Where he says “again” concerning the same one, he indicates that it was said of him. The Father says: “I will be a father to him,” that is, for his honor, “and he shall be a son to me” (2 Sam. 7:14), for my glorification. He used “I will be” and “he shall be” not because this Father was not Father, and that one Son, from eternity, but with regard to the common knowledge of human beings. He was not then Father to them, nor was this one then Son; but on the day of judgment he will be Father and he will be Son, when all the ungodly recognize Christ to be Christ, the Son of God—something they denied while living. These two statements were made concerning Christ according to his divinity.

And again the Father says concerning the same Son: “Let all the angels of God adore him” (Ps. 96:7); but he first indicates when this was said. “When the Father introduces,” that is, shows that he is to introduce, “his Firstborn, his Christ, into the world.” He says “introduces” because he was led into the innermost places of hearts. When, I say, he shows that he is to be introduced, he says: “Let all the angels of God adore him,” namely, the Son according to his human nature. This too must be understood of him after the resurrection.

The preceding statement, “I will be a Father to him,” is found in Isaiah; it is also found in the Psalm “The Mercies of the Lord,” where the same meaning is expressed: “He shall call upon me: You are my Father” (Ps. 88:27). The following statement, “Let them adore him,” is found in the Psalm: “The Lord has reigned; let the earth rejoice” (Ps. 96:7), except that there it reads “Adore,” whereas here it reads “Let them adore.”

The Father also speaks concerning the same Son in relation to the angels: “He makes his heavenly spirits angels,” that is, he sends his messengers wherever he pleases. And not only those of lower rank, but also “a flame of fire,” that is, the seraphim, whose order surpasses the others in dignity. He made them his ministers, also according to his human nature, serving him. This the Father says in relation to the angels.

But he says the same thing to the Son: “O God the Son, your throne,” that is, your judicial seat, “endures forever and ever.” And rightly so, because “the rod of your kingdom is a rod of equity,” that is, upright and inflexible justice. A king’s rod is straight, and for this reason it is usually made of bronze, so that it may signify upright and inflexible justice. This justice is upright and inflexible in Christ.

Again, rightly is your throne eternal, because you have loved justice, that is, you have embraced every good thing not under compulsion but out of love. And just as you have loved justice, so you have hated iniquity, that is, every evil. For some love justice in such a way that they nevertheless do not hate certain injustices.

And therefore, so that your throne might be eternal, so that the rod of equity might be yours, so that you might love justice—for all these things to exist in you—“O God the Son, God your God has anointed you”; that is, I, who am speaking, have anointed you. Others, such as David and Saul, were anointed through ministers; but Christ was anointed through the Father’s own operation.

“I have anointed you,” I say, “God your God,” who is consubstantial with you, “with oil,” that is, with the Holy Spirit, because just as oil nourishes the flesh, so the Holy Spirit cherishes and soothes the soul. “With oil,” I say, “of gladness.” It is rightly called “of gladness,” because that man, through the Spirit by whom he was conceived, remained free from sin.

Christ was anointed with the Holy Spirit in his mother’s womb. He received the Holy Spirit again at baptism, when the Spirit was seen above him in the form of a dove (Matt. 3:16)—not that he received the Spirit at baptism as though he needed a new justification, but to show that in baptism he would give the Holy Spirit to human beings for their justification.

“God has anointed you with the oil more than your companions,” that is, more than the apostles and the others who received the Holy Spirit. He is above them because Christ was conceived from the Holy Spirit, whereas all the others were conceived from the seed of the flesh. All these things were said of the Son according to his humanity.

The Father said these things concerning the Son; and again the prophet speaks to the Father concerning the same Son according to his divinity.

“O Lord Father, you founded the earth,” that is, you firmly established this Church, which is called “earth” in comparison with the higher Church of the angels. “You founded it,” I say, “in the beginning,” that is, through the Beginning, who is the Son, according to what he himself says concerning himself: “I am the beginning, who also speak to you” (John 8:25).

“You founded the earth and the heavens,” that is, the greater saints, such as the apostles, who pour out your mysteries upon their subjects. These, I say, you not only founded, but they should be called the proper work of your hands. For in the excellence of these people it is apparent that your hand has worked, just as any craftsman might say: “This outstanding image is my work,” but in one made less well he might not recognize himself, although both are his work.

“And the heavens themselves shall perish,” that is, whatever they will be according to their nature will be destroyed by death; “but you shall remain in them,” that is, justice and the other things that you will work in them will remain in them. “And all of them, whether heavens or earth, shall grow old,” that is, they will gradually be corrupted through the misery of the flesh.

[Col. 0495A] “They shall grow old,” I say, “and they shall perish like a garment,” that is, according to the body that is in them and surrounds the soul like a garment. “They shall perish, and you shall change them like a cloak,” that is, the body, which is like a cloak for the soul. You will change them after they have become incapable of suffering and immortal.

They will also be changed according to their souls, which will be made more glorious and will advance in the knowledge of God. “They shall perish and grow old, but you are the same,” that is, immutable, in contrast to the fact that they grow old; “and your years shall not fail,” that is, your eternity remains.

In contrast to the fact that they will perish through death, he is shown to be superior not only by what has already been said, as greater than the angels, but also by this statement made to the Son: “Sit at my right hand,” which was said to no angel. For “to which of the angels,” as we noted above concerning the same word, “did the Father ever say: Sit,” that is, judge and rest, “at my right hand,” that is, among my superior things, “until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet” (Ps. 109:1–2)—that is, so completely subjected to you as a footstool is subjected to feet? By “feet,” however, Christ’s humanity is understood, since it is the lowest part in him.

This complete subjection is to be accomplished at the last judgment according to the Son’s humanity. Truly he said this to no angel, what he said to the Son: “Sit at my right hand,” because the angels are ministers of the Son; but it is contrary to reason that they should be ministers of Christ and of the same dignity as he.

He says this as follows: It is therefore clear that this was not said to any of the angels, because all the angelic spirits, however many there are, are ministering spirits, that is, appointed to minister to Christ. And because certain ministers have been appointed whom masters do not dare command, he adds, to remove this objection: “They are ministering spirits,” I say, “sent out for service wherever it pleases him, even for the sake of those”—that is, for the sake of human beings.

It is clear that they are greatly subjected to Christ, at whose command they serve even human beings, who are lower than the angels. “For their sake,” I say, “who are to inherit salvation,” that is, who will possess eternal salvation as an inheritance, namely, as a possession firmly secured for them.

## CHAPTER II

> “Therefore we ought to observe all the more carefully the things we have heard, lest perhaps we drift away. For if the word spoken through angels was made firm, and every transgression and disobedience received a just recompense of reward, how shall we escape if we neglect so great a salvation? This salvation, having first begun to be proclaimed through the Lord, was confirmed to us by those who heard it, God bearing witness by signs and wonders and various powers, and by distributions of the Holy Spirit according to his own will.
>
> “For God did not subject the world to come, of which we speak, to angels. But someone testified in a certain place, saying: ‘What is man that you are mindful of him, or the son of man that you visit him? You made him a little lower than the angels; you crowned him with glory and honor, and you appointed him over the works of your hands. You subjected all things beneath his feet.’ For in subjecting all things to him, he left nothing that was not subject to him. But now we do not yet see all things subjected to him.
>
> “But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death, so that by the grace of God he might taste death for everyone. For it was fitting that he, for whom all things exist and through whom all things exist, who had led many sons into glory, should perfect the author of their salvation through suffering.
>
> “For the one who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all from one. For this reason he is not ashamed to call them brothers, saying: ‘I will proclaim your name to my brothers; in the midst of the Church I will praise you.’ And again: ‘I will put my trust in him.’ And again: ‘Behold, I and the children whom God has given me.’
>
> “Therefore, since the children shared in flesh and blood, he himself likewise partook of the same, so that through death he might destroy him who held the power of death, that is, the devil, and might free those who throughout their whole life were subject to slavery through fear of death. For he nowhere takes hold of angels, but he takes hold of the seed of Abraham.
>
> “Therefore he had to be made like his brothers in every respect, so that he might become a merciful and faithful High Priest before God, to make propitiation for the sins of the people. For in that in which he himself suffered and was tempted, he is able also to help those who are tempted.”

## EXPOSITION

He infers this from everything stated above. For to establish this he brought forward all these arguments, saying: Since God has spoken in the prophets and in the Son; since all things were made through the Son; since he is greater than the angels; since it was said to the Son, “Sit at my right hand,” which was said to no angel; therefore we ought to observe more carefully the things we have heard from the Son than those we have heard from the prophets.

We ought to hear the prophets abundantly, but the Son more abundantly, lest, by not hearing the Son, we drift away completely. We drift away daily through many miseries and sins; but if we do not observe Christ’s commandments, we drift away completely, because every good thing will slip away from us, and the punishment of all righteousness will remain for us.

He proved that the Son ought to be heard both because God spoke in the Son, just as he did in the prophets, and because the Son is greater than the angels; and he proved this through the testimonies of those same authorities. Now he says that the Son’s commandments must be observed because those who neglect the salvation proposed to them by the Son will not escape punishment.
