He proves it as follows: Truly, if we do not observe what we have heard from the Son, we shall drift away completely, that is, we shall be punished, because if the word of the angels brought punishment upon those who did not fulfill it, then the salvation of the Son, who is greater than the angels, will bring punishment upon those who neglect it.

This is how he puts it: “If the word”—that is, the manifestation of God’s will, whether in the Law or in the prophets—a word said to have been spoken through angels. For angels ministered both the Law to Moses and the other teachings to the prophets. Whatever they taught, if, I say, “this word was made firm,” that is, confirmed, as the Law given to Moses was confirmed by certain miracles, namely by the thunder heard there, and also by certain threats and promises.

If, I say, the word spoken through angels was made firm, then every transgression and disobedience received its recompense. He calls it “transgression” not only when someone abandons what is commanded in the Law, but also when someone acts against the Law—for example, one who is commanded to love his neighbor not only fails to love him but even kills him.

“Disobedience” means failing to fulfill what is commanded in the Law, even if one does nothing contrary to the Law—for example, one who is commanded to love but does not love. Therefore he says “every transgression and disobedience,” rather than “every transgressor and disobedient person,” signifying that a single transgression or act of disobedience does not escape punishment. A transgressor or disobedient person, however, can be guilty of many transgressions or acts of disobedience.

If, I say, every transgression and disobedience received “a recompense of reward,” that is, a reward repaid—“reward” means what is returned according to the quality of the deed, whether it is evil or good. “Recompense” signifies that as much as someone deserved, so much was returned to him. I say, a just recompense, because in recompensing in this way God acts according to justice. Do not suppose that he is so merciful that he forgets justice.

If, I say, transgression or disobedience of the word spoken through angels received a recompense of reward, how shall we escape that complete drifting away if we neglect—not, I say, if we become transgressors, but, what is less, if we merely neglect—that is, if we disdain to understand—not, I say, the word, but salvation?

For the word of Christ, believed by believers, is the efficient cause of salvation. I say, a salvation so great, that is, unfailing. This salvation has its beginning when sins are forgiven; it has its growth in the establishment of virtues; and its completion in eternal blessedness.

Nor does the fact that they cannot object that they heard this salvation from those who were far removed from them make them inexcusable. He says: This salvation, when it received its beginning—not its institution, since it had been ordained from eternity that it should happen in this way—but the beginning of its proclamation through the Lord of angels, that is, through Christ, whom Christ began to proclaim as this salvation, was then confirmed to us, that is, to you Jews, by those who heard it from Christ’s own mouth, namely through the apostles, whose righteousness and authority commended the firmness of this salvation to you.

It was confirmed, I say, with God bearing witness. The apostles themselves sufficiently bore witness to it by their authority, but God also bore witness together with them through signs and wonders.

He calls “signs” such things as driving away illnesses, which medical skill might accomplish. “Wonders,” however, are things contrary to nature, such as opening the eyes of one born blind and raising Lazarus; these also signified something else.

He also says that God bore witness through various powers. Here he means true virtues, such as justice, prudence, and the like, which he supplied to his faithful people. He also bore witness through distributions, that is, through distributions of the Holy Spirit: to one he distributed kinds of tongues, to another revelations of the Scriptures, and to the others their various gifts.

[Col. 0498A] Having done all these things according to his own will—for he did not consider merit but the good pleasure of his mercy—he said that those who neglect Christ’s salvation will not escape his vengeance.

Now he adds that he has power to avenge all. I said, “How shall we escape?” And truly, those who neglect the Son’s salvation will not escape vengeance, since transgressors of the word of the angels were punished, because he will subject the world to come to the Son, which he did not subject to the angels.

This passage establishes the point by an argument from the lesser. He says it as follows: God the Father did not subject the world to angels. Many things are indeed done in the world through their ministry, but everything pertains to God’s command. I say, the world is to be subjected to him of whom we speak, namely Christ.

Or understand it this way: He did not subject the world to angels; that world, namely, is to be subjected to him of whom we speak, Christ.

That the world is to be subjected to Christ he proves by the authority of David, who nevertheless speaks of this future subjection as though it were past, as if he had been admitted into the divine council. And to prove Christ’s exaltation over all things more certainly, he first sets forth his humiliation, lest, if he asserted the exaltation while leaving the humiliation unmentioned, it should be doubted whether the one who was humiliated was different from the one who was exalted.

Therefore he says: “I alone do not say that the world is to be subjected to Christ; someone else also testified with me, saying in a certain place” (Ps. 8:5–6). This testimony was so well known that it did not require the name of its author or of the place in which it occurred.

David, I say, testifies to this while speaking to the Father: “O Lord, what is that man, Christ?”—he asks this in admiration, meaning that he is destined to be something great; yet how great he is is wholly due to your being mindful of this man.

God was mindful of Christ as man when he preserved him free from sin. I call him a man—or, to speak more explicitly, “that man, the Son of man”—and he is something great in that you visit him.

Just as a physician enters the sick person in order to visit him, so God visited Christ in the tomb, entering to him so that he might rise incorruptible. When he says “the Son of man,” he shows both that he was truly human and that he was not born from the seed of a man: he is the Son of man, not of men.

And just as I have acknowledged his incarnation, so also his humbling: for you humbled him, the Son of God in power, through the assumed nature of passibility and mortality. “You humbled him,” I say, “a little lower,” that is, lower by a little, because although mortal, he nevertheless ruled over the angels in this mortality.

You humbled him a little lower, separated from the angels, that is, from the dignity of their position; for God, having become man, lived among human beings.

Having set forth Christ’s humiliation, he begins to speak of his exaltation, saying: “You crowned him with glory,” that is, with the splendor of immortality, “and honor,” because every knee is bent to him. He says “crowned” by analogy with the way in which a victor returning from a triumph receives a crown; so Christ, having triumphed over death, deserved to be crowned with glory and honor.

And you appointed him over the works of your hands, over human beings and angels—works that are properly called the works of God’s hands—and in such a way over these works that “you subjected all things beneath his feet,” that is, subjected them to him with complete subjection.

For someone could be superior in dignity while certain lower beings were nevertheless not subject to him in any way. Now Paul explains how David’s statement, “You subjected all things,” is to be understood. David says: “You subjected all things.” But in saying that Scripture subjected them, that is, showed that all things were subjected to him, it left nothing that was not subject to him, because when it says “all things,” it excepts nothing.

For, if this is so understood, it is joined with what precedes: I rightly say that the world is to be subjected to Christ, because in subjecting all things to him, he left nothing that was not subject to him.

And although he said, “You subjected all things,” we nevertheless do not yet see all things subjected to him. This is why I said that they are to be subjected to him. Today one thing is subjected, but not yet everything; tomorrow something else, and still not everything; and this “not yet” will continue until, at the judgment, the ungodly also are subjected to him.

Someone might object: Just as they are not yet subjected, so they will never be subjected. To this Paul replies: Although all things are not yet subjected to him, nevertheless, because we see one part of the prophecy already fulfilled—namely, that he has been crowned with glory and honor—we are certain that the remaining part will be fulfilled, namely, that all things will be subjected to him.

He says it as follows: “We see him who was humbled a little,” that is, made a little lower than the angels. For he could have been humbled from what he was while nevertheless remaining greater than the angels; but he says that he was made lower than the angels.

Him, I say, we already see—Jesus, that is, the one who saves his own—crowned with glory and honor, that is, with the splendor of immortality, and with the fact that every knee is bent to him.

He was crowned, I say, not without merit, but because of suffering; and this suffering was not merely tolerable suffering, but the suffering of death. Here he begins to show that Christ’s commandments ought to be observed not only because of his power and vengeance but also—leaving those considerations aside—because of the love with which he loved us so greatly that he chose death for our salvation.

He was humbled in order to taste death for all the predestined, or for everyone universally. The price was given for everyone and is sufficient, if they are willing. He says “taste” because of the bitterness of death, which he experienced inwardly. Or he says “taste” because that death passed quickly and was like a taste, not an intoxication prolonged by delay.

He tasted death, I say, “by the grace of God,” that is, through grace; for man had not deserved this. He therefore tasted death for everyone because it was fitting that he—God the Father, for whose glorification all things were made and through whom all things were made—should do so.

I speak of him who had led, that is, predestined to be led, many sons, that is, justified human beings, into glory, that is, into salvation. It was fitting that he, I say, should perfect the author of the salvation of those sons—namely, Christ—through the suffering of death, as he had promised.

For all things would have been made in vain if the unredeemed human being had perished. Every earthly creature serves man, so that man may have in them the material for praising God. But if man were not saved, God’s plan would fail: he had made all things for his own glorification, yet he would be glorified in none of them if man were condemned.

And since all things were made for the glorification of God and through God, his plan had to be fulfilled so that he might be glorified in his creatures; otherwise it would be absurd for him not to provide salvation for those whom he had made. Christ’s completion begins in the resurrection and will attain perfection on the day of judgment, when all things will be subjected to him.

He proves that it was fitting for Christ to be perfected through sufferings, because they might say that it was wholly unfitting for the one who was the author of salvation, to whom all things ought to be subjected, to be brought down into the disgrace of suffering.

Therefore he says: Truly, it was not disgraceful for him to be perfected in this way, because the one who sanctifies those predestined to glory—that is, Christ—and those who are sanctified—that is, all the predestined—depend upon one source, that is, upon God the Father.

Thus Christ as man was subject to God’s power, just as those who are saved through him are. And since Christ depends upon God, it was not disgraceful if God arranged concerning him whatever pleased him.

He proves through authorities that the one who sanctifies and those who are sanctified depend upon one source, saying: “For this reason”—because the one who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are from one source—“for this reason, I say, he is not ashamed,” that is, Christ does not blush, “to call them brothers,” saying in the Psalm: “I will proclaim your name”—that is, your honor—“to my brothers, and I will praise you in the midst of the Church” (Ps. 21:23), as a pillar supporting and upholding the house so that nothing in it may fall.

Again he proves the same point by the authority of Isaiah, speaking in the person of Christ: “I, Christ, will put my trust in him” (Ps. 17:3), that is, in God the Father. And when he says that he trusts in God, it is evident that he depends upon God like the others.

Again he proves that the one who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are from one source, saying in Isaiah: “Behold, I, Christ, am ready for God’s service, and my children, whom God has given me” (Isa. 8:18). When he says “Behold, I” and “God has given me,” he shows that he depends upon God.

Having proved that it was not disgraceful, he now concludes that through suffering Christ had to be the author of human salvation, saying: Since Christ, who sanctifies, and human beings, who are sanctified, are from one source, Christ therefore partook of those same human beings in order to become capable of suffering and mortal.

And why did the one who sanctifies partake of those same human beings? Because the children whom he sanctified shared in flesh and blood, that is, in body and soul. He speaks of “blood” with reference to the soul, not because blood is the soul, but because it is the seat of the soul. To share in flesh and blood means to be truly human.

And why did Christ therefore partake of humanity? Because the children whom he sanctified were human beings—namely, so that through the death he suffered for the children’s salvation he might destroy him who held the power of death, that is, the devil, who ruled every human being by the law of death.

For he could not destroy death except through death; but he could not die unless he became human. Therefore he had to partake of those same things in the same way.

God created the first man pure and in freedom. The devil, having seduced him because he transgressed God’s command, enslaved him to his own power as a servant. But man, corrupted through sin, could not escape this slavery by any virtue of his own.

Since man had made himself a slave, if he were freed by someone other than a human being, it would be an act of violence, and the devil could justly complain that an injury had been done to him.

Therefore, so that man might be redeemed, it was necessary to find a human being in whom there was no sin. Then, when the devil usurped power over him in whom, because there was no sin, he had no rightful power—by inflicting upon the sinless man death, which is the punishment of sin—he would, through usurping what did not belong to him, justly lose on account of this presumption every human being whom he had justly possessed.

But a sinless human being could not be found among human beings, because all are born in concupiscence. If, however, as some object, the angelic nature were to become incarnate, since both the angel and the human being possess a nature capable of sinning, it would fall very easily, since it is clear that each nature had fallen by itself.

Thus it remains that human nature can in no way exist without sin unless divinity were united to it. Therefore also, as the saints say, God wished to become man so that by this means he might make human beings more indebted to his love.

He shows that Christ not only destroyed the power of death through his death, but also, by the merit of his death, abolished the Law—which had held the Jews in slavery. Therefore he says: He destroyed the devil through death, and through death he freed those Jews to whom this word was addressed, who throughout their whole life had been subject to slavery through fear of death—that is, to the Law, which compelled them as slaves, saying: “If you do this, you shall surely die.”

But Christ, unwilling that you should serve through fear of death, abolished the Law, so that, just as you formerly feared as slaves, now, through grace, you might love as free people.

Truly he partook of humanity in the same way in order to sanctify human beings. For nowhere does he take hold of angels—that is, nowhere in Scripture is he said to have taken hold of the angelic nature in order to redeem angels—but he takes hold of the seed of Abraham, taking flesh from Abraham, so that he might save those who are Abraham’s seed through faith.

Therefore, because he took hold of Abraham’s seed, he had to be made like his brothers in every respect, becoming capable of suffering and mortal, so that he might become merciful—which he possessed by nature—through the manifestation of his work, and a high priest, that is, one made for us a bridge by which we might cross to God.

A faithful high priest, I say, because he sought nothing either from those whom he led or from God to whom he presented the offerings of his leadership. He was also made like them so that he might make propitiation, that is, by propitiating, forgive the sins of the people.

And truly he is able to make propitiation for the sins of the people. For in that nature of his in which he himself suffered under Pilate and was tempted by the devil, he is able to help all who are tempted and to free them from temptations.

## CHAPTER III

> “Therefore, holy brothers, sharers in a heavenly calling, consider the apostle and high priest of our confession, Jesus, who is faithful to him who made him, just as Moses was in all his house. For this one has been counted worthy of greater glory than Moses, just as the one who built the house has greater honor than the house. For every house is built by someone. But the one who created all things is God.
>
> “And Moses indeed was faithful in all his house as a servant, for a testimony of the things that were to be spoken; but Christ as a Son in his own house. And we are his house, if we hold firmly to the confidence and the glory of hope to the end.
>
> “Therefore, as the Holy Spirit says: ‘Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts, as in the provocation, according to the day of temptation in the wilderness, where your fathers tempted me, tested me, and saw my works for forty years. Therefore I was offended [or: angered] with that generation, and I said: They always err in heart. But they did not know my ways. As I swore in my anger: They shall not enter into my rest.’
>
> “See, brothers, lest perhaps there be in any of you an evil heart of unbelief, departing from the living God. But exhort one another each day, as long as it is called ‘Today,’ so that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin. For we have become partakers of Christ, if only we hold the beginning of his substance firm to the end, while it is said: ‘Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts, as in that provocation.’
>
> “For some, after hearing, provoked him, but not all who went out of Egypt through Moses. With whom, then, was he offended for forty years? Was it not with those who sinned, whose corpses fell in the wilderness? And to whom did he swear, “They shall not enter” [or: that they should not enter], into his rest, except to those who were unbelieving? And we see that they were unable to enter into his rest because of unbelief.”

## EXPOSITION

From what precedes he infers that Christ is to be feared because of his vengeance and power; and again that he is to be loved in return by you because, out of love, he tasted death for you and is powerful and ready to help those who are tempted.

Therefore—that is, through all these things—you, holy brothers, have become participants in a heavenly calling. For you have been called to participate in heavenly goods.

You, I say, by loving him and doing what he commands, “consider Jesus,” that is, the Savior; the Apostle whom the Father sent to you; and the high priest, that is, the one made for us a bridge by which we may cross into glory. Jesus is the high priest of our confession because, whatever others may do, we confess him by faith as our Savior.

He compared Jesus with the prophets, and he compared him with the angels, in such a way as to show him greater than all of them. Now he compares him with Moses, again in such a way as to assert that he is more worthy than Moses, just as a son is more worthy than a servant who administers the household.

Therefore he says: “Consider Jesus.” Jesus is faithful to him—that is, to God the Father—who made him, that is, who united a human creation to the Son. He is faithful because he always sought not his own glory but the Father’s, and because he neither concealed the Father’s commandments, terrified by fear nor seduced by love.

He is faithful, I say, just as Moses was faithful in all the house of that one, Jesus or God the Father, in which Moses was not master but minister.

“In all,” because in everything that was necessary—in teaching, feeding, and leading that house, that is, the Jewish people—he faithfully nourished it.

Or let us construe it this way: Jesus is faithful to God, just as Moses was faithful. Jesus, I say, is faithful in all his house, among both Jews and Gentiles, not in one house only, as Moses was among the Jews.

The word “as” indicates similarity only, not equality of measure. He proves through the result what he has said: Truly Jesus is faithful, like Moses. For Jesus was counted worthy—this Jesus, I say, who as Son far surpasses the minister—and was counted worthy of glory, just as Moses was also worthy of glory, though Jesus was worthy of greater glory than Moses, or existed above Moses in merit.

His glory is so much greater insofar as the one who built the house has greater honor concerning the house, that is, in the house among those who are in it. Or “house” means the house that was built: the one who built that house has greater honor than the one who is its steward.

I say, he has greater honor than the one who is its administrator. Two points remain to be proved: that the house was built not by itself but by another, and that Christ built it.

All these things, however, are to be understood of the spiritual house. For it often happens that, in our houses, the person who serves in it is more honored than the one to whom the house belongs. He seems to say: “I rightly say ‘the one who built it’; for a house cannot be built by itself, since every house is built by someone.” To this one might reply: “If it is built by someone, nevertheless it is not necessarily built by God.” Paul responds: “Indeed, the house is built by God; for God is the one who [Col. 0503C] created all things. And if he created all things, it is clear that he also created the house. Since he built it, it follows that he is regarded as possessing greater glory in it than the one who merely serves in the house.”

Because he built the house in which Moses served, he was therefore considered worthy of greater glory than Moses. He is also worthy of greater glory because Moses was a servant in a house not his own, whereas Christ is a Son in his own house. “Moses indeed,” and “Christ truly,” are distributive conjunctions.

Moses was indeed faithful in all his house, namely, the house of God the Father or of Christ, as a servant, because he served in it alone. But a servant who is in a house today may perhaps be expelled tomorrow; he will never be as faithful as a son who is destined to possess the house by inheritance. [Col. 0503D]

Moses was like a servant in testimony to them—that is, merely so that he might bear witness to those things, not so that he could give assisting grace for carrying out the commandments. I mean those things that had to be spoken, that is, those things appropriate to be spoken to that carnal people, who could not grasp spiritual matters.

Moses was like a servant in a house not his own; Christ, however, was faithful like a son, to whom the inheritance of that house remained. I mean a Son in a house belonging not to another but to himself.

We, reborn through grace, are Christ’s house. I say that we are his house on this condition: if we hold fast the confidence of hope—that is, the hope of future blessedness, held with confidence, so that we hope confidently—and if we hold fast the glory of hope, that is, glorious hope, because it concerns heavenly joy.

I say that we must hold fast the firm confidence of hope—that is, confidence enduring to the end of life, when we shall receive what we now hope for. [Col. 0504A] Therefore, because we hold fast the confidence and glory of hope, we are Christ’s house.

For this reason, brothers, see to it that perhaps what can happen does not occur in any one of you. He says “in any one” because he knew that many in the Church could become perfect. I say, then, see to it that there is not in any one of you a heart of unbelief, so that you become unbelievers, thinking that Christ is insufficient for justification and that the law is necessary.

I call it an evil heart of unbelief, that is, a heart plunged into many evils. For as soon as someone becomes an unbeliever, he rushes headlong into sinful action. Nor is the heart of unbelief a small danger: it means having a heart inclined to depart from God. And it will go badly with you if you depart from God—for I mean the living God. Whoever departs from him loses life; whoever advances toward him finds life. [Col. 0504B]

See to it that there is not in any one of you the heart of unbelief that I forbid, just as the Holy Spirit, while issuing the same prohibition, says through David in these words (Psalm 94:8, 11):

“Today”—that is, in the time of grace; for David spoke as though spiritually present in the days of Christ. By “today” the whole time of grace is understood, from Christ to the end of the world. “Today,” I say, in the days of Christ, “do not harden your hearts. If you hear his voice”—and in fact you will hear it—do not harden your hearts. The word “if” is affirmative.

“Do not harden your heart, acting as they did in the provocation”—that is, as your fathers provoked me many times. Of their many provocations he mentions one, saying: “Do not harden your hearts as on the day”—that is, as they hardened their hearts on the day of testing, when they tested me, saying: “Can this man perhaps prepare a table for his people?” (Psalm 77:19). [Col. 0504C]

I mean a testing that took place in the wilderness, where it would have been more appropriate for them to flee to God for help than to provoke him by testing him. You, however, placed in the wilderness of this world, see to it that you do not anger God through your tests. This is the wilderness in which your fathers tested me.

See whether they are fathers according to the flesh, lest they be fathers according to imitation. They tested me, I say, and proved me—that is, they found me trustworthy—for they saw my works for forty years, during which they experienced that I could do all things.

Therefore, because they tested me, I was offended—that is, I was angry with that exceedingly evil generation—and I said concerning them: “These people are always going astray, and that in their heart,” that is, by their own deliberate choice, because they sinned knowingly and intentionally, even though they were able to act rightly. [Col. 0504D]

And although I said this to them, nevertheless they did not recognize my ways—that is, they did not wish to recognize my works, in which they ought to have walked. But because they did not recognize them, shall they enter into my rest, which I had promised them?

This is an interruption in the prayer, so that every kind of incongruity may be understood, as though he said: “If they enter, let no one believe me any longer.” Or it may have any similar meaning. Some say that the word “if” here has the force of “not,” attending to the force of the sentence rather than of the word itself.

I say “if they shall enter” in the sense of “as I swore,” that is, as I firmly established that they would not enter. I swore, to be sure, in my anger—that is, when I was angry with them. Both the anger and the oath exclude them from entering the rest. [Col. 0505A]

If the words “if,” “those,” and “there” are taken together, the same meaning remains: “If those to whom I swore in my anger that they would not enter the rest shall enter my rest.”

And because, brothers, rest was denied to your fathers on account of a heart hardened in unbelief, therefore, brothers, see to it that perhaps there is in any one of you an evil heart of unbelief, departing from the living God, as has been explained.

I say, do not be unbelievers; rather, exhort one another by increasing in virtue, saying each day: “Come, let us rejoice,” and so forth, until—that is, as long as “today” is named among you, that is, the time of grace.

He says “is named” so that those who were far removed from the days of Christ would not think that Christ contributed less to them than to those who lived in his own time. I say that “today” is named because this grace, which is also granted to those who come last, is related to the grace given in the days of Christ and is as powerful for those who come later as for those who came first. [Col. 0505B]

I say, exhort one another so that none of you may be hardened by deceit. For know that the devil deceives you if you should become hardened. I call it deceit because it is a cause of sin: once someone has been deceived, he is thereafter plunged more and more deeply into sin.

You ought to exhort one another and not become hardened, because by grace we have become what we were not: participants in Christ, that is, sharing with Christ in the inheritance of the Father.

I call you participants on this condition: if we hold firm to the end of life and never abandon the beginning of his substance—that is, faith, which is the beginning of good things and through which we are already being made divine and in some way share in the divine substance. [Col. 0505C]

I say that we must hold fast while—that is, as long as—it is said among us: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts,” as your fathers hardened theirs in the provocation mentioned above.

I rightly speak of provocation. For some of them, when they heard the Lord’s commandments, provoked God. Yet not all who went out from Egypt through Moses—that is, under Moses’ leadership—provoked God, for neither Caleb nor Joshua did so.

Likewise you, who have gone out from Egypt through Moses—that is, from the darkness of unbelief through Christ, who consecrates for you the water of remission—do not provoke God.

Some truly did provoke him, since God was angry for forty years with those who sinned—and not with impunity. Do not promise yourselves immunity, because their corpses, the corpses of those who sinned, were struck down in the wilderness. God was certainly angry with them. [Col. 0505D]

Again, returning to the same point: To whom did God swear that they would not enter his rest—that is, the heavenly Jerusalem, where true rest is found—if not to those who were unbelievers and had no faith in the Lord’s words?

Just as he struck down those who sinned and thereby took away the promised land from them, so also he took away the true rest signified by that land. Therefore see to it that you, who are in fact unbelievers if you restore the law as necessary and do not believe that faith can justify, do not fail to enter the rest because of unbelief.

God indeed swore that they would not enter the rest, and we see that his oath was fulfilled, because they were unable to enter the rest on account of their unbelief. [Col. 0506A]

# CHAPTER IV

> “Let us therefore fear, lest, while the promise of entering his rest remains, someone among us be thought to have fallen short. For the good news was announced to us just as it was to them; but the word they heard did not benefit them, because it was not joined with faith by those who heard it. For we who have believed shall enter the rest, just as he said:
>
> ‘As I swore in my anger: If they shall enter my rest’ (Psalm 94:11).
>
> And yet his works were completed from the foundation of the world. For somewhere he spoke concerning the seventh day in this way:
>
> ‘And God rested on the seventh day from all his works’ (Genesis 2:2).
>
> And again in this passage:
>
> ‘If they shall enter my rest.’
>
> Since, therefore, it remains for some to enter it, and since those to whom it was first announced did not enter because of unbelief, he again appoints a certain day, ‘today,’ saying through David, after so long a time, as was said above:
>
> ‘Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.’
>
> For if Jesus had given them rest, he would never afterward have spoken of another day. Therefore a Sabbath-rest remains for the people of God. For whoever has entered his rest has also rested from his works, just as God rested from his own.
>
> Let us therefore hasten to enter that rest, so that no one may fall into the same example of unbelief. For the word of God is living and effective, sharper than every two-edged sword, penetrating to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart (Ecclesiasticus 15:20). And no creature is invisible in his sight; all things are naked and exposed to his eyes, to whom our word is directed.
>
> Therefore, since we have a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast the confession of our hope. For we do not have a high priest who cannot sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who was tested in every respect according to likeness, without sin.
>
> Let us therefore approach with confidence the throne of his grace, so that we may receive mercy and find grace for timely help.” [Col. 0506B–C]

# EXPOSITION

And because they were unable to enter on account of unbelief, let us therefore fear lest someone among us be thought, in truth, to fall short of that rest. [Col. 0506D]

But he first sets forth the possibility granted to us of entering, saying: “Let us fear,” I say, “lest, while the promise”—that is, the frequent promise—“of entering his rest,” namely, God’s rest, remains, someone among us be thought, because of unbelief, to have fallen short of the rest.

I rightly speak of a promise. For the good news was announced to us, just as it was to them, that we could enter the rest through faith. It was indeed announced to them, but the word of the announcement that they merely heard did not benefit them, because it was not joined with faith by those who heard it.

I mean faith accepted on the basis of what they heard, so that, just as they heard, they would believe that God would fulfill it. [Col. 0507A]

Or the passage may be understood this way: “The word they heard, and which was not joined to faith, did not benefit them because of what they heard,” that is, because of what they heard from the returning spies.

According to this interpretation he sends us back to the historical account, when the twelve spies sent by Moses returned and terrified the children of Israel, saying (Numbers 13:28, 34) that the land was indeed fruitful, but that the sons of Anak were there, of gigantic stature, and that the Israelites could not stand in their presence. When they heard this and similar things, they said:

> “Let us appoint a leader for ourselves and return to Egypt” (Numbers 14:4).

Thus, in unbelief, they provoked God.

The word was truly merely heard, because it was not joined to faith, and therefore it did not benefit them. But because it is joined to faith in us, it will benefit us. This is an argument from opposites. [Col. 0507B]

He says it in this way: “We who have believed”—that is, who have joined faith to what we heard—“shall enter the true rest,” whose figure and reality they lost because they were unbelievers.

“We,” I say, “shall enter, just as he said that we would enter through faith,” when he said:

> “As I swore in my anger: If they shall enter my rest.”

This statement was made by opposition: where he said that they would not enter the rest because of unbelief, in the same place, by contrast, he said that we, because we believe, would enter the rest.

Or let us match each statement with its corresponding one. The good news was announced to us concerning that rest, because we who have believed shall enter the rest. The word heard by them alone did not benefit them, just as he said:

> “As I swore in my anger: If they shall enter my rest.” [Col. 0507C]

He said above: “See to it that there is not in any one of you a heart of unbelief,” because they did not enter the promised rest on account of unbelief. You have been told about that rest, namely, that if you have faith, you can possess it.

He now adds in what ways and at what times it was announced, showing that two announcements concerning this rest were made in figure, because no one could yet possess that rest. A third announcement of the rest was made not in figure but in the reality itself, when the rest could already both be possessed and was being possessed, namely, in the days of grace.

The text is joined as follows: “We were indeed told about that rest: here, and there, and elsewhere.” The first “and” indicates the diversity of places where the rest is discussed; the second distinguishes the times. The time when this rest was first announced—namely, the establishment of the world—was far removed from the time of its fulfillment, namely, the days of Christ. [Col. 0507D]

Thus he says: “We were told about the rest, and indeed after the works had been completed, beginning from the foundation of the world.” We were told about that rest.

After the human being was made, the works of God are said to have been completed, since the whole creation of the world was made for the human being. If the human being, the head of creatures, were absent, everything created for the human being would be incomplete.

And because, according to the opinion of some, things could be perfected and completed by God without having their beginning from God, he says “beginning from the foundation of the world.”

We were truly told about it after the works had been completed. Scripture, or Moses, said in a certain passage concerning the seventh day:

> “And God rested on the seventh day from all his works.” [Col. 0508A]

For this reason he does not specify the place but says “in a certain passage,” because this passage of Scripture was well known to them and because it was a distinct and excellent passage, where the subject was salvation. I mean that it was distinguished in dignity from the passage where the sacrifice of a bull is discussed.

Or, if the word “for” is not present there, there is no need to repeat anything; we may simply say: “After the works had been completed.” He said in a certain passage concerning the seventh day. The word “and” that follows has force in the order of the text from which it was taken, as though he said: “God did this and that; and when these things had been done, he rested on the seventh day.”

It is not said that God rested as though he had been wearied by some labor. Rather, by this he signified the future rest when he said: “God rested,” that is, “he ceased from all his works,” so that he would undertake no subsequent work whose material or likeness had not preceded in the first creation—material in bodily things, and likeness in nonbodily things such as souls. [Col. 0508B]

Immediately after creating the human being on the sixth day, he rested on the Sabbath, as though by this he were saying to the human being: “If you are obedient to me, this same rest is prepared for you after obedience has been completed.”

When he says, “He rested on the seventh day,” the rest was announced in such a way that the figure of the rest was also expected, namely, the promised land. The reality signified by that figure was to appear in the days of Christ; before him no one possessed true rest.

As in the passage mentioned above, so also in this passage the rest was again announced. Or Scripture speaks of that rest when it says “again,” indicating that the same thing was said. [Col. 0508C]

Thus, I say, it was announced:

> “If they shall enter my rest.”

For when, by saying this, he denied rest to unbelievers, he signified that the rest was to be possessed by the faithful.

This Scripture is found in David, who could no longer be prophesying about the figure, namely, that promised land, since the children of Israel had already possessed it for a long time. Thus, according to David, this prophecy concerned not the figure, which was already possessed, but the reality of the matter, which was awaited in Christ.

According to Moses, however, who said this same thing to the children of Israel, the prophecy concerned both the figure, which had not yet been possessed, and the reality to be received in Christ.

After presenting two announcements concerning the same rest in figures, he adds a third according to the truth of fulfillment, saying: Since this rest was announced in this way and in that way, therefore, so that what had been said might be fulfilled, he again establishes a day while speaking of the same rest, saying through the Holy Spirit in David: “Today.” [Col. 0508D]

He calls this a certain day, that is, a distinct day superior to all who came before, because on this day salvation is fulfilled, whereas in earlier days it could only be announced and never fulfilled.

He says “today in David, after so long a time.” For much time had passed from Joshua, who distributed the promised land to the Jews, until David’s day. Hence it is clear that David understood another future rest, different from the land they had already possessed for a long time.

He says “today,” as was said above in that passage:

> “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.” [Col. 0509A]

For just as the earlier fathers, because of unbelief, lost even the figure, so you too, if you become unbelievers, will not possess the true rest.

He adds “after so long a time” because it remains—that is, it is still left—for some to enter that rest.

For this reason he also says, “Do not harden your hearts,” because those to whom the rest was first announced, on account of their unbelief, did not enter even the figure, much less the reality itself.

Or the meaning may remain the same in this way: Because that rest was promised in this and that manner, therefore, so that the promises might be fulfilled, it remains for some to enter that rest.

And because it remains for some to enter, he again establishes a certain day, after so long a time, saying through David: “Today.”

And because those to whom the rest was first announced did not enter it on account of unbelief, therefore: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts,” as was said above concerning their fathers. [Col. 0509B]

It truly remains for some to enter that land. For Jesus—that is, Joshua—did not give them that rest, as some falsely suppose.

If this Jesus, that is, Joshua, had given them that rest, David would never have spoken, long after Joshua, of another rest, saying “on this day,” that is, “today.”

Or the passage may be understood in this way: David would never afterward have spoken of another day if he had understood that Joshua had distributed true rest.

Let it therefore be taken in this way: Jesus, Joshua, did not give them true rest.

And because it was promised but not yet granted, the only thing left from what has been said is the Sabbath-rest for the people of God.

“Sabbath-rest” signifies joy, and the delight that occurs on the Sabbath signifies the joy of the true Sabbath. [Col. 0509C]

And I rightly speak of Sabbath-rest. For whoever has entered his rest, whether Abraham or any other saint, has found this Sabbath-rest.

He says it in this way: Not only Christ, but also the one who has entered the rest has rested from his works, that is, from every labor, just as God rested from his works.

The Lord’s rest was both a sign and a cause of our rest. For God made the human being on the sixth day; in the sixth age he came to redeem him; on the sixth day, at the sixth hour of that day, he redeemed him; and by resting in the tomb on the Sabbath he signified that those who are with him will rest in the eternal Sabbath.

And because rest remains for the people of God, and whoever enters it rests as God rested, let us therefore hasten to enter that rest by doing good and believing rightly. [Col. 0509D]

Let us hasten in such a way that none of us falls into the same example of unbelief—that is, into the same unbelief into which our fathers fell.

We, I say, offend more gravely now, because we have them as an example by which to guard ourselves, whereas they fell without a preceding example.

We must hasten toward rest and not fall into unbelief, because the word of God—that is, the word of the Father—is as it says:

> “Your almighty word, O Lord, came from the royal throne” (Wisdom 18:15).

This word of God, I say, is living, that is, possessing life and supplying life to his own. And since it is living, it is also effective, that is, accomplishing whatever it wills: rewarding the devout and condemning the impious. [Col. 0510A]

And since it possesses such great power, it possesses no less wisdom. For it is more penetrating than every sword—that is, than every human intellect. Because it penetrates hidden things, it is called a sword piercing the interior.

I call it a two-edged sword, because just as a two-edged sword, held at the middle, strikes in front and behind, so does the human intellect. He understands this both of spiritual wisdom and of human knowledge.

The word of God also reaches to the division of soul and spirit, because it knows how to distinguish well what belongs to the soul—that is, to sensuality—and what belongs to the spirit—that is, to reason.

It also distinguishes the acts of sensuality among themselves and their dispositions, because sometimes sensuality drags reason with it into sin, while at other times, by acting well, it consents to the spirit.

It also knows how to distinguish the things belonging to the spirit among themselves: how the spirit now resists sensuality and at another time consents to it; how at one time it compels sensuality to act well. [Col. 0510B]

It reaches to the division of joints—or, equivalently, it is the discerner of the joints of soul and spirit—because it knows that sequence joined together in a certain order: now in sensuality, now in spirit.

This occurs when sensuality ceases to act badly and thereafter, by acting well, consents to the spirit; and so, step by step, the spirit also ascends. First it begins to act well; afterward it contemplates heavenly things; then, passing beyond the heavenly things, it fixes its eye upon God himself.

It is also the discerner of marrow, that is, of every subtlety of soul and spirit, because no subtlety can remain hidden from it.

It is also the discerner of all thoughts, because it knows whatever a human being thinks; and not only of thoughts, but also of the intentions of the heart, because it knows whatever a person intends through his thoughts. [Col. 0510C]

And, to summarize its wisdom briefly, there is no invisible creature—that is, no creature that does not appear—in his sight, for he is so great that he comprehends all things simultaneously.

And since the word of God is so effective that it possesses the power to accomplish whatever it wills, and since it is so wise, it both can and knows what it ought to repay to each person.

No creature is invisible in his sight; rather, all things are naked—that is, revealed—and, what is more, exposed internally to his eyes, that is, to his perspicacity. To him who is so powerful and sees all things so subtly, our word is directed; for to him we shall render an account of each thing.

Therefore hasten to him, abandoning the evil of unbelief. [Col. 0510D]

He compared Jesus and showed him to be greater than the prophets and angels by calling him the Son of God. But he had not yet said how the entire salvation of human beings depended on him. They could object: “What benefit is it to us if the Son of God is greater than the angels, when God has not arranged in him that we should be saved?”

To this Paul responds by saying that God established all salvation in him through Christ’s priesthood, destroying the Levitical priesthood and, through Christ’s grace, rendering the burdensome weight of the old law useless.

The text is joined as follows: Because our word is directed to one so powerful and wise, therefore let us hold fast the confession of our hope, that is, the faith through which we are permitted to hope for future glory.

Let us hold fast, I say, since we have a high priest who has become a bridge for us to salvation. [Col. 0511A]

I call him a great high priest, far above all Levitical priests. Our high priest has passed through the heavens in the sublimity of his power, whereas the priests from Levi were permitted to enter once a year into the Holy of Holies, where, nevertheless, the things present were only made by human hands.

But this one, having passed through the heavens by his power, sits at the right hand of the Father.

I call this high priest Jesus, that is, our Savior, powerful to save because he is the Son of God.

Since we have such a high priest, let us hold fast the confession of our hope.

Again, lest weaker brothers despair because of Jesus’ greatness—saying that, because he is the Son of God and has passed through the heavens, he would never deign to condescend to our weaknesses—Paul says:

Let us hold fast the confession without distrust, because although we have a high priest who is the Son of God, he is nevertheless able to sympathize with and condescend to our weaknesses, both according to the frailty of nature and also toward those who have fallen. [Col. 0511B]

We have a high priest who was tested in the flesh through every kind of testing.

I say “tested according to likeness,” that is, because he was like us, mortal and subject to suffering.

Or “tested according to likeness” may mean that he gave us in himself an example of resisting temptations, and yet was tested without sin.

From the fact that he was tested, he knows how to sympathize; from the fact that he was without sin, he is able to deliver.

Therefore, since we have a high priest who both sympathizes and is powerful to deliver, let us approach with confidence the throne of grace—that is, Christ, in whom there is not merely a certain grace, but the throne and seat of all grace.

“For from his fullness we have all received” (John 1:16). [Col. 0511C]

Let us therefore approach so that through him we may obtain mercy for what we have committed and find in him grace for help—that is, assisting grace for acting well in the future.

I say “help,” not according to our own desire, but timely help, because however God sees it to be timely, he will never abandon his own without assistance.

# CHAPTER V

> “For every high priest taken from among human beings is appointed on behalf of human beings in matters pertaining to God, so that he may offer gifts and sacrifices for sins. He is able to have compassion on those who are ignorant and who go astray, since he himself is also surrounded by weakness. And for this reason he ought to offer for sins, just as for the people, so also for himself.
>
> And no one takes the honor upon himself, but only one called by God, as Aaron was. So also Christ did not glorify himself to become high priest, but the one who said to him:
>
> ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you.’
>
> And as he says in another passage:
>
> ‘You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.’
>
> In the days of his flesh he offered prayers and supplications, with a loud cry and tears, to the one who could [or: could have] saved him from death; and he was heard because of his reverence.
>
> And although he was the Son of God, he learned obedience from the things he suffered. Having been perfected, he became the source of eternal salvation for all who obey him, being called by God a high priest according to the order of Melchizedek.
>
> Concerning him we have much to say, and it is difficult to explain, since you have become slow to hear.
>
> For although you ought to be teachers by this time, you again need someone to teach you the elementary principles of the beginning of God’s words. You have become people who need milk, not solid food.
>
> For everyone who partakes of milk is inexperienced in the word of righteousness, since he is a child.
>
> But solid food belongs to the mature, to those who, through practice, have their faculties trained for distinguishing good and evil.” [Col. 0511D–Col. 0512A]

# EXPOSITION

Above he said: “Let us approach Christ with confidence, so that through this high priest we may obtain mercy and grace for help.”

Now he proves from the lesser that through this high priest, Christ, we can obtain mercy, saying: “Indeed, through Christ we can obtain mercy in help. For through the ministry of every high priest, those subject to him can obtain mercy, although that priest is far lesser, since he is taken from human beings, whereas Christ is a high priest from God.” [Col. 0512B]

In some statements he will compare this high priest with Christ, and in others he will show him to be lesser.

Nor should what he says—that every high priest is appointed so that his subjects may obtain mercy through his ministry—appear contradictory to the fact that this has been lacking in many cases. For although it may have been lacking, either because of the sin of the minister or of the people, the high priest was nevertheless consecrated for this purpose: so that through his ministry the people might obtain mercy, unless they sinned in another matter.

He says it in this way: “We shall obtain mercy through Christ the high priest. For every high priest is taken from human beings.”

Before he is chosen, he is so entirely from among human beings that he cannot confer more upon another than he possesses himself.

This high priest, I say, is taken—that is, chosen by divine will. For the divine election by which he is taken produces in him the ability to intercede for the people. Before he is thus taken, he is powerless in this respect, like any other human being. [Col. 0512C]

Taken, I say, he is appointed on behalf of human beings, although shortly before he was “from among human beings.”

He is appointed on behalf of human beings, I say, not to preside over them in secular matters, but in those matters that are—that is, that pertain—to God, namely, to entreat and sacrifice on their behalf.

He is appointed in matters pertaining to God so that he may offer gifts and sacrifices for the removal of the people’s sins. [Col. 0512D]

In the old law, the lesser offerings were called “gifts.” “Sacrifices,” however, referred to the immolation of a bull or something similar.

In Christ’s case, the prayers and everything he did up to the hour of his Passion are called gifts. The sacrifice, however, was when he offered himself on the altar of the cross.

Where he says “taken from among human beings,” he shows Christ’s superiority, since Christ was taken by God’s choice. In the matters mentioned above he shows similarity: if through that high priest, when he offers gifts and sacrifices, people obtain mercy, why should they not similarly obtain it through Christ, who offers these same things?

He is appointed as high priest who is able—that is, who habitually knows how—to have compassion on those who are ignorant, that is, who sin ignorantly out of simplicity, and on those who go astray, that is, who knowingly fall into sin. [Col. 0513A]

Such a person ought to be chosen: one who knows how to sympathize with all the weaknesses of the brothers, not one who impatiently rushes to pronounce a sentence of condemnation upon his subjects.

In this respect Christ is similar, for, having been tested in every way, he sympathizes with our weaknesses.

I say that he is able to have compassion, and certainly he ought to do so, because, just as his subjects are, so he himself is also surrounded by weakness—that is, by the frailty of the flesh and, frequently, by the act of sin.

In this respect Christ is greater, because he was without sin.

And because he himself is surrounded by weakness, he ought, just as he offers for the people, both to absolve them from sins and to preserve them in the future, so also to offer in the same way for himself, in whom there is weakness, in order to preserve himself for the future and to remove past sins.

Here again Christ is greater, because he does not need to offer for himself, but only for the people. [Col. 0513B]

He now explains how this high priest is to be chosen, saying: This high priest ought to offer in this way, and none of these priests takes—that is, thrusts himself forward to take—the honor.

He takes it for himself, I say, with regard to what belongs to him.

He would take it for himself if he entered upon the honor for money, because of a person, because of lineage, because of secular power, or for any similar reason.

For all these things are derived from him. But whoever, on account of virtues, patience, humility, and the like, is chosen for honor, such a person would not take honor for himself—that is, from what belongs to him—but from the virtues, which belong to God. No one takes honor for himself, but only the one who is called by God—that is, the one chosen by divine calling.

It is not said that he is called by God because a divine voice is heard there, but if he is chosen by those who are spiritually sound on account of the virtues of God, this has the same force as if God said: “Come, because you are worthy to receive the pontificate.” He is called by God just as Aaron was called by God. Yet Aaron was not chosen by a common election, because the sons of Korah opposed him. Therefore, when they brought in alien fire and offered incense, they were consumed by fire; and Dathan and Abiron, murmuring for the same reason, were swallowed up by the earth (Num. XVI, 31). But Moses, by God’s command and through a miracle, appointed Aaron to the priesthood.

For God commanded that twelve rods belonging to twelve men from the twelve tribes be placed in the tabernacle, so that the one whose rod blossomed might, in accordance with the manifest will of God, become pontiff. In the election of Aaron he showed that, if there are a few who choose justly while the multitude objects, nevertheless the judgment of the few who choose canonically must be followed, and the error of the multitude rejected (Num. XVII, 2, 10).

If that pontiff has been called like Aaron, not thrusting himself into the honor, he can benefit human beings. So also Christ, for a similar reason, can assist his own: Christ did not glorify himself—that is, he did not thrust himself forward by magnifying himself in order to become pontiff—but the Father glorified Christ, who spoke to him, saying: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you,” as we explained at the beginning of the Epistle.

These, however, are not the words by which the Father glorified him, but words in which he showed Christ worthy of the priesthood. When Christ was being baptized, he said: “This is my Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. III, 17). In these words he glorified the Son. By adding, “Hear him” (ibid.), in this word he consecrated him as pontiff. The Father showed the dignity of the Son by saying: “You are my Son.” Thus he speaks of Christ, just as elsewhere in the same Scripture he speaks of his pontificate: “You are a priest, destined to endure forever according to the order”—that is, according to the dignity of the order—“of Melchisedech.”

The Levitical priesthood, however, was destined to endure not forever but for a time. Therefore Christ’s priesthood must remain forever, because just as blessedness cannot be obtained except through him, so, once obtained, it cannot be retained except through him. In this too he is superior: he was placed over the Levitical priesthood, because that priesthood was temporary. And if the priesthood that was to be destroyed could be beneficial, how much more beneficial is Christ’s eternal priesthood, which also belongs to another dignity, since it is according to the order of Melchisedech.

Christ—so that you may be certain that in him you will obtain mercy—during the days of his flesh, that is, of his suffering and mortality—for it is natural for flesh to suffer and die—in those days, I say, offered prayers and supplications to God. He calls “prayers” all the petitions he made before the moment of his Passion. By “supplications” he means that, when the hour of his Passion was at hand, he prayed with such intensity that he shed bloody sweat.

He offered them, I say, to the one who was able to save him from death—not so that he would not die, but so that death would not long dominate him. He intended that, by being freed from death in himself, the human race might be freed from it as well. He offered them, I say, with a loud cry—not because he cried out so loudly, but with a powerful cry, that is, with the greatest intensity—and with tears.

Nowhere else is Christ found to have wept at that same hour except in this Gospel of Paul. It deserves no less belief, because if he is said to have wept for Lazarus and for the destruction of Jerusalem, showing pity everywhere toward human weakness, he must all the more be said to have wept in order that, by completing his obedience, he might heal the weakness of the human race.

Offering prayers with tears, he was heard because of his reverence—that is, because of his religion. Or, “because of his reverence” means because of the obedience by which he proved that he had always revered the Father. He did not merely offer prayers with tears; he also learned obedience—not by acquiring knowledge, but through experience of the matter—from what he suffered, that is, through death. Although he was the Son of God, powerful over all things, he nevertheless wished in this way to fulfill his priesthood.

And when he himself had been perfected—that is, had died—or, “perfected” means established at the right hand of the Father, so that he lacked nothing imperfect—he became the cause of eternal salvation for all who obey him, not for those who refuse to obey him. He could indeed rightly be the cause of salvation, because he was called pontiff not by human beings but by God, and not according to the Levitical order but according to the dignity of the order of Melchisedech.

He is about to tell them how his priesthood destroys the legal priesthood, how all legal observances reach their end in him, how his priesthood preceded the legal priesthood, and how it will remain forever. First, however, he attacks them with a harsh rebuke—though only in part—and appropriately corrects them before anything else, so that, once corrected, they may be more devoted to listening and more ready to believe. He says:

Concerning this—that is, concerning how Christ is pontiff according to the order of Melchisedech—we have much to say: a great discourse, comprising many things, and difficult to interpret—that is, one which cannot now be interpreted, neither by me, because I do not have suitable hearers, nor by you, because you cannot comprehend it. I call it difficult to interpret for the purpose of speaking—that is, of explaining it to you—because you have become weak in hearing, that is, in understanding.

Or this discourse is great and interpretable, because it contains many mysteries that ought to be explained. I call it great because you have become weak in hearing.

Truly you are weak, for although you ought to be teachers because of the time—the long period you have had for learning, since you were converted at the very beginning of the preaching—although, I say, you ought to be teachers, you now again need to be taught what are the elements of the beginning of the sayings of God.

There are many levels in the sayings of God: first, simple instruction; then instruction of an intermediate kind; and finally, perfect instruction. By “beginning” he means what is appropriate when someone is taught to believe in the incarnation, the Passion of Christ, and similar simple matters. The elements of the beginning are such things as recounting sequentially the subject of the Passion, or something of that kind.

You have also become people who need milk—that is, childish instruction—and milk in such a way that you do not need solid food, that is, perfect teaching. Truly you need milk rather than solid food. For everyone who partakes of milk—that is, for whom childish instruction is necessary—is inexperienced in the word of righteousness, that is, in the teaching of the righteous, meaning the perfect. He is inexperienced because he is a child in understanding.

You are perfect in wickedness, but in understanding you are children. Milk belongs to children, but solid food belongs to the perfect—that is, solid teaching. The perfect are those whose faculties, that is, their understanding, through habit—that is, through constant study—have been trained to discern good and evil, so that they know how to distinguish good from evil, and also among good things which are better and which are less good; and likewise among evil things they know how to distinguish.

## CHAPTER VI

“Therefore, leaving the beginning of Christ’s teaching, let us advance to perfection, not again laying the foundation of repentance from dead works and of faith toward God, of the teaching of baptisms, of the laying on of hands, and of the resurrection of the dead and eternal judgment. And this we shall do, if God indeed permits. For it is impossible for those who have once been enlightened, who have also tasted the heavenly gift and become participants in the Holy Spirit, who have likewise tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come, and then have fallen away, to be renewed again to repentance, crucifying the Son of God again for themselves and holding him up to contempt.

“For the earth, often drinking in the rain that comes upon it and producing [generating] suitable vegetation for those by whom it is cultivated, receives blessing from God; but, producing thorns and thistles, it is rejected and near to a curse, whose end is burning.

“But we are confident concerning you, beloved, of better things and things nearer to salvation, although we speak in this way. For God is not unjust, so as to forget your work and the love that you showed in his name, when you served the saints and continue to serve them. But we desire each one of you to display the same diligence, for the fulfillment of hope to the end, so that you may not become sluggish, but imitators of those who through faith and patience will inherit the promises.

“For when God made a promise to Abraham, since he had no one greater by whom he could swear, he swore by himself, saying: ‘Surely, blessing I will bless you, and multiplying I will multiply you.’ And so, patiently enduring, he obtained the promise. For human beings swear by one greater than themselves, and the oath is the end of every dispute among them, serving for confirmation.

“In this matter, God, desiring to show more abundantly to the heirs of his promise the unchangeableness of his purpose, introduced an oath, so that by two unchangeable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we might have the strongest consolation, we who have fled for refuge to hold fast the hope set before us. We have this hope as a safe and firm anchor of the soul, and it enters into the inner part of the veil, where Jesus, our forerunner, entered on our behalf, having become pontiff forever according to the order of Melchisedech.”

## EXPOSITION

377. Having rebuked them severely, he again speaks gently, including himself, and says:

“Therefore”—that is, because you ought to be teachers on account of the time, and because you ought to have faculties trained in the law of the Lord—“leaving the discourse of the beginning of Christ,” that is, the elements of the beginning by which someone begins to acquire knowledge of Christ, and abandoning this childhood, let us advance to perfection, so that we may know how “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was God,” and so forth.

Let us advance, I say, to perfection, not again laying the foundation of repentance from dead works, and so forth. He calls “dead works” either sins, which cause death, or earlier good works rendered dead by the sin that followed. Repentance from dead works is a foundation, because unless this stone is laid first, nothing will be built.

It is also the foundation of faith toward God. For whoever seeks justification from elsewhere, or does not believe all the parts of the faith, does not have faith toward God. It is also the foundation of the teaching of baptisms. He speaks in the plural, “baptisms,” because there is baptism in water; baptism is also spoken of in the tears of repentance; and in a third way, in the shedding of blood for Christ.

It is also the foundation of the laying on of hands. Unless someone believes that through the laying on of hands sins are forgiven by receiving the Holy Spirit, and that we are strengthened against future evils, he does not have the foundation, because whatever he builds upon it is invalid.

It is also the foundation of the resurrection of the dead. Unless someone believes that the resurrection of Christ brought about the resurrection of the dead, he has lost the faith and has nothing upon which to build. It is also the foundation of eternal judgment. He calls the judgment eternal because whatever is established for such people, whether concerning good or evil, will endure forever. Whoever does not believe in the judgment to come has no foundation, because he is an unbeliever.

All these things are called a foundation because, unless these things precede in the foundation, no one can otherwise do good. All these things were necessary for them: the foundation of repentance from dead works, because they had sinned grievously; and the good works that had previously existed in them had been nullified by sin, since, as he said above, they had suffered many things for Christ from their fellow tribesmen.

Again, faith toward God was necessary. If they understood how every justification is obtained through the faith of Christ, they would not have returned to circumcision as though it were necessary for them. If they had again been well instructed concerning baptism—how all sins are forgiven in it—they would confess the legal observances to be superfluous.

If they also knew how, through the laying on of hands, the Holy Spirit both forgives earlier sins and strengthens against coming evils, they would not concern themselves with the legal observances. Again, if they believed that the resurrection of Christ is the efficient cause of our resurrection in glory, they would seek nothing apart from Christ.

Again, if they considered how Christ would be the future judge of all, through faith in the Judge they would strive only to please the Judge. Because they needed all these things, he therefore says: “Let us advance to perfection,” laying down—as a stone is laid in a foundation—the foundation of repentance and what follows, as these have been explained.

He says “laying,” not “again,” that is, not repeating the former manner, so that, just as we previously laid all these things in you, and they were destroyed when you sinned, the same things might again be laid and destroyed. According to this interpretation, we deny only the word “again.”

Or, if the negation is applied to everything, the meaning remains the same in this way: Let us now advance to perfection, so that we may not again be laying the foundation of repentance. We shall lay it now, but see that it should not be necessary to lay it again. In this way the negation is applied to everything, while the meaning remains unchanged.

I urge that we advance to perfection, and indeed we shall do this—that is, we shall advance to perfection—if God permits, that is, if he grants us time in this life in which our sins can be redeemed. I say “if God permits” because in the other life it is impossible to be renewed through repentance. There is the place of receiving what one has earned; here is the place of earning. That is why he says: “If God permits”: I say this because in the future life he will not permit it.

378. For it is impossible for some who have been moved to repentance in the other life to be renewed through recovered righteousness; that would be to renew them again. Here it is permitted, whereas there it cannot be repeated, namely that someone should be renewed there.

He says “renewed” concerning those who were once enlightened through faith because they believed, and who, after confessing the faith, also tasted—as though a sweet and pleasing taste—the heavenly gift, namely forgiveness of sin through baptism. This gift is from above.

These are the two matters concerning faith. They also became participants in the Holy Spirit, since they possessed various kinds of tongues and the other gifts. They also—and this is something greater—tasted, no less than we did, the good, that is, the pleasing, word of God: they understood the divinity of the Son.

They also tasted—that is, by a kind of anticipation they sampled beforehand—the powers of the age to come, that is, freedom from suffering and immortality. Those who possessed all these things and then fell away cannot be renewed again, moved to repentance.

Nor is it possible for them again to be crucifying the Son of God for themselves, that is, in the other life to make themselves incapable of benefiting any longer from Christ’s crucifixion; nor can they again hold the Son of God up to contempt, that is, to display, so that they might imitate his display. As though he were saying: “They are again incapable of imitating the Son of God.”

Or, alternatively, let us deny the repetition of baptism in this verse: It is impossible for those who were such as these—and even for those who were inferior to them—to be renewed again, that is, to be rebaptized, when moved to repentance. If they are rebaptized, they are again crucifying the Son of God for themselves—not because they crucify him again in reality, but because of equality in sin. For there is one faith, one baptism, and Christ, who consecrated it, died once for our sins.

They are therefore said to crucify the Son of God again for themselves through equality in sin because, if they were first justified through baptism and afterward sinned, they think that the first baptism has thereby been rendered invalid, so that repentance in the future cannot avail for their justification. Such people wish to crucify Christ again, so that from a repeated crucifixion they may obtain repeated forgiveness, not knowing that one baptism and the one death of Christ suffice for every justification after sin just as before it, provided only that there is repentance.

In the earlier interpretation, *ostentui* is used instead of the unusual *ostensioni*, but it is quite appropriate according to the origin of the word, from *ostendo, ostendis* (“I show, you show”). Where he said above, “those who have fallen away,” the preposition *pro* indicates the gravity of the fall, namely into a serious offense.

Above he said: “Let us advance to perfection,” and after inserting certain remarks he added: “This we shall do, if God permits.” He now continues concerning the same matter: Truly we shall do this, that is, we shall advance to perfection; and this is just, because “the earth drinks in the rain.”

By “earth” he means human beings, who are cultivated by the word of God so that they may produce fruit.

This earth, I say, drinks in the rain—that is, it receives the teaching of the divine word with great desire. Just as rain moistens dry and hardened earth, so the word of God makes the hardened heart soft and tempers it, so that it can produce fruit.

The earth, I say, drinks in the rain that often comes upon it. He says “often” because divine teaching should be neither constant, lest it become cheap, nor too infrequent, lest it lose the opportunity to produce fruit. It should be frequent, so that it may be more suitably tempered in both respects.

It comes upon the earth because teaching descends both from God and from prelates, who are superior in the Church. The earth, I say, thus drinks in the rain and produces vegetation, that is, the fruit of good works.

He calls this vegetation suitable for those by whom the earth is cultivated, that is, for preachers who cultivate it. It is suitable because it does not produce something degenerate, but the fruit of divinity—that is, it causes people to act according to what they are taught and to what they see in their teachers.

This earth, I say, producing such fruit receives blessing, that is, an increase of good things from God. Good earth receives blessing.

But earth producing thorns and thistles is rejected. Or, if the text reads that way, the clauses may be joined without altering the meaning: Truly the earth producing suitable vegetation receives blessing. For earth producing thorns and thistles is rejected.

379 “Producing” indicates sinning so wickedly that one corrupts others by a bad example. By thorns he means less piercing sins; by thistles, which pierce more harshly, he means more serious sins.

The earth, I say, producing thorns and thistles is rejected, that is, it is hostile to God, and near to a curse, that is, to destruction. When he says “near,” he indicates that the punishment is indeed close, but that it can still be escaped through repentance.

Its end—that is, the end of this rejected earth—will be burning, that is, everlasting fire, unless it repents. The same verse is joined to the preceding words, although that connection is not equally suitable.

Truly no one can be renewed to repentance in the other life. For the earth—that is, a human being—drinks in the rain that comes only in this life; that is, a person can strive for amendment here. Here is the place of earning; there, the place of receiving.

Or, according to another interpretation, “it is impossible to be renewed” means “to be rebaptized.” For the earth drinks in the rain once; that is, a human being receives the water of baptism once.

Because he rebuked them rather harshly above, saying, “Although you ought to be teachers, you again need to be taught,” and so forth, and because by speaking of the good earth’s blessing as being near he urged them to produce suitable fruit while frightening them away through the contrary example, he now speaks gently to them. Just as he had shaken them with threats, so now he encourages them with soothing words, saying:
