Although we speak in this way—rebuking you above—nevertheless, beloved, we are confident concerning you of better things than burning, and things nearer to your salvation than thorns and thistles. When he says “concerning you,” he indicates that they possess a nature suitable for correction.

“Better” and “nearer” are not comparisons between participants in the same category. We are therefore confident concerning you because you formerly performed many good works. If God did not reward these works after you had repented, he would be unjust. But God is not unjust, so as to forget your work, by which you made all your possessions common to everyone, and your love, because this work proceeded not from fear but from love.

You showed this love in his name, that is, for the honor of God. I rightly call it your work, because you served the saints with your possessions and still serve them with the same love. He indicates three kinds of goodness in them: good work, love, and the honor given to God in his work.

You served them formerly and remain engaged in the same work. But concerning the future, we desire each one of you—not one being absent from this work—to display, that is, frequently to demonstrate, the same diligence in serving the saints until the end of your life.

He says “to display” for the fulfillment of hope, that is, so that in future blessedness what you now hope for may be completed in you. We desire you to display it in such a way that you do not become sluggish in this diligence, but become imitators of those—that is, of the saints—who will inherit the promises, that is, the promised blessedness, not on account of their lineage but through faith and patience, that is, through faith and because, by enduring for a long time, they did not grow weary.

Because Paul knew that it would greatly please them if he said that salvation had been promised to their fathers, he speaks as though someone were asking: “Have the promises been made?” Indeed they have, for they were made to Abraham.

He adds three things: that the promises were made, that they were confirmed by an oath, and that they had already been fulfilled in Abraham. He says:

When God made a promise to Abraham, he swore by himself—and he swore by himself because he had no one greater by whom he could swear. Why? Because he had no one greater, he swore by himself. But he first gives the words of the oath:

He swore, I say, saying: “O Abraham, unless I bless you,” that is, unless I enrich you with an increase of virtues in this life. He says “I will bless,” blessing—that is, in such a way that I shall always remain in the office of blessing—and unless I multiply you by rewarding your faith in future blessedness.

“I will multiply you,” he says, “multiplying”—that is, I will not bring this multiplication to an end unless I do this; an incomplete expression, after which whatever suitable conclusion is understood.

And so Abraham, having been assured, and Abraham patiently enduring—for he endured many adversities for a long time—finally obtained the promise, that is, the blessedness often promised.

He swore because human beings swear. He swore by himself because there is no one greater than he. Human beings swear by one greater than themselves. Therefore, after making the promise, God swore, accommodating himself to human custom. Human beings are accustomed to establish certainty through an oath, just as Jesus, during his earthly life, spoke to them according to the custom of that region in parables and comparisons. Yet God’s oath means nothing other than establishing something unchangeably.

Human beings swear by one greater than themselves, and the oath is the end of every dispute—that is, of their disagreement—serving to confirm one party. In this matter, namely through the oath, God wished to show more abundantly.

He showed abundantly through the promise, but more abundantly through the oath. He wished to show the immutability—that is, the unchangeableness—of his purpose. God’s purpose was to save human beings through faith in Christ, a purpose that scarcely anyone had understood.

This purpose, I say, he showed to be immovable for the heirs of the promise, that is, of the repeated promise, by placing an oath between the promise and its fulfillment.

He placed it for this purpose: that through two unchangeable things, namely the promise and the oath, in which it is impossible for God to lie—for he cannot lie in either of them—we might have the strongest consolation. That is, these things should make us strong in every adversity, since we are willing to suffer for a time so that we may reign forever.

An oath is called *jusjurandum*, as though it were “what is right for swearing.” Perjury, however, is called not *jusjurandum* but *jus non jurandum*, “what is right not to swear.”

In this oath of God we have authority to swear, but in such a way that we neither swear needlessly, even when we speak the truth, nor, when it is necessary, neglect to confirm the truth by an oath.

Let us have this consolation—we who flee in every tribulation to hold fast the hope, not abandoning it on account of adversities. I call it the hope already set before us in Abraham and fulfilled. Or, “set before us” means offered to all who hope in faith.

The person who flees to hope is the one who scorns tribulation because of the joy of the blessedness that he hopes will be his. We have this hope as a safe and firm anchor of the soul, so that, just as an anchor holds a ship and prevents it from sinking, hope may make our soul safe, preventing it from sinking by consenting to iniquity, and firm, so that it never refuses to suffer, even wavering in the least.

I also call this hope something that enters into the inner part of the veil, that is, into the inward and veiled blessedness that none of the living has seen. The inner part of the veil referred to the place called the Holy of Holies, which lay behind the veil. The place before the veil was called the Holy Place, where the priests stood; but the pontiff entered the Holy of Holies once a year. This inner part of the veil signified the heavenly blessedness veiled from us in this life.

And just as we hope to go there, so we shall indeed enter, because Jesus, our forerunner—that is, running ahead of us so that we may follow him—entered into that place, or into those inner parts. He is called a forerunner because no fault ever turned his course aside.

He entered, I say, in order to introduce us. I rightly say “for us,” because he became our pontiff, destined to endure forever according to the dignity of the order of Melchisedech.

## CHAPTER VII

“For this Melchisedech, king of Salem, priest of the Most High God, who met Abraham as he was returning from the slaughter of the kings and blessed him, to whom Abraham also apportioned tithes of all things—first, indeed, whose name is interpreted ‘king of righteousness,’ and then also king of Salem, which is ‘king of peace’—without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, but made like the Son of God, remains a priest forever.

“Consider, moreover, how great this man is, to whom even Abraham the patriarch gave tithes from the choicest spoils. And indeed those of the sons of Levi who receive the priesthood have a commandment to take tithes from the people according to the law, that is, from their brothers, although they too came forth from Abraham’s loins. But he whose descent is not reckoned among them took tithes from Abraham and blessed him who had the promises. And without any contradiction, what is lesser is blessed by what is greater.

“And here mortal human beings receive tithes, but there one testifies that he lives. And, so to speak, through Abraham even Levi, who receives tithes, was tithed; for he was still in his father’s loins when Melchisedech met him.

“If, therefore, perfection was through the Levitical priesthood—for under it the people received the law—what further need was there for another priest to arise according to the order of Melchisedech, rather than to be called according to the order of Aaron? For when the priesthood is transferred, it is necessary that there also be a transfer of the law.

“For he of whom these things are said belongs to another tribe, from which no one attended at the altar. For it is evident that our Lord arose from Judah, concerning which tribe Moses said nothing about priests. And this is still more evident if, according to the likeness of Melchisedech, another priest arises, who was made not according to the law of a carnal commandment, but according to the power of an indissoluble [dissoluble] life. For he testifies: ‘You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchisedech.’

“There is indeed a rejection of the preceding commandment because of its weakness and uselessness; for the law brought nothing to perfection. But there is an introduction of a better hope, through which we draw near to God—and this is not without an oath. For the others were made priests without an oath, but this one with an oath, through him who said to him: ‘The Lord has sworn and will not repent: You are a priest forever.’ Jesus has thereby become the guarantor of a better covenant.

“And the others were made priests in greater number, because death prevented them from remaining; but he, because he remains forever, has an everlasting priesthood. Hence he is also able to save forever those approaching [approaches] God through himself, since he always lives to intercede for us.

“For such a pontiff was fitting for us: holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, and made higher than the heavens. He has no need, as the priests do, to offer sacrifices daily, first for his own sins and then for those of the people. For he did this once, by offering himself. For the law appoints as priests human beings who have weakness, but the word of the oath, which came after the law, appoints a Son made perfect forever.”

## EXPOSITION

[Col. 0522D]

After many intervening matters, he finally sets out how he is according to the order of Melchisedech, saying: I rightly call Jesus pontiff according to the dignity of Melchisedech. For this Melchisedech was king of Salem, which is now Jerusalem but was then called Salem. Later, because the Jebusites inhabited it, *Hieru* was added to Salem, and thence it received the name Jerusalem.

This king of Salem, I say, was priest of the Most High God, that is, not appointed by human beings nor through a human being, but, trusting in his own dignity, he assumed for himself the priesthood of God. This Melchisedech came to meet Abraham when he was returning from the slaughter of the kings who were leading his nephew Lot captive; and Melchisedech blessed Abraham. To him, as he blessed him, Abraham apportioned tithes of all the spoils (Gen. XIV, 20).

He was first called Melchisedech, a name which is interpreted ‘king of righteousness.’ He was then called king of Salem, which is interpreted ‘king of peace.’ Again, this Melchisedech was without father and without mother, not because he had no parents, but because Scripture says absolutely nothing that he had them. He was also without genealogy, having neither sons nor daughters; nor did he have a beginning of days or an end of life of which Scripture speaks, perhaps deliberately omitting these matters. But this Melchisedech, made like the Son of God in the points already stated, remains a priest—that is, his priesthood endures forever.

Let us return and set out point by point how he was made like the Son of God. Melchisedech is called king of righteousness; but who is king of righteousness except Christ, who guides his own through the storms of the world in righteousness? Christ is also king of Salem, that is, of peace, because, after ruling his own in the righteousness of this life, he does not cease to rule them, placed in the true peace of angels.

He is priest of the Most High God: but what priest is as great as Christ, who, because of disobedience to the Father, offered himself on the altar of the cross, and who came to meet Abraham as he returned from the slaughter of five kings? The five kings are the five bodily senses, through which all vices rule in a human being: through sight, for example, desire rules when it desires what it has seen, and so through the other senses, as it was said to the woman in the Gospel: ‘You have had five husbands’ (John IV, 18).

By Abraham every faithful person is understood. Christ comes to meet every faithful person returning from the slaughter of enemies—that is, of vices ruling through the five senses—by giving an increase of good work. It is also read there that he offered Abraham bread and wine (Gen. XIV, 18), though this is not contained here. That bread and wine signify the body and blood of Christ; through participation in them sins are forgiven, and the recipient is strengthened against vices by what is to come.

To him Abraham apportioned tithes of all things (ibid., 20), that is, the faithful person attributes to Christ every perfection that he has. For every faithful person attributes all his perfection to Christ through the number ten, which is a perfect number; for number increases to ten and goes no further, but begins again, saying eleven, that is, one and ten. Perfection is thereby signified.

Melchisedech was first called one whose name is interpreted ‘king of righteousness,’ and then king of Salem, which is ‘king of peace.’ Thus Christ first rules his own in the righteousness of this life; in the other life he rules them in peace. Christ is without father according to the flesh, without mother according to divinity, without genealogy because he had no children of the flesh, and without beginning of days or end according to divinity, being coeternal with the Father.

The preceding points have sufficiently commended the dignity of Melchisedech; but now, for a further increase of his dignity, consider how great this Melchisedech is, to whom Abraham the patriarch—that is, the chief of our fathers, Isaac and Jacob—gave tithes, as though he were his servant and tributary, and gave them from the choicest things he possessed.

Consider Melchisedech’s greatness also in another way: some of the sons of Levi, receiving the priesthood, have a commandment to take tithes from the people; they would not dare to do so otherwise, and this is according to the law, under which they are servants. I say, from the people, that is, from their brothers, who contribute to them willingly because they are brothers. In taking tithes they differ from the people, although the sons of Levi themselves came forth from Abraham’s loins, like the rest of the people.

The sons of Levi take tithes from their brothers; but Melchisedech, whose genealogy is not reckoned among them—that is, among the Jews—took tithes from Abraham and blessed him at the time of his greater dignity, namely when he already had the promises from God.

Now he gathers from what has preceded that Abraham gave, and Melchizedek blessed, without any contradiction. For no one can contradict the proposition that the lesser is blessed by the better. Even if, in another respect, the one who is blessed is greater, he is nevertheless plainly lesser in this respect: he receives from the one who blesses what he did not possess. Observe Melchizedek’s dignity in this way also: here, that is, in the Levitical priesthood, mortal men receive tithes. But there, in the earlier passage of Scripture, Moses testifies that Melchizedek lives, since, while speaking of life, he added nothing concerning death. Observe his dignity in this way as well: Levi, who receives tithes, and the Levitical order itself, were tithed—that is, they gave tithes. I say this so that Levi may be said to have given tithes through Abraham, that is, through a material cause. For when Abraham gave tithes, they were all still in Abraham’s loins. This seems to follow very well. For if we all sinned in Adam because we were in his loins when he sinned, why should Levi not be said to have given tithes, since he was in Abraham’s loins when Abraham gave tithes? And truly Levi gave tithes through Abraham’s giving, because Levi was still in the loins of his father Abraham when Melchizedek came to meet Abraham as he was giving him tithes. For if Isaac had then existed, Levi would not be said to have been at that time in Abraham’s loins, but in Isaac’s loins. But because he was still in Abraham’s loins through Isaac, Levi likewise was there.

Levi is said to have been tithed in Abraham’s loins, but not Christ, although he was Abraham’s son, because Christ was not born from Abraham’s loins according to the lust of the flesh [Col. 0524D]. Levi, however, was born from Abraham’s loins through the law of the members, which is the lust of the flesh.

He showed above that Christ is priest according to the order of Melchizedek, and proved sufficiently that this priesthood is superior to the priesthood of Levi both in time and in its great dignity; he also emphasized this in many ways. Now, having commended Christ’s priesthood, he proceeds to show how the Levitical priesthood is destroyed through Christ’s priesthood. Once that priesthood has been destroyed, he necessarily proves that the destruction of the law follows.

The text is connected as follows: Since Christ was made priest according to the order of Melchizedek, and since it has been sufficiently proved that this priesthood is altogether superior to the Levitical priesthood [Col. 0525A], you who uphold the law, answer me concerning what follows: If perfection—that is, perfect justification—had existed through the Levitical priesthood, then it was right to say that perfection should come through the priesthood, because the people received the law while subject to that priesthood. For the law was in the priest’s hand, and the law could neither be fulfilled nor even minimally put into practice except through the priest’s ministry.

If, then, perfection existed through the Levitical priesthood, why, after the old priesthood had brought perfection, was it still necessary for the prophet David to say that another priest would arise, one different from the Levitical priests and belonging to another tribe? He says that this priest would arise according to the dignity of the order of Melchizedek. And lest someone say, “Let him arise according to this order, but in such a way that he may at the same time retain the order of Aaron,” he says that it is according to the order of Melchizedek precisely so that he may not in any respect be according to the order of Aaron.

He says “arise” because the Levitical priests had been brought low: they were unable to shake off, either from themselves or from the people, the yoke of sin through the law. But Christ arose, and through his priesthood the faithful, shaking off the yoke of sin, rise to blessedness. It is as though he said: If perfection existed through the Levitical priesthood, another priesthood according to Melchizedek would arise in vain to bring perfection. But another priesthood arose; therefore the Levitical priesthood did not bring perfection. We have the assumption: “the priesthood being transferred,” and so forth.

The text, however, is connected as follows. Someone might say: Why do you say that the law is subject to the priesthood and that the priesthood is destroyed when another priest arises? What are you intending by this?

I say that the law is subject to that priesthood and that the Levitical priesthood itself is destroyed for this reason: when the priesthood is transferred, the law of that priesthood must also be transferred, since the law is in the priest’s hand. I intend to prove the destruction of the law by destroying its priesthood.

Truly another priest arose, and truly the priesthood was transferred, which amounts to the same thing: another according to tribe and according to rite. Or it was transferred because it was changed both according to tribe and according to rite.

He first shows that it was transferred according to tribe, saying: Truly it was transferred; or, truly another priest exists, for Christ—“in whom,” that is, in whose regard these things are said—is from another tribe and not from the tribe of Levi. From that other tribe no one was present, that is, no one had previously been appointed to the altar. And truly he is from another tribe, because it is manifest that our Lord Christ arose from Judah, concerning which tribe Moses said nothing about priests, so that anyone from that tribe ought to become a priest.

The transfer of the priesthood according to tribe had already occurred in Samuel, when the sons of Eli were rejected, although according to their hereditary line they were heirs of the priesthood. That change signified the true transformation [translation], which was to take place in Christ.

He proves again that the priesthood was transferred according to rite, something that had not previously been seen, because, although the tribe was rejected, the rites were not changed. Hence he says: I have proved that the priesthood was transferred according to tribe. It is still more manifest [Col. 0526A]—that is, by a more extensive and firmer argument—because proof concerning the rite is stronger than proof concerning the tribe.

It is manifest, I say, that the priesthood has been transferred if another priest arises according to the likeness and rite of Melchizedek, as was foretold. This other man was not made priest according to the law of a fleshly commandment, that is, according to a law that merely commanded and promised fleshly things, but was made priest according to power, that is, according to the divinity that was in him.

By “power” I mean the power of indestructible life, that is, the power by which he gave those who believed in him indestructible life, namely, eternal life.

Or understand it this way: He is not according to the law of a fleshly commandment, that is, according to the fleshly understanding of the law, but according to the power of the law itself, namely, its spiritual understanding. I call it the power of indestructible life because the spiritual operation of the law promises eternal life, just as its weakness promises fleshly life.

I say that the priesthood has been transferred if another priest has arisen. But another priest has arisen, and he proves this from authoritative testimony, saying: Truly another priest has arisen, because David testifies—that is, testifies with me and with many other Scriptures—“You, Christ, are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.”

Although he ought to have said, “Christ is a priest,” in order to reproduce the prophet’s words faithfully, he says, “You are a priest.”

He then adds the reason why the old priesthood was destroyed and the new one introduced, lest an opponent object: Why do you say that God gave another priesthood for the rejection of the old one, when he himself instituted the old priesthood?

In response he says: The rejection of the preceding commandment and of the old law occurs because of its weakness—that is, because it was weak even during the time when it was observed—for although it gave some justification, it did not give perfect justification. It was rejected because of its uselessness, because now, if it is observed, it is not merely weak but harmful.

It truly possessed weakness. For during the time when the law was observed, it brought nothing to perfection—that is, it could bring nothing to perfection. For even if some people were perfect under it, they were not made perfect through it, but through faith in the one who was to come. In calling the law “preceding,” he signifies that something else ought to follow in order to correct the law’s imperfection.

The preceding commandment is rejected, but a better hope is introduced. To commend it more strongly, he does not call it merely a commandment but a hope, because this new commandment of Christ contains hope—not a fleshly hope, but hope of heavenly glory. Through this hope we not only approach God but draw near to him. That the law was weak, while Christ’s commandment is the means by which we draw near to God, greatly enhances the praise of the new priest.

And how much this contributes again to his commendation: Jesus was not made priest without an oath. Others, that is, the Levitical priests, were made priests without an oath, as though they were something destined to be changed. But Jesus was made priest with an oath, by him—that is, by God the Father—who said to Jesus: “You are a priest forever.”

And that your priesthood is eternal: “The Lord swore, and he will not repent of it,” that is, he will not change your priesthood.

David says that God swore this, but he does not say where, when, or in what words God swore it. To the extent that Jesus was made priest with an oath, while the others were made priests without an oath; and to the extent that through Jesus we draw near to God, while through the law no one was brought to perfection; to that extent Jesus became the guarantor—that is, the confirmer and defender—of a better covenant, namely, of one promising better things because they are eternal.

As he surpasses them in promises, so also in the dignity that follows: Jesus surpasses the Levitical priests because the others, that is, the Levitical priests, were made many. They were many because death prevented them from remaining alive. But Christ has an everlasting priesthood, since he remains forever.

Therefore, because he remains forever and possesses an everlasting priesthood, he is also able to save forever [Col. 0527B], whereas it is agreed that the mortal priests of the law could confer certain salvations only during the period of their priesthood.

Having shown how the old priesthood and the law are destroyed through Christ’s priesthood, and having sufficiently commended Christ’s priesthood itself, he now also commends the exercise and fulfillment of the priestly office in Christ by disparaging, through contrast, the operation of the old priesthood. He says:

Jesus is able to save forever—he, I say, who approaches God, not through the alien offerings of animals, but through himself, a living sacrifice offered on the altar of the cross.

Jesus, I say, is always living to intercede with the Father for us, because his flesh lives forever in heaven for this purpose: by presenting himself, it continually appeals to the Father on our behalf.

I say that he approaches through himself. For it was fitting and necessary that such a one, approaching through himself, should be our high priest: holy in himself through the possession of virtues, innocent toward his neighbor, and, being holy in the character of his goodness, also undefiled through the absence of vices.

Nor merely undefiled in the sense that he had once been defiled, but separated every day from sinners, that is, separated from the flock of sinners, and made higher than the heavens, that is, higher than every heavenly creature.

Such a high priest has no need to offer daily for himself, as the Levitical priests have need to offer sacrifices, first interceding for their own offenses and then for the offenses of the people.

He does not say “daily” as though Christ needed to offer for himself on some particular day, but in order to remove from Christ what he attributes to those who have a daily need to offer for themselves. Christ does not have this need.

For he did this—namely, offer—once, not for his own offenses but for the offenses of the people. He did it, I say, by offering himself. His one offering was sufficient for everyone, for the remission of all sins. It is therefore unnecessary for it to be repeated.

Those priests have a daily need to offer for themselves because the law constituted as priests men possessing the weakness both of nature’s frailty and of sin. The law constituted such men as priests, but the word of the oath, spoken through David after the law had been given, constituted as priest not a man but the Son of God [Col. 0528A], who does not possess weakness but endures forever and is perfect.

## CHAPTER VIII

> “Now the main point of what is being said is this: We have such a high priest, who has taken his seat at the right hand of the throne of Majesty in the heavens, a minister of the holy places and of the true tabernacle, which God established, and not man. For every high priest is appointed to offer gifts and sacrifices. Therefore it is necessary that this one also have something to offer. Now if he were on earth, he would not be a priest, since there are those who offer gifts according to the law, who serve a copy and shadow of the heavenly things, just as Moses was instructed when he was about to complete the tabernacle. ‘See,’ he says, ‘that you make everything according to the pattern shown to you on the mountain’ [Col. 0528B]. But now he has obtained a more excellent ministry, just as he is mediator of a better covenant, which has been established on better promises. For if that first covenant had been faultless, no place would have been sought for a second. For finding fault with them, he says:
>
> ‘Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will complete a new covenant over the house of Israel and over the house of Judah—not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt; for they did not remain in my covenant, and I neglected them, says the Lord. For this is the covenant that I will establish with the house of Israel after those days, says the Lord: By giving (Dando) [I will give (dabo)] my laws into their mind, and I will write them upon their hearts; and I will be their God, and they will be my people. And they shall not teach each one his neighbor, and each one his brother, saying, “Know the Lord,” because all shall know me, from the lesser (minore) [the least (minimo)] to the greatest of them; because I will be merciful toward their iniquities, and I will no longer remember (memorabor) [call to mind (commemorabor)] their sins (peccatorum) [sin (peccatum)].’
>
> By saying “new,” he has made the first old. Now what is becoming old and growing aged is near destruction.”

## EXPOSITION

Although he had said little about this priest, he now briefly gathers together the dignity of which he has spoken in the preceding discussion. It is as though he said: I have said many things in praise of this priest, but now I shall make a summary—that is, a brief gathering of many things.

I call it a summary concerning what is being said, that is, something higher and more worthy in praise of Christ, containing everything that has been said above. This, I say, is the summary.

We have such a high priest who has existed for a long time, one who has taken his seat with the Father, resting and judging. He has taken his seat, I say, at the right hand, that is, in equality with the seat of Majesty, that is, with the divinity of the one who sits. For the Father is called Majesty, since, sitting in the same way, he rests and judges.

He has taken his seat, I say, in the heavens, that is, either above those material heavens or above the thrones and dominions.

This high priest, I say, is there a minister of the holy places. For in the heavens he ministers the glory signified by the Holy of Holies. He is also a minister there of the true tabernacle, that is, of the truth prefigured by the old tabernacle: namely, righteousness in the present Church and glory in the future.

The Lord established this true tabernacle so that it would remain forever. But the shadowy tabernacle of the law was not fixed; it was portable, carried from place to place.

A Jew might say: The Lord also established the legal tabernacle through Moses as its minister.

Paul replies: Certainly, but the Lord established this tabernacle in such a way that no one was present whose ministry he employed in establishing it; rather, he established it in his own person.

Christ is truly a minister, for every high priest is appointed to minister, namely, to offer gifts and sacrifices. Therefore, since every high priest is appointed to offer, this high priest Christ must also have something to offer. And since he must have something to offer, it will either be earthly or heavenly—but it is not earthly.

For if it were earthly, he would no longer be a priest, much less a high priest. Therefore what he offers must be heavenly.

He calls “earthly” whatever he would offer in carnal things and for carnal things. If what Jesus offered were earthly, I deny not only that he would be a high priest, but that he would even be a priest, since there were many priests who offered gifts according to the law, that is, upon the earth.

Someone might say: There are indeed many who offer, but because no one can offer worthily in this manner, it would be good for Jesus to offer according to the law.

He removes this objection, saying: Since there were those who offered according to the law, and who serve a copy.

A “copy” is that according to whose likeness something is made. An “example,” however, is the likeness taken from the copy.

When God called Moses to the mountain, he revealed to him there the whole truth concerning the worship of God that was to be fulfilled. But God, understanding with Moses that this carnal people could not immediately grasp spiritual things, told Moses to make figures for that carnal people corresponding to the truth he saw there. In these figures the childish people would be nourished for as long as necessary, until they could pass from the childhood of figures to the maturity of virtue.

In this way, the truth first shown was the copy of the figures that were made according to the likeness of the truth previously shown.

Again, in another respect, the figures are called the copy of the truth according to the fulfillment of that truth, and according to the likeness of the preceding figures. In this sense he calls the figures here the copy.

In what follows, however, he calls the truth previously revealed to Moses on the mountain the copy with respect to the figures made according to the likeness of the virtue [truth] that had been shown.

They serve, I say, the copy—that is, the figures. And because a copy is sometimes the truth and not a figure, he adds “and shadow,” because those figures were a copy possessing not the truth but the shadow of the truth, a shadow lightly dispelled through Christ.

Since there were, I say, those who served the shadow of heavenly things, fulfilling everything just as God instructed Moses, and since those priests properly fulfilled the law, Jesus would assume this priesthood in vain.

Moses was instructed not when he began but when he completed the tabernacle. For he was able to devise certain figures by himself; but since he could not devise all of them by himself, he returned to God so that he might be instructed concerning the figures as he had been concerning the truth.

The Lord said to him: See, Moses, make everything—that is, all the figures—according to the copy, that is, according to the truth, the copy that was shown to you on the mountain.

Those priests have the ministry of serving the copy and shadow; but Jesus has obtained a better ministry, because he ministers in spiritual things and gives spiritual things.

He obtained this ministry, I say, now that it has been shown that he does not offer something earthly.

His ministry is so much better because Jesus himself is the giver of a better covenant, that is, of better things, since he promises eternal things. He does not call him “giver” but “mediator,” because, standing between God and humanity, he receives from God what he grants to humanity.

This covenant has been established—that is, confirmed—and will endure forever. It has been established, I say, through promises, that is, through many and varied pledges. These promises are better, as has often been said.

He said that Christ is the giver of a better covenant, and he proves this by saying: Truly Christ’s covenant is better than the earlier covenant. For the earlier covenant was not free from fault, whereas Christ’s covenant is free from fault.

If that first covenant had been faultless, a place would not have been sought for a second covenant. But since a second was given, it is evident that the first was imperfect and the second perfect. For the first covenant would be destroyed in vain unless it were imperfect. And the second would be given in vain to correct the imperfect first covenant if it were not perfect.

He says this in the following way: If that first covenant had been faultless, he does not say, “If the people under it had been faultless,” but, “If that covenant itself had been faultless,” that is, if it had been free from fault. For in this respect the law itself appeared not to be free from fault: it commanded, but did not possess the assisting grace that it could provide, thereby making all who were under the law liable to guilt.

If, I say, that first covenant had been faultless—I say the same thing to you with certainty—the opportunity for the giving of a second covenant would not have been sought.

He says “would have been sought” because God first through Noah, then through the patriarchs, and afterward through the law and the prophets, gradually instructing the carnal immaturity of human beings through the law, was seeking the opportunity at which, once they had been instructed toward perfection, he might suitably give the spiritual covenant.

If, I say, the first covenant had been faultless, the opportunity for the second covenant would not have been sought. But the opportunity for the second covenant is sought, and he proves this through the testimony of Jeremiah, who says: Truly it is being sought.

For the Holy Spirit, finding fault with those under the law, says through Jeremiah: Behold, days are coming, gradually drawing nearer and nearer. He calls the time of Christ “days,” because when Christ came, the darkness was driven away. And the day dawned, that is, the knowledge of truth.

And that these days are coming is said not by me but by the Lord: believe him. “In those days I will complete,” that is, I will give a new covenant, which will complete the old, because it will lead it to perfection. How it is new he will explain sufficiently in what follows.

I will complete it, I say, in the house of Israel and in the house of Judah. Literally, by Israel and Judah only the Jews are understood; but according to the interpretations of the names, every person who sees and confesses God is understood.

He divides Israel and Judah because, after the death of Solomon, who had ruled over both, his son Rehoboam possessed only the tribe of Judah and half the tribe of Benjamin, while the other tribes of Israel withdrew from him from that day and adhered to Jeroboam (1 Kings XII, 19).

I will give this new covenant over the house—that is, so that, as though coming from above, it may rule over Israel and Judah and not be like the old law, a handmaid in the priest’s hand.

And because it could be a new covenant by promising and commanding new earthly things, he defines it by saying: new in such a way that it is not like the covenant that I made with their fathers.

And because he had made a spiritual covenant with certain fathers, such as Abraham, he therefore specifies that it is the covenant he made on the day when he took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt.

He says “took them by the hand” by the analogy of someone taking by the hand a person lying in mud and unable to rise by himself, and lifting him up. In the same way God took hold of them, powerless by themselves, and brought them out of the misery of the Egyptians.

He now explains how he found fault with them: I took them by the hand, but because they did not remain in my covenant, they neglected me, and I neglected them.

And if I tell you that you have been neglected by God, do not be troubled, for this is what the Lord says: Truly I will give a new covenant, not like the one I gave their fathers.

For this is the covenant that I will establish—that is, give in an orderly manner—to the house of Israel, that is, to all who see God; and not merely now, but after those appointed days. Believe this again, because the Lord says so.

I will establish it by giving my laws into their minds, that is, into their understanding. I will not merely establish them, but I will also write them so that they may remain forever, in their hearts, that is, in their wills. For they will both understand my laws and carry them out willingly.

I will write them, I say, as something that ought to remain over them and rule them. And after they have my laws written in their minds and hearts, I will be their God, because it will be said: Truly God dwells in these people, who shine with so many miracles. And they will be my people; it will be said of them: These truly are the people of God.

This part of the prophecy is fulfilled in this world; what follows remains to be fulfilled in the future.

“They will be my people, and each one shall not teach his neighbor.” Someone might say that he will not care about his neighbor. Therefore he adds that no one will teach even his brother, whom he loves greatly, saying: “Brother, know God.”

The one will not teach the other because they will all know me, from the least to the greatest of them. This will be fulfilled on the day of judgment, when even the wicked will confess Christ as the Son of God.

The saints note that he says “from the least to the greatest,” and not the reverse, in order to show that all will then know God perfectly. For it is impossible for the greater to be taught by the lesser.

“And I will be their God”: again, all will know me. And I will do all these things for them because I will be merciful toward their iniquities, and I will no longer remember their sins.

He says “iniquities” when they do not observe equity toward their neighbor; “sins” when they act wrongly in themselves. Or, if we take “sin” and “iniquity” as referring to the same thing, we explain the passage in this way: He says, “I will be merciful toward their iniquities.”

And because “mercy” could be understood as forgiving without punishment in the present, he therefore adds: I will be merciful in such a way that in the future I will no longer remember their sins.

Some books have “their sin,” and according to this reading the original sin is understood.

From this point Paul begins: The prophet said, “I will give a new covenant.”

By saying “new,” he made the first covenant old in the active sense. Or “he made old,” that is, the first covenant became old, in the passive sense.

And I rightly say that he made the first old, because it is near destruction. He says this in the following way: Whatever is becoming obsolete, as happens with living things, and grows old, as happens with living things, is near destruction. For old age and obsolescence foretell death.

## CHAPTER IX

> “The first covenant indeed had regulations for worship and a worldly sanctuary. For a first tabernacle was prepared, in which there were the lampstands, the table, and the presentation of the loaves; it is called the Holy Place. Behind the second veil was the tabernacle called the Holy of Holies, having a golden censer and the ark of the covenant covered on every side with gold, in which were a golden urn containing manna, Aaron’s staff that had blossomed, and the tablets of the covenant; above it were the cherubim of glory overshadowing the mercy seat. Concerning these things there is now no need to speak individually.
>
> These things having been arranged in this way, the priests always entered the first tabernacle, completing the services of worship. But into the second tabernacle only the high priest entered once a year, not without blood, which he offered for himself and for the people’s ignorance. By this the Holy Spirit signified that the way into the holy places had not yet been made manifest, while the first tabernacle still had its standing.
>
> This is a parable for the present time, according to which gifts and sacrifices are offered that cannot perfect the worshiper with respect to conscience, but only with respect to food and drink, various washings, and regulations of the flesh imposed until the time of correction.
>
> But Christ, appearing as high priest of the good things to come, entered once for all through the greater and more perfect tabernacle not made by hands, that is, not of this creation, and not through the blood of goats [bulls] or calves, but through his own blood, having obtained eternal redemption.
>
> For if the blood of goats and bulls and the ashes of a heifer, sprinkled upon those who are defiled, sanctify for the purification of the flesh, how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the Holy Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, cleanse our conscience from dead works to serve the living God?
>
> And therefore he is mediator of a new covenant, so that, with a death having intervened for the redemption of the transgressions committed under the first covenant, those who have been called may receive the promise of an eternal inheritance.
>
> For where there is a covenant, the death of the one who made the covenant must necessarily intervene. For a covenant is confirmed over the dead; otherwise it has no force while the one who made the covenant is alive.
>
> Hence not even the first covenant was inaugurated without blood. For when every commandment of the law had been read by Moses to all the people, he took the blood of calves and goats, with water, scarlet wool, and hyssop, and sprinkled both the book itself and all the people, saying: ‘This is the blood of the covenant that God commanded for you.’ He likewise sprinkled the tabernacle and all the vessels of the ministry with blood.
>
> And almost everything is cleansed with blood according to the law, and without the shedding of blood there is no remission.
>
> Therefore it is necessary that the copies of the heavenly things be cleansed with these, but that the heavenly things themselves be cleansed with better sacrifices than these.
>
> For Christ did not enter holy places made by hands, copies of the true things, but into heaven itself, now to appear before the face of God for us. Nor did he enter in order to offer himself often, as the high priest enters the holy places every year with another’s blood. Otherwise he would have had to suffer often from the foundation of the world.
>
> But now, once at the consummation of the ages, he has appeared for the abolition [destruction] of sin through his sacrifice.
>
> And just as it is appointed for human beings to die once, and after that comes judgment, so Christ also, having been offered once, will appear a second time, without sin, for the salvation of those who await him through faith [‘through faith’ is absent].”

## EXPOSITION

Although the first covenant is near destruction, it nevertheless had regulations—not true justifications, but justifications suited to its worship, that is, carnal ones, because its worship was carnal. And it had a sanctuary—not a spiritual one, but a worldly one, because human beings considered holiness to be present there, although it was not truly there.

He proves this. Truly the first covenant had a sanctuary, for it had a first and a second tabernacle.

He says it in the following way: A first tabernacle was made, in which at first there were lampstands. Although he uses the plural “lampstands,” there was in fact one lampstand, with a central shaft on which six branches rested, three on the left (Exodus XXV, 32).

In that tabernacle there was also a table immediately after the entrance, and upon this table was the presentation of the loaves, that is, twelve loaves presented to God through sanctification. If one of them happened to be consumed because of necessity—for this sanctified bread was necessary for sacrifices—another loaf, similarly prepared from fine flour, was immediately substituted in place of the one taken.

These twelve loaves were placed on the Sabbath. When they were removed on the following Sabbath, another twelve were put in their place (ibid., 30).

This tabernacle, containing these things, is called the Holy Place [Sancta]. Outside this tabernacle there was an altar under the open sky, upon which animals were sacrificed.

Behind the veil was a second tabernacle. A veil had been placed between them, separating the first tabernacle from the second. This second tabernacle is called the Holy of Holies.

The second tabernacle, I say, had a golden censer and the ark of the covenant, that is, the ark containing the covenant, covered all around with gold.

And because it could have been covered with gold on the outside but not within, he therefore adds that it was covered with gold on every side, inside and outside.

In the ark was a golden urn, that is, a golden gomor, containing manna, so that they might remember the bread with which God had fed them in the desert.

In the same ark was Aaron’s staff, which had blossomed—that is, through which he was chosen as priest. There were also the tablets of the covenant, on which the law had been written.

Above the ark were cherubim, that is, two angels. I call them cherubim of glory, that is, gloriously adorned. Those cherubim were overshadowing the mercy seat.

There was a tablet above the ark called the mercy seat, because an angel used to appear fixed between the two cherubim upon that same tablet and give divine responses.

In this second tabernacle there was also an altar of incense. In the temple, however, there were two tabernacles, separated by the intervening veil.

In the first tabernacle, near the entrance, was a table, and upon it twelve loaves, with incense upon each one [Col. 0534C]. There was also a lampstand, with three branches attached to the central shaft on each side. On these branches were small spheres; after the spheres came lilies, and after the lilies came cups.

The first tabernacle, therefore, signifies the Church of the faithful that exists in the world, in which the ministers of the Church offer prayers and sacrifices each day. The table in the temple beside the entrance signifies divine Scripture, which is ministered, according to their capacity, to those who enter the Church through faith. The twelve loaves are the twelve apostles, by whose teaching the faithful are nourished in the Church. The fact that, when some necessity arose, one of the loaves was taken and another substituted in its place signifies this: when one of the apostles or of their successors has been taken from the world, another who is to serve in his place must be substituted for him.

All these loaves are consumed on the Sabbath, because after the rest of true glory has been reached on the day of judgment, no episcopal office or ecclesiastical administration will any longer be exercised. These loaves are said to have been made of fine flour because in the apostles there was nothing but the purity of innocence and the perfection of virtues; and this ought also to be found in their successors. The incense placed above them, whose odor is pleasing, signifies their prayers, which are acceptable to God and pleasant and useful to those subject to them.

The shaft of the lampstand, to which three branches were attached on the right and an equal number on the left, is Christ. Both the faithful of the old Church and those of the new cling to him as to a firm trunk, and everything that they are or have been they have from him. The three branches on the right signify the three orders of the faithful of this Church, which is more worthy than the old one. You find these in the Gospel, where it is said:

> “Two will be in bed: one will be taken, the other will be left. Two in the field: one will be taken, but the other will be left. Two at the mill: one will be taken, and the other will be left” (Luke 17:34–35).

The two in bed are the continent. Those who are left are the ones who, whether they abstain for the sake of worldly favor or do so for God, nevertheless fail. But those who do this for Christ and persevere will be taken up into glory. The two in the field are those laboring in the Church, which is God’s field; of them, as has been said concerning the others, some will be taken up into glory and some will be left for punishment. The two at the mill signify the possessors of this age, remaining amid the whirl of worldly affairs, who labor to please the man with the woman and the woman with the man. Those among them will be left whom the pleasure of the world draws into crimes and ruin. But those will be taken up who do not fall into crimes and who, from the mammon of iniquity, make friends for themselves (Luke 16:9). 391

Those three branches attached to the left side signify the three orders of the faithful under the old covenant, whom you find represented by Daniel, Noah, and Job. Daniel, who lived chastely, represents those who practiced continence under the old law. Noah, builder and craftsman of the Lord’s ark, prefigured the teachers of the law. Job, who lived in marriage and possessed worldly goods, represents those who pleased God while living in marriage and possessing worldly things.

In all these branches there were small spheres, because the roundness of perfection and the equality of justice were present in all of them. Lilies followed these spheres, because after someone has become perfect, has become a pleasing odor to God, and in the Church has become fragrant through the example of good works, lilies follow. After the lilies come the cups, because when someone is proved perfect and, like a lily, is recognized by the fragrance of good conduct, it remains for him to become a preacher and a pourer-out of Catholic teaching for those in need. Having become such through action and teaching, he kindles himself with the fire of charity and displays light to others in the darkness.

The second tabernacle was divided from the first by the interposition of a veil; into it the high priest alone entered, and only once a year, with blood.

That tabernacle is the heavenly Church. It is covered by a veil because, while we are still in this mortal flesh, or in the Church, we cannot, through the blindness of ignorance, know what and how great a reality God is preparing for his own. The high priest who entered once a year and with blood is Christ, who, at the completion of the ages, offering his blood once for all, inaugurated for us the way to the heavenly homeland.

The fact that the same sacrifice was repeated each year showed the imperfection of that sacrifice, and by its very repetition it commanded that another sacrifice be awaited, one that would not have to be repeated. The golden censer is Christ, who, because he possessed perfect wisdom and had rightful authority over both earthly and heavenly things, is said to have been golden. Because he was full of the fire of charity toward God and neighbor and poured out for the world before God the pleasing fragrance of prayers, he is rightly compared to a censer containing fire and sending the odor of incense upward.

He is likewise the ark of the covenant, that is, the ark in which the covenant was kept and hidden, because in the wisdom of the Father, with whom he personally existed, the commandments of the old and new laws were hidden, and already depended upon his ordering. He also shuts, and no one opens; he opens, and no one shuts (Revelation 3:7). This ark was covered with gold on every side, both inside and outside, because he shone in soul and body with the consummation of every virtue, and no justice was lacking in him.

In this ark was a golden urn, because in Christ’s body there was a true human soul, and that soul was full of every virtue and of perfect wisdom. In the urn was hidden manna, because in Christ’s soul is the divinity itself, which is the bread and nourishment of the angels. There were also in the ark Aaron’s rod and the tablets of the Covenant. Aaron’s rod signified the true priesthood. The tablets of the Covenant are the hearts of the faithful, in which the commandments of the law sit and rest.

Thus Aaron’s rod and the tablets of the Covenant are in the ark, because in Christ there is the true priesthood, and each believer is in him. Hence he says in the Gospel: “Remain in me, and I in you” (John 15:4).

Above the ark was the tablet called the mercy seat, upon which God, appearing through an angel, was reconciled concerning their sins. Above the mercy seat were two cherubim, always looking upon it with bowed faces and overshadowing it with the joining of their outstretched wings.

Christ himself is the mercy seat, insofar as we ask from him what we desire and, by his mercy, he is reconciled concerning our sins. Above him are two cherubim, because even the higher powers of heaven lean upon him and have in him the foundation of their stability. These same cherubim always look upon the mercy seat; 392 but they overshadow it from above, because the heavenly powers always contemplate God’s mercy, yet the more intently they look upon him, the more obscure and unknown he becomes: “For the mercy of the Lord is a great abyss” (Psalm 35:7).

In the ark there were four rings into which the carrying poles were inserted, and thus the ark was carried wherever circumstances required. The four rings are the four Gospels; the carrying poles are the holy preachers who, inserted into the teaching of the Gospel, carry Christ and his faith wherever God wills and ordains.

The fact that it was made of setim wood, which is imperishable, prefigured that Christ’s body would after the Passion be immortal and incapable of suffering. These things are found in the first and second tabernacle; as we proceed to interpret each of them, it is not necessary now to discuss every individual detail. Rather, we must speak of the way in which these things were arranged: in the first tabernacle the priests always entered, completing the duties of the sacrifices—that is, performing the sacrifices according to the rite of their office—in the first tabernacle continually.

But into the second tabernacle the high priest alone entered once a year, and not without blood. After receiving it from an animal sacrificed outside, he dipped it upon the horns of the altar of incense. The priest offered this blood for his own ignorance and for the remission of the people’s ignorance. Through this, the Holy Spirit signified that, whereas everyone entered the first tabernacle, no one except the high priest entered the second: the way of the holy places had not yet been revealed, that is, the saints could not enter heaven. This way was to be revealed to them in Christ when he rose again.

And while the way of the holy places had not yet been revealed, but Abraham and all the saints were being held in darkness, the earlier tabernacle then retained its established condition. For until the way of the holy places was revealed, when Christ celebrated the new Passover, the old law possessed its established status from God.

All these things concerning the entire former and true tabernacle are a parable of the present time, that is, a figure referring to the time now at hand, because whatever was there prefigured has now been fulfilled in Christ. In the first tabernacle the priests always entered, completing the sacrifices, because in the present Church we enter daily, completing Christ’s spiritual sacrifice. But into the second tabernacle the high priest entered once a year, because Christ, the true high priest, entered the heavenly Church once and will not return again from glory.

The fact that the true priest repeated that entry into the second tabernacle each year signified that Christ, the true high priest, had not yet entered his tabernacle in heaven but was still awaited. The legal high priest did not enter without blood because Christ did not penetrate the heavens until he had first poured out his own blood for the redemption of all. Christ offered this blood not for his own ignorance, of course, but for the removal of the ignorance of the whole people.

In accordance with this parable, that is, this figure, gifts are offered under the old law—that is, lesser offerings. Sacrifices of animals are also offered. So, in the present Church, our gifts are prayers as a fragrance of sweetness to God, and the sacrifices are those who are slaughtered for Christ, such as Laurence, and also those who slaughter themselves through fasts, vigils, and manifold afflictions.

These gifts and sacrifices under the old law cannot make the one serving in them perfect. Even if he is perfect according to human judgment, he is nevertheless not perfect according to his own conscience, because his conscience continually whispers to him that he has become guilty of crime and has not been cleansed through the legal rites.

Nor is it surprising that he is not perfect, since I speak of one who serves only in foods and drinks: he eats and drinks abundantly, and in various baptisms—that is, washings performed according to the rites of the legal observances. He also serves in acts of righteousness, but of the flesh, because those acts of righteousness are carnal: they free the body from the punishment of the law, but leave the soul in the bonds of sin.

I speak of the righteousness of the flesh as imposed so that it might endure until the time of correction, that is, until Christ, by the perfection of the covenant through which the imperfection of the old covenant would be corrected. The legal gifts and sacrifices can make no one perfect, but Christ found eternal redemption—which is to say, Christ makes perfect.

He introduces by what means Christ found eternal redemption, saying: “Christ assisting.” He does not specify whom he assists. We can say: Christ assists the Father by his representation, always interceding for us. Or: Christ assists by raising our weakness toward heavenly things, extending to us the hand of assistance. Christ, I say, assisting as high priest not of carnal things but of good things to come, that is, of heavenly things. Or “of good things to come,” that is, of present righteousness and eternal blessedness; all these things were future in the time of the law.

Christ, I say, such a high priest, entered the tabernacle—the name of the sign designates the thing signified.

I say “a much larger tabernacle,” because if that old tabernacle held a thousand people or several thousand, the heavenly tabernacle is also much larger, broadly encompassing the infinity of all who enter it. It is a more perfect tabernacle because in that tabernacle the perfection of complete blessedness is received. In the legal tabernacle there was imperfection everywhere.

I say “a tabernacle not made by hand.” And lest anyone understand this perversely, supposing that it was not made by hand—that is, by the operation of God—he specifies by saying: What I call “not made by hand” means that this tabernacle is not of this creation, that is, not of human creation, like the old one. In the old tabernacle women wove the curtains, craftsmen worked according to their particular trades, and likewise the other artisans.

He entered this tabernacle, not through the poured-out blood of goats and calves, which had to be used in entering the second tabernacle, but through his own blood poured out into the heavenly tabernacle, namely, into the Holy of Holies. He entered once, and through blood poured out once. By saying that he entered once and poured out his blood once, he signifies the perfection of that sacrifice, which did not need to be repeated.

The fact that the old sacrifice was repeated so many times signified that perfection was not present in it and had not yet come. He entered the Holy Places, having found redemption. He does not specify by whom it was found—whether by himself or by another—and we can state either. Redemption was found by Christ because this high priest, in his sacrifice, found the redemption of human beings from sins; in finding it, the legal high priests always failed. Or redemption was found by us, because we find our redemption in Christ.

I speak of eternal redemption because he makes those whom he redeems eternal. He proves this from the lesser, saying: Truly redemption was found through Christ’s blood, because if the blood of goats and bulls, and if the ashes of a burned heifer sprinkled upon the people, sanctify the defiled—that is, cleanse the pollution of sins—if, I say, they sanctify, being effective for correction not of the soul but only of the flesh, because they free the flesh from the punishment of the law while the polluted soul remains, how much more will the blood of Christ cleanse us?

Christ offered not a goat, not a bull, but himself to God. I say “himself immaculate,” something that no sacrifice in the law could be. I say “immaculate through the Holy Spirit,” united to him in the womb of the mother from whom he was conceived, and through this made free from sin. Or he offered himself through the Holy Spirit, who instructed him to obey the Father in all patience.

How much more, I say, will Christ’s blood cleanse—not merely the flesh, but also our conscience, leaving no cause for the conscience to fear for itself. It will indeed cleanse us from dead works, that is, from sins that produce death, so that we may serve the living God. These are the two things Christ’s blood accomplishes in us: it cleanses us from sins and restores the power of free choice, so that we may be able to serve God.

I say “the living God,” placed here to indicate the purpose, because he will give eternal life to those who serve him. He offered himself, and he is the mediator, that is, the giver of the New Testament. He stands between God, from whom he receives it, and the human being, to whom he grants it. Therefore he is the giver of the New Testament, so that, with his death intervening—that is, standing midway between the disposition and the completion of the covenant—the covenant might be established.

I speak of a death necessary for redemption—not, obviously, the redemption of the Gentiles, concerning which the matter is clear, but the redemption from those transgressions that existed under the former [old] Testament. For that earlier law, by issuing commands, increased transgressions from which it could in no way release anyone.

Thus, with death intervening, they may receive the promise of the eternal inheritance, that is, the eternal inheritance repeatedly promised to them. They receive it not all, but those who have been called by God and chosen from eternity.

After Christ had established the New Testament, it was necessary for him to die for the confirmation of that covenant. This was necessary because, if he had been seized by the Jews and denied what he had previously said, and had shrunk from suffering in support of those things, the disciples would have thought that Christ had not understood that what he taught was true, since he denied it out of fear of death.

Moreover, he had to die so that, rising from death, he might bring to completion what he had foretold that he would accomplish—namely, the redemption of Israel.

The heifer of which we spoke above was red, bearing the type of Christ’s blood, and it was burned entirely and reduced to ashes so that it might be a holocaust for the Lord. Its ashes were sprinkled with water. Thus Christ, worn down by many tribulations and finally reduced by death, as it were, to ashes, underwent this.

The ashes of the heifer, which were cast upon human beings, signify the remembrance of Christ’s suffering, which must always be impressed upon people. Therefore, brother, remember that Christ suffered and was crushed for you, and do not provoke him by sinning. If the ashes of a heifer cleansed the flesh, how much more worthily do Christ’s ashes cleanse the soul.

He said above that Christ is the giver of the New Testament, with death intervening; now he proves, from the custom of human law, that he had to die for the confirmation of the New Testament. Someone might say, as it were: “What need was there for Christ’s death to intervene for the confirmation of the New Testament?” Paul says that it was indeed necessary for him to give the Testament with death intervening [Col. 0540A], because wherever a testament is made under human laws, it is necessary that the death of the testator—that is, the maker of the testament—intervene, namely, come between the disposition of the testament and its completion. The testator’s death must intervene because every testament is confirmed in the death of testators—that is, by the death of those who make testaments. Otherwise, that is, if the testator’s death does not intervene, the testament that has been drawn up is not yet valid while—that is, as long as—the person who made the testament lives. For if the testator escapes death, he will alter the testament again if he wishes.

Therefore, because every testament is confirmed by blood and death, the first testament too was not dedicated—that is, confirmed—without blood. Certainly it was not dedicated without blood: for, after every commandment of the law had been read—every one, because if he omitted certain ones, he might seem to disapprove of those omitted and confirm only those read—Moses read every commandment while all the people listened. Then, after he had read it, Moses took the blood of calves and goats mixed with water; he also took scarlet wool and hyssop, from which the sprinkling instrument is made, and sprinkled with blood both the book itself and all the people, saying: “This blood with which I sprinkle you is the blood of the testament,” that is, for confirming the testament which God commanded to you. As he sprinkled the book, so also he sprinkled the tabernacle and all the vessels of ministry with the same blood. And Paul says that almost everything [Col. 0540C] is cleansed in blood according to the old law; and, whatever may be the case with other matters, under the old law remission of sin does not occur without the shedding of blood—that is, no sin was remitted unless some animal was slain in sacrifice.

Likewise Christ, who is signified through Moses, after every commandment of his new law had been read at supper while the whole people of disciples listened: after he had read everything, Jesus took the blood of calves and goats—that is, his own blood. Christ is called a calf because of the strength of the cross, with whose horns he scattered the ungodly. Christ is also called a goat because of the likeness of sinful flesh and because he was a sacrifice for sin, while he bore our sins upon the wood. Christ, I say, took his own blood together with the water [Col. 0540D] which came forth from his side on the cross: through the water sanctifying baptism, and by the price of his blood redeeming us from sins. He took it with scarlet wool, whose color is fiery, and with hyssop. For the wool signifies Christ’s charity; its scarlet, resembling fire, signifies the ardor of Christ’s love; and hyssop, which is effective in driving away swelling of the lungs, signifies Christ’s humility. Through the ardor of love and humility he poured out his blood for our redemption. He sprinkled also the book itself, that is, his Gospel, which he confirmed by his intervening death, and all the people of the faithful—that is, he sanctified them—with his blood, saying: “This is the blood, the confirmer of the New Testament, which Testament God commanded to you.” Here Moses proved very faithfully, speaking the same words as Christ when, after supper, he gave the cup of his blood and said: “This cup is the New Testament in my blood.”

He sprinkled the book; likewise he sprinkled the tabernacle with blood. The same allegory is understood through the tabernacle, namely, the Church of Christ redeemed by his blood, which above was understood through all the people. He also sprinkled all the vessels of ministry, because Christ redeemed by his blood the teachers of the Church, in whom his ministries are contained; and, to those redeemed, he gave the spirit of wisdom and knowledge. All things are cleansed in his blood according to Christ’s law. The word “almost” has no allegorical significance. And without the shedding of Christ’s blood there is no remission of any sin. And because all things must be cleansed in blood and no remission occurs without the shedding of blood,

it was therefore necessary that the copies of the heavenly things—that is, the legal things which are figures of spiritual realities—be cleansed by the things mentioned above, namely, calves and goats. The copies of the true things had to be cleansed by these sacrifices; but the heavenly things themselves, of which these were figures, had to be cleansed by better sacrifices than those just mentioned, goat and calf. And truly the sacrifice by which the heavenly things were cleansed was better: for Jesus entered—and truly these are heavenly things, for they are not made by hand, and so forth. He says this as follows: Jesus entered, not remaining in holy places made by hand. Those holy places made by hand were indeed copies of the true things, but he entered heaven itself. He entered for this purpose: that now, after it has been shown that the holy places made by hand are useless, he might appear before the face—that is, the good pleasure—of God for us, so that we might be brought into heaven with him [Col. 0541C].

He did indeed enter heaven, but he did not enter in such a way that, often returning from there, he might offer himself again, as though his sacrifice once offered were not sufficient for all people and for all time. He did not enter in order to offer himself often, as the legal high priest enters the Holy of Holies every year, repeating his sacrifice because it is insufficient—not with his own blood, as Christ did, but with another’s blood. Because it is another’s blood, it cannot justify. In this he shows both that his own sacrifice is sufficient and that the legal sacrifice is insufficient.

Otherwise—that is, if you wish to say instead that Christ ought to offer himself often—then without doubt, if this is so, he would have had to suffer repeatedly, beginning from the origin [Col. 0541D] of the world. For if his Passion benefited only those who lived in his own time, and he must suffer again in each future age, then surely it would have been necessary for him, beginning in the days of Abel, to bear a cross in every age; or else Abraham and the other saints will not have been redeemed. This indeed would have been necessary. But now, since it has been shown that such a great absurdity follows from this, it must be said that Christ appeared once at the consummation of the ages. Christ’s time is called the consummation because Christ fulfilled everything that had been foretold concerning him. And whereas before there had been no consummation—that is, no true perfection—he brought the perfection of all things. He appeared, I say, for the abolishing—that is, the destruction—of sin by a sacrifice not another’s but his own. Because he completely destroyed sin, Christ need not suffer again; accordingly, he ought not to die a second time, because other human beings too die only once. And just as it is appointed for human beings to die once, after which, when they have died, judgment remains for them, so Christ too was offered once to God through death for the exhausting—that is, emptying—of the sins of many [Col. 0542A]. In that he died once, he is like a human being; but in that a human being dies in order to be judged, while Christ is to judge, he is unlike one. For thus it says: At his second coming, when he comes for judgment, Christ will appear without sin—that is, not in the likeness of sinful flesh, but of flesh glorified by the brightness of immortality and incapacity for suffering. Or he will appear without sin, that is, not coming so as again, as before, to become a sacrifice for sin. He will appear, indeed, for salvation—not to the ungodly, but to those who await him in righteousness and fear.

## Chapter X

> “For the law, having a shadow of good things to come, not the very image of the realities, can never, by the same sacrifices which they offer continually year by year, make those who approach perfect. Otherwise they would have ceased to be offered, because the worshippers, once cleansed, would have no further consciousness of sin. But in those sacrifices a remembrance of sins is made year by year. For it is impossible for sins to be taken away by the blood of bulls and goats. Therefore, when entering the world, he says: ‘Sacrifice and offering you did not desire, but you prepared a body for me. Whole burnt offerings and offerings for sin did not please you. [Col. 0542C] Then I said: Behold, I come. In the head of the book it is written of me: to do your will, O God.’ Saying above that sacrifices and offerings and whole burnt offerings and offerings for sin you did not desire, nor were pleasing to you—things which are offered according to the law—then he said: ‘Behold, I come to do your will, O God’: he removes the first in order to establish the following one. By that will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once. And every priest indeed stands daily ministering and often offering the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins. But this one, offering one sacrifice for sins, sits forever at the right hand of God, henceforth waiting until his enemies are made [Col. 0542D] the footstool of his feet. For by one offering he has perfected forever those who are sanctified. The Holy Spirit also testifies to us. For after he said: ‘This is the Testament which I will make with them after those days, says the Lord: I will give my laws in their hearts, and I will write them upon their minds,’ and, ‘I will remember their sins and iniquities no more.’ Now where there is remission of these, there is no longer an offering for sin. Therefore, brothers, having confidence in entering the holy places through the blood of Christ, by the new and living way which he inaugurated for us through the veil, that is, his flesh; and having a great priest over the house of God, let us approach with a true heart in fullness of faith, our hearts sprinkled from an evil [Col. 0543A] conscience and our body washed with pure water. Let us hold unwaveringly the confession of our hope, for faithful is he who promised. And let us consider one another so as to provoke love and good works, not abandoning our assembly, as is the custom of some, but consoling one another, and all the more as you see the day approaching. For if we sin deliberately after receiving the knowledge of truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins, but a certain fearful expectation of judgment and zeal of fire which will consume the adversaries. Anyone who makes void the law of Moses dies without any mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses; how much worse punishments, do you think, will he deserve who has trampled the Son of God underfoot, considered unclean the blood of the Testament by which he was sanctified, and insulted the Spirit of grace? For we know him who said: ‘Vengeance is mine, and I will repay.’ And again: ‘The Lord will judge his people.’ It is dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God. But remember the former days, in which, after you had been enlightened, you endured a great contest [Col. 0543B] of sufferings: on the one hand made a spectacle by reproaches and tribulations, and on the other made companions of those so treated.
