For you also had compassion on those in bonds and accepted with joy the plundering of your possessions, knowing that you have a better and abiding possession. Therefore do not cast away your confidence, which has great reward. For you have need of patience, so that, doing the will of God, you may receive the promise. For yet a little, a very little while, and he who is coming will come and will not delay. But my righteous one lives by faith; and if he draws back, my soul will not be pleased with him. But we are not children of drawing back unto destruction, but of faith unto the gaining of the soul.”

## Exposition

Christ was offered in order to exhaust sins, because the law cannot make persons perfect, that is, cannot exhaust sins. He first explains why the law cannot make perfect, saying: The law has a shadow of good things to come, that is, of future righteousness in the present Church [Col. 0543D], and of salvation in the future Church. It has a shadow in such a way that it does not even have the image itself of realities, that is, it has within itself no part of truth. For an image at least displays each individual outline of the members, whereas a shadow confuses everything indiscriminately. The law, I say, has a shadow by means of the same sacrifices, which were always the same—that is, imperfect—which sacrifices they offer year by year, and this continually, that is, either every month or every week. The law, I say, by the same sacrifices repeated so often, can never make perfect those who approach it. He proves that it does not make perfect as follows: if they should now sacrifice for some sin and, according to the law, be absolved from it, then if they sinned again and sacrificed again for the new sin, the priest made remembrance of the former sin for which he had already sacrificed, thereby showing the imperfection of that sacrifice; for if the person had been justified by it, it would be pointless to recapitulate the old sin. He says this as follows: Otherwise, that is, if the sacrifices of the law made persons perfect, those sacrifices would undoubtedly have ceased to be offered for past sins. Accordingly, worshippers of sacrifices, cleansed by the sacrifice once offered, would have no further consciousness at all of past sin. They would indeed have ceased to offer them; but the sacrifices for past sins would not cease to be offered, for in the sacrifices offered every year for recent faults there is a remembrance of past sins. Therefore those sacrifices cannot make persons perfect. And remembrance of past sins must be made each year because it is impossible for sins to be taken away by the blood of goats and bulls [Col. 0544B].

Therefore, because sins cannot be taken away through the blood of bulls and goats, when entering the world—that is, the Prophet, introducing the Son of God as entering the world by the assumption of flesh—he says in the Son’s voice to the Father: “O Lord Father, you did not desire sacrifice and offering according to the legal tradition.” By sacrifices he means those from animals, and by offering those from breads and lamps. You did not desire those, but you prepared—that is, wished to prepare—a body for me, so that a sacrifice from my body might be made pleasing and pure to you. Christ’s body is said to have been prepared because it was both free from sin, capable of suffering, and mortal. For unless it were without sin, it could not be a pure sacrifice. But if it were made incapable of suffering and immortal, it would not destroy death, since one who is immortal cannot taste death. But because it was free from sin, capable of suffering, and mortal, he fittingly says: “You prepared a body for me; you did not desire sacrifice and offering; nor did whole burnt offerings”—that is, a sacrifice wholly burned—“and offerings for sin”—that is, a sacrifice called “sin” or “for sin”—“please you.” These things, I say, did not please you, and then, after I saw that this displeased you, namely, that a pure and pleasing sacrifice should be offered to you, I said—that is, I resolved within myself—this: “Behold, I come at the fitting time, because now that those legal things have been rejected, I shall be a new sacrifice pleasing to God.”

I come in order to do your will, that is, in accordance with the measure of your will to offer myself to you as a new sacrifice, a fragrance of sweetness. That we must construe it thus—“I come in order to do [Col. 0544D] your will”—he himself teaches in what follows: “I shall do your will; for thus it is written of me in the head of the book.” Christ as man is called the book, set forth before all as an example of righteousness. The divinity dwelling in Christ, which governs him in all perfection, is called the head of the book. Or “in the head of the book” means in the beginning of Genesis or of the Psalter, where his will is written in the law of the Lord, and so forth. Paul explains how the authority quoted above must be understood. Thus the Prophet, in the Son’s voice, says above with reference to the preceding passage. Saying above, I mean, that you, Father, did not desire offerings and whole burnt offerings and offerings for sin—that is, you did not require these from them in order that they should be done for you, nor, even if they do them unbidden, are they pleasing to you. Someone might perhaps say: “They are displeasing because they are not performed in an orderly way according to the law.” To remove this objection, he says: “The things offered according to the law are not pleasing to you”—that is, even though they are done according to the institution of the law. Then, once the legal sacrifices had been rejected, I said: “Behold, I come to do your will, O God.” By saying these things, he removes the first testament in order to establish—that is, to make permanently enduring—the following one, namely, the New Testament. By that will—that is, in that New Testament established by God’s will—we are sanctified by the placing of virtues after the cleansing away of evils. I say that we are sanctified through the offering of Christ Jesus, that is, through the body of Christ offered once; and that offering, once made, was sufficient [Col. 0545B] for the cleansing of all stains.

Someone might object: The high priest’s sacrifice was insufficient because it was performed only once a year; but the daily sacrifices were useful for taking away sins. To remove this objection he says: Just as the high priest, after making one sacrifice, could not take away sins, so every legal priest, ministering daily, stands ready—and he too, by repeatedly bringing the same sacrifices, yesterday a goat and today another goat, since just as it did not help yesterday, so neither does it help today—offering, I say, the same sacrifices, which sacrifices can never take away sins. The high priest, or any legal priest, repeating the sacrifices, cannot take away sins; but this high priest, Christ, offering a sacrifice not repeated but one alone for the sins of all, sits—that is, rests and reigns—placed at the right hand, that is, seated in equality with God the Father, to remain there forever. Nor will he return to offer again, as though his sacrifice had been insufficient; rather, from now on—that is, in the future—he waits there at God’s right hand until his enemies are placed as a footstool for his feet, that is, until they are subjected to him in every manner of subjection, which will occur on the day of judgment. He offers one sacrifice—one for this reason: because by one offering alone he sanctified and perfected those who had been sanctified through the perfection of virtues, so that they would remain forever.

We indeed say that Christ perfected those sanctified by one offering. In this matter, however, the Holy Spirit bears witness—that is, confirms us—affirming the same thing together with us, because after he had said through Jeremiah, “This is the covenant that I will make with them, and this, says the Lord: After those days I will give my laws in their hearts, and I will write them upon their mind,” the Holy Spirit added: “And I will no longer remember their sins and their iniquities.” By these words the Holy Spirit bears witness that one offering perfected those who had been sanctified, because where there is forgiveness of sins, an offering for sin is no longer necessary.

After he had sufficiently destroyed the old priesthood through Christ’s priesthood, rejected the former sacrifices, and declared that all justification consists in Christ’s sacrifice, offered once for all, he brings this discussion to an end and turns to moral instruction, exhorting them first of all to hold the integrity of faith with a pure heart; and, if persecution should arise, to confess boldly, rejoicing to suffer for Christ, and thus to possess firm hope in faith and confession. Hence he says:

Since Christ the high priest, offering himself once, sanctifies, and the daily sacrifices cannot avail, therefore, brothers, since we have confidence in the entrance—that is, concerning the entrance into the holy places, namely, that we shall truly enter the Holy of Holies—since, I say, we have confidence in the blood of Christ, which he poured out once for our cleansing, I call that way—that is, the way into the holy places—new, that is, newly opened in Christ. No one, even before Christ, walked along this way, which Christ inaugurated for us. I call it a new and living way, that is, one enduring forever.

He inaugurated it, I say, through the veil—that is, through what that veil signified—which divided the two tabernacles, namely, through his flesh. For that veil, which concealed the Holy of Holies, prefigured Christ’s flesh, which veiled the divinity united to it. Therefore, when Christ expired on the cross and everything had been completed, the veil of the temple was torn (Matthew 26:51; Mark 15:38; Luke 23:45), signifying that in Christ the way of entering the Holy of Holies had been opened.

Or he inaugurated the way for us through the veil—that is, through his flesh—and at the approach of death we receive his flesh and blood as provisions for the journey to our homeland. I speak of flesh and blood veiled under the appearance of bread. He inaugurated the way for us through his flesh and through himself as priest, daily interceding with the Father for us. I call him a great priest in comparison with the legal priests. I call him great because he has been appointed over the house of God, that is, over the present and future Church.

We, then, brothers, possessing such confidence, let us approach—that is, draw near to—the Lord with a true heart, that is, with right understanding, in the fullness of faith, that is, possessing faith not merely concerning certain matters but fully concerning everything that must be believed. Let us approach, I say, with our hearts sprinkled—that is, with hearts cleansed not only from sin but also from an evil conscience, so that the conscience of no evil may bite us—and with our body washed in pure water, that is, possessing flesh purified by baptism, which cleanses us. Let us hold fast in deed and in heart to our confession; and if evils press upon us, let us not therefore fear to confess Christ.

I call it an unshifting confession, one by which we turn neither to the right nor to the left; and this confession is the cause of our hope. For if we are not afraid to confess Christ in the presence of persecutors, then we may confidently hope for the glory that is to come to the saints. Someone might say: Who could hope for something perhaps never to be obtained after enduring such great sufferings for so long? To this Paul replies: If you confess boldly, your hope is secure, because God is faithful and cannot lie; he promised good things to those who confess him, the very things that you hope for.

Let us hold fast to our confession and consider one another—that is, each one the other—not in quarrels and slander, but in an incitement to love and good works; that is, let each one be urged by the example of the other to love and to act rightly.

I say that we should not abandon our assembly—that is, the congregation of the Church—frightened by fear of the persecutors who press upon us, as is the custom of certain people, “to believe for a time, and in the time of temptation to withdraw” (Luke 8:13). Let us not abandon it, but console the assembly of the Church, laboring in this all the more as you see the day of death approaching.

Or let us understand it in this way: Let us urge the brothers to love, not abandoning our assembly; that is, if the brothers have sinned, let us not, for that reason, separate ourselves from them in proud indignation, as some are accustomed to do, disdaining to show compassion to a fallen brother. Rather, let us console our assembly and recall them from their evils through compassion all the more as we see the day of retribution approaching. Evil awaits the wicked, good the good. Therefore, let us hold fast to faith and confession, not abandoning our assembly.

Let us do all these things because, if we sin voluntarily—that is, if we remain in sin by our own will and deliberate choice—after receiving knowledge of the truth, that is, after we have come to know Christ, who is the truth itself, and have received the faith, if the will to sin persists in us, no sacrifice remains that will benefit us: Christ, made a sacrifice for the destruction of sins, will profit us nothing.

Or understand it in this way: “No sacrifice remains” means that Christ is not reserved to become a sacrifice again for those who sin again. Rather, what remains for us is a certain fearful expectation of the future judgment; and there remains for us a rivalry—that is, an envy—of fire, a rivalry that will consume the adversaries of the truth.

He proves from the greater case that those who sin against Christ must be punished, saying: Truly, whoever sins voluntarily will be punished in the truth. For if someone, transgressing the law of Moses—which was nothing but a shadow of the truth—dies without mercy when convicted of sin on the testimony of two or three witnesses, and if one who transgresses the law of Moses dies, how much worse punishments do you think he deserves who has trampled upon the Son of God?

He understands the Son of God as trampleable and utterly worthless who says that Christ is unable to forgive sins unless circumcision is added. He also tramples upon him who regards—that is, understands—the blood of the covenant as polluted, namely, the blood of Christ by which the new covenant was confirmed. That person calls Christ’s blood polluted who says that no offense can be cleansed by it. For if Christ was a pure sacrifice, he was also able to cleanse from every guilt; but if he could not cleanse, it follows that the sacrifice was polluted—the blood in which everyone who has been baptized was sanctified.

He likewise deserves worse punishment who has insulted the Holy Spirit. Whoever says that sins are forgiven by some means other than through the Spirit acts insultingly against the Spirit. I speak of the Spirit of grace, who is given freely and freely forgives sins.

Someone might say: Although the law of Moses, which was without mercy, condemned its transgressors, Christ, who brought mercy and grace, nevertheless, even if we sin, will not only fail to condemn us but will forgive us. To remove this objection Paul proves that Christ is judge and that he did not abandon judgment on account of his mercy, saying: Truly, the one who tramples upon the Son of God will suffer worse things.

For we know the one who said this in Deuteronomy (Deuteronomy 32:35): “Reserve vengeance for me”; if a neighbor sins, vengeance against the neighbor belongs to me, and I will repay them in due time and according to the measure of their offense. If he does not leave sin against a neighbor unpunished, how much more will he punish sin against himself? And again, Scripture, affirming God’s judgment, says: “For the Lord will judge his people.” And since the Lord, judging, will return to each person the vengeance due for sin, Paul says: See that you do not sin. For it is fearful to fall into the hands of the living God, that is, of the one who is powerful to do whatever he wills.

After rebuking them rather severely, he now recalls their former good deeds and speaks gently to them, so that those whom he had shaken by fear of judgment might be drawn by certain consolations. He says: See that you do not fall into the hands of God, but remember the former days in which, after you had been enlightened through faith, you immediately endured a great struggle of sufferings upon receiving the faith. For at that time you suffered many things from your fellow citizens.

You certainly endured sufferings; on the one hand, you became a spectacle to the world—that is, because of the reproaches and tribulations inflicted upon you. On the other hand, you became companions of those who lived in this manner, as we did—that is, of all those who lived together with you in the religion of faith.

Truly you were their companions. For you also shared the sufferings of prisoners, supplying them in their imprisonment with what they needed from your possessions; and you suffered reproaches and tribulations. For you accepted with joy the seizure of your possessions, knowing that you had a better substance in heaven, because it was spiritual and enduring.

Since you were such people at the beginning of your faith, therefore do not lose your confidence by degenerating—that is, your good works, through which one may rightly have confidence. If this confidence endures, it possesses a great reward.

They might say: It is difficult to suffer so many afflictions for so long. To this Paul replies: Do not lose your patience, but be long-suffering in enduring, because patience is necessary for you, so that, by enduring and doing the will of God, you may receive the promise—that is, the promised glory.

Nor will it always be necessary to suffer, because only a little while and a small amount of suffering remain: it is light and momentary. After this, the one who is to come will come to you. And after he has come, he will not delay—that is, he will not be slow to give you the glory he promised. Glory is not delayed for martyrs; it is given to them immediately when they depart from the world. To those who rest in the peace of the Church, however, it seems to be delayed, because they must first do penance for certain things they have contracted unlawfully.

“The one who is to come will come and will not delay”; and meanwhile, while he is coming, “the just will live by faith,” because God said through the prophet: “My just one lives by faith” (Habakkuk 2:4). But if the just person withdraws from faith, he will not please my soul—that is, my will. I say, “if he withdraws”; but we are not children of withdrawal, destined thus for destruction. Rather, we belong to faith, for acquisition—that is, in order that through faith we may acquire the salvation of our soul.

## CHAPTER XI

“Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the proof of things not seen. For by it the elders obtained a good testimony. By faith we understand that the ages were formed by the word of God, so that visible things came to be from invisible things. By faith Abel offered to God a greater sacrifice than Cain, through which he obtained testimony that he was just, God bearing witness to his gifts; and through it, though dead, he still speaks. By faith Enoch was translated so that he should not see death, and he was not found, because God translated him. For before his translation he received testimony that he had pleased God. But without faith it is impossible to please God. For the one who approaches God must believe that he exists and that he is a rewarder of those who seek him.

“By faith Noah, having received an answer concerning things that were not yet seen, and fearing, prepared an ark for the salvation of his household; through it he condemned the world and was appointed [made] heir of the righteousness that is through faith. By faith Abraham, who is called, obeyed by going out to a place that he was to receive as an inheritance, and he went out not knowing where he was going. By faith he dwelt in the land of promise as in a foreign land, living in tents with Isaac and Jacob, co-heirs of the same promise. For he was awaiting a city having foundations, whose craftsman and founder is God.

“By faith Sarah herself, though barren, received power for the conception of offspring, even beyond the proper time of her age, because she believed that he who had promised was faithful. Therefore from one man—and that one as good as dead—there arose descendants as numerous as the stars of heaven and as the sand along the seashore, which cannot be counted.

“All these died according to faith, without receiving the promises, but seeing them from afar, greeting them, and confessing that they were strangers and sojourners upon the earth. For those who say such things show that they are seeking a homeland. And if they had remembered the one from which they had departed, they would certainly have had time to return. But now they desire a better one, that is, a heavenly one. Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared a city for them.

“By faith Abraham offered Isaac when he was tested, and he offered his only-begotten son, he in whom he had received the promises, to whom it had been said: ‘In Isaac your offspring shall be called.’ He reasoned [thought] that God was able even to raise him from the dead; hence he received him back also as a figure. By faith Isaac also blessed Jacob and Esau concerning future things. By faith Jacob, when dying, blessed each of the sons of Joseph and worshiped the top of his staff. By faith Joseph, when dying, remembered the departure of the children of Israel and gave orders concerning his bones.

“By faith Moses, when he was born, was hidden for three months by his parents, because they saw that the child was beautiful, and they did not fear the king’s edict. By faith Moses, when he had grown up, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, choosing rather to suffer affliction with the people of God than to have the pleasure of temporary sin. He considered the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of Egypt, for he looked toward the reward.

“By faith he left Egypt, not fearing the king’s anger; for he endured as though seeing the invisible one. By faith he celebrated the Passover and the shedding of blood, so that the one destroying [who would destroy] the firstborn might not touch them. By faith they crossed the Red Sea as through dry land; when the Egyptians attempted this, they were swallowed up.

“By faith the walls of Jericho fell after they had been encircled for seven days. By faith Rahab the prostitute did not perish with the unbelieving, having received the spies in peace. And what more shall I say? For time will fail me if I recount the deeds of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel, and the prophets, who through faith conquered kingdoms, practiced righteousness, obtained promises, stopped the mouths of lions, extinguished the violence of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, grew strong from weakness, became mighty in war, and routed the camps of foreigners.

“Women received their dead back through resurrection. Others were stretched upon the rack, refusing release, in order to obtain a better resurrection. Others experienced mockeries and scourging, and in addition bonds and prisons. They were stoned, they were cut apart, they were tested, they died by the killing of the sword. They wandered about in goatskins and in garments of hair, needy, afflicted, tormented—of whom the world was not worthy—wandering in deserts and mountains, in caves and in the caverns of the earth.

“And all these, approved by the testimony of faith, did not receive the promise, since God had provided something better for us, so that they should not be perfected without us.”

## EXPOSITION

Because he has begun a discourse on faith, saying, “We are children of faith,” and so forth, he adds what appears to be a definition of faith. Yet this is not a definition but a commendation of faith. In commending this faith, he will linger at length and set forth many examples from the ancients.

He says: We are children of faith. Faith, however, is the substance—that is, the existence and acquisition—of things hoped for, that is, of future goods, which are especially and above all to be hoped for. Faith, I say, is thus the substance of future goods, because they neither subsist in anyone without faith nor are acquired except through faith.

Or let us understand it in this way: Faith possessed in the present is, in the future, the substance of things—that is, of heavenly goods. For those goods rightly subsist then in the one who possessed faith in this world; I speak of things now hoped for through faith.

Faith is also the proof—that is, the approval—of things not seen, that is, of goods which, while we remain in this world, we cannot see. For if someone considers how Abraham, by the merit of faith, possessed glory, he can likewise hope for himself that, if he imitates Abraham through faith, he too will possess through faith the glory that Abraham did not see.

I say that faith is the substance and proof of future goods. For this reason I commend faith in this way: in it—that is, in faith—the elders obtained a good testimony. He calls them elders not on account of age but on account of precedence in time. Abel, although younger in years, was nevertheless older than Abraham in the antiquity of the time that preceded him.

Someone might object: You say that faith is the proof of things that do not appear. But how can things that cannot be seen be believed? To this Paul replies: Faith truly is the proof of things not seen. For by faith—that is, through faith—we understand that the ages were formed, that is, fittingly shaped. They were formed, he says, by the word—that is, by the Son—or by the command of God; these are the same thing.

And if we believe concerning the ages that they were formed by the word of God—something that no human being saw—let us likewise believe through faith concerning things that have not yet appeared. We believe, I say, that the ages were formed by the word of God so that visible things might come to be from invisible things.

For when chaos existed, as it is written, “Darkness was over the face of the abyss” (Genesis 1:2), there was darkness because those elements could not be seen, even if someone possessing human sight had existed at that time. But after the elements were separated and, as creatures were formed, grew together into a kind of density, the elements that had previously been invisible became visible.

Nor is it surprising that they could not be seen, although they were bodily things, since we cannot see or discern the moisture contained in a grain of seed, from which the stalk and ear spring forth, even though it is contained within that mass of grain.

Or let us understand it in this way: They were formed by the word of God so that visible things might come to be from invisible things—that is, according to the invisible forms that had preceded them in God’s plan. For first, from eternity, God arranged in his plan the forms of all creatures; and in accordance with the way each had been preordained in that plan, things that were still invisible became visible in time, when each was formed.

Truly the elders obtained testimony through faith. For Abel, by faith—that is, through faith—offered a greater sacrifice, that is, one more acceptable to God than Cain’s sacrifice had been. Abel’s sacrifice is known to have been pleasing to God because the lamb he offered was consumed by divine fire. Cain’s sacrifice was rejected because, when no fire came upon it, the sheaf of grain he had offered remained intact.

Through this faith Abel obtained this testimony: namely, that he was just. For Christ says in the Gospel, “From the blood of Abel the just” (Matthew 23:35), and so forth. Moses also commends Abel’s righteousness, as do many of the prophets. Abel obtained testimony from God, who bore witness to his gifts, as we have said; and through that faith Abel, though dead, still speaks, because he causes us to speak about his faith.

Enoch too, through the faith he possessed, was translated to another homeland, so that he would not see death. After being translated he was not found, because God translated him; if he had been translated by a human being, he would easily have been found. God translated him because, before his translation, he had testimony that he pleased God.

Through faith these men pleased God. But without faith it is impossible for anyone to please God. Truly, without faith no one will please God; for the one who approaches—that is, wishes to draw near—to God must believe that God is one and that God is the rewarder of those who seek him. If the pagans believed only this, that there is one creator and that he repays each person according to his deeds, that would be sufficient for them.

Noah too, after receiving an answer concerning things not yet seen—that is, concerning the future flood—feared that flood and, through the faith he had in the Lord’s words, prepared an ark for the salvation of his household, that is, in which he might save his sons and daughters. Through that faith, because he believed according to God’s word that the flood would come, he condemned—that is, made the world condemnable.

For while Noah believed, and human beings believed that what he was preparing was foolish—the ark in which he would save his household—they were condemned by comparison with his faith. Noah himself was made heir of the righteousness that is through faith.

He now descends to the ancestors of the Jews, showing that in them and in those who came before, all righteousness originated from faith. The one who is now called Abraham on account of the merit of faith, formerly called Abram, obeyed by faith when he went out from Ur of the Chaldeans to that place which, on account of the merit of faith, he was to receive as an inheritance.

He obeyed, I say, and went out from the land of his nation, not knowing where he was going. This same Abraham, by faith, dwelt in the land of promise as in a foreign land, living there in tents with Isaac and Jacob—not because Jacob was there at the same time as Abraham, but because Jacob inhabited the same land as Abraham, seeking with his ancestors not that earthly land but the true land of promise.

I call Isaac and Jacob co-heirs of the same promise, for God frequently promised it to them just as he had to Abraham. Abraham lived in tents because he was awaiting a city having foundations—that is, the stability of eternity—the heavenly Jerusalem, whose craftsman is God, arranging each thing by his art, and whose founder is likewise God himself, fashioning the things he arranges.

By living in tents Abraham showed that he did not care for the earthly Jerusalem but sought the heavenly one.

Sarah herself, though barren and ninety years old, also received through faith the power of conception—that is, the power to conceive offspring. I say that she was not only barren but also beyond the proper time of life, because, as was said, she was ninety years old. She received this power because she believed that God was faithful—that is, truthful—who had promised her offspring.

Therefore, because she believed God to be faithful, children arose from one womb or from one father, and that father or womb being as good as dead, like the stars of heaven. I do not compare them with the stars according to the brightness of their virtues, but according to the growth of their number. They also arose like sand—not again according merely to the barrenness of sand, but according to their innumerability—the sand that is along the shore of the sea, that is, beside the coast of the nations.

For many of Abraham’s children shone with virtues like stars; many barren and fruitless people were cast upon the shore [or: rites] of the nations.

And all these—Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—died while still remaining according to faith, that is, believing that they would receive God’s promises. They died without receiving the promises during life, but seeing those future promises from afar—that is, in the days of Christ—and greeting them, as sailors greet their homeland, which they see from far away and greatly desire. They confessed concerning themselves that they were strangers upon the earth, always passing on to other places, and sojourners—that is, people coming from elsewhere.

They confessed this for a reason: those who say such things, namely, that they are strangers and sojourners, signify by these words that they are seeking the true homeland.

Someone might say: They were seeking a foreign homeland because perhaps they could not return to their own. To this Paul replies: They said these things, and if they had remembered the homeland from which they had departed, wishing to return there, they would certainly have had time—that is, the opportunity—to return.

But now, because they did not remember that homeland, they desire a better one, that is, a heavenly one. And because they desire the heavenly homeland, God is not ashamed—that is, he does not blush—to be called their God, so that he may be called the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. He is called their God because he prepared a heavenly city for them.

Again Abraham, by faith, offered Isaac when he was tested. God did not test Abraham as though he were ignorant of his faith, but so that Abraham himself and the world might know the power of his faith.

And lest it be thought that Abraham intended to sacrifice Isaac because he expected the promises to be fulfilled in another son, Scripture says that Abraham himself, who had received the promises and to whom it had been said, “In Isaac your offspring shall be called,” offered this only-begotten son, reasoning that God was able to raise him from the dead and that, once raised, through him Abraham’s offspring would be called.

Therefore, because he believed in this way, he received him back as a son, both for the multiplication of his offspring and as a figure—that is, in the figures of Christ. For the ram found caught by its horns among the thorns and Isaac signified one Christ, God and man.

Thus, by the fact that the ram was sacrificed while Isaac was withdrawn from death, it was signified that Christ would suffer according to the flesh, but according to his divinity would not experience the danger of death. The sacrificed ram prefigured Christ’s flesh, which was to be sacrificed; Isaac, withdrawn from death, prefigured Christ’s divinity, which would not be harmed by the Passion.

Isaac also blessed Jacob and Esau, possessing faith concerning them and concerning future things: how the elder would serve the younger, and concerning the future realities of which they bore the type—namely, how the Jewish people, the firstborn, would abandon its birthright, namely the worship of God, and the younger, the Gentile people, would appropriate it for itself.

Jacob, dying in Egypt, by faith blessed each of Joseph’s sons, namely Manasseh and Ephraim, and worshiped the top of Joseph’s staff. Joseph, who was second to the king of Egypt, carried a scepter as a sign of his dignity. Jacob worshiped the top of the staff—that is, Christ prefigured by Joseph—for the scepter of righteousness is the scepter of his kingdom (Psalm 44:7).

Joseph, dying in faith—that is, through faith—remembered the departure of the children of Israel, that they would depart from Egypt; and while remembering this, he gave orders concerning his bones, that they should be carried away for burial with Abraham, trusting that those to whom the promise had been made would also rise with Christ if their bodies were found in the land of promise.

Moses, when born, was hidden for three months by his parents through faith, because they believed that this child would become great when they saw his beauty. They did not fear the king’s edict, by which he had ordered every male child among the Hebrews to be killed.

Moses, when he had grown up, by faith refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, choosing rather to suffer affliction with the people of God than to possess the pleasure of temporary sin. He regarded the reproach of Christ—which he prefigured in himself while suffering for Christ—as greater riches than every treasure of the Egyptians.

He regarded it so because he looked toward the future reward, not toward present labor or pleasure.

Moses, through faith, left Egypt, leading the Jewish people out from there, and did not fear the anger of the Egyptian king. He did not fear it because he endured the invisible one—that is, awaited God, whom he could not see—as though seeing him bodily, placing faith in God’s words.

The same Moses, through faith, celebrated the Passover by the shedding of the lamb’s blood, so that the one who was destroying Egypt’s firstborn might not touch the Jews. He had faith in the lamb’s blood, believing that through the power of the lamb of innocence—that is, of Christ, whom the lamb prefigured—he could be saved.

The children of Israel crossed the Red Sea by faith as through dry land. And lest anyone say that this was chance: when the Egyptians attempted to cross the sea, they were swallowed up.

The walls of Jericho fell by faith after seven days of circling. Rahab the prostitute, receiving the Jewish spies in peace, did not perish with the unbelieving because of the faith by which she believed that God would deliver the city into the hands of the Jews.

I have said much in praise of faith; and what more shall I say? For time will fail me—that is, abandon me—if I recount everything concerning faith: Gideon, who placed the fleece in the threshing floor; Barak, who by faith delivered the people; Samson, who accomplished many things through faith; Jephthah, who, as leader of the people, delivered the people, although he sacrificed his daughter through a foolish vow. More is found concerning these four in the Book of Judges.

I would also speak of David, who did many things through faith; and of Samuel and the other prophets, who conquered kingdoms—that is, overcame kings—through faith. They also practiced righteousness through faith, obtained the blessedness that had been promised through faith, and stopped the mouths of lions, as Daniel did; extinguished the force of fire, as the three young men did; escaped the edge of the sword, as Judas Maccabaeus did; recovered from weakness, as Hezekiah did; and many became strong in war.

They overturned the camps of foreigners after putting them to flight. Women received their dead back when they returned from resurrection, as the widow of Zarephath received her only son through Elijah, and the Shunammite woman received hers through Elisha.

Others were stretched upon racks, as the seven Maccabees were, refusing release—that is, unwilling to be freed from their torments—in order that, through the merit of their sufferings, they might obtain a better resurrection. For the more one suffers, the better one will be crowned.

Others experienced mockeries and scourging, and in addition bonds and prisons. They were stoned; they were cut apart, as Isaiah was; they were tested to see whether, through fear of punishment, they would deny the faith; they died by the killing of the sword; they wandered here and there in flight, wearing *melotae*. A *melota*, as they say, is a garment made from camel hair. Or *melus* is an animal called the badger, and from *melus* the word *melota* is derived.

They also wandered in goatskins, lacking temporal goods, afflicted in mind and tormented in body. The world was not worthy to possess such saints—or, according to the words of the impious, the world was not worthy of them, for they said: “Such people are the pollution of the world; let the world be cleansed of them.”

They wandered in deserts, like Mattathias and those who were with him, and in mountains, caves, and caverns of the earth. Natural hollows are called caves; caverns are hollows made by human art.

And all these, approved by the testimony of faith, did not receive the promise—that is, the promised inheritance—because God had provided something better for us: namely, that the former saints should not be perfected in the fullness of blessed joy without us.

For if they had received eternal blessedness without the incarnate Christ, Christ would not have become incarnate—for he would have become incarnate in vain, since salvation would have existed by another means—and thus the former saints would have been saved without us.

## CHAPTER XII

[Col. 0555C]

“Therefore we also, having so great a cloud of witnesses set over us, laying aside every weight and the sin that besets us, let us run with perseverance the contest set before us, looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith, who, for the joy set before him, endured the cross, despising the shame, and sits at the right hand of the throne of God. Consider, then, him who endured such contradiction from sinners against himself, so that you may not grow weary, fainting in your souls. For you have not yet resisted unto blood, struggling against sin, and you have forgotten the consolation that speaks to you as sons, saying:

‘My son, do not neglect the discipline of the Lord, nor grow weary when you are reproved by him. For whom the Lord loves, he chastises; moreover, he scourges every son whom he receives.’

Persevere in discipline. God offers himself to you as sons. For what son is there whom his father does not correct? But if you are without discipline, of which all have become participants, then you are adulterous children and not sons. Furthermore, we had the fathers of our flesh as instructors, and we revered them. Shall we not much more obey the Father of spirits and live? They, indeed, for a few days and according to their own will, instructed us; but he does so for what is useful, so that we may receive his sanctification. Now every discipline, at the present time, seems not to be a matter of joy but of sorrow; afterward, however, it yields to those exercised by it the most peaceful fruit of righteousness. Therefore lift up the hands that hang down and the knees that are loosened, and make straight paths for your feet, so that what is lame may not go astray, but rather may be healed. Pursue peace with all and holiness, without which no one will see God. Take care lest anyone fall short of the grace of God; lest any root of bitterness, springing up, cause hindrance, and through it many be defiled. Take care lest anyone be a fornicator or profane, like Esau, who for one meal sold his birthright [al.: his firstborn rights]. For you know that afterward, when he desired to inherit the blessing, he was rejected. For he found no opportunity for repentance, although he sought it with tears.

For you have not approached a tangible mountain, and an accessible fire, and a whirlwind, and darkness, and a storm, and the sound of a trumpet, and a voice of words. Those who heard it excused themselves, so that the word might not be spoken to them. For they could not bear what was said: ‘And if even a beast touches the mountain, it shall be stoned.’ And so terrible was what was seen that Moses said: ‘I am terrified and trembling.’

But you have approached Mount Zion and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and the gathering of many thousands of angels, and the church of the firstborn, who are enrolled in heaven, and God the judge of all, and the spirit [spirits or spirit] of the perfected righteous, and Jesus, the mediator of the New Testament, and the sprinkling of blood that speaks better than Abel. Take care that you do not refuse him who speaks. For if those did not escape who refused him who spoke on earth, much more shall we, who give heed to him speaking to us from heaven, not escape—him whose voice then shook the earth, but now promises, saying: ‘Yet once more, and I will shake not only the earth but also heaven.’ The phrase ‘yet once more’ declares the removal of things that can be shaken, as things made [or: creation], so that those things that cannot be shaken may remain. Therefore, receiving an unshakable kingdom, we have [or: let us have] grace, through which we may serve God acceptably, with fear and reverence. For indeed our God is a consuming fire.”

## EXPOSITION

[Col. 0556D]

Having brought forward so many commendations of faith, he draws the conclusion from them all: Since faith is commendable on the testimony of so many witnesses, therefore, like those who came before us, we too have so great a cloud of witnesses set over us, commending the faith entrusted to us. He calls it a cloud because, just as a cloud protects from heat and rain, so the examples of the saints mentioned above fortify us against the evils that rush upon us.

We too, like them, must lay aside through repentance every burden of sin that we have committed. We must also lay aside the sin that surrounds us on every side—that is, every evil suggestion—and run with perseverance, not turning back from the good contest set before us. For we have not been called to indulgence, but to endure hardships.

Let us run, I say, looking in imitation toward Jesus, the author of our faith—that is, he who will perfect us in glory if our faith endures whole. Jesus endured the cross, despising not only its bitterness but also its shame, that is, the disgrace associated with such a dishonorable kind of death. He endured it, I say, for the joy set before him in the glory merited by his passion.

Alternatively, the joy set before him may mean earthly joy, that is, the earthly possessions offered him by his crucifiers if he were willing to deny himself to be the Son of God. And because he endured the cross and despised the shame, he sits at the right hand of the throne—that is, in equality with God the Father who sits upon the throne.

Let us run the appointed contest, imitating Jesus, who despised shame and endured the cross. As you look upon him enduring the cross in death, consider also that same Jesus who endured contradiction, so that, just as you imitate him in death, you may also imitate him in enduring contradiction.

Everything adverse that Jesus endured up to the hour of his passion is signified here by “contradiction.” Or, if the reading is *enim* (“for”), it should be joined in this way: You ought to look upon Jesus enduring the cross, for you should also consider that which is lesser in Christ—namely, the contradiction that he endured. You should frequently commit it to memory.

Thus he says: “Consider Jesus, who endured such contradiction”—that is, so contemptible and difficult a contradiction—which was all the more grievous because he, who knew no sin, endured what was inflicted upon him by sinners, not against Peter or any other disciple, but against himself.

Consider this contradiction, I say, so that, remembering it, you may not grow weary—that is, so that you may not be exhausted by enduring adversity. Or, if you grow weary in body, do not grow weary in your souls; let the flesh be weak, but the spirit nevertheless be ready.

For if the contradiction is so great that souls grow weary, as Paul himself says of himself: “We were burdened beyond measure, so that we were weary of living” (II Cor. I, 8), they must nevertheless not faint, just as Paul did not faint, although his soul was weary. They would faint if, through fear of tribulations, they denied the faith. You ought, therefore, to endure without weariness and without fainting, because, even if you have resisted, you have not yet resisted unto blood—that is, your blood has not yet been shed, although, if necessary, it must be suffered for the sake of faith.

You have not yet resisted to the point of shedding blood, although you have fought against sin. In saying this, he praises them in one respect, because they have resisted; in another, he shows that they can still ascend higher, namely, to the shedding of blood.

They have fought, I say, against sin so that it might not gain a place in them. For when they refuse to consent to the impious, they stand against sin; if they consented to them, sin would immediately gain a place in them.

You formerly resisted sin; why, then, have you now forgotten the consolation—that is, the divinity that consoles you in tribulation? This divine consolation speaks to us not as to strangers but as to sons whom it intends to cherish. It says through Solomon (Prov. III, 4): “My son, do not neglect discipline”—that is, persecutions and blows, which constitute discipline.

Through these a person learns how great his frailty is and how little he can accomplish by his own strength [Col. 0558A] unless the grace of God is present. I say “discipline,” not the discipline of persecutors but of the Lord. For they can do nothing except by God’s permission; in this way he wishes to cleanse his sons.

“Do not neglect discipline, nor grow weary”—that is, do not, when you are reproved, grow tired and shrink from suffering. You are reproved when, through this discipline, you are convicted by God as guilty, while he grants you pardon. Through this discipline a person comes to know both his own frailty and, if he endures patiently, obtains pardon for his sins.

You must not grow weary when you are reproved. For the Lord chastises the one whom he loves—that is, through discipline he leads him into chastity and restraint from vices. The one whom he loves he chastises; moreover, every son whom he receives he scourges before receiving him.

Although he forgives sins, no one is exempt from punishment; punishment must be paid either in this life or in the future, either voluntarily by the person himself—which is the more acceptable work—or through the infliction of another.

We can prove this from original sin: it is indeed forgiven in baptism, but the punishment of that sin—namely, mortality and liability to suffering—remains.

Since, then, the discipline of the Lord is so commendable, persevere in discipline—that is, in patience amid tribulations. You must certainly persevere in it, for God offers himself to you as a helper in tribulations, as to sons.

I rightly say “as to sons,” because what son is there whom his father does not correct? God certainly will not have an uncorrected son. No one will be a son except one who is corrected.

But if—that is, if you truly are—outside discipline, by withdrawing yourselves from the discipline of the Lord, of which all the sons of God have become participants, then, if you are outside discipline, you are not legitimate sons but illegitimate children. These are children whom a father does not entrust to tutors because he does not care for them.

Or you are adulterous children in the sense that you are children of the devil, adulterating yourselves.

He has proved through testimonies from Scripture that they ought to persevere in discipline. Now he confirms the same point by arguments drawn from human custom, as if he were saying: I have shown by authoritative texts that we must persevere in discipline; next, after the testimonies of Scripture, I introduce arguments from human custom to prove the same thing.

We had fathers, not of our souls but of our flesh. For we derived the line of our flesh from them, and God bestowed a soul upon our flesh, which had been derived from the flesh of our parents.

We had these fathers as instructors, and we revered them, showing them honor and fearing them. To revere is to offer honor with fear.

If, then, we revered the fathers of our flesh, shall we not much more obey the Father of spirits—that is, God, who gives souls far more excellent than the body—and, obeying him, live forever, something the fathers of our flesh can confer neither upon themselves nor upon us?

The Father of spirits must certainly be obeyed more, because those fathers of the flesh instructed us for a short time and according to their own will: one taught grammar, another the craft of a smith, and often they taught things of no use. But this Father of spirits instructs us for what is truly useful, through discipline, in receiving his sanctification—that is, patience and the other virtues, by whose establishment he sanctifies his own.

Since they could object, saying, “Who can endure such discipline, in which there is always sorrow and never joy?” he himself anticipates the objection and resolves it, saying: I indeed commend to you patience under discipline, but I confess that every discipline at the present time appears—not to those who look only at the surface of things—to be a matter of joy, but solely of sorrow. Here there is always sorrow and never joy.

He then supplies the solution: It appears at present to be sorrow, but afterward—that is, in the future—God will render to those exercised by this discipline the fruit of righteousness, not to cast-off illegitimate children but to legitimate ones.

I say “fruit,” not like the fruit of this world, which is never at peace, but the most peaceful fruit, to be possessed in complete tranquillity.

Therefore, because righteousness will be so fruitful for those exercised by discipline, lift up the hands that hang down—that is, the works of charity, formerly vigorous but now relaxed.

Lift up also the loosened knees—that is, the strength formerly possessed but now weakened by fear of discipline. By the loosened knees he signifies the loss of virtue, because trembling first appears in the knees when they have been weakened; they are raised when they have been strengthened.

Raise the knees and make straight paths for your feet—that is, for the affections of your faith. The first step of faith is confession; afterward, if necessary, suffering. Make the paths straight so that none of you may go astray by departing from the way of faith, nor even limp along that way.

Someone might hold the faith, believing rightly, and yet limp in it if he were afraid to confess it. Let no one go astray in defending the faith; rather, let him be healed from error if he has happened to err.

For your paths to be straight, pursue peace with all, even with enemies. Pursue holiness as well—that is, complete sanctity—without peace and holiness no one will see God.

He indicates how holiness is to be pursued, saying: Pursue holiness, taking care lest anyone among you fall short of the grace of God. The grace of God is prepared for you; see that you do not reject it.

Take care also lest any root—that is, any suggestion of sin—spring up. I call it a root of bitterness, although some think it means sweetness. See, I say, that such a root does not hinder you by springing upward—that is, by bursting forth into an act of sin.

A suggestion springs upward when it brings to completion through action what it wrongly urges. See that no such root hinders you, so that, springing upward through it, many may be defiled—being more inclined to imitate disgrace than honor.

Take care also lest anyone among you be a fornicator or profane, abandoning the worship of God, as Esau was. For one meal of lentils he sold his birthright to his brother Jacob.

We do not find fornication attributed to Esau elsewhere. Or, if we pursue the allegorical meaning, let us say that no one should be a fornicator in the worship of God. Those were fornicators who believed that circumcision was necessary for the faith of Christ.

Or let no one be profane, abandoning the faith entirely. Do not be like Esau, supposing that you can escape condemnation through an unfruitful repentance.

For know this about Esau: both before the sale and afterward, when he desired to inherit the blessing of the firstborn, he was rejected—if not by his father, nevertheless by God.

He was truly rejected, for he found no opportunity for repentance. He did repent of having sold his birthright, but this repentance found no suitable opportunity, although he sought it with tears.

If he had wept while confessing his sin and punishing his iniquity, his repentance would have found an opportunity. But because, even in those tears, he was indignant at his brother’s election and was thinking of killing his brother if he could, the opportunity for repentance was denied him.

You ought to pursue peace and holiness. See that the root of bitterness does not spring up in you, and so forth, because you have not approached an unbearable and terrifying law, making it burdensome and useless, as the former law was; rather, you have approached a law made joyful by great ease, assisting grace, and the promise of heavenly things.

He sets this out at length, beginning in this way: You have not approached a tangible and accessible fire.

At the giving of the old law there was a bodily fire which, if God permitted, could be handled by human hands and approached. Nor have you approached a whirlwind, darkness, and a storm. There was a whirlwind there—that is, a stirring of winds—along with dark gloom and a storm. As the winds struck one another, there was a crashing of hail.

Nor have you approached the sound of a trumpet and a voice of words. The blare of trumpets and audible words were heard there. The Jews who heard that voice excused themselves, pleading their frailty so that the word might not be spoken to them—that is, so that the Lord would not speak to them, but to Moses, and Moses to them.

They excused themselves in this way because they could not bear what was being said to them. God gave them the law amid such harsh terror because he knew that, through the gentleness of love, they would accomplish nothing good, and therefore, like slaves, they had to be compelled by punishments. The multitude of terrors also foreshadowed that they would never be able to bear that law.

It had also been said at the reception of the law that, if a beast touched that mountain on which the law was given, it would be stoned (Exod. XIX, 12)—according to some, by judicial sentence; according to others, because of the confusion of the hail.

[Col. 0560D]

All these things, by contrast, represented the giving of the new law. For we, receiving grace, have approached fire—that is, the burning of the Holy Spirit—neither tangible nor accessible, but spiritual.

The sound of the trumpet that was there signified suggestion, which provokes one to the act of sin as a trumpet summons to war. The more the Jews were forbidden, the more ardently they rushed toward what was forbidden.

There was also a whirlwind there—that is, a stirring of suggestions, namely, the act of sin. In the new grace both the suggestion and the act of sin are removed.

There was also a storm there—that is, the crashing of hail, namely, the habit of sinning. There was also darkness—that is, blindness proceeding from the habit of sinning. In this grace the habit of sinning has been removed and every blindness illuminated.

There was there a voice of words, which they were able to hear. Here there is an inner inspiration; whoever has a foretaste of it runs with great desire to grasp it.

They could not bear what was said. But here the burden is light and the yoke is easy (Matt. XI, 30).

There it was said: “If a beast touches the mountain, it shall be stoned” (Exod. XIX, 12), because here, if anyone of bestial life and understanding sets his mouth blasphemously against the mountain—that is, against divinity—he will be stoned, crushed by the power of the Godhead.

And because what was seen was so terrifying, Moses himself said: “I am terrified in spirit and trembling in body.”

You have not approached a law of terror and uselessness, but Zion—that is, the contemplative life. I call Zion a mountain, that is, one eminent in the height of virtues.

You have approached the city of the living God, who gives eternal life to its citizens—namely, the heavenly Jerusalem—and the gathering of many thousands of angels, so that with them you may resound in the glory of God.

You have approached the church of the firstborn—that is, of the patriarchs and prophets—who are enrolled as senators in heaven; God the Father, the judge of all; and the spirits of the righteous and perfected, that is, those whom the Holy Spirit makes righteous and perfect through the diversity of gifts. As John commonly does, he uses “Spirit” in the plural.

You have approached Jesus, the giver of the New Testament. Or let us say instead: you have approached the Lord of all and the God of spirits—that is, of the souls of the righteous and perfected.

You have also approached the sprinkling of blood—that is, the blood of Christ, by which you have been sprinkled and cleansed.

I call Christ’s blood that which speaks better than Abel’s blood, of which it is written: “The blood of your brother Abel cries out to me from the earth” (Gen. IV, 10). It speaks better because Abel’s blood cries out for vengeance, whereas Christ’s blood cries out for remission.

And because Christ’s blood speaks on your behalf, see, then, that by doing evil you do not reject the one who speaks on your behalf—for your rejection would be to your own harm.

For if those who rejected him who spoke on earth—that is, Moses or an angel—did not escape punishment, much more shall we not escape if we turn away from God, who speaks to us not from earth but from heaven.

His voice, when he spoke, shook the earth then, at the giving of the old law; but now he promises through Haggai, saying: “Yet once more.” “Yet” because he had already shaken the earth. “I will shake not only the earth,” which I once shook, “but also heaven” (Hag. II, 7), transferring their mutable state into immutability.

Paul now explains: The prophet’s saying “yet” and “once more” declares, through the word “yet,” the removal of things that can be shaken. Once the elements have been transferred, they will become immutable instead of mutable.

I call it the removal of things that can be shaken as things made—that is, as things that he created. For the one who made them from nothing could transfer them all the more easily after they had been made.

He says “once” so that, after the transfer has taken place, the things that are now mutable may remain immutable.

And since everything will be transferred into immutability, let us therefore, as those who are to reign in that unshakable kingdom, have some grace already bestowed upon us by God. For unless some grace of God preceded in us, we would not be received by him to reign in immutability.

Or let us understand it this way: Since, once transferred, all things will remain immutable, let us who will then receive that unshakable kingdom have grace, through which we may serve God acceptably, with fear of soul and reverence—that is, fear in the body and the offering of honor.

For it is necessary that we serve God with fear and reverence. Indeed, our God is a consuming fire—that is, one who smelts away all the rust of sin. Therefore it is necessary that he find us purified, not still in need of purification.

## CHAPTER XIII

“Let brotherly charity remain among you, and do not forget hospitality. For through it some, having received angels as guests, pleased God. Remember those in bonds, as though bound together with them, and those who suffer, as though you yourselves were dwelling in the body. Let marriage be honorable in all, and the marriage bed undefiled. For God will judge fornicators and adulterers. Let your conduct be without avarice, content with what is present. For he himself said: ‘I will not abandon you, nor forsake you,’ so that we may confidently say: ‘The Lord is my helper; I will not fear what man can do to me.’

Remember your leaders, who spoke the word of God to you. Looking to the outcome of their way of life, imitate their faith. Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today, and forever.

Do not be led away by various and foreign doctrines. For it is best to establish the heart by grace, not by foods, which did not benefit those who walked in them.

We have an altar from which those who serve the tabernacle have no authority to eat. For the bodies of those animals whose blood is brought into the holy place for sin by the high priest are burned outside the camp. Therefore Jesus also, to sanctify the people through his own blood, suffered outside the gate.

Let us therefore go out to him outside the camp, bearing his reproach. For we have no abiding city here, but we seek the one that is to come.

Through him, therefore, let us offer a sacrifice of praise to God continually—that is, the fruit of lips confessing his name. Do not forget beneficence and communion. For by such sacrifices God is pleased.

Obey your leaders and submit to them. For they keep watch as those who will give an account for your souls, so that they may do this with joy and not with groaning. For this is not beneficial for you.

Pray for us. For we are confident that we have a good conscience, wishing to conduct ourselves well in all things. Moreover, I earnestly ask you to do this, so that I may be restored to you more quickly.

Now may the God of peace, who brought back from the dead the great Shepherd of the sheep, our Lord Jesus Christ, by the blood of the eternal covenant, make you fit in every good thing, so that you may do his will, accomplishing in you what is pleasing in his sight through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.

I ask you, brothers, to bear with the word of consolation. For indeed I have written to you in very few words.

Know that our brother Timothy has been released; if he comes more quickly, I will see you with him.

Greet all your leaders and all the saints. The brothers from Italy greet you. Grace be with you all. Amen.”

## EXPOSITION

Serve God with fear and reverence. Let charity also remain steadfast among you. I speak of brotherly charity, which brotherhood demands. The fact that you are brothers requires you to love one another.

And do not forget hospitality, which is a part of charity and in which you formerly excelled. By saying “do not forget,” he indicates that they had previously been devoted to hospitality but had now become lax.

Hospitality must therefore be pursued, because through this virtue some pleased God, such as Abraham and Lot, whom God showed to have pleased him by receiving angels as guests. He sent his angels in the guise of guests so that through this they might learn that hospitality was pleasing to him.

Let charity remain among you. Remember also those in bonds—that is, minister to those oppressed in chains—as though bound together with them, remembering that you too are bound together with them. For while they are bound in prison, you are bound by the burden of the flesh.

Or understand it this way: “Remember those in bonds as though bound together with them”—that is, as you would wish to be remembered if you were similarly in bonds.

Remember also those who suffer under any kind of worldly misery, as though you yourselves were suffering. He says the same thing by adding “as though dwelling in the body.” For whoever is oppressed by the burden of the flesh is never free from hardship and labor.

Let marriage also be honorable among all of you. Here he removes fornication. And, once marriages have been entered, let the marriage bed be undefiled. Here he rejects adultery.

I commend marriage and the chastity of the marriage bed, removing fornication and adultery, because God will judge—that is, condemn—fornicators and adulterers. This does not mean that he should not judge murder and the other evils, but only that the discussion here concerned these two.

Let your conduct also be without avarice, so that you do not desire what is excessive. I say that you should be content with what is present; it belongs to God to provide for tomorrow.

You ought to be without avarice. For God himself said to Joshua, and through him to every believer: “O Joshua—or whoever is faithful—I will not wholly abandon you as rejected, nor even for a single hour leave you without help.” God said this so that, in addition to what we have already said—namely, that we should be content with what is present—we may now confidently say: “The Lord is my helper,” and therefore “I will not fear what man may do to me,” even if he takes away what is present.

Remember also your leaders, so that you may conform yourselves to the one who spoke the word of God to you, looking to the outcome of their life—that is, seeing that their end was good.

I say “the outcome of their way of life,” that is, of the good conduct in which they live. Imitate their faith first, so that good conduct and a good end may likewise be found in you.

They might say: “We cannot follow their perfection, because they were taught by Christ himself and possessed a greater abundance of grace than we can possess.”

To this Paul replies: “You can indeed imitate them. For Jesus Christ, who was present yesterday in relation to them, is also ready today in the same way in relation to you. He will likewise be present throughout all ages for those who hope in him, to whom he says: ‘Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age’ (Matt. XXVIII, 20).”

Imitate the faith of your leaders by following their teaching. Do not be led away by various doctrines, which now assert one thing and now another, or by foreign doctrines—that is, doctrines proceeding from elsewhere rather than from us. By such doctrines, I say, do not allow yourselves to be led away from what you received from us.

There were certain seducers who argued from Paul’s statement that all foods are clean and sanctified by God that, the more they stuffed their bellies with an abundance of foods, the more pleasing they were to God, who had sanctified all foods for eating.

Therefore he says: Do not be led away by doctrines of this kind, because it is best for the heart—not the body—to be established and strengthened by grace, that is, by the freedom that God has bestowed upon us in the use of all things, rather than to be established by foods—that is, by an increase of pleasure. Such foods did not benefit those who walked in pleasures and gave them excessive room.

We ought not to establish the heart by foods, because we have an altar—that is, the body of Christ, which is consecrated on the altar—upon which we offer vows and prayers to God as our chief offerings.

From this altar, that is, from the body of Christ, those who serve the tabernacle have no authority to eat—that is, those who serve bodily pleasures. For in the body we shall remain only for a time, just as a soldier remains in a military tent.

He proves this point first by a double authority from the old law and then from the new law, drawing the same meaning from both authorities. He had promised this when he said: Truly, those who serve the tabernacle of pleasure do not have the power to eat from this altar, because they do not go outside the camp—that is, they do not withdraw their bodies from the indulgences of pleasure.

He says it in this way: The bodies of those animals whose blood is brought by the high priest into the Holy of Holies for the remission of the people’s sin—and this once a year—are burned outside the camp.

It was customary, as we have often stated, for the legal high priest once a year to bring blood into the Holy of Holies. This blood was taken from animals burned outside the camp.

That high priest, however, is Christ, who brought into the Holy of Holies his blood, poured out on the cross, for the remission of the sins of all.

The fact that the animal was burned until it became ash signified Christ’s contrition, which he endured. Its ash—that is, the memory of his passion—ought to be sprinkled upon the heads, that is, in the minds of individuals.

The fact that it was burned outside the camp signified that everyone who wishes to be cleansed must go outside the camp—that is, outside carnal pleasures.

He now adds the authority of the New Testament, which has the same meaning as the Old, saying: “For this reason”—namely, to prove that those who serve the tabernacle have no right to eat from this altar—or because what was prefigured in the Old Testament was now to be fulfilled.

Jesus also suffered outside the gate, signifying that those who participate in his altar must be outside the gate—that is, outside the senses of pleasure. For the senses are the gates of the soul, since through the eyes a person is led to desire what he sees, and likewise through the other senses.

Jesus suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood. Since Jesus suffered outside the gate, let us therefore go out to him, placed outside the camp—that is, outside the pleasures of the tabernacle.

And not only this: let us also bear, if necessary, his reproach—that is, the death of the cross.

We certainly ought to go out in this way, because even if we wish to remain here, we have no abiding city here, but seek the one that is to come—that is, the eternal city.

And since we seek the city that is to come, let us therefore, in order to grasp it, offer through Jesus himself sacrifices of praise—that is, praises no less pleasing to God than sacrifices—and let us offer them continually.

When I say “sacrifices of praise,” I mean: Let us offer the fruit of our lips. “Of lips” signifies ease; “fruit” signifies usefulness. I say “of lips confessing the name,” that is, the glory, of God.

Let us offer praises. Do not forget beneficence—that is, the generosity of almsgiving—and communion, since you have said that things are not private but common.

You ought not to forget these things, because through such sacrifices—that is, through beneficence and communion—God is pleased. The wording is passive in sense: God is made well-pleased by such sacrifices.

To ensure that you remember these things, obey your leaders, who are perfected and instruct you well, and submit to them—that is, obey them, showing them every submission in word and deed.

You ought certainly to submit to them, because they keep watch over you as those who will give an account for your souls entrusted to them.

Therefore submit to them in such a way that they may do this—that is, keep watch over you—with joy and not with groaning, because of your stubbornness and lack of restraint.

I say “not with groaning,” for it is not beneficial for you to make them groan.

Obey your leaders, and pray for us.

They might say: “You persecute our nation and our rites, so how can you say, ‘Pray for us’?”

To this Paul replies: You ought to pray for us. For we confidently tell you that we have a good conscience in all things, wishing to conduct ourselves well toward everyone.

Where the conscience is pure and the work is clean, do not, then, be troublesome to me.

[Col. 0566A] Above he said, “Pray for us”; now I beseech you to do this still more, that is, to pray for us more earnestly, so that—that is, in order that—I may be restored to you more quickly, bringing with me the fruits of almsgiving, if I should perhaps be released from my bonds. I say, “Pray for us”; but I myself pray thus for you: “May the God of peace equip you in every good thing”—the God who brought our Lord Jesus Christ back from the dead, that is, from the number of the dead. I call Jesus the great Shepherd, that is, exalted above all things. I call him a shepherd not of wolves but of sheep, that is, of the meek. I call him a shepherd made in blood, that is, through the offering of his blood. I call his blood the confirmer of the eternal covenant, that is, of the covenant destined to endure forever.

This God, I say, may equip you in every good thing. He understands them to be equipped if good will is found in them. [Col. 0566B] May he equip you so that you may do his will—not by your own strength, but in such a way that he himself may do in you what is pleasing in his sight, that is, according to his good pleasure. He does this, I say, through Jesus Christ, who is glory for ever and ever. Amen.

Because he had corrected them somewhat harshly, he now speaks soothingly to them, lest they be disturbed by the apparent severity of his words, saying: “May God thus equip you. But I, brothers, beg you to bear this word—not of reproof, as perhaps some of you think—but the Epistle of consolation; that is, receive it with all patience.” And you can bear it easily, because I have written to you very briefly. Here he indicates that they are impatient: he would have written much more to them if he had known that they would listen patiently.

Bear also your brother Timothy, who has been sent to you by me, [Col. 0566C] or released from the bonds in which he was bound with me, now set free. Receive him, I say, as the bearer of this Epistle—that is, receive him honorably and with every expression of love. With him I shall see you, as I suppose, if, returning more quickly from you, he comes to me.

Greet all your superiors. For he did not write the Epistle to them, since they were perfect, but to certain of their subjects who needed correction. Greet also all the holy ones in your Church. For there were certain perfect persons among the subjects, to whom likewise he did not write. The brothers from Italy greet you. The grace of God be with you all. Amen.

The sign of Paul, showing that the Epistle was his.

## THE EPISTLE OF BLESSED PAUL TO THE LAODICEANS

Recently found in an ancient library; but since it is not commonly read among the catholic books, it has not been elucidated by Blessed Bruno.

[Col. 0565]

[Col. 0565D] Paul, an apostle not from men, nor through a man, but through Jesus Christ, to the brothers who are in Laodicea. Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

I give thanks to Christ in all my prayer, because you remain in him and persevere in good works, awaiting the promise on the day of judgment. Nor let the empty talk of certain persons who insinuate themselves lead you away from the truth of the Gospel preached by me. And now God will cause those who are of me to serve the advancement of the truth of the Gospel and to perform works of kindness that belong to the salvation of eternal life.

And now my bonds are openly known, which I suffer in Christ; in them I rejoice and exult. This has happened to me for perpetual salvation, through your prayers and through the ministry of the Holy Spirit, whether through life or through [Col. 0567A] death. For me, to live is life in Christ, and to die is joy—or gain. And he himself will show his mercy in you, so that you may have the same love and be of one mind.

Therefore, beloved, just as you have heard of the presence of the Lord, so hold fast and act in the fear of God, and it will be life for you forever. For it is God who works in you, and do whatever you do without hesitation or sin. And, what is best, beloved, rejoice in Christ, and guard yourselves against all sordidness in the pursuit of gain.

Let all your requests be made openly before God. Be firm in the mind of Christ, and do what is whole, true, modest, chaste, just, and lovable. Retain in your hearts what you have heard and received, and you will have peace.

Greet all the brothers with a holy kiss. All the holy ones greet you. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. And have this read to the Colossians, and the Epistle of the Colossians read to you.

**END OF THE EPISTLES OF BLESSED PAUL THE APOSTLE.**

[Col. 0567]

## 415. APOLOGETIC HECATOSTICHON [HUNDRED-LINE POEM] OF LORD JAMES JEROME, ALUMNUS OF THE CARTHUSIAN HOUSE OF PARIS
