By which he defends Blessed Bruno’s phrasing, which may seem inferior to sharp-witted people, against slander, and weighs the substance of his sentences in a just balance.

[Col. 0567B]

Who is this new lyre-player, soothing with harmonious sound,

leaping across the snowy rocks of the long Allobrogian ridge,

springing over hills and mountains? O how he holds back

all the winged birds beneath the sky,

professing in face, dress, and emaciation that he is a hermit,

yet sounding nothing rustic upon a rustic instrument!

His brow is raised toward heaven; honors are trampled beneath his feet;

the sevenfold star is fixed upon the crown of his head.

No one will accuse him of using delights or a soft couch,

or of being idle in study and devotion.

His fingers have no gold; his divine lyre has no emeralds,

nor does the holy Muse seek foreign-colored cosmetics.

Sacred truthfulness has not concealed his baldness for him,

nor does he seek to arrange his hair with artistic reeds.

Is he another Amphion, or the famous Orpheus restored to life,

[Col. 0567C] drawing deaf elements by the seduction of his strings,

restoring sense to those to whom nature denied it?

Or does his lyre possess greater power than nature?

Let the cities now rot uncultivated: the desert smiles,

while the foolish world roars in the whirlwind of arms;

while the woods sing such welcome victory songs to the heavenly powers

and fill inaccessible groves with angelic choirs,

so that all learning may now serve the holy father,

turning the eagle’s standards toward the cross.

O may I see the Graces pledged in marriage to Christ,

and the Castalian maidens likewise make chaste covenants.

Indeed, I shall see them all in the deserted Helicon,

and I now know how to raise the structure of the desert:

to mingle alternating melodies under Christ’s name

[Col. 0567D] through the temple in facing, divided choirs.

Nor will singing symphony be absent from silent cells,

with the Spirit, and reading joined to alternating prayer.

Is this Bruno, head of the Carthusian order, once

a famous name in sacred biography throughout the world,

with whom the school of the Franks in no way envied Athens,

and whose speech was no less divine than the Roman forum?

Behold, the prophetic helmsman, leader of the order,
moves the citharas and strikes the strings consonant with his life.

He leaves to his own an illustrious example and sign

of how to live and to speak words worthy of the heavenly Prince.

It will be pleasant to address the man and hear him more closely.

Indeed, unless I am deceived by what I hear, he himself is calling:

[Col. 0568B]

“Come in abundance, you wanderers,” he says, “and listen, tender ones;

with the Lord’s lyre-playing king I shall teach you fear.

I am the one who, preferring to withdraw dishonored from honors,

went there where the breath of the Godhead called my vessel.

The horror of the world drove me, a fugitive from Paris,

from the funeral rites, so that I might follow these stars of heaven.

The stars opened the way; the gods smiled at the thought that so many thousands

were to be caught in my hooks.

I am driven by these auspices. Like the voice of one crying in the desert,

weary of the world, I lay out the path of the Thunderer.

Restoring the ways of John the Baptist and his scattered members,

I establish separate camps for my solitary warriors.

The deserted Carthusian desert pleases Christ;

its halls glow with praises by night and day.

It is the inaccessible and waterless desert of the psalmist,

where the living virtue and glory of God may be revealed.

Therefore, eagerly, it equips its sides with dove-like wings,

so that, fleeing here, one may learn to enjoy oneself and God.

[Col. 0568C]

The same glory shone upon the three disciples on the mountain,

where Peter wishes three camps to be made.

Zacchaeus is unable to see Jesus through the crowd;

to Jesus the disciples say, “You are being pressed by the crowd.”

So, monk, fleeing the hostile things opposed by the world,

diligently fulfill the meaning of this name.

Jesus has therefore assigned these tasks to me:

to lay smooth paths through rough groves,

to level the harsh thickets with Christ’s lyre,

raising here new standards of holy warfare.

I have none of the Milesian tales of the Madaurian ass,

[Col. 0568D] nor any weapons conscious of Lycambes’ death.

The seeds of the divine flame are most abundant for me;

nothing is more worthy than devoted leisure.

I burn and compel those lying cold to rise;

now I employ enticements, now force.

Now the lyre of David, now the trumpet of Paul:

the one resounds fully through my fingers, the other through my mouth.

This is the rule of silence prescribed for you, Carthusian house:

while closing your lips to men, speak to God.

For to speak to him, with Paul or David as interpreter, is to suffer no loss through silence.

Nor should the less cultivated use of the Latin tongue offend,

if the language of the worn body is suited to the worn garment.

[Col. 0569A]

I adapt lofty thoughts to humble language;

my words flow not from my mouth but from my heart.

Let others adorn temples with Egyptian trophies;

I praise that, but for the present it is not my concern.

Unwilling to become illustrious through the words of human wisdom,

Paul is present, indebted both to the learned and to the unlearned.

When David bristles in ashes and a hair shirt,

who would wish to be adorned with rhetorical roses?

[Col. 0570A]

Now cleanse my ears and shake the dregs from my palate,

or rather, return within the enclosure of your own spirit.

In these matters it is not the tongue but the heart that must be judged;

for my whole struggle has been with realities.

Do not taste these things merely with the understanding,

but savor them with the Spirit by whom they were revealed,

and nourish the inward parts of your soul with this good.

I wished to offer counsel alike to the greatest and the least,

and every kind of understanding had to be taken into account.

## [PART III OF THE WORKS OF SAINT BRUNO.]

[Col. 0569]

## [NOTICE.]

There follows in the Cologne edition volume, or part, III of the Works of Saint Bruno. Besides certain sermons, it contains the short works *On the Praises of the Church*, *On the Ornament of the Church*, *On the New World*, and *On the Feasts of Feasts*. These, however, are not by Bruno the Carthusian but by Bruno, bishop of Asti, and are numbered among his works. (See below under the year 1125.) The works mentioned above are followed by two letters of Saint Bruno, a sermon *On Contempt of Riches*, and an appendix *On the Origin of the Sacred Carthusian Order*.

[Col. 0569]

## THE TWO LETTERS OF THE DIVINE BRUNO

Which he wrote from the wilderness of Calabria after he had withdrawn again from the city of Rome into that solitude in which he also died.

### I. To Radulphus Viridis, provost of the Church of Rheims

An exhortation to contempt of the world, to the contemplative eremitical life as the better part of Mary, and, further, to fulfillment of his vow.

(See among the *Acts of Saint Bruno*, no. 683, in this volume, col. 420.)

### II. To his sons of the Major Carthusian House

(See above, col. 418.)

[Col. 0569]

## A SERMON ON CONTEMPT OF RICHES. (G)*

[Col. 0569B]

“It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 19:24). This was signified by that jar in which wickedness was shut up, whose mouth a mass of lead closed so that she could not come out (Zechariah 5:6–7). From this it is understood how difficult it is for a greedy person either to be drawn out of or separated from the belly of greed.

The prophet Zechariah tells us that he saw a jar going forth. When he asked what it was, he was told: “This is the jar that goes forth, and this is their eye throughout the whole earth; and behold, a talent of lead was being carried; and behold, one woman sitting in the middle of the jar” (ibid.). When he asked who she was, he was told that she was wickedness. The mouth of the jar was closed with a mass of lead. [Col. 0569C] And behold, two women came forth, who had wings like kites; they lifted the jar between earth and heaven, so that a house might be built for it in the land of Shinar, and it might be established and placed there upon its base, and so forth.

What, indeed, is signified by the jar except greed? “This is their eye.” Whose eye? Clearly, the eye of those who love it throughout the whole earth. For all look toward it; all strive toward it, since, as it is written, [Col. 0570B] “Money is obeyed in everything” (Ecclesiastes 10:19).

In this jar wickedness sits, because the rich and greedy, since they do not possess mercy and piety, are rightly called not only wicked but wickedness itself. But what can be understood better by the two women carrying the jar than anxiety and deception? For greedy people are always anxious in acquiring, and deceivers seize what belongs to others by making it their own.

Therefore these women are said to have wings like a kite, because the kite is among the most rapacious of birds and always lies in wait for small and gentle birds. These women—that is, deception and evil anxiety—carry the jar to the land of Shinar, or Babylon, because by these two vices the rich and greedy are carried away to destruction.

For it is written of this Babylon [Col. 0570C]: “Babylon has fallen, has fallen, that great prostitute, and has become a dwelling-place of demons” (Revelation 14:8). Wretched, therefore, and unhappy in every respect are those who have found for themselves a house in the land of Shinar, where they will dwell among demons. May our most gentle Lord Jesus, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout the eternal ages, rescue us from it. Amen.

[Col. 0571]

## THE CONFESSION OF SAINT BRUNO

(Edited by Mabillon, *Analecta*, new edition, p. 447.)

[Col. 0571A]

We have taken care to preserve in writing the faith of Master Bruno, which he professed publicly to his brothers when he sensed that the hour was approaching for him to enter upon the way of all flesh, because he earnestly asked us to be intimate witnesses of that faith before God.

I firmly believe in the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit: the Father unbegotten, the Son only-begotten, and the Holy Spirit proceeding from both; and that these three persons are one God.

I believe that this same Son of God was conceived by the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary. I believe that the most chaste Virgin was a virgin before childbirth, a virgin in childbirth, and remained a virgin forever after childbirth. I believe that this same Son of God was conceived among human beings as true man, without sin.

I believe that this same Son of God was treacherously seized by the faithless Jews, shamefully treated, unjustly [Col. 0571B] bound, spat upon, scourged, put to death, and buried. He descended into hell to free his captives from there; he descended for our redemption, and he rose again. He ascended into heaven, and from there he will come to judge the living and the dead.

I believe in the sacraments that the Catholic Church believes and venerates, and specifically that which is consecrated upon the altar is the true body, true flesh, and true blood of our Lord Jesus Christ. [Col. 0572A] We receive him for the remission of our sins and in hope of eternal salvation. I believe in the resurrection of the flesh and eternal life. Amen.

I confess and believe in the holy and ineffable Trinity: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, one natural God, of one substance, one nature, one majesty, and one power.

And we profess that the Father was neither begotten nor created, but unbegotten. The Father himself derives his origin from no one; from him the Son received birth and the Holy Spirit procession. He himself, therefore, is the fountain and origin of the whole Godhead.

The Father himself, in ineffable essence, [Col. 0572B] begot the Son ineffably from his own substance, yet not anything other than what he himself is. God begot God, light begot light. Therefore every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is from him. Amen.

[Col. 0571]

## APPENDIX TO SAINT BRUNO: ON THE ORIGIN OF THE SACRED CARTHUSIAN ORDER, BY ZACHARIA BENEDICT, OF VICENZA, A CARTHUSIAN

[Col. 0571C]

Do you wish to know who first laid the foundations

of the Carthusian order, and what cause gave rise to it, traveler?

Follow this history, and read these verses also.

If you seek its fruit, holy compunction will be present.

On the plains of the Senones a most distinguished city,

the marketplace of wisdom, rises with its turreted summit.

They say that Paris, fleeing the Trojan fires,

built it and, remembering his father, called its inhabitants Parisians,

giving them insignia and arms.

There the Seine washes the citadels with many eddies

and sends foreign merchandise to its own seas.

Here is a fertile academy, cultivated by constant care;

here Pallas, too, was transferred from the shores of Cecrops,

and immense wisdom was sent down from the highest matters.

Here he was so distinguished in every virtue and in those disciplines

that require freedom of time, that when he ascended the platform or chair,

he seemed to be the famous voice of the great Paul,

[Col. 0571D] and, in his modest conduct, another Joseph.

The whole people worshiped him as though he had fallen from the summit of heaven,

for he was a priest.

A thousand and eighty-two years after the birth

from the Virgin’s sacred womb had passed

when the final hour came upon this man.

He had to undergo the grave command and harsh laws of death;

now the cold, bloodless body lies there alive no longer.

Rumor resounds everywhere; anxious grief remains everywhere,

[Col. 0572C] and the lamentations of both sexes echo throughout the city.

“Alas! The good shepherd has perished; the holy man has died,”

they cried through the marketplaces. “No one will give us again

those learned and golden words of saving speech.”

Meanwhile the mournful procession of the funeral is prepared.

The obsequies and funeral chant are conducted with great pomp;

citizens, clergy, and the entire learned school gather from every side,

and bronze instruments clang with resounding blows.

The honored corpse is carried to the greater churches,

to be buried beneath Parian marble, with spices placed below.

The priests recite the sad fate in song;

they carry burning torches and waxen lights.

The sorrowful bands proceed together in a long procession

and fill every street with black coverings.

Amid so many events there occurred something astonishing to relate,

a heavenly judgment, dreadful to all:

truly, the very sentence of God, the great abyss

to which alone the secrets of the heart lie exposed (Psalm 35).

Those whom he chooses, or those whom he deprives of heaven,

he alone knows; he alone has distinguished them from eternity.

We blind human beings see the secrets of things

as an owl discerns the light of Apollo.

Behold, the dead man carried beneath silver and purple,

heaped with so much honor,

when he had been placed in the lofty mass of the sanctuary

so that he might be seen more clearly and be visible to all,

answer me: while the reading was being performed, behold a wondrous thing—

he raised his face from afar, lifted his bloodless breast,

and, looking around at the crowds with a grim gaze,

[Col. 0573A] spoke from above the bier in a terrible cry:

“By the secret counsel of the heavenly powers and by just laws,

alas for me! I have been accused; I appeal to the face of the dreadful Judge.”

Then he lowered his head and fell silent, his limbs dry and lifeless.

At the first sight of this everyone trembled and fell speechless.

All were silent; all were afraid; the people strained their ears.

The unaccustomed miracle was scarcely believed by minds reeling with shock.

The embalmers stood trembling, overcome by terror,

and scarcely dared to touch the dead body.

Their hair stood on end, and their voices stuck in trembling throats.

After the silence there arose enormous commotion,

a confused sound of the voices of young and old;

it was heard farther and farther away, and the report ran throughout the city.

The marketplace people [Note: [Col. 0573D] Ἀγοραῖος, that is, “of the marketplace” or “forensic.”] came;

the panting crowd hurried forward.

The vaulted churches rang with various rumors, and the people

could not contain themselves; foot pressed against foot and back against back.

By force they made entrances; the doors fell from their hinges.

[Col. 0573B] Some climbed the highest steps, others the pinnacles,

to look down from above upon these new marvels.

Again the dead man lifted his livid face,

looking here and there with terrifying eyes at everyone,

and said in an unfamiliar bellow:

“Woe, woe is me! For judgment has already been pronounced against me

by the holy Godhead.”

Then he lay as before, without a murmur of speech.

A deep, icy trembling and weakness ran through their bones.

Hearts were afraid; children trembled; the old themselves were terrified

by this novelty. The sacred hall was filled with the sharp cries

of married women, infants, and young men.

They pleaded for mercy with the heavenly powers and beat their breasts,

and, with ears suspended in expectation, said to one another:

“What can this be? This man always gave the holiest commands

to these peoples and lived honorably,

yet he confesses in a pitiable voice that he has been accused

and has heard the final judgment from heaven.

These portents certainly signify something extraordinary.”

[Col. 0573C]

Everyone was uncertain whether he should be entrusted to a consecrated tomb.

The venerable bishop, troubled and uncertain, advised that he be kept above the earth

until God from on high should declare what was to be done.

Then again the lifeless man raised his head high from the bier,

and, contemplating his own misfortune, spoke thus

with immense grief and a great bellow:

“Spare yourselves the funeral rites; you can do nothing for me.

Why did my parents beget me, unfortunate man?

Ah, wretched that I am, I go condemned to eternal fires.”

Then he fell permanently silent and lay on his back.

Ecstasy and lamentation seized the crowd; the entire

sacred building resounded with groans and varied tumult,

and the halls echoed far and wide with women’s wailing.

Some clung to the doors in embraces, others to the columns,

and, with eyes weighed down by grief, seemed to be having a nightmare.

They marveled at the destruction of so great a teacher,

and could not sufficiently marvel that so many good works

and so many pious labors for religion had been extinguished.

[Col. 0573D] At once the people, drenched in tears,

dragged the corpse from the edge of the blessed sacred ground

and enclosed it in a pit of profane earth.

From there a fragrant elder tree grows, and gloomy hemlock.

The sun had sunk into the Oceanid waters,

and the Delian goddess was displaying her pale face from the sky,

when the idle crowd, the citizens, and the learned bands

returned to their own homes with minds stunned.

After their weary limbs had yielded to the bed,

they saw in dreams torches and dreadful shapes,

ghosts wandering in Erebus and threefold Furies,

which at night struck them with something like Lethean terror.

Paris has not yet forgotten those days;

for, utterly shaken from that time, it refuses

to sing these things (answer me); but the fourth lesson

begins here. A thing mournful for all ages!

Bruno, the splendor of priests and rector of schools,

[Col. 0574A]

whom his celebrated German native city had brought forth,

a pious and wise man, outstanding in every gift of learning,

an alumnus of the church of Rheims,

was then teaching the sacred disciplines to the people of Paris.

He attended the funeral with great honor,

and, unable to conceal the grief conceived in his mind

at such portents, as soon as he reached his own quarters,

wept alone in an inexhaustible stream of tears.

“Alas for me,” he said. “Woe, woe, because I have wasted my years!

What shall I, a madman, do? If he who was revered by all the people

as holy burns so unhappily

in the places of Cerberus, in the monstrous abyss,

what will happen to me?” With these words he divided his mind,

now this way, now that, remaining awake and wishing to change his life for the better.

In the morning Bruno returned to the schools, surrounded by a large number of servants.

He mounted the chair, clothed in a mournful cloak,

with eyes fixed upon the ground, red and swollen with grief,

[Col. 0574B] such as one has who, deprived of sleep,

has sighed through cruel nights of vigil.

He addressed his followers in these words.

The countless assembly remained silent:

“I have not come here to utter empty words.

Until now, accustomed to employ human reasoning,

we learned men have all gone astray together.

But enough and more than enough! Let us now follow the commands of heaven.

I have come to report what I feel, and what counsel I have judged

we must hold, and whatever may be useful to us,

so that we may flee the snares of this age

and the dreadful, pitiable fate of yesterday’s light.

Who among us, I ask, would have reckoned that a man destined

for the burning throats of Styx and Cocytus

could be so distinguished in character, so brilliant in teaching,

and so richly endowed with the gifts of nature?

We have seen, alas, how greatly we bleary-eyed people are deceived,

and how our false opinion wanders through so many errors.

What will happen to us wretched people, sinning through long habit,

if such a perpetual condemnation has been given to a man?

If this has happened to the green wood, what will happen to the dry?

(Luke 23:31.) See what vengeance awaits us, dear disciples;

weigh for a little while how many enormous purgations

will cleanse so many stains.

For the wisdom of this world is nothing here

except to appear outwardly holy and just.

O dear companions, take pity on your own condition.

See: death is on the neighboring threshold, extending its curved sickle

and cutting down the green grasses.

Despise riches, which you cannot carry away with you after death,

I beg you, if you value your master’s words;

and if you preserve me in an honor worthy of me,

leave Pentapolis and the fugitive ages with me,

and, with Lot, enter caves and climb the hidden mountains.

You see how fleeting this present life is;

indeed, I will confess that it should be called death more than life.

Raise your minds to heaven; there is our homeland;

there is our rest and eternal dwelling of peace.

This life is exile for us and an oppressive burden,

where there are so many disasters and so many hostile weapons.

But where are now all those kings who once held power on land and sea?

Where, I ask, are the commanders? Where is the proud diadem

of emperors, visible throughout the whole world?

Where now are those once skilled in the valor of war?

Where are the orators, and the famous poets?

The painters, the serious physicians, and the teachers of wisdom?

They have all perished and gone down beneath the lowest

caverns of the earth, where savage death waits,

leaving only tombs as monuments of themselves,

unclean ashes and fetid bodies in sepulchers.

Alas for the love of deceptive life, which seems to scatter flowers

and violets through the fields, and fragrant lilies,

but at the harvest gathers thorns, yew, and poisons,

turning laughter into tears and joys into anxieties.

To serve God while alive is a most sweet thing.

[Col. 0575A] There are sweet tears, sweet sighs,

sweet prolonged vigils, sweet fasts,

sweet submission to commands, and sweet dwelling within enclosures.

What must the heavens now be like, where those released from the flesh

and received from wretched cares into a secure place

see, with clear eyes, the joyful face of the supreme Prince,

from whom happy joys continually flow?

What are we doing, dear companions? The Almighty Godhead

calls us to quiet cloisters through so many signs.

Why are we sluggish before the breath of so great a breeze?

We must go where the stars call us with their right hand,

where the dew-bearing west wind drives us and the northwest wind assists.

Let us leave our homeland, warned to pursue better things.

For my mind is set on leaving the urban buildings

and seeking uncultivated entrances and silent rocks;

among Fauns and the hard offspring of lions

I shall embrace the way of Antony,

and, unknown, I shall hide in Paul’s Nitrean haunts,

beneath the hollowed-out caverns.

But you, excellent companions, noble offspring,

[Col. 0575B]

who have experienced human dangers so often with me,

do you wish to follow me through so many hazards?

Do you wish, as you have always done, to have me as leader,

faithful father, and loving teacher?

I shall be your leader. Now, now I shall accompany you as you go.”

Thus he spoke, and Bruno repeatedly wiped his eyes,

which poured forth warm tears, with the edge of his garment.

From so great a number, six leaders rose,

distinguished in intellect and wisdom, in possessions and ancient blood:

Andrew, holy Hugh, Vegetus, Garinus of Laon,

Stephen of Bourges, and likewise Stephen of Die.

The last two were pupils of the Libyan teacher

and followers of the great canonist Rufus,

from the celibate monastery; they were powerful in the art

of doctrine, and successively broke their silence

in this order:

“Master, to whom no one in the world can be compared,

we have followed you from our earliest years

and have always been ready to obey your commands and words.

By the gods, by all the stars that glitter through

[Col. 0575C] the Olympian expanses, we testify

that without you we could never live.

Through fire, through the midst of arms, we shall follow you.

Whatever adverse fortune may come to you,

our mind is set on dying with you and sharing your life.

Live happily and fare well in true peace,

O companions; without such a master

we cannot spend our lives in these bodies and enjoy the welcome light.

Wherever he wishes to go, we shall follow rejoicing.

Therefore we too shall seek caves and caverns together.

You again, companions; you, earthly things, farewell.

And you, city of Paris, repository of our labors, farewell.

Let our relatives be well; let both our parents be well.

Riches and homes and fertile fields, farewell.

We follow the heavenly powers; we despise the fields that perish.

We flee the earth and hasten toward the citadel of heaven.”

They had finished, and all rushed into the sweet

kisses of peace; both sides were drenched with tears in their embraces.

And so, returning to their own homes, they lamented.

Bruno found no rest in the silent night,

but anxiously considered what place he might discover

where he would be safe from all the noise of the people

and remain more hidden; he pondered and reconsidered it repeatedly.

Meanwhile the sky revolved, and the moon’s lamp,

at its rising, first split the opposing clouds.

After he had long prayed to the heavenly powers and offered

mystic libations at the altars with groans,

and nourished the law of Minerva, he held up the burning lamp,

keeping watch alone far into the night.

Sleep overcame him, and he gave his limbs to the warm bed.

He sank down exhausted, and as soon as rest covered his eyes,

he saw angelic faces walking forward

and mingling wise words with modest lips.

He fixed the seals of shining faith upon his forehead

and said:

“O joyful souls, who bear yourselves in such an appearance,

I adjure you by the greatest scepters of the Thunderer:

have you been sent from the Stygian regions or from heaven?

[Col. 0576A] The figures, cheerful in countenance and beautiful

in face and brow, said:

‘Do not fear, consecrated minister of God.

We have indeed been sent here to you from the highest seats,

and we bring commands from the heavenly Father.

Happy are you, whom heaven has chosen from so many thousands

to restore fallen monks!

Proceed; fulfill your heart and bring your vows to completion.

The divine Sower commands you: go quickly to Granopolis—

the Gauls call it by that common name—

and seek Bishop Hugh. He will show you

the place we have established for you on a lofty height.

In Hebrew speech it is called Carthusia;

in Ausonian speech, that is, Latin, it means

“the perfect calling of the divine powers.”

You too shall take a name from so great a title,

and your students shall be called Carthusians.

Go, therefore, happily. All heaven honors you.

Bruno, it will give you a divine name forever.’”

After they had spoken these words, the angelic faces

flowed into the clouds, and their forms dissolved into the thickened air.

Soon they departed, and the whole bed breathed of amomum.

[Col. 0576B]

He groaned, wavering under the sweetness of so great a message,

sprang from his bed, stretched his upturned hands

toward heaven with a cry, and returned thanks.

“Gods of heaven,” he said, “who possess the threshold of heaven,

if I had as many tongues as Argus is said to have had eyes

in his limbs, I could not render praises worthy

of the gift by which you make me worthy of this task.

These are your gifts, Christ.

There is nothing excellent in me; you bring everything.

Grant success to the good beginning and prepare favorable steps,

heavenly inhabitants who care for human salvation.”

Bruno ordered his companions to be summoned to him at dawn.

They came at once, and he told them every detail.

Amid abundant tears and warm dewdrops,

amid embraces and holy kisses,

they joined hands, pledges of faith, and a covenant of love.

They all decided to hasten the work that lay ahead,

retaining only a few possessions for the building of churches,

and distributing the rest of their goods throughout the city to the poor.

[Col. 0576C]

They ordered the servants to make every effort to bring the horses

and to prepare saddles and bridles.

Then all hastened to obey the command and carry out the orders.

They loaded the books upon pack animals and wagons without delay.

A din arose, and voices rolled through the lofty buildings.

The servants marveled at their masters’ sudden departure from the house,

and could not restrain their tears or their wretched grief.

They turned their pious faces toward the great palace

and said with heavy sobs and open lamentation:

“Proud hall, farewell; halls crowned with hangings, farewell.

You will no longer be seen by us.

We leave you to be inhabited by foreign occupants; farewell.

We are going to unknown shores, and shall never return.”

Thus they took the road and drove their spurs into the horses.

Then the heavenly powers sent down from the highest sky

seven stars, one of which shone more brightly than the others.

From the rising place of the newborn Phoebus

it seemed to carry its step toward the lofty buildings

[Col. 0576D] of Bishop Hugh and to climb the steep path,

which was nearby and rested upon a lofty rock.

While he was lying in sweet sleep, Hugh received such a vision.

After he awoke from sleep, he turned the whole event over

in his mind, weighing and reweighing it.

“What does God the Good One wish by this wondrous sign?” he said.

“What, I ask, do these seven stars portend to the world?”

While he considered these things more deeply, the group approached the city:

the teacher accompanied by six companions entered the bishop’s house,

and told the bishop privately that he wished to see him.

He was led inside to the inner chambers of the hall.

The companions bowed to the old man; Bruno kissed his consecrated hands

and began to speak:

“Great glory of the faith, most upright model of our fathers,

Hugh, warned by the heavenly gods through dreams,

we have come here to you, and disclose to you all our mind,

which the heavenly powers have touched with their inspiration.

The supreme Power has terrified us with a dreadful portent,

[Col. 0577A] which I think cannot be unknown to you, since all Gaul

has been filled for many days with the novelty of this event.

O how cruel and dreadful a day, with great fear,

was that day which inflamed us with so great a love.

You know each detail better, most holy shepherd,

whom God has made illustrious with greater light.

These six disciples wish to climb with me

the steep mountain of religious life in these regions.

With one mind we all wish to live in a vast wilderness

and lead our lives within strict enclosures.

Now satiated with the world, we despise everything that is in it,

and all of us are inflamed with equal love.

Therefore, illustrious Father, reveal to us a place suitable for us;

reveal it, I beg you.

For we know that heaven has disclosed great things to you,

and that it has promised you agreeable assistance in this work

and that you will be our guide into the deserts.”

Thus Bruno spoke. His companions assented to his words.

When the Father heard them, he could not restrain the streams

falling from his eyes; he raised them up and embraced them.

Looking toward heaven, he immediately burst into these words:

[Col. 0577B]

“O supreme Giver, rolling the spheres of heaven,

pouring your influences into them, which supply joyful seasons

and lead down golden ages flowing with peace,

by what worthy word, deed, or affection could I praise you,

who in our age perform such wonders

and deem a human being worthy of so great a love—”
to remove from the muddy places and raise them toward the pole of heaven, away from cares.

Those seven stars appeared to me in a dream. What else? Do they not signify these men, do these seven hearts not show themselves—hearts full of God, destined to illuminate the western dwelling? For the East has sent their honors to us. Fortunate Gaul, which rejoices in so great a shoot, and which peoples from a foreign climate adorn!

Then he addressed them in these gentle words:

“I believe there is a place divinely suited to you, where seven stars have descended from the clouds. I remember the site and keep it in my faithful heart: a steep, humped path leads there over the rocky mountain. It is a barren and cold place beyond what can be said; there are rocks that are always white, deprived of the rising sun by continual snows.

[Col. 0577C]

“In the morning we shall go together and inspect it; we shall survey whatever narrow fields there may be. Meanwhile, my sons, remain with me in the palace, and remember me and my people.”

Thus they rested there when their conversation had ended.

When the intervals of daylight returned with the new sun, they all made for the mountains and the sunlit summit. At last they reached the highest peak. They saw the Hernican rocks and terrifying cliffs everywhere. There were no shrubs there, no fruit-bearing trees. Scarcely were there any green herbs or low broom plants.

Here the bishop, terrified by the harshness of the place, said:

“How deeply I grieve that the beloved company of the brothers has come to such barren hollows and lofty enclosures! Look: unproductive cliffs surround us everywhere. We scarcely see the sun, and evening seems always to remain here; heavy mists hang over the place, and here I see no lairs of wild beasts, no approaches, no tracks.

[Col. 0577D] No bird, no human being, perhaps no animal at all, has come here. Truly these cold places are dreadful, forever deprived of the rising sun by perpetual snows.

“Will human beings live where brute creatures refuse to live? Tell me what you are doing, and whether you can live here.”

So he spoke. As he repeated each point, Bruno interrupted him with these words:

“O noble prince, do you not think it better to endure the hardships of this mountain and its icy cold than to suffer even a single day of the torments and manifold pains of hell? I raise my eyes to heaven and turn over in my mind the joyful days without death, and the gifts that will endure forever and see no end.

“The Almighty calls us here, and heaven has given manifest signs. Shall we be frightened by the small losses of this unhappy life, a life deprived of beauty? Far from it! I would rather go forward into every danger. Let this, then, be our rest and our holy delight.”

[Col. 0578A] He spoke, and all unanimously agreed with him. Immediately the distinguished man Hugh, together with Bruno and all his companions, joyfully uttered these words in song with one voice:

“Hail forever, safest region of the world; hail, long-sought rocky mass, destined to purge pious minds of their long rust and to send many souls into the dwellings of the gods.

“Hail, mountain of the heavenly powers, enriched by love, whose soil, though barren in the gift of its earth and lacking cultivation and crops, will nevertheless never lack those groves and that greenery from which holy fruits are produced in heaven.

“The ground may be parched of herbs, but the field will always grow rich in noble virtues, heaped high with excellent merits.

“Hail, silent woods and slender tamarisks! Receive us into your fellowship with joyful faces. We have come here to live and die together.”

After this the craftsmen began to cut the rocks from the high stone masses and to prepare durable lime.

[Col. 0578B] Some dug, while another piled up heaps of sand. One leveled the ground; another carried bricks and water. Chisels rang, as did heavy mattocks and hard double-bladed axes. The noise and clamor of the men could be heard farther away. On the high plateau cells and shrines were constructed, and an altar was dedicated to the sacred Mother who bore Christ.

That place was deprived of rainwater. There were no cisterns there, nor any well. Only in a hollow did rainwater remain, stagnant, and at times it gave off a muddy stench. Everyone endured these great hardships in sorrow.

But what does steadfast faith not obtain and deserve? That illustrious man Hugh gave himself to tears and prayer, and as a suppliant obtained from heaven what he had asked.

For immediately they dug into the hard base of the rock. Without delay, fresh waters began to flow, and they forced out broad streams like a river. That spring still washes the summits in a winding course and flows around the gardens of the cells in a glassy stream.

The sign still endures, renewing the miracles of Moses, who drew sweet waters from barren marble when the Hebrew host journeyed through the deserts of Arabia.

The solemn day had now arrived on which the rising structure could provide the monks with suitable lodging. Hugh summoned the clergy and invited the citizens from the town to the highest approaches and uncultivated threshold of the mountain, to witness the consecration of the festive church, and to see such men assume the habit of holy rusticity and hide themselves among the rugged Alps.

[Col. 0578C] With the clergy accompanying him, he climbed the forested heights. But Bruno and the brothers bore with difficulty the crowds of so many people and the tumult throughout the holy dwellings.

The bishop arrived, assumed the sacred vestments in the customary order, placed the insignia upon his head, and put on the two-pointed tiara. Fragrant smoke rose from Sabæan incense and climbed higher, filling the folds of the shrine. One prepared a chair for the pontiff; another spread the coverings.

[Col. 0578D] The priests now began their chants with voices in measured harmony. The prior rose to the gleaming altars and, raising his palms toward the heights of heaven, offered the sacred mystical sacrifice and presented gifts to the heavenly powers.

Meanwhile the priest consecrated the church and cloister and decreed that the new house should be called the Carthusian house, and that the houses to be founded should bear that name. He donated estates and bestowed fertile fields, so that the monks might live without complaint.

Then Bruno and his elderly companions entered the sanctuary. Each was stripped of his precious, soft cloaks, and all immediately drew their shoes from their legs. They cut the hair from their noble heads. The handsome, milk-white limbs of the young men appeared; stripped, they remained bent at knees and body.

Then the grieving prior covered the doctor’s white body and the tender backs of the brothers with a rough, hairy garment. He placed upon them a coarse sackcloth and a white mantle of virgin wool, then bound it with white hemp and covered their shoulders with a white, closed hood, as a sign of perpetual enclosure and purity.

[Col. 0579A] Countless crowds stood by, and everyone groaned. Pious hearts could not restrain their pious lamentation.

Then choirs of angels came from the shining summit of heaven and celebrated the festival with sonorous song. David, radiant in purple and scarlet, preceded them, striking an ivory harp. John too had come, girded with the hairy skin of a camel, about to embrace his most beloved disciples. Paul was here, covered with a palm-leaf garment; here was Hilarion and the famous hero Antony; and Benedict, venerable in his shining robe and countenance. They had once followed hiding places and forests and had come as witnesses to such solemn rites.

Learn from this, you who labor for worldly honor, who lift up your heads and possess swollen hearts, moved by the present spectacle and by so great a sweetness: lower the lofty brows of your raised foreheads.

[Col. 0579B] At that time Victor, the father who presided over Christ’s lofty palace, was perhaps gazing upon the heavenly spheres. He saw blessed choirs flashing with radiance, joyfully joining the Thunderer from their highest seats, as he went to visit the holy hills of Carthusian territory.

He was astonished, marked those mountains and that climate, and sent there a swift messenger and swift tablets. He wrote to Hugh about the miracles he had seen.

Hugh, astonished, wrote back everything that had happened at that time and what the Almighty had accomplished in those regions. With his swift pen he recorded the doctor and his six companions turned away from the world’s whirlwind, the lights of the seven stars, the progress of the order that had begun, and its strict rigor.

The messenger departed and returned to the Latin city. When the supreme shepherd received the new report, he rejoiced and immediately summoned the Fathers, the holy senate whom Roman purple makes sublime. He disclosed everything that had happened and confirmed, with the unanimous votes of the court, that the work had been divinely strengthened.

[Col. 0579C] Having completed the document, he fortified it with divine gifts and enriched it with various endowments. Bronze tablets marked with double-headed signs are preserved.

Several other supreme Fathers likewise did this, those who encircle their exalted heads with a triple diadem.

Hugh, however, could never abandon those whom he had once helped; he always supported and increased their strength. Constantly he sought to remain among them, enclosed in the cloister. He too took from them the white tunics and wished to end his life among them and nowhere else.

For forty years he never looked upon a woman’s face and sought no honors. At last, after his holy death, he was received among the saints.

At that time William, the great abbot of the blessed Theofredus, also relinquished the mitre and laid down the sacred staff, as well as the wealthy monasteries of the monks. He chose to live alone beneath a poor roof, under Bruno’s guidance, and accepted the white mantle.

After Victor’s elevation, Urban, prince of the Cluniac order, succeeded to the honors of Rome. He was distinguished in every kind of wisdom. Bruno had once been his teacher, and therefore Urban, wishing to use his master’s help, wise counsels, and advice in conducting affairs, sent a messenger from the Roman city to the freezing heights of the Carthusian mountain, to summon Bruno to service in the holy court.

The messenger went and reached the desired dwelling. Bruno received the pontiff’s letters and, as he read them, anxiously wondered what he ought then to do: whether to attempt the journey or to answer by prayer, lest he withdraw from his purpose or abandon the beloved caves, in which nothing could be sweeter than to remain hidden.

But after he had weighed both sides, Bruno thought it impious to resist the wishes and commands of the supreme pontiff and concluded that he must go.

Thus, though unwilling, he left the fields of the Carthusian house.

Alas, what sighs, what lamentations did Bruno utter, hating the Roman offices, cares, and harsh exile from his cell! What sighs and lamentations did his companions utter? Like a ship whose fastening had been lost and whose tiller had been broken, they suffered very great losses.

[Col. 0580A] At that time Laudumnus was the shepherd’s overseer. As soon as Bruno reached the supreme pontiff’s palace, he prostrated himself with his whole breast and fixed kisses upon the sacred feet. But the pope raised the man who lay there with his hands and applauded his arrival as a friend.

He granted him easy access and received his teacher as a guest with a joyful face and much honor. As his most faithful counselor, Bruno remained close beside the pontiff.

Moved by Bruno’s urging, Urban undertook various measures. Placentia, noble city, bears witness to them; Melfi bears witness, and the famous mountain there bears witness as well.

Under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit he decreed many things. He instituted the daily recitation by the clergy of the Hours of the Virgin Mary and dedicated every Saturday to her.

He armed many thousands of men against the Muhammadans—“the people hostile to Christ”—men inflamed by love of the faith, who took up the sign of the cross and were ready to give their mortal lives for immortal Christ.

Godfrey of Bouillon was their leader, outstanding in arms. Great in ancient lineage, courage, and boldness, he defeated the Turks with heavenly aid. After entering the holy city, he refused to have a royal diadem placed upon his head, since Christ had been crowned with thorns in that city in a different form.

Meanwhile the doctor, unable to endure the city’s tumult, is said to have appealed to the apostolic Fathers, asking that they allow him to visit his beloved forests and enjoy the sweet comfort of the peace to which he was accustomed.

But the Fathers, unwilling that so much splendor should be hidden beneath a cloud, refused. They made him bishop at Rheims, amid the rejoicing of the entire people. Yet he yielded and declared himself unworthy of so great an honor and burden. For he recognized how great a distinction and weight each person must bear who assumes the name of prelate.

When he persistently begged to depart from the city, he obtained his request and immediately went out to the Calabrian shores. He did not return to his former dwelling in the Carthusian mountain, lest he seem secretly to have followed the court of the Roman prelate by design; for the pope had then approached the peaceful regions of Gaul and left the city.

[Col. 0580C] Bruno wrote to the inhabitants of the Carthusian wilderness, explaining what prevented his return and what reason had carried him away to Calabria. His will remained firm: someday to revisit the ancient hills, whenever a favorable opportunity for his desired purpose should arise.

Rejoicing in the freedom he had long desired, Bruno addressed his beloved companions in these words:

“You have seen, my companions, all the evils of the Roman people. Who could count them? When I wish to describe them, tears prevent me. There are a thousand dangers, a thousand snares, and a thousand hardships in our life.

“We have seen wars, deaths, quarrels, the contentious disputes of the populace, jealousies, inveterate hatreds, tumults, and certain men swelling with miserable ambition.

“Therefore, I beg you, let us turn our path away from here. God calls us away from this place; he rescues us from darkness. While the light goes before us, let us depart.

“Let us return to our former path, return to the love of our purpose, to humble cells and quiet forests, and to the sweet consolations of the life we interrupted.”

He spoke and urged them on by his words, ready for the journey. With united minds they followed the desired roads.

After this he gathered other disciples from various places. Some abandoned wealthy inheritances, bodily adornment, concern for the belly, and the richest strongholds.

Finally they utterly despised whatever worldly glory possesses that is deceptive and followed Bruno through inhospitable rocks wherever the divine hand called him.

Purple was trampled underfoot. Bruno happily covered his limbs with a white garment and gave them the clothing of salvation. Marking these men as innocent and humble, he taught that they would inhabit narrow caves and lairs.

With this ardor of spirit—the same with which Bruno had earlier formed the six companions while he lived in the Carthusian caves—

[Col. 0581A] they built caves for themselves through the shady forest in Calabria. Compelled by poverty, they could not raise their cells with lofty roofs.

But Roger, the prince ruling Calabria, prepared to go hunting in the forest. A joyful youth accompanied him. They carried fine nets and hunting spears, and led out troops of keen-scented hounds. The horsemen rushed forward, their horses chewing foaming bits and their quivers strapped to their backs.

When they reached the leafy heights of the mountain, pathless lairs opened before them, falling away from the rocky summit. Behold, the wild animals fled, tiring their dust-covered legs over the ridges and seeking the valleys and open fields.

Weapons rang, the men shouted, and arrows flew. The nimble hunting dogs leapt and pursued the deer. They came to the caves where Bruno and his holy companions were hiding.

Moved by the majesty of the man, the dogs fell to the ground, bent their knees, and, wagging their tails beneath him, worshiped the divine power, filling the air with their barking.

Meanwhile the duke wandered on horseback through the valleys and heard various barks. Perhaps he thought that a boar had been found, or that some lion was descending from the rock.

He pursued them at a run, passing now one group, now another. At last he reached the hiding place and saw the hunting dogs applauding the saint with their tails and lying fixed upon the ground with bent knees as he prayed.

He immediately dismounted, contemplated the venerable face and features, fell to the ground, and asked the reason for their daring to hold such vast wilderness.

The blessed doctor recounted everything and proclaimed the word of salvation, warming the duke with love for the heavenly powers.

Soon the prince ordered shrines, cells, and houses to be built, and gave wealth, lands, towns, pack animals, and various livestock. This Carthusian house became fruitful for us and famous for its many virtues.

From that time the duke, trusting in Bruno’s prayers and those of his holy companions, hoped for their aid whenever he might need help in uncertain outcomes of war.

Neither hope nor empty expectation deceived him. For when he was besieging Capua, surrounding its walls on every side and filling the towns far and wide with numerous forces,

[Col. 0581C] Sergius, whom he had placed in charge of the night watches, violated the sacred obligations of the sworn trust that had been given him. Falsely—

[Col. 0582A] by an oath he had promised at the altars of the gods to the prince of Capua that, under cover of night, he would betray to him Roger’s entrusted camp.

An abominable deed! He promised the access out of avarice.

The night was now approaching when the impious traitor was to carry out the entire fraud—unless the divine powers intervened. The opposing armies stood ready, and the wicked Sergius was hastening secretly to introduce the enemy troops.

The duke had lowered his eyes into a light sleep.

Bruno suddenly stood beside him as he slept—an astonishing event—shedding tears. Tearing open his garments and exposing his anger against the Capuan soldier, he said:

“Rise, take up your arms, prince, and see whether the powers of heaven wish to rescue you and your men from the treachery that has been prepared.”

Startled, he shook off his sleep and roused the army, so that he might learn what truth the vision contained.

He took up his arms. A din arose, and shouting went up into the air. The anxious crowd followed its leader, though unaware of the cause of so sudden a movement. Soon Sergius and his followers fled toward Capua; the tireless duke pursued them. The Capuans resisted, and battle was joined on both sides.

Weapons clashed with weapons. At last Roger was victorious, and the defeated and captured enemies revealed the treachery behind the attack.

Remembering with certainty that he had escaped this fraud through Bruno’s help, Roger visited him and offered him great thanks.

“Not I,” Bruno said, “but the angel sent from heaven who stands beside princes in time of war showed you the wicked treachery beforehand in your sleep.”

After Bruno’s victorious struggles of long toil, he chose to restore his holy soul to the heavenly powers and his innocent spirit from the foul odor of the flesh. His glorious death was exalted everywhere.

Companies of spirits honored him with heavenly song and accompanied him as far as the starry council, where the exalted Father beholds the triumphs of the saints in eternal peace and their faces with wondrous sweetness.

Here he gives great prayers to the Thunderer for the hermits.

Even after his illustrious death he continues to shine through countless wonders, for a living spring flows immediately from the mouth of his tomb, suitable for curing many illnesses, and is still called the Brunonian water.

**In the year of the Lord 1037. Guigo I, fifth general prior of the Grande Chartreuse.**

[Col. 0581]

## Notice

*(Literary History of France, vol. XI, p. 646.)*

### I. Life

[Col. 0581D]

Guigues, surnamed, according to some, “of Châtel,” and according to others, “of Pin,” was born in 1083 of a noble and virtuous family in the village of Saint-Romain, in the diocese of Valence, in Dauphiné (MART. *Ampl. Coll.*, vol. VI, p. 163; LABBE, *Bib. mss.*, vol. I, p. 639; *Ann. Carth.*; MIRAEUS, *Script.*, p. 431). He received an education appropriate to his birth and to the piety of his parents. When he was about to establish himself in the world, he left it in 1107 in order to bury himself in the wilderness of the Grande Chartreuse.

The details of the virtues he practiced in that holy retreat do not belong to the scope of our history. We shall merely say that study—such study as suits a solitary—was not excluded from his exercises. It is known that the first Carthusians spent the time left to them by prayer copying books. Guigues was greatly attracted to this kind of work because it enabled him to become familiar with the word of God and the finest monuments of tradition. In this way he accumulated, in silence, a treasure of learning that he thought would serve only his own edification.

But Providence had arranged otherwise. Scarcely three years had passed since his entry into religious life when the pious companions of his retreat chose him to place him at their head. The wisdom of his government showed that the Holy Spirit had presided over this choice. Powerful in words and deeds, he showed through his instructions the path that had to be followed and made it passable by his example.

The order was still confined to the Grande Chartreuse. Guigues’s reputation helped to extend and multiply it. Pressed by people of merit and influence, he successively sent seven colonies from his wilderness into different regions of France.

Nevertheless, it was wrong to conclude from this that he was the first general of the Carthusians. D. Martène (*ibid.*, preface, no. 37) has solidly proved that the disciples of Saint Bruno did not properly form a congregational body until under Guigues’s successor, in 1140; that it was then that they began to recognize the prior of the Grande Chartreuse as their common head and to hold general chapters in which everything was determined without the authority of the diocesan bishop.

But what Guigues lacked in jurisdiction he regained through the attachment, trust, and respect shown him on every occasion by the monasteries that owed their foundation to him. His talents shone no less in the administration of temporal affairs than in the government of souls. Through his care and skill the exterior of the Grande Chartreuse took on a new appearance. He had its buildings, overturned in 1133 by a terrible accident, reconstructed and given a better form, and he supplied everything necessary for maintaining good order and meeting the needs of those who were to occupy them (MART. *ibid.*, p. 164; LABBE, *ibid.*, p. 639).

[Col. 0583C] The progress of the Carthusians and the fame they acquired in his time and through his care inspired in him no sentiment contrary to humility. He always considered himself and his own to be inferior to the other monks, far from regarding his order as the center and sole refuge of the virtues of the cloister.

He had an exceptional veneration for the Cistercian order, of which he gave marked proofs on various occasions. On his advice Pons, lord of Lazare in the diocese of Lodève, embraced that institute in 1135, after distinguishing himself in the world by his courage and intelligence (History of Languedoc, vol. II, p. 422).

When Étienne of Obazine came to consult him that same year about the observance he ought to establish in his house, Guigues gave him the following reply (MABILLON, *Annals*, LXXVI, no. 72):

“The Cistercians follow the royal way. Their statutes can lead to every perfection. Among us the number of persons whom we can admit is fixed, just as is the amount of property we are permitted to possess. For you, who already have several monks under your government and are resolved to add many others, you ought to prefer the cenobitic life, whose merit depends neither on the number of those who practice it nor on the possessions they enjoy, but on the religion and exercise of the virtues it prescribes.”

Such was Guigues’s modest, equitable, and disinterested way of thinking.

Among the illustrious friends whom his merit attracted, none appear to have been more closely united with him than Peter the Venerable and Saint Bernard. Not content merely to correspond with him, both wished to obtain the satisfaction of seeing him and of being edified in the midst of his respected community.

The abbot of Cluny often traveled to the Grande Chartreuse during Guigues’s lifetime. It is good to hear him himself recount the charms he experienced in Guigues’s conversation:

“The frequent conversations I had with this incomparable man,” he says, “carried me, as it were, outside myself. His words inflamed me as though they were sparks issuing from his mouth. While listening to him I no longer clung to the earth, and all the thoughts of this world vanished from my mind.”

The final years of his life were marked by frequent illnesses. He compensated by courage for the strength he lacked. At last, however, he succumbed beneath the weight of his weakness on 27 July 1137, in the fifty-fourth year of his age (BOLLANDISTS, 1 April, p. 37).

### II. Genuine writings

Guigues distinguished himself in literary activity under two titles: that of editor and that of author. What chiefly earned him the first was the care he took to gather into a single body the letters of Saint Jerome, previously scattered among various manuscripts; to correct their text, which had been grossly corrupted by the ignorance of copyists or the malice of heretics; and to separate from them those falsely bearing the holy doctor’s name.

He gives an account of this work in a letter to the Carthusians of Durbon, published for the first time in D. Mabillon’s *Analecta*, p. 464, and afterward inserted in volume VI of the new edition of Saint Bernard (BERNARD, *Works*, new ed., vol. VI, p. 1056). Guigues tells us there that such an undertaking was not his first effort of this kind and that he had already rendered the same service to other Fathers:

“Among the works of Catholic writers that we have undertaken to collect and correct, the letters of Saint Jerome especially fixed our attention. We had them sought out everywhere, and after purging them, according to the measure of understanding God has given us, of the errors and falsehoods that had slipped into them, we arranged them in a single large volume.

“Now, in examining them, since some appeared to us very little worthy of so great a man, whether because of differences in style and thought or because of comparison with the writings of other doctors, we thought that we ought to remove them.”

He names eight of this kind and gives critical reasons demonstrating their spuriousness. We cannot say whether copies of this manuscript edition still exist. They would easily be recognized by Guigues’s letter to the Carthusians of Durbon, which he expressly recommends placing at the head of his collection as its preface. The new editor of Saint Jerome does not identify any such copies, and it does not appear that the Carthusian libraries provided him with the slightest assistance for the publication of that Father’s works.

As author, Guigues composed:

1. A large number of letters, of which only six, including the one just mentioned, have survived the injuries of time. The first, printed among the letters of Peter the Venerable (*Cluniac Library*, p. 654), is a reply to that abbot, who, in sending a crucifix to the prior of the Grande Chartreuse, had accompanied the gift with a letter full of esteem and affection for him and for his entire community.

Guigues says that he is as grateful for the gift as he is embarrassed by the letter. He begs his friend in future to be more sparing with his praise of persons so little deserving of it; when writing to them, to consult their interest as much as his own edification; and to fear that, through expressions too flattering, he might expose them, weak as they were, to the danger of vainglory.

“Above all,” he adds, “spare yourself—this is a favor I ask of you on my knees—from honoring with the name of [Note: [Col. 0583] D. Mabillon (*Notes on the Works of Saint Bernard*, no. 28) remarks that until the thirteenth century, the name of [Col. 0585] ‘Father’ among monks was given only to abbots. This is why our author refused it.] Father a man as unworthy as I am of that title. It is enough, indeed it is more than enough, that you deign to call me your brother, your friend, your son. The name ‘servant’ would still be above what is due to me.”

This is the only letter we possess from Guigues to Peter the Venerable. But it is certain that they wrote one another a very large number of letters. “I used to write to him frequently,” says the abbot of Cluny, speaking of Guigues to Saint Bernard, “and often I delighted, with him … in familiar letters, and in my letters I called him father” (*ibid.*, p. 895E).

2. Guigues’s second letter, addressed to Hugh of Payns, prior and founder of the Knights Templar, contains a very sound instruction on the duties of this new militia (BERNARD, *Works*, vol. VI, p. 1054). It was written shortly after the Council of Troyes, held in 1128, which Hugh attended and at which he obtained confirmation of his order.

3. His third letter, written to Pope Innocent on behalf of all the solitaries of the Grande Chartreuse, concerns the affairs of the Church of Grenoble. It does not, however, explain the nature of those affairs, because Hugh, abbot of Pontigny, who was carrying the letter, had undertaken to explain them in detail to the Holy Father.

Guigues confines himself on this subject to describing the debilitated condition of Bishop Hugh, a condition that placed him almost among the dead with respect to the exercise of his ministerial functions:

“He who, as we write without tears, is dissolved by illnesses and old age may be numbered among the dead, insofar as the episcopal office is concerned.”

From there he passes to matters concerning Innocent himself and the schism provoked by his rival Anacletus. He then expands upon the prerogatives of the Holy See and concludes by commending to His Holiness the two newly founded orders of Cîteaux and Fontevrault.

This letter, delivered to the pope during the Council of Rheims, celebrated in 1131, was read in full assembly by Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres. Innocent and all those present appeared extremely satisfied with it (MABILLON, *Annals*, book LXXV, no. 121). It is reproduced in full in the second book of the *Chronicle of Morigny* (*Chronicle of Morigny*, p. 379, in DUCHESNE, *Writers of the History of the Franks*, IV, 379).

4. The fourth bears the names of Hugh, bishop of Grenoble—Hugh II—Guigues, and the community of the Grande Chartreuse. It is addressed to the council assembled at Jouarre in 1133 to deliberate on what ought to be done regarding the murder of Thomas, prior of Saint-Victor.

The similarity of style that we observe between this letter and Guigues’s other letters leads us to believe that it too is his, at least in its wording. The author insists on the necessity of punishing the murderers by showing the disastrous consequences of impunity. The issue here is not secular punishment but canonical penance.

Guigues asks especially that the leaders of the attack, who were ecclesiastics, be deprived of their benefices. The council granted these requests. It appears from Innocent’s reply that the same severity was exercised against the assassins of Archambaut, subdean of the Church of Orléans.

Jean Le Picard was the first to make this document known to the public, in the notes on the letters of Saint Bernard (BERNARD, *Works*, vol. I, extensive notes, p. 25). Father Labbe reproduced it in the tenth volume of the councils, p. 975.

The fifth letter is addressed to Cardinal Haimeric, chancellor of the Roman Church (BERN. OP. vol. VI, p. 105, 1053). This prelate, having come to the Grande Chartreuse, had formed a very close friendship with Guigues. Some time afterward—around the year 1134—the latter wrote to him to thank him for his visit. [Col. 0586A] But with his thanks he thought he ought to mingle a genuine expression of gratitude, in the form of advice concerning the cardinal’s situation and the state of religious affairs. Everything was then in turmoil because of the open war that Innocent and his rival were beginning to wage against one another, with temporal arms in hand. Although the prior of the Grande Chartreuse was as firmly attached as Haimeric to the former’s party, he nevertheless could not approve the violent means being employed to restore peace to the Church. He believed that he saw the source of this abuse in the morals of the Roman court. Accustomed to imitate secular courts in the pomp and softness proper to them, it had, in his view, finally become indistinguishable from those dangerous models by using their weapons to fight its enemies.

This is the subject of the letter, in which Guigues undertakes to make the cardinal understand the two inward enemies whom man has most to fear: pride and [Col. 0586B] sensual pleasure. He shows how hateful these two vices are in themselves, and especially how out of place they are in times of calamity. On this point he recalls the conduct of the Jews on similar occasions and, comparing it with that of Christians, laments to see the latter surpassing in hardness that crude and carnal people.

“For the Jews,” he says, “had recourse to fasts and hair shirts to appease divine anger, whereas we, amid the dangers surrounding us and beneath the weight of the sins with which we are burdened, set no limits to our pride and sensuality. It is no longer a sheep or a calf that we take from the flock to satisfy our greed; it is the entire flock that we devour. Like Amalek, we drag along an innumerable multitude of men and horses, with which we flood every diocese, seizing whatever falls into our hands, sparing neither profane nor sacred things, stripping churches, overturning altars, carrying away [Col. 0586C] holy tables, crosses, images, and chalices—and for what purpose? Is it to relieve the poor, found monasteries, or ransom captives? Certainly not, but to assemble engines of war, to hire archers, cavalrymen, and infantry, and employ them to destroy Christians; employ them, I say, to plunder and slaughter those for whom we ought to be ready to sacrifice our lives. O indescribable grief! Today the supreme pontiffs and, following their example, the other pastors throughout the world do not blush to arm brother against brother—I mean Christian against Christian—and the gold of the sanctuary becomes the sinew of these disastrous campaigns. These are the triumphs in which the Church, our mother, now takes pride; and blindness has become so great that, with consciences stained by murder and hands dyed with blood, men ascend without hesitation to the altar to celebrate the divine mysteries there.

“Ah! If such excesses are to be tolerated, what is there left now to reproach? Nevertheless, I foresee what you are going to answer me. ‘These weapons,’ you will say, ‘are taken from the emperor’s palace.’ I grant it. But would to God they had always remained there, instead of being carried into holy places! For which of the two, tell me, is preferable: that the Church should give laws to palaces, or that she herself should receive them from a palace? Were the Churches entrusted to palaces so that they might instruct them, or do the palaces themselves have the right to be taught by the Churches? Did the palaces give Jesus Christ to the Churches, or did they learn from them to know him? Ah! How much more fitting it would be for kings to receive the hair shirt from our hands than for us ourselves to borrow the kings’ purple! How much more beneficial [Col. 0587A] it would be for us to communicate to them our poverty, our fasts, and our humility than to adopt, as we do, their greed, their delicacy, and their vanity!”

The rest of the letter is equally forceful. It appears that it was not intended for Haimeric alone, but for the entire Roman court. Guigues asks him, if it makes no impression on the others, to apply to himself the truths it contains. We owe it to Horstius that this important piece was brought out of darkness and joined to the second and third letters in his edition of the works of Saint Bernard. D. Mabillon gave it the same place in his own edition.

2. Guigues committed to writing the customs of his order, which Saint Bruno had been content to sketch orally and by his example, leaving to the fervor of his disciples the task of maintaining and perpetuating them. It was at the command of Blessed Hugh I, his bishop, and at the request of the three priors of the Gates, Saint-Sulpice, and Meyria—around the year 1128—that our author undertook this work (FLEURY, *Ecclesiastical History*, book LXVII, no. 58).

In his preface he declares that, until then, the Carthusians had observed nothing except what is contained in the Epistles of Saint Jerome and the Rule of Saint Benedict. D. Mabillon draws from this his principal proof that the first Carthusians recognized Saint Benedict as their father (MAB. *Annals*, book LXXVI, no. 75); he reinforces this proof with the authority of an ancient manuscript whose title is: *The Statutes of Guigues, Prior of the Chartreuse, and of the Other Fathers According to the Rule of Saint Benedict* (*Statuta Guigonis Carthusiae prioris et aliorum Patrum secundum regulam sancti Benedicti*).

The author of the *Annals of the Carthusians* (*An. Carth. mss.*), however, maintains the contrary: neither Saint Bruno nor his first disciples ever claimed to bind themselves preferentially to any of the monastic rules established before them. They always reserved, he says, the freedom to take everywhere and without distinction, from the writings and examples of the ancients, whatever they found most consistent with the perfection of the eremitical life. This is a question that the plan of our history does not allow us to pursue further.

The body of the work is divided into eighty chapters, of which the following are the passages that seemed most worthy of notice.

**Chapter 1.** The brothers, dispersed one by one in their cells—under Saint Bruno they had lived two by two—left them on working days only to go and recite Vespers and Matins together in the church. They recited the rest of the Office privately. On Saturdays they confessed to the prior or to the person whom he had appointed to hear them.

**Chapter 34.** On Sunday after Prime they assembled in the chapter house. Conventual Mass was celebrated before Terce, unless the celebrant had some reason for postponing it. After None they returned to the cloister [Col. 0587D] to converse about useful and edifying matters. There the sacristan gave each person ink, parchment, pens, chalk, and books, either for reading or for copying. The cook likewise distributed vegetables and salt; and in the evening, after supper, they received another brown loaf, *tortam*, and returned to their cells.

**Chapter 31.** They did not use signs to replace speech, as in most monasteries, “because, living alone,” says our author, “they have no need of any contrivance to communicate their thoughts, and because, moreover, they believe the tongue to be the most natural and appropriate instrument for this function.” Thus, whenever they had something necessary to say, they said it aloud and in few words.

**Chapter 33.** The fasts were continuous, as in the Rule of Saint Benedict, from 14 September until Easter. During the rest of the year they fasted only three days each week. [Col. 0588A] The midday meal consisted of eggs or vegetables, which each person prepared himself when eating in his cell. In the refectory, where they assembled on feast days, cheese and fruit were added.

**Chapter 38.** Remedies were rarely used, except for cauterization and bloodletting. The latter, called *minutio*, was practiced five times a year at appointed times. Those who wished to abstain from it benefited from the same relief granted to the others for three consecutive days.

**Chapter 28.** Their clothing and furniture were poor. Among other things, they used skins for bed coverings and pelts because of the great cold of the mountains. “For,” says Guigues, “it is especially fitting for us, among monks, to wear coarse garments and to express poverty and humility in everything that serves our use.”

**Chapters 12, 13, and 14.** When a brother was dangerously [Col. 0588B] ill, they began by administering extreme unction to him; then they wiped his face, and each person came to give him the kiss as though bidding him farewell. After this he received the viaticum. As soon as he entered his agony, they laid him upon ashes. On the day of his burial the community ate in the refectory as on a feast day.

**Chapter 77.** Fugitives, when they returned and gave signs of sincere repentance, were received, but in the last rank; alternatively, they were permitted to pass into another order.

**Chapters 4 and 14.** The church possessed no silverware other than the chalice and a reed tube for receiving the precious blood at Communion. The weekly priest celebrated one Mass during the week for all the monastery’s benefactors, for the inhabitants of the place, and for the dead. “For Mass is celebrated here rarely,” the author adds, “because the principal emphasis here is placed on silence and retreat.”

**Chapter 36.** No outsider was permitted to enter the choir; only religious could do so, and only they could sleep in the upper house. Laypeople slept in the lower house. This was where the lay brothers lived, under the direction of the procurator. The prior went down there from time to time, and this was the farthest he could go, for he was not permitted to leave the boundaries of the Chartreuse.

**Chapters 78 and 79.** The number of choir religious was fixed at thirteen, and that of the lay brothers at sixteen. Guigues advises his successors to reduce this small number still further if the monastery’s resources are insufficient to maintain it, rather than be driven by necessity to beg and wander. “For we detest,” he says, “the custom of going from place to place and begging, as highly dangerous; it grieves us to see it established among several people whose holy manner of life we otherwise praise, under the pretext of charity, in order to have something to give to newcomers.”

Such are the principal articles of the customs of the Grande Chartreuse drawn up by Guigues. The tone in which he expresses himself throughout is more that of a historian than of a legislator. Content to report what was observed at the Grande Chartreuse, he does not seem to wish to subject the other houses to the same usages, doubtless because, having no jurisdiction over them, he believed that he ought to leave it to the local superiors to make similar laws for those under their authority.

For the rest, when proposing each rule, he always takes care to explain its spirit in a few words and to ennoble even the smallest cloister practices through insights drawn from the purest sources of Christian morality. We have just given examples of this.

To understand how faithfully Guigues’s customs were respected by the ancient Carthusians, despite the alterations they suffered in practice, it is appropriate to report the decree that the order issued on this subject in the chapter held in 1259:

“Although some changes have been made regarding observance in the customs of D. Guigues, nevertheless the chapter orders that each house preserve them without changing anything in the text and that, if any passage has been erased, it be restored as soon as possible” (OUDIN, *Writers*, vol. II, p. 1133). “It further orders that every leap year they be read aloud in community, so that all may learn from this how far we have fallen from the perfection of our first fathers.”

It was doubtless in conformity with the spirit of this decree that D. Grior, prior of the Chartreuse of Mount Saint John near Freiburg, placed them at the head [Col. 0589B] of his collection of the ancient and new statutes of the Carthusians, printed in 1510 at Basel, by Amerbach, in a large folio volume. This edition [Note: [Col. 0589D] It should be noted that not all copies of this edition are complete. In some—for example, that at Saint-Germain [Col. 0590D] des Prés—one would search in vain for Guigues’s work; in others, the order’s privileges are missing.] now extremely rare, also contains the order’s privileges, preceded, like the statutes, by a full repertory or table of contents.

Not content with reproducing the text of Guigues’s customs in its original purity, the author of the first volume of the *Annals of the Carthusians*, published in 1683 at La Correrie, thought it appropriate to append a commentary in which he compares them with the regulations made since then. Finally, in 1703 D. Innocent Masson reissued the 1510 edition, with a preface and remarks of his own, in Paris, at Dezallier’s, in a folio volume entitled: *The Discipline of the Carthusian Order Divided into Three Books* (*Disciplina ordinis Carthusiensis in tres libros distributa*).

3. Guigues composed the *Life of Saint Hugh* (BOLL. I Apr., p. 37), Hugh I, bishop of Grenoble, [Col. 0589C] father, protector, friend, and for some time even companion of the solitaries of the Grande Chartreuse.
