As soon as the illustrious prelate had departed this earth, our author wished some skillful pen to make his virtues known to the public. But although Hugh II, successor of the first, and the bishop of Maurienne strongly urged him to undertake the work himself, he did not dare, he says, to assume it, so far did he believe the subject beyond his powers. An express order from Pope Innocent II was required to overcome this scruple.

In his letter dated at Pisa on 1 May 1134, the pontiff informed him that, having learned the details of Hugh’s life and the wonders God worked through his intercession, he had thought it appropriate, on the advice of the archbishops, bishops, and cardinals assembled in council in that city, to order that Hugh be honored with public worship and to assign the day of his feast to the anniversary of his death: “Accordingly,” he adds, “we enjoin upon you, since you are informed of everything concerning this prelate and of the miracles that have manifested his holiness, to set down in writing what you know about these matters, for the edification of posterity.”

Such was Guigues’s submission to the will of the Holy See that neither his conviction of his own incapacity nor the illnesses with which he was burdened allowed him to evade or even delay carrying it out. He immediately took up his pen and, in the same year, sent the pope the first part of his work—that is, the history of the saint’s life as we have it in Surius and Bollandus. His miracles still remained to be treated. We do not know whether he completed this part; at least, no trace of it remains.

[Col. 0590A] 4. Guigues composed meditations whose merit led to numerous editions. They were printed and reprinted at Antwerp in 1550, 1554, and 1589, each time in a twenty-fourmo volume, which, besides these meditations, contained those of William of Saint-Thierry. The same collection was put to press again in Paris in 1600, in a smaller format. In a fourth edition, which appeared at Munich in 1685, two other short works were added to Guigues’s writing, one by Saint Eucher of Lyon and the other by Saint Martin of Braga. Finally, these meditations were included in the three great *Libraries of the Fathers* (Bibl. PP. Paris., suppl. vol. I, p. 787; Cologne, vol. XII; Lyon, vol. XXII, p. 1104).

The author divided them into twenty chapters, each of which, except the last three, which form continuous discourses, consists of separate thoughts relating to a single subject. These thoughts, [Col. 0590B] short, noble, and substantial, are expressed with force and unction. In this work Guigues seeks equally to convince the mind and to touch the heart.

Father Labbe (*Bibl. mss.*, suppl. 8) says that he saw, in the library of the Carthusians of Paris, a manuscript containing one hundred meditations by John of Stotterien, together with an equal number by the venerable Guigues. The manuscript is no longer there; but it is highly probable that Guigues’s meditations are the same as those of which we have just given an account.

Here ends the list of our author’s genuine writings that have survived to us. They are few in number, but sufficient to justify the praise that has always been given to the beauty of Guigues’s genius and the excellence of his piety. One indeed finds in them very fine sentiments, a certain air of nobility, and those lively and penetrating strokes that Saint Bernard admired in the [Col. 0590C] letters he received from him, traces of which are seen only in the saint’s replies.

The freedom with which Guigues rises against the abuses of the Roman court when writing to Cardinal Haimeric shows a soul elevated above the prejudices of his age and incapable of disguising the truth. He was the only person who dared openly to condemn the use Pope Innocent made of temporal arms in defense of his cause. His morality is drawn from the great principles of religion. His applications of Scripture are frequent and almost always apt. His diction is not the same in all his writings: it is more correct in his letters, because they were addressed to educated persons; elsewhere it is more careless. One must forgive him the barbarous expressions that he occasionally employs in the collection of his order’s customs. More recherché terms would not have been as easily understood by all those for whose edification [Col. 0590D] this work was intended.

## § III.—Spurious Writings

We have no hesitation in placing at the head of the works falsely attributed to our author a writing that the public, nevertheless, no longer seems to dispute to him and that is, in many respects, genuinely worthy of his pen: the celebrated letter to the Carthusians of Mont-Dieu on the excellence and duties of the solitary life.

Before Dom Mabillon, critics attributed it at different times to Saint Bernard, Guigues, or William of Saint-Thierry. But this learned scholar claimed it for the last of these on the basis of arguments that won the unanimous approval of his contemporaries (BERN. *Works*, third correction, vol. II, preface to this treatise, p. 196). Dom Martène later came forward and declared for Guigues with equal success, so that to this day he has carried all men of letters along with him in his opinion.

Yet the reasons on which he supports it are more specious than solid; to destroy them with a stroke of the pen, it would be enough to observe that the letter in question is addressed not to Geoffroi, the first prior of Mont-Dieu, but to Haimon, who succeeded him in 1144—that is, eight years after Guigues’s death. It is astonishing that Dom Martène and those who followed him did not notice this anachronism, of which Dom Mabillon had warned them.

It is no less astonishing that none of them perceived how poorly suited to our author’s sentiments and language are the praises bestowed upon the life of the Carthusians in this writing. How, for example, could one attribute to Guigues this opening?

“Brothers of Mont-Dieu, bringing eastern light and that ancient Egyptian fervor in religion into western darkness and Gallic cold . . . come and join me in the joy of the Holy Spirit, my soul . . . We had heard with the ear, but did not believe; we read in books and marveled at the ancient glory of the solitary life . . . when suddenly we found it in the fields of the forest, at Mont-Dieu.”

Does one recognize here the man who was accustomed, in his letters, to style himself “the humble prior of the poor Carthusians”; who considered himself and his companions unworthy of all praise, and who regarded as the most dangerous of temptations the praise he was obliged to receive?

Is it still the prior of the Grande Chartreuse who speaks thus of his house: “With all the holiness owed to the Chartreuse preserved, and with every commendation of the reverence due to it” (*Salva per omnia Carthusiae debita sanctitate et cum omni laude praedicanda reverentia*)?

Let us add one final point, which shows with equal clarity that this piece is foreign to Guigues. In the prologue the author says that he had made a journey to Mont-Dieu. Yet the statutes of the Grande Chartreuse, drawn up by Guigues, forbid the prior to pass beyond the limits of the mountain. Is it likely that Guigues violated a law that [Col. 0591C] his predecessors had observed so religiously and that he himself had just renewed?

These observations spare us from entering into the discussion of the evidence drawn, on either side, from the authority of the manuscripts. There are copies attributing it to Guigues, others to William, and some that designate the author only by the initial letter W, common to the names of both our writers. The latter [Col. 0592A] prove nothing; but among the second group, the manuscript of the abbey of Signy, where William ended his days, deserves all the more consideration because it is above all at that place that the memory of his genuine writings must have been preserved.

Another work that we likewise believe must be denied to our author is a moral treatise in the form of a letter, found in all editions of Saint Augustine and Saint Bernard. In the earlier editions it is entitled *The Ladder of Paradise*, and in the later ones *The Ladder of the Cloister*. D. Mabillon showed (BERN. *Works*, vol. II, p. 311) that it belonged to neither of these Fathers, but to a Carthusian Guigues, according to the inscription it bears in a manuscript of the Cologne Charterhouse:

“Letter of Lord Guigues to Brother Gervasius on the contemplative life” (*Epistola domni Guigonis ad fratrem Gervasium de vita contemplativa*); and afterward: “Brother Guigues to his beloved brother Gervasius: rejoice in the Lord” (*Dilecto fratri suo Gervasio frater Guigo, delectari in Domino*).

It remains to determine whether this was the first or the second of the two Guigues who governed the Grande Chartreuse. Dom Mabillon says nothing on this point. But the following reasons seem sufficient to decide in favor of the second.

First, this letter contains several thoughts and expressions borrowed from Saint Bernard, as anyone familiar with his writings can perceive on reading it. Moreover, when it was written, there must have been other Charterhouses besides the Grande Chartreuse, since it assumes that Gervasius, to whom it was sent, was himself a Carthusian.

The author nevertheless composed it in the first years of his conversion. For not only does he tell his fellow brother that he is dedicating to him the first fruits of his work, but he also presents himself as a plant newly established in solitude:

“These beginnings of our labor I first offer to you, so that you may gather the first fruits of a new planting” (*Haec nostri laboris initia tibi primitus offero ut novellae plantationis primitivos fructus colligas*).

This, therefore, was not the same Guigues under whose government the order’s first colonies were founded. We could add a third reason, but it will find a more appropriate place in the article on Guigues II. It is also there that we reserve the task of proving that Duchesne confused one Guigues with the other when he attributed to the first a treatise *On the Four Spiritual Degrees* and a short work *On Truth and Peace* (Bib. Clun., p. 112, note).

[Col. 0591]

## ANOTHER NOTICE

*Works of Saint Bernard*, Mabillon edition, notes, p. XV.

[Col. 0591D] Guigo I, surnamed “of the Castle,” a Gaul by nation, a Dauphinois by country, and Valentinian by birth; the fifth prior general of the Grande Chartreuse after Blessed Bruno; very dear to Bernard, as is evident both from Letter 11 and from Book III of the *Life of Saint Bernard*, chapter 1; a man of remarkable modesty, as he himself portrayed himself in a letter to Peter of Cluny (Book I of the Letters of Peter the Venerable, letter 25):

“We ask, by the love with which your ardent heart burns toward us unworthy men, that whenever your serenity deigns to write to our lowliness, you should think so much of your own edification that you do not inflate our weakness with dangerous elation. And above all and before all we ask, and on our knees fixed to the ground we beseech you, no longer to consider our lowliness worthy of the name of FATHER. It is enough, and more than enough, if he is called brother, friend, or son who is not considered worthy even of the name of servant.”

The venerable Peter himself later used this example when writing to Bernard, as may be seen in Letter 388; perhaps both were imitating Bernard, Letter 72.

Guigues himself wrote several works by which, as Trithemius says, “he bestowed immortality upon his name”: namely, the *Life of Saint Hugh, Bishop of Grenoble*, dedicated to Innocent II and found in Surius, volume II, on 1 April; the *Meditations*, which are extant in the *Library of the Fathers*; a *Treatise on Truth and Peace*, in manuscript in the library of the Cologne Charterhouse; one book of the *Institutes of the Carthusians*; also a book *On Contemplation*; and various letters, four of which are included here in volume VI, while others were sought by me after Horstius with fruitless diligence.

For when I wrote on this subject to the most reverend Father D. John Pegon, prior of the Grande Chartreuse and general of the order, I was honored to receive this reply: namely, that after six fires, which that holy house had suffered from its beginnings, scarcely anything remained of its extremely well-equipped collection of manuscripts, which its predecessors had assembled with the greatest care and diligence.

The book *The Ladder of the Cloister* (*liber de Scala claustralium*), reproduced in volume V, is also attributed to this same Guigues. Nor should we omit what Trithemius reports about him: that he carefully corrected the letters of Saint Jerome, which had been corrupted by the great negligence of copyists, according to the rule of truth, and collected them into one volume. Guigues’s letter on this subject is included here from volume I of the *Analecta*.

Moreover, Sutor says (*Life of the Carthusians*, book II, chapter 5) that, at the age of fifty, in the thirtieth year of his conversion and the twenty-seventh, or thereabouts, of his priorate, he gave up his spirit to the Lord in the reputation of holiness, in the year of Our Lord 1137, and in the fifty-third year from the beginning of the order. So he says.

[Col. 0593]

## LETTERS OF GUIGO I, FIFTH PRIOR OF THE GRANDE CHARTREUSE AFTER SAINT BRUNO (G)*

### I. To the brothers of Durbon [Note: [Col. 0593] The Chartreuse of Durbon was in Provence, in the diocese of Gap.]

*On the spurious letters of Blessed Jerome*

(MABILLON, *New Analecta*, new edition, p. 464.)

[Col. 0593B]

To our most beloved friends and brothers in Christ, Lazarus, prior of Durbon, and the others serving God in the same wilderness: Guigo, called prior of the Chartreuse, eternal salvation from the Lord.

Among the works that Catholic men have undertaken for the instruction of the faithful—works that our own smallness has also endeavored to collect or correct—we have gathered into one large volume the letters of Blessed Jerome, as many as we could find wherever they were available, and, insofar as God granted us the ability, purged them of falsehoods.

We have removed from them certain letters that, whether from the writings of other teachers or from differences of style and thought, we found unworthy of bearing the name of so great a man. Among these is the letter entitled *To Demetrias*, which begins: “If, relying on supreme talent and equal learning” (*Si summo ingenio parique fretus scientia*). Blessed Augustine, in his work against Pelagius, *On the Grace of Christ and Original Sin*, says that this letter belongs to Pelagius, introducing and refuting several of his arguments uselessly into his own treatise.

To this may be added the following letters:

*To Titatius, on the death of his daughter*, beginning: “I have received your letters of affection” (*Charitatis tuae scripta percepi*);

*To Oceanus, a letter of consolation*, beginning: “The reproaches of various people, manifold tribulations” (*Diversorum opprobria, tribulationes multiplices*);

*To a widow*, beginning: “Great confidence in writing to our humility” (*Magnam humilitati nostrae fiduciam scribendi*);

*To the virgin, or to the daughter of Mauritius*—for it is found with both titles—beginning: “How great is the blessedness in the heavenly places” (*Quantam in caelestibus beatitudinem*);

also *On the Fall of the Virgin, or On Repentance, to Susanna*, since both titles are found in different manuscripts. This letter is ascribed to such different authors that it should be adorned with the name of none of them; in certain books it begins: “I think it a slight sin” (*Puto leve esse crimen*). In others it begins: “What are you doing, soul? Why are you agitated by your thoughts?” (*Quid agis, anima? quid cogitationibus aestuas?*)

*To Desiderius, on the Twelve Readers*, was composed by some unknown person as a mockery of teachers.

*To Celantia*, beginning: “It is a celebrated saying of ancient Scripture” (*Veteris scripturae celebrata sententia est*). This is indeed written in a nobler style, but even so it is unworthy of Blessed Jerome.

The last is a disputation on the origin of the soul, supposedly between Blessed Jerome and Augustine. Although many passages from their writings are inserted into it, it is nevertheless false: first, because the teachers just mentioned never spoke to one another in person; and second, because this question has never yet been clearly defined, either by them or by any other adherents of the Catholic faith. The disputation begins:

“When heavenly eloquence, from its purest fountain, was with you …” (*Cum apud vos coelestis eloquentia purissimi fontis*).

So that the letters of the aforesaid teacher may not appear, without reasonable cause, to be reduced in number in the eyes of the uninformed, place this letter of our smallness at the beginning. Farewell. Pray for us.

### II. To Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny

(*Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*, p. 653.)

To the most reverend lord and father in Christ, Peter, abbot of Cluny: his servant and son, the unworthy servant Guigo of the poor Carthusians, wishes perpetual peace and joy through Christ.

You sent the Crucified One—yourself also crucified—to those who must be crucified. We therefore return thanks for the character of the gift, to the love of the giver. Yet the love expressed in the letter you sent, although it provides great consolation to our weakness, also causes no less confusion to our lowliness through your humility.

Therefore, by the love with which your heart burns toward us unworthy men, we ask that whenever your serenity deigns to write to our smallness, you should think so much of your own edification that you do not inflate our weakness with dangerous elation.

And above all and before all we ask, and on our knees fixed to the ground we beseech you, no longer to consider our lowliness worthy of the name of Father. It is enough, and more than enough, if he is called brother, friend, or son who is not considered worthy even of the name of servant.

Farewell. Greet our revered fathers and lords, for whom you exercise a father’s care; and we ask that, through both their prayers and yours, our blindness may be enlightened, our weakness strengthened, and our iniquity abolished.

We sympathize in our sorrow with the illnesses of Lord Albert, the greater prior, as with those of an old and familiar friend. We also specially greet Lord Peter, specially mentioned in your letter.

We thank your fatherhood also for the visit recently paid to us by the distinguished prior of the cloister and Lord Hugh of Crécy. May divine mercy preserve you in health, advancing continually in virtue, for our joy and that of the whole Church.

You have no need of our recommendation among our brothers. By your merits and your letters you yourself have indissolubly bound the memory of you to their hearts.

### III. To Cardinal Haimeric, chancellor

He warns that there are two enemies with whom one must chiefly struggle, and that against the adversaries of the Church one must use not bodily weapons but humility and repentance.

(*Works of Saint Bernard*, Mabillon edition, vol. II, p. 1051.)

#### 1.

To the most reverend lord and friend in Christ, Haimeric, chancellor of the Apostolic See: his friends—if indeed they are worthy of this name—and his Carthusian brothers wish that he despise earthly things and love heavenly things.

[Col. 0595B] We perceive by recollection how welcome your presence was to us; therefore, we ask, act in such a way that, when you have passed from these days—which, according to the Apostle, are evil, and, according to the Psalmist, fade away like a shadow—to good days and eternal years, you may rejoice not in the vision and companionship of us—for what are we, or what shall we be?—but in the vision and companionship of Him, together with all the saints, on whose account your loftiness has not disdained to know our obscurity, to supply our need, and—something we value far more—to penetrate our retreats, not merely humbly but laboriously, despite the many and great ecclesiastical affairs with which you are never without occupation; to visit us ourselves face to face, and to speak mouth to mouth; from Him alone we are separated by the merits of our sins—not by distances of place or time, for He is always and everywhere, and in Him we live and move and have our being—from that supreme benefit and good, namely, the companionship and vision of God. As it is written: “The Lord’s hand is not shortened, so that it cannot save; nor is his ear made heavy, so that it cannot hear; but your sins have separated you from your God” (Isaiah 59:1).

Since nearly all these sins arise either from exaltation of mind or from the will of the flesh—one of which we share with beasts, the other with angels, though with the rejected—we must strive with the utmost diligence both to crush the pride of the mind by humility and to restrain the lust of the flesh by sobriety. Hence the Lord says: “See that your hearts are not weighed down with gluttony, drunkenness, and the cares of this life” (Luke 21:34). And again: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matthew 11:29).

2. Let our attention, then, not be dispersed among many things. There are only two things against which we must fight with all our strength: exaltation in the mind and pleasure in the body. Once these have been overcome, nothing will remain to conquer, nothing will remain to fear. The desire for external things is inflamed for no other reason than that they may be served in every possible way. If we feel that our effort against these is insufficient, let us implore divine help; but let us implore it humbly, devoutly—with heart, mouth, action, and bearing.

For it was said to the Israelite people when they had sinned: “Now remove your adornment.” Therefore, they removed their adornment from Mount Horeb (Exodus 33:5). Elsewhere, too, the people mourned, and none of them put on any of their adornment. Likewise, the king of the Ninevites, a Gentile, at the voice of one unknown and shipwrecked man, came down from his throne, cast off his garments, put on sackcloth, sat in the dust, and cried out to the Lord (Jonah 3:6), compelling not only people of every age and sex but also the animals to undergo the same austerity.

Let us, then, also look upon the bloody rending of the Lord’s body, which is the Church—something that must be believed to have befallen us because of our merits—not with unmoved hearts or dry eyes. Otherwise, while adorned with precious garments, wrapped in ermine and gray furs, replenished with numerous and exquisite dishes, and not so much placed upon soft feathers as sunk into them like Sardanapalus, how do we suppose that divine indignation can be appeased by our prayers? Should we not rather fear that the prophetic denunciation may then be directed against us, and that it may be said:

“Woe to you who are wealthy in Zion and trust in Mount Samaria, nobles, chiefs of the peoples, entering pompously into the house of Israel; who eat lambs from the flock and calves from the midst of the herd; who sleep on beds of ivory and live luxuriously on your couches!” (Amos 6:10),

of whom it is concluded that “they suffered nothing for the ruin of Joseph.”

3. Let us be ashamed of this, dearest one—known late, seen briefly, snatched away quickly, and perhaps never again to be seen by our bodily eyes, yet never to be torn from the embraces of our love by any circumstance or any time. Let us be ashamed of this and, if we can, mourn over ourselves: we appear to have surpassed both Jewish and Gentile hardness, since they mitigate divine severity by the moderation of their food and by the poverty and roughness of their clothing, whereas we, amid many sins and dangers, observe no limit either in glory or in pleasures.

For we no longer consume merely a lamb from the flock or calves from the midst of the herd, but entire flocks and whole herds. Indeed, like Amalek, when we descend upon the churches with an innumerable multitude of people and animals, we fill everything, devastating whatever we touch. Nor are we satisfied with this: we strip away panels, crosses, chalices, and sacred images. And for what purpose? Perhaps so that the poor may be supported, monasteries built, and captives redeemed? Not so. Rather, it is so that archers and crossbowmen, horsemen and lancers may be hired to kill Christians; and that they may seize their property and souls—property and souls for which they ought to have offered their own.

Alas! Today, from the highest pontiffs and throughout almost the entire world, following the example of the Apostolic See, sacred money is used to hire and arm brother against brother—that is, Christian against Christian. The mother Church rejoices in such triumphs, and after this, with bloodied conscience, one proceeds with all one’s hands to the divine sacrifices. If this is to be endured, what is there left to condemn?

4. “But these,” they say, “are royal possessions, taken from the emperor’s palace.” We do not deny it. And would that they had always remained in palaces, not in sanctuaries—or rather, would that they had never been in palaces or in churches! How much better would it have been for the churches to give laws to palaces than for palaces to give them to the churches? Were churches entrusted to palaces, rather than palaces entrusted to the churches for instruction? Or did palaces give Christ to the churches, rather than the churches give Christ to palaces?

How much more rightly, then, would kings receive hair shirts from us than we receive purple garments from them! How much more beneficial it would be if they themselves embraced our poverty, fasts, and humility, rather than we embrace their avarice, luxuries, and exaltation!

But if anyone in the churches or among ecclesiastical persons attempts to criticize any of these things, will they not immediately answer the person doing so: “What are you doing? Why do you wish to make me better than my teachers, contrary to the evangelical judgment? Does not the Roman Church make use of various furs, gray furs, ermine, marten skins, throat-cut and *lumbatae* garments [Col. 0597B] [Note: [Col. 0597D] *Lumbatae* are small and short trousers.], and also silk clothing? Does not the Roman Church refrain from rejecting banquets, hire an army, and wage wars? Yet a disciple is not above his teacher, nor an apostle greater than the one who sent him; rather, everyone will be perfected if he is like his teacher.”

What can be said to this? You see the narrow straits in which we are placed. Either we must call evil good, or, with God ruling, we will simply not do it; or we must criticize the Apostolic See—which who would dare?—or, perhaps the safer course, we are compelled to remain entirely silent.

O most unhappy times of the apostles, in which the way to God’s kingdom was open only through hunger and thirst, cold and nakedness! O men enveloped in the darkness of ignorance and worthy of every compassion, who, in order to reach life as well, guarded such hard paths for the sake of the words of God’s lips, and knew nothing of our shortcuts!

5. We have poured forth these words not with the authority of a teacher or critic, but with the feeling of one who grieves and laments. The zeal for God’s house, whose beauty we love, gnaws at our entrails, and we ask and implore that, if not elsewhere, at least in you they may produce some fruit.

If those with whom you live show no concern, or only slight concern, or insufficient concern, for their salvation, you nevertheless, without forgetting yourself, must not neglect your own soul. For it is written: “Guard yourself and your soul diligently” (Deuteronomy 4:9); and again: “Have mercy on your soul by pleasing God” (Ecclesiasticus 30:24); likewise: “Guard your heart with every vigilance” (Proverbs 4:23). And the Lord says: “What does it profit a man if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul? Or what exchange will a man give for his soul?” (Luke 9:25).

Therefore, let neither the favor of princes, nor the splendor of ornaments, nor the multitude of business affairs, nor the glory of processions, nor the pleasures of banquets, nor any quantity of gifts offered deprive you of care for it. Let this always and everywhere be present in your mind: you do not know at the dreadful judgment of Christ with whom you will be—whether with those to whom it is said, “Go, accursed ones,” or with those who will hear, “Come, blessed ones.”

[Col. 0598A] Farewell. May God the Father, who brought from the dead the great Shepherd of the sheep, through the blood of the eternal covenant, our Lord Jesus Christ, make you fit for every good thing, so that you may do his will, accomplishing in you what is pleasing in his sight, through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory for ever and ever. Amen.

As for us, may that same almighty God have mercy on us through your intercessions and through the sacred works of the whole Roman Church, gladdening our hearts with the most fragrant and wholesome fragrance of your reputation and with continual progress in truth. Farewell again. Greet for us the reverend Fathers, namely, the bishops of Albano and Ostia [Matthaeus and Albericus], and any others whom your discretion may deem appropriate. Farewell a third time. We ask you to keep this house in your memory, just as it has itself enclosed you within its walls.

IV. To Hugh, Prior of the Holy Militia.—He teaches by what method spiritual warfare should be waged.

To our dearest and most reverend lords and friends in Christ, HUGH, prior of the Holy Militia, and all who are governed by his counsel: the poor servants and friends, the Carthusian brothers, wish a complete victory over the spiritual and bodily enemies of the Christian religion, and peace through Christ our Lord.

1. Since, on your return as on your arrival, we were unable to enjoy the very welcome conversation of your presence, it seemed fitting to us that we should at least converse with you briefly by letter. We do not know how to exhort your affection to bodily wars and visible battles; but concerning spiritual ones, in which we are engaged daily, although we are not capable of stirring you to action, we desire at least to admonish you.

For we attack external enemies in vain if we do not first overcome those within. It is exceedingly shameful and unworthy to wish to subject the armies of anyone whatsoever to our authority if our own bodies have not first been subjected to us. Who could tolerate our wishing to extend our rule outwardly over broad lands while suffering the shameful slavery of vices in our small plots of earth—that is, in our own flesh?

Let us therefore, dearest brothers, acquire ourselves first, so that thereafter we may fight external enemies securely. Let us first cleanse our minds of vices, and then our lands of barbarians.

2. Therefore, let sin not reign in our mortal body so as to make us obey its desires, nor let us present our members as weapons of wickedness to sin. Rather, let us present ourselves to God as those living from the dead, and our members as weapons of righteousness for God—even if the flesh rebels against the spirit without restraint. For, as the Apostle says, these are opposed to one another, so that you do not do whatever you wish.

We would wish, if it were possible, to be free from every desire. But if, in this life, which is entirely temptation, we cannot be wholly free from desire, let us at least not serve our desires. Since we are insufficient in strength for this, let us be strengthened in the Lord and in the power of his might, and let us put on the armor of God, so that we may be able to stand against the snares of the devil.

For, as the same passage continues, our struggle is not against flesh and blood but against rulers and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places—that is, against vices and their most wicked inciting spirits. If these have not—as David also asks—dominion over us, then we shall be blameless and cleansed from the greatest sins.

3. Let us therefore stand with our loins girded in truth, and our feet shod with the readiness of the gospel of peace. In all things let us take up the shield of faith, with which we can extinguish all the flaming arrows of the Evil One; let us have our head covered with the helmet of salvation and our right hand armed with the sword of salvation.

Let us run, not as though uncertainly; let us fight, not as though beating the air. Rather, let us chastise our body and bring it into subjection. For this is the most orderly condition of a human being—that is, of an animal created in the image of God: the flesh serves the spirit, and the spirit is subject to the Creator.

In this battle, each person will be the stronger and, with God ruling and protecting, the higher in a more glorious triumph over the many enemies laid low, the more diligently he strives to be humble in all things. Conversely, he will be weaker and more unstable in every good thing the more he wishes to be proud. For God resists the proud. There is therefore no need to seek elsewhere a fighter to defeat those against whom the almighty warrior himself fights.

Against them David says: “The Lord watches over the little ones”; and, having experienced this in himself, he adds: “I was humbled, and he delivered me.” Let us use this example if we desire to use the same remedy. Let us do what he did if we desire what he received; let us humble ourselves so that we may be delivered from every evil.

The Apostle also says of the Lord Jesus Christ: “He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross.” Nor was this without purpose. “For this reason,” he says, “God also exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father.”

From this example above all let us also take instruction if we burn with desire for the reward. Let us do what he did, so that we may follow where he went before us. Let us pursue the path of such great humility, so that we may arrive at the glory of God the Father. For everyone who humbles himself will be exalted, and whoever exalts himself will be humbled, as the same Lord Jesus Christ testifies, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God for ever and ever. Amen.

May the most powerful mercy and the most merciful power of God make you always fight with the greatest success and triumph most gloriously in both spiritual and bodily battles. We wish you good health, and, in the holy places that you protect, we ask you, dearest, most distinguished, and most meritorious brothers, to remember us when you pray.

We have sent this letter through two different messengers, lest—God forbid—it fail to reach you because of some impediment. We ask you to have it read aloud to all the brothers.

V. To Pope Innocent II.—He consoles the Supreme Pontiff amid the troubles of the schism.

To our dearest and most reverend lord and Father, INNOCENT, Supreme Pontiff of the Apostolic See: the poor servants and sons of the Carthusian house send the peace which the world cannot give, and the devoted service of their fatherhood, together with an obedience that, though not necessary, is willingly offered.

“Many things to your sacred apostolic ears,” etc. See under Innocent II, for the year 1143.

VI. Letter of Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, Guigo, and the Carthusian brothers to the Fathers gathered in the First Synod of Otranto because of the murder of Thomas, prior of Saint-Victor of Paris, cruelly killed by the wicked.

(Labbe, *Councils*, vol. X, col. 975.)

[Col. 0600B]

To the most reverend lords and Fathers in Christ—the archbishops, bishops, and other religious persons gathered in this place for the defense of justice—HUGH, called bishop of the Church of Grenoble, and his sons, GUIGO, the useless servant of the poor Carthusians, and the brothers who are with him, send the knowledge of what must be done and the strength to carry out what has been understood, through Christ our Lord.

That we are human pertains to nature; that we are just, to merit; that we are bishops, priests, archdeacons, or something of this kind pertains to ecclesiastical office. In the first we exist, in the second we are saved, and in the third we receive the power to provide others with what is more subtle. Thus the first two concern us, while the third concerns our neighbors.

If it becomes evident, following the example of the evangelical fig tree—which, after being awaited for so long, produced no fruit—that we have undertaken our office uselessly, no just reason will remain for our being allowed to continue in it. What, then, if we have proved not merely useless to the Church but even harmful, whether by words or by examples? Are we not worthy not only of being removed but also of being punished?

Although the death of blessed Thomas and of the others who have recently departed to the heavenly places in robes washed in the blood of the Lamb is precious in the sight of the Lord and does not require worldly vengeance, nevertheless, if the Church of God—which alone preserves both public and private affairs from ruin—is deprived of the benefit of discipline, we humbly ask and implore you that, protected by the armor of faith, inflamed by zeal for rectitude, and encouraged by the examples of the holy Moses, Phinehas, and Mattathias, as well as of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, who piously raged against Simon, Ananias, and Bar-Jesus, and especially by the example of the Lord himself, who drove the sellers from the temple with blows, you boldly draw forth the sword of ecclesiastical severity against sacrilegious murderers.

If possible, deprive them of every sacred office and benefice, so that all Israel, hearing of it, may fear and no one ever again dare to do anything similar. For they are worse than murderers: in order to satisfy their bloody pleasures, fulfill their wishes, and satiate their hatreds, they have torn apart the bodies of the saints. Unless they not only lose the profit of such great wickedness but also experience punishment, similar things must be feared by all defenders of justice among us.

[Col. 0601A] Farewell. Pray for us, and, raising your sacred right hands over the part of the world in which we are situated, pour forth blessing and supplication. Farewell again. May God make us participants in your holy works, those accomplished and those yet to be accomplished. Farewell a third time, together with the reverend princes, the bishops of Blois and Nevers.

[Col. 0601]

THE MEDITATIONS OF GUIGO, FIFTH GENERAL PRIOR OF THE GRANDE CHARTREUSE.

(*Library of the Fathers of Lyon*, vol. XXII, p. 1164.)

CHAPTER ONE. On truth and peace, and how peace is possessed through truth alone.

[Col. 0601B]

Truth must be placed in the midst, like something beautiful. Do not condemn anyone who abhors it; rather, have compassion. But when you desire to come to it, why do you reject it when you are rebuked for your vices?

See how much truth suffers. The drunkard is told, “You are drunk”; the sexually immoral person, the proud person, and the foul-mouthed person are addressed similarly. Yet this is true. Immediately they go mad, and they persecute and kill truth in the person who proclaims it.

See how much honor is paid to falsehood. The worst people and slaves of every vice are told, “Good masters.” They are appeased, rejoice, and revere falsehood itself in the one who speaks in this way.

[Col. 0601C] Without appearance or beauty, fastened to the cross, truth is to be adored.

The nobler and more powerful each creature is, the more willingly it submits to truth—or rather, it is powerful and noble for this reason: because it submits to truth.

Temporal things prick you. Why do you not flee to other things—that is, to truth?

Truth is therefore more bitter to us than every adversity, because individual adversities attack one or several pleasures, whereas truth reproves them all at once.

If you had experienced all colors and the other things that can be perceived through the eyes, or if you had experienced through the other bodily senses all the reports that you either recited or heard, what benefit would there be? So also with all the many things that you have experienced or heard.

[Col. 0601D] You can hate no one except because of your own wickedness. For even to wish good to the wicked is characteristic of the saints. You ought to love only truth and the peace that proceeds from it.

Let the minister of truth love what he ministers and the one to whom it is ministered. And when the same thing is ministered to him by another, let him receive it with thanksgiving, as something he loves.

Let charity be your reason for speaking the truth, as though you were healing. If someone does not accept it, either you have compassion for him, or you do not love him, or you consider the thing he rejects worthless—just as if a sick person were to reject wholesome medicine.

[Col. 0602B] Truth is followed without end by peace shared with the angels; falsehood, by toil and pain shared with the devil. Truth is not defended; you are the one who needs it.

Truth is exceedingly bitter and unpleasant to your race—not on its own account, but because of their fault—like shining light to weak eyes. Therefore, take care not to make it more bitter while speaking it in a manner contrary to what is required, namely, without charity. For a compassionate physician, giving a sick person a wholesome but bitter potion, smears honey around the rim of the vessel, so that what is sweet may be willingly swallowed and what is wholesome may thereby be received easily. Your entire duty is to benefit people.

[Col. 0602C] If you speak the truth not out of love for truth but from a desire to harm another, you will obtain not the reward of one who speaks truth but the punishment of one who insults.

See how great a punishment you will suffer when the true light perfectly reveals you to yourself, if a person is tortured merely because you show him one of his evils with a single word. Then the thoughts of hearts will be revealed.

You sin equally whether you reproach another or are reproached by another; in either case you either receive truth as an evil or inflict it as an evil. Therefore, if someone wishes to flog you, let him seize your life—that is, truth; let him beat and torture you through it.

Truth is life and eternal salvation. You ought therefore to have compassion on the one who is displeased by it, for he is dead and lost to that extent. But you, being perverse, would not tell him the truth unless you thought it bitter and intolerable to him. You measure others by yourself.

Yet this is most evil: when, in order to please people, you speak the truth that they love and admire as though you were speaking lies or flatteries. Truth is therefore not to be spoken either because it displeases or because it pleases, but so that it may benefit. It is to be kept silent only lest it do harm, like light to weak eyes.

Bread—that is, truth—strengthens the human heart so that it does not succumb to bodily forms.

[Col. 0603A] Blessed is the person whose mind is moved and affected solely by the knowledge and love of truth, while the body is moved solely by that mind. Thus the body too is moved by truth alone. For if there were no movement in the mind except that of truth, and none in the body except that of the mind, there would likewise be no movement in the body except that of truth—that is, of God.

You do everything for the sake of peace; the way to it is through truth alone. Truth is your adversary in this life. Therefore, either subject truth to yourself or subject yourself to it. Nothing else remains for you.

Adversity urges you to desire peace. But, blinded, you desire what makes it altogether impossible for you to have peace while you love and desire it.

[Col. 0603B] Why do you seize within yourself what displeases you so much in another—that is, anger? You are angry because he is angry. Rather, now be angry with yourself because you are angry. If anger truly displeased you in this way, you would not admit it but would flee from it. This happens only by holding fast to peace.

A lake does not boast because it is full of water; it comes from a spring. So it is with your peace. There is always something else that is the cause of peace. Your peace is therefore weaker and more deceptive in proportion as the source from which it arises is more changeable. How worthless it is, then, when it arises from the pleasure of a human face!

Every person desires to be safe. But a person is safe to a lesser degree the more he can be disturbed. He can be disturbed to a greater degree when the things he loves are more ready to be other than he wishes.

Suppose someone says to you: “I will do you harm; I will take away your peace. I will think or speak evil of you.” See how ready you are to be mortified and disturbed.

[Col. 0603C] Let temporal things not be the cause of your peace; it will be as worthless and fragile as they are. This peace will be shared by you with beasts; let yours be shared with angels—that is, let it proceed from truth.

Whatever you had held and loved for the sake of peace and blessedness, despise it unless you want altogether to lose peace and blessedness.

Peace is the good of the soul in which it exists. It is therefore to be desired for its own sake, like a good flavor. [Col. 0603D] Let it be so abundant in you that you do not exclude even the wicked.

“Let not your heart be troubled, nor let it be afraid” (John 14:27). This is the true Sabbath. The person who celebrates it is neither enticed nor compelled; he has himself under his own authority; he can give alms from himself—that is, he can allow himself to be angry or appeased, as another may see to be expedient.

Love of temporal peace necessarily produces unrest of mind. Whoever therefore possesses and loves this peace necessarily lacks peace.

If you do not envy those who do you harm, you will have peace with them.

Just as all things subsist through likeness and peace, so all things perish through unlikeness and discord.

CHAPTER TWO. On the useful displeasure with oneself and on humble confession of sin.

[Col. 0604A]

The beginning of returning to truth is to be displeased with oneself in falsehood. Reproof precedes correction. For one does not wish to change what does not displease.

Since, therefore, you always need to be changed, you always need to be displeased with yourself.

In every care you take for your salvation, no duty or medicine is more useful to you than reproving and despising yourself. Whoever does this is your helper. For he does what you were doing, or ought to have been doing, so that you might be saved.

[Col. 0604B] You please yourself because you do not understand that you possess no good thing from yourself. From yourself you have nothing but evil. You therefore owe yourself no thanks. All evil that you have is from yourself and belongs to you. Thus you owe great punishments as retribution.

The road to God is easy, because one travels it by laying down burdens; it would be difficult if one traveled by taking on burdens. Therefore, unload yourself to such an extent that, having dismissed everything, you deny yourself.

Whoever knows himself to be worthless quietly and humbly receives his reproaches as his own judgments. But he rejects praises as judgments that do not belong to him.

When someone says something bad about you, if it is not true, it harms him, not you. If he calls gold dung, what harm has he done to the gold? If what is said about you is bad but true, you are taught what to avoid.

But whoever says what is good does not benefit the one whom he praises but himself. When something good is said about you, why are reports—things you know better than anyone—being told? Reproach only yourself.

Let each person flee his own vices; for the vices of others will not harm him.

Your habit and your crown are a continual falsehood, since they signify what is lacking.

When someone is grieved that he has committed a theft because of the disgrace that arose from it, he is not repentant of the theft but grieves that he has incurred disgrace. He does not shudder at sinning or regard sin as evil, but at being punished.

For the just, however, sinning and being punished are not two different things. They regard sin itself as the most atrocious punishment, and therefore believe that no wickedness can remain unpunished, since the wickedness of sin is a great punishment, and nothing worse than it can be inflicted on anyone. For this reason they judge that sin itself must be avoided and fled above all evils, even if no other evil follows it.

If you must hate someone, hate no one as you hate yourself. No one has harmed you so greatly.

If nothing is improved unless it has first been reproved, then whoever does not wish to be reproved certainly does not wish to be improved. For it is written: “Whoever hates reproof is foolish” (Proverbs 12:1); “Whoever accepts reproof possesses a heart” (Proverbs 15:32).

On confession.

No return to salvation was possible for the publican unless he had humbly confessed what the Pharisee proudly reproached him for.

You are just in this one respect: if you acknowledge and say that you must be condemned for your sins. If you call yourself just, you are a liar, and you are condemned by the Lord in truth as his opponent. Call yourself a sinner, so that as one truthful you may agree with the Lord’s truth and be liberated.

It is a mark of the great to intercede for those who confess, so that they may be forgiven; but it is a mark of the greater to plead benevolently even for those who do not yet recognize their guilt, so that they may recognize it, and for those who do not confess either because they are ashamed of their guilt or because they love it, so that they may confess.

[Col. 0605A] Every rational soul that wishes to avenge itself inflicts upon another what it fears, abhors, and considers evil in itself. But nothing does it seize more willingly for vengeance than truth, nor does it inflict any evil with a more poisonous mind. Therefore, it abhors nothing more than having truth spoken to it.

The adversary says about another what, if the person to whom it is said humbly acknowledges it, may earn eternal salvation. For when someone calls an adulterer “adulterer,” he says to him as an evil something that the other ought freely to confess for his own salvation. Let him therefore receive it willingly, attending not to the intention with which it is said but to what is said to him.

Whoever genuinely loves not to seem truthful but to be truthful, and genuinely fears not to seem a liar but to be a liar, as soon as he realizes that he has lied, contradicts himself; neither reproaches nor losses of any kind can turn him back from this. For he would rather die truthful than live a liar—if, indeed, a liar lives, since it is written: “The mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wisdom 1:11).

[Col. 0605C] What you wish to conceal—that is, your sin—denounce it, and then it will no longer be something you ought to conceal. You can erase it; you cannot conceal it. For nothing is covered that will not be revealed, nor hidden that will not be known. Why, then, do you prefer to hide the disease rather than heal it? How willingly do you show the diseases of your body to others so that they may have compassion on you—and if they refuse to believe you, you consider yourself miserable, your pain increases, and you also become angry. Do the same with the illnesses of your soul.

CHAPTER THREE. On the pleasures and worthless delights of the five senses.

[Col. 0605D] Consider the two experiences of taking in and expelling: which experience makes you happier, what you experience through the one or through the other? The one burdens you with useless things; the other unloads you. Consider what benefit each provides.

To have swallowed something is simply to have experienced it. Nothing further remains to be hoped for. So it is with all sensual things. Consider, then, what happiness all such things—whether hoped for or possessed—have produced in you, and think in the same way about future things. I say, think about past prosperity, and judge the future accordingly. Everything you hope for will perish. And what will you be after this? Love and hope for something that does not pass away.

You wish wood to be painted with colors, although it is destined to be consumed by fire, and you want the things you consume—whether food or [Col. 0606A] clothing—to be attractive. You need clothing against the cold, not this or that color; likewise, food against hunger, not this or that flavor.

Bestial pleasure comes from the senses of the flesh; diabolical pleasure consists in every arrogance, envy, and deceit; philosophical pleasure consists in knowing the creature; angelic pleasure consists in knowing and loving God.

The things that give greater pleasure in transitory matters are more deadly.

It is equally or even more foolish to kneel before things that you yourself have made and to incline your mind toward things that you destroy—that is, flavors or other sensible objects.

He gathered them from the regions, namely, drawing holy minds away from flavors, odors, and carnal touches; he gathers them into himself.

[Col. 0606B] People thus attempt to make true pleasure or blessedness, as though either it did not exist or it could be made, although it alone truly exists and cannot in any way be made. To make blessedness for oneself is to make God for oneself; to suppose that blessedness does not exist is to suppose that God does not exist.

Consider whether, if all people dismissed every other matter to which they devote themselves and devoted themselves entirely to one color or one flavor alone, they would not be wretched, vile, and foolish. Such are people now, when they devote themselves to so many different qualities of things. For neither many creatures nor all creatures together are our God or our salvation any more than any single one of them is.

When we take pleasure in what beasts also enjoy—that is, in lust, like dogs, and in gluttony, like pigs, and so forth—our soul becomes like their souls, and we do not shudder. But I would rather have the body of a dog than its soul. Yet if our body were transformed into as great a likeness of a dog’s body as our soul is transformed into the likeness of a dog’s soul through lust, who could tolerate us? Who would not recoil?

It would be better and more tolerable for our body to be changed into a beast while the soul remained in its own dignity—that is, in the image of God—than for the body to remain human while the soul became bestial. This transformation is all the more horrible and deserving of lamentation because the soul surpasses the body.

Hence David says: “Do not become like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding” (Psalm 31:9). This cannot be understood as referring to bodily likeness, since that would be absurd.

To modify something, such as food or drink, merely so that it gives greater pleasure is to cooperate with the devil to our destruction and to sharpen the sword so that it may more easily and deeply pierce our entrails. For the more we delight in these things, the more severely and deeply we are wounded.

CHAPTER FOUR. On the empty fears, pains, and torments of the children of this age, which they incur through desire for and love of perishable things.

A person willingly entangles himself in love of bodies and vanity, but, whether he wishes it or not, he is tormented by fear and grief over their destruction—either when the bodies themselves are taken away or when he himself is reproached. For love of perishable things [Col. 0607A] is like a fountain of useless fears and pains and of every anxiety.

The Lord therefore delivers the poor from the powerful by freeing him from the bond of worldly love. For whoever loves nothing perishable has nothing by which he can be harmed by any powerful person, and he is altogether inviolable, because he loves only things that are themselves inviolable and therefore worthy of love.

If someone cuts off all the hairs of your head, he will not harm you unless he touches those that are attached to your head. Likewise, people will not harm you unless they touch the things that have struck roots in you through desire. The more numerous these things are and the more deeply they are loved, the more numerous and violent the pains they will produce.

Either extinguish desire altogether, or prepare yourself to be thrown into confusion—that is, to fear and grieve—over things you ought not to fear or grieve over. [Col. 0607B]

The human soul is tormented within itself for as long as it can be tormented—that is, for as long as it loves anything apart from God. For it cannot unwillingly lose God. It can abandon him, therefore, but it cannot lose him. No one is harmed except by himself.

From as many loves of things that were either to perish for you or by which you were to perish as the Lord has freed you, from just as many fears, sorrows, and pains he has released you.

While the shapes and forms of bodies to which your attachment disfigures you perish—as syllables perish at their appointed times while God conducts the melody—you are tormented. For the rust that has grown within you is being torn away.

Nothing is more laborious for you than not laboring—that is, than despising all the things from which labors arise, namely, all mutable things. [Col. 0607C]

See how vast a multitude of your kind has labored for the world, and not only failed to attain what it sought, but even lost themselves. If you apply yourself, however, you will acquire something incomparably greater than that for which everyone labors or has labored.

The disturbance of the mind is itself foolish and wretched. It nearly always occurs in you when God corrupts the causes of your death—that is, the things to which you had become wrongly attached—so that, abandoning them, you may live.

You love a servant-girl shamefully—that is, a creature. Therefore you are tormented whenever her Lord, that is, your God, does with her what he wills for good.

You have attached yourself to one syllable of a great song; therefore you are disturbed [Col. 0607D] when the wisest singer proceeds with his singing. The syllable you alone loved is taken away from you, and others follow in their proper order. For he does not sing for you alone, nor according to your will, but according to his own. The syllables that follow are hostile to you because they drive away the one you wrongly loved.

What a syllable is in a song, each thing is in the course of the world. You are therefore tormented because you have clung to inferior things, and they pass in their proper order like syllables in a song.

All these things that are called adversities are adversities only to the wicked—that is, to those who love the creature instead of the Creator.

If this man or that man labored for God as much as he labors for the world, his birthday would be celebrated as that of a martyr. [Col. 0608A]

Just as cold comes from ice, so useless fear and the other miseries invade the soul from love of temporal things. Remove from yourself everything that gives you cause for fear, just as you remove things that cause cold. I say, remove them not from a place but from your mind. For nothing is to be feared except what can and ought to be avoided, namely, sin. Whatever ought to be avoided can, with God’s help, be avoided—that is, iniquity.

See how much you are in the power of human beings to be disturbed and tormented. Just as easily as they can disparage you by their words or by their opinion, so easily can they unsettle you. What follows? If you displease them, you are disturbed. Therefore you are in their power. Whether someone does these things [Col. 0608B] or not, you are nevertheless exposed to them through your mental preparation. If you displease them in what is good, this harms them, not you. Labor, then, at that time to change their hearts, not your goodness. If you displease them in what is evil, it is not the fact that you displease them that harms you; rather, it benefits you. Your evil itself is what harms you.

The martyrs say to God: “For your sake we are put to death all day long” (Psalm 43:22); but you say to any worthless things: “Because of you I am disturbed all day long.”

Contract yourself and gather yourself in from every side, lest the whirl of mutable things find you among them and you be tormented.

Whatever way you are tormented—whether through fear, anger, hatred, or any other kind of grief—attribute it solely to yourself, that is, to your desire, ignorance, or sluggishness. If someone wishes to harm you, attribute that to his desire. Your being harmed and your pain are indications of your sin: namely, that you loved something capable of harming you after abandoning God. [Col. 0608C]

You grieve when spectacles are damaged. Attribute this to yourself and your error, because you clung to things capable of harm. For human beings have become so accustomed to turning every evil against something else that, if they stumble against a stone or are burned by fire, they dare to blame and curse God’s creatures. Were those creatures not to do this, they would rightly be blamed as feeble and lifeless; the human being ought rather to mourn the misery of his own weakness.

See how, like a sea of innumerable bodily forms and human souls that never remain in the same condition, you are never allowed to rest. [Col. 0608D]

Although a nurse knows that a little child will be delighted if given a sparrow, she is nevertheless extremely afraid to give it to him—and all the more afraid the more she thinks he will delight in it. Certainly everyone wishes both himself and those he loves to rejoice. Why, then, does the nurse not merely refrain from wishing this joy for the child, but even takes care, as though it were a great evil, that he should not have it? Certainly she wants him to rejoice. Why, then, and from where does she know he will rejoice, does she take it away? Why, except because she considers the grief that will follow, and knows that this joy will be its cause? For she knows perfectly well that a more severe grief will later enter the child’s mind in proportion to the intensity of the joy that preceded it; from the magnitude of the present delight she measures the magnitude of the future sorrow. What else does this woman [Col. 0609A] suggest by her action should be done, except that all those joys followed by lamentation should be avoided as plague and poison? One should not consider how pleasant they are while they are present, but what bitterness they generate in us when they depart.

Such are all temporal joys. Why, then, should I not avoid, with the same prudent caution, a vineyard, a meadow, a spacious house, a field; gold and silver; human opinions and praises; and other similar things? O who will give to the decrepit yet foolish child—that is, to the whole human race spread throughout the world—a certain great and supremely wise nurse who, with such care and solicitude, will take away from it, or recall it from, the joys that are the seeds of future sorrows? But from where comes such a great groaning of tears throughout the world, except because this most devoted and powerful nurse never ceases—whether through herself or by other means—to take away from the human race, or refuse to give it, the causes of sorrow, namely temporal things, just as one takes a sparrow away from a child? [Col. 0609B]

## CHAPTER V. On the desire, love, and boasting associated with earthly and temporal things, and how true misery is not removed by them but increased

When two things are equal, one can become greater than the other in two ways: either through its own increase or through the diminution of its companion. In this latter way all the rulers and powers of the world either rejoice or strive to be greater than all the rest—through the latter’s abasement and diminution, not through the elevation or increase of their own body or [Col. 0609C] mind. For neither their bodies nor their minds are improved in any way; they merely seem to themselves to have advanced and grown because the others have declined and diminished. But if everything else were so reduced that it had been brought to nothing, in what respect would your soul or body grow by this?

Just as someone who wishes to make bricks prepares a yard in which to place them temporarily—not because they are to remain there, but because, once dried, they are to be moved elsewhere—so that yard is not prepared for any particular bricks but equally for all the bricks that are to be made. In the same way God made this place of human habitation for human beings who are to be created and, once their appointed time has been completed elsewhere, transferred. And just as a potter removes some bricks so that newly made ones may take their place, so God, through death as the transfer of those who came before, prepares a place for those who will follow. The fool, therefore, is insane who clings lovingly to the yard of his heart and does not instead constantly consider with concern where he is to be transferred from here. Nor should it seem unjust or harsh to bricks when they are removed from here, since they were plainly placed here for that purpose. It will seem so only to those who do not consider that they must necessarily be transferred from here—those who, in mad desire, claim as their own what is common and belongs to no one in particular, but is jointly assigned to countless future occupants. Consider in this same matter another madness no less serious. Although these bricks are almost all of the same size, scarcely any one of them is content with the space of a single brick; rather, after ejecting or breaking [Col. 0610A] others, each claims for itself as much space as it can from many bricks. [Col. 0609D]

What do you think of someone who devotes all his attention and time to propping up a house that cannot be propped up with the things from which nothing at all can be propped—or, if it can be propped, whose props themselves require just as many other props as the house that is to be supported by them, and those props in turn require as many more, and so on to infinity? This life is the house; you are the one who props it up; the props are temporal things, which never remain in the same condition and cannot either support or be supported at all.

He who seeks a long life seeks a long temptation. “For man’s life upon earth is a temptation” (Job 7:1). [Col. 0610B]

What God did not love in his friends or relatives—that is, power, nobility, riches, and honors—do not love in yours.

You eat, drink, dress, and sleep traps; everything is a trap.

You are exiles through love, pleasure, and affection, not through place. You are exiles in the region of corruption, passions, darkness, ignorance, evil loves, and hatreds.

Love transitory things, without which you cannot exist, only insofar as you love yourself—that is, this temporal life. And insofar as you despise this life, [despise] its supports—

It is grievous to you to have lost this or that. Do not therefore seek to lose it. Whoever loves and acquires things that cannot be retained seeks to lose them.

All misery consists in this. Everyone loves something as his chief concern, fixing his attention there continually. But you—what do you do? Look: everyone, as though having found a treasure, seizes a separate portion of the world and devotes himself to it; or else they are divided among several things, as when a dog placed between two pieces of meat does not know which to approach first, fearing to lose the other.

If the things in which you trust or delight were to do this to themselves, you would laugh at them as foolish, or rather mourn them as lost. And if everyone is insane in this way, is it ever good for you to be insane? If you tolerate yourself, so unclean as you are, why not tolerate anyone else? As many misfortunes as the things you love are subject to, so many is your mind subject to. [Col. 0610D]

He who loves what ought not to be loved is wretched and foolish, even if neither he nor that thing ever perishes. Is an idolater wretched only because what he worships is destined to perish? Then would he not be wretched if it did not perish? Certainly, while his idol remains, its worshiper is utterly wretched, even if sound in body and full of temporal goods.

Adversities do not make you wretched; they reveal and teach that you already were. Prosperity, however, blinds the mind by concealing and increasing misery, not by removing it.

See how the soul is captured by bodily things and, once captured, is tormented, as happens in the case of a child. It is captured by seeing a sparrow and, once he has received it, becomes subject to as many contingencies as the sparrow itself. How, then, is it safe before it is captured by such things? Things that please hold it fast, so that it may be punished by adversities. [Col. 0611A]

Once the ship was given to us, we were carried by the winds toward joy or sorrow, according to the succession of the forms that came before us.

How could a person not boast or be proud of strength or beauty when he boasts of weakness or ugliness? He boasts if he is carried on a horse, or if the ugliness of his clothing is concealed by its finery, whereas he would seem more able to boast if he himself carried the horse by his own strength, or at least did not need it; if he himself adorned his clothing with his own radiance, or at least did not need its adornment. For these things and similar ones proclaim his neediness and ugliness.

How gladly would a person display his own beauty, if he possessed it, who so gladly displays another’s—namely, in clothing, whether furs or garments of any kind! [Col. 0611B]

No less ought one to grieve for the person who rejoices at acquiring temporal things than for the person who grieves at losing them. Both are afflicted by a fever—that is, by love of the world.

## CHAPTER VI. On the useless and worthless desire for praise, glory, or human favor

If you knew the nature and power of human opinion or favor well, you would never, or only very slightly, labor, rejoice, or grieve on their account. They benefit nothing to whom they are given, just as colors and other forms disfigure the bodies or things in which they exist, while benefiting or harming those bodies and things in no respect. What did it benefit the sun or moon that the pagans thought them gods? Or [Col. 0611C] what harm does it do them that you know them to be creatures? And if you thought them to be dung, what harm would that do them? Therefore examine the nature and power of these things as you would that of this or that plant or tree. With God’s help, you will easily be able to do so; from people’s opinions or favors, all other things must be assessed.

By this you recognize what is owed to God alone, because when these things are directed toward any other entity they are of no benefit: knowledge, love for the sake of showing favor, fear, reverence, admiration, and so forth. For by the very fact that they benefit nothing to the one to whom they are offered, they show that they belong only to the one who is not in need of anything. If being praised, known, or admired were beneficial, who would not hire people every day, paying them like laborers, to offer these things continually, so that he might progress without interruption? What mother would not lavish them on her children without ceasing? Who would not praise his clothing, estates, beasts of burden, and himself day and night, so as to make them better by praising them? None of these things, therefore, benefits the one to whom it is offered. But the one who offers it becomes either worse or better by offering it. If he loves, admires, or fears what he ought to love, admire, or fear, he becomes better; if he does not ought to do so, he certainly becomes worse. The same applies to the rest. How compassionate, then, is the Lord, who demands nothing from us for his own benefit and counts himself greatly served if we always do what is useful to us! [Col. 0611D]

Consider the nature of opinion, favor, praise, or blame as you would that of roots, herbs, or other things.

The love of any one human being belongs to everyone. For each person ought to love everyone. Whoever wants this love to be offered to him specially is a robber and therefore becomes guilty against all. [Col. 0612A]

Look: while mingled with this body, you were sufficiently wretched, for you were subject to all its corruptions, down to the bite of a flea or a little mouse. This was not enough for you. You mingled yourself with other things, almost as though with bodies: human opinion, admiration, love, honor, fear, and other similar things. Just as you are afflicted by the injury done to your body, so you are afflicted by injury done to these. You yourself supplied the wood with which you are burned. Your honor is harmed when you are despised; the same applies to the rest. Think in the same way about the forms of bodies.

By the same vice with which this or that person despised you, you, like a coward, grieved at being despised—namely, pride. And by the same vice with which someone took something away from you, you grieved that it had been taken away—that is, through love of things destined to perish. [Col. 0612B]

Unless you despise whatever human beings can do, whether by opposing or assisting you, you will not be able to despise their affections—that is, their hatreds or loves—and therefore neither their good nor bad opinions.

See how you sell your love and the other affections of your mind for pennies or coins, just as wine is sold in a tavern. Again, observe how you purchase opinions, loves, and the other affections or movements of human minds for pennies and coins, just as wine is purchased in a tavern.

This man gave all his possessions for praise; that one, for the pleasure of his belly and throat. Which of them acted worse? I do not know that, but I do know that one was driven by a swinish pleasure and the other by a devilish one. [Col. 0612C]

Do you wish to be loved by human beings? Certainly—to be present for me, that is, for this life of mine. Therefore you feel yourself weak and ready to succumb to their violence. It is as though you were saying: “If people wish it, I shall die; if they wish it, I shall live.” This is false. You will necessarily die, whether they wish it or not. What will you do so as not to die? Therefore you wish people to hold a high or favorable opinion of you, so that they may love or fear you. But you want them to love or fear you so that they may benefit you or not harm you. Conversely, you fear or dread that people may hold a shameful or bad opinion of you, lest they hate or despise you, lest they harm you, or at least lest they fail to benefit you. This comes from the very experience of weakness and frailty that you contracted by withdrawing from God and clinging and relying upon unstable and weak things. For if you did not perceive their worthlessness and weakness, you would not fear on their account or grieve. But you fear on their account and grieve when they perish or are taken away. Therefore you recognize their worthlessness and weakness. Consequently you can offer no excuse at all for loving or relying upon them. Yet it is exceedingly strange to perceive the weakness of something and nevertheless rely upon it, to know its worthlessness and nevertheless love or admire it. When, therefore, you grieve or fear on this account, you show two things in yourself that seem unable to coexist: namely, that you know and perceive their weakness and worthlessness, and yet love and rely upon them. For unless one of these two things were present in you—unless you either did not love them or did not know their worthlessness—you would in no way grieve when they perished. [Col. 0613A]

## CHAPTER VII. On the true praise of the just and the blame of the wicked, and who is worthy or unworthy of praise

Be the kind of person who is praised. For no one is rightly praised except the good; but the person who desires praise is not good, and therefore is not praised. When you flatter the one who praises you, you are no longer flattering your praiser; for you are no longer being praised, since you are so vain.

When it is said, “How good, how just,” the person who is such is praised—not you, who are not such; rather, you are also greatly blamed, since you are so wicked and unjust. The praise of the just is the blame of the unjust. Therefore it is your blame, insofar as you are unjust. When, then, you applaud the just person who praises you, you applaud your truest critic, because you are unjust. For no one is just who thinks himself just—not even an infant of a single day. [Col. 0613B]

He who rejoices in praises loses praises. If you love praise, do not wish to be known for praise; that is, if you wish to be praised, do not wish to be praised. For the person who wishes to be praised cannot truly be praised. The one whose good deeds are proclaimed is praised. But the person who wishes to be praised is not only empty of every good; he is also full of a great and devilish evil, namely great arrogance. He is therefore not praised. The just person, on the contrary, is always praised; there can be no blame of him. For blame is the rejection of evils, and what the just person does not possess cannot be reproached to him; therefore he cannot be blamed. Universally, all praise of the just is blame of the unjust, and all blame of the unjust is true praise of the just. When someone is praised for a good quality, the benefit goes not to the one praised but to the one who praises. [Col. 0613C]

Someone praises you for holiness; he is reaching upward. What pleases him is beyond you, namely holiness. But if you love him not as one who is pleased by holiness, you are reaching downward.

Whoever grieves or becomes angry at losing some temporal thing thereby shows himself worthy of having lost it. Likewise, whoever becomes angry or grieves when insulted demonstrates that he deserved it. He would wish to be praised as much as he did not wish to be insulted.

You grieved at being despised or held in low esteem; by this very fact you show that you ought to have been despised and held in low esteem, and that it was therefore rightly done. For if you had not deserved to be despised and held in low esteem, you would never have feared or grieved at being so treated. By this fact alone—or most of all—you deserve to be despised and held in low esteem: that you fear or grieve at it. In short, no one fears being considered worthless or being despised unless he is worthless and worthy of contempt. [Col. 0613D]

## CHAPTER VIII. On those who wish to be loved and admired, and how through such desire a person becomes like the devil and makes himself an idol for others

He alone truly worships God who truly directs himself toward him with the affection of fear, love, honor, reverence, and admiration. For this alone is true and perfect worship. Whoever offers this to anything other than God is therefore a true idolater.
