But whoever wishes these things to be offered to himself—whose place does he truly occupy, if not that of the devil, who strives by every means to extort these things from human beings? Thus all human complaints amount to this: either their gods—that is, the creatures to which they had offered this true and divine worship—perish or are taken away from them, or such worship is not offered to them. See, then, how greatly idolatry still reigns in you and throughout the world. [Col. 0614A]

No thing ought to wish to be loved as a good except that which, by the very fact that it is loved, makes its lover blessed. But nothing does this except what has no need of a lover—that is, what gains no benefit either from being loved by another or from loving another. The most cruel thing, therefore, is that which wishes someone to place his attention, affection, and hope in it, although it cannot benefit him. This is what demons do: in place of serving God, they wish people to be occupied with them. Cry out, then, to your lovers: “Cease now, wretches, to admire, revere, or honor me in any way, since I, wretched as I am, can bring no help either to myself or to you; indeed, I need your help.”

As far as it lies within you, you have destroyed all human beings, for you have placed yourself between God and them, so that, turning their gaze toward you and abandoning God, they might admire, contemplate, and praise you alone—something wholly useless to you and to them, and I will not say harmful. [Col. 0614C]

Nothing is more worthy among rational creatures, especially devout minds; nothing is baser than the corruptions of bodies. Since, then, you wish to be admired by human beings, blinded by this very pride, see to what misery you have descended. See, therefore, the justice of God. You set yourself up as God—that is, as one to be admired by the most excellent part of creation—and he subjected you to the lowest part. For you wished and did everything in your power to be known, seen, praised, admired, revered, loved, feared, and honored by all human beings. All these things are owed to God alone by the most excellent part of all creatures, namely rational minds. It was therefore just that you, who set yourself up as God before the most worthy parts of creation, should receive as God what is most worthless in it; and that you, who by perverse usurpation wished to extort from the most excellent beings whatever was owed to God alone, should bestow whatever you yourself owed upon the most worthless things, namely the corrupt corpses of bodies. For everything you placed above yourself—love and so forth, which belongs to God alone—you offer wholeheartedly to these things. Thus, while you usurp what belongs to God—being praised and so forth—you have lost what belongs to humanity: praising God, for which you were created, and so forth. And because there is no place above the highest or below the lowest, while you strive above the highest you are again below the lowest. For whoever enjoys something must necessarily be subjected to it through love. But you enjoy the lowest things. Therefore you have been thrust beneath the lowest, where there is no place. [Col. 0614D]

Friendship with this world, as blessed James says, is hostile to God. “Whoever wishes to be a friend of this world is constituted an enemy of God” (James 4:4). Whoever loves even one fly in this world must necessarily love the whole world. For the entire world is necessary to the thing he loves. As long, therefore, as there is love of this world, there is hostility between God and human beings. When, then, you wish to be loved by them so that they may become enemies of God, that is what you wish. Yet you preach that everything created should be despised so that they may be reconciled to God. Will you, then, be the sole exception? Will you say to people: “Despise everything for God’s sake except me,” so that nothing else prevents people from being reconciled to God except you, and thus, because of you alone, hostility between God and human beings may continue, with no one being saved, since by loving you they are compelled to love the whole world as necessary to themselves? But it is one thing to love people in the world or for the sake of the world, another to love them in God or for the sake of God, and another to love them greedily or mercifully. [Col. 0615B]

## CHAPTER IX. On the soul that withdraws from God through enjoyment and love of temporal things and is defiled by demons

Let temporal goods say: “If God heals us from the disease of corruption, what will you do? In your actual use of us, consider in what respect you become better through us, or what you hope to gain from us in the future. You have tested us. What, then? Do you wish to be changed into us, or us into you? What have you to do with us, and what have we to do with you? Why do you grieve over our passing away? We preferred to perish according to the Lord’s will rather than remain according to your desire. For this love of yours we offer you no thanks; rather, we laugh at you as a fool. Whom ought we chiefly to obey, God or you? Say, if you dare: is it not almost your entire function to turn us, by devouring us, into corruption?”

“This is your usefulness, your power: that through you our putrefaction may pass abundantly. You cannot cause your concern for this to remain. This is your blessedness: that you should not lack our filth, to which you willingly submit, while through it the devil corrupts and defiles you—not without great pleasure for himself and joy at your deception and destruction.” [Col. 0615C]

Whatever form you enjoy is, as it were, male in relation to your mind. For the mind yields and submits to it; it is not conformed and assimilated to you, but you to it. An image of that same form remains impressed in you like an idol in its temple. To that idol you sacrifice not an ox or a goat, but a rational soul and a body—that is, your entire self—when you enjoy it.

See how, as in a tavern, you prostitute your love as though it were for sale and distribute it to human beings according to the measure of their gifts. No one receives anything in this tavern who gives nothing or is not expected to give something. Yet you would not possess what you could sell unless it had been freely given to you from above when you gave nothing. You have therefore received your payment.

Emptying and distancing oneself from God prepares one for desire.

Whoever wishes to enjoy you in yourself has earned from you the thanks that flies and fleas receive when they suck your blood. [Col. 0616A]

If these things—which, impressed upon your mind, make you submit through admiration and love, the worship owed to God alone—were worshiped by you in some corner of a house, whether carved or painted, through admiration, love, or bodily prostration, and this became known to the people, what would they do to you?

A woman who, for this reason, does not commit fornication and abandon her own husband—because she cannot find an adulterer who will remain with her for long—is not avoiding adultery but seeking a lasting adulterer. You, however, to increase your evil, have spread the legs of your mind to every passerby, so that you might enjoy even momentary adulteries because you could not enjoy lasting or eternal ones.

This is precisely the sum of human depravity: to abandon what is better than oneself, namely God, and to direct oneself toward lesser things and cling to them by enjoying them, namely temporal things. [Col. 0616B]

As a beetle flies overhead, looking at everything, it chooses nothing beautiful, sound, or lasting; but wherever it sees foul-smelling dung lying, it immediately settles there, rejecting so many beautiful things. In the same way, your mind flies over heaven and earth and the great and precious things in them, yet clings to none of them. It despises everything and gladly embraces many worthless and filthy things that occur to it when it thinks. Be ashamed of these things.

## CHAPTER X. On the shamelessness and brazen-facedness of the soul that commits fornication and asks God to foster it in its crime

When you ask God not to take away something to which you have greedily clung, it is as though a woman, caught in adultery by her husband, instead of seeking pardon for her crime were to ask him not to interrupt the pleasure of her adultery. [Col. 0616C]

It is not enough for you to fornicate away from God unless you also incline him to increase, preserve, and arrange for you the things by enjoying which you are corrupted—that is, bodily forms, flavors, and colors.

What woman is so shameless that she says to her husband: “Find me this or that man with whom I may sleep, because I have found him more pleasing than you; otherwise I shall not rest”? Yet you do this to your husband, namely the Lord, when, loving something besides him, you ask him for that very thing.

When you say to God, “Give me this or that,” you are saying: “Give me something in which I may offend you and fornicate away from you.” For when you ask him for something other than himself, by that very petition you reveal to him your guilt and your fornication away from him, without knowing it. [Col. 0616D]

It is a merciful vengeance if a bridegroom, discovering his bride in adultery, merely takes away from her the things with which she was fornicating. How shameless and unchaste she would be if she took this as an injury! You have scarcely any other reason for grieving except this: over the things taken away from your fornications. Your very griefs therefore convict you of your fornications, so that no other witnesses are needed.

Any shameless and unchaste woman ordinarily conceals from the eyes of her bridegroom the tears she sheds over the losses that befall her adulterer, and over the injuries inflicted upon her by the adulterer when he is angry with her; she likewise conceals the injuries themselves and her joys. See now whether you at least do this toward God—whether you do not openly mourn before him over the losses of your adultery, namely this world, and rejoice in its prosperity. “You have the forehead of a prostitute” (Jeremiah 3:3). [Col. 0617A]

## CHAPTER XI. On ignorance of oneself, through which a person, poured out of himself by love of earthly things, cannot contemplate himself

The poverty of the inward spectacle—that is, of God—not because he is not within, but because, through your inward eye being bleary, he is not seen within—causes you willingly to go out from your inner self, or rather makes you unable to remain within yourself as though in darkness. You spend yourself admiring the outward forms of bodies or human opinions. Do not blame bodily forms for holding, frightening, or otherwise moving you; blame your own blindness and your emptiness of the highest good. [Col. 0617B]

See how greatly you are ignorant of yourself. For no region is so remote and unknown to you that you would more readily believe a false account concerning it.

Sometimes evil displeases someone without the reward of good—for example, when two people wish arrogantly to exercise their own will in the same house, and both wish what is evil. If the will of either displeases the other, this does not happen from hatred of pride but from love. The one who loves his own pride hates the other’s pride because it obstructs his own. This is a very hidden trap.

This is how you conduct yourself in the world, as though you had come here to look at and admire bodily forms.

If you did not lack inward spectacles, you would never go out to external ones, even for leisure.

Just as the girl in the story fainted while gazing at the sun, so you are devoted to the necessarily perishing forms of bodies and to human opinions.

This spectacle is open in this life to the eyes of no one except, above all, God, and to your own eyes according to your capacity—namely, insofar as your mind rises above bodies and their forms, or human opinions and favors, or submits to them.

See how, turned away from God, you entered this world with your mouth open wide toward everything except him. [Col. 0617D]

## CHAPTER XII. On humanity’s true usefulness, and how the usefulness of all human beings is one and the same

Blessed is the person who chooses to labor securely. This is the secure choice and useful labor: to wish to benefit everyone, in such a way that you wish to be useful even to those who do not need your help. For the more people seem to attend to their own interests, the less they do what is expedient. The proper usefulness of each person is to wish to benefit everyone. But who understands this? Whoever seeks to pursue his own usefulness therefore not only finds none for himself, but also incurs great harm to his soul. For while he seeks his own usefulness—which cannot exist—he is excluded from the common usefulness, that is, from God. For just as all human beings have one nature, so they have one usefulness. [Col. 0618A]

Everyone who wants nothing that benefits himself is happy. Can a person, then, wish for something that either does not benefit him or harms him? Would that at least once in your entire life you might will what is expedient, in the way it ought to be willed! O miserable condition: not to be able to refuse what harms you!

If you ask people why they are miserable—whether because they do not want what is useful to them, or because they do not possess what they do not want—they will immediately answer that they cannot have what they want. But this amounts to saying: “We have indeed been enlightened; we know and love well what is useful to us, but we are weakened.” This is false [Col. 0618B]. For who among all worldly people loves anything that can make him better? People desire nothing that is not inferior to themselves. And how can what is better, more precious, and more worthy be improved by things worse, cheaper, and less worthy?

Alas, how many do what they want, and how few want to attain what is useful to them! Yet who could ever persuade this to the sons of Adam? When will they be believed not to love their own utility, when they are ready to swear that they wish themselves no evil and that they endure everything they suffer through so many hardships for their own benefit? It is as though you told an idolater that he does not worship God. He would immediately leap forward, swearing that he does worship God, and would count up how much he spends in his worship [Col. 0618C], even pointing out with his finger the god whom he worships. Yet he does not worship God; deceived by error, he takes something else for God.

So human beings undoubtedly do not love or want their own utility, but what, in their error, they think is their utility. And therefore, whatever they do or suffer for such a thing, they think they are doing or suffering for their own benefit. But no one wants or loves his own utility except one who loves God. For God alone is the entire and sole utility of human nature. It is written: “Whoever remains in charity”—that is, whoever loves God—“remains in God, and God in him” (1 John IV, 16). Human utility is therefore such that no one can love it unless he possesses it, and it cannot be separated at all from the one who loves it.

[Col. 0618D] This very claim that people say they love their own utility—who is there who is not even ready to swear this?—but that they do not possess it, is itself evidence that they love something else, not their own utility. For a person has to do nothing else in order to possess his utility except love. Yet people constantly try to make it as though it did not exist, just as the pagans do with God. For if God alone is the utility of human beings, and no one can lack him except one who does not love him at all, then he does not need to be made, since he is eternal, but only loved.

This alone is entirely the cause of all our misery: namely, that we either do not know and love our utility, or do not know and love it to the degree or in the manner in which it ought to be known and loved.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the prudent caution to be used for one’s own benefit amid all prosperity and adversity

[Col. 0619A]

Behold: distressed and troubled, you complain about this or that person because he has spoken insulting and hateful words to you. You grieve, then, either that he spoke such words to you or that he spoke to you with such an intention. That is entirely good, if you grieve on account of his benefit.

For this is not useful to him. But if you grieve on your own account, that is wrong. He could not have said anything so holy and good to you, with such holiness and goodness, that it would have been more useful to you than these things will be, if you use them well. Whether someone speaks or does good or evil to you, the things will be for you as you use them. [Col. 0619B] But for the one who did or said them, they will be such as the intention was with which he did or said them.

For just as iniquity lies only to itself, not to you, if you do not consent and if you rebuke it, so it does and says all evil to itself—that is, for its own destruction—if you do not consent piously and compassionately, but rebuke it. You ought therefore to grieve with the one who has done or said evil to you, not with yourself, since even another’s evil will turn to your good if you use it well, and to as much good as well as you use it. Conversely, it will turn to as much evil as you use it badly, whether the things done or said to you are evil or good, because “all things work together for good for those who love God” (Romans VIII, 28)—all things to such an extent that even other people’s evils do so. But for those who hate God, conversely, all things work together for their evil [Col. 0619C], and all things to such an extent that even good things do so.

Turn, therefore, your entire complaint against yourself, who are using things badly. For even if the things done or said to you really are evil, they can in no way be evil to you unless you use them badly; likewise, good things are not good unless you have used them well.

You must always observe what is happening in your own mind—not what others do, whether good or evil, but what you do with their actions: how, that is, you use their good and evil deeds, and how much you advance through them, whether by favoring and helping, or by compassionating and correcting. You act well with regard to all human actions when you are enticed by none of their benefits into favor, and are deterred by none of their harmful acts from love [Col. 0619D]. For then you love gratitude. It is no achievement to have peace with those who have peace with us.

Whatever happens to you, provided that your mind does not fall into a movement of anger, hatred, sadness, or fear, nor into the cause of these things, it will harm you nothing in the age to come.

Place two balls before a ray of sunlight, one of clay and the other of wax. Although the ray is one and the same, it cannot work in the same way in both; according to their preparations, it does different things in them, hardening the one and melting the other. For it cannot melt an earthen ball or harden one of wax.

So too, one and the same kind of metal—gold, namely—seen by many people arouses different movements in them, according to the preparation of their minds [Col. 0620A]. One is inflamed to seize it, another to steal it, and another to distribute it to the poor. The foolish person calls its possessor blessed; the wise person mourns for its lover.

Neither in a good mind can it arouse an evil will, nor in an evil mind a good will. Rather, both this and all other kinds or causes of bodies or other things move human minds according to their respective preparations. And therefore the entire cause of our wickedness must be attributed to ourselves, not to the things in which we sin. They do nothing else for us except put us to the test. They reveal what we were secretly; they do not make us such.

The glances of other men test how firmly and immovably a bride clings to her bridegroom. For if she is truly chaste, she is moved by the beauty of no other man. So too, if you clung to God with the firmest affection, you would not be enticed by the sight of any creature. All these things test how great your chastity toward God is.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the adversities of this age, how they are to be endured, because through them we are usefully compelled to return to God

See how God pricks you wherever, through desire for created things, you extend yourself outside him, like a nurse pulling back a child’s arm stretched outside the cradle so that it will not perish from the cold.

May God be gracious to you, so that he does not find a place where the foot of your mind can rest [Col. 0620C], and so that, at least under compulsion, O soul, you may return to the ark like Noah’s dove.

Poverty itself, or hardship, in the place of a temporary torturer compels us to desire good things and things different from these. But because we are accustomed only to temporal things and know nothing else, we do not desire things very different from what we suffer. We wish either to interrupt their anger—that is, their hardships—for a moment by some mitigation, as though by a kind of reconciliation, or to undergo things not very different from them.

O man who suffer pain, do you wish to ease it? “I do.” Temporarily or eternally? “Eternally.” Then desire the eternal ointment, that is, God. For he struck you so that you would desire him, not herbs, not bandages [Col. 0620D].

A single fever removes all the things against which you struggle—that is, the pleasures of the five senses. What remains, then, except that you give thanks to God for the victory he has granted? But you instead seek someone to whom you may succumb, hating freedom.

What hope is there if you freely throw yourself upon the enemy’s snares and arrows, if you not only fail to avoid these things but gladly embrace them, expose yourself to them, and flee from them to them? You think they are a remedy, a consolation; you desire them and cannot bear their absence.

Prosperity is a snare; adversity is the knife that cuts this snare. Prosperity is the prison of the love of God; adversity is the battering ram that breaks it.

Adversity says to you: “You strive for me to depart. You would certainly prevent this in no way; if you will rightly, you can. For I cannot remain while the Lord sets the measure”—indeed, I am only a syllable [Col. 0621A].

If you must be like a lamb toward the worst of human beings, what should you be toward God when you are corrected by some scourge from him?

See how you are as though in a battle: thirst scorches you, and you set drink against it; hunger torments you, and you set food against it; cold assails you, and you set clothing or fire against it; illness, and you set medicine against it. Against all these things you need patience and contempt for the world, lest you be defeated in another battle that arises from this one, namely, by whole ranks of vices.

Since you are captivated by pleasure alone, only pleasurable things are to be avoided. Nowhere, therefore, is the Christian soul secure except in adversity.

From the things you love, God has made rods for you. By fleeing prosperity and rushing into adversity, you are tormented. Everything is a scourge except him who destroys the scourge itself—he is like the son who breaks the rod with which his father is beating him [Col. 0621B].

A body is conquered by stronger things and is either pushed or pulled; so too is the will. But you must take care not about what moves the body by conquering it, but about what moves the mind and will.

Woe not to those who have lost temporal things, but to those who have lost endurance. No suffering is overcome except through suffering itself. Hunger is not reduced by eating; rather, it is served, just as thirst is served by drinking. For these things aim at inclining the mind toward enjoying the outward forms of bodies. When this happens, they are not overcome but reign, attaining their end—that is, the mind’s inclination and preparation for an easier and greater inclination [Col. 0621C].

The sole medicine for all pains and torments is contempt for the things by which one has been hurt, and the turning of the mind toward God.

As many carnal pleasures, and as vehemently, as you despise, so many and such strong snares of the devil do you avoid. As many tribulations—especially those endured for the sake of truth—as you flee, so many medicinal remedies do you reject.

## CHAPTER XV. On true patience, by which sinners and the weak are to be endured and loved, while piously hoping for their correction

[Col. 0621D]

See how, in hope, you can love wheat while it is still grain in the grass, bent over; so love those who are not yet good. Be toward everyone as Truth was toward you. As it sustained and loved you in order to make you better, so sustain and love them in order to make them better.

By despairing of the sick person, you blaspheme the physician. His recovery is as easy as the physician’s power and goodness in healing are great.

Take care that, because of a human being’s work, you do not despise God’s work. A human being’s work is murder, adultery, and other similar things; God’s work, however, is the human being himself. Whoever loves something such as a house or anything of that kind [Col. 0622A] also loves the material from which it can be made, namely wood or stones. Therefore everyone who loves the good must also love the wicked, since they never become good from anywhere else. Why do you not love that from which an angel can be made, if you love that from which a cup can be made? For it is written concerning human beings: “They will be equal to the angels of God” (Luke XX, 36).

What a beautiful art it is to conquer evil with good! For opposites are overcome by opposites.

You have been placed like a target to blunt the enemy’s arrows—that is, to destroy evil by opposing it with good. You must never return evil for evil, unless perhaps medicinally; but then it is no longer evil for evil, rather good for evil, that you return [Col. 0622B].

Those who love the world laboriously learn the art by which they may obtain or enjoy what they love. You wish to attain God, yet you despise the art by which he is acquired, namely, returning good for evil.

Either withdraw from here, or perform the task for which you have been placed here: namely, heal and endure.

This one is foolish—that is, the hostile human being; the other is crafty, namely the devil, who attacks you through him. Be gentle toward the former, so that you may free him; be cautious against the latter.

“You are troubled because I am troubled; being troubled, you rebuke one who is troubled. What shame! Let the straight-legged mock the crooked-legged, the white man the Ethiopian. I will indeed be corrected and will no longer do this evil. But what will you do about your own vice, by which you are not only unable to heal me but cannot even tolerate my recovery?” [Col. 0622C]

Why do you wish to dismiss that brother? “Because he is full of anger and every vice.” Then let God do the same to you. You have proved from your own mouth that you ought not dismiss him. “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Matthew IX, 12). If you ask a mother why she abandons her son, and she answers that he is weak and ill, ask whether she would herself want her son to do the same to her. When she says, “No,” add: “Then you hate him for a bad reason.” So it is with the physician.

Let the one who asks forgiveness not be an exactor of vengeance.

If you tolerate yourself, so unclean as you are, why not also tolerate anyone else?

Let others go to Jerusalem; you go as far as patience or humility. The former is going outside the world; the latter, within it [Col. 0622D].

Whatever your offense may be, and however you may offend, wish to have toward yourself the same will from God and from human beings; display that same will toward others, however great or however grievous their offenses may be.

## CHAPTER XVI. On pious compassion and the healing of the weak, and how to live among them with an incorrupt mind

A mother wounded by her son does not demand his wound in vengeance, because she counts that wound as her own also. Therefore, if someone injures her son while wishing to avenge her, he must not be thought to have taken vengeance for her, but to have repeated her injury. So every Christian ought to be toward all human beings: namely, to pity the one who longs for the most certain causes of his own pain—that is, things that are perishing.

It is as easy to distinguish your brother from his vice as good from evil. After all, when a person is seen, who becomes angry or indignant? When his vice is seen, who is not offended, except one who is very wise and good, who knows that this vice harms the person himself more than anyone else, and therefore that he should be pitied?

Your brother is filled with charity and wisdom, and you do not share in them; he is filled with anger, hatred, and rage, and you cannot avoid sharing in them. The insane need the healthy, so that the healthy may either preserve or heal them [Col. 0623B].

Whatever you desire God to show toward you alone—namely, kindness—show this toward all human beings, whether through severity or gentleness. Why do you insult the blind and the weak? You are the same; or, if you are different, it is not through yourself or from yourself.

Consider what you would have to do if all human beings were always driven by such insanity. Would you therefore have to be troubled? Why, then, when one person is troubled on some occasion, are you troubled? You owe him medicine, not agitation. For how can insanity be cured by acting insanely?

Why do the sufferings of those of your own kind please you? Is it because it is just? Then let your sufferings too please God, because it is just. But this judgment delivers you to eternal fires [Col. 0623C].

A foolish physician, unwilling to diminish his own reputation, imputes to the sick themselves whatever does not turn out well, even when it is his own fault. You do the same to those subject to you.

What attitude would you have toward all human beings if you were removed from them, contemplating their sins and miseries? At least now, when you see with your own eyes that they are perishing through blindness or weakness, have that attitude entirely. For either they are deceived by the devil through temporal things, or they are overcome.

Stand in awe of God’s inscrutable judgments concerning you. Whatever you are in relation to others, you do not know why they have not been above you. Be toward them, then, as you see they ought to have been toward you if they had been above you [Col. 0623D].

Your reward will be according to your desire and effort, not according to the progress of those subject to you, whether they advance or not.

Once you have rightly proved that he is wicked, it will be necessary for you to mourn his sin, because the Lord also mourned yours. Why do you examine the illness of a sick person if, once you have recognized the illness, you not only do not grieve and heal him but even insult him?

While you see or hear of another’s evils, look back at your own mind, to test how much true love for human beings it contains.

You ought not to rejoice if it happens that you are better than others; rather, you ought to grieve that they possess less goodness, and count this as something lacking in yourself [Col. 0624A].

First put on the person whom you wish to judge or correct, so that, if you were in his condition, you might act toward him as you would sense to be appropriate for yourself. “In the measure with which you measure, it will be measured to you, and by the judgment with which you judge, you will be judged” (Matthew VII, 2). For Christ also first put on the human being before he judged.

You must not try to make your masters—whose service has been assigned to you by their Father, that is, by the Lord your God—do what you want, but what benefits them. You must incline yourself toward their benefit, not them toward your will, because they have been entrusted to you not so that you may rule over them, but so that you may benefit them, just as a sick person is entrusted to a physician not so that the physician may dominate him, but rather heal him [Col. 0624B].

The physician is not against the sick person but for the sick person—that is, against his illness—and he has his entire and sufficient vengeance for everything he suffers from him in the sick person’s recovery. He imputes nothing to the sick person, but everything to the illness; and therefore his full revenge is the destruction of the illness itself.

Four people were entrusted to two physicians: one healthy person with one sick person to one physician, and another healthy person with another sick person to the other. A reward was promised for caring either to preserve or to restore health. One physician accordingly did everything that ought to have been done to preserve or restore health, and yet both patients died. The other did none of the things that ought to have been done, and yet the one who was healthy remained so, while the sick one recovered. Which of these physicians deserves the reward [Col. 0624C]: the one whose two charges died, or the one whose charges are alive and well?

Without doubt, the one who did what ought to have been done with a pious intention is no less worthy of praise and reward than if his patients had lived and been healthy. But the one who was unwilling to do what he ought to have done deserves punishment no less than if his patients had died.

Two things therefore perfect a physician: good will and complete knowledge. But healing all those for whom he cares is not within his power. For no one can know who is sick beyond hope and who is sick with hope of recovery. Therefore care must be given to all, and in every case the whole art must be carried out with complete kindness. Thus, before the Father of all, we shall merit no less grace and reward for the dead than for the healthy.

[Col. 0624D] Prepare yourself to dwell among the wicked with an incorrupt mind; this is angelic. But what glory is there in doing this among the holy?

It is the virtue of angels to live among the vicious without being corrupted by their vices. It is the mark of the highest physicians to dwell among the sick and insane and not only to remain entirely uncorrupted but to restore health to them.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the virtue and effect of the love of God and neighbor, and how charity is to be desired and bestowed

Whoever enjoys some bodily form, whatever he sees as good in it he attributes not to himself but to that form, and for this reason praises and loves it in his mind. He does not consider himself good, but the form; yet he considers himself good because of it. He does not remain in himself but tends and passes into that form, with as much effort of mind and movement of will as the more he marvels at and loves it in enjoying it.

Therefore, if someone injures or removes that same form, he thinks the injury has been done not to the form but to himself. And because the form was his paradise and blessedness, clinging to it is hell and misery for him, while being separated from it is misery. So be toward God.

If an image of dung is made of gold, it is certainly better substantially than imaginatively: substantially it will be gold, but imaginatively it will be dung. If, however, an image of an angel is impressed upon gold, it will be better imaginatively than substantially. For imaginatively it will be a living, spiritual, rational substance; substantially it will be an insensible and lifeless body [Col. 0625B].

Therefore, when your mind is affected with love toward dead and perishable bodies, it is better substantially than imaginatively. Substantially it is rational life made in the image of God; imaginatively it is such as the things to which it attends and in which it delights. When, then, poured out from itself through the bodily senses, it attends to those things, it moves from the better and perfect—that is, from the living and rational substance that it is itself—toward inferior things. The more vehemently it does this, the worse it becomes.

But when, poured out above itself, it is affected by the truth—that is, by God—it is better and more precious formally than substantially. Substantially it is a soul; formally, if one may say so, it is God. For I said: “You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High” (Psalm LXXXI, 6). When, therefore, it tends from itself toward him, it tends from the inferior toward that than which nothing can be better; and the more effectively it does this, the better it becomes.

When a good that needs some other good is desired, misery is not excluded; rather, need is increased and accumulated. Therefore desire the good that needs no other good. All things are good through goodness. All things, therefore, need goodness in order to be good. Goodness itself needs nothing, for it is good through itself. Love this, then, and you will be blessed.

See what kind of good it is whose final traces—the temporal things, that is—are sought by so many rational and irrational beings amid so many and such great dangers of labors and errors [Col. 0625D].

You should rejoice in nothing at all, either in yourself or in another, except in God.

All vices and sins, because they are committed for the sake of a creature—that is, the lowest good—are opposed to the goodness of the Creator, that is, the highest good.

If the breath of our kind—that is, human opinion or praise—is desired so greatly, how much more ought the salvation of our kind, namely the Creator, to be desired! If it is so sweet to be called good that even those who do not wish to be good rejoice in being called so, how much sweeter it is to be good! And if it is so bitter and shameful to be called evil that even those who rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst things (Proverbs II, 14) cannot endure this, how much worse it is to be evil!

[Col. 0626A] A human being desires some created thing, or clings to it through bodily sensation, and forgets himself. When will you turn in this way toward the Creator?

The Lord commands blessedness for you—that is, perfect love of him—from which come freedom from fear and trouble, that is, peace and security.

Only truth knows how to turn away from evil, and only love of truth can do so. Therefore one does not turn away from evil spatially.

Love what you cannot lack by loving—that is, God.

If clinging to God is your whole and only good, then being separated from him is your whole and only evil, and nothing else. This is your Gehenna; this is your hell.

From now on, wean yourself from these bodily forms. Be ashamed that you cannot be without them. And because, whether you wish it or not, you will one day lose them, do willingly now, with great reward or grace, what you will eventually do even under great punishment. Even if no one takes this life from you, will you not eventually abandon this life and everything belonging to it? Behold, possess everything: will you not at some time lack all these things? Do now, then, what you will do when you have lost everything: learn to be without these things; learn to live and rejoice in the Lord.

### On the gratuitous love of neighbor

Whoever loves everyone will undoubtedly be saved; but whoever is loved by human beings will not for that reason be saved. Just as hatred of you is an impediment to life for everyone, so everyone’s hatred is an impediment to life for you. It is therefore useful for you to love everyone [Col. 0626C]; it is also beneficial for them to love you.

Love given freely is to be desired for its own sweetness, like the sweetest nectar; even if everyone goes mad, it must not be sold for any price. For it is useful to us and makes us blessed, whatever others may do.

If you love because you are loved, or so that you may be loved, you do not so much love as love in return, repaying love for love; you are a money-changer—you have received your reward.

Toward the one who has injured you, show yourself more affable and intimate; toward the one whom you have injured, submissive and ashamed.

Just as you regard whatever good is done to you by human beings as God’s gifts and believe that all thanks should be returned to him, so regard whatever good you show to human beings as his benefits, not yours [Col. 0626D].

When you love someone as a friend but wish wealth for him as a good, you love wealth more excellently than you love him. You love him as one in need, but wealth as sufficiency; clearly, you are more prepared to be without him than without wealth.

Whoever kills an unrighteous person while remaining in his own unrighteousness, because he hates unrighteousness and wishes to destroy it, is deceived. When the unrighteous person dies in his unrighteousness, the unrighteousness is eternal. Therefore let the one who hates unrighteousness take care that the unrighteous person be corrected; then his unrighteousness will perish.

“God is love” (1 John IV, 8). Whoever therefore shows charity to someone for any reason other than charity itself sells God; he sells his own blessedness. For he is well only through loving.

[Col. 0627A] If charity and its signs—that is, eagerness and so forth—please you so much in another person, why is it not much sweeter in your own mind?

Whoever gives something to someone either because that person has given something or because he is going to give something has no grace from God. So it is with you concerning peace and love.

If you love so much that you are compelled by love itself, rebuke and strike; if you act otherwise, you condemn yourself. Do everything toward others with the intention with which you wish God to act toward you.

“The charity of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Romans V, 5). But you love neither God nor your neighbor except for the sake of temporal benefits. It is therefore poured into you through temporal things, not through the Holy Spirit. What is poured in this way is not charity but desire.

[Col. 0627B] Behold, your duty is no different from what it was before you became a superior. Through vows, prayers, and affections you were doing what you have now begun to do through deeds: namely, benefiting human beings. Your actions ought not diminish those affections, but increase them by their encouragement.

In whatever matter you can preserve chastity toward God, in that same matter you can also preserve justice toward your neighbor; this is done by not coveting.

People find it difficult to believe that something burdensome to them is done out of charity.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the perfect justice of the angels, and the difference between their justice and ours

When someone perfectly enjoys any thing, forgetting himself, he tends toward it as though he had abandoned and despised himself, and he attends not to what is happening in himself but to what is happening in it, nor to what he himself is like but to what it is like [Col. 0627C]. Therefore the angels despise themselves more than we do.

For, tending toward God with their whole effort, they leave themselves behind, together with all other creatures, with their entire attention. They do not even deem themselves worthy of looking back at themselves, so worthless do they consider themselves. Despising themselves with their whole mind and forgetting themselves, they go wholly toward him; they attend not to what or how they themselves are, but to what he is. And the more they despise themselves, turn themselves away from themselves, and forget themselves, the more like him—and therefore the better—they become.

Christ leads the angels into the embrace of their bridegroom; he tears us away from the adulterer, that is, from the world. He makes them strong and steadfast for enjoying the bridegroom, and us for renouncing the adulterer, that is, the world. He holds them in vision, or in reality; us in faith and hope. He gives them perfect joy in true blessedness; us endurance in tribulation. To them, blessed life; to us, at best, precious death. To them, living for themselves—that is, for God; to us, dying to the world. To them, rejoicing in their good things; to us, grieving over our evil things. To them, joyful hearts; to us, contrite hearts. To them, justice; to us, repentance. To them, the end; to us, the beginning of good.

I confidently swear that the angels have received from God no gift greater, worthier, more precious, more useful, and therefore more desirable, or more beautiful, than charity. Who could understand or believe this? For God is charity. Therefore whoever possesses something greater or better than charity possesses something greater or better than God.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the true and inward beauty of the soul, and in what the true perfection of every human being consists

[Col. 0628A]

You see no thing that does not possess, within its own kind, a certain natural beauty and perfection. When this is lacking or diminished in some way, it rightly displeases you; for example, if you happen to see a human being whose nose has been cut off, you immediately condemn the sight. You perceive what he lacks for the natural perfection of human nature. So it is with all things, down to a nettle leaf or any other herb.

Who, then, would deny that the human mind possesses a certain natural and proper beauty and perfection? Insofar as this is present in it, it is rightly approved; insofar as it is lacking, it is justly censured. Consider, therefore, with God’s help, how much of this beauty and perfection is lacking from your mind, and do not cease to condemn this lack.

What is the soul’s natural beauty? To be devoted to God.

And to what degree? “With all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength” (Luke X, 27). The same beauty also includes being kind toward one’s neighbor. To what degree? Even unto death.

And if you are not this way, whose loss will it be? God’s, none; perhaps your neighbor’s, somewhat; but certainly your own, supremely. For being deprived of natural beauty and perfection cannot fail to be harmful to anything. If a rose ceased to be red, or a lily to smell sweet, it would seem to me to be some loss to a person who loves such pleasures; but it would be much more and much more grievous a loss to the rose or lily themselves, deprived of their natural and proper beauty [Col. 0628C].

The true perfection of a rational creature is to regard each thing as much as it ought to be regarded. To regard it as more or less than this is error. Now every thing is naturally either above it, beside it, or below it. Above it is God; beside it is one’s neighbor; below it are all other things.

You must therefore regard God as much as he ought to be regarded. He ought to be regarded as great as he is. But no one can regard him as great as he is unless he knows how great he is. And how great he is can be known perfectly only by himself. For as much as his essence surpasses ours, so much does his knowledge of himself surpass ours [Col. 0628D]. In comparison with his essence, ours is nothing; and if our knowledge is compared with his knowledge of himself, ours is blindness and ignorance.

Only his perfect knowledge of himself, equal to himself, exists. Hence the Lord says: “No one knows the Father except the Son” (Matthew XI, 27). Therefore, just as his knowledge of himself alone is perfect and equal to himself, so his love of himself alone is equal and corresponding to himself in its entirety. For he alone, knowing perfectly how great he is, loves himself perfectly according to his greatness.

Return now to that definition which I gave at the beginning. For, when examined more subtly, it is proved to belong not to a rational creature but only to God. To say nothing of the rest, as has been shown, He alone knows and loves Himself wholly, exactly as great as He is. What, then, is the perfection of a rational creature? It is this: that it value all things above it—that is, God—things equal to it—that is, its neighbor—and things below it—that is, irrational spirits, and so forth—as much as they ought to be valued by it, that is, by a rational creature.

How much they ought to be valued, gather as follows. Nothing is preferred to God, nothing is equal to Him, nothing is compared with Him as half, as a third, or as any fraction, however infinitely small. Therefore, let it value nothing more highly, nothing equally, nothing as half or as any fraction, however infinitely small, in comparison with Him. Let it love nothing more, nothing equally, nothing in any proportion whatsoever in comparison with Him. Hence the Lord Himself says: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength, and with all your mind” (Luke 10:27)—that is, you shall love nothing else as something in which to delight or upon which to rely. You have what concerns things above.

[Col. 0629B] All human beings, however, are naturally equal—that is, equal insofar as nature is concerned. Therefore, it ought to value everyone as much as itself. Thus, just as with respect to what is above, that is, God, it ought neither to prefer anything in love to Him, nor to equate anything with Him, nor to compare anything with Him in any respect, so too it ought not to value the salvation of any human being less; and whatever it ought to do or suffer for its own eternal salvation, it ought to do or suffer wholly for the eternal salvation of any human being. Hence the Lord says: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” You have what concerns things in between.

Things below, however, are whatever comes after the rational spirit: the sensual life, which is shared with animals; that which gives life to the body, shared with herbs and trees; and the substance of the body, shared with forms and qualities, metals, and stones.

Therefore, just as it ought to love nothing more than what is above, nothing equally in comparison with what is above, so it ought to value nothing below less, nothing as insignificant, nothing in comparison with things below as worthless by any proportion, however infinitely small. And this is what is written: “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world” (1 John 2:15). You have what concerns things below.

Such a person, then, will have things above for joy, things equal for companionship, and things below for service. He will be devoted to God, benevolent toward his neighbor, sober toward the world; God’s servant, humanity’s companion, the world’s master; subject to God, not arrogant toward his neighbor, not subjected to the world; reducing things below to the usefulness of things in between, and things in between to the honor of what is above.

[Col. 0629D] He will be neither impious, blasphemous, nor sacrilegious toward what is above; neither arrogant, envious, nor wrathful toward what is equal; neither frenzied nor disgraceful toward what is below. He will receive nothing from things below, nothing from things equal, but everything from what is above; impressed by what is above, impressing what is below; moved by what is above, moving what is below; affected by what is above, affecting what is below; following what is above, drawing along what is below: possessed by the former, possessing the latter; reduced by the former to their likeness, reducing the latter to his own likeness.

Toward this perfection we strive in this life, although we shall obtain it perfectly only in the life to come. We shall obtain it there more fully in proportion as we desire it here more ardently. Then there will be no movement in the mind except from God; none in the body except from the soul, and thus neither in soul nor in body will there be any movement except from God. Nor will there be sin—that is, perversity of will—nor the punishment of sin, namely, the corruption, pains, and destruction of the flesh.

The naked mind will cling to naked truth, needing no words, sacraments, likenesses, or examples in order to reach it. For there “a man shall no longer teach his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord.’ For all shall know me, from the least to the greatest, says the Lord” (Jeremiah 31:34); “for all shall be taught by God” (John 6:43).

## CHAPTER XX. On the incarnation of the Word, and how He most fully demonstrated the perfection described above in Himself

[Col. 0630B] Even now, in this mortal life, if the soul were very pure, it would see these virtues, or lines of justice, by itself in the very truth and wisdom of God. It would see not only that it—that is, the human soul—would be immortal and eternal, but also that its flesh would be such in the resurrection. Indeed, it would clearly behold that resurrection itself there, that is, in the Word and Wisdom of God. But because, on account of its impurity, it could not see these things, the human mind was joined to the Word. It received the very Word of God most fully, became wholly conformed and similar to Him, and was wholly and entirely impressed by Him. As it is written: “Set me as a seal upon your heart” (Song of Songs 8:6).

[Col. 0630C] Thus, having been wholly reduced to His likeness, just as wax is reduced to the likeness of a seal, it would present Him for us to see and know in itself. But we were so blind that we could see not only not the Word of God, but not even the human soul; therefore a human body was added as well.

Consider, then, these three: the Word of God, the human mind, and the human body. If we could see the first clearly, we would not need the second. If at least we could see the second, we would not need the third. But because we could see neither the first nor the second—that is, neither the Word of God nor the human mind—the third was added, namely, the human body. And thus “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), in what is external to us, so that in this way He might eventually lead us into what is inward.

[Col. 0630D] A rational soul possessing flesh was therefore joined to the Word; through that flesh it would teach, accomplish, and suffer whatever was necessary for our instruction and correction. In that soul alone the qualities we discussed above were present most perfectly: devotion toward God, benevolence toward one’s neighbor, and sobriety toward the world.

For it preferred nothing to God, equated nothing with Him, compared nothing with Him in any proportion, and compared nothing with Him as any fraction, however small. Hence He says: “I always do the will of Him”—that is, the Father—“who sent me” (John 8:29).

He loved His neighbor most perfectly as Himself. For He spared none of the things that were below Him—that is, below the rational mind—but turned everything to the benefit of His neighbor: both life, though sensual; that which gives life to the flesh; and the flesh itself. For He endured sharper pains for us, death against the vegetative life, and wounds against the flesh itself.

[Col. 0631A] Toward the world He possessed such sobriety and such contempt that the Son of Man had nowhere even to lay His head. He received nothing from things below, nothing from things in between, but everything from what is above—that is, from the Word of God, with whom He was joined in the unity of person.

He was not taught to understand, nor kindled to love, by sacraments, words, or examples, but solely by the presence of the Word of God. Through that soul, the Word and Wisdom of God showed us in three ways—namely, through sacraments, words, and examples—what must be done, what must be endured, and by what means it was to be done.

For a human being ought to follow none other than God, but could follow no one except a human being. Therefore a human being was assumed so that, while following the one whom he can follow, he might also follow the one whom he ought to follow. Likewise, he could be conformed only to God, in whose image he was made, but could be conformed only through a human being. Thus God became human so that, while being conformed to the human being whom he can follow, he might also be conformed to God, to whose benefit this is.

[Col. 0631]

# THE CUSTOMS OF GUIGO, FIFTH PRIOR OF THE GREATER CHARTERHOUSE

*(Annales of the Carthusian Order, edited by D. Innocentius Lemasson, Correriae, 1687, folio volume I, p. 30.)*

## NOTICE. TO THE CARTHUSIAN BROTHERS

[Col. 0631B] Before we proceed to elucidate and explain the Customs of our reverend Father Guigo, we too ought, in imitation of so great a man, to say a few words to you, so that you may more perfectly understand both the author’s mind and the purpose of the work we have undertaken, now that we are presenting these Customs—commonly called statutes—and having them printed anew.

“He who does the truth comes to the light, so that his works may be manifested” (John 3). Taught and invited by this voice of Christ, we have therefore brought our treasure, that is, the first beginnings and instructions of our institution, out of darkness, as it were, so that we may no longer seem to wish to hide it, especially for the following reasons:

First, so that it may be for you like a lamp lit and placed upon a lampstand, by whose light you may be instructed, guided, and kindled.

[Col. 0631C] Instructed in the religious conduct of the Order’s first Fathers; guided in the manner and fidelity with which you are to fulfill your vocation; kindled to imitate them and to rival them in sincere charity.

Second, so that from the light of the truth set forth before you—by which you will see how the Order was preserved, through God’s singular protection, in the vigor and spirit of its institution—you may receive consolation; and so that, once the clouds of anxieties have been dispersed, which a certain opinion of the Carthusian Order’s decline had cast into the minds of some fainthearted persons, you may conceive a new fervor for honoring our institution, honored and preserved to this point by such singular divine protection, and for walking worthily before God in this holy vocation to which you have been called, never degenerating from the ancestral Carthusian observance.

The reverend Father Guigo had foreseen the criticisms of censors, and perhaps had already experienced them in his own time. Therefore he wished to fortify the tender consciences of good Carthusians against their arguments, lest they fall from them into scruples or mental perplexities, as will appear to you from various passages, especially chapter 20 and chapter 57, no. 4, and elsewhere.

Third, so that we may finally restrain the fervor conceived by many and displayed in various ways concerning the Order’s ancient statutes. Some, out of devotion to the Order, have taken certain copies from our cells and bought them from merchants at great price, desiring to know, as it were, their very elements; others, however, have formed from those ancient statutes sinister opinions against the Order’s present condition.

[Col. 0632C] What was therefore in some way concealed, we make public, so that the rash suspicion may no longer enter certain minds that we are regarded as degenerate sons who try to conceal the glorious deeds of our Fathers lest their decline become apparent.

For in these last times—something we report with sorrow and mourning—thus, dearest friends and brothers in Christ, charity has grown cold. Indeed, that excellent gold of charity, of which the bride of the Song says that the head of the heavenly Bridegroom is made (Song of Songs 5), has been darkened, and its beautiful color changed, so that some now think it permissible not only to seek iniquity in the house of the just and to devastate his rest, contrary to the utterance of the Holy Spirit (Proverbs 24), but also—by a new rule, which certainly belongs neither to God nor to the Church—to interpret in the worse sense rather than the better even those things that seem doubtful in some respect, and to consider themselves free to do so.

[Col. 0633A] Indeed, they think they may, without any scruple, besmirch by sinister interpretation even things that are truly and unquestionably good, as though they could make them begin to stink; and thus what was previously of good odor and edification begins to provoke nausea.

Let the Gospels be read and the apostolic books carefully examined. There we read: “Charity does not envy, does not act wrongly, does not think evil” (2 Corinthians 13), along with many similar statements. But we shall find nothing there establishing that it is permissible to injure one’s neighbor’s reputation and to spread his faults, whether true or false, far and wide, as though climbing upon the rooftops.

If Sacred Scripture declares that it is unlawful to act thus toward an individual person, what must be thought of a community, or of an entire Order whose reputation is intact?

[Col. 0633B] D. Thomas followed the meaning of Christ and of the Sacred Scriptures when he used, as a paradigm, a man who had thirty faces and who would unquestionably appear more beautiful to observers when viewed from a distance, in order to express his view on this matter. We ought to embrace and follow that view in all things.

We have not said these few words about the unaltered color of charity in order to become angry with those who think less well of us, but so that we may always strive after the better gifts and beware of the perverse interpretation of the Apostle’s words: “The spiritual person judges all things, and is judged by no one” (1 Corinthians 2). Through these words spiritual men sometimes fall, deceived and blinded by their own judgment, into the devil’s snare.

[Col. 0633C] Spiritual temptations must be guarded against no less than carnal ones—indeed, much more carefully and subtly, especially by those who profess the solitary life. For, withdrawn from carnal objects and desires, they would easily dissipate themselves in their thoughts and fall into rash judgments unless they carefully guarded themselves against the midday demon, which lays before them the snares of their own opinions and judgments.

For Satan himself, transforming himself into an angel of light, deceives those who are less cautious and who in this respect trust themselves; and once he has cast them into error, then, having blinded them through their own judgment, he binds them more tightly and finally makes them almost wholly incapable of correction.

[Col. 0633D] These are the wretched steps of descent that spiritual persons construct for themselves when they do not guard sufficiently carefully against their own judgment. We shall remain far from them if we always keep before our eyes the words of Christ our Savior: “Do not judge, and you will not be judged” (Luke 6); and those of D. Paul: “Who are you to judge another’s servant? He stands or falls before his own master” (Romans 14). Likewise: “Do not judge before the time, until the Lord comes, who will bring to light the hidden things of darkness and will reveal the counsels of hearts; and then each person will receive praise from God” (1 Corinthians 4).

Now, therefore, those who wished with such eagerness either to read or to criticize the statutes of our Order will, as we hope, be quiet when they see that we ourselves set everything forth openly and sincerely, sparing ourselves in nothing, concealing nothing, but rather, when occasion permits, reproving ourselves—to the extent that truth, justice, and charity allow.

[Col. 0634A] Far be it from us to claim for ourselves that holiness which is rightly attributed to our first Fathers. We ask only that we be granted what no one who is not an enemy of justice can deny: namely, that the body of the Order and, so to speak, the soul of our institution not be charged with what is owed solely to the faults of individual persons. It will be clear from chapter 77 of these Customs that the Order was not exempt from such faults even in the time of the reverend Father Guigo.

Let them cry out as much as they wish, “Take away, take away,” against transgressors of the Order’s statutes and those who stray from its spirit—we shall not object. But we too shall cry out: “Let them be punished, let them be punished.” For in this way, with no small consolation to us and to all good people, it will become evident that this was done in the Order from the day of its institution down to our own times, as will be shown by the charters and ordinances of the general chapters, which, when occasion offers, we shall append expressly to the ancient statutes, so that these writings, having been made public, may endure in the next generation, and the people who shall be created may praise the Lord, who gave such zeal, unanimity, and steadfastness of purpose to miserable little men so diverse in nation, upbringing, and natural disposition.

[Col. 0634B] This was even at a time when the Church of God, divided into several parts by a lamentable schism, had drawn our Order after it, likewise split into several parts, toward the end of the fourteenth century and the beginning of the fifteenth, until the Council of Pisa was celebrated, as will be said in its place.

This appears to the eyes of the mind as a great miracle wrought by the Lord. When I contemplate it, I am astonished and cry out: “This is the finger of God.” For the earth of the human heart, which of itself produces only thorns and thistles, does not yield fruits like these. Those who read this work in a spirit of piety and charity will judge of the truth of the matter.

Before we proceed to interpret these Customs of our reverend Father Guigo, I wish to give you a few further admonitions, so that through them you may arrive more easily at an understanding of the meaning and words of this most devout writer.

First, it should be noted that he writes in a very concise manner, both to show that in writing too he wishes to observe the laws of silence, striving to cut away superfluous words and to utter only what seems necessary, and because he is writing for observers of the Carthusian way of life. They therefore understood whatever the reverend Father Guigo wished to say from a single—or, so to speak, half—word, and did not need him to express everything in minute detail.

[Col. 0634D] He therefore communicates the Customs only in their essentials to the companions and brothers of the Greater Charterhouse, who had asked this of him, so that the uniformity which had been held in such high regard and continually preserved by diligent effort from the beginning and thereafter in the Order might be introduced.

Second, the fact that many things contained in the ancient statutes are not expressed in the Customs of R. P. Guigo is no reason to accuse them of novelty, since that reverend Father makes no mention of them. Rather, they belong to the manner in which statutes are composed.

[Col. 0635A] As the number of the Order’s houses and persons increased, it became necessary to establish statutes that would turn simple customs into fixed rules, as it were, and bring the actions of many people in various matters into a single harmony and uniform practice, so that they might aim toward one common rule. It was therefore entirely necessary that the expression of individual actions and of the manner in which each was to be performed become more explicit, lest, in this multitude composed through the greater multiplication of individuals, individual persons be given easier access to interpreting and twisting certain matters according to their own judgment.

[Col. 0635B] Everyone can see that this would corrupt uniformity in practice through a distortion of meaning.

Third, that holy man, who was supremely learned in both divine and human letters, sometimes abandoned the elegance of style readily available to him in order to pursue simplicity in writing the Order’s Customs, and thereby to instruct us how greatly we ought to abstain from modes of speaking or writing that give off some scent of ostentation.

Nevertheless, sparks of heavenly and human eloquence, with which he was endowed like glowing bronze, often burst from his pen, as may be seen in that marvelous chapter “On the commendation of the solitary life.” From it we learn how practiced he was at gathering flowers from the field of Sacred Scripture, from which, prudently collected and beautifully woven together, he knew how to compose garlands exhaling a heavenly fragrance.

[Col. 0635C] We are thereby also instructed that we do no harm to Carthusian simplicity if we learn the eloquence of these sacred books, so that, since we already have hope through the consolation of Scripture, we may also strive in speech to pour forth those pure utterances of the Lord, and thus the wish of Blessed Peter the Apostle may be fulfilled in us: “If anyone speaks, let him speak as the words of God” (1 Peter 4).

Fourth, many things are found in the Customs themselves that can be properly understood only by observers of the Carthusian way of life. They are sometimes expressed in sufficiently barbarous language and, as we said above, are not sufficiently explained for their genuine meaning to be grasped by those who do not know Carthusian rites through practice, even if they are otherwise learned and sensible men.

[Col. 0636A] Hence there arises a reason for indulgence toward those who might wish to understand and apply these Customs in certain places according to their own judgment. In this matter, with due respect to them, the apostolic statement could be applied: “Understanding neither what they say nor what they affirm” (1 Timothy 1).

As for the time when R. P. Guigo wrote these Customs, nothing absolutely certain can be assigned. But, reckoning the years from the arrival of our holy Father Bruno at the rocks of Chartreuse, he seems to have written them approximately forty-four or forty-five years after the Order began.

[Col. 0636B] For Saint Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, was still living, as is evident from the text of the Prologue itself. Saint Father Bruno came to the wilderness of Chartreuse with his companions around the year 1084, and from the day of his arrival until his death seventeen years elapsed.

Blessed Lauduinus, one of his companions, presided over the house of Chartreuse for ten years. But Saint Bruno, while living in Calabria, was still alive; indeed, he outlived Blessed Lauduinus, who deservedly belongs among the martyrs, by a full year and nineteen days.

Blessed Lauduinus was succeeded by the reverend Father Petrus Francus, who presided for only two years. He was succeeded by the reverend Father D. John I, who received R. P. Guigo into the Order from the deanery of the Church of Grenoble. Guigo advanced so far that after three or four years he was elected prior of Chartreuse, namely in the twenty-sixth year after the Order’s birth.

[Col. 0636C] If eighteen or nineteen years are added to these twenty-six years, until he, being prior, wrote these Customs, it will be clear that they were written in the forty-fourth or forty-fifth year after the Order’s birth, as we said above.

It also appears from this that R. P. Guigo came to the Order only five or six years after the death of Saint Bruno, and that from his disciples—who had themselves lived with the holy founder—he learned through both their deeds and their words all that he left to posterity in these written Customs. They would not deserve the name of Customs unless they had already been established for many years and approved and confirmed by the practices of those who used them.

With these matters prefaced, let us now come to the subject itself.

## PROLOGUE OF D. GUIGO

[Note: [Col. 0635C]

**PROLOGUE—No. 2. “The Customs of our house …”** What had been instituted by Saint Father Bruno and observed both by him and by his companions in the house—or rather, hermitage—of Chartreuse was faithfully guarded by their successors.

At that time charity and piety served in place of statutes. Moved by them, the successors put into practice what had been handed down and commended by the Fathers. They had not yet committed anything concerning their observance to writing, because their way of life was still, as it were, in its infancy; and the Order’s observance was still being worked out under the anvil and hammer of experience.

They did not regard their humble way of life—as the most devout writer says elsewhere—as that little spring which was destined to grow into a river; indeed, they did not even think about this matter. They imitated the sons of Rechab, for whom what their father had commended and handed down to them served as law and statutes. At that time the Carthusian institution, which the writer everywhere expresses simply by the name of its way of life, consisted solely in tradition.

[Col. 0637B] The matter here, therefore, concerns the Customs to be written by R. P. Guigo, not statutes properly speaking. Why, then, is “Statutes of Guigo” printed in the page headings of the book? Here is the reason.

When the Order had grown and it seemed necessary to establish statutes expressing and committing to writing both external administration, the form of regular discipline, the Carthusian observance—or the manner of austerity and solitary life—and finally the spirit of the Carthusian institution, and handing all these matters over to everyone for observance as a legal institution, R. P. D. Rifferius composed those first statutes which we call ancient.

In them he transcribed everything contained in the Customs of R. P. Guigo, with a very few exceptions, which we shall expressly note, so that it may be clear to everyone how mistaken were those who, on the occasion of the chapter “On Reproof”—which is numbered as the fourth chapter in the second part of those first statutes—might think, contrary to the author’s meaning, that the Order’s decline had already occurred from the beginning.

[Col. 0637C] Thus what under the reverend Father Guigo was initially called simply a custom gradually passed, through the practice of those who used it, into a kind of law, in accordance with the very definition of custom among jurists.

After a certain approval by our holy lord Pope Innocent II, and also after the ordinance of the general chapter celebrated under Saint Anthelm around the year 1143, where it is said that the prescribed customs were to be observed, they had already passed into statutes by the time of the reverend Father Rifferius.

[Col. 0637D] For this reason, when the statutes were printed around the year 1509, the name “statute” was also prefixed to Guigo’s Customs in the page headings, just as it was to the ancient statutes, which had expressly been composed to be genuine constitutions or statutes of the Order, although the title still includes the word “custom.”

**In the same place. “To commit to memory in writing.”** That is, by writing, we have set forth and handed these matters over to human knowledge and the memory of posterity for preservation. This is a monastic expression, adapted more to the understanding and manner of speaking customary at that time than to the rules of pure Latin. Let this be noted once here for all such cases, for the holy man uses similar phrases and words in many places.

**In the same place. “Because we believed that almost everything was contained in the letters of Blessed Jerome …”** Here it becomes clear how freely Saint Bruno and his successors wished to choose and shape their way and manner of life according to what spirit and prudence suggested, rather than binding themselves to specific rules or constitutions that had long before been established in various monastic orders, whether in the East or in the West.

Saint Bruno chose nothing for his manner of life that had not been praised in the writings of Saints Jerome, Benedict, and others; but he did not for that reason bind himself to their rules, although, like a spiritual bee, he gathered from them material from which to compose his own honey and wax.

[Col. 0638C] It cannot therefore rightly be reproached to those who profess his institution that they do not follow these or those institutions and practices of the saints—whether Antony, John Climacus, Benedict, Bernard, or the ancient Eastern Fathers—for these are not their way of life, nor did they choose them for their own observance.

**In the same place. “And we, who might be able to do something of this kind …”** It also appears from this that they were not thinking of establishing a new and distinctive rule, but only proposed to fashion for themselves a certain form of life that was at once eremitical and cenobitical.

Attracted by their example, Bernard of Portes and the others named in the Prologue likewise formed fellowships of pious men bound together in the same kind of life, and each chose hermitages for himself, where they built settlements that are today the Order’s older houses.

[Col. 0638D] **No. 3. “Because it belongs more to be taught than to teach.”** To lie hidden in the concealment of God’s face; always to seek a life in heaven; to love being unknown and counted as nothing by human beings; and to embrace in all things whatever leads to true and profound humility—the root of all virtues and, as it were, the channel of God’s grace—this is the substance and goal of the Carthusian institution.

**No. 4. “But because we ought not resist the prayers of such great men …”** Here you have the form of holy freedom that must be fulfilled, and of obstinacy in one’s own judgment that Carthusians must avoid. You also have how charity and obedience, knowledge and humility can and must be harmonized by us in the state of the solitary life, and how Carthusian simplicity is thereby composed.

Thus a true Carthusian should never seek, at the prompting of his own will, anything that draws him away from the center of the hidden life; but neither should he obstinately avoid anything when the judgment of his superiors urges him to act or speak. This will become still clearer below, where Carthusian obedience is discussed.

**In the same place. “… in which we agree greatly with the others …”** He does not say “entirely,” because in composing the Carthusian divine office, a monastic rite was indeed adopted—twelve psalms, three canticles, twelve lessons, and similar elements—but quite a few things were also added from the rites both of the Church of Lyon and of Grenoble, in whose diocese Chartreuse is situated.

[Col. 0640A] This can be proved from the ancient missals of the Church of Grenoble and from the manner of celebrating Mass then customary there, which are reproduced almost exactly in our own; likewise from the old antiphonaries and prayers which, as is known, were transferred from the Church of Lyon for our use.]

[Col. 0635]

## Here begins the Prologue of the Customs of Lord Guigo, Prior of Chartreuse

1. To our most beloved friends and brothers in Christ, Bernard of Portes, Humbert of Saint-Sulpice, Milo of Majoravia, priors, and all the brothers who serve God with them: Guigo, called prior of Chartreuse, and the brothers who are with him, everlasting salvation in the Lord.

2. Obeying the commands and admonitions of our most dear and reverend Father Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, whose will we are not permitted to resist, we have undertaken to commit the Customs of our house to writing, as your affection has requested more than once [variant: “we undertake”].
