[Col. 0637] We long delayed this task for reasons that, as we think, were reasonable: namely, because we believed that almost everything we customarily practice here in a religious manner was contained either in the letters of Blessed Jerome, or in the Rule of blessed Benedict, or in the other authoritative Scriptures [variant: “other books”]. And we considered ourselves entirely unworthy to do or to be obliged to do something of this kind.

3. In addition, we knew that being taught rather than teaching belonged to the purpose of our humility, and that it was safer to praise the good things of others rather than one’s own, Scripture saying: “Let another praise you, and not your own mouth; a stranger, and not your own lips” (Proverbs 27:2).

[Col. 0639] The Lord likewise commands in the Gospel: “See that you do not perform your righteousness before human beings, in order to be seen by them” (Matthew 6:1).

4. But because we ought not resist the prayers, authority, or affection of such great men, let us say, with the Lord’s help and with His own assistance, what He grants us to say. Let us begin from the more worthy part, namely, the divine office, in which we are found to agree greatly with the other monks, especially in the regular chanting of the Psalter [variant: “we agree”].

## THE CUSTOMS OF D. GUIGO BEGIN

[Col. 0639]

## CHAPTER I. On the divine office

[Note: [Col. 0640A]

**CHAPTER I—Chapter.** This word, by which distinctions of subject matter are marked in our statutes, is now commonly expressed by the word “chapter.” But out of reverence for the ancient Fathers we have retained this word in the Order, as well as other similar usages. Indeed, we have retained even certain modes of pronunciation that were expressly designated in the ancient statutes, so highly has steadfast adherence to venerable antiquity and stability always been valued among us.

**No. 1. “From the Kalends.”** This entire chapter is found transcribed in the first part of the ancient Statutes, chapter 21, nos. 8 and 9. There is no difference except that what is said concisely here is explained more fully there, as the purpose of composing statutes requires. We still observe precisely the same practice.]

[Col. 0639]

1. From the Kalends of November until the octave of Pentecost, every day, except on solemnities of twelve lessons, we say three lessons with three responsories. We observe the following arrangement: if the Kalends of the aforesaid month fall before Thursday, we begin the responsories and the prophets on the preceding Sunday; on the following day and thereafter we recite three lessons with responsories from the same books.

2. But if they fall on Thursday or later, we begin those same prophets with their responsories on the following Sunday. We spend the days between the Kalends and Sunday in two ways: one with three lessons, on account of the martyrs, and another with one lesson.

## CHAPTER II. Also on the same subject

[Note: [Col. 0640B]

**CHAPTER II.** The same chapter is found transcribed in part I of the ancient Statutes, chapter 2, nos. 3, 5, 6, 8, and 9.

**No. 2. “The Gloria in excelsis, remaining silent until …”** From this passage and others to be noted below it will be clear that those who think that Mass was formerly rarely celebrated by our members in the Order are mistaken.

It is certain that at that time they had only one altar, and rarely two. This is proved by the charter of the general chapter of 1250, where it says: “Regarding the acceptance of two altars, the consent of the communities is to be sought.” We therefore think that this rarity applied not to conventual Masses, but only to private Masses, which were celebrated by monk-priests only on the days prescribed by the statutes.

This entire chapter was therefore transferred into the ancient statutes.]

[Col. 0639]

1. From the Saturday adjoining the first Sunday of Advent until the second weekday after the octave of Easter, we omit the commemoration of the Cross; but we omit the commemoration of Saint Mary until the first day after the octave of Epiphany.

2. On the aforesaid Sunday, after finishing Ezekiel and the twelve prophets—for we read Daniel in the refectory—we begin Isaiah and continue with it until the vigil of the Nativity. Throughout this entire period we use the chapters, verses, and prayers belonging to Advent, remaining silent about the Gloria in excelsis until the first Mass on the Nativity.

[Col. 0641] 3. We begin the antiphons “O Wisdom,” together with the other six, and the proper antiphons for the morning praises in such a way that they are completed on the day before the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity.

4. Each Sunday of Advent is adorned with its own responsories and antiphons at the morning praises; on the other days as well, we always say Advent antiphons at the Magnificat and Benedictus.

## CHAPTER III. Also on the foregoing subject

[Note: [Col. 0641A]

**CHAPTER III. Also on the foregoing subject.** That is, on the same matter that has already been treated above.]

The text of this chapter is found reproduced word for word in chapter 3, part I of the ancient Statutes, no. 8; chapter 11, part I, no. 10; chapter 19 of the same part, no. 7; and chapter 27, no. 5. The same matter concerning sleep is reported in chapter 34 of that part.

Thus, this entire chapter was incorporated into the ancient Statutes, and we now observe precisely the same provisions, except for the daytime sleep, which has been abolished.

[Col. 0641B] No. 1. “In the first month,” etc. From this it is proved that March was still then regarded as the first month, since the seasonal fasts commonly occur in that month.

No. 2. “We celebrate Mass.” Here mention is still made of a Mass celebrated communally, and it is listed among the divine offices assigned to particular days.

[Col. 0641]

1. On the Saturday of the seasonal fasts we sing Sext and Mass in the church, with five lessons, excluding the Epistle, and then None without interruption; and we do the same during the other similar fasts, except that in the first month, after None, we do so on account of Lent.

2. On the Saturday within the octave of Pentecost we celebrate that Mass between Terce and Sext, and in the seventh month after Sext; we defer None, to be said in the cells, until after sleep.

## CHAPTER IV. Likewise concerning the foregoing matter

[Note: [Col. 0642A]

**CHAPTER IV.**—The text of this chapter, up to the words “The following Saturday,” etc., is reproduced word for word in chapter 5 of part I of the ancient Statutes, no. 56; chapter 7, no. 1; chapter 9, nos. 1 and 2; and chapter 10, nos. 1, 2, 3, and 4.

No. 5. “Sext, Mass, and None.” Here too mention is made of Mass as being celebrated in an orderly manner.

No. 8. “The following Saturday lacks a Mass.” This passage is expressed as follows in part I, chapter 11, no. 1, of the ancient Statutes: “It lacks its proper Mass, and the Mass of Blessed Mary is sung in the community.” These words express more clearly the meaning of Guigo concerning the Mass of the fast, which is now also omitted in our Missals, while the celebration of the Mass of the Blessed Virgin Mary is assigned to that day.

No. 9. “On this Saturday,” up to the words “if there are priests.” The same text is reproduced word for word in chapter 11 of part I of the ancient Statutes, nos. 2, 3, 5, and 10.

[Col. 0643A] No. 12. “If there is an abundance of priests, or if those who are present are not prevented by some reasonable cause.” These words are not found reproduced in the ancient Statutes. From them, and from the condition added here, it may be inferred that, although not all the monks in Guigo’s time had yet been promoted to the priesthood, there were nevertheless several priests, and all were suitable for the clerical state, as will be evident from chapter 73 of these Customs. From the omission of these words—omitted from the ancient Statutes—one may infer only that, when the ancient Statutes were composed, priests celebrated among us more frequently than in Guigo’s time. Hence it may have seemed almost superfluous to retain that condition. The reasonable cause that constitutes an impediment will be discussed in its proper place.

[Col. 0643B] The remaining provisions are reported in nearly the same words in the first part of the ancient Statutes, chapters 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 17, 18, and 19.

No. 13. “Partly in the church, partly in the refectory.” The custom begins to become apparent which has always prevailed in the Order: that the Bible should be read through completely each year, whether in the church, in the refectory, or at the conference.

Ibid. “Because of the shortness of the nights.” What he says here about the shortness of the nights refers to the vigils, which formerly were arranged in the Order according to the length or [Col. 0644A] shortness of the nights; the lessons at Matins were made longer or shorter according to the character of the nights. The reference here is to the end of Lent, at which time the days are known to become longer and the nights shorter. These vigils will be discussed below in their proper place.

No. 19. “Content with nine … lessons.” By these words he wishes to express that on these days alone our stricter vigils are somewhat relaxed and the lamp is extinguished at Benedictus; thus, on those three days—which are a very small part of the entire year—our Matins conform to the usage of the Church.

No. 20. “Each of us performs the washing.” This can be understood only of the Carthusians, and it signifies the custom preserved in the Order up to the present day on Maundy Thursday: that we privately wash and cleanse our feet in our cells before coming to chapter, where they are to be washed by the prior. Guigo calls this “performing the washing.”

[Col. 0644B] No. 24. “On this day after dinner, or … not returning to the cloister.” Here he obscurely indicates the custom of the conferences held in the cloister. He does not express it fully because the matter was common knowledge to those to whom he was writing. This also reveals how Guigo was sometimes content to hint at a matter rather than explain it at length. What these conferences were, and how they were to be conducted, is set out at length under the special title of chapter [Col. 0645A] 35 of the first part of the ancient Statutes, as the purpose of composing statutes required. The monks assembled together in the cloister on appointed days and did other things that will be discussed in their proper place. Here we merely note that later Fathers after Guigo, who dealt with the conferences in the ancient Statutes, should not be charged with introducing anything new on the basis of this passage: they merely explain and confirm at length the ancient custom of the conferences indicated here. It is expressed more clearly, though briefly, below in chapter 9.

No. 28. “On Saturday, after singing in the cell.” That is, after completing the office, since among us divine offices were never sung outside the choir; and the most devout writer uses the word “to sing” almost everywhere in the sense of “to complete.”

[Col. 0645B] No. 29. “With two or three monks assisting the priest.” It appears from this that at that time they sang this Mass only on a simple reciting tone; now all the monks assist at this Mass and sing it with musical notation.

[Col. 0646A] No. 31. “On Monday, etc., two candles, etc.” Here the usage of solemn feasts begins to appear. In the ancient Statutes and old books of the Order they are therefore called “candle feasts,” because candles were lit at Matins and Vespers of those feasts as a sign of solemn joy.

No. 33. “On Tuesday of the Rogation Days we eat once, but we prepare food.” In the ancient Statutes, part I, chapter 17, no. 6, we read: “On Tuesday and Monday of the Rogation Days we eat once, but on Tuesday it is permitted to use cheese and eggs.” To understand what Guigo means by the word “food preparation” here and elsewhere, one should know that it was then customary among us—and this continued for several centuries—for the monks to cook part of their food in their own cells: namely, portions (*offae*) and certain vegetables; and only bread, wine, and what in many passages of Guigo’s Customs is called *pitantia* were supplied to them by the cook and the common dispenser. They therefore always prepared this food for themselves, except on days of abstinence and on refectory days, when they ate together in the refectory. The passage of the ancient Statutes expresses [Col. 0647A] only what is implicit here, but the same matter is sufficiently expressed elsewhere in Guigo’s Customs, where it is explained when the use of eggs and cheese was permitted.

The same provisions contained in this chapter are still observed, indeed more strictly, because the custom of assembling together in the cloister for the conferences has been abolished.]

[Col. 0641]

1. From the fourth day before the Nones of January until Septuagesima, we read the Epistles of the blessed apostle Paul.

2. From the day after the octave of Epiphany until Septuagesima, we say the ferial responsories, beginning on the first Sunday after them with *Domine, ne in ira tua* (“O Lord, rebuke me not in your anger”).

3. On the Saturday preceding the first Sunday of Septuagesima, we say *Alleluia* only at Vespers, and likewise at Mass, which we shall resume on Holy Saturday.

4. From that Sunday until Passion Sunday we read the Heptateuch both in the church and in the refectory, singing *In principio* (“In the beginning”) on the first and second Sundays, and the customary responsories on the other Sundays.

5. On the beginning of the fast we change the nocturnal and daytime chapters and the prayers; we sing Sext, Mass, and None in the church.

6. On this day we cover the crosses, to be uncovered on Good Friday.

7. Before the beginning of Mass, ashes are brought to the priest to be blessed after the confession. After they have been blessed and sprinkled with holy water, all in turn receive them, kneeling before the priest, who says: “Recognize, O man, that you are dust, and to dust you will return” (*Recognosce, homo, quia pulvis es, et in pulverem reverteris*). Meanwhile the others sing these antiphons: “Hear us, O Lord” (*Exaudi nos, Domine*); “By the vestibule,” etc. When these have been completed, the priest adds: “The Lord be with you,” and the following prayer: “Grant us, O Lord” (*Concede nobis, Domine*). At the same hour on the two following days we celebrate Masses.

8. The following Saturday has no Mass.

9. On this Saturday we change the Sunday chapters at Vespers.

10. We say the chapter *Domine, miserere nostri* (“Lord, have mercy on us”) at Prime on feast days in Lent and Advent.

11. From the following Monday until Maundy Thursday, we perform the seven psalms with the litany daily in the cells after Prime, except on feasts of twelve lessons.

[Col. 0643] 12. We sing None and Mass, with the Lenten preface, and Vespers in the church every day, provided there is an adequate number of priests, or those who are present are not prevented by some reasonable cause.

13. On Passion Sunday we change the chapters and suspend the customary suffrages until the Monday after the octave of Easter. From that day until Maundy Thursday we read Jeremiah partly in the church and partly in the refectory, because of the shortness of the nights. During this period, unless a solemnity of twelve lessons intervenes, we do not say the *Gloria* at the invitatory, the responsories, or the introit.

14. On a feast of three lessons we make only a commemoration.

15. On the Saturday joined to Palm Sunday we do not celebrate Mass.

16. At Vespers we use the chapter *Hoc sentite* (“Have this mind”), and the responsory *Fratres mei* (“My brothers”), until Maundy Thursday.

17. On Palm Sunday, after Terce has been sung and the priest has put on the chasuble, the branches are blessed after the confession and, once sprinkled with blessed water, are distributed to everyone by the priest. Meanwhile the antiphon *Collegerunt* (“They gathered together”) is sung, followed by “The Lord be with you” and this prayer: “Almighty and everlasting God” (*Omnipotens sempiterne Deus*).

18. If the Annunciation or the feast of Saint Benedict falls after Wednesday of this week, we make no further mention of it.

19. On Maundy Thursday we celebrate a feast, content with nine lessons, as the clergy are, and extinguish the lamp at *Benedictus*, imitating the custom of the Church to this very limited extent.

20. We assemble at Prime; after the chapter we say Terce in the cells and each of us performs the washing, also singing Sext there. We celebrate None, Mass, and Vespers in the church.

21. At Mass, an entire host of the Lord’s Body is preserved for the priest to consume on Good Friday.

22. After the meal, all the monks and lay brothers, insofar as possible, assemble in chapter for the Mandatum. There the feet of all are washed by the prior or by someone to whom he has entrusted this task; the feet of the prior himself are washed, dried, and kissed by the one who is first in order, while the others sing the appropriate antiphons. Then, while the prior pours water, everyone’s hands are washed, a candle is lit, and the Gospel is read. All remain standing until the words “When he had reclined again” (*Cum recubuisset iterum*).

23. From that point we hear the same reading seated, until it is said: “Rise, let us go from here” (*Surgite, eamus hinc*). Then, with the deacon leading, we go to the refectory, where we hear the remainder of the reading seated. When it has been completed, wine is served to each person by the ministers. After the priest has given the blessing, we drink and depart. After this the altar is stripped.

24. On this day after dinner, or after the Mandatum, the brothers prepare the readings and responsories for the following two days, as though they would not return to the cloister until after the meal on Saturday.

[Col. 0645] 25. Compline is rung later.

26. On Good Friday we kneel and say *Miserere mei, Deus* (“Have mercy on me, O God”).

27. Throughout all these three days, each person says the prayers silently at every Hour, content with this one prayer: *Respice, quaesumus, Domine* (“Look upon us, we beseech you, O Lord”). We carry out almost the entire office according to the custom of the clergy. We devote ourselves to the Psalter, omitting other works; the church is cleaned by the sacristan with the assistance of the lay brothers. After the signal has been given somewhat later than usual, Sext and None are said consecutively in the cells. Meanwhile the priest vests, and after the signal is given again we assemble in the church and celebrate the office according to custom.

A reading precedes, followed by the tract and the prayer *Deus a quo et Judas* (“O God, from whom Judas”); then another reading and tract; then the Passion, without “The Lord be with you,” followed by the prayers. When these have been completed, the priest removes his chasuble, we uncover our feet, and reverently kiss the cross brought by the deacon, each one saying inwardly: “We adore you, O Christ, and we bless you, because by your holy cross you have redeemed the world” (*Adoramus te, Christe, et benedicimus tibi, quia per sanctam crucem tuam redemisti mundum*).

Meanwhile the community sings the antiphon *Nos autem gloriari oportet* (“But it is fitting for us to glory”), and the responsories *Popule meus* (“My people”) and *Expandi manus meas* (“I have spread out my hands”). After the cross has been returned to its former place, the priest washes his hands, puts on his chasuble, and receives from the deacon the chalice with wine and the Lord’s Body placed upon it. The deacon begins the Communion: *Hoc corpus* (“This Body”). When these have been placed on the altar, after a brief silence he begins: “Let us pray, instructed by saving precepts” (*Oremus, praeceptis salutaribus moniti*). The *Agnus Dei* is not said, nor on Holy Saturday. After the priest has received the Lord’s Body, we say Vespers alternately and in silence.

28. On Saturday, after Sext and None have been sung in the cells and while the priest is vesting, we assemble in the church. After four readings, three tracts, and a very short litany have been given beforehand, we solemnly begin Mass with *Kyrie eleison*. We say *Gloria in excelsis Deo* (“Glory to God in the highest”), light two candles, receive the kiss of peace, but do not burn incense. When these things have been completed, after the bell has been struck, we sing Vespers most solemnly according to monastic custom.

29. On the holy day of Easter, between Matins and Prime, with all the lay brothers present and receiving Communion insofar as their obediences permit, Mass is sung with the same solemnity customary on Sundays, with two or three monks assisting the priest.

30. At the principal Mass the community receives Communion, as do any lay brothers who are to communicate.

31. We observe all these four days with the greatest solemnity. On Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday we light two candles at Lauds and offer incense. On Wednesday the lay brothers depart. On Thursday, Friday, and Saturday, while singing Sext in the church, we eat together. During the first four days of the weeks of Easter and Pentecost we celebrate no feast of a saint at all. On the final three days, if a feast of three lessons occurs, we make only a commemoration; but if one of twelve lessons occurs, we celebrate it in full. We sing the Easter responsories for fourteen days.

32. We read the Acts of the Apostles for three weeks, then the Catholic Epistles until the Ascension; and from the Ascension until Pentecost we read only the Apocalypse, partly in the church and partly in the refectory.

33. On Tuesday of the Rogation Days we eat once, but prepare food.

[Col. 0647] 34. On the vigil of the Ascension we sing Sext and Mass in the church; we celebrate the Ascension with the greatest solemnity.

35. On the vigil of Pentecost we say None and Mass in the church, and observe the entire week as we do Easter Week, except that on Wednesday and Saturday we sing Sext immediately after Mass. During this week we observe the Ember fasts.

## CHAPTER V. Likewise concerning the foregoing matter

[Note: [Col. 0647A]

**CHAPTER V.**—Everything contained here is also found in the ancient Statutes, chapter 21 of part I, nos. 1, 2, 3, and 4; likewise chapter 20, no. 1; chapter 21, no. 13; chapter 30, no. 1; chapter 5, no. 42; and chapter 4, no. 4.

No. 7. “If there is to be one meal, but if otherwise, twice.” That is, if it is a day on which food is taken twice, with supper served just as dinner is, so that there are two meals. Hence the custom became established in the Order of calling days on which there is no fast “days of two meals.”

No. 8. “The Lord reigns,” etc., at Lauds. This passage indicates that he is speaking only of Lauds, since elsewhere he uses these words, namely, “at Lauds.”]

[Col. 0647]

1. After this week, on whatever day a feast occurs, we begin the Books of Kings, while the responsories for the same history begin on the following Sunday.

2. From the Kalends of August until the Kalends of September, we read Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, the Book of Wisdom, and as much of Ecclesiasticus as time permits.

3. From the Kalends of September we read Job for two or three weeks, and during the following two weeks Tobit, Judith, and Esther.

4. From the Kalends of October until November, the Books of Maccabees.

5. Throughout this entire period—that is, from Pentecost until the Kalends of November—we are content with one lesson, unless a feast intervenes, as are the other monks.

6. We never omit the lessons of the History because of a feast of three lessons, except on the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity; on the three days after the feast of the Innocents; during the weeks of Easter and Pentecost; and during the octave of the Assumption of Blessed Mary.

7. Accordingly, only the invitatory and versicles, the responsories and prayers, and Lauds, as well as the antiphon at Prime and also at Terce and Sext if there is to be one meal—but at Terce alone if there are to be two—are said according to such a feast.

8. We say *Dominus regnavit* (“The Lord reigns”) daily at Lauds not only on such feasts, but also from the Nativity until the octave of Epiphany, and from Easter until the octave of Pentecost.

## CHAPTER VI. Likewise concerning the foregoing matter

[Note: [Col. 0647B]

**CHAPTER VI.**—The same matter is reported in chapter 2 of part I of the ancient Statutes, no. 16. We now make some processions, both as prescribed by the Church, such as on the solemnity of Corpus Christi, and sometimes out of devotion; this pertains more to the increase of piety than to a defect.]

[Col. 0647]

And this must be understood: on no solemnity do we make a procession, nor do we transfer any feast or vigil.

## CHAPTER VII. Concerning the Sunday office

[Note: [Col. 0648A]

**CHAPTER VII.**—No. 1. “Every Saturday after None,” etc. In the ancient Statutes, chapter 35, it reads as follows: “Every Saturday, and on the vigils of feasts of twelve lessons, and on the vigil of Maundy Thursday.” Guigo likewise expresses the same thing below, chapter 9, no. 3. Here, however, he mentions only Saturday, in order to indicate that the conference was held first on Saturday, followed by sacramental confession.

No. 2. “And because throughout the whole week we keep silence in the cells,” [Col. 0648B] etc. Understand: unless an occasion should arise on which, according to Guigo’s Customs, silence is permitted to be broken, as will be noted below. The same is reported in chapter 11 of part II of the ancient Statutes.

Ibid. “To the prior or to those appointed by him.” It is clear from this that at that time certain men were appointed to hear confessions, as is done now, and penitents were given the freedom to choose whom they wished.

[Col. 0649A] No. 4. “If Mass is to be sung on that day,” etc. This passage appears obscure. Yet it does not concern the conventual Mass, but the private Mass that was customarily celebrated on that day in addition to the principal, or conventual, Mass. This is sufficiently proved by the words that follow: “After this the priest, at the appropriate time.” From these it is clear that what was said above is entirely distinct from the conventual Mass, whose celebration and manner of celebration, as well as the offices to be said after Mass, are fixedly prescribed. This is further proved by no. 4 of chapter 8, where it is said: “We sing the second Mass after Matins, at daybreak, as is customary on Sundays.”

Ibid. 4. “That interval, insofar as illness or necessity permits, for spiritual progress . . .” From this it begins to become evident—and it will become clearer from what follows—that the first founders of our way of life always held discretion in high esteem, as especially necessary for the solitary life. They wished to guard themselves and their successors against every excess and extremity, so that everything might be adapted to human strength assisted by heavenly grace, and to the condition of the persons involved, as they frequently intimate. They therefore wish the measure of spiritual exercises to be adapted to the measure of illness or necessity.

No. 8. “After leaving the refectory … immediately None,” etc. We now observe this only on non-feast days within the octave of the Nativity of Christ. On other feasts occurring during the same period we make the same interval that Guigo later specifies. “From which,” etc.

[Col. 0649C] Ibid. “From then throughout the whole summer, a shorter or longer period is given to rest according to the length of the days.” From the Purification until Easter, an interval between dinner and None is said to be provided, and the activity to which that interval is assigned is specified. Then it adds: “From then throughout the whole summer,” etc.—that is, from Easter until the Kalends of October, as may be inferred from chapter 29—a daytime sleep is arranged between dinner and None. Our monks piously observed this sleep as a regular observance, and so strictly that Guigo, speaking of it in chapter 29, no. 5, says: “For we are not merely admonished, but commanded, during the hours assigned to rest, to devote great attention to sleep.” From this it is clear how great was the discretion of the Fathers, who did not wish anything to be taken away by personal choice from those things they knew to be necessary for preserving the strength both of body and soul.

With regard to the longer or shorter period to be devoted to sleep, some prescription undoubtedly existed by which all could regulate themselves uniformly. Yet we have found nothing written about this matter, and therefore think it was left to tradition, as certainly happened in many other cases. Let abstinence from meat, even in illness, serve as an example; Guigo makes no mention of it. Moreover, that daytime sleep, which had been regulated by the Statutes, was abolished among us long ago, at the time when the order of the vigils was changed, as will be said in its proper place. It was granted in summer so as to make up for the shorter period assigned to sleep at night because of the shortening of the nights. For after Matins they never returned to bed; and just as the nights gradually lengthen and shorten, so the period of daytime sleep followed the course of the nights, becoming shorter or longer, so that the time allotted for sleep by night and by day would be equal and would come to approximately the same total. In winter, however, that alternating arrangement of daytime sleep was unnecessary, since the long nights provided enough time for sufficient sleep [Col. 0650C] without dividing sleep, as will become apparent from what is said below.

No. 9. “After None … to speak about useful matters.” It is therefore evident that their silence was not perpetual, and that conversation had been customary in the Order from the beginning. Thus a time for speaking and a time for silence had always been observed among us. Indeed, at that time they were permitted to do what is not permitted now: to ask for and receive several things from the cook.

[Col. 0651A] Ibid. “Vegetables, salt, and other things of this kind.” From the words “and other things,” it appears that the monks were then able to ask the cook-brother for and receive several things not specified in these Customs. From these they could prepare for themselves in their cells the food preparation mentioned above, in chapter 4, at the end, and season certain foods for themselves.

No. 10. “After supper, individual flat cakes.” What that flat cake was, and from what grain it was made, will be explained below in chapter 34, no. 2. Here it is in no way said that the flat cake was given for the whole week, as some have judged. It was merely a pious ceremony introduced for the purpose of honoring more fully, by this act of begging, the poverty that we have vowed, and of declaring that we are Christ’s beggars. This ceremony [Col. 0651B] is still fully preserved. This is clearly proved by chapter 31, no. 2, and chapter 46, no. 1, where mention is made of asking for and receiving bread.

Furthermore, all the matters contained in the present chapter 7 are [Col. 0652A] reported in the ancient Statutes almost word for word: chapter 35 of part I, no. 1; chapter 11 of part II, no. 1; chapter 20 of part I, no. 12; chapter 34, no. 3; chapter 43, no. 5; chapter 32, no. 3; chapter 34, nos. 12, 13, 3, 7, 10, and 9. Likewise chapter 6, no. 6; chapter 17, no. 19; and chapter 5, no. 43. Let the reader not be troubled because here we cite the passages of the ancient Statutes in an inverted order. This is done so that we may follow the order of composition observed by Guigo and thus make comparison of the passages with one another more easily.

It is therefore evident that nothing contained here was abrogated by the ancient Statutes. These provisions are still fully observed among us, indeed more strictly, since permission to sleep during the day has been taken away from us; likewise the permission to speak with the cook and to ask him for and receive the ingredients of some food; and finally the freedom to prepare food for ourselves in the cell.]

[Col. 0647]

1. Every Saturday after None we assemble in the cloister; we review the lessons and whatever else is necessary.

2. And because throughout the whole week we maintain silence in the cells, we confess our sins to the prior or to those appointed by him.

3. If new responsories are to be begun, we sing the great responsory at Vespers.

[Col. 0649] 4. On Sunday, after Prime, we hold chapter. Then, when the brothers have returned to their cells, if Mass is to be sung on that day—that is, if the priest or priests are not prevented by some reasonable cause—the signal is immediately rung; otherwise it is deferred until Terce is to be said. The interval is assigned to spiritual progress, insofar as illness or necessity permits.

5. After this, when the priest has returned to the church at the appropriate time, he vests. When the signal has been rung with a third [variant: “threefold”] stroke, water is blessed in the presence of all. As the priest sprinkles it, he goes around the altar; he sprinkles the monks before the altar and the lay brothers at the entrance of the choir, while the others sing the antiphon *Asperges me* (“You will sprinkle me”). Returning to the lectern, he adds the prayer *Ostende nobis, Domine, misericordiam tuam* (“Show us, O Lord, your mercy”), followed by “The Lord be with you” and this prayer: *Exaudi nos, Domine, sancte Pater* (“Hear us, O Lord, holy Father”). Then he begins Terce, which is followed by Mass.

6. We sing *Gloria in excelsis Deo* (“Glory to God in the highest”) on all solemnities except Advent and Septuagesima.

7. We say *Credo in unum Deum* (“I believe in one God”) both on Sundays and on other days, except on the feasts of confessors and martyrs and on the three days of Easter and Pentecost.

8. After Mass, carrying holy water to the cells, we make a short interval. Then, when the signal has been rung, we return to the church and sing Sext; and so we proceed to the refectory to receive food for souls and bodies alike. From the Kalends of November until the Purification of Blessed Mary, we sing None immediately upon leaving the refectory. From that day until Easter, the interval that we make there—that is, between dinner and None—is assigned to reading or to similar exercises. From then throughout the whole summer, a shorter or longer period is given to rest according to the length of the days.

[Col. 0651] 9. After None we assemble in the cloister to speak about useful matters. During this period we ask the sacristan for and receive ink, parchment, pens, chalk, and books either to be read or copied; from the cook we ask for and receive vegetables, salt, and other things of this kind.

10. After supper, receiving individual flat cakes as Christ’s beggars, we return to our cells.

11. On all similar feasts we proceed in almost the same way.

12. On Sundays within the octaves of the Nativity, Epiphany, or Ascension of the Lord, we say the antiphons, responsories, versicles, and the first eight lessons from those solemnities, and the final four from homilies on the Sunday Gospels. We also read the Gospel itself after *Te Deum laudamus* (“We praise you, O God”); the antiphons at *Benedictus* and *Magnificat*, the prayer, and the Mass are those of Sunday. Afterwards, however, a commemoration of the solemnities is made.

The same is done on the Sunday that falls between the octave of the Lord’s Nativity and Epiphany, except that we also read the first eight Sunday lessons—that is, from the Epistles of the blessed Paul—and we make no commemoration of the Nativity.

13. Only a commemoration is made of Saint Sylvester. But concerning those feasts that we celebrate with a certain special dignity, we think that something should likewise be said separately.

## CHAPTER VIII. Likewise concerning the divine office

[Note: [Col. 0652B]

**CHAPTER VIII.**—Everything contained in this chapter is reported almost word for word in the ancient Statutes, [Col. 0653A] chapter 14, no. 1 of part II; likewise part I, chapter 4, nos. 4 and 10; chapter 5, nos. 2, 3, 19, and 38; and chapter 32, no. 1; chapter 8, no. 4.

The ancient Statutes add only this condition concerning the abstinences from bread and water to be observed on these vigils: unless they fall on feasts of twelve lessons. This circumstance is not explicitly mentioned in Guigo’s Customs, but it is sufficiently implied by chapter 52, no. 1.

Moreover, we still observe the same provisions, except for the abstinences from bread and water, the manner—and indeed the necessity—of whose dispensation will be discussed in its proper place.]

[Col. 0651]

1. Accordingly, we observe the vigils of All Saints, the Lord’s Nativity, Easter, the Ascension, Pentecost, Saint John, the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and the Assumption of Blessed Mary with bread and water; and we continue the Masses by adding Sext in summer and None in winter. We prepare the altar; at Vespers, Matins, Mass, and again Vespers we light two candles and burn incense.

2. On the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity, however, we do not kneel at Lauds; we say *Dominus regnavit* (“The Lord reigns”) and remain silent during *Miserere mei, Deus* (“Have mercy on me, O God”); we light two candles at Mass, but do not burn incense, and receive the kiss of peace.

3. If a Sunday falls on this vigil, from the versicle before the Gospel onward we say the entire office from the vigil, making only a commemoration of Sunday. We celebrate Masses in the same way on the vigils of Easter and Pentecost.

4. At Matins we read the final four lessons from the Gospels. We celebrate the first Mass with the greatest solemnity between the nocturn and Lauds; we sing the second after Matins, at daybreak, as is customary on Sundays. The lay brothers receive Communion at this Mass, and a commemoration of Saint Anastasia is also made.

5. At the principal Mass the community receives Communion, and all the monks receive the kiss of peace from the priest and from one another. We do the same on all such feasts, except the Circumcision of the Lord, the Nativity of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, the Dedication, and Saint Michael. We celebrate the following three days in almost the same way. On the fourth day the lay brothers depart, as at Easter and Pentecost.

6. On the remaining three days we say Sext in the church and make dinner and supper together.

7. We celebrate the Circumcision, Epiphany, Purification, Annunciation, Ascension, Nativity of Saint John, the Nativity of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, Assumption, Dedication, Nativity of Blessed Mary ever-Virgin, and the feast of the angels with a similar rite.

8. At the Purification of Blessed Mary, before Mass and after the confession, we monks—and the lay brothers who are present—receive blessed candles from the priest’s hand [Col. 0653], singing the antiphon *Lumen ad revelationem gentium* (“A light for revelation to the Gentiles”) and the Gospel *Nunc dimittis* (“Now you dismiss”), repeating the antiphon after each versicle. “The Lord be with you” follows, together with the prayer *Exaudi, quaesumus, Domine* (“Hear us, we beseech you, O Lord”), and then Mass. We offer the candles after the Gospel.

## CHAPTER IX. How often we are shaved each year

[Note: [Col. 0653A]

**CHAPTER IX.**—No. 1. “Six times a year.” The same provision is found in the ancient Statutes, chapter 15 of part II, no. 16; and from chapter 28 of the present Customs it appears that each person had a razor for his head.

No. 2. “On the vigils of the blessed,” etc. The same is reported in chapter 14 of the same part II: “If it is such a day”—that is, if it falls on a day when preparing food is permitted, and not on one of the days assigned to abstinence, which are noted in the present Customs.

Ibid. “We do not sing Masses.” This is omitted in the ancient Statutes. Whether it should be understood of both the principal Mass and private Masses—since, on the specified days, which were assigned to fasting, private Masses were omitted in Guigo’s time—there is some reason for doubt, especially because of the expression “we do not sing,” which appears capable of applying only to the conventual Mass. Yet, as we noted above at the end of chapter 4, Guigo commonly uses this expression [Col. 0653C] also in the sense of “we complete” or “we say.”

It may therefore be understood of private Masses, since even during the Lenten fast a conventual Mass—that is, the principal Mass—was celebrated every day, as is proved by chapter 4, no. 12. It is nevertheless more probable that on these days they celebrated the conventual Mass only when a proper Mass was assigned by the Missal then in use. Masses for the dead were also celebrated conventually, as will be clearly seen in other passages.]

3. “On the others, etc., nor do we say Mass.” Here there is an opportunity for easy error unless what follows is prudently harmonized with what precedes; one might then conclude that in the time of Reverend Father Guigo conventual Mass was not celebrated even on feast days with twelve lessons. We believe that this conflicts with the truth, since it is clearly evident from the passages cited both above and below that among us the principal Mass was frequently celebrated even on ordinary days. We therefore think that this must be understood of private Masses, from which at that time they commonly abstained even on those feasts with twelve lessons, though not always, as will appear below from no. 1 of chapter 14.

This abstention from celebrating Masses was not approved by the ancient statutes, and therefore the matter was subsequently arranged in a better way: for the celebration of Masses contributes to the increase of devotion and spiritual exercise. From the ancient custom of the Order, also recorded in old manuscripts, the calendars note a Mass beneath the feasts of the saints entered there as to be celebrated with only three lessons. This distinguishes such feasts, which have a conventual Mass of the feast, from others, which do not. Nothing similar, however, is noted either for solemnities, chapter feasts, or feasts with twelve lessons, the last of which are equivalent to double feasts. It is certain, moreover, that they would not omit conventual Mass either on days of solemnities or on days of chapter feasts. It may therefore be concluded that all these feasts equally had both a proper Mass and a conventual Mass, as we see universally observed in the Church concerning double feasts.

**[Col. 0654A]**

**The same section, no. 3. “Only on the vigil, after None.”** There you have clearly expressed the practice of holding commemorations on those same days, which are specified in the ancient statutes. From this you will perceive that the ancient statutes set down in an orderly and explicit manner what had been written in the Customs of Reverend Father Guigo only here and there, briefly, and as if implicitly. You will thereby have proof of what we said about this in the Prologue.

Why is shaving now performed more frequently among us? This concerns the greater reverence now shown in the celebration of Masses, which is more frequent among us than in the Order’s earliest times, as will be seen in its proper place. But from the very multiplication of shavings, those who wish to call the matter into doubt will easily learn by their own experience that the rigor of our observance has rather increased than diminished.]

**[Col. 0653]**

1. Six times a year we are shaved while silence is observed: on the vigils of Easter, Pentecost, the Assumption, All Saints, Christmas, and at the beginning of the fast.

2. On the vigils of the blessed James, Lawrence, Bartholomew, Matthew, Simon and Jude, and Andrew, we do indeed eat once, but, if it is such a day, we prepare the kitchen and do not sing Masses.

3. On the other feasts with twelve lessons, on which we do not hold chapter, nor say Mass, we assemble in the cloister only on the vigil, after None, for the commemoration.

## CHAPTER X. What sort of guests are to be admitted into the choir

**[Note: [Col. 0655A]]**

**CHAPTER X—No. 1. “Into our choir, etc.”** Since entry into the choir was at that time connected with permission to break silence through ordinary conversation with certain guests, it is not surprising that persons who might enter the choir were selected. Otherwise silence would have been endangered, and for this reason other persons were rigorously barred from entering the choir.

In the present circumstances, when permission to have ordinary conversation with guests has been abolished, we do not allow everyone indiscriminately to enter the choir, but we do not prohibit it with the same rigor. Formerly that entry belonged to personal regular observance, because of the guardianship of silence; now that permission to converse has been removed, it belongs merely to external propriety, which, with due regard to circumstances and reasons, can be relaxed without any injury to regular observance. By personal observance I mean practices that in themselves tend to mortify the flesh and break one’s own will.

**No. 2. “To take someone aside . . . unless the prior gives permission, etc.”** It is therefore evident that in the time of Reverend Father Guigo, as is still observed today, outsiders could converse privately with us only after first asking the prior for permission and obtaining it—not by our own initiative. It is likewise still observed that secular persons must obtain permission from the prior before they may be admitted by us into a cell for conversation.

That in those earliest times outsiders could also be received into our cells is evident from the example of Saint Bruno himself. When both the holy bishop Hugh and the most devout prior of Saint Lawrence were, in turn, taking away the small daily occupations of his cell, he would piously send them away, saying: “Go to your sheep,” etc.

Exactly the same provisions are found in the ancient Statutes, part 2, chapter 9, nos. 1 and 28.]

**[Col. 0655]**

1. We admit into our choir only religious guests with whom it is permitted to converse ordinarily in the cloister.

2. It is not permitted, however, to take anyone aside, or to be taken aside, or to disclose or entrust anything to anyone as though secretly, unless the prior gives permission. It is not for us to seek this permission, but for them, if they consider it important, to request it. We must now say something about what we do for the dead and concerning the dead.

## CHAPTER XI. The Office of the Dead

**[Note: [Col. 0656A]]**

**CHAPTER XI—** Everything contained in this chapter is likewise recorded in the ancient Statutes, part 1, chapter 28, no. 5, and chapter 49, nos. 1, 14, 7, and 11.

**No. 1. “The Office after Matins.”** *Agenda*—the name by which we have long called the Office of the Dead, that is, Vespers, Matins, and Lauds—was then said in choir only from the fourth day before the Nones of November until Septuagesima. At the other times of year it was said in the cell after Vespers, unless that office had to be rendered in convent for an anniversary. Now, however, we always perform the Office in choir, except during Lent.

**No. 3. “But if it is an anniversary . . . with nine lessons.”** By this expression, “with nine lessons,” specifically assigned to anniversaries, he indicates a practice explained more fully in the ancient statutes. At that time it was such that the common Offices of the Dead were rendered with only three lessons and nine psalms.

Nothing, therefore, has been relaxed in this respect; rather, something has been increased, since the Office is now always said in choir after Vespers, and always with nine lessons.]

1. On the day after the feast of All Saints, unless it falls on a Sunday, we say the Office for all the dead after Matins, with nine lessons, content with this one prayer alone: “God of all the faithful” (*Fidelium Deus omnium*). Then, after Prime, we celebrate Mass with the convent present.

2. On no feast with twelve lessons, nor within the octaves of Christmas, Easter, or Pentecost, do we perform the Office of the Dead, unless perhaps the deceased is present or a thirtieth-day observance happens to be held. Even then, during the three days before Easter, and on Easter Day itself, or on Pentecost or Christmas Day, if such a case should occur, we would not perform it at all as regards the Mass [alternative: “the Mass office”].

3. From this day, therefore—that is, from the fourth day before the Nones of November until Septuagesima—we say the Office in church after Matins. From Septuagesima until the aforesaid day, on days of fasting we perform the same office in the cells after Vespers; on other days, after supper [added in a manuscript: “or beforehand”]. If it is an anniversary, it is held in church immediately after Vespers, with nine lessons and antiphons.

4. During Lent, however, so that the brothers may not be burdened, it is said in the cells after the meal.

## CHAPTER XII. Visiting the Sick

**[Note: [Col. 0656B]]**

**CHAPTER XII—** This chapter is reproduced in full in the ancient Statutes, part 1, chapter 47.

**No. 2. “Then he confesses his sins.”** This is not understood of sacramental confession. To prevent any suspicion of public confession—which was never in use among us except for a certain kind of fault specified in the statutes and acknowledged in chapter—the matter is expressed more clearly in the modern statutes, where it says that the sick man says, “I confess to God” (*Confiteor Deo*), and the priest adds, “May he have mercy,” etc.

We now observe exactly the same practice.]

1. When a brother is thought to be near death, the convent is summoned to visit him; **[Col. 0657]** and the priest says, “Peace to this house and to all who dwell in it” (*Pax huic domui et omnibus habitantibus in ea*), sprinkling holy water; the response is: “Amen.”

2. Then he confesses his sins, and after absolution the same priest says: “Save your servant” (*Salvum fac servum tuum*); “Be with him, O Lord” (*Esto ei, Domine*); “Let it profit nothing” (*Nihil proficiat*); “The Lord be with you” (*Dominus vobiscum*); “O God, who for your servant . . .” (*Deus qui famulo tuo*); “O God, who through your apostle . . .” (*Deus qui per apostolum tuum*).

3. Then the psalm “O Lord, rebuke me not in your anger” (*Domine, ne in furore tuo*), the first, is said. At its conclusion his sight is anointed, and it is said: “Through this anointing and his most merciful compassion, may God forgive you whatever you have sinned through sight.”

4. Thus, after the end of each of the seven psalms, this same prayer is repeated for each of the places where he is anointed: for hearing, smell, taste or speech, touch—that is, the hands—walking—that is, the soles of the feet—and the heat of lust—that is, the loins.

5. Afterwards his mouth is wiped, and he receives Communion, being devoutly kissed by all as one who is about to depart, while those present sing the Communion: “This body” (*Hoc corpus*).

6. After this these prayers are said: “Look upon us, O Lord” (*Respice, Domine*); “O God, who are the maker of your creation” (*Deus, qui facturae tuae*); “O God, who for the human race” (*Deus, qui humano generi*).

## CHAPTER XIII. How the Dying Man Is to Be Treated

**[Note: [Col. 0657A]]**

**CHAPTER XIII—** This chapter is likewise reproduced in full in the ancient Statutes, part 1, chapter 47.

**Nos. 2–5. “After this, the Psalterium, etc.”** Every effort is made to ensure that at least two Psalters are said: one in the church and another in the cells, with prostrations. Here you have the origin of the suffrage that we call the *monachatus*—the “monastic” suffrage—which at that time was rendered only for deceased persons actually present. It was a devout occupation of those who kept watch over the body of the deceased.

Later, through a custom introduced by individual houses, it was converted into a certain benefit that was sometimes granted even to secular persons. The ancient Fathers protested against this custom lest it grow and thereby burden the monks, as may be seen in the ancient Statutes, part 1, chapter 49, nos. 15 and 16, and in the ordinances of several general chapters, which will be discussed more fully elsewhere.

The same provisions are given in the modern statutes, but arranged more extensively and distinctly.]

1. When he already seems to be dying [alternative: “just about to die,” *jamjam*], all those who serve him give the signal and everyone hurries to him, setting aside every other concern, unless divine worship happens to be taking place in the church.

2. In that case the prior, or the person whom he appoints, hastens to the dying man with two or three others. After placing him upon blessed ashes, they perform a litany, long or short as circumstances permit. This is followed by the *Pater noster* (“Our Father”) and the prayers “Save [your servant],” “Be with him,” and “Let it profit nothing”; then this prayer: “Your mercy” (*Misericordiam tuam*). After it come five psalms: “Hear my words, O Lord” (*Verba mea*); “O Lord, rebuke me not in your anger,” the first; “I have loved” (*Dilexi quoniam*); “I believed” (*Credidi*); “Out of the depths” (*De profundis*); the *Pater noster*; “From the gate of hell” (*A porta inferi*); and the prayer “O God, whose property it is” (*Deus, cui proprium est*). Thereafter the full Office of the Dead is said, with Lauds and Vespers; after this, the Psalterium.

3. Meanwhile the deceased is washed and clothed: a monk in a hair shirt and cuculla, with stockings and foot coverings; a layman in a tunic and hood, with stockings and foot coverings. He is then placed upon the bier. The psalmody being interrupted, the priest says: “In everlasting remembrance” (*In memoria aeterna*); “Do not hand over to beasts” (*Ne tradas bestiis*); “Do not enter into judgment” (*Ne intres in judicium*). After these he says the prayer: “O God, for whom all live” (*Deus, cui omnia vivunt*).

4. When these things have been completed, he is carried into the church, and the responsory “I believe that my Redeemer lives” (*Credo quod Redemptor*) is sung. After this the priest says: “From the gate of hell” (*A porta inferi*); “Let it profit nothing” (*Nihil proficiat*); “Do not enter” (*Ne intres*); “Let us pray” (*Oremus*); “Receive, O Lord, the soul” (*Suscipe, Domine, animam*).

5. Once the deceased has been placed in the church, the psalmody is resumed where it had been interrupted. Every effort is made to ensure that at least two Psalters are said: one in the church and another in the cells, with prostrations. If something remains of the Psalter that is to be said in the church, it is completed in the cells. If time permits, he is buried that same day, but only after the Mass sung for him. Otherwise the burial is postponed until the following day. The monks and lay brothers divide the night among themselves according to their number and its duration, frequently reciting the Psalter around the body.

6. On the following day, after Mass has been sung in the presence of all, he is buried in this manner. The choir stands beside the body, and the priest says the *Pater noster*; the prayer “From the gate of hell” (*A porta inferi*); the prayer “O God, giver of life” (*Deus, vitae dator*); the responsory “I believe that my Redeemer lives” (*Credo quod Redemptor*); “Lord, have mercy” (*Kyrie eleison*); the *Pater noster*; the prayer “Do not enter” (*Ne intres*); the prayer “O God of souls” (*Deus, qui animarum*); the responsory “Do not hide me” (*Ne abscondas me*); “Lord, have mercy”; the *Pater noster*; the prayer “Do not hand over to beasts” (*Ne tradas bestiis*); the prayer “Do not enter into judgment” (*Non intres in judicium*); the responsory “Do not enter” (*Ne intres*); “Lord, have mercy”; the *Pater noster*; the prayer “Eternal rest” (*Requiem aeternam*); and the prayer “Grant, we beseech you, O Lord” (*Fac, quaesumus, Domine*).

7. He is then carried to the tomb with these psalms: “When Israel went out” (*In exitu Israel*); “Have mercy on me, O God” (*Miserere mei, Deus*); “Give thanks” (*Confitemini*), Psalm 117; “As the deer longs” (*Quemadmodum*); “Remember, O Lord” (*Memento, Domine*); “You have tested me” (*Probasti me*); “Incline” (*Inclina*); “Praise the Lord from the heavens” (*Laudate Dominum de caelis*); “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel” (*Benedictus Dominus Deus Israel*); and the *Magnificat*.

**[Col. 0659]**

8. When they have come to the grave, the priest says the *Pater noster* and “From the gate of hell” (*A porta inferi*), followed by the prayer “To you, O Lord, we commend” (*Tibi, Domine, commendamus*). He then blesses the grave, sprinkles it with holy water, and incenses it. The body is placed in it. As it is covered, the priest says these prayers while the others sing the psalms mentioned above: “We beseech” (*Obsecramus*); “O God, with whom” (*Deus, apud quem*); “To you, O Lord” (*Te, Domine*); “Let us pray, brothers” (*Oremus, fratres*); “O God, who [does something] for the just” (*Deus qui justis*); “The debt of the human race” (*Debitum humani*); “Indeed, presumption” (*Temeritatis quidem*); “Almighty God” (*Omnipotentis Dei*); and “Incline, O Lord” (*Inclina, Domine*).

9. When these prayers and the psalms have likewise been completed, the *Pater noster* follows, together with the prayers “To you, O Lord, we commend” (*Tibi, Domine, commendamus*) and “O God, by whose mercy” (*Deus, cujus miseratione*). They then return from the grave singing “Have mercy on me, O God” (*Miserere mei, Deus*), and in the church complete the entire office with this prayer: “God of all the faithful” (*Fidelium Deus*).

## CHAPTER XIV. Likewise, Care of the Dead

**[Note: [Col. 0659A]]**

**CHAPTER XIV—No. 1. “From the very day of burial until the thirtieth.”** Here you have the origin of the suffrage that we now call the *tricenarium*, the “thirty-day observance,” which is rendered through private Masses, except for the first, which is said conventually on the day of burial. This chapter also provides fuller proof that the custom of frequently celebrating conventual Masses among us, and even of celebrating private Masses not rarely, had been observed from the beginning.

**No. 2. “The brothers [shall hold] the cells, etc.”** This practice was subsequently corrected among us, and now on burial days no conversation is held. Nevertheless, we still eat together twice in the refectory.

**No. 3. “The same and equal office.”** From this we are shown how diligently the Fathers of the early Order wished equality in the charity shown to their members to be preserved among them. We ought to imitate this and not so readily request or grant particular benefits to be rendered after death. Particularity seems to detract from charity, since one person is preferred to another in the provision of assistance. Here too it becomes clear how far they wished all of us to be removed from favoritism toward persons, and superiors especially from everything that suggests haughtiness, ostentation, or singularity.

**No. 4. “By the weekly priest in summer before Prime, etc.”** Here mention is made of the weekly priest and of the Mass privately celebrated each week for benefactors and for all the faithful departed. What, then, does Reverend Father Guigo mean when he adds, “For rarely is Mass sung here”? It is easy to err here unless one understands what Masses this holy man is discussing. He is speaking chiefly of Masses beyond the common Masses and those designated in these Customs, which secular persons might request, especially those against which he inveighs in chapter 41, no. 4, where he says:

“For we have heard—and we do not approve—that many people feast magnificently as often as some persons wish to provide for them a Mass to be celebrated for their dead,” etc.

Immediately after discussing the special Mass for benefactors and all the faithful departed, to be celebrated only once each week, as is still observed, he turns to those Masses which in those times the relatives of the dead requested the monks to celebrate, while at the same time sending them a good meal. Speaking of this, the holy man says, “to feast magnificently,” etc.

We therefore believe that he had these Masses especially in mind when he says, “For rarely is such a Mass sung here” [understand: “a Mass of this kind”], and then adds the reason: because our principal study and purpose is to devote ourselves to silence, etc. The relatives themselves would come to the monastery to hear Mass and perhaps afterward dine there, which was foreign to the purpose and pursuit of silence and solitude.

But because this passage was very obscure, the words “For rarely is Mass sung here” were not included in the ancient statutes. The remainder, however, is recorded there: part 1, chapter 48, no. 1; chapter 47, no. 28; also chapter 48, nos. 8 and 13; and part 2, chapter 9, no. 26.

**No. 5. “For nothing is more laborious in the exercises, etc.”** Here he begins to speak of the purpose and nature of solitude and silence. Nothing is truly more laborious for human nature than to deprive itself of the society of its fellow human beings and of freedom of speech, because there is nothing toward which it is more strongly inclined. The free practice of socializing and speaking is a kind of seed of natural pleasure. When it is to some extent suffocated by the exercise of solitude and silence, nature suffers, because it is prevented from sprouting upward.

Yet nothing can more fully and securely tame corrupt nature and preserve it from dangers, because through solitude and silence opportunities are removed for dissipating oneself in human conversation and exhausting oneself in an outpouring of words. From these arises the more common material of sin. When both paths—that of society and that of conversation—are fenced off by solitude and silence as by spiritual thorns, a person is compelled to turn toward God and toward himself.

Through silence and solitude, the doors are closed to the world and to the vanities **[Col. 0661B]** it presents. When those things are removed from the human senses that ordinarily arouse carnal desires and even thoughts, the soul learns and grows accustomed to devote itself more freely to itself and to God.

If, therefore, the inclination of corrupt nature is as though oppressed by silence and solitude, and if, since it is a friend of the world, nothing is more laborious for it, according to Saint Augustine cited here, than “not to labor”—that is, to act, speak, and associate according to its own inclination—it is certain that in the exercise of both it suffers more intensely than in any other. Nothing mortifies nature to the same degree. Other mortifications torment the flesh, but this one also reaches the spirit. While the vessels of the flesh are thus constricted, however, the spaces of charity can be enlarged.

Although that exercise appears at present to be one of sorrow and weariness, it nevertheless yields to those who practice it the most peaceful fruit of salvation and inward consolation. Through it one tastes and sees that the Lord is good, and through the sweetest experience one recognizes what that peace of Christ is which surpasses all understanding and guards hearts and minds—provided that the undertaking of this exercise has been preceded by a heavenly calling and that it is observed by us, as is fitting, according to the mind and discretion of the Order, which has provided for everything.

“Nothing in excess.” Even in maintaining solitude, moderation must be used, lest through excess beyond the common condition of human beings the mind become dulled or its natural state be harmed. The Order has prudently provided against these disadvantages. For through exercises that succeed one another and are, as it were, interwoven—with room being given to conversation when sufficient—there arises a kind of salutary composition. It results from the concurrence of bodily and spiritual exercises, prudently mingled and tempered together, and is accommodated to the human condition in due proportion, so that we may safely speak the proverb: “Keep the order, and the order itself will keep you”—not only in the soul, but also in bodily and mental health and in devout cheerfulness.

Everything in our statutes has been discreetly tempered to preserve solitude perseveringly, prudently adapted to human strength, and blessed from above by the Lord. We have proved this through continuous and daily experience in all those who from youth have religiously endeavored to acquire the habit of their profession and to occupy themselves profitably in the cell. The situation is otherwise if the Order is not properly observed.

“Woe to that Carthusian,” we immediately cry, “for he has found tribulation and sorrow.” He often experiences labor and affliction of spirit in his mind, and through his indiscretion—that is, through certain works or exercises undertaken under the direction of his own judgment and will, not according to the Order or beyond the Order—he fails bodily and incurs a spiritual fall in the inner person. Let it suffice for now to have said this little about the labors of the solitary life.

But why did Reverend Father Guigo make no mention here of vigils and abstinences, or of the other difficult and severe practices observed in the Order, as though he considered those austerities worthless? It is because the essence of the Carthusian institute consists in observance of the cell and silence, together with the perfect denial of one’s own will. Hence he values the other austerities only insofar as they are related to obedience, as he himself explains in chapter 35, no. 3, where he says:

“For although the things we observe are many and varied, we nevertheless hope that all of them will prove fruitful for us through the one and only good of obedience.”]

1. From the very day of burial until the thirtieth, a Mass is sung for him every day, though not conventually, and the first prayer in the Office of the Dead is specially assigned to him. His day of death having been recorded in the Martyrology, a Mass is always celebrated for him in convent on the anniversary: in winter after Prime, in summer before Prime.

2. On the day on which the deceased is buried, the brothers are not obliged to keep to their cells. As a consolation, they eat together twice, unless it is a principal fast.

3. It must also be known that, without any favoritism toward persons, we perform the same and equal office for all our dead—nothing more for a monk than for a layman, or for a prelate than for a subject [alternative: “subordinate”].

4. For our benefactors, apart from the continual commemoration made always in the prayers of the ecclesiastical office, the penultimate prayer in every Office of the Dead is said. Each week, one Mass is sung by the weekly priest for them, for all the inhabitants of this place, and universally for all the faithful departed: in summer before Prime, in winter afterward.

5. For rarely is Mass sung here, since our principal study and purpose is to devote ourselves to the silence and solitude of the cell, in accordance with the saying of Jeremiah: “He will sit alone and keep silent” (Lamentations 3); and elsewhere: “I sat alone because of your hand, for you filled me with indignation” (Jeremiah 15). For we believe that nothing is more laborious in the exercises of regular discipline than the silence of solitude and quiet. Hence blessed Augustine also says: “For the friends of this world nothing is more laborious than not to labor.” But enough of this; let us now continue with the rest.

## CHAPTER XV. The Appointment of the Prior

**[Note: [Col. 0662C]]**

**CHAPTER XV—No. 1. “When the prior of this house, etc.”** He speaks only of the house of Chartreuse, because he intends not to prescribe laws for others, but merely to communicate to them a custom introduced and already confirmed by use in the house of Chartreuse. No mention is made of the form of law to be observed among them, nor of confirmation to be obtained, because they were not thinking of conferring among us a fixed superior title.

Thus the name “prior” has always been used in the Order to designate the person placed over others, so that it might be indicated that the one who presides over others among us is merely first among equals, and the director and servant of equals, **[Col. 0663A]** not their master. Here it is fitting to quote that passage from the exhortation which the ancient prior of Chartreuse customarily addresses each year to those present at the end of the general chapter. Speaking to the priors, he says:

“Let them consider themselves ministers of their houses, not masters, to whom, as the Apostle says, the stewardship has been entrusted.”

Behold the mind of the Order and the manner in which it is publicly proclaimed to the priors each year. The same form is now preserved in the election, with only those additions that had necessarily to be made as a matter of law when statutes were established in the Order and the Carthusian institute had long since been enrolled among the monastic orders.

**No. 1. “The principal fast.”** That is, the fast customarily observed by the whole Church under precept, not the fast instituted solely by prescription of the Order.

**No. 3. “Thus, for four weeks . . . he makes a fifth.”** To understand that passage properly, one should know—as will be clear from what follows—that at that time the lay brothers did not have a fixed residence in the monks’ house, which is called the upper house because it is situated in a higher part of the rocks of Chartreuse than the other house, which is therefore called the lower house. They remained in the lower house.

After spending four weeks with the monks, the prior went down to the lower house and stayed there for an entire week with the lay brothers, so that he could exercise pastoral care over them more closely. Thus, while inspecting the lower house, he permitted nothing there to deviate from regular observance.

**[Col. 0663C] The same section. “Someone commanded by him.”** Here the office of vicar begins to appear. At that time it was not fixed, nor assigned to one particular monk; later it became fixed, and rightly so, since this was especially suitable for prudently arranging the administration of the Order.

**No. 4. “Yet he does not leave the boundaries of the wilderness, etc.”** By the term “boundaries” among us are understood certain limits designated within which it was established from the beginning that we might possess lands sufficient for the support of the individual houses of the Order. In this way we would not need to wander about and seek what was necessary for our sustenance, since that would have been contrary to our purpose and would unquestionably have destroyed our institute within a short time.

Among us two kinds of boundaries are distinguished: one called the boundaries of possessions, the other the boundaries of the monks. The boundaries of the monks were formerly much narrower than those of the possessions. They were contained within the latter and designated the space within which the monks, sometimes, though rarely, would walk together for recreation, either in the presence of or with the permission of the prior. Hence arose the name *spatiamentum*, by which that walking within the assigned boundaries is designated; it has been preserved in the Order to the present day.

At that time the prior of Chartreuse did not merely refrain from leaving those boundaries of possessions, as he still does today; the priors of the other houses likewise ordinarily observed the same practice, and the reason was the same in every case. Since the possessions of the houses were contained within their boundaries, there was no need to inspect or exercise pastoral care except in matters concerning us that were contained within those boundaries.

I said “ordinarily,” for it is certain that sometimes priors had to leave their boundaries—for example, to accept and direct the foundations of houses and to carry out similar tasks requiring personal diligence and presence.

During the Order’s earliest times, this care of the possessions belonged exclusively to the priors, as will be proved in its proper place. They nevertheless administered it through a procurator and lay brothers, being content to do and arrange personally only those things within these boundaries that required their presence. The lay brothers, but no others, could sometimes leave the boundaries out of moral necessity, though with great caution and with permission.

More will be said in its proper places about how these boundaries were then assigned in the Order and about the other matters mentioned above. Let us now say a little about the wilderness of Chartreuse, outside which the prior of Chartreuse—now called the Reverend Father—does not go.

That wilderness is extremely extensive, containing several very high mountains and deep valleys, so that it is scarcely possible to believe how much pastureland and woodland is enclosed there among the precipitous rocks, growing and dying there because no route is available for transporting timber away. Only in very recent times, and with great labor, has a road been opened through certain rocks, by which means some part of these forests can be made useful through ironworking facilities.

The whole wilderness does not belong to Chartreuse, but only a large part of it, which gradually came into its possession. When our first Fathers came to Chartreuse, Saint Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, and the venerable Siguin, abbot of Casa-Dei, gave Saint Bruno and his companions whatever rights they had there. Later the Chartreuse possession grew within that same wilderness through the piety of worthy secular persons, who out of charity gave them what they possessed there. At times our hermits themselves requested this, so that they might be freed from disturbances which they not rarely suffered from peasants, and so that the boundaries of the wilderness of Chartreuse, especially on the side of Saint Lawrence, might be marked and enclosed by natural boundaries—that is, by precipitous rocks.

Thus the boundaries of Chartreuse gradually grew, with the illustrious chapter of Grenoble and others also eagerly providing assistance. As a result, Chartreuse acquired those broad pastures situated on the summit of the very high mountain called Charman-son, a name which in Latin means “most pleasant summit.”

For this reason the boundaries of Chartreuse are divided into two kinds: privileged boundaries and boundaries of possessions. Privileged boundaries are those designated at the beginning of the Order, placed under the protection of the Apostolic See through the grace of the supreme pontiffs, and adorned with various privileges—for example, prohibitions against women entering them and against anyone’s being arrested within them, the latter constituting a share in ecclesiastical immunity—and other provisions of this kind, which were granted to those ancient and original boundaries.

The boundaries of possessions are those that were gradually added to the other boundaries over various periods through donations and grants of woods, pastures, and even fields. These are contiguous with the ancient boundaries and are contained within the same great wilderness.

Without this enlargement of the boundaries, it is certain that the house of Chartreuse could never have endured as its burdens increased day by day, without the necessity of wandering and seeking; such necessity is in itself destructive of our institute, as is obvious to every prudent person. For this same reason, in order to avoid wandering and seeking, it was necessary that permission to possess property be increased both in the Great Chartreuse and in the other houses, as will be proved in its proper places.

What and how great those burdens were already beginning to be in the time of Reverend Father Guigo, he himself will relate below, in chapter 19.

As the boundaries of the possessions of Chartreuse thus grew within the wilderness, so too did the reason increase for the priors of Chartreuse to inspect what was being done, or what needed to be done, within those boundaries. For this reason, from the beginning of the Order they preserved for themselves the freedom to inspect personally whatever new territory contiguous with the ancient boundaries was added, since it was always considered to belong to the wilderness of Chartreuse.

Indeed, those possessions stand remote from the gathering of human beings, from villages and hamlets, and here the boundaries are not being understood scrupulously and physically, but morally.

**[Col. 0666A]** The priors of Chartreuse have always observed this praiseworthy custom of not leaving the boundaries—understand, except in cases of urgent necessity, such as the upheaval of wars, plague, a summons from the supreme pontiff, and other circumstances of this kind, which are not governed by an ordinary law and have occurred more than once in the Order.

With God’s protection, they will never depart from this praiseworthy custom, following the example of the other priors of the Order, even though, necessity having compelled it, a different provision may have been enacted concerning them, as will be noted in its proper places.

This strict residence of the prior of Chartreuse within his own wilderness was judged necessary not only so that, by his example, the other priors might abstain from useless journeys beyond the boundaries of their houses and might not abuse the freedom granted by necessity to leave them, but also so that the affairs of the Order, which are brought to him from every direction, either by letters or by special messengers, would not suffer harm from delays in responding. For it is always known with certainty that the prior of Chartreuse is to be found either in the house of Chartreuse or at least within the limits of its wilderness.

Let this brief account of the wilderness of Chartreuse and of the residence of its priors suffice for now.

[The same.] His seat, wherever it may be, or his clothing. From this passage it begins to become clear why, in the order, the title “abbot” was never accepted—not even by the Prior of the Charterhouse himself, the order’s general, although the Apostolic See sometimes urged him to accept it. For the mind of the order, dearest friends and brothers in Christ (for I shall not cease to address you in the same words with which R. P. Guigo addresses his companions), [Col. 0666C] the mind, I say, of the order—later expressed everywhere in the statutes—is that we should walk in charity and humility, and that priors should appropriate nothing to themselves, either in titles or in matters relating to food, clothing, or furnishings, that distinguishes them from the monks. Whatever appears, through the statutes, not to have been granted to the monks, they must likewise regard as unlawful for themselves, except for those things so attached to the duties of the priorate that, without them, those duties could not be properly and in accordance with the mind of the order fulfilled.
