**No. 5. “For this reason we write … that he should take horns for himself,” etc.** R. P. Guigo took this manner of speaking from the Sacred Scriptures, in which the ambition of exalting oneself above others is often expressed by taking up horns, as in Psalm 74: “Do not lift your horn on high.”

**No. 6. “But also at other times, not indiscriminately,” etc.** Here it is evident that, for the sake of hospitality, the prior escorted serious and respectable persons to the lower house, or visited them there. For it is certain that at that time there were rooms there in which guests were commonly received for overnight lodging in this Great Charterhouse, although there were also some guest quarters in the upper house, as will be seen below.

Moreover, everything contained in this chapter is found word for word in the ancient statutes, Part II, chapter 5, nos. 1 and following; chapter 6, nos. 1, 23, 30, 2, 3, and 24. Therefore, nothing at all has been omitted from this chapter that was not transferred into the old statutes.]

[Col. 0661]

**1.** When it happens that the prior of this house dies, after his burial the brothers are summoned and a three-day fast is imposed upon all. Morning and evening, in the church, after the office has been completed, the psalm *Ad te levavi* (“To you I have lifted up”) is sung with common devotion, while all lie prostrate upon the choir-stalls: “Lord, have mercy,” the *Pater noster* (“Our Father”), and the prayers “Save your servants,” “Send them help from the holy place,” “May the enemy have no advantage over them,” together with the prayer “Stretch forth, O Lord,” are added. On the fifth day, in the morning, a Mass of the Holy Spirit, the Comforter, is celebrated most devoutly in the convent. Then, gathering in chapter, they elect from among themselves, with the counsel of the elder and better men, one man—either a priest or one to be promoted to the priesthood—and immediately transfer him to the predecessor’s place. Devoting that whole day to rejoicing, they eat in the refectory twice, unless it is a principal fast.

[Col. 0663]

**2.** Although he ought to benefit everyone by word and life, and diligently care for all, he must especially provide to the monks from whom he was taken an example of quiet, stability, and the other exercises belonging to their life.

**3.** Accordingly, after spending four weeks in his cell with the other monks, he spends the fifth with the lay brothers. During that period, someone appointed by him performs his duty toward the brothers.

**4.** He himself does not go beyond the boundaries of the hermitage. His seat, wherever it may be, and his clothing differ from those of the others by no mark of dignity or luxury, nor does he carry anything by which it might appear that he is the prior. He is bowed to—and even this only moderately—when he goes to and returns from reading, or when someone passes before him; and when he comes to someone, they rise.

[Col. 0665]

**5.** At Christmas, Easter, and Pentecost, and whenever a brother is to make profession, he also sings the principal Mass. We write this so that some future person may not perhaps wish to take horns for himself, or celebrate his own name with any kind of glory or eminence.

**6.** During Advent and Lent, however, for stricter custody of himself, he abstains even from the visitation mentioned above, unless some great necessity or benefit compels it. At other times also, he does not descend to the lower house indiscriminately, lightly, or for just any person or cause.

# CHAPTER XVI. On the Procurator of the Lower House

[Note: [Col. 0667A]]

**CHAPTER XVI.—On the procurator of the lower house.** Everything contained in this chapter can apply only to the procurator of the lower house. For in houses where there was no lower house, he did not perform many of the things mentioned here, as was subsequently determined by the ordinances of the general chapters, as will be seen in their proper places. But why was a lower house constructed at the Great Charterhouse, and later, in imitation of it, in the older houses of the order, which are also called *Correria*, a name taken from that lower house of the Charterhouse which is called *Correria*? We believe this was done so that all the noise naturally associated with managing domestic affairs might be kept away from the upper house, where the monks lived, and so that the monks’ peace in their cells would not be disturbed by the commotion of those going back and forth.

**No. 1. “Who is responsible for everything,” etc., “or outside the customary practice.”** Here the nature and extent of the procurator’s care are expressed: namely, it concerned everything ordinarily done in the lower house and done according to custom. For as soon as anything arose that had to be done outside the customary practice, he referred it back to the prior.

[Col. 0667C]

In this chapter, which you have word for word in the ancient statutes, Part II, chapter 8, nos. 1 and 33, there is an excellent model for carrying out Martha’s ministry [Col. 0668A] in the order. If officials strive to conform themselves to it, they will remain true Carthusians, notwithstanding their administration of external affairs. But if they immerse themselves so deeply in concern for temporal matters that they cast away from themselves the practice of interior prayer, the solitude of the cell, and the occupation of spiritual reading, they have written this judgment against themselves.]

[Col. 0667]

**1.** He appoints over that same house one of the monks as a diligent procurator; for so we wish him to be called. Caring energetically for everything, whenever anything important or outside the customary practice must be done, he always seeks the prior’s advice, and he does not presume to give away or undertake anything substantial without his permission.

**2.** Although, like Martha, whose office he has undertaken, he must necessarily be concerned and troubled about many things, he nevertheless does not usually abandon or shrink altogether from the silence and quiet of the cell. Rather, insofar as the affairs of the house permit, he continually returns to his cell as to a most safe and quiet harbor, so that by reading, praying, and meditating he may calm the turbulent movements of his soul arising from the management or ordering of external affairs, and may store up in the secret places of his heart something salutary that he can gently and wisely pour forth in chapter to the brothers entrusted to him. For they need more frequent preaching in proportion as they know less of letters.

**3.** But if—God forbid—he is found negligent, wasteful, or obstinate, and, after being corrected repeatedly, refuses to amend, a better man is substituted in his place and he is immediately recalled to the custody of his cell, so that, since he cannot work for another’s salvation, he may at least work for his own.

# CHAPTER XVII. On the Sick Brother Who Is Sent to the Lower House

[Note: [Col. 0668A]]

**CHAPTER XVII.—**From this chapter the discretion that our founders adopted as their principal rule begins to appear. It sets out the cases in which they then customarily granted some relief to the sick, while preserving the substance of our purpose. This practice, however, is no longer in use among us, because after the first century of the order, in almost all the houses that were built, no lower house was constructed separately from the upper house. It was judged more expedient, for the perfection of the observance of our institution, that all—monks and lay brothers alike—should live within the bounds of one and the same house, under the eyes of the same prior and committed to the same spiritual exercises. Workshops and other similar places were nevertheless built separately from the cloister, so that guests could be received and domestic affairs conducted without disturbing the monks. Thus that ancient practice has been changed for the better, and assistance can now be given to the sick more carefully within the same house, after the manner of what could formerly be granted in the lower house.

**No. 2. “For it is not expedient for the inhabitant of a cell,” etc.** Here we have an explicit statement of how harmful the curiosity of meddling in the temporal affairs of the houses was judged from the beginning to be for men dedicated to learning and practicing the pious exercise of Mary. This is precisely what our statutes, both ancient and modern, so strongly commend, repeating the same words written here by R. P. Guigo and adding many others.

**No. 2. “With outsiders, unless ordered,” etc.** This means that, when outsiders came indiscriminately to the lower house, the sick monk sent there could not speak with them without permission. This is the meaning of the words “unless ordered”; R. P. Guigo also uses them elsewhere to signify permission. Nor could he speak with just any lay brother. The procurator’s authorization is mentioned because, as will be seen below, in the absence of the prior and the procurator it belonged to the lay brother who held the office of dispenser to give the other lay brothers permission to speak. Without that permission, it was unlawful for them to break silence, except in cases determined by the statutes.

[Col. 0669B]

**[The same.] “If such a person is,” etc.** From this it is clear how much regard must be paid, in granting permission to converse, to the greater spiritual benefit, according to the mind of R. P. Guigo: external consolation should not be left without interior and spiritual consolation, while prudent discretion is maintained according to the condition of the sick person and of the illness.]

**1.** If the prior causes any other monk to descend to the lower house—which happens rarely, because of some great and almost unavoidable necessity, either to relieve unbearable weariness, to calm a dangerous temptation, or to mitigate some extremely serious kind of illness—if, therefore, the prior causes one of such men [variant: another] to descend below, he will not meddle with any curiosity in the arrangements, business, or general care of the house.

**2.** For it is not expedient for an inhabitant of a cell to know such things, and it is also contrary to the peace of the whole house. [Col. 0669] He will not speak with outsiders unless ordered to do so, nor indiscriminately with just any lay brothers, but only with those whom the prior or dispenser approves. Thus, if there is someone capable of teaching and consoling, he should speak with those who need instruction and consolation; but if he himself needs consolation or instruction, he should speak with those who know how to provide these things.

# CHAPTER XVIII. Likewise on the Procurator

[Note: [Col. 0669B]]

**CHAPTER XVIII.—“In the lower house, exercising the prior’s functions,” etc., “he receives guests.”** It is therefore evident that the procurator acted in the prior’s place in the lower house, and that guests arriving at the Charterhouse were first received in the lower house and afterward sent to the prior in the upper house, with the discretion noted here being observed. The prior nevertheless descended to the lower house to visit guests, if they deserved it, as is stated above in chapter XV, no. 6.

**“Around the sixth hour,” etc., “and if it is not a principal fast, he dines,” etc.** Here it becomes clear how far the first professors of the order were from a stubborn attachment to their abstinences. They taught by words and demonstrated by example that these must sometimes yield to charity and always to obedience. Why did they do this? So that the will of the order’s subjects might always be made flexible for every circumstance, and so that it might be shown to belong to the character of our institution that we should strive to do what is sufficient for everyone. Therefore, for the sake of hospitality, they wished arriving guests to be received among us with such tested courtesy of charity that even the order’s fast could be broken by the procurator receiving them. The word *prandet* (“he dines”), by which R. P. Guigo also expresses the evening meal, should not trouble the reader, since elsewhere—namely, in chapter 5, no. 7—he uses the same word to express both the evening meal and dinner.

The courtesy of religious hospitality that has been commended in the order up to this point therefore originated with our first Fathers. If it is always and everywhere observed in the houses according to the moderation and discretion expressed in the modern statutes, we shall then be free from every blemish of just criticism. Otherwise, if we exceed the bounds of honorable moderation, while observing the standing and quality of the persons and places, we deserve blame, since this is forbidden both by the ancient statutes and by the new ones, unless unavoidable necessity compels us to do so.

I shall explain by examples. War is raging; one of the order’s houses is surrounded on every side by soldiers and is in danger of suffering the greatest losses unless it wins the favor of commanders and officers, as we have experienced for many years in the houses of Picardy, Belgium, and Germany. Who, possessing sound judgment, could justly criticize the officials of that house if they invited commanders and prepared certain splendid banquets [ [Col. 0669B] When we speak of arranging splendid banquets for military men, we do not understand this according to the usage of secular splendor, but according to the usage of the order—that is, that these splendid banquets should be undertaken by us with regard to the customary usage of the order. —Thus the Carthusian Editor in the *Admonition to the Reader*, at the end of the volume.] to win the goodwill of military men who do not know how to attend to regular statutes, but think they are being insulted unless they find a richly furnished table? If something is lacking that they think ought to be provided according to their rank, they become angry and seek opportunities for revenge, as we have repeatedly experienced; indeed, they do not even accept excuses based on the impossibility of finding more expensive foods.

The same sometimes happens with certain secular nobles whose favor we absolutely need in particular circumstances. If a table suited to their rank or appetite is not offered to them, they consider themselves offended and become hostile to us instead of remaining friends. What misery! In such cases, then, when we yield only to necessity, those who, seeing these things, condemned us for excessive splendor in those banquets would judge rashly.

When these causes cease—that is, if we did the same things when we had to deal with sensible and pious men who know how to judge properly what true Carthusians may desire, while decency and respect for the rank of the persons are preserved—we would deserve not merely to be accused of relaxation but also to be mocked. Seeing this, prudent guests could rightly and deservedly say in their hearts: “If these were true Carthusians, they would certainly know what things, and of what quality, ought to be provided to their guests so that they might be treated religiously.”

I therefore declare that, if we notably and knowingly exceed the limits in this matter, we deserve mockery rather than approval. Yet it must also be admitted that outsiders can easily err and judge rashly in this matter. Not knowing the causes and reasons that often move us, almost unwillingly, to prepare a somewhat more lavish table, they would immediately condemn us and attribute to our free will what should be attributed solely to necessity.

Everything will ultimately be addressed if the discretion noted in the latest statutes is observed in good faith, where the matter is concluded in these words: “The less frequently, the better.”

Finally, if in some houses and by some officials an error should occasionally be committed in this matter, it should not be attributed either to the order or to the regular community of the houses. The community, which constitutes the body of the order, has absolutely nothing in common with the reception of guests and has no part in these excesses, since all the members of the community always have an equally regulated portion in their cells. Indeed, they do not even know what is served in the guests’ room; this personal transgression belongs only to the priors and procurators. It should be brought before the visitors for examination at the next visitation and punished with appropriate severity.

The same must be judged concerning other similar transgressions that are personal and can never justly be charged to the order, so long as appropriate corrections and disciplinary measures protest against them and punish them as far as possible. For only those who remain silent appear to consent. This entire chapter of R. P. Guigo is reproduced in chapter 8 of Part II of the ancient statutes.]

This also must not be omitted, although we had almost forgotten it: the procurator, exercising the prior’s functions in the lower house, receives guests and kisses them. If they arrive at such a time—that is, around the sixth hour—and are such persons, namely religious persons, and it is not a principal fast, he dines with them, the strictness of abstinence being relaxed, and appropriately sends to the prior those whom he judges worthy.

# CHAPTER XIX. On the Mounts and Riding Animals of Guests

[Note: [Col. 0671C]]

**CHAPTER XIX.—No. 1. “But only the persons of the guests,” etc., “not also their riding animals.”** From this and the chapters that follow, one should draw the material for correctly understanding chapter 41, which deals with the avoidance of acquisitiveness. It is clear that our first Fathers renounced the desire to possess anything outside the boundaries, but not the legitimate desire to have within the boundaries assigned to them what would enable them to subsist peacefully and provide sufficiently for their needs—not merely those needs which we call absolute, but also those called moral. For it is clear from this and the following chapters that they then had not only enough to receive arriving guests honorably, but also enough to give alms.

The pious writer assigns the reason why they did not provide riding animals for guests, and that reason still holds. For, given the great increase in every kind of guest arriving from all directions to visit the Charterhouse—the number sometimes reaching seven or eight thousand persons in a year—neither the revenues nor the economy of the Charterhouse could suffice if we provided or maintained riding animals for noble guests. For this reason, as the number of guests increased daily, in recent years we were compelled to build a public hostel outside the bridge of the Charterhouse, where a public host would receive the guests’ riding animals and couriers, as they are called. If anyone murmurs against us on this account, let R. P. Guigo answer for us; he teaches us that the great influx of guests visiting the Charterhouse had already arisen in his own time, indeed had almost reached maturity.

**[The same.] “And such beds and foods for them,” etc.** This passage must be understood with discretion. It would be absurd to suppose that on days assigned to abstinence they offered their guests only bread and water with salt, as is prescribed for the monks. Rather, it must be understood generally of the foods they ordinarily used, such as fish, eggs, cheese, and fruit, while perhaps observing the appointed seasons, so that during Advent and on other days assigned by the statutes of the order, neither eggs nor cheese would be served even to the guests, except for a reasonable cause.

For preparing beds for secular guests, they did not possess mattresses. Instead, they offered them the same beds, honorably covered, that our own brothers used—beds arranged in the form of a chest, according to the custom that still continues and can be seen in all Carthusian cells. This arrangement is sufficiently comfortable, especially in cold places such as the Charterhouse, because those who sleep in them are enclosed, as it were, in a chest and are thereby protected from the greater cold. If in our own times anything has been granted among us concerning guests’ beds, it belongs purely to external polish and the propriety of the times, and does not in any way harm regular observance, since it does not concern the members of the order, who always use the same beds that the order’s first Fathers used.

**No. 1. “We send our pack animals outside for the winter.”** By pack animals he understands mules, with whose assistance we can still obtain only those things that are born or grow outside the hermitage, such as wine, wheat, oil, and so forth. For carts cannot climb from the foot of the cliffs as far as the Charterhouse; therefore it is necessary for these things to be brought to us on the backs of mules. Even now we are compelled to send cows and other animals outside the hermitage for the winter. The name *sagmarius* [pack animal] is formed from *sagma*, a word used for an animal’s saddle or pack, from which *sagmarius* means a mule assigned to carry a pack.

From this passage it is evident that, although the best Fathers renounced the desire to possess anything outside the hermitage, this must be understood strictly of the kinds of things specified below in chapter 41. For it is certain that at that time they had stables and pastures on the borders of the Charterhouse hermitage, specifically at the foot of the cliffs, by whose means they provided for their animals during winter. It was an unavoidable necessity to possess these; otherwise the stables would have had to be rented at great expense and hay purchased to feed the animals, and the weight of the costs would thus have entirely consumed the domestic resources.

This is sufficiently established by chapter 76 of the present *Customs*. But there is no room for scruple when the ruins of those old stables, which served to house the animals, can still be seen. In that same place wheat and other necessities were gathered, and afterward were carried on men’s shoulders, by the dreadful passage called *le Frou*, to the summit of a certain cliff. From there they were loaded onto the backs of mules and transported through the village called Rucheria to the Charterhouse.

**No. 2. “Of wandering about and seeking,” etc.** R. P. Guigo rightly attacks this practice as something almost dreadful to us, because it directly conflicts with our institution. To preserve that institution, one of two things must be chosen: either there must be enough for the persons and houses of the order to be maintained peacefully, without any necessity of seeking, since the condition of solitary life demands this, and a monk ceases to be solitary as soon as he is forced to seek his necessities outside the house; or, if there is not enough, then, because he must provide for himself out of necessity, he also ceases to be solitary and consequently ceases to be a Carthusian. The same must therefore be said here as about snow: snow cannot be warm; as soon as it is warm, it ceases to be snow.

The holy man exercises his zeal here with discretion. Seeing by what pretext certain monks of that time concealed their itch to multiply possessions and acquire without limit, he confronts us with that concealment, tears it away, and casts it aside, lest the temptation to use it should ever invade our brothers, as is read here. Let the officials of the order who would always admit among us an itch to acquire new things, under that false pretext and guise of piety, have the same response of R. P. Guigo. Let them hear from me that houses and officials of the order depart from the spirit of their institution and profession by the same road and with the same step by which, without a just and necessary cause, they attempt and strive to obtain new and superfluous possessions for themselves. Thus spiritual men gradually become temporal, and monks become secular.

None of this, however, concerns our cloistered members, who constitute the body of the order, but only the officials, who are merely the individual members of that body. The cloistered members, even if possessions increase and, through the multiplication of temporal goods, the officials’ cares also multiply, always remain peacefully in the cloister. None of this reaches them; indeed, they do not know either what the house has or possesses, or what the officials are doing.]

[Col. 0671]

**1.** We provide for the persons of the guests, but not for their riding animals, and we prepare for them beds and foods of the kind on which we ourselves feed. Lest anyone perhaps regard this—that we do not provide horses—as harsh, and attribute it not to sober discretion but rather to vicious hardness and avarice, let him consider, we ask, how narrow, how severe, and almost barren a life we maintain in the hermitage, and that we possess nothing outside it—that is, no possessions and no revenues. Let him also consider the number of guests, for whom our pasture, much less our grain, could in no way suffice, since it is not even sufficient for our own animals; for we send both our pack animals and our sheep outside for the winter.

**2.** In addition, we utterly abhor wandering about and seeking as an exceedingly dangerous practice. We regret that it has become deeply rooted among many men whose pious labors and holy way of life in Christ we cannot praise sufficiently, under the pretext of mercy—namely, that they acquire what can be given to those who arrive.

**3.** We also think that this is not a little beneficial for the guests themselves. They ought to share in our spiritual or bodily goods in such a way that they do not compel us to turn aside toward evil. They compel us to turn aside toward evil if they force us, at their expense, to wander and seek.

# CHAPTER XX. On the Poor and Almsgiving

[Note: [Col. 0674C]]

**CHAPTER XX.—No. 1. “To the poor of the world, bread,” etc., “but to the village,” etc.** By “of the world” he means secular poor people, toward whom he wished the quality of our means and freedom in giving to be observed. [Col. 0675A] But why were they then rarely received under our roof—that is, except in cases of great necessity? This was done most prudently, lest crowds of poor people be drawn to this hermitage and disturb our solitude and consume all our domestic resources; and lest, under the pretext of poverty, wandering and idle people should come to us—indeed, not infrequently criminals who, having committed enormous crimes and not daring to maintain a fixed residence, travel everywhere wearing the insignia of pilgrims.

The holy man foresaw from afar what later happened irreparably to this house through the gathering of every kind of person and pilgrim, to whom, as far as possible, table, lodging, and monetary alms are provided. The revenues and economy of this house would never suffice for them unless it were permitted, by exchange with neighboring peasants, to expend on eggs, butter, cheese, fish, and similar foods what the most illustrious countess of the province had bestowed upon this house from its earliest times.

This practice was therefore gradually introduced. Moved by charity, whose compassion was stirred by the real or feigned needs of these vagabonds, it eventually became customary, so that from a certain fictitious right arising from that custom it sometimes passed, as it were, into a public maxim: anyone was free to come to the Charterhouse and enjoy the benefit of hospitality there for three continuous days, as though such hospitality were owed to those guests by the foundation itself.

What disturbance, labor, and expense this caused the house of the Great Charterhouse—expenses that would have been far better spent on helping the genuinely poor living nearby—can scarcely be explained. To make their poverty appear more convincing, they quite often hide their shoes and leggings among the brambles before approaching the threshold of the house, so that, appearing half-naked and barefoot, even in severe cold, they may be given shoes and other things with which to cover themselves. These details are related humorously, so that the craft and ingenuity of our pilgrims may be recognized.

The holy man foresaw these things. But as the order gradually grew and the reputation of this hermitage spread throughout the whole world, it became morally impossible to avoid this development, and even more impossible ever to free oneself from it. This was one of the principal reasons why the Charterhouse had to increase its possessions. Otherwise it could not have subsisted without the necessity of seeking—a necessity that R. P. Guigo regards as dreadful.

From the beginning of this chapter up to the words “we send them to lodge,” the text is found in the same words in Part II, chapter 26, no. 1, of the ancient statutes. The remainder was not transferred into the ancient statutes because it does not suit the purpose of statutes being enacted: it contains only a certain zealous justification of the reason for his conduct and statement. Nevertheless, we shall not pass over it without examination.

By the time of R. P. Guigo, murmurs and mutterings had probably begun to emerge from those who loudly declared that our institution was useless in the Church of God. They murmured against our solitaries because, wishing to devote themselves to themselves alone, they drove away from their hermitage, as far as they could, the crowds of arriving secular persons—even if those persons were needy—with a certain miserly diligence.

These and similar allegations were spread among the people by indiscreet or envious rivals. To prevent the weak from being scandalized by the rumors they had spread, R. P. Guigo confronted them and refuted their empty arguments in a manner at once candid, prudent, penetrating, and learned.

**No. 1. “For it is not on account of temporal care for the bodies of others,” etc., “if there is more familiarity,” etc.** Here he fully proves that those who attributed to hardness the diligence with which foreign beggars were kept away from their hermitage were mistaken. He explains that it is not foreign to our purpose to receive with pious familiarity those who come to us seeking spiritual progress.

**No. 2. “Let Martha, then, have her place.”** Here, with both piety and learning, he answers the arguments of those who wish to attack the Carthusian life and accuse it of uselessness or idleness. If we may add anything to the irresistible arguments of so great a man, we shall say this:

Certainly, when a preacher withdraws into the privacy of his study in order to devote himself there to composing sermons, no one accuses him of uselessness while he is engaged in so useful a work. He withdraws from the eyes and company of men for this one purpose: to prepare something by which he can explain Christian truths to them in carefully composed words and urge them to do violence to the kingdom of heaven.

The more sublime the truths he is to preach, and the more readily and effectively they lead to the understanding and execution of Christ’s will and can be gathered, as it were, into a synopsis, the more highly everyone must value the labor and application of that preacher who remains hidden and separated from men. Moreover, it is perfectly clear to everyone that preaching through examples far surpasses preaching through words alone.

Once these points have been admitted and established by the agreement of all sensible people, without dissent, it is easy to prove how useful a good Carthusian is in the Church of God, and that his vocation can rightly be compared with the vocation of the most celebrated preachers.

If he remains within the cloister and hidden in his cell, this is to compose a precious sermon of example—not one that lasts merely an hour, as preaching by words commonly does, but one that lasts for whole days, months, years, indeed for the entire course of the life of the person who composes and preaches it.

The material of this sermon is a kind of synopsis of all Christian truths, and among the principal practical truths it is the first: for it concerns perfect self-denial, and through that sermon of example it prepares and makes easier for all Christians the way to self-denial. By his works he demonstrates that among human things—even those whose loss people believe they could scarcely ever endure—there is nothing that cannot be joined to generous self-denial undertaken for God. Thus such preaching by example strongly and gently persuades us that we must renounce all things and perfectly deny ourselves in order to follow Christ everywhere.

Moreover, such a sermon has as many arguments for persuading people to strive to obey and follow Christ by denying themselves as the preacher performs acts belonging to his profession. Through these acts he demonstrates to all people that everything is possible for those who wish to hear Christ’s voice and follow him.

But far be it from me, dearest friends and brothers in Christ, to wish thereby to provoke you to some favorable opinion of yourselves. We say this only so that we may hold a fitting opinion of our institution, esteem and honor it as is proper, and from this also conceive a holy fear lest, through our fault or infidelity in properly fulfilling the duties of our profession, we place an obstacle before the divine ordinance that willed our institution to arise with this purpose: that our life, separated from the world and withdrawn from human affairs, should be a continuous preaching, continually instructing people by its example about the necessity of denying themselves and gently attracting them to the practice of that self-denial.

But if both our own salvation and the usefulness of the order in the Church of God are founded upon self-denial, the former will perish and the latter will be of no value if we depart from the spirit and practice of this precious self-denial.

I shall finally touch on this matter in a few words. A good Carthusian is very useful to the Church of God when he diligently devotes himself to the practice of true self-denial and proclaims it to others by his example; one who acts half-heartedly in this exercise is of limited usefulness. But I declare that one who is utterly negligent in this exercise is useful for nothing, since he can be pleasing neither to God nor useful to others, given that he is not useful even to himself. Nevertheless, although that lazy and useless monk is a member of the Order’s body, this does not prevent God’s purpose in establishing the Order’s body from achieving its effect. For even if the Order has some weak or unhealthy members, its body nevertheless lives and flourishes, and the Carthusian community appears to the Church and to human eyes as a body, not as a member.

**No. 4.** “Therefore I, leaving my cell, etc., because of the *paltonarii*.” This word, *paltonarii*, greatly troubled the minds of some people, who wished to discover what the Reverend Father Guigo meant by it. But such words are more vernacular than Latin. It arose from a nickname imposed on a certain class of people—vagrant, idle, and perhaps begging under some pretext of piety—which was first taken from the common language of that time and later expressed in Latin. It must certainly be regarded as belonging to the same category as the word *Huguenots*, by which Calvinists are designated in France.

Here the good Carthusian officials have an answer to importunate and indiscreet secular people who might imagine that they ought to abandon every business in order to devote themselves to unnecessary conversations with them, that tables should always be set for them in our houses, and that secular services should be rendered to them. “Shall I,” says Reverend Father Guigo, “become secular in order to receive and feed secular people?”

**No. 5.** “What, then, do you do with what remains to you?” Here he very learnedly and courageously dissolves the arguments of those who bite at others, always looking for a knot in a rush, and who often obtain from their clever arguments nothing more than having acquired a bad name for themselves and scandalized their neighbours. He also expresses admirably how we ought to preserve both order and prudence in charity.

**No. 6.** “There are also nearby villages full of poor people, etc., rather than that a multitude be summoned here from there.” This is an excellent and irreproachable proposal. In this way we would know whether we were giving to the genuinely poor; whereas among that multitude attracted to us by almsgiving, we do not know who is truly poor. By sending the remainder of our resources to the homes of the poor, we would free our hermitage and solitude from the crowd of so many arriving people; but by giving here, the multitude is indirectly summoned to us. We would most willingly observe this proposal of so great a man. In this way we would receive in this wilderness only pious and respectable guests who came for reasons of devotion; we could provide more generously for the poverty of the neighbouring poor, of whom we have an abundance; and this house would be freed from great cares and labours. But it is impossible now to change anything in this respect. We have the best arrangement in our desire and intention, but we are unable fully to carry it out in practice. This tumult of guests does not touch or disturb our cloistered members, who, as I have said, constitute the body of the Order, in any way. For the monks of the Charterhouse live in the cloister just as quietly and solitarily as they would if guests very rarely came to us.

**No. 7.** “But whoever knows the expenses of this house, etc.” Readers will readily believe this most devout writer, because they know that at that time the Charterhouse did not possess extensive lands. But now, since we hear everywhere of great estates and accumulated wealth, it might seem paradoxical if we applied the same words to ourselves. Yet I do not hesitate to utter them truly and without any fear of falsehood; Christ is my witness that I do not lie. To open, in some measure, a path to the credulity of those who read this, let us say something, for the sake of illustration, about the daily burdens of this Charterhouse.

The Charterhouse has two hundred and fifty persons and more to feed and provide for every day, not counting arriving guests. These have not rarely numbered fifty, sixty, or even nearly eighty people lodging overnight at the Charterhouse in a single day. How many mules are needed, since everything necessary can be brought here only on their backs? How many oxen and ploughs are required to provide what will suffice for the needs of so many people? Certainly, no sensible person hearing this will fail to judge immediately that an annual income of eighty thousand pounds would be required to support so large a household, so that each person might receive at least a little. Yet I declare that the Charterhouse’s fixed revenues scarcely exceed one third of that sum, while its occasional revenues—from the sale of timber, the rearing of livestock, and similar sources—scarcely rise to six thousand pounds, except for the recently constructed ironworks, which profitably consume timber that would otherwise perish among the rocks. Who would not be astonished on hearing this? The subsistence of the Charterhouse must therefore be attributed solely to divine providence, which disposes and directs our affairs under the rules of honourable frugality and household management. And if others do not wish to be astonished at this, I certainly am astonished myself when I consider the matter, and I apply to ourselves the Prophet’s words: “Thus says the Lord: They shall eat, and there shall be some left over” (2 Kings 4:43).

But someone may say: Why do you have so many members of your household among you? It will become clear from what follows that we retain no one who is entirely superfluous.

Three houses are now united, as though fused into one, in the Charterhouse: the Charterhouse itself, the house of Currière, and the house of Calesium. The latter two are now situated within the broadly understood boundaries of the Charterhouse wilderness, and formerly each had its own community. Since these houses were small—especially after the house of Calesium was burned by heretics in the last century—it was judged most fitting to unite the house of Calesium also with the Major Charterhouse, just as the house of Currière had already been united to it three hundred years earlier. Consequently, the cloister of the Charterhouse had to be enlarged by constructing new cells, as though for three monasteries.

The number of monks living in the Charterhouse itself ordinarily rises to forty-five. Since Mass and the other divine offices had to be celebrated in the houses of Currière and Calesium in the proper tone, or at least in a subdued voice, it was prudently arranged that the senior, weak, and infirm monks and lay brothers should be sent to the house of Currière, together with a sufficient household to serve them. For this reason, about ten persons, both monks and lay brothers, ordinarily reside there. In the house of Calesium there are three monks, together with three or four brothers, more or fewer. In the Charterhouse itself there are almost as many lay brothers as monks. Thus, when the monks of the Charterhouse, Currière, and Calesium are counted together, their number rises to approximately fifty-five, and there are just as many brothers. The total number of members of the Order who constitute the Charterhouse community, inside and outside, therefore reaches one hundred and ten.

But one hundred and forty persons still remain if the number of people stated above is to be made up. Why do you need so many hired workers and servants? If anyone wished to accuse us of having an excessive number of servants, let him inhabit this wilderness for a time. There, because of the ruggedness and unevenness of the roads and places, where tasks can be accomplished only with great labour, he would soon fall silent. More than twenty-five servants, working without interruption, are needed merely to transport burdens. More than forty woodworkers, masons, and hired labourers are continually needed to arrange and cut timber—for fuel, for shaping, and for repairing the roofs of the granges—and for other such tasks. A considerable number are needed to feed and care for the animals. I would certainly run out of time in recounting these matters, and I would find more than ten or fifteen beyond the number specified if I wished to count them individually here.

If one adds to all these the number of stonecutters and smiths who, from the year 1676, when the total burning—or rather incineration—of the Charterhouse occurred, until this day have received and continue to receive wages, it will seem almost miraculous how provision could have been made for so many expenses. But those who know with what charity all the houses of the Order came to the aid of the mother Charterhouse in this crisis will not be so greatly astonished. Their assistance was such that we had to say to some of them: “It is enough”—as though the oil of charity flowing into our vessels had remained until such time as we had an empty vessel and were in need. Yet it would be far from the tender maternal charity of the mother toward her children ever to wish to abuse their willingness to give to her. For she says to them all: “We do not seek what is yours, but you yourselves” (2 Cor. 12:14). She accepted only as much as was sufficient to enable her to complete the rest from her own resources. We have explained these matters somewhat more fully for the consolation of our successors. And if we have spoken a little too diffusely about this subject, we ask that we too may be forgiven, together with Reverend Father Guigo.]

**1.** We give the poor of the world bread or something else, as our means allow or our goodwill suggests; we rarely receive them under our roof, but usually send them to the village for lodging. For we withdrew into the seclusion of this wilderness not for the sake of caring for the temporal bodies of others, but for the eternal salvation of our own souls. It is therefore not surprising that we show more familiarity and comfort to those who come here for the sake of their souls than to those who come for the sake of their bodies. Otherwise, we ought once to have settled not in such harsh, remote, and almost inaccessible places—where anyone who came for bodily comfort would undergo more labour than he would obtain relief—but rather on the public road.

**[Col. 0675] 2.** Let Martha therefore have her praiseworthy service, though not without anxiety and disturbance; but let her not trouble her sister, who clings to Christ’s footsteps. For, because he himself is God, she sees him by being at leisure, cleanses her spirit, turns her prayer into her own bosom, listens to what the Lord says to her within herself, and thus, insofar as she can through a small portion see through a mirror and in an enigma, tastes and sees how sweet he is, and prays both for herself and for all who labour in this way.

**3.** And if Martha does not cease troubling her, Mary has not only a most just judge but also a most faithful advocate—namely the Lord himself, who deigns not only to defend her purpose but also to commend it, saying: “Mary has chosen the better part, which shall not be taken away from her” (Luke 10). By saying “better,” he not only commended it but also preferred it to her sister’s laborious activities. By saying “shall not be taken away,” he defended her and excused her from allowing herself to become involved in Martha’s anxieties and disturbances, however pious they might be.

**[Col. 0677] 4.** “Therefore, leaving my cell and my cloister, and forgetting what I had resolved, shall I become a wandering monk because of the *gyrovagi*, a *paltonarius* because of the *paltonarii*, and a secular person in order to receive and feed secular people? Let them—those very people—go on as they have begun and wander around the world, lest, if I too go, they increase their number by adding me. Or, if they insist absolutely that I go, let them stop themselves and do what I do, so that they may rightly be fed at the labour and risk of religious.”

**5.** Here someone may perhaps say: “What, then, do you do with what remains to you?” Let the person who asks this with a biting intention hear that he ought to care rather for the beam in his own eye than for the speck in another’s. Those who say this with friendly goodwill should know that there are holy men or congregations in abundance whose poverty we ought to pity much more than that of secular people, according to the Apostle’s saying: “Let us do good to all, but especially to those who are of the household of faith” (Gal. 6).

**[Col. 0679] 6.** There are also nearby villages, known to us and full of poor people, to which whatever remains to us may be carried and distributed. We think it better and more proper that, if something somewhat greater is to be distributed, whatever it may be should be carried there rather than that a multitude should be summoned from there to us.

**7.** But whoever knows the expenses of this house will not ask what we do with our surplus; rather, he will be astonished that we are not in need.

**8.** Dearest brothers, if we have perhaps pursued these matters at greater length than was proper and spoken more volubly than we should, bear with us and forgive us.

# CHAPTER XXI. On Women

**[Note: [Col. 0682A] Chapter XXI.—No. 1. “We by no means permit women to enter our boundaries,” etc. For this reason our first Fathers took care to obtain privileges from the Holy Apostolic See, as was mentioned above when the boundaries were discussed. But these privileges belong only to the Charterhouse itself and cannot apply to the other houses, since everything in the Charterhouse wilderness is united and contiguous, and no secular person there possesses anything that interrupts that continuity. In the other houses, however, within the assigned boundaries, several secular people possess their own estates, and they cannot be prevented from entering them with their wives and children of either sex. Reverend Father Guigo explains this here so that everyone might know with what vigilance our first Fathers strove to drive women away from their wilderness. The holy man clearly assigns the reasons, which are known to all human beings, the children of Adam: whatever virtue they may possess, the less they distrust themselves in this matter, the more they approach the ease of falling. We must therefore always keep before the eyes of our mind the words of Saints Augustine and Gregory: “The sons of men are human beings.” We must remember that we are flesh.]

**[Col. 0681]**

**1.** We by no means permit women to enter our boundaries, knowing that neither a wise man, nor a prophet, nor a judge, nor a guest of God, nor sons, nor even the first man formed by God’s hands, could escape the blandishments or deceits of women.

**2.** Let Solomon, David, Samson, Lot, and Adam—who took wives whom they had chosen—come to mind; and let us remember that a man cannot hide fire in his bosom without his garments being burned, or walk upon coals without scorching his feet, or touch pitch without being defiled.

**3.** Having completed this, let us discuss the observances of the cell. And since we call beginners novices, let us first explain what concerns them.

# CHAPTER XXII. On the Novice

**[Note: [Col. 0682C] Chapter XXII.—No. 1. “Mercy to the novice,” etc. From this expression, which our first Fathers used to signify in general whatever they were requesting, arose the custom in the Order that whatever we request in chapter we should request under the name of “mercy.” And because at each General Chapter the priors ask to be released from their offices under the title of mercy, it follows that in the chapter documents of the houses of the Order the names are written individually in order of seniority, and each entry says to the prior of House N.: “Mercy is not done”; that is, the petition by which the prior asked to be released from the priorate under the name of mercy has not been admitted. But when it says, “Mercy is done,” this indicates that his petition was admitted and that he has been released from the priorate. We mention this so that outsiders may cease to marvel at this “mercy,” as they call it, of the Carthusians.

Here Reverend Father Guigo begins to lay down the form that we ought to follow in examining—or, rather, testing—young men who come to us seeking admission to the Order, so that we should try rather to frighten them than to entice them by flattering words. Otherwise, as the holy man wishes, a postulant would not remain undaunted if we did not, through the exercise of charity and prudence, try in a sense to frighten him; and rightly so. For since our institution is hard and austere, it ought to admit no one who does not appear not only to have been preceded by a heavenly vocation, but also to possess a certain natural strength of spirit and a sound and cheerful bodily constitution. Those of a melancholic constitution, or of black bile, are not suited to our solitude. If this rigor in testing—or rather frightening—postulants, which the holy man recommends, were once relaxed among us under an indiscreet pretext of charity, we would fill our houses with weak and feeble people, by whom the observance of the Carthusian way of life could not be maintained. And what would follow? Everyone can see. For repeated dispensations give rise to customs; customs once introduced against monastic institutions give rise to corrupt freedom; and from this freedom comes the ruin of regular observance. See where a certain softness in testing and educating novices would ultimately lead if it were admitted among us.

**Ibid., No. 1.** “And because the number of this community,” etc., “is fixed,” etc. The number of monks among us cannot exceed the number of cells constructed in each house. Since we live alone in individual cells arranged for the preservation of solitude, novices, like monks, must live alone. This is why we assign a term—that is, a definite period—to postulants. When it has elapsed, if the postulant is absent and another suitable person presents himself, we freely receive the latter, because we are released from our promise.

**No. 2.** “That this is granted to him only under such a promise,” etc. This is something exceptional, and must be believed to have been permitted only in those times; for it somewhat curtailed the freedom of those wishing to enter our Order. Hence this condition was not included in our ancient statutes, because it had been corrected.

**No. 3.** “One of the seniors is assigned, who for one,” etc., “week.” Here begins the practice thereafter always observed in the Order: that one of the monks is assigned to say the Hours with the novices, so that they may learn how and with what ceremonies they ought to perform the Divine Office. Accordingly, according to the novice’s greater or lesser aptitude in learning this, the monk goes to him more or less often.

**No. 4.** “Who nevertheless gently,” etc., “nor is he immediately permitted to undergo the whole austerity of the institution,” etc. See how our ancient Fathers proposed for themselves rules of discretion to be observed in all things. They wish at first sight to frighten the postulant, so that they may thereby discern by what spirit he is led and why he seeks entry into the Order. But afterward, knowing that everything concerning human weakness must be ordered gently if the end is to be reached firmly, they observe stages in the exercises of probation. The novice is visited more often by the prior in order to be instructed in spiritual matters, and thus, nourished with spiritual food, he may grow in his purpose until, by profession and vows made, he binds himself to observe the institution. Such permissions to speak with the cook are no longer granted to our novices, and full observance is required of them, because it is deemed sufficient if they have recreation with the monks once a week.

This discipline of our ancient Fathers concerning novices, for good reasons confirmed through various experiences, was in some respects changed for the better by later statutes, just as we see happened through later sacred councils, which determined the period of probation and the age for profession differently from earlier ones. Monks could then be expelled from the Order if they became very unruly or vicious, as will be seen below in Chapter 77, and thus the monastic sheepfolds could be cleansed of sheep infected with disease. But now ecclesiastical and civil laws have established otherwise.

**[Col. 0685A] No. 5.** “Or another, if he does not know how to write.” This is not to be understood as total inability to write, for someone who did not know how to write would have been unfit for the clerical state, to which all who were admitted to the condition of monks had to be suited, as will be proved below in Chapter 73. Rather, it refers to inability to write beautifully, as our men were taught to write when copying books, as stated in Chapter 28, No. 2.

Moreover, you will find this entire chapter, except for the condition noted above, reported in the second part of the ancient statutes, Chapter 23, Nos. 5, 9, 16, and 20, and likewise in Chapter 24, No. 1.]

**1.** When a novice therefore asks for mercy, hard and harsh things are proposed to him, and the whole lowliness and austerity of the life that he desires to undertake is placed before his eyes as far as possible. If he remains undaunted and unmoved by these things, and, according to blessed Job (7:15), his soul chooses hanging rather than the love of temporal things, and his bones death, of which it is said, “If we have died with him, we shall also live with him” (2 Tim. 2:11), and if he readily promises that, for the sake of the words of the Lord’s lips, he is prepared to guard difficult ways, then at last he is advised, according to the Gospel, to be reconciled with all who have anything against him. If he has defrauded anyone, he is to restore, if he has the means, at least the equivalent amount, if not fourfold as Zacchaeus did. And because the number that this community ought to contain is fixed, a definite limit is assigned to him, up to which the number must come.

**[Col. 0683] 2.** When he comes at the appointed time, after humbly petitioning in chapter, he is placed under examination for at least a year, with all his possessions fully reserved to him until the day of profession. This is granted to him only under such a promise that, if he should be unable or unwilling to endure our way of life, he will by no means return to the world, but will instead accept some other form of religious life that he can bear. If he dies while conducting himself commendably during the examination, whatever we do for a professed monk wearing the sacred habit, we shall likewise do for him.

**3.** When he has been introduced into his cell, one of the senior monks is assigned to him. Visiting him at the proper hours for one week, or longer if necessary, he is to instruct him in what is required.

**4.** At first, however, he is treated especially gently and mildly. He is not permitted to undergo the entire austerity of the institution all at once, but gradually and as reason or necessity appears to require. For at times he is permitted to speak with the cook, and he is visited more frequently by the prior.

**[Col. 0685] 5.** When the time has approached at which he is to receive the blessing, if he appears promising and has been diligent in asking for mercy, a day is fixed on which, if he perseveres, he is to be fully received. Then, having likewise humbly asked for mercy in chapter, he is freely granted the opportunity either to leave, if he wishes, or to distribute all his possessions as and to whom he pleases. If he perseveres in knocking, the desired consent is granted to him; and then either he himself, or another if he does not know how to write, writes this profession for him.

# CHAPTER XXIII. The Novice’s Profession

**[Note: [Col. 0685A] Chapter XXIII.—No. 1. “I promise stability.” Omitting the discussion of what various writers have said in different places about the vow of stability, we shall present only those matters that, among us, are to be regarded as certain, whether from the wording of the statutes, the ordinances of the General Chapters, or finally the practice of the Order.

First, by that stability is recognized a fixed and in a certain sense indissoluble adherence to the monastic and Carthusian state. By making profession, the monk knowingly and willingly binds himself to it by a vow. Hence we do not hesitate to say that monks called to the episcopate cannot in any way be exempted from those observances of the Carthusian institution that can be reconciled with episcopal duties, such as abstinence from meat. By the vow they have made to preserve stability in the Carthusian way of life, they are bound to this, and the obligation to keep a vow is of divine law. For the conditions required for a valid dispensation in a matter belonging to divine law, I refer the reader to Thomas, Toletus, and those most approved theologians.

Second, stability means adherence to a place—that is, to the house in which the monk makes profession or to which he is sent through the obedience of the Order. He also binds himself by vow to this stability or adherence, as Saint Father Bruno himself sufficiently explains in the passage cited below; and it is evident both from the ancient chapter documents and from the ancient statutes that our members must abstain from instability—that is, from the itch or importunate petition to change houses—as from something opposed to the vow of stability, as will be proved more fully in its proper places. But it is certain from the continuous practice of the Order, which is the best interpreter of laws, that the vow, so far as this aspect of changing houses is concerned, is made only under the condition that no change of place be made without a reason that the Order has judged just. Hence it is certain that a Carthusian monk who, without necessity and by his own will, whether under fictitious pretexts or by underhanded means, obtains—or rather extorts—permission to change houses sins against the vow of stability.

This stability, understood in this way, is essential to our institution, because it is necessary for the manner of solitary life and for assuming its habits.

First, it closes the entrance to the human mind, which is extraordinarily inclined toward novelties, and by the practice of stability mortifies and subdues that inclination, so that the mind may learn to acquire, from senses already withdrawn from external objects, a habitual estrangement that allows the solitary’s spirit to act more peacefully.

Second, through a firm and stable dwelling in the cloister, it prevents the monk’s spirit from being wounded again by so many troublesome phantasms, arising from the objects of abandoned things that strike the mind anew through their presence and impress themselves upon it more violently because of their novelty. For this reason he ought not even wish to see the world in passing.

The purpose of that stability is therefore overturned when a Carthusian monk desires and obtains a change of house. By desiring it, he has already fallen mentally into the temptations of novelty and has begun to walk through the world; by obtaining what he desires, he brings those temptations into action. Then, when nature has returned to the cell and been reduced to its former state of deprivation, it begins to quarrel there—or rather, through collisions of the imagination, to rage anew—against this wanderer who has set out. He therefore receives in himself the just reward of his instability. It is no wonder, then, that the words of the author of the book *The Imitation of Christ* have become a proverb among us: “Those who travel much are rarely sanctified,” since experience has taught us that this is true of those among us who—understand, of their own will—seek to go from house to house at their own insistence.

If some press the matter and say that they are surprised that certain things are treated among us almost as crimes which in other Orders are judged lawful and harmless and readily permitted, we shall answer them briefly that the diversity of states must be considered here. Just as in the secular state many things are not regarded as harmful to certain persons but are judged very dangerous or unbecoming for others and are therefore forbidden, so many things are harmful to professors of the solitary life and therefore must be prohibited, although they are not merely harmless to other religious but often useful to them and therefore imposed upon them by their superiors. It would be easy to prove this with examples, but it does not concern our present purpose.

This stability is therefore regarded in the Carthusian Order as the nerve on which its perseverance in its institution depends. From the making and observance of this vow, with God adding a special grace to it, arose that praiseworthy tenacity in adhering to the Order’s ancient customs and in introducing no innovations in matters belonging to the nature and substance of its institution. From this arose that firmness in preserving the ancient observance which has endured to the present time.

For if something appears to have been changed in the number and quality of abstinences involving bread and water, which are treated in their proper place, it should really be regarded as almost unchanged, because from the beginning they were to be observed only at the superior’s command. If they are now not observed fully as they were formerly, this resulted from the necessity of assisting the needy and preserving bodies; and, as experience required, it was legitimately ordered by the superiors assembled in General Chapter, as we said already in Chapter 7.

Nothing at all has been changed in the Order except what many years of experience first taught could be improved; and even this was done not by the will of inferiors but by the judgment of the General Chapters. Let the form of electing priors serve as an example, as it is established in Chapter 2, Part II, No. 33 of the new collection of statutes made a hundred years ago. There the permission is granted—which was not granted in the ancient statutes—to repeat the scrutiny four times on the same day. But the freedom to postpone the act of electing until the following day is removed, because experience had shown that considerable harms resulted from this, through agreements and other similar devices that kept the Holy Spirit away from the election, to use the words of the statutes themselves.

Indeed, if anything appears to have been added through the ordinances of the General Chapters, this was done only because of abuses that had crept in. To prevent or correct their effects, or to destroy erroneous interpretations, a remedy was supplied through those ordinances, as may be seen in the new edition of the statutes, in which several ordinances have been inserted. This should therefore not be regarded as something new or opposed to stability, since, on the contrary, it is a remedy provided to prevent anything from being gradually changed through human weakness that would conflict with the ancient Carthusian purpose.

This vow of stability, I say, contributes greatly to preserving the Order’s ancient purpose unimpaired. It is therefore clear that this is what Saint Father Bruno himself had in mind when, speaking of monks in his homily on the Purification, he explicitly said: “The axles are broken, because the license to wander is removed, and stability of place and purpose is imposed.” By adding place to purpose in these words, he indicates that, in his view, stability must be preserved in both. This is further proved by the new collection of the Order’s statutes, where it says in Chapter 22, No. 61: “Those who presume, by letters written under suppressed names, to defame our Order, or its prelates, or any of them, or who attempt to overthrow and alter the nature of our institution, shall by that very fact be deprived of every office and vote and incur the sentence of excommunication, from which they may not be absolved except by the Reverend Father or one of the Visitors.” Such an attempt is therefore regarded as the matter of a sin, indeed a mortal one, since it is subject to the penalty of excommunication; and rightly so, because it concerns the violation of a vow in grave matter, such as the attempt to bring about the overthrow and breaking of the ancient and holy institution that has remained in force for so many years through stability. For if those who plot something against the peace and welfare of the citizens of a single city sin gravely, what are we to think of monks who, after making a vow to adhere stably to the purpose of their institution, attempt to overthrow and alter it?

To seek changes and alterations in the ancient use and institution of the Carthusians and to overthrow it are one and the same thing. For from this the Order’s praiseworthy tenacity and stability in its ancient usages begin to be destroyed. If solitary monks once tried in this matter to obtain something through their own insistence, or even obtained it from the Holy Apostolic See by underhanded means, the door would thereby be opened to them for devising, desiring, and seeking every kind of novelty. Their minds, given to speculation within the walls of the cell, would compose a thousand inventions which, urged on by the devil and flattered by private love, they would regard as entirely just and most suitable. They would not rest until they found means to obtain their purpose, and until at last, completely blinded by private love, they judged that they were even rendering service to God if they tried to overthrow the ancient institution.]

**Ibid.** “And obedience.” The words “according to the Rule” are not added, because we vow obedience absolutely and without any condition. Among us it is above the Rule and is, as it were, the substance of the Rule, as Reverend Father Guigo will make clear below in Chapter 35, where we shall discuss this matter more fully.

**Ibid.** “And the conversion of my ways.” By this vow a promise is expressed always to strive toward better things and never to depart from the purpose of correcting oneself. Hence it must be concluded that a monk among us who by his will alone or by his actions abandoned the purpose of making progress or correcting himself would sin against this vow, gravely or lightly according to the nature of the matter involved. If he wished to remain in a simple imperfection, he would incur a similar fault against the conversion of his ways; if the matter concerned a venial sin of weakness, the same sin would result; if a voluntary venial sin, likewise; but if it concerned some mortal sin, he would also sin mortally against the vow of conversion of life. The guilt is therefore doubled on account of the vow, just as merit is doubled through faithful fulfilment of the vow that has been made. In light of this, let those consider how they could extricate themselves or excuse themselves from sin who wished to neglect certain observances of the Order’s statutes and remain at rest in that negligence, under the pretext that a simple statute in itself does not impose an obligation under pain of sin.

The vow, therefore, requires Carthusians to aspire to the perfection of their profession and virtues, and by continual study and effort to strive toward it, doing violence to themselves and to their corrupt nature. What sort of violence this must be is beautifully expressed in the new collection of the statutes, chapter 19, no. 5, where it says:

> For all professed members ought—indeed, by the necessity of the vow of their profession, they are bound—to have their minds prepared to resign willingly and freely into the hands of the superior everything that has been granted to them, whether books or anything else, precious or worthless, whenever the superior wishes and commands it to be done. Nor, if he does this, ought they to murmur or complain; otherwise they have not yet abandoned themselves and what is theirs, and therefore cannot follow poor Christ, become his imitators and disciples, or be enriched by his poverty.

There poverty is under discussion; nevertheless, it is also clear from this passage how earnestly our members ought to strive toward perfection in all things.

[Col. 0689D] If, then, as is evident, the entire basis of the merit of a Carthusian monk’s actions consists in obedience, and if, by the force of the vow of conversion of life, he is bound to aspire to attain its perfection, he must continually ascend through the stages of obedience described by the holy Fathers and arrange them devoutly in his heart. If, on the contrary, he arranges for himself stages of descent, seeking means of carrying out his own will more freely, or even of breaking the bonds of his institute, in which and according to which he promised to serve God, it is evident that he sins both against the vow of obedience and against the vow of conversion of life, by which he is bound. He is bound by the force of the vow he has made in such a way that, according to the norm of the Carthusian institute, he has devoted his own will whole and entire, without any restriction or exception, to the sacred virtue of obedience. The stages of obedience assigned by the holy Fathers are as follows.

The first is that the things commanded by the superior be diligently fulfilled outwardly [Col. 0690B].

The second stage is that the will of the subordinate inwardly conform itself fully to the will of the superior, so that he renounce his own will when it resists. The blessed John Climacus speaks of this in *The Ladder*, step 4, article 3, when he says: “Obedience is the tomb of one’s own will and the awakening of humility.”

The third stage is that the understanding of the obedient person conform itself to the understanding of the one who commands, so that he may now be, according to Saint Bernard, like the Apostle Paul, of whom it is said in the Acts of the Apostles (chapter 9:28): “With his eyes opened, he saw nothing; but they led him by the hand,” and so forth.

Behold the stages, and their character, which a Carthusian monk ought to arrange for himself, by the obligation and necessity of the vows of obedience and conversion of life that he made according to the form of the statutes—a form he did not ignore; indeed, knowingly and willingly, with reference to it, he made his profession in the Carthusian Order.

You will find this entire chapter reproduced in the ancient statutes, part II, chapter 24, nos. 4 and 5, and precisely the same provisions are still observed among us.]

1. “I, Brother N., promise stability, obedience, and conversion of my way of life before God, his saints, and the relics of this hermitage, which has been built in honor of God, the ever-blessed Virgin Mary, and blessed John the Baptist, in the presence of Dom N., the prior.” +

[Col. 0687] 2. During the Mass at which he is to be received, after the Offertory he comes to the step before the altar. Bending down, he repeats the following verse three times, and the choir responds with the same words each time:

> Receive me, Lord, according to your word, and I shall live; and do not put me to shame in my hope.

After its third repetition are added: “Glory be to the Father,” “Lord, have mercy,” and “Our Father.” Meanwhile, the novice kneels before each monk in turn and says, “Pray for me, Father.” After this, returning, he remains standing in the same place as before, bent down. Then the priest turns toward him and says: “And lead us not into temptation. Save your servant. Send him help. Be with him. The Lord be with you.” He then blesses the cowl, which has been placed on the step before the novice, saying:

## CHAPTER XXIV. Prayer over the cowl

[Note: [Col. 0690C] CHAPTER XXIV.—The same matter is reported in the ancient statutes, part II, chapter 24, no. 5, and the same form is observed by us. By the name “cowl” we understand that outer, ankle-length garment to which the hood is attached, and whose two sides are joined by a broad ribbon. Thus, when we appear in public, we wear before and behind something resembling the form of a cross. [Col. 0690D] When, however, we sit alone in the cell and are not occupied with the recitation of the divine offices, we remove that ankle-length cowl and put on the short one fastened with cords, so that we may work more freely.]

[Col. 0689]

Lord Jesus Christ, who deigned to put on the covering of our mortality, we beseech the abundant greatness of your immeasurable generosity: deign so to bless this kind of garment, which the holy Fathers decreed that those renouncing the world should wear as a sign of innocence or humility, that this servant of yours, who makes use of it, may deserve to put you on. You who live and reign with God the Father.

Then, after removing the cope [variant: “drawing off the cope”], he clothes the novice in the cowl. Going to the corner of the altar, he reads his profession openly and distinctly in the hearing of all. After it has been read, he offers it upon the altar, which he has kissed. Bending down at the priest’s feet, he receives the blessing with the following prayer:

## CHAPTER XXV. Prayer over the novice

[Note: [Col. 0691A]

CHAPTER XXV.—No. 1. The same form for blessing a newly professed member is reported in the ancient statutes, part II, chapter 24, no. 5.

No. 2. “And at this time,” etc. Here the holy man expresses in clear words that obedience is, as it were, the center of the Carthusian institute. We defer discussion of this matter until below, under chapter 35. The same material is reproduced word for word in both the ancient and the new statutes.]

[Col. 0691]

1. Lord Jesus Christ, who are the way without which no one comes to the Father, we ask your most gracious mercy to lead this servant of yours, withdrawn from carnal desires, along the path of regular discipline. And because you deigned to call sinners, saying, “Come to me, all you who are burdened, and I will refresh you,” grant that the voice of your invitation may grow so strong in him that, laying down the burdens of his sins and tasting how sweet you are, he may deserve to be sustained by your refreshment. And just as you deigned to attest concerning your sheep, recognize him among your sheep, so that he may know you [variant: “recognize you”] in such a way that he follows no stranger and does not listen to the voice of strangers, but to yours, by which you say: “Whoever ministers to me, let him follow me.” You who live and reign, and so forth.

2. From this time onward, the one who has been received understands himself to be so alienated from everything belonging to the world that he has no power whatsoever over anything—not even over himself—without the prior’s permission. For although obedience must be observed with great zeal by all who have resolved to live according to a rule, it must be practiced by these men with so much greater devotion and solicitude because they have undertaken their purpose more strictly and severely. Otherwise, should obedience—God forbid—be lacking, such great labors would not only be deprived of their reward, but they would also incur the punishment of condemnation.

3. Hence Samuel says: “For obedience is better”—[variant: “he says, obedience is better”]—“than sacrifice, and to listen better than to offer the fat of rams. For rebellion is like the sin of divination, and refusal to submit is like the crime of idolatry” (1 Samuel 15:22). This single testimony contains both praise of obedience and sufficient condemnation of disobedience.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the order of the community

[Note: [Col. 0691A] CHAPTER XXVI.—Rank and place, attached in a certain sense to natural right, are assigned here, but everything is subjected to the service of obedience, since one is said to be subject to the prior’s judgment for a reason whose validity or sufficiency is left to him without any condition. Precisely the same provisions are found both in the ancient and in the new statutes.]

In the refectory, or anywhere else, we all observe the order given to each person by his arrival, unless the prior happens, for some reason, either to place someone below him or to put someone before him.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the age of those to be received

[Note: [Col. 0691B]

CHAPTER XXVII.—Through experience over time one gradually learns what the weakness of human beings can bear and what is more suitable for it. Therefore it is not surprising if, according to differences of time and experience, certain things that previously seemed very good come, through experience of events, to appear not so good as they had been thought, and are even later judged harmful, and are consequently changed or abolished. Hence the greatest care must be taken in the Order lest we rashly criticize or attempt to correct changes made with mature counsel and deliberation.
