Otherwise, through our own experience and at our own cost, we may learn again what our Fathers perhaps learned at theirs, and the common proverb may apply to us: “We must buy at an even higher price what already cost them dearly.” Why does divine providence permit us gradually to arrive at knowledge of the unsuitability of certain things that once seemed highly suitable? It must be judged that this happens so that it may become evident to us how uncertain our plans are, how much we must guard against relying on our own judgment and obstinately clinging to our own opinion, and how much the hardness of our hearts in many matters needs experience, by which it is beaten and softened as by a hammer, so that it may not easily trust itself or follow its own desires, and may purchase through its own experience the firmness by which it clings to truth recognized through its own labors and, so to speak, at its own expense. Nor should it rashly criticize changes that it sees by its own experience to have become necessary. In this way it will recognize how exceedingly imprudent those are in their thinking and conduct who wish to cling too tenaciously to antiquity and never to admit any change in the ancient practices of monastic life.

Our Fathers, therefore, instructed by the experience of others, reject boys and do not wish to admit them among themselves, even under the pious pretext of raising them from childhood in the discipline of the Lord. They admit only men, or at least young adults, who are believed to possess the maturity of deliberation necessary for undertaking our way of life. This must now be observed by us all the more strictly [Col. 0693A], since the door for expelling and rejecting disorderly members from among us has now been closed. In the time of R. P. Guigo that door was not merely open, as is shown by chapter 77 of these Customs; it remained open in the Order for several centuries afterward, as we shall see from what follows. Given, then, this necessity that has been introduced—the necessity of keeping both good and bad members in religious orders—I do not hesitate to declare that, for the good of the entire Carthusian Order, it would be preferable to set fire to one of the cells of our cloisters and let it be consumed by the flames than to admit into it a monk who does not have, insofar as possible, a good and well-tested vocation, and who is lacking the appropriate gifts of mind and body and the devoted will to serve God in the Order as he ought. When I reflect on this, I seem to be filled with fervor, and I do not hesitate to affirm that greater damage to religious orders has arisen and continues to arise from this source. But let us restrain the pen here, lest we write at greater length on the matter.]

We do not receive boys or adolescents, because we grieve that many and great evils have occurred in monasteries through them, and we fear many spiritual and bodily dangers. We receive men who, according to the Lord’s command given through Moses, are at least twenty years old and able to go forth to the sacred wars. With this completed, let us carry out what we promised concerning the cell.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the utensils of the cell

[Note: [Col. 0693B]

CHAPTER XXVIII.—No. 1. “For the bed: straw,” etc. Among the furnishings customarily granted for arranging the bed and for clothing, it is clear that our members never renounced the use of pelts but used them from the beginning. Indeed, at that time two fur garments were assigned to each person in the Grande Chartreuse. One was worn every day and served as an ankle-length outer tunic; the other was used on feast days. Thus they were well protected against the cold in these frigid places. Now our clothing differs from theirs: we use the fur tunic as an outer garment only in winter and at night, while during the day we use another garment made of coarse local cloth. Yet the practice of wearing fur garments even during the day still prevailed in this house not long ago, as we have heard from eyewitnesses and still read in the account books of the Charterhouse. It was changed in accordance with the circumstances of the times, when people appeared to judge more delicately and subtly and to criticize more readily, lest they be scandalized by it. We likewise no longer use sheep pelts for the bed.

“Of whatever thickness or color it may be, he shall not be concerned.” This should not be understood as referring to differences of color, as though one person might be supplied with a red garment, another a black one, and another a white one. It would be ridiculous even to imagine such a thing. Rather, it must be understood as referring to a greater or lesser degree of whiteness within the same kind of material.

“Humility and the wearing out,” etc., “of everything we use.” Here we have a written judgment against us if we employ curious and costly objects for our use beyond what honest decency permits.

No. 3. “Books as everlasting,” etc. By this expression he wishes to indicate that books are a kind of food that is not consumed through use. From this passage it is clear how much the first Fathers wished our members to be occupied with writing books; indeed, this was then their more common occupation, as the chapter plainly shows.

“Thus, because we cannot preach with our mouths, we preach the word of God with our hands. For as many books as,” etc. Our Fathers therefore also devoted themselves to the public good, especially since at that time the art of printing had not yet been invented, and no avenue to reading and study was available except through the possession of manuscript codices. If the ancient Fathers thought in this way and wished us in our own manner to devote ourselves to preaching by copying books composed by others, they did not refuse to allow books composed by our own members also to be copied. Accordingly, those who would wish to exclude our members altogether from composing books must be judged to speak more harshly than is appropriate, and those who, under the pretext of a hidden and solitary life, would think that they ought to speak to God for human beings but not speak of God to human beings—not even by means of the pen—would depart excessively from the mind of R. P. Guigo and would tacitly condemn so many distinguished and devout writers who are numbered among the Order. Yet it must be admitted that great caution must be exercised among us in this matter, lest the itch to write and publish books give room to an empty opinion of oneself, or lest, because of the lesser mastery of the sciences—which rarely abounds in solitary men removed from academic exercises—certain works insufficiently polished be brought into public view. But in these matters the modern statutes have established and prescribed the wisest methods, by adhering to which everything will be accomplished moderately and prudently. The writings of Carthusians, therefore, are not to be entirely excluded from the press, provided that nothing is written in them contrary to the intention of R. P. Guigo, and that a Carthusian treats only those subjects that contribute to the assertion of Catholic truth, the eradication of vices, and the cultivation of virtues.

No. 5. “Let anyone who reads this neither ridicule it,” etc., “unless he has first spent time in a cell,” etc. The holy man attempts to anticipate human weakness—or rather, human foolishness—which, when it wishes to follow its own judgment concerning matters of which it has no experiential knowledge, often raves in its thoughts and opinions. The holy man therefore wisely challenges such judges to an experiment: if they were confined within the walls of a cell for even one week, then the eyes of the blind would be opened and the ears of the deaf unstopped, and they would declare that what they had previously considered superfluous in a Carthusian cell—the little garden and the tools suited to manual labor—was entirely necessary. As for why our solitaries are so provided with things necessary for external occupations, he adds the reason: “lest,” he says, “we should be compelled to leave the cell for what we consider unlawful.” For it must not be believed that a person can remain for a long time within the walls of a cell unless he has there certain well-ordered means of occupying himself. Since he cannot always apply himself to spiritual matters, and human frailty cannot undertake this without the danger of losing both mental and bodily health, he must also have something by which he can relax and refresh his spirit through some external occupation. Those who, when they see a Carthusian monk occasionally occupied with small carpentry tasks, are annoyed by this and think that such less serious activities disgrace a monk who ought to be wholly spiritual, are therefore thinking imprudently, indeed foolishly. These are the people whom R. P. Guigo challenges to put the matter to the test.

From this chapter it is evident how prudently the first Fathers always taught us to act in everything, and how much we must avoid extremes, lest that philosophical axiom apply to us: “Whatever is forced is not lasting.” We see here that they provided for the bodily needs of solitaries with honorable moderation. They were content merely to keep luxury away from us in this respect and, lest we should ever remain idle, they specifically assign so many tools to each monk and prescribe that other tools also be granted as needed, when they say that a person unable to write books, but skilled in another craft, is to be supplied with tools appropriate to his craft.

No. 6. “For this is by no means permitted except when he is summoned to the cloister,” etc. This must be understood morally, for it is certain that at that time our members could also leave the cell for other reasons, as is plainly evident from chapters 17 and 32 and from various other passages, and as reason itself suggests. They could approach the prior to explain their needs to him and request permissions. The departure from the cell that was not permitted was therefore the same departure that we still call an irregular departure from the cell—that is, a superfluous departure made without moral necessity—for which we ought to confess our fault in chapter. Indeed, I am convinced that they were sometimes given permission to walk about within the hermitage for recreation, as appears from a very ancient manuscript that was unhappily consumed by the flames in the last fire of the house. There I read how matters were arranged when walking among the rocks of the Grande Chartreuse was permitted, especially when they went to the mountain called *le Grand Son*, which in Latin means “the great summit” and which overlooks the Charterhouse. Climbing it requires more time and labor.

You will find this entire chapter reproduced in the ancient statutes, part II, chapter 16.]

[Col. 0693]

The inhabitant of the cell therefore receives for the bed straw, a felt covering, a pillow, and a mattress or blanket made of the coarsest sheep pelts and covered with coarse cloth. For clothing he receives two hair shirts, two tunics, two fur garments—one poorer and the other better—and likewise two cowls; three pairs of leggings, four pairs of socks, pelts, a cope, night and day shoes, grease for anointing, two loincloths, and a belt—all made of hemp and coarse material—and everything that pertains in any way to the bed or clothing [variant: “bed or garment”]. He shall not be concerned about the thickness or color of these things. For it is certain that humility and the wearing out of our clothing and of everything we use, together with its baseness, poverty, and lowliness, belong to all monks, and especially to us. He also has two needles, thread, scissors, a comb, a razor for the head, a whetstone or sharpening stone, and a strap for sharpening.

2. For writing, he receives a writing desk, pens, chalk, two pumice stones, two horns, one knife, two knives or scrapers for scraping parchment, one pricker, one awl, lead, a ruler, a board for ruling, tablets, and a stylus. If the brother belongs to another craft—which happens very rarely among us, since we teach nearly all whom we receive to write, if possible—he shall have tools appropriate to his craft.

3. He also receives two books from the cupboard for reading. He is commanded to take every care and precaution that they not be stained by smoke, dust, or any other dirt. For we wish books to be guarded with the greatest care as the everlasting food of our souls, and to be produced with the greatest diligence, so that, because we cannot preach with our mouths, we may preach the word of God with our hands.

[Col. 0695] 4. For as many books as we write, so many heralds of truth do we seem to make for ourselves, hoping from the Lord a reward for all who through them have either been corrected from error or advanced in Catholic truth, and for all who have either been pierced with remorse over their sins and vices or been inflamed with desire for the heavenly homeland.

5. And because, just as we ourselves provide the other necessities that pertain to lowliness and humility, we also prepare our own food, two pots are provided, two bowls, a third vessel for bread—or, in its place, a cloth—a fourth, somewhat larger, for cleaning; two spoons, a knife for bread, a measure, a cup, a water vessel, saltcellars, a pan, two small sacks for legumes, and a towel. For the fire: a fire-steel, tinder, a stone [variant: “a firestone”], wood, and an axe. For work, an adze. We ask that whoever reads this neither ridicule nor criticize it, unless he has first spent a considerable time in a cell amid such great snow and such dreadful cold.

6. For this reason we grant so many things to one person, lest he be compelled to leave the cell for what we consider unlawful. This is by no means permitted except when he is summoned to the cloister or to the church; and this is the customary procedure in the Order.

## CHAPTER XXIX. When one may leave the cell, and concerning vigils and the division of the hours

[Note: [Col. 0696C]

CHAPTER XXIX.—No. 1. “Except at all times,” etc. From this exception an opportunity for error might arise, and one might believe [Col. 0697A] that on the days excepted one had to proceed to the church immediately after the first signal, unless R. P. Guigo’s meaning of “vigils” were explained.

By “vigils,” therefore, we must understand that period of time extending beyond what is necessary for reciting the Matins of the Blessed Virgin Mary. These are said by us every day in the cells between the first and second psalms of Matins. Thus, when only enough time is given for devoutly reciting these Matins, these vigils are “ordinary”; when they extend beyond that, we call them “extended vigils.” R. P. Guigo’s meaning, therefore, is that, on the days excepted here, whether they occur in summer or winter, no vigils are ever to be kept beyond the time necessary for reciting the Matins and Lauds of the Blessed Virgin Mary.

“Which gradually and little by little increase from the Ides of September,” etc. He is now about to explain how these vigils were arranged. For easier understanding, we must recall what was said above in chapter 7, no. 8, concerning longer and shorter nights. They considered the nights to increase gradually from the Ides of September—that is, from the vigil of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross—until the Kalends of November, or the feast of All Saints. From that day until the feast of the Purification of the Blessed Virgin Mary, they arranged matters as though the nights remained at the same length. From then until Easter they considered the nights to decrease; but from Easter until the Exaltation [Col. 0697C] of the Holy Cross, they judged that the nights remained at the same length with respect to the hour of rising during the night.

No. 1. “With fifty psalms.” This requires a full hour and more. It therefore signifies that these vigils gradually increased from the Exaltation of the Holy Cross until they reached the length of a full hour on the very Kalends of November. They remained at the length of a full hour until the feast of the Purification. From that day, these vigils gradually decreased, like the nights, until they returned to their former length at Easter—that is, around Easter; for on the day of the Lord’s Supper these vigils cease.

We now observe precisely the same arrangement concerning these vigils, and the ringing for Compline follows the course of the vigils. The signal is gradually moved earlier from the feast of the Exaltation [Col. 0697D] of the Holy Cross, as it was observed by the ancient Fathers, until the feast of All Saints is reached [Col. 0698A]. From then it remains at the same time on weekdays until the feast of the Purification of the Blessed Virgin Mary. From that day it is gradually moved later until Easter, when it returns to its former time. We explain all this somewhat more fully so that what follows may be more easily understood.

No. 3. “When the nocturns have been sung, a short interval,” etc. This expresses the duration of the interval. But it does not say what was done during it. We believe that they wished in this way to relax the mind’s attention, and that they could therefore return to the cell during the interval, as will be clear from the ancient statutes.

“Then the morning Lauds follow, which light brings to an end from the Kalends of October until Easter.” That is, they ended at the hour when daylight was already bright, or at least beginning to brighten. “Then it begins.” That is, they began at the hour of the day when daylight appeared. From this passage it is clear that the nocturnal vigils were then observed by them in a different manner from ours today, and that they slept without interruption for as long as necessary throughout the entire period between the Kalends of October and Easter. From Easter until the aforementioned Kalends, they remained in bed according to the greater or lesser length of the nights; the shorter or longer duration of Matins also followed this pattern, for at that time they lacked readings unless a feast occurred. Since they slept less at night, however, they made up for it by daytime sleep, which was assigned to them between Sext and None. It is therefore not surprising that they never returned to bed after Matins.

We can establish only by conjecture at what hour the signal for Matins was given, and from those conjectures we may judge that their nocturnal vigils then differed little from those prescribed in the Rule of Saint Benedict. To make the matter clearer, we shall note here what we have tried to learn not only through conjecture but also through experiments undertaken on the basis of experience.

Taking the Kalends of November as a kind of reference point—a time when, as in summer, the signal for Compline should be given while it is still possible to read, that is, while day is turning into night but the letters of a book can still be read—we carefully investigated at what hour this occurred. We found that on a clear day, among the mountains of the Grande Chartreuse, at the very place where the chapel of Saint Bruno stands, it occurred shortly after Sext. At that time, indeed from the Kalends of October, as stated above, daylight brought Matins and Lauds to an end. We must therefore believe that they ended at about the sixth hour of the morning. If we calculate the hours during which the nocturnal divine office lasted, adding the vigils mentioned above, we shall find through the experience that we still undertake today that ordinarily four full hours were counted. If these are subtracted from the approximately eleven hours extending between about six in the evening and six in the morning, more than seven hours remain, which were assigned to uninterrupted sleep. Yet in a very ancient codex we found it written that around the feast of All Saints eight uninterrupted hours were assigned to sleep.

We do not know when that change took place, although we believe it can scarcely be more than two hundred years old, since we possess a manuscript that does not appear especially ancient, in which we customarily admonish all those present in the general chapter, among other matters, concerning the daytime sleep of the monks, which must not be disturbed by moving about or walking in the cloister. At the same time that we believe the order of the vigils was changed through interruptions of sleep, we also think that the custom of daytime sleep ceased.

We have found no written account of the reason why that change from the ancient vigils to stricter vigils through interruption of sleep was made. We conjecture, however, that it was done so that, although nature might suffer somewhat greater tedium from this divided sleep, the powers of the mind would not be overly fatigued by such prolonged application to the divine office, which was then almost joined to the nocturnal office, but would be discreetly restored and preserved through the interposition of sleep. This was especially so because Gregorian chant was in use among us—a practice we do not believe was admitted into the Order in the time of the first Fathers—and through that chant the length of the divine office had been increased to no small degree.

No. 3. “From the aforementioned Kalends, daylight begins Prime.” It follows that, after a short interval had been made following Matins, Prime was rung when the day was somewhat more fully light during this part of the year. “Then it awaits sunrise.” That is, during the other part of the year, from Easter until the Kalends of October, the signal for Prime was given according to the varying times of sunrise, earlier or later [Col. 0700A]. They observed this in such a way that they could truly and literally say, “The star of dawn having risen,” in the hymn that is sung every day at Prime.

“Except only on solemn days.” The meaning is that solemn days occurring between the Kalends of October and November followed the rite of the summer days.

“But also in Lent, so as to devote more time to prayer,” etc. This passage closes the mouths of those who say that no fixed time for mental prayer appears among the Carthusians. We answer them briefly that this explicit determination of time seemed almost superfluous to R. P. Guigo and the others because the life of a good Carthusian is almost continual mental prayer. Nevertheless, this passage makes it clear that time for this pious exercise was always specifically assigned in the Order.

“On the other days, however, on which chapter is held.” That is, on the feasts that we call “chapter days” because chapter is always held on them. “Until it is possible to read in a book,” that is, around the sixth hour. This is still observed by us in the same way, except for the rising of the sun, which we can no longer follow in summer because the interruption of sleep has been introduced. At almost the same hour at which the ancient Fathers rose in summer, we now return to bed after completing Matins.

“At what hour, however, from Easter until the Kalends of October,” etc. “When the sun shines upon the highest mountains.” He is not speaking of only one mountain but of several. There is a very high rock called *la pointe du Midi*, as though one were to say, “the peak marking the southern line,” upon which the sun casts its rays as soon as it rises at the summer solstice, shortly after the fourth hour. But before the mountains have been illuminated in this way, it is the fifth hour. From this we infer that in summer scarcely an hour, or at most an hour and a half, often intervened between the end of Matins and Prime.

“Spiritual exercises.” Here the time customarily assigned among us for mental prayer and devout reading is expressly noted. And if several hours are not assigned among us for mental prayer, let the reader remember that we stated above that the life of a good Carthusian is continual mental prayer [Col. 0701A], as will immediately be proved more fully.

“From the third hour until Sext in winter,” etc. Here you have the time assigned in the morning to manual work. Such work must never be separated from the practice of prayer among us. In this way R. P. Guigo shows us how we can and ought to fulfill Christ’s words: “We must always pray and not lose heart” (Luke 18:1).

“And how Sext and None in winter can be explained as neighboring,” etc. By “the regular hour” he means the office that is said; by the two hours of Saint Mary he means the Sext and None of the Blessed Virgin Mary. From this it follows that the interval between the summer Sexts was only about half an hour, for half an hour is all that is needed to recite those brief offices devoutly.

[Col. 0701B] “The interval between Sext and None is assigned to rest.” Here is the daytime sleep assigned for the summer season, which we have already discussed in chapter 7, no. 8.

“And that between None and Vespers,” etc., “to manual work.” From this it is clear that at every season our monks devoted themselves to manual work twice a day: once in the morning, as stated above, and once in the evening, between None and Vespers.

“From Vespers until Compline, to spiritual exercises,” etc. Here again a period is designated for prayer and spiritual exercises.

## Number 4

In Compline, attention is paid to this: it is rung when it is delayed as long as possible while it can still be read. After its conclusion, once the Lord’s Prayer has been devoutly completed three times, we do not delay any longer before lying down.

Nothing certain can be gathered from this passage concerning the hour at which the signal for Compline was given during the summer. For winter, it can easily be determined, as we said above, namely, shortly after Sext. But this is proved even more clearly by the great variation in the time of ringing for Compline: the order of the nocturnal vigils was very different from the one we now follow. In summer we ring for Compline while the sun is still shining, whereas here it is said that they used to ring only when it was still possible to read in a book—something that occurs only after sunset. The time when it is delayed later falls around Easter and continues in the same way until the Kalends of October. At that time, namely around Easter, it is still possible to read in a book at approximately the seventh hour, and this agrees well with the vigil assigned by the Rule of Saint Benedict.

## Number 5

For we are not merely admonished, but also commanded, to devote great attention to sleep during the hours assigned to rest, so that we may remain alert during the other times.

From this we have established that the spirit of the Order requires us not to attempt, under any pretext, to subtract anything from the bodily supports instituted by the Order through our own will. This is the greatest indication of discretion. The ancient Fathers knew from their own experience that such discretion had necessarily to be maintained in properly directing those who profess the solitary life; accordingly, they would not admit any zeal for additional exercises or mortifications in this area. This will be proved further from Chapter 35.

## Number 6

In general, we say Matins and Vespers in the church, but Compline is always said in the cells. We do not come to the church at other times except on feast days, for vigils, or for anniversaries.

Nothing concerning Mass appears in the printed edition; but in the oldest manuscript codex we read: “Matins, Mass, and Vespers.” We therefore rightly believe that the omission is a typographical error. Whatever the case may be, he had already said enough about Mass in the earlier chapters. If he omitted Mass here, it may be said that he wished to speak here only of the canonical hours, so that his meaning would be that, generally, Matins and Vespers are said in the church every day, while Compline is always said in the cells. This is observed today in exactly the same way.

This entire chapter is reproduced in full in Part I of the ancient statutes, Chapter 41, numbers 4, 9, 10, 12, and 13.

## [Col. 0697] 1

At all times, except on feasts with twelve readings and during the weeks of the Nativity of the Lord, Easter, and Pentecost, once the signal has been rung we anticipate the church office at night with suitable vigils in the cell. These vigils gradually increase from the Ides of September until they reach their full measure at the Kalends of November, when they are sufficient for fifty psalms sung without excessive haste. From that time until the Kalends of February they continue in this form. From then until Easter, they gradually decrease and are reduced to a period sufficient for the Matins of Holy Mary. From Easter until the aforementioned Ides of September, they continue at that same measure.

## 2

After the second signal has been rung, we hasten to the church and strive to arrive before the end of the third signal. There, after the prior—or whoever has been charged with this—has gone ahead, we prostrate ourselves upon the choir stalls and devoutly and solemnly recite the Lord’s Prayer three times, and once at the other hours. Then we rise and begin to sing the psalms with reverence for God.

## 3

After the nocturns have been sung, we take a short interval, long enough at most for seven penitential psalms. Matins praises then follow. From the Kalends of October until Easter, daylight ends them; thereafter, daylight begins them. After Matins, we never return to our beds.

From the aforementioned Kalends until Easter, daylight likewise begins Prime; thereafter, we await sunrise, except on solemn days, until the Kalends of November, when those days follow the pattern of the remaining summer days. During Lent also, on solemn days, it is delayed almost until sunrise, so that more time may be devoted to prayer. On the other days, when Chapter is held—from the Kalends of November until Lent—it is prolonged until it can be read in a book.

At whatever hour Prime is rung from Easter until the Kalends of October, at that same hour Terce is rung from the Kalends of October until Lent, namely, when the sun is shining upon the highest mountains [or, “specifically”]. The interval either from Prime to Terce in winter, or from Matins to Prime in summer, is devoted to spiritual exercises.

From Terce to Sext in winter, and from Prime to Terce in summer, the time is assigned to manual labor. We nevertheless wish these works to be interrupted by brief prayers. The same intervals that lie between Sext and None in winter correspond in summer to those between Terce and Sext. They are separated from one another by an interval long enough for the regular hour and the two Offices of Holy Mary to be completed.

The interval between Sext and None is assigned to rest in summer, sometimes shorter and sometimes longer. The interval separating None and Vespers [or, “determining” them] is occupied by manual labor; while working, one may always return to brief, almost ejaculatory prayers. From Vespers until Compline, time is devoted to spiritual works.

## [Col. 0701] 4

At Compline, attention is paid to this: whenever it is delayed later, the signal is rung while it is still possible to read. After its conclusion, once the Lord’s Prayer has been devoutly completed three times, we do not delay any longer before lying down.

## 5

For we are not merely admonished, but also commanded, to devote great attention to sleep during the hours assigned to rest, so that we may remain alert during the other times.

## 6

In general, we say Matins and Vespers in the church, but Compline is always said in the cells. We do not come to the church at other times except on feast days, for vigils, or for anniversaries.

# CHAPTER XXX

## Concerning those who intrude upon those remaining in the cell, and concerning the kitchen steward

### [Note: [Col. 0702B]]

### Chapter XXX

**Number 1. “If someone is importunate.”** Here he is speaking of outsiders who come to the Charterhouse and, after entering the cloister, do not find anyone with whom to speak. They proceed to the door of a cell; when they knock, the monk comes, and, having heard the knocker’s request, knows from this passage how he ought to conduct himself, even with a blood brother.

**“Unless commanded.”** That is, unless it is with special permission requested from the person who wishes to speak with us, in accordance with what we said above in Chapter 17, number 2.

**Number 2. “The kitchen steward,” etc.** At that time the kitchen steward was the general administrator, acting in the superior house in the procurator’s place.

**[Col. 0703A] Number 3. “But if one of our own,” etc.** He is first asked whether the prior has given the order, etc. It is therefore evident that the monks would also sometimes visit one another with the prior’s permission. This should always be understood whenever Reverend Father Guigo uses the word “command.”

**Number 4. “To sit and converse,” etc., “unless someone should happen to be ill,” etc.** The kitchen steward, then, who at that time acted in the superior house in the procurator’s place, had permission—just as the procurator does now—to speak a few words at the cell door and perhaps also to enter the cell, in order to arrange the kitchen equipment. For at that time each monk prepared his own food in the manner described above, in Chapter 28. He did not, however, have permission to sit there or converse; by the word “converse” are meant words spoken beyond what necessity required.

When monks were ill, however, the kitchen steward could freely enter the sick man’s cell and provide him with appropriate assistance.

This entire chapter is reproduced in the ancient statutes, Part II, Chapter 17, number 5, and likewise in Part III, Chapter 10, number 1. The same rules are now observed in an even stricter manner, because, except in the case of illness, the kitchen steward never enters the monks’ cells without special permission.

### [Col. 0703]

1. If someone importunate comes to the cell, we send him to the kitchen steward, either by gestures or, if he does not understand, by words. We speak no further with him—or with that person [variant: “him”]—unless commanded to do so, even if he is a blood brother.

2. The kitchen steward guards the gate, answers those who arrive, and sends those seeking alms to the lower house. He cares for the houses and for everything belonging to common use. No one, unless commanded, crosses the limits of the kitchen, namely, the door of the refectory through which one proceeds to it.

3. If one of our own comes to the cell wishing to speak with us, he is first asked whether the prior has commanded it; otherwise he is not admitted to conversation.

4. The kitchen steward himself is not permitted to sit and converse in the cells, unless someone should happen to be ill.

# CHAPTER XXXI

## Also concerning the cell

### [Note: [Col. 0703B]]

### Chapter XXXI

Nothing needs to be added to the words of Reverend Father Guigo, who expresses clearly and concisely what a person professing the solitary life must observe if he wishes to form good habits and pass his life peacefully and quietly in his state.

**[Col. 0703C] Number 1. “Except those things which have been generally instituted.”** The most devout and experienced professor of the solitary life always brings this forward in order to drive indiscreet singularities from solitaries’ minds and eliminate excesses, for the reasons that we shall discuss below in Chapter 35.

**“To be requested at the appointed hours,” etc.** From this it is clear that they could ask the kitchen steward for necessities in conversation not only on feast days, but also whenever necessity required it, though at specified hours.

**[Col. 0704A] Number 2. “But if through any,” etc., “bread, wine,” etc.** Here he removes every occasion for scruple by making clear that the Carthusian is not deprived, through the imposed observance of the cell and silence, of the freedom to leave the cell or even to speak when a just reason or necessity demands it, such as the one expressed here.

From the bread mentioned here, and from the freedom to request bread when it runs out, it is suggested that the loaf of bread mentioned above in Chapter 7, number 10, as being given to each monk after the refectory meal, as to a beggar of Christ, was not given for the entire week. Rather, once that bread had been consumed, another was supplied on the days appointed during the week.

**[Col. 0704B] Number 3. “Those living alone know the signals of the cenobites.”** From this we learn how much the first Fathers loved simplicity and sincerity, and how much they wished to transfer both to us. They did not wish to use anything else to express their meaning, when necessity required it, than the bodily member appointed by God for that purpose; and they rejected everything that could give rise to an opportunity for deception or lead gradually away from the purpose of our Institute.

For just as we see the mute communicate through gestures, so those bound to silence could also learn and practice the same thing if, once the freedom to speak had been removed, the use of signs had been introduced and permitted everywhere.

This entire chapter is reproduced in the ancient statutes, Part II, Chapter 17, number 1 and following.

### [Col. 0704C]

1. Having laid these matters out beforehand, let us return to the cell. Its inhabitant ought to watch over it diligently and carefully, lest he either devise or accept opportunities for going outside, except those generally instituted. Rather, just as water is necessary for fish and enclosures for sheep, so he should regard the cell as necessary for his salvation and life. The longer he remains in it, the more willingly he will inhabit it; but if he becomes accustomed to leaving frequently and for trivial reasons, he will quickly come to hate it. Therefore he is commanded to request at the appointed hours whatever must be requested, and to guard with complete diligence what he has received.

2. If, through his own negligence or that of another, he lacks bread, wine, water, or fire; if he hears an unusual noise or cry; or if there is a danger of fire [variant: “if the danger has arisen”], he may leave the cell, provide or request assistance, and, if the magnitude of the danger demands it, even break silence.

3. Living alone, we know only the signs of the cenobites—or none or very few—and we consider the tongue alone sufficient, without involving the other limbs in the guilt of speaking. Therefore, when such great necessity presses, we have preferred that what the matter requires be indicated in one or two words, or certainly in as few words as possible.

# CHAPTER XXXII

## Concerning brothers occupied in some task

### [Note: [Col. 0704C]]

### Chapter XXXII

This chapter makes it plainly evident that the first Carthusians were permitted not only occasionally to visit one another when the prior allowed it for a reasonable cause, but also that several monks would not infrequently gather together to complete some task entrusted to them by the prior. When gathered in this way, they could then speak freely among themselves, the law of silence being suspended, but not with those who came upon them, unless the prior was present or had given permission.

The same text is reproduced word for word in the ancient statutes, Part II, Chapter 18, number 2. It is still prescribed and observed in exactly the same way.

When some of the monks are occupied in correcting or binding books, or in any similar task, they speak with one another, but not at all with those who come upon them, unless the prior is present or commands it.

# CHAPTER XXXIII

## Concerning fasts and food

### [Note: [Col. 0705A]]

### Chapter XXXIII

**Number 1. “On the second, fourth, and sixth feria,” etc.** It must be understood that this does not apply if a feast of the Chapter occurred on those days. This is plainly evident from Chapter 52, where the brothers are exempted from the abstinence to be observed even on the sixth feria—commonly called Friday—because of an intervening feast, although they observed that abstinence only once a week.

Here he explains what those abstinences were and of what kind, which it is established were observed by our members at the beginning of the Order. Some now accuse us of relaxing them because they are not observed in the same way. Before we give the reason for this in its proper places and prove that the Carthusian Institute has not thereby been relaxed in any way, since this observance was introduced and maintained in the Order not absolutely but always conditionally, let the reader note that the condition is expressly declared in the following chapter, where it says: “But if the prior wishes to provide anyone with some pitantia, whether of food, sleep, or anything else—that is, to grant it—we have no right to resist,” etc.

From these words it is clearer than daylight that these abstinences were to be and were observed by all and by individuals only when, and for as long as, the prior judged that they were possible and appropriate without detriment to their health. I say “health,” because this condition would have been entirely superfluous and useless if no consideration were to be given to bodily health. Here the great discretion of the first Carthusians shines forth: they established it as the foundation of their Institute, wishing to prevent many of their members from failing in the solitary way of life through excessive attachment to bodily austerities, just as they already knew had happened to certain ancient anchorites and others. This discretion proved wonderfully beneficial for preserving the Order in its vigor.

**Number 2. “On the third, fifth, and Saturday we cook legumes, or something of this kind, for ourselves,” etc.** Here we must recall what we said above in Chapter 7 concerning the kitchen that each monk prepared for himself in his cell. To prepare it, the kitchen steward regularly supplied them with provisions of certain edible things, which they kept with them, as will be said below, until they ran out; then they requested and received new supplies.

Notice that up to this point there has been no mention of a pitantia. From the words “something of this kind,” we cannot know with certainty what else they could cook for themselves.

**“From the kitchen steward, wine,” etc. “On Thursday, cheese or some more choice food,” etc.** It begins to appear that on Thursday a portion of cheese beyond the ordinary amount was regularly supplied, or some more choice food. Yet there is still no mention here of eggs and fish, although it could also be said that these were indicated by the expression “some more choice food.”

**[Col. 0706B] Number 3. “From the Ides of September,” etc., “except on solemnities, only once,” etc.** “Solemnities” must mean feasts of the Chapter. Reverend Father Guigo uses this word also when speaking of feasts with twelve readings, as is proved from Chapter 4, number 13. Here he indicates the period during which the fast of the Order is observed, which has always been and still is observed at the same time.

**Number 4. “From Easter, however, on the third and fifth feria, and likewise on Saturday, we eat a second time.”** That is, we take not only lunch but also supper; hence these days are called among us “days of two meals.”

**Number 5. “At supper or lunch, when we eat only once, we take raw greens or fruit, if there is any. Retaining these,” etc.** This passage should not be understood to mean that on the fast days of the Order, when they ate only once at lunch, they used only raw greens or fruit, if available. The contrary is plainly evident from number 2, where it says that they cooked legumes for themselves.

It means only that they were freely permitted to use raw greens—that is, vegetables whose supply was given to them—or fruit when they had it. They could therefore keep these with them for as long as they lasted. This is stated to distinguish edible things that they could keep in the cell from prepared foods, which they had to return after eating; concerning these, he adds what follows.

**“For of cheese, fish, eggs, or anything of this kind, which we call pitantias, we take once, and return what remains.”** Here he clearly states that they used not only cheese but also fish, eggs, and other things of this kind for food. From these was composed the portion of food supplied to each monk, which they called a *pitantia* and sometimes a *pulmentum*.

On which days was such a *pitantia* supplied? It is certain that it was given in the refectory on Sundays and feast days. It was also given on Thursday, as may be inferred from number 2 of this chapter. It will also become clear from what follows that it was sometimes supplied on other days, according to the resources of the house and the prior’s arrangement, except on the days assigned to abstinence.

**Number 5. “We take once; we return what remains.”** That is, after eating the *pitantia* supplied to them, the monks could not reserve any of it for supper or for the following day. They had to place whatever remained in the little window, for the kitchen steward to collect. This has always been and still is observed in the Order.

From these words it is clear that they received *pitantias* from the kitchen steward not only on feast days but also on weekdays. They cannot be applied to feast days on which they ate in the refectory, because there the *pitantia* was supplied to them, and after the meal the attendants collected what remained, so that the table would be empty when the signal was given to the refectory lector to end the reading. It would have been superfluous to say of *pitantias* supplied in the refectory, “we take once; we return what remains.” When he ate in the refectory, this was not left to the diner’s discretion. It is therefore necessary to apply the statement to *pitantias* supplied in the cell.

**[Col. 0707C] Number 6. “We drink wine only at lunch or supper.”** This means that we ought not ordinarily to drink wine outside lunch and supper. It also appears from this that the first Carthusians, except on the days assigned to abstinence, commonly used wine with their meals both morning and evening.

**Number 7. “What remains of the bread and wine is returned on Saturday.”** This seems to indicate that they could also keep some of the wine supplied to them in the cell, but had to return it on Saturday, just as they returned the remainder of the bread supplied. We are not now permitted to keep wine in the cell in this way.

**“When we eat in the refectory, cheese,” etc., “is added to the vegetables or legumes.”** It appears from this that two courses were served in the refectory: the item they called a *pitantia*, and, in addition, legumes or vegetables.

This entire chapter is reproduced in the ancient statutes, Part II, Chapter 14, numbers 5, 6, 9, 10, 11, 13, 17, and 19. To make the way clear, through a correct understanding of this chapter, to correctly understanding many other passages that occur throughout Reverend Father Guigo’s *Customs*, and to remove any occasion for error, we add here an index of its contents.

The following points, therefore, are drawn from this chapter:

1. The first Fathers received from the kitchen steward a supply of legumes—that is, beans, peas, and so forth—as well as vegetables, which they cooked for themselves, and also fruit. They kept these with them until they had been consumed; once they were consumed, they requested and received more.

2. They received wine and bread and could keep them in the cell until Saturday. They used wine both at lunch and at supper, except on the days assigned to abstinence.

3. In addition to what they cooked for themselves in the cell, on appointed days they received a *pitantia* from the kitchen steward. They could not reserve any of it for the next meal—understood, always, without the prior’s permission. This *pitantia* consisted of cheese, eggs, fish, or some similar item.

4. On refectory days, legumes were added to the *pitantias* at lunch.

5. From the feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross until Easter, they observed the fast that we call the fast of the Order. The fast that the procurator, and sometimes the prior, was permitted to break for the sake of guests was called a non-principal fast. The principal fast was the one that had to be observed by command of the Church.

6. From the feast of Easter until the feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, they took two meals, that is, lunch and supper, except on days assigned to abstinence or fasting.

More will arise to be said about this matter under Chapter 52.

### [Col. 0705]

1. Now we must speak of fasts and food. On the second, fourth, and sixth feria, we are content with bread, water, and salt, if anyone wishes it.

2. On the third and fifth feria and on Saturday, we cook legumes or something of this kind for ourselves, receiving wine from the kitchen steward and, on Thursday, cheese or some more choice food.

3. From the Ides of September until Easter, except on solemnities, we eat only once a day.

4. From Easter until the aforementioned date, however, we eat a second time on the third and fifth feria and likewise on Saturday.

5. At supper or lunch, when we eat only once, we take raw greens or fruit, if there is any. While retaining these for as long as they last, we do not receive other items of the same kind. Of cheese, fish, eggs, or anything of this kind, which we call *pitantias*, we take once and return what remains.

6. We drink wine only at lunch or supper.

### [Col. 0707] 7

What remains of the bread and wine is returned on Saturday. When we eat in the refectory, cheese or some such *pitantia* is added to the vegetables or legumes; and at supper, either fruit or raw greens, if available, are served.

8. During Advent we eat neither eggs nor cheese.

# CHAPTER XXXIV

## Concerning the measure of wine and cheese

### [Note: [Col. 0708C]]

### Chapter XXXIV

**Number 1. “The measure of wine.”** There was therefore no distinction between feast days and other days concerning the measure of wine, since it was always the same. The new statutes add a prohibition and penance for any of our members who drinks pure wine.

**Number 3. “Although the bread is made of wheat, it is a loaf,” etc.** By “loaf” he means reddish-brown bread, such as is still made in the Order; it retains the same name, *torta*. The same quantity of the *torta* is always supplied to the monks together with a small white loaf, so that half of the bread supplied to us is *torta* and the other half white bread.

Most of us prefer this *torta* to white bread because it certainly has more flavor. But because white bread is lighter and weighs less heavily on the stomach, its use was introduced and became established in the Order, so that a portion of white bread would be supplied to the monks together with the *torta*.

From this concern to transport wheat to these rocks of the Charterhouse, so that bread could be made for the monks, it is plainly evident how wisely our founder, Saint Bruno, taught that everything should be arranged for his disciples. In this way they could persevere in serving God in their vocation with unimpaired health, proceed with equal steps in the practice of their Institute, and avoid what he knew had happened to many who, delighting in extremes, undertook severe abstinences and practiced them stubbornly for a time, but afterward, having damaged their bodily health thereby, gradually became incapable of all observances. Thereafter they were compelled not only to abandon spiritual exercises but also to care for and nourish the body diligently.

Wishing therefore to close the way to such inequalities, he wanted good wheat bread to be provided for his monks. Wheat, however, does not grow in the desert of the Charterhouse, any more than wine does. Access to these rocks was then very difficult, and wheat could be brought here only on the backs of animals or, in part, on the shoulders of men. Wheat and wine were very expensive. Nevertheless, he wanted bread made from wheat to be prepared for the monks, for them always to use, and he wanted wine always to be supplied.

Knowing that good bread, wine, and eggs are among the principal means by which we are sustained and preserve firm health, he prescribed that these be supplied to our members. We do read that fish used to be purchased only for the sick, but nothing of this kind is written concerning eggs.

**Number 4. “Cheese, both in the cells,” etc.** From this we see the well-ordered stability and suitable proportion that he wanted us to maintain everywhere, rejecting peculiarities—that is, things undertaken by one’s own will rather than by the permission or prescription of a superior—which he knew those professing the solitary life had to proscribe with great care.

For from such practices there not rarely arises a kind of proud vanity or a disturbance of peace. From the following chapter it will become even clearer with what circumspection the successors of our first holy Father Bruno wished to eliminate voluntary peculiarities and indiscretions from their members, and how they placed the whole substance and rationale of Carthusian life in obedience alone.

This entire chapter is reproduced in the ancient statutes, Part II, Chapter 14, numbers 15, 16, and 18.

### [Col. 0709D]

1. The measure of wine, both in the cells and in the refectory, remains the same and is diluted in the same manner.

2. For we do not use it pure [variant: “for we do not use pure wine”].

3. Although the bread is made of wheat, it is a *torta*; for we do not make white bread.

### [Col. 0709] 4

Cheese is given in the same weight, both in the cells and in the refectory.

# CHAPTER XXXV

## That no one may undertake greater exercises without the prior’s approval

### [Note: [Col. 0710A]]

### Chapter XXXV

From these words of Reverend Father Guigo it becomes known that, from the beginning of the Institute, Carthusian obedience has been held among us in such esteem, and ought to be of such a character, that nothing apart from it is considered useful or valid in the Order. It is regarded, as it were, as the heart of the Carthusian Institute.

This chapter is reproduced not only in the ancient statutes, Part II, Chapter 14, numbers 25, 27, and 28, but has also been transferred word for word into the new collection of statutes. No one is counted among the Carthusians who has not knowingly and willingly made his vows with reference to the words contained in this statute. From these words it is clear:

First, that through his profession of obedience the Carthusian monk has renounced even certain works of piety, which he cannot undertake unless the prior knows of them and approves them. This is the greatest prudence, since it removes from solitaries the opportunity to fall into serious indiscretions, to which the solitary state would be more vulnerable than other states unless it were governed by obedience.

Second, he must be prepared to receive indulgently from his superior certain alleviations in food, drink, or sleep beyond what the statute prescribes. This too is true discretion, so that the care of the solitaries’ health may depend upon the superior’s judgment and every occasion for obstinacy in one’s own judgment and for indiscretion may be removed from the solitary monk. As has already been said, that state requires discretion, so that God may be served continually in it with health and alertness, without interruption or relaxation.

Third, he is likewise bound to obey in difficult and burdensome matters beyond the statute that are imposed upon him by his superior. Hence it is clear that, by the force of his profession, the Carthusian has subjected his own will to the virtue of obedience in such a way that he has offered it to God, to be valued as a sheep for slaughter.

Fourth, the force of obedience in that state establishes the Carthusian monk in such a condition that he must regard God himself in the person of his superior.

Fifth and finally, it must be held as certain that the sense of the Order and the spirit of the Carthusian Institute consist in obedience in such a way that through obedience alone Carthusian observances acquire the force of merit, while outside it they possess no merit.

For this reason, those who established the form for celebrating the General Chapter, adhering to the footsteps of Reverend Father Guigo and the first Fathers, explicitly noted there the form and circumspection to be observed when the General Chapter judged that the rigor of the Order ought to be diminished in some matter. At the same time, they preserved the freedom to add something new and more demanding to the ancient observances if, after considering the circumstances of times, persons, and experience, it appeared to them more conducive to attaining the end of our Institute.

It will be proved in its proper places that this has likewise been observed up to the present. Thus it will be clear to anyone of sound judgment who wishes to consider the matter peacefully and in a spirit of charity that the General Chapter of the Order—and therefore the body of the Order—has departed neither from the meaning nor from the letter expressed by Reverend Father Guigo in this Chapter 35.

### [Col. 0711A]

1. None of us may undertake abstinences, disciplines, vigils, or any other religious exercises that do not belong to our institution unless the prior knows of them and approves them.

2. But if the prior wishes to provide anyone with some *pitantia*, whether of food, sleep, or anything else—that is, to grant it—or to impose something difficult and burdensome, we have no right to resist. Otherwise, when we resist him, we may be found to have resisted not him but the Lord, whose place he occupies toward us.

3. Although there are many and diverse things that we observe, we nevertheless hope that all of them will be fruitful for us through the one and only good of obedience.

# CHAPTER XXXVI

## Concerning the reception of guests

### [Note: [Col. 0711B]]

### Chapter XXXVI

**Number 1. “For bishops and abbots and all,” etc.** Chapter 18 had already explained how and with what kindness guests were to be received by the procurator. Reverend Father Guigo now declares how they ought to be received by the prior. For the sake of hospitality, the prior also breaks the fast of the Order and must receive at his table not only bishops and abbots but all who are in religious habit.

This is now practiced in a more measured way, lest the prior himself be drawn away from the duties of his office by the necessity of receiving guests so frequently. Thus the modern statutes restrict it to guests to whom this cannot suitably be refused, and they add: “The less frequently, the better.” How much time is spent on such matters that could be more profitably employed elsewhere? How many superfluous words are spoken? The thing speaks for itself.

**“For neither gyrovagues,” etc., “nor lay persons,” etc., “are accustomed,” etc.** It is not said absolutely that lay persons are never received at his table. It is said only that it is not customary to receive them there in the way that others in religious habit are received. All those in religious habit are received; lay persons are not, unless they are of such a character that this cannot suitably be refused to them.

In this the meaning of Reverend Father Guigo agrees with the modern statutes, where it is said in Part II, Chapter 3, number 31: “The prior in his house ought not to eat indiscriminately and without distinction with guests who arrive, but only with honorable persons and such as cannot suitably be refused this; and even then, the less frequently, the better.”

The change should also be attributed in part to the circumstances of the times, since it has been made for the better, provided that the matter always remains within the limits of the intention of the statutes.

**[Col. 0712A] Number 2. “Bishops and abbots, however,” etc.** From this we are taught how far we must stand from every appearance of quarrelsomeness, which nowadays often arises over the preservation of rank.

We see that our first Fathers honored the dignity of the episcopal character equally in all bishops, while always preserving a special reverence for the diocesan bishop. We must never depart from this spirit. By giving honor abundantly rather than sparingly to those to whom honor is due, we should show in all things humility of spirit, kindness in our dealings, hospitality, and sincere affection, so that everyone may recognize in this that we are disciples of the first Carthusians.

**“The weekly priest, however, gives the blessings according to custom.”** This passage confirms what we have already said about the frequent celebration among us of conventual Masses, since explicit mention is made of the weekly priest. The rarity of Masses of which Reverend Father Guigo speaks in certain passages must therefore be understood in a very different way from that in which some have interpreted it.

**Number 3. “Whom,” that is, bishops, etc.** Here we learn how the spirit of humility, with which we ought to be inwardly filled, must also be expressed outwardly in action. We must never admit among us anything that bears even the slightest shadow of secular arrogance or haughtiness.

“Supplicating” signifies among us a bowing of the body with which we offer greetings; indeed, we use it in the church in place of genuflection. “We kiss”: from this it is evident that the form of greeting with a holy kiss, as the Apostle says, has always been in use among us. This form of greeting, however, is to be used only with due regard for the persons involved and for propriety, as well as for the times and regions.

### No. 4

“In the upper house, however, only religious persons…” Thus only those lodged there who were to be received at the prior’s table, enter the choir, and be admitted to conversation with the monks; for we see these things joined together in this passage and in chapter 10.

Moreover, this entire chapter is reproduced in the ancient statutes, Part II, chapter 9, nos. 27, 3, 2, and 28.

[Col. 0711]

1. For bishops, abbots, and all persons living in religious dress—for such persons are received by the prior at table—if they arrive at that hour, the fast is broken by him, unless it is an especially important one [al., “unless it was”]. For neither gyrovagues, nor those who have deserted religious life, nor lay persons have customarily been received at his table.

2. Bishops and abbots also occupy the prior’s seat, both in the church and in other places. Bishops, however, also give blessings; abbots are content with the honor of the seat alone. The blessings, moreover, are given according to custom by the priest serving that week.

3. When these persons—that is, bishops and abbots—come, we kiss them while inclined and kneeling all the way to the ground; other persons, however, we kiss only while making reverent supplication.

4. In the upper house, however, only religious guests are accustomed to lodge. And since the discussion has turned to the prior, it should be added how he is accustomed to conduct himself in the affairs of the house entrusted to him.

### CHAPTER XXXVII. On Taking Counsel

[Note: [Col. 0713A]]

**CHAPTER XXXVII.**—This entire chapter is reproduced in the ancient statutes, Part II, chapter 7, no. 1, and is expressed still more fully in the modern statutes.

From this chapter it appears that formerly among us, without any distinction of matters or consideration of the number of votes, after all had freely stated what they thought, the prior carried out whatever he judged to be better and more correct, without favoritism toward persons. R. P. Guigo gives the reason why they observed the matter in this way. But because ecclesiastical law subsequently established many regulations concerning the reception of novices and similar matters, which the Order was obliged to observe, certain provisions were consequently added to the statutes that compel the prior, in particular cases, to accept and follow the monks’ votes.

[Col. 0713B] **No. 4.** “So that, perhaps burdened by the care and anxiety of temporal matters…” From this it is evident that at that time the care of temporal affairs belonged to the prior. He is therefore warned to appoint over each obedience—that is, the kitchen, the bridge gate, agriculture, and so forth, as will be clear from what follows—such brothers whose diligence and industry could lessen and moderate his anxiety. This will be clearer from the ancient statutes, as will the fact that the prior himself wrote and rendered the accounts—that is, the accounts of receipts and expenditures.

This passage also opens the way to a correct understanding of what the ancient statutes and general chapters mean when they appear to rebuke officials. They are not speaking of clerics or monks, from whose number only one procurator was appointed, who never [Col. 0713C] went beyond the boundaries, but of lay brothers, who, from the earliest institution, as will be seen in these customs, necessarily went outside.

[Col. 0713]

1. If, therefore, anything important or serious had to be discussed, the prior ordered all the monks to assemble together. There, after all had freely stated what they thought, he carried out what he judged to be better and more correct, without any favoritism toward persons.

2. And this was observed absolutely as most useful and most correct: that no one should presume contentiously to defend either another person’s opinion or his own, lest the good of counsel—God forbid!—be turned into discord and frenzy.

3. In lighter and more customary matters, however, he is content with his own counsel and that of the more mature brothers.

4. So that he might not, perhaps, being weighed down by the care and anxiety of temporal affairs, be less able to attend to spiritual matters, he diligently appoints over each obedience brothers to whose fidelity he can safely entrust it.

### CHAPTER XXXVIII. On Care of the Sick

[Note: [Col. 0713C]]

**CHAPTER XXXVIII.**—**No. 1.** “Who, since he knows that toward everyone…” [Col. 0714A] Here we see the form of humanity, discretion, and charity that the priors among us must always observe according to the needs of particular cases, especially toward the sick; reason itself recommends this. Since a solitary person needs both spiritual and bodily occupation in order to pass time profitably in solitude, and therefore, so to speak, ought to make use of himself, but cannot fully accomplish this while ill, the prior’s pastoral providence must then supply what is lacking, both personally and through others. If he ought to act as a father in other matters, in the cases expressed here he ought to conduct himself as a mother, and prove by his actions that, if he could bring the stars of heaven to the aid of the afflicted sick man lying in bed, he would do so most willingly. Behold what the prior’s charitable affection ought to be, and what R. P. Guigo requires of him—he who almost seems to forget Carthusian austerity when the care of the sick is under discussion. Nevertheless, both the prior himself and the sick subject must always bear in mind the rationale of the undertaking we have embraced and never depart from the practice of Christ’s virtue; and he explains this immediately and very well.

**Ibid.** “Who nevertheless themselves also…” Here he gently urges the sick to avoid certain things: namely, not to ask for what is superfluous or impossible, nor, perhaps by murmuring, distress those who serve them, and not to demand in the desert what is scarcely found in cities. To this end he uses these words: they should consider that, just as the healthy ought to differ from healthy secular persons, so the sick ought to differ from sick secular persons. From this it is evident how far R. Father Guigo’s mind is from the view of those who would use his authority [Col. 0714C] to prove that a harsh and almost inflexible manner of acting must be maintained even toward sick monks. This has always been foreign to the Carthusian spirit and practice. Moreover, nothing more religious or eloquent can be written than what the holy man says here concerning the conduct that both our priors and our sick brothers ought to observe.

**No. 3.** “For these alone…” We are accustomed to buy fish. It must not be concluded from this that our first fathers ate only fish when they were ill. That is disproved by chapter 33, nor does it mean that they ate only fish when fish were given to them by outsiders. It should be known, however, that a stream flows within the Carthusian wilderness and carries excellent fish, in such abundance that at that time it certainly sufficed ordinarily for the small community. The author’s meaning, therefore, is that they were accustomed to buy fish only in this circumstance—that is, for the sick—when they did not have fish available from their own stream (for at certain times fishing is impossible), or offered through the charity of their neighbors. He says nothing similar about eggs.

This entire chapter is reproduced in the ancient statutes, Part I, chapter 44, nos. 1 and 4.

1. Since he knows that he ought to show himself solicitous, kind, and merciful toward everyone, especially toward the sick and weak and those placed in temptations—for, according to the Lord’s saying, “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Matt. 9:12)—the sick themselves are nevertheless more carefully admonished, according to the words of blessed Benedict, to take heed lest, by asking for what is superfluous or impossible, or perhaps by murmuring, they distress those who serve them. They are also admonished to remember the undertaking they have embraced and to consider that, just as the healthy ought to differ from healthy secular persons, so the sick ought to differ from sick secular persons, and not to demand in the deserts what is scarcely found in cities.

2. To these, therefore, they recommend attention to the sufferings of Christ; to those, attention to compassion. Thus the former are strong to endure, the latter ready to help. And while both consider that, for Christ’s sake, the former are served and the latter serve, neither do the former grow proud nor the latter fail, each awaiting from the same Lord the reward of his service: the former for suffering, the latter for showing compassion.

[Col. 0715] 3. For these alone, if the illness is severe, we are accustomed to buy fish.

### CHAPTER XXXIX. On Bloodletting

[Note: [Col. 0715B]]

**CHAPTER XXXIX.**—**No. 1.** “Medicines… very rarely…” Understand: outside the time of illness, for then one must follow the physicians’ orders.

**Ibid.** “We are bled five times a year…” We are all astonished at this passage, for we are quite certain that our predecessors did this solely to preserve sound health. This is sufficiently proved by the chapter itself, since they appear to have been more indulgent toward themselves in food, sleep, and other matters. It would certainly be absurd if, on the one hand, from a spirit of mortification they had treated themselves by the opening of a vein and the removal of blood at fixed times, while on the other hand they had sought certain bodily comforts outside the common rule. If we were to attempt anything of the kind today, we would kill almost all the monks in a short time. Indeed, great caution is now necessary before we allow even one or two bleedings a year for any monk without the necessity of illness.

From this necessity—which gradually became apparent—of refraining from this recurring practice of bleeding monks, we have established that the strength of human bodies has declined, as though the world were growing old, and that it is now far less than it was then. Thus the words of St. Gregory are literally true. Comparing the bodily vigor of his own time with that of the ancients, and wishing to prove that the world too grows old and decays, he speaks as follows:

> In its earlier years the world flourished as though in youth; it was strong for propagating the human race, vigorous in bodily health, rich in the abundance of things. But now it is weighed down by its own old age and, as though approaching death, is pressed by ever-increasing troubles.

The difference in bodily stature may also be brought forward as evidence. We preserve with reverence the bones of the first Fathers in a certain chapel beneath which there is a crypt. If they are compared with ours, it is evident that we possess the bones of adolescents, while they possessed the bones of fully mature men, in comparison with ours.

Why, then, has there been this diminution of bodily strength, which was once so great that the first Fathers prescribed for themselves bloodletting five times a year without danger of diminishing their strength? We scarcely dare permit it once a year, even without a cause, having learned by experience that we must abstain from bloodletting because it weakens the strength of our men, so that, if it is permitted, they fail and not infrequently fall into chronic illnesses. In the end, these illnesses make them incapable of observing the Order’s practices, and some become useless persons. I am persuaded that this has occurred for three reasons, of which:

I believe the first proceeds from nature itself, which is gradually failing together with the world.

I judge the second, which seems to me the principal one, to have arisen from a practice gradually introduced, increased, and daily growing: the more delicate way of living and of raising children in the world. From this more delicate custom of living and raising children various needs have arisen. The manner of nourishing bodies has passed from custom into habit, and from habit into necessity. Consequently, our bodies, which before we were brought into the Order had for at least twenty years been more delicately [Col. 0716C] nourished in the world and accustomed to these needs, are now generally unable to endure what the bodies of the ancient Carthusians could easily endure, such as those abstinences involving bread and water of which we shall speak in their proper places. We scarcely dare permit these abstinences now; indeed, when some request them, we are compelled to refuse, even prohibit, them, so thoroughly has experience taught us what such abstinences would accomplish in these times in the bodies of most solitaries if they were maintained on bread and water.

What we have said is proved by country people, whose children, nourished on bread, water, and cheese, are much stronger than the sons of respectable townsmen and endure and accomplish more than the latter. Why, then, are younger Carthusians unable to arrive at the same way of life, which is ordinary for country people, because of their having lost the habit of living as they had lived in the world? We answer that a limit and mean must be established in these matters, beyond which it is vicious to proceed.

Young men coming to us from the world undergo a very considerable change through labor, vigils, and fasts, to which they are immediately committed in the Order; through their manner of life; and through the application of the mind, whose labor greatly surpasses bodily work. If stronger country people were subjected to all these things, some of them would immediately fail. It is therefore obvious that discretion is necessary, lest one depart from a just mean that is tolerable, portable, and durable, without either alteration or relaxation.

Almost all of us come to the Order in adolescence, around the age of twenty, when life is vigorous and requires suitable nourishment. For this reason, nourishment should at least in some measure correspond to the natural practice adopted in the world. If it were not discreetly provided in our solitary state, the greater part of our young men [Col. 0717B] would be incapable of many regular observances before reaching the age of thirty. What would follow from that, and what would become of our observance, everyone can see.

But it belongs especially to the prudent governance of those who profess the solitary life in general, and to the discreet conduct of individuals in particular, that our Carthusian affairs should always be established at a mean which the less robust can attain just as the stronger can. As will become clearer from what is said below in chapter 54, by all thus conforming to the same measure, everyone can serve God cheerfully, persevere in good health, remain always in the same observance, avoid the need for more frequent dispensations, refrain from aspiring to the consolations forbidden in our Order—such as leaving the monastery—and walk unanimously in the house of God without singularity.

This has always been the Order’s aim in arranging our affairs. That aim was long ago assigned to us by R. P. Guigo, has thereafter always been pursued by the general chapters, expressed in the statutes, and finally must always be kept in view by our successors, so that, adhering in all things to the footsteps of the Fathers, both ancient and recent, they may preserve the Order in its integrity, avoiding excess and deficiency alike.

Finally, I believe the third reason for the enervation of bodily strength proceeds from the greater liveliness of the intellect, which exhausts the bodily powers themselves. We have noted these matters at somewhat greater length in order to meet the indiscreet arguments of certain persons.

**No. 2.** “And on the first day, lest anything adverse…” Here he [Col. 0718A] explains the permissions and recreations granted on the days of bloodletting.

**Ibid.** “But not in another’s cell…” It clearly appears from this that permission was also given by the prior for the brothers to visit one another in their cells, but never to eat or drink there, as is still strictly observed. For R. P. Guigo would mention that wine was never drunk in another’s cell in vain if entering another’s cell with permission had not been allowed.

Moreover, this entire chapter is reproduced in the ancient statutes, Part II, chapter 15, nos. 3, 6, and 7.

[Col. 0717]

1. We use medicines very rarely, except for cautery and bloodletting. We are bled five times a year: after the Octave of Easter, after the solemnity of the apostles Peter and Paul, in the second week of September, in the week before Advent, and in the week before Quinquagesima. During this period of bloodletting, for three consecutive days we take two meals, receiving some better food.

[Col. 0717] 2. On the first day, lest anything adverse occur because of the bloodletting, after eating we assemble for conversation; after dinner we also have permission to drink wine, but not in another’s cell.

3. For we are never permitted to consume any food in another person’s cell.

4. During these three days we return to our beds in the morning and tell the cook what is necessary. From him, on each of the first two days, we also receive three eggs for supper.

### CHAPTER XL. On Ornamentation

[Note: [Col. 0718A]]

**CHAPTER XL.**—**No. 1.** “Except for the chalice and the tube…” There is no mention of this tube, by which the blood of Christ was received, in the ancient statutes, but only of the chalice. From this it may be inferred that in R. P. Guigo’s time the practice still existed of communicating sometimes under both kinds, although we believe this was permitted only to the deacon.
