We think that this practice had already died out among us in the time of R. Father Rifferius, who, approximately one hundred and twenty years after the Consuetudines were written by R. P. Guigo, issued those statutes that we call ancient, since they no longer mention the tube.

Here the simplicity appears that the first Fathers wished to maintain even in ecclesiastical furnishings. It should be noted, however, that in those times, when our people had not yet discovered the East and West Indies, gold and silver, and also silk fabric (*bombycinum*) or silk, were very rare in these regions, so that silk garments or garments woven with gold were used only by kings and princes. It would therefore have been quite unusual if the first Fathers had admitted this kind of silk clothing, since their riches consisted in poverty and simplicity.

By “cloaks and carpets,” perhaps the holy man means hangings and similar things, which we use nowhere in our houses, although in some houses, and only on solemn days, a carpet is placed over the steps or footpace of the altar. Why, then, do silver candlesticks, lamps, and similar furnishings now exist in most houses of the Order? It should be believed that this first arose from the founders of the houses, who gave such things for the use of the Church. Later, because several churches of the Order were built near large cities, to which many secular persons came out of devotion to attend the sacred offices, it seemed appropriate to use somewhat more valuable ecclesiastical furnishings, even in our churches, so that divine worship might be carried out more decently and honorably in the presence of these secular persons. This was especially so because silk garments and silver vessels had by then become so common that there was justifiable fear that abstention from silk garments and silver furnishings might be interpreted as contempt for divine worship. In some regions, moreover, matters had through the custom of the times reached the point that secular persons would be greatly scandalized unless they saw everything shining with silver and gold on our altars and among the ecclesiastical furnishings.

Nevertheless, we reject excessive extravagance in this matter, especially when the needs of the poor are pressing. Everything of this kind ought to be sold for their relief and expended on their food. We greatly praise those houses, however, that—while preserving religious decency in all things and taking account of local circumstances—always strive to imitate the ancient simplicity, even in these matters.

Whether more or less is used in this area contributes nothing to the monks’ personal observance, since they derive no personal advantage from it.

**No. 2.** “Of usurers…” There it appears how scrupulously the good Fathers were unwilling to share in the sins of others.

1. We have no gold or silver ornaments in the church, except the chalice and the tube by which the Lord’s blood is received; we have abandoned hangings and carpets.

[Col. 0719] 2. We do not accept gifts from usurers or excommunicated persons.

3. We also inserted into this writing a little document that we had composed concerning certain such matters.

### CHAPTER XLI. That Nothing Be Possessed Outside the Wilderness, and on the Burial of Strangers

[Note: [Col. 0719B]]

**CHAPTER XLI.**—Before we proceed to explain this chapter, certain points must be noted, so that the reader may be prepared to grasp R. P. Guigo’s meaning without danger of error. For this reason, we do not hesitate to repeat here matters touched on above.

[Col. 0719C] First, it is certain that nothing is more opposed to those who profess the solitary life than the desire to acquire and possess temporal goods beyond what is necessary for living honorably and peacefully in their state, taking into account the circumstances of persons, times, and regions. For why does a monk come to the cell if, enclosed there, he longs in mind and desire to possess temporal things? How will he withdraw with Mary to the feet of Christ and enjoy her devout leisure, listening to Christ’s words, if in mind and desire he wanders throughout the world? It must be said that it is not merely useless but foolish to enclose oneself in a cell in order thereby to loosen the reins of desire.

Second, daily experience shows how many anxieties, labors, and endeavors the care of temporal affairs requires, and how many journeys and difficulties it produces. Therefore, when one of the solitaries is chosen for an office of the Order that includes the responsibility of providing for others, so that through the ministry of one person the others may be free in their cells for the exercise of Mary—for if one were not appointed for this purpose on behalf of all, each would be forced to provide for himself, and thus all would be barred from the quiet of the cell—if, I say, one is appointed to such an office and loosens the reins to the desire to have, acquire, and possess whatever he can and whatever comes his way, he must immediately plunge into distractions, journeys, wanderings, and similar things, which are as contrary to the spirit of his profession as the noise of the law courts or military exercises is contrary to the guarding of the cell.

Hence it is evident that such a man is deprived of the Carthusian spirit and consequently ceases to be a Carthusian as soon as he falls into this desire, which the Apostle—and after him R. P. Guigo—rightly calls the root of all evils. For monks, and especially Carthusians, I do not hesitate to call it the root of perdition, since by monastic profession and the state they have freely undertaken they have promised God to renounce this most wretched desire, and those who afterward wish to pursue it in contempt of their profession deserve to be handed over by God to a reprobate mind.

Third, in order to moderate the anxieties of those appointed to provide for the needs of the entire community of solitaries—who, according to the prescription of their institute, ought to have no concern either for temporal affairs or for themselves—and to assist the whole household and the monastery’s burdens, both fixed and occasional, it is certain that an honestly sufficient quantity of temporal goods must be possessed. I call that sufficient which has a reasonable degree of latitude, so that when, whether through common calamities or through the tenants’ failure to pay what they owe us, the annual income is not received in full, the common needs of the house may nevertheless be supplied without the necessity of wandering and seeking.

This ought all the more justly to be admitted in our houses because, according to the spirit of our profession, we must abhor more firmly the practice of wandering about, seeking, and procuring external favors and gifts for ourselves in order to subsist; and rightly so, since this is utterly contrary to our solitary profession and the Carthusian institute. It follows that one of two things must be chosen: either renounce the Carthusian institute, or possess holdings and revenues sufficient—within the moral latitude established above—to support the entire community and bear its burdens.

With these points established, it must be said that the mind of our holy founder, and after him that of R. Father Guigo, consisted in the three matters noted above. This can be proved from what has already been said and will be proved more fully by what follows. From what has already been said it is clear:

First, that the first Fathers renounced the detestable practices, as they call them, of wandering and seeking, and that for this it was necessary for them to have the means by which they could live peacefully in their solitude without such alternation;

Second, that they wished the procurators of the Order always to aspire and return to the quiet and secrecy of the cell, as to the harbor of their salvation;

Third, that they possessed a sufficient quantity of temporal goods, understood within the moral latitude explained above. For it is clear that they had enough to provide for themselves, their guests, and their household, and also to distribute alms to the poor.

**No. 1.** “The occasions of desire…” “the inhabitants of this place…” Here he speaks specifically of the Carthusian house, for it is almost the only one among all the houses of the Order situated in a vast wilderness, and therefore capable of having extensive boundaries within which no co-possessors would be found. This could certainly not apply to the other houses. The founders of those houses were not free to gather together, as into a single mass, the possessions necessary for the houses’ support. Consequently, in establishing the foundations of the houses they were forced to provide revenues scattered here and there. This is the first reason why, in the Order’s early centuries, special permissions were granted to certain houses to possess something outside their boundaries. Nevertheless, they usually gave such goods in emphyteusis, as far as they could, in order to free themselves from these concerns. [Col. 0721C] It is nevertheless certain that the Order religiously observed the rule that fixed boundaries were assigned to each house, outside which no landed possessions could be held, as we said above in chapter 15, no. 4.

When R. P. Guigo wrote this, it is beyond doubt that he sincerely believed that the goods our Fathers then possessed within the Carthusian wilderness, together with the others that will shortly be mentioned, ought always to have sufficed for living peacefully and bearing the burdens of the house in the moderation he expresses below by saying: “Our humble undertaking, whatever it may be, rarely experiences want or abundance, thanks be to God.” It should be noted that this renunciation concerns only what lies outside the boundaries. Thus, when he immediately names two things specifically, it must be understood, with regard to the other houses of the Order, that this applies unless such things are within their boundaries; for here he is concerned only with not possessing such things outside the boundaries.

**Ibid.** “Let them possess absolutely nothing”—that is, neither fields, and so forth, nor anything of this kind. Among the things he specifies, and which the holy man asserts that the inhabitants of the Carthusian house renounced for themselves and their successors, he does not include pasture for feeding animals, nor fixed revenues that can be held without ownership of land or any possession—for example, the assignment of a fixed annual rent to be received from certain places or estates, or to be paid by a cathedral or collegiate church.

That Carthusian house then possessed such things is proved not only by reason but by experience. For, as we said above in chapter 19, in R. P. Guigo’s time it is certain that the Carthusian house possessed pasture and grazing rights at the foot of the cliffs, located outside the boundaries, as well as barns to which it was necessary to bring the animals for wintering. For on the cliffs of the Carthusian wilderness, from the beginning of November until the end of May, there are no grasses on which the animals can be fed. It is therefore necessary to seek them outside, as R. P. Guigo himself explains sufficiently.

As for those revenues held without ownership or possession of land, this too is established by experience through those revenues that this Carthusian house still enjoys, and that are still paid to it annually by the chapters of both the cathedral church and the church of St. Andrew of Grenoble. Certainly, those who know the condition of the Carthusian wilderness will readily regard it as beyond doubt that the Carthusian house could never have subsisted under these burdens of guests and the poor unless it had possessed such supports outside the wilderness. This was therefore expressed more clearly in the ancient statutes.

**No. 2.** “No one at all…” He speaks in relation to the practice of that period, when the clerics and parish priests strictly insisted that the rights specially assigned to them concerning burials be preserved and not violated in any respect; for this reason quarrels and lawsuits easily arose then. He also speaks in relation to the state of our solitary life, which they did not wish to have disturbed by the burial of secular persons. This is sufficiently indicated by the liberty left here to bury not only someone belonging to our undertaking—that is, any member of the Order who happened to end his life here—but also religious persons of any religious order, if it happened that they died here.

**No. 4.** “They will not write anyone’s name…” “nor celebrate anyone’s anniversary according to custom…” We have heard that certain persons… Here R. P. Guigo gives the reason why he rejected these anniversaries. A custom was prevalent in those times, which we discussed above in chapter 14; there we explained how the passage “rarely is Mass sung here” is to be understood. It would be superfluous to repeat that explanation here.

**Ibid.** “This custom removes abstinence and makes prayers venal…” From this it is clear with what zeal our Fathers always burned—a zeal that we also see expressed in both the ancient and modern statutes—in order to eliminate from us anything that smacks of a bargain in exchange for the benefits of the dead. Here it appears what sort of custom the holy man attacks, though modestly, for he immediately adds: “If anyone obstinately swears that such a custom is praiseworthy, we do not resist,” and so forth. Nevertheless, he does not cease to remain within the bounds of generous zeal, calling upon the authors and supporters of such customs to consider the judgment of God.

**No. 5.** “Our humble undertaking, whatever it may be…” “rarely experiences want or abundance.” Here it appears how modestly and humbly our first Fathers thought of themselves. They attach the epithet “lowly” to their undertaking in order to show how far they stood from any intention of winning human esteem by means of it, and how highly humility, abasement, and lowliness were always to be valued by true Carthusians. It also appears that they wished our affairs to be established in the moderation for which Solomon prayed, saying: “Give me neither poverty nor riches…” (Prov. 30:8).

**Ibid.** “For if anyone sends us fish or something of this kind…” Here he speaks in opposition to the custom he condemned above of preparing lavish meals and Masses—in other words, of feasting splendidly as often as someone wished to provide such things to them for his dead. He explains how we ought to use gifts sent to us for the community’s food: they are served only on those days on which the statutes permit it.

[Col. 0724A] This chapter is reproduced in the ancient statutes, Part II, chapter 19, no. 1; Part I, chapter 49, nos. 20, 21, and 17; and Part II, chapter 14, no. 20.

1. Cutting off, as far as we can with God’s help, the occasions of desire for ourselves and our successors, we establish by the sanction of this present writing that the inhabitants of this place shall possess absolutely nothing outside the boundaries of their wilderness: neither fields, nor vineyards, nor gardens, nor churches, nor cemeteries, nor offerings, nor tithes, nor anything of this kind.

[Col. 0721] 2. It has likewise been enacted that they shall bury no one at all, whether he died within or outside this wilderness, in their cemetery, unless perhaps someone belonging to this undertaking happened to die here.

3. But if someone from another religious order should die here, and his community were either unable or unwilling to carry him away, they shall bury him.

4. They shall not write anyone’s name in their Martyrology, nor celebrate anyone’s anniversary according to custom. For we have heard—and we do not approve it—that many people feast splendidly and prepare Masses as often as someone wishes to provide such things to them for his dead. This custom both removes abstinence and makes prayers venal, since the number of Masses is exactly equal to the number of meals, and no fixed intention of fasting or supplication is established where the matter depends not on the devotion of the one who performs it but rather on the discretion of the one who provides the food. For no day will lack a banquet or a Mass if one who provides the food never fails. But if anyone obstinately swears that such a custom is praiseworthy, we do not resist him; let him act as he wishes, since he will have to render an account to the one who searches hearts and tests the reins, and who will repay each person according to his way and according to the fruit of his inventions.

[Col. 0723] 5. Our humble undertaking, whatever it may be, rarely experiences want or abundance, thanks be to God. For if anyone sends us fish or something of this kind, it is brought to the brothers to be eaten in the measure and on the day that the undertaking and the institute require.

### CHAPTER XLII. On the Divine Office of the Lay Brothers

[Note: [Col. 0724A]]

**CHAPTER XLII.**—**No. 1.** “And indeed, if the monk who is appointed over them…” He performs the divine office for them almost as it was written above, but more quickly. By “the procurator monk” he means the procurator, and from this passage it can be inferred that the first Fathers sang on a plain tone. For since it is certain that the procurator alone could not have performed the entire office with musical notation, and since it is said here that he performs the divine office for them almost as it was written above concerning the monks, with only this difference—that he performs the office more quickly—it is clearly apparent that the procurator sang on a plain tone, [Col. 0724B] as is explicitly expressed in the ancient statutes.

There is, nevertheless, a certain prologue placed at the beginning of some antiphonaries and attributed to R. P. Guigo. But since it deals only with the composition of the Antiphonary, and appears there to make little of the study of chant, the authority of the present passage seems stronger than that of this prologue. The prologue can be understood as referring only to the selection and composition of the text of the Antiphonary; or, if it admits any kind of chant, we have no doubt that it was different from the Gregorian chant we now use and more concise.

Ibid. “Which they themselves imitate with the greatest diligence.” From this passage and the following chapter it appears that, when a cleric was present to perform the divine office for them in this manner, they themselves said nothing on their own part; rather, by their mere attendance, attention [Col. 0724C], and imitation of the ceremonies—which the reverend author expresses through religious bodily movements—they fulfilled the office.

**No. 2. “Among whom, on the vigils of solemnities on which chapter is held,”** etc. From this passage it is evident that R. P. Guigo calls every feast of the chapter a “solemnity.”

Ibid. “In order to hear Matins and the rest of the sacred office,” etc. Here mention is made only of hearing the office, not of any recitation. Why this was later changed, so that now our lay brothers perform their office while the convent sings, is described in the following chapter, where they are said to have done so at that time [Col. 0725A] in the absence of a cleric. We believe that this resulted from the disuse of building lower houses in our monasteries. Consequently, all the lay brothers staying in the upper house had to attend the nocturnal offices there; and when these became longer because of the singing, this occupation with vocal prayers was assigned to them, so that during Matins they would not lapse into idleness, boredom, or sleep.

Ibid. “And if they have any faults, they confess them.” This may be understood both of sacramental confession and of public acknowledgment of faults, since both are customarily practiced among us after chapter. On Saturday, after the commemorations, time is assigned to the monks above, chapter 7, no. 2, for sacramental confession. But [Col. 0725B] because the lay brothers were not present then and were occupied with other matters, another time—namely, after chapter—is assigned to them.

**No. 3. “When they are about to go up to the kitchen,”** etc. We have already said that the cook was, as it were, the chief steward, who also acted in the procurator’s place and granted permissions in many matters.

Ibid. “There too—that is, above—as everywhere from Compline,” etc., “and from chapter,” etc. The meaning of that passage is that the brothers staying in the upper house must observe silence from chapter until after None in the same manner as, everywhere outside the upper house, they must observe it from Compline until after Prime.

**[Col. 0726A] No. 4. “To hear Vespers in the chapel,”** etc. Here again mention is made simply of hearing the office.

You will find this entire chapter reproduced in the ancient statutes, part III, chapter 1, no. 1 and following.]

1. Having explained, as best we could, what pertains to the customs of the monks, let us now, with the Lord’s help, speak of what belongs to the lay brothers, whom we call *conversi*. Whenever it is time to rise for Matins, the signal is rung twice, with a short interval between. At the first signal they prepare themselves; at the second they proceed to the church with due seriousness. If the monk appointed over them is present, he performs the divine office for them, almost as it was described above, but more rapidly. They themselves imitate him with the greatest diligence, maintaining silence and quiet, carefully reproducing his bows and the other religious movements of the body.

2. Of these brothers, on the vigils of solemnities on which chapter is held, half—so far as their obediences permit—when they are separated from their work toward evening, go up to the upper church to hear Matins and the rest of the sacred office. There, after the monks’ chapter, they hear the word of God from the prior or from whomever he has appointed for this purpose; and if they have any offenses, they confess them.

**[Col. 0725]**

3. When they are about to go up, they come to the cook; with his permission, they proceed in silence, carrying whatever he has ordered them to carry. There too—that is, above—as everywhere, they remain in silence from Compline until after Prime, and from chapter until after None.

4. They may speak, however, with the cook and with his assistant or assistants about necessary matters. They also descend in silence, carrying back whatever they have been ordered to return, in order to hear Vespers in the chapel from the monk assigned to them.

**CHAPTER XLIII. Also concerning the same matter, and at what time they return to their beds.**  
**[Note: [Col. 0726A]**

**CHAP. XLIII.—No. 1. “Whenever, however,”** etc. From this it is evident that only in the absence of the procurator did they themselves perform Matins at that time, using the Lord’s Prayer in place of the psalms and reciting it in the manner and number specified here. Hence it is clear that the office of our lay brothers was then much shorter than it is now. At that time they repeated the Lord’s Prayer 58 times and the *Gloria Patri* 12 times for the entire nocturnal office; for the daytime office, however, they recited the Lord’s Prayer 25 times and the *Gloria Patri* 21 times. They said nothing for the office of Blessed Mary.

**[Col. 0726B] No. 3. “After Matins they hasten to the appointed prayer,”** etc. This concerns a certain formula of devout prayer, which they still call “maternal,” because it is said in the mother tongue and they teach it to one another.

**No. 4. “And because from the Kalends of October,”** etc. At that time there was no need for them to return to their beds, because, imitating the monks’ custom, they slept without interruption for as long as was sufficient.

Ibid. “They devote themselves to prayer as much as they can.” Nothing fixed is assigned to them in this matter, because, according to the amount of manual work and the necessities that arose, they had more or less free time.

**No. 5. “From Easter until the Kalends of October they return to their beds,”** etc. Why was this permitted to them when it was not granted to the monks [Col. 0727A] at that time? Because daytime sleep was not permitted to the lay brothers, who were assigned to manual labor; they were occupied with work throughout the entire day.

Ibid. “After Compline, their beds,” etc. They are also instructed to devote diligently to sleep the time assigned for sleeping, so that everything, each thing at its proper time, may be carried out in an orderly manner.

You will find the same chapter reproduced in the ancient statutes, part III, chapter 2, no. 1.]

1. Whenever they are without a cleric, they use the Lord’s Prayer in place of the psalms and, wherever they may be, complete all the hours and the entire office with it.

2. At Matins, therefore, if it is a feast of twelve lessons, they say the *Pater noster* only once, bowing; otherwise, while seated in their stalls, they say it once, with great attention. Then, standing, they repeat the same prayer six times, petitioning at each repetition and saying the *Gloria Patri*. Then they sit down and repeat the same prayer twenty-two times. Afterwards they rise and repeat it six times with petition and the *Gloria Patri*; thereafter, continuing to stand, they say the same prayer twenty-two times without the *Gloria* or petition. They add it once more as the collect.

3. After Matins they hasten to the appointed prayer. We do not wish to write it down because it is communicated from one person to another in the vernacular.

4. Since from the Kalends of October until Easter they do not return to their beds, during the interval remaining until Prime—long or short according to the length of the nights—they sew their garments, grease their shoes, peel turnips, or perform any other work assigned to them, provided that they do so without noise. If no such task is pressing, they devote themselves to prayer as much as they can.

5. From Easter until the Kalends of October they return to their beds; throughout this entire period, once the sun has risen, the signal for Prime is rung. During harvest, however, it is rung earlier, as necessity requires. From that time until Easter they begin Prime very early in this manner: “Our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth”; then the *Pater noster* with the *Gloria Patri*, and the *venia* or petition according to the season, three times; and a fourth time for the collect. The other hours are conducted similarly, except that one *Pater noster* is added at Vespers. After Compline they go to bed and take care to sleep, lest, when they ought to be awake, they be forced to sleep.

**[Col. 0727]**

6. Whether they sleep or remain awake, they are ordered to remain quietly and, insofar as possible, without any noise.

**CHAPTER XLIV. Who should preside or respond.**  
**[Note: [Col. 0727A]**

**CHAP. XLIV.—No. 1. “When, in the absence of the one appointed over them,”** etc. By the term “superior,” therefore, R. P. Guigo understands one who has been placed over others, whether over the lay brothers generally, as the procurator is, or over only certain individuals, such as a lay brother to whom an assigned task has been entrusted in obedience and to whom assistants are given for completing it. The person entrusted with directing such an obedience is then called the superior of that work, with respect to the assistants assigned to him.

Ibid. “While the others remain silent, he responds to those who come and meet him.” The silence required there concerns those who arrive or encounter them, not brothers working together, for at that time they may speak among themselves, with the moderation described in the following chapter. In this chapter and the next, the manner in which the lay brothers are to speak and remain silent is prescribed. The same material is found in the ancient statutes, part III, chapter 3, no. 1.]

1. When, in the absence of the monk appointed over them, they gather in the church, the one who is senior in rank presides over the office. The same applies in other places or works, unless the obedience in which they are engaged has been specially assigned to someone. Then the person to whom it has been specifically entrusted presides over the others; while the others remain silent, he responds to those who arrive or meet them.

2. They are not permitted to speak indiscriminately or without permission, whether with whomever they wish, about whatever they wish, or for as long as they wish.

3. Accordingly, when they meet or are overtaken by someone, they may return the greeting only by bowing the head, show the way, answer questions with “yes” or “no,” and explain that they have no permission [variant: *habeant* for *habent*] to speak further with them.

**CHAPTER XLV. When the brothers may speak with their superior.**  
**[Note: [Col. 0728A]**

**CHAP. XLV.—No. 1. “For they have many rustic signs,”** etc. It should therefore be noted that the first lay brothers of the Carthusian house were for the most part pious peasants from the same region. We record this here to facilitate understanding of chapter 53 of these *Customs*.

**No. 2. “But to learn the signs of others,”** etc. This refers to what was already stated for the monks in chapter 31. For if they learned certain signs from one another, they could thereby converse mutually through agreed signs, as is customary with the mute; this would be contrary to the purpose and conclusion of silence.]

1. In whatever obedience they have been placed, the brothers [variant: “a brother”] may speak about necessary matters with the superior appointed over them, after requesting permission by a sign. They have many rustic signs, free from every kind of joking or wantonness, by which they can indicate to one another without speaking matters concerning their duties, their tools, or their work.

2. They are not permitted to learn the signs of others or to teach their own signs to outsiders.

**CHAPTER XLVI. Concerning the cook.**  
**[Note: [Col. 0728A]**

**CHAP. XLVI.—No. 1. “Who prepares and distributes the customary foods,”** etc. We have seen that the monks prepared their own food in their cells above, but [Col. 0728B] the same arrangement does not apply to the lay brothers, because, dispersed here and there for manual labor, they could not prepare food for themselves. One brother, therefore, does this for them all.

**No. 2. “To give or receive,”** etc. Our rule of obedience is prescribed always and in every matter, not only in giving but also in receiving, because obedience—as the foundation, so to speak, of the Carthusian institution—is to be attended to and considered, as R. P. Guigo himself expressly states above, chapter 35.

**[Col. 0729A] No. 4. “To those arriving from the neighboring village,”** etc. That is, from the settlement of Chartreuse, situated among the rocks of Chartreuse toward Grenoble, now called the parish of Chartreuse, to distinguish it from the Carthusian house. This chapter is reproduced in the ancient statutes, part III, chapter 11, nos. 1, 2, 4, and 5.]

1. Let us now go through the individual obediences. One of the brothers presides over the kitchen; he prepares and distributes to the brothers the customary foods, namely legumes and similar items. At the appropriate hours he rings the signal. From him they also receive bread, wine on the appointed days, salt, a spoon, bowls, *lumbaria* (waist-cloths), a needle, thread, and wax for waxing. He may give them nothing else without the procurator’s permission. Whatever he generally distributes to the others, he takes for himself as well.

2. He dares neither give nor receive anything from those who do not belong to this house without the procurator’s command. If the procurator should happen to be absent and some necessity arise in the meantime, he shall act as he thinks the procurator himself would have acted had he been present, and, when the procurator returns, he shall report what he did and how he did it. He may not bring any of the brothers into the kitchen except for a just necessity; once the necessity has passed, he immediately sends out the one brought in, preserving silence inviolate as far as circumstances permit.

**[Col. 0729]**

3. He guards the church, is in charge of the gate, responds to those who arrive, and keeps the common tools. He takes care of the house and all the common furnishings. If anything should be lost from among these things, he will throw himself prostrate on the ground and loudly declare himself responsible and guilty. Whoever performs his duties in his place observes the same requirements.

4. On solemn days, neither he nor the one who takes his place may give or lend anything to those arriving from the neighboring village. He is ordered only to tell them to leave, so that they do not become accustomed to causing disturbance and inconvenience on such days.

**CHAPTER XLVII. Concerning the baker.**  
**[Note: [Col. 0729A]**

**CHAP. XLVII.—**You will find this chapter reproduced in the ancient statutes, part III, chapter 12, no. 1. A lay brother was assigned to these particular offices; he completed the work himself, although assistance was given to him whenever he could not complete it alone.]

The baker receives the grain, dries it, guards it, winnows it, mills it, makes the loaves, bakes them with assistance when provided, and returns them to the cook in the bakehouse.

**CHAPTER XLVIII. Concerning the shoemaker.**  
**[Note: [Col. 0729A]**

**CHAP. XLVIII.—**By *sotulares* understand shoes. This exceptionally learned man used that word because it had been introduced through common usage and was more similar to the French idiom; in those times it was more readily understood. Nor did he fear [Col. 0729B] being accused of corrupt Latin, just as he did not seek praise for elegance of speech.

The same matter is found in the ancient statutes, part III, chapter 13.]

The shoemaker keeps the leather, cuts it, and makes and repairs shoes.

**CHAPTER XLIX. Concerning the superintendent of agriculture.**  
**[Note: [Col. 0729B]**

**CHAP. XLIX.—**Agriculture was practiced in the place called Chartreusette, where the ox barn still stands, and also on the slope of the mountain extending from Correrie to the mill. But [Col. 0730A] those fields produce only oats, and sometimes beans and similar crops; they never produce wheat.]

The person in charge of agriculture takes care of the grange, the oxen, and everything belonging to that obedience.

**CHAPTER L. Concerning the master of the shepherds.**  
**[Note: [Col. 0730A]**

**CHAP. L.—**These provisions reveal the economic manner of acting and arranging affairs that R. P. Guigo and his predecessors had established, so as to advance the household’s resources and protect them from waste, while preserving the religious and harmless manner of proceeding described here. This will greatly refresh the minds of pious readers through the fragrant simplicity it breathes.

**No. 1. “He conducts business with outsiders. He has no permission to chat with them,”** etc. How admirable it would be to see such merchants today, who even in their business dealings abstained from words unrelated to the matter at hand.

**No. 2. “But he is to avoid oaths and lies,”** etc., “which commonly accompany such transactions,” etc. See how [Col. 0730B] sincerely our founders wanted our members to conduct their harmless business, and how entirely they wished them to abstain from secular ways of acting and speaking.

Ibid. “When they go outside for the winter, they are to receive or give nothing,” etc. Here what we touched upon above, in chapter 41, becomes evident. They went outside—that is, beyond the boundaries of the desert—and led the sheep to neighboring places to spend the winter. [Col. 0731A] From the prohibition against receiving or giving anything there, we learn how carefully the first Fathers wished to withdraw our lay brothers from, and preserve them against, the familiarity with secular people that could be fostered by gifts given or received. They knew what danger could gradually arise for their lay brothers from such familiarity. Because of the somewhat more pleasant character of the location, because they had been released—though necessity required it—from the common exercises of the monastery, and because familiarity with outsiders might be added to these circumstances, they could easily first fall into the snares of nature, which flees labor and seeks relaxation, and afterwards even into the snares of the devil.

[Col. 0731B] Would that we always kept before our eyes the example of those first Fathers and continually strove never to depart from it, carefully ensuring that, following their example, we permit none of our members to remain outside the monastery except insofar as, and for as long as, unavoidable necessity requires. For it is beyond doubt that more serious losses to the Order, both temporal and spiritual, could result from this.

I said “unavoidable necessity,” because whenever something can be avoided or supplied by some resourcefulness, that should be considered—and I mean, considered—the greatest gain. Let it suffice here to touch again on one reason, already given above among many others. People accustomed to the exercises of the monastery, and removed and unaccustomed, by their profession of solitary life, to seeing secular objects, [Col. 0731C] are later affected more vividly and intensely by those objects when they encounter them than are those accustomed to seeing them. For, as the philosophers say, “passion does not arise from what is familiar”; therefore such objects must be avoided with greater caution, rejecting a thousand fabrications of private affection, which knows how to invent necessities where in truth none arises.

Ibid. “From a hired boy,” etc. These excellent shepherds did not then trail behind them a crowd of servants; they did everything themselves. Otherwise, hired servants would quickly have consumed their modest household resources. The labor of a hired boy was provided for this one reason: so that they themselves would not be forced, insofar as this could be avoided, to go to the villages, which is dangerous. These holy men considered it dangerous to allow the most devout lay brothers to remain outside the monastery for a time in the neighboring villages, even though not continuously—which point should be noted—and they therefore permitted them to go there only insofar as, as they say, it could not be avoided. For they never departed from the rules of sound judgment. [Col. 0732A] Let us now consider whether we believe ourselves better than such men, so that we need no longer fear what they feared and guarded against with such care concerning their own members who stayed outside the monastery for a time, as though habitually. Elsewhere R. P. Guigo will speak of those who traveled outside the boundaries merely in transit.

Ibid. “On Tuesday and Saturday, beyond the common custom of the brothers,” etc. This custom will be discussed in the following chapter. By “mercy” is meant some indulgence, which, as seems evident here, was discreetly granted according to the mind of the first Fathers whenever a reasonable cause demanded it. For they avoided every extreme and followed the proper mean.]

1. The master of the shepherds guards all the property and tools belonging to that obedience. He conducts business with outsiders, buying and selling what pertains to his ministry. He has no permission to chat with them about other matters. No one may involve himself [variant: “involves himself”] in that business or in its conversations unless the master summons him.

2. He is instructed to avoid oaths, lies, frauds, and the other evils that commonly accompany such transactions, and to place the eternal salvation of his soul before temporal possessions and advantages. He and his companions also guard the grange for the most part. The house in which the cheeses are made, which we call the *arcella*, belongs particularly to their care, as is likewise prescribed for the guarding of certain cells. In general, no one enters another’s cell unless ordered to do so. When they go outside for the winter, they are commanded neither to receive nor to give anything. A hired boy who is with them goes to the mill; bread is baked and wine is purchased, so that they themselves are not forced, insofar as this can be avoided, to go to the villages, which is dangerous. On Tuesday and Saturday they have wine beyond the common custom of the brothers. They also receive wine on the day when they change places, because they cannot prepare food for themselves. This indulgence is granted to them because of their continual labors and the many hardships they endure there.

**CHAPTER LI. At what times the brothers may have wine.**  
**[Note: [Col. 0732A]**

**CHAP. LI.—No. 1. “Only on Thursday, and on solemnities that have chapter, once a day,”** etc. As we have already noted, R. P. Guigo understood by “solemnities” all feasts of the chapter. [Col. 0732B] It should not be thought, however, that the wine served to the brothers once a day was given only in an amount sufficient for one meal, but rather in an amount sufficient for both dinner and supper, as will become clear from what follows and is still confirmed by the ancient custom of this Carthusian house, according to which wine was served to the brothers for both meals and they kept it in their cells.

Why is wine assigned less frequently to the brothers, who are devoted to arduous manual work, than to the monks? Because the labor of the mind is far heavier than that of the body, and wine contributes greatly to the restoration of exhausted spirits.

[Col. 0732C] Ibid. “On the Nativity of the Lord, however,” etc., “they have wine twice.” Here R. P. Guigo lists the principal feasts that we now call solemnities, distinguishing them from feasts that are only feasts of the chapter. On these days, since there were two meals in the refectory—namely, morning and evening—wine was likewise served to the brothers twice.

**No. 2. “Also when they go up,”** etc. “If the monks happen to take supper in the refectory,” etc. This agrees with what precedes, for since the monks then eat in the refectory, wine is also served to the brothers going up to the upper house, so that there may be a certain conformity of observance between the two groups.

You will find this chapter reproduced in the ancient statutes, part III, chapter 19.]

**[Col. 0731]**

1. The other brothers who remain at home receive wine only on Thursday and on solemnities that have chapter, once a day. On the days of the Nativity of the Lord—four days—on the Circumcision, Epiphany, Purification, and Annunciation, if the latter falls on a Sunday; during the four days of Easter; on the Ascension; during the three days of Pentecost; on the solemnity of Saint John; of the apostles Peter and Paul; of the Assumption; of the Dedication; of the Nativity of Blessed Mary; of Saint Michael; and of All Saints, they have wine twice.

2. When they go up because of a feast to be celebrated on the following day, if the monks happen to take supper in the refectory, wine is given to them. This occurs only when two feasts on which food is eaten in the refectory follow one another.

**CHAPTER LII. Concerning the fast of the brothers.**  
**[Note: [Col. 0733A]**

**CHAP. LII.—No. 1. “Every Friday,”** etc., “except on solemnities,” etc. Thus they practiced abstinence only once a week, namely on Friday, unless a feast of the chapter occurred; in that case they were exempt from the abstinence. There is no doubt that the same was observed concerning the monks. For why would the monks not have been exempted on the same principle, since they practiced abstinence three times a week, when the brothers, who observed it only once, are here exempted because a feast of the chapter intervenes? No mention is made of transferring the abstinence, and so it is clear that in such a case it simply passed unobserved. Now, however, the practice is different: when a feast of the chapter falls on Friday, the abstinence is transferred to another day.

Ibid. “In Advent also,” etc., “on Wednesday as well.” [Col. 0733B] This is still observed, and the brothers practice abstinence on the same days, in the manner in which this observance of abstinence is now maintained among us.

**No. 2. “On the vigils of the apostles James,”** etc. “But they have *pulmentum*,” etc. By *pulmentum* is understood *pitantia*, since the two words are shown to be almost synonymous by this same chapter. This further confirms what we said above, under chapter 33, and explains how the words of R. P. Guigo in no. 5 of that chapter are to be understood: “At supper, or at dinner when we eat only once, we take raw herbs or fruits, if any are available.” He calls them “raw herbs” to distinguish them from cooked ones. It would be absurd to believe that they ate these raw herbs without any seasoning, as animals do, since some of them would have been very harmful to their health.

[Col. 0733C] Ibid. “On the other days, however,” etc., “they eat twice, but receive *pulmentum* only once.” The meaning is that the fasts of the Order observed by the monks from the feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross are not observed by the lay brothers, except during Advent. Nevertheless, *pitantia* is served to them once, and in addition they receive herbs, fruits, or roots for supper; these are also added to the *pulmentum* at dinner on fast days when they eat only once. This is what is meant by the words “at dinner, if they eat only once.” Since they were expressly exempted from the Order’s fast so that they would not be weakened by excessive labor, it would be incongruous to believe that on fast days, when eating only once is permitted, they were fed solely on raw herbs, fruits, or roots, since they had the same need to work as on other days.

**No. 3. “In general, the common foods of this house are seasoned only with salt.”** [Col. 0734A] There was a great difference between the manner of seasoning food in those times and the manner we now see observed everywhere. Spices were not then available, and butter was scarcely used. Then, as we now see in various regions, there was great diversity in this matter according to different customs of seasoning food. From the use of such customs, once nature has been steeped in them, arises a distaste for food prepared otherwise—a distaste that can scarcely be overcome. We have repeatedly confirmed this by experience in our own house [Col. 0734B] during the general chapter, when German, Italian, Spanish, Belgian, Polish, and French Fathers assemble. They nevertheless become accustomed to the French custom more readily than to that of other regions. To come closer to the point, our good Spanish Fathers can scarcely tolerate butter in seasonings; fish cooked with water, salt, herbs, and similar ingredients tastes good to them, but they are astonished when it is cooked with wine. We note these things only so that it may be understood that distinctions in such matters must be made according to differences of time, region, and custom. Moreover, he is speaking here of common foods, and it cannot therefore be concluded that they used neither oil nor herbs in seasoning the *pitantiae*. They used salt [Col. 0734C], and not the other kinds of spices, which were then rare and perhaps supplied only by those who feasted splendidly and delicately.

Ibid. “On Thursday and on solemnities of the chapter,” etc. Mention has already been made above of the *pulmenta* ordinarily served on fast days, and here it is also stated that on Thursday something beyond the usual fare was given. What this was, we do not know; but it is certain that they received something better than usual.

Ibid. “But on Easter and Pentecost,” etc., “without,” etc. On those feasts they were in the upper house, and on the days noted here they left it to return to the lower house, where their customary food was served. This is why on those days they received only wine and nothing else.

**[Col. 0735A] No. 4. “Raw herbs, fruits, or roots, when available, only at supper, or at dinner if they eat only once,”** etc. Here R. P. Guigo explains more clearly what he had stated more briefly and therefore more obscurely in chapter 33 when speaking of the monks. Here the difference is clearly visible between the edible things that monks and lay brothers could keep with them for as long as they lasted—which the monks prepared and cooked for themselves in their cells—and the *pulmentum* or *pitantia* supplied to them from the kitchen. Join this passage with what is said here in no. 2, and you will see that even on ecclesiastical fast days *pulmentum* or *pitantia* was served to them, regardless of which particular day of the week those fasts occurred, except only on the days assigned to abstinence. From this conclude, all the more strongly, that the same arrangements were observed for the monks as for the lay brothers.

Ibid. “The wine given is to be drunk only at dinner,” etc. If they were permitted to drink wine at supper as well as at dinner, and yet [Col. 0735B] ordinarily received wine only once a day, it may be inferred that wine was given to them in an amount sufficient for both meals. The word “or” should not be taken disjunctively but conjunctively, so that the meaning is that they were not to drink wine outside dinner and supper; the same was prescribed for the monks.

**No. 5. “Whatever remains from the *pitantiae*,”** etc., “lest anyone perhaps secretly practice an unapproved abstinence,” etc. From this passage it is evident how carefully and subtly the first Fathers wished to restrain our members from indiscreet abstinences, and how completely they wished nothing in this area to be admitted [Col. 0735C] that was not entirely subject to obedience, direction, and discretion. For them it was of the greatest importance to restrain those who professed the solitary and Carthusian life from voluntary and arbitrary practices, lest they injure their head or body and, under the pretext of abstinence, substitute and nourish in place of obedience singularity, private attachment, subtle vanity, and obstinacy in their own judgment—things that are truly the cancers of the solitary life.

They therefore require everything to be returned daily to the cook, so that he may know whether each person has eaten suitably from the *pulmenta* or *pitantiae*, and so that an explanation may immediately be demanded from anyone returning his portion as to why he had not eaten it [Col. 0735D]—whether he was ill—and so that the superior might immediately be informed of the matter. This passage is highly noteworthy and clearly demonstrates what the spirit of the Order has always been regarding abstinences and other exercises, which R. P. Guigo expressly notes in chapter 35 are not part of our institution.

**[Col. 0736A]** You will find this chapter reproduced in the ancient statutes, part III, chapter 20, no. 1.]

**[Col. 0733]**

1. Every Friday they are content with bread, water, and salt, except on solemnities. During Advent, Quinquagesima, and the Ember fasts, they also practice the same abstinence on Wednesday. They live in the same manner on the vigils of Easter, the Ascension, Pentecost, Saint John, Peter and Paul, the Assumption, All Saints, and the Nativity of the Lord.

2. On the vigils of the apostles James, Bartholomew, Matthew, Simon and Jude, Andrew, and Saint Lawrence the martyr, they eat only once but have *pulmentum*. On the other days, so that they may not be broken by excessive labor, they eat twice but receive *pulmentum* only once.

3. In general, the common foods of this house are seasoned only with salt. On Thursday and on solemnities of the chapter, they receive something better than usual. On Thursday of Easter and Pentecost, and on the day after the feast of the Innocents, if that day falls on Thursday, they take wine without any *pitantia* [variant: “without any other *pitantia*”].

**[Col. 0735]**

4. When available, they receive raw herbs, fruits, or roots only at supper, or at dinner if they eat only once. Whatever remains from the *pulmentum* or *pitantia* of one dinner, they return. They drink the wine given to them only at dinner or supper.

5. Whatever remains from the *pitantiae* or *pulmenta* and is suitable for use is returned to the cook, lest anyone secretly practice an unapproved abstinence.

**CHAPTER LIII. At what time they eat oat bread.**  
**[Note: [Col. 0736A]**

**CHAP. LIII.—No. 1. “They eat bread made from oats,”** etc. This passage sounds almost intolerably austere to those who do not know the customs of this region. In other regions where wheat grows abundantly, peasants can scarcely eat such bread even in times of famine, because they are unaccustomed to it and do not know how to make good bread from oats. But they will cease to wonder when they learn that in this region oat bread is the customary food of the peasants and even of respectable townspeople from the neighboring villages. They have been accustomed to eat it from the time they first leave the cradle, and consequently they become strong and vigorous—so much so that it would be difficult to find people in wealthy regions who live more healthily [Col. 0736B] and longer, or whose offspring multiply more.

Why is oat bread eaten there? Because wheat is very scarce among these rocks. The peasants save it for occasionally making cakes, whereas they use oats for making bread. Oats grow sufficiently abundantly in these mountains and are superior to the oats that grow elsewhere. Moreover, necessity, the teacher of all things, taught them how to make sufficiently good bread from it. Before taking the oats to the mill, they dry them in a warm oven; as a result, they are milled perfectly and yield very white flour, from which they later make bread. Such is the ordinary bread of the region.

It is therefore not so surprising that the lay brothers, who for the most part were natives of the region, as we noted above in chapter 45, [Col. 0736C] ate oat bread for five months, when their neighbors eat similar bread throughout the entire year. In the time of R. Father Guigo, however, lay brothers who came from another region, and who were not accustomed and could not become accustomed to this kind of bread, were given the same bread on which the monks were fed.]

In Advent, etc., they receive individual wheat loaves from the pittance allowance, etc. Those who inferred from this passage that, during these seasons of the year, a wheat loaf was distributed to each person only once a week as the entire substance of the pittance would be greatly mistaken. For it is clear from the foregoing that they were served a cooked dish, or pittance; but the meaning is that during Advent and Lent wheat bread was given to them as an addition to the pittance, and that, on the first day of the week, when they received their pittance for dinner, they also received that wheat loaf for the whole week. In memory of this practice, it is still maintained among us in most houses of the Order that during Advent and Lent the brothers are served, on Monday at dinner, a small wheat cake mixed with a little oil and salt, from which they may eat throughout the week; for they keep it with them just as they do bread. We have often eaten from such loaves.

The same matter is reported in the ancient statutes, part III, chapter 20, no. 12.]

From the Kalends of November until Easter they eat bread made of oats. During Advent and Lent, however, they receive, each week, individual wheat loaves from the pittance allowance.

## CHAPTER LIV. On Their Bloodletting

[Note: [Col. 0737A]]

**CHAPTER LIV.—No. 1.** “Four times a year,” etc. The monks were bled five times a year, but the lay brothers only four times, perhaps for this reason: through strenuous labor they more easily discharged excess humors. Here, moreover, the bodily supports and refreshments granted to them are specified; they were not unlike those which, as we saw, were granted to the monks in chapter 39.

**No. 2.** “But whoever is not bled is compelled to receive the same meal as those who have been bled,” etc. From this passage it is evident how far the mind of the first Fathers, and the spirit of our institution, stood from a scrupulous and obstinate interpretation of bodily austerities, from a spirit of coercion and singularity; and, conversely, how they wished us to observe a devout and discreet freedom of spirit, flexibility of mind, and the elimination of singular practices, even when those practices are good.

For here we see a lay brother in good health who has not been bled and therefore has no need of these supports and refreshments. Nevertheless, the good Fathers wish—in fact, if he refuses, they compel him—to use the same benefits as the others. Why is this, unless to teach us, as we have said, how earlier Carthusian solitaries ought to direct their charges, and how Carthusian monks ought to allow themselves to be directed by their superiors? It is therefore not surprising if prudent superiors today sometimes deny certain monks permission to maintain abstinence on bread and water, because that practice has rightly fallen into disuse and would be something singular, which neither others observe nor could observe. Thus, in accordance with what is expressly stated here, they are compelled to receive the same food as the others.

I also believe that our holy Father Bruno, a man endowed equally with holiness, prudence, and learning, impressed this spirit and manner of acting upon his successors, especially because he knew that the spirit of holy freedom was necessary for properly directing solitaries, so that they would not fall into scruples and anxieties of mind, would be preserved from obstinately clinging to their own judgment, and would be removed from those things that can arouse or nourish a hidden self-satisfaction.]

[Col. 0737]

1. They are bled four times a year: around the Kalends of May, around the Ides of July, around the Kalends of October, and around the Kalends of February. For those who have been bled, pottage is given for three days in the morning, and wine is given twice. On the first two days, three eggs, if available, are added to supper.

2. If they become thirsty after dinner, they drink wine, but not in another person’s cell. For it is by no means permitted that anyone drink or eat anything in anyone else’s cell. They are free from work, return to their beds, and from after dinner until Vespers converse about good things. Whoever is not bled, however, is compelled to receive the same meal as those who have been bled.

## CHAPTER LV. On Silence at Dinner

[Note: [Col. 0738A]]

**CHAPTER LV.—No. 1.** “While eating … they maintain silence.” Here we have the law of silence to be observed by them at table, [Col. 0738B] but it plainly does not apply to other times and exercises, during which they were not bound to silence in the same way.

**The same place.** “Although this was permitted earlier, nevertheless after the example,” etc. By this example he wishes to urge the lay brothers to observe more strictly what they already observed by the institution of the Order.

**No. 2.** “Our own brothers also, regardless of the obedience in which they are placed, with brothers of another obedience,” etc. They may, however, speak among themselves while working together in the same obedience, as is evident from chapters 44 and 45 and other passages.

The same matter is reported in the ancient statutes, part III, chapter 3, nos. 8 and 3.]

1. Wherever they may be, they maintain silence while eating. Although this was permitted earlier, nevertheless, after the example of the most reverend and God-beloved Cistercian monks [variant: “the most beloved-of-God Cistellensians”], whom we rejoice to see have greatly increased in both religious observance and number in a short time, we observe it more perfectly. For their lay brothers and monks do not speak at dinner.

2. Our own brothers also, regardless of the obedience in which they are placed, are not permitted to speak with brothers of another obedience.

## CHAPTER LVI. What Is to Be Done in Dangers

[Note: [Col. 0738B] **CHAPTER LVI.**—The same matter is reported in the ancient statutes, part III, chapter 22, no. 1. [Col. 0738C]]

If anywhere the urgency of a sudden illness, fire, or some such danger should arise, whoever can help first does so, with silence suspended.

## CHAPTER LVII. On the Brothers’ Clothing and the Utensils of the Cell

[Note: [Col. 0738C]]

**CHAPTER LVII.—No. 3.** “In the upper dormitory,” etc. From the title itself it is clear that the lay brothers then had individual, separate cells. Nevertheless, the dormitory [Col. 0739A] was in the upper house—that is, a large room filled with beds separated from one another—which the brothers went up from the lower house to occupy on feast days. It was impossible for each person to have two cells, one in the lower house and another in the upper house. By “common beds” he means beds occupied by individual brothers as circumstances required, so that no bed was assigned permanently to a particular person and could not be occupied by someone else in his absence.

**No. 3.** “In all such matters nothing else is considered except that cold,” etc. Here those who among us would wish to seek something elaborate either in the cloth from which garments are made or in the construction of the garments themselves—something redolent of worldly elegance [Col. 0739B]—would find judgment written against themselves. But, as R. Father Guigo wisely adds immediately, if vanity and pleasure are to be removed from our clothing, necessity and usefulness are not to be rejected.

**No. 4.** “Whoever reads these things,” etc. Here he repeats concerning the brothers what he had already said concerning the monks in chapter 28. For the holy man knew that the world abounds in indiscreet censors who, while neglecting themselves, nevertheless spend almost their entire lives in judgments, censures, and indiscriminately criticizing the deeds of others. To prevent our people from being disturbed by such criticism and falling into scruples, he anticipates the objection and speaks here at length.

This entire chapter is reported in the ancient Statutes, part III, chapter 23, nos. 1, 4, and 5.]

1. For clothing they have three tunics, three pairs of leggings, two pairs of foot-cloths, indoor and outdoor shoes, a fur garment, skins, a mantle, a hood, one pair of woolen mittens (*mitanas*; variant *mitaneas*), two loincloths, and two belts. Their shoes are made of oxhide.

2. From the Kalends of November they return one old tunic and receive one new one; likewise, they return one pair of leggings and receive one pair of leggings and one pair of foot-cloths. They receive old skins and fur garments—namely, those which the monks return when they receive new ones. They also have straw, a felt cover, a pillow, and a mattress for their beds.

3. From Easter until the feast of Saint Michael, from Prime until Compline, they do not use night shoes. In the upper dormitory they also have common beds, fur garments, and indoor shoes. In all such matters nothing else is considered except that cold be kept away and nakedness covered. For the straps of their shoes and the belts around their waists are made of raw hemp, and the loincloths themselves are hempen. Thus no thought is given to what vanity or pleasure might demand, but only to what necessity or usefulness requires [or: what necessity or usefulness alone demands].

4. They also have two bowls for food; one, in place of a tablecloth, for bread; one larger bowl for washing; a pitcher, a salt-cellar, a spoon, and a knife; a water vessel; and tools as well: an axe, a spade, an adze, an awl, a small sickle, two needles, thread, scissors, and a gimlet. Whoever reads these things should not hasten to laugh at or criticize them unless he has first lived in such a solitude and endured such great cold.

## CHAPTER LVIII. That They Do Not Seek Permission to Speak with Outsiders

[Note: [Col. 0739B]]

**CHAPTER LVIII.—No. 1.** “With those who do not belong to this house they do not seek permission, nor with,” etc. R. Father Guigo has already said the same concerning the monks in chapter 3. A lay brother, like a monk, is not required to seek permission in order to speak even with his blood brother. Nevertheless, both the blood brother and others may request that permission from the superior and obtain it, as is evident from chapters 10 and 30. It is not so with those who belong to the house: we find no prohibition, either here or elsewhere, against requesting permission to converse with them.

**No. 3.** “When accused, without delay,” etc. “The one who reproves,” etc. Here we have the form of interior mortification professed by our first Fathers. In observing it they did not impose the limits that they clearly and carefully imposed upon bodily austerities, but wished private attachment to excuses to be dismissed absolutely. This kind of mortification far surpasses all bodily austerities and concerns the work of converting our conduct, concerning which we make a vow. Thus, by this example, they taught that we must aspire to the very marrow of true mortification and self-denial in the inner person, where God is found, as is explicitly explained in the prologue to the modern statutes, where the search for God in the inner person is discussed.

The same matter is found in the ancient statutes, part III, chapter 3, no. 4; also chapter 23, no. 5; and likewise part II, chapter 12, no. 13.]

1. They do not seek permission to speak together with those who do not belong to this house, not even with a blood brother.

2. They keep absolutely nothing with them unless they have permission.

3. When accused, they immediately prostrate themselves and ask pardon. They do not rebuke the person who reproved them on that same day.

## CHAPTER LIX. What Is to Be Done with Something Sent to One of Us

[Note: [Col. 0740B]]

**CHAPTER LIX.—“It is given not to him but rather to another,” etc.** From this it is clear how strictly they wished to exclude every appearance of ownership [Col. 0741A] from themselves. If someone were to ask me in what I believe the austerity of the first Carthusians consisted, I would answer without hesitation that it consisted:

First, in the denial of one’s own will, as required by R. Father Guigo;

Second, in the suffocation, so to speak, of private affection, as he describes in the preceding chapter;

Third, in the renunciation of every form of ownership, as he notes here;

And fourth, in the devout observance of solitude, accompanied by devotion to interior prayer and withdrawal from useless concerns and desires relating to temporal things; for if these are lacking, solitude can be neither devout nor tranquil.

[Col. 0741B] Each of us ought to bring his intention, actions, and voluntary affections to these standards, and, according as he deviates more or less from them, confidently determine whether he approaches more or less closely to the spirit of our institution and of the first Fathers, or stands farther from it. Little attention should be paid to the reduction of abstinence on bread and water, because our first Fathers established that practice under the governance of obedience and admitted it only on the condition that we should not imagine that our possessions consisted in such things. It is clear from chapter 35 that R. Father Guigo regarded them as almost nothing in comparison with obedience. Therefore no relaxation can justly be charged to the Order on this account, as will be proved in its proper places.

Nor should attention be paid to the increase of temporal goods [Col. 0741C] and concerns, provided that these remain within the limits established and expressed by the modern statutes, because this must be attributed to the circumstances and necessities of the times. Moreover, this matter concerns only a few officials, not the cloistered members, from whom the regular community and the body of the Order are formed. Rather, all our arguments concerning the perseverance of individuals in the first Carthusian institution must be derived from the four principles noted above. Arguments concerning the perseverance of the Order as a whole, however, must be gathered from its statutes and the ordinances of the general chapters, because only what can be attributed to the entire Order is to be drawn from them, not the actions of particular individuals.

These four principles compose the goal toward which we must strive. Saint Father Bruno and his successors established it for themselves as well as for us, and we must set it before us as the target toward which they directed the arrows of their efforts and affections. Yet since it is certain that, as human beings, they nevertheless sometimes sinned, we should not now assess matters as though we could or ought to be incapable of sin.

If, then, we sometimes err as human beings, let us never depart from this goal, but always keep in our intention and endeavor:

[Col. 0742B]

First, the denial of our own will;

Second, love of correction and the pursuit of continual amendment, in relation to the vow of conversion of conduct that we have made;

Third, the renunciation of ownership;

And fourth, the observance of a devout solitude removed from the concern for and desire of temporal things.

The same matter is reported in the ancient statutes, part II, chapter 22, final number.]

If something—a garment or anything of that kind—is sent to one of us, whether lay brother or monk, by a friend or relative, it is given not to him but rather to someone else, so that he may not appear to possess it as his own.

## CHAPTER LX. What Is to Be Done with Something Found

[Note: [Col. 0742B]]

**CHAPTER LX.—No. 1.** “Otherwise it is left untouched.” Here it is evident with what vigilance of purity of conscience our people refused to possess another’s property, since they did not even wish their own members to touch it in this circumstance. By this example they demonstrate [Col. 0742C] how free we ought to be from desire for earthly things.

The same matter is reported in the ancient statutes, part II, chapter 22, no. 2.]

[Col. 0741]

1. If anything is found within (*intra*; variant *infra*) our boundaries, it is immediately returned to its owner, if he is present; otherwise it is handed over to the procurator. If something is found by one of our people outside our boundaries, it is immediately returned, if possible, to the brothers or to its owner, or entrusted to someone through whom it is thought it can be returned more effectively and faithfully; otherwise it is left untouched.

2. They lie in their cells and in the dormitory dressed in a single tunic and wearing a belt.

## CHAPTER LXI. On the Brothers’ Breeches and Small Fur Garments

[Note: [Col. 0742C]]

**CHAPTER LXI.—Linen is distinguished from hemp, and the former’s use is rejected because it is more delicate.** Here, however, they specify whatever contributes to warding off cold and preserving modesty in the work under discussion.

[Col. 0743A] The same is found in the ancient statutes, part III, chapter 18, no. 17; chapter 3, no. 2; and chapter 18, no. 18.]

1. The shepherds have hempen breeches, which they put on when they make cheese; otherwise they do not use linen garments at all [or: we do not use them], not even undergarments.

2. We have also granted the shepherds small fur garments, which can be made from approximately two sheepskins; they do not use them except when they go outside in winter.

3. Wherever they may be, they always maintain silence while milking.

## CHAPTER LXII. On the Brother Who Looks after the Pack Mules

[Note: [Col. 0743A]]

**CHAPTER LXII.—** From this chapter it is plainly evident, as we said above, that the term *sagmarii* refers to mules, and how much our people were to guard against the itch to learn curiously what was happening in the world or to attend to public rumors.

The same matter is reported in the ancient statutes, part III, chapter 26, no. 1.]

1. When the brother who looks after the pack mules goes outside, he does not sleep on a mattress and seeks nothing except lodging, unless the prior or procurator has specially assigned something to him.

[Col. 0743] 2. He neither carries nor brings to any outsider any words or greetings from any of us, nor from any outsider to any of us, unless the prior or procurator orders it. When he hears worldly rumors, he is ordered to leave them there.

## CHAPTER LXIII. On the Garden

[Note: [Col. 0743A]]

**CHAPTER LXIII.—** From this chapter and from others dealing with the administration of household affairs, it is evident how orderly they wished everything to be arranged and placed under the merit of obedience.

The same matter is reported in the ancient statutes, part III, chapter 15, no. 1.]

The garden and the things belonging to it are assigned to one of the brothers, who refers all matters to the procurator and renders him an account of everything.

## CHAPTER LXIV. On the Keeper of the Bridge

[Note: [Col. 0743B]]

**CHAPTER LXIV.—** This bridge is situated between two steep and lofty cliffs along the road to Grenoble. Between them flows a torrent formed by waters converging from the surrounding mountains and springs. When the torrent swells through an abundance of rain or melting snow, it falls and rushes among the rocks with such force and roar that it rivals the crashes of thunder.

In this chapter there is nothing else to note except the same form of silence and obedience that R. Father Guigo assigns throughout these *Customs*.

[Col. 0744A] The same is found in the ancient statutes, part III, chapter 27, no. 1; chapter 28, no. 30.]

1. The keeper of the bridge has permission to converse with absolutely no one unless he has been specially ordered to do so. By signs alone—or, if he is not understood, also by words—he turns away those who ought not to cross. Whoever takes his place is ordered to observe the same rule.

2. Absolutely no one who serves as another’s substitute in any obedience is permitted to change anything in that obedience without permission. In the cells themselves, whether above or below, nothing may be changed or done unless it has first been shown and ordered, lest the house, laboriously constructed, be damaged [or: worn away] or destroyed through curiosity.

## CHAPTER LXV. On the Brothers’ Disciplines

[Note: [Col. 0744A] **CHAPTER LXV.**—The same is reported in the ancient statutes, part III, chapter 4, no. 1, and is still observed in the same manner.]

1. During Advent and Quinquagesima, each person receives one discipline each week.

2. If they are not at home, they say the Lord’s Prayer seven times in place of the discipline, with acts of supplication.

## CHAPTER LXVI. On Ashes

[Note: [Col. 0744A]]

**CHAPTER LXVI.—** R. Father Guigo is speaking of the Wednesday before Lent, which is called Ash Wednesday because ashes are placed on the head on that day.

The brothers who are present in the lower chapel receive ashes from the procurator’s hand. Those who are absent say the Lord’s Prayer three times, with acts of supplication.

## CHAPTER LXVII. What They Do for the Mass

[Note: [Col. 0744A]]

**CHAPTER LXVII.—** Here a devotional obligation is prescribed, which they discharge for the Lenten Mass that was celebrated daily in the upper house for the community.

The same is reported in the ancient statutes, part III, chapter 6, no. 1.]

They also say the Lord’s Prayer three times, prostrate, after None, from the beginning of the fast until Easter, in discharge of the Mass.

## CHAPTER LXVIII. On Maundy Thursday

[Note: [Col. 0744B]]

**CHAPTER LXVIII.—** The lower house could not be abandoned by everyone. Therefore, when most had gone up to the upper house, those who remained at home performed the ceremony of washing the feet, which R. Father Guigo seems merely to indicate here, writing about it so briefly, as he did in several other matters.

Wine was then offered to each person, and after drinking they withdrew. In this they imitated the rite prescribed above in chapter 4, no. 23, for the monks.

The same matter is reported in the ancient statutes, part III, chapter 7, no. 3.]

On Maundy Thursday, those who remain below come after dinner to the kitchen, where the brother who is first in rank washes the feet of the others. Wine is offered to each person, and after drinking they withdraw.

## CHAPTER LXIX. On Good Friday

[Note: [Col. 0745A] **CHAPTER LXIX.**—Certain public devotional exercises to be performed by those remaining in the lower house are noted here. The same matter is reported in the ancient statutes, part III, chapter 7, no. 4.]

[Col. 0745]

1. On the following day, that is, on Good Friday, those who are there—that is, below—come to the church after None, which is delayed longer on that day than on the others. There they say the Lord’s Prayer once for the Church; once for the pope, the bishops, and all the sacred orders; for the emperor; for catechumens; for all afflictions and dangers; for heretics; for Jews; and for pagans, with acts of supplication added after each petition except that for the Jews.

2. Then they reverently kiss the cross brought by the kitchen worker, saying inwardly: “We adore you, Christ, and we bless you, because by your holy cross you redeemed the world.” Whoever does not know this says the Lord’s Prayer once.

## CHAPTER LXX. How They Are to Conduct Themselves on Solemnities

[Note: [Col. 0745A]]

**CHAPTER LXX.—** Here it is clearer than daylight that by the word “solemnity” the devout writer understood any feast on which a chapter meeting was held. Here too it is established how those who remain in the lower house on feast days are to spend their time.

The same matter is reported in the ancient statutes, part III, chapter 8, no. 1.]

On every day of the entire year on which chapter is held, those who do not go up, unless obedience prevents them, remain in their cells and devote the interval between Terce and Sext to prayer.

## CHAPTER LXXI. What They Do for the Dead

[Note: [Col. 0745A]]

**CHAPTER LXXI.—** This was all that they rendered for those recently deceased in their own house, for at that time there was no mention of benefits to be rendered for others through suffrages.

[Col. 0745B] By “acts of supplication” we understand the devout ceremony in which we bend the knees and kiss a bench or the ground.

The same matter is reported in the ancient statutes, part III, chapter 9, no. 1.]

For one recently deceased they owe three hundred Lord’s Prayers, half of which they perform with acts of supplication. At each anniversary they say nine, with the same number of acts of supplication.

## CHAPTER LXXII. On the Shaving of the Brothers

[Note: [Col. 0745B]]

**CHAPTER LXXII.—No. 1.** “But they also wash their heads.” Nowadays everyone’s head is washed and shaved. He makes no mention of the longer beards of the lay brothers, because at that time they were generally similar to those of the monks, since they were shaved only six times a year. We assigned the principal reason for this change above, in chapter 9.

**The same place.** “All the services, however,” etc. Here we have the form of humility and charity that we must follow in the mutual services we render to one another.
