**No. 2.** “When they meet one another,” etc. Here we see how foreign to the spirit and practice of the first Carthusians was the harshness of face and gesture that carries the odor of a melancholy spirit. On the contrary, they wished their members to adopt, when meeting brothers, a face expressive rather of joy and devout cheerfulness, and they required us, far removed from rustic discourtesy, modestly to observe practices of courtesy and, so to speak, civilized charity.

Those therefore misunderstand the statutes who, finding the expression “holy rusticity” there, suppose that everything must be done by us with unpolished rusticity. Not so, beloved friends and brothers in Christ, not so is that rusticity to be understood. By “holy rusticity” we should understand simple, sincere, and candid ways of acting, which testify that we stand far from the spirit and vanities of the world; these we ought to preserve in all things.

The same matter is reported in the ancient statutes, part III, chapter 21, nos. 1 and 4, and chapter 3, no. 2.]

1. As often as the monks are shaved, so often are the lay brothers shaved. But the lay brothers also wash their heads. All services, however private, which individual brothers do not themselves attend to or cannot perform, are humbly and devoutly completed by others, so that the person to whom such a task has been assigned considers himself fortunate.

2. When they meet one another, they pass by in silence, giving way to one another with friendly eagerness and humble deference. In this the younger brothers—that is, those who arrived later—take care to anticipate their elders.

## CHAPTER LXXIII. On Receiving a Novice

[Note: [Col. 0746B]]

**CHAPTER LXXIII.—No. 1.** “For laymen received for conversion,” etc. From this arose the custom in the Order of calling those brothers “lay brothers” who are not suited or prepared for the clerical state.

**The same place.** “Almost the same thing is done as with clerics.” By “clerics” R. Father Guigo means the monks. It is therefore clear that at that time, as is still observed, they would receive no one into the state of monks who was not suitable for the clerical state. From this arose the old question put to a novice in the Order before he is admitted: “Can you advance to sacred orders?” The meaning is whether he has any impediment, bodily or spiritual, that would prevent him from receiving sacred orders.

Thus, in R. Father Guigo’s time, all could be advanced to the priesthood. Yet although there were many priests in the monastery, it is certain that not all celebrated Mass at that time; they were content to celebrate in the manner and at the times specified in the first chapters of these *Customs*.

**The same place.** “For hard things are likewise proposed,” etc. The testing of lay brothers ought to be no less severe than that of monks. Unless lay brothers have been brought to the monastery by a good vocation—that is, a heavenly vocation, or one believed to be such—and unless they devote themselves energetically and intensely to fulfilling the obligations of their vocation, they can more easily fall, through the external exercises to which they are assigned, into dissipation, then into habitual relaxation, and afterward into various occasions of sin. This cannot happen so easily to monks who always remain in the cloister.

**No. 2.** “And for as long a period as the prior should wish, but not,” etc. At that time, therefore, the prior had discretion to extend the period of probation beyond a year for as long as he wished. The matter concerned receiving testimony only from lay brothers, not necessarily requiring a formal vote, as we have already said something about in chapter 37. It is therefore not surprising that, for good reasons and on the basis of experience, a probation of five years in the state of donors should commonly be assigned among us in these times before a lay brother is admitted to the state of lay brothers.

**No. 3.** “He asks someone in his own voice,” etc. This was established because the greater part of the lay brothers at Chartreuse came from a mechanical or peasant condition, although later men of very noble birth embraced that state out of humility and devotion and adorned the Order with great splendor of virtue.

The same chapter is reported in the ancient statutes, part III, chapter 24, no. 1.]

1. For laymen being received into profession, almost the same thing is done as with clerics, for hard and severe things are likewise proposed to them.

[Col. 0747] 2. They are also ordered to reconcile anything they may have against one another. They are also ordered to be reconciled with those against whom they have anything, and are admitted to probation for as long a period as the prior wishes, but not less than a year; they are received on the testimony of those among whom they have lived—namely, the lay brothers—just as clerics are received on the testimony of the monks.

3. On the day on which someone is to make their profession, the candidate is led to the monks’ chapter, where, after hearing about stability, obedience, and the other necessary matters, he remains immovable and undaunted. He asks someone in his own words to write his profession for him, and at its end he himself draws the sign of the cross with his own hand. Carrying it in his hand, he approaches the right side of the altar after the Gospel and the offertory. The deacon then reads it aloud, while everyone listens, holding it in his right hand, and says as follows.

## CHAPTER LXXIV. The Profession of a Lay Brother

[Note: [Col. 0748A]]

**CHAPTER LXXIV.—No. 1.** “And perseverance.” This is equivalent to the word “stability,” which the monks pronounce in their profession; indeed, in expressing stability of remaining in the same place, it in some way goes beyond it.

**The same place.** “But if at any time,” etc. This extension of the wording was made so that they might understand more fully the obligation of stability to be observed by them. By expressly consenting to the condition that they could be forcibly returned to the service of the house, they were to know that through their expressed vow they had entered the service of God and the Order and had voluntarily assumed, for the love of God, the condition of servants. From this condition it seems that they are not included among the fugitives mentioned below, in chapter 77.

The same matter is reported in part III of the ancient statutes, chapter 24, no. 5.]

1. I, Brother So-and-so, promise obedience, conversion of my conduct, and perseverance all the days of my life, in this desert, before God and his saints and the relics of this desert, which has been constructed in honor of God, blessed ever-virgin Mary, and Saint John the Baptist, for fear of our Lord Jesus Christ and the remedy of my soul, in the presence of Lord So-and-so, the prior. If at any time I should attempt to flee or depart from here, may the servants of God who are here have full authority in their own right to seek me out and recall me, forcibly and violently, to their service.

2. After this he offers the same document upon the altar, and, after kissing the altar, he bends down at the priest’s feet to be blessed with the following supplication: “Save [him]; send [aid] to him; be [a protection] to him; the Lord be with you; let us pray. Lord Jesus Christ, who are the way.” See above.

## CHAPTER LXXV. How a Brother Is to Conduct Himself after He Has Been Received

[Note: [Col. 0748B]]

**CHAPTER LXXV.—** “Not even a staff,” etc. “Without having the prior’s permission,” etc. R. Father Guigo indicates to the newly professed what their self-denial ought to be: possessing nothing as their own and abandoning their own will.

Here mention is made only of the prior’s permission insofar as it concerns obedience, but perfect observance of poverty is also involved. The reason is that, although we do not explicitly make a vow of poverty, just as we do not make a vow of chastity, it is certain that both are contained in the vow of obedience like an infant in its mother’s womb; and this has always been the understanding in the Order.

It is therefore not surprising that R. Father Guigo everywhere considers and proclaims obedience as the fountain of all our goods, because it is like a mother who holds the other vows—of poverty and chastity—and all the observances of the Order in her bosom. But if the mother is injured or dies, what can be hoped for from her offspring? This comparison, if not completely, certainly very closely accords with R. Father Guigo’s meaning and helps us to explain and rightly understand our institution.

The same matter is reported in part III of the ancient statutes, chapter 25, no. 1.]

From this time onward, let him know [or: let him recognize] that he has absolutely nothing—not even the staff on which he leans while walking along the road—without the prior’s permission, since he does not even belong to himself. With regard to him, the same provision will be observed that we stated above concerning a monk: namely, that if he dies while acting acceptably during the time of examination, nothing less will be done for him than if he had been professed.

## CHAPTER LXXVI. On the Lodging of Brothers Who Are Sent Outside

[Note: [Col. 0749B] “They are sent outside”: that is, beyond the boundaries. Here the places situated in the neighboring mountains or plains are specified, to which lay brothers could more commonly be sent. They were forbidden to receive lodging or food from anyone, for the reason mentioned above: lest they fall into occasions of familiarity and, consequently, relaxation.]

[Col. 0749]

When some are sent outside into the neighboring mountains—that is, above Cornillon, and at Bocoiron, Intermontes, and Scales—they receive neither food nor lodging from anyone unless they have been specially ordered to do so or are compelled by some unavoidable and unforeseen necessity.

## CHAPTER LXXVII. On Fugitives or Those Who Have Been Expelled

[Note: [Col. 0749B]]

**CHAPTER LXXVII.—** “Whether he has fled or has been driven out.” Here we have the method of dealing then customary with those who were either fugitives or expelled from the monastery because of depraved conduct. It is not surprising that in any communities, even those established in the native fervor of their purpose, there should be found people who fall into similar situations.

For the monastic state, however holy its institution and however well suited to acquiring and preserving holiness, cannot cause human beings to cease being human, since even the apostolic state did not prevent Judas from becoming a betrayer and afterward his own murderer.

Why, then, do people cry out so loudly over the fall of some monk? Because they do not know themselves. Blinded by their own opinion, they pay no attention to themselves; and, falling daily like wretched human beings, they still do not understand what it means to be human. If they were wise and understood, [Col. 0749D] they would indeed exercise zeal against sin, [Col. 0750A] but they would mourn over the sinner, sympathize with him, and take care for themselves.

Here it appears what was then done so that the monastic enclosures might be cleansed of infected sheep, lest they infect others. The particular case for which a monk or lay brother might be expelled is not specified, but the terms “perversities” and “vice” are used generally. Nor is it said that they sought out fugitive monks. Yet this seems to be implied, since it is hinted at in the form of profession for lay brothers, although the following words seem to oppose this interpretation. Everything can be reconciled, however, if a distinction is made between a fugitive simply and one who is at once fugitive and perverse: the former could have been forcibly recalled even against his will, whereas the latter they would not have wished to recall, because, on account of his perversity, he also deserved to be expelled. [Col. 0750B]

“And if, led by repentance, he returns.” Here the matter is not a forced return, but one proceeding from the free motive of repentance and inward conversion.

“Promising the correction of his perversities.” The word “perversities,” placed in the plural, indicates serious faults, as though they had become habitual. For from the mere habit of sinning a person is called perverse and, as it were, depraved in character; whereas one is called a sinner who falls into sin through human weakness but does not persist in sinning.

“The prior shall handle his case, etc.” Such a fugitive or expelled person, even if he returned voluntarily and was moved by repentance, was therefore not immediately received. From this it is clear how cautiously the good Fathers acted in those times [Col. 0750C], and how scrupulously they wished to guard against receiving a diseased sheep that might harm others, preferring the good of the community to the advantages of a private individual.

“And according as the number of the brothers, or the usefulness of the house, or even his salvation, etc.” From the number of the brothers, R. P. Guigo wishes to express the weight of the counsel arising from the united judgment of several persons. Here he assigns various points to be considered or weighed, from which, as from principles, a more suitable conclusion might be drawn, so that the usefulness of the community and what was more advantageous for the salvation of the expelled or fugitive might be reconciled together.

“And if the counsel should favor receiving him, he shall be placed last as a test of humility, etc.” From this it appears that, before an expelled or fugitive person was admitted to his former status, his humility was tested, so that the truth of his conversion might be recognized from his proven humility. In this testing, which should be carried out in the manner of the testing undergone by novices before they are admitted to profession, it must be believed that, if they failed, they would again have been expelled and not admitted to full reconciliation in the order.

“But if not, permission shall be given to him, etc.” At that time, therefore, it was permitted to give someone permission, on one’s own authority, to transfer to another order; this is no longer permitted.

In this chapter one can see what monastic polity then existed, a polity also approved by the ancient canon law, by which the first Fathers could cleanse the monastic enclosures of diseased sheep and render the rest of the flock immune from the many harms, vexations, and scandals [Col. 0751B] arising from the lukewarm or evil conduct of persons of different character. It is certain that, by this cleansing, monastic discipline could then be maintained in a sounder, purer, and more durable condition: they had at hand an effective remedy by which they could remove evil from their midst. Now, however, for weighty reasons pertaining to the public good of both the ecclesiastical and civil orders, that jurisprudence has been changed. If any of the sheep once admitted to profession become diseased or vicious, we are now compelled to keep them in the same enclosure mixed with the good, the former remedy of purification having been cut away and now being granted only for rare causes.

The monastic order seems to have suffered great ruin from this. But it is entirely just that lesser harms should be set aside in favor of greater ones. For, with the multiplication of monasteries and religious persons, and also with the greater ease of admitting young men to religious profession, under the confidence that they could be expelled if they did not live religiously, the number of those expelled and of those to be expelled also multiplied. After returning to the world, they not infrequently scandalized and disturbed the Church and families by a wandering, idle, and disorderly manner of life. As the number of those expelled from monasteries gradually increased, and the public scandal arising from this also grew, the Church’s concern gradually increased about closing the door of expulsion.

If we complain about this matter, the following answer will be made to us: “Take heed for yourselves, and by careful discussion and rigorous examination [Col. 0751D] test those whom you admit to profession. No force is imposed upon you to receive monks. Therefore bear those whom you have freely and voluntarily made monks; for it is not right that, for your convenience, the commonwealth should suffer harm and the Church scandal from so many religious persons stripped of their habits. Act cautiously when you receive novices for profession; educate them well in regular discipline; correct and imprison [Col. 0752A] the disorderly. It is better that vicious persons should be confined and restrained within the monastery’s walls than that, placed at liberty, they should be allowed to compensate for their former practice of a stricter life by vicious conduct.”

What shall we answer to this? With due deference to better judgment, only one objection occurs to me. Certain cases arise in which the monastic orders truly deserve great compassion, and in which some provision for a suitable remedy would be desirable. These cases result from deception and from the sheer fault of secular people who, in order to provide for their own affairs, strive to make unhappy monks. There are young men who, whether urged on by their parents, compelled by sheer necessity, or led by other purely human motives, come to the monastery without any heavenly vocation [Col. 0752B]. There, restraining themselves during the year of novitiate and living with sufficient modesty and religious observance, they deceive both the regular community and, even more, themselves. For after making profession, no longer able to endure themselves, they begin to reveal what they are; and instead of zeal always to advance on the way of God, they substitute and put into practice the skill of seeking relaxation. Let us cease discussing these grievous harms and the remedies to be applied to them, and take care to do what belongs to us.

In these times, then, when the remedy of cleansing our enclosures has been taken away, what must be done? If, in the time of R. Father Guigo, when they had the remedy in their hands, they acted so cautiously concerning the reception of those who wished to become Carthusians [Col. 0752C], let us now act much more cautiously and rigorously with those who petition, and strive with every effort to test them and to discover whether they come, drawn by a heavenly vocation, to seek God in Carthusian profession, and whether they possess the dispositions necessary to bear the burdens of the order.

To speak humanly, then, let us conclude this question with the Apostle, on account of human weakness, in these words. There never was, nor will there ever be, a monastic congregation, however well ordered, which, along with good and ordinary members, does not contain some who through their own fault have neglected or lost the grace of their vocation. From this cause, from the other matter noted above concerning those who enter religion without a heavenly vocation, [Col. 0752D] and from excessive indulgence in punishing excesses and transgressions, almost all the more serious harms in monasteries arise.]

If any inhabitant of this place should flee or be expelled, and, moved by repentance, should return, promising to correct his perversities and the particular vice on account of which he had been expelled or had fled, the prior shall handle his case in common counsel. According as the number of the brothers, the usefulness of the house, or even his own salvation seems to require, he shall act toward him; and if the counsel favors receiving him, he shall be placed last as a test of humility. But if not, permission shall be given him to go to some other religious house, in which he may save his soul.

## CHAPTER LXXVIII. On the Number of Inhabitants

[Note: [Col. 0752D]]

### Chapter LXXVIII

In this chapter nothing is laid down from which it could be concluded that the intention of the first Fathers was that each house of the order should admit only a fixed number of monks, beyond which it should not proceed. [Col. 0753A] R. Father Guigo merely explains what he had established for the house of the Carthusian Charterhouse, harmonizing the number of persons and the burdens of the Charterhouse with its resources, as will immediately be seen. But these matters will be found expressed more explicitly in the ancient statutes.

You have this chapter reproduced in the ancient statutes, part II, chapter 25, numbers 1 and 3, and chapter 34, part III, number 2.]

[Col. 0751]

1. The number of inhabitants of this wilderness is thirteen monks—not because we are always so many, for at present we are not so many, but because we have decided to receive that number if God should send them. But if some such person should ask for mercy—someone whose usefulness and worth seem scarcely capable of being recovered—he shall be added as a fourteenth, provided that the resources of the house are thought capable of bearing it.

[Col. 0753] 2. The number of laymen, whom we call lay brothers, has been fixed at sixteen. At present, however, there are more, for some of them were old and weak and could not work, and for that reason we were compelled to receive others. Therefore, when those who are now frail have died, we shall not accept others in their place.

## CHAPTER LXXIX. Why the Number Is So Small

[Note: [Col. 0753A]]

### Chapter LXXIX

Here R. Father Guigo openly explains why the number of inhabitants of the Carthusian wilderness was fixed at thirteen or fourteen monks and sixteen lay brothers: “lest,” he says, “being compelled to seek and wander in order to meet expenses greater than this place can bear, we should begin what we dread.” Both the old and the modern statutes repeat and frequently inculcate the same point, and it has always been carefully observed in the order. Thus, if all the inhabitants of the houses of the order were brought together, there would be approximately 2,500 monks, approximately 1,300 lay brothers and donates, and 170 nuns; distributed among the individual houses, this would amount to scarcely twelve monks and nine laymen per house. [Col. 0753B]

The Charterhouse, as I have already said, must be regarded as capable of having forty-five monks, but this number is reckoned for three houses, namely the Charterhouse, the house of La Courrerie, and the house of Cales. The Parisian house accommodates forty monks, as does the house at Avignon, Pavia, Naples, and at most four or five others built near very large cities; these too can have the same number. Some houses, however, can receive from twenty to thirty monks. But most of the remaining houses were founded and built for thirteen monks—that is, twelve monks together with the prior—which number agrees with that expressed here by R. Father Guigo. Nevertheless, there are quite a few that have only eight, nine, or ten monks. But we must make every effort to bring them eventually to that number of thirteen monks [Col. 0754A], so that they may be able to fulfill the complete regular observance in chant and the reading at table. This can rarely be required reasonably of a small number because of the old and infirm; hence the entire burden of chant and readings falls upon the shoulders of four or five monks. For this reason the statutes of the order direct that, in houses which do not have eight monks, the singing is to be done on a single note.

The number of inhabitants in the houses of the order is therefore, by God’s providence, only moderate. Large buildings and considerable expenses are needed to construct and endow a house in the order, because according to our Institute each monk must have a small house, or cell, separated from the others, as is seen in our cloisters [Col. 0754B], for which a large cloister enclosure is necessary. Moreover, the support of Carthusian monks costs more than that of others, since each must have in his cell an individual fireplace, furnishings, and similar things that elsewhere are provided communally. We note these matters more fully so that the mind of the order, as it has always been and still is concerning the number of monks, may be recognized more clearly; this pious writer also explains it sufficiently in number 2.

### Number 2

“Should our successors, etc.” The holy man does not seem satisfied with repeating those activities of seeking and wandering, which he calls hateful out of the abundance of his heart. So firmly was he convinced that these things ought to become objects of horror to his successors—and so it has happened. For the Fathers [Col. 0754C] of the order speak of this matter even more severely in the old and new statutes.

### Number 3

“Considering, therefore, not the gifts that are sent, etc.” Here it is evident how great was the prudence of R. Father Guigo and how suited he was to arrange and foresee everything discreetly. Gifts were indeed being received at that time, for he speaks of the present; yet, foreseeing that they would cease, he arranges everything as though they had already ceased.

[Col. 0755A] “We think that the aforesaid number of people can live here, provided that, etc.” Here we have a most beautiful passage, which we ought to read written everywhere in our houses and keep before our eyes. From it we shall learn by what method it can be possible to do much with few revenues, as we see and marvel at in many houses of the order, especially those removed from the crowds of people. One example among many will suffice here. A certain house of nuns has approximately sixty members of the order. If the number of servants and hired workers necessary for the administration of domestic affairs is added, the number rises to seventy or more. Yet this house scarcely has six thousand pounds of annual income, apart from what it takes for its own use from agricultural management. Who would believe that such a large household could subsist on such small revenues? Nevertheless, the situation is certainly so. I could cite a hundred houses of the order in which the same thing is proved by experience; and I rejoice at this, and shall continue to rejoice. The greater burdens of the houses of the order generally do not arise from within—for when things are done in an orderly and religious manner, secular people could scarcely believe how much can be accomplished with little—but from without: namely, from the almost unavoidable expenses which they are compelled to incur because of external circumstances involving times, places, business, and persons. Hence very few are found that could, within ten years, accumulate enough to support themselves for one year [Col. 0755C] if their annual revenue were entirely to fail.

Moreover, the same matters that R. Father Guigo says here are not only reported in the ancient statutes, part II, chapter 25, number 5, but are also expressed more fully in the modern statutes [Col. 0756A], where they may be read with great spiritual consolation.]

1. We have chosen this small number for the same reason that we neither provide mounts for guests nor maintain an almonry: namely, lest, being compelled to seek and wander in order to meet expenses greater than this place can bear, we should begin what we dread.

2. But if our successors should be unable, for certain reasons unknown to us, to maintain this same very small number in this place without the hateful duties of seeking and wandering, and if they are willing to follow our counsels, they should return to the number which they could bear without the dangers mentioned above. For we who now live here, although we are few, would much rather be fewer still than arrive at those evils while preserving or increasing our number.

3. Considering, therefore, not the gifts that are sent—for it does not seem right to us to undertake, on the basis of uncertain benefits, certain burdens that cannot be assumed or laid down without great danger—but considering not the gifts, rather what this wilderness in which we live can produce, whether from agriculture or from the raising of animals, we think that the aforesaid number of people can live here, provided that the same zeal that has existed until now continues in humility, poverty, and moderation in food, clothing, and the other things pertaining to use, and provided finally that contempt for the world and love of God—the reason for which everything must be borne and done—increase daily toward perfection.

## CHAPTER LXXX. On the Commendation of the Solitary Life

[Note: [Col. 0756A]]

### Chapter LXXX

#### Number 1

“There are many lowly and minor matters, etc.” He wishes to speak of matters concerning the duties of the shoemaker and the baker. Concerning the brothers’ *brachae*, that is, breeches, and similar things, he said, etc. “To judge nothing” means to distinguish nothing, but to embrace without discrimination all the things which we believed you wished to have.

#### Number 2

“Yet not everything in such a way, etc.” This refers to what we have said: that he did not undertake to set out everything in detail, but only in a manner sufficient for the purpose, according to the proverb: “For the intelligent, a little is enough.”

#### Number 3

“As for the commendation of this life, etc.” This commendation of the solitary life has a relationship with the sacred Scriptures such that whenever it is read, it always awakens a new taste of sweetness in the soul of the reader [Col. 0756B], even if he has already read it a hundred times. For there is in it a certain sweetness of style which, by sincere and almost natural arguments and methods, anticipates and convinces reason itself, and finally, carrying the reader away gently, compels him to declare that the man who wrote these things was certainly inspired by the Holy Spirit—one for whom Scripture was, as it were, his mother tongue, and who dipped his pen into the ink of the heavenly writing desk. It is certain that he is speaking here of physical solitude—that is, of the solitude which truly makes a person alone, separated from companions, existing with God alone—and that he says absolutely nothing that could in any way apply to another kind of solitude. The matter is so evident in itself that we consider it superfluous to prove its truth here by various glosses.

[Col. 0756C] #### Number 7

“Almost everything that is best in our institution consists in quiet and solitude, silence and the seeking of higher things, etc.” Here the most devout writer very briefly lists the principles of Carthusian life, which are quiet from worldly matters and affections, solitude from human company and the sight of vanities, silence from useless words, and the seeking of higher things—that is, seeking and setting one’s mind on the things above. He does not speak of the rest, because they are referred almost as accidents to the substance of the Carthusian purpose, which is obedience rendered in quiet, solitude, and silence.

#### Number 12

“Since by its rarity and by the small number of its followers it sufficiently commends itself, etc.” R. P. Guigo immediately shows where he obtains this argument, lest he seem to be putting forward something paradoxical or offensive to some people. From this argument we ought to draw the following conclusions for our own progress. It belongs to God alone to make monks, and whenever an attempt is made by human counsel or human industry to multiply monks, the number of miserable persons rather than of holy men will be increased. Let us therefore always follow the mind of the statutes strictly, both regarding new houses, which should be received only with great discernment, and regarding subjects to be admitted into the order.

[Col. 0758A] “The Lord knows those who are his own” (II Tim. 2:19), and we do not know whom he wishes to include in this our Carthusian vocation. Let us therefore beware, in a matter of such importance, of following our own judgment or inclination. Instead, attending solely to the fulfillment of God’s will, let us strive to carry it out uniquely concerning those who come to the order, observing and carrying out these things devoutly and sincerely, in the spirit of true charity, by which both a heavenly vocation and the will of God can be recognized in this life.

Nor should we ever be deceived by arguments drawn from that Gospel passage: “Compel them to enter, so that my house may be filled” (Luke 14:32). This applies only to the call to Christian faith, which is altogether necessary for salvation and imposes no moral obligation [Col. 0758B] that cannot and ought not to be fulfilled by all with God’s grace. It does not apply to the call to the monastic state, and especially not to the Carthusian state. For that state requires not merely people steadfast in faith, but those who, through a singular vocation from God, are called to that manner of life which he has established in his Church in order to shine there in a special way [Col. 0759A], and for this purpose he wished them to be placed and kindled upon a lampstand. In this manner of life there are many things to which human strength is unequal and in which a person cannot be preserved in a virtually continuous practice without special grace; and we firmly believe that this grace is attached to God’s call to that state. Many are called to the faith, but few are predestined to the Carthusian order.

Let us remember those men mentioned in the First Book of Maccabees, chapter 5. When certain people wished to act bravely and enter the contest, they brought disaster upon many; and the reason given there is that they were not of the stock of those men through whom salvation had been accomplished in Israel. I do not hesitate to declare that the same thing will happen to us if we attempt by human industry to make Carthusian [Col. 0759B] monks.

God knows how long the Carthusian order should endure and with what number of monks it should be composed. Let us therefore entrust the whole matter to divine providence and religiously strive to do only what belongs to us [Col. 0760A], always keeping in mind this point: if, by God’s disposition, the order is to decline because of a shortage of subjects, then the matter will occur without injury to God, without scandal to the Church, and without any disgrace to the order; for it will die honorably, as though in its own bed. But it will not be so if, through the careless and indiscriminate reception of subjects, we fill it with people who have been called by God only to the faith and not to the Carthusian religion. For they will display a slaughter in the order instead of a good contest, through relaxations and the carrying out of disordered affections, and perhaps even through wars declared against the order that seeks to restrain them. The result will be that the order will finally perish miserably, with injury to God, with scandal to the Church, and with its own disgrace. I ask that I be forgiven, following the example of R. Father Guigo [Col. 0760B], if I write somewhat more extensively on this subject.

Behold, most beloved brothers and friends in Christ, the first institutions of the Carthusian purpose, to which, as to principles, everything subsequently introduced and ordered in the order is related.]

[Col. 0755]

1. You have, most beloved, as you requested, our customs described in whatever manner was possible. Many of them are lowly and minor matters, which perhaps ought not to have been written down, except that your affection compelled us to judge nothing but rather to embrace everything that was ready to hand.

2. We do not think, however, that everything has been set down in such a way that nothing at all remains. But if anything has escaped us, it can easily be pointed out in a present conversation.

3. As for the commendation of this solitary life, we have almost remained silent, knowing that it has been abundantly commended by many holy and learned men of such great authority that we are not worthy to tread in their footsteps, and judging it superfluous to show you what you know equally well or better.

4. For you know that, in the Old and especially the New Testament, almost all the greater and more subtle mysteries were revealed not amid tumultuous crowds but when the servants of God were alone. You also know that the servants of God, whenever they wished either to meditate on something more subtly, to pray more freely, or to be separated from earthly things through an ecstasy of mind, almost always avoided the hindrances of the multitude and sought the advantages of solitude.

5. Hence, to touch on something from this subject, Isaac goes out alone into the field to meditate (Genesis 32); and we must believe that this was not accidental but customary for him. Jacob, after sending everything ahead, remains alone, sees God face to face, and is made happy at once by a blessing and by a change of name for the better (Genesis 24). Alone, in one moment, he attained more than he had attained throughout his entire life in company.

6. Scripture also bears witness to how greatly Moses, Elijah, and Elisha loved solitude, how much they grew through it in revelations of divine mysteries, and in what manner they were continually endangered among human beings but visited by God when they were alone.

7. Jeremiah also, as we mentioned above, sits alone because he is filled with God’s threats (Jeremiah 15), asking that water be given to his head and a fountain of tears to his eyes, so that he might mourn those slain among his people. He also asks for a place where he may exercise himself more freely in so holy a work, saying: “Who will give me a travelers’ lodging in the wilderness?” (Jeremiah 9). It is as though he had no leisure to do this in the city; in this way he indicates how much companions hinder the grace of tears. After saying, “It is good to wait in silence for the salvation of God” (Lamentations 3)—an occupation for which solitude provides the greatest assistance—and after adding, “It is good for a man to bear the yoke from his youth,” in which he greatly consoles us, since almost all of us undertook this purpose in youth, he further says: “He shall sit alone and be silent, because he shall lift himself above himself.” In this way he signifies almost everything that is best in our institution: quiet and solitude, silence, and the seeking of higher things.

8. He later shows what kind of people these practices make his disciples, saying: “He shall give his cheek to the one who strikes him; he shall be filled with reproaches.” In the first there shines the greatest patience, and in the second perfect humility.

9. John the Baptist, also, than whom, according to the Savior’s proclamation, no one greater has arisen among those born of women (Matthew 11), clearly shows what security and usefulness solitude provides. Though he was assured neither by the divine oracles that had foretold that, filled with the Holy Spirit from the womb (Luke 1), he would go before Christ the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah, nor by his miraculous birth, nor by the holiness of his parents, he fled the company of human beings as dangerous and chose the deserted solitude as safe. As long as he dwelt alone in the wilderness, he knew neither danger nor death. What virtue and merit he gained there, the baptism of Christ and the death he accepted for justice demonstrated. For he became such in solitude that he was worthy alone to baptize Christ, who washes away all things, and for the truth to avoid neither prison nor death.

10. Jesus himself, God and Lord, whose power could neither be aided by secrecy nor hindered by public exposure, nevertheless, in order to provide for us by his example, was first tested in solitude by temptations and fasts before he preached or performed signs. Scripture also reports that, leaving the crowds and the disciples, he went up the mountain alone to pray (Matthew 14). At the time when his passion was already approaching, he likewise left the apostles and prayed alone. By this example above all he indicated how much solitude benefits prayer, since he did not wish to pray together with companions, even though they were apostles.

11. You yourselves, holy and venerable Fathers—Paul, Anthony, Hilarion, Benedict, and the countless others—consider for yourselves how greatly they advanced in mind in solitude. You will prove that the sweetness of psalmody, the study of readings, the fervor of prayers, the subtlety of meditations, the ecstasies of contemplation, and the baptisms of tears can be aided by nothing more than solitude.

12. Let these few examples that we have mentioned not suffice you for the praise of the purpose you have undertaken. Rather, gather more for yourselves, either from present experience or from the pages of the sacred Scriptures. Yet this purpose itself does not need such commendation, since it sufficiently commends itself by its rarity and by the small number of its followers. For if, according to the Lord’s words, the way that leads to life is narrow and few find it (Matthew 7), while conversely the way that leads to death is broad and many go by it, then among the institutions of the Christian religion each one shows itself to possess greater and higher merit in proportion as it admits fewer people, and lesser and lower merit in proportion as it admits more. We wish you always good health and ask that you remember us.

Here end the Customs of Guigo, Prior of the Charterhouse.

[Col. 0759]

# LIFE OF SAINT HUGH, BISHOP OF GRENOBLE, BY GUIGO, PRIOR OF THE CARTHUSIANS

(Bollandists, *Acta sanctorum*, April, vol. I, p. 36.)

## Prefatory Notice

1. Among the illustrious men who flourished with an exceptional splendor of holiness in the eleventh and twelfth centuries of the Christian era, Saint Hugh may be counted: bishop of Grenoble in the upper Dauphiné, a friend of Saint Bruno, founder of the Charterhouse, and of Saint Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux. Saint Hugh was born in the year of Christ 1053 and was ordained bishop in 1080, when he was nearly twenty-seven years old, as is read below in the *Life*, number 5. He departed to the Lord in the eightieth year of his age, the thirty-second of his episcopal consecration, in the year of Christ 1132, on the Kalends of April, the Friday before Palm Sunday, as is read below in number 33. That year was a leap year; the lunar cycle was 12, the solar cycle 21, and the Dominical Letters were CB. Easter was celebrated on 10 April. These are the facts concerning his age.

2. In the sixth year of his episcopate he received Saint Bruno and energetically assisted him in founding the Charterhouse. When Bruno was summoned to Rome by Urban II, the supreme pontiff, Lauduinus, the first companion of Saint Bruno in the religious life, governed the Charterhouse. After he and two others who had succeeded to the supreme government of the Charterhouse had died, Guigo, the fifth prior of the Carthusians, was appointed around the year of Christ 1110. He died in the year 1137, and thus survived Saint Hugh’s death by only five years; he had always been joined to him by the holiest friendship. Saint Bernard of Clairvaux explains the affection with which he embraced both of them in the *Life* of Saint Hugh, in these words. The monk Gaufridus writes:

“When the servant of God, Bernard, had already spent several years at Clairvaux, it came into his mind to visit Saint Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, and the Carthusian brothers out of devotion. The bishop mentioned above received him so gratefully and reverently, recognizing the divine presence in the visit of such a guest, that he prostrated himself and adored him, touching the ground. When the servant of Christ saw the bishop, advanced in age, renowned in reputation, and distinguished for holiness, prostrate before him, he was greatly alarmed. He too fell down before him, and, having at last been received with the kiss of peace, he complained with deep sighing that his humility had been put to shame by the veneration shown to so great a man. From that time Saint Bernard obtained a special place in his heart, so that thereafter those two sons of splendor became one heart and one soul and enjoyed one another in Christ. For, just as the queen of Sheba testified concerning Solomon, each rejoiced to find in the other far more than fame had proclaimed. At the Charterhouse also, the servant of Christ was received by the most reverend man Guigo, the prior, and by the other brothers, with the same affection and veneration. They rejoiced with joy when they found him present just as they had previously known him through his letter.”

3. Thus far Gaufridus. Among the letters of Saint Bernard there are two addressed to the aforesaid Guigo, numbers 11 and 12, from which anyone can easily perceive how greatly the holiness and purity of life flourished at that time in the Charterhouse under Guigo. But how greatly Guigo and the other monks of the Grande Chartreuse shared all things with Saint Hugh for the defense of the Church is indicated by a letter from all of them, written in the year 1130 to the Council of Jotrum, which had assembled for the defense of justice, when Blessed Thomas, prior of the Abbey of Saint Victor in Paris, had been cruelly killed by impious men because of his defense of justice. The letter bears this inscription:

“To the most reverend lords and Fathers in Christ, archbishops, bishops, and other religious persons assembled in this place for the defense of justice: HUGH, called bishop of the Church of Grenoble, and his sons; GUIGO, the unworthy servant of the poor Carthusians, and the brothers who are with him: knowledge of what must be done, and courageous fulfillment of what is known, through Christ our Lord.”

We omit a transcription of that letter, since it is included in the Council of Jotrum. We shall speak of Blessed Thomas on 20 August; his *Life* and martyrdom, published by himself in the year 1665, were supplied to us by Philip Gourreau, prior of the aforesaid abbey.

4. At that time, when the Council of Jotrum was being held, Pope Innocent II was in Gaul. He sent letters to the archbishops of Reims, Rouen, and Tours, and to their suffragans, urging them to avenge the death of the aforesaid prior. This pontiff was thoroughly acquainted with the holy character and virtues of Guigo and the other Carthusians, as well as with their intimate spiritual bond with Saint Hugh. He enrolled Hugh, who had died piously and holily in the third year of his pontificate, in the catalogue of the saints in the fifth year of his pontificate, at the Council of Pisa in the year of Christ 1134, as he indicates in a letter written at Pisa on the tenth day before the Kalends of May to Guigo, prior of the Charterhouse. In that letter he commanded him to describe diligently the life and miracles of Saint Hugh.

Guigo fulfilled the first part of the apostolic command, recounting Saint Hugh’s deeds from his birth to his death. The second part, which was to encompass his brilliant miracles, he did not undertake—perhaps, as we think, prevented by illness and death, for he died in the year 1136, as we have said. “Guigo,” writes Peter Sutor (*Carthusian Life*, book II, treatise 5, chapter 7), “was from a castle in the diocese of Valence, born of distinguished parents, outstanding in intellect, retentive in memory, eloquent in speech, exceptionally effective in exhortation, remarkably learned in secular and divine letters, and no less venerable in conduct than in teaching. Having become the fifth prior of the Great Charterhouse after Saint Bruno, he far surpassed his predecessors in reputation and authority, and observed the rigor of the order to the letter.” So much for that.

We possess this Life in two ancient parchment manuscripts of excellent quality; after comparing it with the Surian edition, we have illustrated it with our annotations. Vincent of Beauvais, book XXII, chapter 8 of the *Speculum historiale*; Peter de Natalibus, book IV, chapter 22; Peter Dorlandus, book II, chapter 1 of the *Carthusian Chronicle*; Zacharias Lippelous; Franciscus Haraeus; and many other collectors of Lives of this kind published the same work in abridged form.

5. The name of Saint Hugh is entered in various sacred calendars, both handwritten and printed. Among these are Grevenus and Molanus in the *Auctarium* of Usuard; Maurolycus, Galesinius, and Canisius; and, among monastic writers, Wion, Menardus, and Dorganius. Bucelinus composed a lengthy encomium of him; Constantine Ghinius entered him among the feast days of the canons; and Saussay praises him extensively in the *Gallican Martyrology*. With all of these, he is thus celebrated in the *Roman Martyrology*:

> At Grenoble, Saint Hugh, bishop, who spent many years of his life in solitude and, renowned for the glory of his miracles, departed to the Lord.

# LETTER OF POPE INNOCENT II

[Col. 0761]

[Col. 0761A] Innocent, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Guigo, prior of the Carthusians: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Responding to divine benefits, having learned of his life and heard of the miracles performed through the merits of Blessed Hugh, we have jointly praised the clemency of the heavenly Majesty. After consulting with the archbishops, bishops, cardinals, and others who were present with us, we ordered that he be honored among the saints and the elect, and that the day of his assumption be solemnly celebrated with joy.

Since, therefore, the life which he piously led in the body, and the splendor of the miracles by which God causes him to shine forth brilliantly among men, [Note: [Col. 0761B] Guigo seems to have wished to describe the miracles in a separate treatise, since he does not touch on them in this Life; [Col. 0762B] but we have not yet found any trace of it.] are especially well known to your devotion, by the authority of Blessed Peter and our own we command you to commit carefully to the memory of posterity whatever you know concerning these matters. Thus God may be honored in His saint, and the clergy who read and the people who hear may give thanks to the Lord and, through Hugh’s intercession, merit to receive forgiveness of sins.

Praying for you, through you we greet and bless in the Lord our beloved sons, the Carthusian brothers.

Given at Pisa, on the tenth day before the Kalends of May.

[Note: [Col. 0762B] In the year 1134.]

# HERE BEGINS THE LIFE

[Col. 0761]

## PROLOGUE TO THE ROMAN PONTIFF

[Col. 0761B]

To the most beloved and most reverend lord and father, Innocent, pontiff of the Apostolic See, Guigo, useless servant of the poor Carthusians: perpetual salvation and peace in the Lord, and, if it has any power before God, the prayer of so great a sinner.

[Col. 0762B] 1. The commanding graciousness of your apostolic office did not spare either our modesty or our incompetence. For, as the letters of your serenity prefixed to this little work indicate, by the authority of Blessed Peter and your own you commanded us to commit to writing, for the knowledge of posterity, the life of Blessed Hugh, bishop of Grenoble.

Several others had indeed requested the same thing long before, [Col. 0763A] but especially Arialdus, whose authority could by no means be disregarded, and Hugh, bishops respectively of Maurienne and Grenoble.

[Note: [Col. 0763D] Arialdus, in our manuscripts Airaldus and Ailardus, elsewhere Ayrardus, formerly a monk and prior of the Charterhouse of Portes in the diocese of Lyon, became bishop in the year 1145 and died in 1167.]

[Note: [Col. 0763D] Hugh II, formerly a professed monk of the Great Charterhouse, bishop of Grenoble, and later, in 1153, made archbishop of Vienne.]

[Note: [Col. 0763D] Maurienne, commonly Saint-Jean-de-Maurienne, on the Arc River flowing down from Mount Cenis, in the Duchy of Savoy toward the east, eleven miles from Grenoble, although the route is interrupted by mountains.]

The former, regular in habit and life, had been the blessed man’s companion for nearly thirty years in the conduct of ecclesiastical affairs. The latter, formerly a monk among us, succeeded him in ecclesiastical government in such a way that, because of his prolonged and severe illness, he was consecrated in his place—at Hugh’s own request and by your gracious command—before Hugh himself died.

As for those whom, because of long familiarity or shared life, I could not keep in the dark, my incompetence or modesty—and perhaps, no less, the weakness of the flesh—could sufficiently excuse me. But before the weight of such authority, we did not dare even to murmur, lest by disobeying him to whom the whole world has been entrusted we offend Him by whom the world was made, and lest, while avoiding before men the disgrace of incompetence, we incur condemnation before God.

We beseech those who read these things not to measure the holiness of so great a Father by this writing—holiness far greater not only than our eloquence but even than our thought—and especially not to suppose that we have been able, by our words, to exalt him beyond what his merits require. For we are so far from having been able, as though favorably disposed, to magnify his holiness more than was fitting that, as we truthfully say, because of our incompetence and the poverty of our speech, we could not explain even the excellence of his holy conduct as fully as it deserved.

# CHAPTER ONE. SAINT HUGH’S PARENTS, STUDIES, AND CANONICATE

[Col. 0763C]

2. Since the character and deeds of that most holy Father, pleasing to God, provide such abundant material for speech that they surpass not only our eloquence but that of anyone, we would have considered his fleshly origin entirely unworthy of mention. Everyone knows that, through the inscrutable depth of divine judgment, the good are daily born from good, the wicked from wicked, the wicked from good, and the good from wicked indiscriminately. It matters little from what kind of parents a person is born, but rather with what kind of conduct he lives; and power, riches, and earthly nobility do not increase one’s merits by making one illustrious, but rather their rejection for Christ’s sake does. For we see both that the Lord was born of poor parents, [Col. 0763D] and that the more distinguished apostles were chosen from among fishermen.

Thus Blessed Paul, writing to the Corinthians, says:

> “Consider your calling, brothers: not many are wise according to the flesh, not many powerful, not many noble. But God chose what is foolish in the world to confound the wise; God chose what is weak in the world to confound the strong; God chose what is low-born and despised in the world, and things that are not, to bring to nothing the things that are, so that no flesh may glory in His presence” (I Cor. 1:26).

Yet since those who have written about the virtues of the saints are also found not to have kept silent about their earthly births, we too shall briefly say that Blessed Hugh, a native of Valence, had parents in a place situated beside the river Isère, called Châteauneuf, who were not lowly according to worldly rank and, more importantly, were distinguished by the excellence of holiness.

[Note: [Col. 0764D] Above Valence, the Isère flows into the Rhône; Châteauneuf, still called by that name today, lies beside it. Wion, in his notes on the Benedictine Martyrology, wrongly assigns this place to Spanish Valencia.]

His father, named Odilo, was, in addition to the many things he honorably did or possessed while wearing military dress, a lover of truth and chastity. Indeed, with the open-hearted affection of an upright mind, he avoided lies more carefully than many religious men. Although, after the death of his first wife, he soon took two wives, he nevertheless experienced no embraces except those of his wedded wives—something regarded in these times and in this corrupt age, especially among the powerful, as almost monstrous.

When he had grown old, at the urging of his most holy son, he despised the world with such fervor that, forgetting old age and refined habits, he did not hesitate to undertake the harsh paths which the Charterhouse keeps because of the word of God. There he lived for nearly eighteen years with such sobriety and such humility that he was dear to all who served God there and was regarded by everyone as most worthy of veneration.

When he was entering upon the way of all flesh—he was nearly a hundred years old—the venerable son was present. With his own hands he anointed him and filled him with holy Communion. After completing his father’s holy funeral with fitting veneration, he made the day of his death, as also that of his mother, memorable throughout his life by almsgiving and sacrifices.

3. His venerable mother, after her husband’s departure—for she had known no other man at all—wished likewise to abandon everything. Since monasteries for religious women were then rare, she spent the remainder of her life in her own home, instructed by her pious son in salutary counsels, in continence and almsgiving, prayers and fasts, and other holy works. She also restrained, as far as she could, her sons, brave in military exploits, from immoderate excesses.

When she lay ill with the sickness of which she died, her longed-for son came to her. He administered the holy mysteries; not long afterward he fulfilled the final duties of burial, readily rendering obedient service to God’s command in the Mosaic Law:

> “Honor your father and your mother, so that you may live long upon the earth” (Exod. 20:12).

Of this earth the Psalmist is believed to say to the Lord:

> “You are my hope, my portion in the land of the living” (Ps. 141:6).

She used to say that, while she was carrying him in her womb, she had seen in a dream that she had given birth to a beautiful child. The saints—including Blessed Peter—were carrying him into heaven to be presented before God. Because of this, and with her support, he was directed toward the study of letters; for it was hoped—and not without reason—that he would become singularly favored and meritorious before God.

4. He loved literary studies greatly; for their sake he even traveled to foreign regions and endured much. He possessed a modest sobriety which remained with him until extreme old age. It often forced him, even among his own people, to endure deprivation of necessities, since, overcome by shame, he could not confess to his friends if something troubled him. By this restraint, as by a bridle, he was held back from many unlawful things.

When he returned from the schools and stayed at Valence—where, although still young, he was a canon of the principal church—among secular and dissolute people, he remained modest and sober. For, as he himself said, he had resolved from that time onward, with God’s help, to preserve himself free from every contamination.

It happened that Hugh, papal legate throughout Gaul by command of blessed memory Pope Gregory VII, came to that same city: a man vigorous and renowned in ecclesiastical affairs, then bishop of Die, [Col. 0765B] later archbishop of Lyon.

[Note: [Col. 0765D] Hugh was made bishop of Die in 1073 and transferred to the archbishopric of Lyon in 1092. The city lies in the middle of the Dauphiné, [Col. 0766D] a day’s journey from Valence.]

Seeing a young man handsome in face, tall in stature, measured in speech, and modest in conduct—and having learned from those who knew him of his learning and lineage, and recognizing in him, since he was keen-minded in both human and divine matters, certain great signs of future goodness and holiness—he embraced him cheerfully and affably, asking him to come to him as a companion and participant in his struggles.

With the help of only a few men, he was laboring with great zeal not only against laymen who sacrilegiously retained churches, tithes, and cemeteries, but also against priests whose lives were stained by dishonorable marriages, and against simoniacs who, blinded by greed, mixed sacred and profane things together.

Hugh gladly accepted this invitation.

# CHAPTER TWO. ASSUMPTION OF THE BISHOPRIC OF GRENOBLE

5. Some time afterward, the same legate held a great council at Avignon, a distinguished city of Provence.

[Note: [Col. 0766D] In the year 1080. At that council, after Achard was deposed, Gibilinus was made archbishop of Arles.]

At this council he accomplished many things worthy of praise, for the honor of God and the benefit of the Church. The canons of Grenoble, lacking a bishop and seeking one, came to the council. When they learned that the aforesaid young man was present at the assembly, they humbly petitioned his venerable patron, in whose service he joyfully shared, with the council’s support, to give him to them as bishop without delay.

The patron immediately and gladly consented, rejoicing in the honor of his beloved companion and favoring the advancement of the Church, whose sacred offices he did not doubt the young man would serve advantageously.

But Hugh, shaken by sudden fear from the depths of his being, began to resist with his whole body, crying out loudly and affirming that he was unequal to such mysteries in age, knowledge, and finally in character and life. He could not in any way endure that, to the peril of his salvation, his unworthiness should defile venerable offices.

He never abandoned this judgment about himself, formed in the deepest humility. For throughout every increase in holiness and good works, he was never ashamed to declare himself an unprofitable servant and unworthy of administering the episcopate, and he was always ready to resign it, as what follows will make clear.

The man of profound counsel who had granted him to the aforesaid clergy, although pleased that at such an age and in such a condition—for he was still a layman and about twenty-seven years old—he not only did not seek undeserved honors but rejected those offered to him, nevertheless began, with the reasonable eloquence in which he excelled, to raise his courage, comfort his modesty, and break down his stubborn resistance.

He maintained that, in burdens of this kind, whether undertaken or borne, no one ought to rely on his own virtue but rather on God’s goodness. From God he ought to hope for the good he lacked, and to refer to Him whatever he had received.

At last, overcome by the consolations and exhortations of this man and the other serious men present, he yielded to the election.

[Col. 0766C] 6. At that time the Church of Vienne was governed by an archbishop named Garmundus.

[Note: [Col. 0766D] Called Guarmandus by others; he held the see from 1077 to 1083.]

Because he was under the disgrace of simony, Hugh did not permit him to lay hands upon him. Thus, after receiving all the orders except the episcopate from the legate—who deserves to be remembered with reverence—he set out in the legate’s company to be consecrated by the supreme pontiff of the Apostolic See.

While he was staying there awaiting the appointed day of consecration, at the very beginnings, as it were, of divine service and in the first training of the sacred warfare, inexperienced and unaccustomed to such matters, he encountered the gravest assault of the ancient enemy. This assault did not cease to torment his holy soul, sometimes more fiercely and sometimes more gently, day and night, until the illness in which he later lay dying.

Because, through the distinguished merits of his holy conduct and illustrious works, he was destined to have great fame and glory among God’s people, he received, lest he should perhaps be exalted, an angel of Satan to buffet him, as did the blessed Apostle who said that such an angel had been given him (II Cor. 12:7).

Likewise, in the prophet Zechariah, Satan stood at the right hand of Jesus the high priest, who prefigured the mystery of the true Savior, to oppose him (Zech. 3:5).

Nor is this surprising, since Satan had dared, in wicked presumption, to tempt God, clothed in human flesh, the Creator and ruler of all things. Finally, after showing Him all the kingdoms of the world with their glory, he attempted to persuade Him even to the crime of idolatry, saying:

> “All these things I will give you, if you will fall down and worship me” (Matt. 4:9).

Thus, just as he had suggested idolatry to the Lord with incredible presumption, so by a viper’s cunning he suggested blasphemy to the Lord’s servant: namely, that he should think something unworthy about God or about the things belonging to God. But just as he had been defeated and confounded by the Lord, so, with the Lord’s help, he departed defeated and confounded by His servant.

7. When, as we have said, Hugh had experienced the unexpected assault of the ancient enemy, he considered whether the Lord might have been angered against him because he had yielded, even unwillingly, to those who elected him. He therefore resolved by every means to renounce the election made in his favor and to avoid entirely the sacred offices to which he felt himself increasingly unworthy to be assigned.

He hastened to disclose this decision, which he considered most salutary, to the man who had brought him there, pouring out tears and sighs from the depths of his heart together with the temptation itself.

The latter, having partly calmed his weakness and excessive fear—although the fear arose from religion—with a reasonable reply, urged him to go to the pope and reveal everything that troubled his mind to him as Christ’s vicar.

When Hugh had done this humbly and devoutly, he was so filled by the nourishment of consolation from the pope’s mouth and experienced such an outpouring of affection toward him that he was compelled to rejoice over the very temptation which had nearly driven him to despair and to take from it material for an even more confident hope.

For the blessed pope, experienced and not ignorant in such matters, taught him that the Lord reproves and chastens those whom He loves and scourges every son whom He receives (Heb. 12:6). Therefore, the more harshly He had laid the scourge upon Hugh’s heart, the more clearly He had given him a sign of fatherly love.

The pope also taught that the devil had already foreseen how many losses he himself would suffer through Hugh and how much growth in virtue God’s people would receive through him. For this reason, with God’s permission, the devil had employed every effort of his ancient malignity to deter Hugh in any way from the sacred offices—to the devil’s own disgrace and punishment, but to Hugh’s crown and glory.

8. Strengthened by these words, full of truth and supported by authority, though the temptation was not completely extinguished, Hugh became more even-tempered through the consolation he had received and shortly afterward accepted episcopal consecration from the same pontiff.

Both at the consecration itself and throughout the entire time he remained there, the love of that great man for him was shown so strongly that it plainly appeared that he had perceived in Hugh some great sign of present divine grace.

The countess Matilda also—of feminine appearance but entirely manly courage, who knew wisely to calm and bravely to endure the tumult and dangers of human affairs, like the prophetess Deborah—venerated God in His servant and supplied everything necessary for the day of his consecration.

[Note: [Col. 0767D] Franciscus Maria Florentinius collected and published her acts in Italian. Much is said about her in the Life of Saint Anselm, bishop of Lucca, published by us under 18 March, especially chapter 2.]

She gave him the pastoral staff which he used for a long time, together with explanations of the Psalms according to Saint Augustine and Saint Ambrose’s volume entitled *On Duties*. Throughout the remainder of his life she honored and cherished him with sincere devotion as a true servant of God, eagerly thirsting to be instructed by his counsel and defended by his prayer.

9. After these matters had been accomplished not only successfully but religiously, Hugh returned to the Church entrusted to him. He found the clergy and people exceedingly inexperienced and disorderly in divine matters, and so ignorant of holy observances that not only clerics of the lower orders but also [Col. 0768B] priests took wives and publicly celebrated marriages; they did not hesitate to buy and sell sacred things; laymen possessed churches, offerings, tithes, and cemeteries, while priests were subject to their authority; and usurers or lenders at interest accumulated unjust profits from the losses of others. Nevertheless, some of these people still entered churches and received the sacred mysteries.

Everyone was so entirely lacking in discipline.

Moreover, the substance of the episcopal household had almost entirely been consumed, not so much by bishops as by the tyrants who had preceded him. As a result, for many years Hugh endured great deprivation even of necessary food, since he did not wish to supply his needs through unlawful contracts, as many do, and did not dare to borrow, thinking that he had nothing with which to repay.

But with what vigilance and by what scourges of preaching and discipline he pursued the vices and sins of the people entrusted to him; what labors, journeys, and anxieties he undertook there; what fasts, vigils, psalmody, groans, prayers, and showers of tears he poured out for them, in fatherly compassion, to appease the Lord on their behalf—it is beyond our power to recount.

Nor can it, or need it, be expressed in our words what fruit came from such great labors, since the evident transformation of all things for the better plainly places it before the eyes of those who witnessed it.

# CHAPTER THREE. A YEAR AS A CLUNIAC MONK; FREQUENT ASSOCIATION IN THE CHARTERHOUSE WITH SAINT BRUNO AND OTHERS; THE GIFT OF TEARS AMID AFFLICTIONS

[Col. 0768D]

10. Meanwhile, Hugh diligently imitated the winged living creatures in Ezekiel, which always moved forward with their faces before them. He never ceased to set himself before his own eyes and examine with subtle scrutiny either his dangers or his progress.

Considering his age, the imperfection of his conduct—for he himself kept the eyes of his mind fixed upon this especially until death and persuaded others to do the same—and the burden of the office he had undertaken, before two years had elapsed after his consecration, [Col. 0769A] he abandoned everything and became a monk of Casa-Dei, of the Cluniac order.

[Note: [Col. 0769D] Casa-Dei monastery in Auvergne, founded by Saint Robert, its first abbot, who died on 24 April 1058; more is said about that monastery in his Acts. Wion wrongly calls Saint Hugh abbot of Casles.]

There, at that time, a greater devotion to poverty and humility seemed to flourish. Inflamed by the examples of the holy men who were numerous there, and himself no less inflaming them, although a novice, he remained for a year. He became beloved by all for his many virtues, but especially for humility, whose tireless practitioner he was above all virtues.

He conducted himself in such a way that he was worthy both of everyone’s imitation and of everyone’s veneration.

After this, compelled by Gregory VII, the aforesaid pontiff of the Apostolic See who had consecrated him, he returned from the monastery—into which he had entered fervently—to the episcopate even more fervent than before. From the practices of a single year he brought back such growth in virtue as many scarcely attain through the labors of a long life.

In place of a cloister he had vigilant watchfulness, by which he restrained not only the senses of his body but also the thoughts of his heart; in place of an abbot, justice, from whose commands neither prosperity nor adversity could ever draw him away; and in place of a community, religious people, whom he never wished to lack because of the saying:

> “With the holy you will be holy, and with the innocent man you will be innocent” (II Kings 22:26).

Indeed, he regarded the whole universal Church as his community. He embraced it with such sincere affection that he could not bear its adversities or prosperities with an unmoved heart. In accordance with the Apostle’s words, “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I am not inflamed?” (II Cor. 11:29), he always rejoiced in the Church’s prosperity and was tormented by its adversity.

[Col. 0769C] 11. He was living in this way when, before three years had yet been completed after his return from the monastery, Master Bruno arrived: a man renowned for religion and learning, almost a living image of honesty, seriousness, and complete maturity.

[Note: [Col. 0769D] These matters are related more fully in the Life of Saint Bruno, under 6 October, where this passage deserves notice for its sincerity and antiquity. In book I, chapter 5, of the *Speculum Carthusiae*, it is said that “Saint Hugh is believed to have been Master Bruno’s companion at the schools.”]

His companions were Master Landuin, who later became prior of the Charterhouse after him; two Stephens, one from Bourges and one from Die—both had been canons of Saint Rufus but, with the abbot’s approval, had joined him out of a desire for solitary life; Hugh, whom they called the Chaplain because he alone among them exercised the priestly office; and two laymen, whom we call Conversi, Andrew and Guarinus.

[Note: [Col. 0770D] At that time the monastery of Saint Rufus stood beside the walls of Avignon; later it was devastated by the Albigensians and subsequently transferred to Valence.]

They were seeking a place suitable for the eremitical life, but had not yet found one. Drawn both by this hope and by the sweet fragrance of his holy way of life, they came to the holy man.

He received them, treated them, and enabled them to attain their desire, not only gladly but reverently. With his counsel, help, and companionship, they entered the solitude of the Charterhouse and built it.

At about that time, Hugh had seen in a dream God constructing a dwelling-place for His own gracious presence in that same solitude, with seven stars also providing him guidance on the journey. There were indeed seven of them. For this reason he gladly embraced the counsels not only of these men but also of their successors, and until his death he continually supported the inhabitants of the Charterhouse with counsel and benefactions.

12. Although he had previously burned wholly with the fires of divine love, he was inflamed by their example and companionship for the exercises of heavenly discipline no differently than if someone were to place several other burning torches around one already aflame.

He lived among them not as a lord or bishop but as a most humble companion and brother, ready, as far as he could, to serve everyone. Thus the venerable William, then prior of Saint Lawrence and later abbot of Saint Theofredus, himself bound by considerable religious devotion to Master Bruno, and Hugh’s cellmate—for at that time two lived in each cell with Master Bruno—would complain rather bitterly that Hugh took from him almost every duty belonging to humility within the cell.

[Note: [Col. 0770D] The monastery of Saint Theofredus, built by Saint Calminius, duke of the Auvergnats, lies six leagues from Le Puy, in whose diocese it is situated. Saint Calminius is honored on 19 August and Saint Theofredus on 18 August.]

William complained that the bishop did not associate with him, at least as a companion, but rather as a servant, and sadly asserted that he was not permitted to perform any of the menial tasks which, according to custom, they ought to carry out by turns, because Hugh took them all away from him.

Hugh was so devoted and diligent in living in the hermitage that Master Bruno sometimes compelled him to leave:

> “Go,” he would say, “go to your sheep, and render them what you owe them.”

At that time, inflamed by great zeal for poverty and humility, Hugh wished to sell all his horses and, distributing the proceeds to the poor, travel about on foot preaching.

But Master Bruno, a man of profound understanding, whose counsel Hugh obeyed no differently from commands, did not consent. He feared that Hugh might perhaps become proud in his own eyes, or be judged by the other bishops as a singular eccentric, or—as was beyond doubt—be unable to complete the undertaking because of the roughness and unevenness of the roads.

13. As he pursued spiritual things with ever greater zeal and despised carnal things, it happened that, through excessive vigils, fasts, readings, prayers, meditations, and other sacred exercises, he fell into a very serious illness of the head and stomach. From the discomforts and torments of this illness, more frequent and more severe than anyone could believe, he was never free for at least forty years, as long as he lived.

Thus another was added to the angel of Satan mentioned above, by whom he was buffeted so repeatedly that he might not become exalted.

How greatly he grew, purified and refined by these two afflictions—temptation and illness—as gold in a furnace—in devotion to God and in true compassion for all the afflicted, he himself, even while alive, could not fully express, even had he wished to do so.

For the more he was afflicted by these things, the more vehemently, rejecting what belongs to the world, he turned wholly toward God, his true and only refuge. From this he drew, as he used to say, a pleasure all the fuller and sweeter the harsher the anguish he had suffered, according to the Psalm:

> “According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, Your consolations have gladdened my soul” (Ps. 93:19).

Such alternations continued in him until the end.

[Note: [Col. 0771D] *Alteritas* means alternation or change. Saint Augustine, *On Music*, book VI: “When things are applied which affect the body with a certain alternation, so to speak.”]

Sometimes, with the eyes of his spirit raised with all their strength toward heavenly things, tasting and seeing that the Lord is sweet, he was refreshed by ineffable joys. At other times, weighed down by human weakness, he fell back into his usual state and was not free from his former anxieties.

In both states there were tears: there, tears of joy; here, tears of weariness.

What more is there to say? His tears had become his bread day and night. Prosperity did not dry them, nor adversity. He could scarcely read, scarcely sing psalms, scarcely meditate on divine things without them.

The grace of tears had grown in him to such an extent that often they did not leave him even while he was eating, unless he restrained them. Many times, especially during several years near the end of his life, they either interrupted or darkened the meal he shared with himself and his companions.

14. He had a reader who read to him at table, both elsewhere and especially there, from the sacred books—of which he had had quite a few copied—so that he might nourish himself and his companions with a double delight.

Whenever the reader encountered something remarkable concerning divine severity or mercy, Hugh compelled him to repeat it two or three times. No sooner had he tasted the spiritual pleasure offered by Scripture than, shaken from the depths of his being, he was flooded with such torrents of tears that they completely removed from him the pleasure of eating and drinking and moderated it among his companions.

Thus, having learned by experience what happened, his companions, when they saw such movements approaching, signaled to the reader to yield and stop reading for a while, so that they could temporarily avert this kind of difficulty.
