Sinners who came to him for confession felt this grace of divine favor especially strongly. He received them kindly and humbly and listened to them with the greatest patience: sometimes weeping himself with those who wept, and sometimes stirring them to tears by his own weeping. One example will make this sufficiently clear.

Gauterius, surnamed Calnesius, beloved by God, who lived and died among us after a long and praiseworthy monastic life, used to relate that, when he was still in the world and confessed his offenses to Hugh—for he was distinguished in learning and honor in the Church of Grenoble—Hugh leaned over his head and poured such an abundance of tears upon his crown that, once his hair was soaked, little streams ran downward even over the face of the penitent.

[Note: [Col. 0772D] Others call him Galterius and Gualterius.]

He received women’s confessions no less cautiously than kindly. He was not accustomed to hear them in corners or obscure or secret places, but rather where he could be seen by many. He applied his ear quite familiarly, but turned his eyes in the other direction, asserting that, because of the devil’s snares, only the hearing should be applied to such matters.

# CHAPTER FOUR. THE HOLY CUSTODY OF THE EYES, THE OTHER SENSES, AND THE TONGUE
15. He always maintained the aforesaid vigilance over his eyes, everywhere and with incredible circumspection. Thus, when powerful and noble women, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying, “Honor to whom honor is due” (Romans 13:7), frequently came to converse with him, and he received them honorably and cheerfully, he would remain for a long time discussing many matters with them without seeing their faces at all. For he said that illicit thoughts could scarcely be avoided unless one restrained the bodily senses with great vigilance; and that, according to the Prophet, through these senses as through windows death enters and comes into our houses (Jeremiah 9:21).

On one occasion, while he was conversing with certain religious men—including a man distinguished for learning and purity, namely Lord Airaldus, then his own archpriest and now bishop of Maurienne—the same Lord Airaldus replied that he looked freely at women and that their gaze did him no harm, for he was exceedingly chaste. To this he answered that the gaze of a religious mind ought to be turned away not only from women’s faces but from men’s as well. He maintained—and anyone may infer this from his own experience—that through the fellowship of human mutability and through compassion, the emotions of the person seen frequently pass over to the one seeing with immeasurable speed: thus, for example, a person becomes angry from looking at an angry person, sad from looking at a sad person, and licentious from looking at a licentious person. It is enough, he said, for anyone to possess his own passions, without copying alien ones into himself in this way.

He added that throughout his entire episcopate he had looked upon the face of only one woman in such a way that, if she encountered him again, he could recognize who she was from the consideration of her features. What could be chaster than this response? What more circumspect? What more filled with true philosophy? To have shown himself toward women in this manner was supremely chaste; to have noticed such things in human emotions was supremely wise.

Hence came the following incident. When I asked him about my mother—who had spoken with him about whatever she wished, for as long as she wished—whether extreme old age had greatly broken her, he reflected briefly and said, “I do not know whether she is old or not.”

Hence also came this other incident. A certain woman, distinguished by power and nobility, whose name we do not wish to disclose, was speaking at considerable length in his presence, as she pleased. When he too had answered as he wished and she had departed, his companions—whom he always took care to have as prudent and religious men—asked why he had not rebuked her for adorning herself and her face so cleverly and so wantonly. He replied, with a certain horror and detestation, that he had not seen her face at all.

[Col. 0773A] Is it not remarkable that he had not seen the face of that one woman, when he knew the face of no woman? Where now is the inquisitive wantonness of priests, and the wanton inquisitiveness of so many who wear the sacred habit? Let them attend to these things and imitate them, if they can; let them marvel and reverence them, if they cannot.

But those who consider holiness worthless without miracles—miracles which we do not greatly value for the reason that we know both the elect and the reprobate to possess them in common, while among the greater patriarchs and many other saints who greatly pleased God we find either none or few—those who nevertheless seek miracles should consider again and again whether anything more miraculous ought to be demanded of a human being enclosed in mortal flesh; and whether it could seem anything but impossible for any man to govern a great bishopric for fifty years and more, while knowing the face of no woman whatsoever except one.

And in truth this woman herself was not particularly beautiful, but she was very much in need of his counsel. Nevertheless, people came to his presence not only from his own diocese but also from other bishoprics, whether for confession or for innumerable other reasons, with a devotion and frequency proportionate to their recognition of his holiness.

16. He restrained not only this sense—that is, sight—but all the others with similar care. He curbed his ears and tongue, not merely from other unlawful things but especially from detraction. He used to say that each person’s own sins were sufficient, and that there was no need to contaminate one’s conscience by listening to the sins of others or to pollute one’s tongue by speaking of them. He neither inquired into rumors nor readily repeated them.

How can we prove more certainly than by the testimony of an enemy that he was truthful in his speech? Count Guigo—an adequately capable man in worldly affairs, yet during a period of peace very devoted to this same servant of God, against whom he had vigorously resisted in the cause of justice—inflicted many and considerable troubles upon him. To say nothing of much else, he was twice excommunicated by him for his offenses and twice expelled him from the episcopal residences.

Thus, when a major dispute arose between them in the presence of Guido, archbishop of Vienne—who later became Pope Calixtus [Note: Guido, of the most noble family of the counts of Burgundy, was made archbishop in 1083, then apostolic legate, and was elected pope in 1119 under the name Calixtus II; he died in 1124.]—and the man of God, in accordance with what is written, “The righteous is as confident as a lion and shall be without fear” (Proverbs 28:1), was defending justice against the count with open opposition, the latter, angered and inflamed with the fires of rage, and prepared, as it appeared, to bring forward whatever accusation he could, introduced the following as though it were a serious crime:

“I once heard you say something that was not true.”

Then the holy bishop asked, in the presence of all who were there—and there were many people of various ranks—whether he had ever heard him knowingly tell a lie. Although the count was angry and filled with fury, he was nevertheless weighed down by the force of truth, and replied that he had never heard him knowingly tell a lie.

For the truthfulness of the bishop’s speech, then, let this one testimony from an enemy in anger suffice.

[Note: Count Guigo. At this time there flourished Guigo Crassus, son of the elder Guigo, who was also Count of Albon, and Guigo, Count of Forez; Nicolas Chorier discusses them in Book II of *Delphinatus*, p. 797. But which Guigo, the count, is here designated by antonomasia (ἀντονομαστικῶς), let others decide.]

17. Although we may perhaps be accused of digression, since the truth of the holy man was made evident through the count, let his charity likewise be shown through the same man.

As has been said, the count was extremely hostile to him, so much so that the holy man lived either with us or at Lyon rather than in his own residences. For the Church of that city always showed him great reverence and great assistance in his troubles, and considered it a pleasure to make use of his counsel in more serious matters.

One day, then, when we were speaking together about the count, he said that he entertained good hope for the man’s salvation and did not despair of his attaining the mercy of God, because he had never been accustomed to pray for anyone more pleasurably or more fervently than for him.

Wonderful charity—and no less astonishing humility! What could be fuller of charity, or more singular among men, than to pray no less earnestly for one’s persecutor than for one’s benefactor? And what could be humbler than to attribute this very devotion not to his own merits but to those of the other—not to merits he already knew to exist, but to those he hoped would come to exist?

Since it is therefore certain that he fulfilled the commandment which says, “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you” (Matthew 5:44), there can be no doubt that he also attained the reward which follows: “So that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and sends rain upon the just and the unjust” (ibid., 45).

No reward, surely, is more blessed, just as no commandment is more sublime. Let those who are not lacking the eyes of the heart approach, so that they may see what merit belongs to one who fulfilled such a commandment and obtained so great a reward.

18. It would be superfluous to speak of his sense of touch or of smell. He cultivated the latter only so far as not to admit foul odors that might aggravate the disorders of the brain; as for the former, namely touch, he had entirely renounced it even before he was ordained.

He did not restrain himself and his senses from looking upon women with such discipline because he felt himself weak with regard to lust—for the temptations and afflictions of the weakness already mentioned, the many cares of ecclesiastical administration, and especially his constant devotion to reading, singing psalms, praying, meditating, and contemplating divine things had rendered him almost insensible to such pleasures—but in order to preserve the maturity and severity appropriate to his habit and office, and to offer the weaker, against the snares of the aged enemy, examples of circumspection for them to follow.

He taught that no one ought to presume upon any degree of purity or strength, since, as Job testifies, a human being does not remain in the same condition (Job 14:2), and since the adversary, prowling about like a roaring lion, continually seeks someone to devour (1 Peter 5:8). He placed David and Solomon before their eyes: because they had conducted themselves too freely toward women, the one fell from the height of innocence into adultery and murder, while the other, from the wisdom by which he had surpassed all mortals, descended into such folly that he became enslaved to idols.

How greatly the blessed man repressed the desires of the belly and throat is proved more certainly by the facts themselves, without our saying anything. For the headaches and stomach disorders produced especially by these disciplines show clearly—indeed, more than clearly—that he abstained from such delicacies.

## CHAPTER V. Almsgiving; contempt for gifts; the removal of disputes; preaching; the defense of the authority of the supreme pontiffs.

19. He was himself a diligent practitioner of almsgiving and also an ardent exhorter of others to it. Except for the necessities of his own household, he stored up almost nothing of what he was able to acquire in treasuries to be squandered by his descendants in lawsuits or consumed in luxury. Rather, remembering the Apostle’s saying, “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7), he gladly distributed it to the needy.

Indeed, during a time of great famine, when the granaries threatened to fail, he sold gold and jeweled rings, as well as a similarly gold cup, and spent the proceeds on feeding the poor.

Powerful and noble people also greatly assisted this grace in him. Having perceived the fragrance of his holy way of life, which spread far and wide with beneficial and pleasing effect, they sent him many gifts from distant regions, although they had never seen him, out of reverence for God.

Far from his table—and even from his entire courtyard—he kept actors, as vessels of destruction and instruments of falsehood; far away also military retainers, as instruments of robbery, slaughter, and every kind of cruelty; and even knights, except for a few, and those only rarely, and only in view of some very particular benefit.

[Note: In another of our manuscripts, *spiritualis* is read instead of *specialis*, and this reading has also been written in the margin of Surius.]

For he did not consider it right that the goods of churches, which ought to be regarded as the patrimony of the poor, should be spent for the uses of other people—especially bad people. Indeed, he accused himself severely, as though he were one of the poor, because he took for himself and his companions an adequate supply from the resources entrusted to him, rather than enduring poverty with the poor and becoming poor himself.

Thus, as we have said, he gladly gave alms, diligently recommended them, and imposed them upon penitents as a satisfaction. For these three things above all he prescribed to those who wished to amend their sins: prayer, fasting, and almsgiving. In doing so he followed not human rashness but evangelical authority.

For the Lord says that the worst kind of demon cannot be driven out except through prayer and fasting (Mark 9:28). Elsewhere, speaking to the Pharisees, he says: “Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you” (Luke 11:41).

20. If we wished to write about the moderation with which he was accustomed to distribute these very things according to persons, strength, inclinations, and resources, and about how wisely and soberly he distributed his possessions for the needs of his household, his spiritual and bodily companions, and also for the relief of the poor, it would provide the clearest evidence not only of his holiness but also of his prudence. But we must avoid wearying the reader.

Certainly, how can we pass over, even if we touch upon it only briefly, the fact that although he very frequently heard, discussed, and settled the worldly and ecclesiastical cases of his own people and of others, and although, throughout so long a period of life, he repeatedly performed consecrations, degradations, and reconciliations among the clergy subject to him, according to the appropriate causes and needs of persons and churches, nevertheless, in accordance with the prophetic proclamation, he shook his hands free from every gift (Isaiah 33:15)?

In his judgment, neither the dignity of a person nor the amount of money ever benefited anyone; poverty benefited no one, nor did any extreme lowliness of office, birth, or worldly condition harm anyone. A friend did not find him more lenient, nor an enemy harsher. He imposed no monetary penance upon the convicted or confessing, and he neither defended nor pronounced a profit-making sentence in lawsuits. He did not regard the person of the poor, nor honor the face of the powerful.

This makes the merit of the blessed man all the more illustrious, since it has so rarely had an example either in the present or in the past.

How much material this passage would offer us, if we wished to praise good things by comparison with evil, for attacking the filth of the present age! In it, with the disgrace and overthrow of honesty and justice, money enters temples, stains altars, sells priestly offices, drives out innocence, and contaminates everything divine and profane. Gifts now blind the eyes of the wise and overturn the words of the just. Everyone loves gifts and pursues rewards; from the least to the greatest, all are devoted to greed; from prophet to priest, all practice deceit. Usury and fraud do not cease from our streets; finally, greed stands at the head of all things, and everything obeys money.

But enough of this; we have not undertaken this work for such matters.

21. Let us therefore turn our words to the man of God, who had learned, under the instruction of piety, to tolerate—not to love—the contentious causes of temporal affairs for the love of eternal things.

For he used to say that lawsuits were more troublesome to him than every fever, and that he would renounce them in every way if he did not know that by doing so he would offend God. He involved himself in them only for the sake of peace, especially for the sake of the poor and the churches; for he knew that these suffered more grievously from the movements of wars.

But whenever he found in some people implacable hatreds and irreconcilable anger, then, trusting most firmly in God’s help and wholly released into an attitude of charity and humility, he pleaded most urgently and devoutly with those who had been offended, on behalf of those who had given offense.

How many times, as though blinded by his desire for human salvation, did he throw himself into muddy places for such causes! How many times did he lie prostrate for a long time at the feet even of contemptible persons!

He was not easily—indeed, scarcely ever—frustrated in his wishes. For even when some had refused, they later offered, repentant and making satisfaction, not merely freely but without being asked, what they had denied when he had pleaded.

Every class of people showed him such reverence that anyone who denied him what he requested believed that he had gravely offended God.

22. He was also an outstanding preacher, for he was by no means unlearned. He was well endowed with intelligence and memory, insofar as his head pain did not dull them; indeed, he dictated his own letters, especially those about which he was more deeply concerned.

He persuaded more easily in preaching because he displayed through his deeds what he said in words. In order to instruct the people entrusted to him more effectively, he anticipated his speech by his actions, just as it is written of the Lord: “Jesus began both to do and to teach” (Acts 1:1).

He therefore instructed people toward confession and stirred them to repentance by displaying the divine clemency, which was ready to forgive. He did not seek to be praised by the learned as a wise man, but rather sought what his hearers would understand better and retain more usefully.

Indeed, his preaching sometimes moved his hearers so deeply that certain people publicly confessed even capital crimes, fearing God more than human beings. The following example will make this clear.

At the fortress of Vinnaicum, when a large crowd had gathered for the dedication of a church, he delivered a sermon that dissolved the hearts of his listeners into many tears.

[Note: The fortress of Vinnaicum, commonly called Vinay, lies six Roman miles from the monastery of Antonianum. Another manuscript reads *Insuaicum*, while Surius adds *Jusnaicum*.]

There two women who, as became evident, had taken his words more deeply into the ear of their hearts, confessed before many hearers the crimes they had committed. We do not know with sufficient certainty what the second woman said; the first, however, disclosed that she had killed her husband.

When the man of God asked how she had killed him, she replied that she had given him poison in his food. After this, he ordered those present to withdraw, so that the others could more freely reveal whatever they wished to him.

Such was the eagerness of the rest of the people to confess that the endurance of the priest could not listen to even half of them, although they were exceedingly devoted to this task.

We heard this from the reverend man William, distinguished by age and holiness, now abbot of Saint Theofredus and then a monk, who had been the inseparable companion of the blessed man for more than twenty years.

23. But when will we be able to commit all his virtues to memory, even by touching upon them briefly? Divine grace had gathered together in that one man so many adornments of virtue that, if distributed among individuals, they would have been enough to make many people illustrious and renowned.

If chastity is praised, who was purer than he? If truthfulness in speech, who was more cautious in speaking? If love of God, who was more fervent? If love of neighbor, who was kinder? If humility, who was more abased? If almsgiving, who was more generous? If prayer, who was more devout? If the grace of tears, in whom was it more abundant? If contemplation, in whom was it more sublime? If endurance, who was stronger in tribulation? If justice, who was stricter? If prudence, who was more circumspect? If temperance, who was more moderate?

Yet although he was such and so great, he nevertheless, in accordance with the Gospel saying, “When you have done everything, say: We are unprofitable servants” (Luke 17:10), never ceased to accuse himself as fruitless and useless: he occupied the position of bishop, received the honor of a bishop, consumed episcopal goods, but possessed neither the merits nor the fruits of a bishop.

Certainly, there were things at hand that could not merely have brought solace to his mind but, unless it had been so firmly grounded, could also have lifted it into pride. To say nothing of the benefits that had come through him to clergy and people alike, the desert of Chartreuse, the abbey of Cales, the desert of Excubiae, and the houses of regular canons at Miserenum and Saint George had begun through his efforts and had advanced through his spiritual and bodily support.

But he thought only of his imperfection, from which even the Apostle was not free, saying, “Not that I have already received it or am already perfect” (Philippians 3:12). And, together with the Psalmist’s words, “That I may know what is lacking in me” (Psalm 38:5), he considered with extremely careful examination not what virtue he possessed but what he lacked. In every way he desired to cast off the episcopal burden. As we said at the beginning, he never lacked this conviction or desire from the beginning of his promotion until his death.

24. As this desire increased day by day, he sent envoys and letters to Rome for this very purpose, to Pope Honorius of venerable memory.

[Note: Honorius II succeeded Pope Calixtus II in the year 1124, on 14 December, and died in February 1130.]

But when the envoys failed to obtain what he requested and instead received from the pope letters of consolation and exhortation to persevere, he himself, although burdened by illness and old age, nevertheless strengthened by the hope of future rest, took care to visit the Roman pontiff. He humbly begged and implored that his old age be granted permission to rest and that a better shepherd be appointed in his place for the Church of Grenoble.

But even he was unable to obtain permission to devote himself solely to himself and to God, although he presented, as he thought, many just reasons both of body and of mind.

[Col. 0778D] It was believed that, through the sole authority and example of his holy way of life, he could benefit the people subject to him more, even though weak and sick, than anyone else, however strong and healthy.

Thus, after granting the other things he requested, and after honoring and consoling him as best he could, the supreme pontiff sent him back home. Nevertheless, he did not lay aside the desire, conceived long before, to relinquish the episcopate.

25. After Honorius died, Innocent II succeeded him in the month and year already mentioned.

[Note: Innocent II succeeded him in the month and year already mentioned.]

Then, when Peter of Leon [Note: Peter Leonis, a Roman, was made cardinal in 1120 and became the antipope called Anacletus II. We discussed him on 10 February in the Life of St William the Hermit, in connection with William, the last duke of Aquitaine, whom St Bernard brought back from this schism to obedience to Innocent II.], supported not by his own merits but by the assistance of his relatives and brothers, had risen up through tyrannical and schismatic madness against your innocence, which had succeeded the blessed Honorius—and when the man of God had learned this with complete certainty—although, as we have said, he was worn out by illness and age, nevertheless, through zeal for the house of God, whose beauty he loved, he went to Anicium so that, together with the other bishops, he might excommunicate that schismatic.

[Note: Anicium, or Le Puy of Blessed Mary in Auvergne, where Gerard, bishop of Angoulême, was deposed.]

That excommunication, owing to the authority of so great a man, contributed greatly both to the advancement of the Catholics and to the harm of the schismatics.

Certainly, both Peter himself and his father had previously shown the holy man many acts of reverence and service. But in such a matter—that is, wherever justice was at stake—the blessed man was swayed neither by friendship nor frightened by power.

For some years earlier, when the emperor Henry had seized Pope Paschal, together with the clergy and part of the citizens, in the church of Saint Peter through an unspeakable act of treachery, and, overcome by pity for those captured with him, had forced them into unlawful agreements, the holy man ensured above all that Henry should be excommunicated at Vienne.

[Note: In the year 1112, under Guido, archbishop of Vienne, and with the great assistance of Saint Godefredus, bishop of Amiens, whose feast is celebrated on 8 November.]

Through that excommunication, with the Lord strengthening the judgment of His Church, the prosperity of that tyrant was turned into its opposite, and his descendants were deprived of imperial dignity.

When your serenity, fleeing from the persecution of the aforesaid schismatic, entered Gaul, Blessed Hugh met you at Valence. With tears he begged and implored you—as he had previously requested from your predecessor—that he be released from all ecclesiastical burdens and honors, and that a more useful shepherd be chosen for the Church of Grenoble. But not even then was he able to obtain what he had requested so effectively and humbly.

## CHAPTER VI. Illness; admonitions given to visitors; death; burial.

26. From this time onward he began to fail more and more each day and to draw nearer to death as his ailments increased.

Of the two angels of Satan whom, as we related above, he had been given to buffet him lest he become exalted—namely, temptation and illness—one, temptation, was extinguished so completely that no trace of it remained; the other, illness, did not cease increasing day by day until, when he died, it too ended with him.

Although it had always been clear through his words and deeds that God dwelt in his blessed soul, this became especially evident in the final affliction of his illness. It could not remain concealed what sort of merit he possessed, with how sincere an affection he revered the Lord, and with what true love he had defended justice and truth throughout his long life.

For through the excessive violence of the illness, almost the whole of his memory was destroyed or disturbed—but only that part which is common to good and evil people alike, and serves indifferently for good purposes among the good and evil purposes among the wicked: the part that retains the forms of local and temporal things.

When that portion of memory had been obliterated or confused, the other portion—imprinted with the lines of truth, justice, and the whole worship of God, which is appropriate only to acts of piety in holy human beings and angels—not only became known as clearly as before but at times even more steadfastly and fervently. Thus, by continually appealing to the ears of divine mercy with litanies, psalms, and the beating of his breast, by day and by night, he often became burdensome to the religious men who served him.

27. Eight or nine men were present to serve him, and sometimes even ten, drawn partly from his own companions and partly from our house, the house of Cales, and the house of Excubiae. Some were learned and some unlearned, but all were religious brothers. No secular person at all was admitted to his service.

They served him most devotedly, day and night, in his bodily and spiritual needs. Toward these servants of his he showed, by clear signs, how far he had advanced in humility—the virtue which, as we related above, he pursued above all others—and how deeply he had impressed it upon the sacred recesses of his pure heart.

If he needed anything, he did not command any of them as a master, but asked; and he prayed for a divine rather than a human reward. For example: “Show or do this or that for me, for God’s sake, so that God may repay you for it in the future.”

They marveled and were utterly astonished that the man who had been accustomed to govern all his subjects, and especially his own household, with such authority and severity, had clothed himself during his illness—when others are usually more prone to anger and indignation under the goad of disease—with such gentleness and humility.

For if anyone even mildly rebuked him or said that he had endured some annoyance in serving him, he immediately struck his breast violently with his fists, proclaimed himself guilty, and most devoutly begged that the discipline of rods be imposed upon him.

Since everyone refused to do this out of their great reverence for him, he wept abundantly and repeated countless times the confession which he had been accustomed to use before celebrating the sacred mysteries.

He also recited psalms and passages from the divine Scriptures, as well as litanies and ecclesiastical prayers, day and night with incredible persistence. We were credibly told that on one night he completed three hundred Our Fathers.

When those serving him rebuked him because by doing these things he was not only tiring his body but also increasing his illness, he replied that these practices not only did not increase his sufferings but brought him great remedies.

28. He had become so accustomed to these exercises and had absorbed so deeply the sweetness of divine praise and supplication that, although almost everything else had fled from his memory through the illness, as we have said, neither delirium nor the force of any other disease could erase these things from his most holy mind.

Rather, he went over them with greater persistence and delight, since the others came to him more rarely, aided as they were by forgetfulness.

Although, often compelled by this same forgetfulness, he did not know where he was or with whom he was, when questioned about matters relating to justice and religion he answered without hesitation, with complete truth and great wisdom.

When a false report had spread that a son had been born to Count Amadeus [Note: This is Amadeus II, count of Savoy, son of Humbert II, whom he succeeded upon his death in 1103; he died on the island of Cyprus on 1 April 1149.]—who, following the example of his father, Count Humbert, showed considerable reverence to the blessed old man—and those attending him asked whether he himself wished to baptize the child, he immediately replied with some disdain:

“No. It does not matter by whom someone is baptized, since baptism, conferred by anyone, is always the same.”

[Note: That is, whether the baptizer is a bishop or a parish priest.]

Likewise, when those present were disputing among themselves which person should ordain as priest the successor whom he himself had already requested and who had been elected, he answered with similar indignation that an ordainer ought not to be chosen within the Catholic Church, since, although the priesthood is conferred on different persons and by different persons, it cannot be different.

He was more easily and more vehemently indignant in such matters because he considered it blasphemy even to doubt them.

29. Clerics and laypeople also came in considerable numbers to visit him, with great reverence and devotion. According to their persons and offices, he poured forth most salutary admonitions.

Among them was Guigo Desiderius, one of the more important men after the count and especially devoted to him. When Guigo, kneeling—for everyone did this—before his bed, asked for his blessing, the holy man rebuked him severely, saying that by imposing unjust exactions upon his subjects he was earning eternal torments for his soul.

Astonished, Guigo replied that these words were being spoken to him not by one who could now almost be counted among the dead, but rather by God, who had revealed the matter to him. He confessed that he had indeed recently imposed a very heavy fine upon his land, that he had not yet received it, and that after this admonition he would never receive it.

30. The bishop of Chartres, Lord Gaufridus, had been especially known and dear to the servant of God from the time of their acquaintance.

[Note: Gaufridus held the see from 1116 to 1138. He was the apostolic legate of Innocent II, whom he received at Chartres in 1130 and was already escorting back into Italy.]

After his visit—which he had made all the more welcome because it was so greatly desired—he was returning from Valence, where you were then staying, to your presence. When he asked what message he should deliver to you on his behalf, the holy man said that your kindness should pray to God’s mercy for him.

But when he then asked what he wished prayer to be offered for him, he replied: “That God may extinguish what is worldly in me and kindle His own love.”

He very frequently made the same request of the religious brothers who rendered him diligent service, declaring, with beating of his breast, that he was guilty and unworthy of divine benefits.

On one occasion, one of his companions, moved by his many tears and sighs and wishing to console him, said: “Why, Father, do you weep so much, when you have committed neither murder nor perjury nor any other criminal act?”

He immediately replied: “What does that matter, when desire and vanity alone, if divine mercy is absent, can suffice for human destruction?”

What wiser or more concise answer could have been given by a man in sound health and with an unimpaired memory? Everything that the good avoid through pious efforts and the wicked pursue through destructive endeavors, he enclosed in two words: desire and vanity.

31. The bishop of Die, Lord Odolricus [Note: Also called Odoricus and Uldricus; he is said to have lived until 1144.], was also one of his pupils. In the Church of Grenoble he had advanced him through every office up to the deanship—the highest dignity there after the episcopate.

Desiring to receive the habit of the regular life from the venerable hands of the most holy old man, he came devoutly, although the bishop was already greatly weakened and burdened by increasingly severe illnesses.

When the blessed man learned from his attendants why he had come, he rejoiced with such great joy and was immediately so filled with happiness that, forgetting his illness and eager to go out to meet him, he nearly threw himself from his bed.

When Odolricus approached, the holy man kissed him and, shedding tears for joy, said:

“May God strip you of the old man with his deeds, and clothe you with the new, who was created according to God in the justice and holiness of truth.”

His memory, as has already been said, was now failing beyond what concerned ordinary matters, while in divine matters it sometimes overflowed more abundantly than usual.

After giving him many most holy and salutary admonitions, when Odolricus was leaving, the holy man had not yet crossed the entire courtyard when he took care to give him one further instruction: that he should cut the foot coverings from his leggings, so that, except for his feet, his entire body would lie clothed. For he grieved that some people in the religious habit slept with their legs exposed, to the injury of holiness.

After this, with the help of his attendants, he descended to the level floor. Prostrating himself face down, he gave great thanks to God with tears for what had taken place. By these signs, although he was almost already dead, he showed how greatly he desired human salvation.

32. But he could not tolerate his servants laughing, indulging in idle talk, or repeating useless rumors with any patience. For he immediately restrained this by a stern rebuke, declaring that the times owed to tears and penitence must be occupied with lamentation, not worn away by laughter, frivolous reports, or idle conversation. Therefore, we ask, let those who know no cause for wonder except what is extraordinary consider again and again whether they could have found anything like this either in Scripture or in human accounts—and whether it does not seem altogether impossible and contrary to nature, and therefore incredible, that a man could lose from memory bodily things and those customary from childhood, yet not lose divine things, when reason rather demands that spiritual and divine matters, being subtler, less familiar, and more difficult to grasp, should depart first, while bodily matters, as more familiar and easier for human weakness to contemplate, should remain longer.

But if the events that ordinarily occur among the saints are more wondrous in proportion to their rarity, what could be more wondrous than this, for which, because of its rarity, there is no example either in Scripture or in human affairs? Let each person judge as he wishes; but it seems to us—and we think that those more experienced, especially those versed in natural philosophy, will judge no otherwise—that it was no less singular and no less wondrous, indeed perhaps even more so, that amid so many and such long-lasting and severe afflictions of the brain he did not lose divine knowledge and invocation, nor his devout religious devotion, than that amid torture-horses, burning plates, and glowing grates someone should refuse to deny the Christian faith with unconquerable steadfastness.

There, everything that torments is imposed wholly from outside; here, the very instruments of reason, and the very senses of divine and human things, the memory’s storehouse, are attacked from within. The mind presiding over them is assailed nowhere and from nothing other than those very bodily parts by which it ought to have been helped—parts that are more excellent and sublime, and more closely joined to it because of their subtlety. We marvel at the one in the revered martyrs, at the other in Blessed Hugh.

Yet this was neither new nor recent for him. For in the ecstasies of his mind—which were frequent and sublime—he had been accustomed to taste heavenly sweetness with delight, leaving beneath him not only everything else but even himself. Thus, when afflicted, he returned to that which had been sweeter to him when he was in health.

It is therefore evident that Blessed Hugh, like holy Job, was harried by such great storms of tribulation and refined in such furnaces of suffering, as gold is refined, so that he might emerge from this life purer and brighter for the fellowship of the saints, and so that the world might recognize that he had loved God not superficially but from the very marrow of his being, since neither the force of pain nor that of madness could restrain him from invoking Him. What more is there to say? He persevered in these things to his final breath. Toward his Carthusian house, and toward its unworthy prior—which we do not write of without tears—he displayed a special affection, not ceasing to remember them amid such great afflictions.

33. Thus, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1132, being at least eighty years of age, in the fourth month, and likewise at least in the fifty-second year after his consecration, on the Kalends of April, the Friday before Palm Sunday, around cockcrow, Blessed Hugh—outstanding among the bishops of his time in works and reputation—departed to the Lord. His household was peaceful and filled with every good thing, the Church entrusted to him was secure, and the people were enjoying tranquil peace. He left behind a Carthusian already appointed as his successor, as he had long and earnestly desired.

His body was kept unburied until the Tuesday of the following week, during clear and warm days, so that no one wished for summer; many marveled that it did not decay either from the mildness of the air, from the heat of the densely packed crowd surrounding it, or from the warmth of the candles. Three bishops hastened to his venerable funeral rites: the bishop of Die, the bishop of Grenoble, and the bishop of Chartres. The last of these had scarcely withdrawn on the preceding day, after paying him a second visit during his final weakness, and had asked that, if Hugh should soon die, word should immediately be sent to him—as indeed happened.

34. As soon as the news of his death spread widely, innumerable crowds hurried to him, not only from his own episcopate but also from distant regions, bringing candles and offerings of various kinds. People of every age, sex, and condition most devoutly kissed his feet, so much so that the sandals themselves, as though they had been dyed, became darkened alike by saliva and tears. Even nursing infants were brought, so that they might be protected against every adversity by touching so holy a body.

Some, kissing the sandals with even more ardent faith, bit them, wishing to carry away with them something for sanctification. Rings, coins, and other objects were applied to the saint’s body, so that, once he had been buried, they might be kept as relics. From among our own monks, and from those of Cales and Excubia, there were many lay brothers, constant guardians of the most holy remains; there were also very numerous companies of monks and clerics in ecclesiastical vestments.

So great was the crowd gathering from every direction, and so welcome to everyone was even the dead man’s presence, that they scarcely allowed him to be buried at last. Finally, on the fifth day after his death—the Tuesday after Palm Sunday, as we have said—they deceived the crowds, promising that they would carry him outside the church so that they might look upon and touch him more freely. When they had gone out in this hope, and the Church of Blessed Mary ever-virgin, where he was to be buried, had thereby been partly emptied, the doors were immediately and firmly closed. Then the venerable relics of the sacred body were placed in the prepared sarcophagus with great reverence and with an immense outcry of lamentation mingled with psalm-singing.

The gathering of crowds around his tomb, sometimes thinner and sometimes denser, because of their hope of divine mercy being shown toward them on account of the holy man’s immense merits, continues to this day.

**In the Year of the Lord 1188. Guigo, second prior general of the Carthusian Order of this name; Bernard, John, Stephen of Chalmeto, Carthusians**

[Col. 0785]

## Notice concerning Guigo

*(Fabricius, Bibliotheca mediae Latinitatis, III, 135. For other matters, see below the Preface of Pierre-François Chifflet.)*

Guigo II, prior general of the Grande Chartreuse, who resigned the generalate in 1176 and died in 1188, is regarded as the author of a book divided into thirty-six chapters, *On the Fourfold Exercise of the Cell*: withdrawal from worldly affairs, meditation, prayer, and manual labor. Pierre-François Chifflet, S.J., published it together with other ancient monuments of similar subject matter at Dijon in 1657, in octavo, in a book entitled *Manual of Solitaries*, drawn from the cells of the ancient Carthusian Fathers. It was reprinted with the same materials in the *Bibliotheca Patrum* of Lyons, volume XXIV, pages 1468–1501.

Perhaps Guigo should also be credited with the *Ladder of Paradise*, or *Ladder of the Cloistered*, that is, a treatise on the manner of praying and on the contemplative life, addressed to Brother Gervase. It was published among the works of Saint Augustine in the appendix to volume VI, page 643, Amsterdam edition, and among the works of Saint Bernard, volume II of the new edition, pages 325–330.

[Col. 0785]

## The Ladder of Paradise, or Treatise on the Manner of Praying and on the Contemplative Life, perhaps to be attributed to Guigo II

*(It is found among the works of Saint Augustine, volume VI, or volume XL of the *Patrologia*, appendix, column 997.)*

## Book of Guigo, second prior of the Grande Chartreuse of that name, on the Fourfold Exercise of the Cell

There are added the letters of Bernard, first prior of the Charterhouse of Portes; of John and Stephen of Chalmeto, monks of the same Charterhouse; and also a letter of Pope Alexander III to Arthaud, prior of the Charterhouse of Alvernia.

*(Bibliotheca Patrum XXIV, 1463, from the *Manual of Solitaries*, edited and prepared by Pierre-François Chifflet, priest of the Society of Jesus.)*

[Col. 0787]

## Preface concerning the following short works

[Col. 0787A] Since these short works are now seeing the light for the first time through our press, and since they appear to have been unknown even to Theodore Petraeus, who nowhere mentions them in his *Carthusian Library*, we believe it is certainly in our interest to make clear at the very entrance to the work from which libraries and from what ancient manuscripts they have emerged, by which authors they were written, and what their character ultimately is.

### I. Book on the Fourfold Exercise of the Cell, by Guigo, apparently, second prior of the Grande Chartreuse of that name

We transcribed this book from a manuscript of the Charterhouse of Portes. We then obtained from a manuscript of the Charterhouse of Parc, at Le Mans, several variant readings, which, wherever necessary, we either attached to the text as the sounder readings or recorded within brackets in our copy, preceded by the letters “Par:” to indicate the Parc manuscript.

The exceptionally cultivated and deeply venerable Dom John Chauvet, general secretary of the Carthusian Order, who transmitted these variant readings to me, also informed me that the Parc manuscript belongs to the number of those which Saint Geoffrey of Loudun, bishop of Le Mans—so he is commonly called, although he was not established by any authority of the Roman See—the second founder of the Charterhouse of Parc, gave to that house around the year of Christ 1244. If this is so, it will be necessary to affirm that this Parc copy was made approximately four hundred years ago.

The Portes manuscript is shown to be even older by the fact that it contains certain words belonging to a more remote age and more alien to pure Latin, words which are found corrected in the Parc manuscript. Following these traces, we judged that the Blessed man to whom this treatise is dedicated, the prior of the Charterhouse of Witham, was none other than Bovo, a man of great religious devotion and prophetic spirit. The longer Life of Saint Hugh, bishop of Lincoln, divided by its author, Hugh’s household companion, into five books, confirms that Bovo succeeded Hugh, formerly prior of Witham and later elevated to the episcopate, in the administration of the same Charterhouse of Witham around the year of Christ 1186.

About five years earlier, Bovo had strongly influenced the decision that the same Hugh should be granted to the English king to preside over the house of Witham. For the Life of Saint Hugh says the following, in Book II, chapter 3, during the consultation of the Carthusian Fathers concerning that matter:

> A certain Bovo, whom we later heard frequently relating this when he was prior of Witham, asserted that the king’s word had come from God; concerning Hugh he added: “Believe my humble judgment. Before long you will hear that he is among the chief lights of the holy Church, raised upon the candlestick of ecclesiastical governance. Long ago Hugh seemed to me, by his virtues, more a bishop than a monk.”

It is worth noting that the dedication says: “The Blessed Prior of Christ’s poor, who, while dwelling at Witham, professed the Carthusian Order.” In the same form Guigo, fifth prior of the Grande Chartreuse, begins the prologue to the Life of Saint Hugh, bishop of Grenoble:

> To the most beloved and most reverend Lord and Father, Innocent, pontiff of the apostolic see, Guigo, unworthy servant of the poor Carthusians, perpetual salvation, etc.

And the Carthusians of the Grande Chartreuse, in the letters of Peter of Cluny, Book VI, Letter 23:

> To Peter the Venerable and honored abbot of the Cluniacs by the grace of God, the humble brother, called prior of the poor of the Grande Chartreuse, with those same poor, eternal salvation from the Lord.

Thus it is entirely clear that, in ancient times, the Carthusians were commonly called “the poor,” evidently because the meagerness or austerity of their food and clothing stood out above that of others. On this matter, besides others, one should consult Peter the Venerable, *On Miracles*, Book II, chapters 28 and 29, who frequently elsewhere declares how highly he esteemed the Carthusian institute, and especially his sixth book of letters: Letter 12 to Pope Eugene, Letter 24 to the brothers of the Grande Chartreuse, and Letter 40 to Basil, prior of the Grande Chartreuse.

Let us now proceed to investigate the author of this work. Although neither manuscript gives his name, certain details scattered through the work have led us, as though by the hand, to Guigo, formerly prior of the Grande Chartreuse and second of that name. After resigning the generalate, he lived twelve years longer in private retirement at the Grande Chartreuse. He died on the fifth day before the Kalends of October, in the year of Christ 1188, by which time Bovo had already begun to serve as prior of Witham two years earlier.

First, in chapter 15 and in many other places, the author reveals himself to be a Carthusian. Moreover, since he repeatedly cites, according to their ancient form, the statutes of Guigo, which were later rearranged in the year of Christ 1259, it is necessary that he wrote sometime between the first Guigo—who wrote around the year 1130—and 1259.

Furthermore, in that same chapter 15 and elsewhere, he speaks as one possessing authority and addresses the priors of the entire Carthusian Order as though they were present in a general chapter. He addresses them with a gravity of judgment that suggests either the authority of a general superior or at least the remnants of an office that he had formerly held.

The author, then, was both an inhabitant of the Grande Chartreuse and a person of the highest dignity there. All these features would scarcely be found to fit anyone appropriately once this one Guigo is excluded. Concerning him, a writer of that order relates:

> He was certainly a great man, of admirable teachability and, without doubt, of a prudence greater than human prudence. He was deeply devoted to contemplation and quiet. He asked and received absolution from the general chapter, thereby casting off that burden, which he considered far too heavy for him because of his inexperience in human affairs, which he had neglected through much contemplation of divine things.

At last the devout Guigo sent forth his spirit into perpetual light on the fifth day before the Kalends of October 1188, twelve years after his absolution: commendable not so much for his manner of life as admirable for certain words and deeds beyond the ordinary course of human nature. For this reason many, not without an omen, called him “the Angel”; because of the innocence of his life, he merited, on the day after his death, to celebrate the angels’ festival among the blessed.

Thus, if there is room for our conjecture, Guigo published this work for Bovo, prior of Witham, around the year of Christ 1187, calling him “the son of his spiritual womb,” perhaps because, while Bovo was superior, he had used him in the Charterhouse as a confidant and arbiter of the secrets of his spirit or conscience.

Certainly, an indication of Bovo’s considerable superiority to Guigo is found in the records of a legal matter between the abbot of Bonnevaux and Jocelin, prior of the Grande Chartreuse, dated to the year 1185. The witnesses are listed as follows: first Bovo, a monk of the Grande Chartreuse; then Guigo, formerly prior of that house.

This, for the present, is conjecture. If in the future any new light should shine upon a different conclusion, we shall readily and gladly accept it.

Moreover, one may wonder that the author says in chapter 28 that the reprobate angels never possessed charity, and therefore were capable of charity but did not receive charity. He cites Ezekiel, chapter 28, verse 13, together with an interpretation of Pope Gregory.

The author certainly seems to have followed Rupert’s footsteps—Rupert having asserted the same thing in Book I of *On the Works of the Trinity*, chapter 16, and from the same passage of Ezekiel, indeed also from Pope Gregory, whom the author here cites closely and almost transcribes.

Some, however, whether Fathers or teachers, explain this as referring to actual charity, which it is not implausible that the reprobate angels never possessed, especially given the opinion of certain writers who assert that they persisted only for a single instant from their first creation until their fall.

Since it is more probable, however, that the angels’ way was not so brief, and since supernatural habits would seem to have been infused in vain if they had never burst forth into any act, I would prefer to say, with John Martinon, *Disputation 43, On the Angels*, section 5, number 41, that Ezekiel, together with Gregory, should rather be understood as speaking of charity not simply, but increased through merits, as the word “filled” indicates; or even perfected through blessedness and glory, where charity in second act is so much greater and more intense as the vision of God surpasses the act of faith.

Less probable is the opinion expressed by Hugh of Saint-Victor in *Summa of the Sentences*, tract 2, chapter 2; Peter Lombard in Book II, distinction 3, part II; Bonaventure in the same distinction, article 1, question 2; and several others, namely, that the evil angels were created in a state of pure nature and were endowed with no grace or habitual charity. This conflicts with the Angelic Doctor, *Question* 62, article 3, and also with the holy Greek as well as Latin Fathers, if their meaning is properly understood.

See the commentators on Ezekiel at the passage in question, and the scholastic theologians at the cited passages of the Master and Saint Thomas, as well as Petavius, volume III of *Theological Dogmas*, Book I, chapter 16.

### II. Three letters of Bernard, first prior of the Charterhouse of Portes

[Col. 0790D]

We owe the letters of this Bernard, first prior of Portes, and of his disciples John and Stephen, which we publish here, to a single parchment manuscript of good quality belonging to the renowned monastery of Jura. This monastery was formerly called Condat from its earliest foundation, then Saint-Oyend or Eugendus, and most recently Saint-Claude.

From the founding of the Charterhouse of Portes—that is, from the year of Christ 1115—until approximately 1260, we have determined that exactly five Bernards presided as priors over that house. We learned this either through the guidance of Dom Hugh Buat, coadjutor at the Grande Chartreuse, a most cultivated man and exceptionally learned in the history of his order, or through examination of the ancient original records themselves.

There was little difficulty in distinguishing the fourth and fifth. The fourth, surnamed “de la Tour,” is known to have presided over the entire Carthusian Order, after serving as prior of Portes, from 1253 to 1258. The fifth was surnamed “de Samia”; he also served as prior of Portes from approximately 1256 to 1260.

It is, however, exceedingly difficult to distinguish the three earlier Bernards who were priors of Portes—whom most writers have conflated into one. I shall explain the matter briefly, insofar as the nature of the subject permits.

The first Bernard, prior of Portes, was also its founder. He came from the Benedictine monastery of Ambronay in the year of Christ 1115. Thus the Charterhouse of Portes holds, by right of antiquity, the first place after the Grande Chartreuse among the Carthusian houses in the Alps, and is third in the entire Order after the second house of Calabria.

I read the record of his death in this form in the necrology of the Grande Chartreuse, whose name and origin we shall explain in the appendix to this *Manual*, number 31:

> On the day before the Ides of February, Bernard died, first prior of Portes, 1152.

But he had resigned long before. For, according to the records of the Grande Chartreuse, on the feast of Saint Thomas the Apostle in the year of Christ 1147, Bernard de Portis, who had resigned the bishopric of Belley and was then prior of Portes, is mentioned.

Yet William was already bishop of Belley on the Kalends of September 1141. For Falco, archbishop of Lyons, testifies that in that year, 1141, in the fourth indiction, in the twelfth year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent II, and in the second year of his own episcopate, on the Kalends of September, on the twenty-seventh lunar day, Bernard, prior of Portes, came to him with Pons, Boso, and Stephen, monks of the same house. For more than twenty-five years, beginning in the year of Christ 1115, they had served Christ the Lord in the wilderness of Portes, and had come so that a dispute which had arisen among their neighbors concerning the boundaries of their jurisdiction might be settled by the judgment of Falco himself, archbishop, together with William, bishop of Belley, and Ismion, abbot of Ambronay.

William was bishop of Belley at least until the year 1157. Since Bernard de Porta—whom we do not distinguish from Bernard de Portis—is read as merely a monk of Portes in a charter of Portes dated to the year 1135, on the third day before the Nones of May, the charter discussed below in connection with Stephen of Chalmeto, it is necessary that he was bishop of Belley sometime between the third day before the Nones of May 1135 and the Kalends of September 1141; indeed, sometime between 1135 and 1138.

For Bernard de Portis is also said to have been bishop of Maurienne after Airald, whose death the people of Maurienne assign to the year of Christ 1138. Geoffrey, abbot of Hautecombe, certainly mentions Airald and Bernard, bishops of Maurienne drawn from among the monks, in the Life of Saint Peter, bishop of Tarentaise, as it appears in my manuscript copy, Book I, chapter 16. The people of Maurienne likewise affirm that both were taken from the Charterhouse of Portes.

It therefore appears that Bernard de Portis became bishop of Maurienne after having been bishop of Belley, from the year 1138 until at least 1146. For we have read him called “Bernard, bishop of Maurienne” in manuscripts of the Church of Vienne, in a privilege granted to that Church by Conrad, king of the Romans, in the eighth year of his reign, on the Feast of the Epiphany—that is, 6 January—in the year 1146 from the Incarnation of the Lord.

He must have resigned in that same year or shortly afterward, in 1147, when we find him merely prior of Portes, on 21 December. This is Bernard de Porta, or de Portis, to whom, while he was still a private person, Saint Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, addressed Letters 153 and 154. In them he testifies that, urged by Bernard’s encouragement and frequent letters, he had composed several sermons on the Song of Solomon.

Some say that this same Bernard de Portis was summoned by Pope Innocent II to a bishopric in Lombardy, specifically Milan; I do not know on what certain and trustworthy authority. Saint Bernard himself bears witness to the matter in Letter 155, in which he earnestly asks Innocent that Bernard de Portis be reserved for a more suitable place and another people.

Nor was this request in vain, for at the time indicated he received the bishopric of Belley instead of a Lombard bishopric.

Was he called de Portis from some estate bearing that name? Perhaps from the very place where the Charterhouse of Portes was founded and to which he devoted himself. For that mountain pass was already long ago called “Portes,” because the natural rocks there, raised in certain places as though by an artisan’s hand, imitated gates.

Someone might say that Bernard, bishop of Maurienne, was entirely different from Bernard, bishop of Belley, on the evidence of the necrology of the Grande Chartreuse, where, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of January, only this is recorded:

> Bernard de Portis, monk and bishop of Belley, died, 1152.

The bishopric of Maurienne should also have been noted if it had fallen to the same man. But when Bernard de Portis died, he was neither bishop of Maurienne nor bishop of Belley, but merely prior of Portes; he therefore had to be designated by the bishopric of Belley, to which he had first been consecrated.

Let us now continue with the rest. Bernard de Portis was prior of Portes in 1147, having been bishop of Belley and Maurienne. Therefore, Bernard, the first prior and founder of Portes, who lived until 1152, had already appointed Bernard de Portis as his substitute by at least 1147.

Both Bernards died in 1152: the founder on the day before the Ides of February, and the other on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of January. Yet the latter died first, because according to the ancient Gallic custom that year, 1152, is to be reckoned from Easter, or from the Incarnation—that is, from 25 March—not, as now, from the Kalends of January.

From the death of Bernard de Portis to the death of Bernard, founder of the house of Portes, there were exactly fifty-eight days. During this period, the surviving founder Bernard substituted for Bernard de Portis in the priorate of Portes his former novice Anthelm, or Nanthelm, then formerly prior of the Grande Chartreuse.

It is one and the same Bernard, prior of Portes, whom the contemporary author of the Life of Saint Anthelm says, in chapter 2, received Anthelm into the Charterhouse of Portes, and in chapter 10 says, when already weighed down by old age, transferred the administration of the house to Anthelm.

Anthelm presided for almost two years, until 1154, and then returned to his own cell in the principal Charterhouse. After nine years, in 1163, he was consecrated bishop of Belley by Pope Alexander III himself, on the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary, which at that time fell on a Sunday, when the Dominical Letter was F.

He died in 1178, in the fifteenth year of his episcopate, on the sixth day before the Kalends of July, after Compline. His deposition, or day of burial, is recorded in the necrology of the Grande Chartreuse as follows:

> On the fifth day before the Kalends of July, Nanthelm, bishop of Belley, died.

In the Church of Belley, however, he is honored on the very day of his death, the sixth day before the Kalends of July, under the name Anthelm, although both the Carthusians and he himself called him Nanthelm. See the appendix, number 2.

[Col. 0793B] When Nanthelm left the priorate of Portes in 1154, Bernard, the third prior of Portes bearing that name, succeeded him. He later became bishop of Die. The list of the priors of the Charterhouse, attached to the ancient statutes and printed manuscripts under Guigo, second prior of the Grande Chartreuse of that name, around the year of Christ 1176, says:

> At that time Lord Bernard flourished, formerly prior of Portes and afterward bishop of Die. He raised the dead, cleansed lepers, and shone forth through countless other miracles.

And Dom Hugh Buat, whom we mentioned above, says that he read these same words on page 42 of a manuscript of Portes:

> Under the blessed pontiff Alexander III, Lord Bernard, once our prior, was taken from us so that he might be appointed bishop of Die—a true man of God and a saint.

Then, on the following page:

> Thus the holy man Bernard governed the bishopric of Die with wondrous patience, greater piety, and most ardent charity; with marvelous skill he snatched and rescued his sheep from the jaws of Tartarus.

When this third Bernard was called to the bishopric of Die, his successor appears to have been Stephen, prior of Portes, who is mentioned in a bull of Pope Alexander III dated to the third day before the Nones of February 1171. Perhaps this is the same Stephen of Chalmeto, concerning whom we shall speak below.

Stephen was succeeded by Rostannus, whom the bull of Pope Lucius III, dated to the third day before the Nones of February 1182, in the first indiction, calls by name.

Since nearly all writers, including more recent Carthusians such as Peter Sutor, Peter Dorlandus, Theodore Petraeus, and Laurentius Surius in the Life of Saint Stephen, bishop of Die, together with our Canisius and Saussay in their martyrologies, and many others, have confused the third Bernard now with the first and now with the second, we must distinguish them on the basis of what has been said.

The first Bernard, founder of the house of Portes in 1115 and formerly a monk of Ambronay, had already resigned the priorate on the feast of Saint Thomas the Apostle in 1147, appointing Bernard de Portis, formerly bishop of Belley, as his substitute.

When Bernard de Portis died in 1152, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of January, the first Bernard, who outlived him, appointed Nanthelm, formerly prior of the Grande Chartreuse, as prior of Portes. Not long afterward—namely, fifty-eight days after the death of Bernard de Portis—the first Bernard departed this life, on the day before the Ides of February, in the year which, as we reckon it today from the Nativity of Christ or from the Kalends of January, was 1153, although it was still 1152 according to the reckoning of the Gauls, who began their year 1153 on the following 25 March.

After the second Bernard, surnamed de Portis, Nanthelm was the third prior of Portes, for nearly two years, from 1152 to 1154. When he resigned in order to return to the solitude of his Charterhouse, Bernard the third succeeded him. Bernard was later made bishop of Die by Pope Alexander III and became renowned for his virtues and miracles.

Concerning the first Bernard, Dom Hugh Buat testified to me that he had read the following in a manuscript of Portes:

> He wrote several letters encouraging virtue and the religious life. The principal ones were addressed to Falco, dean of Lyons, and to the same man after he had become bishop; to Aymon de Rohières; to Rainaldus the enclosed recluse; to the nuns of Lyons; to Berlion, bishop of Belley; to the nuns of Blesio; to Pope Eugene; to Saint Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux; and to Ismion, abbot of Ambronay. The most beautiful of all is the letter in which he explains the reasons why he left the monastery and fled to the wilderness of Portes. It begins with these words: “Escape to the mountain, lest you too perish with them.”

Only three of these letters have come down to us.

The first is addressed to Aymon de Varennes and Aymon de Rohoria, *On Fleeing the World*. The records of Alveria mention these men among the benefactors of that house in the following words:

> Aymon and Hugh de Varennes built the church, namely that of Alveria. Aymon de Rivoria built the brothers’ dormitory.

The second is addressed to the nuns of Lyons and exhorts them to undertake with great courage the regular discipline which they had recently embraced.

Leidradus, archbishop of Lyons, mentions two convents of maidens in Lyons in his letter to Charlemagne:

> In the same city I restored other churches. One, indeed, in honor of Saint Eulalia—where there had been a monastery of maidens—I dedicated in honor of Saint George. I reroofed it anew and rebuilt part of its walls from their foundations.

A little later he says:

> I also restored from the foundations both the churches and the house of the monastery of maidens dedicated in honor of Saint Peter, where the body of Saint Annemundus the martyr was buried—a monastery founded by that holy martyr and bishop himself. Thirty-two nuns now appear to dwell there, living according to the regular institution.

Since Lyons is now overflowing with convents of nuns, I understand Bernard of Portes’ letter to concern the Benedictine monastery of Saint Peter, still renowned for its wealth and religious observance, because I believe that in his time it was the only convent of nuns in Lyons. Leidradus indicates that the old monastery of Saint Eulalia—where the Church of Saint George now stands—had already ceased to exist in his day. It is beyond doubt that all the others, such as those of the Poor Clares, Carmelites, Annunciates, and so forth, were founded after Bernard’s time.

[Col. 0795A] The third is addressed to Rainaldus the enclosed recluse, *On How One Should Live before the Lord*.

Who this Rainaldus was, an ancient parchment from the archives of the Grande Chartreuse has taught me. It begins, “Guido de Aranda,” and we have transcribed it in the appendix to this *Manual*.

That charter bears no date, but it has among its witnesses Hugh, procurator of the Grande Chartreuse, whose office other documents indicate he held around the year of Christ 1134. From this indication alone one may determine the period of Rainaldus, the recluse at Saint Ragnebert; the same may also be inferred from the script of the records themselves.

This Rainaldus, then, was an enclosed hermit who had a cell apart from the brothers, not far from the Benedictine monastery of Saint Ragnebert, which is about two league-hours from the Charterhouse of Portes. It took its name from Ragnebert, son of Duke Radebert, whom the wickedness of Ebroin once made a martyr.

The monastery had previously been called Bebronnum, after the stream by which it is watered, and had been founded by Saint Domitian, whose name is entered in the martyrologies on the Kalends of July. In his Life, which we once transcribed from an old manuscript of the same monastery, the statement that Saint Domitian fled the persecution of Julian the Apostate must be corrected. For this cannot agree with what is added concerning Domitian’s encounters with Vincent of Lérins, Hilary of Arles, and Eucherius of Lyons, all of whom are universally known to have flourished approximately a century after Julian.

### III. Five letters of John, monk of Portes

[Col. 0795C] This John professes himself a monk of the Charterhouse of Portes at the beginning of his fifth letter to his nephew Bernard, whom he addresses in these words:

> For we know that from the house in which you are, from the Carthusian house, from our own house, and from other communities of this purpose, certain individuals have departed; some of them died after a few days, others after a few months.

This indicates that he was a Carthusian, though not necessarily from the principal Charterhouse or even from the house of Portes.

He calls himself a brother in flesh and spirit of that Stephen whom his first letter strongly urges to renounce the vanity of the world. I am therefore inclined to the conjecture that this is the same John of Montemedio, monk of the Charterhouse of Portes, who is mentioned at the beginning of the first letter of Bernard, prior of Portes, and who was the adviser and encourager of his brother Stephen of Chalmeto in casting off the burden of secular life.

For brothers were distinguished by different surnames, especially in noble families, just as we commonly see today; this practice was likewise current in earlier centuries.

I think the ancient author of the Life of Saint Anthelm, bishop of Belley, chapter 13, in Surius under 26 June, should be understood to refer to this same John. He says:

> After Anthelm, formerly prior of the principal Charterhouse, had become prior of Portes, succeeding Bernard, who, weighed down by old age, had transferred his office to him, Anthelm showed reverence to Lord Bernard, placing him before himself. He behaved in the same way toward John, a religious servant of Christ, and whenever John arrived, Anthelm would reverently rise before him. He never omitted this, even when bishops, abbots, or persons of any rank were present.

Saint Anthelm had left the priorate of the Grande Chartreuse in the year of Christ 1151. He was then prior of Portes as a private monk for two years, from 1152 to 1154; these dates correspond suitably with John of Montemedio.

I can scarcely bring myself to recognize the author of these letters as a certain John who had been abbot of Abundantia and became a monk of Alveria—that is, a Carthusian who had come from the Augustinians and whom some records say died in the year of Christ 1202. For, on the evidence given above, our John is found to have been both a Carthusian of Portes and older than that John.

## IV. Letter of Stephen of Chalmeto, monk of Portes, to the novices of Saint-Sulpice, On Perseverance in the Order

[Col. 0796B]

Richard of Benuntia—as I read in the autograph documents, dated on the third day before the Nones of May in the year of Christ 1135—gave several estates to the Charterhouse of Portes, into the hands of Dom Bernard, the prior, in the presence of the monks of that place: Bernard of Porta, Boso the procurator, and Stephen of Chalmeto, still a novice. Elsewhere too, not infrequently, you may find this Stephen entered in the Portes archive, now as a novice, now as a monk of Portes.

Moreover, the codex of that same Charterhouse contains the following. Stephen of Chalmeto, noble by birth and nobler in piety, became a monk of Portes in 1135. He composed several pious works and sent letters to various people, fragrant with holiness. This Stephen is different from the first and fourth priors of the same name, of Majorey, and from both of the younger ones. For it is certain that Stephen of Majorey, the first prior, died on 4 January 1118. The fourth had begun to preside in the year 1130 or 1131.

It is more plausible to question whether Stephen of Chalmeto was himself that Stephen, prior of Portes, who is mentioned in Pope Alexander III’s Bull issued to the monks of Portes in 1171, when he was in the thirty-sixth or thirty-seventh year since his conversion to monastic life.

Saint-Sulpice, however, whose novices this letter concerns, was a house of the diocese of Belley and belonged to the Cistercian Order. It was founded by Amadeus, count of Savoy, in the year of Christ 1130, with monks brought there from the monastery of Pontigny, as the old foundation records teach, preserved by the learned Samuel Guichenon in his *History of Bresse and Bugey.

Certainly, that these novices to whom Stephen of Chalmeto writes were not Carthusians may also be understood from his words:

> “Since some, when they have come to our or to your way of life, customarily sigh either from ours toward yours or from yours toward ours, lest the tempter deceive us through such suggestions, let us hear the Apostle saying: ‘Let each person remain in the calling in which he was called’” (1 Corinthians 7:20).

Nevertheless, it seems possible to prove that during these very years there was some house of the Carthusian Order bearing the same title. For around the year of Christ 1130, Guigo, fifth prior of the Grande Chartreuse, dedicated the statutes of his Order, newly compiled by him, to Bernard, prior of Portes, Saint-Sulpice, and Milo of Majorey.

[Col. 0797A]

How could so prudent a man have sent the secret laws of his own domestic discipline to be reviewed by an outsider? Or how could he have allowed a third Cistercian to sit in judgment on them together with two Carthusian priors?

Some claim that traces of this Carthusian house of Saint-Sulpice still survive, not far from the Cistercian abbey of Saint-Sulpice in the diocese of Belley, in a very secluded and almost inaccessible place on the same mountain, which, they say, is still called *Carthus* by the local inhabitants. Guichenon, however, says in the history cited that in the bishopric of Grenoble there exists a monastery called Saint-Sulpice, which he asserts formerly belonged to the Carthusians.

If this is true, I suppose that Humbert was prior of one or the other of these Charterhouses, the man whom Guigo mentions in the preface to the statutes.

## V. Letter of Pope Alexander III to Arthaud, prior of Arvière, concerning the schism of his time

We ourselves read the old autograph of this pontifical letter in the Charterhouse of Arvière.

After the council celebrated at Tours around the year 1163, Pope Alexander went to the city of Sens to remain there, since that metropolis was very beautiful and fertile. He stayed there for a long period, from the Kalends of October until Easter of the following year, conducting there, in accordance with his duty, the affairs of the universal Church. Thus runs the *Acts of this Pontiff*, from a Vatican codex, as cited by Baronius under the year of Christ 1163, no. 18.

Since it is therefore clear from these sources that Pope Alexander lived in the city of Sens from the Kalends of October 1163 until Easter 1165, and since this letter to Arthaud was dated at Sens on the fourth day before the Kalends of March—a date which he spent there in each of the two successive years—it remains uncertain whether it should be assigned to the year 1164 or 1165.

The following is recorded in the sacred calendars concerning Arthaud, or Arthold, prior of Arvière, who is venerated among his own people as blessed on the day before the Nones of October:

> “The man of God Arthaud, drawn from the Carthusian community into the episcopate of Belley, and worn out by old age, returned to the quiet of his cloister and surrendered his spirit to God in peace in the desert of Arvière.”

He is said to have been bishop of Belley after Rainald, from the year of Christ 1184 to 1190. Thereafter he lived as a private person until the very end of his life, reaching the year of Christ 1206.

Indeed, when Saint Hugh, bishop of Lincoln, visited him hidden away in the desert of Arvière—surely in the summer of the year 1200—Arthaud had advanced far in age, as the author of the *Life of Saint Hugh*, his contemporary, says; he adds:

> “Nor were their minds unlike that of our bishop, although their ages were unlike.”

Saint Hugh was then sixty years old, about four months before his death, while Blessed Arthaud was already advanced in years and perhaps more than ninety.

Meanwhile, even from the subject of this letter you may understand how truly the ancient author of the *Life of Saint Anselm*, chapter 15, says that Alexander was greatly assisted by the Carthusians and the Cistercians in the exceedingly difficult affair of the schism. The same may also be gathered from Geoffrey, abbot of Hautecombe, in the *Life of Saint Peter, archbishop of Tarentaise*.

## VI. Appendix containing proofs of what was argued, in the second section of this preface, concerning the first three priors of Portes named Bernard, and Nantelmus associated with them

[Col. 0798A]
