At this point one might pause over no. 4 of this Appendix, the diploma of Rainald, archbishop of Lyon, concerning the name and origin of Majorey, and concerning the matters described in it that belong to an earlier age.

We certainly saw with our own eyes in the archive of Majorey Rainald’s autograph documents, dated in April of the year 1213 and authenticated by his seal. Thus there can be no reasonable doubt that, if an error was made in examining and testing Valentinian’s privilege, that error must be attributed to Rainald himself, the archbishop, or to his chancellor.

Yet Rainald does not transcribe Valentinian’s own documents. He transcribes only a certain declaration of the benefaction granted by Valentinian to Majorey, which could have been written many centuries after Valentinian by some notary at Isarnodorum, or Isarnorum, and which recalled the privilege formerly granted to Majorey.

I mention this so that no one may look here for a consular dating or for the other formal features of imperial rescripts, or complain that Valentinian was absent from Isarnodorum—the town of the Gallic island and of the Sebusians, or, if you prefer, of the Segusians—in the year 385, since, while the tyrant Maximus controlled the Gauls, Valentinian remained in Italy. For Valentinian’s privilege could have been issued at Rome, Milan, or some other place in Italy, and later documents issued at Isarnodorum could have recorded it long afterward.

[Col. 0798C]

If Rainald, the archbishop, had described in this declaration the figures on the golden seal he had seen, it would be possible to reason confidently about its authenticity and antiquity. In all other respects, I recognize nothing in the document that would prove it false.

Valentinian the Younger was treacherously killed by Arbogast in the seventeenth year of his reign, during the consulship of Arcadius II and Rufinus—and indeed, as Epiphanius notes in his little work *On Measures and Weights*, on the Ides of May, a Saturday, the day before Pentecost, which at that time fell on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of June. All this assigns the event to the year 392 of the Christian era.

For some time, however, hatred and suspicion had already arisen between Arbogast and Valentinian, as may be gathered even from Zosimus, book four. Valentinian had entered upon his office after the death of his father of the same name, on the tenth day before the Kalends of December in the year of Christ 375, and, in the tenth year after the consulship of Gratian III and Equitius—that is, in the year of Christ 385—Majorey’s Valentinian, the chamberlain, could already have had his loyalty tested by Arbogast, and rewards for his proven fidelity decreed.

As for Jovinus, the priest of the temple of the Mountain of the Sick, for whose suppression of brigandage the fortress of Majorey is said to have been built, I believe that he was none other than Jovinus who, having long before been promoted by Julian to be commander of the army throughout the Gauls—as Ammianus says in book 26—served faithfully in the same office, as commander of both armies, under several succeeding emperors.

He was also consul with Lupicinus in the year 367 of the Christian era. In that same year two rescripts of the emperors Valentinian and Valens were issued to him at Reims, in laws 9 and 10 of the *Theodosian Code*, *On Military Affairs*.

The wife of Consentius also derived her origin from him; concerning her Sidonius writes at Narbonne (poem 23):

> “To this man of supreme talent, and likewise  
> of supreme nobility and beauty,  
> a woman was joined who, transferring to her husband’s house  
> the distinction of ancient Jovinus,  
> filled the sophist’s home with the robes of office.”

He is also called “most Christian” in the testament of Saint Remigius and, in Flodoard, book 1 of the *History of Reims*, chapter 6, is the founder of that basilica of Reims which was once called after Blessed Agricola and is now named after Saint Nicasius. His anniversary is also commemorated there on the seventh day before the Ides of September.

I therefore believe that there can be no doubt that a marble monument was carved for this same Jovinus. It is now seen beyond the main entrance of his church, on the right, set upon several columns. Its sculpted design, expressed in bronze, was published and illustrated with an elegant commentary by Tristanus Sanctamantius in his work *Hadrian*.

I would add only this: the figures on that monument do not represent an actual hunting expedition once undertaken by Jovinus against wild beasts, but merely something symbolic and emblematic.

For scarcely anyone could believe that a lion was killed by a Gallic man of whom no exploits are recorded by Ammianus—in books 21, 22, 26, and 27, where he discusses him—or by other writers outside Gaul, Italy, Germany, and Britain, regions that do not abound in lions.

To have pierced a boar, doe, or stag with a hunting spear would have been a very modest distinction for a most Christian man and commander of the army, and hardly worthy of being commended to all posterity by so elaborate a mausoleum for eternal remembrance.

[Col. 0799C]

Since, then, I read in the passages cited from Ammianus that in the regions mentioned Jovinus repeatedly subdued the enemies of the Romans, and since Prosper, in book 3 of *On Promises and Predictions*, chapter 38, says that under the rule of the devout emperor Theodosius all the temples were stripped by the counts Jovinus and Gaudentius, I finally understand why he is displayed in eternal marble as the conqueror of the boar, stag, doe, and lion.

No one will deny that by these animals the barbarian peoples whom he defeated, or the evil spirits whom he deprived of office and expelled from their dwelling places, may fittingly be signified.

At the same time I understand why Jovinus was insultingly called so by Majorevus. Majorevus was evidently, like most people who at that time pursued either palace or military service, devoted, after the custom of his ancestors, to the worship of idols. He took it very badly that Jovinus was destroying the idols and stripping their shrines of their wealth and ornaments.

For that reason he called him, impious and savage as he was, “the priest of the temple of the Mountain of the Sick,” while nevertheless acknowledging him to be so powerful that he thought he had to protect himself from his attacks even by building a fortress.

That insult is plainly the language of a pagan and a military man. Solinus, chapter 7 of the *Polyhistor*, and Plautus in the *Curculio*, indicate that sick people used to keep watch in the temple of Aesculapius.

That a temple was consecrated to Aesculapius on a mountain in Libya is attested by Trismegistus in the *Asclepius*. The ancients generally observed the practice of establishing temples to Aesculapius both on mountains, for the benefit of the healthy air, and near water, for the convenience of the sick.

Today the French common people call many fortresses *Aigremont*, that is, “Mountain of the Sick,” because of the custom I have described.

Perhaps our Jovinus had once been in charge of some temple of Aesculapius before he devoted himself to Christ; or, already a Christian, he may have founded a hospital in an elevated place, together with a sacred building, according to Christian rites.

Hence he was called by Majorevus, mockingly and insultingly, “the priest of the temple of the Mountain of the Sick,” because by order of the most Christian emperor he was overthrowing the temples of the idols.

This is enough by way of conjecture, lest you rashly condemn the prudence of Rainald, archbishop of Lyon, who appears to have trusted this diploma concerning the fortress of Majorey, where a Carthusian house was established as early as the year of Christ 1116 and ranked sixth among all the houses of the Order according to antiquity of foundation.”

[Col. 0799]

# The Book on the Fourfold Exercise of the Cell, Apparently by Guigo, Second Prior of the Charterhouse of That Name

From manuscript codices of the Charterhouse of Portes and the Charterhouse of Parc.

## Prologue

[Col. 0799D]

To the most reverend lord and most beloved father in the heart of Christ, B., prior of the poor of Christ who dwell at Wittheam and have professed the Carthusian Order: from an unworthy servant of God and God’s servants, the son of your spiritual womb, holiness in the present life as merit and happiness in the future as reward.

If it were permitted to summon before a court either a father by his son or a master by his servant, perhaps my insignificance, reverend Father, would have something over which it could bring suit against your greatness before the judge—not, as it seems to me, unjustly. For behold: while your powerful authority considers what it is permitted to demand from me, it has ceased to consider what the moderation of your discretion should recognize my weakness to be capable of doing.

Hence that outstanding preacher, while asserting that everything is permitted to him, plainly denies that everything is expedient. For although it belongs to a father with respect to a son, and to a superior with respect to a subject, to impose by command what is appropriate to the time and place, the cause and the matter, one must first consider whether each of the two is sufficiently able, in knowledge and power, to bear what is imposed.

Certainly, willingness must never be lacking—not even when knowledge and ability happen not to be present.

I have prefaced these remarks because your venerable fatherhood ordered me to attempt in writing to show what exercises the person who has professed the holy Carthusian Order ought chiefly to pursue in his cell, where he must remain as a solitary, and from which he should not leave at any time except when reasonable causes require it, as expressly provided according to the tenor of that Order.

It is a useful work, to confess the truth; but for it an experienced person alone is sufficient. I, however, am not unaware that I am unfit for it, since I know that honey is sweet, but know this more by hearing than by tasting.

I also know, as that philosopher says, that I do not know—namely, that I speak these things from personal understanding. Nor do I know how to speak with my mouth, as though reading what the prophet’s secretary asserts that he did.

Certainly, Wisdom’s destruction and death said:

> “With our ears we have heard its fame” (Job 28:22).

Did they see its beauty with their eyes? Certainly not. Did they experience its sweetness with their throats? Not even that. Among them hearing alone was active in relation to its fame; neither sight in relation to its appearance nor taste in relation to its sweetness.

And what could I worthily say about the sweetness of the cell, when it is evident that I have heard something about it, however faintly—as I cannot deny and do not wish to deny—but have experienced little or nothing of what it is, what kind it is, or how great it is?

Yet, fearing that I might incur the sin of divination and the crime of idolatry, and choosing rather to be found empty of those things that puff up than of those that build up, I compelled myself, so that I might now be willing when previously I had been unwilling. I persisted as best I could: teaching what I had not learned and handing on what I had not received.

It follows, therefore, that unless obedience with charity, and charity with obedience, come forward to excuse this great rashness and presumption in me, I must rightly be counted among those whom the Apostle says have turned aside to vain talk, wishing to be teachers of the law while understanding neither what they say nor the matters about which they make assertions.

But so be it. Behold, I have become foolish—but wisely, because you compelled me. Thus, if presumption accuses me, compulsion excuses me.

For although my ignorance demands silence from me, your command opened my mouth. Thus I was placed in the position of fearing to be silent, though ashamed to speak: preferring through ignorance to give room to confusion in myself rather than, by resisting authority—and therefore the ordinance of God—to subject myself to condemnation.

Accordingly, attempting to carry out your command as far as I could, I took care to apply both my mind to study and my hand to the pen. What occurred to me for the present concerning this subject, because your fatherhood compelled me to treat it, I arranged in writing just as I discovered it in study.

Since there is no doubt that the strength and power of the entire Order reside in the strictness of the general chapter, which the priors of that Order, from far and near, assemble each year at the Charterhouse in the same place, I took care to begin this discourse of mine from that point.

I then attempted, as far as I could, to show in what the very essence of the Order consists, and especially what those exercises of holy religion are to which the inhabitant of the cell ought to devote himself, introducing testimonies from Sacred Scripture wherever the argument required.

Those exercises are four: devotion to sacred reading, the maturity of purified meditation, the devotion of pure prayer, and the vigor of useful action. Of these four, prayer is the greatest.

For this reason I judged it fitting to place before this book the following title: *On the Fourfold Duty of the Cell*, unless your fatherhood should have thought otherwise.

The chapters too have all been placed before the beginning of the book, in the order in which they follow one another, so that when something is sought it may immediately be found without difficulty. Not only that: in the book itself the same chapters are inserted in the places appropriate to each, so that when the heading set before a section is considered, it may clearly be recognized what the following discussion treats.

Let your fatherhood, beloved by me in the Lord, now accept this small gift, offered with devotion that is not small. If perhaps you see in it little that you ought rightly to approve, may you at least deign to accept the devoted intention of the one offering it.

I also ask you that, since I have carried out your command—omitting certain other matters in which it might have been sweeter for me to engage, though perhaps not more useful—though not as I ought, certainly as I was able, you return me this reward for my labor: that you be willing to remember me in your prayers.

Let the recompense for my ready obedience be the devoted persistence of your prayer for me before God.

May God almighty the Father, through his beloved Son, in the holy Spirit of both, guard your reverend fatherhood from every evil, order your days in his peace, rescue you from eternal condemnation, and command that you be numbered among his elect. Amen.

## Table of Chapters

I. The manner and reason for the arrival of the priors of the Carthusian Order at the annual chapter, and the threefold fruit of their arrival.

II. The sublime sweetness and the sweet sublimity that in the Carthusian Order consists especially in three things.

III. The spiritual way of life of the Carthusian brothers, in which they go after Christ, through Christ, and to Christ.

IV. What should be understood spiritually by the meanness and harshness of the Carthusian habit, and concerning their frugal food.

V. The purity of inward contemplation, which chiefly concerns the solitude of the cell.

VI. How the sweet repose of the cell, and its restful sweetness, are expressed in certain passages of Sacred Scripture.

VII. Concerning the same repose of the cell: how its secret was expressed by holy men from Moses to Isaiah.

[Col. 0803A]

VIII. Concerning certain holy men who lived from Isaiah to Christ, and certain others who lived after Christ’s coming, and how through them the repose of the cell was prefigured.

IX. Concerning the repose of the cell, and that it is not expedient for one who lives in it to remain outside it too long through rash curiosity.

X. That the cell must be continually kept by the person who inhabits it, and what danger comes to him if he rashly leaves it.

XI. The great and many dangers incurred by the inhabitant of the cell who leaves it wrongly, and how the complete and perfect rejection of worldly affairs brings great repose to the holy soul.

XII. The rejection of worldly affairs, anxieties, and possessions—matters to which the Carthusians devote particular attention.

XIII. The place of holy pleasure, and the spiritual flight of holy Job.

XIV. How spiritually a river flowed from the place of pleasure to water paradise, and what that river is.

XV. That the priors who assemble for the annual chapter ought diligently to devote themselves to the renewal of the Order, and concerning the four holy exercises to which everyone who wishes to dwell fruitfully in the cell ought carefully to apply himself.

XVI. A commendation of the cell, and concerning those four divisions into which the river is divided that flows from the place of pleasure to water paradise.

XVII. That the inhabitant of the cell ought to avoid every illicit word, and what good things sacred reading advances us toward.

XVIII. The kinds of holy meditation to which the solitary seated in the cell ought to devote himself, and concerning the diligent recollection of Sacred Scripture.

XIX. The mode of meditation that produces in the mind of the one meditating the occasion of fear and sorrow, and its division into eight modes.

XX. The general resurrection of the dead and the punishments of the condemned, and how those eight modes in which fear and sorrow arise should be recalled.

XXI. How fear drives pride from the mind of the person meditating, and concerning the third mode of meditation, which provides an occasion for love and consolation.

XXII. The fourth mode of meditation, which produces in the mind of the person meditating the causes of pity and compassion; and that certain things which we see others doing badly ought generally to be excused within ourselves rather than rashly judged.

XXIII. How we ought to set the fifth mode of meditation in our mind against the temptation of the flesh, the devil, and the world by which we are continually assaulted.

XXIV. Concerning the weariness suffered by someone who inhabits the cell, and how he can drive it away from himself, renew himself, and restore himself.

XXV. Concerning what Christ performed in the flesh, and concerning the labors of his saints.

[Col. 0804A]

XXVI. The seventh mode of meditation, which produces in the mind of the person meditating the causes of astonishment and wonder, and how through the things that have been made the one who made them is perceived.

XXVII. Concerning the voices and words that the soul hears spiritually, and how the soul was made in the image of God, what movement it receives, and what movement it is incapable of receiving.

XXVIII. Concerning those blessed spirits: what they are and what things pertain to them, and what the inhabitant of the cell ought to turn over within himself concerning them in pure meditation.

XXIX. The kind of meditation that we ought to possess within ourselves, in the inmost places of our heart, when we endeavor to think about God, and how it is fitting and permissible for us to conceive of him.

XXX. Concerning the Trinity of Persons and the unity of the substance that is God, and that neither the Trinity prejudices the unity nor the unity the Trinity.

XXXI. The diligent concern and concerned diligence that we ought to devote to our prayer when we apply ourselves to it; and concerning the great instability with which, at the time of prayer, we wretchedly and miserably fluctuate through idle and harmful thoughts scattered in our heart, and wander through countless things.

XXXII. Concerning the wandering of the mind that we perceive to be present in us during prayer, and how and why the devotion of prayer should be understood through the third river flowing from the place of pleasure, which is also called the Tigris.

XXXIII. What kind of people we ought to show ourselves to be before approaching prayer, so that when we come to it we may offer it to God in such a way that he makes it acceptable to himself and mercifully fruitful for us.

XXXIV. That when we approach prayer we ought from a pure heart to forgive those who have offended us, and, if there are people who hold anything against us, to be wholly and perfectly reconciled with them.

XXXV. The four kinds of thoughts that it is necessary for us to keep in mind if we wish to pray to the Lord purely, devoutly, and fruitfully.

XXXVI. Concerning manual labor, to which the inhabitant of the cell ought to devote himself; at what hours he ought to apply himself to spiritual exercises and at what hours to manual labor; and many other matters concerning the same inhabitant of the cell.

# The Book on the Fourfold Exercise of the Cell

## Chapter One: The Manner and Reason for the Arrival of the Priors of the Carthusian Order at the Annual Chapter, and the Threefold Fruit of Their Arrival

[Col. 0804D]

The arrival of our venerable fathers, the priors of the Carthusian Order, at the annual chapter produces great fruit for the whole of that Order.

They assemble in the Carthusian desert, all of them from different places and many from distant ones. And, not to deny what is true, they assemble not without great labor, with immense devotion, cheerfulness, eagerness, humility, simplicity, kindness, piety [Cod. Parc., purity], and charity.

This, then, is the reason for their arrival.

First, they come to show that they ought to offer prompt and humble obedience—as befits men of such sincere conscience—to the ancient institution of the Order. It is this institution that obliges them to assemble each year at the appointed time, when the general chapter is to be held in the aforesaid place.

Those are excepted who, because they are often unable to be present, have a just occasion and reason, and to whom the chapter itself has discreetly and mercifully granted permission to remain away.

Second, they come so that, in every spiritual joy, they may also see one another bodily and may increase more and more among themselves the sweetest charity of brotherhood in the Lord.

Third, they come so that, to the best of their knowledge and ability, with zeal according to knowledge and with prior discretion, they may renew the Order they have professed by common counsel and consent, and stabilize and strengthen it in a good condition.

In destroying what is harmful as well as in constructing what is useful, they should show themselves intent upon everything with fervent concern and concerned fervor according to God. Thus they should diligently imitate in this twofold work of salvation the one whom the Lord appointed over nations and kingdoms “to uproot, to tear down, to destroy, to demolish, to build, and to plant.”

This is the threefold cord by which our fathers and lords, bound together in Christ, assemble: the strength of profound humility, the sweetness of fraternal charity, and the anxious care of the charge entrusted to them.

This cord is difficult to break—indeed, wholly impossible to break among holy men alone—when the Lord strengthens it and preserves it more and more in its integrity.

For since he himself, the lover and author of humility, says, “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matthew 11:29), it is plain that those who are known to be disciples of the truth persevering to the end are consequently bound by the gentle bond of humility.

Likewise, since according to the Apostle, “Whoever loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law” (Romans 13:8), and, as he immediately concludes, “Therefore the fullness of the law is love” (Romans 13:10), it is plainly evident that the integrity of this cord cannot be dissolved in anyone in whom—or rather, within whom—the perfection of fraternal charity is known not to diminish.

And what can we, or what ought we, to say about the one who presides in anxious care?

Does not the angel stand beside shepherds who are keeping watch and guarding the watches of the night over their flock, and does not the glory of God shine around them?

It is clear that those who have an angel standing beside them do not fear any injury to themselves, nor do those who have the glory of God shining around them fear any darkness.

And from where do they receive these two outstanding blessings? Certainly from the fact that they were keeping watch and guarding the watches of the night over their flock.

Moreover, what is it to keep watch and guard in this way other than to destroy what is evil and build what is good?

## Chapter Two: The Sublime Sweetness and Sweet Sublimity That Consist Especially in Three Things in the Carthusian Order

[Col. 0806A]

We have said something about the manner and reason for the arrival of our lords and fathers—namely, the priors—at the general chapter, and what fruit comes from their arrival.

Do we think that when they assemble in this way and for this reason we ought to say to them what the Apostle says to certain Corinthians: “It is no longer possible to eat the Lord’s Supper”? (1 Corinthians 11:20.) Certainly not.

Rather, when they assemble in unity in this way, it is already possible to eat the Lord’s Supper.

We have called it the Lord’s Supper, not the supper of Holofernes, which is full of pleasure, nor the supper of Herod, which is polluted with blood, but the Lord’s Supper, at which, girded with the linen cloth of purity, they wash the feet of their disciples—their own affections and intentions.

Rising at dawn and offering holocausts individually, they should resist by every means possible lest they sin, and bless God in their hearts.

Thus they will be worthy to reach that supper which a certain man prepared as a great feast.

Even today many are prevented from wishing to come to it by the estate of vanity, the yoke of fivefold curiosity, and the wife of pleasure.

Therefore let these holy men diligently do what they can for the sake of the reason for which they have assembled.

They obey the institution of the Order in assembling. In an orderly manner they visit one another bodily, and thus multiply within themselves the mutual love of fraternal charity.

It remains for them now to fulfill the third reason for which they assemble. They do so when, in their discussions concerning the Order, they all strive together, with devoted care and devout concern, both to uproot whatever evils appear among them and to add whatever is good.

Therefore, let a river flow from the place of pleasure to water paradise.

What should we suitably understand by this paradise according to the tropological sense, which we propose to follow?

Let us understand by it the sublime sweetness in the Lord, and likewise the sweet sublimity, of the Order we have professed—unless someone should think that something else is better, truer, and more fitting.

Certainly, if someone else thinks differently, God has revealed this to him. It seems to us that we may meanwhile hold this view without prejudice to a better judgment.

For we observe what privilege, what kind, and what extent this twofold good possesses in the Order, and this is why we dare to think in this way.

Not only that, but sometimes—although very rarely—we have been permitted to experience it ourselves, if only faintly.

The privilege of this twofold good consists especially in three things: external discipline, the perpetual solitude of the cell, and the complete rejection of this world.

These three particularly commend the sweet sublimity and likewise the sublime sweetness of the Order that we have compared to paradise, among the many great goods that are found in it: a commendable external discipline, the perpetual solitude of the cell, and the perfect rejection of the world.

Of these three, the solitude of the cell is the greatest. It is greater because it is what makes possible both the usefulness of external discipline and the perfection of the rejection of the world.

For it provides the occasion and cause by which external discipline can please both God and human beings and benefit the person who practices it, and it brings the rejection of the world to completion without exhaustion.

To touch briefly upon this first great good, we refer external discipline to meanness, harshness, and frugality: meanness in clothing, harshness in the use of the hair shirt, and frugality in food.

## Chapter Three: The Spiritual Way of Life of the Carthusian Brothers, in Which They Go after Christ, through Christ, and to Christ
And now we beseech you, venerable Fathers in the Lord and beloved brothers, to allow us calmly to bring forth into the midst and raise up on high your religious and holy manner of life. This is partly for your own small consolation [Col. 0807B], but chiefly for the glory and praise of him who is its cause, that it exists, and likewise its pattern, that it is such. He is the one whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world (John 10:36), so that we might live through him. This happens when, as Ecclesiastes says, the eyes of the wise man are in his head (Eccles. 2:14); and when, as John instructs, “whoever says that he remains in him ought to walk just as he walked” (1 John 2:6). Hence also these words of his: “No one comes to the Father except through me,” but also this other saying, spoken at that time: “You are unwilling to come to me, that you may have life?” (John 14:6).

To the two brothers whom he made fishers of men he also says, “Come after me” (Matt. 11:28)—O, after me; O, through me; O, to me [Col. 0807C]. You too walk along these three ways, coming after him, coming through him, and finally coming to him. Thus he says: after me, through me, to me.

Why must we go after you, O sweet and good Jesus? Certainly because you are the way. And why through you? Surely because you are the truth. Why also to you? Certainly because you are the life. “I,” he says, “am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). This is true, because you are the way, you are the truth, and you are the life: plainly, the way in example, the truth in promise, and the life in reward.

You are the way for us, O mediator of God and human beings, God and human, Christ Jesus, in your humanity, which you took from us for our sake, because in it you showed us the example of a holy manner of life. You are life for us in your divinity, in which you are coequal, coeternal, and consubstantial with the Father. For just as the Father has life [Col. 0807D] in himself (John 5:26), so he gave you, the Son, to have life in yourself. He gave it because he begot you. He did not give the Son something he had not previously possessed; rather, that giving was his eternal begetting—indeed, it is his begetting from eternity. And he gave life, not another life than the one he himself is, so that the life given might be life from Life, the Son begotten from the Father, God from God, light from light; and that the one who gave and the one to whom he gave might be one and the same life, just as there are not two different gods, but one and the same God, both begetting and begotten.

Hence, just as the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son also to have life in himself [Col. 0808A], so that we may believe that the begotten is not later than the begetter, just as the begetter is not earlier than the begotten—although the Father is from no one, because he is the Father, whereas the Son is from the Father, because he is the Son. In what we have heard—“just as the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son also to have life in himself” (John 5:26)—we understand that the Father and the Son are one, coequal, coeternal, and of one substance.

In the vision and participation of this life alone consist both the fullness of our joy and our entire blessedness. Moreover, you are the truth, O good and kindly Jesus, in both your natures, the assuming and the assumed, because what you promise us as a human being, you restore to us as God.

You, therefore, O our lords and brothers—you, I say, go after him; you go also through him, so that you may arrive at him. He himself desired to go in this way, whose prayer had this form: “Lead me in your way, and I shall enter into your truth. Let my heart rejoice” (Ps. 85:11). In this way there is sincerity in uprightness; in this truth there is brightness in knowledge; in this joy there is true happiness in the blessed and beatifying vision of God.

Addressing the same person in another psalm, he says [Col. 0808B]: “You have held my right hand, and in your truth you have led me, and with glory you have received me” (Ps. 72:24). “You have held, you have led, you have received.” He who is the way holds your right hand, so that you may go after him; he who is the truth leads you by his good will, so that you may go through him also; and he who is the life receives you with glory, so that at the end you may arrive at him and remain with him without end.

And indeed your excellent religious life never ceases to proclaim that these words are true. Its good reputation flies far and wide. You, however, strive in every way so that your holy manner of life may not be inferior to that reputation. Otherwise, if the reputation spread about you were false—which God forbid—would it not become disrepute? [Col. 0808C] It would also be the occasion and cause of the greatest shame. For, as Boethius says: “Those who are falsely praised must themselves necessarily blush at their own praises” (*On the Consolation of Philosophy* III, prose 6). Therefore take care that those who hear about you what is praiseworthy may be able to say of you what the queen of Sheba once confessed about herself to that magnificent king Solomon: “I have proved,” she said, “that not even half was told me” (3 Kings 10:7).

## CHAPTER IV. What is to be understood spiritually by the lowliness and roughness of the Carthusians’ clothing; and concerning the poverty of their food

This exceedingly excellent manner of life of yours [Col. 0808D] is also completely separated from the world and from the things that belong to the world. Hence it rightly can and ought to be regarded as paradise—but only by one who loves it and practices it with immense fervor and with all his efforts.

There is, then, lowliness, and there is also roughness in your clothing. What do your clothing signify to you in these matters, except those two outstanding goods that are gifts of God alone: namely, humility of heart and mortification of the flesh? We refer lowliness to humility, and roughness to mortification. The former suppresses the swelling of exaltation in the mind; the latter destroys the stench of corruption in the body.

These are indeed the two bonds of its depravity by which that ancient enemy binds the human race among the reprobate. He is truly the serpent, real and crooked, creeping on his breast and belly, as the old translation reads [Col. 0809A]. For that ruler of the world, of this darkness, raises some vainly above himself, while he weakly casts others down beneath himself. In this way he conquers both: these by the strength he has in his loins, because of the higher sex; and those in his navel, because of the lower sex.

But he who was born of a humble and incorrupt girl comes to break these bonds in his elect: that humble mediator of God and human beings, holy, teaching them above the beasts of the earth and instructing them above the birds of heaven. He expressed this supremely also in his own cross and death.

“Let us condemn him to a most shameful death” (Wis. 2:20). These are the words of the Jews conspiring against the death of the Savior. In hearing that they wished to condemn him to death, observe the roughness [Col. 0809B]: for what is rougher than death? But in their proposal and decision that this same death should be not merely shameful but most shameful, understand that you ought to recognize his cross. For what kind of death is more lowly than the cross? The cross is a disgraceful punishment. Refer the disgrace to lowliness and the punishment to roughness.

Thus the Son of God became obedient to the Father even unto death; and lest anyone should regard this as something insignificant, the Apostle deemed it worthy to add, “even death on a cross” (Phil. 2:8). By suffering such a death for us, he prefigured in himself what you may appropriately observe in your clothing.

And what does this have to do with your benefit? Very much, throughout the whole world: namely, that by humbling yourselves [Col. 0809C] under the mighty hand of God, you may deserve to be exalted by him at the time of visitation. Likewise, by mortifying the deeds of the flesh through the spirit, may you arrive at life. As has already been said, the lowliness of your clothing signifies humility, and its roughness signifies mortification.

Certainly the sparingness of your food resists the prince of cooks, lest he destroy the walls of Jerusalem; and this is exceedingly necessary for us. For if what Solomon says is true, “Whoever pampers his servant from childhood will afterward find him rebellious” (Prov. 29:21), is possessing such and so great a good not in some sense possessing paradise?

You have been raised above the world, of whose lover the Lord says: “He was clothed in purple and fine linen, and feasted splendidly every day” (Luke 16:19). In purple there is color; in color, beauty; in beauty, brilliance; in brilliance [Col. 0809D], vanity; in vanity, pride. In fine linen there is softness; in softness, pleasantness; in pleasantness, the itching of the flesh; in itching, titillation; in titillation, pleasure; in pleasure, wantonness.

Thus the purple displays him as lofty, and the fine linen as slippery. But the fact that he feasted splendidly not on occasional days but every day shows that he was subject to gluttony. You, however, are not like this. Rather, we liken you to that beggar, because begging also involves a certain lowliness. He was full of sores, and in this respect we correctly assert that he was in roughness. For in not receiving the crumbs that fell, he was far removed from the one who feasted splendidly every day.

## CHAPTER V. Concerning the purity of interior contemplation, which pertains chiefly to the solitude of the cell

[Col. 0810A]

After this, we must consider that the continual solitude of the cell is the second good that we have assigned to the spiritual paradise. Certainly I do not think that one deviates from the truth who calls the continual solitude of the cell paradise. But now someone who knows by experience what and how great are the goods contained in it may ask: Why should I hesitate to call that a paradise which is plainly heaven itself?

For, if a thing is to receive its name from its reality and to be called what it sounds like, what is a cell except the hall of heaven? Truly, the Lord is in the cell, because it is nothing other than the house of God and the gate of heaven (Gen. 28:17). In it there is an ascent and descent of angels above the Son of Man on the ladder of charity [Col. 0810B].

What the beautiful appearance of lovely Rachel prefigured in herself; what the joyful and joy-giving rest of Mary, sitting and listening, possesses—continual solitude of the cell possesses all of this, and in reality more than in symbol: not only in its fragrance but also in its taste. It is ignorant of Martha’s laborious agitation, but rejoices greatly in Mary’s peaceful, tranquil, quiet, gentle, sweet, pleasant, good, serene, lovely, beautiful, luminous, delightful sitting.

And when shall we be able adequately to admire, recount, and praise the goods that are in this hall of heaven? Their greatness exceeds all measure, and their multitude exceeds all number, so that in explaining their immensity, some tongue is like a tiny drop falling feebly in comparison with a very broad and very deep river flowing perpetually [Col. 0810C].

Are we speaking hyperbolically or flatteringly? Far from it. In this we imitate, as far as we can, the one who—as the son of Neriah says of himself—“spoke from his mouth as though he were reading” (Jer. 36:18). For divine reading, which can neither be deceived nor deceive, is abundant experience. It is this that makes us learned, to some extent, concerning these matters and gives us certainty; therefore we speak.

Let us now, if you please, proceed in our customary way through the pleasant and fruitful meadows of the Scriptures, and see with what and what kinds of little flowers—beautiful and fragrant, sweet and wholesome—this hall of heaven is strewn, and the little bed that is in it, so that each one of you may say with conviction [Col. 0810D]: “Our bed is flowering” (Song 1:16).

In your love of this practice and of such a wholesome and religious study, you show that you fully understand how holy Scripture habitually both portrays and approves this peaceful rest of the saints. Behold: when sleep is cast upon the first-formed man, he immediately sees the woman formed from him. There is in him something masculine that rules, and something feminine that is ruled.

As long as holy Abel was within, he was certainly not in death but in life. Once he went out at Cain’s suggestion, he also encountered death itself. Cain’s voice, therefore, is this: “Let us go outside” (Gen. 4:8).

This is the suggestion of those who possess earthly things unlawfully—who are farmers and therefore earthly, not heavenly inhabitants [Col. 0811A]. They strive to deceive those who mourn their present exile, so that, abandoning interior things, they may pour themselves wholly into exterior things through desire and action. For Cain’s name is interpreted as “possession,” whereas Abel’s is interpreted as “mourning.”

But hear what follows, and strive by every means to avoid what you hear. What does the truthful history say? “And when they were in the field, Cain rose up against his brother and killed him.” It is no wonder that he was killed, since he went out into the field. For, as the Truth himself says, “The field is this world” (Matt. 13:38). Since the whole world, as the Apostle John says, lies in the power of the evil one (1 John 5:19), how can anyone escape death who enters it and remains there through will, pleasure, and wicked action?

## CHAPTER VI. How the sweet rest of the cell, and its tranquil sweetness, are expressed in certain passages of Sacred Scripture

[Col. 0811B]

It is still pleasing to direct our attention to the matters before us, so that we may demonstrate what and how great the rest of the cell is. Behold, holy Enoch, because he walks with God, does not appear, for God takes him away (Gen. 3:24). According to the tropological sense, what else is this than that those who devote themselves to God alone, while serving him, do not entangle themselves in worldly affairs? And, in order to please him from the depths of their being, they exclude from themselves, as far as possible, all external things.

Thus, while they devote themselves to interior things alone, they refuse to appear publicly amid excessive occupation. Righteous Noah before God, so that according to the interpretation of his name he may have rest, hides himself more willingly in the recesses of the ark [Col. 0811C] the more vehemently he observes the waters of the flood inundating the earth. The dove too, finding no place outside where its foot may rest, seeks rest for itself within (Gen. 7–8), because the holy, simple, and innocent soul rests more delightfully in interior things the more diligently it empties itself completely of the pleasure of all exterior things.

A sleep falls upon Abraham, and in it a great terror seizes him (Gen. 15:12). As he hears a hidden word spoken to him, his ear receives its whispering veins as though secretly. This means that the holy mind, the father of holy thoughts, elevated through contemplation, is often compelled to tremble inwardly all the more as every concern for external affairs is lulled within him, so that he may attend to God freely and fully [Col. 0811D]. Thus, while he is raised by the infusion of inner inspiration into the sublimity of contemplation silently speaking within him, he delightfully examines its causes and origins, its occasions and modes, in the innermost secret of holy purity.

Sarah dies, and after her death she is buried in a double cave (Gen. 23:2, 19). This takes place spiritually when, in a holy and pure soul, perfect contempt and rejection extinguish all affection and desire for visible things. Thereafter let it devote itself diligently to this twofold holy practice: purified contemplation and excellent action. In this way, though dead in a living manner, it may have in God the life hidden with Christ.

Isaac, whose name means “of the living one and seeing,” dwells beside a well [Col. 0812A] (Gen. 25:11), so that in the devout soul—which hastens toward the laughter of eternal exultation—there may be both living vision, lest it limp blindly away from the truth, and likewise seeing life, lest it grow sluggishly torpid toward the good.

Jacob, fleeing from his brother’s anger, sleeps with a stone at his head (Gen. 28:11–12), his mind resting in Christ. With pure eyes he beholds holy messengers ascending and descending on the ladder of charity above the Son of Man, so that on the one hand they may transcend themselves in mind toward God, and on the other remain soberly present for us.

Holy Joseph dies, but dies in a life-giving manner, at the age of one hundred and ten years (Gen. 50:25), preserving the Decalogue in the perfection of holiness, since the number one hundred signifies perfection and ten signifies the law. Prepared with the fragrant spices of spiritual virtues, he is laid within himself, in the little chamber of the inner secret [Col. 0812B], while he is bodily in the Egypt of this age; and thus he is in the world without being of the world.

## CHAPTER VII. Likewise concerning the same rest of the cell, and how its secret was expressed through holy men from Moses to Isaiah

Moses feeds sheep, driving them into the interior of the desert, so that, seeing a great vision, he may perceive fire burning in the bush without consuming it (Exod. 3). The holy mind nourishes within itself simple and innocent thoughts by the word of God, and, leading them into the innermost secret, observes them with the pure gaze of true faith. It sees the divine and human natures in the one same person of Christ, and the two united to each other in so great and such a covenant that neither glorification consumes [Col. 0812C] the lower nature nor assumption diminishes the higher.

Not only this, but in one girl of singular merit, shining above all who belong to her sex, it sees virginity, yet fruitful; fruitfulness, yet virginal. Thus she possesses both in herself, so that neither injures the other. Another matter was also prefigured for the same Moses in this vision: namely, that he should know he was to lead that people which would receive the fire of the law without avoiding the thorn of sin.

Caleb and Joshua see the land of promise from afar, and they affirm that it flows with streams of milk and honey (Num. 13). This could be recognized through the cluster of grapes carried on a pole—namely, Christ worshiped on the cross.

The boy Samuel sleeps in the tabernacle where the ark of God is [Col. 0812D] (1 Sam. 3). He deserves to be called by the Lord, and, taught by the old man what he should answer the one calling him, the boy says: “Speak, Lord, for your servant is listening.”

Holy David is seized and burns with immense and holy desire when he says: “Who will give me wings like a dove’s? I shall fly away and rest” (Ps. 54:7). To show us where he can find rest on these wings of the dove and in this holy flight, he adds: “Behold, I have fled far away, and I remained in the wilderness” (ibid., 8). His rest, therefore, is in departing or fleeing far away, and especially in remaining in solitude.

He is rightly said to have many days of age—that is, many splendors of spiritual virtues—and to have no delight in the deceitful goods of this world, because, when he was covered with clothing, he was not warmed (1 Kings 1:1). For all earthly things are, as it were, garments of the body [Col. 0813A].

Therefore he sleeps in the sweet embraces of Abishag, whose name is interpreted as “the growling of my father,” and through whom true wisdom is signified. She is the beautiful young woman sought in all the borders of Israel. When found, she is brought to the king. She stands before him for uprightness, warms him for sweetness, sleeps with him for rest, and heats him for true and chaste love. She is so warm that she kindles in him the ardor of divine charity, and so chaste that she neither pricks nor arouses him toward the lust of worldly, carnal, or diabolical vanity, pleasure, or curiosity. For, as Scripture says, “King David did not know her” (ibid., 4). He would have known her if he had taken vain pride in the wisdom given to him from above.

Holy Elijah, fearing the threats [Col. 0813B] of a harlot and sorceress (1 Kings 19), leaves his servant—that is, his childish understanding—and goes to the hiding places of the desert. Throwing himself down, he sleeps under a broom tree. Desiring to depart and be with Christ, he asks that his soul be taken away, and, establishing all that belongs to him in love of God and neighbor, he is twice put to sleep, twice awakened, and finally twice refreshed; then he goes on in the strength of that food.

After observing the Gospel and the law, as though after forty days, he comes to the mountain of God. There, remaining in a cave of the flesh, after a great and mighty wind—which casts down heights and crushes hardness—after the shaking of fear, after the fire of love, he hears the sound of a gentle breeze in the subtlety of pure contemplation. On hearing this sound, like one who desires to leave the prison of the flesh, he goes out [Col. 0813C] and stands at the entrance. And lest the investigator of majesty be overwhelmed by glory, he also covers his face with a cloak.

Elisha dies, and after his death is buried (2 Kings 13:20). Why did this need to be said, since it is not something new but ancient, not something unique to one person but common to all without exception? It was said so that his tomb might be shown to be greatly venerable, because when some dead man is thrown into it [Cod. Parci: “that”], he is restored to his former life even by touching his holy bones.

The religious king Hezekiah receives from the prophet, in the promise, that what is saved from Judah and what remains will send its root [Col. 0813D] downward (2 Kings 19): this refers to the hidden purity of thought; and it will produce fruit upward: this refers to the public excellence of action.

He also turns his face toward the wall that divides him from God because of his sins (2 Kings 20:2), and first confesses his iniquities so that he may be justified, imitating the one who says: “I acknowledge my iniquity, and my sin is always before me” (Ps. 50:5). Therefore he prays while weeping, and weeps while praying; striving to wash away great sins with great weeping, he cries out like a swallow’s fledgling and meditates like a dove.

## CHAPTER VIII. Concerning certain holy men who lived from Isaiah until Christ, and concerning certain others who lived after Christ’s coming, and how through them the rest of the cell was prefigured

Isaiah saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up (Isa. 6:1) [Col. 0814A], perceiving him in the purity of interior contemplation: the Creator of the universe presiding in understanding over the angelic creation, remaining in his own sublimity, and over the human creation, raised from its fall through one mediator.

But this occurred only in the year in which King Uzziah died—that presumptuous and leprous man. And why is this mentioned? Clearly, so that we may know that the purity of contemplation cannot be present in one in whom the swelling of exaltation and the stench of corruption still dominate and live through affection and action.

Finally, after this he says: “My secret to myself. My secret to myself” (Isa. 24:16).

Josiah strikes his heart when he hears the reading of the book that Hilkiah found in the house of God (2 Kings 22); and Huldah consoles him, although she is a woman who lives in the Second Quarter [Col. 0814B].

Jeremiah sees a vigilant rod (Jer. 1:11), so that he may know that the Lord watches over his word to perform it. Ropes raise him from a muddy depth and a deep mud, with old rags interwoven among them or lying beneath them [Par. “supporting them”]. This is so that, ascending from the valley of weeping and singing the Songs of Ascents, with his heart wounded by the love of Christ, he may carry his words in his innermost being like sharp arrows.

This concerns the ropes. As for the old rags, he also carries the examples of God’s servants, whom God makes alive from the dead and radiant from the black, like consuming coals.

A likeness of a hand sent to Ezekiel seizes him by the lock of his head (Ezek. 8:3). Lifted between earth and heaven, he is led in spirit from Chaldea [Col. 0814C] to Jerusalem, so that, seeing the abominations there, he may make a whip from the cords and drive the buyers and sellers from the temple, saying: “The zeal of your house has consumed me” (John 2:17).

Daniel, with his three companions, abstains from what is pleasant to the belly so that he may attain what is truly sweet to the mind; and from then on he is made worthy to perceive the meaning of all visions and dreams.

Not only this, but sitting beside the rivers of Babylon and weeping in remembrance of the heavenly Zion, with the windows of his heart opened toward God, he prays three times a day against Jerusalem, sighing in the true brightness of his spirit for the security of heavenly peace and for the blessed and beatifying vision of the eternal Trinity [Col. 0814D].

Ezra, the most learned and swift scribe, prepares his heart to seek out the law of the Lord (1 Esdr. 7:10), doing and teaching commandment and judgment in Israel. He knows that the animal is clean which both chews the cud and divides the hoof. It is right that he should first do and then teach, so that he may both understand from the commandments of the Lord and recognize that in the adornment of the priest the shoulder-piece (*superhumerale*) is to be placed first and the breastpiece (*rationale*) afterward.

Nehemiah the consoler, according to the interpretation of his name, repairs the walls of Jerusalem (2 Esdr. 3), building in them six gates, which are perhaps sight, hearing, taste, smell, speech, and touch. Behold: the Sheep Gate, the Fish Gate, the Old Gate, the Valley Gate, the Dung Gate, and the Fountain Gate.

And, coming to the times of grace, Jesus, seeing the crowds, goes up onto a mountain (Matt. 5:1); and on another occasion he goes up onto a mountain alone to pray (Matt. 14:23) [Col. 0815A].

The blessed John, destined to be the Lord’s forerunner, while still a boy, grows and is strengthened in spirit, remaining in the desert until the day of his manifestation to Israel (Luke 1:80).

Peter goes up to the upper room to pray, and not without hunger; afterward, through the splendid faith of Cornelius (Acts 10:9), he is soon to be satisfied.

The excellent preacher Paul urges Timothy (1 Tim. 4:13) that, when he comes, he should attend to reading, exhortation, and teaching (ibid., 16), asserting that by doing this he will save both himself and those who hear him (ibid., 8). He also says that bodily exercise is useful for a little, but that godliness is useful for all things, since it has the promise of the life that now is and of the life to come.

When the doors are closed, where the disciples have gathered because of fear, Jesus comes, stands in their midst, and says to them: “Peace be with you” (John 20:26). These three things will follow—coming, standing, and speaking—if these three things have preceded: in the evening, on that day, the first day of the week [Col. 0815B].

From the hand of the angel standing upon the sea and upon the earth, the apostle John receives a book in the Apocalypse (10:9); when he devours it, it makes his belly bitter. Yet it is sweet in his mouth, like honey.

The Lord Jesus, that angel of great counsel, mighty in deed and word, fulfilled Sacred Scripture: justifying by faith circumcision, which refers to the earth, and the foreskin, which refers to the sea, through faith, so that when the north wind gives way to the south, it may not hinder him.

When John receives this book, there is bitterness in his belly but sweetness in his mouth: one in fulfillment and experience, the other in remembrance and understanding.

If you attend diligently to all these things and to each one of them [Col. 0815C], O Carthusians, you will clearly perceive what kind, what quality, and how great the rest of the cell is. For, as the person who has experienced it knows, the more earnestly you attend to it, the sweeter, gentler, more pleasant, more serene, more delightful, easier, and clearer you will find it.

## CHAPTER IX. Concerning the rest of the cell, and that it is not beneficial for one who lives in it to remain outside it too long through rash curiosity

Everyone who dwells in a cell must know this and carefully store it in tenacious memory: the cell of which we are speaking does not wish the person who lives in it to remain rashly outside it for too long [Col. 0815D].

And who loves to remain rashly outside it for long, except one who is utterly ignorant of how many and how great are the goods contained in it? Indeed, just as it is fruitful to remain in it, so it is dangerous to wander outside it for a long distance or a long time. For the inhabitant of a cell cannot live spiritually outside the cell any longer than a fish can live bodily outside the water.

Consider that for the little fish called the herring, one and the same moment means both being outside the water and breathing its last. And indeed the word *cella* is formed from *halec* (“herring”) when it is reversed.

Some, however, who do not consider the matter correctly, think that they are advising those who sometimes become weary in the cell [Col. 0816A] if they make them go outside. But these people are deceived by a mere appearance of insufficiently careful discretion. This is utterly unbeneficial.

For a certain momentary rest without rest, sweetness without sweetness, and consolation without consolation may be felt for a while; but without delay disturbed bitterness, bitter disturbance, and altogether intolerable desolation follow. As soon as he returns to the cell, the harshest agony and the harshest anguish of spirit, the gravest weariness of heart, and the most atrocious disembowelment of mind will seize, penetrate, and surround him within.

For whenever someone rashly leaves the cell to wander outside it for a shorter or longer time in curious and vain fashion, he returns like a new inhabitant, and when he comes back he feels and discovers himself to be another person from the one he was before he went out [Col. 0816B].

To this may be added what one woman says concerning herself: she went out full, but the Lord brought her back empty; henceforth she did not wish to be called Naomi but Mara (Ruth 1:21). For she had been beautiful before going out, but after returning she experienced herself, both to herself and within herself, as bitter.

And from what place did she go out? Was it not Bethlehem? And what was the cause of her departure? Was it not famine? And where did she go out to? Certainly, to the region of Moab. In that place, as the truthful history says, she lived in such a way that she was a sojourner there. And as long as she was there, she was a stranger. Why a stranger, except because she was not in what belonged to her but in what belonged to another? For her proper dwelling was nowhere else than Bethlehem.

What do you think these things signify? Why, then, do we hesitate to call the cell [Col. 0816C] a kind of Bethlehem—yet a spiritual, not temporal [Par. “bodily”], not a historical but a moral one?

In historical Bethlehem, the blessed Mother gave birth to Jesus Christ once. In this tropological Bethlehem, as everyone who has experienced it several times knows, the Mother bestows on us daily, indeed without ceasing, the grace of holiness, a fruit at once sweet and wholesome [Col. 0816D]. It is sweet because of the anointing, which is what the name Christ signifies; and wholesome because of salvation, which is contained in the name Jesus. For, as you know, the name Christ signifies “Anointed,” while the blessed name Jesus signifies “Savior.”

Therefore, if you wish to receive it, the one who inhabits the cell in the manner in which he ought to inhabit it receives from the mother of grace the spiritual fruit of true holiness, both delightful and sweet because of the exultation with which he rejoices inwardly. This means that, according to the tropological sense we are now following, blessed Mary gives birth to Christ in Bethlehem, delightful and sweet because of the inward exultation; and, according to the same sense, that blessed Mary feeds Jesus in Bethlehem, useful and wholesome because of the religious practice exercised outwardly.

But when we say these things, let no one think that we are making any distinction or division between Jesus and Christ, insofar as the one person who is so called is concerned. For there is no doubt that the one who is Christ is also Jesus. But because of the different interpretation of these names, we also understand a different signification in them.

The person is one, but the meanings of the names belonging to the same person are different. Thus [Col. 0817A] the name Jesus signifies one thing, and the name Christ another; yet one person is not signified by Jesus and another by Christ, because Jesus Christ, the Son of God, our Lord, Redeemer of the world, God and human, mediator of God and human beings, is not one and another, but one and the same.

Insofar as he is human, he pleads with the Father for us; insofar as he is God, he is propitious to us together with the Father, to whom he is equal in all things.

Thus, for the one who dwells fruitfully in the cell, grace confers through the mother a spiritual fruit that is sweet and wholesome. This is, according to a certain moral sense, in a certain manner, Christ Jesus being born in Bethlehem.

But although, according to the interpretation of its name, Bethlehem [Col. 0817B] is “house of bread”—since it is called the house of bread—there is nevertheless sometimes the presence of famine in it. Famine is present to it when the absence of bread is present to it.

Let me speak boldly to you: when weariness of heart, as sometimes happens, falls upon the inhabitant of the cell because a person, filled with many miseries, never remains in the same condition, and when torpor of spirit comes upon him, then there is famine in Bethlehem. Nevertheless, Naomi must not leave Bethlehem because of this famine—I advise you—but must know that after a time of want a time of abundance will come.

If she does go out, she should know that she will return altogether bitter and, as Naomi herself says of herself, will come back empty though she went out full [Col. 0817C]. She will go so far as to judge herself no longer to be called Naomi, but rather Mara.

Behold: where once there was beauty, now there is bitterness; likewise, where there was fullness before, there is now emptiness. The cause of so great and so horrible an evil is that departure alone, made according to this meaning.

## CHAPTER X. That the cell must be continually held by the one who inhabits it; and what danger comes to him if he leaves it rashly
We have said some things about the cell, and that it is wholly inappropriate for anyone who inhabits it to leave it too childishly; and that, once outside it (which ought nevertheless to happen rarely, and only for rational reasons), he should not remain away from it through excessively reckless wandering. For, to show more fully now—as we have already shown in part—how dangerous such a departure is, behold: the truthful history says that Dinah went out, and that she went out to see—not men, but women (Gen. 34:2)—and she herself was a woman. Nor is this surprising, for it is commonly said: “Like seeks like”; and this testimony is true.

And what do we understand by “woman” except softness? For we are not now dealing with sex, but are indicating, by what may be understood from her natural weakness, the reprehensible weakness of either sex. Everyone, therefore, who is reprehensibly soft is, in a certain manner, a woman: not naturally, with regard to sex, but reprehensibly, with regard to conduct. The wise man says:

> He who is soft and negligent in his work is a brother to him who dissipates his own work. (Prov. 18:9)

Does this man not seem to you, in some way, to be a woman, whom we know to resemble one who is soft, negligent, and dissipating? Such is Dinah as she goes out: by her is signified the person who reprehensibly leaves the cell. And one who is such goes out for this purpose: to see such persons—namely, women.

And what is it for her to see except to love? For wherever love extends itself, there the eye also turns; and where there is sight, there too is affection. Indeed, “love iniquity, and iniquity will love you.” Thus she who went out to see was herself also seen; for Scripture says: “When Shechem had seen her, he added that he loved her” (Gen. 34:2). That seeing was plainly loving, because, wherever reckless sight has gone before, illicit love subsequently follows.

David would not have illicitly desired the woman as she bathed if he had not first seen her incautiously. And he slept with her—there can be no doubt that Shechem did likewise with Dinah. This is nothing other than for the soft and negligent man, resembling one who dissipates, because he has not avoided a reckless departure from the cell, to admit into himself and toward himself an illicit sweetness, by damnably consenting to the flesh, the world, and the devil; and through experiencing it to reach eternal perdition [Par.: damnation].

> As one who ravished a virgin.

Behold: before her departure she was a virgin, but afterward she was corrupted. For what is it for her to be ravished except to be corrupted? Yet she was overcome by force, and it is evident that she did not go out for the purpose of being ravished; nevertheless, because she admitted a reckless departure, because she aspired to illicit sight, through this twofold preceding guilt she was judged worthy and deserved to encounter that ravishment—which followed, or rather came upon her—even though it was violent.

But what does the history say at the end about her who thus went out, was thus seen, thus loved, thus corrupted, and thus ravished? Observe: “He soothed her grief with caresses.” Behold: Dinah is indeed grieving, but her corrupter and ravisher attempts to soothe her with caresses. This is the seductive speech with which he strives to soothe her grief:

> Why is your soul sad, O Dinah, and why do you trouble yourself? Are you grieving because you went out? What wrong have you done in this? What religious obligation is it that you should sit shut up alone in the house? What authority supports such a religion, if indeed it is a religion, that you should remain alone in the house night and day? Did blessed Benedict institute it? Did that great Augustine? Are the religious and holy Cluniacs, Cistercians, and the many other orders who do not lead such a life therefore not religious and holy? And if this is perhaps tolerable in certain others, it is by no means tolerable in you, who are such and so great. For in you, more than in many others, there abounds profound knowledge, polished eloquence, discernment in the heart, and a word of learning on the lips. Yet what use is there in all these things? All of them are hidden. Therefore manifest yourself to the world, and be in the world—in which, if you wish, you can be without being of the world. Do not remain shut up in the house any longer, knowing that it is far more useful and fruitful for you to save many with yourself than yourself alone.

Soothed by these caresses, this foolish woman gladly listens to the seductive songs of the Siren; she now saves no one, and moreover loses herself. Behold what and how great, how many and how grievous evils she has already incurred who went out recklessly. For all these things that have been said about Dinah we refer to the person who, with curiosity excessively reckless and with recklessness no less curious, leaves the cell in mind as well as in body.

## CHAPTER XI. On the great and numerous dangers incurred by one who inhabits a cell but leaves it wrongly, and on the great tranquillity of soul conferred by the complete and perfect rejection of secular things

Accordingly, as Scripture says, Dinah went out, and she went out to see. Having gone out to see, she herself was seen, to her great harm. Having been seen, she was also loved. Having thus been loved, she suffered corruption; to this she was drawn by a certain violent compulsion, though perhaps also voluntarily. For carnal pleasure was the cause that she could be drawn in this way; and she could be so drawn because she did not resist very strongly and did not oppose it with her whole will.

Indeed, long ago it was first said: “Each person is drawn by his own pleasure.” And lest, after all these things, this wretched and foolish transgressor should return to her heart and, grieving according to God, turn toward repentance, even in her sadness she is soothed with caresses.

O how great and how numerous are the evils! And what was the occasion and origin of all of them, or what was their cause? Certainly, her reckless departure; for she would have incurred none of these evils if she had kept herself inside. But because she went out curiously, she came damnably to these evils. Since curiosity was the cause of her going out, this is plainly shown by the testimony of Scripture: she went out in order to see. Pleasure was also joined to this curiosity, because she went out to see women.

O curiosity, dangerous beyond measure! For it lost outside the precious deposit that afterward it could never recover. A virgin went out, and returned corrupted; and she grieved that outside she had lost that lofty state of purity to which she could no longer climb.

So too that hairy man, bristling like a skin [i.e. Esau, Gen. 27], by remaining too long outside, made himself alien to his father’s blessing and could not thereafter attain it. For, as the Apostle says, “desiring to inherit the blessing, he was rejected.” For, as the same Apostle adds, “he found no place for repentance, although he sought it with tears” (Heb. 12:17).

Therefore, as was said much earlier, departure from the cell does not bring consolation to one who is perhaps sometimes afflicted there by weariness; rather, it brings a twofold desolation. This happens like what happens to a dropsical person: the more eagerly he drinks, the more violently he kindles thirst within himself, so that to drink much is for him to thirst more greatly.

What, then, should be done? Whenever anyone feels himself afflicted by weariness, let him, as though placing his body there as a pledge, entrust it to the wall of the cell; and, thinking not at all about going out, let him return to prayer, reading, meditation, and some useful activity. Certainly, without delay, according to his custom, that Father of mercies and God of all consolation will come. After the storm he will make things tranquil; he will turn the cloudy sky into clear weather; he will strengthen the fainthearted, gladden the sorrowful, fortify the weak, confirm the wavering, lead the faltering to stability; and, driving away the winds on every side and calming the waves, he will transform the turbulent sea into a calm and secure shore.

Go, therefore, and learn what this means:

> He is my God, my Savior, my helper; I shall not depart. (Ps. 61:7)

Keep yourselves more strictly in the cell whenever you feel that some weariness has arisen there, as often happens. Recall that the maiden who was soon to become the Mother of God, while preserving her virginity, was found within, in the innermost chambers, when she was visited by Gabriel. For you read:

> The angel entered to her. (Luke 1:28)

It is clear that she was not outside but within; the angel could not, as it were, come to her unless he entered.

But it is more than enough to remind you of this. For in the complete and perfect practice of these things you have anticipated both us and our discourses. We have said these things, nevertheless, so that we might show you in some measure what spiritual fruit there is in the silence and solitude of the cell. They are more old than new to you, since, by the Lord’s favor, you have already learned them through long and continuous experience. Hence you do not need to be instructed about them through the ministry of our speech.

But how great and how tranquil is the fruit of the soul in the complete rejection of the world, and how fruitful is that tranquillity, we can clearly estimate from the many forms of distress endured by those who are entangled in the world’s cares and anxieties. Since it is too lengthy—indeed impossible—for us at present to express these distresses one by one, I wish now to offer one sufficiently appropriate example, by which those who need it may learn how great is the difference between the occupation of such people and the tranquillity of the saints who serve God in leisure without idleness.

Behold: those lukewarm people, often wholly uncertain about their own life and generally frustrated in every hope, labor anxiously against the storms of tempests, the savagery of waves, and the violence of winds. These others, however, wholly free from all such things and from the other dangers of this kind, stand secure and joyful in the serene and pleasant tranquillity, in the tranquil and pleasant serenity, in the serene and tranquil pleasantness of some most peaceful shore.

O what loss there is among the former, and what gain among the latter, who are “as having nothing and possessing all things”! For the former despair and no longer live; they rejoice greatly at finding a grave, their soul choosing hanging and their bones death; and therefore, sleeping, they are silent and rest in their sleep, the fear of evils having been removed.

For they know that wisdom must be written in a time of emptiness, and that “he who is diminished in activity will find it”; and that they must have leisure so that they may see God, because the Lord himself is God. For the abyss says of Wisdom, “It is not in me,” and the sea says, “It is not with me” (Job 28:14).

## CHAPTER XII. On the rejection of secular business, anxieties, and possessions, to which the Carthusians devote special attention

[Col. 0821A]

You possess this separation from the world in abundance, since you do not concern yourselves with the revenues of churches, parishes, or tithes, content with your poverty, which is full of riches. You do not wish to possess anything outside your boundaries, nor ought you to do so, so that you may provide more abundantly for your tranquillity and peace.

In order that you may proceed by this short, secure, and undefiled way toward the kingdom of God, your predecessors and Fathers instructed you by both example and word—men who preferred to be poor rather than rich. For, if Paul is not mistaken:

> Those who wish to become rich fall into temptation and into many useless and harmful desires, which plunge people into destruction and perdition. (1 Tim. 6:9)

And he adds:

> For the root of all evils is greed; by desiring it, some have wandered from the faith and pierced themselves with many sorrows. (1 Tim. 6:10)

And immediately there follows a salutary admonition:

> But pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, patience, and gentleness. (1 Tim. 6:11)

And earlier:

> Having food and clothing, let us be content with these things. (1 Tim. 6:8)

Concerning this rejection of secular business and earthly possessions, so that it might be held, maintained, and guarded unchanged and inviolate in the order for all time, that venerable man of holy memory, the lord Guigo, a man of great religious devotion, writes as follows (Statutes, ch. 41):

> Cutting off, as far as we are able with God’s help, occasions of greed for ourselves and for our successors, we decree by the sanction of this present writing that the inhabitants of this place shall possess absolutely nothing outside the boundaries of their wilderness: neither fields, nor vineyards, nor gardens, nor churches, nor cemeteries, nor offerings, nor tithes, nor anything of this kind.

The man of God also adds the following:

> It has likewise been decreed that they shall bury in their cemetery no one who has died, whether within or outside this wilderness, unless it should happen that someone belonging to this way of life dies here. If, however, someone from another religious community dies here and his own community is either unable or unwilling to carry him away, they shall bury him. They shall not write anyone’s name in their Martyrology, nor shall they celebrate anyone’s anniversary according to custom.

Lest this perhaps seem too harsh and cruel to anyone, the aforementioned servant of Jesus Christ, a man who in his own time—and as is still evident today—was distinguished both for religious devotion and for learning, clearly shows by what reasonable cause, with what prudent intention, and to prevent what evils this institution was established. He adds:

> For we have heard—though we do not approve it—that many people hold splendid banquets as often as someone wishes to provide them in honor of his dead, and have Masses celebrated as often as they are prepared to offer them. This custom removes abstinence and makes prayers saleable, since as many Masses are celebrated as there are courses of food. Nor is there any established purpose of fasting or entreaty where the matter depends not on the devotion of the one who performs it but rather on the will of the one who provides the feast. No day will lack a banquet or a Mass if someone to feed them is never lacking.

And enough concerning these matters.

The same man says earlier, in this way (Guigo, Statutes, ch. 40):

> We possess no ornaments of gold or silver in the church except the chalice and the tube through which the Lord’s blood is received. We leave aside cloaks and tapestries; we do not accept gifts from usurers or excommunicated persons.

Thus the man of God writes concerning these matters.

You, however, O Carthusians, carefully and with every solicitude observe these things, and you do well. You do well for this reason: the less you receive from the world, the less you owe to it. But this must also be added: the less you attend to the world and to the things that belong to the world—not only in affection but also in action—the more freely and purely, the more sincerely and sweetly, the more fully and perfectly you can attend to God alone. Thus, as you advance toward the desert of perfection, you do not permit even a hoof to remain in Egypt of all that is necessary for the divine sacrifice.
