You have fully and perfectly understood all these things that we have said as belonging to these three matters: namely, to your external exercise, to the continuous solitude of the cell that you maintain, and finally to the complete rejection of the world and of the things that belong to the world.

You should not, we think, find it absurd that we have called the lofty sweetness—and likewise the sweet loftiness—of your order, which these three things commend, a kind of paradise.

It truly is paradise: a garden of delights, filled with every pleasure and full of every kind of loveliness. But let this paradise be watered; for that is both reasonable and very good. Its irrigation is its growth; its irrigation is its progress. For it is watered when strength and increase are imparted to it.

It is paradise, and it is necessary that it be watered. For in spiritual conduct, not to progress is to fail. Since, as Scripture says, “when a man has finished, then he begins” (Sirach 18:6), it is clear that paradise is indeed paradise, yet nevertheless needs irrigation.

Furthermore, since, as blessed Job says (Job 14:1), and as we all continually experience, a human being born of woman never remains in the same state, he either rises to higher things by the gift of the grace that strengthens him, or descends to lower things under the weight of his own weakness.

Therefore it is clearer than light from these considerations that those who are not concerned to increase their spiritual progress plainly fall into the most hideous decline. Those who are such, as was said long before us, fall into the danger of failing precisely where they have laid aside the desire to progress.

For this reason paradise must be watered, because the one who has been washed also needs to have his feet washed. And although Paul labored more than all the apostles, he nevertheless declares himself unworthy to be called an apostle.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the place of holy delight and on the spiritual flight of holy Jacob

“How,” someone may ask, “will this paradise be watered?”

What is written in Genesis? How do you read it? Does Scripture not say that a river went out from the place of delight to water paradise? (Gen. 2:10.)

And what river is this—or rather, what is this place of delight? For this must first be investigated, since, just as irrigation proceeds from this river, so the river’s going forth proceeds from the place of delight.

Thus, as is evident from these things, it is difficult—indeed impossible—for this paradise to be watered unless a river, whoever or whatever it may be, first goes forth from the place of delight.

Since this is so, what is this place of delight? It seems to us, if this is agreeable to you, that the sweet and pleasant unanimity of sincere charity which, according to God, you possess among yourselves—pure and cleansed, good and joyful, willing in Christ, as far as knowledge and ability permit, to reject every evil and desire every good—can and ought not inappropriately to be called a place of delight.

Truly, this is a place of delight—of delight, I mean, not carnal but spiritual; not a delight by which flesh or spirit is defiled, but rather one by which both spirit and flesh are purified, adorned, and beautified.

This is the place to which the one who flees from the face of the hairy man threatening him with death comes, and in which he wishes to rest when the sun has already gone down. For the truthful history says:

> When he had come—without doubt Jacob—to a certain place, he wished to rest there after sunset. (Gen. 28:11)

Who is this fugitive except the one of whom Isaiah gives command in the burden concerning Arabia to those who dwell in the south, that they meet him with bread? He is every chosen believer who increasingly withdraws himself from carnal or worldly excess, lest he incur death.

It is very necessary that the inhabitants of the southern land meet him with bread, so that those who are spiritual may instruct such persons in the spirit of gentleness, and so that the Lord may not send away from their houses those who have sustained him for three days fasting, lest they fail on the way.

“They fled,” he says,

> from the face of swords, from the face of the imminent sword, from the face of the drawn bow, from the face of grievous battle. (Isa. 21:15)

All these things concern the death with which the hairy man, Esau, threatens the gentle man, Jacob. To avoid incurring it, he prepares to secure himself by flight.

Thus the fugitive comes to a certain place. And it is the place of delight, because it is a place of rest; for this too follows:

> He wished to rest there after sunset.

When did the sun set? When the heat of temptation subsided. It is impossible for this fugitive to rest here before that sun sets, because as long as the heat of temptation burns the mind, it does not rest in the serenity of inward tranquillity; and consequently it has not yet reached the place of spiritual delight.

For how can there be sweetness where there is no tranquillity?

But this fugitive comes to this place and rests in it when he apprehends a sweet tranquillity according to God and an equally tranquil sweetness—when he apprehends them, holds them, and, holding them, does not let them go.

Now let him take a stone from among the stones that lie there—that is, from among the men of riches who humble themselves in the city of the Lord of hosts, in the multitude of true strength—and let him place beneath the head of his mind, through imitation, that one who is the Holy One of all the saints. Clinging to him, let him sleep in that same place: sleep, I say, with regard to tranquillity; in the same place, with regard to sweetness, so that both his rest may be sweet and his sweetness tranquil.

And in this sweetness and in this tranquillity, with the eyes of his mind purified, let him behold the ladder of charity: lowered at the bottom through compassion for his neighbor and fixed at the top through desire for God. Let him also behold the angels, who are heralds of the truth, ascending through contemplation and descending through action; and let him behold leaning upon that ladder the one who will repay the labors of his saints.

Then, struck with awe and trembling with astonishment, returning to himself through awakening, let him cry out and say:

> Truly, the Lord is in this place.

Where is the Lord, if not in tranquillity from which all disturbance is absent? Where, if not in sweetness in which every delight is present and no bitterness at all?

And he says:

> And I did not know it.

Nor is this surprising, for he could not know it until he was granted the experience of it. But from the time when he came to that place, took stones from it, placed one beneath his head, slept, and while sleeping saw the ladder and what was happening upon it, he knew.

Nor do we mean by this that he knew while coming, taking, placing, and sleeping—as though these actions could confer this knowledge upon him if he had not seen the ladder and the things belonging to it. Rather, these four things preceded so that the fifth could follow; and the sixth, namely knowledge, followed—or rather accompanied—it.

Therefore he knew when he saw; and just as he would not have known had he not seen, so he would not have seen had he not slept, nor slept had he not placed the stone beneath his head, nor placed it there had he not taken it, nor taken it had he not come.

Thus, when he saw, he knew, because when he experienced it—and to the extent that he experienced it—he then knew to that extent. For in a matter so great and such as this, no more knowledge is comprehended than the experience itself perceives.

He also added:

> How terrible is this place!

Nothing is more true. It is terrible to the devil, terrible to the world, and terrible also to the wicked man—terrible like an army drawn up in battle array.

It is lovable only to the one who flees from the face of the hairy man and, although he himself is gentle, is bristling like a skin. It is accessible only to him.

This is nothing other than the house of God and the gate of heaven. And this too is true: nothing beneath heaven is, or can be, truer. For in this place above all God remains, and through it there is also entry into heaven.

## CHAPTER XIV. How the river goes forth spiritually from the place of delight to water paradise, and what that river is

This is especially the place of God, where the voice of a great commotion is heard: “Blessed is the glory of the Lord from his place.” For the cloth that had been over the head of the buried Lord was also found, after his resurrection, wrapped separately in one place.

Why is this place called “one,” unless because it is the place of delight? For God is not in a division of minds but in unity; and where unity is absent, there is no true sweetness of soul.

This place is your unanimity, such as we briefly described above. From this place great and numerous rivers flow forth; for it is a place of rivers, where the streams are broad and open.

But the river that flows most powerfully from that place, so that your paradise may be watered, is not a river that shares, associates, or agrees with those rivers of which the Psalmist says when addressing the Lord:

> You dried up the rivers of Ethan. (Ps. 73:15)

Nor is it like those of which Habakkuk says to the same Lord:

> You will cleave the rivers of the earth. (Hab. 3:10)

Still less is it like those called Abana and Pharpar, the rivers of Damascus.

Rather, it can and ought to be compared to the river called the Jordan, in which Naaman the Syrian washed and, having washed, was cleansed (2 Kings 5:12, 14); and to the waters of Siloam, in whose pool the man born blind washed and was enlightened (John 9:7).

It can also in part be compared to that river of which Saint John writes in the Apocalypse, in the seventh vision:

> He showed me—without doubt the angel—a river of living water, bright, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb. (Rev. 22:1)

For no one who wishes or is able to contradict it will deny that the throne of God and of the Lamb is the place of an incomprehensible delight.

From that throne flows the incomprehensible, abundant, living, and eternal happiness by which the elect will enjoy blessedness forever, in the unceasing contemplation of the divine vision.

For concerning this the Lord says to his elect:

> They will give into your lap a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and overflowing. (Luke 6:38)

Behold the measure without measure, of which what overflows is spoken. But this is not in the present; it will be in the future. Nevertheless, these words can be understood not only of that happiness which those who are judged worthy will enjoy as their reward, but also of the holiness with which they are now enriched as merit.

But, so as not to delay you longer, it seems to us that the fervent and unceasing devotion of your pure minds is a river flowing perpetually. It then goes forth from the place of delight, appearing outwardly among you as though proceeding into public view, yet not departing from it; by going forth it does not leave the secret place of your unanimity, which we described earlier.

The devotion by which you are inwardly inflamed toward God and the things of God is this river. It goes forth when it is manifested by definite outward signs, when the mind itself, because of its excessive force, is not permitted to restrain it.

This is the river that goes forth from the place of delight to water paradise. Behold: we have already told you what this paradise is, what the place of delight is, what this river is, and what it means for this paradise to be watered; and you have heard it.

## CHAPTER XV. That the priors who assemble for the annual Chapter ought diligently to attend to renewal of the order; and on the four holy exercises to which everyone who wishes to remain fruitfully in the cell ought diligently to devote himself

Therefore, if this river exists among you—or rather, within you (and I am speaking to you, our reverend fathers and priors, who have assembled for the annual Chapter)—if, I say, this river exists among you and within you, or rather, because it does exist, know that the time is now present, or rather already at hand, for it to go forth and water paradise.

And you ask: How will this happen?

As was shown above. Come together into one spiritual consensus according to God, from God, for God, and with God, just as you have already come together bodily in one place. Individually and all together, with great devotion and with that zeal which is according to knowledge—that is, with a discerning concern for the restoration, renewal, and strengthening of the order—apply yourselves vigorously both to correcting whatever evils may exist and to establishing, increasing, and confirming what is good.

Therefore lift up your eyes and see the regions, whether they are already white for harvest or—God forbid—dry for burning. Rise early and go to the vineyards; see whether the vine has blossomed, whether the flowers are producing fruit, whether the pomegranates have flowered. There above all the bride will give her breasts to the bridegroom.

As for how these things apply, we avoid explaining them more openly, investigating them more deeply, or declaring them more fully because, so far as actual experience is concerned, you cannot be ignorant of them if you strive to exercise your office continually and manfully, according to place and time, business and circumstance, measure and manner—so far as is permitted, fitting, and useful.

But let this river take the greatest care to go forth in this way from the place of delight to water paradise, so that it may be divided from there into four heads. For the truthful history reports this (Gen. 2:10). We, however, if you have no better interpretation at present, refer these four heads to as many exercises of holy religion, in which the whole form [Par.: *summa*, “sum total”] of our order consists.

They are reading, meditation, prayer, and action; of these four, the greatest is prayer.

Whenever we are free from bodily necessities—for as long as we live here we are compelled to serve them—we must be found in one of these four and attend to it with the greatest diligence.

Reading ought to be clearly understood and retained in memory. Meditation ought not to be obscured by the darkness of any fantasy, but illuminated by the full light of truth. Prayer ought to be inflamed by a heavenly desire in complete purity and pure sincerity, and be moistened by the outpouring of pious tears—whole, upright, direct, and lifted up.

Action, for its part, must be wholly free from lukewarmness, sluggishness, disturbance, and murmuring. It must be corrupted by no plague of wickedness, omitting everything that can do harm and, with perfect solicitude, alacrity, cheerfulness, and vigor, admitting whatever can be beneficial, according to knowledge and ability, and adorning itself with every approved exercise.

Unless we diligently and unceasingly take care to devote ourselves to these four holy exercises of holiness, we cannot remain fruitfully in our cells.

How sweet, how pleasant, how good, how joyful, how delightful, and how lovable it ought to seem to the servant of God, hidden in the cell, to attend to these four things: now to apply himself diligently to reading, now to devote himself to pure prayer, now to give his diligence to necessary action; and so that in each of these his mind may be absent from the meditation that has been cleansed of impurity for no hour or moment.

For whenever meditation is absent from any one of these, that exercise is in no way fully fruitful. Without its presence, reading cannot be grasped and retained through understanding; prayer cannot be suspended and remain in the heights; and action cannot be extended and directed toward what is necessary and useful.

Therefore it is very necessary that meditation precede, accompany, and follow each of the other three. It must precede each one so that it may be begun well; accompany it so that what has been begun well may be fully completed; and follow it so that what has been fully completed may be firmly strengthened.

Take comfort—I speak to you who inhabit the cell—take comfort, I say, and rejoice in the Lord, with the Lord, and for the Lord, because the tranquillity that you hope to possess in the future you already have and hold now, in a certain manner, in some of its first beginnings.

We say to you boldly: if you are in the cell as you ought to be, then, in a certain manner, you are in heaven itself.

Behold: you read and pray, meditate and work. These are the exercises to which you devote yourself in the cell.

How holy is your mouth, and how holy also your ear! When you pray—if, that is, you pray in the manner in which you ought to pray—your mouth is in the ear of God. And should I hesitate to call that mouth holy which I see in God’s own ear?

When you read, the mouth of God is in your ear. And shall I not call this ear holy?

Whether, then, you speak to God—which you certainly do when you pray—or God speaks to you—which plainly occurs when you read—I unhesitatingly declare you blessed.

What shall I say about pure meditation? What about excellent action? The former sanctifies the soul; the latter adorns the hand.

Who could deny that God is within you when in your mind there is nothing that is not good and holy, nothing that is not sincere and religious, nothing that is not gentle and devout, nothing that is not pure and clean, so far as the matter of guilt is concerned; but whatever belongs to holiness and goodness, sincerity and religion, gentleness and devotion, purity and cleanness is active within it?

Who, likewise, could then deny that he is with you when you perform nothing except what is useful?

These, then, are the four exercises to which you, who inhabit the cell, devote yourselves continually in the cell: diligent reading, pure meditation, heartfelt prayer, and necessary action.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the commendation of the cell, and on those four heads into which the river is divided that goes forth from the place of delight to water paradise

[Col. 0827D]

What better, or more agreeable, should you, who are an inhabitant of the cell, judge there to be than diligently to alternate these practices day and night? Indeed, it is so sweet for you to apply yourself to them, and you find such sweetness in each one, that when you devote yourself to one, you can scarcely be torn away from it to turn to another. You perceive each of these to be more flavorful and sweet to you the more you perceive their flavor and sweetness—not merely often, but always; not merely frequently, but without interruption. And indeed, you eat and drink when you devote yourself earnestly to them; [Col. 0828A] but this eating in you increases hunger more than it diminishes it; and to drink much is nothing other than to thirst more deeply. Thus it is found to be true what Wisdom herself says of herself: “Those who eat me will hunger still, and those who drink me will thirst still” (Eccli. XXIV, 29).

When can faintheartedness of spirit, turmoil of mind, agony of heart, or some weariness afflict you, when this fourfold exercise flourishes within you? Why, then, do some people shrink from the solitude and quiet [Par., *silentium*, “silence”] of the cell and consider enduring it burdensome, except because they are entirely ignorant of how great, how excellent, and how sweet its delight is?

To whom shall I compare you, or to whom shall I liken you, who are a lover and inhabitant of the cell; who inhabit it by loving it, and love it by inhabiting it? [Col. 0828B] What person in this life is superior to you in this experience of sweetness? For, as it seems to me, no such person is found. But who could even equal you? Is it perhaps one of those who are supreme lords of worldly affairs? No one at all. To be sure, they may perhaps seem superior to you with regard to a certain dangerous dignity in name and outward appearance, for which and on account of which they will have to render an account at God’s strict judgment. But with regard to this singular sweetness in which you rejoice and exult—this pleasure, delight, joy, cheerfulness, liveliness, beauty, serenity, sincerity, enjoyment, and, finally, to sum up many things in a few words, this fullness of every good and a certain image and likeness of that [Col. 0828C] heavenly blessedness for which we long—all of them are far beneath and inferior to you.

O how great, and how abundant, is the sweetness in these four exercises: in reading, meditation, prayer, and action! Great: no measure reaches it. Abundant: I see that it has no number. And perhaps these four are those four heads into which the river is divided that goes out from the place of delight to water paradise. Let us now see what Scripture says about these four heads:

“The name of the one is Phison, the name of the second river Gyon, the name of the third river Tigris; and the fourth river is Euphrates.”

Of Phison it is said that it surrounds all the land of Evilath; of Gyon, that it surrounds all the land of Ethiopia; and Tigris runs toward the Assyrians. It is not said, however, that Euphrates surrounds any land, or where it goes; [Col. 0828D] it is only said that the fourth river itself is Euphrates. Was any of this said without purpose? Certainly not. Let us therefore attend to it.

They say that the name Phison means “mouth of the pupil.” And if this is true, then just as sight may be referred to the pupil, so speech may be referred to the mouth; for in the mouth is the tongue with which we speak, and in the eye the pupil with which we see. And where do we see what is true, so that we do not wander in the darkness of falsehood, except in diligent reading of Sacred Scripture? And when, by the order’s permission, we come together on feast days to speak, what, I ask, should we speak about except those things contained in the reading of Sacred Scripture?

Appropriately, then, by “mouth” and “pupil” the study of sacred reading is expressed, in which the light of truth shines, through which we attain to the brightness of luminous knowledge; [Col. 0829A] and we read the word of sacred instruction, about which we confer with one another for the edification both of ourselves and of our brothers.

The first of these matters is spoken of by Peter in his Second Epistle: “We have,” he says, “the prophetic word made more certain, to which you do well to attend, as to a lamp shining in a dark place” (II Petr. I, 19). Of the second, holy David speaks, addressing the common Lord of all: “Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light to my paths” (Psal. CXVIII, 105).

## CHAPTER XVII. That the inhabitant of the cell must avoid every unlawful form of speech, and what good things sacred reading advances us toward

[Col. 0829B]

You, therefore, servant of God, who live alone in the cell—and yet do not dwell there alone—if you grasp through full knowledge everything that pertains to Sacred Scripture, you attain to a certain most radiant vision in your mind. And whenever you are granted permission to speak, if you take care to occupy your tongue with these matters, you will have not only an inwardly illumined vision, but also a mouth inwardly cleansed and adorned.

Thus, thus, you will not without reason be able to interpret Phison as “the mouth of the pupil,” through which, as we have said, we can receive sacred reading, since through it you acquire both such clarity in your inward sight and, outwardly in your mouth, the word of truth, for your edification and that of those who hear you.

Far be it—once and again, often and always—that in the cloister, on feast days, when you open your [Col. 0829C] mouth to speak, you should take up disordered loquacity in that same mouth of yours. This is wholly unbecoming to your gravity and maturity. It will scarcely be apparent that on other days you have shown yourself devoted to diligent reading, pure meditation, and heartfelt prayer if, when you open your mouth to speak, you accommodate your tongue, through bad habit, to loquacity or garrulity, and especially to dispute and contention. All these things—and every foolish and empty, lying, deceitful, idle, immodest, excusing, slanderous, threatening, angry, or proud word—are wholly alien to those spiritual exercises to which you ought to devote yourself in the cell.

Remember what Truth herself [Col. 0829D] says: “For every idle word that people speak, they will give an account of it on the day of judgment” (Matth. XII, 36). If an account must be rendered for an idle word, how much more for a harmful one? Although an idle word cannot in fact be harmless. But here we call a word harmful when it is deceptive, flattering, quarrelsome, false, or any other criminal word of this kind; for crime is often present in the mouth just as it is in the body.

The remaining words of this sort, I say, by which God is greatly offended, everyone who hears them is seriously harmed, and the one who speaks them is subjected to grave sin—this is attested by the Lord himself: “By your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned” (Matth. XXII, 37). See with how great care you must beware of falling into that which will condemn you.

[Col. 0830A] Hence the blessed Benedict, father, leader, and advocate of monks, writes in the Rule of Monks: “Jesting, idle words, and speech that provokes laughter, we condemn everywhere by perpetual enclosure, and we do not permit the disciple to open his mouth for such speech” [Rule of St Benedict, chapter 6].

Know, dearest to us, you who inhabit the cell, that the conversations and trifles which are almost continually in the mouths of many secular people are blasphemies in the mouths of religious men, and especially in the mouths of Carthusians. Certainly, as the Lord says, “A good man brings forth good things from a good treasure” (Matth. XII, 35).

If reading, meditation, prayer, and useful action have been stored in the treasure of your heart through ardent love and continual exercise, then when your tongue moves to [Col. 0830B] speak, it will surely bring forth some one of these. If you act in this way, your inner sense will be illumined and your outward mouth beautified; and both these goods will be conferred upon you through diligent reading, so that it is not without a great mystery that Phison is interpreted as “the mouth of the pupil.”

This diligent reading, of which we have now said something, instructs us to sing a new song to the Lord and always to bring forth the newness of a holy life, because Phison also surrounds all the land of Evilath. In this bringing forth of holy newness, the gold of true wisdom is born, and the gold of that land—clearly, of Evilath—is the finest.

For there is a wisdom that is from above: first, pure; then peaceable, gentle, open to persuasion, agreeing with what is good, full of mercy and good fruits, judging without hypocrisy [Col. 0830C] [Jac. XIII, 17]. Is wisdom not, in fact, “sapid knowledge”? And the gold that is not merely good but finest is born in the land of Evilath when it is born both from a devout soul, in which the inward sight has been illumined through diligent reading of Sacred Scripture [Par., *intrinsecus*, “inwardly”], and in which nothing is brought forth outwardly in the mouth except what pertains to edification.

When such a soul devotes itself to bringing forth holy newness, it loves the good; and in its inward palate, after every unlawful sweetness has been completely rejected, nothing tastes sweet to it except God alone. It tastes in him what is the finest of all goods. Thus its name is Phison; thus it surrounds all the land of Evilath, where gold is born, and the gold of that land is finest.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the kinds of holy meditation to which one who sits alone in the cell ought to devote himself, and on diligent remembrance of Sacred Scripture

[Col. 0830D]

Moreover, the name of the second river is Gyon, which, being a bursting forth, surrounds all the land of Ethiopia. This is meditation, which, by resisting manfully and forcefully, breaks through whatever belongs to Ethiopian blackness—that is, to the deformity of sin—before it can, through consent, render the soul deformed.

For when the holy soul applies itself wholly to the purity of inward meditation, no temptation, however violent, can subject it to itself through consent. As soon as temptation begins to knock at the very door of the mind, if the mind has been perfectly occupied in purified meditation [the reading *meus* is uncertain, apparently for *mens*, “mind”] [Col. 0831A], its strength breaks off not so much what has already caused harm as what might newly be able to cause harm [Par., *praerumpit*, “breaks through”].

Therefore, you who inhabit the cell, just as diligent reading, which is Phison, tastes sweet to you when you drink its waters—which surround all the land of Evilath, where the finest gold is born—so let pure meditation, which also surrounds all the land of Ethiopia, taste sweet to you. For you vomit out with great danger whatever you have taken in by writing from the waters of Phison unless you immediately drink from the waters of Gyon.

Just as it is negligence to read without understanding, so surely to forget what has been read and understood is nothing other than to lose entirely whatever you acquired by reading and understanding.

There are, however, many kinds of meditation. When you devote yourself diligently to them, you will be able to draw your mind back toward firm [Col. 0831B] maturity and mature stability. Thus you will compel it to stand solidly within itself, so that it neither raises itself emptily above itself nor weakly casts itself down beneath itself. Nor, I say, will it become sordid when it has been instructed by that supreme Teacher concerning the swelling things of earth; nor will it become empty when it has been taught concerning the birds of heaven.

Just as the meditation of which we propose to speak has various forms, so they also produce various causes in the mind of the one who meditates. We place first the form through which a cause of instruction arises in the mind of the one who meditates; second, that which produces a cause of sorrow and fear; third, that which provides an occasion for love and consolation; [Col. 0831C] fourth, that from which the mind receives a cause of devotion and compassion; fifth, that from which comes a cause of discernment and self-abasement; sixth, that from which comes in the soul a cause of its renewal and restoration; seventh, that from which comes a cause of astonishment and wonder; eighth, that form through which those things are turned over in the mind of the one who meditates that are invisible and spiritual.

We also include that form by which the sober and holy mind, made wholly free and alien not only from every impure affection but also from every idle thought, beholds the Truth itself in those very realities that are true, through a vision not now spiritual, nor rational, but rather intellectual—and beholds it blessedly. Here the pure mind becomes blessedly exalted toward God. This can no longer be called simple meditation, [Col. 0831D] but excellent contemplation.

In this contemplation, and through it, the devout and inflamed mind transcends the whole body and all bodily images and likenesses. In the very light of Truth, in which all things truly are—past, present, and future; not otherwise past than future or present, nor present otherwise than past or future, nor future otherwise than present or past—it contemplates, by a simple gaze, all things that Truth has revealed to it simultaneously, always, and in the same manner.

Whatever has been purely grasped by the holy soul in this vision is clearly luminous and certain. This is the vision that, when imaginary and fantastic vision have been set aside, clarifies both sensory and spiritual vision, so that it becomes one who sees, speaks mysteries, discloses hidden things, or [Col. 0832A] announces things to come.

There are perhaps other kinds of meditation that produce causes reasonable and appropriate to themselves; but these are the ones that have occurred to us at present. And now hear more fully and perfectly, you who inhabit the cell, certain matters pertaining to these.

Therefore, to speak to you first about the first form: sitting in your cell, let your mind travel through all the books of the divine page. Let understanding accompany and illumine this silent rumination and remembrance of yours. Turn over within yourself—in your mind—the things contained in the legal books, the books of the prophets, and the hagiographers; as well as what is contained in the books belonging to the New Testament, namely the narratives and [Col. 0832B] genealogies, events and deeds of the evangelists, apostles, and catholic teachers; whether these things are to be understood historically, allegorically, tropologically, or, certainly, anagogically, rightly and in accordance with catholic teaching.

Lead your consideration from the very beginning of the world through the things that were done and said in four successive variations [Par., “narratives”], through six ages, three periods, and two states; and from the time of Christ’s Incarnation to the dregs of the present age, through the things that pertain to Christ himself, and also to the apostles, martyrs, confessors, and virgins.

How great a multitude of words there is in silence within your heart concerning each of these things! When you turn all these things, each and every one, over within yourself, can you be said to be alone in the cell? Certainly not. For when you apply yourself diligently to these matters, all the persons of whom the Old and New Scriptures speak, and of whom mention is made [Col. 0832C] in the Scriptures of the Fathers who lived after the Incarnation, are in a certain manner with you.

Indeed, this may perhaps be more extensive and more perfect because they are also within you. Here you will receive great and abundant instruction, for you grasp within yourself the entire universe of Sacred Scripture.

## CHAPTER XIX. On that form of meditation which produces in the mind of the one who meditates a cause of fear and sorrow, divided into eight forms

Another meditation follows this one, and it is, O you who inhabit the cell, one that pertains especially to you. Sitting in your cell, therefore, recall in the bitterness of your soul your years and your days; [Col. 0832D] turning over and over within yourself what evils, how many and how great, you have damnably committed, where and when, with what will and intention, and for how long, whether in your mind or in your flesh.

Think and rethink within yourself how weak you are in both mind and body, how inclined toward vices, how powerless for virtues, how burdened with many fears, afflicted by sorrows, wandering through errors, anxious with cares, and troubled by suspicions; to how many and how great dangers you are exposed, with what bonds you are bound, with what filth you are defiled, with what offenses you are filled, and beneath what masses of great and numerous evils you are oppressed.

Consider how you are almost incessantly torn apart by what is alien to you, mangled within yourself, lacerated inside yourself, scattered outside yourself, cast down beneath yourself—and prostrated below yourself, while also being emptily lifted above yourself. And because it would be exceedingly long, indeed impossible for us [Col. 0833A], to number all the calamities that wretched human beings suffer within and without, consider how you yourself are like those descending into the pit; and unless the gracious favor of your Creator assists you, you are in temptation like wax before the face of fire or like the lightest dust in the breath of a most violent wind.

After this, let your meditation represent to you in your mind how terrifying the Creator of the whole creation himself is in his counsels concerning the sons of men: neither washing away the evils of the reprobate nor accepting their good deeds, and moreover, by his just but hidden judgment, neither softening but even hardening their hearts, lest they should turn and be healed.

Consider within yourself what Ecclesiastes says: that there are righteous and wise people, and their works are in the hand of God; yet no one knows whether he is worthy of love or hatred [Col. 0833B] (Eccle. IX, 1). But everything is reserved for the future. Then things will be certain, when a person will no longer have either place or time in which to amend himself.

The same writer also says: “Consider the works of God, that no one can correct the one whom he has despised” (Eccle. VII, 14).

After this, set before the eyes of your consideration the departure of your soul from the body, portraying it now within yourself. How terrifying that hour will be for you—and therefore how greatly it must even now be feared! How great will be the trembling then in your soul and the affliction in your body, when bitter and hostile death separates from one another those two companions, as I may call them, who have been together for some time—that is, your body and your soul.

Meditate now within yourself, indeed inside yourself, on what will then be your state of mind: not only forgetfulness of all the things that exist in this [Col. 0833C] world, but also of all your loved ones, friends, and relatives. Then there will indeed be a departure from here, but it is wholly unknown where the migration will be. As someone says of himself: “I shall depart, but I do not know where; I do not know when.” Nor is any return of the spirit to the body expected before the last day, in accordance with that true saying of the holy man: “When a man sleeps, he does not rise again until the heavens are worn away; he will not awaken, nor rise from his sleep” (II Cor. V, 10).

The spirit leaves the body, and when it has left, the body dies. Thus the body that lived by the soul becomes soulless. For, as blessed Augustine says—and as we observe daily in those who go before us, just as survivors will observe it in us when our time comes—when [Col. 0833D] the soul departs, the one who walked lies down; the one who spoke is silent; closed eyes receive no light; ears open to no voice; and all the functions of the limbs come to rest. There is no longer anything that moves out to walk, hands to work, or senses to perceive.

Is this not the house that some invisible inhabitant adorned? The one who could not be seen has withdrawn; what can be seen with sorrow remains.

These are the things blessed Augustine says about this.

Now let your meditation turn to something else and foresee, as far as it can, the presentation of your soul, stripped from the body, before the tribunal of that terrifying and strict Judge. As the Apostle says: “We must all appear before the tribunal of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that each may receive what belongs to the [Col. 0834A] body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil” (Joan. XIV, 30).

There was one human being who alone entered on behalf of this matter without stain; he alone was free among the dead, and he alone could say: “The prince of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me.” There is no one among us in whom he does not possess something of his own.

After this, in your inward meditation, look with the eye of your consideration at what will become of your body after your soul has departed from it. Your meditation does not need to labor much in foreseeing this, because bodily sight itself makes you certain what you ought to think about it. Go now, open the tomb of whichever dead person you wish, and look inside. If you do this, will it not appear so horrifying to sight and smell that [Col. 0834B] neither sense could in any way endure it even for a moment?

Certainly, you will see a corpse horribly stinking, swarming with decay, and teeming with worms. And this body of which we are speaking will come to such a state that, after the soul’s departure, it will be stench; after stench, decay; after decay, a worm; and after the worm, dust more rejected, more worthless, more foul, and more fetid than every other dust.

## CHAPTER XX. On the general resurrection of the dead and the punishments of the damned, and how those eight forms in which the cause of fear and sorrow exists are to be recalled

Now let your meditation, you who inhabit the cell of which I am speaking to you, show you something about that future general resurrection of the dead on the last day, when, at the end of the age, [Col. 0834C] the King of kings himself and Judge of the living and the dead will come. He will come in great power and majesty to judge—the one who formerly came in weakness and humility to be judged.

And when he comes, as he himself promised, all his angels will come with him, and all nations will be gathered before him. Then he will say to the righteous, and therefore to those who are to be saved: “Come, blessed ones”; but to the unrighteous, and therefore to those who are to be condemned: “Depart from me, accursed ones.” To the former he will say: “Possess the kingdom”; but to the latter: “Go into eternal fire.”

O, possess the kingdom! O, go into eternal fire!

Then will truly be fulfilled what holy John narrated in his Apocalypse as though it were past, although it is still future, concerning the reprobate: “The angel,” he says, “lifted up a stone like a great millstone and cast it into the sea, saying: ‘[Col. 0834D] With such force that great city Babylon will be cast down, and it will no longer be found’” (Apoc. XVIII, 21).

This angel is the one who is called the angel of the great counsel; strong indeed, because the Lord himself is strong and powerful (Psal. XXIII, 8). He will cast that great dry straw of the reprobate, prepared for eternal fires—which is called a stone because of its insensible hardness, and a millstone because the impious walk about in circles [Psal. XI, 9]—into the sea of eternal damnation.

That millstone is the great Babylon, which will be cast into this sea in such a way that it will no longer be found.

This meditation usually occupies the soul for a long time, portraying before it, indeed within it, the supreme terror of the Judge who will then appear and the disclosure of all hidden things. For the judgment will sit, and the books of [Col. 0835A] past conduct and inward consciences will be opened; and each person will be judged according to what the books contain in writing.

Depict also the powers of heaven moved, the heavens and earth burning, and that terrible and dreadful vengeance which he will exercise against the reprobate, placing them like a furnace of fire at the time of his appearing, when he will trouble them and fire will devour them (Psal. XX, 10). It is a fire, as we read, that is not extinguished.

There are many other terrifying, dreadful, and fearsome things that the soul can in some fashion foresee if it applies itself anxiously and diligently to this meditation.

After this, let your meditation go around and traverse that dark land covered by the shadow [Col. 0835B] of death, the land of misery and darkness, where the shadow of death and no order dwell, but everlasting horror (Job X, 21–22). Let it see in that land the eternal punishments of the reprobate, the infernal Gehenna, where the fire will be unquenchable and the worm immortal; where also—to sum up innumerable things in a very few words—no good will be present, and no evil will be lacking.

Behold the eight meditations that I have set before you, who inhabit the cell: six in the preceding chapter, and two in this one. These eight meditations are divided within that second kind of meditation in which the cause of fear and sorrow alike resides.

We also wish to recount these eight meditations briefly by repetition, so that you may retain them more firmly in memory and turn them over within yourself whenever you wish.

The first concerns the many excesses—without number in relation to us, and immeasurable [Col. 0835C] in greatness—that we have damnably committed both in mind and in flesh.

The second concerns the miseries that likewise exceed all measure and admit no number, which we endure in heart and body: both those that pertain to guilt, by which we are defiled, and those that pertain to punishment, by which we are tormented.

The third concerns the most secret, most severe, and immovably fixed judgment in eternity by which that terrifying, just, watchful, and strict Judge, God, watches over the rational creature who is reprobate among the sons of men; whom he rejects from eternity and condemns for eternity. In this meditation we discover, not without great fear and terror, that we do not know on which path light dwells or where [Col. 0835D] the place of darkness is, nor whether we are worthy of love or hatred.

The fourth concerns that terrifying hour of dissolution in which body and soul will be separated from one another.

The fifth concerns the presentation of the soul before the tribunal of the Judge, when it will be presented there as it departs from here. Its enemy will appear there, accusing it of all the unlawful things it has committed that have not been erased through repentance, confession, and satisfaction; conscience will bear witness to them; and the Judge himself will render to it according to its merits.

The sixth concerns the emptied body of the soul being handed over to burial: earth entrusted to earth, ashes returning to ashes, flesh given as food to worms, reduced to decay, and after decay becoming utterly rejected dust.

The seventh concerns the [Col. 0836A] general resurrection of the dead and that dreadful judgment to which the whole human race will be gathered; the terror of the Judge in which he will appear to the reprobate; and the proclamation of the terrible sentence, which will be this: “Go, accursed ones, into eternal fire” (Matth. XXV, 41).

The eighth concerns the punishments of those same reprobates condemned for eternity. To these belongs what Isaiah says: “The fire that consumes, the worm that gnaws” (Isa. LXVI, 24), and the eternity of both: for of the former it is said that it will be unquenchable, and of the latter that it will be immortal.

## CHAPTER XXI. How fear drives out exaltation from the mind of the one who meditates, and on the third form of meditation, which provides an occasion for love and consolation
[Col. 0836B] These meditations, which we have set before you—eight in number, addressed to you who are an inhabitant of the cell—belong to that mode of meditation which we placed second. Of it we also said that it produces the cause of sorrow and fear. And we spoke truly: for what else does the mind of one who meditates find in each of these eight meditations than something that generates and occasions a powerful cause of fear and sorrow for it?

These are the meditations which, when the mind attends to them diligently, prick and strike, beat and scourge, wound and torment; they summon it to compunction and stir it to tears. For the soul suffers beyond measure when it attends diligently to these meditations within itself; it suffers, I say, and fears. It suffers greatly because it feels that it is presently enduring such grievous things; but it fears still more because it dreads that in the future it may endure far worse things. With this sorrow and fear was he filled who, shaken and pierced with compunction, said to that terrifying Judge: “Your wrath has passed over me, and your terrors have troubled me” (Psalm 87:17).

After his wrath has passed over us, his terrors also trouble us, because, although what we now endure seems to us unbearably harsh, we also fear that, as our faults require, we may at the end come to endure things far harsher, without end.

This mode of meditation, which we have divided into eight forms, gives you, who are an inhabitant of the cell, a certain fiery experience; just as the preceding mode leads you to a certain luminous and splendid understanding. And although each mode is exceedingly good, this one is more necessary for you: the former instructs you, but this one moves you; the former displays, as it were, many riches, but this one leads you to possess them. See that the man who possesses many riches should be called rich, not the man who merely sees them with his eyes—since they belong to another and are not his own.

There you will receive knowledge; here, wisdom. There, you receive it so that by recognizing you may know, and by knowing recognize; here, so that by fearing you may grieve, and by grieving fear. What exists there gives off, as it were, a faint fragrance to the sense of smell; what exists here is fully savored by the sense of taste.

It is dangerous for you to attend to the former unless you attend likewise to this one, because the former sometimes produces elation, whereas this one always produces humility. For “knowledge puffs up,” and understanding vainly exalts the mind; but sorrow, while scourging through compunction, causes inflation to subside, and fear, while tormenting as though by threats, presses down the empty exaltation of the mind.

Thus knowledge and understanding are often the cause of elation, but sorrow and fear are always the cause of profound humility. Therefore, in that first mode of meditation, you seem to behold a kind of immense light; in this second one, you feel a kind of immense heat. For that reason, immediately after you have attended carefully to the former, attend with no less diligence to this one also, so that, if you have perhaps soiled your feet in the former, you may wash them in this one as well.

Indeed, just as the first mode needs this second one, lest it raise you too vainly through the swelling of elation, so this second mode likewise needs a certain third mode, lest it cast you down too fatally through the horror of despair. Since, therefore, your mind, O inhabitant of the cell, finds in this second mode of meditation nothing except what belongs to sorrow and what is full of great bitterness, lest—God forbid—it be swallowed up by excessive sadness when it considers these things, it does well to set before itself certain joyful and sweet realities, both to mitigate this sadness and to prevent these bitter things from extending into what is excessive.

Therefore let this third mode of meditation represent inwardly to your mind how great are God’s sweetness and compassion, how great his clemency and goodness; that he is gracious to all; that his mercies are over all his works; that he is abundant in forgiveness; that he is more ready to spare than to punish; that he is long-suffering in waiting; that he is very merciful in forgiving; that he is the Father of mercies and the God of all consolation, who consoles his own in all their tribulation; and that, as a father has compassion on his children, so he also has compassion on those who fear him [Paris manuscript: “he himself also”].

Above all, let this meditation represent to your mind that he did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all, giving us everything in him and reconciling the world to himself in him and through him. Let it represent that the same Son loved us so greatly that he washed us from our sins in his blood; that for us he put on flesh, was disgraced upon the cross, and was subjected to death. He gave us his flesh and his blood, and his soul for us: his flesh for a hard, dreadful, and shameful passion; his blood for the most abundant outpouring from the five places of his most sacred body; his soul for its departure.

And if we wish to examine what lies more deeply within these things, he gave us flesh as food, blood as drink, and his soul as the price. What does this have to do with us? Everything, in every way: namely, so that we who are hungry may be refreshed, we who are dry may drink, and we who are captives may be redeemed.

Do you think that he who suffered so many and such great things for you will abandon you? Far be it from you to think so. How many people who had withdrawn from him farther than you has he called back to himself? For he is the one who, where sin abounded, makes grace abound all the more.

Holy David is a witness, for he committed a great sin. Defiled by adultery and stained with blood through murder, he added to this double evil the abomination of treachery. The cord by which he was bound was threefold: adultery, murder, and betrayal; foul, bloodstained, and deceitful. It was difficult—indeed, impossible—for it to be broken, except that where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more in him.

For these were his sins: incest, cruelty, and deceit. But where incest abounded, purity abounded all the more; where cruelty abounded, compassion abounded all the more; and where the deceit of betrayal abounded, the simplicity of purity abounded all the more.

Certainly those who are such are multiplied beyond number, if we wished—but cannot—to recall to memory all those whose iniquities the merciful and compassionate God forgives, whose sins he covers, washing them, justifying them, and sanctifying them in the Holy Spirit.

Thus, indeed, “as far as the east is from the west,” he has put their iniquities far from them, placing goodness where there was evil, merit where there was injustice, and grace where there was guilt.

This, then, is the third mode of meditation of which we told you, who are an inhabitant of the cell: it generates the opportunity and cause of love and consolation, just as the preceding mode, which is the second, provides the cause of fear and sorrow. And it is most necessary that this third mode follow the first, so that, just as the second empties the swelling of elation produced by the first, the third may remove from the second the horror of despair.

Thus, in these two modes—namely, the second and the third—your mind may sing to God not merely of mercy, lest rash presumption elevate it, nor merely of judgment, lest deadly despair swallow it up, but of mercy and judgment together. In this way it will not limp on one side of itself, nor—God forbid—stray from the straight path, but will strive to walk along the right road, turning neither to the right through foolish rejoicing in empty hope nor to the left through damnable trembling in profound despair.

## CHAPTER XXII  
### The fourth mode of meditation, which produces in the mind of the one who meditates the cause of piety and compassion; and that we should generally excuse within ourselves certain evils that we see being done by others rather than rashly judge them

There is also a fourth mode of meditation, of which you, who are an inhabitant of the cell, must understand that it produces the cause of piety and compassion. This mode appropriately follows the third, which provides you with the cause of consolation, so that, having been consoled, when you see people afflicted by misery or stained by guilt, you may hasten more readily to compassion than to judgment and show yourself more prepared to console than to reproach.

We have said this because those who appear clothed in the habit of religion—whether monks or regular clerics dwelling in their cloisters—or we ourselves, anchorites and hermits who live alone (would that we did so alone!), when they observe something that displeases them, also observe it without any discretion before their eyes and without any compassion. They often hasten to judge rather than to console; and how often do we do the same!

Why do you, who lurk in the corners of your cell, judge others—not indeed now in the likeness of a rapacious wolf, but biting more like a spiteful flea? And you do not judge as that just Judge does, in equity, but rather as an unjust judge, who fears neither human beings nor reverences God, in iniquity.

For you attack your prior, or the one who governs you in his place when he is absent, or your steward, or one of your brothers. You will never find any of these whom you do not often regard as blameworthy, even though each of them may truly exist as irreproachable as a human being can be.

“How can this be?” you ask. “If one of them ought not rightly to be blamed, how can each of them appear to me rightly blameworthy?” It is because you are proud and irascible, harsh and impatient, and you never wish to break your own will, however perverse it may be. Rather, insolent and rebellious, and as far as you are able wholly unconquerable, you always strive to carry it out against right and justice.

Although everything that is in you is in you not because of anyone else but because of yourself, you nevertheless attribute it not to yourself but rather to others. You open your eyes to others, but close them entirely to yourself. Thus it happens that you cannot see yourself for your own good, since you never attend to yourself but always to others.

If your own eye saw you fully, no one other than yourself would so often appear blameworthy to you. But because you are weighed down by a certain exceedingly serious illness, you always reproach those who even serve you well in everything—not because of any negligence of theirs (for there is absolutely none, since they serve you with every diligence), but rather because of your own great infirmity.

We have not said this because everything you see being done by others ought always to be praised and never, according to place and time, person and cause, reproved—for you see things that ought to be reproved rather than praised, not merely often but almost always—but so that, when the reason requires it, you may accuse others in such a way that you never excuse yourself in those matters for which you yourself ought rightly to be accused.

In this way it will happen that, while you constantly consider how grievous your own evils are, the evils of others will seem more bearable to you, and while your zeal is fully moderated, it will not be able to become excessive. Then, never stopping short of the proper measure or extending beyond it, your mind will restrain itself within rule and proportion, walking along the royal road and turning neither too rashly to the right nor to the left.

Therefore, you who are an inhabitant of the cell, when you hear or see certain evils being committed by some people, accuse them through zeal and uprightness in such a way that, in some measure, you excuse them through piety and compassion.

Do not consider worthy of praise what ought rightly to be reproved, just as you should not consider worthy of reproof what deserves praise, lest you incur the prophetic saying: “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who make bitter sweet and sweet bitter, who make darkness light and light darkness” (Isaiah 5:20). But just as, whenever you praise, flattery must be absent, so likewise, whenever you reprove, compassion must be present.

Therefore, when you see something wrong being done, suppose that it happened through weakness, or through a sudden slip, or through chance. Excuse the intention of the one acting, if you cannot excuse the act itself. But if you see that it admits absolutely no excuse, suppose that the temptation was exceedingly violent.

When, then, you see someone spiritually sick, let his sickness displease you in such a way that the sick person himself nevertheless pleases you. Let it not please you that he is sick, but let the one who is sick please you. Thus, yes, love the human being and persecute the sinner; yet he ought to please you not because he is a sinner, but because he is a human being.

Accordingly, in the evils that you see appearing in human beings, let neither zeal nor compassion be absent from you. Let each of them be present in you in such a way that, for the sake of both, sincere and orderly charity may be present as their cause, beginning, middle, and end.

## CHAPTER XXIII  
### How we ought to oppose in our mind the fifth mode of meditation against the temptation of the flesh, the devil, and the world, by which we are continually assailed

The fifth mode of meditation gives rise to contempt and rejection, and it does so in this manner. Constant experience ought to make you certain, you who are an inhabitant of the cell, that you cannot exist without temptation. For if that saying of the holy man is true—“Temptation is the life of a human being upon earth” (Job 7:1)—indeed, because it is true, temptation can never be absent so long as life remains upon earth. It follows, therefore, that when you no longer live upon earth, you should know that you are without temptation—not before then, but only then.

Now the flesh tempts you, the world tempts you, and that ancient enemy also tempts you. The flesh strives to draw you toward pleasure, the world toward vanity, and the devil toward the horror of pride and swelling, envy and spite, anger, hatred, and the other spiritual vices of which he himself is full.

When, then, you feel yourself assailed by any of these temptations, set yourself before yourself, sitting in your cell, and in your inward meditation see and consider how you can despise it and cast it away from you.

When the flesh addresses you by tempting you, do not lend an ear to its wicked voice, but make it fall silent without any delay. Do this in the following way. Consider in your meditation how impure and foul is this flesh that you carry; how unclean and brief is all its pleasure; how, after a short time, it is to be handed over to death; how after death it will become a worm, corruption, and stench; and how, after the worm, stench, and corruption, it will become the most contemptible and worthless dust.

When, therefore, it strives to draw you toward the experience of unlawful, wicked, and therefore deadly sweetness, let the bodily appearance be depicted before the eyes of your mind by that crafty seducer. Consider not merely how it seems in some way to appear outwardly, but rather what it truly is in itself, in the reality of the thing, even now in life, and what it will be after death.

You will see clearly that it appears outwardly like a sack shining on the outside, but within it reeks with every filth, uncleanness, and intolerable corruption. Let it now appear in every respect before the sight of your mind while living as it will be when dead, lying in the tomb and teeming with worms. You will plainly discover that, when it is desired, nothing other than decay and corruption is being desired.

Thus, with blessed Job, you will scrape a potsherd covered with discharge (Job 2:8); thus you will dash the little ones of the wretched daughter of Babylon against the rock.

But when the unclean world opens its mouth in your ears, suggesting that you desire the vanity with which it itself is filled, consider that all its exaltation is like smoke and that all its glory is rushing with the greatest speed toward a shameful end.

When you see someone exalted and raised up in it like the cedars of Lebanon, pass by, and behold, he is no more. For its praise is brief and its joy lasts but an instant. If its pride should rise to heaven and its head touch the clouds, it will be destroyed in the end like dung, and those who had seen it will say: “Where is it?” “Like a flying dream, it will not be found; it will pass like a vision of the night” (Job 20:5–8)—and the rest of what was falsely said about him by the enemies of the holy man, but which is truly applicable to any proud and impious person who, utterly despising heavenly things, thinks about and loves only what belongs to the world.

Now, to destroy the voice of that slippery and malicious friend, nothing, as it seems to me, can be set against it more effectively than the complete perfection of holiness that your Savior possessed in his heart, proclaimed with his mouth, and displayed in his works.

As a nail drives out a nail, let that immeasurable fullness of holiness of our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, always held before the eyes of your mind, wholly reduce to nothing in your heart the abundance of the devil’s wickedness. Nothing pertaining to death will he be able to pour into you through consent that this one’s superabundant holiness will not utterly annihilate in your mind, provided that through pure meditation, with devotion and love, it remains fully and perfectly within you.

This, then, is the meditation that confers upon you the cause of a certain wholesome contempt and rejection: teaching you to despise within yourself and cast away from yourself whatever whispers to you in your inner ear—whether the flesh toward foul pleasure, the world toward unstable vanity, or that great enemy of ours toward utter destruction.

## CHAPTER XXIV  
### The weariness suffered by one who is an inhabitant of the cell, and how he can drive it away from himself, renew himself, and prepare himself

[Col. 0841D]

The sixth mode of meditation belongs to those things in which the cause of your renewal and restoration exists, you who are an inhabitant of the cell. You ought to hold it within yourself in the following manner.

Often, when you are alone in your cell, a certain inertia, languor of spirit, and weariness of heart seizes you. You feel within yourself a very grave disgust; you yourself are a burden to yourself. That inward sweetness which you once used so happily has now failed you. The sweetness that was in you yesterday and the day before yesterday has now been turned into great bitterness. The moisture of tears with which you used to be abundantly drenched has dried up entirely. Spiritual vigor has withered within you; beauty has perished.

You carry your soul torn and lacerated, confused and divided, sad and embittered, and you have nowhere to settle it in repose. Reading no longer pleases you; prayer no longer tastes sweet; you find none of the customary showers of spiritual meditations. And what more shall we say? No spiritual cheerfulness, eagerness, or joy remains in you.

You are ready and quick for laughter, idle talk, and frivolity; but toward silence, toward doing anything useful, and toward every spiritual exercise you are wholly slow and sluggish. O what a wretched change in your pursuits! You are no longer the same person you once were, but entirely another.

But rise up; shake yourself free from the dust; loosen the bonds from your neck. Strive to restore yourself, you who have been so torn apart; and, renouncing this old condition, devote all your strength to your renewal.

“How can I do this?” you ask. Listen and understand how you can do it. Place before your eyes the companions who preceded you [Paris manuscript: “the saints who preceded you”], together with the great labors they endured in time and the far greater rewards they have already received in eternity.

Join bars to bars in the inner tabernacle of your heart; also place golden rings upon them, so that the structure of your mind may be firm and not totter. Bars are joined to bars when virtues are joined to virtues.

See how the chief of the apostles joins bars to bars in his second letter, where he says: “Supply virtue in your faith, and in virtue knowledge, and in knowledge self-control, and in self-control endurance, and in endurance piety, and in piety brotherly affection, and in brotherly affection love” (2 Peter 1:5–7).

He makes clear, by adding what follows, how great a benefit proceeds from this joining together of the bars: “For if these things are present and abound among you, they will not make you empty or fruitless in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ” (ibid., 8).

But place golden rings upon these bars—that is, consider in your mind what sort, what kind, and how great are the rewards they have already received. For gold signifies splendor, while the ring, in which no beginning or end can be found, signifies perpetuity. Thus you may know that the perpetuity of their rewards is ineffably radiant and their radiance perpetual.

The Psalmist also speaks in this way of the bars joined together and the golden rings: “They will go from strength to strength; the God of gods will be seen in Zion” (Psalm 83:8). To go from strength to strength refers to the bars; to see the God of gods in Zion refers to the golden rings.

## CHAPTER XXV
### On the things Christ accomplished in the flesh, and on the labors of his saints

Go, then, and first set before the eyes of your consideration that Holy of holies, who is the head both of you and of all the elect, so that you may prove yourself wise: “For the eyes of the wise are in his head.” Therefore see him conceived and born without any impurity, wrapped in swaddling clothes and laid in a manger, nourished with his mother’s milk, subjected to circumcision; appearing to the faith of the Magi as eternal God, almighty King, and mortal man; presented in the temple, taken with his mother into Egypt, and brought back into the land of Judaea, advancing in wisdom, age, and grace.

[Col. 0843A] Consider him baptized, fasting, hungry, tempted, living among men, weary from his journey, conducting himself in all things holily: working miracles, preaching what brings salvation, teaching truth, suffering harsh things, enduring indignities, silent under insults, bearing reproaches, humbly stooping to wash his disciples’ feet, offering the sacraments of his body and blood, praying more earnestly in his agony, and shedding a sweat of blood.

Look upon him sold, bought, handed over by a kiss, seized with swords and clubs, bound, led away, falsely accused, unjustly judged, cruelly condemned, covered with spittle, struck with fists, veiled, and subjected to slaps. Behold him scourged, made an object of mockery, clothed in a scarlet cloak, his most holy head torn by a crown of thorns, holding a reed sceptre, covered in purple for disgrace, adored in derision, despised by Herod and his soldiers, mocked in a white garment, ill-treated by soldiers, carrying his cross, cruelly fastened to the cross with nails, reviled with harsh words, fed gall, given vinegar to drink, bowing his head, yielding up his spirit, and commending that beloved soul of his into his Father’s hands.

[Col. 0843B] Contemplate him wounded in the side by a soldier’s lance, pouring forth from it blood for our redemption and water for our spiritual washing; taken down from the cross, buried, despoiling hell, biting hell itself, putting death to death, risen again, appearing, eating with his disciples, and ascending where he was before—he who did not depart from there when he came here, nor leave here when he went there. In this way keep your eyes in your head.

If you diligently ruminate within yourself upon all these things, and others of this kind concerning him, with due devotion and pious compunction, we think that you may in some measure be rescued from this inertia of yours. For we cannot possibly comprehend, much less explain to you, in what honor and glory that nature has been exalted at the Father’s right hand—the nature which proceeded from the womb of the Virgin Mother utterly without any contagion of sin, and, enduring the great agony of a dreadful death, hung upon the wood.

[Col. 0843C] Yet this we know without doubt, because he himself truly promises it: where he is, there his servant also will be. And his prayer to the Father is in these words: “Father, I will that where I am, they also may be with me, that they may see my glory which thou hast given me” (John 17:24).

Meanwhile, that we may descend from the head to the members, let John the Baptist, beheaded, appear before the eyes of your inward consideration; Peter, crucified with his feet raised upward and his head hanging downward; Paul, beheaded. Let Andrew appear, living for two days on the cross; James slain by the sword; the other James cast down; John cast into a cauldron of boiling oil and finally sent into exile; and all the other apostles brought to their end; and those two-year-olds who bore witness to Christ not by speech but by death.

[Col. 0844A] Let holy Stephen, stoned, appear, and Lawrence, roasted; and—because it would be too long, indeed impossible, to recount individually the sufferings of all the martyrs who suffered for Christ—set before yourself, as far as you can and insofar as you can, their admirable contests and triumphs, in both sexes and at different ages. Set before yourself also the venerable lives of the holy confessors, who, although they did not depart by the shedding of their blood in open martyrdom, nevertheless led a holy life not unlike martyrdom.

If you linger long over these things, we think that you will immediately be freed from the weariness which burdens and oppresses you, and that you will be able to feel yourself made relieved, cheerful, and lively. We advise you, however, to strive to do this more attentively when something has perhaps been said or done to you against your will—as sometimes happens—by which and because of which you become excessively fainthearted and sad, troubled and angry, miserably devastated inwardly by bitter disputes, whisperings, unjust threats, accusations, and replies.

[Col. 0844B] Run then, when there is such a great storm in the sea of your heart, and, casting away from yourself the silent outcry and the clamorous silence that resounds and horrifically rages in the forum of your mind, awaken pious JESUS, who is a helper in times of need, in tribulation, asking him to aid you in your peril.

Therefore let holy Abel, slain by his brother, come before the eyes of your mind; Jacob, humbly yielding to his brother’s anger by flight; Joseph, sold by his brothers because he would not sin, accused of having sinned, committed to prison without fault, and innocently cast into a pit. Let holy Moses come to your heart—indeed, into your heart—the meekest of all men who lived upon the earth, interceding for an iniquitous people who wished to stone him; enduring contentious contradiction and rebellion from Dathan, Abiram, and Korah, and the detraction of both his brother and his sister.

[Col. 0844C] Let him also come whom no one can justly accuse, who lived without complaint from youth to gray hairs, who declared that he would commit a great sin if he did not intercede for the people who were rejecting him from rule; who did not cease to mourn the king rejected by God, not even when he feared that king would kill him. Let him likewise come who humbly fled his persecutor as his lord, and, having received both opportunity and place for vengeance, did not recognize him as an enemy; who even mourned him in tears when he was slain, although he knew well that he himself would succeed him in the kingdom.

He is the one who, with a breast full of piety, laments his parricidal son when dead; and forbids that the servant who curses him be struck, although that servant has called him a man of blood, a man of Belial. And, to omit mountains and hills that we may not weary you, let us pass over the countless other men of mercy, whose righteousness has not received oblivion, and leap to their head.

[Col. 0845A] You yourself know that he was called a glutton and a drinker of wine, a friend of sinners and publicans; that he was said to have a demon and was called a Samaritan; and that, when accused by many, he answered nothing. He too was led as a lamb to slaughter and did not open his mouth. With these seasonings refresh your inward parts when that disturber of peace and divider of unity, who makes the pot boil like the deep sea, sees everything lofty, and is king over all the children of pride, strives to pollute them with deadly poison.

For it is beneficial for you to do this, so that, once the troubled and dark cloud that covers your mind has been driven away, you may be restored and renewed alike; and, when Jesus rises in the little vessel of your heart, tossed about, reeling, already covered by waves and in peril, and commands the winds of temptations and the sea of deep and swelling bitterness, there may be a great calm.

## CHAPTER XXVI
### On the seventh mode of meditation, which produces in the mind of the one who meditates the cause of astonishment and admiration, and on the fact that through the things that have been made, he who made them is perceived.

The mode of meditation that we placed seventh is that which, when you who inhabit a cell remain in it for some time, produces within you astonishment and admiration. If you desire to possess this mode, you must sit in solitude and lead your pure and steadfast thought from the very beginning of the world, through the ages and generations of each individual thing, up to the present time in which you live; and you must carefully attend to the marvelous things that the Creator and Disposer of all those creatures, himself marvelous, has marvelously accomplished.

Consider without exception that everything besides God came forth and came into being from non-being at his will; and that he, who lives eternally, created everything simultaneously. Yet wisdom was created before all things, since Scripture, which is also truthful, says: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. 1:1). But do not suppose that there is any contradiction here. Rather, recognize that a distinction is made between the beginning of time itself and priority of rank. With regard to the first statement—“He who lives eternally created everything simultaneously”—Scripture says: “He who lives eternally created all things together” (Eccl. 18:1), and, “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.” With regard to the second, wisdom, which is rational creation, was created before all things.

Visible creation first appeared in a crude and, so to speak, formless matter belonging to those four elements: fire, air, water, and earth. Then, over the course of six days, it was brought into form. We properly comprehend the creation of which we are speaking in three ways: in the formless creation of things that did not exist, in the formation of things thus created, and in the ordering of things formed.

At the very beginning of time, before any day, formless and crude matter came forth from non-being into being in those four elements. Afterwards, during the first three days, the elements were arranged in their appropriate places; and thus visible creation was formed. On the first day light was made and divided from the darkness. On the second day the firmament was placed between the upper and lower waters. On the third day the waters were gathered into one place; their gatherings were called seas, and the earth was clothed with grasses and trees.

During the three following days creation was adorned in the proper order. First the luminaries were made—the sun, moon, and stars. On the fifth day the fish and birds were made. On the sixth, creeping things, cattle, and the beasts of the earth were made, together with humanity itself, destined to be lord of all visible things. On the Sabbath, that is, on the seventh day, God is said to have rested, because nothing is read as having been made by him on that day.

Therefore, if you carefully consider within yourself the creation of corporeal creation in its formless state, the formation of things created, the ordering of things formed, the creation and establishment of the first human being, the restoration after the Fall, and the events that occurred in the six ages, we think that you will not lack a cause for astonishment and admiration.

Amid these things, touch and hear within the very meditation of your mind. For your mind itself has a kind of touch and a kind of hearing; both, however, are spiritual, because the mind itself is spirit. Let its spiritual touch therefore encounter the three things that exist in creatures.
