The first is what they are from themselves; the second, what they are from the Creator; the third is twofold, rendering a recompense worthy of its deserts: either life in return for righteousness, or death in return for wickedness. In the first there is contempt for the work; in the second, glory for the Creator; in the third, the benefit of service, the counsel of admonition, and the punishment of condemnation. Of these three, the first assists, the second exhorts, and the third threatens.

Amid these things, let your spiritual touch approach the three visible properties of visible creatures. The first is immensity, the second beauty, and the third usefulness. In the first this spiritual touch finds admiration; in the second, approval; in the third, revelation [Par. *relevatio*, “relief” or “lifting up”].

The first of these claims for itself multitude and magnitude. There is multitude in things alike, unlike, and mixed together. Magnitude is found in mass, which consists in bulk and weight, and in space, which consists in length and breadth, depth and height.

Witnesses to multitude are the stars of heaven, the sand of the sea, drops of rain, the days of the ages, the hours of the days, the moments of the hours, the hairs of animals, the grasses of the fields, the leaves of trees, the scales of fish, the feathers of birds, and everything of this kind. Witnesses to magnitude are the mass of the mountains, the hollows of the valleys, the courses of rivers, the height of heaven, the breadth of the earth, the depth of the abyss, and innumerable things of this sort. As far as we are concerned, the former admit no number and the latter no measure.

Furthermore, admirable beauty comprises four things: position, motion, form, and quality. In position there are arrangement and disposition, which claim for themselves things, places, and times. Motion is fourfold: local, which is forward and backward, upward and downward, rightward and leftward, and circular; natural, by which something increases and decreases; animal, by which something desires and perceives; and rational, by which something discerns and acts.

These five things also proclaim an admirable form: beauty, deformity, vastness, smallness, and rarity. Quality, too, is declared admirable by five things, which nourish the same number of bodily senses: the loveliness of colors, soothing to sight; the melody of sounds, soothing to hearing; the fragrance of odors, pleasing to smell; the sweetness of flavors, pleasing to taste; and the fitness of bodies, pleasing to touch.

The usefulness of creatures is adorned by these four things: fitness, gratitude, pleasure, and necessity.

You cannot fail to be astonished and to admire, you who inhabit a cell, when you carefully think and meditate on these things within yourself. For diligent inspection of God’s visible and perceptible creatures will be for you a great and exceedingly powerful cause and occasion of admiration.

In them, in a certain manner, the invisible wisdom itself is seen—a wisdom that, as it is in itself, can be seen by no one in the blindness of the present exile. Hence the statement that someone made concerning Wisdom: “In her ways she shows herself cheerfully to them” (Wis. 6:17). The ways of invisible Wisdom are its own visible and perceptible creatures. In those ways it shows itself because it appears, in a certain manner, in its works, although it still remains hidden from us as it is in itself. And “cheerfully” is rightly said, because the vision of the Creator in the inspection of his work is like the cheerful delight of an exceedingly pleasing joy.

See, therefore, within yourself in meditation these four elements and all the corporeal things formed from them. See everything that creeps beneath the earth, grows from the earth, walks upon the earth, flies through the air, swims in the waters, and shines in the firmament; and whatever corporeal and visible things have been created, formed, and ordered by God. Know that these are the ways of invisible Wisdom, in which it cheerfully shows itself to you.

For, as the Apostle says: “His invisible things, understood through the things that have been made from the creation of the world, are clearly seen” (Rom. 1:20). The invisible things of God are not one thing and God himself another, because what he has, that he is. Hence the Apostle adds: “His eternal power also, and divinity.” To see these invisible things of God through the things that have been made is nothing other than, in a certain manner, to see the Maker of invisible things in the things he has made and through the things he has made.

These invisible things of God are now seen through the creature of the world in this way because the noble rational creature—namely, the human soul—still living as an exile, sees the invisible one in visible things and apprehends knowledge of the Maker in his works. The creature of heaven—that is, the angelic creature—does not do this, for it does not need to see the Creator in creation, since it continually sees him in himself. You, however, who are not yet able to do this, meanwhile behold the one who made all things in the things he has made.

Someone says:

“He himself gave me true knowledge of the things that exist, so that I might know the arrangement of the world, the powers of the elements, their beginning and consummation, the middle points of times, the changes and transformations of seasons, the courses of the year and the arrangements of the stars; the natures of animals and the ferocity of beasts, the paths of winds and the thoughts of human beings, the varieties of plants, the powers of roots, and whatever things are hidden and unforeseen I learned. For Wisdom, the artificer of all things, taught me” (Wis. 7:17–21).

Therefore, if you diligently ruminate on all these things within yourself, you will certainly possess in this meditation something at which to be astonished and to admire.

## CHAPTER XXVII  
### On the voices and utterances that the soul spiritually hears; how the soul was made in the image of God; what movement it receives; and what movement it cannot receive

It is now time for us to approach the eighth mode of meditation, by which, as we said, spiritual and invisible things are revolved in the mind of the person meditating.

The spiritual and invisible matters that we propose to discuss concern the human soul, the angelic creature, and also the divine nature. In the chapters immediately following, we intend to treat certain matters concerning these three: the human soul, the angels themselves, and God.

You, therefore, who inhabit a cell, dwelling in it alone and yet not alone, first raise within yourself that spiritual hearing which, as we said above, is possessed by the soul, and let it hear the voice of three spirits. The first is ours, the second angelic, and the third is the one who created these two. For concerning that Spirit who is both God and human, Scripture says: “God is spirit” (John 4:24).

Each of these spirits has its own voice, and you hear each voice whenever you meditate carefully and purely upon each one. Since their voices concern the firmament, the first is beneath it, the second from it, and the third above it; and at this point animals are compelled to fix their step and lower their wings.

Let this hearing also perceive and hear the uncreated Spirit addressing four groups: angels, the souls of the saints, the devil, and human beings. In the first address there is an infusion of divine notice; in the second, the insertion of voluntary expectation.

The third contains four modes. The first includes the rebuke of wickedness, the second the praise of righteousness, the third the granting of temptation, and the fourth prohibition.

The word that the Spirit of whom we are now speaking, the uncreated Spirit, as it were speaks to human beings, is distinguished in two ways. It is formed either by itself or through a subject creature—namely, through the angelic creature—and it occurs in eight modes: it is formed through words; through things; through words and things together; through images displayed before the eyes of the heart; through images temporarily assumed from the air and displayed before the bodily eyes; through heavenly substances; through earthly substances; and through heavenly and earthly substances together.

But the animal human being does not perceive into what form that which exists by itself is formed. This remains hidden from the understanding for as long as it also remains untested by experience.

Let the one who speaks to these four groups also hear them addressing him. He hears the angels in one manner and the souls in one manner: the angels by admiring the incomprehensible infinity of the Godhead, and the souls by awaiting vengeance for blood. He hears the devil in three ways: by not wishing to conceal his malice, by unjustly accusing innocence, and by maliciously seeking it for temptation. He hears human beings in as many ways: praying for the forgiveness of sins, the grace of merits, and the glory of rewards.

Read the second and the twenty-eighth books of the *Moralia* of blessed Gregory. In them you will find how profoundly and elegantly that same man discusses these matters; among the other teachers, he is acknowledged to have been keen in intellect and graceful in expression.

Amid these things, see within the inwardness of your meditation that the human being was made from two substances: one corporeal, the other incorporeal. Insofar as he is corporeal—as was said long before us—he shares participation in a nature common with the other animals; but in the composition of his form he differs from the other animals. Their form is inclined and bent toward the earth, signifying that they should seek nothing beyond earthly things. The human form, however, is raised and lifted upward. The human being also, unlike the other animals [Par. *animalia*, “living creatures”], walks upright and directs his gaze toward higher things. This clearly declares both that he ought to set his mind on things above and that he ought, with the whole intention of his mind, to strive toward the place where Christ sits at the right hand of God the Father.

Hence someone says:

“While the other animals look down upon the earth,  
he gave humankind a face held high, and commanded it  
to see [*tueri*, ‘behold’] heaven and to raise its uplifted countenance toward the stars.”  
(Ovid, *Metamorphoses* 1.84.)

Thus, from the form of the body, the human being is admonished to differ from the other animals in the desire for good things, although he shares with them a common bodily nature.

But according to the soul, he has no community of properties with the other living creatures. For the soul alone was made in the image and likeness of God. It is said, as they say, to have been made in the image of God with respect to substance and the purity of reason; but in the likeness of God with respect to the imitation of purity and the love of charity. Alternatively, it is said to have been made in the image of God with respect to knowledge of truth, and in his likeness with respect to the purity of nature and reason.

The soul is an image of God, made according to the image; it is not of the same nature as God, but differs from him by a great distance, because it is capable of progress and decline and is therefore subject to variation. In this respect it is very far removed from God, although it is a certain image and likeness of him. It is also far removed from that Image which is everywhere identical with God himself—namely, from the Son of God the Father, who is everywhere identical with the Father.

The soul possesses natural simplicity of essence. Its being is also identical with its living. We do not, however, say that its being is living in the sense of living well with respect to holiness, or blessedly with respect to happiness. For, although from the moment it was created it cannot ever cease to live, just as it cannot ever cease to exist, it can nevertheless live badly when it is wicked, and wretchedly when it is condemned.

It also possesses freedom of choice, by which it distinguishes between good and evil and loves and chooses whichever of the two it wishes, so that its merit may lie in these choices. Behold in the soul simplicity of essence, perpetual life, and freedom of choice.

It receives variation of movement, because it is mutable. Movement is according to place, according to time, and according to form. Some say that the movement according to form has three species: increase, decrease, and alteration.

Something moves according to place when it passes from one place to another through an intervening place. This pertains only to a body; it is not applicable to the human or angelic spirit. Things are said to move according to time when they receive a before and an after. Those things move according to increase or decrease that grow or diminish in quantity. Those things receive the movement of alteration that are altered in a certain manner by the diversity of forms and activities.

There are certain things capable of receiving every kind of movement, such as corporeal things, because they move according to place and time. Created spirits are also moved by various affections that they begin to possess and then cease to possess. Thus movement according to form is always followed by movement according to time.

Created spirits, therefore, because they move from good to evil, from evil to good, from good to good, and from evil to evil, are moved by two species of movement. Movement according to place cannot belong to the soul; but it is capable of the movement that occurs according to time and according to form. For it is often changed through various affections, and this cannot happen without temporal movement. It does not move from place to place through an intervening place, because it does not move locally.

Blessed Augustine also says: “Nothing that is not a body is in a place.” Boethius too, in his book *On the Trinity*, says that neither quantities nor qualities are in a place, although it is true that they are in a subject. For it is one thing to be in a subject and another to be in a place, just as it is one thing for the soul to be in a body and another for the soul to be in a place.

Things that are in a place fill the place and occupy the place; this belongs only to a body. For the philosopher does not say without reason that “the individual parts of a place contain the individual parts of a body” (*Physics*, book IV). For a body to be in a place is for that body itself to fill the place; it is for the body itself to create extension—upward, downward, backward and forward, rightward and leftward.

This does not apply to the soul, which is in a place and is bounded in such a way that it is not contained and enclosed by the circumference of any place as a body is contained and enclosed. No one who understands how far the nature of spirit differs from corporeal nature says that this is false.

## CHAPTER XXVIII  
### On those blessed spirits—namely, what things pertain to them—and what the inhabitant of a cell ought to turn over within himself concerning them in pure meditation

Now I wish to say something to you, who inhabit a cell, about those heavenly spirits. Your intercourse with them ought especially to be through purity, eagerness, and desire. You must not think that when you are in your cell you are alone in it. For you are never less alone than when you are alone in it—as we put it—if you are in it in the manner in which you ought to be.

Are you then alone when, enclosed in the inner chamber of your pure and cleansed mind, with the door of your heart closed against all useless things, you pray in spirit to your Father? Are you then alone when, in the innermost recesses of your soul, along certain mature and sound paths of luminous understanding and inflamed affection, having at that very hour excluded all frivolous and idle thoughts from yourself, you walk through and go around the bright and most beautiful dwellings of the blessed spirits who always see the face of the Father in heaven?

How are you then alone when, in the broad, purified, and spacious halls of your spirit, in great light and ardor, not without ineffable joy and exultation, you move through the ranks of the patriarchs, the fellowships of the prophets, the senate of the apostles, the lovely roses of the martyrs, the beautiful violets of the confessors, and the pleasant, sweet-smelling lilies of the virgins?

How good it is for you to be here! How sweet and delightful it is for the beautiful and fair dove, and for the soul whose voice is: “My beloved is mine, and I am his” (Song 2:16), and also: “I am wounded by love” (ibid., 5), to sleep between the left hand and the right hand of the same beloved! There she rests the more securely, the more anxiously and carefully he himself strives for her repose, zealously driving far away whatever might disturb, diminish, or impede her vigilant sleep.

Finally, with a certain admirable adjuration she addresses the daughters of Jerusalem: “Do not awaken or rouse my beloved until she herself wishes it” (Song 3:5).

And now, dearest to us, you who inhabit a cell, turning your back as far as you can on transitory, earthly, and lowly things, and your face toward eternal, heavenly, and higher things, raise the thought of your heart toward those things that ought to be thought and held concerning those heavenly spirits.

They came forth from non-being into being at the will of God [Par. *illo*, “that one”], the almighty Creator of all creation. They are not coeternal with God, nor coequal or consubstantial with him, because, although they are exceedingly exalted and worthy, they are nevertheless creatures.

They were created at the beginning of the world, when heaven and earth were first established. They were created simultaneously: both those who persevered and those who fell; both those who turned away and were cast down, and those who turned back and were confirmed. For this is what the Catholic teachers who treated of these matters asserted and left written in their works.

They were created rational, and all of them—both those who would become evil and those who would become good—were created capable of charity. We do not say that all of them were recipients of charity, but that they were capable of charity. Those who turned away from God and were condemned eternally never had charity, nor will they ever have it. Therefore the evil were not created as recipients and possessors of charity, but as capable of charity. They could have possessed it, but, swelling up against their Creator, they did not wish to possess it.

The prophet Ezekiel speaks in this way concerning the one who became the author of their ruin: “Your gold, the work of your beauty, and your settings were prepared on the day on which you were created” (Ezek. 28:13). Behold, he says that his settings were prepared on the day on which he was created, because he was capable of charity; but they were never filled, because he did not receive charity.

Blessed Gregory explains these prophetic words in this way in the thirty-second book of the *Moralia* (chapter 18):

“‘Gold,’ he says, ‘was his workmanship, because he shone with the brightness of wisdom, which he received when he was well created. Settings are made in stones for this reason: so that, bound with gold, they may be joined together in the composition of an ornament, so that those whom the gold poured into the filled settings binds together may not in any way be separated from one another. Therefore, the settings of this stone were prepared on the day of his creation, because he was created capable of charity. If he had wished to be filled with it, he could have remained attached to the holy angels, like stones set in the ornament of a king.

For if he had made himself penetrable to the gold of charity, he would have remained joined to the holy angels, fixed, as we have said, as a stone in the royal ornament. This stone therefore had settings, but through the vice of pride they were not filled with the gold of charity. For since stones are bound with gold so that they may not fall, this one fell because, although pierced by the hand of the craftsman, he scorned being bound by the bonds of love.

But now the other stones, which had likewise been pierced, have been bound together, mutually penetrated by charity; and through the fall of this one they have obtained this gift: that they will no longer be separated from the royal ornament by falling.’”

These are the words of blessed Gregory, and this is how he speaks concerning these matters.

Angels are believed to have received four things in their very creation: a simple and immaterial substance; personal distinction, wisdom, and understanding of divine truth and goodness; a rational form; and freedom of choice—that is, the capacity to distinguish good from evil and, by choice, to incline toward either one.

Their substance is simple and immaterial because they do not subsist through any diversity of parts. From the composition of parts they receive quantity, but no dimensions—that is, neither length, breadth, nor height. All of them, however, differ in personal property.

They possessed an aptitude for knowledge, all the greater in proportion to the purity of their substance. This was the ability to know by which they could understand what they owed to their Creator, what they owed to themselves, and what they owed to their companions.

Their power is said to be threefold: power over themselves, power among themselves, and power over those things outside themselves.

The power they had over themselves was not possessed equally by all, because they differed in this power according to the subtlety of their substance and the purity of their nature. The more subtle and perfect in nature someone was, the more he surpassed another in this power and the more ready he was to despise evil and desire good. By this power, which they are said to have possessed over themselves, they could easily attain the good and reject evil.

The power that they have among themselves is said to be one of dominion. In this power some are superior and others inferior: some command, while others obey those who command, as their duty of submission requires. In this power they are not only distinguished by rank but also differ from one another. For those who are destined to exercise dominion differ from those over whom they exercise it.

The power directed toward external things is called by some the power of administration. Through it they perform those things among the good that are necessary for their salvation, either inclining them toward a good will, supplying strength for the fulfillment of the good will they already possess, or protecting them from the contrary power.

Evil human beings are also very often punished through them, because, as Augustine says: “Through good angels and through evil ones, God sometimes scourges evil human beings.” But, he says, he does not recall having read that God ever scourged good human beings through good angels.

A substantial part of this power is their freedom of choice. Free choice is the free judgment of the will; it is almost in these terms that philosophers too are found to have described it. For they say: “Free choice is free judgment concerning the will.” That is, free choice is the power to distinguish between good and evil, together with the voluntary choice of good and rejection of evil.

For “choice” belongs to discernment and judgment, which is why we customarily call arbiters judges. “Freedom,” however, belongs to the will, which the rational creature possesses freely. The creature that wills good wills it freely, and the creature that wills evil wills it freely.

The former occurs through the prevenient grace of God—that is, when the rational creature wills good. The latter occurs when the grace of God withdraws—that is, when the rational creature wills evil. Yet in both cases the will is involved. For God’s assisting grace does not force the will by necessity, nor does his withdrawing grace strip it of freedom.

Thus the will deserves reward and punishment, because it inclines freely and without any compulsion toward either one, that is, toward good or evil.

It was not without reason that this was called “the free judgment of the will,” or “free judgment concerning the will.” For, as was said, the rational creature always possesses the power freely to will good or evil, with the choice of the former—that is, good—and the judgment of rejection of the latter—that is, evil.

Only the will is always in the power of the rational creature. For the rational creature needs nothing placed outside itself in order to possess a will; we know that this is true in every evil will. The rational creature is sufficient from itself alone to possess an evil will. But to possess a good will, the rational creature is not sufficient from itself alone unless it is aided by the grace of God.

Although it cannot possess a good will without the grace of God, it nevertheless does not need something external in order to possess a good will. For unless the fault of the rational creature obstructs it, the grace of God is never absent from the possession of a good will.

Nothing, therefore, belongs so completely to the power of the rational creature as the will itself, which it always possesses freely, with reason discerning whether it is good or evil. Free choice is therefore rightly called “the free judgment of the will,” or “free judgment concerning the will,” because, as was said, the rational creature always possesses the power freely to will good or evil, with the choice of the one—that is, good—and the judgment of rejection of the other—that is, evil.

Those spirits who turned toward God received the reward of glorification, eternal blessedness, for which they were made worthy by their merits with the help of God’s grace. Without compulsion, they see God eternally and rejoice without end in him, from him, and with him [Par. *gaudebunt*, “they will rejoice”].

But those who turned away from God were handed over to the cords of hell, which they deserved by their fault when God abandoned them, though without oppression; and they will not see God eternally.

The ordering of the good consists in two things: in divine praise, in which they continually persevere, and in the office of administering the many things that must be carried out in this world, whether concerning human beings or any other things, in whose administration they obey the divine disposition.

Their greatest administration concerns human beings, both in the bestowal of bodily benefits and in the bestowal of spiritual benefits. They can fulfill these without any labor, though not by will alone—that belongs to God alone, for whom willing is doing—but through some act, visible or invisible, according to what is appropriate to them.

The orders of those blessed spirits are divided according to three hierarchies, each of which contains three orders. In the first hierarchy are these three orders: seraphim, cherubim, and thrones. In the second are dominions, principalities, and powers. In the third are virtues, archangels, and angels.

For what reason and on what account these orders received such names is sufficiently and abundantly known from the explanations of many Catholic teachers; therefore it is not necessary for us at present to say anything about that reason and cause.

But let us come to you, who inhabit a cell, for whom and to whom we say all these things. Raise, as far as you are able—or rather, as far as it has been granted to you—the cleansed eyes of your pure contemplation toward these nine orders of blessed spirits, so that you may see, in part, what their sublimity and dignity are.

In the inward recollection within yourself, strive, with the sense of memory, to smell at least faintly; and with the taste of love, insofar as you can, to taste beforehand something of the joys of the heavenly spirits who are in the several orders: how each of them is incorrupt and complete in itself, joyful and glad; how, in the sincerest, most ardent, and most enduring love, they are mutually benevolent and kind; tranquil in undisturbed peace; secure in the most perfect certainty; undivided, pure, serene; seeing God himself face to face; clinging to God continually, with no other thing interposed; existing blessed in God and from God; continually occupied with the praises and proclamations of God in the fullness of true and eternally unfailing love and exultation.

To sum up much in a few words: no evil at all is present in them, and no good is lacking to them.

O what sweetness and delight there are in these words! If you are an eagle—or rather, because you are one, provided that you are in your cell as you ought to be—rise, rise above the things beneath you and above the things outside you. Rise through the things within you toward those things of which we speak: sublime and great, perfect and complete, tranquil and quiet, secure and certain, festive and joyful, pleasant and delightful, luminous and splendid, sweetest and most soothing, and, since these are words, finally full of everything that ought to be desired and equally free from everything that ought to be avoided—things that are above you.

Thus, thus make your nest for yourself in high places; remain in the rocks, dwell on the craggy stones and in inaccessible cliffs; from there contemplate your food.

When, therefore, in this way, with pure contemplation, full love, and desire, you sit in your cell and represent those blessed spirits to yourself and yourself to them, know that the King has led you inwardly into the wine cellar so that he might order charity within you. You can now say with Paul: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20), and: “He made us sit with him in the heavenly places, in Christ” (Eph. 2:6).

At that time, as blessed Gregory says, Paul may perhaps have been held in prison when he testified that he was sitting with Christ in the heavenly places. But there he was—Gregory adds—where he had already fixed his ardent mind, not where sluggish flesh still necessarily held him.

Go, and do likewise in your cell. When you return to us, giving glory to God, you will be able to tell us that you made your nest in high places, that you also remained in the rocks, dwelt on the craggy stones, and contemplated your food in inaccessible cliffs.

## CHAPTER XXIX  
### On the kind of meditation that we ought to maintain within ourselves, in the innermost places of our heart, when we strive to think about God; and how it is fitting and permissible for us to think about him

[Col. 0855C]

We have now reached the point where, together with you, an inhabitant of a cell, we may discuss something about the invisible things of God. Concerning these the distinguished preacher says:

> “His invisible attributes, ever since the creation of the world, are understood and perceived through the things that have been made” (Rom. 1:20).

And certainly these invisible things of his are nothing other than what he himself is. Hence the same Apostle, to instruct us what we ought to think about these invisible things, adds: “His eternal power and divinity.” His own eternal power and divinity is himself, who is the eternal God. For indeed he possesses eternal power and divinity; but what he possesses, that he is.

When we are about to speak of God, [Col. 0855D] we cannot say what he himself is, because we are unable to think it. Therefore, what we cannot comprehend with the mind, we consequently cannot express with the mouth. Certainly, whatever exists is either he himself or a creature that he himself made. But the being of a creature is so far removed from his being that it can be said of it that, in a certain sense, it is not, whereas he alone is.

A holy man gives the following judgment on this matter, in this form:

> “For he alone is, and no one can turn aside his thoughts; and whatever his soul has willed, that he has done” (Job 23:13).

And the Apostle says that he alone possesses immortality (1 Tim. 6:16). How is he not alone immortal, who is also alone existent? He alone is, to whom alone being is identical with what he is. He himself is his own being, and he himself is the being of all things. But he who alone is, who alone possesses immortality—what is he? He is none of the things he created, because he is from eternity, not from time. He is the creator of all creatures; hence it is certain that he is not a creature.

We know how to tell you, an inhabitant of a cell, what God is not; but who can say what he is? Blessed Dionysius speaks about this in the second chapter of *The Angelic Hierarchy*:

> “Therefore the mystical traditions of the manifesting utterances, at times praising the blessedness of the superessential divinity as reason, understanding, and essence, declare its divine rationality and wisdom, its truly existing substance, and the true cause of the subsistences of those things which exist; and they fashion it, as it were, as light, and call it life. They prove it to surpass, in some manner, all the more chaste and abiding formations, while material formations fall short of these wondrous forms, and thus they show the divine by way of likeness to the truth. For it is above every knowledge and life, with no light characterizing it, and with every reason and understanding left incomparably behind in likeness to it.
>
> “At other times, however, by dissimilar manifestations from the utterances themselves, they praise it in a supra-worldly manner, calling it invisible, infinite, and incomprehensible; and through things which are, and from which they signify, they indicate not what it is but what it is not. For this, as I judge, is more powerful with regard to it. Thus, according to what the hidden and priestly tradition has introduced, we truly say that it is not, in a certain respect, any of those things which exist. But we are ignorant of its superessential, invisible, ineffable, and unending infinitude. Therefore, if negations concerning divine things are true, while affirmations are inadequate, manifestation through dissimilar forms is more suited to the obscurity of the mysteries.”

These are the words of blessed Dionysius concerning these matters: the words are obscure, but a profound understanding lies hidden within them. See how he says that we are ignorant of its superessential, invisible, ineffable, and unending infinitude, which is to be worshiped. See how, adding to this, he asserts that negations concerning divine things are true, while affirmations are inadequate. And for this reason he says that manifestation through dissimilar forms is more suited to the obscurity of the mysteries.

Certainly, his superessential, invisible, ineffable, and unending infinitude is nothing other than what he himself is. And since we are ignorant of this infinitude of his, while this infinitude is himself, how can we not be ignorant of what he is? But if negations concerning divine things are true, while affirmations are inadequate, our negation is true when we say, “This is not,” because we know what it is not; whereas our affirmation is inadequate when, affirming, we say, “This is,” because we do not know what it is.

And yet, although we do not know that which he is, we certainly know that he is. For unless we knew that he exists, how could we love him? What we do not know to exist, in so far as our thought is concerned, has no existence. And therefore how can what, so far as we are concerned, does not exist be loved by us? But we know that he exists, we love him above all things, and with all our inmost being we sigh for him. Yet when, by loving him so greatly and sighing for him, we know that he exists, what do we know him to be?

Indeed, he told his chosen servant that he is, when he said: “I am who I am.” He also wished this answer to be given concerning himself to those who asked about him: “I am,” he said, “who I am. Thus shall you say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is has sent me to you’” (Exod. 3:14). He said that he is; but he did not say what this “is” is.

Perhaps, however, by saying that he is, he did indeed say what this “is” is—namely, that he said that he is. For whatever can be believed about him in a catholic manner, whatever can truthfully be said, is gathered together in this word *is*: “is.”

And when will the noise of our mouths, where a word begins and ends, utter any word by which we can adequately express God? Indeed, God the Son of God, begotten by God the Father, one and the same God with the Father and the Holy Spirit of them both, is himself the Word. But he is not a word uttered in passing; he is eternally begotten, not made, equal, consubstantial, and coeternal with him whose Word he is. He was “in the beginning,” and “was with God,” and “was God” (John 1:1).

“In the beginning was the Word.” Behold his eternity: whatever was in the beginning was never made, just as it is said of heaven and earth: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. 1:1). But it *was*—that is, it was from eternity.

“And the Word was with God.” Behold that the person of the Word is distinct from the person whose Word he is. For if one was with another, then plainly the one who was there was one, and the one with whom he was was another.

But lest you think him something else, the text says: “And the Word was God.” Behold the divinity of the Word—not a different divinity, but the same divinity as that of him whose Word he is. Therefore the Word who was with God was himself God with the one with whom he was. The Word is another from the one with whom he was—not another God, but another person from the person of the Father; yet with him he is one and the same God: God from God, God the Son from God the Father.

He is certainly not something else, because he has the same substance, eternity, and divinity as the Father. Thus he is another because of the distinction of persons, but not something else because of the unity of the divine substance.

But when we say all this, what are we saying? When will we have words by which we can say what God is? “We shall say many things,” says a certain wise man, “and shall fail in words” (Ecclus. 43:29). Truly, we shall fail in words more than we shall succeed in perfectly stating what we intend, even when we say many things.

And words, however they may be, what are they other than expressions of the mind? Indeed, they either do not yet exist or no longer exist, because they exist only in passing. Before they begin to pass away, they do not yet exist; and once they have passed away, they no longer exist. Where, then, or when shall I find words by which, speaking to you who are an inhabitant of a cell, I may show what God is?

Behold: in your cell you love God most ardently without ceasing, you pray to God most devoutly, and you desire with all your inward being to reach God. But in loving, praying, and desiring in this way, what do you think God is?

You know that he is invisible, and that no creature is invisible before him; that he is a beginning without beginning and an end without end; that he is above all things but not exalted; beneath all things but not subjected; within and outside all things, yet neither enclosed nor excluded; always himself and everywhere himself, yet he is never time and nowhere a place.

He is the one who is, always the same and in the same manner; nothing has happened to him, will inhere in him, pass away, or have inhered in him. “Great is his power, and of his wisdom there is no number” (Ps. 146:5).

And, O hand almighty over all things! O eye likewise seeing all things! There is nothing that can escape that hand, nothing that can remain hidden from that eye. He is full of himself, and without him there is nothing; he is for himself and for all things, because he is his own and all things’ being.

He is nowhere, because he is not confined by place; and yet he is nowhere absent, because no place excludes him. And what place is there without him? “From him, through him, and in him be glory.”

To whom? To the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, the only God.

He is the God of the ages, to whom the ages themselves could neither draw near nor depart from him; yet they are not coeternal with him. For whatever things once were or will be in themselves are always in him—indeed, just as they are from eternity, so also they are into eternity.

For in him neither what was passes away as old, nor what will be comes as something new. Rather, both stand in him and are present to him: what already is no less than what does not yet exist.

And, O how wonderful he is in himself, the creator of all things, since the things created by him are so wonderful! They are indeed exceedingly wonderful, and they proclaim him to be far more wonderful than themselves. For the things he created show themselves to be good because their creator is good. They show themselves, I say, to be good, beautiful, sweet, numerous, and great:

good for use, beautiful to sight, sweet to taste, numerous in number, and great in measure.

These things, I say, display themselves, and they display themselves wondrously. But by displaying themselves, they show their creator to be far better, more beautiful, sweeter, and greater: the best of all good things, the most beautiful of all beautiful things, the sweetest of all sweet things, and the greatest of all great things. He is, as it were, the true, supreme, and eternal goodness, beauty, and—if one may so speak—multiplicity and greatness of himself.

Whatever we see, hear, taste, smell, and touch in this world and of this world is not he. What, then, is he, the Lord our God—what, I ask, is he?

He is not the great and abundant beauty that I behold with bodily sight; he is not the voice that I hear bodily; he is not the odor that I smell, the flavor that I taste, or the texture that I touch.

And yet, in a certain manner, there is something like multiplicity, something like greatness, something like beauty, something like a voice, something like an odor, something like a flavor, and something like texture.

There is something like multiplicity, but with a single simplicity and a simple unity into which no number enters. There is greatness, but without quantity, which no measure can comprehend. There is beauty, which no ugliness obscures. There is a voice, which no time carries away. There is an odor, which no breeze disperses. There is a flavor, which no eating diminishes. There is texture, which no corruption contaminates.

## CHAPTER XXX. On the Trinity of persons and the unity of the substance that is God, and on the fact that neither the Trinity prejudices the unity nor the unity the Trinity

[Col. 0859A]

Behold what we have said to you, an inhabitant of a cell, about God. And indeed we have said many things; but what have we said in all these things? Have we not failed in words? “We shall say many things,” he says, “and shall fail in words” (Ecclus. 43:29).

If the words we speak are many, why do we fail in words? Clearly, because we do not fully express what he is, about whom we speak many words.

We also say—if it is permissible to speak in this way—that although he is one, he is many, but without number; great, but without quantity; simple, but without diminution; good, but without quality; eternal, but without time; everywhere, but without place; in every thing, but without being defined by anything; in every time, but without any change in himself.

He cannot in any way be stained because of his purity, divided because of his simplicity, comprehended because of his immensity, or measured because of his infinitude. Nor can he be altered in knowledge, since he is most wise, or changed in affection, since he is supremely good.

Every effect is subject to his power; every hidden thing is revealed by his wisdom; every event follows his deliberation. Time does not contain his eternity, virtue does not contain his goodness, sense does not contain his wisdom, and action does not contain his power.

To him be glory, for he is the King of the ages, to be worshiped and adored, feared and held in awe, the ruling God, immortal and invisible, from whom, through whom, and in whom are all things.

All things are from him, because he is the beginning and author of all. All things are through him, because through him they are granted existence, just as their being itself was granted to them. But all things are also in him.

We ought, however, to marvel at the greatness of his power rather than imagine the dimensions of some place.

We say further—if we either know or are able to say anything here—God the Father, God the Son, God the Holy Spirit: three persons, none of whom is another person; and one substance. The catholic ear gladly accepts this.

But when we say this, what are we saying? “Something great and profound,” you say, “we are saying when we say this.” We are saying, you say, that in one and the same God, besides whom there is no other, there is both a Trinity of persons and a unity of substance.

“Good,” I say. But are you saying that the Trinity of persons there is something other than the unity of substance?

“No,” you reply, “but these persons have their own properties. For it belongs to the Father alone to beget, and therefore he is from no one; it belongs to the Son alone to be begotten, and therefore he is from the Father; while it belongs to the Holy Spirit alone to proceed, and therefore he is from the Father and the Son.

“But the Holy Spirit is not from the Father and the Son in the same way as the Son is from the Father, because he proceeds from both—namely, from the Father and the Son—but is begotten by neither. The Son, however, is begotten by the Father alone. Therefore the Father is the begetting one, while the Son is begotten; and hence the Father is Father, and the Son is Son. Otherwise there would be several Fathers and Sons in that Trinity; and to believe this would be exceedingly abominable, dreadful, and utterly impious.”

There are, therefore, three persons: the Father begetting, the Son begotten by the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father and the Son.

None of these persons is another person, because there is not one person but three. For one person cannot beget himself, be begotten from himself, and proceed from himself.

Yet these three persons are one substance, one nature, one divinity, one majesty, and one eternity.

You rightly hold the catholic faith, you who are an inhabitant of a cell. But what is this, I ask, that you present to me a number without number, give it to me, and immediately take it away again? If there are three, is there not a number? But if the substance, nature, divinity, majesty, and eternity of the three are one, where is the number?

“The number,” you say, “refers to the persons, because there are three; but it does not refer to the substance, because it is one.”

You speak well. But are these three persons something other than this one substance? Or is this one substance something other than these three persons?

“No,” you reply, “because these three persons are this one substance, and this one substance belongs to those three persons. None of the three persons is the other, yet each is what the other is.

“For the Father is another than the Son or the Holy Spirit, but not something else; and the Son is another than the Holy Spirit or the Father, but not something else. The Holy Spirit is another than the Father or the Son, but he is not something else, because the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are naturally one and the same God.”

Thus we assign to each person his own property without taking away the unity of the substance, because in no respect does the unity of the substance prejudice the Trinity of persons, nor does the Trinity of persons prejudice the unity of the substance.

Therefore the Trinity of persons is not to be conceived or separated apart from the unity of the substance, nor the unity of the substance from the Trinity of persons. Rather, both the unity in the Trinity and the Trinity in the unity are to be venerated and adored.

“If it is as you say, or rather because it is so, how is it so?”

“I do not fully grasp through knowledge how it is,” you say, “but through faith I piously believe that it is so.”

You speak exceedingly well. For believing belongs to piety, investigating to presumption; but to know fully and perfectly is life—and eternal life.

Blessed Augustine says that the Father alone, or the Son alone, or the Holy Spirit alone, is as great as the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit together. It is now fitting to recall to you, an inhabitant of a cell, his words, which he set down in the sixth book of *On the Trinity*, namely in the final chapter of that book, taking occasion from Hilary’s three profound words: “eternity in the Father, beauty in the image, use in the gift.”

Blessed Augustine writes as follows:

> “Having searched out, as far as I can, the hidden meaning of these words—that is, of Father, image, gift, eternity, beauty, and use—I believe that in the word ‘eternity’ he followed nothing other than the fact that the Father has no Father from whom he is; whereas the Son is from the Father, so that he may be, and so that he may be coeternal with him.
>
> “For if an image perfectly fulfills that of which it is the image, it is equal to it; it does not make that of which it is the image equal to its own image. In that image he called ‘beauty,’ I believe, because of its loveliness. There is already such complete harmony, primal equality, and primal likeness that it differs in nothing, is unequal in no way, and is unlike it in no part, but responds in every respect to the one whose image it is.
>
> “There is the first and supreme life, for which living and being are not two different things, but being and living are the same. There is also the first and supreme understanding, for which living and understanding are not different, but what it is to understand is what it is to live.
>
> “This is being: all things one, as a perfect Word, lacking nothing; a kind of art of the almighty and wise God, full of all the unchangeable living principles. All things are one in it, just as it itself is one from the One with whom it is one.
>
> “There God knows all the things he made through it. Therefore, although times depart and succeed one another, nothing departs or succeeds in God’s knowledge. For created things are not known by God because they have been made; rather, they were made—or are mutable—because they are immutably known by him.
>
> “That ineffable union of the Father and the Image is not without perfection, love, or joy. That love, delight, happiness, or blessedness—if anything worthy can be said in a human voice—was briefly called ‘use’ by him. It is the Holy Spirit in the Trinity, not begotten, but the sweetness of the Begetter and the Begotten, bathing all creatures, according to their capacity, in the lavishness and abundance of the Unbegotten [*ingeniti*; perhaps *ingenti*, ‘immense’], so that they may preserve their order and rest in their proper places.
>
> “All these things, therefore, which have been made by divine art, display in themselves a certain unity, beauty, and order. Whatever of them exists is one thing, as are the natures of bodies and the faculties of souls; it is formed by some form, as are the shapes or qualities of bodies and the teachings or arts of souls; and it seeks or preserves some order, as do the weights or arrangements of bodies and the loves or delights of souls.
>
> “Therefore, by perceiving the Creator through the things that have been made and understood, we ought to understand the Trinity, whose trace appears in creation in a manner appropriate to it. For in that Trinity there is the supreme origin of all things, perfect beauty, and most blessed delight.
>
> “Thus those three seem both to define one another and to be infinite in themselves. But here, in bodily things, one is not as much as three together, and two things are something more than one thing. In the supreme Trinity, however, one is as much as three together, and two are as much as one.
>
> “Thus each is in each, all are in each, each is in all, all are in all, and all are one. Whoever sees this, whether partly or through a mirror and in an enigma, should rejoice in knowing God, and should thus honor God and give thanks. But whoever does not see it should strive through piety to see, not through blindness to accuse, because God is one, yet he is also Trinity.
>
> “It must not be understood confusedly: ‘from whom are all things, through whom are all things, in whom are all things’; nor should glory be given to many gods, but to him alone, forever.”

These are the words of blessed Father Augustine, that distinguished teacher, concerning these matters. We do not wish to speak about them any longer, because while so great and such a sun both shines to illuminate and burns to set us aflame, it is fitting for the earthen lamp to withdraw and, no longer appearing, hide itself in the refuge of silence.

## CHAPTER XXXI. On the diligent care and careful diligence that we ought to devote to our prayer when we apply ourselves to it, and on the great instability with which, during prayer, we miserably and pitifully fluctuate in our hearts amid our thoughts, dispersed through idle and harmful things, and wander through innumerable paths

While crossing that second river which flows out from the place of delight, whose name is Gihon, we lingered for some time. We do not think that either the delay itself should be criticized or that anyone should be excessively surprised at it, if he knows only how great its breadth and depth are.

Now let us approach the third river that flows out from the place of delight, whose name is Tigris, so that we may cross through it.

As far as the moral sense alone is concerned, we have said that by this river called Tigris devoted prayer is to be understood, just as by the river called Gihon pure meditation is to be understood.

We have said something to you, an inhabitant of a cell, about the kinds of meditation; and would that what has been said to you has been as fruitful for you as it has been profusely spoken by us!

Now something must be said to you about devotion in prayer. If we either knew or were able to say anything about it adequately, it ought to be all the more necessary for you because, among all the exercises to which you apply yourself in the cell, you are accustomed to practice this one most frequently.

But what do we know or what are we able to say to you about it? Yet, so that you may know, you who are an inhabitant of a cell, how you ought to apply yourself to it, you need more the teaching that instructs all things through anointing than our instruction.

For the Apostle says that “we do not know what we ought to pray for as we should; but the Spirit himself pleads for us with unutterable groanings” (Rom. 8:26). He pleads for us because he makes those whom he fills into petitioners; and through his gift alone and the infusion of his grace, it comes about with us that we know how to pray as we ought.

We ought to lament and accuse ourselves with inward groaning and great sorrow because we almost never pray as we ought, rather than teach others how to pray. For we certainly do not know how to pray as we ought.

Do we then pray as we ought when, during our prayer, we turn over in our hearts either nothing at all or almost nothing—and even that very rarely—of all the things we utter with our mouths?

When, being thus absent from ourselves and utterly unaware of what we say with our mouths, we suppose that we are praying, we are gravely deceived. In every respect we become like those of whom the Lord says through the prophet: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. 29:13).

Blessed Augustine says to his clergy in his Rule (ch. 4):

> “When you pray to God with psalms and hymns, let what is uttered by the mouth be present in the heart.”

Blessed Benedict likewise says this in the Rule for Monks (ch. 19):

> “We believe that the divine presence is everywhere, and that the eyes of the Lord behold the good and the wicked in every place; but let us believe this without any doubt especially when we attend the divine office. Therefore let us always remember what the Prophet says: ‘Serve the Lord in fear’ (Ps. 2:11), and again: ‘Sing wisely’ (Ps. 46:8), and: ‘In the sight of the angels I will sing to you’ (Ps. 137:1).
>
> “Let us therefore consider how we ought to stand in the sight of the divinity and the angels, and let us stand to sing in such a way that our mind agrees with our voice.”

He also says:

> “If we wish to make some request to powerful people, we do not presume to do so except with humility and reverence. How much more, then, must we entreat the Lord God of all things with humility and purity of devotion? Let us know that we are heard not through many words, but through purity of heart and compunction of tears. Therefore prayer ought to be brief and pure, unless perhaps it is prolonged by the fervor of divine inspiration and grace” (*Rule of St. Benedict*, ch. 20).

Thus those outstanding men understood these matters.

But we wretched people, when we pray—or rather, when we are deceived into thinking that we pray—are very often weighed down by sluggish sleep, or, through unstable thought outside ourselves, wander not merely frequently but almost continually through every idle and frivolous thing, through harmful and useless things.

If we think that such prayer is pleasing to God, we are without doubt deceived. But if, persisting stubbornly and pressing forward arrogantly, we contend against our conscience that it pleases God, we lie, do not practice the truth, and the truth is not in us.

For this is not the kind of prayer to which Paul invites us. He urges us to pray in the Spirit and to keep watch in prayer with all perseverance. The Lord himself, addressing the Apostles and exhorting them to pray, says: “Watch and pray” (1 Cor. 14:15). He placed “watch” first, thereby teaching us that if we desire our prayer to be pleasing to God and fruitful for us, we must watch with every effort and exertion against insolent and unstable thoughts, against harmful and useless thoughts, both before the time of prayer and especially during the prayer itself (Col. 4:2; Eph. 6:18; Mark 14:38).

Otherwise, what the tongue seems to utter as prayer is deprived of all spiritual fruit by the wandering of unstable thoughts.

As Ecclesiastes says: “Dead flies ruin the sweetness of the perfume” (Eccl. 10:1). And—as we experience not merely frequently but almost continually—birds descend upon corpses. It is exceedingly necessary that Abram drive them away, lest what he offers be entirely lost if, God forbid, it should happen to be snatched away by them.

The women also—as the distinguished narrator, Saint Luke, makes clear to us in recounting what the Lord did—came to the Lord’s tomb carrying the spices they had prepared (Luke 24:1). And what are these spices except the sweet and fragrant incense of holy prayers?

Hence the Psalmist asks that his prayer be directed before the Lord like incense (Ps. 140:2). And Saint John says in the Apocalypse that the twenty-four elders have golden bowls full of incense (Rev. 5:8). So that we may know what we are to understand by this incense, he adds that they are “the prayers of the saints.”

What are these golden bowls except holy minds, bright with the purity of cleanliness and especially adorned with the precious beauty of love for God and neighbor? In such bowls the incense is preserved whole and uncorrupted, because the incense of devout prayers is received from pure hearts full of charity and sent forth and offered to God.

Hence it is said that the women carried the spices they had prepared (Luke 24:1). For we carry spices that have been insufficiently prepared when we offer God prayers—if they are prayers at all—which the most worthless dust of unstable and unclean thoughts empties of their substance, corrupts, and makes unworthy of the divine ears.

First, therefore, let the spices be prepared, and then let the spices be carried to the Lord. That is, let us first make our prayers pure, and then devoutly offer them to almighty God, so that they may be acceptable to him.

But alas, we wretched people! We carry to him spices that have been insufficiently prepared. When we think that we are praying, we often—and almost always—do not turn over in our hearts, either through understanding or through affection, what we utter with our mouths.

And how can we hope that God will hear a prayer that we offer in such a way that we, who seem in some manner to offer it, perceive it neither through love nor through understanding?

And when did the women carry the spices they had prepared? It was “on the first day of the week, very early” (Luke 24:1).

O stability! O tranquility! O brightness!

On the first day of the week, very early, they carried the spices they had prepared, so that we may know that, when we pray, we ought to have within us unity with regard to the stability of our thoughts, calm with regard to peace, and brightness with regard to understanding.

Thus, during prayer, we should not permit ourselves to wander in the mind through idle or unlawful things, but, as far as we are able by God’s grace, should direct our thoughts solely toward those things that we utter with our mouths.

Nor should we turn over any inward disturbance. Rather, we should be at peace, in complete peace toward all people, and especially toward our brothers and fathers, with whom we are obliged to dwell harmoniously in one household.

Finally, we should not be darkened by the obscurity of any phantasm; instead, we should be illumined by the light of a certain spiritual radiance sent into us by God.

## CHAPTER XXXII. On the wandering of the mind that we feel to be present in us during prayer, and on how and why devotion in prayer is to be understood through the third river flowing out from the place of delight, which is also called Tigris
It compels us, you who inhabit a cell, to do something more with you concerning these matters; it compels us, I say, through the great misery by which we are heavily weighed down, not to forget ourselves. For we cannot help sighing and groaning over the immense instability of our wretched and miserable heart. It is excessively restless and fugitive, and almost [Col. 0865A] incessantly steals itself away from itself; before it realizes or detects what is happening, it is scattered outside itself, broken into fragments, and dispersed among innumerable things. Once broken up and dispersed in this way, it scarcely permits itself to be recalled and gathered back to itself, and to be restored within itself; and if perhaps it has at some time been collected into itself, it does not permit itself to remain within itself even for a single moment, so to speak. And when it is continually and miserably ravaged, burdened, and oppressed by such great and such numerous miseries, it is then tormented by them all the more when it turns to prayer.

For when we read in a book or apply ourselves to some manual task, we are sometimes able to bring our heart to bear upon it to some extent, and we manage to make it remain with the matters in which we are engaged, however much it resists and struggles. But when we approach [Col. 0865B] prayer, our heart, as though it hated this beyond measure and held it in complete and perfect detestation, hastens to steal itself from itself, to withdraw itself from itself, to depart far from itself [Par.: recedere, “to withdraw”], and, fleeing swiftly, to turn its back upon the things uttered by the mouth. And if perhaps it returns to itself, however rarely, it immediately departs from itself again and surrenders itself once more to its former wandering.

O great misery! How aptly it has been said: “There was silence in heaven for about half an hour” (Apoc. 8:1). It is not a full hour, but half an hour of stability and rest takes place in the soul; this is what it means for silence to occur in heaven. Yet even that half hour is not felt as half an hour, because it is almost only anticipated.

O immense sickness of the heart—and entirely incurable so long as the body that is corrupted weighs down the soul, and this earthly dwelling depresses the sense that thinks upon many things. [Col. 0865C] Where is there hope for us amid such misery except in the sole mercy of God, since we are unable, as we ought, to apply ourselves to that exercise which, among all the exercises to which we devote ourselves, is most necessary for us? What shall we say about our manifest evils when we see that even our good deeds cannot be good? What else should we do amid these circumstances? Let us incessantly and sharply rebuke, reproach, and accuse ourselves in the sight of God; and, carrying our miserable soul in our hands, let us tear our flesh with our teeth.

Perhaps our pious Creator, who knows our formation and remembers that we are flesh, will find some excuse for our weakness in this very ardent and humble accusation of ours. Indeed, as Isaiah says, all our injustices are “like a menstruous cloth” (Isa. 64:6), so that we may know without any doubt what judgment we ought to form about our own injustices, since we hear that even our righteousnesses—if they are righteousnesses at all—were compared by so great a prophet to such a thing.

[Col. 0865D] Let us therefore always and everywhere carry before God a severe correction, a sharp reproach, and a biting accusation, inwardly in the heart and outwardly in the mouth. Let us devoutly entreat him to grant us in his mercy that this recognition of guilt—our humble confession, accompanied by inward contrition of heart and pure confession of mouth—may obtain pardon for us; and that he may count us righteous before him in this respect: that we regard ourselves as wholly and perfectly unjust, without any excuse.

[Col. 0866A] But perhaps you, who inhabit a cell, answer us as follows: “You have made me exceedingly anxious and fearful by these words; you have greatly disturbed, stirred, and shaken me. For you have fully and plainly shown me my great misery, by which I am excessively burdened and devastated in this respect, and you have entirely taken away every excuse from me. Indeed, I feel all these things in myself just as I hear you saying them. Whatever you say is certainly true, and there is no falsehood in these words of yours. For my daily—indeed, continual—experience makes me certain, not merely my knowledge, that everything you say is as you say it is. But what does it profit me that you tell me I am tormented by a serious illness—of which I myself know the more fully because I feel it the more painfully—unless you also show me how it can and ought to be cured? Tell me, then, I beg you, as it occurs to you, how I ought to present myself in prayer, so that I may offer it to God acceptably.”

[Col. 0866B] And we answer you as follows: “He without whose gift alone your prayer can be neither acceptable to him nor fruitful for you says this silently in your heart.” For him, what he has generally said is as good as done. Perhaps he would also say it to you through us, although we cannot speak about this without great confusion and shame on our part.

Should we not be ashamed that we teach others but do not teach ourselves; that we paint a handsome man while we painters are ugly; that we restore others with food and drink while we perish from hunger and thirst; that we clothe others in the finest garments while we ourselves walk naked? Indeed, we are so naked that the shame of our nakedness is visible to everyone, and our disgrace appears before all.

[Col. 0866C] Therefore, in order to attend to your edification, you who inhabit a cell, we have applied these matters—as you yourself know—far above, and we continue to apply them, according to the tropological sense, to the purity of devout prayer, represented by this third river that flows out from the place of delight. Its name, as the truthful account says, is Tigris.

Tigris, then, means an arrow: pure and devout prayer. It is swift, piercing and penetrating, cutting through and reaching its destination. Certainly, like an arrow flying with the greatest speed, prayer itself flies all the way to God. In the end, “the prayer of the righteous penetrates the clouds.” What can obstruct it? Everything that appears visibly, as though hard and closed, it pierces and penetrates, sent forth from a pure spirit and not abandoned by that spirit. Whatever seems to stand in its way, it cuts through with the sharpness of its spiritual purity; and it never rebounds if it reaches the one who is above all things.

[Col. 0866D] Not only this: prayer also combats, overcomes, and destroys everything that opposes us, everything contrary to us, and everything harmful to us. Perhaps this is what is meant when it is said of this river that it goes against the Assyrians. By the people of the Assyrians, we think that everything which works for the injury of our spirit is to be understood.

[Col. 0867A] This river, Tigris, goes against those Assyrians because the purity of devout prayer, like a sharp arrow flying with the utmost speed, resists and opposes everything that can harm us—unless, perhaps, it is so disposed that it benefits us, and its harming us consists in nothing other than benefiting us. If the force of some temptation wearies us, if—as often happens—the heavy mass of some raging adversity presses upon us, this river, Tigris, goes against these and all the other Assyrians who are in this world, because the sincere devotion of prayer powerfully withstands them. Although these adversities often weary us, they never overcome us, nor do they ever crush us, even if they frequently press upon us.

Has it escaped our mind that Amalek once came to fight against Israel? This still happens today, when the people of the reprobate, as though licking earthly and passing things through affection and desire, strive by their evil examples and admonitions to drag us, through illicit consent, toward the delight and perpetration of sin.

[Col. 0867B] But so that we may know how the river Tigris goes against the Assyrians: Joshua strikes Amalek to destruction when Moses raises his hands on the mountain (Exod. 17). According to this second sense, which we are now pursuing, the passage suggests one and the same thing: Moses raises his hands on the mountain so that Amalek may be defeated, and the river Tigris goes against the Assyrians.

And who is this Moses? Must we pursue these matters for you, so that you, who inhabit a cell, may be edified? Or should we draw back, lest you become weary, thinking that what we say is excessive? But which wise person would call excessive however lengthy a discourse may be, provided that its individual words can increase the spiritual progress of holy edification in those who hear them?

[Col. 0867C] Who, then, is this Moses, except you who are a true and sincere inhabitant of a cell? For the name Moses, which, as among many people, is well known and common, is interpreted as “taken from the water.” And were you not taken from the waters, when the grace of God visited you, rescued you from the current of worldly conduct, and transferred you to the pleasant and sweet rest of the cell?

Moses is said to raise his hands because you, in your cell, ought to pray without ceasing, according to the apostolic admonition (1 Thess. 5:17). And Moses should raise his hands so that Amalek may be driven away, so that the river Tigris may go against the Assyrians.

But he must climb the mountain; a stone must be placed beneath him on which he may sit; and both Aaron and Hur must support his hands. As long as his hands remain raised, Israel prevails and Amalek is defeated. But whenever he lowers his hands, as though wearied, even for a little while, Amalek prevails and Israel is defeated.

[Col. 0867D] But lest the Israelites suffer this weariness of his hands, which is so dangerous for them, Aaron and Hur must support them. What do these things signify?

Let Moses climb the mountain, so that you, who inhabit a cell, may grasp the height of holy conduct. But sit also upon a stone, so that you may rest in the firm stability of pure thoughts and in their stable firmness. Finally, lest your hands grow weary and, once weary, be lowered, let them be supported by Aaron and Hur.

[Col. 0868A] For lest your thoughts—we speak to you, who inhabit a cell—grow lukewarm in prayer, and thereby become neither acceptable to God nor fruitful for you, let Aaron and Hur make them vigorous and strong: humility must press them down into the lowest place, lest they become proud; the ardor of charity must inflame them toward God and toward your neighbor, lest you grow cold.

For Aaron is interpreted as “mountain of strength.” Indeed, the virtue of true humility is both exalted and strong, because it makes the mind which it entirely occupies both lofty and robust. The truly humble person, the lower he is in his own eyes, the higher he is in the eyes of God; and the weaker he appears to himself, the stronger he is before God. For humility’s virtue contains both strength and humility: a humble strength and a strong humility, so that neither prejudices the other. Thus the virtue of holy humility is lowly in one’s own eyes and exalted in the eyes of God.

[Col. 0868B] Moreover, Hur signifies fire and denotes the ardor of charity. Therefore, let these outstanding virtues—the strong height and lofty strength of humility, and the unquenchable ardor of charity—support the hands of your devotions so that they do not grow weary. We speak to you, who inhabit a cell, who in this sense are the true and sincere Moses.

We have said all these things in order to show how, in the moral sense, we should understand that the third river which flows from the place of delight—the river by which we assert that prayer is to be understood as devout—still today, though spiritually, goes against the Assyrians.

Behold how great and how powerful is the assistance and comfort that the power of prayer supplies against every adversity and every harmful thing when we devote ourselves to it in the manner in which we ought. Thus it becomes clear to us that Scripture does not say idly that Tigris goes against the Assyrians.

[Col. 0868C] And what is the manner in which we ought to devote ourselves to it? You, who inhabit a cell, ask what that manner is, knowing that it is fruitful for you to know this, but still more fruitful to exercise it through experience, in deed and in truth. You ought not to ask this of us, but of someone experienced, for only experience grasps what it is.

Yet because you compel us to say something about it, we shall speak what the Lord grants us, since we do not wish to be thought philosophers—which might perhaps happen if we kept silent.

It seems to us that if you desire to pray fruitfully, you ought to consider three things with the greatest care. First, what sort of person you are when you approach prayer. Second, what sort of person you offer yourself to God as within it. Third, what sort of person you show yourself to be after the time of prayer.

[Col. 0868D] Consider how clean and tranquil you come to it, how pure and whole you remain within it, how grave you are once the prayer itself has been devoutly celebrated and completed, and how mature you remain for as long as you can. Thus, when you devote yourself to prayer in your cell, the more carefully you exercise these three things, the more acceptable your prayer will be to God and the more fruitful for you.

If you ask the Father in the name of the one who is called Jesus both in name and in reality, you will undoubtedly obtain what you ask in this way. You will also be powerfully able to resist all the things—whatever they may be—that strive against you, so that you may overcome and destroy them. Your own experience will make you certain of how this third river, [Col. 0869A] which flows from the place of delight and is also called Tigris, goes against the Assyrians.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. What sort of persons we ought to present ourselves as before approaching prayer, so that when we have come to it, we may offer it to God in such a way that he mercifully makes it both acceptable to himself and fruitful for us

Before we enter that fourth river which we read flows from the place of delight and whose name is Euphrates, you, who inhabit a cell, ask us to discuss something more with you about prayer. For the more frequently you devote yourself to it, the more ardently you desire to be instructed in how you ought to attend to it.

We agree; we accommodate your request and, according to our ability and knowledge, are prepared to fulfill your wish in this matter. [Col. 0869B] You will remember that, near the end of the chapter immediately preceding this one, we said that, for your prayer to be regarded as acceptable to God and to become fruitful for you, you must consider three things with the greatest care.

The first is that you carefully attend to what sort of person you are when you approach it. The second is what sort of person you offer yourself to God as within it. The third is what sort of person you show yourself to be after the end of prayer.

Since we cannot adequately treat all three together in this chapter, let us begin with the first of the first. We earnestly admonish you, who inhabit a cell; we urgently entreat you; and, in the Lord, we command you at a suitable—and even an unsuitable—time: when you hasten to adore the Lord your God, and especially when you intend to approach [Col. 0869C] in order to sacrifice the Son to the Father, where God is especially reconciling the world to himself in that same Christ, carefully keep in mind and know without any doubt that, although the eyes of the Lord observe the good and the wicked in every place, you then appear especially in the sight of God and of the holy angels who are present, and of all the saints.

And what you offer to God in prayer, offer yourself as present both to him and to those blessed spirits of the heavenly court, and also to all the saints—whether you are praying alone in your cell, though not alone, or praying with others in the oratory. If this is so—and indeed, because it is so—pay the greatest attention to how you approach and to what sort of person you ought to present yourself in this approach.

And you say to me: “It is your responsibility to teach me how I ought to present myself at that hour; it is my responsibility to listen humbly and, according to my ability and knowledge, to devote myself faithfully to carrying it out.”

[Col. 0869D] And I reply: “So be it, as you say; and I pray God that we may do so.” Therefore, when approaching prayer, diligently strive and exert yourself with all your strength to bring a completely clean heart, so that you may offer a prayer pleasing to God and salutary for yourself.

“How will this happen?” you ask. Listen, understand, and, having listened and understood, also accomplish it in deed.
