Whatever wounds your conscience—indeed, whatever is able to wound your conscience because you have illicitly committed it by thought, speech, action, or in any other way—strive first to amend and cast it away through full repentance, pure, humble, and faithful confession, and fitting satisfaction, together with a firm resolve, by the grace of God, to exercise restraint from that point onward.

[Col. 0870A] I say “whatever is able to wound your conscience” because there are very many people who scarcely ever endure any bite of conscience amid all their transgressions, although they never cease committing what is unlawful. For there is no fear of God before their eyes, nor any desire for their own salvation. Hence, in none of the unlawful acts they commit do they know how to return to their conscience. They pass blindly through all the evils they commit and do not even consider themselves guilty in anything, although it is clear that they offend in innumerable ways.

But when they seem to do something that is, as it were, good, however slightly and superficially, they also continually turn it over inwardly among themselves, glorying not in the Lord but in themselves; and outwardly, seeking human praise with their mouths, they do not cease to proclaim it arrogantly.

[Col. 0870B] You must not be like this, you who inhabit a cell; no, do not be like this. In everything that you turn over in your mind, say with your mouth, or commit in deed, always and everywhere return to the testimony of your conscience. Seeing it fully in the light of truth, accept as entirely valid what it has truly judged about each of your inward thoughts and outward practices—both in condemning, blaming, and correcting the things it rejects, and in acquiring, retaining, practicing, and increasing the things it approves.

Therefore, always carrying a sharp stake of self-accusation in the belt of your heart, sit by humbling yourself and dig by correcting yourself. In this way cover through repentance what has been brought forth by you foully and stinkingly—not so much by nature as through guilt. Know that blessed are those whose sins are covered, and that, just as in the holy living creatures the two wings of each were joined together, so also two wings covered their bodies.

[Col. 0870C] What these things mean, blessed Gregory will teach you; or rather, your own experience will make you certain of it. But if you see anything that appears good in yourself, know first and most certainly that it does not come from you. Then do not fail to recognize that even Jerusalem itself will be searched by that just and strict judge “with lamps”; and when the time comes, he will also judge the righteousnesses.

For just as, if he comes to you, you will not see him, so also, if he departs, you will not understand it—so that, if he ever smiles upon you, you must not trust him.

[Col. 0870D] Learn in this way, through experience, to reckon fault even among good things, where there is no fault. Therefore cast away from yourself completely those deadly loincloths of the first parents’ excuse-making, by which innumerable people today, to their great foolishness, cover their shameful parts.

Know also that to excuse guilt is nothing other than doubling a simple fault and increasing a small one. Rather, let reason hold a certain strict tribunal within you; but let conscience, which does not know how to spare, remain silent, or conceal, make its proclamations. Let the mind itself fall silent, wholly free from every stain of excuse, defense, contradiction, and evasion. Instead, casting away the garments of the perverse silence by which it has until now been covered, let it make itself naked and stripped through pure confession.

[Col. 0871A] In the presence of reason presiding over this tribunal, let the mind humble itself deeply and stand ready and willing to undergo, according to reason’s judgment, the strict discipline of fitting satisfaction, with a firm resolve to amend from that point onward.

When you, who inhabit a cell, ought to maintain all these things within yourself in this manner, you should exercise them especially when you intend to approach prayer. For the Psalmist says of himself: “If I have looked upon iniquity in my heart, the Lord will not hear” (Ps. 65:19). He immediately adds: “Therefore God heard, and attended to the voice of my petition” (Ps. 65:19). The implied meaning is: “Because I did not look upon iniquity, God heard and attended.”

[Col. 0871B] If, then, you exercise what has been said, and in the manner in which it has been said, confidently rejoice that your prayer will be heard by God, because you no longer look upon iniquity in your heart. For if there was once any iniquity in it, it has already been erased.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. That when we approach prayer, we must forgive from a pure heart those who have offended against us, and, if there are any who hold something against us, become fully and perfectly reconciled with them
Among these matters, you who are an inhabitant of a cell, carefully keep in mind that apostolic command—and indeed a most salutary one—in which, addressing his beloved and chosen disciple in his Epistle, he says: “Lifting up pure hands, without anger and disputation” (I Tim. II, 9).

What difference, we wonder, is there between disputation [Col. 0871C] and anger? It seems to us, certainly, that a person who is moved against someone with excessive injustice and indiscretion, with excessive harshness and cruelty, is in anger. But the person who represents to himself in his mind even the one against whom he has been stirred, although that person is bodily absent, and who addresses him amid the inner whispering of his heart, with a certain silent cry—or, if it may more appropriately be said, with a certain clamorous silence—in tumultuous disturbance and disturbed tumult, uttering many kinds of allegations, all of them—as it seems to him—reasonable, but in truth entirely devoid of reason; who receives answers, with no one present with him except himself: this person is surely in disputation. For he disputes and argues, quarrelling with no one else in a bitter voice, always excusing himself and bitterly accusing the one against whom he has been stirred; silently—since no one hears him except himself—and bitterly, he cries out.

But our hands must be lifted in prayer free from both of these evils: we must cease from being moved against anyone, and must not, in our heart, accuse another while silently clamouring and clamourously remaining silent in our own defence; nor, while accusing another, excuse ourselves, ourselves being in these matters both the sole accuser and no one else—the very person who, by accusing another, excuses himself, and by excusing himself, accuses another. Free from both of these dreadful evils, I tell you, you who are an inhabitant of a cell, you must lift your hands in prayer, so that it may be acceptable to God and fruitful for you.

Against both these evils, which must be driven away from us at the time of prayer, the Lord’s command is twofold [Col. 0872A]. One part is this: “When you stand to pray, forgive if you have anything against anyone” (Mark XI, 25); the other is: “If you offer your gift at the altar,” and what follows. But let us first deal with the command we placed first, before proceeding to the other.

“When you stand,” says the Lord, “to pray, forgive if you have anything against anyone.” And again: “If you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will also forgive you your sins; but if you do not forgive people, neither will your Father forgive your sins” (Matt. VI, 14–15).

See, you who are an inhabitant of a cell: you have heard both what the Lord exhorts us to do and what he threatens us with. He exhorts us, indeed, that when we approach prayer we should forgive; but he threatens that if we do not forgive, neither will we be forgiven. The exhortation, I confess, is exceedingly salutary; the threat, exceedingly terrifying. If we forgive, we will be forgiven; if we do not forgive, neither will we be forgiven. See how it has been placed in our will whether grace should cherish us or anger strike us.

Therefore, as you approach prayer, you who are an inhabitant of a cell, forgive, so that you may be forgiven; but forgive in the manner in which you desire to be forgiven. Perhaps you say: “What does it mean to forgive?” And we answer you in this way: to forgive means to send something out of the mind, so that you retain within your mind and in yourself none of those things that anyone has wrongly said or done to you.

For if, stirred and grieving, sad and complaining, angry and bitter, you turn over within yourself anything that someone has said or done to you rather harshly, or if you seek an appropriate time to repay him in kind and in return; and if, when some adversity befalls him—not inflicted by you, but by someone else—you also rejoice because of it, we say plainly that you do not forgive. Nor can you profitably approach prayer for as long as you feel such things being acted out within you. You have not yet sent from your mind what was done or said to you; rather, you still possess a mind filled with deadly poison, with which you yourself have filled it.

And if you either dare not or are ashamed to do this, or indeed cannot do it, but nevertheless look upon the person against whom you have been stirred with a wounded and grim eye, with lowered brows, depriving him of the serenity of your countenance; and either do not deign to speak with him, or, if you happen to speak, hurl bitter words at him for this reason, and are not inwardly gentle toward him, as you ought to be toward your brother: know for certain that you have not yet forgiven and that you are still unfit to approach prayer.

Perhaps you will answer in this way: “Your speech is harsh; who can listen to you? When, then, do I forgive, if I do not forgive for as long as I feel such things being acted out within me?” And we answer you thus: know that nothing impure pleases God, who is supreme purity, and that nothing feigned pleases him, who is true justice. If you listen to us patiently, we shall tell you when you forgive.

See and pay attention: if you send from your mind something that has been said or done to you so completely that you entirely forget it; and if you look upon the person who has inflicted something contrary upon you, whether by word or deed, with a serene eye, without any recollection of those things; and if you address him with perfect goodwill and gentleness of mind; and if you make no bitter mention of any of those things inflicted upon you, either in his presence or in his absence, whether by speaking or in any other way, it seems to us that you have then forgiven.

For then you forgive not in word and tongue, but in deed and truth, fulfilling what the Lord says: “If you do not forgive each one his brother from your hearts” (Matt. XVIII, 35). Know beyond all doubt that everything which is not sincere cannot please God, just as it cannot remain hidden from him. Indeed, complete such forgetfulness is itself complete forgiveness.

For it is written in the Law: “You shall not remember the injury done by your fellow citizens” (Lev. XIX, 18). And after their father Jacob had died and been buried, Joseph’s brothers sent to him [Col. 0873B]: “Your father commanded us before he died to say these words to you: ‘I beg you to forget the crime of your brothers, and the sin and wickedness which they committed against you’” (Gen. L, 17). But, so that we may know that such forgetfulness is forgiveness, they added: “We also ask you to forgive the servant of God, your father, this iniquity.” See how what they had previously called “forgetfulness” they now call “forgiveness.”

But if you remember, while being touched by no pain at all, we say that you do forgive. For we often remember sad things joyfully, and, now perfectly healthy, recall without any pain that we were once ill; and in our mind, without any darkness, we look upon those former shadows which, insofar as they themselves are concerned, have already passed away.

To bring this matter to an end, it seems to us that you then forgive when, remembering that you endured such things, you rejoice and are glad, imitating the one who says that he gladly boasts in his weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may dwell in him; and who also adds: “Therefore I am pleased with my weaknesses, with insults, with necessities, with persecutions, with distresses, for Christ” (II Cor. XII, 10).

But if you have not yet reached such perfection that you can rejoice and be glad when you remember such things, yet in this recollection turn them over within yourself without any disturbance; and, considering them altogether as nothing, love the person who inflicted some adversity upon you no less than you loved him before—or would love him if he had never inflicted it—then certainly you have forgiven.

Therefore you approach prayer fruitfully when, forgiving in this way, you fulfil the Lord’s command. But just as you do not wish to have anything against another, so also it is necessary that, as far as possible and as much as depends upon you, you do not allow anyone to have anything against you. In this way you will also fulfil that other command of the Lord which we placed second above, namely: “If you offer your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go first to be reconciled to your brother; and then come and offer your gift” (Matt. V, 23–24).

For, as blessed Gregory says (Homily 8 on Ezekiel): “The gift is not accepted unless discord is first driven from the mind.” Here you must understand that you ought to drive discord from your brother’s mind no less than from your own: your brother has something against you because you have injured him, just as you drive discord from your own mind because you have injured him. “Leave it,” he says, “and go first to be reconciled to your brother.”

What does it mean to leave the gift and go to be reconciled to your brother, except humbly to cease from prayer for the time being, until you have been reconciled to your brother? And if this is so, why must prayer be suspended for the time being, unless because you cannot offer prayer that is acceptable to God or fruitful for you until you have first been reconciled to your brother?

You can and ought to do this if your brother is present—the brother whom you remember to have something against you. But if, at the time of this recollection, he is so far absent from you that you cannot immediately reach him by bodily steps, do in your heart, before him who examines that same heart, for your brother—although he is far away—what you ought to do toward him if he were present.

Do this for the time being until you are able to have your brother present, so that you may then do openly, in his presence, what you are now doing secretly before God, in his absence.

“And how,” you ask, “will this be done?” See and pay attention to how it will be done. Intending to offer your gift—that is, the devotion of your prayer—to God, and remembering at that hour that your brother has something against you, postpone offering your prayer for the time being until you have done what we are now telling you.

Go in your very heart to your brother, although he is bodily situated far away from you. In profound humility and true repentance, prostrate yourself inwardly before him, with God, who is present, as witness; and, lying humbly at his feet, sharply reproach yourself, earnestly ask his forgiveness, and promise him amendment thereafter. Thus reconciled to your brother, approach to offer your gift.

The word “then” seems to indicate this. For what does “then you shall offer” mean except that you ought not to offer before doing this? If you acted otherwise, the gift offered would neither please God nor benefit you.

But great discernment must be exercised in this command of the Lord, and some exception must also be understood in it. We are not compelled to do this whenever we remember that our brother thinks he has something against us, whatever the manner.

For example, suppose you correct your brother for the salvation of his soul, at the proper time and place. Suppose you make a just and charitable accusation against him in chapter, and do so in every respect according to the manner required by the order. If, because of this, he becomes disturbed and agitated and thinks that he has something against you, it does not seem to us that you are bound to go and be reconciled to him. For, as far as depends upon you, you have committed no evil against him; rather, you wished to do him a great good. But he, through his resentment and impatience, turns your great good into a great evil for himself; and it is more because of the weakness of the sick man than because of any fault of the physician that he falls ill even from the medicine.

For this reason blessed Augustine writes about the matter in the Rule for Clerics (chapter 8): “Nor should you judge yourselves malevolent when you point this out. For you are rather not innocent if, by keeping silent, you allow your brothers, whom you could correct by pointing it out, to perish. If your brother had a wound on his body which he wished to conceal because he feared being cut, would it not be cruel for you to remain silent about it, and merciful to point it out? How much more, then, ought you to reveal it, lest it fester more dangerously in his heart?”

See how cruel are those who conceal their brothers’ spiritual wounds, and how merciful are those who point them out so that they may be healed.

Again, if some superior corrects one of his subjects for his fault—for this too he is bound to do by reason of the office he has undertaken—and does so piously and fatherly, so that the subject may amend, do you suppose that he must go and reconcile himself to his brother if that brother, unjustly stirred, thinks that he has something against him because of this?

“I do not think so,” you say, “unless he exceeded the proper measure in his correction.” But we say: not even then. It often happens that the more ardently a person loves, the more quickly he exceeds the proper measure in correcting. For because the mind of the superior loves as it ought and as much as it ought, he often exaggerates his correction more than he should.

Nor should he involve himself here in any reconciliation, because this could harm the disciple more than help him. Hence blessed Augustine writes about this in the aforementioned Rule (chapter 54), addressing the superiors themselves:

“When, however, the necessity of discipline in correcting conduct compels you to speak harsh words, if you also feel that you have exceeded the proper measure, you are not required to ask forgiveness from your subjects, lest, while excessive humility is maintained before those who ought to be subject, the authority of governing be broken. But forgiveness must nevertheless be sought from the Lord of all, who knows with what benevolence you love even those whom you perhaps correct more severely than is just. For the love among you ought not to be fleshly but spiritual.”

Certainly, if, while wood was being cut, iron flying from the handle struck and killed a friend, that friend—and yet the killer of his friend—could live if he fled to one of the three cities of refuge (Deut. XIX). So too, we say, if he simply went away into the forest. We have said this so that we may know what kind of people we ought to be when we approach prayer.

## CHAPTER XXXV. On the four kinds of thoughts that we must keep in mind if we wish to pray to the Lord purely, devoutly, and fruitfully

[Col. 0875D]

See, you who are an inhabitant of a cell: to some extent, as we think, you now know how you ought, by the grace of God, to prepare yourself when you intend to approach your God in prayer (chap. 35). Whatever we have said about prayer, and may perhaps still say, we refer to that third river which also flows out from the place of delight and is called the Tigris; of which we also read that it goes toward the Assyrians. We have lingered in it for a long time because, plainly, on account of both its great depth and its great breadth, we could not cross it quickly.

But now you ask us to instruct you, as far as we know and are able, concerning what we placed second above: namely, how you ought to persevere in prayer itself, and what you ought at that hour to turn over in your thoughts [Col. 0876A]. You must know this without doubt—and, unless we are mistaken, you have often experienced it yourself—that in no spiritual exercise do we feel a greater labour or a more arduous struggle than when we persevere in prayer, provided that we strive to make it what it is necessary for us to have.

For then, above all, the great instability of our heart and the malice of the ancient enemy weary and torment us beyond measure. That slippery and malicious one, who has a thousand ways of doing harm, knows that through especially devout prayer his hidden deceits are exposed and his open forces defeated. To empty its fruit completely, he generally makes himself more troublesome to us by then injecting unlawful thoughts into our hearts.

Our own instability and wandering of mind also devastate us more in prayer—as we lamented much earlier with great groaning—than in any other exercise. To such an extent does a multitude of idle, impure, and harmful thoughts then thrust themselves suddenly into our mind, even against our will and despite our resisting with all our strength, before we are able to foresee it; although at other times the mind was free and quiet from them.

Therefore we must know that it is exceedingly necessary, when we feel these things within us, to steady our miserable heart with every effort and, as far as we can, not allow it to cling to the wandering and foolish thoughts that force themselves upon it.

If you, who are an inhabitant of a cell, desire to know how you may pray purely—or rather, since we know with complete certainty that you ardently desire this—strive with all your strength to turn these four things over in your thoughts at the time of prayer: the one whom you pray to, the one through whom you pray, that which you pray for, and you yourself who pray.

Your heart must be very broad, so that it can contain these four things within itself simultaneously.

O how joyful was the mind of blessed Benedict, to whom, while he was praying and saw a holy soul being carried up to heaven, the whole world appeared gathered together beneath a single ray of the sun, so that he might clearly recognize that, for one by whom the Creator of the universe is seen, every creature is small.

Therefore, when you pray, keep before the eyes of your heart the one to whom you pray. And who is that one except God himself?

“What,” you ask, “shall I think when I think of my God?” We answer you that the anointing which teaches about everything will teach you this more fully than any human instruction. That anointing will teach you to think of your God as a certain eternity, because he has neither beginning nor end; as a certain immensity, because he occupies no place; as a certain unchangeableness, because he belongs to no time; as omnipotence; as charity; as the peace that surpasses all understanding; as essentially present everywhere. We love him by desiring him, and desire him by loving him, embracing him as though with certain arms of sincere love. We know that there is no end to his greatness.

Let your mind think of him in prayer, expanded in love for him, so that it may pray purely, representing him to itself alone and solitary. Set him before you and yourself before him; and, because of the great love with which you love him above all things, in the ineffable sweetness that you feel infused into you by him, in a certain joyful and joy-giving jubilation, steal yourself away from yourself, deprived of yourself, cling to him, glued to him.

But do not ask us how, when you pray purely, the one to whom you pray reveals himself to you, for we are completely ignorant of these matters. And we are ignorant because we have experienced them either exceedingly rarely or never.

This, however, we know: when a holy and sincere mind—a clean, purified, and pure mind—prays in complete and perfect love and desire, then, by his secret infusion, he reveals to that mind his own inward and hidden things, most pleasant and sweet.

We placed second that we should consider with the greatest attention the one through whom we pray. Who is this one except the mediator between God and human beings, God and human, Christ Jesus [Col. 0877B]? Insofar as he is human, he is with us and pleads for us before the Father in a far better manner than we do; and insofar as he is God, he is with the Father and the Holy Spirit, with whom he is one and the same God, making propitiation for us.

He is indeed our righteous advocate with the Father; and he is not only the divine propitiator but also the propitiation for our sins.

Behold the golden altar: namely, Christ’s human nature, in which there is absolutely nothing that is not pure and free from every fault. Upon this altar we offer our prayers to God the Father, so that God the almighty and merciful Father may rightly be propitious to that nature which, in the human being who is pure, he sees joined to his divine Son by personal union.

Therefore, you who are an inhabitant of a cell, let the Son of God appear to you through the inner eyes of your contemplation: equal in every respect to the Father and the Holy Spirit, coeternal, and consubstantial. Let him, I say, appear to you as you stand in prayer, presenting before the Father’s face the glory of victorious flesh in great joy.

For he himself is the golden altar: Christ appearing in human nature, which was free from every sin and therefore golden. Upon this golden altar we sacrifice the offerings of our prayers, so that the supreme Father may be propitious to us sinners in the one in whom he sees our nature joined to that same Son—not culpably, but naturally, in the unity of person.

Thus let Christ appear to the inner eyes of your contemplation, conceived by the Holy Spirit, incarnate without corruption, born without injury; appearing to the Magi as the eternal God in the incense, the almighty king in the gold, the true and still mortal human being in the myrrh.

Let him appear to you suckling at the virgin mother’s breasts, wrapped in swaddling clothes, placed in a manger, subjected to circumcision, offered in the temple, fleeing to Egypt in obedience to his parents and returning from there; subject to his parents, advancing in wisdom, age, and grace.

Let him appear to you baptized, fasting, hungry, tempted, living among human beings; in his deeds enduring malicious observers, and in his words obstinate contradictors.

Let him appear to you teaching what is true and salutary, doing new and wondrous things, washing the feet of his disciples, giving them the sacraments of his body and blood, praying at greater length in his agony, so that his sweat became like drops of blood running down to the ground [Col. 0878A].

Let there appear to you, above all, everything harsh, dreadful, disgraceful, and cruel that he endured for you: that he was sold, handed over, seized, bound, led away, questioned, judged, condemned, smeared with spittle, blindfolded, struck on the head, slapped, scourged, clothed in a scarlet cloak, mockingly worshipped, ridiculed in a white garment, holding a reed in his right hand, carrying his cross, and reckoned among the wicked.

Let there appear to you the vinegar mixed with gall offered to him; his most holy blood pouring forth—not a drop but a wave—through the five wounds of his most sacred body; his praying for transgressors; his commending that beloved soul into the Father’s hands; his bowing his head; his giving up his spirit.

Let him appear to you buried, raised again, appearing to his disciples over forty days by many proofs, and then ascending where he had previously been; sitting at the Father’s right hand; coming with great power and majesty to judge—the one who came in humility to be judged; reigning eternally in his chosen ones, making them recline at table, and passing among them and serving them.

Behold, we tell you, you who are an inhabitant of a cell, through whom you ought to pray to the Father. Therefore, when you pray, embrace this advocate of yours with certain arms of your mind, and present him in the very purity of your mind before the Father’s face. Strive to offer him to the Father with rejoicing and faith, such as we have now shown him to you.

What could you fail to obtain from the loving Father that pertains to your salvation, praying and asking in the name of his beloved Son, if faith in you does not waver, hope does not despair, and charity does not grow lukewarm?

Pay attention also, in these matters, to the very words of your petition. Standing before God the almighty Father in the presence of that entire heavenly court, and presenting your advocate to the Father, turn over in your heart what you say with your mouth, so that your voice may agree with your mind, and your mind may think what your voice utters.

This is what we placed third above: that you attend to the one to whom you pray in such a way that you do not fail to attend to what it is that you pray for, so that your mind may understand what your tongue utters.

“But,” you say, “it is not possible for everyone to have the mind understand what the tongue utters—not merely because of the instability that exists in their minds, but because of the ignorance that is in them. For there are very many who are scarcely able to understand anything of what they say, because they possess almost no knowledge of letters, so far as understanding is concerned. Although they may possess the outward articulation of words, they do not possess knowledge of the inward meaning hidden in those same words.

“Do you mean that the prayer of such people is entirely without fruit before God, because they do not grasp in their minds through understanding what they utter with their mouths?”

We answer you concerning this as follows: God forbid that we should say this. We do not think that the saying “The ignorant person will be ignored” (I Cor. XIV, 38) was spoken about them. For although they do not possess this understanding, if with devout hearts, good intention, and proper manner they utter the sacred words with faith, hope, and charity, I am confident in the mercy of the one whom they pray to that he himself will supply in them what they do not possess in themselves; and their ignorance will not prejudice the fruit of their prayer.

For it cannot be believed that what has not been given to them should be strictly required of them, or that this should bring great harm to their salvation because they do not return what they have never received.

But just as they may perhaps have some excuse in these matters, so you certainly cannot be excused, since you possess knowledge and understanding of the things you utter but, through your great negligence, do not care to attend to them.

Therefore, apply your heart to what you utter with your mouth when you pray to your God—not only when you yourself utter it, but also when you hear others reciting psalms or hymns with their mouths.

When in choir you hear something pertaining to the psalms, when you sing, or when you read, let what you utter outwardly in sound be inwardly present in your heart through understanding. But when you hear others reciting verses of the psalms, singing, or reading, attend intentionally to what they utter, and through understanding apply your heart, together with your ear, to what you hear them say.

This is what we have just said: you must also consider what you pray for.

As for what we placed fourth—that you should attend to yourself who pray—you fulfil it when, entreating God the Father in heart and mouth through his Son Christ Jesus, your advocate, you gather and heap up before yourself at that hour your sins and offences, your crimes and disgraces, and the many great weaknesses by which you are weighed down in mind and body. You place before the eyes of your contemplation, as far as you can, your past, present, and future, so that, digging around the unfruitful tree and applying manure, you may compel it to bear fruit, and eat the roasted lamb with wild lettuce.

In this way you will render your prayer pleasing to God. In this way, holding your sins as though sealed in a pouch, rejoice and be glad because your iniquity has been healed. In this way also, with the tax collector who stood at a distance and did not dare to lift his eyes to heaven but struck his breast, you will afterward, and after a little while, go down justified to your house.

But if, as sometimes happens, at the suggestion of the evil enemy—who is always striving to harm us, but is especially troublesome in prayer, so that he may snatch away from us all its fruit—some unlawful thought, formed in any way by anger, agitation, vanity, curiosity, or pleasure, violently intrudes upon you as you settle into prayer and ravages you intensely, so that you cannot turn your mind’s eye away from it, the counsel is that, setting aside the other petitions to which you had been attending, you rise manfully in prayer against this affliction. Do not cease from this rising in any way until, through God’s mercy, you have overcome it and found peace.

See, these are the four things that we advise you, who are an inhabitant of a cell, to turn over in your mind at the time of prayer: who the one is to whom you pray, who the one is through whom you pray, what the thing is for which you pray, and, finally, who you are who pray.

In the first consideration, you contemplate the ineffable majesty of God the almighty Father; in the second, the boundless mercy of your Saviour; in the third, a certain tranquil purity and pure tranquillity; in the fourth, your own weakness, with which you are burdened in heart and body.

Concerning what we said above—that we must know what sort of people we ought to show ourselves to be after the time of prayer—we say this briefly to you, who are an inhabitant of a cell. When prayer has been completed, we ought, for as long as we are able by God’s grace, to preserve ourselves in the same gravity, maturity, and integrity.

For if we immediately admit frivolous thoughts in our hearts and return to laughter and loud amusement, to poisonous detraction and idle chatter [Col. 0880B], we must greatly fear that, by acting in such ways, we may lose the fruit of our prayer.

Let us imitate with what care that woman of whom we read prayed to the Lord, weeping abundantly and speaking in her heart; her lips alone moved, and her voice was not heard at all; and her countenance was no longer changed in different directions (I Reg. I, 13, 18).

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On the manual work to which the inhabitant of a cell ought to devote himself, at which hours he ought to engage in spiritual exercises and at which hours in manual labour, and on several other matters concerning the same inhabitant of a cell

[Col. 0875D]

We have lingered long in this third river, which is called the Tigris [Col. 0880C], and perhaps not foolishly. For it is exceedingly useful for you, who are an inhabitant of a cell, to know how you ought to devote yourself to prayer, since it is clear that you must apply yourself so frequently to this spiritual and holy exercise. But now let us leave this third river and, if it pleases you, enter the fourth. It is called the Euphrates, which likewise proceeds from the place of delight. Concerning it, Holy Scripture does not relate that it circles any land, as it does of the Phison, which circles all the land of Evilath, and of the Gyon, which circles all the land of Ethiopia; nor that it advances against any peoples, as it does of the one called the Tigris, which advances against the Assyrians. It says only, simply and briefly: “The fourth river is the Euphrates” [Col. 0880D] (Gen. 2:14).

This is perhaps because useful and fruitful manual work—which, according to the interpretation of its name, we refer to the river that is the Euphrates—is more common to very many people than any of the three commendable exercises mentioned thus far, according to the tropological sense in which we are proceeding: namely, the study of reading, the purity of meditation, or the devotion of prayer. We do not see all those whom we see clothed in the religious habit to be sufficiently capable of those three at all times, so that all might be able, fully and abundantly, either to devote themselves to the study of reading, or to persist in pure meditation within the mind, or likewise to apply themselves to devout prayer [Par. “or to the devotion of prayer”]. But who is there who, if he is sound in all the members of his body, cannot, according to necessity and the time, perform something good with his hands?

Therefore, because piety—as the Apostle says—is useful for all things, possessing the promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come (1 Tim. 4:8), perhaps it is rightly said of two of the rivers that they circle lands, and of the third that it advances against the Assyrians. We applied that usefulness to those rivers: to the Phison, on account of the study of sacred reading; to the Gyon, on account of the purity of inward meditation; and to the one called the Tigris, on account of the sincerity of devout prayer. But because bodily exercise is useful only to a limited extent—which we refer to the Euphrates, the fourth river—it proceeds, insofar as it is useful, as though from the place of delight.

Yet because it is not useful for all things, as piety is, but only for a little, Scripture does not say of that fourth river, through which we understand action, either that it circles any land or that it advances against any peoples. It says only, as we have already stated, simply and briefly: “The fourth river is the Euphrates” (Gen. 2:14).

And if these things can stand thus—and if perhaps they cannot, but are to be understood in whatever way is more correct and fitting—you, who are an inhabitant of a cell, should nevertheless know this: it is very necessary for you, for many reasons, to devote yourself to manual work at appointed hours and times, insofar as it is permitted, fitting, and expedient. For it removes weariness, produces enjoyment, brings great usefulness, and does not allow idleness—which is the enemy of the soul—to prevail over it [Col. 0881B]. You return to those three spiritual exercises—the reading, meditation, and prayer—with greater desire and pleasure because, for the sake of the fruit of good action, you occasionally interrupt them with greater willingness.

If you ask to what work you ought to devote yourself, we answer you briefly: devote yourself, namely, to the work which your prior has assigned you, so that you may apply yourself to it. Moreover, if the prior has so provided, there is one work to which you ought especially to devote yourself in your activity: namely, that you learn to write, if you can learn it, and, if you can and know how, that you write.

In a certain sense this is an immortal work; a work—not, if one may say so, passing away, but remaining; a work, so to speak, and yet not a work; finally, a work which, among all other works, is especially becoming to learned religious men. For learned religious men always, insofar as bodily health permits them, when they are free from prayer, reading, meditation, and—something that must by no means be omitted—bodily necessities and the necessary supports of the body, ought, as time and reason demand—not indeed as their own will may choose, but rather as the discerning authority and authoritative discernment of the one presiding may dictate—to devote themselves diligently to books: preparing, producing, binding, correcting, decorating, illuminating, giving titles to them, and arranging, making, and completing whatever pertains to these tasks.

Although this is decent and fitting in every order, it is especially appropriate and beautiful in our Carthusian order. Why do I say “appropriate”? Beautiful and suitable—as though that could be enough. Indeed, I say that this is how we ought to act. For who can always apply himself untiringly either to reading, meditation, or prayer, without an occasional interval? And therefore, even if scarcely any fruit came from manual work, it is nevertheless good that at times our diligent concern and concerned diligence should devote itself to it, according to the time and the manner.

Thus we may drive weariness from ourselves, lest we be weighed down too heavily by the burden of faintheartedness, and drive away idleness, which is the enemy of the soul and which, as a certain wise man says, “has taught much evil” (Ecclus. 33:29), lest our mind wither beyond measure through the absence of every useful exercise.

Saint Paul also instructs us how necessary and health-giving manual work is for us. For he writes, as you yourself know:

“We beseech you, brothers, to abound more and more, and to strive to live quietly, to conduct your own affairs, and to work with your hands, as we commanded you; and to walk honorably before those who are outside, and to desire nothing from anyone” (1 Thess. 4:11).

Let us also know that he himself did what he taught. He says: “You yourselves know how you ought to imitate us. For we were not restless among you, nor did we eat anyone’s bread without paying for it; but in labor and toil, working night and day, so as not to burden any of you” (2 Thess. 3:7–8). And to show us that he could have acted otherwise if he had wished, he says: “Not as though we had no authority, but that we might give ourselves to you as a pattern for imitation” (ibid., 9). And again: “When we were with you, we used to command you this: if anyone is unwilling to work, neither should he eat” (ibid., 10).

A little later he adds: “For we hear that some among you are walking disorderly, doing no work, but busying themselves with what does not concern them. Now we command and beseech such persons, in our Lord Jesus Christ, that by working quietly they eat their own bread” (2 Thess. 3:12).

Why do we think that so great and eminent a teacher wished to admonish his disciples about this so earnestly and diligently, unless he knew that it was useful and exceedingly health-giving for them to do it?

Go, then, you who are an inhabitant of a cell, and do likewise. Every day on which it is permitted to work, if you are fully sound in body, perform with your hands some useful work that contributes to the common good—not what you have chosen for yourself by your own will, but what your superiors have assigned to you—cheerfully and in orderly fashion, according to your knowledge and ability.

Remember what the venerable Ivo, bishop of the Church of Chartres, writes about this, among other things, to the virgins living in the monastery at Dun (Epistle 10):

“Be always intent,” he says, “upon prayer, or reading, or work, so that the devil may find you neither idle nor exposing your minds to harmful and wandering thoughts.”

He adds:

“This custom is said to have existed in the monasteries of the Egyptians: they would receive no one who was unwilling to devote himself to work—not because of necessity, but to avoid idleness, which is the enemy of the soul.”

Blessed Benedict also says the following about this in the Rule of Monks [Col. 0883A] (chapter 48):

“Idleness is the enemy of the soul; and therefore the brothers must be occupied at appointed times in manual labor, and again at appointed hours in sacred reading.”

See, then, what great and eminent men think about manual work; see what they have left concerning it in their writings. We understand it through that fourth river, which proceeds from the place of delight, according to the moral sense, and of which Scripture says: “The fourth river is the Euphrates.”

We know with complete certainty that, unless they knew that this exercise was exceedingly fruitful and exceedingly health-giving, they would in no way have agreed so harmoniously about admonishing, commanding, and writing about it.

Meditate on these things, you who are an inhabitant of a cell; remain in them. Pay attention to yourself and to your manual work. Persist in it. This, however, ought especially to be your work: as we told you above, apply yourself diligently to writing books.

This ought indeed to be the particular work of Carthusian recluses. For this reason, the venerable Guigo, of blessed memory and to be named with every honor—the fifth prior of the Carthusian desert, exceedingly learned, as we read, in secular and divine letters, keen in intellect, tenacious in memory, remarkable in eloquence, and most effective as an exhorter—this great and distinguished man, I say, writes about this in the twenty-eighth chapter of the book of the Institutions of the Carthusian Order, which he himself composed:

“We teach almost all whom we receive to write, if it can be done.”

And shortly afterward:

“We wish books to be guarded with the greatest care as the everlasting food of our souls, and to be produced diligently. For since we cannot preach the word of God with our mouths, let us preach it with our hands.”

He shows what usefulness comes from this when he adds:

“For however many books we write, we seem to make for ourselves that many preachers of the truth, hoping for a reward from the Lord on behalf of all those who through them will either have been corrected from error or will have advanced in Catholic truth; and also on behalf of all those who through them will either have been pierced with compunction for their sins and vices or have been kindled with desire for their heavenly homeland.”

In the book of the Life of Saint Martin, too, we read that “no craft was practiced there except that of the scribes.” It is then added: “The younger members were assigned to this work; the elders devoted themselves to prayer” (Sulpicius Severus, Life of Saint Martin, ch. 7).

The venerable Guigo mentioned above shows at what times one ought to devote oneself to this holy manual work. In the twenty-ninth chapter of the aforesaid book he writes:

“From Terce until Sext in winter, and from Prime until Terce in summer, time is assigned to manual work. Nevertheless, we wish these tasks to be interrupted by brief prayers. In summer, the period between Vespers and None is occupied with manual work, and while working one may always have recourse to brief, as it were ejaculatory, prayers.””

Concerning the spiritual exercises to which the inhabitant of a cell ought especially to devote himself, at what hours in winter and summer, he writes as follows:

“The period either from Prime until Terce in winter, or from Matins until Prime in summer, is devoted to spiritual exercises.”

Again, in chapter 7:

“After leaving the refectory, from the Kalends of November until the Purification of Blessed Mary, we sing None immediately. From that day until Easter, the interval which we make—that is, between dinner and None—is assigned to reading or to similar exercises.”

Again, in chapter 29 of the same book:

“From Vespers until Compline, time is given to spiritual work.”

Thus you have learned to what particular work and at what times you ought, according to your knowledge and ability, to devote yourself.

Know this also: what we have drawn from you, we have poured out for you; we have clothed you, but with your own garment; we have fed you, but with your own food; we have given to you, but what you already possessed; we have enriched you, but with what you already abound in.

Let what we have said to you at present about manual work suffice. We receive it through that fourth river which proceeds from the place of delight, concerning which the truthful account says: “The fourth river is the Euphrates” (Gen. 2:14).

Behold: you have something by which you may more fully recognize than learn how you, who are an inhabitant of a cell, ought to devote yourself to those four holy and sanctifying exercises. They are: the study of reading, the purity of meditation, the devotion of prayer, and the usefulness of action.

We have placed nothing new in this little book for you, but something ancient, since, according to the comic poet: “Nothing has been said that was not said before.” And Ecclesiastes says: “There is nothing new under the sun.” Nor can anyone say: “Behold, this is new.” And he adds: “It has already existed in the ages that were before us” (Eccles. 1:10).

We are not conscious of having written anything contrary to the truth. Nevertheless, we do not stubbornly deny that we may have written something that is in some respect otherwise, knowing that it is often characteristic of good people to judge there to be fault where there is none.

For indeed, bearing our soul in our hands, we do not wish to spare our mouth so much that we would not tear our own flesh with our teeth, provided that we find it to be ours. But it will be the task of your prudent sagacity and sagacious prudence to gather the rose without taking a thorn into your hand; or, to speak more plainly, to retain what is good while striving to abstain from every appearance of evil.

But let us now put an end to these matters, since we have said a great deal. Would that what we have said to you, who are an inhabitant of a cell, might be as fruitful as it is abundant.

With devoted humility and, no less, humble devotion, though absent in body yet present in spirit, we beseech you: if your holiness finds in anything written here something from which you can receive some spiritual fruit, may you graciously intercede for the soul of that most wretched sinner who has gathered these things together as best he could—not as he ought, but as he was able.

## [LETTERS]

[Col. 0885]

# THREE LETTERS OF BERNARD, FIRST PRIOR OF PORTES

(From a manuscript codex of the monastery of Saint Oyend of the Jura, or Saint-Claude.)

## LETTER ONE. TO AYMO OF VARENNES AND AYMO OF ROHORIA

### On fleeing the world

[Col. 0885A]

Bernard, prior of Portes, and his sons, John of Montmédy and Stephen of Chalmette, send the most reverend and most beloved in Christ, Aymo of Varennes and Aymo of Rohoria, greetings most devoted in the Lord.

“To seek the Lord while he may be found”: we have taken care, insofar as the Lord has granted us the ability, to exhort those present to this; and through the present letter we wish to invite and rouse those who are absent to the same.

Therefore, as servants of the supreme head of the household, whatever our condition may be, acting as his ambassadors to you, we invite you to his supper and to his wedding feast. At his command we add that his oxen and fattened animals have been slaughtered, that everything is ready, and that one must come to the wedding without delay (Luke 14).

We beseech you, then: put aside those excuses by which certain people commonly excuse themselves. One says: “I have married a wife, and therefore I cannot come.” Another says: “I have bought five yokes of oxen, and I am going to test them.” Yet another says: “I have bought a farm, and I must go out to see it.” Those who make such excuses do not defend themselves; they offend the head of the household who invited them.

Having set aside these and every other excuse, come quickly. For when the angel says to the apostle John, “Blessed are those who are called to the marriage supper of the Lamb” (Rev. 19:9), beware lest he himself—God forbid—justly say in anger: “The wedding is indeed ready, but those who were invited were not worthy” (Matt. 22:8); or, certainly, that statement which seems to sound more terrifying: “Amen I say to you, none of those men who were invited shall taste my supper” (Luke 14:24).

Since Scripture says, “Blessed is the one who speaks in the ears of the hearer” (Ecclus. 25:12), that is, of one who understands, and since we know that we are speaking not to unlearned but to educated ears, we do not think that the weight and gravity of the foregoing statements should be diminished by an exposition of our words.

The invitation just given draws them to follow Christ’s humility, having despised the vanity of worldly pride. However much wealth or luxury may have flowed to them in their worldly way of life, they do not lose their joys but exchange them. Indeed—apart from the eternal goods that “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man, which God has prepared for those who love him”—they find incomparably and unspeakably greater joy and delight in divine service than they were able to experience in worldly pleasures [Col. 0885D–0886A].

For those who say, “I have rejoiced in the way of your testimonies as in all riches” (Ps. 118:14), are not without joy. And: “The law of your mouth is good to me, above thousands of gold and silver” (ibid., 72). And: “The judgments of the Lord are true, justified in themselves; more desirable than gold and much precious stone, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb” (Ps. 18:10–11). There are other such passages that it would take too long to enumerate.

The Holy Spirit, who arranged these testimonies in the Scriptures, does not allow those who have despised earthly things for heavenly things, perishing and defiled pleasures for eternal ones, to remain strangers to and inexperienced in those delights signified in the divine utterances. How much greater they are for the mind than for the belly, and how much more excellent spiritual delights are than bodily ones, the inexperienced may hear, but they cannot understand or know at all [Col. 0886B].

The Apostle knew this when he said: “I am filled with consolation; I abound exceedingly in joy in all our tribulation” (2 Cor. 7:4). He did not say “in prosperity,” but “in tribulation”; nor “in some tribulation,” but “in all.” If he had said, “I rejoice in tribulation,” he would have said something great and astonishing. If he had also said, “I abound in joy in tribulation,” he would have proposed something even more astonishing. But by saying, “I abound exceedingly in joy in all our tribulation,” he could not have expressed the excellence of his joy more clearly.

If, then, he consoles his own people here in all their tribulation, what joys of consolation has he prepared for them there, where no tribulation can exist? If he so gladdens and refreshes them on the road of their pilgrimage, how will he gladden and satisfy them in the homeland of their eternal dwelling?

But enough of this.

Some people, despising the invitation to the Lord’s supper and wedding feast given above, and either not believing or neglecting the joys of the saints—whether those they possess here or those promised to them in the future—fulfill what is written: “They spend their days in good things, and in an instant they descend to the underworld” (Job 21:13).

Because such people do not wish to abandon their evils, whatever good works they may perhaps perform are not acceptable before God. For, as it is written, when God gives them time for repentance, they abuse it in pride; by multiplying their sins they store up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath and of the revelation of God’s just judgment (Rom. 2:5).

When God, not they themselves, wishes to put an end to their evils and repay them what they deserve—that is, near the day of their death—if they are perhaps permitted to confess their sins, then, in accordance with what blessed Augustine says, “They speak, but they do not confess,” because God does not accept the confession of the mouth where there is no sincere repentance and sacrifice of a contrite and humbled heart.

They are not so much sorry that they have sinned as they grieve that the opportunity to sin has been taken away from them. Nor can they leave without sorrow what they possessed with love.

Then, however much money they pour out, as though for the redemption of their soul, the sentence pronounced by the Holy Spirit through Solomon remains hard and terrible against them: “Riches will not profit on the day of vengeance, but justice will deliver from death” (Prov. 11:4).

He called it “the day of vengeance,” meaning the time when, illness already pressing upon them, the necessity of death draws near. But when he says that riches will not profit, he means those who have not practiced justice.

Hear also how terribly Wisdom itself, that is, the Son of God, threatens such despisers through the same Solomon:

“Because I called, and you refused; I extended my hand, and there was no one who looked; you despised all my counsel and neglected my reproaches, I too will laugh at your destruction and mock you when what you feared comes upon you” (Prov. 1:24, 26).

Speaking further about such people, he adds:

“When sudden calamity falls, and destruction rushes upon you like a storm, then they will call upon me, and I will not hear; they will rise early, and they will not find me, because they hated discipline, did not receive the fear of the Lord, did not consent to my counsel, and despised all my correction. Therefore they shall eat the fruit of their way and be filled with their own counsels” (ibid., 27–32).

He adds: “The turning away of the little ones will kill them, and the prosperity of fools will destroy them.” Those whom he signified by the name “little ones,” he explicitly identifies by explaining them as “fools.”

Nor are those little ones excluded from the number of such people concerning whom it is said through Jeremiah: “They are wise to do evil, but they do not know how to do good” (Jer. 4:22), although the Apostle says that “the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God” (1 Cor. 3:19).

Therefore, we beseech you, do not become their companions.

Holy Scripture declares that only those depart this life securely who either have committed no sins after baptism, or at least have had their crimes wiped away through worthy fruits of repentance and have no other sins to confess at their departure, except those about which the apostle John says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8).

By saying this he certainly did not wish to signify any grave crimes, but only those daily and minor sins without which this life cannot be lived, however soberly and justly one may live.

Every crime is a sin, but not every sin is a crime. “Sins” are called those things that we commit even in speaking or thinking vainly, and such sins are forgiven through daily confession and the Lord’s Prayer. “Crimes,” however, are called only those grave offenses that separate a person from God: namely, those prohibited by the Decalogue, or those concerning which the Apostle says: “Those who do such things shall not obtain the kingdom of God” (Gal. 5:21).

After reading through and examining with the greatest care the entire page of the New and Old Testaments, one nowhere finds it promising security or certainty of forgiveness to those devoted to the works of flesh and blood who do not abandon their evils before the time of death.

For then, as was said above, it is not they but God who puts an end to their evils.

What is not found in sacred writings is preached most foolishly and believed most unhappily. God can indeed do for whomever he pleases what he did for the thief in the Gospel. But one unique and singular example must not be accepted as a general doctrine.

Therefore, let what is uncertain be left aside, and let what is full of certainty and security be held fast.

Run, then, run to the merciful one, lest afterward you experience the Judge. Run while it is day, lest darkness overtake you. For when the Lord says, “The night is coming, when no one can work” (John 9:4), whoever delays and neglects until it is said to him, “Fool, this night they will demand your soul from you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?” (Luke 12:20), then calls in vain upon the one already striking him, whom earlier he despised when he mercifully called him.

For the one who now delays his ineffable mercy knows thereafter only how to impose a severe and rigorous judgment.

“Come out,” says the voice sent from heaven, “come out of Babylon, my people, and do not share in her sins” (Rev. 18:4). And the prophet says: “O Zion, flee, you who dwell with the daughter of Babylon” (Zech. 2:7).

Therefore, lest you be found among the sons of Babylon and its ruin overwhelm you, come out, flee, hasten, follow, and embrace with all the depths of your compassion the counsel of Wisdom, which says:

“My son, do not delay turning to the Lord, and do not put it off from day to day; for his anger will come suddenly, and at the time of vengeance he will destroy you” (Ecclus. 5:8–9).

In accordance with your request, we intercede for you daily before the Lord; now we intercede with you yourselves and for you yourselves. We know with complete certainty that we have obtained from the Lord the effect of our petition, provided that you are not more inexorable than he is.

If we are pleading our own case here, do not believe us; but if we are pleading yours, do not neglect it.

If one of you is moved to do what Christ counsels through us, while another perhaps is not moved, we beseech the one who is not yet moved—and, admonishing him before the Lord, testify to him, and by testifying admonish him—not to presume to call back or delay the one whom the Lord deigns to call, but rather to pray that he himself may deserve to be drawn.

For no one comes to me, as the Truth says, unless the Father who sent me draws him (John 6:44).

Let him hear Wisdom saying to him: “Do not prohibit doing good to one who can; if you are able, do good yourself” (Prov. 3:27). The Spirit and the bride say, “Come”; and does anyone dare to say, “Do not”? To one to whom Christ has not promised tomorrow, does anyone dare to postpone it for a second or third year?

For Christ says: “Pray that your flight may not be in winter or on the Sabbath” (Matt. 24:20); and who says, “You will be able to flee with me in the second or third year”?

Let the one whose heart Christ has moved do everything possible so that the one who has not been moved may be moved, or the one who has been moved only slightly may be strengthened.

Otherwise, let him hear not the one who recalls him, but Christ saying: “If your eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and throw it away from you. It is better for you to enter life with one eye than, having two eyes, to be cast into the Gehenna of fire” (Matt. 18:9).

He said the same concerning the hand and the foot.

Some people, while recalling or delaying those whom Christ calls, as though giving them advice, act carelessly and simply, but nevertheless not innocently: they take the part of the devil against Christ.

We know that many who have left everything and devoted themselves to serving God, and even some who have vowed that they will do the same very soon, ardently await and eagerly entreat this consolation from the Lord: that they may be formed by our example, instructed by our speech, and supported by our counsel.

We beseech you: if you have forgotten yourselves, have mercy on them—and also on the many for whom the Lord is prepared to open the door of his compassion through your example and imitation.

Otherwise, you must consider what account you will render to the Lord for the talent which until now you have kept hidden in the earth, when he is already, behold, about to come.

May the Lord cause these things, which we have written not in the learned words of human wisdom but in the teaching of the Spirit, as he has deigned to grant it, with the pen running swiftly, to work in your hearts so that soon we may give him thanks for the result of our purpose, and each of you may deserve to say before him with sincere devotion:

“I have considered my ways and turned my feet toward your testimonies” (Ps. 118:59);

and:

“I have restrained my feet from every evil way, that I might keep your words” (ibid., 101).

Farewell.

## LETTER II. TO THE NUNS OF LYONS

She exhorts them courageously to undertake the stricter discipline they had recently embraced.

Bernard, called prior of Portes, and the brothers who are with him, send to the venerable and most beloved in Christ, the abbess of Lyons and the other nuns serving Christ under her governance, their most devoted greetings in the Lord.

We give thanks to God, who at last has deigned to grant you the grace to live religiously and holily under the discipline of a rule. At this benefit of God’s grace toward you the angels rejoice, the saints are glad, and the Church of Christ glories and exults. Christ himself has already prepared a crown for you in heaven, because, through his gift, you have conquered the world and the devil. You have conquered the world because, although you are still in the world, yet by God’s grace you are no longer of the world. For Christ said to the Apostles, and through the Apostles to you: “You are not of the world, but I chose you out of the world” (John 15:19). Those who love the world and live according to the desires of the world are of the world. You have conquered the devil because you have taken away the weapons in which he trusted: by fleeing the opportunity for sin which he prepares for all whom he is able to deceive, and by breaking the snares which he set for you. Yet it is not you but he to whom, giving thanks, you say: “You have broken my bonds; to you I will sacrifice a sacrifice of praise” (Psalm 115:17). And again, concerning him, you say: “He hid me in his tabernacle; in the day of troubles he protected me in the hiding-place of his tabernacle” (Psalm 26:5).

The most glorious Mother of God, Mary, is also already interceding for you, and rejoices that you are counted among holy women. From now on the Church of Christ, which previously was dishonored by your disorderly way of life, will be helped by your prayers before God; and as much as it was previously saddened by your irreligion, so much will it glory and rejoice in your amendment. Since, then, there is joy over your way of life both among the angels in heaven and among human beings on earth, how greatly ought you to rejoice over your own salvation? How many thanks ought you to give God for your deliverance? You ought most devotedly to say what is sung in the Psalm: “I will confess to you, Lord my God, and I will glorify your name forever. For your mercy is great over me, and you have delivered my soul from the lowest hell” (Psalm 85:12–13).

Know this also: it is greatly beneficial and salutary for you to carry out with cheerfulness and joy the good work which you have begun. For the Apostle teaches that a good work ought to be performed in this way, saying: “Not out of sadness or necessity, for God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7). Hence, in the Psalm: “Serve the Lord with gladness” (Psalm 99:2). If, however, some among you are still saddened by this holy and God-pleasing constraint which has been imposed upon them, you who are wiser and better ought to console them in the Word of God and make known to them what Holy Scripture says: “As the moth harms a garment and the worm wood, so sadness harms the heart” (Proverbs 25:20). The Apostle also says: “The sadness that is according to God produces repentance unto lasting salvation, but the sadness of the world produces death” (2 Corinthians 7:10).

You ought also to pray for them and invite them to pray, so that by God’s grace they may turn necessity into willingness. And, as blessed Jerome teaches (Letter 10 to Furia), let them “make a virtue of necessity.” If you pray earnestly for them, and they pray for themselves, the love of God will be poured out into their hearts through the Holy Spirit, and then they will truly say: “I ran in the way of your commandments, when you enlarged my heart” (Psalm 118:31). For sadness makes the heart narrow, so that a good work becomes a burden and a weariness. Love, however, enlarges the heart, so that the good work may be done cheerfully and without difficulty.

All of you together should also do what the Apostle says: “The unmarried woman and the virgin thinks of the things of the Lord, so that she may be holy in body and spirit” (1 Corinthians 7:34). She is holy in body who keeps her body undefiled. She is holy in spirit who, by thinking about the things of the Lord, keeps her heart clean from unclean and seductive thoughts. Hence the saying: “Guard your heart with all vigilance, for from it life proceeds” (Proverbs 4:23). The heart is well guarded if it is always kept occupied, as far as possible, with holy thoughts, in accordance with what is written: “Holy thought will preserve you” (Proverbs 2:11, according to the Septuagint).

You ought to do this watchfully and diligently: sometimes through prayer, sometimes through holy meditation, and at times through working with your hands in silence, as the Apostle says: “Whoever does not wish to work, let him not eat” (2 Thessalonians 3:10). Often, too, through psalmody, with hearts and voices sounding together, as the same Apostle teaches: “Singing and psalming in your hearts to the Lord” (Ephesians 5:19).

Although you may perform all these things with the greatest diligence, it is nevertheless impossible for you to be entirely free from wicked suggestions. Sin is committed in three ways: by suggestion, which comes from the devil through thought; by pleasure, which comes through the flesh when that same devil inflames desire; and by consent, which comes through the mind. But there is no danger, and no sin at all, if the mind drives away thoughts that rush in importunately like flies, keeping vigilant watch over its own guardianship. If, however, the mind slumbers and permits any unclean and harmful thoughts not only to enter but also to remain in it, the divine word reproves us through the Prophet: “How long will harmful thoughts remain in you?” (Jeremiah 4:14).

If, after a wicked suggestion, pleasure or desire has been stirred through excessive negligence, then at least let the mind awaken and, by invoking the name of Christ, extinguishing the fire that has been kindled, let it bravely resist and drive out the enemies already admitted within the door, lest it too—God forbid—be dragged away captive through consent to sin, or even be destroyed. If, however, consent follows pleasure, so that the mind decides that what the flesh desires ought to be done, then the sin is already fully imputed, even if the deed does not follow; for the evil will is held guilty even without an evil action. Just as God reckons a good will to a person as righteousness, even if that person lacks the opportunity to do good, so he reckons an evil will as sin, even if the person lacks the opportunity to sin.

We have said these things briefly concerning the guarding of the heart so that you may understand how, in accordance with the apostolic testimony quoted above, you ought to pursue holiness not only of body but also of mind. The more diligently you pursue it, the more you will please Christ the Lord, to whom you have been betrothed, and the more worthy you will be to hear from him what is written in the Song of Songs: “Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved; behold, you are beautiful. Your eyes are like those of doves” (Song of Songs 1:24). He said “beautiful” twice: beautiful inwardly and beautiful outwardly; beautiful inwardly through purity of heart, and beautiful outwardly through integrity of life; beautiful inwardly through good intention, and beautiful outwardly through good action; beautiful inwardly through good will, and beautiful outwardly through holy conduct. “Your eyes,” he says, “are like those of doves,” because, like doves, whose nature is simple and without gall, your eyes see nothing that the mind wrongly desires.

When you depart from this life, freed from the eternal torments of the wicked, you will enjoy the eternal happiness of the righteous, and you will see the King in his beauty, into whom the angels desire to look. Hear the Lord saying in the Gospel: “Watch at all times, praying that you may be worthy to escape the evils that are to come in the last days, and to stand before the Son of Man” (Luke 21:36). And the Apostle says: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Romans 8:18). Think upon these things; recall them through continual meditation; and you will consider nothing laborious or burdensome by which you may escape the punishments of eternal fire and obtain the rewards of eternal blessedness.

## Letter III. To Rainald, the Recluse

How one ought to live before the Lord.

### [Col. 0892B]

Bernard, called Prior of Portes, to Brother Rainald, the recluse: to act manfully in his holy purpose.

You ask us to set down in writing how you ought to live before the Lord—a request indeed honorable, but one for which we might perhaps offer a just excuse. Yet lest we seem to have failed in charity rather than excused ourselves reasonably, we undertake to satisfy your request, not indeed as fully as would be expedient, but as charity suggests. We wish to remind you that we are by no means establishing for you a fixed and certain rule of life; rather, from the practices which religious life in the Church customarily observes, we shall briefly indicate to you what seems most concise. If anything we say should seem either too severe or too lenient, it will be your responsibility either to temper the severe things with gentler ones or to strengthen the lenient ones with more rigorous practices, as the Lord grants you both the will and the ability. Everywhere, however—and this we strongly urge—preserve discretion, which is known to be of the greatest value both for progress and for perseverance in religious life.

Beginners, whom they call novices, often undertake things greater than their strength, because their fervor is usually accompanied by lack of discretion. As a result, either—and this is grievously to be lamented—they lose perseverance, or, suffering serious bodily and sometimes mental illness, they are compelled to return to easier and excessively relaxed practices which they ought never to have abandoned.

### On Silence

With these matters prefaced, let us speak first about silence. It seems that you ought to observe it absolutely from Compline until Prime in summer, and in winter until Terce. Since you ought always, insofar as circumstances permit, to seek and pursue silence, it must especially not be violated at night, unless pressing necessity compels it, so that some necessary matter may be indicated in a few words spoken modestly.

You ought not only never to speak idle words, or words bearing no weight of usefulness; you ought not even to listen to them from anyone. Let no one dare to recount stories or vulgarities to you, nor rumors about affairs in the outside world. Listen gladly only to what gives you cause to thank God, if it concerns divine benefits, or to what gives you cause to pour out prayers before God, if it concerns sad or adverse matters. Let everyone who comes to you either hear good from you or say something good to you. If religious or learned men visit you, always be more ready to hear good things from them than to say them yourself.

If you strive to observe these things, fantasies of vanity will not hinder the devotion of your heart in psalmody and prayer. Consider how great the necessity laid upon you of observing these matters is, from the following testimonies of the Holy Scriptures. The Lord says in the Gospel: “For every idle word that people speak, they will give an account of it on the day of judgment” (Matthew 12:36). It is also written: “In much speaking you will not escape sin” (Proverbs 10:19), and: “The man of many words will not be directed on earth” (Psalm 139:12), and: “Death and life are in the power of the tongue” (Proverbs 18:21).

Do, then, what you say in the Psalm: “I said, I will guard my ways, so that I may not sin with my tongue; I set a guard over my mouth” (Psalm 38:2–3). There it continues: “I was mute and was silent even from good things” (ibid., 3). If, then, according to the Prophet, because of the seriousness of silence you ought sometimes to be silent even from good things, how far ought things that are not good to be from you?

### Against Idleness

Let us now continue with the occupation of spiritual and bodily works. Since it is certain that idleness is an enemy of the soul, and the Apostle says, “Whoever does not work, let him not eat” (2 Thessalonians 3:10), the tempter ought to find you occupied in some spiritual work at every hour during which you are awake. It also seems fitting to us that, in accordance with the same Apostle—“all things decently and in order” (1 Corinthians 14:40)—you should distinguish these works according to their proper times.

Spend the morning hours, until Terce in winter and until Prime in summer, in spiritual exercises. By spiritual works we mean prayer, sacred reading, holy meditation, and psalmody. During the rest of the day, until Vespers, be occupied with some useful manual work, interrupting it with brief prayers. After Vespers, devote yourself to spiritual works, but remember then also to apply yourself to silence as much as you can. After Compline, do not delay in giving rest to your limbs.

On feast days especially, you ought to devote yourself to spiritual studies, as the Lord deigns to grant you fervor and grace in them. Nevertheless, you should know that it is better to turn from time to time to some manual work than to persist in reading while dozing and incur weariness through excessive reading. After some work has preceded it, you may rise again to prayer or reading with greater fervor through this pleasant alternation.

At such times do work that can be done quietly and without noise, lest the undiscriminating crowd take offense. Take care never to have such anxiety about any bodily work that it makes you slow or lukewarm in prayer or in the other things that must be done spiritually. Bodily exercises are not to be preferred to spiritual ones; rather, spiritual things are far more excellently to be placed before bodily things. Whatever you do bodily should be done vigorously and diligently at its proper time. But far be it from you to let concern or anxiety about it hinder the fervor or devotion which you ought to have regarding spiritual matters.

“Be anxious about nothing,” says the Apostle, “but in every prayer and supplication, with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God” (Philippians 4:6). Also, by the authority of the same Apostle: “Bodily exercise is profitable for a little, but godliness is useful for all things” (1 Timothy 4:8).

### On the Value of Work

From the proceeds of your work, purchase whatever will be necessary for continuing your work; whatever remains, spend on what will be necessary for your clothing. Do not seek to receive from another the cost of clothing if you can sufficiently provide it for yourself from your own work. For we know that you receive your food from the monastery.

Except for the things just mentioned, beware entirely—and consider it abominable—to store up or retain anything for yourself as though it were your own. Whatever remains for you after the necessary expense of clothing and preparing your work, whether from things perhaps given to you by some servants of God or from the proceeds of your work, spend immediately, as seems appropriate to you, on the needs of the poor.
