Thus, in accordance with the Apostle, by working with your hands at what is good, you may have something with which to give to the one suffering need (Ephesians 4:28).

If at some time someone wishes to give you something which you do not need, remember that it is written: “It is more blessed to give than to receive” (Acts 20:35). Far be it from you to stain your mind even with the slightest desire, or to repel from yourself the grace of the one who called you, by retaining or desiring what you do not need. For you have renounced not only the world and all its desires, but also denied yourself, so that by carrying your cross after Jesus you may attain his promises.

### What Clothing Should Be Used

Concerning clothing, it seems to us that you can and ought to abstain entirely from linen garments and be content with woolen and fur clothing. If this pleases you, have two tunics as shirts. Two or three pairs of leggings, because of the winter cold. Enough foot-coverings. One fur garment, or two if you judge them necessary, together with skins and a cloak.

For your bed have straw, a felt blanket, a coverlet made of thick sheep pelts covered with rustic cloth, or a *cotum* (a cushion) [Note: *Cotum*, in French *coussin* “cushion,” from the Germanic *Kussen*.], and a pillow for your head. Also have two needles, thread, scissors, and such equipment as you see to be necessary, so that you are not compelled to ask others for such things, thereby breaking silence, or to be anxious because of want.

It also seems to us that, when the bishop is present, you ought to receive the canonical habit, so that not only the place but also the habit may remind you to live soberly and devoutly before him who knows what is hidden.

### How to Fast

Concerning abstinence and fasting, understand it in this way. The Apostle indeed says: “I chastise my body and bring it into subjection” (1 Corinthians 9:27). And again: “Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires” (Galatians 5:24).

But because this sort of dwelling, which you have chosen by God’s inspiration, usually harms the health of the head because of the confined air—and frequent fasting is also known to cause this—we do not think it beneficial for you to undertake a great severity of abstinence. We therefore believe it sufficient that, throughout the entire year, you eat only once on Friday: abstaining from wine but taking pottage, unless a feast day or the octave of one of the solemnities of the Nativity of the Lord, Easter, or Pentecost occurs, or you have undergone bloodletting, or perhaps are ill.

If you think that the same abstinence should be observed on Wednesday, we judge that nothing further should be added. We do not think that fasts on bread and water are suitable for you, for the reason stated above, unless you should think that the vigils of these solemnities ought to be observed in that manner: the Nativity of the Lord, Easter, Pentecost, the Ascension, Saint John the Baptist, Saints Peter and Paul the Apostles, the Assumption of Blessed Mary, and All Saints.

We think that you should spend the remaining time of the whole year according to monastic custom: from the Ides of September until Easter, eating once; from Easter until those same Ides, eating twice. Take wine also according to the monastic measure, but never drink it pure; and receive the other things served to you by them with thanksgiving. We think, however, that you ought to abstain from meat and blood, except when you are ill.

At your meals you must always attend to this Gospel saying of the Lord: “Take heed lest your hearts be weighed down with gluttony and drunkenness” (Luke 21:34). And to what the Apostle says: “Do not make provision for the flesh in its desires” (Romans 13:14).

It is very well known that moderate food and drink, moderate sleep, are most healthful both for soul and body, and greatly contribute to purity of heart and flesh. Remember to pursue this moderation, always keeping, as far as the Lord enables you, the same measure in eating. Do not deprive natural necessity of anything among poorer foods, nor, among richer and more carefully prepared foods, indulge the desire of the flesh more than usual or more than nature requires.

This moderation in food will be more acceptable to God, more useful for the purity both of flesh and of heart, and healthier for the body than if, by pursuing more strenuous fasts, you later made up for the fast with indiscriminate satiety.

### [Col. 0895D] On the Divine Office

In the Divine Office, follow the custom of the clerics; therefore, you do not need us to write instructions for you. But in order to observe this division of time in performing the same Divine Office, apply as much diligence as you can, so that you rise at the crowing of the cocks, or at the monks’ signal, or according to your own estimate at that time.

From the Kalends of October until Easter, finish the nocturnal Office before dawn; from Easter until the aforementioned Kalends, finish it shortly after dawn. In winter you shall sing Prime as dawn breaks; Terce at sunrise; and Sext, None, Vespers, and Compline at the monks’ signal.

If you are able to observe the prescribed time for rising for the nocturnal Office, never return to bed in the morning hours. Then, as we said above, you ought to devote yourself to spiritual studies, not to sleep. Those who are diligent in spiritual matters rarely sleep at that time, except perhaps on account of bloodletting.

If occasionally a later hour should remain until daylight and you think you ought to sleep, you should first perform your customary prayer, provided that you are not too weighed down by sleep; and afterward, if it should be necessary, take a little sleep. If you do not have the books necessary for the nocturnal Office—although we do not think you will lack them—you ought to rise either before it or around dawn for prayer and for carrying out some other spiritual activity.

In summer also, something we had almost forgotten, you ought to sleep after midday, as the monks do.

### [Col. 0896B] On Common Prayer

Remember to devote yourself to prayer with the greatest eagerness and concentration. Let no concern, illness, or trouble ever call you away from it. Pray for the salvation not only of yourself but of all the faithful—living, those yet to be born, and the dead—and for those by whose support you are sustained, as well as for us.

Then, trusting in the help of the Holy Spirit, who teaches the saints to pray with unutterable groanings (Romans 8:26), in accordance with the Lord’s exhortation, enter the chamber of your heart. With the door of your breast closed against vanities and unclean thoughts, through which the enemy tries to break in, pray to your Father in secret. At every hour, as far as the Lord enables you, but especially then, guard your heart with all vigilance.

### [Col. 0896C] That There May Be Concord between Mind and Tongue

When you stand before the Lord to sing psalms, apply every effort and all vigilance so that your mind agrees with your tongue, and so that you may do what the Apostle says: “Singing and psalming in your hearts to the Lord” (Ephesians 5:19), and what he said of himself: “I will psalm with the mind also” (1 Corinthians 14:15). Also heed what he says: “Sing psalms wisely” (Psalm 46:8), and: “In the sight of the angels I will sing to you” (Psalm 137:1).

When you do these things, as the Holy Spirit pours in the dew of his sweetness, you will often seem not to be producing prophecy or words dictated by another, but to be pouring forth before God the very words of most devout prayer.

### On the Morning Hours

After psalmody or prayer, meditate especially in the morning on the law of God, according as he himself grants you grace. Search in the secrecy of your heart to learn what the Lord commands you and how you may fulfill it. Direct the strength of your heart and your conduct according to the rule of the divine commandments and the example of the holy Fathers.

When you are unable to sleep in bed, strive to do the same without interruption, following what Scripture commands and what we mentioned shortly before: “Guard your heart with all vigilance, for from it life proceeds” (Proverbs 4:23).

The human mind is an unstable thing, and unless it is always held with great diligence, insofar as the Lord deigns to help, occupied with holy meditations, after it has flowed away into the vanities and impurities which the tempter never ceases to suggest and thrust upon it, it is not easily found devout in prayer or psalmody.

### On Reading

Approach reading also with devotion and spiritual desire, so that you may either hear there something which you can draw upon as an example for your conduct, or, according as the Lord deigns to dispense it to you, be refreshed by the sweetness of the divine words and mysteries.

With this zeal and intention, read in turn all the divine Scriptures that you are able to possess—not so that you may be puffed up with knowledge, but so that you may be built up in love. Whatever Scriptures you do not penetrate with your understanding, reverence humbly as divine secrets, and piously defer understanding them until you enter the sanctuary of God and understand at the end.

For whatever you have understood, humbly give thanks to the author of the gift. Apply every care to books lent to you, so that they are not stained by smoke, dust, or any other dirt.

### On Bodily Trouble

If at any time you suffer bodily trouble or illness, or perhaps are injured by someone either in word or deed, you ought to remember the sufferings and injuries of Christ. The hardships which you will endure by the Lord’s arrangement, not only bear patiently but also give thanks to him who chastises every son whom he receives, if he deigns to inflict upon you the chastisements of fatherly loving-kindness.

In what you suffer from those close to you, do not return evil for evil or cursing for cursing. On the contrary, bless them—not merely with your words but from the innermost part of your heart and with genuine good will—and pray for those who slander and persecute you, so that you may be a son of your Father who is in heaven.

Although we do not think you will suffer such injuries from human beings, or will suffer them only rarely, nevertheless, if anything should happen—as human affairs go—we want your breast to be free from such disturbances. Nor should you become angry with yourself, as sometimes happens to people lacking discretion, when they encounter difficulty in carrying out some task.

### Hindrances to Prayer

Those who live alone also commonly become troubled within themselves and, through the devil’s agency, contract a kind of cloud of sadness. The old enemy knows how to hinder the prayers of God’s servants and their holy pursuits by various kinds of harm.

Sometimes he tries to introduce sadness or irrational anger; sometimes proud exultation; sometimes the memory of an injury; sometimes a vain recollection of things once said, done, or yet to be done; sometimes unclean thoughts; sometimes lukewarmness of spirit or the torpor of sleep. In this way he may turn the mind away from its holy intention or impede it.

If he finds that he is not resisted in lesser matters, he immediately weaves stronger bonds of temptation. For he prefers to overthrow rather than merely impede. Those whom he cannot overthrow, he does not cease to impede as far as he can.

“But God is faithful,” says the Apostle, “who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can bear, but with the temptation will also provide a way out, so that you may be able to endure it” (1 Corinthians 10:13).

Against these things, and indeed against every kind of temptation, and also against nocturnal illusions, arm yourself with the strength of prayer and take up that shield of which the Apostle says: “In all things take up the shield of faith, with which you may be able to extinguish all the flaming arrows of the wicked one” (Ephesians 6:16), and so forth.

For sincere love and fervent faith in the cross of Christ render all the enemy’s devices ineffective; and prayer poured out with tears overcomes and repels every kind of temptation.

### On Humility

These are the spiritual instruments and contests of your warfare before the King whom you have begun to serve. You must know that for this reason you are confined in body and separated from external cares: so that in heart you may be free for these things.

You are considered great among human beings because you are called a recluse; but unless you carry out these things before God with every effort and all vigilance, you will in no way be great. Human beings notice only outward things; the Most High, however, will judge what is inward.

When you see that you are unequal to these examples, humbly confess your lack of devotion and your imperfection before God, and with complete devotion ask earnestly for the help of his grace, for he says: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).

You must often find yourself lukewarm, often sluggish. For this reason his grace sometimes withdraws for a time, so that you may trust in his help and not presume upon your own strength. Thus the most merciful Father knows how to heal pride by humility.

For if he did not sometimes withdraw his grace, the human mind, lifted up and believing that it was sufficient in itself for righteousness, would fall more seriously into pride. But he abandons the proud in such a way that he returns to the humbled with more merciful grace. Thus he sleeps in the storm, so that, awakened by prayers, he may command the winds and the sea and bring about a great calm.

The Scriptures will teach you most fully that humility is the guardian of all virtues, and that every virtue without it is widowed and weak—indeed, is not virtue at all. When you fast, pray, and sing psalms, invisible enemies will not be lacking to applaud you and say: “Well done, well done! Who is like you? Who pleases God in this way? If only people knew your holiness!”

To them immediately answer in your heart with the prophetic voice: “Let those who say to me, ‘Well done, well done,’ be put to shame at once” (Psalm 39:16). And add: “For I am a beggar and poor” (ibid., 18).

In truth, however far you advance by walking from virtue to virtue, you will always be needy and poor, and you will not be able to obtain complete victory over the invisible enemy until you reach him to whom you say: “You will fill me with joy in your presence” (Psalm 15:11), and, “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears” (Psalm 16:15).

If someone should praise you to your face, do not believe the words of others more than your own conscience, remembering the Scripture that says: “Those who call you blessed are themselves deceiving you” (Isaiah 3:12).

Therefore, so that you may not become exalted in your own estimation over your progress, keep in mind what the Apostle says: “What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you glory as though you had not received it?” (1 Corinthians 4:7).

To avoid the desire for human favor, hear the Lord saying: “Take heed that you do not do your righteousness before people in order to be seen by them” (Matthew 6:1). Otherwise, “you will have no reward with your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 6:5). Of such people he also says: “Truly I tell you, they have received their reward” (ibid., 5).

Do not think, however, that it is evil to be praised by people, provided it is not done for the sake of flattery; for, on the contrary, it is written: “Woe to the person through whom the name of the Lord is blasphemed” (Romans 1:24; Isaiah 52:5). What is evil is to desire or love praise.

### On Charity

After you have learned from Christ to be gentle and humble of heart, he who resists the proud and gives grace to the humble will give you, when you ask, seek, and knock, through the Holy Spirit, that charity than which he gives no greater grace to any human being in this life.

When this love begins to burn in your heart, it will enlarge it so that whatever seems hard or difficult to you in the divine commandments will become very easy. In this way, I say, it will enlarge your heart and make whatever seems hard or harsh to you pleasant and light, so that you may truly say: “I ran in the way of your commandments, when you enlarged my heart” (Psalm 118:32). And: “I delighted in the way of your commandments, as in all riches” (ibid., 14).

Understand this charity as nothing other than love of God and neighbor. For there are two commandments, but one charity. When the Lord spoke of the two commandments, he said: “On these two commandments depend the whole law and the prophets” (Matthew 22:40). When the Apostle spoke of charity, which is one, he said: “Love is the fullness of the law” (Romans 13:10).

There are therefore two things commanded, but there is one charity through which they are fulfilled. The commandments that are given are in the law, but the charity through which they are fulfilled is in the heart. Yet it cannot be in our hearts from ourselves or through our own powers. Rather, “the love of God,” says the Apostle, “has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans 5:5).

Ask for this most earnestly, continually, and devoutly from him from whom comes every good gift and every perfect gift. How no good work can be perfect without charity—indeed, how nothing can be beneficial without charity—the apostolic reading that begins, “If I speak with the tongues of human beings and of angels” (1 Corinthians 13:1; Romans 8:38–39), and so forth, will be able to teach you.

Blessed is the person whose soul is so full of charity that he can truly say: “I am certain that neither death nor life nor any creature will be able to separate me from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.”

### On Confession

You shall ask a spiritual man from the monastery to come to you at appropriate times, as seems suitable both to you and to him—not just anyone, but a religious and discerning man. To him you shall humbly confess, as to a father, the offenses by which you recognize yourself to be blameworthy before God.

You must examine not only negligences in actions and rashness in speech, but also sins of thought; you should record them on wax or parchment so as to confess them from memory. You should devoutly carry out whatever he enjoins upon you, and humbly ask him to pray for you, in accordance with the saying: “Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, so that you may be saved” (James 5:16).

Through confession and penance, together with the sacrifice of prayer, past sins are washed away, future sins are guarded against, and the snares and illusions of demons are both avoided and rendered powerless.

You must know that among religious men devoted to a great and arduous way of life, certain offenses are reckoned as serious faults which are considered light and venial in secular life. Therefore remember what blessed Job said to the Lord: “I feared all my works, knowing that you would not spare the one who sins” (Job 9:28).

Take courage, then, in the Lord and act manfully. Christ will not be lacking to you, nor will he cheat you of his promise, for he says: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age.” May he himself, who called you through his grace, deign to be present as a help to you and to us, aided by your prayers, so that he may cause us to rejoice forever in mutual vision within his kingdom. Amen.

[Col. 0899]

## Five Letters of John, Monk of the Carthusian Monastery of Portes

(From the manuscript codex of the monastery of Saint-Oyend of the Jura, or Saint-Claude.)

## Letter I. To Stephen, His Brother in Flesh and Spirit

On the flight from the world.

### [Col. 0899D]

John, brother to Stephen, most beloved in Christ, both in flesh and in spirit: may you be found in Christ’s mercies, and not fear an evil report.

How is it, dearest and most ardently desired in Christ, [Col. 0900D] that, although all around us we are professors of the Christian religion, such a great multitude of those contained within the Church is found not only to refuse obedience to the Lord’s commands by doing what has been ordered, but even to oppose them with obstinate minds by doing what has been forbidden? Both groups—the ones who do not do what has been commanded and the ones who do not [Col. 0901A] fear doing what has been forbidden—if there is in us any compassion, any godliness, must be mourned and lamented with continual weeping and continual grief. For both, even if they do not perhaps incur the same punishment, will nevertheless incur the same condemnation unless they persevere in repentance.

For the earth has been so filled with iniquity, and what the Lord foretold would happen in the last days (Matt. 24:14)—“because iniquity will abound, the love of many will grow cold”—has begun to take place, that you will more easily find someone praising the sinner in the desires of his soul than someone correcting him for the error of his way. If we are to give an account on the day of judgment even for idle words, what will become of those who love pleasures and the unlawful desires of this world more than God? Where will they go from his spirit, and where will they flee from his presence? He who was judged in humility will come with power and majesty to judge the world by fire.

How will they be able to dwell with consuming fire and everlasting flames? If there is no place to flee from God the Judge, neither from east nor from west, when “the righteous will scarcely be saved,” where will the impious and sinners appear? The expectation of that judgment, then, at which all of us must be presented before Christ’s tribunal, is exceedingly terrible and more fearful than can either be said or imagined, even to the righteous. For it is dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God.

But those who serve the various and unlawful desires of this life do not wish to consider these things. What is said about that terrifying examination they either do not believe or despise; or, even if they believe, they nevertheless, through a diabolical inspiration that dulls their fear, [Col. 0901C] reduce it to contempt and forgetfulness—although, as far as possible, they ought to keep these matters before the eyes of their minds even while sleeping.

If the reason for lessening this fear is that the day of judgment seems far away, then that final day of one’s departure, which is certainly near to each person although its time is uncertain, ought to terrify everyone, make everyone solicitous, and rouse the torpor and lukewarmness of minds to vigilance. On that day each person must be found according to his merits—merits that can no longer be increased or diminished—whether good things that can never be changed for the worse, or evil things that can never be converted into good.

There are many—indeed, an innumerable multitude of people—who multiply their evils through their continual sins. They acknowledge that they are sinners, [Col. 0901D] yet pretend not to turn back. They cling too closely to the example of that Gospel robber, trusting, through a kind of presumption concerning divine mercy, that by one final confession at the time of death they can have the multitude of their sins erased, although they cannot even comprehend it by estimation. Many of these, while carelessly trusting in mercy, incur condemnation through the exceedingly fearful and hidden, yet just, severity of divine judgment.

Sudden accidents and untimely death, as well as the impenitent hearts of many during the time granted for confession, reveal this fact all too frequently, in pitiable and lamentable ways. How impenitent a heart many possess at the time of that final [Col. 0902A] confession is especially revealed in those who, after despairing of life, recover from their illness after whatever confession they have made, return to their customary sins, and sometimes commit worse ones than before. For if they had truly repented, they would have avoided committing again the things that must be mourned and lamented.

If they had died during that illness, God would know whether they were destined to reach Christ’s kingdom. Those who depart this life in such a condition, even though they have not been without such a confession, have a salvation as doubtful as their condemnation is uncertain: just as one must not despair of them, so one must not presume concerning them. For how will those find an end to punishments who never put an end to sins? If they lived longer, perhaps they would sin more.

Why the confession of that venerable [Col. 0902B] robber ought not to be compared with their confession belongs to another place and time to discuss. In this matter we are guided not by our own opinion but by the authority of the holy Fathers. The Apostle gives a terrifying judgment concerning such people: “Do you not know, O man, that the kindness of God leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness and impenitent heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of God’s just judgment” (Rom. 2:4–5).

The wise, therefore, who have not received their soul in vain, and who have laid for their work that foundation besides which no one can lay another—that is, Christ Jesus—have never placed their salvation in such uncertainty. Firmly clinging immovably to the strongest anchor of their hope, they order their [Col. 0902C] life in this way: according to the rule of the divine commandments, they direct not only all their actions but also their thoughts and words, so that, as certainly and securely as possible, they may await the final hour of their departure and likewise the final day of the great judgment. Thus they may speak confidently and without shame at the gate of their departure and say: “The prince of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John 14:30).

Desiring, with the Apostle, “to depart and be with Christ,” they not only do not fear that final day of the dreadful examination, but await it with the greatest longing, knowing that the crown of righteousness is laid up for them, which the Lord will repay them on that day. Even now, when their voice has ceased, they do not cease frequently to repeat in the desire of their heart:

[Col. 0902D] “When shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Ps. 41:3.) When will you fill me with joy by your countenance? When will I appear before your sight and be satisfied when your glory appears? When will I be intoxicated with the abundance of your house and drink from the torrent of your delight?

I know that you are surprised—or perhaps even complaining—at the length of my words. But consider that the matter about which I am speaking is great and demanding. The business with which I am concerned is your salvation. Can so great a concern weigh upon you? Do not, then, be annoyed at reading what I was not annoyed to write. I judged it useful for you. This is what compelled me to write these things to you, and this is the reasoning that persuaded me: because I desire the salvation of all people, if that were possible, and especially of the faithful [Col. 0903A], I cannot fail to be concerned for your salvation, and to implore it from the Lord with whatever affection and desire I can.

I do not cease to ask this of God in my prayers. Rarely do I pray to God for myself without remembering you. By the inspiration of God’s grace, it seemed to me insufficient merely to persevere in prayers unless I also stirred your mind and, insofar as the Lord might deign to grant it, roused you by a word of exhortation.

Having therefore requested and received permission from the prior, I have undertaken what the Lord will deign to inspire. May the life-giving Holy Spirit be present, and may he deign, by his inspiration rather than by my exhortation, to breathe upon your breast with the breath of holy desire.

Behold, then, with the Lord inspiring and the Holy Spirit favoring the undertaking, in the name of the Lord [Col. 0903B] Jesus Christ I exhort you—and I exhort you not with my own voice or authority, but with the Lord’s: “Go, sell all that you have, and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven” (Matt. 19:21), and “come, follow me.” “For unless someone renounces all that he possesses, he cannot be my disciple.”

Does what he commanded seem harsh or difficult to you? My most beloved, observe in regard to this command of the Lord, insofar as the author of the command himself will deign to show us, these five points: first, that it is not difficult; next, who it is that commands; then, the reason for the command; fourth, its rationale; and fifth, what he who commands did for you. Let us consider these in the same order, with his help.

If it seems difficult and burdensome, think [Col. 0903C] that the labor is brief, the reward great, the work lasts only a few days, while the recompense is everlasting and the rest without end. If you weigh the labor, weigh the reward as well. Labor that is commended by such great rewards is not to be feared.

But the difficulty is either nonexistent or slight. The way has already been trodden by many, and the daily examples of converts make this clear. Even if all else were lacking, to show that it is not difficult, the testimony of the one whom not to believe is to recoil from salvation would be sufficient: “My yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matt. 11:30). Only those who have experienced it can readily understand the power and truth of this saying.

Or perhaps he commands you to abandon something you will not receive? “You will have treasure in heaven” (Matt. 19:21), [Col. 0903D] where thieves are not feared and the deposit is faithfully guarded. Do you think you will receive merely onefold? “You will receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life” (Matt. 19:29).

Or does he command you to relinquish what you would always have possessed? No. “Naked you came from your mother’s womb, and naked you will return there” (Job 1:21). And the Apostle says: “We brought nothing into this world; it is beyond doubt that we can take nothing away.”

Who, knowing and understanding these things, hesitates to abandon—or rather, to exchange for eternal goods—goods that not only cannot be eternal but cannot even be lasting? O hope, O love, O empty fruit of temporal things—if only it were merely empty and not also harmful! “When a man has become rich, and the glory of his house has multiplied, when he dies he will not take everything with him, nor will his glory descend with him” (Ps. 48:17–18). [Col. 0904A] Where, then, will it descend? To the place where he will not see the light forever. He will leave his riches to others; his chest will indeed be empty, but his conscience will be emptier still.

“But many,” you say, “repent afterward.” And some, after making it, look back and abandon their resolution. Do you not know that some bits of chaff are so light that they do not even wait for the winnowing of the threshing floor, but depart at the slightest breath of wind? When the chaff has gone, do not the grains remain to be stored in the granary? Why should the apostasy of a few who depart contribute more to despair than the examples of the many who persevere contribute to confirmation in their resolution? Surely, because of the crime of one Judas, Christ’s apostles are not themselves guilty?

[Col. 0904B]

But let us consider who delivered that command to renounce one’s possessions, and of what authority is he who gives the command. The Almighty commands this—your God, who joined you together with bones and sinews, who will reduce you to dust, and who will bring you to an end from morning until evening. He is one whose authority would have to be obeyed even if no benefit followed from obedience.

Look at all living things, both those endowed with sensation and those without sensation; look at the very mass of the elements and everything made within them. “All things,” says the Prophet, “serve him” (Ps. 118:91).

Woe to us wretched sinners! Every irrational creature [Col. 0904C] does not resist, even in the slightest, the will and command of its Creator; but we, who were made in his image and likeness and to whom it has been granted to enjoy his eternal blessedness, not only do not obey, but also—and this is most wicked and more impious than can be expressed—do not cease to resist and oppose him. As the Prophet says, “They honor me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. 29:13). And again: “They profess that they know God, but by their deeds they deny him” (Titus 1:16).

But what of this? According to the Apostle, he is faithful and cannot deny himself. The impious and sinners, however, will be received by Gehenna.

We said a little earlier that we should consider, in the third and fourth places, the reason and rationale of the command. It is easy to consider its reason. Its reason is eternal life. For the Lord, who does not need our goods, commands nothing [Col. 0904D] for his own sake but for ours—not that it may be well with him, but that it may be well with us.

Let us therefore consider the rationale somewhat more attentively. We are commanded to renounce all worldly things. As was said a little earlier, even if the authority of the one commanding were the only reason, and even if there were great difficulty and labor, no hope or reason for reward, no persuasive rationale, and even if the command seemed somehow irrational, we ought nevertheless to fulfill it with every effort and diligence.

The reason why he commanded this is also great, forceful, and weighty with immense necessity, pressing upon our sluggishness. To show the rationale of this command, the Apostle James cries out, saying: “Adulterers, do you not know that friendship with this world is enmity with God? Whoever wishes to be a friend of this age will be constituted an enemy of [Col. 0905A] God” (James 4:4).

The first and greatest commandment of the Law is love of God. Since, then, according to James, we cannot love God and the world at the same time, and since we cannot reach God except by loving him according to the commandment of the Law, the clearest and most forceful reasoning compels us to leave everything and follow Christ, so that by loving him we may reach him.

“Adulterers”—for in holy baptism you betrothed your soul to Christ, the heavenly and true Bridegroom. There you renounced the devil, all his works, and all his pomps. But what is it to renounce the devil except to renounce the world? And what are the works and pomps of the devil except the works and pomps of this world? For, as the Lord testifies, the devil is the prince of this world: “Now the prince of [Col. 0905B] this world will be cast out” (John 12:31). Someone has also said:

“Entangled with the world, one is part of the world’s prince.”

If, then, you love anything other than Christ; if you follow and embrace the world, to which you renounced yourself in baptism, you make your soul guilty of adultery and are proved to be an adulterer—not of a human being but of God, which is most serious.

What else, then, do I advise, or what else does Christ demand from you, except what you vowed in baptism? “He will be constituted an enemy of God.” Do you therefore wish to be a friend of the world so that you may be constituted an enemy of God?

It is easy to consider the same reasoning concerning love of one’s neighbor that was demonstrated concerning love of God. How many hatreds, angers, quarrels, disputes, and hostilities arise among neighbors [Col. 0905C] because of temporal possessions—so much so that even harmony among brothers is rare—is not something to be demonstrated by argument but observed in the daily conduct of people.

As for the extent to which temporal goods impede the effect of the twofold love, and the extent to which renunciation of them advances it, only those who, having left everything, have devoted themselves to loving the Lord and their neighbor have experienced it.

If, then, according to the Lord’s saying, the whole Law and the Prophets depend upon these two commandments—that is, love of God and love of one’s neighbor (Matt. 22:40)—and, according to the Apostle, “the fullness of the Law is love” (Rom. 13:10), while riches and charity can scarcely, or not at all, be possessed together, and riches cannot be loved while charity is retained [Col. 0905D], what wise person, understanding these things, hesitates even briefly to leave everything, love the Lord, seek him by loving him, find him by seeking him, and reign without end with him once he has been found?

Our evasion, then, is hemmed in and surrounded on every side. The authority of the one commanding presses upon us; no difficulty obstructs us; the reason persuades; the rationale convicts; and finally, the inexpressible necessity of rewards and punishments compels, constrains, and drives us with inexpressible force.

For either, if obedient, we shall obtain rewards “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart—things which the Lord has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. 2:9); or, if disobedient, we shall pay everlasting penalties. Once those who fall into them by an irreversible fall have been placed in eternal torments [Col. 0906A], no consolation will remain for them, no hope of remedy at all, and no respite, even for a little while, will be granted.

Do this, then, my beloved; think upon this; keep this incessantly before the eyes of your heart. If rewards do not invite you, let punishments at least frighten you. If love does not draw you, let the fear of the greatest of all things—the dreadful judgment and everlasting torments—drive you. For “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Prov. 1:7). Through fear you will reach love.

If, in some way, as often happens, the fear of eternal judgment is dulled in your mind, keep before you the day of your departure. Its time is uncertain, but you know with certainty that it is near. On that day you will find, according to your merits, either good or evil things—as was said above—which will not be changed forever.

For just as the hope of good things is joyful, [Col. 0906B] so the uncertainty of evil things is terrifying. If you do not guard against falling here, after you have fallen there you will beg in vain for the assistance of friends and implore divine mercy in vain. There your friends and brothers will not be able to help you; nor will all the saints, nor the choirs of angels—I say this boldly—nor will God himself be able to rescue you from there. He is just; he cannot save the unjust and impenitent.

There you will not find remedies that you did not seek earlier in life. If, then, you acknowledge that you are a sinner—or rather, because you truly are a sinner, for there is no one without sin, not even an infant whose life upon the earth is but one day (Job 14:4, according to the Septuagint)—because, I say, you are a sinner, you will repent either here or there; but there your repentance will be fruitless, for in hell there is no redemption.

Will Christ [Col. 0906C] suffer again for those who descend into hell? “Having risen from the dead, he dies no more.” See, therefore, and observe with every effort and vigilance how great a necessity rests upon you to produce worthy fruits of repentance, whether for light offenses or for grave ones.

But why did I say “light”? Would that the Lord considered any sin light! How can any sin be thought light, when Christ died for our sins? Sin is so grave, so great, so difficult a matter that the sins of the world could not be wiped away unless the Son of God tasted death for all. And yet a human being dares to consider any sin light?

All sins are indeed light and venial in those who produce worthy fruits of [Col. 0906D] repentance; but in the impenitent, all sins—even those that seem light—are grave and full of condemnation.

How could you produce worthier fruits of repentance than by leaving everything, according to the Lord’s command and his will, and, naked, following the naked Christ; by fleeing not only the will but also the place and opportunity of sinning; and by devoting yourself to God in heart and body?

“It is a harsh lot,” you say, “if only those who renounce the world are saved.” This is the voice of one who is pretending not to hear, not of one who fears God. Whoever says this does not strive to be crowned with those who contend in the arena; defeated by the mere name of the contest, he collapses.

Do not, my dearest and most ardently desired one, do not consider what others do. Look instead, attend to, and consider more attentively what you yourself ought to do. What folly [Col. 0907A]—or rather, what madness—would it be, if the blind fall into a pit, to wish the sighted person to fall as well? If those driven by insanity leap into the fire, would it be for the prudent and knowledgeable person to wish to leap in likewise? And if everyone is condemned, not to avoid or fear condemnation?

Why do you not hear: “Narrow is the way that leads to life, and few are those who find it”? (Matt. 7:14.) Why do you not hear: “It is a little flock to which the Lord has been pleased to give the inheritance”? (Luke 12:32.) Why do you not hear: “Many are called, but few are chosen”? (Matt. 22:14; the printed citation reads XXVIII, 10.)

My beloved, I can do nothing except admonish you. If I could both advise you toward what is salutary—and would that it were salutary!—and compel you more effectively toward it, believe me, we would scarcely grant you a delay of two days. These things would seem sufficient both for me to persuade and for you to consent. [Col. 0907B]

But there still remains what I said above should be examined in fifth place: namely, to consider what the Son of God has done for you, insofar as he will deign to enlighten the eyes of your heart; so that we may see whether perhaps he has commanded you to do something greater for him than he himself first did for you.

First, then, contemplate him made man, so poor and needy that he had nowhere to lay his head. After this, observe him and consider more attentively, as though in a certain treasury of your mind, suffering from hunger, thirst, and weariness; treated with reproaches, insults, blasphemies, and abuse; enduring even his betrayer as far as the table, and in the betrayal itself as far as the kiss; finally, [Col. 0907C] bound, smeared with spittle, struck with blows, beaten with scourges; enduring false witnesses, utterly wicked accusers, and an unjust judge; crowned with thorns; carrying his own cross; counted among thieves; hanging naked upon the cross; there made a mockery of by the people; given vinegar to drink; and at last dead.

Consider all these things concerning him, I say, as carefully as you can, as though they had been set before your eyes. By enduring all these things, he was both fulfilling the mystery of redemption and showing you the way of imitation.

But what is this? What, I ask, is it for God to suffer these things? Attend; observe more attentively. What, then, is it for God to become man? Consider what God is; consider what man is. What is it for God to become man? What is it for him to suffer all those things, him who rules and created all visible [Col. 0907D] and invisible things? What is it for him to be crucified, him who could not only have prevented his crucifiers from committing their crime, but by a mere nod could have crushed them all as one crushes a single gnat?

What such humility, what such patience, could otherwise even be imagined? And what goodness, what clemency, that God should suffer these things for man, the Creator for his creature? In meditating upon this, in wondering at this, does anyone’s spirit grow lukewarm, does anyone’s mind languish in sluggish torpor? And does anyone dare call one of his commands harsh or difficult?

For what shall we repay the Lord for all that he has repaid us? If you find something that you can do for him greater than what he has done for you, I approve your counsel. For this, surely, you owe your Creator and Redeemer. What servant, indeed, is grateful to his lord if he does not do more for his lord than the lord has done for the servant? [Col. 0908A]

But if you can find nothing of this kind either in his commandments or by devising it yourself, you owe your Creator at least equal for equal. And if you can find not even this—or if you are unwilling to do that small thing which I advise, and which he himself commands—do not dissemble any longer.

You owe this to him because you are reckoned, as was said above, among Christians by profession—if only you had persevered in the innocence which you received in holy baptism. But if you are a sinner, fulfill the command whose fulfillment you owe, and seek what you can do in satisfaction for your sins. If you have nothing greater or more effective for you in either respect, do the Lord’s will by fulfilling the command, and it will be reckoned to you as satisfaction for your sins. [Col. 0908B]

If I were advising you as one inexperienced, you might perhaps more reasonably bring forward a calculation of the difficulty. But now, since I give this advice as one experienced, and have removed the fear of difficulty and—as one speaking with little wisdom—have shown you an example, so that you may follow the one whom you ought to have preceded, no room remains with me for calculation, with God for excuse, or anywhere at all for dissembling.

Do you not know that your judgment depends upon my deed? If you persist in dissembling even now, I am certain that the Lord will grant me some additional reward for this present exhortation; but your sin will be increased through contempt.

And what shall I say? The hand grows weary, but affection does not fail; the right hand grows weak, but charity does not grow cold—rather, it grows fervent and bursts into flame.

Let us therefore return to the mystery of redemption, [Col. 0908C] which was discussed above, and see what the Lord has bestowed upon you by suffering the things already mentioned, if perhaps your charity may thereby catch fire or your affection be moved.

May he therefore be present who makes the tongues of infants eloquent and grants them to say what pleases him. May the Spirit, I say, be present and kindle the inmost parts of your soul and mine alike with that fire which the Lord Jesus came to cast upon the earth and desired greatly to burn.

First, then, O man, you were without God in the world, ignorant of God and your Creator. You were born in this present life for labors and dangers, but from the misery of the present life you were falling irretrievably into everlasting torments. And—what is more pitiable—you were ignorant of this very condition of your perdition, and therefore did not know yourself. For since you knew neither your end nor your beginning, how could you know yourself?

Then, taking pity from on high, the Son of God came to you. He came as the true light shining upon you, who dwelt in the region of the shadow of death, and drove away the darkness of your ignorance, showing you your God and Creator and making known to you your condition—namely, from where you came and what you were.

You who were a son of perdition, who were a vessel of wrath and dishonor, he placed among vessels of honor and mercy, not only rescuing you from eternal damnation but mercifully restoring you to eternal life. You had lost paradise; you received heaven. You who had been a companion of demons became an associate and companion of angels.

But what shall I say? I shall say still more: from a servant you were adopted [Col. 0909A] as a son. What did I say? Yes, I say it. You who were a servant—not of God, for to serve God is to reign, but a servant of sin and a servant of demons—were adopted as a son.

But whose son? Boldly I say it, confidently I say it, joyfully I say it: a son of God. For he says: “As many as received him, to them he gave power to become sons of God” (John 1:12).

Do you wish the matter to be stated more plainly? Again I say it with confidence and exultation: the Son of God became the Son of man, so that you might become a son of God. “I will declare your name to my brothers” (Psalm 21:23), and: “Go, announce to my brothers” (Matthew 28:10).

But if a son, then also an heir—indeed, an heir of God and coheir with Christ.

And what shall I say further? The Son of God, coeternal, co-omnipotent, and consubstantial with the Father, united your nature to himself in one person and exalted it above all the heavens, above every principality and power, as far as the session with the Father, as far as the right hand of Majesty. [Col. 0909B]

Your nature, to which it had been said, “You are earth, and into earth you shall go” (Genesis 3:19), has been raised to such glory and such honor—not merely to equality with the angels, but above every height of the archangels—that it has heard: “Sit at my right hand” (Psalm 109:1).

But for what purpose? So that he alone should be there? No; rather, so that you might be there with him. “That where I am,” he says, “they also may be with me” (John 17:24). And: “I will, Father, that where I am, my servant also may be there” (John 12:26).

But what is this? Open the eyes of your heart—of your heart, I say, open your eyes. Awaken faith, kindle charity; let desire catch fire, let tears of devotion and humility flow—tears of devout longing.

What, then, is this? What, I ask, is it for a man to become a son of God? What is it for the son of man—or rather, the son of perdition—to become the brother and coheir of the Son of God, in order to possess the Father’s inheritance?

What is this dignity bestowed upon our nature, that it should sit at the right hand of the Most High? What is this excellence, that man should be exalted above the entire angelic nature as far as the right hand of Majesty, when he had been oppressed to the lowest depths of hell under the tyranny of demons?

And what great piety, what great clemency of divine goodness, that not only should the dignity which we had lost in our first parent be restored to us, but that gifts and benefits should moreover increase more magnificently and abundantly?

Where is piety? Where is devotion? Where are praises? [Col. 0909D] Where is thanksgiving? Where is the jubilant rejoicing of gladness and exultation?

O mystery ordained from eternity, promised from ages and generations, wondrously prefigured by signs and enigmas, and more wondrously fulfilled at the end of the ages! For when the almighty Father, through the only-begotten Word, had created all visible and invisible things, the work of our redemption appears to me to be the most wondrous of all the things he wondrously created.

I do not know whether others feel the same way. For me, however, it is devout and sweet to feel this way.

O joy with which the heavens rejoice and the earth exults! “Rejoice in the Lord, all the earth; sing, exult, and sing psalms” (Psalm 97:4).

Recognize, O man, to what dignity and to what joys you are called! In contemplating your restoration, may the unconquerable fervor of your faith increase; and, forgetting passing goods, may the unwavering expectation of your hope rise toward heavenly things.

Through constant meditation on such great benefits, may desire grow fervent like a revolving chariot; may charity catch fire, knowing how to love only such heavenly goods, and wisely avoid the adulterous desires for visible things.

Wonder at, proclaim, and praise the divine goodness without ceasing. For what praises, what thanksgivings, can you worthily offer your Creator? What will you repay the Lord for all that he has repaid you? What worthy thing will you be able to do, so that you may be considered worthy of such benefits?

“For the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that shall be revealed in us” (Romans 8:18).

What shall I say, my dearest and most desired one, [Col. 0910B] if you do not strive to hasten toward such salvation and such joys, as certainly and securely as you can? What shall I say if the companion of angels does not fear—or even strives—to become the companion of demons? If the heir of heaven, indeed the heir of God and coheir of Christ, wishes to remain on earth? If the son of God wishes to serve the world?

What shall I say if you still wish to entangle in the world, its deeds, or its unlawful desires the nature of your humanity, which you ought to have preserved in sanctification and honor for the sake of the honor and reverence of that man who sits at God’s right hand?

How will you escape if you neglect so great a salvation? If those who have not heard the ways of life and truth are condemned without end, what sentence of condemnation will those receive who hear, understand, and neglect?

Come, then, my beloved, come, and let us strive together with every effort and devotion toward such great and ineffable joys; and, with God’s help, let us arrive there together.

I exhort you in Christ. Once, if I am not mistaken, I used to rejoice more than you yourself in your progress in temporal goods. Now, however, I consider everything as refuse, in order to gain Christ.

Come, come; the angels invite you. They rejoice over one sinner who repents; and if you make them rejoice over your repentance, they will undoubtedly make you a sharer in their joys.

Will you not abandon the vain joys of the world in order to be joined to the joys of the angels? Come; Christ calls you. What? Rather, he also appears before the face of God for you and intercedes for you; for he does not wish the price of his blood [Col. 0910D] to be ineffectual in you.

Will you, then, make Christ’s outpouring of blood ineffectual for yourself? I beg you—indeed, I entreat you—for his sake and through him, not to deprive him of what he purchased in you. He gave his soul and his blood for your soul. Do you not see at what price you were valued?

What will you do, O man, if you deprive Christ of his rightful claim? “Behold,” he says, “I stand at the door and knock; if anyone opens to me, I will enter in to him and dine with him” (Revelation 3:20).

Run, dearest one, run; hasten to open to Christ who is knocking. Believe me, you will taste and see how sweet the Lord is.

But if you despise me as I admonish you and pour out devout prayers and pious tears to the Lord for your salvation; if you despise the angels who invite you and stand ready to bring you help; if you despise Christ who calls you, intercedes for you before the Father, [Col. 0911A] and, should you neglect him, charges the price of his blood to your account—then I use the apostolic word: “I am clean from your blood” (Acts 20:26). Your blood be upon your own head.

God is my witness how, longing for you in the bowels of Jesus Christ, I have asked this of God with prayers and tears, and have earnestly entreated it in the present exhortation, not without labor.

But I do not doubt—indeed, I am certain—that you will do what I urge, or rather, what such a multitude of necessities presses you on every side to do. For the Spirit of the Lord, who was present with me as I wrote these things—for I am not conscious of having brought them forth from my own heart—the Holy Spirit, I say, who granted confidence for writing, has also granted confidence that he will be present with you in the tears poured out through writing and prayer.

Whatever, therefore, you resolve to do under the inspiration of that same Holy Spirit, although I give many admonitions, this is the first thing I admonish you: do not prefer human counsel to divine counsel. Beware, I say, of human counsel, for “they are iniquitous lips and a deceitful tongue.” If perhaps you cannot entirely avoid it, shoot against it “the arrow of the mighty one and desolating coals.”

Next I admonish you not to propose doing what is easier and less conducive to salvation. Let faintheartedness be far from the strong. “Cast your care upon the Lord, and he will nourish you” (Psalm 54:23), and “he will save you from the faintheartedness of your spirit” (ibid., 9).

Do not suppose that faintheartedness does little harm, since so great a prophet gloried in having been saved from it by the Lord.

The time is short; salvation is everlasting. The Lord’s yoke is easy. Believe one who has experience.

Keep the Lord’s sufferings in mind. Observe also what you yourself have done and what you ought to have done. For some, noticing the magnitude of the commandment and forgetting the greatness of their sins, attend not to what they have done but to what they are commanded.

While they tremble at the light burden and easy yoke of the Lord, they remain in their own filth and do not fear increasing the heap of condemnation for themselves. In them that saying of the Prophet is apparently fulfilled: “There they trembled with fear where there was no fear” (Psalm 13:5). And this saying: “Let the one who is filthy be filthy still” (Revelation 22:11).

Consider also what tranquility of a good conscience comes from walking by a surer and nearer way to salvation and awaiting the final hour confidently, resting as though in a harbor of salvation.

Consider, I say, how much confidence a good conscience has before God: namely, to live so that, according to the apostolic judgment, “in the things that we do, our heart does not condemn us” (1 John 3:21).

Seek, therefore, a safe harbor. A sailor is rightly accused of inexperience if, when he could enter the shelter of a safer harbor, he does not fear entrusting himself to a stormy shore.

What good is it to have sailed across the sea and escaped the storms if, upon reaching shore, you fear the same shipwreck, and an inhospitable cliff of the wrecked shore shatters the ship’s hull?

Take these things into consideration, then, and attend carefully as a faithful counselor of your soul; and if perhaps you are fainthearted—though may this be far from you!—cease to be so.

Third, I also admonish you to devote yourself to prayer very frequently and fervently. If there you wish to act confidently rather than fearfully, courageously rather than falsely, you will have the Holy Spirit as your counselor. For “the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit” (Wisdom 1:5).

Whatever the breath of his most kind and merciful inspiration suggests there, undertake without hesitation and without any delay, strengthened by divine counsel. For this is the fourth thing I wish to commend to you: flee delays.

Many, while seeking delays, have fallen into a snare. For it has always been harmful for those prepared to postpone matters. “Let the dead bury their dead,” says the Lord (Matthew 8:22); “but you, follow me.” The one to whom he said this was seeking delays.

“Tomorrow, tomorrow” is the voice of a raven, as blessed Augustine said (*Sermon 71, To the Brothers in the Desert*). The raven sent out from the ark did not return, but the dove returned, because the Lord does not love delay in a raven-like voice, but confession in a dove-like groaning.

Do these things, then; watch carefully over them, my dearest one. For we remember, hear, see, and grieve how many who had already made a good beginning of willing have either turned away from a holy purpose or been led to decline what was less suitable—and I do not know whether they were even driven into damnation—because they failed to take these matters into consideration.

But when you have brought the matter to completion, see what fruits of the blessed life you will immediately begin to receive.

First, every page of sacred speech, which now, because of the dissimilarity between your conduct and your life, you feel resisting you like an unconquerable adversary and struggling against you, will become so fitting for you and will harmonize so well with your life that, when singing the psalms, you will not seem to be composing a prophecy or words dictated by someone else, but rather pouring forth before God the words of your own most devout prayer. Whenever what is said is moral instruction, you will resound as though with a certain harmony of voice and life, most sweet to you and most pleasing to God.

With what banquets, what musical instruments, what joys, or what delight of human life can this pleasure be compared?

Observe also another joy, filled with no lesser delight—indeed, preferable to all riches and to everything whatsoever that is considered pleasant or enjoyable in human life.

The most blessed Fathers Ambrose, Augustine, Jerome, Gregory, and others, each offering in God’s tabernacle whatever he can, will compete to unfold the enigmas of Scripture for you, explain the oracles of the prophets, and strive to show you a harmony of the New and Old Testaments filled with ineffable joy.

One will explain to you the retributions of the wicked; another will show you the joys of eternal life; one will carry you away into contemplation; another will draw tears of devout compunction from you; one will form you in humility, another in patience, another in chastity; this one in modesty, that one in kindness, this one in gentleness, another in faith, another in hope. All of them, however, will shape you for charity.

Nor will they cease before you are found so perfected, with the Holy Spirit working everywhere and dispensing everywhere, that you may attain “to a perfect man, to the measure of the fullness of the age of Christ.”

Christ dispenses these joys to his soldiers while he delays the eternal ones. In the meantime he has set this table before them, until they feast, rejoice before God, [Col. 0913A] and delight in gladness.

With these joys he comforts them for the time being; indeed, he multiplies these joys, compensating them with abundant interest, in place of the joys of the present life which they have abandoned, until they receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life.

These are indeed few things that I can say to you, since I am still a soldier inexperienced in new battles. But weigh great things from small ones, and many from few.

You will grieve that you have been absent from these joys for so long and will say: “Woe is me, for my sojourning has been prolonged” (Psalm 119:5), and so forth.

You thought you were being called to labors; I invite you to joys. Come, therefore, do not delay, and let us together taste the first fruits of these joys and likewise of the hope of eternal things.

Those who serve secular affairs and business, and the various pleasures and cares of life, cannot even dream of these joys. Having lost their senses, they are dull of heart and like people suffering from fever. Even if you offer a feverish person savory and sweet dishes and drinks, they have no taste for him because he has no sense of taste.

“For the Lord hides the abundance of his sweetness for those who fear him”—that is, he hides it from others, so that these may perceive it while the others do not.

I ask you not to measure the length of my words as though it were the measure of my charity. I shall never seem to myself to have said enough or done enough until you have fulfilled Christ’s will and my desire.

Farewell. May the Lord lead you out of the pit of misery and the mud of filth, set your feet upon a rock, and deign to direct your steps. May he rescue your soul from death, your eyes from tears, and your feet from falling. Amen.

## LETTER II. TO LATOLDUS  
### On the Manner of Praying

[Col. 0913C]

Brother John sends greetings to his dearest brother Latoldus.

Recently, when I had answered your inquiry concerning the manner of praying with what the Lord had enabled me to see, you earnestly asked me to send you in writing the three petitions in which, as I had said, the substance of the prayers that each of us makes for ourselves ought to consist.

And because I had said that, for arousing the affection of devotion, it is of great value not always to follow the same wording, but, as affection dictates, to vary our words and formulate our petitions either from the very prayers which we use in the Church or from the words of sacred Scripture, you also very devoutly asked me to write out some prayers for you in this manner, so that, reminded by them, you might be able to follow this form of prayer.

Therefore, setting aside excuses, lest I seem rather to have failed in charity than to have made a just excuse, I shall strive to satisfy your desire according to the strength which the Lord will deign to grant. For I prefer that my lack of skill should accuse me rather than that the charity which commands this from your heart should accuse me.

### Here he proposes that three things are to be asked.

Therefore, insofar as the Lord has granted my smallness to understand, each of us ought to ask three things for ourselves in prayer.

First, forgiveness of sins. Second, knowledge and performance of the divine will. Third, eternal salvation, which is in Christ.

In asking for these things, one should dwell on them sometimes at greater length and sometimes more briefly, according to the opportunity of the time or the feeling of devotion.

But we should be more concerned with the affection and desire with which these things are to be sought than with the words by which they are to be sought. For God does not need us to make our need or our will known to him in words, as though he did not know it; rather, as it is written, he knows what we need before we ask him. But we have an ineffable need to implore his benefits with ardent desire.

We can do this all the more effectively insofar as the grace of the Holy Spirit deigns to assist our weakness. For the Apostle says: “We do not know what we ought to pray for as we should, but the Holy Spirit himself pleads for us with unspeakable groanings” (Romans 8:26).

He said “pleads,” that is, he makes us plead, or grants the disposition to plead.

Let us now return to the three petitions set out above.

First, then, we must ask forgiveness of sins—not only of those of which we are conscious, that is, in which we recognize that we have sinned, but also of those in which we have fallen unknowingly.

For if the faults which we have committed unknowingly were not to be feared, it would not be said in the Psalm: “Remember not my ignorances” (Psalm 24:7).

And when the Apostle had said, “I am conscious of nothing against myself,” he immediately added: “But I am not thereby justified” (1 Corinthians 4:4), thereby indicating that he had sinned, or might have sinned, in many things through ignorance.

Accordingly, another Apostle said: “In many things we all offend” (James 3:2).

In the second petition, I said that two further things were to be requested: not only the performance but also the knowledge of the divine will. For a person easily goes astray in what he does not understand and can be deceived by the appearance of what is right, so that what is good may seem evil to him and what is evil good.

Hence the Prophet says: “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil” (Isaiah 5:20).

To prevent this from happening to us, we are commanded in the Gospel to possess the prudence of the serpent together with the simplicity of the dove (Matthew 10:16). The Prophet laments those who lack this prudence, saying: “Ephraim has become like a dove seduced, without understanding” (Hosea 7:11), because some, wishing to follow the simplicity of the dove, are led astray and fall into error because they do not have a heart—that is, understanding of the truth.

So that we may not fall into such darkness of error and ignorance, we must pray with every persistence and effort that we may be worthy to follow, in the sincerest and most persevering imitation, him who says: “Whoever follows me does not walk in darkness but has the light of life” (John 8:12).

The performance of the divine will consists in those two things which are briefly expressed where it is said: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Psalm 36:27). Anyone can easily observe how comprehensively these two commands embrace whatever is prescribed anywhere in Scripture.

Third, as I said, we must ask for eternal life, so that with a simple eye—that is, with a sincere intention—we may seek God, and so that in everything we do our intention may be directed neither toward the desire for human praise, which is hypocrisy, nor toward anything else, but solely toward possessing God.

“In simplicity of heart,” it says, “seek him” (Wisdom 1:1). And: “Do not approach God with a double heart” (Ecclesiasticus 1:36).

### Concerning those things found in the Psalms

Anyone who knows how to give attentive hearing to the divine words can easily observe how these three, or four, things are requested in Scripture in many different ways, especially in the Psalms.

From these, in accordance with your request, I shall set down some examples, so that, as the Holy Spirit deigns to inspire you, you may learn from them to vary your words in prayer—as I said is useful for arousing devotion—and may be able to shape your petitions.

### Concerning those things useful for asking forgiveness

For asking forgiveness of sins, the following passages found in the Psalms are useful:

“Cleanse me, Lord, from my hidden faults” (Psalm 18:13).

And: “Remember not the sins of my youth and my ignorances” (Psalm 24:7).

And: “For your name’s sake, Lord, you will be favorable to my sin, for it is great” (ibid., 11).

And: “See my humility and my labor, and forgive all my sins” (ibid., 18).

And: “Remember not our former iniquities, but be favorable to our sins for your name’s sake” (Psalm 78:8–9).

And: “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, Lord, for no living person shall be justified in your sight” (Psalm 142:2).

And: “Turn your face away from my sins, and blot out all my iniquities” (Psalm 50:11), and so forth, as it is written in that Psalm and in others.

Likewise elsewhere: “Do not remember, Lord, my sins or those of my parents, and do not take vengeance for my sins” (Tobit 3:3).

### What should be used for asking understanding?

For asking for understanding of the truth, we may use the following passages, of which I shall mention a few from many:

“Enlighten my eyes, lest I ever sleep in death” (Psalm 12:4).

And: “For you enlighten my lamp, Lord; my God, enlighten my darkness” (Psalm 17:29).

Likewise: “Make your ways known to me, Lord, and teach me your paths” (Psalm 24:4).

And: “Make known to me the way in which I should walk” (Psalm 142:8).

And: “Teach me to do your will” (ibid., 10).

And: “Teach me your ordinances” (Psalm 118:26).

And: “Give me understanding, that I may learn your commandments” (ibid., 73), and so forth.

There is also the one who says: “Would that my ways were directed toward keeping your ordinances” (ibid., 5).

And: “Lead me in the path of your commandments” (ibid., 35).

And: “Direct my steps according to your word” (ibid., 133).

Other passages of this kind, especially in this Psalm—which is more moral than the others—and in other Psalms, can indeed be understood, but can scarcely be numbered.

Therefore, whoever says these things and things like them seeks nothing other than to do God’s will. But whoever says with devout groaning, “Woe is me, for my sojourning has been prolonged!” (Psalm 119:5), and: “Do not put me to shame in my expectation” (Psalm 118:116), and: “When shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Psalm 41:3), and other things of this kind, certainly desires the vision of God and the promises of eternal life.

We have shown how these things are requested individually in Scripture. Anyone can ask for them all together in a single prayer, saying as follows:

### Prayer to the Father

Holy Father and Lord, who give life to the dead and call those things which are not as though they were: mercifully absolve me, your sinful servant, whom you have deigned to call from the death of my sins to your mercy, from all my guilt and sins.

And, having given me understanding by which I may see and charity by which I may serve you and your servants, make me always progress toward better things in your service, so that in your kingdom you may complete in me the work of your mercy which you have begun.

Through the Lord, etc.

### Another prayer to the Father

Holy Father and Lord, who seek what was lost, bring back what was cast away, and guard what is fat and strong: guard around me the works of your mercy. You have deigned to seek me when I was wandering and to lead me back to your sheep.

Having granted me full forgiveness of all my sins, give me such understanding and such perseverance in doing your will that you may have mercy on me with everlasting mercy.

Through the Lord, etc.

### Another prayer

Holy Father and Lord, who do not desire the death of sinners and do not delight in our destruction: blot out my iniquities like a cloud and my sins like a mist.

And in the knowledge and performance of your will, make me persevere with such sincere humility and progress that you may save me in your heavenly kingdom.

Through the Lord.

### Prayer to the Son

Lord Jesus Christ, who came to seek and save what was lost: give life to me, your sinful servant, whom you have called.

Granting me understanding and observance of your commandments, make grace abound where sin abounded, so that with your elect you may make me truly a participant in your redemption and resurrection.

You who live, etc.

### Another prayer to the Son

Lord Jesus Christ, who are the true light that enlightens every person coming into this world: take away the darkness of my sins, and give me enlightened eyes of the heart, so that I may know you and understand and do your will.

Do not permit me ever to be separated from you.

You who live, etc.

Since many more things can be said in this manner, let it suffice that we have set down these.

### Concerning prolonged prayer

Some pray at greater length and more earnestly when imploring forgiveness of their sins. Considering the greatness or multitude of their sins more attentively, they offer God not so much words as groaning and tears—the sacrifice of a contrite and humbled heart—yet they are not able to pray with the same fervor as in the other matters set out above.

This commonly happens to beginners, that is, to those recently converted. To such people the Apostle James says: “Be miserable, and mourn, and weep. Let your laughter be turned into mourning and your joy into sorrow” (James 4:9).

### Concerning the tears of the perfect

Others, once they have begun to make progress in the way of God, in understanding, and in performance, are surprised that they have no tears, or only rarely have tears, for their sins.

But when temptations and weakness hinder them from fulfilling what they understand as fully as they wish, they pray more attentively and fervently against those temptations and against their own weakness, so that, with the help of God’s grace, the struggle with temptations may be overcome, understanding may be increasingly enlightened, and weakness may be strengthened.

Of such people it is written: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied” (Matthew 5:6).

[Col. 0917B]

### Concerning those who desire to be with Christ

Others, having already overcome temptations and having grown stronger through God’s grace in fulfilling what they understand, sigh toward eternal things with the great heat of burning desire.

Groaning that their sojourn is being prolonged, they desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ. Their voice is:

“As the deer longs for springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God” (Psalm 41:2);

and:

“How lovely are your tabernacles, Lord of hosts” (Psalm 83:2), and so forth.

These, then, are the three stages: beginners, those making progress, and the perfect.

### Another manner of praying
We find in the Scriptures other forms of prayer as well. Although in them the things set out above are not expressly requested one by one, nevertheless all that is conducive to salvation is understood to be sought in a concise prayer, as in: “Let your mercy, O Lord, be upon us, just as we have hoped in you” (Ps. 32:22); and: “Have mercy on me according to your word” (Ps. 118:58); and: “Deal with your servant according to your mercy” (ibid., 24); and: “Have mercy on me according to the judgment of those who love your name” (ibid., 132).

Following this form, we can pray for others in any circumstance, saying: “Make them, O Lord, appear in righteousness before your sight, so that they may deserve to be satisfied when your glory appears.” Or: “Make them, O Lord, participants with all who fear you and keep your commandments.” Or: “Deal with them, O Lord, according to your mercy, just as you are able to do abundantly more than we can ask or understand.” Or: “Give them, O Lord, your kingdom and your righteousness.” Or: “By that abundance of your goodness by which you surpass both the merits and the desires of those who entreat you, make them walk so in accordance with your good pleasure that they may please you in the land of the living.” Or: “Guide them on the straight path, so that they may deserve to see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living.” Or: “Establish them, O Lord, in the firmness of your love, so that neither death, nor life, nor any creature, nor any temptation may be able to separate them from you and from your love.” Or: “Grant them, O Lord, both to seek you with their whole heart and to accomplish with complete love the things pleasing to you.” Or: “Guide them, O Lord, according to the good pleasure of your will, into the way of eternal salvation” [Col. 0918A]. Alternatively: “Make them, O Lord, worthy of the promises of the life that now is and of the life eternal.” Or: “Make them pass through temporal goods in such a way that they do not lose eternal ones”; this seems especially suitable as a prayer for those who live in secular society. And also: “Make them, O Lord, so merciful that they may obtain mercy.”

For those, however, who pursue what is more perfect, one may pray that they become poor in spirit so that they may possess the kingdom of heaven; meek, so that they may deserve to possess the land of the living; mourners, so that they may deserve eternal consolation; hungry and thirsty for righteousness, so that they may obtain the promised satisfaction; pure in heart, so that they may deserve to see God; and peacemakers, so that they may deserve to be sons of God. May they advance by walking from virtue to virtue, until they reach the vision of the God of gods in Zion [Col. 0918B].

### That prayer should be offered for the prelates of the churches

Prayer should be offered for all the governors of the Church, so that they may administer the charge of government entrusted to them in such a way that they may deserve to work for the salvation both of themselves and of those subject to them. For all who live either according to our way of life or in any holy manner, one should pray that they may deserve to walk worthily in the vocation to which they have been called. For all the orders of the Church, one should pray that the Lord may deign to increase his servants in them both in number and in merit, and that, according to the riches of his grace, he may advance those who walk well in them toward better things, while bringing those who have gone astray back to the way of truth.

For those who are placed in any spiritual or bodily tribulation [Col. 0918C], one should pray that all may feel the Lord’s mercy present to them in their needs.
