Or: “May the Lord, according to the riches of his grace, in his favor remove everything adverse to them and grant everything that will benefit them.” For those who have fallen into heresies or schisms, one should pray that they may be brought back to the way of truth. For unbelievers, that they may be led to the portion and fellowship of the elect.

Just as prayer should be poured out for obtaining divine benefits, so thanksgiving should be offered for those already received. I would write about this at greater length, were it not that what has been set out above already seems excessively long.

I have written these things to you in one way or another, with a hurried hand, not knowing how much they will benefit you. But this I certainly know, and I want you to know it with complete certainty: insofar as the Lord has granted me the ability, I have taken care to satisfy your desire [Col. 0918D]. If I learn that these things have been useful to you, I shall hope to receive from Christ, through your prayers, compensation for my labor—Christ who commands through his Apostle that “through love we serve one another” (Gal. 5:23). I desire that all the brothers be greeted in my name through you—not all together, but each individually by his own name. How much I need to be helped by their prayers and yours, I have been unable adequately to indicate either while present or to express sufficiently while absent.

## LETTER III. TO HUGH  
### On the manner of praying, and especially on thanksgiving

To his most beloved brother HUGH, brother John sends greetings.

[Col. 0919A] I once wrote a letter on the manner of praying to brother Latoldus, when he had most devotedly requested this of me. In it, following the form of prayer that I was discussing, I set out, by way of example, three prayers addressed to the Father and two to the Son. When that letter came into your hands, you urgently requested that we add some prayers specifically concerning the person of the Holy Spirit.

Although the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are inseparable and therefore also work inseparably, and whatever the Father or Son gives is likewise given by the Holy Spirit, nevertheless, yielding to your request, I added after the prayers already given two prayers addressed to the Holy Spirit and a third to the Holy Trinity. Later, when you noticed that at the end of that same letter I had mentioned thanksgiving in such a way as to suggest that, if place or time permitted, I could say more about it, you again pressed me insistently, indeed altogether importunately, to write something more laborious for you on this matter—that is, on thanksgiving.

In response to what you ask, I find myself inadequate; but, supported by your prayers, I hope for sufficiency from him from whom comes every good gift and every perfect gift.

*[Here he inserts the whole of Letter II, addressed to Latoldus, On the Manner of Praying, to which he attaches the following three short prayers, placing them between the second prayer to the Son and the section on prolonged prayer.]*

### Prayer to the Holy Spirit

Holy Spirit, God, who regenerated me, born carnally into the world, through spiritual birth in the sacred font, grant me full forgiveness for all the sins that I have subsequently contracted in any way, and make me persevere so steadfastly in advancing both in understanding and in action through your justifications that I may deserve truly to belong forever to the portion and fellowship of your elect. You who with the Father and the Son possess one divinity and an undivided unity of the same majesty and power, throughout all ages of ages.

### Another prayer to the Holy Spirit

Holy Spirit, who are both the gift of God and God—God with respect to yourself, gift with respect to us—grant, I beg, through the grace of your indwelling, that the mind of this poor little servant of yours may shine with understanding of the truth and burn with the fire of love, so that, mercifully cleansed by the benefit of your grace from all the stains of my sins, I may deserve to be in the body whose head is Christ, and here live well and live blessedly forever [Col. 0919D], with whom, and with the Father, glory and undivided honor belong to you throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

### Prayer to the Holy Trinity

Holy Trinity, one God, who first gives life and sanctifies all whom you make blessed in the heavenly homeland, marking them with the Spirit of adoption on the way, give me, your little servant, that same Holy Spirit as the pledge of our inheritance, so that, as he pours into my heart the love that covers the multitude of my sins, confirms me in every understanding, word, and good work, and remains with me forever, I may deserve to praise you throughout the ages of ages with those who dwell in your house. Amen.

[Col. 0920A] What I said at the end of that letter, then, I repeat at the beginning of this one: just as we pour out prayers to obtain divine benefits, so we are bound to offer thanks for those we have received. If any person is ungrateful toward another person from whom he has received benefits, who would not judge this evil and unjust? If, then, it is evil to be ungrateful toward a human being, how much more toward God?

How, except by giving thanks, do we show that we are not ungrateful for his benefits? Scripture accuses those of ingratitude of whom it says: “And they forgot his benefits and his wonders that he showed them” (Ps. 77:11). In the Gospel, too, when the Lord had cleansed ten lepers and only one gave thanks, he complained that the other nine had proved ungrateful, saying: “Were not ten cleansed? And where are the nine?” (Luke 17:17), and so forth.

Let the discerning reader or hearer of the holy Scriptures therefore observe that whenever we are commanded or admonished to praise God, bless him, magnify him, exalt him, glorify him, sing to him, rejoice, exult, or give thanks, substantially the same thing is signified by different words. For example: “Bless our God, O nations” (Ps. 65:8); “Magnify the Lord with me, and let us exalt his name together” (Ps. 34:4); “Sing to him and sing psalms to him” (Ps. 105:2); and “Come, let us rejoice in the Lord; let us shout for joy to God our salvation” (Ps. 95:1).

“Confession” in the Scriptures also often signifies praise, as in: “I will confess to you, Lord my God, with all my heart” (Ps. 86:12). For, as though explaining what he had said, he adds: [Col. 0920C] “and I will glorify your name forever.” And the Lord says in the Gospel: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth” (Luke 10:21). He was not confessing sins, since he committed no sins, but was giving thanks to the Father.

People commonly recall the benefits of their friends or lords, so that from the magnitude of the benefits they may consider how much love or service they ought to return to them. We, therefore, must not merely call to mind but most diligently consider and seek out what and how many benefits and gifts have been bestowed upon us by God, and most devoutly render their author the praise and thanksgiving due to him.

For by recalling heavenly gifts we kindle the love of God in our hearts. By giving thanks for them, we merit both that what we have received may be preserved for us and that what we have not yet received may be increased for us. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “To the one who has, more will be given, and he will abound; but from the one who does not have, even what he seems to have will be taken away” (Luke 19:26).

For he is truly said to possess the gifts of God who uses them through devout thanksgiving for the purpose for which they were given—that is, to seek God—and who merits grace in return for grace. But whoever abuses them in seeking something else, being ungrateful, deserves to be deprived even of what he has received.

Some gifts of God are given commonly to the good and the wicked, while others are peculiar to the elect. External riches of gold and silver and other things, bodily health and strength of the limbs, intelligence and memory, knowledge of letters, and other things of this kind [Col. 0921A] are given alike to the reprobate and to the elect. But it is clear that faith working through love, piety, charity, holy fear, and the other gifts of true virtues are given only to the elect.

Let us therefore hear someone recalling with rejoicing in a psalm the divine benefits bestowed upon him. “Waiting,” he says, “I waited for the Lord, and he inclined toward me; he heard my prayers and brought me up from the pit of misery and from the mud of filth” (Ps. 40:2–3). Up to this point he shows from what depth of evils he has been liberated by God’s grace. In the following two verses he describes his establishment, direction, and renewal, saying: “And he set my feet upon a rock” (ibid.), and what follows.

Although nothing is stated there that signifies blessing or thanksgiving, the devout recollection of divine benefits is nevertheless counted as thanksgiving. In another psalm also he glorifies God, saying: “Who is God besides the Lord, or who is God besides our God?” (Ps. 17:12). It is as though we were asking, “What has he done for you? Why do you magnify and praise him in this way?” He enumerates many works of divine grace toward him and adds: “God who girded me with strength and made my way blameless” (Ps. 17:12), and so forth, up to: “and my footsteps were not weakened” (ibid. 33:37).

The Apostle says: “I give thanks to him who strengthened me, who judged me faithful and appointed me to the ministry.” By adding, “although I was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an insolent man” (1 Tim. 2:12–13), he shows God’s grace toward him to be the greater in proportion to his unworthiness to deserve receiving it. He also gives thanks when he says: “Blessed be God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies” (2 Cor. 1:3), and so forth.

### The difference between one who prays and one who praises

There is this difference between the disposition of one who prays and that of one who praises: prayer contains contrition and groaning, especially when sins are being mourned or when divine help is sought amid temptations and tribulations. But one who praises and gives thanks is filled with spiritual joy and gladness.

Therefore, for those who are deeply contrite over their sins, it seems beneficial that, after the sorrow experienced on account of their sins, they turn to thanksgiving, so that thanksgiving may console the soul sorrowing over its sins. Otherwise, someone of this kind might be swallowed up by excessive sadness. Thus the mind afflicted by sins may be renewed in hope of forgiveness by giving thanks for the benefits it has received.

For others, it seems that prayer should begin with thanksgiving, so that the mind of the one praying, filled with spiritual joy and confidence, may pour forth the whole prayer that follows from a kind of inward richness.

### We must always give thanks

We must give thanks to the Father not only in prosperity but also amid chastisements—to the Father who chastises every son whom he receives—as it is written in the person of the righteous: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise will always be in my mouth” (Ps. 34:2). Whoever blesses him at all times gives thanks not only in prosperity but also in adversity.

The wicked, too, praise God amid prosperity, as it is written: “He will confess to you when you have done good to him” (Ps. 49:19); but in adversity they are accustomed to murmur and blaspheme.

### On the same subject

One who is diligent and devoted in thanksgiving should first of all recall the greatest and most excellent of all divine benefits and give thanks for it with as much devotion and piety as possible: through the most sacred mystery of Christ’s incarnation and passion, we have been redeemed from eternal death and restored to eternal life.

For in Christ salvation itself came to the sick, mercy itself to the wretched, wisdom itself to fools, life itself to the dead, the way itself to those who were wandering, truth itself to liars, the Redeemer himself to captives, and God himself to human beings.

That majesty of divine wisdom, coeternal, consubstantial, and co-omnipotent with the Father and the Holy Spirit, which carries all things by the word of its power, and reaches from end to end mightily while ordering all things sweetly, wished in such great compassion and such abundant goodness to come to the aid of our misery that it deigned to humble itself not only to the assumption of our nature but even to insults and death on the cross, for our redemption and salvation.

The Only-Begotten of the most high Father, since he had nowhere further to descend by humbling himself than to die, as though guilty and condemned, the most shameful death in the human being whom he united to himself in one person, so our nature had nowhere further to be exalted than to sit in Christ at the right hand of the Father, to have the name that is above every name, and to have every knee bow to him—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth.

He gave us the firmest hope that, if we faithfully cling to him, we shall follow him to where he went before us. “Father,” he says, “those whom you have given me, I will that where I am, they also may be with me, so that they may see the glory that you have given me” (John 17:24).

Who could worthily contemplate such great grace? Who would be sufficient to render worthy praise and thanks for it? Even if we are unable to offer worthy praise, we must nevertheless not cease giving thanks until, with him as our guide, we reach the place where we may do so without end, as it is written: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, Lord; throughout the ages of ages they will praise you” (Ps. 84:5).

Now is the time both for praying and for praising; then it will be a time only for praising. For then, just as blessedness will succeed misery, praise will succeed prayer. Once all God’s promises have been fulfilled, nothing will remain to be requested, as he himself says: “On that day you will ask me nothing” (John 16:23).

The more we love him, the more diligently we ought to attend to the canonical—that is, prophetic and apostolic—and also the other Scriptures, and listen most attentively to what they suggest to us about him, or what he himself speaks to us in them.

Who, hearing him say through the prophet, “I will free them from the hand of death; I will redeem them from death. I shall be your death, O death; I shall be your sting, O underworld” (Hos. 13:14), would not burst into this joyful and praising utterance, saying: “Thanks to you, Lord, for such great goodness, which you have deigned to expend upon our redemption; and I pray that you may make us truly share forever in that redemption and eternal salvation which is in you”?

Who, hearing the Apostle say, “The saying is trustworthy: Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners” (1 Tim. 1:15), would not pour forth praise together with prayer and say: “To you, Lord, praise; to you thanksgiving, for in such great compassion you seek the life of sinners, not their death. May it please you, Lord, to deign to justify us from sins and save us with eternal salvation”?

When we hear the words in which his benefits are either recounted or promised, we ought, as the Apostle teaches, to “abound in him in thanksgiving” (Col. 2:7). But the soul that loves and longs for him, after offering thanksgiving, must also add prayers, so that it may be made worthy of his promises.

Whoever, on hearing the divine words, is inflamed to pray, praise, or love God can truly say what is written in the Song of Songs: “My soul melted” (Song 5:6)—that is, it dissolved into tears of love.

I know that a certain prudent and religious man said: “He does not have the Spirit of Christ who, on hearing Christ’s words, does not burn.” But the man who said this seems to me to have judged others by what he experienced within himself, which is characteristic especially of very many people.

Knowing, however, that many good and just people have either no gift of tears or only rarely possess it, I say the following for the consolation of such people. Some love Christ with the ardent affection of charity; others do not feel a great affection of love for him, but show that love in the effect of their works. Of these he himself says: “Whoever has my commandments and keeps them is the one who loves me” (John 14:21). And again: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word” (ibid., 23). Hence Gregory says: “The proof of love is the manifestation of the work.”

In the person of those who love Christ with ardent affection it is also said: “As the deer longs for the springs of water” (Ps. 41:8), and so forth.

Finally, I say that each person is better and holier in proportion as he is more devout and ardent in loving and seeking God [Col. 0923D].

For just as we sometimes offer prayers to the Father and sometimes to the Holy Spirit, although more often prayers are offered to the Father through the Son in the Holy Spirit, so the same should be done with thanksgiving, as the Apostle says: “Giving thanks to God the Father through him” (Col. 3:17)—that is, through Christ.

As far as I have been able to experience both activities, namely praying and giving thanks, each person performs them better in his own words—that is, words arising from the inmost heart—than in the words of others. For neither in prayer nor in thanksgiving is ornament of language sought, but the disposition of the mind.

If someone does not have words of his own at hand, let him pray and give thanks through psalms and by whatever other means he can. I have done what I could, as you requested. You are forceful. May you, by this forcefulness, deserve to seize the kingdom of heaven! I shall await from the Lord, through your prayers, the fruit of my labor.

## LETTER IV. TO BERARD  
### On guarding the heart

To his most beloved brother BERARD, brother JOHN sends greetings.

By this brief writing I discharge the request of your petition and the debt of your promise. When I had offered you and the brothers who had come with you to us an exhortation on guarding the heart, and had shown how the soul or the flesh ought to obey reason, you earnestly asked that I send you in writing what I had expressed in words.

Observe, then, that the human being consists of two things, namely soul and body. But the soul, although it is not divided, is again distinguished into two, namely soul and spirit.

There is a certain lower power of the soul that gives life and growth to the body and, favoring the senses of the flesh, longs to flow immoderately into carnal pleasures. In the Scriptures it is called “soul,” because it animates—that is, gives life to—the body. Some have preferred to call it “sensuality.” In this respect we do not differ from animals, since animals too have a soul that moves and gives life to the body, seeks what is useful, and flees what is harmful.

There is also a certain higher power of the same soul, which is called spirit or reason. Through it we differ from animals; for according to it we have been made in the image of God, because through it we distinguish between good and evil and between the Creator and the creature.

The Apostle distinguishes these three—namely, the spirit that understands, the soul that gives life, and the body that is given life—in one passage, saying: “May your spirit and soul and body be preserved blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Thess. 5:23).

Our governing principle, then, is the spirit, which is also called mind, reason, and intellect. It is not something different from the soul itself, but something belonging to the soul that ought to preside over it.

Our lower element is the life of the body itself, that is, the soul, which, because it desires carnal things, is also called “flesh.” Hence the Apostle says: “With my mind I serve the law of God, but with my flesh the law of sin” (Rom. 7:25). And again: “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. 5:17). The flesh, however, desires nothing without the soul.

Our final element is the body, which is also visible. Often, however, the Scriptures speak in such a way that, without observing this distinction, both are signified together under the single name “soul” or the single name “spirit.” When the Lord says in the Gospel, “I lay down my soul for my sheep” (John 10:15), by the one name “soul” he designates the whole of what consists of soul and spirit. Likewise, when he says, “Into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke 23:46), he did not intend to distinguish the spirit from the soul, but expressed both together under the single name “spirit.”

Therefore, when a human being lives according to the body, he is called carnal or animal. He is called carnal because he pursues carnal things; animal because he is carried along by the unrestrained license of his soul, which the spirit does not govern, since the spirit itself does not submit to being governed by God. This is the disordered life of the human being, exposed to destruction.

But one who governs his soul by the spirit, and through the soul also restrains the body within the limits of the natural order—which he cannot do unless he himself has God as his ruler—is called spiritual.

This, then, is the ordered life: that the spirit of the human being submit itself to God, that is, present itself ready to do God’s will. Then, by divine gift, it will also have the flesh and soul subjected to it, that is, obedient to reason.

As long as the first human being kept the commandment of obedience in paradise, he was spiritual. After he sinned and was dismissed from paradise, he remained in the condition of being animal. Therefore, all of us who are born from him through sin first live as animal beings, until through God’s grace we become spiritual. Hence the Apostle says: “Not first what is spiritual, but what is animal; afterward what is spiritual” (1 Cor. 15:46).

Even now, whenever any human being falls into sin, nothing other than what happened in paradise among those three—namely, the serpent, the woman, and the man—is taking place.

First, the serpent makes a suggestion, either through thought or through the bodily senses: by seeing, touching, hearing, tasting, or smelling. When this suggestion has been made, if desire is not moved toward sinning, the serpent’s cunning is driven out. But if desire is moved, it is as though the woman has already been persuaded.

Sometimes, however, reason also restrains and checks the desire that has been stirred, manfully. When this happens, the person does not fall into sin but is crowned after a certain struggle. If reason consents and decides that what lust has stirred up ought to be done, the human being is expelled from all blessed life as though from paradise.

For sin is already imputed even if the act does not follow, since conscience is held guilty in the mind. Sin is therefore committed in these three ways: by suggestion, which occurs through the devil; by desire or delight, which occurs through the flesh and the soul; and by consent, which occurs through the spirit.

That persuader of wickedness knows that reason cannot be led to consent to sin unless pleasure or desire has first been stirred in that part of the soul which ought to obey reason as its governing man. Therefore, in marvelous ways he does not cease to suggest through thought whatever he can and, unless he is repelled, after suggesting to the flesh, to inflame desire, so that afterward he may be able to drag the captive mind into consent to sin.

He knows whom to inspire with the swelling of pride, to whom to suggest the appetite for empty glory, to whom to offer the poison of envy, whom to inflame with lust, whom to provoke to anger, and whom to contaminate with the plague of one vice or another, according as he can detect the dispositions of different people to receive the fuel of various vices.

Thus he—as it is written of him—lies in wait for the heel, that is, for our fall (Gen. 3:15). We, however, must crush his head, that is, the beginning of his evil suggestion, always keeping at hand the sword of the Spirit and the rest of the armor about which the Apostle instructs us (Eph. 6).

Scripture says: “Guard your heart with all vigilance, for from it the sources of life flow” (Prov. 4:23). The heart is guarded in no better way than by keeping it always occupied with holy thoughts, insofar as this can be done by God’s grace, as we read: “Holy thought will preserve you” (Prov. 2:11).

Even if we do this most diligently—now through reading, now through prayer, sometimes through psalmody, and at other times through holy meditation—it is nevertheless impossible for us to be entirely free from evil thoughts. But there is no danger and no sin at all if the spirit, or reason, keeping most vigilantly on watch, promptly drives them away when they attack insolently, opposing to our seductive and harmful thoughts the shield of prayer and the defenses of holy thoughts.

But if reason grows drowsy and allows any unclean and harmful thoughts not only to enter but also to linger in the mind, the divine word rebukes us through the prophet, saying: “How long will harmful thoughts remain within you?” (Jer. 4:14).

If, after an evil suggestion, desire has also been stirred through excessive negligence, then at least the mind must awaken and, extinguishing the fire that has been kindled, forcefully resist and drive out the enemies already admitted within the door, lest it too—God forbid—be destroyed by consenting to sin.

I have written these things briefly for you, taking care, insofar as I could, to satisfy your request. If I learn that they have pleased you, I shall obtain my reward through your prayers [Col. 0926C].

## LETTER V. TO BERNARD, HIS NEPHEW, WHO WAS THINKING OF TRANSFERRING FROM THE CARTHUSIAN ORDER TO ANOTHER  
### On steadfastness in one’s vocation

Brother JOHN, an undistinguished monk of the house of Portae, sends to his most beloved spiritual son and bodily nephew BERNARD the perseverance and progress due in divine service.

I have heard that you wish to withdraw from the purpose to which Christ’s grace had called you, and to transfer to another order. This persuasion does not come from him who called you, but from the serpent who deceived Eve by his cunning and now wishes to deceive you also, and to lead you back from the narrow way that leads to life, along which you had begun to walk, to the broad [Col. 0926D] and spacious way that leads to destruction. Hear, therefore, rather Christ saying: “Strive to enter by the narrow gate, because many, I tell you, will seek to enter and will not be able” (Luke XIII, 34). He does not merely say, “Enter,” but “Strive to enter,” because great striving and struggle, great exertion and conflict, are certainly necessary: against the weakness of both mind and body; against the innumerable weaknesses, difficulties, and impediments that arise; against the darts of tongues, the insults, and the slanders of those who speak evil; against carnal and earthly desires; against the innumerable temptations, deceits, and snares of the invisible enemy.

As someone has said: “The exile from heaven knows what is being done in heaven.” Envious of the blessedness that [Col. 0927A] he himself lost, he never ceases—through innumerable kinds of temptation, both by himself and through his agents—to strive so that, just as by deceiving our parents he drove them from paradise, so by ensnaring some who live well he may exclude them from that paradise. Of it Christ says in the Song of Songs: “A garden enclosed is my sister, my bride; a garden enclosed.” For *paradise* is interpreted as “garden.” Christ’s garden, therefore, is the holy manner of life of the elect in the present Church. It is enclosed—that is, fortified by divine protection. In this garden lilies of chastity, hyssop of humility, roses of patience, and fir trees of contemplation grow; the myrrh of abstinence or sobriety also gives forth its fragrance, as does the frankincense of prayer, together with the other adornments of the virtues, which in Scripture are signified by various names of spices, aromatic trees, and herbs [Col. 0927B] are signified.

In this garden, the more the servants of God deserve to advance, the more sweetly and effectively they gather those fruits of the Spirit which the Apostle enumerates, saying: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience” (Galatians V, 22), and so forth. They love the sweetness of these fruits so greatly that, even if no blessedness of the future life were to follow, they would confess that they have already received from God a great recompense—indeed, one abounding in multiplied return—in place of the riches, pleasures, and joys of the world which they renounced.

For it is certainly a large portion, and in some sense an imitation, of future blessedness: not to be puffed up by any pride; not to be gnawed by envy; to be free from slavery to sin; not to be carried away by ambition, avarice, or any other desires; [Col. 0927C] not to be elated by prosperity; not to be broken by adversity; to harm no one and to wish to benefit everyone; when someone injures us or inflicts any wrong upon us, not merely not to return injury or wrong, but in addition to repay evil with good; to show the affection of love toward all; to be nourished by the feasts of the holy Scriptures; to enjoy the consolations of the Holy Spirit; and not only not to fear departure from this life, but even to await it with desire, on the testimony of a good conscience.

The Apostle calls these and similar things the fruits of the Spirit because no one can be such except through the grace of the Holy Spirit. The more abundantly a person receives him, the more easily and effectively that person deserves to fulfill these and the other things taught by the holy Scriptures.

The devil, therefore, rises up against those whom he seeks to drive from the paradise of the present Church—that is, from holy conduct—and draw into a rejected way of life, chiefly through two kinds of temptation [Col. 0927D]. For, as blessed Augustine says, “He either frightens in order to break, or flatters in order to deceive.” He frightens through adversities, persuading us that the things which prove troublesome, hard, and laborious are unbearable and impossible to endure, so that, broken and dissolved by despair, we may recoil from our holy purpose. He flatters through prosperity, inviting us to carnal pleasures and to the things that appear desirable in the world.

You, therefore, observe what surrounds you, and beware lest you be deceived by the serpent. For the Father, who rebukes those whom he loves and scourges every son whom he receives, has begun to scourge you through the bodily affliction that you endure. If what scourges you seems hard, it ought to be incomparably [Col. 0928A] sweeter to you because he receives you; and you ought to give thanks if you deserve to be scourged as a son.

If you do this, the Father’s scourge accomplishes two things for you: namely, past sins are cleansed and future sins are guarded against. Past sins are cleansed because there is no doubt that God, as it is written, “will remit sins in the time of tribulation” (Ecclesiasticus II, 13). Future sins are guarded against because it is likewise written: “Before I was humbled”—that is, before I was afflicted by the scourge—“I sinned” (Psalm CXVIII, 67).

For here, and where it is said, “I have been humbled exceedingly” (ibid., 107)—that is, very greatly—and, “See my humiliation and deliver me” (ibid., 153), and, “See my humiliation and my toil, and forgive all my sins” (Psalm XXIV, 18), as also in many other [Col. 0928B] passages, *humiliation* is not the name of a virtue but of affliction. The righteous man, in whose person that entire psalm was written, by saying, “Before I was humbled, I sinned,” indicated that he was scourged for this reason: so that he would not sin. Once scourged, he ceased to sin; hence he adds: “Therefore I kept your word.”

Hear, then, not the serpent but the Apostle saying: “Persevere in discipline”—that is, do not lose perseverance under the scourge. And he adds: “God offers himself to you as to sons” (Hebrews XII, 7). But if, he says, you are without discipline—that is, if you refuse to be scourged—“then you are adulterers and not sons” (ibid., 8).

If, however, you prefer to believe the serpent, who is attempting through the accumulation of temptations to bring you to despair, you will be his food, as it is written: “Dust shall be the serpent’s bread [Col. 0928C]” (Isaiah LXV, 25). For “dust”—that is, those compared to dust—are the people of whom it is said: “Not so the wicked, not so; but like dust which the wind drives from the face of the earth” (Psalm I, 4). The wind is temptation; “from the face of the earth” means from the stability of the Church; dust means the wicked, who do not resist temptations, just as dust cannot resist the wind.

If you believe the serpent, you will be counted among the enemies of God, of whom it is said: “The enemies of the Lord have lied to him, and their time shall be for ever” (Psalm LXXX, 16). For if you invalidate what you promised on the day of your profession, you will be guilty before God and human beings of both a broken vow and a lie.

You will not only harm yourself, but will also become for many a rock of stumbling, and you will injure far more people by scandal than you could have benefited [Col. 0928D] by your example. Therefore you will be judged not only for your apostasy but also for their destruction. For the Lord says: “Woe to the person through whom scandal comes” (Matthew XVIII, 7).

Job, covered with worms and struck with a most grievous ulcer from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head, said: “My justification, which I began to hold, I will not abandon” (Job XVII, 6). When his wife also suggested blasphemy, he said: “If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not also receive evil?” (Job II, 10.)

The Apostle says: “In hunger and thirst, in many fasts, in cold and nakedness, in prisons and beatings, and in frequent deaths” (I Corinthians XI, 27). Serving Christ amid dangers, tribulations, and innumerable persecutions, he did not fail but said: “We glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces patience [Col. 0929A], and patience proven character, and proven character hope” (Romans V, 3–4), and so forth. Elsewhere he says: “I am pleased with myself in weaknesses, in insults, in necessities, in persecutions, in distress for Christ” (II Corinthians XII, 10).

And why did he not fail amid all these things? Elsewhere he gives the reason, saying: “I can do all things in him who strengthens me” (Philippians IV, 13). He not only strengthened him, but also, he says, “he comforts us in all our tribulation” (II Corinthians I, 4).

You, however, afflicted by a bodily trouble, although it is bearable, have failed in spirit because you have lost the hope and trust that you ought to have in God concerning all that surrounds you and all that is to come. You have become weakened, and the strength of your body and soul has begun to diminish, as the sacred Scripture says: “If you lose hope, being weary in the day of [Col. 0929B] distress, your strength will be diminished” (Proverbs XXIV, 10).

For if you had not despaired, you would truthfully say: “Hoping in the Lord, I shall not be weakened” (Psalm XXV, 1). Therefore recover your senses and fear what is written: “Woe to the fainthearted, who do not believe God; therefore they shall not be protected by him” (Ecclesiasticus II, 15); and again: “Woe to those who have lost endurance” (ibid., 16).

Recover your senses, I say, and because you have given assent to the enemy’s suggestions, do penance. Believe Christ, who says: “All things are possible to the one who believes” (Mark VII, 22); and, “Whatever you ask for in prayer, believe that you will receive it, and it will be done for you” (Mark XI, 24).

Ask him, therefore, together with me, earnestly and devoutly, to grant you perseverance in his service and continual progress toward better things; and in your bodily illness may he deal with you—according to the most merciful disposition of [Col. 0929C] his grace—as he himself knows to be expedient and salutary for you.

As you pray these things, believe that he will either heal the illness, or relieve it, or bring it to an end through a swift death. For perhaps Satan knows that you will die sooner; therefore he is so importunate that he may deprive you of the good of perseverance. For we know that from the house in which you are, from the Carthusian house, from ours, and from other houses of this purpose, certain men have departed, some of whom died after a few days and others after a few months.

Hear, therefore, the Scripture saying: “Believe God, and he will restore you” (Ecclesiasticus II, 6). And again: “The Lord is good, and a strengthener in the day of tribulation, and he knows those who hope in him” (Nahum I, 7). And this: “Hope in him, and he will act” (Psalm XXXVI, 5). [Col. 0929D] He did not say what he would do, but this was so that we might understand that he will do all the things that will be necessary and salutary [Col. 0930A] for those who hope in him.

Meditating on these and similar things, then, strengthen yourself in the Lord and act manfully. If you cannot fast as much as others, fast as much as you can, knowing with complete certainty that no one can be perfect in any virtue while the vice of gluttony rules him. Believe me, it is not beneficial for your youth to abandon your customary fasts altogether.

Do not therefore prefer the temporary and momentary health of the body to the eternal salvation of the soul. For the Apostle says: “Those who belong to Christ crucify their flesh with its vices and desires” (Galatians V, 24). And the Lord says: “Whoever has not taken up his cross and follows me is not my disciple” (Matthew X, 38; Luke XIV, 27).

As for healing or easing bodily illness, fasting, and absolutely everything that pertains to the Lord’s [Col. 0930B] ordinances, hope in him, and he will act (Psalm XXXVI, 5). For he, as we read in Isaiah, “gives strength to the weary, and to those who have no strength he increases power and might” (Isaiah XL, 29).

Hear, therefore, what the Scripture says: “The one who is slack and negligent in his work is a brother to the one who wastes his own work” (Proverbs XVIII, 9). Do not be useless or remiss in your works. Pursue spiritual things as diligently and devoutly as you can; and pursue bodily matters at their proper time, energetically and as usefully and well as you are able, always invoking divine assistance.

Meditate on these things; occupy yourself with them, lest—God forbid—if the unclean spirit finds you unoccupied, he return to the house from which he departed, taking with him other spirits more wicked than himself, and your last state become worse than the first.

But ask the Lord with the greatest urgency and devotion that you may deserve to be rooted and grounded in love [Col. 0930C]. Once you have obtained this, then, as it is written, “you will run and not be weary; you will walk and not faint” (Isaiah XL, 31).

If you believe that you will see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living, do what follows: “Wait for the Lord; act manfully” (Psalm XXVI, 14), and so forth. If you act in this way, then, strengthened at once by the principal Spirit, you will rejoice while giving thanks to God and will taunt your enemies, saying: “Those who trouble me, my enemies, they themselves were weakened and fell” (ibid., 1). And again: “They were confounded because I hoped” (Job VI, 20).

Giving thanks to God, you will say: “Bless, peoples, our God” (Psalm LXV, 8), and so forth, as far as: “and he has not allowed my foot to be moved” (ibid., 9). You will add the remaining words that follow, up to: “I will repay you my vows, which my lips have distinguished” (ibid., 14). [Col. 0930D]

Farewell, and pray for me. Greet the lord prior for me, and the others by their names.

[Col. 0931]

## Letter of Stephen of Chalmeto, monk of Portes in the Carthusian order, on perseverance in the order, to the novices of Saint-Sulpice of the Cistercian order

*(From a manuscript codex of Saint-Oyend of the Jura, or Saint-Claude.)*

[Col. 0931A]

To my most beloved brothers in Christ, Bonoamicus and his companions at Saint-Sulpice, placed under annual examination, Stephen of Chalmeto sends confirmation by the principal Spirit.

Some of your friends asked me—perhaps considering me more capable than I am—to devote whatever effort I could to strengthening or encouraging you. Therefore, wishing not so much to meet your need as not to fail in charity, I consulted the lord prior. It seemed good to him that this little document should be sent to you in my name.

Thus I am not instructing recruits as a veteran of a completed military service, but, like a soldier still inexperienced in new battles, I am offering things that may serve equally for my own confirmation or exhortation and for yours. We must therefore, both you and I, consider with attentive devotion the works of divine mercy toward us.

First, that he did not shut us into the hands of the enemy, as we deserved, so that—as it is written [Revelation XXII, 11]—those who were filthy might continue to become filthier; but, contrary to our merits, he mercifully and powerfully led us out of the pit of misery and the mire of filth in which we lay.

Next, he granted us such an opportunity to live soberly, justly, and piously. His grace went before us, so that we would not choose whatever was easier and lighter in a spirit of cowardice, but would undertake with constancy that particular way of serving the Lord which, the narrower it is, is the more certain for salvation; the more arduous, the safer; and the more direct for reaching the goal.

For all these things, let us daily offer him, who called us, the thanksgiving that is due, and let us hear the Apostle saying: “We exhort you not to receive the grace of God in vain” (II Corinthians VI, 7). Whoever does not act according to the preparation or opportunity for God’s grace that he has received from God receives God’s grace in vain.

He also receives God’s grace in vain who, having put his hand to the plough, looks back (Luke IX, 62). Such people, as the Lord says, are neither worthy nor fit for the kingdom of God; they have condemnation because they have made their first faith void (I Timothy V, 12).

With great weight and a dreadful proclamation of the divine voice it was said: “Remember Lot’s wife” (Luke XVII, 31). “Do not look back,” the angel said to Lot, “and do not stand anywhere in the surrounding region; save yourself on the mountain” (Genesis XIX, 17).

We who, when divine grace called us, climbed the mountain—that is, took up the arduous and highest path of virtue and justice—for “your justice is like the mountains of God” (Psalm XXXV, 7)—must not descend to the level ground of the region, that is, decline to any easier or less laborious way, lest the fires of Sodom engulf us, or lest, just as Cain killed Abel, the devil kill us.

For Abel was killed in a field. The field is the broad and spacious way that leads to death and destruction. Although Abel’s death was precious in the sight of the Lord, it is nevertheless not inappropriately understood as signifying the destruction of those who undertake nothing arduous or laborious and are killed by the devil in the field—that is, on the broad way of the world.

The Lord therefore says to Moses: “You shall not boil a kid in its mother’s milk” (Deuteronomy XIV, 21). By the name “kid,” sinners are understood. For the kids will stand on the left at the judgment, and in the Law a goat is commanded to be offered for sin (Leviticus XXIII, 19).

But the mother’s milk is the easier teaching of the Church, according to which those who have committed no grave offenses are rightly permitted to live. Therefore, the less we abstain from what is illicit, the more justly we cut ourselves off from what is lawful and belongs to the mother Church’s milk, so that by producing worthy fruits of repentance we may obtain forgiveness and mercy from the Lord.

In accordance, therefore, with the apostolic exhortation, let us see lest there be in any one of us an evil heart of unbelief, causing departure from the living and true God (Hebrews III, 12). Rather, let us exhort one another every day, so that none of us may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin.

If the flatteries suggested by the tempter do not capture us and seduce us; if the things he presents as difficult and intolerable do not frighten and break us; then, with the Lord’s help—for he has become our refuge—we shall easily overcome all the snares of temptation. For those who hope in him will not be weakened, and all who hope in him will not go astray.

He is faithful and will not allow us to be tempted beyond what we can bear. The Apostle says: “You have need of patience, so that, doing the will of God, you may receive the promises” (Hebrews X, 36).

Let us therefore, through patience, run toward the contest set before us (Hebrews XII, 1), considering how much patience and obedience Christ displayed for us, even unto insults and the death of the cross, so that we may not grow weary and fail in spirit.

For it was not said, “the one who begins,” but “the one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew X, 22).

When the experience of our own weakness teaches us how true is that saying of the Lord, “Without me you can do nothing” (John XV, 5), and when his mercy has gone before us, it is certain that he will not withdraw from us the assistance of his grace unless we first withdraw ourselves from him.

Hence the Apostle says in the person of the Lord himself: “My righteous one lives by faith” (Hebrews X, 38). “But if he withdraws himself, my soul will not be pleased.” Immediately, adding in the voice of himself and the elect, the Apostle continues: “But we, brothers, are not children of withdrawal, unto perdition, but of faith, unto the gaining of the soul” (ibid., 39).

By these words he indicated clearly enough, and very terrifyingly, that those who are children of withdrawal are also children of perdition.

But unless we walk with due perseverance in the vocation to which we have been called, then, as the Apostle Peter says: “It would have been better for us not to know the way of justice than, after knowing it, to turn back” (II Peter II, 21).

Hence Solomon also says: “As a dog returns to its vomit, so a fool repeats his folly” (Proverbs XXVI, 11). And again: “A man who wanders from the way of instruction will dwell in the assembly of giants” (Proverbs XXI, 16). Here, by the name “giants,” the proud and alienated from God are signified, whether demons or human beings.

Since some people, when they have come to our purpose or yours, are accustomed to sigh either from ours toward yours or from yours toward ours, let us beware lest the tempter mock us through suggestions of this kind. Let us hear the Apostle saying: “Let each person remain in the calling in which he was called” (I Corinthians VII, 20).

Hence Solomon says: “As a bird migrating from its nest, so is a man who leaves his place” (Proverbs XXVII, 8). And again: “If the spirit of one who has authority rises against you, do not leave your place” (Ecclesiasticus X, 4).

Since, moreover, as iniquity increases, the love of many grows cold, and since some, deceived by the serpent and recoiling from both your purpose and ours, do more harm by scandal than they had done good by example—for they do not fear that frightening and terrible sentence of the Lord’s proclamation: “Woe to the person through whom scandal comes” (Matthew XVIII, 7)—we must take great care that the levity and inconstancy of the few who go back do not disturb us more than the gravity and constancy of the many who persevere strengthen us.

Indeed, just as the perseverance of the good ought to strengthen us, so that we may stand perseveringly and manfully, the apostasy of the wicked ought to make us cautious and watchful, lest we fall and, according to the Lord’s word in the Gospel, our last state become worse than the first (Matthew XII, 45).

For the rest, we must listen with a most faithful ear to the holy Scriptures as they are read, heard, and meditated upon. Whatever we find in them concerning the destruction of pride through humility; the overcoming of anger or impatience through the gentleness of meekness and patience; the driving away of sluggishness and lukewarm negligence through spiritual fervor; the repelling of the envy of jealousy through the grace of kindness; the trampling down of the desire for empty glory through the testimony of conscience; perseverance in prayer; continual guardianship of heart and mouth; acquiring the four virtues—prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice; observing gravity and modesty in walking, silence, conversation, and every condition and action; avoiding the evil of disobedience through submission in sincere obedience; acquiring, with proper pious progress, the good of perseverance; and finally, love, which is the end of all perfection and the fullness of the Law—all this ought to appear before God through daily progress and growth in our conduct and character.

Farewell. Through your intercession I commend myself to your prayers and to those of the entire holy community.

[Col. 0933]

## Letter of Pope Alexander III to Arthaud, prior of Alveria, concerning the schism of that time

*(From the archive of the house of Alveria, of the Carthusian order.)*

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son A., prior of Alveria: greetings and apostolic blessing. “While considering the pious simplicity,” and so forth. *(See this letter among the works of Pope Alexander III.)*

[Col. 0933]

## Appendix

Containing proofs of the matters discussed in the preface to the reader concerning the three Bernards, priors of Portes, and Nanthelmus linked with them.

### I. Rainaldus, recluse of Saint-Ragnibert, around the year of Christ 1134

*(From the archive of Majorieu Carthusian house.)*

[Col. 0933C]

Guido of Aranda abandoned every claim that he had been making against the brothers of Majorieu concerning their pastures, and swore into the hand of Rainaldus, recluse of Saint-Ragnibert, that he would be their faithful helper and friend. For this he received three shillings, twelve coins, and seven denarii. Witnesses: Bernard, prior of Portes; Hugo, procurator of Majorieu; and Donatianus, monk of Saint-Ragnibert.

### II. Bernard of Portes, prior of Portes, formerly bishop of Belley, in the year of Christ 1147

*(From the archive of Majorieu Carthusian house.)*

[Col. 0935A]

Bernard of Portes, called prior of Portes, to his most beloved in Christ, Humbert, prior of Majorieu, and his brothers: greetings and every good.

Let it be known to you that G. of Benuntia approved everything that his father had granted to you in perpetuity on the mountain of Chevillac, at my request, when I was still bishop of Belley. The same Giraldus likewise promised you complete fidelity and protection for all his days, just as his father had promised.

This was done in our church on the day of Saint Thomas the Apostle, in the year of Christ 1147, before our entire community, and before Paul and Anthony *los Forts*, squires, and Peter Moschet of Latinia.

### III. Nanthelmus, bishop of Belley, commonly called Antelmus, in the year of Christ 1164

*(From the archive of Majorieu Carthusian house.)*

For the concord and peace of those who would come later, so that they might live more quietly in silence, the ancients decided to commit their deeds to writing for remembrance.

Therefore let everyone who reads or hears this charter know that I, Nanthelmus, humble bishop of the church of Belley, came to the house of Majorieu on account of certain disputes that had arisen between that house and the knights of Roubemont. Among them peace was restored in the following manner, by God’s gift.

When every complaint had been removed and all resentment and discord had been quieted, Lord William and Lord Garnerius, together with their sons, for themselves and all their living and dead, granted and freely gave to the brothers of Majorieu everything that they or their predecessors had acquired, whether by gift or by purchase, and in which they had been invested on that very day.

Namely, lands and woods, and the use of pasture throughout all the land enclosed within those same pastures; on the condition that they receive no person of any order or religious affiliation to dwell in the aforesaid land, but rather resist with all their power anyone wishing to do so.

The exception is that Lord Garnerius may receive for habitation in the village of Mionz, on that portion which belongs to him, whatever religious persons he wishes—not to devastate the pastures granted to the hermits, except insofar as concerns the village itself. Passage there is not denied even to the livestock of Majorieu.

Furthermore, they took under their protection and custody everything belonging to the brothers of Majorieu. To those going to and returning from the aforesaid house they gave firm security from themselves and their men; and if they had ever inflicted any injury upon the aforesaid brothers, or upon those coming to or returning from them, they humbly asked forgiveness.

Lord William of Roubemont and his sons William and Aimo, Lord Garnerius, and his sons William, Guiffredus, Garnerius, and Gaucerannus faithfully understood, promised, and swore these things into our hand. Their wives also approved the same, although they were unable to come to the hermitage.

These matters were settled at Majorieu, in the lower house, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1164.

Those present with me at this settlement were: William, our chaplain, a monk of Portes; Master Anselm, canon of Belley; Andrew, monk of Saint-Sulpice; and Willencus, a monk.

From Majorieu: Humbert, prior; Hugo, procurator; and the lay brothers Bonfils, Philip Girard, and William.

Secular priests: Vicardus of Balmeto; Jordan and William of Breuno; Humbert of Burco; Dua; and John of Isinana.

The knights: Hugo and Vicardus of Balma; Aalardus of Biliniac; Garnerius of Balmeto; Jordan of Chamberiac; Erardus of Martiniac; and Jordan and Aimo of Enflafol.

Also present were Guido, provost of Belley; Lambert, cleric; and his brother Poncius of Balmeto; and William, furrier of Nantua.

It should be known, moreover, that in exchange for the aforesaid concession and gift, six pounds of Genevan currency were remitted to William of Roubemont. The sons of the aforesaid Lord Garnerius also approved the foregoing in the monks’ assembly and received from it nearly forty Genevan shillings.

### IV. Origin of the castle of Majorieu in the valley of Meria, where the Carthusian house of that name now stands

*(From the archive of Majorieu Carthusian house.)*

Rainaldus, by the grace of God humble minister of the first church of Lyon.

We make known to everyone that we saw and carefully read word for word certain letters, sound, intact, not erased, violated, or corrupted, secured by a very ancient golden seal, whose tenor is as follows:

“Let all present and future know that the emperor Valentinian, in the tenth year of his reign, granted to Majorieu, his chamberlain, whatever he had previously given him in the mountains and valleys near the valley of Helnon, near the valley of Michalia, and near the mountain of Cambes, with every authority, high and low: to build houses, towers, castles, and cities; to enact laws; to mint his own coins; and to act as though he were emperor.

“For he preferred to have his right eye blinded rather than to hand over the key of the emperor’s chamber to the enemy Arbogast.

“At Isernori, on the Kalends of April.”

On the back, however, the following had been written:

“Majorieu built the city of Balmeto, from which he took his name, and the castle called Majorieu after his own name in the valley of Meria. The valley was so called from the trunks of trees that had been uprooted, for the suppression of the brigandage of the wicked and savage Jovinus Popa of the temple of Montisaegrum.

“Majorieu begot Ginioldus of Balmeto; after thirty-seven descendants directly descended from him, Ginioldus begot Pontius. Pontius begot Ritboldus, and Ritboldus begot Nortboldus.

“At the request of Aimo, squire of Balmeto, we caused this present copy to be sealed with our seal, as agreeing with the original.

“Witnesses were William of Cologne; Albo of Golden Mountain; G., penitentiary; and Le., seneschal of the refectory.

“Given in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1213, in April, with the seal of the same pontiff.”

## In the year of the Lord 1200: Saint Hugh, bishop of Lincoln in England, of the Carthusian order

[Col. 0937]

## The Life of Hugh, written in five books by Alexander, apparently a monk and later abbot of the monastery of Saint Augustine, Canterbury

*(Edited by the Reverend Father Bernard Pezius, Bibliotheca ascetica, vol. X.)*

### Notice

As soon as the Most Reverend and Most Illustrious Prince of the Holy Roman Empire and Bishop of Passau, Joseph, Count of Lamberg, saw this work in the renowned library of the Carthusian house of Gaming in Austria, he immediately judged it highly worthy of publication. This is not surprising. For that most devout prelate at once recognized in it the image of his own soul, as well as that of our German Altmannus. Inspired by the encouragement of so great a prelate, the venerable and universally learned vicar of that celebrated place, the most Reverend and illustrious Father Leopold Widemann—already known throughout Europe for more than one reason—soon set himself to extracting these books from an old codex of his library, and, having furnished them with most learned notes and observations, generously and affectionately entrusted them to me for publication in print.

This Life resembles a broad and most delightful meadow from which not only private ascetics and those devoted to Christian piety, but also prelates of the Churches, may gather little flowers of every kind of virtue. From it the latter will easily learn how much strength and courage can be brought to the soul—even against the most powerful—by contempt for the empty things of the world and by a mind conformed to divine principles.

The customs of our own age do not permit us to review here in greater detail all the individual examples of this kind found in the great Hugh. Those who are interested in French and English history will learn from this work many things about the affairs of Henry II, John, and the other princes of both kingdoms that are found nowhere else. But it is scarcely appropriate to say more about these matters here.

The work derives considerable authority from the fact that its author indicates in several places that he was not only a contemporary of Saint Hugh but also his intimate companion (see Book I, chapter 9, and Book V, chapters 2, 20, 23, and 24). It is also clear from this that he had been the holy bishop’s chaplain.

He himself should be heard in the prologue to Book II, col. 961:

“When Hugh had administered the bishopric of the Church of Lincoln for twelve years and fifty-three days with the greatest religious devotion, it pleased his holiness to take my humble self from the sweetness of cloistered life as some sort of solace amid his anxieties, and to associate me inseparably at his side. From that time I was never absent from his company, except for one single night, for the three years and five days during which he afterward lived in the body; day and night I was always attached to him and ministered to him personally.

“Throughout this period, therefore, almost everything that this little book will contain about him I either saw with my own eyes or heard from his holy lips.”

Moreover, it is plainly established from the prologues of Books I and II, as well as from Book V, chapter 23 (see note 343 there), and from chapters 12 and 22 of the same book, that the author of this Life of Saint Hugh—of which we here present an epitome made by another Carthusian, though its original phrasing has been preserved—was a Benedictine monk, specifically of the monastery of Saint Augustine at Canterbury. These points are beyond dispute. Only his personal name can be questioned, because in the original and more extensive Life, according to Molanus in his Notes on Usuard’s Martyrology under 17 November, he expressed his name only in this fashion: “To the lords and friends most dear in Christ, Q., the prior, and the monks of Witham who are with him, the least of brothers, A.” Nor is the abbreviated version that we present here identified differently by its abbreviator, as is clear from the abbreviator’s prologue.

Theodore Petreius, in the Carthusian Library, while expressing some doubt, calls the writer of the Life of Saint Hugh, bishop of Lincoln, Adam; the abbot Morotius does likewise. But since they wish this Adam to have flourished around the year 1340, it is manifestly impossible that he was Brother A., the author of the great original Life epitomized here, since that author testifies that he transmitted what he had himself seen with his own eyes or heard from the lips of the most holy bishop, and indeed that he had remained constantly with him for more than three years, as we saw in the preceding section. The author of this abbreviated version, however, may have been Adam, a Carthusian theologian who must have flourished around 1340, the date assigned to him by Morotius. For in a parchment codex of the Carthusian house at Gembloux there is another extensive abbreviation of Hugh’s Life, bearing this title: “Here begins the second abbreviation of the Life of Saint Hugh, bishop of Lincoln. Thus Hugh, born of noble and religious parents, etc.” Since this second abbreviation, written in a fourteenth-century hand, exists in the aforementioned Gembloux codex, the first abbreviation cannot belong to a later century.

So much concerning the author of the abbreviation of the great Life of Saint Hugh. How faithfully and carefully he reduced that larger work to an epitome, he himself explains sufficiently in the preface to Book I, and the distinguished Father Leopold has accurately observed it in his Notes. Yet it must certainly be admitted that this abbreviator would have deserved more from posterity if, after removing only the moral digressions and commonplaces, he had preserved for us the preface of Brother A. to Book I, together with everything else—even if little of it—which nevertheless sheds some light on the history. But we must return to Brother A., the principal author of the great Life of Hugh, and consider who probably lies concealed under this initial, the first letter of his name.

I have always thought it extremely likely that this Brother A. was none other than Alexander, “an Englishman by nation, a monk by profession, of the Order of Saint Benedict at Canterbury, and eventually abbot there in the monastery of Saint Augustine,” as John Pits reports in *On the Illustrious Writers of England* under the year 1217, p. 287. There he also records the following about Alexander:

“He was endowed with a fortunate intellect, and, as they say, from almost the tenderest age had received careful training in the liberal arts; he grew into a most learned man. When he had attained eminent erudition, he was also found to possess sound judgment, mature prudence, remarkable skill in practical affairs, great devotion toward God, and charity toward his neighbor. By the unanimous agreement of his brethren he was considered worthy to be placed over the entire community.”

Anyone who has examined even one or two of Alexander’s books among us will soon discover that these characteristics of mind and spirit attributed to him by Pits correspond admirably with Brother A., the author of the principal Life of Saint Hugh. Almost every page of that work displays notable signs of learning, prudence, judgment, and integrity for his age.

Pits continues concerning Alexander:

“When he had conducted himself vigorously and prudently for several years in this office—that of abbot—and the fame of his virtues had reached the ears of King John himself, the king consulted him concerning the disputes which at that time he was having, with great seriousness, with the supreme pontiff. Alexander encouraged the king to hope for a favorable outcome, repeatedly asserting that the whole matter could be settled. When the king discovered that the man was somewhat inclined to his side, in the year of the Lord 1206 he sent him as ambassador to Rome concerning this affair. In that embassy he declared himself so openly to be on the king’s side, and clung to him so faithfully in everything, that he incurred the great hatred of the opposing party. Consequently, in the course of time, after the king’s death, he was excommunicated by Pandulf, the legate of the supreme pontiff in England, and deprived of every ecclesiastical benefice, office, and function. Thus, they say, he ended his life in poverty and misery.”

Thus far Pits concerning Alexander. At the place cited he also compiled a catalogue of his other literary monuments, and adds that “he is said to have lived until the year of Christ 1217, when Henry III happily began his reign in England.”

These facts provide fresh support for our conjecture that Alexander was the author of the great Life of Hugh. For it is clear from Book I, chapter 9, that he lived not only until 1217 but even until 1220, since there he reports that Hugh was canonized by the pope, an event which, according to Raynaldus, certainly occurred in that year under Honorius III. If anyone regards this passage as suspect and thinks it may be a gloss by the abbreviator, it is at least clear from the prologue to Book V that the author was still alive and writing in 1212, the fourteenth year of King John of England, precisely the year in which he there testifies that he was writing. See the notes of the most learned Wydemann on this passage.

Thus, since his age, learning, and initial all fit Alexander, the monk and abbot of Saint Augustine’s at Canterbury, and since no other distinguished writer of that monastery at that time is known whose name began with A., it scarcely seems possible to doubt any longer that Brother A., the author of the great Life of Hugh, was the same person as Alexander. But concerning Brother A.—whose complete work Lawrence Surius undoubtedly saw and reduced in his own style to another epitome—enough has now been said.

# Dissertation on the Year in Which Saint Hugh Was Consecrated Bishop of Lincoln

[Col. 0939]

It is the unanimous opinion of writers that Saint Hugh was consecrated bishop of Lincoln on the feast of Saint Matthew the Apostle and Evangelist, and that he died in the year 1200, on 16 or 17 November. But they do not all agree about the year in which that consecration took place. Baronius, Raynaldus, and Antonius Pagius in his criticism of Baronius, following Roger and Matthew Paris, maintain that Hugh was consecrated in 1186. There would be little dispute about that year were it not that the author of the Life presented here, and with him Lawrence Surius, provide grounds for doubt.

Although the author of the Life nowhere mentions the aforesaid year, nor definitely any other year of the consecration, it can nevertheless be clearly inferred from various passages, which will be brought forward shortly, that he favored 1185 rather than the following year. Surius himself does not state the year in the text. But when he adds together the years and days given by the author of the Life in the prologue to Book II, he correctly writes: “Hugh occupied the episcopal see for fifteen years and fifty-eight days.” The years and days mentioned by the author in the prologue, and calculated by Surius, amount precisely to that total. If they are counted backward from 16 November, the day on which Saint Hugh died in 1200, it is necessary that he was consecrated in 1185, not in the following year.

Raynaldus, volume XIII of the *Annals*, p. 48, thinks that the text suffers from an error in the number of years and supposes that “fourteen” should be read in place of “fifteen.” But no error entered the Acts as published by Surius, unless perhaps one was committed by the principal author before Surius—an error scarcely credible. I would attribute to the author at least as much, if not more, credibility than is granted to Roger or Paris. He was familiar with Saint Hugh for more than three years and, as is clear from our notes and observations, performed the duties of a careful historian. Roger, although he was nearly contemporary—for according to Oudinus, volume III of the *History of Ecclesiastical Writers*, col. 96, he died in 1237—nevertheless did not live with the saint, nor did he compose his life with particular diligence. Paris, later than Roger, transferred much from him into his own history, as Oudinus likewise reports in the cited place, col. 211.

These points having been established, we must now produce the passages from this very Life which show that Saint Hugh was consecrated bishop precisely in 1185.

## I

In the prologue to Book II, the author of Saint Hugh’s Life acknowledges that Hugh had been a bishop for “twelve years and fifty-three days” before the author came to him. He adds that from that time he had been absent from Hugh’s company for “three years and five days,” except for one single night, for as long as Hugh thereafter lived. These years, together with the days, amount to fifteen years and fifty-eight days; counted backward, they lead us to 1185 and prove that Hugh became a bishop in that year, as is evident to anyone who considers the passage.

## II

In Book V, chapter 7, we read:

“Thus far, for nearly thirteen years, I have not departed from the upright footsteps of my predecessors.”

And:

“Meanwhile the period extends from the feast of Saint Nicholas almost to the Kalends of September.”

And again:

“On the day of the outstanding doctor Saint Augustine, he immediately greeted him”—that is, Hugh greeted the king.

Before these statements, in the same chapter, the following is prefaced:

“One year and almost four months before his death, King Richard of the English burned with fierce anger against him—Hugh—for the following reason.”

We shall now see how the year 1185 is to be deduced from these statements.

Richard, king of England, died, as everyone acknowledges, in 1199, on 6 April. From the feast of Saint Nicholas, that is, 6 December 1197, to April 1199, one year and four months elapsed—the period from which the king is said to have burned with fierce anger against Hugh. Meanwhile, the period from the aforementioned feast of Saint Nicholas in 1197 extended almost to the Kalends of September 1198, that is, to the feast of Saint Augustine, which falls not far from the Kalends of September. On that feast Hugh greeted the king as he listened to the solemn Mass, and asked him for and received a kiss.

If, therefore, Saint Hugh had been consecrated bishop in 1186, on the feast of Saint Matthew, as the learned men cited above maintain, he would certainly not have completed his twelfth episcopal year on Saint Nicholas’s day in 1197, nor even on Saint Augustine’s day in 1198; still less would he have begun his thirteenth. But if he became bishop in 1185 on the aforesaid feast, then by Saint Nicholas’s day in 1197 he had begun his thirteenth year more than two months earlier, and by Saint Augustine’s day in 1198 he had almost completed it, lacking only one incomplete month.

## III

In Book V, chapter 12, there is an account of a woman deceived by a demon and freed through the prayers of Saint Hugh. This liberation either took place while Hugh was still prior at Witham, or shortly after he had been consecrated bishop.

The first possibility conflicts with the author’s intention, both because of the words “After the bishops had departed from one another,” and because of the statement, “And this the bishop of Oxford reported to our bishop.” The second possibility depends on the year in which Bartholomew, bishop of Oxford, died. That he did not survive into 1186 is clear from Trivet’s Chronicle, in Acherius, volume III of the *Spicilegium*, p. 165 of the new edition. Under that year we read: “John, cantor of Exeter, was made bishop of that same Church.” If John became bishop in that year, Bartholomew had either already died or had resigned the bishopric. That Bartholomew died in that year is attested by the Winchester Annals in Part I of *Anglia Sacra*, p. 302, in these exact words: “In the year 1186 Bartholomew, bishop of Exeter, died.” Learned men will certainly judge this evidence more trustworthy than Oudinus, who, while expressing doubt about the matter, assigns his death to 1185.

Perhaps Bartholomew died in the final days of 1185, or before 25 March 1186. Hence a slight disagreement about the year may have arisen, since some formerly began the year at Christmas, others on 1 January, and others at Easter. Let us therefore suppose that Bartholomew died either after Christmas, in the final days of 1185, or before 25 March 1186 according to the present reckoning. In that case Oudinus can indeed be reconciled with the Winchester Annals.

But from the history narrated here we have a clear basis for proving that Hugh was consecrated bishop not in 1186 but in 1185. Bartholomew could have attended the consecration held in 1185, reported the woman’s case to Hugh at that time, and, after some time had passed, added the account of the rescue of the unfortunate woman. He could in no way have been present and reported the case to Hugh already as bishop if Hugh had first been consecrated in 1186, because, as we saw from Trivet, John had already become bishop of Oxford in that same year, having previously been cantor, and Bartholomew, his predecessor, must already have died.

## IV

In Book III, chapter 1, concerning the vacancy of the see of Lincoln, we read:

“Shortly before, that most distinguished see had been vacant for approximately eighteen years—namely, two and a half years after the translation of the aforementioned bishop Walter, and fifteen years before that bishop’s consecration.”

To derive the year 1185 from this passage as well, several preliminary points must be made.

First, the period of the vacancy must be reckoned from the year in which Robert, bishop of Lincoln, died, up to the year in which Saint Hugh succeeded him in that bishopric.

Second, Robert must have died either after Christmas in 1166 or at least before 25 March 1167, so that the Winchester Annals, which assign his death to 1166, may be reconciled with Trivet, according to whom he died in 1167.

Third, Geoffrey, who was bishop of Lincoln in name alone in 1181, as Baronius holds under that year, was ordered by the Apostolic See either to seek to obtain the office of blessing or to resign the bishopric.

Fourth, Geoffrey actually resigned, and did so into the hands of Richard, archbishop of Canterbury, “in 1182 on the Epiphany of the Lord,” as Wharton attests in Part I of *Anglia Sacra*, p. 73, in the notes.

Fifth, although it is not certain, it is nevertheless probable that when Geoffrey’s resignation was being discussed, Walter’s promotion to the bishopric of Lincoln was also under consideration, and that he was consecrated in that year, perhaps even in the month in which Geoffrey resigned, so that the see, which had already been vacant for so long, might not remain vacant any longer.

Sixth, Walter presided over the bishopric of Lincoln for scarcely one complete year, since Giraldus of Wales, his contemporary, says that he was bishop there for one year.

Seventh, according to the Rouen Chronicle, published by Labbe in volume I of the *New Bibliotheca*, Archbishop Rotrodus died in 1183 and Walter succeeded him; but the month in which the former died or the latter succeeded is not given.

With these points established, let us now suppose that Robert of Lincoln died, if not in 1166, as the Winchester Annals maintain, at least before 25 March of the following year. Accordingly, the fifteen years during which, according to the author of Saint Hugh’s Life, that distinguished see was vacant before Walter’s consecration had elapsed, if not at the end of 1181, certainly before the corresponding date in 1182.

To these fifteen years let us add one year—not to be counted as part of the vacancy—in which Walter, according to the Welsh historian, governed the see of Lincoln. To these sixteen years let us also add two and a half years during which, after Walter’s translation, the see again remained vacant. These years together amount to eighteen years and six months; and, if counted from 21 March 1167, they are completed precisely on 21 September 1185.

But if we wish to begin the calculation from that date and year up to 21 September 1186, we shall find nineteen years and six months, and shall be forced to assign the entire two years to Walter’s episcopate at Lincoln. This would contradict Giraldus, who, as noted above, says that he was bishop there for only one year. Indeed, Walter would have to be assigned more than two years if Robert had died either in 1166 or in January 1167. This argument therefore supports 1185 much more strongly than the following year, and agrees with the years which the author of the Life counted either before Walter’s consecration or after his translation.

Meanwhile, a difficulty arises concerning the year and month from which the two and a half years during which, according to the author of the Life, the see of Lincoln was vacant after Walter’s translation should be reckoned. In the Rouen Chronicle cited above, under the year 1185, we find this statement: “In this year Walter was received, etc., as archbishop of Rouen on the feast of Blessed Matthias.”

If that two-and-a-half-year period of vacancy had to be reckoned from the feast of Saint Matthias in 1185, we would be forced to assert that Hugh first became bishop in 1187, which is universally contradicted. Therefore that period must be reckoned not from Walter’s reception on the feast of Saint Matthias, but from the king’s nomination, which could have taken place immediately after Rotrodus’s death. Rotrodus may have died in the first months of 1183, although the reception of his successor was delayed by other obstacles. In this way we are correctly brought to the year 1185.

That Walter could have been nominated by the king in 1183, around March, may be inferred from the fact that Geoffrey resigned on the Epiphany in 1182, that Walter succeeded him but was bishop of Lincoln for only one year, and that Rotrodus died in 1183, though in an uncertain month. Since Walter was therefore transferred from Lincoln to Rouen, according to Giraldus, so that he might be nearer to the king in councils and difficult affairs, this may have been the reason why the king nominated him archbishop not long after Rotrodus’s death.

These four arguments lead me to believe that, according to the intention of the author of the Life, Saint Hugh was consecrated bishop of Lincoln in 1185, on the feast of Saint Matthew.
