The first and second arguments for this year are sufficiently clear and evident, and the third is no less weighty, since Bartholomew of Oxford died in 1186 according to the Winchester Annals, and John succeeded him in the same year according to Trivet. The fourth argument, however, depends on many circumstances, which may be either true or false; it is therefore submitted to the judgment and examination of the learned reader.

Furthermore, I do not see what can be set against our opinion in favor of 1185 from this Life itself. The only difficulty is raised by Trivet, who writes under that year:

“The king of the English, crossing the sea, celebrated Easter at Rouen.”

And again:

“The king of the French visited the king of the English, who had been struck by illness, on 12 November.”

Finally, under the year 1186:

“The king of the English, crossing into England together with the queen, landed at the port of Southampton on 27 April.”

If, therefore, the king remained in Normandy for an entire year, it does not seem that the events narrated in Book III, chapter 1 of this Life as having taken place in England could have occurred in 1185.

Yet it is scarcely credible that the king remained outside England for the entire year. He could have celebrated Easter at Rouen in 1185; after celebrating it, returned to England in May, supported Hugh’s election, and, after Hugh’s consecration, returned to Normandy, where he fell ill, was visited by the king of the French, and finally returned to England in the following year. On this assumption, the clouds which Trivet seemed to raise against our opinion and against the author of the present Life disappear.

Still lighter is the objection that might perhaps be raised against 1185: namely, that in that year the feast of Saint Matthew, on which Saint Hugh was consecrated according to everyone, fell on a Saturday, whereas in the following year it fell on a Sunday, the day appointed for the consecration of bishops. For, apart from the fact that neither the author of the Life, nor Roger, nor Paris, nor anyone else asserts that Saint Hugh received the episcopal consecration on a Sunday, it seems beyond dispute that episcopal consecrations could also take place on the feasts of the apostles. But enough on this subject.

# The Life of Saint Hugh, Bishop of Lincoln in England, of the Carthusian Order, Written in Five Books

[Col. 0943]

# Prologue to the Abbreviation of the Life of Hugh, Bishop of Lincoln

Having examined the sequence of the description of the Life of Blessed Hugh, composed by Brother A., who is explicitly mentioned in the greeting before the prologue, it was found to contain expansions of language which the aforesaid brother added for ornament and edification, although they are not essential to the substance of the events. Various digressions are also inserted in which the lives of persons other than our Hugh are described. Moreover, matters less significant, though connected with our Hugh, are interspersed—things which, to avoid excessive length, seem better omitted.

Indeed, this previously mentioned prolixity is thought to have been the reason why the book containing the aforesaid account has hitherto been read and heard with less eagerness. Therefore, for the honor of the saint and to remove the weariness of both reader and hearer, it seemed to me highly expedient to insert into the present volume, in a shorter compilation, those matters concerning the life and conduct of the saint in question which were found to be more noteworthy. I have included nothing in this volume except what was taken from the aforesaid account.

This abbreviated volume is divided into five little books, just as the book containing the larger account mentioned above is divided. The first treats of the life and conduct of our glorious Hugh, from his childhood until his migration to England. The second concerns his migration and his deeds while governing the house at Witham before his episcopate. The third explains how he was made bishop and how vigorously he began to exercise the episcopal office. The fourth and fifth add accounts of many of his praiseworthy deeds, both miraculous and otherwise.

There appears to be no other reason for distinguishing these little books from one another, and from the third, than that the distinction itself might lessen the weariness of reading and hearing, which would be greater if three books were contained in one. The prologues, however, are placed before each little book here word for word, just as in the larger volume mentioned above. The order of some chapters is not preserved. Nor are all the chapters inserted, since some have been removed, and certain contents found under particular chapters have been transferred to other chapters.

[Col. 0943] Here ends the abbreviator’s prologue.

# Book One

[Col. 0945]

## Chapter One  
### How Hugh, deprived of the comfort of his mother and joined with his father to a regular community of clerics, bore the yoke of the Lord from infancy; and words of his own concerning his childhood education are inserted

Hugh [Note: [Col. 0945D] From the lineage of Avalim. Hence Book II, chapter 1: “Though illustrious by birth, he is said to have been far more illustrious through the excellence of his character, Hugh of Avalim by name.” And Abbot Morotius, in the *Theatre of the Carthusians*: “Hugh was a nobleman of Dauphiné, whose father was lord of the town commonly called Avalon, three miles distant from the city of Grenoble.”] was deprived of the comfort of his mother before he had yet passed the limits of childhood, and shortly afterward was joined, together with his father, to a community of regular clerics.

He was nearly eight years old when he entered the novitiate of spiritual warfare. Through the diligence of his good father, who watched over him beneficially, he was taught to serve God before he had learned to live for the world. Thus the tutor’s lashes touched his childish body; thus the fetters of discipline restrained his youthful movements, so that he overcame vices by virtues, and his entire life, from its beginning to its end, became one continuous martyrdom.

He himself often related the following about himself when speaking familiarly with his companions:

“Indeed,” he said, “I never touched the joys of this world, never learned its games, and never knew how to play. When I had entered childhood and had already learned the first elements of letters, my father divided his patrimony among his children by allotment; but the portion that fell to me, the smallest among the brothers, he gave to the community of regular clerics.”

[Note: [Col. 0945D] At least to William and Peter, who are praised in Book III, chapter 13, and Book IV, chapter 4.]

[Note: [Col. 0945D] To the clerics of the canonical profession. Hence it is clear that Hugh was initially a regular canon. The text immediately adds: “Senior among the canons of that place.”]

Without lingering, he completely rejected everything belonging to the world. He was about to enter Christ’s soldiery, and, though already a veteran in worldly matters, suddenly became a recruit in the heavenly camp. He assumed the garment of the regular life, whose spirit he had long possessed, and, grieving from the depths of his being that he had not been granted the opportunity to leave the world at its very entrance, he readily persuaded me—who knew nothing of the things of the world—to become with him a companion of the spiritual life.

[Note: [Col. 0946D] Thus the father surrendered himself together with his son to the community mentioned above, not after him, as some assert.]

There is a church [Note: [Col. 0946D] Named Villa Benedicta, commonly Vilar Beneith. There Hugh, as is related in Book V, chapter 22, tasted the first beginnings of the sacred life; and he also gave it a library, as is mentioned there.] in the territory of Grenoble that supports clerics of the canonical profession, numbering at least seven.

[Note: [Col. 0946D] The number seems to be corrupt, and “seventeen” should be read.]

The place itself, together with its inhabitants, is also subject to the mother and cathedral church of Grenoble. My father had always cherished it with particular affection; it bordered on his castles [Note: [Col. 0946D] Among these was the castle of Avalim, “whose stronghold,” Hugh says in Book III, chapter 13, “our brother William is known to hold.”] and lands. As a devoted son, he rejoiced to embrace the favor of the greater church through reverence for its daughter. Among the canons of that place there was a certain man, highly distinguished for religious observance and also regarded as superior to the others in learning.

[Col. 0946A] The children of noble families were eagerly entrusted to him by their parents, to be instructed both in secular and ecclesiastical letters and also trained in moral discipline. From the very beginnings of my education he impressed sacred learning upon me with the greatest care. By whatever encouragements and admonitions he could use, he strove to kindle my tender mind with love for a sounder and spiritual doctrine. He diverted my attention from the vanity of playing and joking by various methods, involving me in honorable exercises of every kind.

When boys of my own age and companions were frequently playing according to custom, he gently instilled in me these exhortations of paternal affection:

“Do not let the foolish and wandering frivolity of your companions allure you, my dearest son. Leave them alone. The pursuits of such boys are not suited to your lot.”

He would also add:

“Hughlet, Hughlet, I am raising you for Christ; it is not your role to play.”

## Chapter Two  
### On his progress in knowledge and virtue, and how devoted and diligent he was in divine offices and in serving his brethren

When he had reached the time of puberty, with adolescence dividing the middle years of his life, no pen could easily describe how much discretion and knowledge, how much virtue and grace, the fountain of life whom he thirsted for poured into him.

At that time he flourished with great sharpness of intellect and learned more quickly whatever he wished. He rejoiced in the vast storehouses of his memory, where he could deposit whatever he had learned so that it would not be lost to forgetfulness. Yet these natural gifts would have been of no importance had the addition of grace not both suggested excellent things to be learned and, by extending them, increased more abundantly what it had suggested. Swarms of blessed meditations seethed in his breast; the fragrances of heavenly joys burned within him.

Meanwhile, he began to attend the divine offices with such diligence and to serve his brethren with such care that in both matters he devoted nothing less than his whole self. Neither forgetfulness nor any occupation could ever steal anything from his diligence, so that he would not remember to render to God the things that belonged to God, and to his neighbors the things that belonged to his neighbors, without omission or offense, as was appropriate to him according to time and place.

Nor did he strive merely to perform the duties assigned to him. Rather, he believed that everything which, as his conscience testified, he could provide for anyone’s benefit or relief was demanded of him as though it had been specially assigned to him.

[Col. 0947A] Finally, when the brethren who had known him at that time repeatedly recounted such things about him in his presence, when he was already bishop, and I too was present, he said:

“Certainly, after I entered the Carthusian order, I do not know whether even once there crept into me any delay in carrying out some duty that I ought to fulfill.”

Among monks, the term *morantia* is commonly used when someone omits the task assigned to him—reading, singing, or serving—and consequently the regular function suffers delay.

He said these things about himself not boastfully but firmly:

“When, during the dedications of churches, the celebrations of ordinations, or any of the daily or nightly offices, some delay arose through the carelessness of ministers, singers, or readers, wishing to rebuke such negligence in his brethren, he would point out to them that they ought to take from his own conduct an example of diligence in the divine offices.”

This diligence continued in him to the end, astonishing to all who knew him and easier to admire than to imitate. Never could the present disturbance of a noisy crowd, the complications of any past or present dispute, or any other circumstance of that kind arising from whatever source steal upon him in such a way that he did not always have ready in his heart or on his lips whatever, at the proper time and hour, had to be performed either at the altar or in any other ministerial duty.

## Chapter Three  
### On the praise of his father, and how humbly and devotedly our Hugh served him, being specially assigned to his service

[Col. 0947C]

To continue the sequence of the narrative we have begun, when Hugh had reached adulthood, his father began to be afflicted by frequent ailments of extreme old age.

[Note: [Col. 0947C] Hugh was nearly eight years old when he entered the novitiate of spiritual warfare, and at that time, as was reported in chapter 1, his father assumed the garment of the regular life. Since Hugh, when already grown, served him during his illnesses, his father must have lived in the religious life for several years.]

His father had won such a crown of virtue in both forms of service—first in worldly warfare and afterward in spiritual warfare—that nothing was more pleasing to his fellow soldiers than to offer him agreeable companionship in every respect. He had been a man of singular moderation, gentle and honorable in conduct, vigorous in courtesy, and most welcome for his kindness.

Accordingly, Hugh, who devoted himself to all the brethren with filial dedication and all his strength, was specially commanded by his prior to serve his father above all others and more particularly in whatever he needed.

“For you will offer neither to me nor to the other brothers anything more welcome than to deny no desired service to so distinguished a man. Among the brothers no one is more devoted than you, nor more inclined to humility, nor more prompt in helpfulness. To no one could we more gratefully entrust the care of this man.”

The pious youth gladly accepted the command and carried it out still more gladly, serving the needs of his bodily and indeed spiritual parent. Through that father, he rejoiced that he had been begotten and offered to God, rather than previously begotten for the world.

You would now have seen him—he who had won the greater favor of all through his service to each of the brethren—pleasing everyone above all by surpassing each of them in his attentiveness to his father’s needs. Whatever all and each of them would have preferred to provide for that most vigorous man, he alone fulfilled on behalf of them all.

He himself often recounted this with gratitude: thereafter, for as long as his father lived, he led him, carried him, covered him with clothes and shoes, undressed him, washed him, wiped him, made his bed, prepared food for him in his weakness, and, once it had been prepared, fed the debilitated man himself.

These and similar services were sweeter to him when he performed them than honey is to one eating it, or any spices to one intensely thirsty. A thousand times over, for each of these acts, he received blessings from his father’s mouth, and he drank them eagerly into his thirsting heart. For he knew that the blessings of fathers establish the houses of their children. Indeed, since the Lord was going to give him the blessings of all nations, He went before him with blessings of sweetness, displaying him to everyone as sweet, lovable, and worthy of blessing.

[Note: [Col. 0947D] His father therefore died before Hugh’s withdrawal to the Carthusian order, not afterward, as some imply.]

## Chapter Four  
### How, after being ordained a Levite, he immediately instructed the people through his zeal for preaching, received the cell of Saint Maximus to govern, and governed it commendably; and under this heading the fifth chapter of the Great Life is included

[Note: [Col. 0947D] From the title of this and certain other chapters it is clear that the abbreviator shortened some material, retaining the author’s words but cutting out what he considered superfluous.]

But when he had already entered his nineteenth year [Note: [Col. 0947D] If Hugh died in 1200, as Surius testifies, already sixty years old, he seems to have been born around 1140 and ordained a levite in 1158 or the following year.], at the request of the entire community of brothers, he was compelled, through the venerable bishop of Grenoble, to ascend, [Col. 0949A] against his will, to the levitical order [Note: [Col. 0947D] This was Gaufridus, formerly a Carthusian and at that time bishop there. He is also the man of whom the following is read in the acts of Saint Anthelm in the Bollandists: “Anthelm, together with his associate Gaufredus, a man of outstanding eloquence and highly learned in the Scriptures,” etc. The abbot Morotius likewise celebrates him: “Godefridus, bishop of Grenoble, formerly the colleague of the aforementioned Othmarus in the parent house of this institution—the Carthusian order—received him, when he was yielding to fate, into pastoral care. In the Grenoble archives there is an imperial charter of Frederick dated 1161, in which he is distinguished by the title of prince. What sort and how great a man Godefridus was may be recognized from the anonymous author of the Life of Saint Anthelm, bishop of Belley, who raises him up with this eulogy: ‘The Carthusian order, first before all others in the Western Church, as is sufficiently evident, confirmed that Alexander should be regarded as the Catholic and true pontiff, and that obedience should be rendered to him. But who was the author of this action? Surely Anthelm, and with him Gaufredus, a wise man of outstanding eloquence and most learned in the divine Scriptures.’ He is also mentioned in the list of pastors of this flock published by Jean Chenu, Claude Robert, and Scaevola and Louis Sammarthanus.” Morotius wrote this in the third part of his *Theatrum Ordinis Cartusiensis*, published at Turin in 1681. In his annotations on the Life of Saint Anthelm, p. 234, Henschenius writes: “Elsewhere we are astonished to find no mention whatsoever of this Gaufredus.” [Col. 0949D] Taking this occasion, in addition to Abbot Morotius’s eulogy, I add a testimony extracted from thirteenth-century manuscripts and statutes, which reads as follows: “For the tenor and confirmation of our entire purpose, I, Basil, called prior of the Carthusian house, and our other brothers, with one mind and one voice, commit our house to be corrected by the common chapter, while preserving the constitutions which we now religiously observe in writing or by custom. For the same tenor of our purpose, B. of Portes, the prior, promised obedience to the common chapter on behalf of himself and his house. The other priors likewise made the same promise, each in his proper order. Furthermore, for confirmation of the aforesaid chapter of the Carthusian house, the lord Gotfredus, bishop of Grenoble, sent a letter containing the following: ‘I, G., by the grace of God bishop of Grenoble, at the request of B., prior of the Carthusian house, and of the other brothers serving God there, grant that the aforesaid house is to be corrected by the common chapter, as has been decreed by the general council of the whole order through episcopal authority, and that it is to be preserved forever in the Carthusian purpose. We further decree that, if the aforesaid house should ever attempt to transfer itself from its purpose to another purpose—which God forbid—or if the prior, or any person belonging to that house, or even the whole house, should refuse to obey the aforesaid chapter, it shall be subject to the sentence of excommunication, both ours and that of the entire chapter.’”]. He soon began, with zeal for holy preaching, to instruct the people and to stir more earnestly toward love of the heavenly homeland the hearts that lay sluggish. He publicly rebuked sinners before everyone. All indeed rejoiced in the words of grace that proceeded from his mouth; but above all, his own prior, a religious and devout man who had educated him and loved him as his own soul. Seeing his pupil elevated by the sublimity of his life and by his word of glory, he himself also strove to raise him still higher.

Accordingly, he entrusted to him the governance of a nearby cell called Saint Maximus, because its basilica had been consecrated to Saint Maximus, the noble patron of that place. Hugh accepted it almost entirely empty of necessary resources [Col. 0949B]—for it was not lawful for one devoted to obedience to refuse obedience—and within a short time filled it abundantly with good things. The little possessions of the place itself scarcely seemed sufficient to support even a single respectable inhabitant with a small household. But Hugh, knowing that two are better together than one, did not wish to be alone, lest it should someday be said to him: “Woe to the one who is alone, because if he falls, he has no one to lift him up” (Ecclesiastes 4:6). Knowing also, according to the judgment of a most learned man, “that just as the companionship of a younger person is more pleasant, so that of an older person is safer,” he took as his companion a fellow canon, venerable in years and character. Entrusting the care of the fields and vineyards to conscientious peasants, he himself devoted his time to reading and prayer. It came about that within a short time the place, together with its inhabitants, enriched by the resources of their goods and the merits of their conduct, acquired a celebrated reputation for goodness throughout the surrounding region. He and those who were with him, living soberly, devoutly, and justly amid their abundance, supplied nourishment to the needy while showing honor to the rich. With zeal for sacred exhortation, he instructed not only the parishioners of his little church but also the crowds who came from every direction to hear the word of God, earnestly warning each person, according to the condition of his station, to show himself blameless in following Catholic tradition and a devout way of life in every respect.

## CHAPTER V. How he carried out the Gospel command, “If your brother sins against you,” in the case of a certain parishioner of the said cell who had been publicly accused of the sin of adultery

[Note: [Col. 0950D] Of the events narrated in this chapter, nothing is found in Surius except the following brief notice: “He was entrusted with the administration of a certain parish, which he discharged so perfectly that everyone alike said he would become a man of great prudence and holiness.”]

[Col. 0949D]

[Col. 0950A] Among the little sheep entrusted to his care there was a diseased and wandering sheep, thrusting itself willingly into the jaws of wolves. One of his parishioners was obstinately afflicted by the crime of adultery. But what care, what concern, and what persistence this good imitator of the Good Shepherd devoted to him, we have thought best to relate in his own words. Once, while many learned men were seated together, and Hugh was present and conversing familiarly with them on various matters, some experts in both canon and civil law proposed that Gospel question in which the Lord says to Peter: “If your brother sins against you, rebuke him between you and him alone” (Matthew 18:15). As for what follows—namely, the bringing of two or three witnesses with him, or the manner of declaring a brother’s sin to the Church—some defined the matter one way and others another, without coming to the same conclusion. The bishop then stated what seemed right to him and supported his judgment by pursuing this example.

[Col. 0950B] “When I was once a young man and myself, though only a deacon, was administering the governance of the parish entrusted to me, while a certain simple priest performed what belonged to his office in the celebration or administration of the sacraments and ecclesiastical services, it happened that one of my parishioners incurred the stain—or rather, what is worse, the guilt—of adultery. I endured the report of this evil with great difficulty. I investigated the matter with the utmost care and, once it had been discovered and acknowledged, corrected it with the cooperation of the grace of our Lord, proceeding as follows.

“I summoned the man privately, between myself and him alone, and said what I thought ought to be said, appropriate to the matter and the place. He, on the contrary, began stubbornly to deny his guilt, to become angry, and, so far as his blind obduracy suggested daring to his mind, even to threaten and insult me. When he departed for his home, he left me as sad as he showed himself, for the time being, incorrigible.

“Remembering the Gospel command, I first brought with me two witnesses, and afterward three, who knew the matter equally well. I rebuked the man, urged him to correction, and promised him forgiveness once he had been corrected through satisfaction. He delayed promising correction, and would not allow even the suspicion or basis of the crime to be removed. [Col. 0950D] At last, when his guilt had become known to everyone, I publicly exposed the enormity of his crime before all who were listening—I openly convicted him one day in the middle of the church during a solemn feast—and I solemnly denounced that he would be handed over to Satan for the destruction of his flesh unless he repented quickly. Terrified and confounded by these words, he sprang forward into the midst, renounced his sin with groans and a flood of tears, and performed penance. Thus corrected and reconciled, he received forgiveness.”

[Col. 0951A] These are the things that the holy man related. We have thought it right to insert them into the present history so that the reader may see more clearly from them what care and zeal, what discernment and diligence, this man filled with God had shown from his earliest years concerning the salvation of souls. Thus, not undeservedly, having been found faithful in little over many of his Lord’s goods, he appears at the proper time to have been set over them. [Col. 0951B]

## CHAPTER VI. How he visited the Carthusian house with his prior and loved it when he had seen it

But, as Holy Scripture says, “When a person has finished, then he will begin” (Ecclesiasticus 18:6), although everyone proclaimed Hugh already perfectly completed, according to the measure of his profession and beyond the measure of his age, at the summit of virtue, he himself thought that he had not even reached the beginning of perfection or of a worthy manner of life. Once he had learned of the holy and exalted reputation of the Carthusian monks, he longed with an insatiable desire of heart to be formed by their example. At first, concealing the intensity of this desire, he sought to obtain the opportunity, together with his prior already mentioned above [Note: [Col. 0951D] That is, the superior of Villa Benedicta, who is honored by the title of prior above, in chapters 3 and 4.], to enjoy the sight and affection of those men. When this had been accomplished, such a love for their spiritual way of life was immediately kindled in his breast that he could in no way contain its flame within himself. He was already happily experiencing the truth of the words spoken by one who was unhappily burning:

> The more the fire is covered, the more fiercely it burns beneath its covering.

He gazed upon the place and, as he gazed, marveled at it: by its very situation it almost surpassed the clouds, touched the heavens, and was completely removed from every earthly disturbance. He considered how great an opportunity there was there to devote oneself to God alone. This purpose seemed to be especially supported by the abundance of books, exceedingly rich, by the ample opportunity for reading, and by undisturbed leisure for prayer. As far as the arrangement of the place was concerned, these things were indeed recognized to be so. But in the inhabitants of the place he observed mortification of the flesh, serenity of mind, freedom of spirit, cheerfulness of countenance, and purity of speech. Their constitutions commended solitude, not isolation; they separated their dwellings but joined their minds. Each person lived with himself, yet no one did or possessed anything as his own. All lived separately, and each lived in common. Each remained apart so as not to experience hindrance from another; each lived in common so as not to be deprived of fraternal consolation. These things and others like them, observed there, as well as the secure protection of obedience—which has often failed many solitary persons and exposed them to extreme danger—pleased Hugh, seized Hugh, and claimed him wholly, as though he had been carried outside himself.

Among that company of holy men there was a certain elder [Note: [Col. 0951D] In all likelihood this was Basil, then prior of the Carthusian house, whose particular responsibility was to test and receive novices.], formerly of great reputation in the world and at that time also of the highest renown in his holy vocation. Hugh opened to him, in confidence, the burning of his heart. He asked not so much whether he should do what he desired as how and how soon he might accomplish it. With groans and tears he sought the elder’s advice, but received an answer far different from what he had hoped.

The prudent man observed that the young man, as his appearance indicated, was delicate in constitution and tender in age [Note: [Col. 0952D] Namely, about twenty-three years old, since, as is established below in chapter 9, he had not yet been ordained to the priesthood.]. He also knew that Hugh was distinguished by birth and did not believe that the rigor of the order could suit his character or correspond to his strength. Seeking, therefore, by this terrifying answer to restrain him from so presumptuous an undertaking—or rather, testing the constancy of his spirit—he said:

“Dear little son, how do you dare even to think of such a thing? The men whom you see inhabiting these rocks are harder than all stones; they know neither how to spare themselves nor how to pity the others who live with them. This place is dreadful even to look upon, and the order is exceedingly burdensome in practice. The rough covering of its hair shirt would scrape the skin and flesh from your bones while you were still alive; the rigor of its discipline would utterly strip away the tenderness that I see in you.”

But this soldier of Christ, a familiar and devoted follower and imitator of the most blessed Martin, made more steadfast by the terror inflicted upon him, silently turned over in his heart the words of the unconquered Laurence, who, when every kind of torture had been set before him by those wishing to frighten him, said: “I have always desired these feasts.” For just as a furnace leaps up when water is thrown into it and raises its locks of flame high into the air, so the burning desire of the saints grows stronger when adversity confronts it.

## CHAPTER VII. How, at the insistence of his prior, he swore on faith that while the prior lived he would never enter the Carthusian order; how he did not keep his pledge, yet felt no scruple over violating it, and thereby gained such great spiritual benefit

[Col. 0952D]

Avoiding the elder just mentioned, as though he were cruelly opposing his wishes, Hugh immediately disclosed the burning of his heart to some of the other brothers. They did not delay but, with immense approval and urgent encouragement, persisted in supporting his salutary purpose, promising him both their assent and their assistance. Then Hugh, exulting with boundless joy, begged them most earnestly to conceal these things from his prior [Note: [Col. 0952D] The superior at Villa Benedicta.]. A diligent imitator of Gospel teaching, he remembered that a treasure which has been found ought to be hidden until, after abandoning everything he possessed rather than selling it, one might deserve to purchase it and possess it more securely.

Nevertheless, although he tried to conceal what he was planning with great dissimulation, he could not escape the suspicion of his watchful shepherd, who loved him exceedingly. When they had therefore returned hurriedly to their own house, the elder, his face covered with tears, addressed him:

“Most beloved son, I know—indeed, I know—that I brought you to the Carthusian house to my great misfortune and to the irreparable loss of my church. The Carthusian house has snatched you wholly for itself; it possesses you entirely. In the meantime we scarcely retain you bodily, but your soul is not with us. Nor, I fear, will even this last long. For since you have followed the spirit from your earliest age, dragging your flesh along like a burden, by the force of that spirit and not under the guidance of this place you will surely soon be taken away from us.

“Alas! The light of my eyes is suddenly extinguished, and the staff of my old age is snatched away from me, tottering as I am and now needing it more than usual. But will the sweetness of my honey suddenly turn into wormwood, and will my glory—by which a father took such pride in his wise son—be reduced to nothing? Have pity, son, have pity rather on your father. Do not, by depriving my gray hairs, already near the tomb, of the consolations of your great vigor, pass beyond the bounds of the piety and compassion innate in you.

“If the maternal compassion of the Church, which gave birth to you for God, and the paternal sweetness of devout men, which gently nurtured you, have not wholly recalled your soul, burning for higher things, at least yield in this matter to your father’s old age. Do not abandon me while I am still breathing, since now it is only through you that I ought to breathe.”

Amid these and similar words, grief absorbed the spirit of both men. When the elder had scarcely recovered his breath, he spoke again:

“I hope—I hope, trusting in the goodness implanted in you, dearest son, that you have heard me. Let my son, then, swear to me in the name of the Lord his God that, after abandoning his father, he will not join himself to the observances of the Carthusian house while I live [Note: [Col. 0953D] His spiritual father, not his natural father.]. Otherwise, the dart of suspicion with which fear has cruelly pierced the inward parts of my spirit will in no way be removed.”

Good God! What was happening to the mind and spirit of your servant amid these things? What a conflict between two loves was raging in his heart! O marvelous event! O marvelous perplexity! [Col. 0953D] On both sides there was storm, and on both sides calm; from either direction the waves drove the wavering man both toward shipwreck and toward harbor. If he did not obey God calling him to higher things, one love would be abandoned; if he resisted the authority ordained by God, a twofold love would be wounded. One love, which belongs to God, would be abandoned; the twofold love, which belongs both to God and neighbor, would not be fulfilled. O distress on every side—but, strangely, because of an excess of spaciousness, distress amid vast freedom! What, then, would he do, so enlarged and so constricted? He might say:

“O enlarged soul, and O constricted soul, I do not know what I should choose. Nevertheless, I say that whichever of these you choose, whether you perform or refuse to perform what is being demanded, life and not death is yours. But what you did, what outcome you found, and how you escaped these importunate hands, let us now see.”

Accustomed and habituated to obey superiors and submit to them, unable to contradict and unaware of how to refuse assent, he gives his hand to the one demanding it and, having physically pledged his faith to the one commanding, fulfills his obligation. He then leaves the rest of his affair entirely to divine judgment.

But shortly afterward, when he had hesitated for some time and did not know what to do, when he endured daily losses in his spiritual life and shrank from violating the faith he had given, heavenly mercy suddenly poured into his heart a ray of the truest and clearest discernment. It inspired him and fully assured him that a pledge extracted without due consideration, against the usefulness of the soul or to the detriment of true salvation, was not to be observed.

Knowing, therefore, and rejoicing because the Lord his God was truly speaking these things within him, hearing and obeying him, he abandoned the house entrusted to him. No one knew, because no one was lying in wait or suspected anything of the kind. He departed secretly, went to the Carthusian house [Note: [Col. 0953D] In 1163, as may be inferred from chapter 12; he became procurator after approximately two lustrums from his entrance into the order, in 1173.], and, welcomed with joy, remained there amid great grace.

When he was frequently asked by your young servant [Note: [Col. 0953D] That is, by the author of the *Life*. Hence what follows: “He always said to me.”] whether this violation of his pledge had ever produced in him any scruple, as such things usually do, he always answered me:

“Certainly I never felt a scruple because of it, but rather a jubilation of mind whenever I remember the deed, from which I gained such great spiritual benefit.”

## CHAPTER VIII. Concerning the gravest temptation that seized him after he entered the Carthusian order, and how he was nevertheless not deprived of saving protection

After he had transferred himself to the Carthusian order, a very grave temptation seized him, concerning which he himself used to relate the following:

“Immediately,” he said, “when I set my foot across the threshold of the cell [Note: [Col. 0954D] The temptation described here is different from that related below in chapter 13. This one afflicted him immediately after his entrance into the order, while Basil was still alive; the other came after Basil’s death and around the beginning of Hugh’s priorate.], I felt a new movement of temptation rising in my heart. That temptation was not uniform. Rather, when I entered upon a new warfare, the tempter renewed all the ancient instruments of his malice. Above all, as though he were stretching against me a most powerful ballista, which he hoped would be insuperable for me, he drew—indeed kindled—against me the spur of my flesh. Day and night it did not depart from me—the angel of Satan stood over me, pressing me hard and buffeting me.

“What could I do in the face of this, good Jesus? Or rather, what did your goodness do in the face of this, as you acted kindly with your servant? I watered the earth with my knees, heaven with groans, my breast with blows, and my cheeks with tears. I beat, struck, and fell upon it. But I did all these things and countless others as though beating the air, until you, who neither sleep nor slumber and who guard Israel, blessed Samaritan, laid your hand upon me.

“You, the guardian through the night, as you laid your hand upon one half-dead, whom I thought you were scarcely leaving behind after robbers had suddenly crept in from every side and broken in violently, immediately dispelled every evil. Then, seeing the field of my heart dried up and the furnace of my flesh collapsing, with fluid thoughts flowing away on one side and fiery impulses on the other, I marveled at what I had been and what I had suddenly become.

“As these things alternated in me and, rather, within me, I often forgot myself, remembering you from the land of Jordan. From that river, which derives its name and origin from two sources, I seemed to double my confession of my humiliation and your glorification: singing your mercies to you and proclaiming my injustices against myself. I perceived that you were forgiving the wickedness of my sin.

“While I remained in Hermon and on the little mountain, detesting and cursing every slippery path of obscene depravity, humbling myself and, after the deadly fire, recognizing that I was dust and ashes, you soon dealt kindly with your servant, opening my eyes so that I might contemplate the wonders of your law. Sometimes, though fatigued and exhausted, you allowed me at least to taste in advance that hidden manna.

“This tiny portion that I was permitted to sample here was so great and so immeasurable that, to obtain it more fully and for a longer time, I could easily despise everything the world knows, whether sweet or bitter, gentle or harsh. Yet for me there was rarely an hour or a brief pause in these things. Again I was carried away to struggles, again to wars.

“Nowhere, and never, did the compassion of the most merciful Redeemer fail me, unworthy though I was. His voice was always in the ear of my heart, teaching and consoling me; his hand was always with me, rescuing and strengthening me.”

With a contrite mind he secretly related these and many other things of this kind, not only for our consolation but also out of devotion and humility concerning his own condition—a condition whose alteration he lamented after becoming a bishop. He would recall what he had endured through human weakness or received by divine gift in his earlier life. He introduced these matters as a vehement reproach against himself, as though he had not responded suitably to God for his benefits, or as though, after his Lord’s more generous gifts, he had shown himself, now in mature age, weaker in the powers of his spirit than he had been in earlier years.

## CHAPTER IX. Concerning the praise of the Carthusian order, Hugh’s progress in it, and how the elder to whose service he had been assigned tested him concerning the reception of priestly orders and foretold that he would become a bishop. Chapters 10 and 11 of the longer *Life* are included under this chapter

[Col. 0955D]

[Col. 0956A] At that time, as always, there were in the Carthusian house men of the highest holiness and gravity, both clerics and laymen, greatly revered even by the highest princes and prelates of the churches. It would not have been easy to discern who among them could be regarded as more fervent or more perfect. There was such rigor in disciplining the body and such discretion preserved within that rigor that, by maintaining the mean between the two extremes, no one was content to undertake anything beneath his strength, nor was anyone permitted or willing to practice anything exceeding the limits of his strength.

Concerning this order, in the register of the pope during whose time our Hugh was canonized [Note: [Col. 0955D] In 1219 Pope Honorius III entrusted the examination of the Life of Saint Hugh to Stephen of Canterbury; and, according to Raynaldus, enrolled him in the number of the saints in the following year. Thus the author of the *Life* was still alive during these years while writing this account, or had inserted it into writings composed earlier.], it is written:

“The Carthusian order surpasses the other orders in this respect: it has placed a limit upon desire.”

What do we think Hugh accomplished here, and how greatly did he progress, when the love of learning implanted in him from his earliest months, so to speak, could be continually and almost fraternally assisted and advanced by books, teachers, an exceptionally gifted intellect, and leisure as opportune as it was abundant? He continued in these pursuits by day and in these studies by night. He blamed the brevity of time alone for being hostile to his progress and his joys, since, in an astonishing way, all the length of days and nights seemed too short for him as he read, meditated, or prayed.

[Col. 0956C] At some point he was assigned the care and service of an elderly monk, a man of great virtues. The old man was so sickly and, because of extreme age and weakness, so confined that he never went beyond the walls of his cell. During the chanting of the canonical hours and in supplying whatever necessities were required, Hugh assisted and soothed him as a devoted and tireless servant, like a nurse caring for a foster child or a mother for her son; in everything he served him no otherwise than as he would have served the Lord Jesus Christ himself.

After several years had already passed in this manner of life, it happened that the time approached when the bishop of that place was to celebrate the conferral of holy orders. Knowing this, the man of God, who was at once Hugh’s teacher [Note: [Col. 0956D] The name of this man of God is given neither by Surius nor by Dorlandus. But Bzovius, under the year 1200, writes from Dorlandus as follows: “While he was doing these things at that time [Col. 0956D] when holy orders are customarily conferred, it happened that the holy Father Basil, the prior, as though testing Hugh, said to him: ‘Behold, son, the time has come for you to decide whether you wish to become a priest.’” These words are Dorlandus’s, except for “the holy Father Basil, the prior”; in its place Dorlandus has “that holy elder,” understanding, as Dorlandus had stated earlier, the man whose care Hugh had undertaken with the permission of the prior, that is, Basil. That elder must therefore be distinguished from Basil the prior, although his name is unknown.] and foster child [Note: [Col. 0956D] “Teacher,” as I think, in spiritual matters; a foster son, since Hugh, as stated above, assisted and nurtured him in his infirmity like a nurse caring for a foster child or a mother for her son.], began to say to him, as though testing him:

“Behold, son,” he said, “it is now for you to decide whether you wish to become a priest. If you consent, you will now be advanced to this rank.”

Hugh had long desired nothing in life, and nothing was equally dear to him, as to serve in sacred ministries, to be nourished by the divine sacraments, and, because Jesus was most sweet to him—as will be explained more fully below—to touch his own Jesus more freely with the mouth of his heart and with his body in the saving host. Burning with desire at what he had heard, he immediately and humbly revealed what he wished:

“As far as it depends on me, Father,” he said, “there is certainly nothing I desire more in this life.”

Then the elder said to him:

“What have you said? What, I ask, have you said? What a marvel! You have read so many times that whoever approaches the priesthood unwillingly approaches it unworthily, and now you do not fear to approach it not unwillingly but eagerly, as you yourself admit?”

Terrified by these words and as though struck by lightning, Hugh fell prostrate at the feet of the man rebuking him, flinging his whole body to the ground. [Col. 0957B] He wept profusely and, with groaning words, begged pardon for so great a presumption. The elder, as though pretending for a little while not to notice his distress, though he himself was shaken to his very inward parts by Hugh’s devotion and humility, at last addressed him gently and tearfully:

“Rise,” he said, “rise.”

When Hugh had sat down at his command, the man of God spoke these words in a prophetic spirit:

“Do not be troubled. No longer merely ‘son,’ but ‘my lord,’ do not be troubled, I say. I know, and truly know, with what spirit and affection you have spoken these words. Therefore I say to you: soon you will indeed be a priest, and afterward, when the time foreknown by God arrives, you will also be a bishop” [Note: [Col. 0957D] Hugh became bishop of Lincoln in 1185 or the following year.].

## CHAPTER X. Concerning his progress in devotion after he became a priest, and the rigor of his bodily austerity and abstinence

[Col. 0957C]

Having therefore been advanced to the priesthood according to the word of the man of God, he progressed in sacred devotion as much as he advanced in rank. In the service of the altar he behaved as though he were handling the visible Lord and Savior with his hands. To those standing nearby, when he celebrated the divine mysteries, he seemed in deed and truth to sing with the bride that nuptial verse: “My beloved is mine, and I am his” (Song of Songs 2:16).

He disciplined the members of his body by vigils, fasts, and scourging, and, according to the custom of the order, by the use of a hair shirt and by drinking water with dry bread. He omitted none of the austerity that the common rule or the examples of his predecessors allowed.

Not ceasing to add many personal practices beyond what was required, he bent his knees frequently, laid his entire body upon the ground, and, lying prostrate with Moses and Aaron, with Joshua and Daniel, implored divine mercy to turn away his wrath from his people and hasten propitiation. During every week of Lent [Note: [Col. 0957D] Thus, by Hugh’s time, the rigor of the first fathers had been moderated. They had been accustomed to fast in this way on three days of every week throughout the entire year, not by precept but according to personal choice. Hence Guigo, the fifth prior of the Carthusian house, writes in the customs he published: “On Monday, Wednesday, and Friday, we are content with bread and water and salt, if anyone wishes.”], he was accustomed to spend three days eating only bread and water, without any seasoning whatsoever, unless perhaps a little salt was tasted. In the final week, the observance of the same diet was extended to Saturday. Before he became a bishop, neither illness nor weakness nor any other circumstance ever compelled him to relieve this four-day fast with any other food or drink.

The physicians attributed to this abstinence an excessive cooling of his stomach in advancing age. Consequently, he often endured pains and almost constant discomforts. They also identified it as the cause by which his appetitive faculty, stronger than his digestive faculty, made him, when he was about fifty, more corpulent than he had formerly been as a young man.

## CHAPTER XI. How he was assigned to the service of Peter, archbishop of Tarentaise, and ministered most devotedly both in searching the Scriptures and in everything that could be fitting for reverence or pleasing to the spirit, daily receiving from him blessing, absolution, and salutary instruction

At the same time [Note: [Col. 0957D] Surius’s Life of Saint Hugh makes no mention of the material inserted in this chapter, nor does the Life of Saint Peter among the Bollandists.], the most holy man Peter, archbishop of Tarentaise [Note: [Col. 0957D] Peter presided over the archbishopric for thirty-three years. He became archbishop in 1141 and died on 14 September 1174, as Pagius reports in volume 4 of his *Critique of Baronius*, p. 644, against Henschenius, who argued that he died on 8 May 1175.], a Cistercian monk, frequently used to visit the Carthusian house [Note: [Col. 0958D] There is no doubt that he had inherited from his parents an exceptional affection for the Carthusians. Concerning them, the following is found in his Life: “They strove not merely to receive religious men but to seek them out, especially the Carthusians and the monks of Bonneval, in whom they took particular pleasure; they brought them suitable provisions and brought back from them counsels for salvation, not only to follow themselves but to communicate to many others,” etc.], and there remained in a solitary cell below the dwellings of those holy men. Hugh likewise was assigned to his service and appointed to wait upon him.

If a reading was to be recited, or if any passage in that vast sea of books was requested and had to be sought out and found, Hugh was ready for it: every Scripture that might be requested was at hand for him. If the discussion concerned the pages of the Old or the New Testament, or if the deeds of the saints or the treatises of the teachers prompted inquiry, nothing escaped Hugh’s diligence. When that holy man spoke, Hugh was a gentle and teachable listener; when he was ordered to speak, he was a keen interpreter, remarkably effective and pleasing in expression.

He served him graciously in everything that could be fitting for the holy man’s reverence or pleasing to his spirit. He frequently washed his feet and kissed with the kiss of his heart those feet which he was not permitted to kiss with the kiss of his mouth.

[Col. 0958D] Hugh, now a bishop, was also heard relating these and other things about his former archbishop, who was by then reigning [Note: [Col. 0958D] Namely, at the time when the author was writing this.] in heaven. He also recalled this about him: after entering his bed, so that he might relieve his limbs, wearied by the day’s labor, through nighttime rest, while Hugh arranged him in bed and covered him with his garments, he heard him say this prayer every day:

> “Grant, we beseech you, Lord, that, giving thanks for the gifts we have received, we may receive greater benefits.”

Every day he also strengthened his servant Hugh with a powerful blessing, absolved him from all sins by pontifical authority, and instructed him with spiritual admonitions. Finally, he withheld nothing useful from him, but carefully revealed to him every plan of God that he knew would benefit him and, through him, many others.

## CHAPTER XII. How, after becoming procurator of the Carthusian house, he governed it energetically in both spiritual and temporal matters, rendering himself deservedly commendable to all.

[Col. 0959B]

After this, when Hugh had spent approximately two lustra [Note: [Col. 0959D] From this passage it is clear that Hugh came to the Charterhouse in or about 1163. For he completed approximately two lustra in the cell, in the year 1173, when Basil, prior of the Charterhouse, died and Hugh was appointed procurator by Guigo, the new prior. See, however, what I have observed below concerning the lustra, in Book V, chapter 20, note 306.] in the nest of his solitude and, having died fully to the world, was supported on every side by the most solid feathers and plumage and had become perfectly fit for flight, his prior entrusted the administration of the whole house to him, although he resisted as much as he could. [Note: [Col. 0959D] For at least four years, before he was sent to England.] He therefore governed the household committed to him with diligence, instructed the brothers carefully, and, in accordance with that saying about Saint Honoratus of Arles which he often had on his lips and greatly praised:

> “Always shaking the sluggish out of their laziness, he compelled those fervent in spirit to rest.”

[Col. 0959C]

The Lord, however, blessed the house, causing it to abound exceedingly in every good. Who, after being deprived of Hugh’s counsel even in temporal matters, did not receive from him advice useful for his needs, advice that even the wise of this age would admire? And whom did he instruct in temporal matters without immediately inflaming him toward eternal things? In chapter he spoke the word of God—things unheard of—to monks, brothers, and laypeople who happened to arrive. He refreshed the poor, as far as the rigor of the order permitted, even with daily assistance. When he could not help these people with material goods, he consoled them with words, fulfilling the saying of the wise man:

> “Behold,” he says, “a good word is better than an excellent gift” (Ecclesiasticus 18:17).

Meanwhile everyone spoke of Hugh: whether prior, monk, or lay brother, they extolled the grace bestowed upon him. The rich exalted Hugh with praises; the poor commended Hugh to the Lord in their prayers and begged that he be commended to their fellow sufferers. But he called this votive praise, as though he also despised it as frivolous.

## CHAPTER XIII. Concerning another temptation of his, different from the one discussed above in Chapter VIII, and how he was freed from it through that former holy prior of the Charterhouse, Basil, whom he called his foster father. This temptation is also inserted in the Great Life, Book II.

[Col. 0960A]

A temptation of the flesh suddenly arose against him, and it raged against him so continuously and so relentlessly that he would have preferred, for the time being, to be handed over to the punishments of Gehenna rather than be pressed by such flames. The struggle was so immense and the contest so fierce that it cannot be doubted that it was by divine power alone that he did not yield as a human being; instead, by resisting manfully, he carried away the victory. No one could fully recount the manner of this encounter: with what tears, how many groans, how frequent a confession, how harsh a scourging, he either sought divine assistance, crushed his heart, or tormented his own body. At dawn one day, however, the Sun of Justice, rising from on high, visited him in this manner, sending his angel and rescuing him from the power of these darknesses.

[Col. 0960B]

He had spent that night in darkness, remaining awake through almost all of it. At last, when the strongest athlete had been thrown down but not overcome—not defeated, but exhausted—a light sleep stealthily came upon him. Immediately, as though placed in an ecstasy, he saw that man of God, the former holy prior of the Charterhouse, Basil, who had received him into the order, standing before him, radiant in face and angelic in clothing, and addressing him in a gentle voice: [Note: [Col. 0959D] A notable testimony concerning Blessed Basil, drawn by our author from Saint Hugh’s account. It agrees with the description of Basil by the author of the Life of Saint Anthelm as “a man of wonderful holiness and devotion.” Accordingly Sausseius writes in the supplement to the Gallican Martyrology, p. 1125: “On the day before the Nones of June, at the Greater Charterhouse, the deposition of Saint Basil, confessor, general of the same order; through whose holy institutions and examples the order wonderfully flourished.” And again, ibid., fol. 1134: “At Grenoble, the commemoration of Blessed Basil, eighth general of the Charterhouse, who died there on the day before the Nones of June.” The distinguished Bollandists also mention him among those omitted on 4 and 14 June.]

> “What is the matter with you, dearest son? Rise and confidently tell me your will.”

He replied:

> “O good father and most devoted foster father, the law of sin and death that is in my members afflicts me unto death. Unless you help me in your customary manner, behold, your child will die.”

He had scarcely finished speaking when the saint said briefly:

> “Good; I will help you.”

Then, with his entrails laid open by the razor which he seemed to hold in his hand, he appeared to cut from them something like an inflamed swelling and cast it far outside the cell. After giving his blessing, the physician withdrew. The sick man, healed and restored to himself, sat up as sleep fled; and, rejoicing beyond measure at the radiant appearance granted him of his foster father, who had departed to the Lord several [Note: [Col. 0960D] Not merely a few days earlier, as Surius has it. For at least four years had elapsed between Basil’s death and this temptation, which is distinct from the one mentioned in Chapter VIII.] years before, he found himself wholly changed in heart and flesh.

Having several times received the substance of these events from Hugh’s own mouth, when he was speaking with me privately, I finally had him recount, during his last illness, the entire sequence of events more clearly and carefully, just as I have now arranged it.

When I asked whether he had afterward felt any movement of this kind in his flesh, he replied:

> “Indeed, I do not deny that I felt something, but it was very slight, and it was no less easy to despise than to suppress. I say this because I learned that someone else had written about these matters differently, asserting that, after being visited by the Blessed Virgin, Our Lady, the Mother of God, who appeared to him, he had been castrated and cured of his anger, so that thereafter he experienced no bodily stirring at all. But what I heard from his own mouth concerning his cure, I have expressed with complete truth.”

[Col. 0961C] [Note: [Col. 0961C] It is still unknown who wrote this. Giraldus Cambrensis, in Warthon, Part II, p. 432, mentions “a certain Angelic man,” but without a name, and says nothing about the Mother of God. If he differs in any respect from what is stated here, greater credence should be given to the author, who learned Hugh’s account from him during his final illness.]

We shall now treat of the transfer of our Hugh of Burgundy [Note: [Col. 0961C] Understand Burgundy in its broad sense, insofar as the Dauphiné is included under it.] to England and of his subsequent deeds, and, bringing the preceding book to a close, let us turn to another.

[Col. 0961] The First Book ends.

# PROLOGUE TO THE SECOND BOOK

[Col. 0961B]

When Hugh had most religiously administered the episcopate of the Church of Lincoln for twelve years and fifty-three days [Note: [Col. 0961C] By calculating the years and days indicated in the prologue, Surius correctly writes in the Life: “He held the episcopal see for fifteen years and fifty-eight days.” If this is so, Hugh must have been consecrated bishop on the feast of Saint Matthew the Apostle in 1185, not the following year, to which, following Roger, nearly everyone commonly assigns his consecration. This question is discussed more fully in the dissertation prefixed to this work.], it pleased his holiness to take my lowliness, whatever its worth, as a kind of assistance in the care of his life in the cloister’s sweetness [Note: [Col. 0961D] By these words the author sufficiently indicates that he was a monk; this is confirmed elsewhere, especially in Book V, chapter 23, where, after the words “He who wrote these things spoke with him,” he adds shortly afterward: “under the prior testimony of the same monk and priest with whom he was speaking.”], and to attach me inseparably to his side. From that time until he later lived in the body for three years and five days, I was absent from his company only for one single night, always clinging to him and serving him by day and by night. During this period, therefore, I saw with my own eyes almost everything that this present little book will contain, or heard it from his holy lips.

[Col. 0962B]

I learned from him and from others who had acted as procurators for his arrival the reason why he came into our world [Note: [Col. 0962C] From the Greater Charterhouse to England. By calling England “our world,” he indicates that he was English by nationality. It seems possible to infer from Book V, chapter 22, that he was a monk of Canterbury.] and likewise the manner in which he departed from his beloved Charterhouse, arranged for the house at Witham to be built from its foundations, established it, filled it with excellent men, and afterward proceeded to the episcopate.

As for the things he did in the episcopate before I began to follow him, I deliberately pass over countless matters, certainly known and highly worthy of everyone’s knowledge. For I learned that many of these things had been committed to writing by men much more learned than I. [Note: [Col. 0962C] I read that Giraldus Cambrensis, Roger, and Paris wrote about Saint Hugh. The first was published by Warthon in Anglia Sacra, but reports rather little about the saint. The second is cited by various writers and seems to have written about the saint incidentally. The third borrowed much from Roger and is later than our author. Whether others wrote about Hugh in that age, I do not know. See the observations of another on Book III, chapter 6, note 96.] I judged it superfluous, indeed presumptuous, to repeat in blunter speech what others had explained more appropriately.

But for those matters which we believe those writers did not fully know, let us now direct both pen and mind to recount them in order, and, invoking the assistance of the Holy Spirit, let us make such a beginning.

[Col. 0961] The Prologue ends.

# BOOK TWO

## CHAPTER I. How Hugh was sent to seek a founder for a house of the Carthusian order to be built in England at Witham.

[Col. 0961C]

At that time the fame of the virtues of our Hugh reached the knowledge of Henry II, king of the English, on this occasion. [Note: [Col. 0962D] “In the month of August,” says Trivet in his Chronicle for the year 1177, published by Luc d’Achery in vol. III of the Spicilegium, “Henry the elder, king of the English, crossed to Normandy with his son Geoffrey, duke of the Bretons.” Baronius adds for this year that the king was still there on 21 September.] While the king was abroad, across the sea, a certain nobleman from the regions of Normandy came to him. The king, among other words of mutual conversation, began to make extensive inquiries of him about the Carthusian order.

[Col. 0962C] [Note: [Col. 0962D] It is believed that this nobleman came before the king in praise of Hugh in the year 1177, and that near the end of that year or the beginning of the next Hugh was requested through envoys to become prior.]

For, having long before been informed of the fame of that holy way of life [Note: [Col. 0963D] Apparently in 1175. For, according to Pagi, King Henry visited the tomb of Saint Thomas at the beginning of July 1174; after visiting it, according to Trivet’s Chronicle, he returned to Normandy. After Easter 1175, “the elder king,” in Trivet’s words, “and his son the younger king crossed into England.”], the king had summoned several brothers from the aforesaid house and had granted them, in England, a village called Witham, situated in the territory of Bath, at the place they themselves had chosen, together with fields, woods, pastures, vineyards, and whatever else was necessary for founding that house of the order.

[Col. 0963D] [Note: [Col. 0963D] Or, as it is read in the Monasticon Anglicanum, in the county of Somerset.]

The man designated as prior for those brothers [Note: [Col. 0963D] When the first prior at Witham returned from England to the Charterhouse, and another sent there from the Charterhouse died soon afterward, nearly three years passed before Hugh was sent to Witham as the third prior.] had agreed to remain in England for only a very short time. Accustomed as he was to the leisure and repose of solitude, he could not, with his delicate disposition, endure the burdensome care required by so great a construction. He and nearly all his companions were wearied by the customs of a foreign people, an unfamiliar diet, and the other things that easily give rise to offense in the habits and wishes of outsiders on foreign soil.

Some of the local inhabitants were also afraid of their arrival in their territory, foolishly fearing that, dissatisfied with their own boundaries, the newcomers might desire to seize their acres. When the innocent men perceived this hostility of the natives growing against them, they allowed their prior to return to the house, so that, after taking counsel with holy men, he might either return in a more peaceful frame of mind or obtain the appointment of another more capable of the task in his place.

He therefore returned, and another was sent in his place. Affected by a similar weariness, he soon received, through a blessed death, the end of his labors and the beginning of life. Meanwhile the remaining brothers were united in wavering amid various storms of disturbance.

The king himself was distressed to the depths of his heart by this. He began to imagine and fear the future mark of disgrace with which he knew he would be branded among the magnates of the many surrounding nations if he were unable to complete an undertaking so salutary and so favorable to all foreign peoples.

From the aforementioned man, therefore, he received this counsel:

> “From these waves, my lord king, you can free yourself by one single and most effective course. There is a certain monk in the Charterhouse, noble by birth but far more distinguished by the excellence of his conduct, named Hugh of Avalon. Adorned with every grace of virtue, he is so beloved and gracious to all who know him that by his appearance alone he draws everyone’s affection to himself. Those who are worthy to hear a word from his mouth rejoice as though they had received a divine or angelic oracle. If this newly planted foundation of our most holy order in these parts should be granted such a cultivator and ruler, you will see it suddenly prosper, bearing the most joyful fruit of every grace. Moreover, as I am certain, the entire English Church will be adorned more beautifully by the splendor of that pure religion and most religious purity.

> “Nevertheless, his own people will not easily release him from their house. He himself also will not take up residence elsewhere except under compulsion and against his will. A favorable and vigorous embassy is therefore needed; it is also necessary to strive through an industrious pursuit of entreaties, so that, once this sole request has been obtained as quickly as possible, your mind may thereafter be relieved of the burdens of this anxiety, and this sublime religion may be propagated more conspicuously for the glory of your excellence.

> “For in this one man you will find, together with a host of other virtues, whatever patience and sweetness, whatever greatness of soul and gentleness can be found in any mortal. The nearness or companionship of this man cannot be disagreeable to anyone. No one will shun him as a foreigner; everyone will regard him as a citizen, everyone as a member of the household, a brother, and an intimate friend. For he himself regards the entire human race no differently than his own entrails; he embraces and cherishes all people in the arms and bosom of a single charity.”

He had said many other things in this vein. The king applauded him greatly as he spoke and thanked him, then sent as quickly as possible, with royal letters, venerable envoys to the holy house of the Charterhouse—namely, Lord Reginald, bishop of Bath, surnamed Lumbrach, and with him certain vigorous and industrious men.

[Col. 0963D] [Note: [Col. 0963D] According to Baronius, Reginald was designated bishop in 1173 and consecrated the following year by Saint Peter of Tarentaise, as Henschenius reports in the preliminary material to his Life. Since he was sent as legate against the Albigensians of Toulouse in 1178 and attended the Lateran Council the following year, it can be inferred with some certainty that he was sent to the Charterhouse to request Hugh as prior near the end of 1177.]

## CHAPTER II. How the envoys, coming to the Charterhouse concerning their request, found the brothers divided; what Hugh himself thought about granting it; and this is Chapter 3 in the sequence of the Great Life.

The king’s envoys came to the Charterhouse, bringing with them the venerable bishop of Grenoble, the diocesan of that place. They presented their lord’s letters to the prior and brothers, and followed them up earnestly and persuasively with humble words.

[Col. 0964D] [Note: [Col. 0964D] At that time John, descended from the lords of Sassenage and a Carthusian bishop, presided over the bishopric. Concerning him, the succession of bishops taken from the order records: “Lord John, bishop of Grenoble, a Carthusian, distinguished at home and abroad for the highest character, from the year 1165 until the Kalends of June, on which day he went to heaven in the year 1194.” Abbot Morotius, speaking of his death, which he places several years later, writes: “Then, having completed the course of his years, he prepared himself for eternity with the most peaceful close of life.”]

When all were saddened at the first hearing, the prior was especially disturbed. Their response was delayed, while the consciences and wishes of each individual concerning such a matter were examined.

The first prior wholly opposed the request, and the brothers’ opinions varied in different directions. Some said that such a man, so beneficial to the whole order, ought by no means to be sent to such distant regions. [Note: [Col. 0965D] From this it is inferred that Guigo, then prior of the Charterhouse, who contemplated—as he did shortly afterward—resigning the priorate, wished to transfer it together with the generalate to our Hugh. It is therefore no wonder that he resisted the envoys’ request as much as he could and did not dismiss Hugh except under compulsion.]

Others, one of whom was Lord Bovo [Note: [Col. 0965D] This is the Bovo who succeeded Hugh in the priorate of the Witham Charterhouse and whom we often heard recounting these events. Guigo, former prior of the Charterhouse, is believed to have dedicated to him the “Treatise on the Fourfold Exercise of the Cell,” edited by Chiffletius, S.J.], asserted that the king’s word had proceeded from God and explained on many grounds that it was unsafe to oppose it. Bovo said:

> “You neither know nor consider anything, because heavenly providence is accomplishing all this so that the holiness of this order may shine more splendidly through a holy man to the farthest boundaries of the world. Nor should you think that he can long be confined beneath the bushel of our hiding place. Believe my littleness: before long you will hear that he has been raised among the principal lights of Holy Church upon the candlestick of ecclesiastical governance. For Hugh has long seemed to me a bishop by his virtues rather than a monk.”

[Col. 0965D] [Note: [Col. 0965D] This is a second prophecy of Hugh’s future episcopate. The first, in Book I, chapter 9, was made by an old man who, because of his age, never left the walls of his cell. The second was made by Bovo, who some years later went from his cell to England, succeeded Hugh there in the priorate, and presided over him until the year 1200.]

At last Hugh was asked to state his opinion and disclose his wishes. He immediately replied:

> “I was taught long ago to reserve nothing of my will concerning my own condition. I shall freely explain what I truly think about this matter. Having lived so long in the midst of your holiness and been so greatly assisted by your admonitions and examples, I have never known how to guard my own soul for even a single day. I therefore wonder how it could enter the mind of any wise person that I should be sent farther away to govern the souls of others by myself.

> “How could I be capable of establishing a new house, when I have been unable to preserve the institutions of the old ones? These things I hear are childish and, without prejudice to your reverence’s good pleasure, are in no way worthy of such lengthy deliberation.

> “Let us therefore set aside concern for such matters from now on. The undertaking is difficult and does not tolerate delay, and it is your responsibility to provide diligently lest the king’s undertaking be prolonged in an unfinished state, to the danger of souls and the disgrace of the holy order. Choose from among yourselves, or from your other houses, some man suitable for this work and send him with these men.

> “As wise men, answer these men wisely as well: say that you wish to fulfill their desire better than they themselves ask, assigning them not the man whom, being deceived, they seek, but the kind of man whom, as religious and discerning people, they require. For it is not expedient to grant the request for the person sought without greater deliberation, since they themselves do not wish to be deceived concerning the person’s quality. Thus let their request be granted in such a way that they rejoice at having received more usefully than they asked.”

## CHAPTER III. How it was finally obtained that Hugh should go to England and come to the king, and how he was escorted honorably to Witham.

Although Hugh insistently pursued these and other arguments in his defense, nevertheless, through the inward disposition of the wisdom of God, who moderates all things gently, his intention could in no way deprive the divine decree of its effect. Nor could the protection of the prior, who wished to retain Hugh, prevail against the order of things arranged by God.

The opposition of both—the prior’s and Hugh’s—while unknowingly striving to resist, was necessarily compelled to serve the Majesty working invisibly. For the more stubbornly the prior resisted, and the more insistently Hugh declared himself unequal to the task, the more vehemently the bishops present, with their advisers and finally joined by certain senior brothers of the community, pressed for the fulfillment of what so great a king had requested.

What more is there to say? At last the whole body of the brothers, overcome both by the prayers and by the arguments of those who had come, yielded to their request.

When all urged Hugh to consent, he transferred his opinion to the prior, since he could do nothing else. For he knew that the man who loved him as his own soul and did not wish him to be separated from him in any way could scarcely, or never, impose this upon him.

[Col. 0966B]

They say that, urged by the admonitions of his bishop and by the groaning prayers of all who were present, the prior answered those around him as follows:

> “As the Lord lives, this word will never leave my mouth: that I should order Hugh to abandon my old age [Note: [Col. 0966D] He was therefore burdened by old age, since he was then prior of the Charterhouse—not Basil, as Dorlandus reports, for Basil had died four or five years earlier, nor Jancelinus, who was still vigorous at this time and died thirty-three years after Hugh. Rather, it was Guigo, the intermediate prior between the two, a thoroughly old man and apparently prior of the Charterhouse twice; he must not be confused with Hugh, who preceded Saint Anthelm in governing.] and deprive the Charterhouse of his most sweet and absolutely necessary presence.”

At last, overwhelmed by the excessive persistence of everyone and finding no way at all to proceed, he turned to the bishop of Grenoble and said:

> “It is already settled what I have said about myself: neither my voice nor my mind will ever remove Hugh from me. You must now decide. You are our bishop; you are our father [Note: [Col. 0966D] Father as diocesan bishop; brother as a fellow-professed religious, having become one, as Morotius says, “when, leaving the headship of the monastery of Saint Robert, he sought more secluded hiding places among the Carthusians.”] and brother.” If you impose this upon him, if you command it, I do not contradict or resist.”

He said no more. His voice interrupted by weeping, he gave himself over to tears, by which he might ease the pain of his anxious mind.

[Col. 0966D]

You would have seen streams of tears flowing from everyone’s faces.

[Col. 0967A]

The bishop himself, being exceedingly compassionate, a very honorable and gentle monk, was compelled by all to exercise the authority over Hugh that the prior had promised him. He first addressed everyone in this way:

> “Dearest brothers, it is evident that you have climbed to the summit of Christian perfection no less through your way of life than through your profession. We, who are idle and far inferior to the height of your holiness, need not explain to you what you ought to do in matters belonging to God, nor even admonish you to complete vigorously what you know better than we do, since throughout your whole life you have shown that you seek not your own interests but those of Jesus Christ.
