> “I thought it necessary to recall one thing to the prior, and also to your entire community, brothers: let me place before your eyes how your predecessors acted in a case very similar to this one.

> “When, at the insistence of Saint Bertirraminus, then bishop of Le Mans, the most holy Benedict sent his beloved and holy disciple Maurus to the western regions of Gaul to establish monastic religion, you read that a similar grief and a cause of grief not unlike this arose there. The holy man of God restrained both his own grief and that of the brothers in such a way as to show that the servants of God must not be saddened by matters in which they know their Lord’s will.

> “There he also added a saying worthy of remembrance: ‘Let us beware,’ he said, ‘lest, God forbid, we be found to oppose God by this very sadness of ours.’

> “But you, dearest brother Hugh, must also imitate in this the one whom you have always delighted to follow: the only-begotten Son of the supreme Father, who, for the salvation of many, deigned to leave the height of his divinity and enter publicly into human life.

> “You too, therefore, must not hesitate to wander for a short time away from your dearest companions, setting aside for the moment the silence of the solitude you love so greatly, so that you may be joined to him forever afterward in the kingdom of his blessedness, in this exile of the present life.

> “I, though unworthy, impose this upon you in his place, for the remission of your sins and also in exchange for eternal rewards, and I firmly command it under the obligation of obedience.

> “Go therefore safely and happily with these venerable men who have come to summon you. Take charge, with the Lord’s favor, of the house to be built at Witham in England. Preside there steadfastly and serve diligently the place and the brothers gathered there, and those who are to be gathered, in the name of the Lord.”

[Col. 0967D]

Hugh tried for some time to annul this decision by throwing himself at the bishop’s feet, but he achieved nothing. At last he yielded. Commending himself to the prayers of all who were present and bidding farewell to the brothers with the kiss of peace, he departed with those envoys [Note: [Col. 0967D] One of them, and the principal one, was Reginald, bishop of Bath. Since he acted against the people of Toulouse in 1178 and attended the Lateran Council the following year, as I have already noted, there is scarcely any doubt that he came with Hugh to the king near the end of 1177.] and came to the king.

At last, dismissed by the king with the greatest favor and escorted honorably to Witham, he was received with ineffable joy as an angel of the Lord by the few brothers who were then there, and installed as prior.

## CHAPTER IV. How, after inspecting the condition he found at Witham, Hugh returned to the king and arranged for the inhabitants of the village of Witham, who were to depart, to be provided for with the greatest generosity.

He found the brothers like another Joseph in Dothaim, which is interpreted as “defect.” They were indeed settled in a forest not far from the royal village then called Witham, a name which the place is believed to have received as a kind of prophecy of what was to come.

For the name is said in Latin to mean “dwelling” or “habitation” [Note: [Col. 0967D] *Ham* among the Anglo-Saxons means the same as *Haim* or *Haimat* among the Germans—that is, dwelling or homeland. *Wit* means the same as *Witz*, sense.], because, through the arrival of this man, a Christian philosopher, the place deserved to become extraordinarily so in reality: men of understanding, outstanding in every word and every sense, were drawn from all sides by the fragrance of knowledge of him. Though remaining and dwelling there bodily, they did not cease to yearn in thought and desire for that eternal homeland whose joys they were already beginning to taste with perfected understanding.

The brothers whom he found had cells woven from boards, enclosed by a very small rampart and stakes. [Note: [Col. 0968D] The cells made of planks, the church not yet laid out, the cloister not even begun, the many approaches to the king, the other matters related in this and the following chapter, and finally the buildings completed under Hugh, easily required seven or eight years for completion. I say this so that no one may suppose that Hugh came to England later than 1178.] In these, taking shelter as best they could until the time of correction, they were, in brief, lacking all—or nearly all—the supports necessary and proper to their order.

Nor had it yet been determined where the major and minor churches, the monks’ cells, and the cloister with the brothers’ little houses and guest lodgings ought most suitably to be built.

The inhabitants who had formerly occupied the aforementioned village, which was now about to pass into their possession, still lived there. No provision had yet been made to ensure that they would be willing or able to yield their homes to their new successors without complaint or injury to themselves.

After Hugh had carefully examined and individually recorded these and other matters concerning the site, the character of the place, and the other things that the needs of the order demanded or that could serve the welfare of those living there, it had been agreed among them that Hugh would promptly return to the king.

When he had explained each matter as it seemed to him, the king admired his prudence and moderation in everything. He approved whatever Hugh arranged and willingly granted whatever he requested.

First, he summoned all the owners of estates or other property who had to withdraw from the place, lest by any disturbance or the arrival of any crowd the deep silence of their solitude should be interrupted, or at least disturbed or even slightly broken.

On behalf of the king, these people were collectively offered a choice: each might select whichever of two options he preferred. They could receive fields and dwelling places on equal terms in whatever royal manors they chose, as they had held them at Witham; or, freed from the yoke of their former servitude, they could freely go to inhabit whatever regions they wished.

Then, when some requested land and others liberty, Hugh, a most tenacious champion of benevolent justice, said to the king:

> “Now, my lord, this too must be provided for: compensation in money must be given for the houses and for whatever expenses or labor these people have incurred in cultivation and in various constructions, so that we may not succeed those who have suffered any loss through us as people who are ungrateful, but as joyful people succeeding the joyful and benevolent.”

When the king initially presented himself as though this were difficult, Hugh, preeminent in goodness and vigorous in intervention, added:

> “Indeed, my lord, unless these men are first compensated in full for everything down to the last penny, this place cannot be granted to us.”

Thus the king was compelled to purchase a benefit which, as he thought, would be of no advantage to him: for old huts, decayed beams, and half-ruined walls he poured out a great quantity of bronze for a brief convenience.

But this good merchant, not content with so small a profit—unless he seemed to himself to have preserved justice rather than shown mercy—again addressed the king with a smiling expression:

“Come now, my lord king: behold, in your own land I, myself a stranger and needy, have made you rich in numerous houses.”

The king smiled at this and replied: “I did not wish to become rich in this way. These riches have almost made me poor. Yet I do not know what use these possessions are to anyone.”

Then Hugh, finding in the king’s answer the opportunity he had been seeking, said:

“Indeed, as I see, you set little value on this transaction. Let it therefore be done in a manner worthy of your greatness, and let these houses be given to me, since I have nowhere to lay my head.”

Astonished at this request, the king gazed at the petitioner in wonder and said:

“O remarkable lord! Do you suppose that we are unable to build new houses for you? Tell me, nevertheless, what would you do with them?”

He replied: “It is not fitting that royal greatness should inquire about every trifling matter. This is my first request to you; and since it is a small one, why should I suffer delay in having it granted?”

The king then jested—for, being exceedingly prudent, he gladly tested the man’s intelligence through a long exchange of words:

“O man who, on foreign soil, has almost become a violent one! If he relies on force, what would he do, when by words he extorts things in this fashion? So that he may not inflict anything harsher upon us, let what he demands be done.”

Then he gave the houses which had been granted to him to all their former owners. Since they now possessed the price of the houses, those men either again sold the houses for a price or moved elsewhere to live. Hugh himself hurried to construct the site as it may now be seen.

## CHAPTER V. How, when the construction of the site made no progress at all because of a lack of funds, Brother Girard approached the king with our Hugh and addressed the king with very harsh words; how Hugh’s patience was thereby approved, and from that time his intimacy with the king was greatly strengthened

Meanwhile, after a considerable portion of the principal construction had been suitably completed, the king—occupied with various affairs of the realm—paid less attention to the completion of certain buildings whose use appeared extremely necessary. Because funds for the workers’ wages were running short, the artisans repeatedly harassed the prior and the brothers with insistent complaints. The prior therefore sent some of the brothers to court, so that they might appropriately inform the king of this shortage and obtain its remedy. He promised that he would attend to the matter and send the necessities very soon. Those who had been sent returned, bringing back nothing but words.

In the meantime, while the ruler pretended not to notice that he had promised to fulfill his undertaking, work ceased altogether. The prior thought that the matter should be endured in silence, so that the king might of his own accord undertake what he knew to be expedient. But when he continued to neglect it for too long, another embassy was sent to him; and once again, as before, it brought back a promise that was not fulfilled.

Meanwhile, after the matter had been prolonged by many delays, weariness crept over the brothers. Some of them, stirred even to anger, attacked the prior with harsher words. They accused him alike of sloth and negligence, because he had not long ago gone in person to the king—even though the king was in distant regions—to deal with so important a matter.

But one of the brothers, named Girard [Note: The same man of whom the Life of St Anthelm writes: “There were present two brothers from the Charterhouse, noble by birth but nobler in humility and steadfastness of faith—namely Aymo, once a distinguished and powerful man in the world, and Girard, his equal in virtue,” etc. Thus, as he stood by St Anthelm until his death, so after Anthelm’s death he stood by Hugh in England. There Peter of Celle, who knew him, praises him in his Commentary on the Book of Job, book II: “The day before yesterday I saw a certain Gerard by name, a brother of the Carthusian order. Who above all …,” etc.], a man indeed of austere character but deeply religious, and exceedingly effective in speech among nobles and princes, addressed the prior in these words:

“How long, my lord prior, do you judge that this most hard-hearted man should be coaxed, rather than publicly warned to complete as quickly as possible the buildings without which the outward form of our order ought not to remain? Or, if he prefers to delay any longer, bid him farewell and hasten to return with all of us to our homeland and our own house. Do you not perceive that such great negligence toward us reflects dishonor upon our order, and that we ourselves are exposed to the mockery of everyone around us, since, after living here for so many years, we have been unable to put a roof over these tiny dwellings? If your innate modesty restrains you from saying to this man what is fitting, let us approach him together, and you shall hear what I have to say to him.”

When all the brothers had been summoned and the matter laid before them collectively, they all agreed that Girard should go with the prior to the king. The prior said:

“I too gladly accept your counsel. Nevertheless, Brother Girard, you must see to it that, just as you speak freely, so you conduct yourself with moderation in your speech. For, as I have truly discovered, this prince is exceedingly shrewd in mind and almost inscrutable in spirit; perhaps he pretends not to hear us in order to test us. Without doubt he knows how greatly the perfection which we have professed depends upon fulfilling that divine teaching which says to us, ‘In your patience you will possess your souls’ (Luke 21:19), as well as that saying of blessed Paul: ‘In everything let us show ourselves as ministers of God, in much patience’ (2 Corinthians 6:4). Much patience is demonstrated when great endurance bears many contrary and adverse things with great gentleness. For patience without endurance is not great but short-lived; without gentleness, it is altogether no patience at all.”

The prior therefore took with him the aforementioned Girard and another brother named Cynard [Note: See more concerning him below, book IV, chapter 12.], an old man of thoroughly proven virtue in the holy religious life, and set out for the king. The king received them all reverently, as though they were heavenly angels. In response to their presentation of the urgent matter, he spoke graciously, made good promises, excused the cause of the delay, and promised that everything would be completed promptly; yet he provided no funds for the present, nor did he state with certainty when he would provide them.

Then Brother Girard, grinding his teeth and remembering rather his earlier resolution than the admonition given to him, began to rebuke the king more severely. Finally he said:

“Whatever may henceforth seem good to you, my lord king, whether you complete or abandon the work already begun, will no longer concern me. I yield your entire kingdom to you in peace, and, bidding you farewell, I shall immediately return to our Carthusian wilderness. Do you think you are showing us favor if you support us with your bread, when we have absolutely no need of it? Indeed, it is better for us to flee to the rocks of our Alps than to contend with such a man, who regards as lost everything that is done for his salvation. Let him keep his riches, which he will soon lose and leave to someone he does not know, though he loves them so much; neither does Christ deem them worthy to be shared, nor does any Christian.”

Girard’s words—and others like them, harsher still—were reported as the consolations he offered to so great a ruler.

What the pious and moderate prior felt during these events, he himself, by then a bishop, often recounted. He said that Girard had spoken so many and such strong words that, whenever he later remembered them, he shuddered from head to foot. At that moment, while that heroic man—who had received such great freedom of speech from the Spirit of God—was uttering these things, Hugh was so suffused with shame on the king’s behalf that he could scarcely endure the confusion of his own heart. He urged his brother to spare such expressions or to remain entirely silent.

But Girard, being a man of purer conscience, of venerable gray hair, and also of noble blood [Note: He appears to have belonged to the family of the counts of Nevers. He is called a count of Nevers by Dorlandus and Morotius; yet they confuse him with William, likewise a Carthusian and a count of Nevers, conflating the deeds of the two. They must plainly be distinguished, both from the Life of St Anthelm, which mentions each of them, and because Pope Eugenius III’s letter and another of St Bernard to Countess Ida, in Achery, *Spicilegium*, vol. II, p. 513, new edition, establish that William died before 1153, whereas Gerard certainly still lived under Hugh. Concerning William, William of Nangis writes under the year 1138 in Achery, *Spicilegium*, vol. III, p. 5: “William, the distinguished count of Nevers, also flourished; his devotion shone forth wonderfully when, from being a powerful prince of the world, he became in the Charterhouse a humble poor man of Christ.”], did not refrain from saying yet other and other things—whatever he had said—by which he might correct or instruct the prince, and from adding still further words.

Meanwhile the king neither changed his expression nor uttered a word. Rather, silent and calm, he endured the speaker until the brother had brought forth with his mouth everything he had conceived in his mind. At last, satisfied and relieved by the labor of giving birth to what was in his heart, Girard ended his reproaches; surrendering his lips, which had been scourging, to silence, he restrained his spirit and suppressed his voice.

After this all remained for some time in profound silence. The prior lowered his face in embarrassment while looking at the king and judging the agitation of his mind from his gestures. At length the king began to speak:

“What are you deliberating within yourself, good man?” he said to Hugh. “Are you too preparing to depart and yield our kingdom to us?”

Hugh replied softly and gently:

“I have not despaired of you so completely, my lord. Rather, I sympathize with your impediments and occupations, by which the endeavors beneficial to your soul are obstructed. You are occupied; and, when the Lord assists you, you will carry forward well the salutary undertakings you have begun.”

Then the king embraced him and said under oath:

“By the salvation of my soul, as long as I breathe the air of life, you shall not depart from my kingdom. I shall share with you the counsels beneficial to my salvation, and with you the concerns necessary for my soul.”

He immediately sent funds and ordered the work to be completed with the greatest urgency.

## CHAPTER VI. How the king trusted Hugh above all others in matters concerning the salvation of his soul; how many believed him to be the king’s son; and how, by reproving him for various transgressions, Hugh never ceased to instruct him through holy exhortations—for the king bore adversity more lightly through Hugh’s varied consolation, overcame it more easily by relying on his prayers, and avoided it more prudently when guided by his counsels

After this the great prince enjoyed the man of God’s conversation more frequently and took even greater pleasure in his counsel. Nor were there many such counselors; indeed, as many believed, there was scarcely anyone under his entire authority in whom his spirit found greater rest than in the prior of Witham.

His power was extensive. Almost the whole of England, together with the greater part of Ireland, served him; Normandy with Anjou, Aquitaine with Gascony, and many large territories of the neighboring regions were also subject to him.

Yet throughout all these lands there was no person, whatever his rank or order, to whom he listened more willingly or obeyed more readily than this man whenever Hugh required him to inquire into or heed whatever concerned the salvation of his soul. He entrusted himself to Hugh with such intimacy and preferred him to almost everyone else with such singular privilege of affection that some obstinately believed and asserted that Hugh was his natural son and that the king had been his bodily father.

After the death of King Richard [Note: King Richard died in 1199, on 6 April; St Hugh attended his funeral, as is related in book V, chapter 15.], the son and successor of the king of whom we are speaking, we saw innumerable groups of people of different conditions and ranks hastening to Hugh when he was in the regions of Aquitaine, consulting him about their affairs as they would have consulted the brother of the deceased king.

Many argued with us, calling him the king’s brother; and they would not believe us when we asserted what we knew to be true about his kinship and lineage. They said:

“We know better what is true in these matters, and we have recognized it more clearly. Our former lord King Henry never loved an outsider as he loved this man, never honored one as he honored this man, trusted no one as he trusted this man, or entrusted himself to anyone as he entrusted himself to this man. If he were not his son—which the similarity of their physical appearance also seems to acknowledge—he would never have exposed himself and his affairs to him so specially, nor advanced a foreigner to such an honor with such insistence.”

Such was their claim.

“But we firmly assert what we know most truly: it was not flesh and blood that won him this favor with the king, but the revelation of the Father who is in heaven. For He who is in the heights, knowing him, clearly knew with what sincere and perfect affection of heart, after leaving everything, he followed Him—for, except for Him, he knew how to love nothing.”

The king himself also clearly saw and discerned this. As he is known to have received from God the grace of loving more closely men approved by the testimony of a good way of life, so he honored Hugh more preeminently than others because he perceived him to burn more brilliantly with the flames of divine love.

For Hugh was never with him in a spirit of flattering speech, much less of adulation. Wishing him to be the sort of man he knew to be expedient—first for himself, then for his household, and finally for everyone—Hugh pressed his point opportunely and importunately, according to the cause and matter, the time and the place, reproving, beseeching, and rebuking him in all patience and gentle instruction. In accordance with Saint Benedict’s excellent maxim, he mingled occasions with occasions, terrors with consolations.

Hugh therefore discussed with the king only those of his affairs and concerns that touched upon Christ, the Church, the peace of the kingdom, the peace of the people, and, finally, his own salvation. He never discussed earthly concerns with him, because he himself cared only for heavenly things and continually urged him to love, seek, and obtain them by every possible means.

It would take too long to enumerate individually how many earthly benefits the king bestowed at Hugh’s urging, how often through Hugh he changed his anger into clemency and granted pardon to those who had offended him, and how many churches and religious places he protected through Hugh’s intercession and enlarged with necessary resources.

Hugh constantly warned him not to trust in the empty and more fleeting prosperity and power of the world, nor to place his hope in uncertain riches, but in the living God, who is true strength and the certain and eternal blessedness of those who hope and confess in him. He urged the king readily to give, to exchange perishable things for those that endure, and to share temporal goods with the needy, so that he might share eternal goods with them.

Hugh frequently reproved him for various transgressions and diligently invited him to reform. He rebuked him most vehemently concerning vacant cathedral churches and monasteries, which the king often and for a long time unlawfully kept in his own hands and treated most wickedly through his agents. He also proved to him that, in appointing bishops and abbots, he was abusing the power usurped by his predecessors.

Hugh pointed out that almost all the causes and sources of evil among God’s people sprang up through unworthy prelates, were fostered by them, increased through them, and flourished through them. He asserted that divine judgment would especially turn the punishments for all these things back upon those who were not afraid to present themselves as the authors or supporters of such men’s promotion.

“And what need is there,” he said, “most wise prince, for you to inflict pernicious death upon so many souls for the empty favor of some individual? Why should you bring upon God such losses from the destruction of so many people redeemed by Christ’s death, and thereby store up for yourself such heaps of punishments in the future? How much better it would be for you to leave elections free to everyone according to the decrees of the canons, thereby extricating yourself from the labyrinth of so many evils, and to intervene only to this extent: that those whom the people entrusted and subject to you would choose as acceptable to God and beneficial in matters belonging to God might prevail, while those striving in the opposite direction would be crushed in their schemes and fail.”

By this principle, the prudent dispensation of the holy Fathers is known to have assigned Christian princes a significant role in appointing the governors of churches: through their most sincere diligence, the rashness of ambitious men, if it emerged, could more easily be restrained, while the unanimity of the religious could more readily gain strength in their endeavors and fulfillment of their wishes.

Hugh persisted in such speeches and devoted himself to admonitions of this kind toward the prince whenever any opportunity brought him into familiar contact with him, or whenever he obtained more private conversation with him. He approached him frequently for many reasons: sometimes summoned by the king himself, sometimes going to him voluntarily on account of the various needs of the house that Hugh had founded and governed.

At that time many adversities repeatedly arose for the king from every direction. He bore them continually more lightly through the spiritual man’s varied consolation; at times he overcame them more easily by relying on Hugh’s prayers; and most often, instructed by Hugh’s counsels, he avoided them with greater foresight and prudence.

## CHAPTER VII. How, when the king was in danger on the British Sea, he attributed his deliverance to Hugh, and was said to have vowed that he would hasten to promote him to the episcopal rank if he reached the harbor safely

On one occasion the king was crossing the open sea with a sizable fleet, between Normandy and Brittany, when a violent storm suddenly arose and he was nearly shipwrecked. At the first watch of the night the sea swelled, and, driven by raging winds and enormous waves, seemed either to resist or to batter the ships. It labored now to thrust the vessels into the midst of the stars, now to plunge them into the abyss.

I do not know whether the human condition has ever endured anything more grievous in this play of the elements. Under that death—and under an image of death more bitter than death itself—a considerable portion of time was spent, teaching each sailor that, to a discerning observer of the end of things, the whole span of mortal life is scarcely reckoned a brief moment.

King, counselor, powerful man, strong man, rich man, old man, or young man—none complained of all that he had lived until then, or that he had ever seen a calm and tranquil day. The immediate image of death before their eyes compelled some to wish that they had already endured the sting of the death that was now upon them. Those whose minds were sounder devoted themselves to confessing their sins, deriving concern for the future from despair of the present life. Most cried out with groaning prayers and vows to the Lord, to the saints, and to the holy women.

At last the king himself burst into these words:

“O, if only my Carthusian Hugh were keeping vigil now! If only he were at this moment devoting himself to secret prayers! If only he were taking part with his brothers in the solemn watches of the divine offices! Then surely God would not so greatly forget me!”

Then he prayed and groaned more deeply:

“God, whom the prior of Witham serves in truth, through his intervention and merits mercifully have pity on us, who have justly been brought into such distress because of our sins.”

Some also report that he vowed that he would hasten to promote Hugh to the episcopal rank if he deserved to reach the harbor safely. Immediately the roar of the sea and the whirlwind of the winds subsided and vanished. The waves fell, a gentler breeze returned, and the strait became completely calm. All the ships reached the desired shore. Everyone offered thanks to divine mercy, and thereafter the king devoted himself entirely to reverence for the man of God.

## CHAPTER VIII. How Hugh devoted himself wholly to prayer, so that by habit he uttered the word “Amen” in his sleep; how he conducted himself at table; and how, whatever occupation he had in hand, he gave himself to it entirely

[Col. 0976A]

When the construction of both dwellings—the brothers’ and the monks’—had finally been completed [Note: As I have stated elsewhere, its completion required seven or eight years.], Hugh devoted himself to the customary exercises of holy living, with greater freedom and therefore greater intensity. All the time that the mere necessity of sleep did not claim from him he gave to prayer, reading, meditation, or spiritual conversation and exhortation.

Yet if one had been closely associated with him, had watched him more attentively while he slept, and had carefully listened when he reported what his waking spirit had perceived while free amid the bonds of sleep, one might have thought that the mind’s constant wakefulness never deserted his sleeping body. Whether resting by day or by night, one could hear him a hundred times, with a powerful impulse of the spirit and a firm pressing of the lips, uttering with his mouth that mystical word so often repeated by the Lord: “Amen,” as though it were the conclusion of a preceding prayer.

Nothing else came from the mouth of the sleeper, as happens with many who utter voices or words in their dreams. Rather, he repeated it gently and very peacefully, pausing, sometimes at longer intervals and sometimes more frequently, prolonging the first syllable slightly and sending the last upward as though shooting it from a bow, countless times.

Nor is it surprising that his inner serenity, deepest clarity, and pure sweetness did not desert him in sleep, since, while awake, external vanity, blind curiosity, and impure pleasure could in no way entangle him in their allurements.

When he took bodily nourishment and ground earthly food with his jaws, then above all his ears hungered for and drank in the word of God. If, as was customary on feast days, he entered the refectory with the brothers and dined with them, he had his eyes on the table, his hands in the dish, his ears toward the book, and his heart toward God, just as he himself admonished and instructed the others.

If he ate alone in his cell [Note: That is, on weekdays, according to Carthusian custom; they ate together in the refectory only on Sundays and feast days.], the book and the little table divided the duties of his eyes between them. His eyes moved back and forth: on one side lay the open book, on the other the bread that had been set before him. Pottage was added only rarely; more often water served as both drink and broth. The most precious seasoning of these meals was never absent: the word of God.

At every time and in every place, whatever the reason of the place and time required, he did himself and urged others to do. He had so thoroughly converted this orderly and salutary discipline into a habit that he always seemed wholly and undividedly present to whatever the arrangement of the place or hour prescribed that he attend to. He observed the same practice even while resting in bed.

As long as he was in good health, his bed never held him awake even for a moment. As soon as his limbs had been received by the bed, they too immediately received sleep. If he was ever awakened untimely by some circumstance, he promptly either rose to pray or, within a moment, fell back into sleep.

## CHAPTER IX. How people flocked to Hugh at Witham to receive consolation; how many wished to live the religious life with him, though he did not quickly or readily receive those who knocked

While Hugh flourished at Witham in these and similar pursuits of spiritual discipline and profitably pursued the study of the spiritual life with his fellow disciples, many religious men [Note: Among these were Andrew and Alexander, mentioned in the following chapter; Prior Robert and Sacristan Ralph, in chapter 12; and Walter—who, according to Wharton, *Anglia Sacra*, part I, p. 586, became a Carthusian after having been prior of Barthon, though he later returned to the priorship.] of different conditions and professions flocked to him. They confidently expected to be edified and instructed by seeing and hearing him, and to be refreshed by the gift of the consolation they desired.

No one’s hope deceived him, and no one was deprived of the pious desire of his heart. At Witham everyone was given examples of perfect religious life; all carried away sound instruction; and each person was filled with the affection of holy devotion.

From there the fragrance of this holy reputation spread gently throughout all the regions of Britain. Its sweetness affected the hearts of many so powerfully that highly learned men, richly endowed with various revenues, abandoned the pomp of this world and sought with complete devotion the humility of Hugh’s holy and sincere way of life, embracing it with complete eagerness.

The most illustrious masters of the liberal disciplines rejoiced under the teaching of so great a master to fulfill the apostolic saying:

“If anyone among you thinks that he is wise, let him become a fool, so that he may be wise” (1 Corinthians 3:10).

Having renounced the world’s empty wisdom under the discipline of such a teacher, they themselves became so learned and teachable by God that they pursued the path of Christian philosophy with the unvarying straightness of their lives.

Some monks also, as well as members of the regular clergy, desired to place themselves under the discipline of the diligent shepherd. They wisely recognized that although the bodily pasture found with him was arid, it was more abundantly compensated by the richness of spiritual nourishment.

But Hugh, the superior, being prudent and circumspect in every respect, did not open the door quickly or readily to those who knocked. As the Apostle advises, he tested the spirits to see whether they were from God, and did so not without sweetness and a certain gentle severity. To some he opened only after they had persevered in knocking through more extensive testing.

## CHAPTER X. On the apostasy of the brothers Andrew and Alexander, and on their insults and blasphemies against Hugh and the Carthusian order

As became clear from the outcome, it did not please the Lord that all those to whom our Hugh had opened the door should persevere. Some turned back, among them Andrew and Alexander.

Andrew was regarded as a monk and sacristan of the monastery called Mulchelney [Note: In *Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. I, pp. 194 and 197, it is called Michelniense and Micelnense, in Dorsetshire.]. Alexander [Note: A letter of Peter of Blois survives, no. 86, encouraging him to constancy.] had been, as the common expression has it, a secular canon.

Having turned to rebellion, they provoked Hugh harshly. Andrew raged with somewhat greater moderation, but Alexander, without any appearance of restraint, did many evils to his Paul [Note: An allusion to Timothy, chapter IV: “Alexander the coppersmith did me much harm.”]—that is, against Hugh.

“You have most wickedly deceived us,” he said, “and led us into a place of horror and vast solitude, deprived and stripped of pleasant dwellings and abundant possessions. As though there were no dwelling places of religious quiet in the world, you prescribe that we hide here among the thickets in a beastly manner and fashion.

“The whole earth abounds in communities of living religious, where both the multitude of those living together would provide us consolation and the perfection of their life would sufficiently serve us as an example. Yet here we are, alone and without consolation, languid and sluggish through listlessness. For whole days we see no one whom we might imitate; we look only upon the walls enclosing us.

“Nor are your cleverly argued reasons allowed to prevail over us indefinitely. Your speech always contradicts our clear and most reasonable judgments. Yet the yoke of this still exceedingly rare and novel rule is imposed upon us as though Christianity had perished everywhere except among the Carthusians, and as though the path of salvation had been discovered by scarcely a few insignificant men. But those who are not blind to what is better neither ought nor are able to remain any longer under these useless and empty practices.”

With these and similar words he attacked that holy order with blasphemies and, in the madness of his obstinacy, assailed the man of God with such insults.

Meanwhile Hugh grieved over the dangers of those who had already established within themselves the wicked discourse of apostasy. He also feared the scandal to the weak and newly converted, whom the tempestuous storm of such men’s behavior more violently afflicted amid the unavoidable waves of temptation arising from every direction.

Their spirit—for they were badly strengthened—was like a whirlwind striking the wall of that holy society and tearing apart its structure with all its might. How much sadness and weariness occupied that holy breast, so tender in fraternal compassion and true piety, because of their bitter obstinacy, even he who endured it could not, as he often confessed, express in words.

Later we saw this same Alexander [Note: During the last three years of St Hugh’s life, in which the author of the Life was attached to Hugh.], by then a Cluniac monk, when circumstances had turned out somewhat against his wishes, overcome by regret for his change of order and seeking the favor of Hugh, then a bishop, with ambitious entreaties. He repeatedly begged us also to intervene so that he might deserve to return to the dwelling in the true paradise which, as he claimed, he had foolishly lost.

But, as it is said of Esau through the Apostle, “he found no place for repentance, although he sought it with tears” (Hebrews 12:17).

The aforementioned Andrew also returned, deprived of the honor of his name, to the familiar cradle of his childhood [Note: That is, as I interpret it, to Mulchelney.].

## CHAPTER XI. How difficult our Hugh was in receiving those who had once apostatized, and how tenderly he loved the peaceful perseverance of those who remained in their religious life

Hugh was always found exceedingly reluctant to receive those who had once departed from the order, whether monks or lay brothers. He maintained that this religious life must above all carefully guard against the fickleness of unstable men, whom he described by the name “chaff.” By this he meant those who, at the slightest movement of temptation, separated themselves from the fellowship of the good, shaken out from the threshing floor of their undertaken profession.

He said that such men might live more suitably in other religious places, where the discipline of the active life could sometimes advance even these people toward salvation. He maintained that, precisely because such a society—tested and proved by experience—was rejected by the Carthusian order, this was beneficial both to those who were turned away lest they enter and to those admitted within who remained in interior peace: when the former were not entrusted with what they were less suited for, their arrival caused no hindrance to the others.

In this matter he never admitted the pleas of anyone, however beloved or eminent. He closed the door of a return to all who had voluntarily abandoned the enclosure of his sheepfold and had previously shown themselves unmanageable within it.

In every respect he guarded the peace of his people as though it were his own salvation. It seemed to him that not only those disturbed this peace who presumed, through some wickedness, to assail their holy and delicate Sabbath, but also those who pretended not to notice the attackers, failed to restrain those already within, or negligently prevented those who would attack them—though excluded—from entering.

## CHAPTER XII. How, although he was concerned to acquire the books necessary for his community, Hugh nevertheless, through an extraordinary impulse of charity, voluntarily had returned the library [Note: That is, the Holy Bible, which the ancients commonly called “the library.”] which the king had acquired for him from the monks of Winchester; how from that time a special affection grew between the monks of Winchester and the hermits of Witham, through which Prior Robert of the cathedral church and Sacristan Ralph became solitaries at Witham; and how the author of this Life asserts that he wrote it at their request

[Col. 0979D]

It is pleasing to relate briefly certain deeds of this man, filled with a twofold love—namely, love of God and of his neighbor—which provide a notable sign of the most sincere charity that shone forth so powerfully in him.

By this time, with the number of brothers nearly complete according to the custom of that order and the regular buildings also suitably finished, the diligence of this good shepherd kept watch continually over the souls of the sheep entrusted to him, which had to be built up without interruption in their holy purpose.

As a considerable aid in this work, he devoted no sluggish effort to preparing, purchasing, and acquiring by whatever means he could sacred books. He used to say that these were to religious people, especially those living a solitary life, what delights and riches were in peaceful times, what weapons and armor were in wartime, what food was in famine, and what medicine was in sickness.

From this it happened that, when on one occasion he was speaking more familiarly with the king and introduced a mention of the scarcity of books, the king urged him to devote himself to having books copied by hired scribes. He replied that he lacked parchment. Then the king said: “And how much money do you wish to have given you to make up this deficiency?” “One mark of silver,” he replied, “will suffice for a long time.” At this the king smiled and said: “Oh, how immoderately you burden these men!” He immediately ordered ten marks to be counted out for the brother who was with him. He also promised to send him one library containing the complete text of both Testaments.

The prior returned home. The king, not forgetting his promise, diligently sought a library of excellent workmanship which he could give him. At last, when he inquired more carefully, he was told that the monks of Saint Swithun had produced an outstanding library, newly and suitably made, in which it was intended that the brothers should read at table while eating.

[Note: [Col. 0979D] Elsewhere in the Roman Martyrology, under 2 July, Saint Swithun. Concerning him, see the Bollandists under that day, and Mabillon, volume III of the *Annals*, p. 98.]

When he learned this, he was exceedingly pleased. He went as quickly as possible to the prior of that church and, promising a generous recompense, asked that the desired gift be given to him—and obtained it without delay. Thus the prior of Witham, together with his brothers, received and inspected the library as a royal gift. They themselves were greatly delighted, and especially rejoiced that more painstaking correction would enhance still further the elegance of the script and the beauty of the entire work.

[Col. 0980C]

After this it happened that one of the monks of the church of Winchester came to Witham for the sake of edification.

[Note: [Col. 0980D] Or Winchester, concerning which see the *Monasticon Anglicanum*, volume I, p. 31, and the additions at folio 979.]

The prior, as was his custom, refreshed him with the utmost friendliness and with a conversation suited to his holy discretion. He suddenly learned from him with what great supplication the Lord King had deigned to request that very library from his prior.

“And indeed,” he said, “we rejoice all the more at this, that he has bestowed it upon your holiness. If it pleases you in every respect, matters have proceeded well. But if not—if in some part it differs from your customary practice—we shall promptly produce another, far better, to be arranged according to your wishes in every respect. For we made this one correspond to our own use and custom, and not without the expenditure of great toil.”

[Col. 0981A]

At this the prior, astonished—for he had not previously known by what means the king had obtained it—addressed the brother at once:

“Is it so? Has the lord king founded our church upon the fruit of your indispensable labor? Believe me, dearest brother: your library shall be restored to you immediately. But we also earnestly beseech, through you, the whole community of your brothers to deign to pardon our humility, because, through our agency, though we ourselves were unaware of it, they have suffered the loss of their book.”

When the monks heard this, they were profoundly alarmed. With groaning voices they begged him not to think or speak of such things, declaring that it would in no way benefit their church if the favor of the king, usefully won for them through such a gift, were for any reason to be forfeited.

“Is it true,” he said, “that you presume more than usual upon his favor, and that you are not distressed that he has been made well disposed toward your affairs by such a gift?”

When the monk declared that joy had arisen from this among all his brothers, Hugo continued:

“If this joy is to endure for a long time, it is necessary that the restitution made to you remain hidden from everyone. But if you are wholly unwilling to receive this library secretly, I shall restore it to the one who sent it here. If you take it back, however, he shall in no way learn of this through us.”

What more need be said? The monks received their book as though they had acquired it by a recent gift. They were greatly gladdened by the book, but much more by the sweetness of the one who had sent it and restored it, and by the fullness of his charity.

[Col. 0982B]

From that time forward, especially, there grew among the inhabitants of both places—namely, the monks of Winchester and the hermits of Witham—a prerogative of exceptional affection which, by God’s grace, would endure forever.

Afterward, the men worthy of every praise, Robert, prior of the cathedral church of Winchester,

[Note: [Col. 0981D] Of Winchester, and afterward prior of Witham, unless he was someone other than the man mentioned in book V, chapter 24.]

and Ralph, sacrist of that same church,

[Note: [Col. 0981D] The abbreviator says that the *Life of Saint Hugh* was written at the request of this man and the said Robert. He seems to have learned this from the author’s first prologue, which is absent from the manuscripts.]

having become solitary inhabitants of Witham, made excellent progress in their solitude.

“The author of our great Life of Hugh says that, at their request, he committed to posterity in writing those things which he wrote about him.”

[Col. 0981]

Here ends the second book.

# PROLOGUE TO THE THIRD BOOK

[Col. 0981B]

Since, by the Lord’s favor, we have sketched in a summary fashion, in whatever style, the deeds of the blessed man by which he deserved to please almighty God from the very time of his childhood up to his episcopate, let a brief account now run through how, with heavenly grace attending him, he ascended to the episcopate, and how he lived and taught in that office.

For we do not now promise to recount each individual deed, nor even the principal ones among his deeds and words. Rather, we shall recount only those things—not all of them, even so—which we have learned with greater certainty from his actions and memorable sayings and retained in our memory. In doing so, we do not seek to arouse the reader’s or hearer’s excessive wonder, but rather the edification of those who desire to know and imitate what is holy and salutary.

For in this matter also he had deeply and perfectly absorbed the gravity and humility handed down by the holy founders of the Carthusian order:

[Note: [Col. 0982D] It is clear from this passage that the Carthusians have always sought, not so much miracles in the eyes of men as a holy life in the sight of God.]

he seemed to wonder at or emulate nothing less than miraculous prodigies, although he would recount with pleasure and venerate more profoundly those things read or learned about holy men.

[Col. 0981D]

I say that he recounted these things to commend those who displayed them and to stimulate those who admired such deeds, whereas for him the holiness of the saints alone was a miracle, and alone was sufficient both as a miracle and as an example.

[Col. 0982C]

For him there was one universal miracle of his Creator: the inward remembrance of his Maker, which never left him, and the astonishing and inexplicable multitude of his mighty works.

It was also known to everyone who had been more closely attached to him that, through him, while he lived—whether he knew it or not—the Lord had displayed many miracles, sometimes for his own relief and more often for the assistance of others. Nor, with heavenly grace providing aid, will certainty concerning this matter be denied to anyone among the faithful to whom we shall communicate these things in some fashion through writing.

Let this preliminary account from the preface of this third little book concerning the life of the blessed man suffice. Now, however uncultivated the style may be, let it unfold the sequence of the history.

[Col. 0981]

Here ends the prologue.

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 0983]

## CHAPTER ONE  
### How Hugh was elected bishop

[Col. 0983A]

After the venerable Walter, bishop of Lincoln, had been advanced to the archiepiscopal see of the church of Rouen,

[Note: [Col. 0983C] In the year 1183 Rotrodus, archbishop of Rouen, died, and Walter of Coutances, bishop of Lincoln, succeeded him. Thus says the *Chronicle of Rouen*, edited by Labbe, volume I of the *Bibliotheca nova*, p. 369. The same is confirmed by the *Chronicle of the Monastery of the Dead Sea*, p. 1440, in Martène, volume III of the *Anecdota*. The *Chronicle of Rouen* adds: “In this year, 1185, Walter of Coutances was received as archbishop of Rouen on the feast of Saint Matthias.” Trivet agrees with this as to the year, but omits the day.]

Henry II, king of the English, held discussions at Eynsham for nearly eight continuous days with bishops and the magnates of the realm concerning various affairs of the kingdom.

[Note: [Col. 0983C] Two monasteries bearing almost the same name are recorded in the *Monasticon Anglicanum*, volume I: Evesham in Worcestershire, p. 144, and Eynsham in Oxfordshire, p. 258. It appears that this assembly was compelled to meet at the latter.]

At that same monastery, at that time, Baldwin, archbishop of Canterbury, of pious memory,

[Note: [Col. 0983C] Baldwin was archbishop from 1184 until 1191, when he died in Palestine, according to Pagi in his critical notes on Baronius, p. 701. Wharton, however, in *Anglia Sacra*, part I, p. 113, maintains that he died in 1190.]

and some of his suffragan bishops had gone there as guests. The king also arrived there each morning and, after holding discussions with the men mentioned above, returned again to his palace at Woodstock.

[Note: [Col. 0983D] Possibly the same place as Wodestkam, mentioned below in chapter 8, and also Wdestoc, where, according to Henry of Huntingdon in Acher’s volume III of the *Spicilegium*, p. 503, Robert, bishop of Lincoln, is said to have been struck by apoplexy while speaking with the king.]

At that time several elections of bishops and abbots were held there.

[Note: [Col. 0983D] Trivet reports in his *Chronicle* that the prelates and nobles were summoned by the king in 1185, but he does not specify the place to which they were summoned. Baronius says, on the authority of Roger, that they were summoned to London, and, together with Trivet, assigns as the reason the collection of an aid for the Holy Land. No one asserts or denies that they were also assembled at Eynsham in this or the following year.]

[Col. 0983B]

The canons of Lincoln had also come there to elect—or rather to receive—the bishop elected by heaven.

At that time there were not a few persons of influence in that church, bound or devoted to counsels and services, including courtly services. In secular affairs they were renowned, excelling particularly in abundance of literary learning and worldly wealth. Most of them considered no bishopric, however extensive, to be greater than their own importance, since they themselves were furnished with revenues greater than those of any large bishopric.

Some of them, whether for the “good work,” in the Apostle’s phrase, or, in accordance with worldly ambition, for the dignity of honor and power, would by no means have refused to become bishops had someone been present to compel them.

But with the Lord holding the king’s heart in his hand and inclining it wherever he wished, with the metropolitan and several other religious persons agreeing—above all, through the urging of Reginald, bishop of Bath, who has been mentioned earlier—the king himself took care to provide a more suitable shepherd for the guardianship of so many of the Lord’s sheep.

That diocese contains four pairs of archdeaconries,

[Note: [Col. 0984C] Henry of Huntingdon enumerates these, together with the archdeacons, in the volume cited above, p. 504.]

and extends across nine counties and more. It contains very large cities and innumerable parishes; nor is another bishopric easily found that is larger or more populous.

The distinguished see had been vacant for approximately eighteen years—ten years before the consecration of the aforesaid bishop and two and a half years after his translation.

[Note: [Col. 0984C] The calculation begins in the year 1167, when, according to Trivet, Robert, bishop of Lincoln, died, though neither month nor day is added or has yet been discovered. If so, not approximately eighteen years but nineteen would have elapsed if Hugh had been consecrated bishop on Saint Matthew’s day in 1186.]

[Note: [Col. 0984C] It requires examination from what point this two-and-a-half-year period after the translation should be reckoned, especially since Walter did not preside over the church of Lincoln for long, existing there for only one year, as the Cambrian says in Wharton’s *Anglia Sacra*, part II, p. 418.]

Fifteen years, moreover, had passed before his consecration.

[Note: [Col. 0984D] Fifteen years had elapsed since the death of Robert, who, as I stated above, died in 1167 or 1166, in an uncertain month, by the year 1182. Yet I have found nowhere whether Walter was consecrated to Lincoln in that year. It nevertheless appears probable from the fact that, according to Roger as cited by Baronius, Geoffrey received a mandate from the pope in 1181 either to receive holy orders or to resign the bishopric; he chose the latter in 1182, on the Epiphany of the Lord. Walter succeeded him and was bishop of this church for one year.]

Through so many years that field of the Lord had been deprived of cultivation and industry. It is therefore hardly surprising that it lay foul and overgrown with the thorns of vices and the many shoots of abuses. The king, perceiving that the danger of so great an evil was attributable to him—since it was clear that he had been the author of so ill-considered an appointment—strove by every means, through the vigor of an exceptionally worthy cultivator, to compensate for the losses caused by the neglect of cultivation for so long.

The clergy therefore, while vainly striving toward divergent preferences, and while none of them, as was said, sincerely desired anything except his own advancement, pressed many of their number to advise them insistently to seek as their pastor the prior of Witham, a man of incomparable goodness.

[Col. 0984C]

His holiness was praised by many, his discretion, his affability; his religious devotion was exalted without measure. In short, it was proclaimed that every elegance of character and the complete square of every virtue had come together in this one man. By the unanimous voice of many he was acclaimed as no less than worthy of the highest priesthood.

At this point you might have seen the aforesaid men at first seemingly overwhelmed by a kind of horror—men, to be sure, who perceived the things of the flesh; men, I say, who even in the cause of God sought what belonged to men rather than what belonged to God. Finally, they declared, not without mocking laughter, that the culture of that region, its customs, and its language were either wholly contrary to their own or entirely unknown to them.

But their mockery was salutarily mocked, to their great advantage, by those who judged soundly. They too, suddenly changing their minds, unanimously elected the man whom they had childish­ly despised, to the immense honor not only of themselves but of the entire holy Church.

Thus the one whom the Lord had chosen from eternity for this very purpose was, at the divinely appointed time, chosen by men. Those who knew him rejoiced; those who had not known him marveled; and all together praised the Lord God with the loudest voice.

## CHAPTER TWO  
### How Hugh, considering the first election made concerning him invalid and void, persuaded those who came to him to return to the cathedral church and hold a canonical election there

At the request of the clergy, with the king’s approval and the nobles’ acclamation together with the bishops, the election was immediately confirmed by the metropolitan, while Hugh meanwhile remained hidden in his hermitage, entirely unaware of what those men far removed from him were doing concerning him.

[Col. 0985C]

From the very place where the election had been held, certain leading electors were sent to him, already hopeful clerics and sons of their church. Bringing the lord archbishop’s mandate, together with royal letters, they reached him and explained the circumstances of his calling to the higher office.

When he had heard this and examined the letters they had brought—for among other things they announced that he was to present himself with all speed to the king and the archbishop in order to discuss the matter of his consecration—he immediately gave the following response to what he had heard and read:

[Col. 0985D]

“It is not surprising,” he said, “if the lord archbishop, or even the lord king, gladly wishes to see my person, unworthy though I am of such an honor and altogether unequal to so great a burden, advanced to a higher rank.

“For who would doubt that it would please the king if he saw men whom he had summoned from distant regions under pretext of religion flourishing with happy success in his kingdom? Likewise, who does not know that it would be welcome to the lord of Canterbury, who appears almost alone among the bishops of this land to display the religious habit,

[Note: [Col. 0985D] Baldwin belonged to the Cistercian order. Besides him, there were still living Gilbert, formerly abbot of Gloucester and first bishop of Hereford, later bishop of London, and John, formerly of the Cistercian order and bishop of Norwich—perhaps also some others.]

that he should receive as coadjutors in the pastoral office he has undertaken men who are experienced in the regular discipline?

“Nevertheless, these wishes or efforts of theirs cannot prejudice your rights. It is your responsibility to choose freely a rector whose governance and character you will thereafter necessarily have to endure.

“In short, the election of an ecclesiastical rector must be held not in the royal palace, nor in a pontifical council—provided no danger of schism or other crime intervenes—but rather in the chapter of the particular church.

“Therefore, to make known to you the opinion of my insignificance, know that I consider everything done concerning the election invalid and wholly void. You too, treating as undone whatever a part of your assembly is known to have attempted in this matter, return, with God’s blessing, to your own church.

“There, relying equally upon the counsel and assistance of the Holy Spirit, solemnly celebrate the canonical election of your pastor. To accomplish this worthily, keep before your eyes not the will, grace, or favor of the king, the prelate, or any other human being, but solely the will, grace, and favor of almighty God.

“You will obtain no other answer from my insignificance. Go, then, and may the good angel of the Lord accompany you.”

Since he persisted in this decision and could not by any means be induced to present himself to the king or archbishop for such a matter, the men who had been sent to him returned as quickly as possible. They were extraordinarily edified in every respect by what they had heard from him and observed about him.

Not they alone, but everyone who heard of it marveled and rejoiced greatly. All praised and magnified in him the sincerity of his spirit, the excellence of his discretion, the liveliness of his counsel, and his zeal for ecclesiastical liberty.

## CHAPTER THREE  
### How, after the second election had been held at Lincoln, he replied to those sent to him that he would not undertake the episcopal burden without the obedience of the prior of the Carthusian house

When these matters had been reported to the chapter of Lincoln, the whole body of that college rejoiced all the more, as though it had received in its elected man a pledge of future vigor and certain first fruits of virtue. Those who had previously complained that they had been badly led astray and deceived into choosing as their rector and lord a man barbarous by nature and, as they feared, rough and uncivilized in conduct now, having discovered the power of his goodness and wisdom, hastened to elect him anew and most devoutly begged him to deign to undertake the ministry of pastoral care over them.

Again, several more messengers than before were sent, bearing letters from the chapter and also from the king and archbishop. Since everyone believed that the matter was now completed and that he had no further means of postponing it, the fully instructed envoys came to him cheerful and happy.

The blessed man had long before foreseen that he would one day be brought by divine providence to the office of pontiff.

[Note: [Col. 0987D] This was based on the prediction of the old man mentioned in book I, chapter 9, and of another, Bovo, in book II, chapter 2, and perhaps on another revelation known to him but unknown to us.]

Thus, because he grieved that what could not be avoided would eventually occur, he wished, as far as he could, to delay its happening and prevent it from happening too soon.

After hearing the envoys’ words and examining the letters mentioned above, he addressed them as follows:

“It is astonishing,” he said, “that wise and civilized men should so urgently solicit an uncultivated and ignorant man such as I, seeking to deprive me of the quiet of solitude, familiar and dear to me since my youth, and endeavoring to thrust me into public gatherings and entanglements of affairs wholly unfamiliar and untried by me.

“But since, as I see, my arguments cannot dissuade you from this, know for certain that the end of your labor does not lie within my own power. You cannot be unaware that I am a man placed under another’s authority.

“You know me as a monk subject to the commands of my prior,

[Note: [Col. 0987D] Namely, the prior of the Greater Chartreuse, since he was the prior-general of the whole order.]

bound to preserve obedience until death and wholly submissive to the command of the man who sent me to these lands.

“My superior has entrusted me with the custody of this house, and reason does not permit me, while neglecting it, to take up the governance of any other house or church.

“The lord of Canterbury, primate and chief of the English Church, is subject to the supreme pontiff; nevertheless, in a matter of this kind there is another authority intermediate between us. Either you must abandon the purpose of this petition, or you must undertake the labor of a burdensome journey as far as the Chartreuse. For no one shall place the burden of your load upon my shoulders without the command of my prior.”

## CHAPTER FOUR  
### How the men sent to him sought the prior of the Chartreuse, and how Hugh himself, devoting himself more vigorously to religion, prepared to face the episcopal yoke impending over him

When they received this reply and saw that his word could not at all be changed, they returned—saddened by the failure of the business for which they had come, but made cheerful by the virtues and remarkable steadfastness of their future pastor, from which they had received no small evidence.

But, not to linger over many details, honorable envoys were promptly dispatched to the Chartreuse. On arriving there, they presented in writing and orally the petition of the church of Lincoln, the king’s prayers, and the archbishop’s injunction.

[Col. 0987D]

They were received with due honor and graciously heard.

[Note: [Col. 0987D] That is, of the Greater Chartreuse, then headed, from 1178 onward, by Jancelin. Saussay, in the supplement to the *Martyrologium Gallicanum*, p. 1093, writes of him: “At the Greater Chartreuse, in the diocese of Grenoble, Jancelin, of blessed memory, the tenth prior general of the Carthusian order, piously breathed his last. For almost sixty years he presided over it, not without outstanding praise and holiness of life, as his *Mnemosynon* in the catalogue of the Fathers of that order records.” Thus he writes there. He died on the stated day in the year 1234.]

They hastened back, carrying to Hugh the prior’s and the brothers’ mandate that henceforth he should offer canonical obedience to the lord of Canterbury,

[Note: [Col. 0987D] The obedience which a bishop owes to an archbishop; the bishop of Lincoln owed it to the archbishop of Canterbury.]

and that, for the present, he should simply obey him in this matter, setting aside all hesitation and humbly accepting what it was clear had been divinely imposed upon him: the yoke of the Lord.

[Col. 0988A]

While they were dealing with these matters, Hugh did not give himself over to leisure. With every effort, by day and by night, he devoted himself to compunction of heart and purity and prepared himself through continual prayer—not for the adornment of costly garments or the splendor of vessels, as an occasion for empty glory, but for his soul, in view of temptation.

He awaited the impending change in his condition as a sailor watches a storm threatening beneath gathering clouds, or as a soldier, long kept in reserve, fears the encounter with enemy columns that he had once dreaded.

With God, his familiar provider and nourisher, he carefully discussed the expenses necessary for the feast on which he was to be anointed with the oil of gladness.

[Col. 0988B]

By expenses, I mean not those with which he might restore his bellies, themselves destined to be destroyed, with food likewise destined to be destroyed, but those by which he might strengthen with unfailing virtues the immense multitude of his inner senses and affections.

He considered nothing more pitiable than, on the day of so great a solemnity, to be outwardly drenched with the richness of sacramental oil while inwardly wasting away in the foulness of a burning conscience.

Seeking to guard against this monstrous misery, he conducted himself in procuring and preparing the resources necessary for this very purpose as though none of the study and labor he had devoted to the matter from his earliest age had accomplished anything.

Moreover, there continually passed before the eyes of his mind not the allurements of pleasures or riches desired by most people, not dignity or the excellence of power, and not even the assiduous attentiveness of servile obedience, but the bitter losses of the contemplative life and the detriments to peaceful and serene meditation and prayer.

No one, as he himself often confessed to us more privately and not without a groan, could adequately describe the daily anguish of his heart, by which he was tormented to the marrow, when he imagined that he would soon lose the fruitful leisure of his cell, to be replaced by the burdensome business of palaces.

He also feared that, when psalmody yielded to disputes and sacred reading ceased in favor of superfluous chatter, inward contemplation might likewise yield to other fantasies, and inner purity to external vanities.

[Col. 0988D]

Finally, when he learned that the messengers had returned—messengers whom he certainly would have preferred to return only then for the first time—he did not cease strengthening the brothers in their holy purpose with paternal exhortations and commending his own fear more earnestly to their prayers.

Let those who desire the episcopate so greatly, and those who aspire to the heights of prelacies by so many winding turns of crooked paths,

[Col. 0989A]

now see by what kind of virtues, with what riches of character, and with what rewards of merit they surpass this man.

Having been perfectly taught both to keep himself unharmed by wounds and to heal the wounds of others, and being so abundantly supplied with the nourishment of salutary doctrine, he spoke with the innermost affection of his heart and with the clearest effect in his actions:

“I am not a physician, and there is no bread in my house; do not appoint me ruler of the people” (Isaiah 3:7).

Yet the more deeply the blessed man attended in everything to his own deficiency, the more abundantly he deserved to receive the supplement of divine fullness, singing the words of the Teacher of the Gentiles:

“Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think anything as from ourselves; but our sufficiency is from God” (2 Corinthians 3:5).

Because he knew that this sufficiency came to him not from himself but from God, he did not wish to grow proud of what was borrowed or even given by another, nor to walk in great matters. Rather, attending to himself as being within himself, but regarding the gifts of God that he received as above himself, he strove with the whole affection of his mind to hold the lowest place at the Church’s wedding feast.

But the one who had set him apart from his mother’s womb and called him by his grace, so that through him he might glorify his name among many nations, compelled him by a friendly invitation to ascend higher, so that from the sufficiency bestowed upon him from heaven he might give food in due season to his fellow servants.

## CHAPTER FIVE  
### How, after the return of the messengers from the Chartreuse, Hugh was compelled by a third summons to leave his house; how, as he transferred himself toward London to receive consecration, he did not abandon the humility of his former order, but rather carried his bundle behind his saddle; and how at his consecration he was lavishly honored by royal munificence

[Col. 0989C]

After three months had elapsed from the day of his first election,

[Note: [Col. 0989C] After the first election at Eynsham they went to Witham for consent; from Witham, for the second election, to Lincoln; from there again to Witham; from Witham to the Greater Chartreuse; and from there they returned to Witham for the third summons; from Witham to London for the consecration. I remain uncertain whether all this could have been completed within the narrow space of three months.]

the aforesaid envoys returned from the Chartreuse, and by a third summons he was compelled to leave his house—he who long before had left his country and his kindred.

He therefore went forth to receive the blessing of episcopal consecration. As he proceeded to receive the heights of such great success, he did not abandon the depths of humility. Fulfilling in deed what he always revolved in his heart, he followed the advice of the wise man:

[Col. 0990A]

the greater he was, and the higher he climbed, the more he humbled himself in everything.

Retaining his customary gravity of spirit together with an outwardly humble appearance, he sat upon a horse adorned not with ornamental trappings but burdened behind the saddle with what he would use by day and by night, a bundle wrapped in skins and blankets.

[Cod., wrapped in blankets.]

Thus, while his clerics rode horses decorated with golden pack-saddles, the chosen one of the Lord rode among them. They tried by various devices to take his little bundle away from him and place it on their own pack-saddles.

But since it could be extracted from him neither by serious pleading that he permit this nor by joking—for before ascending to a higher rank he was careful not to abandon or alter, even slightly, the practice he had previously observed—they were overcome with intense worldly shame at the humility of the spiritual man.

When he was approaching the city of Winchester,

[Note: [Col. 0989D] Where the cathedral church was located. For more concerning it, see the *Monasticon Anglicanum*, volume I, p. 31, and Mabillon, volume III of the *Annals*, p. 567.]

where the royal household and a large crowd of citizens would be coming out to meet him, one of the clerics, unable to endure the embarrassment to his vain heart, secretly cut the straps by which the bundle mentioned above was fastened and became an unexpected thief, stripping the unwitting man of the burden he was carrying.

At last, arriving in London on the feast day of the blessed evangelist Matthew,

[Note: [Col. 0989D] Everyone agrees about the day, but not about the year.]

he was consecrated with episcopal blessing and most worthily joined to the apostolic order for preaching to the poor.

The king,

[Note: [Col. 0989D] Either the king was present at the consecration, or he was not far from it.]

rejoicing that his desire concerning Hugh’s promotion had been fulfilled, celebrated his joy with infinite gladness. He also bestowed upon him, with the greatest generosity, certain golden vessels, many silver ones, and various utensils for every necessary use, adding abundant funds for all the expenses of celebrating the solemnity.

## CHAPTER SIX  
### How, when enthroned at Lincoln, Hugh replied to the archdeacon of Canterbury that he would give him as much for the chair as he had given for the mitre; how he also replied to the steward of his household concerning the number of does to be taken; and concerning the marvel of the birds at Stow, as reported by the archdeacon of Menevia

[Note: [Col. 0989D] The archdeacon of Menevia was Gerald of Wales, a contemporary of Saint Hugh. Henry Wharton, in the preface to part II of *Anglia Sacra*, p. 20, rightly notes that he was archdeacon of Brecon in the church of Menevia—not archdeacon of both Brecon and Menevia, as Bale has it, nor first archdeacon of Brecon and afterward of Menevia, as Pits has it. Gerald held only the one archdeaconry of Brecon, although he is frequently called archdeacon of Menevia by the cathedral church in letters of bishops, kings, and himself. Furthermore, in the part of *Anglia Sacra* cited above, Gerald’s book *On the Lives of the Bishops of Lincoln* appears from p. 410, and from p. 420 his threefold work, or book *On the Lives of Six Contemporary Bishops*. In both places Gerald celebrates our Hugh with high praise, but he describes the story of the swan only in the latter work, p. 431 and following, in almost exactly the same words as the author of the *Life*. The same Gerald, in both his longer and shorter catalogues of his books, pp. 442 and 445, testifies that he also wrote “the Life of Saint Hugh, fifth after Remigius, of that same place,” namely, “bishop of Lincoln.” Yet this *Life* nowhere appears in *Anglia Sacra*, nor does Wharton observe in his general preface where it exists today. Perhaps this Life of Hugh is not different from the eulogies generously bestowed upon him by Gerald in the two works mentioned above, whatever Gerald’s words may seem to suggest otherwise.]

When he had been enthroned in his church, the archdeacon of Canterbury, who according to custom was requesting a solemn gift, is reported and known to have received this reply:

“Whatever I gave for the mitre, I shall give no more than that for the chair.”

When the steward of his household, whom the king had appointed for him, suggested that some of his does enclosed in his park ought to be caught to prepare a solemn banquet, and that it was not lawful for more to be captured than he himself had ordered, Hugh replied:

“Let three hundred be caught; and, if you see fit, do not hesitate to add to this number.”

What he had said simply, in accordance with the magnificence of his heart, was turned into a proverb for amusement by the king and courtiers to whom the remark became known.

Therefore, while everyone at Lincoln was celebrating with the greatest joy of heart the feast marking the arrival of the ruler appointed for them from heaven [Col. 0991B], the kindness of Christ appeared first to have alluded to it, not far from the city itself, by a clear and highly memorable sign. For on that day, or very near it, on which Bishop Hugh was first received at Lincoln and enthroned, a new swan—never before seen there—flew to his manor, situated about eight miles from the city of Lincoln, near Stow, delightfully covered with woods and ponds.

[Note: [Col. 0991D] “At his manor,” that is, at his estate or village. Ordericus Vitalis, Book IV, in Du Cange’s *Glossary of Medieval and Late Latin*: “He obtained two hundred and eighty estates (which, from *manere*, ‘to remain,’ we commonly call *maneria*).”]

[Note: [Col. 0991D] “Near Stow,” formerly a monastery restored by Remigius and transferred by his successor Robert to Eynsham. Hence it is read in the *English Monastic*, vol. I, p. 262: “Stow in the county of Lincoln, a cell of Eynsham.” And again: “A monastery of monks at St Mary’s of Stow. Remigius, bishop of Lincoln, built it anew.” See also Gerald of Wales, *Sacred History of England*, part II, p. 417: “He prudently transferred the monks of Stow to Eynsham, in a laudable exchange, which was highly advantageous to the Church of Lincoln both because of the proximity and pleasantness of the manor and because of the nearness of the prebends.”]

Within a few days it had crushed by the weight of its great bulk all the swans it found there, except for one female, which was spared for companionship, not for the increase of its breed. For it was almost as much stronger than an ordinary swan as a swan is larger than a goose. Yet it was superior to a swan in every respect, especially in color and whiteness. In addition to its size, it differed in this respect: it did not display, as swans do, a swelling on its bill or any blackness. Rather, it had the same flat surface of the bill, marked with a becoming saffron color, as were its head and the upper part of its neck.

This royal bird, remarkable both in quality and in size, was brought to the bishop in his chamber at his first arrival at that place.
