It became domestic, as though spontaneously and without difficulty, because of the wonder it inspired. At once it took bread from his hand and ate it, and clung familiarly to him. In the meantime, as it seemed, it had shed all its wild nature and was averse neither to his touch nor to the approach or tumult of the crowds of attendants and onlookers gathered all around.

Sometimes, too, when it was being fed by the bishop, it would thrust its head, together with the entire length of its neck, into his broad and very capacious sleeve and into the inner fold of his garment. There it would remain for some time, as though anxiously congratulating and playfully greeting its master, while muttering and searching for something.

The servants and keepers of the manor also asserted that, when it had been away from that place for some time according to custom, it usually became more lively than usual for three or four days before the bishop’s arrival. It would fly about on the surface of the river, beating the water with its wings and crying out in a loud voice. At times it would even leave the pond and walk with great strides, now toward the hall, now toward the farther gate, as though going out to meet its arriving master.

This too was remarkable: it made itself familiar and entirely tractable to no one except the bishop alone. Rather, while standing beside its master, it would defend him against the approach of others—as I myself witnessed several times with astonishment—crying out, threatening them with its wings and bill, and croaking in a loud voice according to the patterns of its nature. In this way it seemed to demonstrate that it belonged to him personally and clearly to declare that it had been sent to him alone as a sign.

[Note: [Col. 0992D] What has been said thus far about the swan is also found in Gerald of Wales at the place cited. It is uncertain which of the two borrowed it from the other, since both lived at Lincoln under Hugh and could have witnessed the events. The author of the *Life* adds what follows.]

[Note: [Col. 0992D] In the year 1200, when Easter fell on 9 April, and Hugh died in November.]

When the bishop came to that very place around the following Easter, shortly before his departure from this life—his final arrival there—the bird not only failed to offer him its customary greeting, but would not even allow itself to be threatened into coming out of the fishpond in which it was swimming. In the water itself it wore a mournful face and a sickly appearance, displaying no sign of cheerfulness in any movement.

Everyone present was astonished at this. At last, when the bishop ordered that it be brought in, even against its will, many people labored in vain for three days. Finally it was caught in a more remote reed bed, where it had fled and was hiding from its pursuers. When it was brought before the bishop, with its head hanging and its face ill, and with every gesture expressing sickness, it presented a mournful image. At the time the novelty of this spectacle filled those who saw it with amazement.

But when the bishop soon departed from that place and, after the lapse of the sixth month from that time, entered upon the way of all flesh, and was never again seen by the bird that loved him, those who considered the outcome of the matter clearly understood what this mournful behavior had foretold: namely, why it had given its master so sorrowful a final farewell. It nevertheless remained there for a long time afterward.

[Note: [Col. 0992D] The months meant here are evidently the complete intervening months between April and November.]

## CHAPTER VII

How solicitous our Hugh was to place suitable persons in the Church of Lincoln and to join them to his side for the support of the burden imposed upon him. This is Chapter Eight in the sequence of the longer *Life*.

[Col. 0993A]

Having thus briefly introduced the sign displayed to all in wonder by the famous bird on behalf of the man of God, let us proceed, with the help of the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, to make known to the faithful, insofar as we can, other notable signs of his merits.

First of all, it seems especially worthy of remembrance how much effort and concern he devoted to adorning the Church entrusted to him with distinguished men. For he weighed and considered deeply that without the assistance of good men he could benefit neither the people nor the clergy whom he governed, and could not adequately assist those who sought the justice of ecclesiastical jurisdiction. He therefore earnestly endeavored to associate with himself men endowed with wisdom and knowledge and, what is more important, highly approved in the fear of the Lord. Relying on their counsels and accompanied by their assistance, he most vigorously fulfilled the office of government he had undertaken.

Finally, through these men he made the Church of Lincoln more glorious and more richly furnished than all the Churches throughout the world. When prebends or other benefices became vacant, he bestowed them upon these men. He placed them in various dignities and appointed them to the several ecclesiastical functions. Such men he sought out with every effort, not only throughout the whole English world but also in foreign lands and in schools overseas, and incorporated them into the bosom of his Church.

He also approached his venerable metropolitan, Archbishop Baldwin, his brother mentioned above, and addressed him as follows:

“Reverend Father, your discernment knows how greatly it is expedient—not only for my soul, not only for the Church entrusted unworthily to me, but rather especially for us, and thereafter equally for the whole of holy religion—that I should strive not to show myself wholly useless in the office committed to me.

“I give thanks to God, the author of every good thing, because by his gift I do indeed desire this very thing. But how to fulfill what I have been granted to desire, I do not know; and that I am unequal to it by myself, you know first and better. Nor do I possess sufficient knowledge or ability for this; indeed, I have not sufficiently recognized by whom my deficiency in this respect may more fittingly be supplied.

“For I am a foreigner, and the less I know the natives of this land, the more imperfectly do I know by what supports of merit and by what proofs of learning they excel. Your long experience has procured you fuller knowledge of this matter. You were brought up among them; you presided over them for a long time; you know them, as the saying goes, inside and out.

“Therefore, looking not merely to my own danger but rather to yours—for you did not fear to promote so ignorant a man to this arduous task—entrust to me as assistants from among those who, by remaining at your side for a longer time, have shown themselves worthy in every respect and have been especially formed by your example. Let them be men whom I may safely admit to share the concern imposed upon me, and who may laudably support with me the burden of pastoral care.”

When the archbishop heard these words, he rejoiced greatly. From this single request of the holy man he clearly perceived many good qualities in him.

First, he saw how great was Hugh’s humility: that so great a man should think so meanly of himself, and should consider himself alone unworthy of the honor by which divine and human testimony alike proved him most worthy. He was astonished that, contrary to the usual course of human prosperity, a man raised from lowliness to the highest rank had grown more through humility than through dignity, more through gentleness than through domination.

He saw how zealously Hugh sought the salvation of his subjects, since he so earnestly desired the assistance of good men for securing it. He observed what benevolence Hugh possessed toward his primate, being conscious of his own purity, and what prudence he displayed in all things, since he wished those whom the metropolitan had employed in his own household to become his personal companions and foremost counselors.

Accordingly, he assigned to him as masters two of those who had been attached to himself: Robert of Bedford and Roger of Royston. Both of them appeared to excel throughout the entire clergy of England with distinguished prerogatives of grace.

[Note: [Col. 0993D] Robert appears to have received this surname either from the district of Bedford or from the monastery of St Alban’s, which is situated in the county of Bedford.]

[Note: [Col. 0993D] The same Roger as the one concerning whom Bzovius, in his *Annals* under the year 1200, p. 86, records: “Within fifteen days after the death of Master Roger of Roleston, dean of the Church of Lincoln, Hugh appeared to him, saying: ‘The Lord has granted me,’” and so forth.]

## CHAPTER VIII

How our Hugh incurred the king’s displeasure by excommunicating the king’s chief forester and excusing himself, when pressed by that same king, from conferring a prebend.

With these and other outstanding men carefully attached to his side, Hugh possessed the Spirit of God, of whom it is written, “Where the Spirit of God is, there is liberty” (II Cor. 3:19). He freely rebuked sinners and deferred to no powerful person against justice.

Thus it happened that, at the beginning of his promotion, while he was exercising strict ecclesiastical discipline against certain exalted powers of the kingdom, he appeared to have offended the king himself to no small degree.

[Note: [Col. 0994D] Baronius, drawing more briefly on Surius in this and the following chapter, and on Peter of Blois, explains who the foresters are and why they are so called.]

Among the other destructive abuses, the first plague in the kingdom of the English is the plague of the forest officials, which devastates the provinces. For this plague, violence is law, robbery is praised, equity is detestable, and innocence is guilt. No condition or rank, and no one inferior to the king—to express the whole matter briefly—remained or escaped unharmed when that injurious jurisdiction had not often attempted to crush him.

Hugh’s first encounter was with this destructive force. It was both his first cause for battle and the subject of his triumph. It first compelled him to wield the two-edged sword of the Spirit.

For when the forest officials began to rage, as they did against others, so also against Hugh’s own men, contrary to the liberty of his Church, matters eventually proceeded to the point that Hugh bound the king’s chief forester, named Geoffrey, with the bond of excommunication.

[Note: [Col. 0995D] As the next chapter states, he submitted to being beaten with rods and thereafter supported Hugh in conducting business.]

When the king learned of this, he blazed with violent anger. Meanwhile, one of the prebends of the Church of Lincoln became vacant through the departure of the canon who had held it and awaited a new dispenser. When the courtiers heard of this, they quickly begged the king to request in writing that it be conferred upon one of them. They thought that by this they would also be doing a service to the king, since they would give him an opportunity somehow to mitigate the royal indignation aroused against himself.

The king did not hesitate to favor their request, for in this matter too he was eager to test the bishop’s mind and purpose. At that time the king was staying at Wodestkam, while the bishop was at Dorchester, residences believed to be thirteen miles apart.

[Note: [Col. 0995D] Dorchester, once the episcopal see, which was transferred to Lincoln under Bishop Remigius.]

[Note: [Col. 0995D] From the distance between the two places it could perhaps be inferred whether Wodestkam is the same as Woldestok or Wdestoch, mentioned in Book III, chapter 1.]

When the bishop read the letters of request sent to him, he said:

“Ecclesiastical benefices ought to be conferred not upon courtiers but rather upon ecclesiastical persons, whose holders should serve not the palace, the treasury, or the *stacearium*—or *scocarium*—but, as Scripture teaches, the altar. My lord the king has means with which to reward those who serve his business; he has means with which to compensate in temporal matters those who labor for him in temporal service.

“It is good for him to allow those who are to serve the supreme King, after provision has been made for their needs, to enjoy their revenues, and not to consent to deprive them of their rightful stipends.”

[Note: [Col. 0996D] Or *scocarium*. On this word, see the note at the same place in Book V, chapter 13.]

Having said this, he did not fear to send the royal messengers back to him empty-handed and without result.

## CHAPTER IX

How, when summoned by the king because of the offenses just described, he answered in such a way that he departed free, with the king’s goodwill.

When these matters had been made known at court, concerning the new and still almost recent bishop of Lincoln there were people who, as it seemed, endeavored by poisonous speeches to incite the king, already sufficiently angered against him, to even greater fury.

“Now, my lord,” they said, “it is manifest how ungrateful this man is for your great benefactions. It is now clear where you have placed your labor and expenditure, while you watched so carefully over his promotion. Would that this inhuman man were content merely not to return thanks, and were not also bent on repaying such honor with injury!

“What can we hope he will do for you hereafter, or how can we trust that he will defer to your commands [*jussis*, supplied in the text], when we now see him, after so many benefactions—and benefactions still fresh—show such irreverent contempt for your excellence over such a small matter? We grieve that he has confused your prayers and your intimate bailiffs with such an insolent judgment.”

[Note: [Col. 0996D] Elsewhere called *ballivi*, German *Landvogt* or *Amtmann*.]

Although that prince was greatly disturbed by this, he did not exceed the bounds of moderation. He immediately sent for the bishop and summoned him to appear before him.

Knowing that the bishop was already approaching the doors, the king withdrew with the whole company of nobles then present into an adjoining wood, having mounted their horses. There, taking his seat in a pleasant place, with the councillors and other magnates seated around him in a circle, he ordered that no one rise to greet the approaching bishop and that no one salute him when he arrived.

Without delay Hugh appeared, stood before them, and greeted the king and those seated with him; but no one returned his greeting. When he saw them sitting silent and unconcerned about him, he approached more closely. Gently placing his hand on the shoulders of a certain great councillor who was seated nearest the king’s side, he made a place for himself beside the king.

When everyone persisted in obstinate silence for a long while, the king at last raised his lowered face and ordered one of the attendants to give him a needle and thread. Having received them, he began to sew with his own hand a wounded finger of his left hand, wrapping it in a small piece of cloth.

He did this so that, for a while, something might be happening, saying nothing in the meantime. He conducted himself as people who are exceedingly angry ordinarily do, when the rancor of their minds absorbs the function of their voice and their breath is obstructed in its passage.

When the bishop observed this, and recognized that all this pretended display was being made on his account, he looked down from a higher watchtower of inward reason upon the schemes of carnal thoughts. Then, turning to the king, he shattered the proud elevation of his heart with these very few words, and struck him down bodily, so that he could not withstand the force of the words, even falling backward upon the ground.

We shall give the words themselves, taking nothing away from them and adding nothing. He said:

“How like you are now to your kinsmen from Falaise!”

As though pierced through the heart by this weapon—gentle and light, indeed, but wonderfully penetrating and exceedingly sharp—the king stitched his fingers, then burst into laughter. Throwing his head back, he lowered his neck toward the ground and for a long while gave free rein to his laughter in that posture.

Those seated with him who understood the bishop’s words were held in extraordinary amazement. They marveled beyond measure that, at such a moment, such a reproach had been directed against so great a prince by such a man.

Yet they too, unable to restrain themselves from smiling, began, with astonished minds, to await [probably *exspectare*, rather than the printed *exspectantes*] what the king would finally answer. Several who did not understand the meaning of the words that had been spoken were even more astonished at the sudden change in the king’s behavior.

At last, realizing their ignorance, the king himself became the interpreter of the insult, so as to instruct them. Deeply stirred by the novelty of such a polished taunt, and himself admiring the man’s confidence, he began to speak:

“Do you understand what sort of insult this barbarian has inflicted upon us? I shall explain his words to you. It is established that the mother of our great-grandfather William, the conqueror of this land, came from a humble family and was born in the famous town of Normandy called Falaise.

[Note: [Col. 0997D] She was Hervela, or Harlotta, daughter of a furrier, by whom Robert, duke of Normandy, fathered William the Conqueror, the great-grandfather of King Henry II.]

“This town is especially renowned for the craft of furriery. Since this mocker saw me sewing my finger, he therefore said and reproached me as being like the people of Falaise and related to them.”

[Note: [Col. 0997D] A famous Norman town, together with its castle, otherwise called Falaise. Concerning it someone writes: “Falaise, with its castle, the homeland of William the Conqueror, is surrounded by very deep ditches and enclosed by two ponds.”]

“Nevertheless,” he said to the bishop, “tell me, good man, what did you think you were doing when, without consulting us, you subjected our chief forester to an anathema? Why did you also treat our little request with such contempt that you neither came to us yourself to explain the reason for your refusal nor sent us through our messengers a word that might please us?”

[Note: [Col. 0997D] The request that a prebend in the Church of Lincoln be granted to someone, which Hugh denied in the preceding chapter.]

To this complaint the bishop immediately replied:

“I know that you labored diligently for me to become a bishop. Therefore, in order to free your soul from the danger into which it might fall if I failed to carry out what is known to be my duty regarding the welfare of the Church entrusted to me, it was necessary for me to restrain its oppressor by ecclesiastical censure and not to hear the man who unjustly desired to extort a prebend for himself in that Church.

“As for approaching your excellence concerning either matter, I thought it not only superfluous but also inappropriate, since it is easy for your discernment prudently to recognize what is rightly done, and since your will is nevertheless inclined favorably to approve what you know to be right.”

Finding nothing in these arguments that could be contradicted, the king set aside the cloud of hostility he had rashly conceived. With a serene face he embraced the bishop, earnestly commending himself to his prayers, and left the whole matter to his judgment: namely, how he should restore the man bound by the sentence through the benefit of absolution.

The bishop absolved the man, who was now deeply contrite and humbled in spirit, after he had given the public oath required by the form of the Church, having him and his accomplices beaten with rods. After giving his blessing, he found Geoffrey devoted to himself with a special and increasingly familiar goodwill for the rest of his life, and attentive to his affairs.

[Col. 0997D]

By this single refusal Hugh also sharply restrained the courtiers from their violent demands for prebends, by which, like the rapacious talons of kites, they infested churches everywhere and plundered them, and he drove their importunity far from himself.

Yet even they vied with one another in serving and honoring him, so much so that he himself often highly praised the evidence of their devotion and diligence. He told his familiars that he would more gladly bestow greater benefices upon some of them if they were not entangled in the bonds of the court.

## CHAPTER X

That he considered prebendaries in churches bound to residence; how he answered a Parisian master who desired to become a prebendary in the Church of Lincoln; and how especially he loved unity among brothers and among all people.

Hugh made courtiers—or, indeed, clerics from any cathedral church—canons of his own church only rarely. In the Church of Lincoln especially, he required residence from those to whom he granted the canonical stipends of that Church.

For just as those who serve the altar properly share in the altar’s rights, so he said that the benefits of the altar came to those who did not serve it by an incongruous claim. And when churches happened thereby to be deprived of the due watches of those who served them [the manuscript reads *et ecclesias cum debitis*, “and the churches with due …”], this seemed [the manuscript reads *contingeret et speciem*, “it happened and the appearance …”] to have the character of robbery: men who would not serve were presuming to occupy the stipends assigned to those who were to serve in the spiritual militia.

He also established that the Apostle’s statement should be understood and observed especially in this matter: those who do not labor in the sanctuary should not eat what is consecrated in the sanctuary. For if the Doctor of the Gentiles boasts that he preached the Gospel without expense, how disgraceful, he said, must those be considered who, without zeal for evangelizing and without the service of ministering, presume to seize the expenses assigned to those who evangelize or minister!

We remember that at that time, in the year 1200, when Hugh was in Paris together with the author of the *Life*, a certain man of almost the highest reputation among the Parisian theologians and canonists once said to Hugh:

[Note: [Col. 0998D] The year 1200, when Hugh was in Paris with the author of the *Life*, as is established from Book V, chapter 19.]

“Lord bishop, you have displayed your Church as glorious beyond all the Churches of the entire world, distinguished by its multitude of clerics. It would be quite desirable for me—and I do not wish to conceal this from you—to be associated with their number under some title, however small.”

The bishop immediately replied:

“And we would gladly join you to their number if you are also willing to reside among them, and if your morals likewise answered your learning with equal steps.”

For that man himself presided over the Parisian schools and directed them.

[Note: [Col. 0998D] Let the Parisians determine who presided over the Parisian schools in that year.]

At that time he was more celebrated for learning than for discipline. Having received such an answer, he blushed that he had expressed himself too freely, and learned from his own case the truth of what he remembered having heard more than once in his homeland concerning this man’s most sincere freedom.

He is said to have departed from Hugh and thereafter applied himself to more disciplined conduct.

Hugh loved quiet and chaste men of spirit more closely. He did not admit others to his flock with a clear conscience, no matter how greatly they excelled in industry or in distinction of learning.

He said that nothing in this life was to be preferred to the good of peace, and that nothing was to be avoided more than the plague of sedition and disturbance. For this reason he warned people by every means to avoid the company of those who, possessed by another spirit, longed for schisms and sowed discord among brothers.

He urged all kinds of people without distinction, and especially prelates, to preserve inviolate the bond of unity and concord with their subjects, setting himself before them as an example.

For he said:

“Because I know that I observe the good of peace and unity more tenaciously with our sons, I consider no king and no mortal person whom I ought to fear. Nor do I lose that inner security which is the imitator and preparation of eternal tranquility.

“Nor, he said, is this peace granted to me by my lords—for this is what he called his canons—because they find me gentle and mild, as though wholly ignorant of strife. I am in truth more pungent and biting than pepper, and, presiding over their chapter, I am frequently inflamed to anger over matters of very little importance.

“But they know that they must endure me as they have received me, and so they make a virtue of necessity by deferring to me. I give them abundant thanks. For since I first began to reside among them, have they ever resisted me even in a single word?

“When the chapter has ended and everyone has departed, no one, I think, fears that he should distrust our affection for him; nor do I consider myself unloved by any of them.”

Such and so great was his loving affection for each of the sons of his Church from the beginning of his promotion until the final day of his life that he clearly proved himself an imitator of the one of whom the evangelist John makes this venerable declaration:

“Having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end” (John 13:1).

When he placed himself in their defense, if ever he recognized that one of them was being burdened by any attack, he was accustomed to say, not only by his actions but also in words:

“He who touches you touches the pupil of my eye” (Zech. 2:8).

## CHAPTER XI

How he dissuaded both Baldwin, archbishop of Canterbury, and his successor from persevering in the construction of chapels, which gave rise to the gravest discord between them and their Canterbury monks, and how he restored peace among them.

[Col. 1000A]

When Baldwin, archbishop of Canterbury, of pious memory, was hastening, at the instigation of certain people, to build in the territory of his city a church or chapel in honor of Stephen, the precious protomartyr, and Thomas, the renowned new martyr of the English, the monks of the cathedral church strongly opposed him, asserting that the undertaking was being attempted to their prejudice.

[Note: [Col. 0999D] On this, Baronius under the year 1186 writes: “By the authority of these presents”—the words are those of Pope Urban III—“we command that you may build a church in honor of the blessed martyrs Stephen and Thomas,” etc. But, as Trivet has under the year 1187: “Baldwin of Canterbury was forbidden by apostolic letters to proceed with the new church which he had begun,” etc.]

Hugh of Lincoln, consulted by the archbishop about this matter, gave a most certain prophecy, as the outcome of the affair proved:

“If, my lord archbishop, a schism—which would be disastrous—should arise between you and your chapter because of this undertaking; if the vigor of discipline should wither in your community and the rigor of the order diminish, no one’s judgment would suffice to measure beforehand how many dangers to souls would follow.

“Furthermore, you will have to subject your royal authority to servitude. You will also be exposed to the disdain and fear of the Roman Curia and of many men established in high rank and possessing diverse powers. At every hour and at every moment you will necessarily have to fear the movements and dispositions of the supreme pontiff.

“He himself will order the demolition of whatever he eventually learns has been undertaken prejudicially, whether the work has been completed or merely begun.”

[Col. 1000B]

When the archbishop said that Saint Thomas had conceived the purpose of establishing this building in honor of the holy levite Stephen, the bishop answered with considerable elegance:

“Let it be enough, then, that you have already been made equal to the martyr by a similar purpose. If you wish to hear my ignorance, you will proceed no farther.”

When the archbishop nevertheless relied rather on the counsel of others and pressed forward to bring his intention into effect, he eventually learned by experience how true is what Scripture says:

“The soul of a holy man sometimes declares truths more than seven watchmen sitting on high to observe” (Ecclus. 37:18).

For not one of the evils that the just man had foretold failed to occur. By order of the lord pope, that structure was utterly removed and demolished, its author losing both his labor and the expense of the work, amid shame and repeated lamentation.

The faithful man likewise foretold the same to his successor, who was intent upon a similar undertaking, and its outcome proved him right.

[Note: [Col. 0999D] Hubert. Raynaldus, under the year 1198, reports the following from Paris: “Pope Innocent III protected the Canterbury monks against the favor of Hubert, archbishop of Canterbury, and of the king of England, and ordered the church of Lamelich, the source of the dissension, to be overthrown.” Concerning this Trivet likewise writes under the year 1199: “Hubert, archbishop of Canterbury, demolished, by order of Pope Innocent III, the church founded in honor of blessed Thomas at Lambeth, which his predecessor Baldwin had begun.”]

For he too, not far from London, relying on royal power, erected a contentious chapel like the former one, which had stood near Canterbury.

[Note: [Col. 1000D] Apparently another chapel, not the same one. Baldwin is here said to have wished to build near Canterbury—or, as stated above, in the territory of his city—whereas Hubert wished to build a chapel or church not far from London.]

He established clerics as prebendaries in it, to minister according to the custom of secular canons, either in person or through intermediaries. After several buildings had already been constructed around the site, a bitter lawsuit was prolonged between the Father and the sons, that is, between the archbishop and the monks. Many highly distinguished persons, both monks and clerics, also died in the city from Roman fevers during the civil war then raging.

At last the ill-considered undertaking of that great-hearted man was reduced to dust when he himself demolished it. He did this as unwillingly as he did shamefacedly, compelled, of course, by apostolic severity.

Finally, when the man of God Hugh was hastening through the final illness of his mortal life toward the healthier condition of the happier life, peace was restored between the parties mentioned above, with Hugh himself acting as arbiter together with judges delegated by the supreme pontiff.

[Col. 1001B]

The same most truthful son of peace rejoiced wonderfully at this and gave thanks for it to the divine mercy. He rejoiced especially because, after the likeness of the blessed Martin—whose devoted lover and energetic imitator he had always deserved to be—he had brought his virtues to this good consummation: leaving behind him the peace of the Church of God restored.

[Note: [Col. 1001D] Concerning this peace, confirmed more fully in the second year after Hugh’s death, see the *Annals of the Church of Winchester* in Wharton, p. 305.]

## CHAPTER XII

How Hugh conducted himself at table and regarding food; how forcefully he behaved in carrying out the duties of his office; and how humbly and devoutly he attended to children being confirmed and to others confined by illness.

[Col. 1001C]

At table he was cheerful and pleasant, but not without gravity and moderation. He always kept in mind—and sometimes even expressed aloud when people urged him to be cheerful—the words read in the Book of Esther [Judith]: “Let us be joyful according to the face of the saints” (Judith 16).

Whenever actors or musicians happened to be present at his solemn banquets, whether he was sitting at his own table or at someone else’s, he then devoted himself especially to gravity. He scarcely ever lifted his eyes from the table, and conducted himself in every gesture and word so that it was evident to observers that he then constrained his inner self more tightly, when his outward senses were being more sweetly soothed by such allurements.

[Col. 1001D] While eating, he listened to sacred readings with such attentiveness that, apart from the passions of certain martyrs, the deeds of certain saints, and the more celebrated sermons of the doctors on the principal solemnities, he had almost the whole, or indeed the entirety, of the Old and New Testaments read aloud—except for the books of the four Evangelists [Note: [Col. 1001D] This was according to the custom of the Carthusian order, in which these books are still read each year, either in the church or in the refectory, and are prescribed to be read] [Note: [Col. 1002D] These books are read annually among the Carthusians in chapter after the ninth canonical hour, from Easter until the feast of All Saints]—both during the nocturnal office before him and at dinner. As we mentioned above, he himself continually observed this through uniform instruction, and impressed upon all who desired to offer God reasonable service that they too should observe it, so that at every time and place they might suitably fulfill whatever the urgency of present circumstances required. In order to carry this out with greater dignity, he also took pains to make himself capable and, as far as he could, fit for it.

Recognizing that the episcopal office was a work of great labor and could not be decently fulfilled without bodily strength as well, he provided food for the “beast of the body” so that it might suitably serve necessary purposes. He did this with the greater confidence and sufficiency because there was less reason to fear that, having already been thoroughly subdued by a very long discipline, it would resist its rider through stubbornness. For by continual use of a colder diet he had so worn down the inward powers of his body that, as his natural heat failed, he suffered frequent discomfort from his chilled stomach and was also repeatedly tormented most bitterly by iliac disorders. Nevertheless, amid all this, a singular grace was present and flowed to him, increasing his strength to a degree astonishing even to the strongest. It was almost like witnessing a miracle to see how, at the dedications of churches, the celebrations of ordinations, and other ecclesiastical offices, or in whatever exercises of pontifical ministry involved the greatest labor, he alone surpassed the strength of all who attended him. When everyone was not merely tired but almost collapsing—some withdrawing briefly to recover their strength, others taking turns to serve him—he himself, tireless and cheerful, passed from one task to another and from one labor to the next.

For such duties he sometimes rose before dawn and, fasting and never ceasing from labor, spent the middle of the day until the deep darkness of the following night. Often, when the excessive heat of summer threatened, he compelled some of the altar ministers to taste a little bread and wine [Note: [Col. 1002D] Surius suggests the opposite in these words: “He allowed no one to minister at the sacred offices who had broken his fast on any pretext”], lest, weighed down by heat, fasting, and labor, they should be unable, after so many repeated circuits, to stand at the dedications of churches without danger, and finally to minister at the solemn celebration of Mass. When he perceived that, after tasting the bread at his command, some felt horror and fear at touching during the sacred rites either the chalice or the Lord’s linen cloth [*Dominicam sindonem*], he rebuked them as people of little faith and weak judgment, since they were unwilling to obey the one giving the command without hesitation in a carefully considered order.

Whenever, as commonly happened, people met him while he was traveling and sought to be confirmed through the laying on of his hands, or brought infants to him to receive that sacrament, he immediately dismounted from his horse at a suitable place and, with attentive devotion, fulfilled what belonged to his office, wherever in the diocese this occurred. No weariness or illness, no roughness of the road or bad weather, could induce him to remain on horseback merely to administer the sacrament. After giving the desired blessing to those standing around, and pouring out a prayer to God for any sick people who were present—who, breathing again with joy in the hope of obtaining health—he himself, filled with the blessings of all, resumed the journey he had begun. We have often learned with complete certainty that very many people obtained the hoped-for recovery through such prayer or blessing of his.

## CHAPTER XIII. How, out of the sweetness of his affection, he played with little children, who in turn applauded him wonderfully.

[Col. 1003B] Because of his great abundance of childlikeness and innocence—for he was an exceptional lover and guardian of simplicity and purity—the holy man cultivated infants with extraordinary affection, considering not only their sincerity but also their age. Whenever he encountered little children, he addressed them with a certain spiritual sweetness and drew from those scarcely able to babble fragments of speech of remarkable charm. From time to time he impressed upon their foreheads or other senses the life-giving sign of the holy cross, uttering good wishes for them and strengthening them with repeated blessings. They too delighted in playing familiarly with him in return with astonishing eagerness; although they usually feared the sight of almost every man, they clung to him more eagerly than to their own parent.

[Col. 1003C] We saw a certain infant, six months old from birth [Note: [Col. 1003D] The author implies that what is related here concerning the infant occurred during the final years of Saint Hugh’s life, since he asserts that he himself saw it], applaud the bishop with such movements of all his limbs when the bishop marked his forehead with sacred chrism that he seemed to imitate the singular joy of the Lord’s Forerunner exulting in the womb. He opened the little lips of his tiny mouth in such inexhaustible laughter [Col. 1004A] that it seemed incredible that one of such tender age, accustomed as yet only to cries, could laugh in this way. Then, stretching out his little arms as though to fly upward—now twisted, now flung apart—and tossing his neck this way and that, he seemed to show that the greatness of the joy affecting him was more than he could bear. Drawing the bishop’s hand toward himself with both small palms and squeezing it according to his ability, he brought it to his mouth; once it was there, he hastened to lick it rather than kiss it. While the bishop did these things for a very long time to the infant, and the infant to the bishop, they delightfully presented to one another an unprecedented spectacle. The bishop himself offered the child apples, or many other things that are usually pleasing to children, but the child pushed each one away as though it were burdensome to him. In pushing them away, as though he had won, he gazed open-mouthed entirely at the bishop [Col. 1004B]. Even when he looked with a kind of distaste at the hands of his nurse, who was carrying him, as she reached toward him, he fixed his eyes on the bishop, applauded him with his hands, and smiled at him continually.

When the child was finally carried away and those present marveled at such a prodigy, declaring that they had never seen such immense dancing in so small a body, the bishop related that he had once seen something similar.

“For some time ago,” he said, “when I was prior at Witham [Note: [Col. 1003D] In all probability in one of the leap years, 1180 or 1184, when the English priors were obliged to come to the general chapter], it happened that, at the time of the general chapter, I went to the Carthusian house. While passing on the journey by the castle of Avalim, whose stronghold our brother William is known to hold, I turned aside to his house. There a little boy was presented to us, not yet skilled in speech, the son, plainly, of that same brother of ours [Col. 1004C] [Note: [Col. 1003D] He must be distinguished from another son of that same brother, whom, as is recorded in Book V, chapter 20, Saint Hugh baptized in the year 1200 when the boy was seven years old; the child now under discussion, by contrast, must have been at least sixteen in the year 1200]. He applauded us in every respect with similar movements, so that, after being released by his nurse and placed upon our bed, he could be seen, amid the joys he was displaying, even laughing almost beyond the capacity of nature.”

[Col. 1003] Here ends the third book.

## PROLOGUE TO THE FOURTH BOOK

[Col. 1003C] In order, therefore, that, with the sequence of time briefly interrupted, we may continue as we began and relate a few matters according to the successive stages of life, after completing the history of infancy and also of childhood, we must briefly append the account of adolescence. Thus the narrative must be extended through the successive stages of life up to the burial of the dead. In the diligent performance of these duties, no one after Tobias is found to have equaled Hugh; as was made known above, by dedicating every moment of his life to the divine commands, he rightly earned the privilege of being able to benefit many people himself at every stage of life [Col. 1004C]. Once he had reached full maturity and been distinguished by the pontifical office, he appeared to have devoted such great care to burying the dead that, in return for this mercy reserved for the future, he was also granted in the present a singular honor in burial [Col. 1004D] [Note: [Col. 1004D] The burial accorded to the saint is treated at length below, throughout Book V, chapters 27 and 28. It is also discussed by Ralph of Coggeshall in the English chronicle published by Martène and Durand, vol. V of the New Collection, col. 866]. With the Lord’s favor, this will be explained more fully when this fourth and penultimate book of his deeds reaches its conclusion; at its beginning we have thought it appropriate to offer these preliminary remarks.

[Col. 1003] Here ends the prologue.

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 1005]

## CHAPTER I. The tonsure of Martin, the keeper of our Hugh’s chests; his conversion to religion; and his progress therein.

[Col. 1005A] The venerable bishop Hugh had appointed a certain young man, named Martin, to guard the episcopal chests. He was modest and chaste in conduct, but not entirely free from worldly vanity. These chests contained vessels, vestments, and other sacred objects of this kind used in the ministry of the altar. It was customary for their guardian and bearer, although a layman, nevertheless—because he was engaged with clerics in ecclesiastical ministries—to be tonsured like a cleric and, wearing a linen tunic over his own clothing, to serve in the duties entrusted to him.

Martin, recently appointed to this office, was ordered by the bishop to receive the tonsure [Col. 1005B]. For three days he postponed fulfilling the command, held back by an unworthy shame, trying each day to conceal the matter with various excuses, even though he was accused of deliberately omitting the command through disobedience. The bishop noticed this. One day, when Martin was bringing the chests back from a church after Mass, the bishop observed him and followed him into an inner chamber. Twining his fingers in a lock [*cincinnio*; alternatively *cicinno*] of Martin’s hair, he said: “Since you have not found a barber to give you the tonsure prescribed for you, I myself will tonsure you.” Saying this, he took up scissors and cut his hair all around in a circle.

As soon as this was done, the young man dissolved in tears, threw himself at the saint’s knees, and, clasping his feet tightly with his hands, said: “My lord, by the mercy of God I beseech you to listen to me for a little while [Col. 1005C]. Since the right hand of your holiness has removed from my head the sign of worldly vanity, I beg you to be willing to free me completely from the snares of this world. For truly, once the worldly hair has been cut off by your hands, it will no longer weigh down my neck. To reveal more clearly the purpose of my mind, which has been inspired from heaven through the service performed by your hands: this wicked world has become wholly contemptible to me, and I desire the monastic life. Henceforth I devote myself entirely to God and renounce altogether the pomp of the world. I beg that your grace, through which I have merited being anticipated by God’s grace through you, may continue to accompany me, so that the grace which has now gone before me may also accompany me throughout all the days of my life. Through you may I merit receiving the religious habit, through whom I have just now received the tonsorial mark.”

What more is there to say? Since the bishop regarded these words as childish and received them negligently, he pretended not to have heard anything and proceeded to the dining hall to eat. But while the others were eating, the consuming flame of desire devoured Martin’s inmost heart, so that he could scarcely be induced to take bodily nourishment, because of the intensity of the inward fire with which he burned to the marrow. When the meal was over, he approached privately, one by one, all those whom he judged likely to be more readily heard by the bishop in such a matter. Throwing himself at their feet, he struck their ears, minds, and feelings with sobs, moved them with entreaties, and inclined them by his tears, full of piety, to offer assistance to him who was burning with desire before the bishop, so that through the bishop he might obtain the fulfillment of his saving desire.

Persisting tirelessly in this throughout the days and nights, he finally obtained after three days what he had perseveringly requested. His three-day disobedience having been expiated by a delay in being heard no shorter than the delay of his disobedience, the most merciful man, knowing the proper measure of his mercy, summoned to him the venerable prior of Saint Neot [Note: [Col. 1005D] The priory of Saint Neot, as it is recorded in the *Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. I, p. 368, was in the county of Huntingdon. It was first a cell of the abbey of Bec in Normandy and later became an independent foundation. The Bollandists will treat, or may already have treated, Saint Neot on 31 July. Mabillon is also to be consulted, *Annales*, vol. III, p. 241, and vol. V, pp. 327 and 520] and, to summarize briefly what happened, requested and obtained that his Martin be favorably associated with the holy community of that cell. For in earlier years the young man had learned of the thoroughly praiseworthy formation of the men of Bec, as well as the orderly way of life of the household of Saint Neot. Therefore he had preferred to be bound by their profession and joined to that residence. The kindly provider supplied him with the regular habit and made the day of his reception into the sacred habit a joyful occasion for all the brothers by means of a solemn meal.

[Col. 1006C] Martin, striving tirelessly to do the things of God no less than to know them, and with the grace of Christ furthering his pious vows, made such rapid progress in goodness and discipline, and in knowledge, that his advancement was judged worthy of imitation by all. His former nourisher—his bishop—afterward promoted him to the rank of subdeacon with immense joy. Everyone found it remarkable that, in his own case, what seemed impossible for anyone else had occurred: although already advanced in age, he had learned letters so quickly, letters he had not learned at all in his earlier years. Yet Martin was not, I do not say, exalted by the praises of those who admired him; he was not even lightly moved by them. Rather, he challenged his former contemporaries and companions with the strongest arguments concerning vanity, inviting them to pursue a more reformed life.

He also asked the bishop to obtain through his prayers from the lord abbot of Bec that he be granted permission to go to the mother house at Bec [Col. 1007A] [Note: [Col. 1007D] Mabillon discusses the origin of this monastery in *Annales*, vol. IV, p. 438] and remain there for a longer period, so that he might be more perfectly instructed in the ceremonies of the sacred order and more fully taught by the examples of the most approved monks whom he knew to be there. After a short time, through the intervention of the bishop, he obtained the fulfillment of this pious request. We have recently learned many highly commendable things about his conduct and diligence, both from the abbot himself and from others [Note: [Col. 1007D] Whether the men of Bec know anything about this Martin that has escaped me, I do not know].

## CHAPTER II. The kissing of lepers and the manifold consolation, in the words of our Hugh, concerning the sweetness of the Savior and the most generous distribution of alms. [Note: A memorable saying which Surius reports concerning the difference between the kisses bestowed on lepers by St. Martin and St. Hugh, while the abridger is silent, nevertheless suggests that Surius had before him the longer Life of St. Hugh, as may be inferred from various passages; Petreius also indicates that in his time it existed in the Charterhouse of Cologne.]

—This is also the chapter in the sequence of the Great Life, Book Four.

Among the other marks of his compassion, who could worthily recount how much care he showed the sick and how much kindness he extended to those suffering from the foulness of leprosy? He often washed their feet with his own hands, wiped them, and caressed them with kisses. He also customarily gave coins to those who had been refreshed with food and drink. He frequently did this more privately, before a few witnesses, in his own chamber, to thirteen persons, although as many could have been found in the places where he himself was present.

There were also, on certain estates of the bishopric, hospices in which not a few people afflicted by this disease, both men and women, were supported. In addition to the revenues assigned by his predecessors, he supplied them with various forms of assistance in many matters, with complete diligence. He frequently went to them in person, accompanied by only a very few of his followers—devout and God-fearing men—and, sitting among them in a secluded room, he lifted their spirits with excellent words. With something like a mother’s gentleness he soothed those who were grieving, raising up those who were temporally desolate and afflicted toward the hope of eternal reward. He also interwove lessons in good conduct with extraordinary sweetness among his words of consolation. If he had learned of anything blameworthy in them, he advised them so that it would not be committed again: they should repent more deeply of what they had done, and no courage or desire to commit it again should remain in them.

Before the conversations of exhortation, after ordering the women to withdraw for the time being, he went around to the men one by one and kissed them. He bent toward each of them and embraced for longer and more tenderly those whom he saw already more grievously wasted by the disease [Col. 1007D]. He declared that such people were blessed; he said that they were the flowers of paradise and the precious pearls of the splendid crown of the eternal King. He reminded them that they should confidently and securely await our Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, who would refashion their lowly body [Col. 1008A] to conform to the body of his glory (Philippians 3:21). By contrast, the fearful await the exalted Judge who is to come; those who now glory in the appearance of their bodies shrink, through the pride of their minds, from conformity to his humility and purity.

When he spoke privately with his familiar companions about the great clemency of our Savior—who so often blesses the most wretched in the present life with divine speech in his Gospel, now introducing Lazarus, covered with sores, carried by angels into Abraham’s bosom, now declaring that he himself is sick in the sick—he exalted the Author of all sweetness with extraordinary sweetness.

“O,” he said, “how blessed were those who clung more familiarly to a Physician so greatly loved! How sweet it would be for me to lick with kisses whatever he had trodden with these feet, touched with any part of his body, or handled with his hands, to place it before my eyes, and, if it were possible, to insert it even into my inmost bowels! How wretched are those who fear offending anyone other than one so sweet! How deserving of lamentation are those who consider anything else sweet, and desire anything else, rather than cling sweetly to the Sweet One in this way and obey him sweetly! I do not know what bitterness someone could now taste who, through continual meditation, has learned to chew sweetly upon the sweetness of this Sweet One on the inner palate of his heart.”

As the holy man thought and spoke these things about the heavenly Physician of our wounds, and as he also expressed what we have related above concerning his suffering members, and devoted himself to these people, he clearly revealed how intensely the fire of both divine and fraternal love burned within him [Col. 1008C]. He also distributed such great alms generally to all who were in need that, apart from what he often gave secretly for many particular reasons—sometimes when asked, sometimes anticipating by his own initiative the cries of those suffering need—it is believed that he spent, under a definite provision, as much as one-third of the annual income from all his possessions on works of mercy.

## CHAPTER III. How steadfastly he opposed rebels and punished by ecclesiastical censure those who obstinately offended against God.

After what has been related, it seems appropriate to recall how bravely he acted in restraining the presumption of the proud; how he himself, unarmed, often entered without hesitation among armed troops; and how he stood amid flashing swords and drawn hands, first in the Church of Lincoln, then in Holland [Note: [Col. 1008D] Read “in Hoyland,” a part of England in the diocese of Lincoln, where there was the monastery mentioned in the *Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. I, p. 773: “The abbey of Swineshead, founded in the county of Lincoln in the year 1134.” Vischius writes in his *Chronologia* under that year: “The monastery of Swinshed, that is, Hoyland in England”], and finally in Northampton [Note: [Col. 1008D] Also called Northampton, a county belonging to the diocese of Lincoln. A charter appears in the *Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. I, p. 681, in which our Hugh confirms to the monks of Saint Andrew at Northampton various grants formerly made to them], steadfast and undaunted, with his head uncovered.

Yet I have said too little in saying that he stood there, since, moving back and forth, he brandished the sword of the Spirit with complete freedom against the raging and roaring conspirators or intruders, handing the disobedient over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit might be saved on the day of the Lord (1 Corinthians 5:5). His courage shone forth all the more sublimely because the strength of brave men there yielded more visibly to fear; and his confidence appeared all the more brilliantly because the lack of confidence of his companions and officials was more openly revealed in such great danger. For it was not enough for them merely to flee to the altars; they even seemed to consider it unsafe to hide beneath the very tables of the Lord. While they fled in this way and sheltered themselves in hiding places, Hugh remained alone and struck with his lips at the swords men were threatening against his neck. Broken and confounded by the boldness of his great-hearted courage, as well as by the protection of the angels guarding him and the armor of divine power itself, the clerics and laymen at Lincoln, the soldiers and armed men in Holland, and the burgesses—that is, citizens—at Northampton withdrew in hostility, many giving way to one: the savage were overcome by the gentle, and the disturbed by the tranquil.

At Holland, however, something must not be passed over. William of Avalim, the bishop’s cousin, a very fierce knight, heated by the blood of a noble lineage, when one of the armed men prepared with drawn sword to strike the bishop with deadly audacity, threw himself forcefully in the way of the man already about to strike. He also wrenched the sword from him with great strength and, unless the bishop had strictly prevented him, would not have allowed him to leave without injury.

Hugh was thus prepared, in accordance with the apostolic model, to avenge every disobedience with the sword of the Spirit (2 Corinthians 10:6). His punishment was also so swiftly followed by vengeance that, when people obstinately sinned against God, just as he himself did not spare them in any way, so anyone whom he struck with the spiritual sword in his zeal for justice would, unless he repented quickly, perish also through bodily destruction. Hence he rebuked all rebels and violators of ecclesiastical law—those who sometimes insolently presumed upon their own power and, through the swelling of their minds, occasionally burst forth boldly into threats—with a terrifying voice:

“What do you presume to do with your strength or weapons against the hand of the Almighty, when this hand has given even us, unworthy and weak as we are, weapons of such power that no human armor can in any way equal them? Your darts do not pierce our coats of mail [Col. 1009D], and our helmets do not fear your swords. Our swords, however, are resisted neither by your helmets nor by your breastplates. When you cut the flesh, you cannot touch the soul at all. Our sword destroys the body as well and subjects to death—not passing death, but eternal death—the souls of those whom it strikes.”

## CHAPTER IV. The substitution of a child for the offspring of a knight’s wife; the punishment of those who consented to so great a crime; the title of forest warden; and the cruel death of a certain bishop who retained a curse.

It will not be useless now to mention, by way of example, a few among those whom he handed over to reprobate death by anathema alone and who departed this life by a horrible end. In the territory of Lincoln there was a knight already advanced in age who had a barren wife. He also had a brother, likewise a knight, industrious and prudent, whom he appeared likely to have as his heir by hereditary right if he should die without children. His wife, however, envied this brother, fearing that, if widowed, she might fall under his rule, toward whom she had never felt a pleasing affection.

Incited, therefore, by the cunning of viperous wickedness, and wishing to block his access to the inheritance he sought, she substituted another’s child for her own, since she had no child of her own [Note: [Col. 1009] As may be inferred, this occurred in the year 1195. For a girl scarcely four years old is betrothed, and the fraud is exposed in the year 1199 in the author’s presence]. With her inward organs stuffed and swollen through this deceit, she bound a cushion around herself externally. She also pretended that her womb was swelling with childbirth, although she was bearing only the monstrous crime of her wickedness [Col. 1010B]. The knight, against whom the trick of this crafty malignity had been contrived, detected that a deception was being prepared for him but was unable either to convict or restrain the maker of the deception, and therefore brought the matter to the knowledge of his friends. He searched anxiously for a remedy in counsel but found no suitable one.

Meanwhile the woman took to her bed and indulged in the sighs of a fictitious labor. She brought out publicly a female newborn child obtained from a certain poor woman in a nearby village and, as though she had truly given birth to it herself, raised it with the utmost care. She also summoned the child’s real mother to herself and entrusted to her the care of nursing her own offspring.

While these things were happening not far from Lincoln, it happened that the Easter festivals of the Lord’s Resurrection were already approaching [Col. 1010C]. The knight, deceived by feminine cunning, therefore approached the bishop, with discreet men supporting him—men whom a more reliable report had informed of so great a crime—and, before all who were listening, disclosed the entire account of the highly suspicious affair. It was not yet known with certainty whose daughter the child was, or how she had been acquired by the false mother, through whom the knight’s disinheritance was being arranged.

Deeply moved by what he heard, the just and devout man ordered the husband of the wicked woman to be summoned to him without delay. Calling him aside, he questioned him more insistently, instructed him, and refuted him, earnestly striving to draw from him a confession of so great a crime. But the man feared the quarrels of his excessively insolent wife more than the justice of God; bewitched as well by her viperous hissing [Col. 1010D], he first denied that he had any knowledge of this crime. At last, when the bishop pressed him and forcefully presented the evidence of public opinion—evidence showing that it was most probable that, being already sickly and old, he could not have fathered a child, and that he could not have been ignorant of his wife’s contrivance—he was compelled by the evident reasoning and finally deceived himself with this answer:

“Because for a long time I have been burdened by bodily illness and have known my wife’s secrets less than perfectly, I wish, if it pleases you, to learn the truth about them more closely from her. Whatever I discover from her, I will report to you tomorrow morning and will undoubtedly follow your counsel concerning everything that, according to the course of the investigation, ought most usefully to be done.”

The bishop, having sufficiently warned him, allowed him to depart with these words:

“Know that tomorrow all those who were the authors or supporters of this evil will be solemnly and terribly struck by us with the sentence of excommunication, unless perhaps you carry out what you promise.”

Thus dismissed, the man returned to his household and explained in order to the barren woman what he had heard from the bishop and what he himself had reported to the bishop. At this she gnashed her teeth and insolently rebuked the unhappy man, utterly dissuading him from returning to his trustworthy counselor. He foolishly obeyed his mistress, whom he had long been accustomed, in an inverted order, to serve as a servant, and remained at home [Col. 1011B], adding the crime of lying to his earlier error.

The following day arrived, a day made glorious by the paschal solemnity of the most holy Resurrection of the Lord. After delivering a sacred exhortation to the people, the bishop disclosed to everyone the outcome of this affair, magnified the enormity of the crime, and declared that, insofar as he could, he would not fail to oppose so great a sin through the censure of his pastoral office. When he had explained fully how great a crime it was to attempt anything of this kind not only against one’s own brother but against any neighbor—an act that necessarily causes the perpetrator, together with all his posterity, to suffer irremediable loss—he also said that this kind of sin, under the weight of its wickedness, often bound its perpetrators irrevocably to death [Col. 1011C]. He bound all those by the bond of anathema who had not feared to bring about the disinheritance of the aforementioned knight through the substitution of the child.

Nor did he delay long before allowing Satan to exercise the tyranny of his cruelty against those handed over to him by the sentence of the just man. During the following night Satan attacked the husband—the man who, by concealing rather than correcting his wife’s perversity, had fostered it—and suddenly tore out his soul. For he suddenly appeared dead in the little bed into which he had lain down, as he believed, to rest peacefully.

The woman’s persistent fury and exceedingly harsh anger were such that it was not enough for her to have destroyed her own husband so fatally unless she also carried out her initiated wickedness against his brother in a hostile manner [Col. 1011D]. She persisted in maintaining her wicked claim, retaining the curse that was due to her and asserting an inheritance that was not due to her foster daughter.

After the lawful heir had thus been excluded from his brother’s succession, the little girl, together with the inheritance, was granted by royal favor to a certain young man who was the brother of Hugh of Newtown, namely, the kingdom’s chief forest warden [Note: [Col. 1011D] He had succeeded Geoffrey in this office, of whom mention was made in Book III, chapter 8]. The same man planned to solemnly betroth her to himself in the manner of marriage when she had scarcely completed her fourth year [Col. 1012A], evidently taking precautions lest he should be deprived by some circumstance of acquiring so valuable a patrimony.

When this became known to the bishop—who, by a general statute previously established, had often prohibited marriage with persons of indiscreetly young age—he immediately issued a special prohibition as well, forbidding any priest or any Christian faithful person to presume to attend this marriage in particular. In doing this he looked ahead to the lasting as well as temporal security of many, and also safeguarded the common law: such a marriage should not be entered into to the prejudice of either party before the truth of an affair of this kind had been more fully learned and examined.

But soon afterward, when the bishop had departed for the king in Normandy on certain business [Note: [Col. 1011D] Hugh came to Normandy in Septuagesima of the year 1199, as related below in Book V, chapter 15, intending to go to King Richard], the aforesaid young man’s supporters and relatives gathered in a more remote village [Col. 1012B]. There, taking advantage of the simplicity of the local priest—or of his greed—they solemnly joined the little girl to the knight before the face of the Church: an illustrious woman of peasant status, born free yet descended from servile condition. Their eagerness to seize another’s right was so great that neither her degenerate condition, despite her free birth, nor the manifest destruction of salvation prevented the ill-omened marriage.

Meanwhile the bishop returned from overseas, and what had been done soon became known. The priest who had officiated at such a marriage was punished by the bishop with suspension both from his benefice and from his office. Against the other transgressors of his prohibition, when the men stubbornly refused to appear before him, the sentence of excommunication was promulgated.

[Col. 1012C] Meanwhile, the chambermaid of the pretended mother—the woman through whose agency the child of another mother had been sought and found—terrified by her conscience, first went to the penitentiary of the Church of Lincoln, Master William of Bredefeld, subdean [Note: [Col. 1011D] Perhaps also chancellor, who, according to Surius, tried Hugo [Col. 1012D] concerning the difference between the kisses exchanged by him and those of Saint Martin.]; and finally, at his urging, approached the bishop himself. With a great outpouring of tears she disclosed the entire sequence of events. When the bishop had thus been informed of everything, he kept secret within himself for the time being what he had heard more secretly; but he ordered that the sentence previously pronounced be publicly renewed throughout the churches on each successive Sunday.

After this had been carried out for some time, the unhappy woman who had contrived and brought about this evil finally came to recoil from the exceedingly pernicious deed she had committed. At last, encouraged by prudent advice, she went with the aforementioned chambermaid, her accomplice and conscious minister of her crime, to the bishop. First to him alone, and then to several discreet men—including the man who wrote this account [Note: [Col. 1012D] From this I infer that the adulteress’s repentance occurred in 1199, after Hugo returned from Neustria to England.] and who was present—she tearfully confessed her guilt. With lamenting voice she declared that she had ruined her own husband, deceived his brother, and brought death upon the one and outlawry and disinheritance upon the other. All these matters were carefully made known by the bishop to the metropolitan of Canterbury [Note: [Col. 1013D] Hubert, mentioned again in the following chapter and elsewhere.], who at that time was justiciar of the whole kingdom, as well as to the brothers and friends of the man whose patrimony had been treacherously obtained, as has been said, and to nearly all the leading men and barons of the English court.

Nevertheless, the girl’s bridegroom, though innocent of the crime, together with his advisers, persisted in holding the property he had wrongfully acquired. For they asserted that, according to the laws of England, any offspring was to be deemed legitimate whom the husband of the wife would have legitimately regarded as legitimate during his lifetime. On this pretext, therefore, the legitimate heir was barred from entering into possession of his hereditary property. Meanwhile, however, out of respect for the bishop rather than because the matter was unknown—for it had become almost universally known—a judicial decision against him was not permitted to be formally issued.

But when the most steadfast defender of justice again crossed over to Normandy [Note: [Col. 1013D] In the year 1200, when he went with King John on the business indicated below, Book V, chapter 19.], and repeatedly declared at his departure that, if the knight took this woman as his wife, as he proposed, he should know that he would certainly have a peasant woman and would derive little joy from her, the wicked men again formed a conspiracy. They fixed a day for the parties and announced that the final judgment in this dispute was to be delivered at London without further postponement.

Thus Adam of Newtown—for that was the name of the man who had married the girl—hurried to London surrounded by crowds of relatives. On the night before the day on which the judges had promised to adjudicate that land to him in full—for up to that time he possessed only its custody—he was received at an inn not far from the city. While his supporters and advisers were anxiously discussing in the city with the judges the form of the judgment to be pronounced, he, cheerful and drunk, was taken to bed at the lodging-house; but, sleep suddenly joined to death, he expired [Note: [Col. 1013D] During the period in which Hugo was staying in Normandy and Gaul.]. Alone, before the tribunal of the more righteous Judge, to receive the return due for his deeds, he was immediately brought forth wholly unprepared and expecting nothing of the kind.

There is reason to fear that he may there have heard, to his reproach, the judgment expressed by that strict Judge which his own truthful herald so often had upon his lips. For when the holy man frequently heard the previously unknown and foreign name “foresters,” and when complaints from those oppressed by them were increasing everywhere, he used to allude to the barbarous designation and say:

“Rightly and quite appropriately are these men called foresters. For they will stand outside the kingdom of God.”

Another of the bishop’s foresters, who had incurred his curse, died a cruel death within a few days after he had deserved to be handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh (1 Cor. 5:5). For he had decided, in his customary insolent manner, to treat more harshly certain men whom he had found in the forest he guarded. They killed him in such a way that, after his arms had been cut off and his head torn away, they left certain quite small sticks—on account of which those who killed him had been greatly wronged by him—between the mutilated corpse and the severed head, together with other limbs hideously cut off and laid here and there in three places, as a sign and testimony of his wickedness. For he had been accustomed to exercise tyrannical rage against all his neighbors.

## CHAPTER V. Concerning a certain deacon who fiercely prosecuted a knight on the charge of treason against the king

This chapter is also inserted in the Great Life, Book IV, chapter 6.

A certain deacon named Richard of Wara prosecuted a knight named Reginald of Argentem on the charge of treason against the king. Both belonged to the diocese of Lincoln. It was known to many, however, that the knight was falsely accused by the cleric. When the bishop learned of this, he sought through ecclesiastical censure to restrain the deacon from his rashness. Accordingly, under threat of anathema, he prohibited the deacon from bringing him before a secular court, especially for a judgment involving blood.

But the deacon, emboldened by the royal favor that protected him, disregarded both the bishop’s warnings and his threats. The archbishop of Canterbury [Note: [Col. 1013D] Hubert, elected archbishop in 1193 and deceased in 1205. Thus Wharton, Part I, page 114, *Anglia Sacra*.]—who was also then regarded as the public justiciar of the kingdom, and to whose protection King Richard had especially commended the deacon—is said to have instructed the bishop not to compel the cleric, contrary to royal honor, to abandon the prosecution of the accusation he had begun.

But, in this as often in similar commands of that man, the bishop, an imitator of Peter, paid attention rather to the rights of his own office than to the words of a human being. For that great man, as he himself truthfully used to testify, had both swords entrusted to him: he was metropolitan by ordinary authority and legate of all England by apostolic authority [Note: [Col. 1014D] “This Hubert,” says Ralph of Diceto in Wharton, Part II, *Anglia Sacra*, p. 693, “in the year of the Lord 1195, obtained from the same Celestine, with the favor of all the cardinals, the fullness of power in the office of legate, both in the archbishopric of York and in his own.”]. Thus, by royal commission, he was also supreme judge over secular courts. The bishop therefore carefully and prudently sought to distinguish by which sword he was speaking.

Accordingly, whenever he advised or commanded something that belonged more properly to the material sword than to the spiritual one, the man of God was not afraid to say to him what is recorded as having been said by the chief of the apostles to the pontiffs: “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29).

For this reason he did not delay striking the rebellious cleric, who stubbornly resisted ecclesiastical discipline, with pontifical severity. He therefore suspended him from office and benefice because he refused to submit to the canonical yoke. The cleric then went to the legate and obtained from him, in fact, a release from the suspension. Thereupon, swelling with pride, he approached the bishop and, in the presence of many of the kingdom’s leading men—both nobles and bishops—began to utter great threats.

He boasted that he had now been so exempted from the jurisdiction of the bishop of Lincoln by the legate’s authority that henceforth he would in no way refrain, on the bishop’s account, from showing every loyalty to the lord king and striving to obtain justice from him against his betrayers. He also insulted the bishop, asserting that he had been released from the suspension by which, as he said, the bishop had punished him unlawfully.

At this, the bishop—who, in his customary manner, was no feeble pilot of Peter’s little boat, but became even more steadfast when fear had been introduced—spoke before all who were listening:

“You flatter yourself in vain about this release. For you should know that you will be excommunicated immediately if you continue to refuse obedience to justice concerning your offenses.”

What more need be said? When the cleric stubbornly shouted back and thundered furious threats as though speaking with the king’s own mouth, the bishop neither feared nor delayed to bind him with solemn anathema.

The cleric then went to the legate and complained that the bishop had excommunicated him with such insolence, as he alleged, to his own detriment and the king’s injury. From the legate he eventually obtained letters to the bishop instructing him to regard the cleric as absolved, since the legate himself had absolved him.

When the bishop had read this command, he said:

“If the lord archbishop should decide a hundred times that you are to be absolved, you should know that we shall excommunicate you a hundred times, or even more often, as long as we see you irrevocably hardened in the madness of your presumption. You may judge how highly you value our sentence; for our part, we hold it wholly valid and firm.”

The cleric departed, somewhat broken in spirit by fear of such steadfastness, and promised that he would consider whether, as justice required concerning obedience, he wished to give security before the bishop. Shortly afterward, however, one of his own servants struck him lethally on the head with an axe. Alas, he breathed out his soul before he could make known any repentance for his error. His brain was split by a single blow, and he died instantly.

## CHAPTER VI. Concerning a young girl at Oxford who, rejecting her first betrothed, was in fact married to another and, when convicted of this, refused to obey blessed Hugo

This chapter likewise appears in the Great Life under chapter 6.

[Col. 1015D]

A certain young woman of Oxford, the daughter of a townsman, had been lawfully married to a young man from her neighborhood. Inflamed with a greater love for another young man, she rejected her first husband and was in fact married to the other. After the first husband brought a charge against her and she was convicted, the bishop diligently admonished her to return to her first husband.

Her mother, however, dissuaded her and, in this wicked counsel, showed herself another Herodias to her daughter. The girl brazenly proclaimed that she would die before marrying him. Then the man of God took the right hand of that first husband and, mingling encouragement with threats, said:

“My daughter, if you wish to be my daughter, obey my command and receive your husband with the kiss of peace and with God’s blessing. Otherwise, truly, henceforth I shall spare neither you nor your pernicious advisers.”

He ordered her husband to receive her with the holy kiss. While he was attempting to fulfill this command, the unhappy woman most shamelessly spat in his face, although the altar was nearby, the great priest was present with many most reverend men, and a large crowd of the faithful was gathered in the church itself.

Then, while everyone was deeply ashamed at the insult inflicted upon the man, the bishop said in a terrible voice:

“Because you did not wish for blessing but loved a curse, behold, a curse shall seize you.”
