And immediately he excommunicated her. She departed stubbornly to her own home. After a few days granted to her by heavenly mercy, so that she might deliberate more profitably with herself, her heart became still more hardened and she did not repent in any way. Choked by the evil enemy, she suddenly exchanged her unlawful and fleeting pleasures for punishments both everlasting and just.

## CHAPTER VII. Concerning a cleric of the diocese of York who refused to obey the judgment concerning the surrender of a church, which had been issued against him by blessed Hugo under delegated authority

This chapter is still found under the same chapter 6 in the Great Life.

Similarly, Hugo had decreed by apostolic authority that a certain cleric of the diocese of York, named William, should have restored to him the church of which he had been unjustly dispossessed through the violence of certain men. For a long time the opposing party, armed, drove him away from entering the possession adjudicated to him [Col. 1016C].

The knight who was lord of the village in which the disputed church stood was protecting his brother, who had entered the church by intrusion, with arms, striving unlawfully to secure for him the possession he had seized. Both ecclesiastical and secular judges and leading men of that region supported the intruder’s party.

At last William, exhausted by excessive labors, also appealed in person to the assistance of the Roman court and sought the aid of many others here and there through vigilant but scarcely fruitful efforts. Completely drained, he turned wholly to the one refuge of the oppressed, the unconquerable patron of justice, and appealed to him for help with tearful words.

The good man, an ardent imitator of Elijah and Elisha in zeal [Col. 1016D], indignant and supported by apostolic authority, struck the aforesaid intruder and his accomplices with a sentence of severe malediction.

Nor did divine vengeance delay long in raging against the sacrilegious men. For, as was reported to us by many religious men, some of them were driven into madness; others, overtaken by sudden death, miserably perished; and from others, amid immense torments, their eyes fell from their hollow sockets.

Thus the power of the absent man subdued the present audacity of the proud when they sought to harm the innocent; thus the defended possession of the goods was restored to the rightful possessor; and thus, finally, the strong athlete, most proven in our own time and ambidextrous, trained to fight with both hands and to use either as his right [Col. 1017A], struck and killed some, while he struck others and made them live. They fell from him on the right and on the left. For each person who received a blow from his right hand quickly fell into death. Either he was corrected and died to sin in order to live for God, or, hardened in heart and uncorrected, he was handed over to destruction.

## CHAPTER VIII. How he redeemed the servitude of the pallium from King Richard, how liberally the clergy of his diocese contributed to that redemption, and how he also prohibited the acceptance of monetary penalties for offenses

This is also chapter 7 in the Great Life.

The bloodthirsty enemy of the human race perceived that the strength of the man who was everywhere victorious was advancing to his own great detriment. He therefore tried by crafty art to remove him from the camp of those whom his presence protected, so that, with the unconquerable protector of the entire battle line removed from the place of combat, he might at least rage more freely among the remaining troops.

For the venomous serpent knew that the man of God was an ardent champion of the Church’s freedom. He imposed no monetary exactions whatsoever upon the churches subject to him, nor would he in any way consent to such demands when imposed by secular powers upon any of his churches. The serpent therefore tried to draw him into a predicament from which he could scarcely escape without doing something at least inconvenient.

Armed with the cunning of long-standing malice, he stirred up the perverse minds of certain persons familiar and subordinate to the bishop, so that through them he might excite the king’s feelings against the bishop with new and unexpected complaints. They suggested to the king [Col. 1017C] that the bishop of Lincoln was withholding some enormous debt that he was bound to pay him annually. Thus, as the common expression has it, he had fallen into the king’s mercy and could be assigned to repay the treasury a very large sum accumulated through his prolonged withholding of it.

For it was said that a former bishop of Lincoln named Alexander, who preceded Hugo as the third bishop [Note: [Col. 1017D] Geoffrey, or Gaufridus, is not counted; without consecration and without a pallium, he held the bishopric for several years and finally resigned.], had given the king who then ruled a pallium valued at one hundred silver marks during his own time. His successor, named Robert [Note: [Col. 1017D] Robert II, who succeeded Alexander first.], was also said to have done the same on several occasions.

Thus the calumny descended upon Hugo. They not only anxiously demanded from him what, as they recalled, he had been obliged to provide annually during his episcopate [Col. 1017D], but also maliciously decreed that he should be liable, at the king’s pleasure, to make satisfaction for the insulting withdrawal of a royal payment.

Nor did they allege merely that the bishop was liable; they declared that the Church as well—for he had assumed both its burdens and received its revenues [Col. 1018A]—was liable, during the time of his predecessor Walter [Note: [Col. 1017D] He was Alexander’s second successor, and our third successor was Hugo.], both for the withholding and for the repayment of the pallium, although Walter himself had never given the king the pallium that was due.

When the bishop was summoned by King Richard himself on these matters, he at last freed himself and his successors, despite the opposition of the oft-mentioned archbishop [Note: [Col. 1017D] That is, Hubert. Note here that Baronius, under the year 1189, reported certain things from Surius as though they had occurred at the beginning of King Richard’s reign, whereas from this Life, Book V, chapter 7 [Col. 1018D], it is clear that they first occurred in 1197. Hence Baronius also erroneously writes in the index under the letter B: “He accuses Saint Hugo, bishop of Lincoln, before Richard, the new king of England.”], who, as was said, was especially hostile to him. For three thousand marks he secured release both from the demand for the withheld payment and from the imposition of the same payment in the future, and he freed his Church for all time from the burden of that presentation.

He considered nothing more disgraceful or more intolerable than to make the bride of the eternal King—or himself, her temporary guardian—tributary to a mortal man and, in a certain sense, to exhibit her as subject to a tax [Col. 1018B] [Note: [Col. 1018D] On the pallium and its redemption, see Gerald of Wales in Wharton, Part II, *Anglia Sacra*, p. 419.].

But from where could such a great sum of money come to this exceedingly generous man, who had always been accustomed to pour out all his annual revenues and every kind of income on works of mercy and the expenses of just necessity, and who never had any money left over beyond the period of the present year, especially since he frequently borrowed money from others? Where would he find the many thousands of talents with which to pay the king?

A plan was indeed ready to hand if he wished to extort from the purses of his subjects what was lacking in his own. But how could he extort their substance when he had always desired to lay down not only money but even his own life for the safety of those entrusted to him? And how could he, while striving to free his own Church from an ignoble payment, burden the churches of others in order to relieve himself and impose the yoke of servitude upon others for the sake of his own freedom?

It therefore seemed to the man of God that one remedy alone remained, and it was also entirely to his liking: namely, that he should withdraw for the time being to his Witham [Note: [Col. 1018D] It is stated below, chapter 10, that Hugo withdrew to Witham once or twice a year. Here he was considering withdrawing there so that he might redeem the burden of the pallium without expense to others.], live there in solitude, and order that all the revenues of the entire bishopric be applied to the payment of this debt.

He rejoiced and exulted with all his heart because he thought he had found an occasion that was not only just and honorable but also necessary, an opportunity to withdraw for a while from worldly tumult and cling to heavenly secrets with the greater sweetness because he would do so more freely.

But when he made this intention known to his clergy, all began to resist it most vehemently, declaring his removal wholly intolerable to them. Countless religious persons also strongly dissuaded him from carrying out what he had planned [Col. 1019A].

Finally, all the ecclesiastical persons of his diocese jointly agreed willingly to contribute money from their resources for the exemption of their mother Church. With one accord they also earnestly implored the bishop, as their pious and most valiant father and defender, not to absent himself from them for the sake of this matter.

Thus, although unwilling and compelled by the petitions of his children, he yielded to them, placing the pious decision of the whole community above the desire of his own will. He strictly forbade his officials to presume to demand anything more from anyone than each person voluntarily offered; and he ordered that money be given from his own treasury as far as his resources permitted.

In this way he rescued the provincial churches, rather than merely their mother, the Church of Lincoln, from the disgraceful and burdensome yoke of a long-established servitude and restored them once and for all to perpetual freedom. For, without burdening anyone, he received from the clergy only once what—indeed, more than what—the two previously mentioned inventors and collectors of this tribute had been accustomed to extort, not without imposing a burden upon many: a pontifical ambition disguised under the pretext of the royal pallium.

We do not dare say this on our own authority, but report it according to the judgment of many who often lamented that their poverty was mocked by such collusion among the rich. Indeed, the king himself, having been informed, as was believed, by certain men who willingly and frequently milked the breasts of their sheep to the point of extracting butter [Col. 1019C], had said that it would profit the bishop rather than himself if he took much from his clergy in the manner of his predecessors, so that he might give little for the pallium, weighing it upon his shoulders.

But the true and good shepherd loved the immunity of the sheep entrusted to him as much as he loved the sheep themselves. And, so far as he was concerned, just as he diligently avoided every form of avarice, so he continually uprooted, with all his strength wherever possible, every occasion for avarice.

Accordingly, he prohibited both his archdeacons and their officials and deans from exacting a substantial monetary payment from any offenders. He feared, of course, that for the sake of gifts they might either oppress an innocent person or favor a guilty person in his offenses, in accordance with the saying of the ancient lawgiver: “Gifts blind the eyes of the wise and overturn the words of the just” (Exod. 23:8).

He also frequently impressed upon his officials this other saying of Scripture: “Fire will devour the tents of those who gladly accept gifts” (Job 15:34).

On the other hand, when they often asserted that the wicked were more frightened by the loss of money than by the disgrace of excommunication or the infliction of corporal punishments imposed upon them, he maintained the opposite: negligence should be imputed to the person who was more lenient in reproving those who had sinned and more severe in coercing them, and who did not watch over them as carefully to ensure that they fulfilled the satisfaction imposed upon them as he watched to count out the monetary assessment promised to him.

When they sometimes tried to argue on their own behalf, saying that the most blessed archbishop and martyr Thomas had exacted such fines from offenders, he immediately replied:

“Believe me, he was not holy for that reason. Other merits of virtue made him holy, and by another title he deserved to win the palm of martyrdom.”

## CHAPTER IX. How, against King Richard, who claimed it for himself, he established by a formal inquest the right of advocacy of the abbey of Eynsham

This is chapter 8 in the Great Life.

Since the coming of the Normans into England, after England had been subdued by their martial right, the Church of Lincoln had continuously and without challenge exercised the patronage of the monastery of Eynsham for a hundred years and more [Note: [Col. 1019D] From the year 1066, when William the Conqueror—of whom shortly—crossed from Normandy into England and was crowned king of England in London on Christmas Day. Thus Pagi, *Crit.*, p. 228.], [Note: [Col. 1019D] Gerald of Wales, Part II of *Anglia Sacra*, p. 417: “Robert Bloet,” he says, “prudently transferred the monks from Stow to Eynsham, etc., and reserved to himself and his successors the granting of the pastoral staff.”] Yet certain malicious persons stubbornly undertook to deprive it of this dignity.

The blessed bishop Remigius [Note: [Col. 1019D] Consecrated bishop by Lanfranc of Canterbury in 1067, about the beginning of the reign of the aforesaid William; he died in 1093, on the feast of the Ascension.]—whom, shortly after the glorious conquest of the island, the cathedral church of Lincoln had as its founder [Col. 1020C] [Note: [Col. 1020D] He is so called because he transferred the see from Dorchester to Lincoln.]—restored the aforesaid abbey after it had been laid waste and its brethren driven out in fear of the enemy. It was said that the illustrious conqueror William had confirmed it to him as his own by royal authority in such a manner that, apart from that bishop and his successors, no ecclesiastical or lay person whatever might presume to claim any lordship over it.

It happened in the tenth year of blessed Hugh’s episcopate [Note: [Col. 1020D] This was the year of Christ 1195 or 1196, since there is uncertainty about the year in which Hugh was made bishop.] that the venerable governor and abbot of this monastery, named Geoffrey, departed to the Lord [Note: [Col. 1020D] No Geoffrey appears among the abbots of Evesham at this period; it is therefore clear that this man was abbot of Eynsham.]. From the days of King Stephen [Note: [Col. 1020D] Stephen, king of England, died in 1154.] down to the penultimate years of the reign of Richard, son of King Henry [Note: [Col. 1020D] There seems to be an error, or the sense is rather obscure.], he is known to have presided over that place for about forty-four years [Col. 1020D] [Note: [Col. 1020D] He therefore began to preside one or two years before the death of King Stephen.].

When the bishop heard this, he sent, in accordance with ancient custom, one of his clerics to take the custody of the abbey into his hands and to administer its affairs, together with care for the brethren [Col. 1021A], until the canonical election of an abbot could be held. But those who administered the king’s affairs in England sought to take from the bishop both the custody of the vacant abbey and the lawful power of appointing its abbot [Note: [Col. 1021D] By the right by which Robert Bloet reserved to himself and his successors the granting of the pastoral staff, undoubtedly obtained of old from Remigius.]. For at that time the king was fighting overseas against the king of France [Note: [Col. 1021D] King Richard fought overseas against the king of France every year from 1195 until his death, with peace now made and now broken.].

Accordingly, many prudent men who sincerely loved the bishop tried to persuade him not, as the saying goes, vainly to tire himself by setting his arms against the current of the river, since for the moment they were too weak because of the number and power of his opponents. They maintained that the king’s father, Henry, had decreed by a general ordinance that all the abbeys of his kingdom should remain in his gift. Nor did they think it easy [Col. 1021B] that the son—who, as it appeared, was more obstinate than his father in many matters—would allow him to enjoy this privilege, even though it had been obtained in ancestral times, contrary to his father’s decree.

Finally, they advised that this undertaking, full of labor, of slight profit, and damaging in many ways, should not be attempted at all. They suggested that the fruit of labor too should be measured against the labor, and said that one ought not to incur the greatest losses in innumerable matters, which they already foresaw would arise more rapidly from this controversy for him and his own, where there was almost no hope of attaining what he sought, and perhaps little benefit even if it were attained.

To those who offered such advice, the man of singular confidence and remarkable discernment immediately replied: “Far be it that any mortal should presume to establish such a decree as would enable him to take from our God and from the most blessed [Col. 1021C] queen of heaven what is theirs! Laws of this kind, even if they were just, would give a rule only for future affairs; they would not overturn the enactments of earlier men. Which of my predecessors subscribed to such a decree, by which alone possession hitherto held by them could reasonably be prescribed against their right? Far be it that the ordinance of any lay person should infringe the privilege of ecclesiastical liberty! May it never befall me that, through fear of any power whatsoever or dread of however great a difficulty, I should, so far as lies in me, permit the right of my Church to perish! For if it is shameful enough not to increase the dignities and liberties of the holy Church acquired by our predecessors and defended by the ancients, how disgraceful it is if, through the inertia of a cowardly and useless [Col. 1021D] ruler, those things should fall from their state of integrity which ought to be increased and better advanced by a vigorous steward!”

Pursuing this course for two consecutive half-years [Note: [Col. 1021D] The election of the new abbot was therefore postponed for more than a year at least.], sparing neither expense nor his own labor, and fighting most resolutely both against the king himself and against very many who secretly opposed him by fraud, on both sides of the sea, for the freedom of the canonical status of the aforesaid monastery and for the defense of his own dignity, he at last obtained, by the Lord’s favor, a celebrated triumph [Col. 1022A]. For, after the rights which his predecessors had possessed in that monastery had been established by the sworn testimony of twenty-four trustworthy persons, clerics as well as laymen, the patronage was adjudged to him in the king’s court.

Accordingly, the custody of the vacant abbey and full and absolute jurisdiction to appoint its abbot were restored to him [Note: [Col. 1022D] Gerald of Wales confirms this account in Part II of his *Anglia Sacra*, p. 419, in these words: “Hugh manfully retained the monastery of Eynsham, formerly on the point of being lost through royal power, and by costly labors, but effective and fruitful ones, restored to the Church of Lincoln the granting of the pastoral staff.”]. After this he went there in person and remained for eight days with the brethren of the place like a kindly father among his dearest sons, going in and out, dining with them in the common refectory, and abundantly refreshing them with the wine of gladness and the fare of his generosity.

[Col. 1022B] Meanwhile, by his order the community deliberated concerning the election of the future abbot. When a week had been completed, the neighboring abbots and other religious men having been summoned, the monks’ election was presented to the bishop and solemnly confirmed by him. When these things had been duly accomplished, the distinguished shepherd set out for Lincoln. There, in the cathedral church, the elect of Eynsham was honorably advanced to the abbacy by his sacred blessing, with the approval and joy of all.

After a solemn banquet had been prepared for the clerics, the abbot, and his monks, the renowned leader of both companies reclined in their midst, rejoicing and exulting wonderfully in the Lord because, after the likeness of the supremely good shepherd, he had brought in other sheep that were from another fold, so that henceforth these and those sheep might become one flock and there might be one shepherd for both. Thus he had mutually joined the Church and the abbey in covenant, so that both might forever be one [Col. 1022C]. He also gave the new abbot a pastoral staff beautifully inlaid with silver and ivory, together with a large and distinguished cup. He enriched the place committed to the abbot’s governance with many benefactions and adorned it with gifts, and he always cherished and loved with paternal affection both the abbot himself and the flock subject to him.

## CHAPTER X. That almost every year he withdrew to Witham, where his face seemed to bear horns; and how, while preaching there to laypeople, he especially sought to instruct them in three matters: charity of heart, truthfulness of speech, and chastity of body; and how strictly he sought to preserve truthfulness in his own conduct

This is chapter 9 in the Great Life.

[Col. 1022D]

The holy man was accustomed to withdraw to his Witham once or twice almost every year. There he lived, after the manner of the others, in a solitary cell which was always kept vacant for him, without an inhabitant; there he meditated and prayed, took refreshment, and [Col. 1023A] slept. Sometimes he would come out into public, to greet those arriving and those who wished to speak with him. To attentive observers, from communion with the Lord’s speech he seemed in some manner to bear a horned face radiant with heavenly beams; yet he veiled it with the living grace of a certain cheerfulness and with the sweetness of all gentleness, and moderated his countenance for those conversing with him.”

Although laymen and secular persons were praising the state of that angelic life and complaining about the impediments of their own worldly lives—persons whom he knew neither wished nor were able to pass over to a more perfect way of living—he offered them the following instruction:

“Will only monks,” he said, “or merely hermits and solitaries attain the kingdom of God? In the end, when the Lord judges each person, he will certainly not demand that someone have been a hermit or a monk; rather, every reprobate will be reproached for not having truly been a Christian. For three things are required of every Christian, and if even one of them is lacking when he is judged, the Christian name will be of no benefit to him. The name without the reality will instead harm him, because falsehood is more condemnable in one who professes the truth. It is required, then, that the virtue and truth of this good name be possessed, so that charity may be held unfailingly in the heart, truth in the mouth, and chastity also in the body—not deceptively Christian.” [Note: [Col. 1023D] These words belong not to the author but to the abbreviator, who omits certain matters because of their length.]

Among the many things inserted at greater length in the continuous narrative of the Great Life concerning these three matters, a notable statement is the one he is reported to have made while preaching to women about chastity and the love of God. He said:

“Almighty God has deserved to be loved sufficiently by the female sex, because he did not refuse to be born of a woman. From this he also granted all women a magnificent and truly worthy privilege. For although it has not been granted to a man to be, or to be called, the Father of God, it has nevertheless been granted to a woman to be the parent of God.”

He possessed such great truthfulness in speech that no statement came from his lips in which he sensed there was any falsehood. Even when recounting or reviewing something he had done or heard, he always used some qualification to guard against any falsehood, even in matters he knew to be unquestionably true, saying, “Thus it has occurred to us,” or [Col. 1023D] something similar, by which he entirely avoided the rashness of a false assertion. With no less strict an observance of truth, he guarded the reverence due to his seal, permitting nothing untrue ever to be contained in the letters that were sealed with it. He was so scrupulous that, following the customary formula of writing, when he issued citations to anyone, he would not allow the words “We remember that we once cited you” to be placed in them, lest something that was not in his memory should falsely be said in his written document to be in it.

## CHAPTER XI  
How, when coming to Witham, he possessed an extraordinary brightness suffused with a ruddy color, sensing at the first sight of the place that he was being filled with an ineffable joy of the spirit; and what his manner of life was while he stayed there.—This is Chapter Ten in the Great Life.

[Col. 1024A]

So that no one might find less credible what we have mentioned above concerning a certain spiritual brightness of his countenance shining forth from him when he came out of his cell, we have thought it appropriate to insert briefly into this account another matter about him, very well known to his intimates and repeatedly observed by many, with complete truthfulness and not without astonishment and admiration.

Whenever he was journeying from distant regions toward that solitude dear to him, as soon as, from afar, he entered the neighboring territory, an extraordinary brightness, becomingly suffused with a ruddy color, customarily covered his cheeks together with his whole face. At the first sight of the place, he himself also felt the innermost regions of his heart suffused with an ineffable joy of spiritual gladness, as he very often confessed to his intimates. Once he had arrived at Witham, heavenly grace produced in him such a renewal of all his senses that he seemed suddenly to be renewed inwardly and outwardly at the same time, like the eagle’s youth.

After removing the outer cloak that he wore in public—it was made entirely of somewhat reddish cloth, lined with white lambskins [f. “lined”]—he put on ram skins with no cloth covering over them. As stated above, he wore the hair shirt next to his naked body; over this he wore a tunic, and over the tunic a fur garment. His bedding consisted only of a cloak, a pillow, and skins. In the morning, when he washed his hands as usual, he used neither a servant nor a towel. Each day he celebrated Mass with the utmost devotion, content with two assistants: the sacristan of the place and his own chaplain. [Note: [Col. 1023D] Thus Mass was already being celebrated daily, at least the conventual and public Mass, which is likewise known to have been celebrated daily in former times under Guigo V, although private Masses were celebrated less frequently. [Col. 1024D]]

Except for the pontifical ring, in the other priestly vestments he differed in no respect from the custom of the Carthusians. For he wore an alb and amice, stole, fanon, and chasuble, plain and white, neither decorated with silk nor with gold embroidery or gems. On Sundays, after supper, he proceeded with the other monks in silence and solemnity to the door of the refectory, where bread sufficient for each person’s food throughout the whole week was handed out by a brother standing inside. [Col. 1024D] [Note: [Col. 1024D] To this day the same practice is carried on in the Carthusian order, when bread is distributed to each person—not enough for the whole week, but sufficient for the following day.]

Nevertheless, often with the prior’s permission, he would gather with his own hands from the basket or chest in which the loaves collected from the brothers’ cells or from the refectory were stored, harder crusts and tiny fragments already scorched by dryness. He did this not because his own bread was insufficient, but because it was more than sufficient; rather, he said that these fragments seemed tastier to him than an entire loaf. Indeed, seasoned with blessings, they tasted more pleasantly to his healthy palate.

[Col. 1025A] He took delight in washing bowls—not only those in which pottages had been served to him, but also any that he happened by chance to find unwashed somewhere—scrubbing and polishing them inside and out with such care, using his hands and exceedingly clean fingers, as though he thought he were handling the Lord’s chalice.

At all times, once a week—that is, on Saturday—he regularly attended the bath of the purest confession. Since he carried this out according to the inviolable tradition of his order, he never omitted it; indeed, he did it more frequently whenever, because of some deed, word, or thought, a scruple beyond his usual experience arose in his mind. He also frequently repeated his confession countless times, striving to reveal to the Lord whatever sin he could remember having committed from childhood and to obtain pardon through the prayer of the Lord’s vicar to whom he confessed. As though this were not enough, whatever else he had done during the course of the entire year, he took particular care at that time to confess with great contrition of heart in the ears of the most discerning venerable servants of God, continually complaining that whatever good he possessed, if indeed he possessed any by God’s gift, was rendered impure by his guilt, so that it did not emerge sufficiently pure; whereas his evils were nothing other than pure evils.

## CHAPTER XII  
How, when Brother Eynard had set out on his journey to leave Witham and return to the Charterhouse, he was brought back by Blessed Hugh, after they had entered into a mutual pact that the one would not abandon Witham and the other Lincoln in the future.

When the aforementioned Brother Eynard had become very old—for he had been sent far and wide by his Carthusians for nearly a hundred years into various parts of the world to establish houses of that order, and at last, already decrepit, had come to Witham for this purpose—he wished to return to the Charterhouse. For, with God’s mercy assisting him, he saw that the place itself had now happily advanced toward the summit of perfection, both inwardly and outwardly. He therefore planned to return to his own people and to join his already aged limbs to the tombs of the saints who had once raised him when he was a young man. But when he saw that his intention was being frustrated from day to day by various arguments, and could no longer bear the intensity of the desire that agitated his mind, he bade farewell to the brothers and began to depart, supporting his trembling limbs with a staff.

[Col. 1025D] At that time the bishop was occupied in his cell with his customary exercises and the sweetness of contemplation. For that devoted old man had taken care that what he was planning should not become known to him too soon, since he had already recognized with complete certainty, from many indications, that he would be strongly hindered by him. But the matter could not remain hidden from the bishop for long. He therefore quickly followed him on foot as far as the interior of the neighboring grove and addressed him:

“May almighty God pardon you, Brother Eynard! What is it that you have decided to do? Why have you resolved to depart without your pupil and leave me alone in a foreign land, deprived of the sweet comfort of my teacher? I certainly do not [Col. 1026A] fail to understand how pious a desire leads you, so that you may spend the remaining days of your life among the holy hermits of Burgundy. But reason and will alike compel me rather to do the same.”

Then he removed the pontifical ring from his finger, summoned his clerics, and said to them:

“Go as quickly as possible, taking this ring with you, and greeting our lords at Lincoln in our name, announce to them that they should provide themselves with another and choose another bishop, so that henceforth we may be permitted to cherish a solitude that is friendly to us. It is far too long since I have lived amid the storms of the world, wrongly preferring the vain and bitter occupations of this age to the sweetness of the holy way of life, in which I was formed from the beginning.”

As he continued in this way, that man of desires began to fear and tremble—not because he was led by affection for his native soil, but by a burning love of heaven—and he stood there stupefied. Then, when the clerics complained about such a misfortune, saying that through him they would be deprived of their own shepherd, and vehemently exaggerating the harm of this disaster, the brother, covered with tears and groaning deeply, fell at the holy prelate’s feet.

This layman, with eloquent and most learned speech, tried to persuade the bishop, now by prayers and now by arguments, that he could not lawfully abandon the sheep divinely entrusted to him. When he saw that the bishop could not be moved in this way, he embraced his knees and said:

“Truly,” he said, “as long as the vital spirit animates and governs these limbs, I will not allow you to abandon your flock and, disregarding the salvation of so many, to care only for yourself. It is better for me [Col. 1026C] to remain in a foreign land until the end and finally to be brought to an end by death than to become the author of so great a separation—that is, division. Let us therefore return to our customary duties, lest, while seeking what belongs to us, we be accused of neglecting what belongs to Jesus Christ.”

Thus the prudence of the holy man, in an instant, not only moved the man whom no one had previously been able for a long time to turn from his intention of leaving the place, but also compelled him, through vehement entreaty, to beg that he himself would not leave either, provided that the other did not depart. After they had therefore entered into a mutual pact—that the one would not abandon Witham, nor the other Lincoln—they returned together in high spirits, each rejoicing that he had triumphed over the other.

## CHAPTER XIII  
Concerning the harmless completion of the kitchen fire at the time of our Hugh’s final departure from Witham

[Col. 1026D]

Hugh was accustomed to come to Witham every year, especially in the autumn, so that, while his own people were occupied with particular diligence in gathering their temporal crops, he, having left behind the company of his household in their own homes, might more easily and freely devote himself to gathering and storing the harvest of the spirit in the innermost storehouses of his soul. We shall now relate what happened there at the time of his final departure. [Note: [Col. 1026D] This occurred around the end of the year 1199.]

On the night that concluded the day on which he had last said farewell to the brothers, whom he would never again see bodily, the following event occurred. After he had first commended himself separately to the prayers of each of them in their cells, having confessed beforehand and requested and received their mutual prayers, he eventually asked permission to leave from the community, received the solemn blessing given to all, and exchanged the kiss of peace. Then, using the words that he frequently spoke when about to depart from those dear to him, he left them, saying:

“Now I commend you to God and to the word of his grace.”

From there he went to the lodging of the lay brothers, where his clerics and servants lived, intending to spend the following morning there. After resting, he entered the church to offer God the nocturnal praises. Suddenly, through the glass windows on the western side of the oratory, an exceedingly great blaze shone forth, so bright that its radiance seemed to surpass the sun’s rays. Astonished, some of those standing nearer the church doors rushed outside and saw the kitchen—that is, the cookhouse—which was almost entirely surrounded on every side by neighboring buildings, burning with flames stretching far up into the air.

When the bishop recognized this, he was greatly alarmed, fearing that the devouring fire might perhaps rage against the nearby buildings. Indeed, the position and arrangement of the surrounding structures gave no one reason to suppose that anything else would happen. The little building itself had been constructed for the use of the servants and the bishop’s guests, so that food might be cooked there for them. It was woven together from twigs and branches serving as walls, while a light thatched roof covered it. It stood only six or seven feet from the guest hall, and its roof, made of dry wooden shingles, projected close to the hall’s roof. In addition, wooden cells assigned to the lay brothers were arranged nearby in a circle. The church itself, standing still closer and surrounded on every side by various outbuildings, was also rightly feared.

Seeing, then, that all these things were exposed to inevitable danger on his account unless divine power should restrain it, the prudent man was briefly dismayed, but placed the greatest trust in the Savior’s goodness and several times made the sign of the saving cross against the fire. Interrupting the nocturnal office, which he had already begun in part, he immediately devoted himself to prayer before the Lord’s altar. He did not stop praying until word was brought that the little house had been completely consumed and had yielded to the flames, and that the fire had subsided—indeed, without damage to anything whatsoever except that one building, which, even if it had remained unharmed, would have had to be deliberately demolished by human hands. For he had already repeatedly ordered a stone dwelling to be built there for necessary uses in place of the demolished structure, precisely because he feared that danger might arise from it.

When everyone marveled the next morning that the fire had proved so harmless, he rejoiced in the Lord and said:

“Blessed be God, who not only wished to comfort our present fear in such a circumstance, but also, at last in my presence, completely removed the anxiety of future danger.”

[Col. 1027] Here ends Book Four.

# PROLOGUE TO BOOK FIVE

[Col. 1027C]

Having, with the help of Christ’s grace, brought to some conclusion four little books concerning the life of our holy father Hugh, the bishop, and trusting in his same assistance, we shall now attempt to undertake the fifth—which we intend to be the final book of this little work—in the order set out below.

In its narrative we have decided to recount nothing at all except what we ourselves witnessed in person, or what we clearly remember to have been reported to us as having been done by him shortly afterward. [Note: [Col. 1027D] In this Book V the author relates certain events that he himself witnessed, and others that he heard from other people.]

The beginning of this narrative will be taken from the singular devotion he possessed toward the burial of the dead. At the end, by way of conclusion, there will follow the final account of the incomparable honor and dignity of his burial and funeral rites, with which he deserved to be endowed from heaven after completing the struggle of the present life.

The material between these sections will contain especially those events by which it is shown that, while vigorously fighting for the immunity of the English Church against King Richard, against his justiciar, and against his own metropolitan, he labored greatly and, with God’s protection, successfully overcame them; and that, in the end, by showing humanity in burial to the king himself and to his persecutor, he achieved a splendid triumph.

To these matters there also appear to be added other things worth knowing concerning the beginning of John’s reign—now, in the third month of its fourteenth year, greatly weakening and gradually failing, as he had foretold would happen. [Note: [Col. 1027D] John, king of England, was crowned at London in the year 1199, on the day of, or on the Sunday within the octave of, the Ascension of the Lord, at Westminster. [Col. 1028D] That is, in the year of Christ 1212, while the exile of the Canterbury men and the others was still continuing.]

Next, we shall attempt to explain how he visited the Charterhouse and other places renowned for their religious observance, and how, after returning to England at London, he passed blessedly into the joys of the heavenly Jerusalem through a happy death.

[Col. 1027] Here ends the prologue.

# BOOK FIVE

[Col. 1029]

## CHAPTER I  
On the immensity of divine love for human beings, notably demonstrated in the duty of human burial, and on the immense affection of our Hugh for this duty

[Col. 1029A]

Hugh, the friend of God, drawing sweetly from his inmost secrets the memory of the abundance of divine sweetness toward the human race, very often placed before his hearers, as an odor of sweetness, these and similar thoughts, which we set down below.

As he used to say, among the innumerable things that reveal the immensity of God’s love for humanity, those things are recognized above all the others as displaying the prerogative of singular excellence which he never ceases to bestow upon human beings either before their birth or after their death.

To touch briefly upon the human beings who are now being born and dying: before the birth of each person, God the Son paid on that person’s behalf the price of his own death; God the Father sent that same Son into the world to die for humanity; and God the Spirit even poured himself out as a pledge. The whole Trinity together, one God, established the sacraments by which the newly born person might immediately be cleansed, fortified, and strengthened; he also granted the supports of his law by which the person might be governed and instructed, and bestowed many other things, sufficiently beyond explanation, which would serve that person’s welfare in many ways.

After the unstable course of life, when a person is overtaken by death—when he is received by those once most dear to him with a certain weariness, while he is driven from his former home by the anxious haste of parents and children—the most gracious kindness of his God alone does not reject him, though he is despised by the others.

Immediately, he not only sends angelic spirits to protect the soul returning to its Creator, but also sends his foremost and chief ministers on earth—priests, that is, and others placed in the sacred orders—to serve at the funeral. To them he says, in a manner:

“Do you see, my priests and wardens of my palaces that are in the world? Do you see my work, which I have always loved, for which I did not spare my only-begotten Son, but made it a participant in his immortality and death? Do you see, I say, that this work has become a burden to those who were once its friends and companions, and that it is cast out and driven away from them as though it were troublesome?

“Come, run quickly and go out to meet this image of my Son, crucified for it, as it flees for refuge to me. Take it up with censers and candles; strike the signs of my Church in solemn ringing; resound more loudly with hymn-singing voices; open the doors of my basilica and its hidden inner places; and lay beside the altar that contains the body of my Son the relics of that brother or sister.

“Finally, surround the joy of this person, now at last triumphant, with precious cloths; crowd around it with lamps and lanterns; and, with crowds of attendants standing by, surround it, even though it lies prostrate. Moreover, by a repeated votive offering of my Son, prepare a rich banquet, so that the breathless spirit, still restless and exhausted from the contest of its long-practiced mortality, but now laid aside, may breathe again into strength; and so that the flesh, temporarily emptied of its former inhabitant and soon to be cherished in the bosom of mother earth, may be watered with most welcome sanctification, so that on the final day it may joyfully be joined to its companion, known long ago, and may blossom forth cheerfully, happily to be clothed in eternal freshness.”

By expressing this thought in full and carefully chosen words concerning the compassionate kindness of the benevolent Creator toward the dead, he, who was in many matters a conscious and faithful interpreter of that divine dispensation, clearly indicated to the prudent enough by what feeling and with what regard he was moved to show such care toward those being buried.

For he had established by a general prohibition that in villages where he was present no parish priest should consign any deceased person, especially one already of mature age, to burial, unless perhaps some obstacle prevented Hugh himself from carrying it out, in which case the priest fulfilled that same duty with his permission. He particularly wanted this observed regarding adults, because he knew that, if they had lived praiseworthy lives, they deserved more abundant honor; but if they had led culpable lives, he knew that they required a more abundant urgency of intercession.

He therefore went everywhere to all people, offering them the service required by ecclesiastical custom with the greatest eagerness. For the poor, he arranged through his almoner that lights and other things desired at funerals should be supplied abundantly.

Whenever, while traveling, he saw a funeral being carried to some cemetery for burial, he immediately dismounted from his horse and approached the bier. After praying for a while, if he did not have a suitable book in which he could read without difficulty—for by then, as the end of his days approached, some of his customary sharpness of sight had diminished—he joined the priest celebrating the funeral rites, chanting the psalms with him and responding “Amen” and other responses as the priest began or completed the collects, fulfilling the role of a cleric—or, indeed, of a layman.

If a suitable book was available, he himself carried out what belonged to the priest: reciting the prayers, sprinkling holy water, carrying the censer around, casting earth upon the body, and carefully completing the rest of that office. After the absolution, he resumed the journey he had begun, with a blessing.

Most often, when he was staying in great cities, he would set out to bury one person, and then one report after another would reach him that others were waiting to be buried in various churches. He visited them all with great eagerness, devoutly rendering to each in turn the proper office of burial.

No matter how many there were, he did not cease this work of such great humanity until he knew that no one remained to be buried. Certain powerful men who were dining with him sometimes complained and murmured that, while he prolonged these activities, the hour of dinner had already long since passed. But whether he himself had invited them, or whether he had been invited by them to dinner, or whether it was on account of this matter or any other business, he never omitted to perform this work of piety whenever he could find someone upon whom to perform it. [Note: [Col. 1031D] Our Hugh gave an example of this when he was invited by the archdeacon of Bedford, as is related in the following chapter.]

But it is little that we report these things concerning persons of lesser rank. For it is established that he did the same even when invited to dine by kings. Later, at Rouen, he was invited by King Richard, [Note: [Col. 1031D] In the year 1197 or 1198. For Hugh visited the king overseas in both years, as is established from chapter 8 of this book.] and earlier he had once been invited by Richard’s father, [Note: [Col. 1031D] Perhaps this occurred in the first or second year of his episcopate, when he is recorded to have been with King Henry in Book III, chapter 9.] but he postponed going to the palace for as long as he found in the city people whom he could bury.

Thus he compelled both kings, together with their nobles or their entire households, to prolong their fasting for a long time, while he refused in any way to omit this religious duty, summoned by court officials though he was, whether out of regard for their rank or for human will.

When the court officials pressed him to hasten to the king who was waiting and growing impatient with the delay, and urged him to come as quickly as possible, he, doing nothing more hastily, said:

“There is no need for the king to wait for us; let him eat in the name of the Lord.”

He also said to his intimates:

“It is better for an earthly king to dine without us than for our humility to leave the command of the eternal King unfulfilled.”

From this it may perhaps be understood that it was not undeservedly repaid to him by divine providence that, having neglected two kings on account of the burial of the poor, he himself at last, for the service of his own funeral, should have two kings gathered together with many eminent men. [Note: [Col. 1031D] The kings of England and Scotland, as is stated below in chapter 27 of this book.] But we shall speak of these matters in their proper place; for now, let us continue what we have begun.

## CHAPTER II  
On the burial of a certain poor man in Normandy, of several people in Lincoln, and of a certain prelate in Bermondsey

Since we have reported what happened at Rouen, the metropolis of Normandy, although we did not see it ourselves [Note: [Col. 1031D] From this it may be inferred that the events concerning King Richard reported in the preceding chapter occurred in 1197, when the author had not yet been with Hugh, except during the final months of the year.], but heard it truthfully, we may briefly conclude by relating, in connection with a similar event, what we ourselves saw the same man do in that province. [Note: [Col. 1032D] The author relates in this chapter events that occurred during Hugh’s final years, when he himself remained with the bishop.]

One day, then, while the servant of God was traveling, it happened that not far from the castle called Argent [Note: [Col. 1032D] The same place as “Argentomagus,” or “Argentum,” “Argentomovum,” near which this event occurred in the year 1198, when, as will be said below in chapter 7, Hugh visited King Richard on the feast of Saint Augustine.] he saw close to the public road what appeared to be a recently buried human corpse under a mound. After examining it carefully, he immediately stopped and sent to the country people whom he could see plowing the earth from a distance. He learned that the grave contained the remains of a little man who had formerly begged for alms from door to door.

The same poor man had died in the house of a poor countryman living nearby. The priest of that parish had neglected him because of his poverty, and he had received burial there because no one was available to carry him to the cemetery. When the most merciful man heard this, he groaned deeply. He immediately dismounted, took the book—which he almost always carried with him—and carefully and devoutly went through the prayers and psalms that custom had established for burial. Later, by praying earnestly to the bishop of the place, he urged him to deal more harshly with that priest who, because of the man’s poverty, had denied a Christian a Christian burial.

On another occasion [Note: [Col. 1032D] Namely, in the year mentioned above, when, according to chapter 9, the king asked Hugh to send him twelve of the wealthier men from his Church.] when he was at Lincoln and had celebrated with the utmost devotion, on the day after Christmas, Mass for the glorious first martyr of Christ, Stephen, a certain mason who was laboring on the church asked him to absolve by pontifical authority the soul of his brother, who had been taken from human affairs the preceding night, and to commend him to the Lord with particular devotion.

He immediately fulfilled the request and began to inquire whether his brother’s little body had yet been buried. When he heard that it was still being kept unburied in a more distant church, he ordered a horse to be brought for himself, another for his chaplain, and a third for the servant who was accustomed to ride before him. For he had decided to go to the funeral with these three alone.

But when the horse for the chaplain was unavailable, he ordered the servant’s horse to be brought for the chaplain and told him to go ahead and hurry to the appointed place as quickly as possible. Thus, content with only two horses and accompanied by one monk and two boys, he arrived at the body of the deceased.

After commending it with paternal solicitude to the bosom of mother earth, he proceeded that same day—if our memory does not deceive us—to bury five more bodies successively in different cemeteries, assigned to him by their friends.

But as the hour grew late, and he was delaying his arrival at the solemn meal to which the archdeacon of Bedford had invited him, together with a considerable part of the clergy [Note: [Col. 1032D] He is called Laurence in chapter 4.], many people urged him—and finally the very man who had reported his dead brother to him—to pray for a while for the soul of the deceased, offer the aid of absolution, and commend it to the Creator, so that he would no longer delay coming to those already weary from waiting so long.

He answered those who made this suggestion with a certain sharpness of reproach:

“Why,” he said, “do you not heed the voice of our Lord speaking with sacred lips: ‘My food is to do the will of my Father who is in heaven’?” (John 4:34.)

He said no more. Like Saint Tobias, he interrupted his meal and preferred, as the Wise Man advises, “to go to the house of mourning rather than to the house of feasting” (Ecclesiastes 7:3). He therefore went, greatly consoling the mourners by the presence of his holiness; and, burying the one who was mourned, he released him from mourning through prayer, as is piously believed, by the mercy of Christ.

[Col. 1033B] On another occasion [Note: [Col. 1033D] In the Annals of the Church of Winchester, in Wharton, Part I, *Anglia Sacra*, p. 303, under the year 1198, it is stated: “Simon, abbot of Pershore, died at Bermondsey on the fourth day before the Ides of May.” Again, under the same year, in the Worcester annals, p. 478: “Simon, abbot of Pershore, died. Anselm succeeds and is blessed at Worcester on All Saints’ Day.” From this it may be inferred that the events reported here occurred in May of the year 1198.]

When the prelates and nobles of England had been summoned to a general assembly at London, the bishop of Lincoln also arrived there. The most urgent affairs of his Church likewise compelled him to confer about them with his friends who had gathered at the place.

It happened, however, on the day immediately preceding the appointed day of that assembly, that one of the prelates who had gathered there was suddenly struck by an illness which soon ended his life. Many people reported that he had been more than sufficiently addicted to the enticements of gluttony and excessively devoted to drinking.

When Hugh heard of his death, although the man had been scarcely known to him, he nevertheless sympathized with him from the depths of his compassionate heart and earnestly interceded for him before the Lord. He immediately ordered an investigation into where and by what persons the man should be buried. He was informed that he was to be buried in the Church of Our Lord and Savior at Bermondsey [Note: [Col. 1033D] A monastery in Surrey, begun around the year 1082, of the Cluniac order. Its benefactors, together with certain charters, are listed down to the year 1417 in the *Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. I, pp. 639 ff. [Col. 1034D]], but that no bishop or abbot was expected to celebrate his funeral rites.

None of his neighbors, household members, or former friends wished or dared to be absent from the solemn assembly that was to gather at Westminster on the day of his burial. When the bishop heard this, he said:

“God did not will that such a person, with so many prelates gathered together in this same city [Note: [Col. 1034D] London, from which Bermondsey—or, as it is written here, Bermundesia—was not far distant.], should be abandoned by all of us at this final necessity. We shall not act in this way toward our neighbor; no one would wish such a thing to be done to him by another.”

He therefore arranged to send some of his own people to the court, so that they might excuse his absence in the meantime. At daybreak he set out to provide the deceased with burial.

If we were to bring forward what we learned with our eyes and what we learned through our sense of smell on that day, we would certainly cause horror and astonishment in our hearers. We might also provoke the indignation of some people, who would claim that we were inhumanly forcing upon the public ear the common misery of human disaster and the lot of dying men that we had witnessed. Nevertheless, since a large part of the report we have undertaken depends upon these matters, and since in speaking of them we lament our own misery more than we insult another’s calamity—which God forbid—let what we say be heard for the benefit of all.

Let the living know, for their progress in humility, what became known in the dead man as an accumulation of horror. Let what he displayed to the living, as they looked upon the dead man—may God be gracious to him—also at some time be offered to those who are destined to die, as an incentive toward virtue.

A corpse extinguished in death was seen lying in a coffin, its face—after the manner of certain people—uncovered, but blackened blacker than [Col. 1034B] coal. The rest of the body was indeed clothed in a white priestly alb and also in a chasuble, but because of its excessive swelling it could scarcely be contained within them. For while the spirit still animated it not long before, it had swollen so violently in bulk that it could scarcely breathe. But after it had breathed its last, the internal corruption and the fiery heat of the torrid summer stretched the lifeless body so greatly that it seemed prodigious to those looking upon it.

Yet what was thus plainly visible to the eyes would have been tolerable, if the nostrils could have been spared their own punishment. The others, whom the order of events occasionally required to approach the coffin, closed their nostrils by inserting incense or other aromatics, and also kept various sweet-smelling substances in their hands to place repeatedly before their mouths. The bishop alone—although no one had a keener sense of smell, nor was anyone more averse to the foul stench [Col. 1034C]—stood beside the corpse and walked around it, admitting none of these things, which people ordinarily use by such means to lessen the corruption of the air, as though he were not circling a corpse in a coffin but, like a mother, were tending her little child lying in a cradle.

After this, when he had returned to his lodging, some of his companions, fearing that perhaps the inhaled contagion of the air had affected his innermost organs, began to question him about it. He regarded them as mistaken: they had not inhaled anything unpleasant there, since he himself—whose sense of smell was keener than any of theirs—had perceived nothing disagreeable in the place. Indeed, the good odor of Christ, which was truly for him the odor of life, caused him during life not to sense the stench of death at all.

## CHAPTER III. Concerning the dispute between him and the count of Leicester over a certain estate adjoining Leicester.—This is found as chapter two in the Great Life.

[Col. 1034D]

On the following day [Note: [Col. 1034D] After the burial of the aforesaid prelate. From this it is also inferred that the general meeting of prelates and nobles took place in May 1198; after it was dissolved, Hugh crossed over to the king.] when he had come to court, he began to be assailed by a serious accusation brought by the count [Note: [Col. 1034D] His ancestors founded the abbey at Eton in Warwickshire and the monastery of Luffield in Northamptonshire, as stated by the Monasticon [Col. 1035D] Anglicanum, vol. I, pp. 518 and 520.] of Leicester, who was attempting to take from him an excellent estate adjoining that city. The bishop’s friends and advisers also urged him to come to terms with his adversary under the appearance of peace, setting before him many reasons for fearing the case, although it was sufficiently just.

But he rejected the count’s obstinacy and excessive insolence and said to all his advisers, with great confidence and emphatic assertion:

“Know for certain that, so long as I remain alive in this light, that man will in no way obtain the fulfillment of this wicked intention of his. Let him therefore possess, to the accumulation of his own condemnation and that of his people, the documents violently extorted at some time during a period of war; but we, with the help of our Lady, will retain intact throughout our lives the patrimony entrusted to our protection, diminished in no respect whatsoever.”

[Col. 1035B] At the time, this assertion seemed to many prudent men to have been uttered with insufficient consideration, since the claimant’s action appeared to possess the color of equity, and both the king’s favor and that of almost the entire court were believed to be aligned with the count’s wishes. Nevertheless, the holy man’s words prevailed: he had cast his whole thought upon the Lord.

It also seemed remarkable to many that he never wished, in the famous manner of the secular court where those disputes were being heard, to excuse himself through an intermediary on the ground that it was impossible for him to appear in judgment, however greatly he might be pressed by the litigants’ maliciousness, lest he seem even to incur the appearance of lying.

After his death [Note: [Col. 1035D] That is, after the death of Saint Hugh.] the count indeed obtained the estate he was claiming, but immediately [Col. 1035C] he was struck by the contagion of leprosy; then, deprived first of bodily health and shortly afterward of life as well, he died without children.

Before his death, when many were attempting to place his brother—namely, the bishop of Saint Andrews in Scotland—in the seat of the man of God, who had long since departed to the Lord, a noble and devout matron saw one night in a dream the aforesaid servant of God, the bishop just mentioned, burning with the heat of ambition while attempting to climb onto his throne. He struck him harshly beneath the chest with a pastoral staff, so that the man who received the blow seemed to fall backward onto the ground. [Note: [Col. 1035D] This bishop of Saint Andrews in Scotland must have fallen or died in the year 1201 or 1202, since in the following year William, formerly precentor, succeeded him in the bishopric of Lincoln.]

When morning came and she had recounted the dream to her companions, certain men appeared, publicly announcing the death of that man—to the astonishment of those who heard them. What else, then, does the so abject and so sudden destruction of men so illustrious, so flourishing with the flowers of this world, suggest to those who know of it, except that overturning the rights of Churches and unjustly harassing the servants of God is supremely destructive?

## CHAPTER IV. Concerning a revelation disclosed to a cleric who, during the celebration by the bishop, saw the form of a child beneath the saving Host.—This is the third chapter in the Great Life.

[Col. 1036A]

One day [Note: [Col. 1036D] In the year 1194 or the following year, when this vision occurred, Hubert already being archbishop, but the author of the Life not yet having become Hugh’s companion.] while the bishop was staying at a manor belonging to him called Bukkedena, some monks came to him, presenting for his blessing some priestly vestments and a very beautiful chalice. The bishop had then come into the church from the burial of a servant of Laurence, archdeacon of Bedford, in order to celebrate the solemn rites of Mass.

It was a Saturday, on which day he always used to celebrate, when free to do so, both the daytime and nighttime office of blessed Mary, Mother of God. On that day also many clerics, richly endowed with ecclesiastical revenues, had gathered there from every direction.

When those men were already present in the church, the bishop held the aforementioned chalice in his hands, uncovered, in order to consecrate it. Seeing that it was remarkable for its metal, size, and workmanship, he carried it from the altar into the choir. Displaying it to all the clerics mentioned, he praised the devout diligence of religious men concerning the worship of the divine ministry and its vessels; conversely, he reproached them because, though wealthy in the revenues of many churches, they did not suitably cultivate those churches with books, vessels, or other necessary things, but rather strove to strip Christ’s basilicas of all these things than to adorn them.

After this he entered the sanctuary and began to celebrate Mass with great devotion. When, all the other rites having been properly completed, he reached the point at which it is customary to bless the Host raised on high, soon to be changed by mystical sanctification into the true body of Christ, divine clemency deigned to open the eyes of a certain cleric. Under the appearance of a little child, it showed him his Christ being handled with the utmost reverence by the most pure fingers of the sacred prelate. [Note: [Col. 1036D] This gave occasion for Saint Hugh to be represented with the little child above the chalice.]

The child was indeed very small in form, but through a certain divine radiance and whiteness was exceedingly beautiful, beyond human estimation. The cleric who had seen this, inflamed—as was natural—with extraordinary devotion and deeply moved, spent the entire interval in tears between that elevation and the next time he saw it raised to be broken and received, already divided into three parts.

At that second elevation he again saw, under the same appearance as before, the Son of the Most High, born of the Virgin, offering himself to the Father for the salvation of humankind. [Col. 1036D] Afterward, when everything that had to be done in the church had been completed, the cleric who had witnessed these things approached the true priest of the Lord and spoke to him privately in these words:

“Lord Father,” he said, “I have something to report to you which, if it pleases you, your holiness ought to hear with particular attention.”

When he had related these things to him on bended knees, the man of God withdrew with him from the crowd, [Col. 1037A] sat apart beside the altar, and gently instructed him to say whatever he wished.

Then the cleric said:

“On the day after the feast of All Saints—which was celebrated in this very week—when I was chanting the Psalter in a certain church for the souls of the faithful departed, as their solemn commemoration is customarily observed on that day, a certain voice suddenly came to my ears and said in perfectly clear words:

“‘Rise, my son, and go quickly to the bishop of Lincoln. Tell him, on God’s behalf, to admonish the archbishop of Canterbury more diligently [Note: [Col. 1037D] Hubert, who was elected archbishop on 30 May 1193 and enthroned in the same year on 7 November, Part I of Anglia Sacra, [Col. 1038D] p. 114.] so that together with him he may immediately and more vigilantly devote himself to correcting the condition of the clergy and the Churches.

“‘For the divine majesty is gravely offended by the things that are continually done by the rulers of the Churches and their ministers. Priests and persons of the other orders, stained by every kind of vice, especially by the filth of lust, and made injurious to the divine sacraments by approaching them unworthily, do not hesitate, insofar as they can, to pollute them by receiving and handling them irreverently.

“‘The Churches themselves are everywhere entrusted to unworthy persons, hateful to God because of their depraved conduct. Such persons often pass them on to one another for a fixed rent, in the manner of secular estates; and, like vile taverns, churches are leased under an annual payment for the sake of shameful profit, in what some now call emphyteusis.

“‘There is no discussion of pastoral care or of supporting the needy from the revenues. Instead, they continually long with complete greed to mend their purses—purses that luxury may empty, or that avarice alone may enclose so that they touch only rust.

“‘These and similar vices of rulers, transmitted by contagious imitation to those whom they govern, dominate the hearts of nearly all, both small and great. Hence great fury and the wrath of God threaten both the people and all the inhabitants of this land alike. Destruction will swiftly be brought upon them, and upon this wretched nation—unless hastening action and hastened correction forestall it—the scourge of heavenly vengeance now hangs.’

“After these words, the voice that had been heard fell silent.

“Before I heard these things, I had already completed the Psalter as far as Psalm 101 and, kneeling before the altar of the holy Mother of God, had devoted my mind intensely to prayer. For the memory of my father, who had died in the land of Jerusalem a few years earlier, where he had gone out of religious zeal, had suddenly arisen in my mind. [Note: [Col. 1038D] That is, in the year 1190, when many of those marked with the cross died during the expedition against the Saracens.] From this there suddenly arose such a fervor of compunction that my spirit was absorbed by it. Completely abandoning the psalmody and suppressing every movement of my lips, while streams of tears poured from my eyes in torrents, I poured out prayers to the Lord only through the desires of my heart.

“On hearing this voice, which seemed to come from the nearby altar, a certain horror mingled with astonishment immediately interrupted the force of compunction that had wholly claimed me. I began, stunned, to wonder who had spoken such things and to whom [Col. 1038A] he had spoken them. For I knew that no one except me was standing nearby in that place.

“After long cycles of fearful thought, when I had been unable in any way to discover the author of the voice, I signed myself with the saving sign of the cross and began again to devote myself to the interrupted prayer with greater desire than before. Without delay I again heard the voice, in the same tone and with the same syllables, expressing the same sentence as previously.

“Then, since I could perceive neither the person standing nor the person to whom this speech was addressed, I decided that I should leave the place, thinking only this to myself: that some more sacred mystery was being enacted there by persons whose secrets I was unworthy to witness. Having therefore adored the Lord and signed my forehead, I departed from the place.

[Col. 1038B] “When I reached the church doors, a certain virgin met me, a very devout woman who served the Lord day and night in fasting and prayer, cold and nakedness. She rarely left that church and scarcely ever withdrew from its courts. While the aforesaid events were being heard, she had been devoted to her customary prayers in a remote corner of the church.

“She fell at my knees and earnestly begged me, if possible, to share with her something of what I had learned had been said to me inside. But because I did not yet know to whom the things I had heard had been spoken, I in turn preferred to ask her to reveal to me what she knew of the heavenly voice’s utterance—for she was more worthy than I to hear and know the inner mysteries, and she herself confessed that the voice had been sent from heaven, while I had perceived nothing of its meaning.

“To this she replied: ‘I certainly know that the Lord twice addressed speech to you, commanding you to do something. I paid little attention to it myself, but I understood with absolute certainty that the command was addressed to you.’

“Then I said: ‘Pray, beloved sister, that the Lord may deign to fulfill his good pleasure concerning us. As for the matters of which you now speak, I have received no certainty about them.’

“After I had said this, I myself left the church, while she returned inside to the accustomed retreats of her prayers.

“Afterward, I entered my lodging chamber and spent the day there, fasting and praying until evening. When I had taken refuge only in a little bed, while my mind was agitated by the waves of various thoughts concerning what I have related, I suddenly heard a voice repeating for the third time the very thing it had declared at first and second, though now preceded by an indication that made clear to me that it was speaking to me. For it said:

“‘I speak to you, my son, who are resting there present: go as quickly as possible to the venerable man, the bishop of Lincoln, and do not delay to announce to him, on behalf of the Almighty, all these things that I commanded you twice in the church.’

“To this I immediately replied:

“‘And how will a man of such authority believe my words, when I am weaker both in age and understanding and scarcely know how to say anything?’

“Then the one who was speaking replied to this [Col. 1039A] and added:

“‘That man will have unquestioning faith in your words when, as signs to identify them, you tell him what you will see upon the altar before him on the first day when you reach him and behold him celebrating the solemn rites of Mass. Do not, therefore, delay to obey my words, but devoutly carry out what I command you.’

“After these words the speaker’s voice was taken away.

“But I, greatly encouraged to carry out what had been commanded, rose during the night after taking only a little sleep. Without telling my companions, I set out on foot to seek you. [Note: [Col. 1039D] The place where the admonition was given was one or two days’ journey from the place where Saint Hugh was staying.] I arrived here shortly before the beginning of Mass and devoutly watched your holiness celebrate the divine mysteries.

“Paying especially close attention to the Lord’s table before you, I clearly saw, although with unworthy eyes, our Lord Jesus Christ’s body under the appearance of a little child, twice raised by you above the chalice in your hands. Since you also saw the same thing far more clearly—because you saw it for a longer time, from nearer, and more worthily—there can be no doubt about it.”

The cleric continued in this way, tears flowing down his cheeks. The man of God also wept abundantly during these events.

When they had both wept together for some time and exchanged many words about these things, the bishop wiped the cheeks and eyes of both himself and the cleric with his sacred fingers and kissed him. The cleric was about twenty-five years old. He ordered him to remember to keep these things reverently hidden. Moreover, he earnestly exhorted him to hasten to take the religious habit and to serve the Lord completely in religious conduct. For he maintained that it was not fitting for one who had seen and heard such things to continue wandering in the vanity of the world. The cleric immediately replied that he would gladly obey these admonitions.

Afterward the bishop entered the hall to dine. Surrounded by a large company of diners, he sat down cheerful and happy, ordering the cleric so often mentioned to recline with him in the open area, not far from his own place. The next day he dismissed him with his blessing and sent him to a monk who was acquainted with him. The cleric himself soon afterward became a monk and lived a highly religious life.

We have learned with complete certainty that many mysteries of spiritual visions were later revealed to him; some of them, having long ago been committed to writing at the command of the holy prelate, [Col. 1039D] are known to have been circulated far and wide. We also frequently heard from his own mouth these very things that we have now related.

## CHAPTER V. Concerning the very astonishing miracle that occurred in France, involving the body of Christ in the hands of an unworthy priest, and concerning the remarkable judgment of our Hugh, who was invited to see that miracle.—This is chapter four in the Great Life.

[Col. 1040A]

Concerning the life-giving sacrament of the most holy Eucharist, it does not seem inappropriate to relate one further event that is known to have occurred in Gaul [Note: [Col. 1039D] I do not know whether the event, which is here said to be known to many, had been made public by anyone else.]. Although we consider it most worthy of the knowledge of many of the faithful, it would nevertheless not have been inserted by us into this present history if the judgment of the man who is the subject and cause of all that is inserted on this page had not compelled us to include it—the judgment he remarkably expressed concerning the event itself.

At a certain time [Note: [Col. 1039D] In the year 1200, from which it is clear from this chapter that Hugh was in Paris and Gaul.] after departing from the city of Paris, while traveling toward Troyes, he lodged at his first stopping-place in a certain village called Joi. [Note: [Col. 1040D] Since this village is said to lie between Paris and Troyes, at one or the first stopping-place, let those living nearby determine whether any memory of this event still survives there.]

Wherever he had been received as a guest, it was his custom to invite the parish priest and the ministers of that church to his table. He frequently used to say to his steward, with a certain generous cheerfulness, what the Lord once often said to the Hebrew people:

“Do not abandon the Levites who are within the gates of your city” (Deut. 14:27).

The priest of that place, however, although summoned by the ministers in the customary manner, obstinately refused to come to the bishop’s table. He did come after the meal to visit him—not merely to offer the bishop, whose reputation was exceedingly great, the courtesy of a greeting, but rather to obtain the favor of being commended to the Lord through his prayers.

He also came to explain to him in words a very astonishing event that had happened to him some time earlier [Note: [Col. 1040D] It must have occurred between 1160 and 1170. When the priest related it to Hugh, he was described as very old, though this was attributed more to the severity of his abstinence than to his age.] concerning the sacrament of the Lord’s body, which was to be adored, and to invite him to see the event itself, still displayed before people’s eyes in his church.

The priest was already advanced in age and venerable in appearance. His whole body was emaciated and very dry, not so much from age as, it was said, from the severity of his abstinence, his skin clinging tightly to his bones.
