After greeting the bishop, he was unable, out of modesty, to explain personally what he wished to tell him. Instead, he related the following in order to some of the bishop’s companions:

“When I was a young man,” he said, “and had ascended to the priestly rank, although neither my years nor my conduct yet deserved so high an office, it happened, through the ambush of the ancient enemy, that I committed a certain mortal sin [Col. 1040D]. I had not yet been cleansed from its contagion by the remedy, the washing of penance or confession; yet, polluted in heart and body as I was, and moreover blind in mind and weak in faith, I—horrible to say—customarily approached the ministry of the sacred altar shamelessly and rashly.

“One day, while I was assisting at the sacred secrets of the Mass and silently turning over in my mind the enormity of my crime during the consecration of the saving Host, amid other thoughts of my dark heart this question revolved within me:

“‘Do you suppose that this body and blood is truly made, handled, and received by me, the filthiest of sinners—the one who is described as the brightness of eternal light and the spotless mirror?’

“While I was considering these and other thoughts no less foolish than these, the moment arrived when the most holy Host had to be broken into three parts according to the customary rite. When I broke it through the middle, immediately the most liquid blood began to flow out through the fracture. It suddenly changed the middle portion of the Host, which I was holding in my hand, into the appearance of flesh and stained it with a blood-red color.

“When I saw this, I was completely paralyzed with fear. Almost deprived of my senses and having lost the counsel of reason, I allowed whatever of the sacrament I was holding in my hands to fall into the sacred chalice.

“At that moment there was to be seen—and it remains visible to the present day—a miracle astonishing for all ages: wine changed into blood and bread into flesh, with half of each changed in this way, visibly displaying under the two species both the reality of the sacrament and its form—both the signifying and the thing signified.

“When I saw these things retaining their forms without change, and did not dare touch them at all, I covered the chalice with the paten and the paten with the sacred pall, and completed the office of the Mass. Afterward, when the people had been dismissed, I placed the chalice, together with the sacred elements that are still contained in it today, in a suitable place beside the altar, to be guarded with due reverence.

“After this I went into the presence of the supreme pontiff. Having first confessed my guilt, I explained the whole sequence of the event to him, and returned from him with the benefit of absolution, after an appropriate satisfaction had been imposed upon me.

“Now, in order to behold these great works of God visibly, faithful people come here from many places throughout the surrounding region. They glorify with the utmost reverence the God who alone works wonders.

“Holy bishop, I desire these things to be made known to you through these men, so that I may deserve to be assisted before God by your prayers, and so that you yourself, together with your companions, may rejoice more fully in the Lord when you have seen these things.”

Those who reported this to the bishop, having learned it from the priest, hoped that he would soon proceed to see the event, with eager devotion of heart. But [Col. 1041D] he immediately answered what he had heard in these words:

“Let them have, in the name of the Lord, the signs of their unbelief. What have these things to do with us? Do we marvel at particular images of this divine gift, when every day we behold this entire and complete heavenly sacrifice with the most faithful vision of the mind? Let the man who does not behold the whole thing with the inner sight of faith look at its tiny portions with bodily sight.”

Having said this, he dismissed the priest, who had commended himself to his prayers, after giving him his blessing. He rebuked the curiosity of his companions and strengthened them in the solidity of faith. Indeed, he made it abundantly clear that the faithful ought to hold and understand with greater certainty what faith prescribes than what this visible light displays.

[Col. 1042A] Thus he restrained them from their intended curious sight and instructed the minds of his hearers to awaken both the vision and the embrace of devotion through these words and life-giving nourishment for their hearts. From the foregoing, and also from other words of his, we are more firmly persuaded that it was granted to him not only once, as was shown above, but also frequently, with the face of the inner man revealed, to perceive by a certain inward vision those things concerning this sacrament which we are all taught to retain as invisible realities through the purest faith.

## CHAPTER VI. How our Hugh corrected his metropolitan, and how concerned he was about the conduct of his subjects.—This is chapter five in the sequence of the Great Life.

[Col. 1042B]

But when the man of God, after the divinely given admonition he had received, urged his metropolitan more frequently than usual and with greater insistence than usual to set aside for a while the secular cares to which he clung tirelessly and to devote himself rather to the practice of his episcopal office than to the administration of public affairs, he aroused in him a grave hostility against himself.

As for those subject to his jurisdiction, both clerics and priests, he himself, with all his strength and through his officials, recalled them to the path of a more upright life and to the integrity of regular discipline. Omitting nothing of paternal concern, he poured oil and wine into the weakened conduct of those entrusted to him, so that the severity of strictness might restrain those whom the gentleness of compassion had been unable to heal.

[Col. 1042C] How much he labored, and how much he accomplished in correcting his subjects through this twofold exercise of ecclesiastical administration, it is not within our ability to explain as fully as would be fitting, since even the most skilled minds would scarcely suffice to unravel it in the length of many volumes.

He also took care, as far as he could, to restore the churches of his diocese in every respect to their proper condition. He diligently admitted to their governance men commendable in knowledge and life, while he vigorously excluded from entering them those who lacked these qualities.

How greatly he was driven by zeal in this intention can be better judged from his own words, by which he very often confessed concerning himself:

“I am astonished,” he said, “that some people are said to rejoice when prebends or churches fall vacant, which they can then bestow at will upon new possessors. For I speak truly of myself: nothing in this life has ever afflicted my mind as much as the anxious care of selecting and discerning suitable persons to whom the governance of vacant prebends or dignities of our Church might properly be entrusted.

“Nor has anything worldly ever saddened me so greatly as that error by which, often in response to the recommendation of many, I granted ecclesiastical benefices to men whom I foolishly believed to be diligent in the canonical disciplines, until afterward, enriched with the goods of the Church, their perverse conduct revealed them to have been negligent.”

In this way he lamented, not without a sigh, that certain people had deceived him in this matter.

We know that, to guard more carefully against making this error, he specially instructed one of his associates, in whose sincerity he had considerable confidence, that if he sensed or heard even the slightest unfavorable report concerning anyone whom he intended to provide with a benefice in his Church, he should on no account presume to conceal it from him.

This was not because he would place faith in uncertain rumors about anyone, but so that he might sometimes select certainty even from doubtful reports and meanwhile moderate the favor he had conceived from uncertain praise, until, after the truth of what he had heard had been investigated, he could more freely carry out, with an unimpeded judgment of mind, what reason dictated.

He also instructed many men who feared God and possessed discernment to report carefully to him persons approved in conduct and learning, whom he might gather into the bosom of his Church when a suitable opportunity arose.

[Col. 1043B] But alas for the unhappiness of human weakness and ignorance! For many of those men, under the pretext of kinship, some other connection, or familiarity, strove rather to recommend to him persons who ought to have been blamed. At times he did not hesitate to place confidence in them, even though they were acting faithlessly against him, indeed against God.

Thus he knew and lamented that he had been deceived on several occasions by certain people. He abhorred all the more, with great disgust, the perversity of unfaithful men who had abused God’s patience and his own most pure simplicity, and, insofar as he was able, he excluded them from his counsels.

## CHAPTER VII. How at the Council of Oxford he resisted a request for aid sought from King Richard, by whom nevertheless he was honorably received after the offense.—This is contained under chapter five in the sequence of the Great Life.

[Col. 1043C]

While he was doing these things and devoting himself more diligently to the Lord’s gains through the acquisition of faithful souls, the poisonous schemes of the ancient serpent against him did not cease.

Accordingly, one year and almost four months before his death [Note: [Col. 1043D] King Richard died in 1199, on 6 April. The king’s anger against Hugh therefore broke out in 1197, around the feast of Saint Nicholas the bishop, which is observed on 6 December.], Richard, king of the English, became fiercely angry against him for the following reason.

While the king was engaged overseas and fighting fiercely against Philip, king of the Franks, the whole body of the magnates of England was summoned [Note: [Col. 1043D] In the year 1197, when, according to Trivet in his Chronicle, the king of England was fighting fiercely against the king of the Franks.] by the archbishop of Canterbury, Hubert, to a general assembly at Oxford. The archbishop, who presided over public affairs in the king’s place, laid before them the king’s necessities: he was inferior in money and troops, yet was fighting against a very powerful king who was striving with all his strength for his disinheritance and destruction.

Finally, he asked them to decide collectively by what kind of aid they could assist their lord in such straits. Those who followed every royal command and regarded obedience to it as obligatory had already determined that the barons of England, among whom they themselves were counted, should provide the king with three hundred soldiers, who would serve him continuously for a full year at their own expense against his overseas enemies.

When the bishop of Lincoln’s consent was then requested in that assembly, he remained silent for a while, deliberating within himself. The primate of Canterbury and Richard, bishop of London [Note: [Col. 1043D] Richard was bishop of London from the year 1189, according to the Winchester Annals, p. 302; according to the same source, he died in 1198, on 10 September.], who also held the privilege of the deanery among the bishops, had first declared that they would expose themselves and their possessions in every respect to the king’s necessity.

Then he quickly replied:

“You know, prudent and noble men who are present here, that I am a newcomer in these regions [Col. 1044B] and that I was taken from the simplicity of the eremitical life and appointed to episcopal office. When, therefore, the Church of my Lady, Saint Mary the Mother of God, was once entrusted to my inexperienced governance, I carefully learned its customs and dignities, as well as its obligations and burdens. In preserving and fulfilling these, for almost thirteen years [Note: [Col. 1044D] A clear indication that Hugh became bishop in 1185. For when he came to the king on Saint Augustine’s Day in 1198, he had not yet completed twelve years if he had been made bishop in 1186.] I have so far not departed from the upright footsteps of my predecessors.

“I certainly know that the Church of Lincoln is bound to provide military service for the lord king, but only within this land; beyond the borders of England, nothing is owed by it. Therefore I consider it more advisable for me to return to my native land and inhabit the desert as usual than to exercise the episcopate here while, by losing the ancient immunities of the Church entrusted to me, I subject it to unprecedented exactions.”

Taking this reply rather badly, the archbishop, lowering his voice somewhat and trembling, with lips quivering from indignation, added that he would inquire of the bishop of Salisbury, named Herbert [Note: “Herebertus, archdeacon of Canterbury, was elected bishop of Salisbury in the year 1193.” Thus the Worcester Annals, in *Anglia Sacra*, part I, p. 478], what his own attitude was concerning the provision of assistance to the king. In response to the inquiry, the latter answered briefly:

“It seems to me that, without grave prejudice to my Church, I can neither say nor do anything other than what I have just heard from the reply of the lord bishop of Lincoln to be necessary.”

At this the archbishop became exceedingly indignant. After first venting the bitterest reproaches against the bishop of Lincoln, he dissolved the council and informed the king [Note: Toward the end of the year 1197, as is also clear from the following note] that, because of the bishop of Lincoln, the king’s business had been deprived of its result. When the king had received this message for the second and third time through the archbishop’s messengers, he ordered all the bishop’s possessions to be confiscated as quickly as possible, in great anger and fury. He gave the same order concerning the bishop of Salisbury, who had approved the decision of the bishop of Lincoln by his assent.

What more is there to say? The bishop of Salisbury was immediately outlawed [Note: In the *Winchester Annals*, p. 303, the entry for 1198 reads: “The bishop of Salisbury, etc., having been dispossessed of his possessions, crossed the sea in the month of February.” A little later: “Herbert, the poor bishop of Salisbury, returning from Normandy, etc., landed in England on the sixth day before the Ides of June.”]. After coming to the king and enduring insults, losses, vexations, and very many humiliations, he finally, only with the greatest sum of money, bought back his peace and his possessions. But no one dared to lay hands upon the property and possessions of the bishop of Lincoln, since they feared incurring his displeasure, and feared undergoing his anathema no less than they would fear a capital punishment.

Meanwhile, the period from the feast of Saint Nicholas was prolonged almost until the Kalends of September [Note: Namely, from 6 December 1197 until the day of Saint Augustine in 1198, when Hugh came to the king and was dismissed by him in peace, though not for long]. The king repeatedly ordered that the bishop be outlawed, while the royal officials did not dare in any way to carry out the order. At last, moved by the entreaties—especially of those who pressed the claims of the royal treasury, so that his property might be seized by right of the fisc—he crossed the sea to the king.

At Rouen, two noblemen approached him: namely, William, surnamed Marshal [Note: A man of great authority with the kings of England, and eventually earl of Pembroke. For more about him, see *Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. I, p. 725, and the *Chronicle of Trivet* under the year 1219, when he died in London at the New Temple and was buried on the day after Ascension], and the earl of Albemarle [Note: William by name, surnamed de Fortibus; through his wife Hawise, earl of Albemarle. Trivet mentions him under the year 1221]. Explaining to him through how many insults the king’s fury had raged against the lord of Salisbury, and how many threats he had made against the bishop of Lincoln, they begged him to be willing to indicate to the king, through them, whatever seemed expedient for his own welfare, so that they might communicate it to the king and soften his attitude toward his case or business.

For they asserted under oath that they would rather have bought peace for him with all the resources at their disposal than see the king’s ferocity rage against him in accordance with the movement of his fury.

“And we pursue this course,” they said, “not only because we love you with the utmost fidelity, but also because in this matter we fear greatly for ourselves, for our lord the king, and for all his people. No one can doubt that heavenly vengeance will strike him very swiftly if he presumes—as God forbid!—to harass your holiness with unworthy injuries. Then we and our friends would become a reproach and a spoil for our enemies, who would fight against us.”

When they had continued in this vein, the bishop immediately replied:

“We return immense thanks, with all the affection of our hearts, for the goodwill that you have toward us. I know very well that, above all others, you are necessary to our lord the king in his present distress, for which we have sufficient sympathy. I also know well that, more than others, he is indebted to you for the benefit you have bestowed.

“Therefore I do not want you to say anything on my behalf, against whom the king is so angry. Otherwise, if he gives you a harsh answer, you may become less diligent in his service; or, if he hears you on my behalf, he may consider that he has done something great for you and may prove somewhat less ready to repay you with the benefits you deserve.

“You may tell him only this, if you think fit: that we have come to these regions in order to visit him. If he wishes us to see him, let one of his people inform us where we should meet him.”

After he had said this to them, those noblemen greatly admired both his prudence and his magnanimity. They went to their lord and reported all these things to him. The king himself was also by no means unimpressed by the bishop’s words, and, his mind being suddenly changed toward him in almost every respect by divine providence [Col. 1046B], ordered that the bishop be told to meet him on the following third day at the new castle of Les Andelys [Note: From this place a major dispute arose in 1197 between King Richard and the archbishop of Rouen, as related on p. 840 of vol. V of Martène’s *Thesaurus novus*; it was settled, as may be inferred from Trivet’s *Chronicle* under this year, by means of an exchange].

Our Hugh approached him confidently and found him in the chapel of that place hearing the solemn Mass on the feast of the eminent Doctor, Saint Augustine. He immediately greeted him. The king himself was standing beside the entrance of the doorway on a royal throne, while two bishops—namely, the bishop of Durham [Note: Read “Dunelmensis,” who was Philip of Poitiers; concerning him see *Anglia Sacra*, part I, p. 726 and following] and the bishop of Ely [Note: Eustace, elected bishop in 1197; concerning him also see *Anglia Sacra*, part I, p. 633]—stood beside his feet.

When the bishop had greeted him, the king did not answer him a word. After looking at him for a while with grim eyes, he turned his face away from him. The bishop said firmly:

“Give me a kiss, my lord king.”

The king turned his gaze away from him even more and inclined his face and head in another direction. Then Bishop Hugh seized the king’s garment around the chest and shook him vigorously, saying again:

“You owe me a kiss, because I have come to you from far away.”

The king replied:

“You have not deserved to be kissed by me.”

Shaking him still more strongly by the cloak, which he held tightly in his hand, Hugh said confidently:

“Indeed, I have deserved it.”

And he added:

“Kiss me.”

Then the king, admiring the bishop’s confidence and steadfastness, smiled slightly and kissed him.

Two archbishops [Note: Walter of Rouen, already reconciled with the king, and, apparently, Hubert of Canterbury; for Geoffrey of York was in the king’s disfavour that year] and five bishops were also present there. They had taken their stand between the king’s throne and the steps of the altar. Wishing among themselves to summon the prelate, who had now triumphed over the king in this manner, they made a place for him to sit not far from the king. But he passed directly by them, planted his feet beside the corner of the altar, and, with his eyes stubbornly lowered toward the ground, devoted his attention solely to the celebration of the divine mysteries.

Meanwhile, the king watched him with considerable curiosity and almost without interruption. When, at the threefold invocation of the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world, the priest had given the kiss of peace to an archbishop who was, according to custom, about to bring the peace to the king, the king advanced to meet him as far as the steps. He took from the archbishop the sign of the peace received through the immolation of the heavenly Lamb, and with humble reverence offered it to the bishop of Lincoln by kissing him on the mouth.

Thus the most illustrious prince himself chose to offer to the holy bishop the sign of veneration which the archbishop was preparing to bring to him. For he went eagerly to the bishop and, while the latter suspected nothing of the kind but was earnestly entreating the Lord, paid him honour—as the Lord Himself had plainly ordained—so that what the Lord says might be fulfilled: “Those who glorify me I will glorify” (1 Samuel 2:30).

## CHAPTER VIII. How, after the king’s anger had been calmed, he reproved him and departed honoured by him; and how, after his departure, the king reported to him the victory over his enemies that had befallen him.

When the sacred service of the altar mentioned above had been completed, Hugh approached the king and made a brief but forceful complaint concerning the indignation that had been stirred up against him without cause. He demonstrated with the clearest reasoning that he had done absolutely nothing wrong against the king.

Since the king could offer no reply to the contrary, he shifted the blame for this offence onto the archbishop of Canterbury, who, he said, had repeatedly made sinister reports about Hugh to him in letters. The bishop promptly proved, with the greatest ease of reasoning, that all these reports were devoid of truth, and said:

“Subject to the honour of God and the salvation of my soul and yours, I have never opposed your interests, either wholly or even in the smallest matter.”

When the king’s indignation had thus been calmed, the bishop was honoured with royal gifts. The king also sent him, for the purpose of lodging, to the castle he called the Harbour of Joy [Note: Apparently the same as the castle of Les Andelys, since the former is called new and the latter recently built], which he had recently constructed on a certain nearby island. He asked him to come to him again the following day, so that, after another conversation, Hugh might return to his own lands with the king’s grace and favour. Hearing this gladly, Hugh promised that he would return on the following day.

Yet, being piously concerned in pastoral solicitude for the salvation of the king’s soul, Hugh took his hand, raised him from his seat, and drew him aside to a place near the altar. There he told him to sit, and, sitting beside him himself, addressed him more privately:

“You are our parishioner, my lord king, and by reason of our pastoral care we are bound to answer at the dreadful judgment of the Lord for your soul, which the Lord of the universe redeemed with His own blood. I therefore want you to tell me how the inward state of your soul is, so that I may effectively offer it counsel or assistance, insofar as heavenly inspiration may help.

“For a year has now passed [Note: From this it may be inferred that Hugh was also with the king in 1197] since I spoke with you on another occasion.”

When the king told him that his conscience was good in almost every respect, except that he was troubled by hatred of his enemies, whom he found injurious and wickedly hostile toward him, the bishop said:

“If you please the Ruler of all in every respect, He will easily either make your enemies peaceful toward you or subjugate them after defeating them. But you must take the greatest care lest you—as God forbid!—be injurious in any matter to your Creator, or commit any injustice against your neighbours.

“Concerning you, however, I speak sorrowfully: it is now a public rumour that you neither preserve marital fidelity toward your own wife in the marriage bed [Note: Richard married Berengaria, daughter of the king of Navarre, in 1191. Hugh visited and consoled her at Beaufort Castle, as related in chapter 15 of this book, in 1199], nor keep the privileges of the Churches inviolate, especially in appointing or electing their rulers.

“For it is said that you are accustomed to promote certain men to the governance of souls through the intervention of money or favour—a crime that is certainly highly distinctive. Without doubt, if this is true, peace cannot be granted to you by the Lord.”

After carefully admonishing and instructing the king for the time being on these matters, while the king wholly excused himself concerning some points and earnestly sought Hugh’s intercession concerning others, Hugh dismissed him with his blessing and happily withdrew to the lodging provided for him by the king.

The king meanwhile spoke about Hugh with his attendants and praised his courage at length:

“Truly, if all the other bishops were everywhere like this man, no king or prince would dare to raise his neck against them.”

Then some of the king’s advisers suggested that he send letters to England through Hugh and request from the great men of the realm assistance in the form of some kind of subsidy. They particularly advised him to send Hugh on this mission because, without doubt, the letters would be received more favourably by everyone if they were delivered through so important a messenger. Some also hoped that the bishop would carry out this commission more willingly, so that he might thereby be further commended to the king’s favour.

But, as the Wise Man says, “In vain is the net spread before the eyes of the winged creatures” (Proverbs 1:17), for Hugh was immediately informed of all this by the king’s household. When his clerics suggested that, in so easy a matter, he should eagerly comply with the king’s wishes, he rejected their words with great disdain, saying:

“Far be this from me! It is not my role to become the bearer of royal letters. This cannot agree either with my purpose or with my office. It is not my role to become even slightly a collaborator in exactions of this sort.

“You are not unaware that this powerful man always begs as though with a drawn sword; and especially when this power continually asks, it presses. Our Englishmen are first enticed by flattering solicitations, but eventually they are driven by the harshest coercion to contribute, not what they themselves wished, but what pleases the king. Often they are forced against their will to carry out what they know that they or their predecessors once did voluntarily.

“Therefore let me not become involved in matters by which the favour of an earthly king would cooperate in the loss of one’s neighbour, and the indignation of almighty God would follow and be incurred.”

The bishop therefore warned the king’s advisers to ensure that such orders were not imposed upon him, lest, by contradicting the king’s decision, he should once again be forced to forfeit the king’s favour. When this became known to the king [Col. 1049B], he immediately ordered Hugh to return to his Church with God’s blessing and not to undertake the trouble of coming to him again on the following day as they had agreed, but instead to pray continually and wholeheartedly to the Lord for him.

Thus Hugh, freed in the Lord’s name from the courtiers’ snares, returned joyfully with all his people to his own lands, magnifying God.

Scarcely had the bishop returned to England—indeed, he had not yet reached his Church—when the same king attacked the king of France [Note: Philip. On this battle and victory, see Trivet in his *Chronicle* under the year 1198, where he confirms what is related here] near Gisors and put him to flight after capturing several of his nobles. At that time the count of Nevers was also thrown into the castle ditch and died by drowning.

The king soon informed the bishop of Lincoln of the sequence of this triumph [Col. 1049C], earnestly asking him to continue praying for him as he had begun to do. He also set down in a letter the names and number of the brave men whom he had captured, writing among other things that King Philip himself had also drunk quite deeply from the ditch into which he had fallen, and that he would have met his death in a headlong flight had he not escaped through the assistance of his men.

Many of the king’s people asserted that this honour and trophy had been granted to the king from heaven through the merits of the holy prelate, whom the king had resolved to venerate more earnestly for the Lord after abandoning their former hostility.

## CHAPTER IX. How steadfastly he excused himself in response to the kings’ command, by which he was ordered to send twelve members of his Lincoln Church who would be most suitable for dispatching the king’s messages, and how he exercised ecclesiastical censure against the officials appointed to confiscate all his goods.—This is chapter 7 in the sequence of the *Great Life*.

When the enemies of the man of God had devised what was thought to be an irrefutable stratagem of crafty subtlety, it was suggested to the king that there were many canons among the clergy of the Church of Lincoln who were wealthy in countless revenues [Note: Concerning the wealth and extent of the bishopric of Lincoln, Gerald of Wales writes in *Anglia Sacra*, part II, p. 417: “Thus the diocese of Lincoln grew through Remigius, but declined enormously through Robert and Robert. Yet, still containing within itself seven and a half counties of the entire kingdom, and possessing populous lands and, besides various dignities, seven or eight other archdeaconries, it far surpasses all the cathedral churches of the kingdom in the breadth of its diocese”], and rich in gold and silver as well, so that they could contribute considerable sums from their treasuries without suffering serious loss.

“By such a device,” they said, “it will be easy to extort these sums from them. Let our lord the king write to the archbishop of Canterbury [Note: This is thought to have been done in the year 1198, after Hugh’s return from the king, although it could also have occurred before his departure in that same year] that he hasten to send to him from the bosom of the Church of Lincoln twelve men distinguished in prudence and counsel, and also endowed with eloquence—men whom he himself knows to be suitable for the king’s service—who, adequately supplied with the necessary resources, may competently and diligently conduct the king’s business, at their own expense, in the Roman Curia, in Germany and Spain, and elsewhere, wherever he should judge it appropriate to send them.

“Why delay with further details?” At last the archbishop’s messenger came to the bishop, presenting twelve pairs of letters, enclosed with the archiepiscopal seal, to be delivered to twelve of the most eminent persons of his Church. He also brought a special letter for the bishop, in which the wording of the aforementioned letters was set out according to the formula given above. At the end of it, by both royal and his own authority, he ordered the bishop to send each letter to those to whom it had been written and to send those men also into his presence, ready, in accordance with the form of the royal command, to cross the sea to the king as quickly as possible.”

When this became known, those who happened to be present there at the time were especially troubled, since they heard that they were being summoned to an unwelcome mission.

The bishop, however, made no reply to what he had heard—for it was the hour of dining—but went to the table that had already been prepared. During the meal the clerics murmured among themselves, saying that they feared the bishop might give the messenger a harsh answer, since in so alarming a case what was needed was not pontifical severity but rather subdued gentleness, to discover first whether the lord of Canterbury might perhaps be softened by humble entreaty. If he wished, he could easily alter this plan for the better.

While they were discussing these matters among themselves, Hugh, a man of resolute heart, quickly dispelled their fearful hesitation. He did not seek advice from any of them about revising his reply. As soon as he rose from the table, he addressed the messenger who had come:

“New things, and things never before heard anywhere, are being imposed by our lord of Canterbury—both those he imposes by the authority of the king and those he imposes by his own will. Let him know, however, that I will never be, nor have I ever been, the bearer of his letters; nor have I ever subjected our clerics to royal services, nor will I do so.

“I have often forbidden clerics—even those from elsewhere who hold benefices in our bishopric—to dare to make themselves obligated to secular patronage in public duties, such as the leasing of forests and other administrations of this kind. Some who were less obedient to our salutary warnings in this matter we punished by the severe deprivation of their benefices.

“By what reasoning, then, should we tear from the innermost bosom of our Church those whom we are ordered to send to royal services? Let our lord the king be satisfied that the archbishop has already devoted himself wholly to carrying out the king’s business, neglecting the duty of his profession and certainly placing his own soul’s salvation in danger.

“Yet, if this seems insufficient to him, he may come with his men. Here is the bishop; I will come, I say, to hear the king’s commands from his own mouth. I will also come, in accordance with those commands, ready to carry out most promptly whatever is just.

“But you: take back with you the twelve letters that you say you brought to us, and do with them whatever you please. Report to our lord archbishop, in due order, everything that I have said to you. At the end tell him this: if our clerics are to go to the king in this manner, I myself will go with them. They will not go without me now, nor have I ever gone elsewhere without them.

“For this is the relationship of a good shepherd to his sheep, and of good sheep to their shepherd: the shepherd must not scatter them by exposing them carelessly, nor must they stray by rashly fleeing from him.”

The bearer of the letters was breathing anger at this. He was a court cleric, deliberately chosen for the very purpose of undertaking such an embassy. He was also, as could be understood, swollen with innate arrogance, and even more swollen by the breath of the courtly spirit.

When he prepared to launch threats—which, because the breath was obstructed by the swelling of his heart, he could scarcely utter— the bishop cut short his venomous words and ordered him to leave immediately. He departed at once, bewildered and confused.

The bishop then sent some prudent men from among his own people to the archbishop, asking and warning him to measure in advance and guard against the evident prejudice to ecclesiastical immunity—which he was bound to protect—that would arise from such edicts, and not to give any assent whatsoever to such measures.

The archbishop was moved by their entreaties or arguments more outwardly than from the heart, and, concealing for a while the resentment which he said he had conceived openly because of the disobedience of his suffragan, promised that he would take care that, provided the king’s interests were preserved, the present business might either be completely brought to peace with the lord of Lincoln or be arranged in a more moderate fashion. For both authority and sound reasoning prescribe that evil must never be done through obedience, and that good must sometimes be left undone.

But the peace that had been promised did not last long. Soon afterward, public edicts were issued ordering that the bishop’s possessions be taken into the hands of the royal officials. When the bishop heard this, he said to his clerics:

“Did I not tell you that the voice of these men is indeed ‘the voice of Jacob, but the hands are the hands of Esau’?” (Genesis 27:22.)

To summarize the events briefly: those to whom the execution of the tyrannical edict had been entrusted, overcome by excessive fear, first suggested to the king that they should suspend the order. Then they pointed out how dangerous it would be, both for those who gave the order and for those who carried it out, to attempt anything that might cause them to fall under the curse of that man.

They said that it was perfectly clear that, whoever he cursed, the Lord would curse also, and that this curse, as the prophet says, would soon consume him (Isaiah 24:6).

At that time there was in the army a prince of the Rutenians named Marchadeus [Note: Trivet calls him Mercader under the year 1197. Raynaldo, however, calls him Marchadeus in the annals under the year 1199, where he discusses his cruelty, p. 31], a man wholly given over to bestial savagery and a ruined conscience, rushing headlong into every crime and sacrilege.

The king, however, little or not at all moved toward better counsel by what his officials repeatedly urged upon him, said:

“These Englishmen are cowards. Let us therefore send Marchadeus, who knows how to play with that Burgundian.”

Immediately one of his friends said to him:

“Marchadeus is necessary to your war, my lord king. But you will certainly be deprived of his services and obedience if he becomes subject to the anathema of the bishop of Lincoln.”

The king declared that this would in no way be expedient for him. Fearing Marchadeus’s danger even more than his own, he refrained from sending him, lest he should perish; but he did not refrain from undertaking that by which the king himself would be ruinously endangered.

Accordingly, the king gave orders to one of his officials, Stephen of Curneheya, a faithful and God-fearing man, and also sufficiently devoted to our bishop, that, if he valued his life and limbs, he should immediately take the goods of the bishop of Lincoln into his hands.

At last, compelled by fear of the king, Stephen sent some of his men to seize the lands and all the movable goods they might find, together with the villages and castles of the bishop. As they were first making their way to take possession of the town of Lafford, the bishop’s retinue happened by chance to meet them not far from the borough of Saint Peter.

Terrified by this encounter, they turned aside a little from the road and, having summoned certain ecclesiastics, explained to them how great a threat their lord the king had made against their master because he had delayed dispossessing the bishop [Note: *Desaisire*, that is, to deprive someone of possession], and that they were now going to carry out the order unwillingly and under compulsion, bound by fear of the supreme danger.

Like the third group of fifty sent by the treacherous king to Elijah, these men humbled themselves and earnestly begged that, through the mediation of those clerics, that true servant of God might take pity on their souls, lest heavenly vengeance consume them because of the offence against him that they feared incurring.

They begged him to hasten rather to soften the king’s animosity, lest he heap losses everywhere, even upon the innocent and those wholly removed from the merits of the dispute between the king and the prelate. They further promised that, to the best of their ability, they would preserve his property inviolate. They asked him to suspend for a time the sentence of excommunication, by which the king would be further provoked and their own innocence consequently placed in danger.

When these things became known to the bishop, he said:

“It is not for these men to preserve our property. Let them go only, and let them deal as they wish with the goods—not so much our goods as the goods of our lady, holy Mary, the Mother of God.”

As he said this, he drew from his breast the fringe of a linen stole, which he always wore hanging around his neck beneath his cloak when travelling. Waving it in his hand, he said:

“This will certainly restore to us, down to the last penny,” whatever these men might decide to seize.

When he came to his own village, called Bugden [where the aforementioned bearer of the archbishop’s letters had come to him, and where he had also received, as mentioned above, the ordeal of a divine oracle through a warning concerning the defence of ecclesiastical liberty], he immediately ordered letters to be written. In them he commanded the archdeacons and deans of the places where his possessions were situated that, having gathered the priests of the neighbouring Churches around them, as soon as the aforementioned officials entered their regions, they should ring the bells and light the candles and subject to anathema all who had presumed, whether by giving orders or by obeying them, to touch violently and seize unjustly the property of his Church.

When these arrangements had been made, and almost all his people were tossed about by fear and intense agitation, he was finally taken to bed. As though he had suffered no disturbance at all, he immediately relaxed his limbs into the sweetest sleep. This matter never penetrated into the depths of his heart. That night, too, he did not cease repeating “Amen” more frequently and more intently than usual, as though moved by a more powerful impulse of the spirit [Note: Concerning “Amen,” see Book II, chapter 8].

## CHAPTER X. How, when the archbishop advised him to send money to the king, who thirsted for it like a dropsical man for water, he replied, “If he is dropsical, I will not be water”; and concerning the healing of a madman at Cestrehant.

At that moment [Note: Toward the end of the year 1197, when, as follows immediately, the king’s anger against Hugh first boiled over], when the storm of royal persecution first raged against the shepherd of the Church of Lincoln, who was exposing himself for his sheep, the event we are about to relate occurred.

At that time the same ever-watchful guardian of the Lord’s fold had gone to London to confer with the archbishop and the other leading men of the kingdom about this great matter. From them he brought back only this advice: that he should demand a large sum of money from his clerics and send it as quickly as possible to the king, through one of his own people, in order to calm the fury of the avaricious king.

The archbishop said:

“Do you not know, my lord bishop, that just as a dropsical man thirsts for water, so the lord king thirsts for money?”

He immediately replied, according to his custom:

“Certainly—and if he is dropsical, I will not be the water for him to swallow.”

Leaving London, he hastened back to his Church, from which he intended, after arranging everything, to cross the sea to the king as soon as possible, as has been said above.

One Sunday morning, therefore, he was travelling through a village which antiquity had established as being called Cestrehant. When almost his entire retinue had already gone ahead, he himself entered the middle of the village with only a very few companions and was suddenly surrounded by the great clamour of a shouting crowd.

The assembled people begged him to deign to bless, by the sign of his sacred right hand, one of their neighbours who was possessed by a most savage demon. When he saw the man lying bound inside the open doorway of his house, he immediately trembled throughout his body with spiritual indignation. Not content to bless him from a distance as he was, he dismounted from the horse he had been riding and said:

“Shame upon this wickedness! This is certainly not right.”

He saw the demoniac lying on his back, with his head fastened to the doorpost and each of his hands tied to one of two pegs driven deeply into the ground on either side. His feet likewise were joined together and fastened to a stake.

His eyes rolled around in a remarkable fashion, while his mouth was twisted now to one side, now to the other, in a pitiable manner. At one moment he thrust his tongue out of his mouth to an immense length; at another he gnashed his teeth. At another he displayed the passage of his throat open in the most monstrous gape of his jaws, as though it were some enormous abyss, a horrifying sight to those who looked upon him.

The prelate ran quickly to him, made the sign of the holy cross over him, bent down, and held his right hand extended near the man’s mouth for some time, meanwhile reciting in a subdued voice the Gospel passage: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1).

During this, he saw that the wretched man’s head—which he had been accustomed to move constantly here and there—was now still and quiet, as dogs are when they fear the blows of those punishing them. His eyes, however, while looking at the bishop, nervously turned in different directions, showing a certain sign of fear.

When the bishop had gone through the Gospel as far as the passage “full of grace and truth” (ibid., 14), he rose and silently observed the patient for some time. Suddenly the man turned his face away from him to the other side and thrust out his tongue from his mouth in the manner of someone mocking.

Then that vigorous warrior against the opposing power, indignantly blessing and mixing water and salt as swiftly as possible according to ecclesiastical custom and rite, sprinkled it over him. He also ordered those standing around to put some of the same water into the man’s mouth. After giving his blessing to everyone, he mounted his horse and departed.

All the people blessed him individually and together, declaring that their bishop, shortly before, while travelling down the same road, had seen the demoniac and, overcome by excessive fear, had driven his horse forward with his spurs. He had not merely passed the wretched man without helping him but, as though he himself were driven by the Furies, had fled at a gallop.

From that moment the man was freed from the demon. Thereafter he diligently strove to amend his life in every respect. Devoutly devoting himself for a long time to pilgrimages to the saints, he lived piously for several years and at last rested in peace with a good end.

We recently learned these facts about his end in the aforementioned village from his neighbours, who said that they themselves had been present at the healing related above.

## CHAPTER XI. How he freed a certain woman from a pythonic spirit.—This is chapter 8 in the *Great Life*.

Now, it must not be passed over that, at the chapter held at Lincoln, he had declared that he would cross the sea to go to the king on behalf of the common need [Note: [Col. 1055D] Above, chapter 9, in these words: “If our clerics are going to the king in this manner, I too will go with them.”]. After giving his sons the solemn ritual blessing—namely, the blessing that the priests under the Law, through Moses, were commanded to give to the sons of Israel, and which he had caused to be written in his book of blessings—and after commending himself to the prayers of each of them and exchanging with one another the holy kiss of peace, he had commended them all to God and to the word of His grace in the words of the Apostle. From there, as was mentioned above, he proceeded directly to the aforesaid manor [Note: [Col. 1055D] Bugden, situated on the road between Lincoln and London.].

While he remained there for a few days, the dean of the neighboring locality informed him that a certain little woman in his deanery, who appeared to possess a Pythonic spirit, was drawing great crowds of people to herself by means of divination. For she openly identified thefts committed by anyone and exposed every kind of hidden sorcery. If, however, she was approached or rebuked on this matter either by the dean himself, as he stated, or by any prudent and educated man, she immediately rendered the person reproving her almost stupefied and speechless by the shameless volubility of her tongue, and so overwhelmed everyone with the flood of her talk that no one could convict her or impose silence upon her. The bishop at once replied: “We shall be going to London in a few days, and as we pass through your district, you shall bring her to a suitable place to meet us.” And this was done.

Accordingly, the bishop himself dismounted from his horse when he saw the woman. A crowd of people was standing there with children who were to be confirmed by the laying-on of hands. When the woman had been brought before him, the man of God, as though angrily confronting her, addressed not so much the wretched woman as the one inhabiting her, the hidden demon: “Come now, you unhappy woman,” he said, “what do you claim to divine for us?” Then, closing his right hand into a fist and holding the end of his stole enclosed within it, he said: “Tell me, seat of the demon, if indeed you know: what does my hand contain?”

As he said this, the little woman, who shortly before had been insolent, immediately collapsed as though lifeless at his feet. At the sudden sound of such power she had become incapable not only of speaking but even of standing. For meanwhile the inhabitant who had wickedly animated her had fled, and she remained healthily weak beneath the hand of the healing physician, although previously, under the attack of the destructive disease, she had been lethally strong.

After she had lain for some time bent down at the feet of the holy man, he ordered her to be lifted up. Then, using the dean as interpreter—for he did not know the language of the rustic woman—he ordered that she be questioned about how she had acquired her skill in divination. When she had been questioned repeatedly, she said in a faint and subdued voice: “I do not know how to divine; I implore the mercy of this holy bishop.” Again she fell face downward at his feet.

After he had laid his hand upon her head and briefly prayed for her, he gave her his blessing and ordered that she be brought to the prior of Huntingdon, the penitentiary [Note: [Col. 1055D] Perhaps the same as the one at Huntingdon, where, according to the *Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. I, p. 530, there was a nunnery founded outside Huntingdon.] of those parts, instructing her to undertake true penance after making a confession of all her sins. This, as we later learned, she faithfully carried out. For he had commanded her never again to presume to divine the sorceries of others, but continually to accustom herself to mourn and confess her own sins. From that time she appeared so modest and silent—although previously she had been exceedingly talkative and insolent—that all who knew her former behavior regarded this very change as a great miracle.

## CHAPTER XII. How he delivered another woman from an incubus demon

This chapter is contained in the great *Life* under chapter eight.

[Col. 1056C] Because of the similarity both of the circumstances and of the persons involved, we have reserved this account of the rescue of another woman from demonic infestation to be rightly numbered among the miracles of this man and set forth here, although it occurred at a different time [Note: [Col. 1055D] In the year 1185 or 1186, and no later, when Hugh was either still prior of Witham or had recently been consecrated bishop. This matter will be treated more fully in the question of the year in which Hugh became bishop.].

At one time, Bartholomew, bishop of Exeter, a man of exceptional learning and education [Note: [Col. 1056D] In the *Annals of the Church of Winchester*, in Wharton’s *Anglia Sacra*, part I, p. 300, it reads: “In the year 1161, Master Bartholomew was made bishop of Exeter.” And again, in the same work, p. 302: “In the year 1186 Bartholomew, bishop of Exeter, died.”], informed him that a certain demon, appearing in the form of a young man, had been accustomed to abuse an unfortunate little woman who lived in his diocese. He also stated that she had often disclosed the misery of this detestable affliction to him and to other venerable persons in a tearful confession, and had earnestly sought advice about how she might be rescued from her obscene oppressor. He added that, through fasts and various forms of bodily mortification, she had subdued her sinful members almost to the point of death [Col. 1056D]. Yet all these things together had done nothing for her against the hateful and wicked lover. He said that she had endured such circumstances for a considerable number of years.

Therefore the venerable Father Hugh, moved both by compassion for the wretched woman and by indignation at the demon’s impurity, said: “If, as you say, she is being raised up against her sin by contrition of heart, confession of the mouth, and bodily affliction, I see nothing else remaining except that prayer should be offered more earnestly for her to the mercy of the most merciful Redeemer.”

The bishop of Exeter replied that he and countless others had already done this, but without success; and he earnestly begged Hugh also to pray for her. Hugh answered him: “Not only I, but every faithful person, ought to do this with the greatest devotion.”

Afterward the bishops went their separate ways [Note: [Col. 1057D] According to the author’s understanding, Hugh was already a bishop when the events here related took place.]. When they met again after some time had passed [Note: [Col. 1057D] The second meeting could have occurred one or two months after the first.], this diligent rescuer of souls anxiously asked the bishop mentioned above how matters stood concerning that little sheep of his flock, whom the destructive wolf had so savagely torn.

The bishop then explained to him not only her deliverance but also the remarkable manner of her deliverance, as follows:

“By your prayers,” he said, “she long ago escaped the yoke of her shameful bondage.” For one day, when that incestuous demon had almost rendered her lifeless by deluding her with an unbelievable frenzy of lust, he departed and vanished, while she remained in her chamber, abandoned to intense grief and sorrow. Then, behold, another spirit in the form of a young man, as it appeared to her, entered and began to ask why she was so sad.

“When she gave no answer, he said: ‘I know, and I know truly, that that wicked one has afflicted you. But this is not surprising, for he is perverse and exceedingly malicious. Yet if you are willing to consent to my desires and counsels, he will never again have access to you.’

“Greatly encouraged by this, she immediately replied: ‘There is nothing under heaven possible for me that I would not gladly do or endure, provided that I could likewise be saved from his approach.’

“‘Come, then,’ he said, ‘do not hesitate to enter into a covenant of love with me. Whatever you ask or desire, I shall grant you; I shall demand nothing from you contrary to your wishes, and I shall inflict upon you nothing that is not pleasurable or lovable.’

“She promised her consent to these and other offers, provided that she might experience the effect of the promised deliverance. Then he led her to a place near her house and, pointing out to her a plant growing at some distance, said: ‘Take that herb, hide it in your bosom, and scatter it throughout your house. When you have done this, you will learn by experience that I have been truthful in my promises.’

“She did what she had been instructed to do. After this, the shape-shifting demon came in his familiar form and stood near the window through which he used to enter and leave. Looking inside, he said to the woman: ‘What is this horrible and rotten thing that you have scattered throughout this house? Throw this hated grass, which you have foolishly brought upon yourself, far away from you and from your house as quickly as possible.’

“She pretended not to hear and did not obey the wicked one’s commands. He then began, now with threats and now with flatteries, to press her more insistently to throw out the herb, which he said he loathed. When he saw that she despised him, he withdrew after a little while, furious and threatening.

“Not much later the other one arrived. As though congratulating his beloved, he said: ‘Have you learned that what I told you was true? Now, while I speak with you more privately, you will temporarily remove from yourself the herb hated by all our people. After I have departed, you will resume the armor of your grass, by which you will remain unharmed from the snares of the poisonous enemy. For that gallows-bird will never dare to approach you in any way while he senses that I am present with you.’

“To this she replied: ‘Come to me if you wish and if you can; for I must not violate my promise. But, as long as I live, I shall never cast this herb away from me, since it alone has been able to provide me security against that most impure oppressor.’

“What more is there to say? This one too, like the first, after prolonged prayers and threats and flatteries vainly continued, finally vanished into the empty air, lamenting for a long time and at great length that he had been outwitted by the little woman. The woman, however, now armed more effectively than by that herb—with faith, devotion, and good conduct—leads an honorable and peaceful life in the fear of God.

“All this, as it is told by us, I heard from her own mouth. She came to me after she had been cured, intending finally to undertake a measure of penance and receive the benefit of absolution” [Col. 1058C]. Thus the bishop of Exeter recounted these things to our bishop, who himself frequently reported them to us, in our presence, before many people.

The woman mentioned above, while traveling through many holy places for the sake of prayer, eventually reached Canterbury. There, while seeking the aid of the prayers of religious men, she showed a monk of St. Augustine’s the herb that she had brought out from her bosom. He showed it to us [Note: [Col. 1057D] “Us,” that is, the author of the *Life*.], and we later showed it to the bishop, for until then he had not recognized it.

The Greeks commonly call this herb *hypericon*; the Latins call it *herba perforata*, “perforated herb,” or “St. John’s herb” [Note: [Col. 1058D] These words appear to have been omitted by the abbreviator.]. This story is inserted in the great *Life*. If anyone should perhaps find these things less than credible, let him read Bede in his *Explanation of the Gospel according to Luke*; there he will find similar events that occurred in Bede’s own time, recorded by so great a teacher.

## CHAPTER XIII. Of the rescue of a thief who was being led to the gallows, and how he spoke to the barons of the Exchequer

This chapter is contained under chapter nine in the great *Life*.

But we must return to the journey our bishop had begun toward the king [Note: [Col. 1058D] Namely, to the events that occurred on the journey undertaken to King Richard around the end of 1198 or the beginning of the following year.] and, with the pen already moving forward, set them forth.

When, as we have said, he had expelled the Pythonic spirit from the woman [Note: [Col. 1059D] This was discussed above, chapter 9.], and on the following day had entered the territory of St. Albans [Note: [Col. 1059D] Once a famous monastery, about which see further in the *Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. I, p. 176, and Mabillon, vol. II of the *Annals*, p. 298, and vol. IV, p. 672. It may be inferred from Giraldus Cambrensis in *Anglia Sacra*, part II, p. 417, that this place had formerly belonged to the bishopric of Lincoln. He writes there concerning Robert de Chesney: “He also lost St. Albans, although that monastery had been joined to the Church of Lincoln with such close familiarity that most of its abbots had been prebendaries in the Church of Lincoln,” and so forth.], behold, a condemned man met him with a crowd of officers. Because of a theft he had committed, his arms bound behind his back, he was being dragged to the deserved gallows.

While the others came forward humbly and customarily to seek the bishop’s blessing, the bound man forced his way through as best he could. First he rushed to the neck of the bishop’s horse, then immediately fell at his feet and called for mercy in tearful words.

The bishop promptly drew back the reins and asked who the man was and what he wanted. His attendants, who knew the matter as it was, replied: “It is not for you, lord, to inquire further about this man [Col. 1059B]; rather, leave him and pass on.”

They spoke thus because they feared that he might attempt to rescue the man from the king, thereby endangering them all. But the bishop inquired all the more closely into the case of the man who was appealing for mercy. When he had learned it fully, he cried out joyfully: “Ah, blessed be God!”

Then he said to the officers who were leading the man to the gallows: “Come back with us, my sons, to the town. Leave him with us, and report to your superiors and judges that we have taken him from you. We shall make you secure.”

Since they did not dare to resist, they handed the man over to him. As soon as the bishop had entered his lodging, he entrusted the man, now freed from his bonds, to his almoner.

When the bishop’s clerical attendants had come to him, they earnestly warned and begged him to allow the judges to carry out what was their duty concerning the accused. They said:

“Until now, lord, neither the king nor anyone else who plots against you has been able to find against us any just cause, or anything resembling a just cause. But if you decide by your episcopal authority to invalidate a sentence already pronounced by the secular judges and already put into execution, your enemies will say that you have offended against the king’s crown itself and have incurred the charge of lèse-majesté.”

He replied: “I know the confidence of your courage. But let those judges be summoned here to us”—for they were already outside seeking to speak with him—“and you shall hear their words and ours.”

When they had been admitted to his assembly, he addressed them as follows:

“You prudent men know that it is the prerogative of Holy Mother Church everywhere throughout the world to provide security and preserve the safety of anyone who flees the danger of condemnation and takes refuge with her.”

When they replied that they knew this well and that it ought rightly to be observed, he continued:

“If you know this, you must also know that wherever a bishop is present together with the faithful of Christ gathered with him, there also is the Church. The man who is accustomed, through his ministry, to dedicate the material stones of a church to the Lord, and who also has the duty of sanctifying the living stones from which the Church more truly consists, through the individual sacraments so that they may become the Lord’s temples, ought rightly, wherever he may be, to enjoy the privilege of ecclesiastical dignity and to assist all who are in peril, according to its established form.”

The judges gladly acknowledged this. They recalled that the ancient laws of the English had expressly established the same principle, but asserted that it had now been abolished, either through the negligence of modern bishops [Col. 1060B] or through the tyranny of princes.

After they had discussed the matter among themselves, they addressed him in these words:

“Lord, we are your sons and parishioners [Note: [Col. 1059D] From this passage it may be inferred that those who were in the territory of St. Albans still remained under the care and in the diocese of the bishop of Lincoln, whom they revered as their father and shepherd.], and you are our father and shepherd. Therefore it is neither our role nor will it be, if you are willing, to oppose or dispute your privilege, nor is it yours to attempt anything that would endanger us. Accordingly, if you free this man, we shall offer no resistance; but we leave it to you to take care that we do not thereby endanger ourselves before our lord the king.”

Then he said: “You have spoken well and rightly. I therefore take him from your hands; for this act of force I shall answer sufficiently wherever it is necessary.”

Thus the accused happily escaped the place of execution. Free, he came with the bishop to London and afterward departed unharmed wherever he wished [Col. 1060C].

The bishop then approached the leading officials presiding over the king’s Exchequer [Note: [Col. 1060D] At that time it was at Westminster near London, but not long afterward it was transferred to Northampton, as reported in the *Chronicle of Trivet* under the year 1209. Among the English, *scaccarium* means the court in which financial matters are handled. It is also sometimes used for the treasury itself, since the treasury of the king of England was kept in the same building where the judges of the Exchequer sat. See Du Cange’s *Glossary* under this word.], and courteously begged them to look kindly to the security of the Church, especially in the king’s absence.

They rose respectfully to greet him and promised obediently to do what he had requested. They then compelled him by many entreaties to sit with them, even if only for a moment. He scarcely consented, but at last sat down.

They rejoiced and said: “Now we shall be able to celebrate a triumph, since we have lived to see the day on which the bishop of Lincoln sat at the king’s Exchequer.”

At this, embarrassed by the place, he immediately rose, offered a kiss to them all, and said: “Now I too shall triumph over you. If, after I have given you the kiss of peace, you admit anything less than peaceful against my Church…”

They were exceedingly astonished at both his action and his words and said to one another: “O the remarkable prudence of this man! See how easily he binds us beforehand, so that even if ordered by the king, we shall not dare to trouble him without great disgrace.”

After giving them his blessing, he withdrew. Intending to visit the king, he soon afterward crossed over to Normandy.

## CHAPTER XIV. Of the young man whom he found in despair near the city of Rochester, whose flesh afterward rotted away beside both thighs, and who was healed by our Hugh in body and soul

This is drawn from chapter 2 of book IV of the great *Life*.

When the bishop reached the city of Rochester [Note: [Col. 1061D] An episcopal city in which a see under the title of St. Andrew was established in 604. It is now called Hrofensis, Roscetrensis, Rovecestrensis, Roffensis, or Rochestrensis.], a certain young man approached him, one whom the enemy of the human race had ensnared most destructively in his deceits. Through an interpreter—for neither the young man sufficiently understood the bishop’s speech nor the bishop the young man’s—he recounted the following pitiable tragedy about himself:

“When I was still a young adolescent, not yet capable of much discernment, I was carried along by empty and wandering movements of the emotions. It happened that, through the ambush of the adversary of human salvation, I incurred the detestable crime of some enormous offense. Not content with a single fall, I added fall to fall, and, what is worse, by adding crime to crime I formed a long-standing habit of falling into crimes.

“My offense was exceedingly horrible in its character. Consideration of its circumstances—place, time, and person—together with its own enormity, had multiplied its seriousness fourfold. Nothing was lacking among the circumstances of my sin to complete the supreme accumulation of evils, except perhaps a partial ignorance of the law. Moreover, persuaded and enticed by another, I almost always sinned first against myself.

“Recently, when a certain priest was preaching the word of God, I, utterly unworthy, happened to be present in a church among the crowds who had gathered. The priest was reviewing a catalogue of capital crimes. Wielding the sword of the divine word with particular force against this offense, of which I was conscious in myself, he so greatly magnified its damnable foulness that I almost believed I would be swallowed up when the earth suddenly opened and would fall alive into hell.

“Finally, I fell into such confusion of mind that I thought I had been completely driven outside myself. I spent that day and the first part of the following night in tears and sobs. Then, behold, after midnight, my little body, wearied by grief, sank into sleep. A woman appeared to me, shining with indescribable beauty, and offered the following counsel to me in my desolation:

“‘Do not despair, poor wretch,’ she said, ‘for the mercy and power of my Son are abundant, and He wishes no one to perish. Rise at dawn, seek the priest whom I identify for you by name, and confess your sins to him faithfully, purely, and completely.’

“After these words, the vision was taken from me together with my sleep. I rose during the night and carried out what had been commanded me. Not long afterward, unable to endure the shame of my confusion and terrified of the place of my ruin, I secretly left my mother’s house and the city in which I had been born and had lived in misery.

“As I traveled, not knowing where I should go or where it would be most suitable for me to stay, a man of terrifying appearance suddenly met me in my anxiety and sorrow. He was very tall, red-haired, and spoke to me with a dreadful face:

“‘Wretch,’ he said, ‘you have grievously offended God and His mother. If you wish to make them favorable to you by any means, you must extinguish that body with which you have so often insulted them. You are mistaken if you believe that, in the same vessel that you have polluted with so many contaminations, you can accomplish anything acceptable to divine purity.’

“He had scarcely finished speaking when behold, pilgrims arrived, seeking the tomb of the blessed martyr Thomas [Col. 1062B]. At their appearance the speaker suddenly disappeared.

“Although I was violently driven into fear and despair, I nevertheless marked my forehead with the saving sign. Continuing sorrowfully on the journey I had begun, scarcely able to guide my own steps because of the pain in my heart, I arrived in this city around the third hour on this very day on which these things were said to me [Note: [Col. 1061D] He was therefore not far from the city of Rochester, in which this wretched man had been born.].

“Even before I visibly received the persuasion of the man mentioned above, the thought had been introduced into my mind that I should kill myself. But afterward this thought prevailed more strongly in me, and I would have done what he suggested if the memory of the vision mentioned earlier had not somewhat encouraged me in my misery, allowing me to take some comfort from the mercy of our Savior and His mother.

“For I had also long accepted as a firm tradition that whoever inflicted death upon himself would undoubtedly perish eternally. Yet so hostile to me was, and still is, as I believe, this suggestion of the enemy, that today I went twice to throw myself from the bridge of this town into the river. The first time I drew back because of the multitude of passersby; the second time, the report of your arrival, conveyed to my ears by your forerunners, suspended me as I was already on the verge of the plunge. As soon as I learned that your holiness would be present, all agitation of heart cast aside, I began to breathe again through the conversation of such great discernment.”

When he had finished speaking, the bishop briefly exhorted him as the circumstances required. After giving him his blessing, he instructed him to follow his footsteps as far as Dorobernia [Note: [Col. 1062D] That is, as far as Canterbury.], where he would receive more fully and freely both counsel and assistance for his salvation.

The young man obeyed these saving instructions. When he came to Canterbury, he was strengthened by the bishop’s sacred teaching and helped by his intercession, and he was completely and permanently freed from the destructive temptation.

While the bishop remained there, waiting for nearly fifteen days for a suitable time to sail [Note: [Col. 1062D] When these days had elapsed, Hugh crossed over to Neustria and arrived there around Septuagesima in the year 1199.], the young man, already very strong in faith and devotion, stayed in the same city for about a week [Col. 1063A]. He intended to visit the threshold of the chief apostles as soon as possible for the sake of prayer.

Meanwhile, we know that an unheard-of event happened to him. Suddenly the flesh beside both his thighs and around his genitals rotted away so completely that two openings, or rather twin pits, of dreadful size and depth appeared on either side. Yet, despite the immense gaping of the wounds, he felt absolutely no pain.

Fearing a more serious danger, he showed the rotten place to a certain most trustworthy man skilled in treating wounds, Master Reginald the baker. From him we learned that the rotten flesh had already flowed away almost to the innermost organs.

This was reported to the bishop [Col. 1063B], who ordered that wax be applied to the wounds. At that time the servants happened to be softening wax by heating it at the fire, as is customary, so that it could be used to make candles for necessary purposes.

A remarkable thing! As Jonah’s ivy sprang up in a single night and likewise withered in a single night when the Ninevites gathered in repentance (Jonah 4:7), so the repentant man’s sudden ulcers were more quickly turned into scars; not even a mark of closure remained upon them.

Now healed entirely according to the Gospel pattern, in soul as well as in body, he solemnly took up his wallet and staff and, as he had intended, set out for the apostolic walls. After receiving the blessing of the supreme pontiff, he returned to England and assumed the habit of the Cistercian Order. By the merit of his good conduct, he steadfastly claimed for himself not only the reality but also the name of a convert [Col. 1063C].

## CHAPTER XV. That he could not be induced to ordain as subdeacon a cleric who was destined to become a leper; how violently he was urged to appease the anger of our king by means of money; and how, when news of the king’s death arrived, he could not be persuaded to visit his burial

This is chapter 10 in the sequence of the great *Life*.

Around this time the king had already launched an expedition against the count of Angoulême [Note: [Col. 1063C] Trivet states that this expedition was undertaken against the count of Limoges in the year 1199, and others generally agree with him.], against whom, it was said, he was preparing to wage an unjust war [Note: [Col. 1063D] The cause was a discovered treasure, which Trivet and Raynald discuss under this year.].

Meanwhile, legal truces that had been proclaimed when the time of Septuagesima had already been announced required a cessation of arms between him and the king of France. When the bishop himself reached Neustria, he remained in that land for nearly three weeks, chiefly because of the presence there of the lord pope’s legate [Note: [Col. 1063D] Namely, Cardinal Peter, who, as reported on p. 33 in Raynald, made a five-year truce between the kings of France and England in this year, confirmed by the pope.] [Note: [Col. 1063D] From Septuagesima until Quadragesima.].

From there, around the beginning of Lent, he set out for Angers [Note: [Col. 1063D] Commonly called Anjou and Angers; formerly a county and now the capital of the duchy of Anjou, where there was also an episcopal see.]. At a manor of the abbot of Saint Nicholas [Note: [Col. 1063D] A Benedictine abbey in the suburb—or, as Mabillon writes, situated west of and overlooking the city of Angers—which was begun by Fulk Nerra and completed by his son Geoffrey in the year 1060.], not far from the city of Angers, he remained for a period of no shorter duration [Note: [Col. 1063D] Rather, including the time spent there, longer than the stay he made among the Grandmontines.], awaiting the king’s return from the distant places where he appeared to be engaged in military turmoil [Note: [Col. 1063D] The king of England was wounded there by a missile from the castle called Caluca by Trivet, near Limoges, and died a few days later.].

Meanwhile, at the request of religious men of the Grandmontine Order [Col. 1064B] [Note: [Col. 1064D] The Grandmontine Order was founded by St. Stephen of Muret around the year 1076 under a strict discipline in a monastery that became the head of the order, in the diocese of Limoges.], who lived in a nearby place [Note: [Col. 1064D] Apparently not far from the city of Angers.], he celebrated holy orders among them [Note: [Col. 1064D] On the Saturday before Passion Sunday.].

The archdeacon of Oxford [Note: [Col. 1064D] One of the seven or eight archdeaconries subject to the see of Lincoln, originally established by Remigius.], named Walter [Note: [Col. 1064D] Concerning him, under the year 1197, Trivet’s *Chronicle* reads: “Walter Map, of whom many amusing things are related, became archdeacon of Oxford after being precentor of Lincoln.”], earnestly begged him to advance to the order of subdeaconate a young man who seemed sufficiently suitable and was known and dear to the bishop himself, who had been placed over the archdeacon’s household, and who was to be presented for advancement to the rank of subdeacon. But Hugh refused in every way and, not without some agitation of indignation, restrained those who were interceding for the young man.

At the time everyone present was astonished by this. But shortly afterward, when that same cleric, in consequence of his sins, was terribly covered with the contagion of leprosy, the outcome made it sufficiently clear to those who considered it that the man of God had foreseen in the spirit what would happen to him, and therefore had not wished the blessing of sacred ordination to be lost upon him [Col. 1064C].

While the bishop remained in the place mentioned above [Note: [Col. 1064D] At the manor of the abbot of Saint Nicholas, or at the Grandmontine monastery; the former seems more likely.], reports circulated everywhere that the king was threatening great things against those who despised him and was plotting savage measures. Hence he was hastening to overthrow completely the count mentioned above [Note: [Col. 1064D] The count of Limoges, as most people say, or the count of Angoulême, whom the author of the *Life* mentions.].

Some also reported that the bishop of Lincoln and his clergy were included among those against whom the king was preparing to inflict every kind of severity as soon as possible because of their contempt for him. Hearing such things about a most ferocious man, the clerics were not a little afraid for themselves.
