At that time certain prominent persons from the clergy of the Church of Hereford were present in the city of Angers [Col. 1065A] [Note: [Col. 1065D] In the *Annals of the Church of Worcester*, p. 477, in *Anglia Sacra*, it reads: “In the year 1186 Robert Foliot, bishop of Hereford, died, and William Le Ver succeeded him.” Trivet adds, under the same year, that William was consecrated on the feast of St. Laurence. Laurence Beyerlinck reports that he died in the theater of human life in the year 1199. If so, he must have died in January or February of that year, as may be inferred from this passage.], intending to come to the king to secure the election of a bishop.

One of them was the aforementioned Walter, who was both archdeacon and a canon of the bishop of Lincoln, and also held a prebend in the Church of Hereford. Since certain people wished to place him in charge as bishop of that church [Note: [Col. 1065D] Without the desired result. For it was not Walter but Giles de Braose who was elected bishop of Hereford in 1199, as recorded in the *Annals of Worcester*, p. 479.], they feared that the present hostility, through which the king’s anger had swollen against the people of Lincoln, might obstruct the fulfillment of their desire.

Therefore, by common agreement, the men of Hereford and Lincoln, taking with them the dean and precentor of Angers, as well as certain other canons of that church, came together to the bishop. With their utmost efforts they tried to persuade him that, because of the wickedness of the present days—as his archbishop had frequently warned him—he should redeem the time by sending messengers to the king, promising him a fixed sum of money toward expenses, and by this expedient recall himself as soon as possible to his own see, freed from the costly labor and anxious concern.

“Already,” they said, “not only kingdoms but individual regions are being shaken by the clash of war on every side; the peoples are disturbed, and fear is invading cities and villages. Nothing is now safe: neither a city in which to dwell nor the open countryside in which to remain. Soon it will be neither safe to stay in these places nor free to depart.”

In such matters, the counselors decided that almost the entire day, until evening, should be spent burdening our Job considerably. For these men had come together from three different places to give him this advice, and to act toward him as though they were consulting him. [Col. 1065C] But he alone, resisting tirelessly—not against three men, but against as many bands of men—demonstrated that their arguments were devoid of reason. For he maintained that this was not, as they thought, redeeming time, but wasting it, and indeed wasting it most shamefully, when the dignity and liberty of the Church were so completely subjected to lay military power that neither ecclesiastical persons nor ecclesiastical possessions could enjoy ecclesiastical peace and tranquility unless peace was bought today, at an intolerable price and according to the whim of laymen, only to be revoked tomorrow.

Such were his thoughts and statements concerning that kind of “redemption.” But for us it is now sufficiently evident what he, filled with the Spirit of God, foresaw would shortly happen in the English Church through such exactions [Note: [Col. 1066D] In 1207 the archbishops, bishops, and monks were sent into exile, where they remained for many years.]; for we now see that, after the monks and clerics had been expelled and driven into exile, and the bishops and archbishops likewise, not merely part but the whole of their possessions [Col. 1066A] fell prey to lay plunderers.

When the counselors mentioned above pressed him still more vehemently to set procrastination aside and immediately accept the advice he had already rejected for so long, he was overcome by profound weariness. He saw that they were as obstinate in their purpose as they would be implacable in spirit if he did not comply with them. At last he concluded the unwelcome conversation in these words:

“Indeed, brothers, let what has been said suffice for the present. Tomorrow, with the Lord’s inspiration, we shall arrive at one sound judgment, which he himself knows will contribute most abundantly to the glory of his name. For night has counsel, as we have learned more than once by experience.”

After they had withdrawn, he himself, distressed and gasping for breath, confessed that he had scarcely ever endured so much weariness in so short a time. He sat for a while in meditation, entreating the Almighty with the deepest affection of his heart to enable him to escape the knot of so great a perplexity in such a way that he would offend neither God nor his friends and sons by appearing to disdain their opinion. At last, when his limbs relaxed into sleep, the innermost recesses of his heart began to dream of the Lord.

Then, after the long and delightful pleasures of a vision, he heard this voice sent down from heaven:

“Wonderful is God in his saints; the God of Israel himself will give power and strength to his people. Blessed be God!” (Psalm 67:36).

At these words he was roused from sleep and left his bed. He went to confession earlier than usual, indeed earlier than he did on any Saturday [Note: [Col. 1066D] It was therefore Friday, the day on which the king was wounded, when Hugh was so greatly distressed by the counselors, as is written here; but not the night on which the king died, as Raynaldus reports from Surius in his *Annals* for this year, p. 35.]. In confession he severely reproached himself [Col. 1066C] for the slightest hesitation of the previous day, by which he had afforded his advisers in harmful things even the appearance of his assent [perhaps, connivance]. “Nevertheless,” he said, “I hope that our merciful and gracious Lord will be propitious to me as I confess and lament my iniquity, and that, according to all his wonders, he will rescue us from our present distress.”

And behold, shortly afterward the venerable abbess of Fontevraud came to him [Note: [Col. 1066D] Matilda III of this name, who presided over that celebrated monastery in that year.]. She secretly informed him that the king, struck by a crossbow bolt, had lingered for several days in the greatest agony, wavering between life and death on an uncertain boundary. As far as we can recall, the king was struck by the fatal missile on the very day on which the bishop had been so sorely tormented by the importunities of the evil counsel. During the interval between the king’s wounding and the arrival of the news of it, no one—notably, to our astonishment—said anything to him concerning the decision of so difficult and urgent a matter [Col. 1067A]; he himself silently awaited the salvation of God.

Meanwhile, the dean and canons of the Church of Angers asked him to perform the divine office among them on the approaching Sunday of Palms, because their bishop had not yet returned from the Roman curia, where he had recently received episcopal consecration. He agreed. But when he was already traveling toward that city on the preceding Saturday, a cleric named Gilbert de Lasci met him on the road and announced in the clearest terms that the king had already paid the debt of death [Note: [Col. 1067D] Concerning this, see the *Annals of Winchester* in Warthon, *Anglia Sacra*, p. 304: “King Richard was pierced by a missile near the town of Châlus on the seventh day before the Kalends of April, and died on the eighth day before the Ides of the same month—that is, on Tuesday.”].

The following day it became known that the king was to be carried to the monastery of Fontevraud and there buried beside his father [Note: [Col. 1067D] “And Richard’s body was buried at the feet of his father, King Henry, at Fontevraud.” Thus the *Annals of Winchester*, in the passage cited immediately above.]. On hearing this, Hugh groaned deeply and immediately announced to his companions that he would go to the designated place [Col. 1067B] to perform the last services. Almost everyone tried to dissuade him from doing so.

When he reached the city, he learned that these rumors had already spread everywhere, that violence was being inflicted on travelers, and that robbery was being practiced on all sides. Some of his own people, who were bringing him money from England, had fallen into the hands of plunderers, who had taken forty marks of silver from them. His friends and household therefore advised him not to expose himself and his companions to such disturbances, but rather to remain in the city until the legitimate prince succeeded the dead king and could suppress the wickedness of the violent. Many asserted that the lawlessness of the offenders was so great that they would show no more respect to a bishop [Col. 1067C] than to any layperson.

“For what advice,” they said, “would be available to you if—God forbid!—in some remote wilderness these men should strip you of your mounts and clothing?”

To this he replied, as a truly righteous man who, like a confident lion, was without fear amid every terror, and who became even more steadfast in the face of terror inflicted upon him:

“It is certainly clear how many dangers may be feared on this journey, but they may be encountered by the fearful. For my part, however, I think that I have more to fear for my character: lest the Lord and once my king should see me cowardly withdraw my presence at such a moment, and lest I fail to resume toward the dead either the loyalty or the favor that I always devotedly showed him.

“What wonder if he has caused us trouble, since he was insufficiently on his guard against the malicious counsels of flatterers? Certainly, he never received my presence without the greatest honor, and never sent me away unheard when I personally offered him advice concerning any of my affairs. [Col. 1068A] If he offended against me in my absence, that ought to be attributed to the spite of detractors, not to his own depravity or malice.

“I shall therefore repay, to the best of my ability, the honors he so often bestowed upon me; and it shall not be through me that I fail to attend his funeral with devotion. If robbers meet us as we go, if they take our horses, if they carry off our clothes, we shall proceed all the more easily as your burdens become lighter. If our feet too are shackled and the ability to walk is denied us, then—and only then—will our bodily absence be legitimately excused, when it has been caused not by our own fault but by obstacles imposed by others.”

With these words, he left his companions in the city [Note: [Col. 1067D] Angers, which Hugh had reached early in the morning.], together with almost all his belongings. He set out accompanied only by one of his lesser clerics and one monk, with a few attendants [Col. 1068B].

On hearing that Queen Berengaria was staying in a castle called Beaufort [Note: [Col. 1067D] Commonly Beaufort, where Berengaria, then the widow of King Richard, was residing.], he turned aside from the public road and traveled through terrifying woodland paths until he reached the town, in order to console her over the death of her husband. Speaking to the heart of the grieving widow, who was almost dismayed to the depths of her soul, he soothed her spirit in a remarkable manner. He instructed her, with excellent words, in endurance amid adversity and caution amid prosperity. After celebrating Mass there and imparting, out of devotion, many blessings to the queen and the others who were present, he immediately departed.

That same day [Note: [Col. 1067D] That is, on 10 April, when, after leaving his companions at Angers and celebrating Mass at Beaufort, he reached Saumur by evening, a city situated on the Loire.] he reached the town called Saumur. The townspeople received him with a litany in a joyful procession. He stayed with the aforementioned Gilbert de Lasci [Col. 1068C] [Note: [Col. 1068D] Descended from a noble family transferred from Normandy to England.], who was then studying there, because he was overcome by Gilbert’s earnest entreaties and was received by him with the utmost generosity.

The following morning, on Palm Sunday [Note: [Col. 1068D] That year it fell on 11 April. Ralph of Coggeshall, in vol. V of Martène’s *Collectio*, p. 857, writes that King Richard’s body was buried on Palm Sunday beside his father, with royal honors, by the bishop of Lincoln among the nuns.], he went to the monastery of Fontevraud. At the very doors of the church he encountered the bearers of the royal corpse. When at last the body had been committed to burial with the greatest honor, in keeping with royal magnificence, the bishop returned to the lodging mentioned above.

For three successive days he continued going to that monastery [Note: [Col. 1068D] Hugh went from Saumur to Fontevraud and returned on 11, 12, and 13 April; on the 14th he also went there with John, the future king, and returned with him to Saumur, as is clear from the following chapter.]. Repeating Masses and psalms, he implored pardon and the happiness of perpetual light for the kings buried there and for all the faithful resting in Christ.

## CHAPTER XVI. How John, the future king, came to Fontevraud after his brother’s burial, and what he promised the nuns through our Hugh; and concerning various deeds of that same John which foreshadowed his future condemnation.

[Col. 1068D]

[Col. 1069A] At daybreak on Wednesday [Note: [Col. 1069D] This was 14 April.], the king’s brother, John, surnamed Lackland [Note: [Col. 1069D] So called either because, while his brothers had been raised by their father Henry to the highest honors, he, as the youngest, possessed nothing, as Trivet writes; or because he was eventually deprived of the lands he had obtained from his brother Richard.], was received at Chinon [Note: [Col. 1069D] “Immediately,” writes Coggeshall in Martène, col. 859, “he went to the castle of Chinon, where the royal treasure was kept; and after Robert of Turnham had handed over the castle and treasure to him, he soon seized other castles, and so forth.”] by certain English nobles who held the castle, so that he might govern everything in place of his brother. The household of the dead king, which was established there, also came to him on the same day.

For he had taken a solemn oath that he would faithfully execute the testament of the dead king, and moreover that he would inviolably preserve the lawful customs of earlier times and the just laws of the lands and peoples over whom he was to preside. Shortly before his death, the dead king had deprived him of all the lands he had possessed, because he had discovered that John had conspired with the king of France for his destruction [Col. 1069B]. At the time when the king died, John was with his nephew Arthur in Brittany. When he heard of his brother’s death, he came to Chinon with only a few companions.

He immediately sent to our bishop, who was staying in the aforementioned town [Note: [Col. 1070D] Namely, Saumur, commonly called Samur and Saumur.], awaiting an opportunity to return to his homeland. He earnestly begged him to grant him his presence as soon as possible. When the bishop met him on the road, he rejoiced at the sight of him with immense joy. He spurred on his horse, left his entire company behind, went to meet him, and, paying him reverence, asked him not to leave him but to return with him to England and provide him, across the sea, with constant companionship.

Hugh indicated, however, with reasons, that he would by no means do this. He nevertheless accompanied John as far as Saumur, after they had first visited at Fontevraud the royal tombs of his father and brother. Since what happened there is worthy of knowledge and imitation, it should not be suppressed in idle silence.

When this new lord of so many peoples, accompanied by a large band of nobles, wished to enter by knocking with his own hand at the choir door [Note: [Col. 1070D] A wholly remarkable testimony to the extraordinarily strict enclosure of the nuns of Fontevraud at that time!], in order to see the tombs mentioned above and commend himself to the prayers of that holy community, two nuns of venerable seriousness replied that no mortal was permitted either to see the convent or to enter the inner enclosure except in the presence [Col. 1069D] of their abbess.

“You must therefore,” they said, “await her return; she is expected back from her journey very soon. Nor should your Excellence consider it harsh that we do not violate the statutes of our order even for your sake. Rather, you should regard your father, of blessed memory, as worthy of imitation in this respect. Among religious men he held it in the highest esteem when they observed the institutions handed down by their forebears with strict and inviolable devotion.”

Having spoken thus, those prudent virgins restrained and excluded the prince who was knocking. Then, carefully closing the doors, they returned to their companions [Col. 1070A].

John then turned to the bishop and asked him to convey to the servants of Christ his request for their prayers before God, and also to disclose to them the many good things he intended to bestow upon them.

Hugh replied:

“You know that I detest every lie. I shall therefore take care not to repeat with my lips your promises unless I can be fully confident that you intend to fulfill them.”

John swore that he would fulfill not only what he was then promising, but also that, as circumstances of time and place allowed, he would increase those promises abundantly. The bishop then explained all this to the nuns in John’s presence. Commending John’s undertaking to their prayers [Col. 1070B] and merits, and giving his blessing to all, he departed together with the king.

He had also spoken at length to John about devotion toward God, clemency toward subjects, and justice toward everyone. John declared that he was prepared and willing in spirit to do all these things, and affirmed that he would always obey Hugh entirely as a father and teacher. He earnestly commended his whole conduct to the bishop’s holiness.

During their friendly conversation, John had also drawn from his bosom a stone enclosed in gold and suspended around his neck. He showed it to Hugh, asserting that it had been given to one of his ancestors from heaven with this promise: whoever among his successors deserved to possess it would never be deprived of the greatness of his ancestral dominion.

The bishop immediately replied:

“Place your confidence not in an insensible stone, but entirely in the living and truly heavenly stone, our Lord Jesus Christ. Fix the foundation of your heart most firmly upon him, and anchor your hope in him. For this solid and living stone crushes all who resist it, but does not allow those who rely upon it to sink away. Rather, continually raising them to higher things, it enlarges and extends them so that they may merit still greater rewards.”

When they had reached the church porch, where the image of the final judgment—at which the elect are separated from the rejected—is represented with elegant workmanship, as far as human art permits, the bishop took his companion, the future king, by the hand and drew him to the judge’s left side. There kings, wearing their insignia, are seized by the infernal torturers and dragged into Tartarus, where they will hear: “Go, you accursed, into the eternal fire” (Matthew 25:41).

Then the bishop said:

“May the lamentations and endless torments of these men be continually present to your mind. May these perpetual punishments constantly pass before the eyes of your heart. The diligent remembrance of these evils [Col. 1071A] should teach you at what cost those are briefly placed over the governance of others who, because they govern themselves badly, are without end subjected to demonic spirits to be tormented. As long as it is possible to avoid these things, it is always wise to fear them, lest, when avoidance is no longer possible, you should afterward be forced to endure them forever.”

He also said that sculptures or paintings of this kind were rightly placed before the entrances of churches, so that those about to enter and pray to God for their needs might know that their greatest and highest need was to obtain pardon for their sins. Once that pardon had been obtained, they would remain secure from the punishments of hell and rejoice in everlasting delights. The bishop continued at length in this vein.

As the companion, soon to be king, passed on, he took the bishop with him by the hand and drew him toward the opposite wall. There he showed him kings crowned with splendid crowns and, under angelic guidance, advancing toward the joy of the heavenly King.

“These men,” he said, “my lord bishop, you ought rather to have shown me, for it is my wish to follow and attain their example and companionship.”

For a few days afterward John displayed such humility and submissiveness in bearing and speech that he seemed to exceed all measure. When beggars encountered him on the road and offered him good wishes, he carefully returned thanks with his body bent and his head bowed very low. He most gently returned the greetings of even poor old women in rags who saluted him.

But after three days, although these things had made both the bishop and the others who witnessed them rejoice considerably, he saddened them much more by other unfitting deeds and words [Col. 1071C]. Omitting many of them for the sake of brevity, we report a few, so that the prudent listener may infer, after considering the root, what kind of fertility can be expected from the fruits that will follow from such a tree.

On the most holy day of the Lord’s Resurrection [Note: [Col. 1071D] That year it fell on 18 April.], as was customary, John approached the bishop, who was standing at the altar, to make his offering. His chamberlain placed twelve golden coins in his palm, as royal custom required. John, surrounded on every side by a considerable crowd of nobles, stood before the bishop, gazing at the coins for a long time and provoking him almost playfully. He delayed making the offering until everyone who was watching him was astonished.

At last the bishop, moved by this behavior at such an hour and in such a place, said to him:

“Why do you look at them in that way?”

John replied:

“I am looking at these gold coins. If I had possessed them a few days ago, I would not have offered them to you but would rather have put them into my own purse. Nevertheless, take them now.”

At this the man of God was indignant and blushed deeply on John’s behalf. Being a man of devout mind and generous heart, he withdrew the arm John had extended toward him. He would neither touch his gold nor allow his right hand, faced with such avarice, to be kissed. He groaned inwardly and shook his head:

“Throw down what you are holding there,” he said, [Col. 1072A] “and leave.”

John threw the coins into the silver basin into which offerings were collected and departed.

None of those who attended the bishop ever presumed to retain for himself anything from an offering in another person’s church, except perhaps when the bishop was dedicating a church. He often said that it seemed wholly unjust to him for those who partook there of spiritual nourishment through the grace of the one who guarded that place to carry away any temporal thing from another person’s altar. He observed this rule everywhere, both in his own diocese and in others, and made his attendants observe it as well.

Thus none of his men took anything from this offering. At the time, some thought that in this matter he was imitating the faithful and prudent servant of the Lord [Col. 1072B]. For just as the Lord once had no regard for Cain and his offerings (Genesis 4:5), so now the servant of the Lord, because he had rightly disapproved of the giver of the offering, scorned even to touch his gift.

The bishop then began to preach the word of the Lord to the assembled multitude. As he discussed at length the conduct of good and evil rulers and the rewards reserved for the future, the people were responding devoutly. But the prince mentioned above, following the custom of princes who eat early in the morning, could not tolerate either the subject or the length of the sermon. He sent to the bishop three times, earnestly begging him to bring the sermon to an end and celebrate the divine office, so that after such a long fast he might be permitted to eat.

But our courageous evangelist, who had climbed upon a high mountain, disregarded his wishes and commands. Indeed, raising his voice still more boldly, he did not cease feeding the great multitude of his hearers with the bread of spiritual teaching until, amid the acclamations of all and the tears of many, he had sufficiently instructed them for the occasion to receive worthily the sacramental bread that descended from heaven and gives life to the world (John 7:33) [Note: [Col. 1071D] With two lines drawn through it, the abridger of the *Life* acknowledges that he has omitted certain matters, which may be sought in the longer work, that is, the *Life* written by the author.].

Here, in the sequence of the longer *Life*, several evil deeds of King John are inserted. Whoever wishes may examine them there.

## CHAPTER XVII. How, after the death of King Richard, he escaped the violence of enemies while returning to his homeland, and was joyfully received by those who met him.—This is also chapter 12 in the longer *Life*.

[Col. 1072D] It should therefore be understood that he, truly an exile from the world and a citizen of heaven, thereafter became especially fearful of the losses arising from his present dwelling-place and burned with desire for his heavenly habitation. He had come to recognize more fully that the change of kingdom desired by some was turning toward worse things, and that the hoped-for improvement of the condition of the Church was moving in the opposite direction [Note: [Col. 1072D] This occurred in 1207, when the archbishops, bishops, monks, and clerics were driven into exile and did not return before 1214.].

He therefore judged that he should return to his own Church as quickly as possible, so that he might provide more diligently for the salvation of the souls entrusted to him and, through the richer fruit of every form of piety, seek more freely for himself a passage to heavenly joys [Col. 1073A].

After taking leave of the prince mentioned above, he departed from him on Easter Monday [Note: [Col. 1073D] That is, 19 April.]. When he reached a village where he had decided to lodge, and which the inhabitants call La Flèche [Note: [Col. 1073D] Now La Flèche, in Latin *Flexia*, a town with a castle about ten miles from Angers.], he entered the church and prepared to celebrate Mass. But before he had put on the sacred vestments, his servants rushed to him in confusion and announced that his horses and wagons were being detained by the guards of that place, and that some of his pack animals had been carried off by robbers.

The bishop Gilbert of Rochester [Note: [Col. 1073D] Otherwise called the bishop of Rovecestre or Rochester. Concerning him, the *Annals of Winchester*, in vol. I of *Anglia Sacra*, p. 302, state under the year 1185: “Gilbert de Glanvill was made bishop of Rochester.” And on p. 346: “In the year 1214, while the interdict still continued, Gilbert, bishop of Rochester, died; he had held the bishopric for thirty years.”] was in his company, together with a great many clerics from various places. They all unanimously begged him, in view of the crisis and disturbance caused by these events, to set aside the celebration of Mass, be content to have the Gospel read to them, and devote himself to freeing himself and his companions from such dangers [Col. 1073B].

But he was not at all disturbed by what the robbers were doing, nor moved by what his companions suggested. Like one deaf and mute toward what he heard, he continued only with what he had begun. He was not content merely and plainly to perform the sacred office. Rather, wearing sandals, tunic, dalmatic, and the other insignia, so as to strengthen everyone more effectively by divine protection, and inserting the pontifical blessing into the proceedings, he devoutly celebrated Mass according to solemn custom.

When everything had been properly completed and he was removing the sacred vestments, the magistrates of the place hurried into the church, humbly and earnestly begging pardon for having presumed to obstruct or disturb his servants. They also promised their services if he would consent to spend the night there. If, however, he decided to continue farther, they promised to provide an escort from among their own people as far as safer places [Col. 1073C].

He addressed them quite cheerfully, being filled with spiritual joy and nourished by a heavenly banquet. He did not refuse their escort, but immediately departed with them. That same day he reached the monastery of Saint Peter [Note: [Col. 1073D] Called *De Cultura*, concerning which Mabillon, *Annals*, vol. I, p. 191, writes: “To Bertichramnus, speaking of him, the noble monastery of Saint Peter, called *De Cultura Dei*, owes its origin; it is situated in the suburb of the city of Le Mans.”] situated in the suburb of Le Mans.

At dawn on the following day, while he was performing the morning office to God and, as usual, having long lessons recited, a great tumult broke out from the city walls. Soldiers with an armed force, sent by the countess of Brittany [Note: [Col. 1074D] Named Constance, daughter of Conan, duke of Brittany, and widow of Geoffrey, son of Henry II, king of England; she transferred the duchy to Geoffrey.], and by her son Arthur [Note: [Col. 1074D] The son of Constance and Geoffrey, then a boy of twelve years.], launched an attack in order to capture the aforementioned John.

John had indeed arrived there during the night, but, sensing that ambushes had been prepared for him, had secretly crossed the city before sunrise [Col. 1073D] [Note: [Col. 1074D] He crossed Le Mans and proceeded to Rouen, where, according to Trivet, John, then a prince of thirty-two years, was girded with the sword of the duchy of Normandy on the octave of Easter, 15 April 1199.].

As soon as a certain Gerard, one of the bishop’s clerics, learned this, he hurried to report what he had heard, in considerable agitation and anxiety. He earnestly begged the bishop to shorten the office he was celebrating by using shorter lessons, so that, by avoiding more easily the bands of armed men moving about in the uncertain light, he might safely complete the journey that was pressing upon him with the companions who had already gone ahead.

But just as he had faced this disturbance without fear, so he calmly and carefully rendered to God the hymns that were due. Nor was this foolish. While he lingered, the abbot of that place [Note: [Col. 1074D] The abbot of Saint Peter *De Cultura Dei*.] arrived. He rode ahead of the bishop and led him unharmed by shortcut paths beyond the city suburbs. Many of those who had gone ahead of him were intercepted and detained by hostile violence.

He left there, in the custody of the aforementioned abbot, two wagons with some horses and various belongings. The countess, arriving at the city itself on the following day, had all these things brought to him, earnestly commending herself and her son to his prayers. He himself was making for the city of Séez [Note: [Col. 1074D] Commonly Séez, in whose suburb stood a monastery dedicated to Saint Martin, whose abbot, as it seems, is here highly commended.].

He had also learned from many reports that the abbot was distinguished by excellent pursuits [manuscript: “that the abbot was one of the best,” etc.] and greatly renowned for upright conduct. On hearing that the abbot’s monastery stood not far from the road along which he was traveling, he desired to make the man of God’s acquaintance and commend himself to his prayers. Neither the urgency of the moment nor the length of the journey could deter him from hastening eagerly to seek him.

Through trackless paths unknown to all his companions, he eventually reached the monastery he had long sought, accompanied by a few of his men [Col. 1074C]. The rest, together with the servants and companions, had been sent ahead by the direct road to the city where he himself was to lodge.

When he learned that the abbot was absent, he celebrated Mass and departed, spending all the devout affection of his heart upon the head of the righteous one and upon our Lord Jesus Christ—the devotion he had intended to share with the abbot, a member of Christ and a most faithful and honorable servant.

After this, when every obstacle of every kind had been removed, he was received into the bosom of his Church, bringing to his sons the peace they had long desired, a peace won through much labor and also through many honors, and destined to endure throughout his entire life.

Crowds of rejoicing and applauding people came to meet him everywhere—in the city, from the city, and throughout his diocese [Col. 1074D]—as though he were an eminent commander returning in triumph. Many men in Normandy, and in England innumerable people from both the laity [Col. 1075A] and the clergy, unanimously proclaimed to him:

“Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Matthew 23:39).

He, attributing everything to God and nothing to himself, blessed the Lord, who always triumphs in all things.

## CHAPTER XVIII. [Note: [Col. 1075D] The events related in this chapter occurred in different years.] How, wishing to visit the Charterhouse, he did not obtain the requested permission to withdraw; how vigorously he conducted the cases entrusted to him, especially against a certain Jordan of the Tower; and how burdensome he found personally involving himself in secular affairs, which he judged ought to be assigned to faithful and prudent men.

For a long time, even before the course of his present life had ended, the bishop had cherished the wish to visit the Charterhouse, which he had always loved, to observe the order’s way of life in person, and, by seeing and speaking with that flock—small but most holy—to allow his inward desires to breathe more freely amid external disturbances and to strengthen them more abundantly.

He had also earnestly desired, if the opportunity were granted, to renounce entirely the burden of pastoral care, since, under the pretext of spiritual office and in an inverted order of priorities, he was compelled to spend almost all his days serving the settlement of worldly disputes.

“Already,” he said, “the magistrates or governors of cities and the prelates of Churches appear to differ almost solely in this: the latter devote themselves to lawsuits continuously, the former on alternate days. The former are sometimes permitted to attend to the interests of their own households; the latter are scarcely ever allowed even to deal with the affairs of their own souls.”

He had also approached the ears of the supreme pontiff, through intermediaries, a second or third time concerning this purpose of his heart. But the pope did not yield in the least. He not only rejected Hugh’s request but also rebuked the intermediaries of the petition rather harshly.

For all the most difficult and arduous decisions of cases that came under apostolic authority to be argued within the boundaries of all England, each of the Roman supreme pontiffs during Hugh’s time delegated to the bishop of Lincoln [Note: [Col. 1075D] The matters entrusted to our Hugh by Pope Celestine in the cases of the archbishop [Col. 1076D] of York are reported by Baronius under the years 1191, 1199, and 1195, who also cites the pope’s letters themselves.].

People of every rank, moreover, both ordinary and lowly, desired to litigate before him against their adversaries in proportion to the confidence they placed in the merits of their cases. Whether their opponents relied upon force or armed themselves with deceit, under the judgment of this most just judge truth more easily convicted them and equity more quickly overwhelmed them.

He had received this gift from God as well: just as no one was more steadfastly attached to what was equitable and right, so no one could easily be found who seemed swifter or sharper than he in examining truth and falsehood. Those who were regarded as more experienced in law and thoroughly practiced in the pleading of forensic or ecclesiastical cases observed this in him and attributed it to miracles. Although he was unaccustomed to such matters and almost ignorant of the laws, he surpassed everyone’s acumen and outstripped the intellects of legal experts.

[Col. 1076A] We saw a certain powerful man in the city of London, called Jordan of the Tower, whom two poor and insignificant orphans, still living under guardians, had summoned to court by authority of the lord pope’s letters, on account of the unjust detention of certain houses belonging to them by hereditary succession. The case itself had been brought into the ecclesiastical forum by the title of usury, on which it was said to rest.

On the appointed day, he came to the bishop surrounded by a very large company—not, as though he intended to litigate, but as though he intended to break off the progress of the suit—men who were more like champions than advocates. When his attendants presented him with written and oral prohibitions and pleas, both on behalf of the lord king and of other exalted powers, and also on behalf of the citizens of London collectively, that he should not proceed in the case—for, they asserted, if he did so, it would rebound to the prejudice of their city—his assessors and household unanimously decided that the case ought to be abandoned. He, however, after deliberating within himself for a little while, finally crushed the oppressor of the orphans with these words.

He remembered that the father of the orphans was the one of whom Scripture says: “You will be a helper to the orphan” (Psalm 10:14). He therefore said:

“Indeed, Jordan, although you have been dear to us, we are nevertheless in no way able to favor you against God. Yet because it is clear that resistance to so many and such powerful supporters of yours would be useless not only to these little ones but even to ourselves and our fellow judges, we do not wish to conceal from you what we shall do. I speak for myself: I shall deliver my soul. I shall write to the lord pope that you alone in these lands resist his jurisdiction, and that you alone strive to nullify his authority.”

At this sentence, as though struck by an arrow, he was touched to the very depths of his heart—for he understood how weighty such a report would be in the ears of the supreme pontiff, especially when it came from the mouth of a man of such great renown—and immediately began consulting with his associates about making restitution to those who had been dispossessed. For he found no other possible outcome. The words of the just man, like goads driven deep, had left men exceedingly prudent in their generation unable even to approach them with arguments or blandishments, much less to yield before them.

Accordingly, he soon satisfied the complainants in a manner worthy of them, and, as he himself declared, not without enormous expense, since he had personally spent money on the property. Thus one brief allegation by the just man obtained what scarcely anyone would ever have believed could be obtained by any multitude of litigators.

Although in similar cases he very often provided assistance to innocence or truth when they were suffering shipwreck, he nevertheless considered it unbecoming for a pontiff to devote his efforts so frequently to earthly and transitory matters rather than to heavenly and eternal ones. He bore the burden of such activities, but under compulsion, expecting from the merit of obedience a plea for excuse rather than a reward for an admirable undertaking.

[Col. 1077A] There is no need to support this with innumerable examples of his words and deeds, which would readily occur to a writer, since his attitude is confirmed in him by such an indisputable proof: he never sat down to his own treasury or accounts, whether of his revenues or expenses, and never deigned to attend to the reckoning of his own household.

As for the Apostle’s instruction that a bishop should rule his household well (1 Timothy 3:4), he taught that it should be fulfilled, and fulfilled it, in such a way that these duties were entrusted to men highly esteemed for faith and discretion. He trusted them as he would have trusted himself, so long as they conducted themselves blamelessly; but if they acted otherwise—which could not remain hidden for long—he removed them immediately. He was not bound by private affection toward any of those to whom he had entrusted the administration of his affairs. He appointed those whom faith and diligence could commend, not those whom, as commonly happens, some closer personal relationship could move him to favor.

## CHAPTER XIX

How, after peace had been restored between the kings of France and England, in which our Hugh also took part, and after obtaining permission from the king and the archbishop to withdraw to the Carthusian house, he came to Paris and there spoke most salutary words to Louis, son of the king of France, and Arthur, nephew of John; and concerning a certain man who encountered him and sought absolution, whom he had excommunicated in England a long time previously.

This is also chapter 13 in the sequence of the Great Life; the preceding chapter is included under it as well.

After a year had already been completed [Note: [Col. 1077D] Perhaps an ecclesiastical year, not a natural one. King John was crowned in London in 1199 on the day of the Ascension of the Lord, which fell on 27 May, or on the Sunday within the octave of that feast, namely, 30 May. And “in the year 1200,” as Trivet writes, “on the Ascension of the Lord, which occurred on 18 May, peace and concord between the two kings were restored between Vernon and the island of Andely in the form set out below.” So he says. Raynaldus, however, following Roger, reports that peace was made on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June, that is, 22 May, in the Annals, p. 47.] after King John’s coronation, the bishop crossed the sea again at his request [Col. 1077C], in order to attend his meeting with the king of France, at which peace was finally restored between them.

Hugh thought that he had now found a suitable opportunity to visit the Carthusian house. Accordingly, after requesting and receiving permission from the king and the archbishop at the castle of Andely [Note: [Col. 1077D] As we have seen from Trivet, the peace in which our Hugh took part was consolidated at this time, and Hugh obtained permission to visit the Carthusian house and the other places mentioned below.], he began his journey on the last day of May [Note: [Col. 1077D] Pentecost fell that year on 28 May, and the Wednesday on 31 May.], which was the Wednesday of Pentecost.

As he was going to Paris, he turned aside to Saint-Denis [Note: [Col. 1078D] For this most celebrated monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, consult Mabillon, vol. I of the Annals of the Benedictines, p. 340 and following.]. After he had left the clerics’ quarter, innumerable crowds came toward him. For scholastics poured out in groups from the city to meet the universal “counselor of the schools” [Note: [Col. 1078D] The whole of chapter 28 may be seen, toward which this is one portion.], as a distinguished versifier called him.

Students from almost every nation desired to see face to face the man through whom, after Saint Nicholas, they had recognized incomparable benefits being bestowed upon clerics [Col. 1078A]. Thus, while all applauded his arrival in the name of the Lord—some joyfully enjoying his kiss and conversation, others merely his appearance together with his blessing—several pressed him most urgently to accept their hospitality. Since it was impossible to satisfy everyone in this, he did not refuse to stay with one man alone, who had previously sought to obtain this by earnest entreaty.

This man was said to be his kinsman, named Raymund, a man conspicuous for great integrity, whom Hugh had promoted first to be a canon of Lincoln and eventually to be archdeacon of Leicester.

A young man of exceptionally promising character came to visit the bishop at his lodging: Louis, son and heir of the king of France, who shortly beforehand [Note: [Col. 1078D] The day after the day on which peace was made between the kings, as Raynaldus reports in Note [ [Col. 1077D] Perhaps an ecclesiastical year, not a natural one. King John was crowned in London in 1199 on the day of the Ascension of the Lord, which fell on 27 May, or on the Sunday within the octave of that feast, namely, 30 May. And “in the year 1200,” as Trivet writes, “on the Ascension of the Lord, which occurred on 18 May, peace and concord between the two kings were restored between Vernon and the island of Andely in the form set out below.” So he says. Raynaldus, however, following Roger, reports that peace was made on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June, that is, 22 May, in the Annals, p. 47.], cited above.] had taken in marriage the niece of the king of England through his sister, namely Candida, queen of the Spains [Note: [Col. 1078D] Others call her Blanca, Blanchia, or Blanda. She was the daughter of Alfonso VIII, king of Castile, by Eleanor, daughter of Henry II, king of England, and mother of Saint Louis, king of France.].

Arthur, nephew of the aforesaid king, also came with him; he was the son of the late Geoffrey, count of the Bretons, and was then about fourteen years old. The pious Hugh embraced both of them and sweetly instilled into each appropriate and most salutary counsels.

Louis listened eagerly to what was said, with a calm expression. Arthur, however [Note: [Col. 1078D] For by hereditary right he laid claim to the kingdom of England.], rejected with disdain especially the counsel that urged him to maintain love and peace toward his uncle, the king of the English.

Meanwhile Louis asked the bishop to visit his newly married wife. Hugh kindly agreed and went on foot to the nearby royal palace [Col. 1078C]. With a few words he so cheered the young woman, afflicted as she was by her recent misfortune, that immediately, abandoning her sorrow, she who for several days had gone about in mourning thereafter displayed both the happiest expression and the happiest spirit.

After this, when he had already passed through the county of Troyes, a certain man came to him [Note: [Col. 1078D] A subject of Robert, count of Leicester, who had formerly committed an offense but now voluntarily undertook the penance once despised.] imploring his mercy in a wretched voice.

He confessed that, because his sins demanded it, he had received a sentence of excommunication from Hugh, and that, as a result, he was continually tormented by fear of final destruction and was constantly afflicted by misfortunes.

The cause of the sentence was this. He had once been custodian of the count of Leicester’s villages. At that time a thief took refuge in the church of a village called Brackley, of which this man himself was the bailiff. The property lay in the diocese of Lincoln [Col. 1078D].

Its principal lord was considered a man of outstanding military ability, and through the line of his noble blood he was connected with the greater nobles of the kingdom. Hence, supported by the king’s favor, he claimed for himself the confidence to usurp certain things contrary to justice, no less for his own men than for himself.

His officials, therefore, contrary to the warning of Scripture, which says, “Do not be excessively righteous” (Ecclesiastes 7:17), exercised cruel justice against a man who was seeking the mercy of the Church. They deceitfully dragged him from Christ’s sanctuary and killed him by hanging.

At that time the bishop was overseas. When he returned and learned what had happened, he pronounced a general sentence against the perpetrators and accomplices of this crime.

The others who bore a seared conscience concerning this sacrilege humbly submitted themselves to ecclesiastical discipline. But this man, abhorring the severity of the required satisfaction, left England and fled to his lord in Normandy [Col. 1079A].

For those who had inflicted the death, as well as those who by treachery had dragged him from the church’s enclosure, had been compelled—stripped naked except for their breeches—to dig up the man’s already decayed corpse and, placing it on a bier, carry it from the place of hanging to the village for almost a mile, with their shoulders thus bare.

They were also compelled, after being scourged by all the priests of that chapter at the doors of all the churches of the village, to carry around the limbs of the body, now dissolved by decay, and to bury them in the cemetery of the church from which they had brought the living man out, using their own hands and, as stated, with their bodies always naked.

After this they were ordered to go barefoot to Lincoln, expose their sides to the lashes before the doors of each church in that great city, and endure other similar things which were sufficiently harsh to bear, especially in winter.

This man, who was one of them, could not endure these things. He preferred to leave England rather than provide the English with the satisfaction of seeing him perform an appropriate penance.

But, as it is said according to blessed Job, “He who fears the frost will be overtaken by snow” (Job 6:16), and as the person who does not tolerate harsh treatment from a physician is often endangered by illness, so it happened to him in a similar way as a result of his own decision.

Because he refused to endure correction for his guilt while he could still preserve the integrity of his position, storms of adversity rose against him from every side. He was afflicted by such losses and various misfortunes that, as he asserted, he became weary of his life.

He also perceived that the favor of his lord—whom he had thought he was serving—had been so completely withdrawn from him because he had tried to resist the bishop that his lord would neither allow him to remain in his service nor willingly have him appear in his presence [Col. 1080A].

At last, returning to himself, he judged that the man whom he had thought must be fled from was now the physician whom he should seek. Breathless and anxious, he finally found him, and from him, though he was in a distant place, scarcely received the remedy which he had scorned to accept when it was freely offered nearby.

He now gladly undertook the burden of seven years’ penance, which he had scorned to complete in a shorter time.

[Note: [Col. 1079D] The abbreviator omits certain matters which, had he added them, would not have made the labor fruitless on account of their antiquity, especially if they were matters unknown to the Bollandists in the Life of Saint Anthony.]

Here, however, the Great Life inserts the pilgrimage that our Hugh made to blessed Anthony, together with a straightforward account of several miracles of the same blessed Anthony. The whole of this is presently judged best omitted in order to avoid a lengthy digression.

## CHAPTER XX

Concerning his arrival and reception at Grenoble and at the Carthusian house, and how he conducted himself in those places; concerning the restoration by him of peace between the bishop and the count of Geneva; and how, when he was about to depart from the Carthusian house, he arranged matters concerning the relics obtained by himself and his monk.

[Col. 1080B]

After he had therefore paid the vows owed to so great a patron, Saint Anthony, and had visited the hospice of that place [Note: [Col. 1079D] “This is the church of Saint Anthony of La Motte near Vienne” (these are Mabillon’s words in vol. V of the Annals of the Benedictines, p. 369), “to which they relate that the body of that great Saint Anthony was transferred in the eleventh century. There a cell was erected by the monks of Montmajour, together with a hospice assigned to receive sick people suffering from Anthony’s fire.” [Col. 1080D]], and had ordered money to be distributed to the attendants for food and relief—for a great multitude of the infirm, whom disease had deprived of various limbs before their recovery, remained there—he set out for Grenoble [Note: [Col. 1080D] Commonly Grenoble, the principal city of the Dauphiné and an episcopal see; after Saint Hugh, six others succeeded there who had been taken from the Carthusian order.].

From there, the natural character of the region and the frequency of travelers made the journey to the Carthusian house, across steep mountains and rugged rocks, more manageable.

As soon as his arrival became known to the people of Grenoble, they all rushed together to meet the highly venerable man outside the city walls. They received him and led him through the center of the city, which had been specially and magnificently decorated in his honor with flowers, silk hangings, and varied ornaments, as far as the cathedral church of Saint John the Baptist, with songs of joy and a solemn procession.

It was the birthday feast of that same forerunner of the Lord [Note: [Col. 1080D] It recurs annually on 24 June; Saint Hugh either arrived there on that day or on the preceding day and was honorably received.], who, after the Mother of God, the sole Lady of the world, was the special patron both of the Carthusian order and of our bishop.

There Hugh celebrated high Mass with the greatest devotion. After the Gospel he preached to the people a sermon seasoned with the nectar of extraordinary sweetness. Thus, by the grace of salutary speech, he doubled and completed their joy—both that of the annual solemnity and that of his first visit to them since becoming bishop—so that he fed them with the bread of tears, giving them drink in tears, but in due measure (Psalm 79:6).

Finally, with such humility and such devotion he sought the prayers of all, emphasizing his own lowliness and unworthiness, while the heavenly favor had raised him from the dungheap and placed him on high, that the eyes of all poured forth tears like springs of water.

[Col. 1081A] On that same day he also baptized a boy already seven years old [Note: [Col. 1081C] This boy must be distinguished from another son of William, the brother of Saint Hugh, mentioned in Book III, chapter 13. The latter was applauding Hugh when he was still prior at Witham; this boy, however, was baptized by him when he was already bishop, in the final year of his life and episcopate.], the son of the most valiant knight William of Avalim, his brother. The bishop of Grenoble received him from the sacred font [Note: [Col. 1081C] The bishop of Grenoble in the year 1200 was either John or William, both Carthusians. Concerning John, consult the notes on Book II, chapter 2. Concerning William, the Carthusians report as follows: “The truly pious Lord William succeeded him” (John, whom they say died in 1194, on the first day before the Kalends of June) “and died in 1223.” Yet for Abbot Morotius, John was still alive in 1219, when he wrote of him: “In the nineteenth year of the following century he restored the city.” Concerning William, the same Morotius writes: “In the year 1221 William, already the sixth bishop taken from the monks of the proto-Carthusian house according to the diptychs of this Church” (Grenoble), “was brought in as bishop; and although he was a brief pastor, being carried off within three years, he nevertheless equaled the virtues of his predecessors and offered an outstanding example of integrity, which he had imbibed in that most complete school of perfection.” Morotius says this while extending John’s administration and shortening William’s.].

When the boy’s uncle strongly insisted that he should be called by his own name, which was Peter, Hugh replied, at the suggestion of the present writer:

“Not at all; he will be called John. The patron of this place and of the present day takes precedence over you.”

We spent the day of so great a solemnity with the bishop of that city, who entertained us so splendidly with everything that the laws of hospitality required that the very manner of it seemed to exceed all measure. You might have said that the generosity of the Burgundians had itself surpassed even the extravagant luxury of the English.

[Col. 1081B] From there, when we set out for the Carthusian house early the next morning [Note: [Col. 1081D] That is, on 25 June they made for the Carthusian house, about three miles distant from Grenoble.], those whom horses carried were compelled to cover almost the greater part of the journey on foot. For the horses, riderless, could scarcely manage the continuous ascent over the steep and broken sides of the mountain; pack-horses or asses, however, pass along this path more freely.

The bishop too, compelled by necessity, became a pedestrian. Although he was exhausted by excessive sweat, he remained ready and cheerful in spirit, and by walking made his companions weary.

He took care, however, to ensure that he reached the brothers while they were sleeping at midday [Note: [Col. 1081D] In Hugh’s time the custom still prevailed among the Carthusians [Col. 1082C] that, after Matins, they did not return to bed but recovered at midday the sleep they had forgone during the night. In the course of time this custom was abolished.]. For he was extremely careful that his arrival should not disturb their rest even slightly.

He remained among them for almost three full weeks [Note: [Col. 1082C] These probably include the several days he spent among the lay brothers; for it follows that, after the period of three weeks, he prepared himself to return.], like one of them. Especially during the nighttime hours of chanting, he was never absent from the brothers’ choir, while he always slept entirely alone in a solitary cell.

During that time, how much he drank in there, and how much he received from the reciprocal conversation of holy men concerning spiritual sweetness, no one expects us to explain in writing. Indeed, not even he himself could have expressed it in words, since he had been privileged to experience it in reality.

[Col. 1082A] Several bishops came there to visit him, as did very many poor clerics and laypeople living in the neighboring parish. They hastened eagerly to him as though to their formerly lamented and now restored own parent.

He embraced and kissed them all with equal affection and, recognizing them as acquaintances, showed that he remembered them. He also engaged them in familiar conversation and, in deeds and words, showed himself like that little one whom the gentle and humble Master set before his disciples in the Gospel as an example to imitate.

He increased the grace of his friendliness by the generosity of his hands, which were not sparing, for in him both a gracious tongue and a liberal hand flourished together.

He also remained for several days in the lower dwelling where the lay brothers lived, so that he might satisfy them too from the abundant breasts of his consolation, while he himself might feast in turn on their conversation and disciplined conduct, as though at the entrance of the glory of the nations.

Some of them had turned aside from the broad road of worldly activity and entered the narrow and difficult road that leads to life. With happy hope they awaited the entrance to paradise.

During those days, at fixed times and hours, he also made himself available to the poor who flocked to visit him. He spoke with them so familiarly that, while sitting among them, he showed by his monastic habit alone that he was no other than one of them.

The bishop of Geneva had also informed him [Note: [Col. 1082D] His name was Antholinus, also called Nantelinus and Nanelmus. He had been prior of the Vallon Carthusian house in 1185 and was elected bishop of Geneva. He died in the twentieth year of his episcopate, that is, in 1205, on the Ides of February.] how gravely his count [Note: [Col. 1082D] William, or Wilhelmus I, count of Geneva. This was the man whom, according to Abbot Morotius, Antholinus, in the second year after assuming the episcopate, obtained, on the sixth day before the Kalends of September, to be subjected to the imperial ban, as one harassing the Church’s property in many ways.] had oppressed him for three times four years, to the great prejudice of the bishop. For this reason he had long before bound the count with the bond of excommunication and anathema [Col. 1082C] [Note: [Col. 1082D] This was at the very time when the aforesaid count was subjected to the imperial ban, namely in 1186, from which three times four years had almost elapsed by the year 1200, though not yet three periods of five years, unless “five-year period,” as learned men more correctly do, is understood to mean a cycle of four complete years.].

Because of this fear, the count did not dare enter his own city. For, if our memory does not deceive us, he asserted that three periods of five years had already elapsed since he had been forbidden to approach the seat of his cathedral church.

Then our strong and faithful man, whom a versifier indeed celebrated as the “shepherd’s staff” [Note: [Col. 1082D] See the final chapter.], greatly consoling and strengthening the afflicted and sorrowful brother, promptly sent two priors from the Carthusian order to exhort the count, worn down by a prolonged bodily illness, to hasten to be reconciled with his father, the bishop, and with his mother, the Church.

He also put words into their mouths, instructing them to impress upon the count above all that he should strive to seek the favor of his scourging father, lest, if death came more quickly, he should become an exile from the inheritance of the children of God.

The count listened disdainfully as they spoke such things to him. But after they had departed, he came to himself, as he himself testified, through the intercession of the man of God. Deeply pierced by the force of the words that Hugh had entrusted to them, he satisfied the Church whom he had injured. Thus he was first absolved from the sentence and afterward, freed from the burden of the flesh, rested in peace.

After the period of three weeks, the bishop, knowing that it is written, “A man shall leave father and mother and cling to his wife” (Genesis 2:24), prepared to return to the care of the Church to which he had formerly been betrothed. Besides other gifts, as he took his final leave of the Church from whose breasts he had grown into a mature man, and as he was already departing, he left behind relics of immeasurably precious worth as a perpetual memorial of himself.

He had in his chests a silver box, which he carried in his hands during the dedications of basilicas, filled with numerous relics of saints and holy women. He himself, or the custodian of these chests, his monk and chaplain, had acquired most of them in various places.

But the bishop gave the relics that he himself had sought to a most devout Carthusian sacristan, in the presence of the prior and the brothers, to be kept in that place. His monk’s relics he left to be carried to his own monastery.

## CHAPTER XXI

How devout he was in visiting the relics of the saints and in seeking them out, and how he finally arranged matters concerning them.

This is contained in the Great Life under chapter 14, around the middle of that chapter.

Because [Note: [Col. 1083D] It is clear from the context that the events of this chapter occurred in other years as well, not only on this journey.] we have mentioned the relics of the saints, it does not seem pointless, but rather conducive to the glory or edification of those who hear, to relate a few more things about them briefly.

The bishop had ordered a ring to be made for him of the purest gold and precious stones. On the part that surrounded the finger externally it had a kind of hollow, which he intended as a repository for sacred relics. This receptacle was about four fingers wide on every side. Into it he had gathered portions of holy relics, numbering as many as thirty.

Since he was moved by the greatest devotion and was deeply concerned to acquire such a salutary treasure, he pressed most earnestly to obtain something from the body of the great confessor of Christ, Benedict, the foremost leader and lawgiver of monks.

Regarding this desire, he sent affectionate letters to the venerable abbot and monks of the monastery of Fleury [Note: [Col. 1083D] This is a monastery of outstanding renown, situated on the Loire in the diocese of Orléans. It is frequently mentioned by writers on Benedictine affairs, such as Pez, Bucellinus, Mabillon, and others.], where the most sacred bones of so great a Father rest. He wrote to them and sent, by one of their brothers, both a monk and a custodian [Note: [Col. 1083D] This monk seems to have been Morinus, who at the end of chapter 26 is said to have died as almoner at Stourport. Certainly he was different from the author of the Life: the latter was a monk of Canterbury, whereas this man was a monk of Fleury. The latter also was away from Hugh for only one night; this man, sent from Lincoln to Fleury and returning from there, presented the sacred relics to Hugh at Dorchester [Col. 1084D].], possession of certain holy relics that he had obtained for himself at Lincoln. He earnestly requested that they deign to share with him some of their wealth in this respect.

Why say more? At last the bearer of the letter returned and brought the holy man the fulfillment of his desire and request: one tooth from the teeth of Saint Benedict, together with a considerable portion of the cloth [Note: [Col. 1084D] Concerning a tooth secretly removed from Monte Cassino, the Bollandists relate in the Life of Saint Benedict that the man who had taken it was compelled to return it. Here, by God’s marvelous providence, a goldsmith is warned and urged to visit Hugh in order to enclose the tooth in a ring.] in which the saint’s hair had been wrapped.

The same bearer also had in his hands the reciprocal letter of those to whom he had been sent. In it they returned the greeting due to so great a Father and, by sending the gifts, offered an unquestionable testimony concerning them.

When the man of God had received and read these letters, he rejoiced with extraordinary delight and immediately ordered his goldsmith to be summoned. The goldsmith lived in Hugh’s castle, called Banvenbiria.

At the time when these events took place, however, the bishop was staying at his manor called Dorchester [Note: [Col. 1084D] This is the place from which the episcopal see was transferred to Lincoln. I cannot discover where the castle of Banvenbiria was situated. Perhaps it was not far from Lincoln, which lies about thirty miles from Dorchester.], which was about thirty miles from the castle just named.

Meanwhile, while a messenger was being prepared to bring the goldsmith, so that Hugh could order him to bring with him the tools by which he could suitably open and close the bishop’s sacramental ring—for that is what he called it, because he used it frequently in the celebration of ordinations and consecrations as an incentive to devotion—suddenly the very goldsmith whom they had been ordered to seek appeared. He brought a presence as unexpected as it was welcome, causing equal joy and astonishment.

When asked the reason for his arrival, he asserted that, while he was sleeping around midnight, someone had appeared beside him and ordered him to hurry at once to the bishop.

“For,” he said, “very precious relics have been sent to him, which you must place inside his ring. [Col. 1084D] Rise, therefore, quickly, and go to the bishop.”

Awakened from sleep by this voice, I was so agitated in mind that I could undertake no task until I came to you to report these things and to test whether what I had heard was true.

“Here I am, therefore, and here are my tools. Use the work of the craftsman, as you know how.”

This revelation and report by the craftsman strengthened the certainty of the relics and increased the joy of all who were present and had learned of these events.

The most generous man distributed to certain abbots and other devout men who were present small portions of the cloth he had received. But the tooth, which he repeatedly kissed with great affection, he had enclosed in his ring.

At Fécamp [Note: [Col. 1085C] Now Fécamp, commonly Fescan or Fécamp, founded for virgins around the year 658; since its restoration in the tenth century it has been a monastery of Benedictine monks. See Mabillon, vol. I of the Annals of the Benedictines, p. 447; vol. II, p. 540; and again vol. IV, p. 152.], too, at the distinguished monastery, he gnawed off two pieces from a bone of the arm [Note: [Col. 1085C] The Bollandists discuss many matters concerning relics, including the arms of blessed Mary Magdalene, in vol. V for the month of July. They make no mention, however, of this arm bone.] of the most blessed beloved of Christ, Mary Magdalene.

At that time none of those present—neither abbot nor monk—had ever seen the bone uncovered. It had been sewn extremely tightly inside two silk cloths and a simple linen one [Col. 1085B].

When no one dared display it for the bishop, who was insisting on seeing it, he snatched a small knife from one of his notaries, quickly cut the threads, and, unsewing the wrapping, reverently applied the most sacred bone to his mouth and kisses.

When he was unable to dislodge anything by pressing with his fingers, he first applied his incisors and then his molars; by their strength he quickly broke off two portions, which he placed in the right hand of the man writing this [Note: [Col. 1085D] The author means himself. This action therefore occurred within one of the final three years of Saint Hugh’s life.], saying:

“Keep these very carefully for us.”

When the abbot and monks saw this—for they had long been astonished and frightened, but now became furious and angry—they cried out:

“Shame upon such wickedness! We thought that the bishop had asked for these sacred things to be brought out in order to venerate them, and behold, he has handed them over to be torn apart by a dog’s bite.”

He calmed them as they continued in this vein with gentle words, saying among other things something memorable:

“If a little while ago we handled the most holy body of the Saint of saints with our unworthy fingers, and transmitted it into our inner selves after touching it with our teeth and lips, why should we not also confidently handle his holy limbs for our protection and to gain their veneration and remembrance more earnestly, and, when the opportunity is given, acquire them so that they may be preserved for us with due honor?”

At another time, at the borough of Saint Peter [Note: [Col. 1085D] “At the borough of Saint Peter.” A monastery in England, belonging from ancient times to the Order of Saint Benedict, otherwise called Peterborough, concerning which Mabillon writes in volume I of the Benedictine Annals, under the year 655. There is another monastery of Saint Peter of the same order at Gloucester. Of the former, namely Peterborough, a fuller account is given in volume I of the Monasticon Anglicanum, p. 63, from which I add this conclusion: “In the year 970, Saint Adelwold, bishop of Winchester, transferred the relics of Saint Swithun from the cemetery into the church, and also began to restore the monastery of Medeshamstede (Peterborough), and called it the borough of Saint Peter, exactly one hundred years after its desolation.” Mabillon assigns this desolation to the year 770, in volume III of the Benedictine Annals, p. 167. Concerning the monastery of Saint Peter at Gloucester, moreover, see volume I of the Monasticon Anglicanum, p. 108, [Col. 1086C] where it is asserted that Ethelfleda, daughter of King Alfred, “transferred the bones of Blessed Oswald the king from Bardney to this Gloucester monastery of Saint Peter.” On the same page, p. 142, the monastery of Bardney in Lincolnshire is described, and among other things it is recorded that “the body of Saint Oswald was first buried at Bardney, where at that time there were three hundred monks,” and so forth. When I read and compared these passages, [Col. 1086D] I began to wonder whether the arm of the said Saint Oswald had been at the Peterborough or at the Gloucester monastery of Saint Peter. But the doubt was resolved by the fact that, as Mabillon reports in volume V of the Annals, p. 473, the head of Saint Oswald was found in the church of Durham together with the body of Saint Cuthbert in the year 1004. If the head of the holy king could be transferred to Durham, why could not his arm likewise have been transferred to the monastery of Peterborough, whether from Bardney or from Gloucester?]

From the arm of the glorious king and martyr Oswald—which is still displayed with its bones and skin, even with bloody flesh, as though it had recently been cut from a living body—the bishop cut off with a knife a projecting sinew, yielding and soft to the touch when handled, and kept it for preservation with every reverence.

He then placed this, together with the other sacred relics—which it would take too long to enumerate—in the frequently mentioned ring. On one occasion, when he had come to Lincoln from overseas, he solemnly offered this ring as a gift upon the altar of the blessed Virgin, so that it might likewise be kept there. Later, having forgotten this offering, he ordered that the same often-mentioned ring, together with the other relics, be given to the Carthusians. When his monk [Note: [Col. 1086D] “His monk.” That the author is indicating himself here is sufficiently shown by what follows: “This was fulfilled through the efforts of that same monk after the holy man’s death.” The extent of what Hugh entrusted to the author before his death will be related below.]—the custodian of those sacred objects—reminded him of the gift of the ring that he had previously made, he ordered that the ring be returned to the Church of Lincoln. But he gave them a small chest, fashioned of gold and gems, which had been kept at Lincoln in his treasury, so that the relics of the saints bestowed by him might be placed in it. This was accomplished, through the efforts of that same monk, after the holy man’s death.

## CHAPTER XXII

On the places through which he passed on his return from the Charterhouse to England, on his deeds in those places, and on how he was gravely afflicted by illness before coming to London

[Col. 1086C]

When the aforesaid distribution had been completed, the bishop immediately descended to the lower dwellings of the lay brothers. On the following day, after invoking God’s blessing upon the Charterhouse and bestowing his own, he departed bodily from the place in which he remained continually in heart and spirit. He had often been most insistently entreated by a devout and energetic man, the prior of Saint-Domnin [Note: [Col. 1086D] This is a cell formerly presided over by Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny. Concerning him Mabillon writes in volume V of the Annals, p. 441: “He was then appointed provost of the cell of Domena in the diocese of Grenoble.”], to honor the house which he governed by visiting it in person. Accordingly, the bishop turned aside to his cell. Receiving him, together with his brothers, in a solemn procession as though he were an angel of God, he spent the day with him in gladness of heart and spiritual rejoicing.

The bishop also intended to visit Villa Benedicta [Note: [Col. 1087C] Consult the notes to Book I, chapter 1]; for that is the name of the cell in which he tasted the beginnings of his sacred religious life. But, following the logic of the route, he first proceeded to a castle that had belonged to his father, where his two brothers, William and Peter, maintained their residence and considerable lordship. These men, always rejoicing—as energetic knights—to spur Hugh onward in the course of truth, as one spurs a horse with a sharp heel, often urged not only the bishop but also his counselors, both in person and by messages when absent, not to let his spirit grow weary amid the persecutions of false brothers or cruel lords. They declared that they would rather he had never been born than that, contrary to his noble birth, he should for even a moment, through a degenerate spirit, have yielded to the oppression of ecclesiastical liberty.

Coming, therefore, to stay with them, he visited not only their places but also the nearby homes of nobles, common people, and the sick, and was received by all the inhabitants with a common rejoicing. They kept him there for two days.

On the third day he finally reached the canons’ house of Villa Benedicta, which the local inhabitants call Vilarboneyth in their vernacular. It is difficult to express how much joy his arrival brought, not only to the inhabitants of that place [Col. 1087C] but also to all the neighbors round about. He also gave that church a library—that is, a volume of the sacred Scriptures—purchased for ten silver marks. He visited as well the cell in which, as we said above, he had once held the priorship as a young man; it is called Saint Maximus.

In these places, decrepit men and gray-haired elders, as well as bent old women and women advanced in years, surrounded him. As they applauded Hugh, they raised to the skies with extraordinary praises the beginnings of Hugh’s life among them, once sprouting like a lily. They also declared that the beginnings of his earliest age had already proclaimed, through certain signs of an innate virtue, the marks of his future holiness. He then returned to the castle mentioned above and rested there for one night.

From there, already hastening toward England, he reached the city of Belley [Note: [Col. 1087C] “Belley,” that is, the city in which, under the archbishopric of Besançon, seven bishops from the Carthusian Order presided over the see of Belley during the twelfth century. Among them was Bernard, a mirror of every virtue [Col. 1087D] and holiness, who presided in the year 1200 and died in 1207, on the day before the Nones of May, or, as some maintain, in 1208.] at his second stage. There he was privileged to receive for kissing the framework of half the Forerunner’s hand, with its three fingers—namely, the middle finger and the two lower fingers—still beautifully covered with skin [Note: [Col. 1087D] Concerning this framework I find nothing among the Bollandists, where they discuss Saint John the Baptist. They report certain things about the arm and right hand, as though these had been transferred in about the year 1263 to Cîteaux and even to Rhodes. Yet, in respect of antiquity, the Church of Belley takes precedence over both translations, unless these relics were perhaps transferred from Belley to Cîteaux or Rhodes.]. For many years no one had dared to uncover it and see it naked. But Hugh’s attendant and servant, burning with a special love for his patron and having acquired an even greater confidence in him, did not hesitate to do so. The canons of the church rejoiced, having found a man of such purity that he could most worthily undertake this act.

After confession of sins had been made, absolution given, and prayer offered, that revered sanctuary, stripped of its covering, was displayed openly for all present to see.
