The bishop did not hesitate to touch with his fingers and kiss with his lips those very joints which had touched the holy head of God’s servant. After giving a blessing to the others who were prostrate in worship all around, he raised those joints on high and signed us above with them in the form of a cross. From a certain very old purple cloth, which had long adhered to the sanctuary by covering it, he cut off a considerable piece and gave it to his monk to embrace with the greatest devotion.

On this journey he visited and entered four houses of his order: the Charterhouse [Note: [Col. 1087D] The Great Charterhouse, founded in 1084, in which our Hugh consecrated himself to God by making his vows], Alveria [Note: [Col. 1087D] Also called Alveria, situated in Bresse; its foundation was begun in 1122, and it was united to the order under Guigo V, prior of the Charterhouse], Jovinium [Note: [Col. 1087D] I believe the reading should probably be Luvinium or Luvigniacum, [Col. 1088C] for whose Carthusian foundation Lucas d’Achery provides the charter in volume III of the Spicilegium, p. 542], and the Valley of Saint Peter [Note: [Col. 1088C] A Charterhouse founded in the diocese of Laon around the year 1140. It was later presided over, as prior, by Engelbert under Basil, who was still prior of the Charterhouse; Engelbert later became bishop of Chalon and, after resigning the bishopric, prior of the Charterhouse of Mont-Dieu. He is said to have died around the year 1200, on 13 February. He is discussed in volume IV of Gallia Christiana, p. 895, though with a slight error, unless he was prior of the Valley of Saint Peter twice, once before and once after his episcopate.].

Although Alveria was difficult to reach because of its mountainous location and lay farther from our route, he sought it for this very reason. The former bishop of Belley [Note: [Col. 1088D] This was Saint Arthaud, or Arthaudus, formerly prior of the Charterhouse of Alveria and later bishop of Belley. Concerning him Pierre-François Chifflet writes in the preface to the Manual of Solitaries: “The man of God Arthaud, who is venerated among his people as blessed on the day before the Nones of October, was drawn from the Carthusian flock to the episcopate of Belley. Worn out by old age, he returned to the quiet of his cloister and peacefully gave back his spirit to God in the desert of Alveria.” According to the Carthusian records, he died “famous for continuous miracles, on the day before the Nones of October, in the year 1206.”], who had been raised from the priorship of that house to the episcopal chair, had now laid down the burden of pastoral care and had once again made himself a simple inhabitant of a cell, so that he might serve his heavenly desires more freely. He had long burned with desire for our bishop and wished to be refreshed by his conversation and sight; he had often made this known to him through intermediaries.

That blessed man had indeed advanced far in his days and, with the setting of worldly light already approaching, sighed for entry into the unending day. Our bishop shared the same disposition, though not the same age [Note: [Col. 1089D] Saint Hugh was then sixty years old, according to Chifflet, citing Surius, while Blessed Arthaud was already advanced in age, perhaps more than ninety. Abbot Morotius calls him an old man with a cowl. I would believe him to have been a centenarian if, as is said, he was the first prior of Alveria.]. For he already held all perishable things—which he had always despised in his early years—in profound disgust.

At last, each having obtained the desired conversation, they made the hidden recesses of their consciences brighter through the radiance of the other’s holiness, as each in turn disclosed his secrets. Finally they came together for the common conference of all the brothers. Then the former bishop of Belley asked the lord of Lincoln, in the presence of the brothers, to recount the terms of the peace concluded between our kings, for he knew that Hugh had been present at their reconciliation.

To the request of so great a man, the most fervent zealot of the order, deeply saddened, replied gently and almost jokingly: “O Father,” he said, “although bishops may hear and report rumors, monks may not. Rumors may not enter cells or cloisters; one may not leave cities and bring rumors into solitude.” Saying this, he turned his words away from rumors and toward the pursuit of spiritual edification.

It follows how devoutly he visited Cluny [Note: [Col. 1089D] “Visited Cluny,” under Hugh V, formerly abbot of Reading and then abbot of Cluny. Cluny and its abbots are discussed in the Cluniac Library of André Duchesne, and in volume IV of Gallia Christiana, cols. 1117 ff. Here a notable commendation of the Cluniacs of that period by Saint Hugh of Lincoln is reported.] and how reverently he was received by the great multitude of that holy congregation, and how insistently the whole community compelled him to remain with them for three days [Col. 1089C] and recover his strength after the journey.

After he had carefully observed and highly commended the discipline of that place—in choir, in the cloister, and in the refectory—celebrating different Masses familiarly among them and dining with them, he finally said: “Truly, if I had seen this place as I see it now, and had not yet fallen in love with the Charterhouse, Cluny would have made me its monk.”

Among other things he saw and praised one particular practice, which we therefore briefly insert in these pages, because it was instituted by blessed Benedict and, although it ought to be read by monks everywhere, we are surprised that it is not read and has almost been consigned to oblivion. For when the most blessed Benedict treats in his Rule of the reception of guests, he says among other things: “Let the divine law be read before the guest, so that he may be edified; then let every kindness be shown him.” [Col. 1090A]

The Cluniacs fulfilled this instruction toward us in the following manner. After the bishop had been received with a festive procession and his blessing had been obtained, the lord prior led him into the parlour. There he sat with him, together with about twelve elders of the community. One of the brothers present opened a copy of the Pastoral Rule of Blessed Pope Gregory, which he had brought in his hands for this very purpose. Coming into the middle, he read aloud and distinctly, for understanding, one chapter from beginning to end. When this was completed, he brought the reading to an end as the prior began; likewise, at the prior’s signal and with the words *Benedicite*, the bishop gave those present permission to speak.

We also passed quickly through Cîteaux [Note: [Col. 1089D] “Cîteaux,” of which Gallia Christiana, volume IV, Benedictine edition, col. 980, also treats. [Col. 1090D] At that celebrated place the abbot was then Guido II, later cardinal-bishop of Palestrina.]. He turned aside there so that he might celebrate the solemnity of Mass on the distinguished feast of the Assumption of the Mother of God. For at that time the whole of Gaul, except for certain monasteries enjoying privileges, was under interdict [Note: [Col. 1090D] This was promulgated in the year 1199 because of the divorce between the king and queen, and was lifted in 1201. So report de Nangis and Trivet in their chronicles.].

Then, having obtained his wish and been commended to the prayers of the brothers of that place, he also visited Clairvaux [Note: [Col. 1090D] Clairvaux, under Abbot Guido, as I gather from volume IV of Gallia Christiana, col. 796.]. The former archbishop of Lyon, John of holy memory [Note: [Col. 1090D] Surnamed “of the warlike hands,” designated from Poitiers first to Narbonne and then, in 1181, made archbishop of Lyon; more is said of him in volume IV of Gallia Christiana, col. 130.], had sent certain venerable men to meet him, earnestly requesting that he offer the benefit of his presence to the archbishop, who was dwelling at the aforesaid place and had long desired it. Since he had already resigned the office of pastoral care because of his advanced age, and had retained his former insignia only by order of the Supreme Pontiff, he devoted himself diligently to sacred contemplation in that holy monastery.

When the bishop asked him to which Scriptures he had now chiefly devoted the work of his meditation, he replied: “The meditation of the Psalms alone has now wholly claimed me. From them, daily and continually, a refreshment that never fails is renewed for me, soothing the palate of the inner man.”

After this, he brought joy to the monastery of Saint Remigius [Note: [Col. 1090D] The monastery of Saint Remigius. Concerning it and the sacred ampulla, see volume I of John Mabillon’s Benedictine Annals, p. 61; Mabillon made his monastic vows to God in this monastery.] situated beside the city of Rheims by his holy and magnificent arrival. He stayed there for three days and marveled at the abundance of ancient books kept there, reproaching the negligent carelessness of modern men, who not only refuse to imitate the industry of the Fathers in composing and copying books, but do not even strive to read, or at least reverently handle, the sacred books prepared through the labor of the Fathers.

Here he also admired and venerated the vessel brought from heaven by a dove to blessed Remigius, in which a renewed abundance of sacred balm continually overflows for the anointing of the kings of France.

When he had reached the castle of Saint-Omer [Note: [Col. 1091D] Audomar, also called Audomaropolis, commonly Saint-Omer, is a city of Artois whose bishop is a suffragan of the archbishop of Cambrai], which lies ten miles from the port of Wissant [Note: [Col. 1091D] In the Chronicle of Saint Bertin, edited by Martène, col. 688, we read: “Immediately, when Lord John the abbot learned that these holy exiles”—the monks of Canterbury—“had landed at Wissant,” and so forth], he took a brief rest there from his prolonged fatigue before entering the sea.

Not far from there was a monastery of the Cistercian Order, called by the inhabitants Clairmarais [Note: [Col. 1091D] In Latin, *Claromariscus*, an excellent Cistercian monastery [Col. 1092D] founded around the year 1140.]. After three days the glorious solemnity of the Nativity of the perpetual Virgin and Mother of Mercy was approaching. The bishop did not wish to move far from the vicinity of a place where he could celebrate the divine mysteries before so distinguished a feast, lest, should the weather turn unfavorable, he arrive in England too late to celebrate it.

On the very day he came to Saint-Omer, therefore, he had blood let from a vein, so that, once the period of observance had been completed—which one customarily claims for oneself in phlebotomy—he might celebrate the desired feast with greater freedom and energy. For several days he had already felt heaviness increasing in every limb and throughout his body, together with a certain dull pain. After the bloodletting, however, this very discomfort increased immediately to such a degree that, after barely tasting anything at the table where he had been reclining, he was compelled to leave while the others were still eating and retire to bed.

As soon as he had reclined his neck, an exceedingly abundant sweat poured over him. It did not cease flowing throughout that entire day and most of the following night. He was also soon seized by such a strong aversion to food that during those three days he tasted scarcely anything.

Toward evening, on the vigil of the aforesaid feast [Col. 1091C], he set out for the monastery just mentioned and spent the night there, retaining with him only one monk and one lay brother of his own household. He ordered the others, with the horses, to return to the lodging from which they had come. The abbot [Note: [Col. 1092D] At that time it was Gerard of Champagne, elected abbot in 1198] and the brothers of the place resisted this as much as they could, striving with all their strength to keep his entire retinue with them.

The bishop preferred to rest in the infirmary, where two brothers were assigned to serve him; they devoted themselves to his service with extraordinary devotion. Since they could not persuade him to take any food, they compelled him to offer his feet to be washed, most diligently warmed, and dried. He was sufficiently pleased by their kindness and repaid them with God’s blessing and his own in return for their devotion.

Not long afterward, by divine favor, one of them was promoted to abbot [Col. 1091D] [Note: [Col. 1092D] Namely, either Nicholas or Lambert: the former was in charge in the year when the Canterbury men were sent into exile, while the latter held office during the exile], and the other to prior of the same place. During the course of our present exile, when we turned aside briefly to visit them, they received us with great kindness.

On the following day, the bishop of Christ celebrated his penultimate Mass there. Having completed it with the utmost devotion, he returned fasting from bodily food to his lodging in the frequently mentioned town [Col. 1092A], where we briefly explain an extraordinary event that became known at that time.

A certain baker had kneaded flour on Sunday and had baked loaves for sale during the following night. When he drew them from the oven the next morning, one loaf, having been struck forcefully against the floor, split open; immediately a stream of blood flowed from it and stained the loaf all around. When the baker saw this, he was terrified by so portentous an event.

He broke the bloody loaf into pieces and saw liquid blood drip from each of the cracks. He broke other loaves, one after another, and saw blood filling every fracture. Terrified by so monstrous an occurrence, he concealed the loaves for nearly a week, so that they would not be seen by others. Meanwhile, however, his hired workers or neighbors brought what had happened to public attention [Col. 1092B].

What more is there to say? The matter eventually became known to all the townspeople. One of these loaves was brought to the bishop by villagers; we broke it, and blood immediately followed the fracture, as though the flesh of a human being or of any living animal had been cut. We also carried away with us from there a sizable piece of this bread in our bosom.

The bread was leavened. Unleavened and leavened loaves had likewise been baked in the aforementioned oven, but the unleavened loaves appeared pure in their own nature, with nothing portentous about them. The leavened loaves, however, all poured forth blood if they were fractured or cut.

For this reason some thought that the avaricious man’s rashness had been punished by such an event: on Sunday he had prepared what he would sell more quickly on the following day. The unleavened bread, kneaded and baked after the twilight of the sacred day, admitted nothing horrible; but the bread that had been kneaded and leavened before evening, contrary to the rule, brought no profit to its maker and instead made him a spectacle.

Several of these loaves were sent throughout the neighboring monasteries and churches, to be carefully preserved as a memorial for posterity, as a warning to presumptuous violators of sacred solemnities, and as an example for correction.

But through the help of the Mother of Mercy, after celebrating the Mass in her honor as we have said, her servant and most devoted vicar Hugh received considerable relief from his illness. When the day of the solemnity had been completed with joy and rejoicing, he went on the following day with his companions to the port of Wissant.

At dawn on the next day, Saint Anne, the mother of Mary the Mother of God, watched him board the ship. At first the wind blew gently, but suddenly it filled the sails. All travelers by sea customarily look to Mary, the star of the sea, so that they may direct their course; likewise, when sinking winds deny them progress on their journey, they call upon Mary’s mother in prayer and seek her favor with offered gifts, so that they may continue their voyage.

Hugh, however, ever since Mary’s birth had rendered her the service of veneration more familiarly and devoutly [Note: [Col. 1093D] Thus, already in Saint Hugh’s time, Saint Anne was venerated in England as the patroness of sailors; her veneration grew considerably toward the end of the fourteenth century.]. In turn, she quickly brought him aid in all his necessities and dangers.

Then, when he invoked her, she hastened to his side and so delighted him by bringing him swiftly, in the calmest course, to the desired shore that, immediately after his feet had pressed the sands, he went to the church to celebrate the solemnity of Mass for the sacred childbirth of Mary.

From this action it became sufficiently clear how great was his devotion to the sacraments of the Lord: neither the tossing of the sea nor the privation caused by illness, prolonged for many days, could restrain him from celebrating the divine mysteries. For just as, formerly as a monk, whenever the permission of his order allowed [Note: [Col. 1093D] See the note appended to Book IV, chapter 12. I add that, even in the time of Guigo V, prior of the Charterhouse, the thirty-day series of Masses granted for the recently deceased was in use; each such series required that a Mass for the dead be offered publicly or privately on thirty successive days], so now as a bishop, whenever circumstances coincided with what was possible, he never at any time omitted celebrating Mass.

Through this especially devout and frequent reception of the sacred ministry he deserved to obtain both an exceptional purity of heart and an unconquerable firmness of constancy and of the other virtues. It was also known to those close to him that the mysteries of invisible things and spiritual secrets had been divinely disclosed to him amid the very revered secrets of the canon.

On one occasion, however, he learned that his chaplain, whom he knew to have had blood let from him the day before, had celebrated Mass. He gently rebuked him then, but when the man attempted it again he reproved him more severely, strictly forbidding him to presume to do so again. He recalled that dangers arising from such presumption had occurred more than once and had come to his knowledge.

But, to resume the thread of the narrative, he spent the day of his arrival in England at Dover [Note: [Col. 1093D] Dover, today called Douvres, is a city and port in southern England, opposite Calais, a celebrated port of France], where he landed, together with his clerics and other members of his household and friends. A considerable crowd had been waiting there for his expected and previously announced presence, and he, joyful among the joyful, spent the day in gladness.

On the following day he came to Canterbury. As soon as he entered the city, he visited the basilica of Christ. There he prayed first at the Savior’s altar, then at each of the memorials of the saints resting there, and especially for a long time and with the greatest devotion at the tomb of the glorious martyr Thomas. He earnestly commended himself and his companions to the divine protection and the patronage of God’s saints [Col. 1093D].

Then, after the prior and many brothers had reverently escorted him as far as the outer courtyard, he turned aside to his lodging. There, the king’s justiciars and many of the kingdom’s nobles—whom some unforeseen circumstance had then drawn to that place—were delighted to visit the bishop in friendly competition, applauding and congratulating his arrival but sympathizing with profound sorrow over the bodily illness they had learned afflicted him.

With great magnanimity and steadfastness of heart and speech, he strove earnestly to console them. With a serene countenance, both by his words and by his own example, he taught and demonstrated that the Lord’s scourges ought to be sweet to the servants of the Lord.

Indeed, dimness of vision had gradually crept upon him. During the journey just mentioned, the continual exposure to dust and heat had greatly impaired the sharpness of his eyes. We repeatedly urged him to allow some medical treatment to be applied, but he always answered in the same words: “These eyes are sufficient for us, as long as their use is necessary for us. While these outward eyes are somewhat dulled, though not outwardly deprived of their former beauty, the clearer brightness of the inward lights is rendered more radiant day by day.”

At Canterbury, however, where the illnesses of certain people are often relieved, his illness became so severe that he had to be transported from there to London, partly on horseback and partly by boat, not without discomfort. Yet none of this ran contrary to his wishes, nor did anything that happened to him conflict in any way with the prayers he had devoutly offered in the church.

## CHAPTER XXIII

How, while ill in London, he foretold the evils that would come upon England, received the sacred anointing, replied to those advising him to make a testament, did not abandon the zeal he had always had for the divine office, and conducted himself when King John and the archbishop came to visit him

[Col. 1094C]

After he had entered his own lodging, which he possessed near London beside the Old Temple [Note: [Col. 1094D] At this place, as is said below in chapter 27, Saint Hugh’s entrails, offered separately from his body, were deposited in a leaden vessel. It is called the Old Temple in contrast with the New Temple; thus Trivet records in his Chronicle under the year 1219 that someone was buried in London “at the New Temple.”], his limbs, panting with fever, were immediately received by the rest of his bed.

Many of his friends, seeing this, were overcome with grief; even in his hearing they entreated divine mercy to command that he be restored unharmed to the sons of his Church, who had long been anxiously awaiting his return. He gently consoled them in a few words, saying: “Whether present in body or absent, I shall never be lacking in spiritual presence to our sons, dearest in Christ.”

But concerning my health or bodily presence, indeed concerning my whole self, may the will of the Father who is in heaven always be done.

After spending one night in the same place, on the following day he said to the man who wrote these things [Note: [Col. 1094D] Namely, the author of the Life, who shortly afterward declares that he had been Hugh’s monk and priest]: “Those who love us temporally, and indeed embrace us spiritually [Col. 1095A], would very much like my temporal life—which in truth has long since begun to weary me—to be prolonged. But our judgment is far different, for we clearly see how lamentable the condition of the Church of England will shortly be.

It is therefore better for us to die than to live and see the evils that threaten this people and its saints [Note: [Col. 1095D] These events occurred after Saint Hugh’s death and lasted for a long time: the clergy, together with the monks, were sent into exile, and almost the whole of England was devastated by war.]. For without doubt, what Scripture foretold must be fulfilled in the descendants of King Henry: ‘Bastard shoots shall not strike deep roots’ (Wisdom 4:3), and ‘the offspring of an unlawful bed shall be exterminated’ (Wisdom 3:16).

Moreover, this present king of the French [Note: [Col. 1095D] Philip II, called Augustus, crowned king of France in 1179; he died in July 1223] will avenge his father Louis upon the offspring of the transgressing woman [Note: [Col. 1095D] She was Eleanor—Alienordis, Alienora, now Eleonora—who, after divorcing King Louis, the father of the aforementioned Philip, took Henry, then duke of Normandy and later elected king of England, as her husband in the year 1152], who rejected her undefiled marriage bed with him and shamefully attached herself to his rival, the king of the English.

Therefore this Philip of France will destroy the royal line of the English just as an ox is accustomed to crop grass down to its roots. For three of his sons have already been cut down by the French: two were kings [Note: [Col. 1096D] Henry the Younger and Richard, both kings of England—the former while his father was still alive, the latter after Henry his father’s death], and one was a count [Note: [Col. 1096D] Geoffrey, son of Henry II, king of England, count and duke of Brittany]. The fourth, who remains, will have only a short peace with them [Note: [Col. 1096D] King John, who died after many disasters inflicted upon England by the French, in October 1216].

You know that two days from now will be the Nativity of my evangelist and apostle Matthew. That day was also the anniversary of my episcopate; for, as you know, on it I received episcopal anointing. I have often been ill since early youth, yet until now I have received none of the anointing properly called that of the sick. Of the anointings that might be appropriate to my person, this alone has not yet been conferred upon me. I therefore desire to merit receiving it tomorrow, on the vigil of the blessed Evangelist.

Now, therefore, we must anticipate the face of the Lord through a pure and true confession, so that, with the Lord himself consenting, we may receive so venerable a sacrament worthily, according to our measure, and beneficially for his household.”

After these things had been said, he began carefully to confess before the Lord everything he knew to be blameworthy in himself, and whatever he might have regretted as lacking in himself at any stage of life, order, or profession. First this was done in the presence and testimony of the same monk and priest of his, with whom he was speaking; then three priests of reverend character joined them.

The first was the dean of Lincoln; the second was the instructor [another reading: precentor], who succeeded him in his episcopal chair [Note: [Col. 1096D] William of Blois, consecrated bishop of Lincoln in 1203; he died in 1206]; and the third was archdeacon of Northampton, a man renowned alike for his life and learning.

In this confession [Col. 1095D] he omitted none of those matters which he had previously confessed countless times to very many devout men. Each of these men used to acknowledge that, up to that time, he had never seen anyone who knew how to accuse himself as this man did, enumerating promptly, penetratingly, and fully, with the circumstances of his offenses, both what he had omitted and what he had unworthily committed [Col. 1096A].

In confessing, he always repeated this: “My true, pure, and sole evils are evils; my good deeds, if there are any, are not good in that way, but are impure through the admixture of evils, everywhere entangled with evils, and therefore are not simply and truly good.”

Having therefore continued this kind of confession for three days, at about the third hour, during the aforementioned vigil, he came out from his little bed to meet the Eucharist that had been brought to him, barefoot, wearing a hair shirt, a tunic, and a cowl. Kneeling before that awesome and divine sacrament, and worshiping devoutly, he prayed for a long time, recalling the infinite benefits bestowed by the Savior upon the human race and giving Him thanks for them. He commended himself, as he said, as exceedingly culpable to His most merciful compassion, and tearfully implored that His protection and help might remain with him to the end and never abandon him. Finally refreshed with the food of eternal life and anointed with extreme unction for the remission of sins, he gave thanks to the Lord and said to us:

> “Now let the physicians and our illnesses come to whatever agreement they can; henceforth our concern for either of them will be less in our heart. I have entrusted myself to Him, I have received Him, I will hold fast to Him, and I will cling to Him whom it is good to cling to and whom it is blessed to hold. Whoever receives Him, and whoever entrusts himself to Him, is strong and safe.”

Later, when his weakness was growing worse, he was advised to draw up a will according to custom. He said:

> “I am truly weary of this custom, now introduced everywhere into the Church. For as far as my soul is concerned, I have never possessed anything at all, nor do I now possess anything, that I would consider mine and not rather the property of the Church that I governed. Nevertheless, lest the treasury seize things as usual, if any temporal goods should be left in the bishopric after my death, I now entrust to our Lord Jesus Christ the distribution to the needy of everything that I appear to possess.”

He summoned the dean and two archdeacons of his Church, and handed over to them for distribution under their supervision whatever could be found among the resources of his possessions. After this he ordered his orarium—that is, his priestly stole—to be brought to him. Hanging it around his neck, he placed under an anathema all those who might fraudulently conceal or forcibly take anything from his property, or attempt to deny the aforementioned executors the free power to carry out what he had ordered.

After receiving the sacrament of extreme unction, while the fever’s heat increased day by day, he remained continuously in bed for two months. He repeated his confession almost daily, and sometimes several times a day, hastening to cleanse even the slightest movements of his thoughts and excesses of speech, if, while distressed, he happened to become angry with his attendants.

His mind was always intent upon prayer. He carefully saw to it that he performed the divine office at the appointed hours, both by night and by day, nor did he allow the hours to be omitted or anticipated because of an attack of feverish heat. When his strength permitted, he himself sang psalms with those who were singing. He immediately rebuked those who read or sang carelessly or hurriedly, with a terrible voice or sound. Throughout all his preceding life he had always shown the greatest concern for both matters: that the appointed praises should be rendered to the Creator distinctly and at the proper time.

As long as he was able, he also observed the alternation between standing and sitting during the psalmody, and compelled his clerics to observe it, so that while one, sitting, restored his tired limbs, another might show reverence by standing before the divine and angelic presence.

[Note: According to the ancient custom of the Carthusian order, which is still observed in the order.]

When he attended great assemblies of nobles or the adjudication of lawsuits, just as others customarily withdrew from time to time to formulate interlocutory decisions, so, whenever the moments of daylight required it, he withdrew to sing the appointed hours. His practice was no different at the dedications of churches and at the celebrations of ordinations.

The king also came to visit him in his illness.

[Note: John, concerning whose manor—that is, if I am not mistaken, his character and disposition—Saint Hugh began to doubt, indeed to despair. Nevertheless, it may be inferred from the vision reported by Raynaldus in his *Annals* under the year 1226, folio 333, that King John was ultimately saved.]

Saint Hugh did not even appear inclined to rise or sit up for him, although he still had enough strength to sit on his bed while taking food. The king spoke to him with the greatest compassion, explaining that he placed himself and his possessions at Hugh’s disposal for the execution of his wishes. But while the king, having excluded all his own attendants, sat for a long time before the man lying there and continued at length with many flattering words, the bishop scarcely replied to what he heard. In the end, commending his own affairs and the executors of his will, together with the whole Church of Lincoln, to the king’s protection, he took his leave.

He had by then certainly despaired of the king’s character, and for that reason said little to him, lest he lose his fine speeches.

His metropolitan also visited him several times while he lay ill.

[Note: Hubert, namely the archbishop of Canterbury, whom Hugh rebuked repeatedly, both here and elsewhere, and did not regret having rebuked.]

He promised to show him, to the best of his ability, every kind of humanity and kindness. Finally, when the archbishop suggested that, if Hugh had perhaps provoked or injured anyone by word or deed in a less than just manner, he should remember to ask pardon from the offended party—and then admitted that Hugh had often and repeatedly provoked him most bitterly, although he was nevertheless Hugh’s spiritual father and primate, so that remorse of heart and a necessary request for pardon seemed appropriate—Hugh replied:

> “Certainly, when I review the hidden recesses of my conscience, I clearly find that I have often provoked you to anger; yet I do not perceive what I should repent of on that account. But I know that I ought to grieve because I did not do this more often and more urgently. If life were still to be prolonged with you, I firmly intend to do precisely this more frequently than usual under the eyes of God, who sees all things. For I remember that, in order to accommodate myself to you, I have often cowardly suppressed things that I ought not to have kept silent about and that, if spoken, you would not have heard with equanimity. Thus, through my own fault, I avoided offending you rather than offending the Father who is in heaven. As a result, I have sinned not only against God—for which I humbly seek forgiveness—but also, and not lightly or as a bishop ought, against your fatherhood and your primacy.”

## CHAPTER XXIV  
### How he instructed the master builder of the Church of Lincoln to prepare for a general assembly soon to be held there; how he described what he wished to be observed concerning his funeral and burial; and how he responded to the advice given him to eat meat

When the final day of this life was already approaching—fifteen days later—

[Note: Thus, around the feast of All Saints, he gave the architect the instructions that follow. Likewise, says Gerald of Wales, page 419 in Wharton, he renewed the chapter house of his church with equal stones and marble columns, by marvelous workmanship, and so forth, as stated there.]

—and when Geoffrey de Voires, the noble builder of the great work which Hugh’s magnificent love for the beauty of God’s house had begun to raise from its foundations in the renovation of the Church of Lincoln, was present, Hugh spoke to him as follows:

> “Since we have learned that our lord king, together with the bishops and all the leading men of this kingdom, will soon assemble at Lincoln for a general conference, hasten and take care to complete everything necessary for the decoration and adornment around the altar of my lord and patron, Saint John the Baptist. We wish it to be dedicated when our brother, the bishop of Rochester, arrives there together with the other bishops.
>
> [Note: He was Gilbert de Glanville, concerning whom see note 277 to chapter 17 of this book.]
>
> For we ourselves shall also be present there at the appointed time of the conference.
>
> [Note: He was present—not in body but in spirit; indeed, he was also present in body, having been buried with the highest honors.]
>
> We truly wished to consecrate it ourselves, but since the Lord has disposed otherwise, we wish it to be consecrated before we reach that place, with every obstacle removed.”

He repeated these very words, and others besides, giving orders to his servants and to all the principal persons of his Church that, even in the final rites, they should show as much honor as possible not only to the king but also to the bishops and his other friends who would come to Lincoln.

Meanwhile, the most violent illness began to press upon him, and, with attacks redoubling each day, a grievous fire ravaged his solid limbs; dysentery drained his vital organs and the marrow of his interior being. Therefore, several days before his death, he again explained to us by explicit instruction everything he wished to be carried out before his funeral and burial:

> “Prepare ashes, blessing them according to the solemn rite. You will scatter them in the form of a cross over the bare ground where you will place me when you see that the hour of my final breath is at hand.
>
> [Note: Even now, when extreme unction is administered to a sick Carthusian, ashes are blessed and then scattered here and there over the bed and body of the sick person.]
>
> A hair shirt is by no means placed beneath those who are dying in our order, as some do. For among us each dying person is content with what he previously used and wore while alive.”

He said this while dressed in a hair shirt and tunic, with a cowl also worn over them. He never lacked these garments—or rather, wrappings—at any moment of his illness. Neither the fever’s heat nor such copious sweating removed any of them from him. He scarcely permitted the hair shirt to be changed once or twice. We found it between his body and his tunic, hardened by sweat almost like mud and twisted like a rope through his frequent turning from side to side; we also discovered that it had rubbed his skin raw in a great many places.

Since we knew that among the Carthusians hair shirts are commonly removed from the sick—

[Note: Nothing is established concerning this custom; nevertheless, the statutes permit hair shirts to be removed after a dispensation.]

—we said to him:

> “My lord, this rough garment injures and ulcerates you excessively as you lie continually in sweat. You ought therefore to remove it and, according to the custom of the order, be entirely without it while the illness afflicts you.”

But he replied:

> “God forbid, and may this never happen! This garment does not injure us but soothes us; it does not ulcerate us so much as it helps us.”

He also instructed the writer of this account, saying:

> “I know that no bishop or abbot will be found in these parts who can perform for me the proper commendatory office for the soul being led out of this prison. For a general edict has drawn all the prelates of this land to Lincoln. Send boys with horses to Westminster—
>
> [Note: This is a monastery built in the western part of the city of London under the title of Saint Peter; Mabillon discusses it in volume I of his *Annals*, page 285.]
>
> to bring seven or eight monks from there, so that they may celebrate our funeral rites with you. You will also send word in my name to the dean of Saint Paul’s—
>
> [Note: The cathedral church in the eastern part of the aforementioned city. The same Mabillon, in the volume just cited, doubts whether monks ever lived there.]
>
> and command him to send here a large number from among the clerics who attend the choir. Thus you will perform a splendid funeral for me.”

> “When the time comes for my lifeless body to be clothed, as customary, in pontifical vestments, you will associate with you one priest in regular habit, who will carefully wash and dry the entire corpse with you.
>
> [Note: From this the reader may infer what affection Saint Hugh had for the author of his life, since he entrusted to him not only the secrets of his conscience but also the care of washing his body after death.]
>
> For I am to be buried in the church of the holy Mother of God, not far from the altar of Saint John the Baptist.
>
> [Note: Namely, in Lincoln Cathedral.]
>
> It is therefore necessary that the remains of this body be presented as clean as possible, since so much sweat has already stained them with great uncleanness. Take care that no negligence of any kind intrude in this matter, by which the sacred dignity of the revered place might be dishonored. Brother Peter, our lay brother, is to supply water to those washing me; and apart from you three who will perform this service for me, no one else at all is to be present when these things are done.”

> “When my body has been carried to the Church of Lincoln, you will bring out from our chests the vestments kept there in which I received episcopal consecration, from the sandals to the mitre, and you will clothe the body to be buried in all of them. They are plain and unostentatious, for I have kept them for these uses until now.”

When his rings were also presented to him, he handed us one of modest weight, though made of gold and containing a lesser stone of watery sapphire. He said:

> “This finger of ours received this one when I became bishop, and this right hand will retain it when I am buried. We provided for ourselves in this matter when we entered this rank, so that our ordination and burial might be honored with the same insignia. While we were living and using them, they would remind us of humility; and when we were finally dead and buried, if someone happened to find them, their value or appearance would in no way provoke him to steal them.”

As he continued speaking about these matters, it was made known to those listening that he had foreseen that, after the first burial, his body would at some point be transferred and consequently inspected, since it was to be placed at first in a double tomb, namely one of lead and one of stone, both sealed most securely, so that no one would be able either to see it or to seize its ornaments.

[Note: Surius reports that the translation took place in the year 1280, at the end of this saint’s Life. The date should be corrected insofar as he calls this year the eighty-sixth after the death of Blessed Hugh.]

He designated the place of his burial as follows:

> “You will place me before the altar of my aforementioned patron, the Lord’s precursor, wherever there appears to be suitable space, beside some wall, so that the pavement may not be inconveniently occupied by a tomb, as we see in many churches, and thus provide those walking there with an obstacle or a fall.”

Whenever he was afflicted more severely by immense pains of this kind, he often repeated:

> “O merciful God, grant us rest! Good Lord, true God, grant us rest at last!”

Once, as we consoled him, we said:

> “Now, my lord, you will rest; the cessation of this attack is indicated by the fact that the beat of your pulse is now coming to an end.”

He replied:

> “Oh truly blessed are those whom even the last day of judgment will grant unshaken rest!”

When we in turn said to him:

> “By God’s will, you will have that day of judgment when you lay down the burden of this flesh,”

he answered:

> “You do not understand rightly. It will be not a day of judgment but a day of grace and mercy on which I shall die.”

It was a source of great astonishment and admiration to those present that, amid the many torments of his most violent illnesses, his courage of mind always remained unconquered. When he wished, he turned himself in bed so vigorously onto his other side; and when he left his bed, he walked away and returned as robustly as necessity required, so that one might think that the strength of his spirit had entered into a kind of encounter and battle with the weakness of his body.

For this reason the physicians, observing his movements, also said:

> “Truly, this man’s spirit sustains his weakness. Truly, with the Apostle he can taunt this body of death and say: ‘When I am weak, then I am stronger and powerful’ (2 Corinthians 12:10).”

His voice, too, was so full and vigorous that, although lower than before, it was nevertheless scarcely less audible than usual. On the very day of his death, after the martyrology, he caused the reading from the Gospel of John to be brought to an end by the sound of his own voice. On the following day, at the Mass celebrated there before his corpse, the Gospel began to be read at the point where, the day before, at his direction, the text of that same Scripture had ceased to be recited.

When we noticed that this had happened without his arranging it, we glorified God, who by a beautiful and wondrous order had always directed all his works and his entire life even to the end. The passage of Scripture itself plainly carried a prophecy of the greatest sweetness in the sequence of the events that had taken place. It concerned the familiar conversation between our Savior and Martha before the raising of her brother Lazarus, which runs as follows:

> “Martha said to Jesus: ‘Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died’” (John 11:32), and so forth.

Since he had established that other canonical Scriptures should be read annually at the appointed times, both at Matins and at his Mass, he arranged for the four books of the four Evangelists to be read through at the four seasons of the year after the first hour of the day, with the reading of the martyrology preceding them.

[Note: Now, each year, the Carthusians read them in chapter after the canonical hour of None on feast days occurring between Easter and the feast of All Saints.]

He never omitted these readings even when traveling on horseback.

One of his friends urged him to complete a confession sufficient, as far as he knew, for the expiation of his sins, saying:

> “My lord, as you yourself know better, that confession is more effective and more pleasing to God which specifies everything individually than that which includes individual matters under a kind of generality. For you were for a long time both an ordinary and a delegated judge over many people, as far as memory recalls. Take care to confess whom, or how many persons, you promoted in their affairs—as commonly happens—because of private love or hatred, or whom you oppressed by using judicial authority less lawfully.”

To this he gave an answer that was both a source of joy and a marvel to many who heard it:

> “I do not remember ever knowingly departing from the truth of judgment through hatred or love, or even through hope or fear of any person or thing. If, in judging, I deviated from what was right, it was the fault of my own ignorance or, certainly, of those sitting beside me.”

Nor should it seem appropriate to pass over without reflection the fact that this man, who had always opposed every kind of vanity and superstition, did not refuse, at the end of this illness, to taste meat rather than eat it, for the good of obedience.

His friends suggested, and the physicians asserted, that he would be more easily cured once winter had passed if he permitted his body, already affected by cold quartan fevers following other fevers, to be nourished with more substantial foods. The archbishop ordered him, and imposed it upon him as a remission of sins, to obey the physicians’ advice even in such a diet.

But Hugh objected that the prescription of the Carthusian order forbade this for him, since the eating of meat was prohibited in common to all who were sick, healthy, or dying.

[Note: From the beginning of the holy order this was forbidden not by precept but by custom. In 1259 a public renunciation was added to the custom, and finally, in 1368, a penalty was decreed for transgressors.]

But, not to delay over many details, at last, at the request of his clerics and also by the command and earnest admonition of the archbishop of Canterbury, after receiving exhortatory letters from Lord Robert—then procurator, and shortly afterward prior at Witham—and from the brothers of that place, urging him to obey his archbishop’s command without hesitation, he took meat as food, although from his youth until then he had never tasted it on any occasion.

He said to us:

> “Know that this eating of meat, however strongly urged, can in no way be either a matter of desire or a remedy for us. Nevertheless, lest we scandalize so many venerable men—or rather, lest even at the point of death we depart from the footsteps of Him who became obedient unto death—let meat be given to us. For now we shall gladly eat it as a seasoning of brotherly love.”

When the physicians asked what kind of meat he would prefer to eat, he replied:

> “Pig’s feet, if you think fit; we read that they were once permitted to the sick by the holy Fathers.”

They therefore served them, but Hugh ordered them removed as soon as they had scarcely touched them with his front teeth. Similarly, he tasted a very small amount of small birds.

[Note: He was compelled by obedience to do so at a time when the order had not yet solemnly renounced the eating of meat.]

When he was in good health, he also used to rebuke certain religious men, especially heads of monasteries, who, contrary to regular custom, told their brothers to abstain from meat in every circumstance. We remember that he once said the following to an abstemious abbot:

> “Brother, from whom your subjects ought to receive comfort and an example, you will sin against them in both respects because of this extraordinary abstinence. You yourself will not cut away luxuries from your diet but will change them, and in this you will scarcely escape the charge of vanity and superstition. For your officials will prepare for you either exotic vegetables or fish more expensive than meat, and instead of fat, various seasonings made with spices and costly ingredients.
>
> By this example your subjects will learn to reject the dishes set before them and always to crave the latest inventions of cooks. Whoever does not wish or is unable to seek any of these things, while utterly rejecting what has touched meat, will leave the table with his stomach poorly strengthened. When he has done this repeatedly, first sleeplessness, then mental sluggishness, and finally weakness of the whole body will take hold of him, already incapacitated for every exercise of the spiritual life.
>
> What comfort will those hope to receive from you who, worn down by prolonged weariness, know with complete certainty that they will never find anything at your table that can bring them any refreshment? For the fact that I do not eat meat depends not so much on my own choice as on the decree of the order to which I once subjected my neck.
>
> Therefore our order admits fewer people into its laws, because the varied multitude cannot contain what it has instituted. You, on the other hand, who have undertaken to govern a multitude, must, just as you ought to serve the customs of many according to the opinion of your legislator, also accommodate yourselves to their manifold weaknesses and provide for their needs.”

And this is what he said.

## CHAPTER XXV  
### How he departed this life

This chapter is contained in the *Great Life*, chapter 16.

But let us now explain, as we began, what remains concerning the departure of our good teacher from us. On the day before he migrated from the body, as he had often been accustomed to do each week previously, he received the viaticum of the body and blood of Christ.

On Thursday, the sixteenth day before the Kalends of December, when the day was already drawing toward evening, he felt his strength failing more and more. He sent some of his servants to the prior of Westminster and others to the dean of Saint Paul’s, to summon, as he had earlier ordered, the clerics and monks for the service of his funeral.

[Note: Hoveden agrees with this in Pagi’s *Critiques on Baronius*, page 708, writing as follows: “In the month of November, on Thursday, the sixteenth day before the Kalends of December, Hugh, bishop of Lincoln, died in London.” Saint Hugh therefore died on November 16, which in the year 1200 fell on a Thursday, not on the following day, on which his feast is commemorated. The explanation is to be sought in the custom of the Carthusian order, which commands that someone who dies today at or after Compline be entered in the book of anniversaries not on the day of his death but on the following day.]

After this, placing his right hand for a long time upon our heads, he commended us and all his sons to God, almost in the last words of his voice. Having received his blessing, we said to him three times, before we could draw any word from his mouth:

> “Ask the Lord to provide your Church with a pastor who will benefit it.”

At last he said:

> “May God do so!”

After he had spoken these words, we had the floor stripped bare before him and marked the figure of a cross there with blessed ashes. He, in turn, blessing them with his fingers, began to worship with his head bowed.

Although at that hour we withdrew from him only with great reluctance, nevertheless, so that on his final day he might hear the divine service no less fully—for he had shown such devoted attention to it throughout his life—we began to chant the hymns customarily sung at Compline.

When we came to the place in the psalm where it says, “He will call upon me, and I will answer him; I am with him in tribulation; I will rescue him and glorify him” (Psalm 90:15), he indicated that this should be done, and he was laid out upon the ashes in the midst of the ashes.

[Note: According to the ancient custom of the order, concerning which Guigo, the fifth prior of the Grande Chartreuse, says the following in the statutes: “The prior, or the person whom he has appointed, hastens to the dying man; after placing him upon the blessed ashes, they recite the litany, long or short according as circumstances permit.” This custom has now been abolished because of the danger of hastening death; nevertheless, as stated above, the ashes are still blessed and scattered, and the Litanies are read.]

As we sang more rapidly, he gradually gathered his spirit with the most peaceful expression on his face, and then delivered it into the hands of the Creator when the chorus of singers began to recite the canticle of Simeon.

Thus both prophetic and Gospel testimony made clear that the Lord had heard him when he so frequently, as we have said, asked that peace be granted him. It was also proved most truly that what he had foretold was so: the day of his death would not be for him a day of judgment piercing him with any bitterness, but rather a day of mercy, graciously forgiving every offense, and a day of grace gently cherishing him in peace. This was granted by Him who throughout his life had given him to love mercy and truth, Jesus Christ our Lord, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives as blessed God forever. Amen.

Here, in the sequence of the *Great Life*, there is inserted a lengthy comparison between our Hugh and Saint Martin. To avoid excessive length, it has been omitted from this present abridgment. From that extended comparison the following verse was taken:

> “Happy imitator, worshiper, and heir of Martin.”

## CHAPTER XXVI  
### Concerning the vision of the falling tree, from which the antiphon “The tree falls, the mystical sign of the sacrament” was taken, and so forth

This chapter is chapter 18 in the *Great Life*.

In the year of grace 1200, on the sixth day of the octave of blessed Martin—

[Note: The feast of Saint Martin in the year 1200 fell on a Saturday, and the sixth day of the octave fell on a Thursday; this confirms note 367, placed in the preceding chapter.]

—a short time after sunset, Hugh, the light of the people of Lincoln, imitator and lover of Martin, the imitator and lover of the true Sun, bade farewell to the light of this world and approached the Sun that knows no setting.

On the night immediately following his passing, as the supreme mercy arranged all things piously, one of those who were staying with him was shown the following vision, as a definite indication of the impending event.

[Note: Apparently the author himself, since below he adds: “No one recognized it before the man who arranged these matters concerning his life.”] When morning came, he disclosed the vision to his companions and took especially careful steps to prepare what was needed for the solemn funeral rites. The physicians who were present mocked and rebuked him, for the doctors promised Hugh health until the final hour of his life and a longer life.

The vision was as follows.

He seemed to be standing in a certain garden adjoining the wall of the house in which the bishop lay. The site was on the northern side; on the west it was enclosed by the fences of the houses, on the east it was bounded, and on the south by a ditch, beside which on one side lay an orchard and on the other a cemetery. The ditch itself was covered with growing bushes and brambles.

From the part of the wall where the head of the bishop’s bed was attached, a pear tree of extraordinary and immense height and beauty appeared to have fallen. It extended far beyond the space of that garden. Admiring its immense beauty and beautiful immensity, he thought to himself:

> “Who has ever seen such a beautiful pear tree? What a loss of noble material it will be if this most splendid tree rots in this hidden place, when so many writing tablets could be cut from it—enough to supply the scholarly studies of all England or France!”

[Note: *Dipticae*, that is, diptychs or tablets for the use of scribes.]

While he pondered these things, asleep in body but anxious in heart, he suddenly saw himself place his arms beneath the fallen trunk. When he tested its mass by moving it slightly, he was astonished to see the entire timber immediately lifted from the ground with the greatest ease into his arms, as though it had absolutely no weight, and carried by him here and there.

Meanwhile, its small branches suddenly fell away from the trunk; the central beam itself, smooth and knotless, remained in the arms of the one carrying it. Astonished and delighted by this miracle, and soon waking from sleep, he found the interpretation of the vision impressed upon his heart, and he spoke these words to himself with his lips and mouth:

> “This man will truly die shortly; this fruitful and most beautiful tree has shown it.”

In the morning he reported to those of his companions to whom he thought it worthwhile to tell it that, for the present, he had understood these things concerning the meaning of his vision.

What that tree’s effortless lifting signified, no one recognized before the man who arranged these matters concerning his life and virtues—even though in an abridged form—with an easy style. For whatever this little book contains excerpted from the words or deeds of the holy man must be judged, in view of the greatness of his virtues and works, as though insignificant and easily falling leaves were being compared with the immense strength of a vast tree.

> “Nor can these things be compared with those great deeds which the memory of the writer carries inseparably, always clinging to his heart; nor with the very things that he committed to parchment, except as one might compare bundles of light twigs with the towering firs and most lofty cedars that touch the sky.”

Here, in the sequence of the *Great Life*, two other visions are placed that attest to Hugh’s glory. Incidentally, there is also inserted the vision that he himself had while staying at Lafford, concerning Brother Morinus, his almoner, who was dying at Stowport.

## CHAPTER XXVII  
### Concerning the preparation of the body of the deceased, the celebration of the funeral as he had described it, its conveyance to Lincoln, the account of miracles occurring on the journey, and the arrival of kings and other eminent persons

This is found in the sequence of the *Great Life*, chapter 19.

We must now return to his funeral. As we have explained, after Hugh, the lover of peace, had fallen asleep in peace in the Lord beneath the song of peace, only a few of his attendants being present, our humble company performed the commendatory office for him with such devotion as it could.

Then we applied our unworthy hands to washing his body, as he himself had arranged. When it had been stripped, it appeared cleaner than could be believed and remarkable for its great brightness; after it had been washed and carefully dried, we clothed it in the pontifical insignia.

Meanwhile, those whom he had sent, as we have said, to summon the celebrants of his funeral returned. They brought seven monks or somewhat more, and a large crowd of clerics.

[Note: This multitude of monks and clerics arrived from Westminster and from the Church of Saint Paul’s, as Saint Hugh had requested in chapter 24, on the very day on which he died, at Compline.]

They spent the whole of that night in hymns and spiritual songs. After the sacred body had been placed in the church, while those men celebrated and continually maintained votive vigils around it, the solemn Masses were celebrated on the following day.

[Note: Namely, on November 17. After that day had passed, the body was transferred toward Lincoln on November 18, to be buried there; it arrived there on November 23. Thus Hoveden, in Pagi’s *Critiques*, page 708, under the year 1194, writes: “In the month of November, on Thursday, the sixteenth day before the Kalends of December, Hugh died,” and adds: “His body was brought to Lincoln on the ninth day before the Kalends of December, to be buried there.”]

On the advice of the physicians—although others thought and asserted that this absolutely ought not to be done—the entrails were removed from his body, since it had to be carried a considerable distance for burial. They were placed in a lead vessel in that same Church of Blessed Mary at the old temple and honorably deposited beneath a marble stone beside the step of the altar.

[Note: This confirms note 342 to chapter 23.]

There they await the glorious temple of his restored body, which is to be happily received at the time of the great resurrection.

Although these things had been done pointlessly and needlessly, as human prudence judged them [Col. 1107A], it soon became clear, when his very entrails were exposed, that they had nevertheless been divinely ordained to happen in this way, for the glory of God, who is always wondrous in his saints, and also for the honor of that same servant of his, as later became known in various ways. Indeed, when the secrets of the internal organs had been laid bare by the surgeon’s hand, they were found to contain nothing superfluous in their accumulation, and absolutely none of the congealed humor that ordinarily collects within them. Rather, they shone with such pure brightness, as though they had been washed and cleansed everywhere by the greatest human care. This was certainly marvelous to those who looked upon it, but for some it lessened the weight of the miracle: they thought that the abstinence of so long a period, together with the force of the dysentery by which he had been afflicted for several days before his death, might have emptied him completely in this way. However it may have happened, this can truthfully be said: outwardly whiter than milk, inwardly and outwardly purer than glass, his body was also shown to resemble that of Martin, so that he may rightly be called in this respect too “the Jewel of priests.” More will be said below, in its proper place, about his wondrous beauty.

After embalming him with many spices, we began to transfer him from the place of his passing to Lincoln for burial [Note: [Col. 1107D] On 18 November, when the first stage was at the monastery of the monks of Bedford—that is, at that celebrated monastery founded long ago at St Albans in the county of Bedford.]. It is unnecessary—and indeed impossible for us—to describe the tears and groans of the peoples who came from every direction. The clergy and people of the city of London followed the bier far outside the city walls, with crosses and candles. [Col. 1107C] As soon as people of either sex and every condition, rank, and order heard of his death throughout the fields and villages, they streamed together within their territories to meet the bearers of the sacred funeral. To touch the bier was regarded as the supreme privilege. Those who were prevented from doing so by the multitude of the throngs pressing together considered it no small triumph even to adore it from a distance and to see it.

Throughout the journey, for four continuous days, by a miracle renewed—or rather continued—each day, the Lord glorified his saint. For four candles burned continually in the hands of mounted boys. Although exposed in the daytime like torches, neither the breaths of the winds nor the drops of rain that sometimes fell thickly from the clouds could extinguish them. [Col. 1107D] The boys held the candles, now dismounting from their horses, now remounting the empty saddles with great force; yet amid all this the fire did not abandon them. The crowds who saw these things were astonished and burst into cries of exclamation, declaring that even a light enclosed within clasped hands could not be kept unextinguished, whereas these candles, sheltered by no covering but relying solely on God’s power, continued to burn; through the merits of the saint, the quality of the threefold element overcame its own nature. For the airy breath, the watery moisture, and the fiery brilliance rendered marvelous services to Christ’s victorious soldier.

Leaving aside the more sacred judgments of others concerning such great works of God, it is enough for the moment to commend the opinion of the simple faithful: it was not without reason that the saint appeared adorned with so pleasant an honor of light, since, for the glory of the mother of the true Light, the perpetual Virgin, he had greatly increased the customary lights of that very church by a very large addition. For he assigned substantial revenues to the treasurer of Lincoln for this purpose, so that the immense space of that great building, with its walls almost bare, might shine with the radiance of candles during the night offices, just as by day it gleamed with the sun’s rays. [Col. 1108B]

The first stage of the conveyance of the body toward Lincoln was therefore with the monks of Bedford. At dusk on the second day, after we had begun the journey, we reached the bishop of Lincoln’s village called Bickleswade [Note: [Col. 1107D] The second stage in November was at the village of Bickleswade.]. There, while a crowd of grieving inhabitants gathered around the bier, at the very entrance of the church in which the venerable body was to rest that night, a certain man’s arm was broken so violently that even those standing farther away clearly heard the crack of the bone as he suffered the fracture. The man’s name was Bernard; he is said still to be alive. His companions dragged him half-dead from the church doors and carried him to his own house, ordering him to endure his suffering until morning and then promising that physicians would come to his aid. Thus, with the place of the fracture neither bound nor treated with any medicine, the severity of the injury compelled him to spend much of the night awake in great pain.

At last, when he had fallen into a light sleep, he saw the bishop touching his arm with the most merciful hands and, after giving him a blessing, withdrawing a little later. Yet when the vision granted to him had departed, the power of the blessing bestowed did not depart. On awakening from sleep, he found that all pain had been completely driven away, the bone firmly knit, and the arm healed, so that he thought he had received in sleep the earlier fracture rather than the subsequent cure. [Col. 1108D]

The third stage was at Buckden [Note: [Col. 1107D] The third stage was on 20 November at Buckden, which is the same place called Buggeden above, in chapter 9 of this book. [Col. 1108D]]. In these two episcopal manors we were received with such wails and lamentations from the inhabitants that it is dreadful to remember them and difficult to write about them.

On the fourth day of the journey we reached Stamford [Note: [Col. 1108D] The fourth stage was on 21 November at Stamford, where there had once been a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict. Mabillon discusses it in volume 5 of the *Annals*, p. 539, where he lists certain monks of this monastery, perhaps responsible for the care of nuns, as will be said in the following note.]. There, while a dense procession of people crowded around the bier, and on one side a choir of virgins consecrated to God from the neighboring monastery [Col. 1109A] [Note: [Col. 1109D] This is discussed in the *Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. I, p. 487, under the title: “Stamford in the county of Lincoln, house of nuns of Saint Michael.” In the charters reproduced there it is now called Stanfard, but more often Staunford, and is said to be situated at Stamford and subject to the abbot of Peterborough.], while on the other the inhabitants of the surrounding villages increased the already populous crowds of the borough, we could scarcely enter the town itself before the deep darkness of night.

There the Lord, through the merits of his servant, deigned to perform such a miracle that no one could rightly hesitate to prefer it even to the raising of the dead. Among those who had gathered for so great an encounter was a man of innocent life, devoted in every way to good pursuits, who earned his living and that of his household by the craft of shoemaking. When he tried to approach the most precious burden that he saw being borne from a distance, he made little progress because of the density of the crowds. Then, with many people listening, he burst into cries such as these:

“O good God, why am I not permitted to approach the body of your best servant, so that I may either deserve to kiss the fringe of the garments with which he is covered, or place my most unworthy head beneath his sacred relics? O Searcher of things and hearts, Jesus, most merciful Savior, fulfill this one desire of mine: let me be able to pass beneath the bier I see, with heart and body bowed down, and thus remove my soul from the filth of this world.”

While he shouted these things and persisted with tireless efforts, the crowds, astonished by his cries, gradually withdrew. At last he thrust himself beneath the bier. After touching it and adoring it with his head bowed, he began to pray in this manner, raising his eyes and hands toward heaven:

“I give you thanks, Father of mercies and God of all consolation, because you have had mercy on me and consoled me so greatly that I have been able to join my body, burdened with so many sins, to the most holy body of your servant—the thing I desired above all else in this world—and have deserved to draw near to him who faithfully served you. I therefore beg you, almighty God, command that on this night my soul be placed with the soul of this man whose body you have enabled me to approach, in everlasting rest, where I do not doubt that it is.”

After he had finished this prayer, we entered with the sacred body into the church where we were to spend the night. He, meanwhile, entered his own dwelling, which was almost adjoining the church, with only one street between them. Immediately his neighbors rushed into the church and, calling out in agitation for a priest, compelled the priest they found to hurry to the man’s house, taking the provision of holy Communion with him. The man was already at the point of death. As soon as he perceived the priest, he made his confession, received absolution, and had his will duly drawn up; then he gave up his spirit in peace. [Col. 1110A]

While he was still alive, the saint had been accustomed, when he heard someone mourning a dead person too immoderately, to say to them, among other words of consolation: “And what is this that you are doing? By the holy nut”—for he sometimes used this expression in place of an oath to confirm his words—“by the holy nut, I say, things would be exceedingly bad for us if we were never permitted to die.”

He also extolled the miraculous raising of the dead, but he praised even more highly the miraculous rescue, on several occasions, of the living from this world: that of Peter, the subdeacon and notary of blessed Pope Gregory [Note: [Col. 1109D] In the *Life of Saint Gregory the Great* written by John the Deacon, a story is related that some reject or doubt.]; that of a certain penitent discussed in the miracles of Saint Projectus, martyr and bishop [Note: [Col. 1109D] The Bollandists preserve two Lives of Saint Projectus for 25 January. From neither have I been able to determine who the penitent mentioned here was, unless perhaps it was Amarinus—though the printed wording concerning Projectus being slain and made a martyr is uncertain.]; that of many monks, as is read in the *Life of the blessed abbot Archadrius of Gemeticum* [Note: [Col. 1109D] See his Life in Surius under 15 September, where the relevant matters are found in sections 20, 22, and 23.]; and also that of the seven sleepers [Note: [Col. 1109D] The Bollandists discuss these in volume 6 of the July *Acta Sanctorum*, p. 375, and in Martène and Durand, vol. V, *Collectio Veterum*, column 928. Their names are given in the Tours chronicle, which says that they were born from two brothers of Saint Martin, the patron of our Hugh.].

But let us now proceed with the remaining matters. At this place our agents bought horn lanterns, in which candles might burn continually around the bier during the day. For the candles, shaken by the various movements of the riders and by the assaults of the rushing winds, dripped excessively from the face of the devouring fire and, through their continual dripping, soaked the hands and clothing of those carrying them in a most troublesome manner.

He appointed Ancaster as our fifth stage [Note: [Col. 1110D] The fifth stage was on 22 November. Wharton, part II of *Anglia Sacra*, p. 409, mentions a certain young man from Ancaster who had been driven mad and was restored to health at the tomb of the holy man (Remigius).]. From there twenty miles [Note: [Col. 1110D] A small distance, certainly, if it was completed in a single day.] were reckoned to the city [Note: [Col. 1110D] Lincoln, which was reached on 23 November—that is, as Hoveden says, on the ninth day before the Kalends of December.]. On the sixth day of the journey, as we were now approaching it closely and, when we were nearly a mile outside the city, were coming to the descent of the hill, we encountered, amid an immeasurable multitude of clergy and people, the king of England [Note: [Col. 1110D] John, who at that time was king of England.], the king of Scotland [Note: [Col. 1110D] William, king of Scotland from 1165 until 1214.], archbishops [Note: [Col. 1110D] Three or four: Hubert of Canterbury, Geoffrey of York, and the archbishop of Dublin or of Ragusa. See Raynaldus, p. 49, in the *Annals*, book 13.], bishops, princes, abbots, and as many nobles as had scarcely ever before been found assembled together in England.

The king of Scotland, mourning because he had always loved that man with such great affection, stood apart and, unable to approach more closely, gave himself over to tears, although he felt that he ought rather to rejoice, if the force of grief allowed him to reason so. The other nobles, both English and Scottish, placed their shoulders beneath the considerable burden [Note: [Col. 1111D] Coggeshall confirms this, column 866, in Martène, vol. V, *Collectio Veterum Scriptorum*, where he says that the king and the archbishops also placed their shoulders beneath the coffin.]. Whoever was granted the privilege of fitting his limbs to the task of carrying that body rejoiced that he had not been unsuccessful, since the merits of the one they served could lift the souls and bodies of his attendants to heaven and raise them above every disaster.

# CHAPTER XXVIII

## The conveyance of the body through the city; its new preparation; the display of miracles; the magnitude of the offerings; and the inscription of the verse, “Staff of pontiffs,” etc.; and his burial in the place where he had ordered it

This chapter is contained in the great Life, chapter 20.

While so many great men eagerly offered their shoulders to carry the funeral bier that no individual could have been selected from such a multitude, the king and the archbishops or bishops, before the entrance to the city, surrendered to others for carrying the precious pearl which they had undertaken to bear, as though others were snatching it away. Thus those whose greater strength had given them the opportunity to take up the bier proceeded full of joy, touching it now with their shoulders, now with their hands. When they had enjoyed this kind of procession for some time, they were suddenly driven away by others and forced to yield their prize to new bearers.

Throughout the entire route to the church—a route extending over no short distance—new bearers succeeded one another at almost every moment. They did not come in equal numbers; rather, as many bearers approached as the structure of the bier could accommodate. Yet no one except men of high rank and distinction dared to enter into these contests.

They proceeded even through streets filled with very deep mud from the winter rains, repeatedly sinking their calves and often even their knees into the mire. Those unable to approach closely threw coins upon the chest enclosing the body; stretching out their hands, they adored it from a distance and commended themselves more devoutly to the saint. The Jews too, mourning and lamenting and loudly proclaiming that he had truly been a servant of the great God, rendered him whatever homage they could by coming to meet him and by their tears. They compelled us to recognize that the saying had been fulfilled in this man: “The Lord gave him the blessing of all nations” (Ecclesiasticus 44:25). [Col. 1111D]

With trumpets sounding through all the churches of the entire city, together with hymns and spiritual songs, he was at last carried into the embrace of his own church. Soon afterward he was transferred to a more secluded chapel, where he was to be clothed in the insignia of his garments, through the service of our insignificance [Note: [Col. 1111D] The author refers to himself; above, in chapter 24, Saint Hugh had entrusted himself to be clothed.], in which he had once received episcopal consecration. [Col. 1112A]

At that time a miracle could be seen there. His flesh shone with such a snowy and uniform whiteness that it plainly displayed, though he had been dead for so many days, a kind of glory of resurrection. Nothing livid appeared in it, nothing pale or withered, nothing dark, nothing that was not milky—or rather lily-white—shone forth. His hands and fingers, his arms and upper limbs, were as perceptible, soft, and pliable as they had long before been in the living man, though now he was dead. Only his face and his right hand had been lightly anointed with balsam. We made no examination of the condition of his other limbs. When we inserted a ring on his finger and gloves and the pastoral staff into his hands and arms, we discovered only in these places that matters were exactly as we have described.

Thus properly adorned with all the pontifical insignia, his face uncovered, he presented the appearance more of one sleeping than of one lifeless. He was carried back into the choir by those glorifying God. Crowds came running from every direction, carrying burning candles in their hands, kissing his feet and hands, and offering gold, silver, and precious stones.

Meanwhile, while we were sitting somewhat farther away with a venerable man, the dean of that church [Note: [Col. 1111D] This was Roger, the man mentioned in note 132 to Book III, chapter 7; at his urging Giraldus Cambrensis acknowledges that he arranged certain matters in part II of *Anglia Sacra*, p. 434.], discussing with one another the wondrous things that had happened concerning Christ’s servant, some people arrived in amazement and astonishment and said to us:
