“Did you see and observe how much beauty has now begun to blossom in the bishop’s face, so that it presents cheeks resembling red roses, and displays the cheerfulness of one sleeping rather than dead, indeed of someone who has just come from the baths?”

The dean was astonished and replied to those who announced these things: “You are certainly mistaken, dearest brothers. His face truly shines with wondrous whiteness, but no trace of red coloring appears in it. A little earlier we carefully observed his entire appearance and beauty.”

Then they almost dragged us along with them and showed us, when they had brought us close, with the evidence of our own eyes, that they had truly reported the grace of the redness with which his face shone. This genuine appearance of heavenly beauty remained, white and ruddy, as long as he was visibly present upon earth before the eyes of the bride entrusted to him. Whether that beauty remained with the body in the tomb or not is not for us to know now; it will be known later [Note: [Col. 1111D] Perhaps in the translation made in 1285, which Surius published with the *Life of Saint Hugh*, although I do not know from where he obtained it and it is not by the author of the Life. Hence Raynaldus, vol. XIII of the *Annals*, p. 48, rightly concludes that this account of the translation of the body was added by someone other than the author of the Life. Petrus Dorlandus also mentions this translation in Book III, chapter 14 of his *Carthusian Chronicle*. Since he is earlier than Surius and says that the translation was made approximately eighty-six years after Saint Hugh’s passing, as does Surius, it seems to have taken place around 1285, not in 1280, as the margin notes at the cited chapter 14; Raynaldus, vol. XIII of the *Annals*, p. 48, may perhaps also need correction.].

If that beauty disappeared, and the glory of his face was taken away with Moses, there will be no reason for those who may one day be granted knowledge of this to be scandalized, since his appearance is perpetually visible and indestructible to the invisible beings of heaven. From there not only the beauty of peace but also the health of weakness continues to flow into him.

The events that follow are known to lend support to these matters with a sufficiently joyful omen. For when we had returned to the place of the gathering just mentioned, several people quickly came to the dean, saying that a certain woman who had been deprived of the light of her eyes for many years had received her sight at the first touch of the holy body. They also suggested that the dean should order the trumpets to be sounded and the *Te Deum laudamus* to be sung in loud voices.

We strongly dissuaded him from this, because the woman herself was unknown to them; it was possible that, having fabricated her blindness, she was pretending to have newly received a light of which she had already been deprived for many years. We therefore advised that [perhaps: for a long time?] the truth concerning this matter, and concerning the other signs that would undoubtedly come to be heard, should first always be investigated most carefully, and that nothing should be disclosed or publicly proclaimed in any way until it had been proved with complete certainty. [Col. 1113B]

While there was some discussion on these matters between us and the clergy, others also came running, reporting an unquestionable miracle concerning another woman. As a certain devout matron stood beside the body after making a pious offering and was engaged in prayer, a clandestine thief suddenly cut away the purse hanging from her belt, which contained several silver shillings. Immediately, before any mortal except himself had yet recognized what he had done, he was struck by sudden blindness. He no longer knew where to direct his steps. Worn down by excessive fear, he tried for some time to move here and there, swaying like a man drunk and overcome by wine, but he could not. His gestures drew the eyes of many people upon him, and the bystanders asked what had happened to him and why he was behaving in this way in such a place.

Without saying anything, he stretched the hand holding the purse upward, revealing by the deed itself what he had done, and then, in a mournful voice, added what he had immediately suffered. The woman looked at the little purse in the hand of the sacrilegious cutter and recognized it as her own. The thief returned what he had stolen, and immediately received back the sight he had lost. She too recovered the money she had lost and extolled with immense praises the clemency of the patron whom she had approached with a devout heart. Shortly afterward it became more certain that the earlier woman truly had been blind for a long time and had received her lost sight there.

Meanwhile the crowd of people became so great that within a short time the amount of the offerings exceeded forty marks. Men and women surrounded the son of light, lying in their midst, day and night, holding burning candles in their hands and continually encircling him as one crowned by the Lord with glory and honor, in the manner of a crown.

At that time the master of Leicester, a learned and industrious man, placed at his feet the following couplet, in which he briefly expressed his manifold distinctions of virtue:

> Staff of pontiffs, standard of monks, counselor of schools,  
> Hammer of kings—Hugh was all these.

On the following day, while he was being carried to the tomb, the sacred garments with which he had been clothed were mutilated by repeated cutting. Whoever was able to commit such a sacrilege by stealing something sacred from a sacred object believed that he was thereby making himself especially sacred or sanctified.

He was buried, as he had ordered us, beside the wall, not far from the altar of Saint John the Baptist. Since it seemed more suitable because of the access of the crowds who gathered, he was placed on the northern side of the church, to the glory of God, who lives and reigns above all things, blessed God forever. Amen.

[Col. 1113] Here ends the Life of Saint Hugh, bishop of Lincoln.

[Col. 1113]

# LETTER OF BLESSED HUGH, BISHOP OF LINCOLN, CONTAINING REGULATIONS MADE DURING A VISITATION

(*Monasticon Anglicanum*, I, 924, edition of 1682.)

[Col. 1113D] To all the faithful of Christ to whom this present writing shall come, Hugh, by the grace of God bishop of Lincoln, greeting in the Lord.

When we came to the congregation of the handmaids of Christ at Cotun, in fulfillment of the duty of our office to conduct a visitation, we took care to apply a remedy to the matters that we learned needed correction there. Therefore, observing that a greater number of nuns were living there than the resources of that house could support, we determined, with the consent of the master, the prioress, and the convent, that from now onward the congregation of nuns should not exceed thirty in number, that the number of sisters should be confined to ten, and that twelve lay brothers should be employed there in rural duties.

The master chaplain, together with only two chaplains, shall be assigned to perform the divine offices. No one shall be given the religious habit in that house until the present convent has been reduced to the number specified above, except for the manifest usefulness of the house and then only by special permission of the diocesan.

The seal of the house shall be kept under the custody of the master, the prioress, and a nun commonly elected for this purpose, whose religious commitment and discretion have been approved. It shall be secured under a triple lock, and no document shall be sealed there without the knowledge of the whole chapter, or of its greater or more sound part.

All rents, *instaura* [repairs or restorations; the reading is uncertain], and every kind of income shall be recorded in writing each year. The record shall be entrusted for safekeeping to the prioress and subprioress and to four others chosen from the better and more prudent members, jointly elected by the whole chapter or by its greater and more sound part.

The master and the administrators of the house shall hand over all the house’s money, in coin or in whatever form it comes to the house for any reason, after it has been counted in the presence of these six women and sealed with the master’s seal. Whenever necessary, and to whatever extent necessary, they shall release it without difficulty for the business of the house, under the trustworthy testimony of both the master and the others; the remainder they shall again deposit under the master’s seal.

Each month these six women shall audit the account of the house’s ordinary expenses. Since renunciation of ownership belongs to the profession of religious persons, we strictly prohibit any woman or man in that house from presuming, after receiving the religious habit, to possess anything as private property. Everything shall be held in common.

Nuns, chaplains, brothers and sisters, and guests shall eat the same bread and have the same drink, except that the needs of the sick shall be provided for more delicately, as may be appropriate.

Since the peace of religious persons is usually disturbed by the frequent presence of secular people, we prohibit any man or woman from being received in secular clothing to stay in the aforesaid house, unless someone should perhaps spend the night there as a matter of hospitality.

Likewise, no one, whether secular or professing religious life and coming from elsewhere, shall speak alone with a single nun, whether man or woman, except in the presence of an honorable witness, such that there can be no suspicion of wrongdoing, and with permission obtained according to their rule from those in authority.

Furthermore, because it is altogether dishonorable for religious persons, especially women, to roam or wander about, we decree that no sister or nun shall stay at a grange for the purpose of caring for animals or for any other reason whatsoever. Nuns shall not be sent outside merely by their own decision or on any slight pretext to visit neighbors or relatives, nor shall they be sent out in any way without the special permission of the master and the prioress, and without the greatest and acknowledged necessity.

Because simoniacal depravity has led many into error and destruction, and because we desire to provide for the salvation of souls, we strictly prohibit any man or woman from ever being received there by agreement in exchange for money or any temporal thing.

Under threat of anathema, we command that all the foregoing regulations, beneficially established by us, be firmly observed forever by everyone of either sex in that house.

[Col. 1115]

# THE CHARTERS OF BLESSED HUGH

## I. Charter Reciting and Confirming the Grants of Donors

(*Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. III, p. 84, edition of 1673; vol. I, p. 84, edition of 1682.)

[Col. 1115C]

To all the faithful of Christ to whom this present writing shall come, Hugh, by the grace of God bishop of Lincoln, greeting in the Lord.

Since benefits bestowed by divine prompting for the support of Christ’s poor must be protected by the assistance of episcopal authority, lest the perversity of malicious people obstruct them, we are bound to strengthen them. We wish it to come to the knowledge of all of you that we approve and confirm by this present writing, for God and the Church of Saint John the Evangelist of Brakeley Hospital and for the brothers serving God there, all the benefits that have been bestowed upon them by the faithful of Christ through divine inspiration and assigned to their uses. So that these may come to everyone’s knowledge, we have judged it appropriate to record them by their proper names.

Having therefore examined the charters held by the aforesaid brothers, from the gift of Robert the elder, of good memory, count of Leicester, and of his son Robert the younger, count of Leicester:

First, we approve and confirm the foundation of the Church of Saint John the Apostle and Evangelist of Brakeley Hospital. We decree that the same church, together with the same hospital, shall be free and exempt from every subjection, as is expressed in the charters of the aforesaid patrons that we have seen.

To Solomon, master of the aforesaid hospital, and to his successors and to the brothers residing in that hospital who have been promoted to the priesthood, we grant permission to celebrate the divine mysteries in that chapel for the honor of God and for the salvation of the founders and of all the faithful. [Col. 1116D] This is provided, however, that if the parish church should at any time be vacant, the aforesaid brothers may, excluding excommunicated and interdicted persons, celebrate the divine offices in a subdued voice, by the authority of the venerable father and lord A., of blessed memory, the third supreme pontiff, as we have seen in the privilege granted to them by that same father. [Col. 1117A]

We also decree that the burial of the poor and guests who die in that hospital, and of those who at the point of death commend themselves to burial in the hospital’s territory, shall be free, without injury to the neighboring churches.

We judge that the liberties and free customs which R., the abbot of Saint Mary of the Meadow at Leicester, of good memory, and the convent of that place have granted to them, as we have seen them arranged in their charter, shall be enjoyed in fortunate perpetuity and strengthened by our confirmation. Namely, that Solomon, the aforesaid steward of the hospital, and his successors shall have, within the enclosure of the court of the aforesaid hospital, a church free and exempt from every subjection, in which the divine office shall perpetually be celebrated, together with burial for the poor, his household, his servants, and pilgrims, and full authority to govern and complete power to dispose of everything belonging to the aforesaid hospital.

They shall also have the complete consolation of the confessions of the poor and sick, and shall preside over them perpetually.

From the gift of Robert, count of Leicester, Robert the second, the younger: two and a half acres of land at Creys beside the hospital court, and all the land at Creys below their court, from the count’s gravel-land, as it is enclosed within its own bounds.

From the gift of the same count: two virgates of land, one namely from the assart land with the freedom from pannage that belongs to Halsow, together with the messuage belonging to the aforesaid virgate, situated at Brakeley at the head of the spring of Gotdewelle; and another virgate belonging to Brakeley, with its messuage, situated below beside the stream of the same spring, which virgate Swerman, the father of Master Solomon, held.

From the gift of Gilbert of Mount: twenty-three acres of land measured in his demesne by the perch, at Stockbridge on the side toward Brakeley and Ringesham meadow, as the charter made by Gilbert himself concerning this matter makes clear.

From the gift of Elias of Hinton: the meadow called Herlesham and another meadow called Ferham.

From the gift of Alice of Romeli: four acres of land in that part of the cultivation-land of Werveldiche and in the part that extends toward Halsow.

From the gift of Thomas Sorel and his son Simon: four acres at Siresham, and all the land that he held at Eswich, as the charters of the donors make clear.

We also decree and command that the liberties and free customs granted to the aforesaid brothers, as they are expressly contained in the charters of the patrons, [lacuna], shall be inviolably observed. Therefore, so that [lacuna] the donations and liberties previously granted to the aforesaid brothers, as the charters of the donors attest, and as they were reasonably made to them, may obtain the support of perpetual stability, we have judged it appropriate to provide them with [lacuna] and, for the knowledge of posterity concerning these matters, to add the testimony of episcopal authority by this present writing and the affixing of our seal.

These are witnesses: R., abbot of Nostell; Master Stephen, chancellor of the Church of Lincoln; Master Womer; Master Gerald of Rowell; Master Richard of Claleveel; and many others.

## II. Charter of Lord Hugh, Bishop, and the Chapter of Lincoln Concerning Two Portions of the Church of Corby

(*Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. I, p. 881, edition of 1673.)

To all the faithful of Christ to whom this present writing shall come, Hugh, by the grace of God bishop of Lincoln, greeting in the Lord.

Let all of you know that, with the assent and consent of our beloved sons in Christ, William [Col. 1118B], dean, and our chapter of Lincoln, out of regard for divine mercy, we have given and granted to our beloved daughters in Christ, the nuns of Saint Michael outside the borough of Stamford, two portions of the church of Corby. These portions belong to the advowson of the said nuns by the gift of Matilda of Diva, by the gift of Ascelina of Waterville and her heirs, and also by the gift of Hamo Peche.

They are to have and possess them forever for their own uses, saving the portion of Hugh of Osberneby there for as long as he lives, and also saving the perpetual vicarage, with a suitable mansus, which Hilary the chaplain holds from the said portions and which has been assigned to him and to his successors, the vicars of those portions.

The aforesaid nuns shall bear all episcopal and archidiaconal burdens relating to the said two portions [Col. 1118C], while in every respect the episcopal customary usages and the dignity of the Church of Lincoln remain preserved. Therefore, so that this may obtain perpetual force, we have deemed it appropriate to secure this present charter with our seal together with the seal of our aforesaid chapter.

With these witnesses: William, dean; John, precentor; and others. Given, and so forth, in the chapter of Lincoln, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the seventeenth year of our pontificate.

### III. Charter of Hugh, Bishop of Lincoln, Reciting and Confirming the Grants Donated to the Monastery of Saint Oswald at Bardney

*(Monasticon Anglicanum, vol. I, p. 850, ed. 1673.)*

**[Col. 1118D]** Hugh, by the grace of God Bishop of Lincoln, to all the sons of holy mother Church, greeting.

Episcopal authority ought diligently to support the just petitions of religious men, lest benefits canonically granted to them be disturbed in any way by the harassment of malicious persons or alienated by untimely vexations. Therefore, by episcopal authority, we confirm and strengthen with the protection of this present document all the goods and possessions of our beloved sons, the abbot and monks of Bardney, gathered by divine grace in the monastery of Saint Oswald—possessions in lands, men, churches, tithes, and other things—which they presently possess justly and canonically and for which they possess authentic documents.

Accordingly, whatever Gilbert de Gaunt the First and Aliz de **[Col. 1119A]** Muntfort, his wife, the restorers of the aforesaid monastery, as well as Walter de Gaunt and Earl Gilbert, his son, and likewise the men of the fiefs, granted to the aforesaid monastery, for the salvation of their souls, by title of donation and as alms, as their charters testify, we have decreed shall remain forever free and exempt from every earthly service and payment. Likewise, we decree that whatever Earl Simon, who had taken Aliz, daughter of Earl Gilbert, as his wife, gave together with the inheritance of the aforementioned men and confirmed by his charters shall remain so.

These are all the possessions granted: Bardney, and Osgotebi with its appurtenances. At Stepings the aforesaid monks have four carucates of land, two bovates, and the church of Frisebi. At Schendelbi, **[Col. 1119B]** the church of Saint Peter, with its lands and tithes; and south of the same village, the chapel of Saint James with the adjacent grove, and its two mills; and Tholi’s land and his service, and Gunnes’s land with its service. At Partenay, the church of Saint Nicholas with its appurtenances, and the chapel of Saint Mary in the same village, and the tithe of the mill of that village. At Braitoft, the whole tithe of the demesne of Simon, son of William. At Croft, by the gift of Philip de Kima, twenty sextaries of salt from the revenues of that village. By the gift of Gatter de Braitoft, ten acres of meadow in the territory of Frisebi. By the gift of Herbert, son of Alard, twelve acres of meadow beyond Scalslet. By the gift of Ralph, son of Gilbert, for the soul of his brother Hugh, the land which he held in Frisebi, and which he possessed at Ingaldelmeles and Derfletes; at Croft, **[Col. 1119C]** the church of Stepinge.

At Wainflet, one bovate with the attached saltworks. At Haltona, by the gift of William de Rumara, five and a half bovates of land, a mill, and a ninth part of another mill. At Hagiordingham, by the gift of Walter de Gaunt, six bovates of land and the church of that village; and by the gift of Gilbert de Gaunt, the knight’s fee which he held in the same village. At Lucebi, two bovates of land and the church of that village with its appurtenances; one dwelling and one mill in the territory of the same village; one bovate at Wincebi; and Tonnecroft. Near Lyme, by the gift of Ranulf, Earl of Chester, the mill of Bradewad and one mark of silver from the **[Col. 1119D]** revenue of the mill of Bracebrigge. The mill of Strattone. Edlingtone, with all its appurtenances. By the gift of Earl Gilbert, a third part of Baumburg and the mill of the same village. The church of Sotteberi, with its lands and tithes. The church of Saint Hilary of Spridelington, with its tithes. At Burtona, three carucates of land. At Schamtona, with its lands and tithes. At Edelingtona, the church with all its appurtenances.

By the gift of Robert Marmiren, Buteyake, with all its appurtenances. At Bartona, the church of Saint Peter, with the chapel of All Saints, its lands and tithes, and all its appurtenances; and the tithe of the mills of that village. Also, by the gift of Earl Gilbert, one bovate of land for the soul of Seer **[Col. 1120A]** de Arcels; and south of the same village, the land which he gave to the monks in exchange. At Horkeston, the tithe of the demesne. At Torpe, the whole tithe of the demesne. At Folkingham, the church with its lands and tithes.

By the gift of Herbert de Gaunt, the church of Irnham, with its lands and tithes. At Afwardebi, two parts of the lord’s tithe. At Wilegbi, two parts of the lord [the source reading is incomplete]. At Staunton, the whole tithe of the demesne. At Surray, all the land that belonged to Ivo, son of Schardman, with its assart; and William, son of Hacon’s assart in the territory of the same village; and William Bigot’s assart, with Gippolf’s land in the same village. At Suttona, half a carucate of land with the adjacent pastures and meadows, and a meadow in the territory of Hotoft. At Scrubbi, two and a half bovates. At Wdetorpe **[Col. 1120B]** one bovate of land; and Thuait with its attached land, and the mill of Wlierne. Hertelholme, with its lands and revenues. The church of Bulthalm with its appurtenances. At Bracebrige, from the estate of William, son of Walter Winterhard, one bovate of land. At Edelesberg, the church with its appurtenances. At Hale, the church with its appurtenances. At Hekington, the church with its appurtenances.

Accordingly, we receive under our protection all the aforesaid possessions which our predecessors reasonably confirmed to them, together with their liberties, customs, and immunities, as their documents testify, and we provide them with ecclesiastical protection—saving in all respects the episcopal customs and the dignities of the Church of Lincoln.

With these witnesses: Hamo, dean of Lincoln; **[Col. 1120C]** William, subdean; Master Stephen; and others.

### IV. Charter of Confirmation by Hugh, Bishop of Lincoln, of the Donations to the Church of Saint Andrew at Northampton

*(Monasticon Anglicanum, vol. I, p. 681, editions 1673 and 1682.)*

To all Christ’s faithful to whom this present document shall come, Hugh, by the grace of God Bishop of Lincoln, greeting in the Lord.

It is our duty to yield to just petitions and to grant whatever assistance we can to the sons of holy Church. Therefore, by the special authority **[Col. 1120D]** with which we are entrusted, we confirm to our brethren, the monks of the Church of Saint Andrew at Northampton, namely: the church of All Saints at Northampton, with all its appurtenances; the church of Saint Giles, with all its appurtenances; the church of Saint Michael, with all its appurtenances; the church of the Holy Sepulchre, with all its appurtenances; the church of Saint Mary, with all its appurtenances; the church of Saint Gregory, with all its appurtenances; and the church of Saint Peter, with all its appurtenances, namely, the church of Thorp and the chapel of Upton, with all their other appurtenances; the church of Saint Edmund, with all its appurtenances; the church of Saint Bartholomew, with all its appurtenances; and the chapel of Saint Thomas, with all its appurtenances; and the **[Col. 1121A]** church of Ryall, with all its appurtenances; the church of Erton, with all its appurtenances; the church of Newenton, with all its appurtenances; the church of Syvell, with all its appurtenances; the church of Multon, with all its appurtenances; the church of Braufelde, with all its appurtenances; the church of Preston, with all its appurtenances; the church of Byllyng, with all its appurtenances; the church of Hawton, with all its appurtenances; the church of Nuenton, with all its appurtenances; the church of Hardyngystorn, with all its appurtenances; the church of Stotysbury, with all its appurtenances; and the church of Sulgrave, with all its appurtenances.

Also, two parts **[Col. 1121B]** of the tithe of the whole demesne tithe of Earl David at Yordele, Bartone, Dodyngtonne, and Haryngwith; a third part of the whole tithe of Earl David’s demesne at Fodryngeya; a third part of the whole tithe of the demesne of Dverton; two parts of the whole tithe of the demesne of Styvede; twenty shillings from the mills of Parton, for purchasing wine for the Masses; three sums of grain from Earl David’s garden at Bertona, for making altar breads; two parts of the whole tithe of the demesne of Wllastona; two parts of the tithe of Walter, son of Winemer, at Throp; two parts of the aforesaid Walter’s demesne tithe at Wuston; two parts of the tithe of Achard de Sproxton’s demesne at Sproxton, Wythyn, and Strattona; two parts of the whole tithe of the demesne **[Col. 1121C]** which belonged to Roger, son of Aze, at Psham; two parts of the whole tithe of Henry de Cogenho’s demesne at Horrowedon; two parts of the whole tithe of William, son of Burchard, at Flore; two parts of the whole tithe of Henry de Armenteri’s demesne at Stowe and Ryslyngburg, which they hold at farm from the monks of Saint Projectus of Vermendes; two parts of Walter Luvel’s demesne tithe at Lyslynghury; and the church of Postona with all its appurtenances, together with two virgates of land and twenty acres of heath in the same village; two parts of Richard de Heyford’s demesne tithe at Herleston; two parts of the whole tithe of Andrew de Braybrooke’s demesne; a third part of the whole tithe of Richard Foxle’s demesne at Forle; and two parts of the whole tithe **[Col. 1121D]** of Little Hoctona near Langeporte, which they have by the gift of Godfrey of Boulogne.

And so that all these things may remain secure and unimpaired for the aforesaid monks of Saint Andrew, just as they were rightly and reasonably granted to them, we strengthen them by the testimony of this document and of our seal, saving in all respects the dignity of the Church of Lincoln.

With these witnesses: Robert, abbot of Nuttelega; Walkelin, abbot of Saint James; Walkelin, prior of Londa; Master Robert de Harding; Master Roger de Rolveston; Master Simon de Sywell; Master William de Monte; Master Richard de Dodeford; Henry, son of Peter; Master Warin de Bedford; Simon, dean of Witlyngbere; Roger, dean of Pateshyll; Master **[Col. 1122A]** Samson de Bereheby; Master Robert de Mellum; and Master Robert Grosteste.

### V. Confirmation of Hugh, Bishop of Lincoln, Concerning the Church of Waldene

*(Monasticon Anglicanum, vol. I, p. 819, ed. 1673.)*

To all Christ’s faithful to whom this present document shall come, Hugh, by the grace of God Bishop of Lincoln, greeting in the Lord.

Let it be known to all of you that, out of consideration for piety, we have granted and confirmed by this present charter to the canons of the order of Sempringham at Malton, serving the Lord, the church of Waldene with its appurtenances in perpetuity, just as it was reasonably granted to them by the gift of Walter de Nevile and Alan Ayruun, **[Col. 1122B]** the patron of the same church, saving the episcopal customs and the dignity of the Church of Lincoln.

With these witnesses, and others.

### VI. Confirmation by Saint Hugh, Bishop of Lincoln, of the Churches of Thorneberg and Dodeford for the Monks of Luffield Monastery

*(Monasticon Anglicanum, vol. I, p. 522, ed. 1682.)*

To all Christ’s faithful to whom this present document shall come, Hugh, by the grace of God Bishop of Lincoln, eternal greeting in the Lord.

So that the things granted by the faithful to religious places for God’s sake might be possessed without disturbance, the prudent care of our predecessors diligently secured this by confirming them to the recipients in authentic documents. Following in their footsteps, we have therefore deemed it appropriate to confirm to our **[Col. 1122C]** beloved sons in Christ, the monks of Luffield, the benefits which the donations of the faithful granted to them, since they were reasonably bestowed upon them and their house, and to record them in this present document.

By the gift of Ralph de Caignes, the church of Saint Mary of Dodeford. By the gift of Hamo, son of Memphilin, the church of Thorneberg. By the gift of Richard, son of Nigel, half of the church of Saint Mary of Beckhampton.

We grant all these benefits, with everything pertaining to them, to be possessed by the monks in perpetuity, as is contained in the charters of the donors and of the archdeacons by whom the aforesaid monks have already been instituted in them; and we confirm them by the protection of this document and our seal, saving the episcopal customs and the dignity of the Church of Lincoln, **[Col. 1122D]** with these witnesses: Robert, abbot …; Roger de Rolveston; Master Richard de Swalewoel; Geoffrey de Leichelave; Robert de Capella; John, dean of Lieston; Eustace de Wiltona; and many others.

### VII. Charter of Hugh, Bishop of Lincoln, Confirming the Donation of Rodulf de Abi for the Construction of an Abbey at Grenefeld

*(Monasticon Anglicanum, vol. I, p. 881, ed. 1682.)*

To all Christ’s faithful to whom this present document shall come, Hugh, by the grace of God Bishop of Lincoln, greeting in the Lord.

The prudent care of the ancients took precautions that donations made by the faithful **[Col. 1123A]** to religious places could not be revoked through any malicious scheme, by having them confirmed by episcopal authority. Therefore, following in their footsteps, and seeing that it is within our power to provide for the house of Genefeld and the nuns serving God there, we have decided to confirm by the authority with which we are entrusted the things piously granted to them, and to set them down in an authentic document under their proper names:

By the gift of Eudo de Grenesbi and his son Ralph, founders of the aforesaid place, the church of Abi with all its appurtenances; the cultivated lands at Boland, Wargarthweit, and Catecrooft, together with the cultivated land beside the wood of Swinewit; and the meadow belonging to Catecroft. Sixteen acres of meadow in the fields of Abi; the wood of **[Col. 1123B]** Aitterlund and Tiedolf Barnewde; the tithe of the mills of Abi; and the whole wood of Croxhage which Normannus held.

By the gift of Roscelin de Riggesbi and his son Jodlan, whatever they held at Wlurikehage. By the gift of Gilbert de Riggesbi and his son Herbert, whatever they held at Wlurikehage and Prestehage; the assart beside Prestehage; and four acres of land at Heregerethage, with all the pasture of Riggesbi.

By the gift of Ainfrid de Hage, fifty-five acres of cultivated land and five acres of meadow in the common pasture of Hage. By the gift of Alan de Munbi and his son Eudo, whatever they held at Wlurikehage; and the church of Combrewrth, insofar as it belonged to them, namely, three parts of that church; and Snoutecroft with **[Col. 1123C]** the common pasture of Sutton; and one toft which belonged to Gunebien; and pasture for three hundred sheep in the pasture beyond Habedic of Munbi.

By the gift of William, son of Otver, thirty-three acres in the fields of Abi and **[Col. 1124A]** Toresbi. By the gift of Ivo de Strubi and his son Henry, forty-two acres of land at Crareker and Croxhage. By the gift of William de Wdetorp and his son Alan, Motteker, and one bovate of land at Farford with one toft.

By the gift of William de Welle and his son Robert, six acres of land in the territory of Wiern, at a place called Harlham. By the gift of Herbert de Alebi, Walter, and William, his sons, whatever they held at Wlurikehage and Prestehage; and whatever they held between Bolandewange and Derwennehille, and between the abbey and the ditch of Crakethweith, within the boundaries laid out from Crakethweit to Trentesic, with the common pasture of Abi.

By the gift of Gunter de Alebi, whatever he held at Wlurikehage, and whatever he held between the cultivated land of Presthage and Gilbert de Campania’s land. By the gift of Picot de Houton and his son Richard, one saltworks in the marsh of Newton; **[Col. 1124B]** and five acres of meadow at Twaflates and Westenges.

By the gift of Thomas Burgefurn, two acres of land in the territory of Hage, and all his land at Northon which lies between the road and his cultivated land. By the gift of Gilbert Testard, three perches of land in the territory of Abi. By the gift of William Burgefurn, one acre of land in the territory of Swabi, in the cultivated field called Brerthebuskewange.

All these things, just as they were rightly and reasonably granted to them, I confirm by this present document and by the protection of my seal, saving the episcopal customs and the dignity of the Church of Lincoln.

With these witnesses: Haimo, dean of the Church of Lincoln; Master Roger de **[Col. 1124C]** Rovelton, archdeacon of Leicester; Master Richard de Swalewecliva; Geoffrey de Lechelade; Robert de Capella; Eustace de Wilton; and many others.

**[Col. 1123]**

# Ancient Statutes of the Carthusian Order

*(Dom Mabillon, Annales Benedictini VI, Appendix, p. 685.)*

## Notice

At first, the monks of the Grande Chartreuse lived under the jurisdiction of bishops, who visited them in their cells and corrected them as they pleased. But when they discovered that the bishops found more to admire in them than to correct, they voluntarily divested themselves of that jurisdiction and placed it in the hands of the general chapter and the prior of the Grande Chartreuse, granting them complete freedom concerning the discipline of governance.

For a long time, other priors of the same institute desired this freedom. They wrote to Anthelm, prior of the Grande Chartreuse, earnestly asking him that the matter be amended in the general chapter, to which they would assemble at the appointed time. Anthelm praised their pious proposal and, after consulting Hugh II, Bishop of Grenoble, who had been a Carthusian monk, replied that they should proceed lawfully in this matter and seek the consent of the bishops in each of their dioceses and of all the brothers in their convents.

Having easily obtained this consent, Bernard, prior of Portes; Sofford, prior of Excubiae; Lazarus, prior of Durbon; Stephen, prior of Majorevi; and John, prior of Alveria, assembled at the Grande Chartreuse and, together with Anthelm, a man of extraordinary holiness, celebrated the first general chapter. We present its acts and statutes, together with those of certain other chapters.

## I. Acts of the First Chapter of the Carthusian Order

*(From the manuscript of Mont-Dieu.)*

**[Col. 1125]**

**[Col. 1125A]** Let it be known to all the faithful of the holy Catholic Church, present and future, that the priors of the Carthusian institute—namely Bernard, prior of Portes; Sofford, prior of Excubiae; Stephen, prior of Durbon; and John, prior of Alveria—had long asked the prior and brothers of the Grande Chartreuse that they be permitted to hold a common chapter in that same house of the Grande Chartreuse, for the correction and amendment of the entire institute.

After this urgent and almost continual entreaty, Anthelm, prior of the Grande Chartreuse, with his brothers, finally consented, on the advice of Hugh II, the venerable bishop of the Church of Grenoble, but on this condition: that each of the priors obtain letters from his archbishops and bishops and from the common **[Col. 1125B]** chapter of his brothers, granting authority to the general chapter over all matters requiring correction and amendment throughout the houses of the institute, and specifying the day on which they were to assemble.

Having received with thanksgiving this much-desired consent and obtained the letters, they assembled on the appointed day. Since similar letters had been issued by the archbishops and bishops and by the chapters themselves, it pleased them to enter one letter from the bishops and one from the chapters in the following form:

“Falco, minister of the Church of Lyons, to the beloved brother Anthelm, prior of the Grande Chartreuse, and to all the priors serving God under the Carthusian order, and to the brothers who are with him: may they obtain from the Lord the reward of poverty. We grant and entrust forever, by episcopal authority, the houses of Portes and Majorevi, **[Col. 1125C]** emulating your religious observance, at their request and petition, as houses emulating your religious observance, to be corrected in perpetuity for the observance and confirmation of your order, as shall have been decreed by the common decision of the chapter.”

“To the most reverend fathers and lords, the prior of the Grande Chartreuse by the grace of God, and the brothers serving Christ under his governance: all the brothers of Portes send peace and eternal salvation from the Lord.

“We not only grant and praise **[Col. 1125D]** your eventual consent that the priors of our house and of the other houses should assemble at your house, which is the mother of our institute, at the appointed time, as has been decreed, so that they may diligently deliberate concerning matters capable of securing the unity, stability, and firmness of our order; we have also received it with thanksgiving.

“Therefore, in all matters pertaining to the observance and confirmation of our order, as shall have been decreed by the common decision of the universal chapter, we grant and entrust our house to you and your successors, to be preserved and corrected forever.”

It therefore pleased them to record the decrees of this universal chapter according to the several divisions of the chapters.

**[Col. 1126A]** The first chapter contains the following: the divine office of the Church is to be celebrated in precisely one rite throughout all the houses, and all the customs of the house of the Grande Chartreuse that pertain to the religious order are to be observed uniformly.

The second chapter concerning priors decreed that if any prior—God forbid!—should act against the religious order and its institute, and, after being privately admonished once, twice, and three times by the brothers and in his own chapter, should remain uncorrected, the prior of the Grande Chartreuse, with the common counsel of the general chapter, shall have authority either to correct him, if possible, or to replace him as incorrigible.

The same was established concerning the prior of the Grande Chartreuse and the correction of that house. Once the aforesaid incorrigible prior has been deposed, he is **[Col. 1126B]** either to remain in the same house, if this can be done peacefully for that house, or he is not to delay transferring to another house of the institute to which he has been ordered to go.

The prior who is to be substituted in that house shall, if reasonably possible, be chosen from among the brothers of the same house, according to the foregoing institutions. Otherwise, according to the judgment of the common chapter, a prior shall be appointed for the desolate brothers from one of the other houses, with the exception of the Grande Chartreuse. The same was decreed concerning the election of a prior after the death of his predecessor.

The third chapter provides that if the prior or brothers of any house of this institute should, of their own will—God forbid!—wish to transfer that house to the religious order of another institute, they shall in no way be permitted to do so, since they are **[Col. 1126C]** confederated in perpetuity with this institute by law.

The fourth chapter therefore decrees that no new house of this institute shall be built without the consent of the common chapter, and that no prior may presume to issue institutions.

The fifth chapter states that if the house of the Grande Chartreuse, which is the mother and nurse of the others, should be compelled to obtain a prior from another house rather than its own, it may take for itself any person from any house of this institute, except the priors of the houses.

The sixth chapter has the following provision: if any matter should arise concerning one of the houses of the aforesaid institute which must presently be addressed, **[Col. 1126D]** the prior of the Grande Chartreuse shall immediately summon to himself, if he cannot deal with it alone, as many priors as seem sufficient to him for resolving it. Their decision shall be considered no less valid than that of the universal chapter.

Finally, the seventh **[Col. 1127A]** chapter provides that neither the prior of the Grande Chartreuse nor any other priors may, without the common counsel of the general chapter, remove or add anything concerning either the divine office or any other institutions of this religious order.

We call “common,” or “universal,” chapter those who have been summoned and assembled. Therefore, so that all these institutions, which pertain to the firmness and unfailing stability of this holy religious order and which have been usefully devised and most beneficially considered by holy men, might have perpetual continuance, all the priors, **[Col. 1128A]** following the path of humility, submitted themselves with complete devotion to this holy discipline and continual correction, and professed in these words that they would bear tirelessly and unfailingly the sweet yoke and light burden of this holy obedience:

“I, Brother Stephen, prior of Majorevi, promise obedience to the common chapter.”

The venerable bishop mentioned above was also present—a father and monk of that same Carthusian house. Kissing his hand, in which he held all these prescriptions, with their knees bent, they made this profession.

## II. Further Chapters of Another Assembly

*(From the same manuscript.)*

**[Col. 1127]**

**[Col. 1127B]** 1. The first chapter provides that the Passion of the Lord is to be sung like the other Gospels.

2. The second chapter provides that when the Nativity of the Lord falls on a Wednesday, on the following Sunday the responsory is to be sung as on the day of the Nativity of the Lord: at Mass, *A Child Is Born for Us*; the prayer, *Grant, we beseech thee, almighty God, that we [of the Only-Begotten—fragment incomplete]*; the Epistle, *The kindness has appeared*; and the Gospel, *In the beginning*, and so forth, as on the Sunday of the Nativity.

3. The third chapter provides that on the Sunday on which the Gospel *There Was a Certain Joseph* occurs, the antiphon *Joseph Was* is to be sung at Vespers on Saturday and repeated at the *Benedictus*. The same is to occur on the Sunday after the Ascension: namely, **[Col. 1127C]** the antiphon from the Gospel is to be sung both at Vespers on Saturday and at the *Benedictus*.

4. The fourth chapter provides that on the sixth Sunday after Epiphany, which precedes Septuagesima, the Gospel *I Will Confess to You, Lord, Father of Heaven and Earth* is to be sung, with antiphons from the same Gospel: *Take My Yoke upon You* at the *Benedictus*, and *For My Yoke* at the *Magnificat*.

5. The fifth chapter provides that the repetition of the responsory *I Said, Lord* is *Heal My Soul, **[Col. 1128B]** for I Have Sinned against You*, and that the same is to be repeated after the *Gloria*.

6. The sixth chapter provides that what has been corrected in the Psalter is also to be corrected in the responsory—for example: *If [They] Have Not Ruled over Me*; *He Himself Delivered Me*; *And I Shall Exalt Mercy in the Morning*; and *From Generation to Generation*.

7. The seventh chapter provides that after *Come*, *Eternal Creator of All Things* is to be sung; at Lauds, *Splendor of the Father’s Glory*; at Vespers, *God, Creator of All Things*, and so forth; at Compline, *Christ, Who Are the Light*.

8. The eighth chapter provides that from the octave of Pentecost until Advent, on all ferial days except feast days, the Sunday prayers are to be said at Vespers and Lauds.

9. The ninth chapter provides that in the responsory of one **[Col. 1128C]** martyr, at the third nocturn, the verse *The Just Man Will Rejoice in the Lord* is to be said.

10. The tenth chapter provides that on the feast of Saint Andrew, if it falls during Advent, food is to be taken only once, but nevertheless the brothers are to come to the collation.

11. It has also been decreed that doing something for the dear ones in the convent is to depend on the judgment of the prior and his chapter.

## III. Other Statutes

*(From the same manuscript.)*

**[Col. 1127]**

**[Col. 1127D]** 1. It was decreed in the Carthusian chapter that, after None in the cloister, a reading should be given for the customary discourse, according to the prior’s judgment.

2. It was then decreed that, just as regulations had been established concerning the riding of the brothers of the other houses, so they should also be observed at the Grande Chartreuse—except that when they have come to the chapter, or when some have been sent by the chapter on a particular business, the houses from which the brothers are sent may, as necessity requires, send a brother out on horseback in the customary manner.

3. We also decreed by common consent that, when Lord P., abbot of Cluny, should die, **[Col. 1128D]** the same office should be performed for him in all the houses of our order as is customarily performed for a prior or professed brother, except for the anniversary and except that his name is not to be written in the martyrology.

For all the other deceased of the entire Cluniac order, besides private prayers, a general office, both of Mass and of the office for the dead (*agenda*), is to be celebrated once a year in the convent. Each priest shall recite one Psalter, and the lay brothers three hundred Lord’s Prayers. We have ordered that this service be completed each year, from the chapter itself until the Nativity of the Lord. For Lord Ainric, Bishop of Winchester, and likewise for the successors of the aforesaid **[Col. 1129A]** abbot, after their deaths a general office is similarly to be celebrated in the convent.

4. It was again decreed that if any house or any person of our order should request letters from the Roman Curia, either personally or through another, against the statutes of the common chapter, that house or person shall be separated from the fellowship of the entire order unless reconciled by the same common chapter.

5. It was further established that, since the number of inhabitants of our places is fixed, a fixed number and limit should also be maintained for animals and hired workers. Therefore, so that moderate unity might everywhere be preserved, it was decreed that no house of our order should have more than twenty-five hired workers, more than 1,200 sheep and goats together—excluding he-goats—more than twelve dogs, more than thirty-two oxen, **[Col. 1129B]** more than twenty calves, or more than six pack animals.

6. Concerning the removal and substitution of priors, we also judged that the following should be observed: no congregation of our order may remove a living prior from his office unless with the consent of the common chapter; nor may the chapter itself, without consulting the brothers of that association and against their will, appoint or remove a prior without a suitable cause.

If a dispute should arise between the brothers of any house and their prior on account of his offenses, and if that prior, after being repeatedly admonished by them, should refuse to correct himself, the matter is to be referred to the council of the common **[Col. 1130A]** chapter and settled by its judgment.

7. It was also stated that no house whatsoever may presume to write to the person of the lord pope concerning its own or another’s business without the counsel of the common chapter.

8. It was likewise decreed that if any prior, either personally or through one of his subordinates, should presume to violate the statutes of the chapter, then, once the transgression has become manifest, he is to confess his fault in the presence of the entire chapter and leave it. Barefoot, with his customary garments removed, carrying rods in his hand, he is humbly to return before the convent to receive discipline. In his own house, he is likewise to impose similar discipline on his subordinates for a similar fault.

**[Col. 1130B]** 9. It was also decreed that if anyone should exceed the prescribed number of animals, whatever is in excess is to be distributed to the poor by decree of the chapter.

10. It was further established that the garments of monks should not come within half a foot of the ground, and those of lay brothers should not descend below the edges of their footwear.

11. We also establish that, out of reverence for and in the interest of peace with the congregations of the Cistercians and Premonstratensians, no person from them is henceforth to be received into our order. If any of our members should violate this institution, he is also to be compelled to expel the professed member and separate him from the entire order.

## IV. Ancient Statutes of the Carthusian Order Concerning Sacred Rites

*(From Colbert Manuscript 3808.)*

**[Col. 1129]**

**[Col. 1129C]** 1. In every Mass for the living that is celebrated in rotation, each person says: *Almighty and eternal God, who [of the living]…*

2. We declare that a Mass for benefactors must never be offered on feasts of twelve lessons, even when a thirty-day observance is in progress, provided that another day is available on which it can be offered.

**[Col. 1129D]** 3. On whatever day the octave of the Apparition falls, if the responsory *Not in Anger* cannot otherwise be said, the octave itself shall be observed on Saturday.

4. We declare that the Sunday Mass is not to be prevented because of an anniversary Mass. Rather, the anniversary Mass is then to be said privately and the Sunday Mass in the convent, unless another day in that week is free on which the Sunday Mass can be said.

5. Since our lord the supreme pontiff has ordered and strictly commanded, under the authority of holy obedience, that the feast of Corpus Christi be solemnly celebrated by all, we, out of reverence for God and for the holy command, establish and command in the same manner prescribed in the decretal that the feast be observed in our order, and that it be solemnly celebrated, with candles, both in the offices and in the other Masses—namely, on the Thursday after the octave of Pentecost. **[Col. 1130C]**

An octave of the aforesaid feast is also to be observed, with the rite and solemnity with which the octave of the Assumption of Blessed Mary is celebrated.

6. We command and admonish all the priors and convents of our order not to omit each year the thirty-day observance formerly granted to Lord Amblard, Bishop of Maurienne.

7. We declare that when the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord falls on a Sunday, the borrowed responsories, namely *Behold, the Days Are Coming* and *Hail, Mary*, are to be said.

8. It is declared that on the day of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross a sleeping period may be taken, according to the ancient statutes.

9. We order that henceforth the kiss of peace be received in the church from a tablet on which an image of Christ crucified is painted.

**[Col. 1130D]** 10. At all times, a candle is to be lit during the elevation of the Body of Christ at conventual Masses, except during a period of interdict and cessation of divine services.

11. We declare that, according to our privileges and statutes, and according to the decretal placed under the title “On Privileges” in the second book, at the end of the said decretal, we may administer the ecclesiastical sacraments to our domestic servants.

12. We declare that priors and vicars of nuns, if they should happen to die in the houses over which they preside, do not lose the associations of their own houses, unless they made profession in the houses in which they are priors or vicars.

13. When the feast of the Annunciation is celebrated within the octave of Easter, at first vespers those psalms are to be said which are said within the said octave, namely, *Dixit Dominus* (“The Lord said”).

14. We declare that the second Mass of the Nativity of the Lord is to be celebrated; and if dawn has not appeared, the monks are to return to their cells before the Mass is celebrated.

15. We prohibit serving any longer in the convent, or even in private, with cowls made of cloth.

16. From now on, priors or monks of our order, or lay brothers, are not to go to burials, except perhaps those of princes and great prelates, or of their father and mother who belong to the order, if they are buried within the boundaries of their houses.

17. The statute made concerning the presence of bishops—that priors should relinquish their seats in the church to the bishops when the latter are present—is understood to apply when the bishops are present in the church.

18. We order that the Ember fasts in September be celebrated in every house of our order according to the custom of its diocese.

19. We order that if a feast of three lessons having its own Mass office should occur, on Wednesday of the general chapter the Mass of the feast is to be said, while the Mass *Salus populi* (“Salvation of the people”) is to be celebrated privately by someone.

[Col. 1131C] 20. According to the custom of the house of Carthusian, the antiphons are to be resumed at the pitch at which the psalmody ended.

21. Those guilty persons who have been reconciled to the order are to have the order’s spiritual benefit, according to the rank to which they have been restored.

22. We order that, when several tricenaries are to be begun, once the first tricenary has been begun by the prior or by the senior member, the others are to be begun by those to whom it falls to celebrate the Mass of the tricenary already begun.

23. It is strictly and effectively enjoined upon all persons of the order that no one, under any pretext whatsoever, whether personally or through another, directly or indirectly, by deeds, words, or letters, induce any person, whatever their condition, to request from the order any spiritual benefit beyond the general recommendation customarily made through the prayers of the order. Nor are they to grant an anniversary lightly in their houses, nor in any way bind themselves to spiritual matters in exchange for temporal things, except insofar as this can lawfully be done, according to the advice of experts.

24. We order that henceforth, because of the Church’s precept—which we formerly did not observe throughout all the houses of the order—on the feasts of the Twelve Apostles, the Evangelists, and the Four Doctors, once each year, a chapter feast be held for the monks. Lay brothers who are occupied with work on the aforesaid feasts are not to cease from it, nor are they to go up to the upper house on account of chapter. The names of the apostles are Peter, [Col. 1132A] Paul, Andrew, James, and John, the sons of Zebedee; Philip, Thomas, Bartholomew, Matthew, James son of Alphaeus, Simon, Judas, and Matthias.

25. So that uniformity may be maintained in the order in divine service, as it is contained in the statutes, let all priors and vicars procure the lesson which is read at Carthusian during the octave and throughout the octave of the Eucharist; a copy of this lesson can be found at Carthusian.

26. The prior and convent of Liminat, and any others whom it may please, are permitted to celebrate solemnly the feast of the Conception of the Blessed Virgin Mary. The office is to be made as on the Nativity, with the name “Conception” substituted for the name “Nativity.”

27. The house of Carthusian is permitted to celebrate a chapter feast for Lord Hugh, Bishop of Lincoln, [Col. 1132B] who was a monk of Carthusian.

28. During Eastertide, the Gospel *Ego sum vitis vera* (“I am the true vine”) is to be said on the feasts of Blessed Ambrose and Blessed Hugh, if those feasts happen to be celebrated during that season.

29. We admonish that in all houses of lay brothers separated from the upper houses, where there is a chapel, and where no legitimate impediment exists, Mass be celebrated by the prior or procurator at least twice or three times. [lacuna] If, however, the prior fails to carry out what was prescribed above, he is to confess his fault in the next chapter.

30. The tricenary granted to Lord Amblard to be paid every year is to be duly paid around the feast of Saint Mark the Evangelist, as is done at Carthusian: namely, for him and his parents the first prayer, *Inclina … famulorum et famularum* (“Incline … of male and female servants”), is to be said; [Col. 1132C] then the customary prayers.

31. Although it has been established that one hundred brief prayers are to be said during the year according to a fixed number, and they must not be omitted, the ancient custom contained in the statutes is also not to be omitted hereafter: namely, sending and announcing through the houses of the order brief notices of deceased persons, so that a special prayer may be said for them, and afterward a general prayer may be said for the others—namely, a singular prayer for one person and a singular prayer for several, as is contained in the statutes.

32. We approve the arrangement formerly made, with the admonition that every day the Mass of the Blessed Mary be said after the conventual Mass, once other impediments have ceased, as is done at Carthusian, and, as prescribed above, let it be done. [Col. 1132D] We further order and wish that it be said.

33. We declare that in the houses of nuns and monks where there are not as many priests as there are Masses owed, even if those Masses are delayed beyond the week in which they are owed, and the houses are unable to discharge them, fifty psalms are to be said for each Mass owed that could not be fulfilled, according to the prior’s or vicar’s ordering and disposition.

34. We approve and confirm as holy and praiseworthy the custom of those houses of the order in which a Mass of the Blessed Virgin Mary is said each day. We admonish in the Lord certain priors and monks of the order who oppose this custom that, for the honor of God and the Blessed Virgin, we should imitate this custom out of special devotion.

[Col. 1133A] 35. Because, by God’s grace, the number of persons and houses is increasing, we briefly order that from the general chapter until the coming Nativity of the Lord, fifty brief prayers may be said each year, and from the Nativity until the next chapter an equal number, with the other brief prayers sent during the year counted within this number; nevertheless, two brief prayers are to be fulfilled each week.

36. We wish to extend to our own monks, out of devotion, the new constitution specially issued by the Apostolic See concerning monks receiving Communion once a month, since we ought to devote ourselves to devotion more than other religious. We therefore establish that every non-priest monk who is a cleric received among us receive the sacrament of the Eucharist on the first Sunday of each month, at least according to the terms of the aforesaid constitution and with due preparation.

37. We admonish priests who celebrate rarely that henceforth they prepare and dispose themselves.

38. On account of the office for the benefactors of Saint Stephen, Cluny, and the general chapter, so that it may not be excessively delayed, it is granted that the anniversary may be transferred. Other non-anniversary offices that are transferred are to be discharged and rendered when and as is contained in our constitutions.

39. In response to the question asked concerning the feast of Blessed Anthony and its office, the following is prescribed, as is done at Carthusian: the sermon at matins, *Omne quod agimus*, etc. (“Everything that we do,” etc.); the Gospel both at matins and at Mass, *Si quis venit ad me*, etc. (“If anyone comes to me,” etc.); and the homily of Pope Gregory, *Si consideremus* (“If we consider”). [Col. 1133C] The introit of the Mass is *Os justi* (“The mouth of the just”), and the epistle is *Justum deduxit* (“He led the just man”).

40. Since, according to the statute of the order, non-priest monks and nuns are bound to say fifty psalms in place of the Mass of a tricenary, we likewise declare that in houses of nuns and monks where there are not as many priests as there are Masses owed, even if those Masses are delayed beyond the week in which they are owed and the houses are unable to discharge them, fifty psalms are to be said for each Mass that could not be fulfilled, according to the ordering and disposition of the vicar and of *rationis* [reading uncertain]. Nevertheless, the nuns are not for this reason to omit rendering one psalter for a brief prayer, as is contained in the new statutes.

41. On the Sunday within the octave of the Eucharist, the title of the first lesson is to be *Ex dictis sanctorum* (“From the sayings of the saints”).

42. We order that the feast of Blessed Hugh, Bishop of Lincoln, formerly a monk of Carthusian and prior of Witham, be celebrated throughout the entire order with candles and chapter. Lay brothers are not to cease from their work, nor are they to have chapter. At first vespers, over the psalms, the first antiphon from lauds, *Ecce sacerdos magnus* (“Behold the great priest”), [Col. 1134B] and the second responsory are to be said, and the Mass is to be celebrated without the Creed.

43. It is declared that when a feast of three lessons occurs on Ash Wednesday or thereafter, it is not impeded by the Mass of the fast but is to be said by the weekly officiant.

44. It is likewise declared that when several brief prayers occur in a week, and the Masses are to be rendered according to the ancient statutes with their proper prayers, this is permitted notwithstanding the statute concerning two brief prayers to be said in a week. If, however, more than two brief prayers happen to occur in a week, as many fewer are to be said in the following week as the number by which they exceeded two.

45. On the feast of the Conception of the Blessed Mary, *Sanctificationis* (“of the Sanctification”) is to be said in place of *Conceptionis* (“of the Conception”).

46. We declare that when an anniversary occurs while the deceased is present, two offices are to be said on the same day: one, namely that of the anniversary, after vespers in the church; and the other, according to the usual custom, near the funeral bier.

# V. STATUTES ISSUED IN THE YEAR 1261 BY THE GENERAL CHAPTER OF THE CARTHUSIAN ORDER

*(From Colbert MS 3807.)*

[Col. 1133]

[Col. 1133C] 1. In the year of the Lord 1261, it was established that the prior and procurator may say *Placebo* and *Dirige* after None when they are outside the convent, and that the sick may do likewise.

2. Likewise, that the house of Green Valley may write to the lord pope concerning what it needs.

3. Likewise, that conventual members are not to eat outside the houses.

4. Those received, or to be received, from the orders of Friars Minor and Friars Preacher may not hold obediences involving pastoral care without a dispensation from the supreme pontiff. Those who have professed in the aforesaid orders or in the Cistercian Order likewise may not hold any obediences, even without pastoral care, in our order without a dispensation from the general chapter.

5. Priors are not to give vicars general authority, except in a case of evident necessity or usefulness.

6. The benefits of private anniversaries are not to be performed on days assigned, according to ancient custom, to abstinence; [Col. 1134C] they may nevertheless be performed on any chapter feast, notwithstanding the custom of any house. What is given on Tuesday or Saturday may also be counted as the benefit of an anniversary, whatever it may be.

[Col. 1134D] 7. The statute requiring monks to prepare the kitchen once a month is revoked.

8. No one is to appeal except to the general chapter or to the prior of Carthusian; anyone appealing elsewhere is to lose the order. If, however, the chapter’s judgment declares that the appeal was unjust, the person who appealed in this way is to be severely punished according to the measure of the fault.

9. No one is to appeal unless the correction contains grave and manifest iniquity. An appeal issued for any reason is not to be pursued in person, but through a messenger and letters; and in this case priors are bound to provide their subjects with a messenger and expenses.

10. Lay brothers and lay affiliates are bound to show and explain to the prior, or even to the procurator, everything they have in their cells or elsewhere, whenever they are requested to do so, lest they incur the sentence of excommunication promulgated against proprietors.

11. When a monk from the Cistercian or Black Monks’ order makes profession among us, he is not blessed if he was blessed in his own order. He nevertheless performs the remaining rites: he asks that the verse *Suscipe me, Domine* (“Receive me, Lord”) be prayed for him, reads the profession, and receives Communion.

12. If anyone becomes so seriously ill within our boundaries that he could not enter the boundaries on foot or horseback, he cannot be received or clothed according to the prescribed rite.

13. Novices are not to make profession unless their own prior is present, or another member of our order is present with his permission if he cannot be present.

14. For each of the states of our order—namely monks, lay brothers, and lay affiliates—three useful members may be added in place of three useless ones.

15. No one is to presume to propose anything for enactment by which the ancient rigor of the order might be diminished. Whoever does so, and refuses to desist after being admonished by the prior of Carthusian or by the definitors, is by that fact deprived of the order.

16. Visitations of the houses of Catalonia, England, and Slavonia, and of Saint Bartholomew’s and the other houses very far from Carthusian, are not to be carried out except in leap years, unless the chapter or the prior of Carthusian should at some time judge otherwise necessary.

[Col. 1135C] 17. Whoever is convicted or confesses to an unspeakable act of incontinence is to be consigned to perpetual imprisonment without hope of release.

18. Each house of our order is to have a sufficient prison in which criminals may be confined to do penance, as well as anyone who threatens death or fire, until the chapter makes another provision concerning them. In incarcerating the aforesaid criminals, subjects are bound to obey their priors or vicars, or the visitors.

19. The prior of Carthusian may reconcile any criminals to the order, while preserving the discipline of the order, in order to avoid scandal and danger to souls; and their own prior may likewise do so at the point of death.

[Col. 1135D] 20. Fugitives found without letters from the prior of Carthusian or from their own priors may lawfully be seized by any priors of the order.

21. The definitors of fugitives are not to involve themselves in the reconciliation or discipline of fugitives who come to the chapter for the sake of reconciliation; this belongs to the definitors of the general chapter.

22. The general chapter, by the fullness of power it possesses, may for a reasonable cause place any person of the order in any house of the order, even for the purpose of making profession.

23. If someone has once professed in one house of the order and professes again in another, it is sufficient for his profession that he promise obedience to the prior in the convent.

24. On the octave of the Nativity of the Lord, the preface of the Nativity, the *Communicantes*, and the *Hanc igitur* are to be said.

25. When the Apparition of the Lord occurs on a Sunday, a commemoration of the Sunday is made, and the antiphons are *Cum factus esset*, etc. (“When he had been made,” etc.).

26. After the lessons from the prophets, when they end with *Explicit* (“Here ends”), *Tu autem, Domine* (“But you, Lord”) is to be said.

27. On the feast of the Finding of Saint Stephen, the antiphons and responsories are to be said as on the octave of his Nativity.

28. On Wednesdays and Fridays of the Lenten fasts, after the other prayers, the prayer *Omnipotens, qui vivorum* (“Almighty [God], who [are God] of the living”) is to be said.

[Col. 1136B] 29. At Masses for the dead at which, according to the order, the tract *De profundis* (“Out of the depths”) should be said, the introit *Requiem aeternam* (“Eternal rest”) is to be said.

30. Every week throughout the entire year two brief prayers are to be said, and no more, until the general chapter, unless several persons should die in one house in a single week, or some other just cause should exist. After the general chapter, more are to be said if those mentioned above should not suffice.

31. Priors are not bound to follow the advice of lay brothers in receiving others, unless they see that it is expedient.

32. Lay brothers and lay affiliates are to receive Communion on the day of their profession.

33. Guests staying at the house of Plantata are not to request anything there beyond what was promised by those of Saint Robert.

34. When standing in the upper church, lay brothers and lay affiliates are to imitate the monks.

35. The number of laymen whom we call lay brothers is fixed at thirteen. Two of the lay affiliates may be clerics and may enter the monks’ choir, even without a cowl; perform the monks’ office except for Masses; attend chapter; and eat in the monks’ refectory, whenever their priors grant them this favor in the matters mentioned above.

36. Lay affiliates are to eat in the refectory with the lay brothers at the time when those lay affiliates themselves eat in the upper house.

37. Henceforth no nun may be elected prioress unless she is thirty years of age. In every house of nuns, the prioress is to promise obedience to the vicar, and the nuns only to the prioress. The monks who are in any house of nuns, as well as chaplains, lay brothers, and lay affiliates, are to promise obedience only to the vicar.

38. Chaplains, clerics, and lay affiliates living with monks or nuns are to observe the order of fasts prescribed above for nuns and monks.

39. We declare that observing the order means being content on Monday and Wednesday with bread, wine, and cooked food; on Tuesday and Saturday, with bread, wine, and cooked food without a *pittantia* (a supplementary dish); on Friday, with bread and water; and on chapter feasts and Thursday, as do the others, according to obligation.

[Col. 1137A] 40. As soon as the *Sanctus* begins, the hood is to be put on.

41. When several tricenaries are begun together, each has its own Mass and proper prayer, and afterward they are to be added together in the plural prayer.

42. All carpets and painted or ornamental tiles are to be removed from the cells.

43. Ornamental paintings are to be erased from the churches and guesthouses.

44. It is established that henceforth no one of our order may be appointed prior until he has lived commendably in our order for two years from the time of his profession.

45. Novices who come to our order are to provide themselves with clothing, if they have the means.

[Col. 1137B] 46. A priest who cannot celebrate Mass is to be considered useless in the convent.

47. Priors are to receive a clerical lay affiliate after consulting the monks.

48. The statute that henceforth the boundaries marked out and written down in the customary manner by two priors be brought to the next chapter, there reasonably examined by all the definitors, approved and sealed, and from that point possess binding force, is approved and confirmed.

49. If a mount should die while a visitation is being made, the compensation is not to exceed fifteen pounds; if it is worth less, the compensation is to be reduced.

50. No house is to have a colloquy except on a feast of twelve lessons.

[Col. 1137C] 51. We exhort and wish that priors whose convents are divided because of poverty receive no novices in the meantime without the permission of the prior of Carthusian or of the general chapter.

52. The admonition is to be effective and strict, so that no prior or other person of the order obstinately appropriate books or anything else to himself through the usufruct granted to him.

53. Anyone who has been reconciled to the order, even if he dies and is buried elsewhere, does not lack the benefit of the order.

54. The procurators of the order in the upper house are neither to give nor able to give anything without special permission, unless it is expressly granted to them in the statutes.

[Col. 1137D] 55. Those who wish to open the choir door are to have the door partly open at the elevation; it is to be opened only at the elevation and closed afterward.

56. Since the common good is to be preferred to ownership, henceforth no one is to advise, counsel, or arrange that alms be assigned for a supplementary dish, infirmary, sacristy, or anything of that kind.

57. We admonish that monks are not to carry drink outside, nor are priors or visiting guests to be trusted in this matter; the fathers of the houses are to discourage the practice as far as they can.

58. We strictly order and irrevocably wish to be observed that lay brothers and lay affiliates who henceforth appeal to secular lords, complaining and denouncing, personally or through another, the orders or corrections imposed upon them, are to lose their house forever; monks, however, are to lose their voice forever.

59. If anyone wishes to leave the order, or persuades another to leave, he is to be deprived of his voice forever by the visitors.

60. We order that when two persons are in a cell, with the first door completely open, the second door is in no way to be locked.

61. We order and wish in every way that clerical lay affiliates, in those cases in which lay brothers lose their beards and cells, now also be punished in this way: they are never to wear any cowl except a gray one; they are to have hoods in the manner of novices; and they are to receive only half a loaf of the monks’ bread together with the household bread. We say the same, in their own manner, concerning lay affiliates who are laymen.

[Col. 1138B] 62. We order and wish in every way that each house keep deposits under two or three locks, one key to be kept by the prior and the other key or keys by those to whom the prior decides to entrust them.

63. We establish that the association of a tricenary is to be made on the first anniversary after the beginning of the tricenary.

64. We do not believe that clerical lay affiliates are bound to psalters.

65. At the altar, when the priest turns toward the people, he is to join his hands and not draw them back to his breast at *Dominus vobiscum* (“The Lord be with you”).

66. Novice lay brothers and lay affiliates may be sent outside the boundaries for the benefit of their house.

67. Lay brothers are to call one another “brothers”; whoever does otherwise is to receive pardon.

68. Neither monks nor lay brothers are henceforth to presume to keep or engrave seals; those who possess them are bound to return them immediately.

69. Whenever someone is appointed a novice, for purposes of the discipline of the novices he is understood to be the last of those whom he finds, unless something else is expressly stated.

70. When it happens that a commemoration is to be made on the feast of the Trinity, it is to be made from the Easter office.

71. We wish and admonish that visitors remain vigilant and attentive, and that they not send guests where they know that three guests are already present.

72. The stole is to be worn not *concellata* [term uncertain], but uniformly.

[Col. 1138D] 73. As far as they can, visitors are to take care that their lay brothers and servants do not learn or investigate and reveal the faults and manner of visitation of the houses they are going to visit.

74. Those who henceforth wish to propose anything to the general chapter are to submit it in writing, in brief terms, and hand it to the reader.

75. Chaplains and clerics living with monks and nuns are to observe the order of fasts as do the nuns and monks. They have temporal benefits like lay brothers, and spiritual benefits like monks, and they are bound to render them for others just as the monks themselves are.

76. No supplementary dish is to be given to monks in the refectory at the supper of the eve of abstinence from meat, nor to lay brothers in their cells.

77. If the feast of the Holy Cross falls on a Sunday, a commemoration is to be made first of the Sunday, then of the octave of Mary, and afterward of the martyrs.

78. Anyone who has made profession in our order, left it, and later returned is not to make profession again, but is immediately to promise obedience.

79. Non-priest monks are to say one psalter for the tricenary granted to those who are not of the house.

80. On the Saturday of the fasts, the prior is to read the fifth lesson, even if he celebrated in the morning.

81. At the request of visiting priors, unless the priors themselves are present, no supplementary dish is to be given to monks on the days granted by the order, nor are they to leave the house for the purpose of taking a walk.

82. It is ordered that novices, after the lesson has been read in chapter and the matters to be proposed by the prior have been presented, be immediately excluded from the chapter, and entirely excluded from the general chapter.

83. The prayer for the vigil of Saint Andrew and that of the feast of Saint Sylea are to be said twice consecutively.

84. Those who knowingly disobey the visitors cannot be absolved by their own priors.

85. Wherever visitors find that monks customarily eat outside the enclosures of the houses, they are to rebuke and punish the custom.

86. The secrets of the order are not to be revealed.
