87. The order believes that the statute of the Council of Lyon does not prevent us from bowing whenever the name of Jesus is heard; it is to be done as before.

[Col. 1139C] 88. No nun is to be sent from her house by visitors except for the establishment of a new foundation, and then only with the permission of the prior of Carthusian or of the general chapter.

89. Monks who have been sent, and those who will henceforth be sent, to houses of the order to make profession are to make it within one month.

90. Priors who are relieved of guests are bound to provide them with the necessary expenses.

91. The Mass of benefactors is to be rendered on a feast of twelve lessons, even while a tricenary is in progress.

92. On whatever day the octave of the Apparition occurs, if the responsory *Domine, ne in ira* (“Lord, do not rebuke [me] in your anger”), etc., cannot otherwise be said, that octave is to be celebrated on the preceding Saturday.

93. We order and wish that henceforth secular prebendaries not be received into the order without the permission of the general chapter or of the prior of Carthusian, granted for a year.

94. All manual games are to be avoided by persons of the order.

95. Servants are not to be permitted to leave the authority of Carthusian while the general chapter is sitting, nor are their priors to give them money for drinking.

96. We order and wish that if any persons from the Mendicant Order have been received, or are received—which is scarcely to be done—they may not hold an obedience without the permission of the general chapter.

97. The prior of Green Valley is granted a third cleric.

[Col. 1140A] 98. We prohibit lay brothers and lay affiliates from henceforth riding in black fields [or, according to the printed variant, “in black cowls”].

99. Priors are enjoined, under the virtue of holy obedience, and commanded not to presume to give their parents or relatives anything from the goods of the house without consent, lest the house be burdened.

100. We declare and wish that henceforth no prior receive anyone into the order without the consent and will of his convent or of the greater part of it.

101. We order that lay affiliates, both clerical and lay, be bound to silence: sometimes because of the place, as in the church, refectory, at table, or in the cloister; sometimes because of the persons present, as when they are with persons bound to silence.

[Col. 1140B] 102. Concerning the feasts of Saints Benedict, Hugh, and Ambrose, whenever they occur during Eastertide, nothing is to be changed: everything is to be done as before Easter with respect to the homilies, Gospels, and epistles, both at Mass and at matins.

103. Visitors may not send guests outside the province they are visiting, unless they send them to the house in which they most recently made profession.

104. The statute concerning the veiling of nuns who have held and relinquished offices is approved and confirmed.

105. We enjoin upon the visitors of the order that they not hesitate to enjoin priors to ask for mercy whenever they see a reasonable cause appearing, and especially those whom they see to be obstinate in this matter.

[Col. 1140C] 106. It is to be prudently established that any subject monk, lay brother, or lay affiliate who commits the crime of theft, alienation, or ownership exceeding the value of three solidi, and does not confess it to his own prior at least at the times established in the statutes, incurs by that very fact the sentence of excommunication. Priors—or, in their absence, vicars in their houses—are to announce this sentence, issued by the general chapter, every year on Palm Sunday. It is added that priors may absolve as before, and vicars until the prior’s arrival.

107. It is established that any lay brother who henceforth commits the sin of incontinence is to lose his house forever and be reduced to the status of a lay affiliate with respect to food and beard; he is also to lose his cell, without hope of dispensation.

108. Likewise, anyone who defames his prior, or causes harm to the house by urging creditors to recover debts, exhorting anyone to seize the goods of the house, or inflicting other damage, loses his cell.

109. The same is to be observed concerning those convicted of theft and ownership.

110. The statute concerning the food of lay brothers is to remain in force: concerning two [lacuna] loaves and oat bread, and concerning wine being given only at the times established, the form contained in the statutes is to be firmly observed. Thus, notwithstanding contrary customs in some houses, the aforesaid statute is henceforth to be followed, unless the priors, having considered the character of the region, the persons, and the houses, decide to dispense mercifully with it. If, however, on this account or for another they withdraw from their work, work less faithfully, or perform [lacuna], and this becomes known to the prior or procurator, and they do not correct themselves after being admonished, the prior, with the counsel of his convent or of the greater part of it, is to send them to the prior of Carthusian to be supported elsewhere.

111. Since lay brothers and lay affiliates are received chiefly for the salvation of souls and for work, and some refuse to work with their own hands, we establish that anyone who is reproved for this by the prior or procurator and does not amend after being admonished is to be deprived of wine [Col. 1141B] and of the supplementary dish for as long as the prior sees fit, unless evident necessity excuses him.

112. Lay brothers are not to ride within the boundaries of their houses unless they are so weak and ill that they cannot walk; nor are they to ride outside except according to what is written in the statutes.

113. Whenever they wish, or at least once a month, the prior and procurator are diligently to visit and inspect the cells and workshops of the lay brothers, and the lay brothers themselves are bound to explain everything to them. If any lay brother has become accustomed to store and keep in his cell food beyond what is permitted and owed, and does not correct himself after being admonished, he is to be deprived of his cell forever. Henceforth they are not to have clandestine locks, under the penalty contained in the statutes. They may have locks on the outer door if the prior considers this expedient; whenever they leave the house, they are to hand its key to the cook. Whoever fails to do this is to go without wine and the supplementary dish on the next day on which wine and the supplementary dish are given.

114. We exhort priors to be exceedingly vigilant and attentive in correcting lay brothers, and they are not bound to follow the advice of lay brothers in receiving them.

[Col. 1142A] 115. To the statute that lay brothers are to call one another “brothers” is added that anyone who acts otherwise is to confess his fault in the following chapter and receive discipline without mercy.

116. The newly made statutes are to be read to the lay brothers immediately after the sermon by the person whom the prior appoints, four times a year or more often if the prior sees fit.

117. Unproductive, remote, and sterile lands may for a time be given in emphyteusis, with the consent of the convents, as seems appropriate. If, however, any lay brothers openly or secretly attempt to impede the aforesaid arrangement, and this can be proved, they are to be made lay affiliates.

118. We further order that the aforesaid statutes be immediately approved and confirmed.

119. Concerning the three persons whom the prior of Carthusian could, for a year, admit by dispensation beyond the number of thirteen lay brothers, for houses that were in great need, we order that those three persons henceforth be received among the lay affiliates. It is added that if any person should appear to be very necessary and useful to the houses, the aforesaid prior, having considered the person’s qualities, may dispense with one or two of those three so that they may become lay brothers.

120. We wish in every way that the aforesaid statutes be observed and confirmed in the following chapter.

121. These statutes are to be read four times a year to all the lay brothers and lay affiliates gathered in their chapter, namely on the feast of the Purification, Saint John’s, and the Assumption of the Blessed Mary.

**NOTE.** Although these statutes have the year 1261 prefixed to them, not all of them ought to have been issued in that year; some were issued in subsequent years. This is clear from statute 87, in which mention is made of a decree issued at the Council of Lyon.

# VI. STATUTES ISSUED IN THE GENERAL CHAPTER OF THE CARTHUSIAN ORDER IN THE YEAR 1289

[Col. 1141]

[Col. 1141C] 1. In the year of the Lord 1289, we newly establish that every house of the order may have two clerical lay affiliates who are included among the seven lay affiliates.

2. Likewise, priors are to pay for persons associated with the houses as they do for their own persons, unless a mutual agreement provides otherwise.

3. Likewise, we newly establish that henceforth the boundaries marked out and written down in the customary manner by two priors be brought to the following chapter, and there, after reasonable examination by all the definitors, be approved and sealed; from that point they are to possess binding force.

4. Likewise, we newly establish that priors and procurators who are found guilty, through negligence or in another way, of the escape of prisoners are to confess their fault in the following chapter and, if the chapter judges it deserved, be deprived of their obediences. Others who caused the escape are henceforth not to have obediences and are to undergo the punishment of the escapee.

5. Likewise, we newly establish that if monks, lay brothers, or lay affiliates convicted or confessing to incontinence should at some time be reconciled to the order, this is in no way to take place in the houses in which they were convicted, except in a perpetual prison. If they are brought out of that prison, they are in no way to remain there, but are to be placed elsewhere under suitable discipline.

6. Likewise, since considerable scandal has arisen among important people in this land on account of silver cups carried away by certain priors, we strictly prohibit anyone of the order from henceforth carrying them outside the houses.

7. Likewise, we newly establish that visitors who happen to die within any house of the order are to have the status of monks there; and if they die nearby, they are to have a tricenary in the house in which they are buried.

8. Likewise, we prohibit anyone from personally obtaining, or causing to be obtained, from princes or any others letters of petition on his own behalf.

9. Likewise, we decree that the association of the thirty-day service be made on the first anniversary after the beginning of the thirty-day service.

[Col. 1144A] 10. Likewise, in response to certain words of the prior of Vallis S. Petri, it is answered that it was not granted by way of statute that the prior of Carthus could compel by ecclesiastical censure those houses that owed him anything; and therefore the statute need not be revoked, since there is none.

11. Likewise, the house of Belli Laris shall henceforth be called Bellus Locus.

## VII. STATUTES ISSUED IN THE YEAR 1290

[Col. 1143]

[Col. 1143A] 1. In the year of the Lord 1290, the statute concerning having two clerics and eating in the refectory with the monks is approved.

2. Likewise, if the feast of the Chair of Saint Peter falls during Lent, its Mass shall be said in the morning, unless it falls on Saturday or Sunday.

3. Likewise, whoever gives the cause of escape to prisoners shall lose his obediences and shall take the place of the escaped prisoner for as long as the general chapter wishes.

[Col. 1144A] 4. Likewise, the statute that monks, converts, or returned members convicted of incontinence, if at some time they should be reconciled to the order, are in no way to be reconciled in the principal houses or in those in which they were convicted, except to perpetual imprisonment, etc., as above, is approved and confirmed.

5. Likewise, the statute concerning giving a brief to those who have participation is confirmed.

## VIII. STATUTES OF THE YEAR 1291

[Col. 1143]

[Col. 1143B] 1. In the year of the Lord 1291, by authority of the general chapter, through definers appointed by it concerning a dispute that existed in the order, on account of a letter obtained from Lord Pope Gregory X, the following were granted to the present prior of Carthus and to all who should be priors in the future: complete power in the penitential forum to hear the confessions of priors and to absolve those who wished to confess to him. Likewise, that he may grant mercy to priors who request it for a year, if he sees that it should be granted for a just or useful reason. Likewise, that wherever matters of the order are discussed, he shall have a double vote for the strict observance of the order. Likewise, that any prior of Carthus may, only once during his entire tenure, send two of his monks to other houses of that order, with the consent of the persons themselves and of the convent of the said house, if it should happen that a good person came to the said house of Carthus and could not be received there because of the large number of monks.

## IX. NEW STATUTES OF THE GENERAL CHAPTER

[Col. 1143]

[Col. 1143C] 1. Profession shall not be made by novices unless the prior is present.

2. Those received who arrive at the appointed term, if the prior is absent and very far away, shall nevertheless be clothed and tonsured by the convent.

[Col. 1143D] 3. The visitation of Scala Dei shall take place in a leap year.

4. It has been granted to the houses of Scala Dei, England, Saint Bartholomew, Ireland, and Sclavonia that the vicar, together with the senior monk, may confirm the election of a prior by the convent, if the prior who could be summoned to confirm the election is not in those regions.

5. Priors are enjoined to defend themselves by means of the privilege granted exempting them from the payment of tithes.

6. After Compline, the antiphon *Sancta Maria* and the prayer *Concede nos* shall be said.

[Col. 1144C] 7. From the fourth day before the Nones of November until Septuagesima, we say the Office for the Dead in the cell, apart from Lauds, after None or after Vespers on feasts of thirteen lessons. On ferial days, however, after Vespers we say the proper or special office with three antiphons and nine lessons, while the daily office is said with the first antiphon and three lessons. It should be understood that during the aforesaid period the first three lessons are said on Sundays, and so forth, in order.

[Note: [Col. 1143D] *Agenda* means the Office for the Dead.]

8. The prior of Carthus may change the visitors for a reason.

9. The Body of the Lord shall be kept in the lower chapel under lock, with whomever it may please, provided that it is renewed every week, if this can conveniently be done. The Mass of Blessed Mary on Saturdays, on the feasts of the chapter, and on the feast of the Candles shall be said privately, except on the days of the Nativity of the Lord, Holy Saturday, and the four feasts of Blessed Mary.

[Col. 1145A] 10. In the absence of the prior, the vicar shall say *Benedicite* even to visiting priors from outside.

11. For a thirty-day service that is being begun, the anniversary may be transferred.

12. Agriculture shall not be carried on in the *agirelaria*.

13. In place of three useless persons, three useful persons may be received, provided that the established number is not exceeded.

14. Novices may celebrate private Masses and serve at them at the prior’s discretion.

15. No one shall presume to argue or play openly or privately with the prior, according to the Rule of Saint Benedict.

[Col. 1145B] 16. The private chapter shall compel the person on whose account it is summoned to pay the expenses incurred in it.

17. At the burial of lay returned members, there shall be no meal in the refectory, nor shall the monks keep vigil, unless the person should die in the upper house.

18. The prior shall not cease from his office on the feast of the Relics of the lower church because of frailty, [Note: [Col. 1145] That is, because of nocturnal illusion, on account of which the monks of old customarily abstained from celebrating,] just as he does not cease on the feast of its dedication.

19. On the feasts of the Purification and the Annunciation, *Gloria in excelsis* shall be said whenever they occur.

20. Without the advice of the procurator, vicar, and sacristan, the prior may not lend more than ten pounds, whether all at once or in portions.

21. The prayers in the Masses shall not exceed the number seven, unless the necessity of the prayers requires it.

[Col. 1145C] 22. The dedication shall not be transferred except because of the feast of the Candles; and then it shall be celebrated with all its solemnity, and there shall be a meal in the refectory. Nevertheless, the converts and the household may work.

23. When a vigil falls on a Sunday, a fast shall be observed and the commemoration of Saturday shall be made.

24. A sick person shall sit in his place in the church, or stand if he wishes; he shall not move to the lower place.

25. A meal shall be eaten in the refectory at the burial of prelates.

26. For a thirty-day service or psalter, clerics or non-priest monks shall say fifty psalms, and laymen fifty *Our Fathers*.

27. When a returned cleric becomes a monk, he shall be tested in his own habit with the cowl.

[Col. 1145D] 28. Within the octave of the Apparition, Ascension, Assumption, and Nativity of Blessed Mary, the ferial *Kyrie eleison* shall be said without *Gloria in excelsis*, unless it is Saturday or a feast of twelve lessons.

29. The prior ought to say the first Mass of every thirty-day service, if he is prepared, even if he is the weekly celebrant.

30. On the feast of the relics and dedication of the lower church, the fast shall not be broken. Likewise, the fast shall not be broken on account of guests.

31. For an archbishop or bishop, the prayer *Da nobis, Domine, ut animam famuli tui sacerdotis et pontificis*—“Grant us, Lord, that the soul of your servant, priest and bishop”—shall be said, and so forth.

[Col. 1146A] 32. All monks shall be buried with a hair shirt, tunic, cowl, stockings, and foot coverings.

33. No convert shall serve at Masses.

34. When it happens that two feasts are transferred, the office of the greater feast shall be held on the first day and the other on the following day; and if an anniversary falls on that day, it shall not be impeded by the transfer.

35. All who threaten death or fire, or anything similar, against any person of the order may be imprisoned at the discretion of their superiors.

36. The Mass of the Chair of Saint Peter on Ash Wednesday and thereafter shall be said by the weekly celebrant, unless it falls on Saturday or Sunday; and the tract shall not be said in it.

37. If a prior relinquishing the priory does not find a vacant place in his own house, the prior may place him in the guesthouse or in a cell, and remove another monk from the cell and place him in the guesthouse, with the monk’s peace and good will.

[Col. 1146B] 38. When the Annunciation of the Lord is celebrated after Easter, the responsory *Prope est Dominus, alleluia. Surrexit Dominus*—“The Lord is near, alleluia. The Lord has risen”—shall be said.

39. Novices shall be excluded from chapter if it seems good to the prior.

40. Converts shall call themselves “brothers”; whoever acts otherwise shall receive a penance.

41. Whenever *In unitate Spiritus sancti Deus*—“In the unity of the Holy Spirit, God”—is said in any prayer, when *Deus in adiutorium*—“O God, come to my aid”—is subsequently to be said, we shall rise at *Misericors Dominus*—“The merciful Lord”—with *In unitate*, and so forth.

42. It is decreed that no one may appeal except to the general chapter; one who appeals justly may not be excommunicated, and a sentence of excommunication issued against someone who appeals justly shall not be valid. Otherwise, the appellant may be imprisoned.

[Col. 1146C] 43. Newly celebrating priests shall not descend from the altar step to receive the offerings.

44. One convicted or confessing to any kind of incontinence, if it happens that he is reconciled, may never be elected prior.

45. Returned clerics shall enjoy the same privilege as converts with respect to provisions, eating in the refectory, and coming when summoned.

46. The feast of Blessed Dionysius may be celebrated with chapter in the houses of our order in the kingdom of France.

47. The word *Litium*, in the plural, shall uniformly be pronounced with *t*.

[Col. 1146D] 48. When two feasts of the Candles immediately follow one another, Vespers of the subsequent feast shall begin with the chapter, except for those cases concerning which the contrary has been expressly enacted.

49. The declaration that, from Easter onward, a double *Alleluia* is to be said in the Office of Blessed Mary is approved, except on the feast of the Annunciation when it is celebrated after Easter, on which the responsory *Prope est Dominus* is said.

50. The statute concerning the construction of prisons is approved. Falsifiers, arsonists, murderers, those who threaten death or fire, vagrants throughout the world, and the others concerning whom it is written and decreed shall be confined in them.

[Col. 1147A] 51. From Quinquagesima until Easter, the fast shall not be broken for any feast.

52. It is decreed that priors shall not allow monks, converts, or professed returned members, for any reason, to keep money set aside or to be set aside for their own or others’ use.

53. It is decreed that whoever lightly says, “I would sooner leave the order than do or omit this or that,” or words equivalent to these, shall, if he is a prior, remain outside his seat in the church for one day; if he is a subordinate, he shall receive discipline in chapter for each occurrence.

54. By the command and decree of the order, priors shall be bound to receive and bring, at the appropriate time, to the general chapter or to the prior of Carthus the reports of the convents, according to the statutes of the order; otherwise, they should know that they will be punished.

[Col. 1147B] 55. The sentence of excommunication issued on Palm Sunday by the prior, in the presence of the monks, converts, and returned members, shall be pronounced in writing.

56. In the Mass, at *Gloria in excelsis* and at *Credo*, a slight bow shall be made at the name of Jesus.

57. We reject fox-fur garments and garments made from wild animals, as well as elaborate and folded footwear; henceforth they shall not be kept.

58. In every Mass to be celebrated for the living, *Omnipotens qui vivorum*—“Almighty God, who [are the God] of the living”—shall be said by each celebrant.

59. Priors may give vicars authority to absolve, in their absence, from any sin; nevertheless, in the case of a certain mortal sin—which may it not happen—he must confess it again to the prior.

[Col. 1147C] 60. The feast of Blessed Magdalene shall be celebrated solemnly with candles; nevertheless, *Credo* shall not be said, nor shall the deacon receive Communion. On the feast itself the proper prayer is *Largire*; at Sext, *Deus qui nos annua*; and at None, *Exaudi*.

61. Simple monks, clerics, or our returned members who come to chapter shall leave chapter after presenting their petitions and shall not return unless summoned, for as long as business is being conducted there. It is granted to every prior of Carthus who shall hold office at the time that, during his tenure, he may receive three monks of the order from the houses of the order, with the peace of the person called, and admit them to profession in the house of Carthus. When one thirty-day service coincides with another thirty-day service for a priest, *Da nobis*—“Grant us”—shall be said for the one being begun, and for the preceding one *Deus cui proprium est ... famuli et sacerdotis tui*—“O God, to whom it belongs ... of your servant and priest.” They are then brought into the plural, namely: *Da nobis, Domine, ut animas*—“Grant us, Lord, that the souls,” and so forth.

62. Converts who are found to have shaved their *grennones* with a razor, contrary to the form of the order, shall abstain from wine on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday until the next shaving.

[Note: [Col. 1147] *Grenones* or *graniones* are the part of the beard that is beneath the nostrils.]

Priors and procurators who, after learning of this, have not caused it to be observed shall abstain from wine once a week until the next shaving, in addition to the abstinences established by the order.

[Col. 1148A] 63. The statutes concerning the number of converts, reduced to thirteen, are confirmed, with the addition that, in a great necessity, the prior of Carthus may grant a dispensation for one year, or the general chapter, together with the house in need, may grant one up to sixteen.

64. Whoever conceals from the visitors things that ought to be revealed to them may not be absolved by his priors unless a penance of seven consecutive abstinences is imposed on him, on the assigned days of abstinence, in addition to the abstinences owed. They shall cause this punishment to be observed carefully and diligently.

65. The statute that priors found guilty through negligence or otherwise concerning the escape of prisoners is confirmed in certain charters.

[Col. 1148B] After the word “prisoners,” the following is added: they shall lose their obediences, and their subordinates shall be subject to the same punishment and shall take the place of the escaped person for as long as it seems good to the general chapter. At the following chapter they shall proclaim their guilt, and, if the chapter judges it appropriate, they shall be punished most severely. Others, however, who gave the cause of the escape shall henceforth have no obediences and shall take the place of the escaped person for as long as the chapter wishes. Procurators shall do and receive the same before the visitors or through them. This is approved and confirmed.

66. The statute that priors must keep any subordinate convicted or confessing to any crime for which, according to the statutes of the order, persons are customarily expelled entirely from the order, in a narrow prison until the general chapter or the general or special visitors, so that the opportunity for wandering may henceforth be cut off, is approved and confirmed. Subordinates are bound to obey in this matter.

[Col. 1148C] 67. The statute that monks, converts, and returned members convicted of incontinence, if at some time they should be reconciled, are in no way to be reconciled in the principal houses or in those in which they were convicted, except to perpetual imprisonment—and, if they are removed from it, they shall in no way remain there but shall be placed elsewhere under due discipline—is approved and confirmed.

68. The regulation that returned clerics may not read the Gospel without the permission of their priors, nor eat in the refectory, nor attend chapter without the aforesaid command, is approved and confirmed.

[Col. 1148D] 69. The statute that nuns must pay the order’s briefs and Masses—namely, one psalter for one Mass—and that we shall act for them according to the statutes of the order, as for other persons of our order, is approved and confirmed. For thirty-day services, each shall pay fifty psalms, like non-priest monks.

70. The statute that the lay sisters of the nuns who are received henceforth shall not wear a black veil, and that if any nun is henceforth convicted of incontinence, she shall, among her other punishments, be deprived of the black veil forever, without any hope of recovering it, is approved and confirmed.

[Col. 1149A] 71. The statute that nuns shall have bands on their scapulars in the manner of monks, but lay sisters shall not, is approved and confirmed.

## X. STATUTES OF THE YEAR 1332

[Col. 1149]

[Col. 1149A] 1. In the year 1332, those who have not constructed a prison in their houses before the arrival of the first visitors shall proclaim their faults at the next general chapter.

2. The feasts of the apostles Peter and Paul, John, both Jameses, Andrew, Philip, Thomas, Bartholomew, Matthew, Simon and Jude, and Matthias, of the four Evangelists, and of the four Doctors shall be celebrated once a year with chapter; and on that account they shall not cease from their business more than usual, nor shall those occupied with work go up to the upper area.

3. The priors of the order shall everywhere wear split shoes and completely black capes; they shall not lie between two sheets, nor shall two people serve guests, nor shall they ever set more than two dishes on the table after the kitchen.

[Col. 1149B] 4. A monk shall be elected by the confirmers to go outside to summon the elected prior.

[Col. 1150A] 5. Whoever has become accustomed to uttering undisciplined or contentious words in conversations shall, at the discretion of his priors, be excluded from conversations.

6. Henceforth no monk shall ever go to the general chapter with the prior.

7. The priors and vicars of the nuns shall obtain for themselves the Legend that is read at Carthus in October and throughout the octave of the Eucharist.

8. Monks summoned to new houses shall immediately make profession there.

[Col. 1150B] 9. Priors writing to one another shall say, “Venerable” or “beloved Father.”

10. Letters concerning the summoning of monks or other persons of the order shall have no validity beyond three years.

## ADDENDA

### IN THE YEAR 1125, MASTER LAMBERT, PRIOR OF THE CARTHUSIAN HOUSE OF SQUILLACE

[Col. 1149]

### NOTICE

(Mabillon, *Annales Benedictini*, vol. VI, book LXXIII, no. 92, from the archive of the Grande Chartreuse.)

In Calabria, after Lanuinus had properly exercised for nearly seventeen years the office of prior or master at the house of Squillace—for that is what superiors were called at that time—he is recorded as having died in this year (1119). Lanuinus is called blessed; his relics are said to be preserved mixed together with the relics of Saint Bruno. Some place his successor as Master Secherus; others identify him as Lambert, who first issued statutes both for the hermits and for the cenobites who lived at Mentauri, not far from Squillace, in the monastery of Saint Stephen.

[Col. 1149]

### STATUTES OF MASTER LAMBERT

(Mabillon, same work, vol. VI, appendix, p. 638.)

[Col. 1149B] **For the hermits.** Let those in the cells maintain continuous fasting and continuous silence, as it was better maintained in the days of Master Bruno.

**For the cenobites.** In the lower monastery, however, it was established that silence should be maintained as it is maintained in regular monasteries during Lent, namely on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday.

[Col. 1150B] **Likewise, for the hermits.** If a feast day falls during Advent, the brothers shall not eat more than once, except on Sundays.

From the Ides of September, therefore, until Advent, Master Bruno established that fasting customarily be observed on Wednesday and Friday with bread and water. On Monday and Saturday the brothers have one dish and wine; on Tuesday and Thursday, two dishes with a portion, if there is anything available.

From Advent, after cheese and eggs have first been put aside, until Christmas, on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday they shall have bread and water; on Saturday they shall have wine and one dish; on Tuesday and Thursday, two dishes and wine.

From Christmas until the octave, they shall eat twice in the refectory, as is customary everywhere. From the octave of the Lord until the octave of Epiphany, the brothers shall eat once in their cells, except on Epiphany and on feasts of twelve lessons.

From the octave of Epiphany until the beginning of the fasts, on Wednesday and Friday they shall have bread and water; during Septuagesima, after cheese and eggs have been put aside, they shall eat once on solemnities, except on the feast of Blessed Mary of the Candles [lacuna].

From the beginning of the fasts, they shall have bread and water three days a week until Easter, except on the day of the Lord’s Supper and on the other feasts on which they ought to eat in the refectory.

From Easter until the octave, the brothers shall eat twice in the refectory, as on the feast days of the Nativity of the Lord.

From the octave of Easter until Pentecost, the brothers shall eat once on four days of the week, with wine and a dish and some portion, if there is anything available; on Tuesday and Thursday they shall eat twice, except on the Greater Litany and the Rogation Days, on which the brothers ought to eat once.

[Col. 1152A] On the feast of the octave of Pentecost, the brothers shall eat in the refectory as on the paschal feast, except during the Ember fasts, when they shall eat once in the refectory, having cheese and eggs.

From the octave of Pentecost until the Ides of September, they shall eat twice on Tuesday and Thursday; on the remaining four days, they shall proceed as from the Ides of September until Advent.

It should be noted, however, that during this period the master—that is, the prior—acted more leniently toward the brothers according to the season, the labor, and the illnesses.

**Likewise, for the cenobites.** The brothers of Saint Stephen shall eat from Easter until Advent as Blessed Benedict commanded, except on the Rogation Days and the Greater Litany, when they shall eat once.

During Advent, on Friday they shall have bread and water; on Monday and Wednesday they shall have wine and one dish.

From Christmas until the octave of Epiphany, they shall eat twice, except on the vigil of Epiphany.

From the octave of Epiphany until Septuagesima, they shall eat once, except on feasts of twelve lessons.

At Septuagesima they shall give up cheese and eggs; likewise when Advent begins.

During Septuagesima they shall not eat twice on any feast, except the feast of Saint Mary.

During Lent they shall eat as during Advent.

When the master travels a short distance, he should make five riding journeys, or fewer if possible; if he travels far, seven or nine.

# INDEX TO THE WORKS OF SAINT BRUNO

Arabic numerals refer the reader to the boldfaced numbers inserted in the text; Roman numerals indicate the part or volume of the works of Saint Bruno.

## A

**Aaron.** “Mountainous” is his interpretation, I, 533. How he was chosen as pontiff, II, 374. His house: a collection of prelates, I, 456. The rod signifies the true priesthood, II, 391.

**Abba.** What it signifies, II, 47.

**Abimelech**, I, 99.

**Abraham.** Had two sons, II, 221. His faith is commended, II, 403.

**Absalom.** A figure of the traitor Judas, I, 7.

**Absolution.** No one can be absolved except through ministers, II, 311.

**Abundant.** Who are called abundant, I, 141.

**Abyss.** Excessive depth, I, 265.

**Achaia.** A province, II, 157.

**Accuse.** What it means, II, 50.

**Adam.** Is called evening, and why, I, 85. He corrupted everyone, II, 31. In him reason was not extinguished after sin but weakened, I, 129. He prefigured Christ, II, 32. Guardian of the Church, II, 32.

**Fat.** What it is, I, 121.

**Adoption.** Twofold, II, 48.

[Col. 1151] **Flattery.** Called oil, I, 560.

**Adulteress.** Prefigures the chaste person; the good [prefigures] the evil without injury, I, 168.

**Egypt.** Signifies darkness, I, 249, and affliction, I, 327.

**Rust.** Signifies lust, and why, I, 311.

**Summer.** Signifies the eternal harvest, I, 285.

**Affections.** Compared with feet, I, 36. Called by the name of hands, and why, I, 51; likewise, I, 75. Compared with lips, I, 265.

**Bodily affliction.** Of little usefulness, II, 325.

**Emulation.** A movement of the soul, II, 192.

**Hagar.** Whom she signifies, I, 11. What she signifies, II, 222.

**Wings.** For protection, I, 194. What they signify, I, 215.

**Alleluia.** Twice placed in the title of certain psalms, and why, I, 427.

**Foreigners.** Denote the Jews, I, 189.

**Alphabet.** Inscription at the dedication of a church, III, 16.

**Amalekites.** Whom they designate, I, 117.

[Col. 1152] **Walk according to the flesh.** II, 189.

**Andrew the Apostle.** His testimony concerning the Eucharist, I, 67.

**Angels.** Called mountains, and why, I, 364. Compared with winds, I, 537. Whether they speak among themselves, II, 136. Their names and offices will cease, II, 147.

**Soul.** Names of the soul, I, 89. Its two powers, I, 336. Its pavement is the flesh, I, 475. Its four principal virtues, I, 484. It is fattened by good works, I, 112. How it is said to have a face, I, 494. Its mouth, I, 552. Its excellence, I, 137. It sometimes designates the whole person, II, 71.

**Passions of the soul.** I, 133.

**Announce.** Said of the future, I, 187.

**Appetite.** Is different from understanding, I, 489.

**Apollo.** Archbishop of Corinth, II, 88.

**Apostles.** Called rams, I, 82. Called gods, and why, I, 153. Called heaven, I, 197. Wise enchanters, I, 99. Fountains of the Church, I, 247. Eyes of Christ, I, 251. Eyes of the Church, I, 350. Fecund, I, 317. Foundations, I, 346. Clouds, I, 386. Knees of Christ, I, 442. Towers, I, 517. Shakers-off, I, 524.

**Waters.** Signify peoples, I, 44. Why, I, 83. Signify prosperity, I, 234.

**Eagles.** Their cunning, I, 403. A type of the devil, I, 411.

**North wind.** The devil, I, 154. Its sides: the devil’s people, I, 154.

**Arabia.** What it signifies, I, 270; II, 222.

**Ark.** Compared with the Church, I, 532, 34. Designates the gentile people, I, 268.

**Bow.** For deception and cunning, I, 112, 151. For hidden defense, I, 138. For temporal tribulation, I, 210.

**Ram.** A rebellious animal, I, 235.

**Rams.** Leaders of the faithful, I, 454.

**Arian error.** I, 515.

**Weapons.** Signify open attack, I, 151. Miracles, II, 189.

**Asaphids.** [They signify] the Synagogue, I, 161, 286.

**Look upon.** For “love,” I, 235.

**Asp.** Cunning, I, 199.

**Atrium.** For spaciousness, I, 228.

**Author of the Epistle to the Hebrews.** 2.

**Hearing.** The understanding of the soul, I, 76.

**Ears.** For understanding, I, 126. The ear of God is called benevolence, I, 87. The power of God is mercy, I, 342.

**Gold.** Signifies perfection of the virtues, I, 146, and charity, I, 147.

**Excessive austerity.** Sometimes generates sin, II, 286.

**The miser.** Makes money his god, II, 249.

**Unleavened bread.** What it is, II, 102.

## B

**Baptism.** Spoken of in three ways, II, 377. The gate of salvation, I, 68. Called a flood, and why, I, 84. The sea, I, 301. For some an occasion of salvation, for others of perdition, I, 542. Through it all sins, including actual sins, are remitted, II, 32. Necessary for salvation even for children, II, 54. Removes sins, II, 280. Those baptized for the dead, II, 148.

**Aaron’s beard.** I, 535.

**Barbarians.** II, 9.

**Bar-Jonah.** Son of a dove, II, 97.

**Basilisk.** Kills by the stench of its breath, I, 371.

**Eternal blessedness.** Compared with spoils, I, 509.

**Blessed.** Who is called blessed, II, 314.

**Bless.** For “exalt,” I, 186.

**Bathsheba.** What she designates, I, 168.

**Temporal goods.** Called false madness, I, 126.

**Good.** Said in many ways, I, 179. Its two kinds, II, 177. What is unknown is loved less, II, 241. Every person is presumed good, 274. Good people are called divine, II, 10. We ought to emulate them, II, 220.

**Oxen.** Signify preachers, I, 22.

**Prize.** Called the reward of labor, II, 267.

## C

**Cancer.** The disease eventually kills, II, 304.

**Caesar and Pompey.** Did not wish to endure one another, II, 13.

**Reed.** Like a tongue, I, 148.

**Slander.** What it is, I, 499.

**Heel.** What it signifies, I, 158. It stands for the end and for a fall, I, 191.

**Dogs.** Talkative, I, 246.

**Song.** What it is, I, 9; II, 250.

XXVII.—On the voices and utterances which the soul hears spiritually; and how the soul was made in the image of God, what movement it receives, and of what movement it is not receptive. 848

XXVIII.—On those blessed spirits: specifically, what things pertain to them; and what the inhabitant of the cell ought to turn over within himself concerning them in his pure meditation. 850

XXIX.—On that kind of meditation which we ought to maintain within ourselves, in the innermost parts of our heart, when we strive to think about God; and how it is fitting and permissible for us to conceive of him. 855

XXX.—On the Trinity of Persons and the unity of the substance that is God, and that neither the Trinity does any harm to the unity nor the unity to the Trinity. 859

XXXI.—On the diligent care and careful diligence that we ought to devote to our prayer when we apply ourselves to it; and on the great instability by which, at the time of prayer, with our thoughts scattered through idle and harmful matters, we wretchedly and miserably fluctuate in our hearts and wander through innumerable things. 862

XXXII.—On the wandering of the mind, which we sense to be present in us during prayer; and how and why the devotion of prayer is to be understood through the third river that goes out from the place of delight, which is also called the Tigris. 864

XXXIII.—What sort of people we ought to show ourselves to be before approaching prayer, so that when we come to it we may offer it to God in such a way that he may mercifully make it both acceptable to himself and fruitful for us. 869

XXXIV.—That when we approach prayer, we ought from a pure heart to forgive those who have offended us, and, if there are any who hold something against us, to be fully and perfectly reconciled with them. 871

XXXV.—On the four kinds of thoughts which it is necessary for us to keep in mind if we wish to pray to the Lord purely, devoutly, and fruitfully. 875

XXXVI.—On manual work, to which the inhabitant of the cell ought to devote himself; at what hours he ought to engage in spiritual exercises and at what hours in manual work; and on several other matters pertaining to the same inhabitant of the cell. 880

BERNARD, PRIOR OF THE CHARTERHOUSE OF PORTES.

THREE LETTERS. 885

LETTER II.—To the nuns of Lyons.—He urges them courageously to undertake the stricter discipline they had recently adopted. 889

JOHN, MONK OF THE CHARTERHOUSE OF PORTES.

FIVE LETTERS. 899

LETTER II.—To Latoldus.—On the manner of praying. 913

LETTER IV.—To Berard.—On guarding the heart. 924

STEPHEN OF CHALMETO.

LETTER ON PERSEVERANCE IN THE ORDER to the novices of Saint-Sulpice of the Cistercian Order. 931

SAINT HUGH, BISHOP OF LINCOLN IN ENGLAND, OF THE CARTHUSIAN ORDER.

**Life of Hugh.**—Prefatory Notice. 937  
Dissertation on the year in which Saint Hugh was consecrated bishop of Lincoln. 939  
Here begins the Life.—Prologue. 943  

**BOOK ONE**

**Chapter 1.**—How Hugh, deprived of his mother’s consolation and associated with his father in a regular community of clerics, bore the Lord’s yoke from childhood; and Hugh’s own words concerning his childhood formation are inserted. 945

**Chapter 2.**—On his progress in knowledge and virtue, and how devoted and diligent he was in the divine offices and in the service of the brothers. 946

**Chapter 3.**—On the commendation of his father, and how humbly and devoutly our Hugh served him, having been specially assigned to his service. 947

**Chapter 4.**—How, after being ordained a Levite, he immediately instructed the people through his zeal for preaching, received the government of Saint Maximus’s cell, and ruled it commendably. The fifth chapter of the longer Life is included under this chapter. 948

**Chapter 5.**—How he carried out, in the case of a certain parishioner of that cell who had been accused of adultery, the evangelical command: “If your brother sins against you.” 950

**Chapter 6.**—How he visited the Grande Chartreuse with his prior and, having seen it, came to love it. 951

**Chapter 7.**—How, at the insistence of his prior, he pledged his faith by oath that, so long as the prior lived, he would in no way enter the Carthusian order; how he did not keep his pledge, yet had no scruple about violating his oath, and thereby made such great progress. 952

**Chapter 8.**—On the very grave temptation that seized him after he entered the Carthusian order; nevertheless, saving protection was not lacking for him. 954

**Chapter 9.**—On the commendation of the Carthusian order and the progress of our Hugh within it; how the elder to whose service he had been assigned tested him concerning the assumption of priestly orders and foretold that he would become a bishop. The tenth and eleventh chapters of the longer Life are included under this chapter. 956

**Chapter 10.**—On his progress in devotion after he became a priest, and on the rigor of bodily austerity and abstinence. 957

**Chapter 11.**—How, assigned to the service of Peter, archbishop of Tarentaise, he served most devoutly both in searching the Scriptures and in everything that could be fitting for reverence or pleasing to the spirit, receiving from him daily a blessing, absolution, and salutary instruction. 958

**Chapter 12.**—How, having been made procurator of the Carthusian house, he vigorously governed it both spiritually and temporally, making himself deservedly commended to all. 959

**Chapter 13.**—On another temptation of his, different from the one mentioned above in Chapter 8, and how he was freed from it by that former holy prior of the Grande Chartreuse, Basil, whom he called his foster father. This temptation is inserted in Book Two of the longer Life. 959

Prologue to Book Two. 961

**BOOK TWO**

**Chapter 1.**—How, for the construction of a house of the Carthusian order in England at Witham, someone was sent to seek Hugh. 961

**Chapter 2.**—How the messengers who came to the Grande Chartreuse concerning their request found the brothers in disagreement, and what Hugh himself thought about granting the request. This is Chapter 3 in the sequence of the longer Life. 964

**Chapter 3.**—How at last it was obtained that Hugh should go to England to the king, and how he was escorted with honor to Witham. 966

**Chapter 4.**—How, after inspecting the condition he found at Witham, he returned to the king and arranged most generously for the inhabitants of the village of Witham who were to depart from it. 968

**Chapter 5.**—How, since construction at the site could not proceed at all because of a lack [Col. 1168] of funds, Brother Girard approached the king with our Hugh and spoke very harsh words to him; how Hugh’s patience was thereby approved, and how from that time his intimacy with the king was greatly strengthened. 970

**Chapter 6.**—That the king trusted Hugh above everyone else in matters touching the salvation of his soul; that many thought him the king’s son; and that, reproving him for various transgressions, Hugh never ceased to instruct him with holy exhortations, because through Hugh’s varied consolation he bore adversity more easily, relying on his prayers overcame it more readily, and, instructed by his counsels, avoided dangers more prudently. 972

**Chapter 7.**—How, when the king was in danger on the British Sea, he attributed his deliverance to Hugh; and how he was said to vow that he would strive to promote him to the episcopal rank as soon as possible if he reached the harbor safely. 975

**Chapter 8.**—How Hugh devoted himself wholly to devotion, so that even in his sleep he habitually uttered the word “Amen”; how he also conducted himself at table; and how, whatever occupation he had in hand, he gave himself to it completely. 976

**Chapter 9.**—How people flocked to him at Witham to receive consolation; how many wished to lead the religious life with him; yet how he received those who knocked neither quickly nor easily. 977

**Chapter 10.**—On the apostasy of Brothers Andrew and Alexander, and on their insults and blasphemies directed against Hugh and the Carthusian order. 977

**Chapter 11.**—How our Hugh was reluctant to receive those who had once apostatized, and how dearly he loved the peace of those who persevered steadfastly in their religion. 979

**Chapter 12.**—How, although he was concerned to obtain the books necessary for his community, he nevertheless, out of an unprecedented charity, voluntarily caused the library acquired for him by the king from the monks of Winchester to be returned to them. From that time, especially, a special affection grew between the monks of Winchester and the hermits of Witham; through this affection Robert, prior of the cathedral church, and Ralph, sacristan, became solitaries at Witham. The author of this Life, our Hugh’s own recorder, says that he composed it at their urging. 979

Prologue to Book Three. 981

**BOOK THREE**

**Chapter 1.**—How Hugh was elected to the bishopric. 983

**Chapter 2.**—How Hugh, at first regarding the election made concerning him as invalid and void, persuaded those who came to him to return to the cathedral church and hold a canonical election there. 985

**Chapter 3.**—How, concerning the second election held at Lincoln, he replied to those sent to him that he would not undertake the episcopal burden without the obedience of the prior of the Grande Chartreuse. 986

**Chapter 4.**—How the delegates sought the prior of the Grande Chartreuse; and how Hugh himself, applying himself more firmly to devotion, prepared himself against the episcopal yoke impending over him. 987

**Chapter 5.**—How, when the messengers had returned from the Grande Chartreuse, he was compelled by a summons for the third time to leave his house; how, traveling toward London to receive consecration, he did not yet abandon the humility of his order, but instead carried his little bundle behind the saddle while riding; and how he was honored most generously by royal munificence at his consecration. 989

**Chapter 6.**—How, when enthroned at Lincoln, he replied to the archdeacon of Canterbury that he would give him as much for the cathedral as he had given for the mitre. How he also replied to the procurator of his household concerning the number of hinds to be taken; and concerning the remarkable birds at Stow, as related by the archdeacon of St Davids. 990

**Chapter 7.**—How concerned our Hugh was to place suitable persons in the Church of Lincoln and to attach them to his side for the support of the burden laid upon him. This is Chapter 8 in the sequence of the longer Life. 993

**Chapter 8.**—How our Hugh incurred the king’s displeasure by excommunicating the chief forester and excusing himself, at the latter’s insistence, from conferring a prebend upon him. 994

**Chapter 9.**—How, summoned by the king because of these offenses, he answered in such a manner that he departed freely, with the king’s goodwill. 995

**Chapter 10.**—That he considered prebendaries in churches bound to residence; and that he replied accordingly to a Parisian master who desired to hold a prebend in the Church of Lincoln; and that among brothers, or among all people, he especially loved unity. 997

[Col. 1169]

**Chapter 11.**—How he dissuaded both Baldwin, archbishop of Canterbury, and his successor from insisting on the construction of chapels, from which the gravest discord arose between them and their Canterbury monks; and how he restored peace among them. 999

**Chapter 12.**—How Hugh conducted himself at table and with food; how vigorously he acted in carrying out the duties of his office; and how humbly and devoutly he attended children who were to be confirmed and others confined by illness. 1001

**Chapter 13.**—How, out of the sweetness of his affection, he played with little children, who in turn applauded him wonderfully. 1003

Prologue to Book Four. 1003

**BOOK FOUR**

**Chapter 1.**—On the tonsure, conversion to the religious life, and progress therein of Martin, our Hugh’s secretary. 1005

**Chapter 2.**—On the kiss given to lepers and the manifold consolation expressed in our Hugh’s words concerning the sweetness of the Savior, and on the most generous distribution of alms. This is Chapter 4 in the sequence of the longer Life. 1007

**Chapter 3.**—How steadfastly he opposed rebels and punished those who obstinately offended against God with ecclesiastical censure. 1008

**Chapter 4.**—On the substitution of a child in place of the offspring of a certain soldier’s wife, and the punishment of those who consented to so great a crime; on the name of the forester; and on the killing of a certain cruel bishop who retained a curse. 1009

**Chapter 5.**—On a certain deacon who vehemently prosecuted a certain soldier for the crime of treason against the king. This chapter is inserted as Chapter 6 of Book Four of the longer Life. 1014

**Chapter 6.**—On a young woman at Oxford who, having despised her first betrothed, was in fact married to another and, after being convicted of this, refused to obey blessed Hugh. This is likewise Chapter 6 in the longer Life. 1015

**Chapter 7.**—On a cleric of the diocese of York who refused to obey the judges concerning the abandonment of a church, regarding which a sentence had been issued against him by delegated authority of blessed Hugh. This chapter also appears under the same Chapter 6 in the longer Life. 1016

**Chapter 8.**—How he redeemed the pallium-service from King Richard, how generously the clergy of his diocese contributed toward that redemption, and how he also forbade the acceptance of a monetary penalty for offenses. This is Chapter 7 in the longer Life. 1017

**Chapter 9.**—How, by a solemn inquest, he established against King Richard, who claimed it for himself, the right of advocacy over the abbey of Eynsham. This is Chapter 8 in the longer Life. 1020

**Chapter 10.**—That almost every year he went to Witham, where he seemed to wear a horned face. How, preaching there to secular people, he strove especially to instruct them in three matters: charity of heart, truth of speech, and chastity of body; and how strictly he himself strove to preserve the truth. This is Chapter 9 in the longer Life. 1022

**Chapter 11.**—How, on coming to Witham, he possessed an unusual radiance, suffused with a ruddy color, sensing himself at his first sight of the place to be filled with an ineffable joy of spiritual gladness; and what his manner of life was while he remained there. This is Chapter 10 in the longer Life. 1024

**Chapter 12.**—How Brother Eynard, while preparing to set out to leave Witham and return to the Grande Chartreuse, was brought back by blessed Hugh; and how they mutually pledged that Brother Eynard would not thereafter leave Witham, nor Hugh Lincoln. 1025

**Chapter 13.**—On the harmless ending of a fire in the kitchen at the time of our Hugh’s final departure from Witham. 1026

Prologue to Book Five. 1027

**BOOK FIVE**

**Chapter 1.**—On the immensity of divine love for human beings, which is notably demonstrated in the ministry of human burial, and on our Hugh’s immense affection for this ministry. 1029

**Chapter 2.**—On the burial of a certain poor man in Normandy, of very many people in Lincoln, and of a certain prelate at Bermondsey. 1031

**Chapter 3.**—On his dispute with the earl of Leicester concerning a certain district adjoining Leicester. This appears as Chapter 2 in the longer Life. 1034

**Chapter 4.**—On a revelation made known to a cleric who, between the hands of a celebrating bishop, saw the form of a child beneath the saving host. This is Chapter 3 in the longer Life. 1035

**Chapter 5.**—On a very astonishing miracle that occurred in France concerning the body of Christ in the hands of an unworthy priest, and on the remarkable judgment of our Hugh, who was invited to see that miracle. This is Chapter 4 in the longer Life. 1039

**Chapter 6.**—How our Hugh rebuked his metropolitan, and how concerned he was about the conduct of his subjects. This is Chapter 5 in the sequence of the longer Life. 1042

**Chapter 7.**—How at the Council of Oxford he resisted a request for aid demanded by King Richard, by whom he was nevertheless honorably received after the offense. This chapter is contained under Chapter 5 in the sequence of the longer Life. 1043

**Chapter 8.**—How, after the king’s offense had been calmed, he rebuked him and departed honored by him; and how, after Hugh’s departure, the king announced to him the victory he had gained over his enemies. [Col. 1170] 1047

**Chapter 9.**—How steadfastly he excused himself from the kings’ command that he send to him twelve persons from his Church of Lincoln who would be best suited to dispatch his messages, exercising ecclesiastical censure against the appointed officials who had been charged with confiscating all his property. This is Chapter 7 in the sequence of the longer Life. 1049

**Chapter 10.**—How, when the archbishop advised him to send money to the king, who thirsted for it as a dropsical man thirsts for water, he replied: “If he is dropsical, I shall not be water”; and on the healing of a madman at Gestrehant. 1053

**Chapter 11.**—How he freed a certain little woman from a pythonic spirit. This is Chapter 8 in the longer Life. 1055

**Chapter 12.**—How he freed another woman from an incubus demon. This chapter is contained under Chapter 8 in the longer Life. 1056

**Chapter 13.**—On the rescue of a thief who was being led to the gallows, and how he spoke to the barons of the Exchequer. This chapter is contained under Chapter 9 in the longer Life. 1058

**Chapter 14.**—On a young man whom he found near the city of Rochester in a desperate condition, whose flesh afterward rotted beside both thighs, and who was cured by our Hugh both in body and in soul. This is taken from Chapter 2 of Book Four of the longer Life. 1061

**Chapter 15.**—That he could not be induced to ordain as subdeacon a cleric who was destined to become a leper; how violently he was pressed to calm the anger of our king by means of money; and how, when news of the king’s death arrived, he could not be dissuaded from going to his burial. This is Chapter 10 in the sequence of the longer Life. 1063

**Chapter 16.**—How John, the future king, after his brother’s burial, approached at the Fountain of Ebrand, and what he promised the nuns through our Hugh; and concerning several deeds of that same John which indicated his future rejection. 1068

**Chapter 17.**—How, after King Richard’s death, he escaped the violence of enemies while returning to his homeland, and how he was joyfully received by those who came to meet him. This is Chapter 12 in the longer Life. 1072

**Chapter 18.**—How, although he had it in mind to visit the Grande Chartreuse, he did not obtain the requested permission to depart; how vigorously he conducted himself in cases delegated to him, especially against a certain Jordan of the Tower; and how burdensome it was for him to involve himself personally in secular affairs, which he judged should be entrusted to faithful and prudent men. 1075

**Chapter 19.**—How, after peace had been restored between the kings of France and England, in which our Hugh also took part, he received permission from the king and the archbishop to go to the Grande Chartreuse; how, while passing through Paris, he spoke most salutary words there to Louis, son of the king of France, and Arthur, John’s nephew; and concerning a certain man who met him and requested absolution, having been excommunicated by Hugh in England many years earlier. This is Chapter 13 in the sequence of the longer Life, under which the preceding chapter is also contained. 1077

**Chapter 20.**—On his arrival and reception at Grenoble and at the Grande Chartreuse, and how he conducted himself in those places; on the restoration of peace by him between the bishop and the consul of Geneva; and how, when he was about to depart from the Grande Chartreuse, he made arrangements concerning the relics that he and his monk had sought out. 1080

**Chapter 21.**—How devoted he was in visiting the relics of the saints and searching them out, and how he finally made arrangements concerning them. This is contained in Chapter 14 of the longer Life, around the middle of that chapter. 1083

**Chapter 22.**—On the places through which he passed while returning from the Grande Chartreuse to England, on his deeds in those places, and on how he was severely afflicted by illness before he reached London. 1086

[Col. 1171]

**Chapter 23.**—How, while ill in London, he foretold the evils that were to come upon England, received extreme unction, and replied to those advising him to make a will; how he did not abandon the zeal he had always possessed for the divine office; and how he conducted himself toward King John and the archbishop when they came to visit him. 1094

**Chapter 24.**—How he instructed the master of works of the Church of Lincoln to make preparations for a general assembly soon to be held there; how he set down in writing what he wished to be observed concerning his funeral rites and burial; and how he responded to the advice given him to eat meat. 1098

**Chapter 25.**—How he departed from this life. This chapter is contained under Chapter 16 in the longer Life. 1103

**Chapter 26.**—On the vision of a falling tree, from which the antiphon “The tree falls, an indicator of the mystical sacrament, etc.” was taken. This is Chapter 18 in the longer Life. 1104

**Chapter 27.**—On the preparation of the dead body, the celebration of the funeral rites as he had prescribed, its conveyance to Lincoln, the account of miracles occurring along the journey, and the meeting with kings and other exalted persons. This appears as Chapter 19 in the sequence of the longer Life. 1106

**Chapter 28.**—On the conveyance of the body through the city, its second preparation, the display of miracles, the abundance of offerings, and the inscription of the verses: “The staff of pontiffs, etc.” On its burial in the place where he had ordered it. This chapter is contained as Chapter 20 in the sequence of the longer Life. 1111
